HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Matthew S. Pleisse, 36, of Shippensburg, Pennsylvania, pleaded guilty yesterday before United States District Judge Robert D. Mariani to possession of child pornography involving a prepubescent minor.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, in April 2025, law enforcement executed a search warrant at Pleisse’s residence and seized several electronic devices including his personal computer and cell phone. Both devices were forensically analyzed and law enforcement found Pleisse utilized cryptocurrency to purchase child pornography from the darkweb and possessed child pornography depicting prepubescent minors.

As part of his plea agreement, Pleisse will be required to resign from his position with the Shippensburg Police Department within 10 days and is required not to seek or accept a position of public trust as a condition of his supervised release.

The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Stephen W. Dukes is prosecuting the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC.

If convicted, Pleisse faces a maximum sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment, a term of supervised release following imprisonment, and a fine. A sentence following the finding of guilt is imposed by the Judge after consideration of the applicable federal sentencing statutes and the Federal Sentencing Guidelines.

# # #
title: Shippensburg Detective Pleads Guilty to Possession of Child Pornography

Tallahassee, Florida – Johnny L. Robinson, 34, of Melbourne, Florida, was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison after previously pleading guilty in federal court to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution and lengthy prison sentence is a yet another victory on behalf of the communities in my district that have been plagued by deadly drugs flooding our streets. President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche have deployed the full might of the Department of Justice toward improving the safety and health of our communities, and my office will continue to aggressively prosecute drug traffickers, like this defendant, to deliver the safe, drug-free streets our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that, beginning in January 2024, the defendant provided co-conspirators with methamphetamine on at least three different occasions. Those co-conspirators then transported the methamphetamine into the Northern District of Florida and distributed it in the Panama City, Florida, area. At the time he provided the methamphetamine, the defendant was aware it would be distributed and specifically agreed that the weight of the methamphetamine was at least 50 grams. In total, the defendant and his co-conspirators conspired to distribute almost 500 grams of methamphetamine.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration, United States Postal Inspection Service, and the Bay County Sheriff’s Office. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Eric W. Welch.

“Our Panhandle communities will be safer with this drug distributor off the streets” said DEA Special Agent in Charge Daniel Escobar, Tampa Field Division. “I’m proud of the way our agents and law enforcement partners worked together for justice.”

“The Postal Inspection Service is committed to identifying and pursuing those who use the U.S. Mail to traffic illegal narcotics,” said Bladismir Rojo, Inspector in Charge, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Miami Division. “Along with our local, state and federal law enforcement partners, we will locate not just the individuals who receive the drugs, but those who go to great lengths to send it.”

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Coast Guard offloads $5.5 million in seized cocaine in San Juan, Puerto Rico
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – Coast Guard Cutter Winslow Griesser offloaded 489 pounds in seized cocaine and transferred custody of three suspects to Homeland Security Task Force San Juan law enforcement authorities at Coast Guard Base San Juan, Puerto Rico, Monday.
The contraband seizure and apprehension followed the interdiction of a go-fast smuggling vessel in Atlantic waters off Puerto Rico, Oct. 10, 2026.  The seized cocaine is estimated to have a wholesale value of $5.5 million.
Federal agents took custody of the three men, including two Dominican Republic nationals and one Chinese national, pending further investigation.
“We are proud of our Coast Guard watchstanders, our aircrew and the cutter Winslow Griesser crew for achieving a successful interdiction,” said Cmdr. Matthew Romano, Sector San Juan chief response. “This interdiction demonstrates the proficiency of our operational crews and valued partners who work tirelessly to intercept deadly narcotics before they reach our shores, protect our citizens, and dismantle the criminal networks that threaten our region."
During a routine law enforcement patrol, the crew of a Coast Guard Air Station Miami HC-144 Ocean Sentry aircraft detected a suspect go-fast vessel transiting in Atlantic Ocean waters north of Isabela, Puerto Rico. Coast Guard watchstanders at Sector San Juan diverted the cutter Winslow Griesser to interdict the suspect vessel. Once on scene, the Winslow Griesser crew stopped the vessel, seized the contraband and embarked the three men who were aboard.
This interdiction is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.
HSTF San Juan comprises agents and officers from the following federal partners: FBI, ICE-HSI, CBP (OFO, AMO and Border Patrol), the U.S. Marshals Service for Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, DEA, ATF, IRS, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the Department of State, and the U.S. Secret Service, the Puerto Rico/U.S. Virgin Islands HIDTA, TSA, FAA, and the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Districts of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
title: Coast Guard offloads $5.5 million in seized cocaine in San Juan, Puerto Rico

text:
Guatemalan National Extradited to the United States Sentenced for Involvement in 2022 Mass Casualty Alien Smuggling Event
A Guatemalan man, Rigoberto Ramon Miranda-Orozco, 39, was sentenced today to 30 years in prison for his involvement in a 2022 mass casualty alien smuggling event in San Antonio, Texas, that resulted in 53 deaths and 11 injured.
“Alien smuggling organizations rely on people like Miranda-Orozco to facilitate their criminal conspiracies and put people on the dangerous path of illegally entering the United States,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “By refusing to secure our borders, the Biden administration empowered human smugglers across the globe to take advantage of our country and break our laws for financial gain. These smugglers value profits over people, and their disregard of the risks or dangerous conditions in which they carry out their schemes too often result in tragic consequences like in this case with 53 people dead. Under President Trump, the Criminal Division and Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA) will sustain maximum pressure on these dangerous criminals to hold them accountable for preventable tragedies and protect our borders.”
“Of the dozens of deceased aliens found in the tractor trailer in June 2022, 21 of those were from Guatemala — a country that Mirando-Orozco called home and a place where he thought he could hide from justice,” said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. “He was wrong. Miranda-Orozco was personally responsible for smuggling two Guatemalans who died in that horrific tragedy, and thanks to our law enforcement efforts and our strong partnership with the Office of the Attorney General of Guatemala, he was found, extradited, and will now spend the rest of his life in a U.S. federal prison. To those who believe they can avoid accountability by cowering in a foreign country, Miranda-Orozco thought the same. Because of this Administration’s commitment to holding accountable all of those who support transnational criminal organizations, he now knows otherwise.”
“This sentencing delivers a measure of accountability for a tragedy that claimed 53 lives and devastated multiple families,” said Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). “Miranda-Orozco and his co-conspirators treated human lives as cargo, knowingly placing vulnerable people in lethal conditions to advance their criminal enterprise. HSI worked relentlessly with our domestic and international law enforcement partners to identify his role in this horrific event, secure his extradition and bring him before a U.S. court. HSI will continue pursuing the transnational criminal networks that profit from human smuggling and threaten the safety and security of our communities.”
According to court documents, Miranda-Orozco conspired with other human smugglers to facilitate the travel of multiple aliens from Guatemala through Mexico, and ultimately, to the United States. Miranda-Orozco organized and facilitated the smuggling of aliens who ended up dying or injured in the back of a tractor trailer that was found in San Antonio on June 27, 2022. The tractor trailer was loaded with 64 aliens, and investigators later determined that it had traveled approximately 156 miles from Laredo, Texas, to San Antonio in 90-degree Fahrenheit heat without functioning air conditioning in the trailer. First responders pronounced 48 aliens dead at the scene and five aliens later died at the hospital, totaling 53 deceased. Among the deceased were six juveniles and at least one pregnant woman. Two of Miranda-Orozco’s clients, both illegal aliens from Guatemala, died in the tractor trailer mass casualty incident, and another sustained serious bodily injuries but survived after a lengthy hospital stay. According to court documents, Miranda-Orozco admitted that he arranged for the aliens’ transportation and accommodations throughout Guatemala, Mexico, and the United States.
Photo depicting size of trailer. Image of claw marks inside trailer.
In August 2024, Miranda-Orozco was arrested in Guatemala pursuant to a U.S. request for his extradition. His arrest was part of a large-scale takedown during which Guatemalan law enforcement executed multiple search and arrest warrants across Guatemala. He was extradited from Guatemala in March 2025.
Miranda-Orozco pleaded guilty on July 2 to conspiracy to bring an alien into the United States resulting in death; aiding and abetting bringing an alien into the United States resulting in death; and aiding and abetting bringing an alien into the United States resulting in serious bodily injury.
HSI San Antonio led U.S. investigative efforts, working in concert with HSI Guatemala’s invaluable team members, and the HSI Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. HSI received substantial assistance from U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s National Targeting Center/Operation Sentinel; U.S. Border Patrol; the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; the San Antonio Police Department; the San Antonio Fire Department; and the Palestine Police Department. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs worked with law enforcement partners in Guatemala to secure the arrest and extradition of Miranda-Orozco and, along with the Criminal Division’s Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training (OPDAT), provided crucial assistance in this matter.
The case is being prosecuted by Trial Attorney Alexandra Skinnion of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section (HRSP), First Assistant U.S. Attorney Eric Fuchs for the Western District of Texas, and Assistant U.S. Attorney/JTFA prosecutor Jose Luis Acosta for the Western District of Texas, with assistance from HRSP Historian/Latin America Specialist Joanna Crandall.
The Justice Department thanks its Guatemalan law enforcement partners, who were instrumental in arresting Miranda-Orozco, and the Guatemalan Attorney General’s Office and Anti-Human Smuggling Unit for making the extradition possible.
This case was supported and prosecuted by JTFA, the U.S. Department of Justice’s lead effort in combating human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations throughout the Americas. In partnership with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking networks that impact public safety and border security. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by other Criminal Division components, JTFA has dedicated prosecutors from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices along the Southwest border, Southern Florida, Northern New York, and Vermont. JTFA partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, HSI, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, and the Office of Field Operations. JTFA also partners with FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 486 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and trafficking; more than 447 U.S. convictions; and more than 374 significant jail sentences imposed and forfeitures of substantial assets.

President Donald J. Trump was returned to office with a clear mandate to end the invasion that Democrats allowed to overwhelm communities, drain public resources, and endanger public safety. In less than two years, the Trump Administration has delivered the largest reduction in the illegal alien population in modern history, driven illegal crossings to an all-time low, and enacted sweeping reforms that finally put American citizens first.
Historic Progress: The Numbers
The Trump Administration reversed years of open border policies and produced the largest sustained drop in the illegal alien population in modern American history.
- The illegal alien population has been reduced by at least 2.3 million, with more than three million migrants leaving the country during President Trump’s second term — the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.
- Nearly 1.2 million illegal aliens have been deported or removed, and nearly 1.3 million illegal alien arrests have been carried out.
- The United States recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least 50 years.
- Catch-and-release was ended, delivering 17 straight months of zero releases at the border and zero Border Patrol releases in FY2026 — the first fiscal year in U.S. history with that result.
- Illegal southern border crossings were cut by 95% from Biden-era levels in FY2026, recording the lowest number of illegal border crossings in American history.
- Nationwide encounters in FY2026 were the lowest in agency history (under 380,000), compared with roughly 2.7 million per year under Biden.
- Entries by asylum seekers at U.S.-Mexico entry points have been slashed by 99.9%.
- Asylum is now granted in just 7% of cases, down from more than 50% under Biden.
- The immigration court backlog has been reduced from more than 4.18 million cases to under 3.09 million — the sharpest decrease in the Executive Office for Immigration Review’s history.
- More than 12,100 gang members have been arrested, including more than 1,500 Tren de Aragua affiliates and nearly 2,000 MS-13 affiliates, along with more than 2,200 known or suspected terrorists (more than 2,000 of whom have been removed).
- Nearly one million pounds of narcotics have been seized through Customs and Border Protection in FY2026 (63% above the prior four-year average), and more than 624,000 pounds have been interdicted by the U.S. Coast Guard, including more than 260,000 pounds of cocaine in Operation Pacific Viper alone — preventing over 219 million lethal doses from entering American communities.
- Fentanyl trafficking at the southern border collapsed by 56%, and fentanyl-linked deaths plunged 22% in a single year.
- Drug overdoses have fallen by more than 40% from the Biden-era peak.
- America recorded its lowest overall death rate ever in 2025, driven in large part by sharp declines in drug fatalities.
- Migration from majority-Muslim countries has been cut by 96% since 2024 and overall migration roughly in half, with visa issuances down 89% for Africa and 81% for the Middle East.
- Border-related deaths fell nearly 80% in FY2026 compared to the Biden Administration
- International student enrollment is projected to decrease by another 111,000 compared to last year.
- More than 300,000 visas have been revoked, including at least 4,000 tied to birth tourism and 6,000 from foreign students who committed crimes or have ties to terrorism. More than 700 visas from Chinese nationals have been revoked by President Trump’s Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force since it launched in August.
- More than 157,000 unaccompanied alien children who were lost under the Biden Administration — often to sex trafficking, forced labor, and other atrocities — have been located.
Securing the Southern Border
On Day One, the Trump Administration declared a national emergency, restored physical barriers, and deployed the military to restore control at the southern border.
- President Trump declared a national border emergency on Day One and deployed thousands of military personnel to protect the southern border against invasion.
- Border wall construction was immediately ordered to resume. Approximately 290 miles of new border barriers have been constructed, including 131 miles of primary wall, with $34.3 billion obligated from the Working Families Tax Cuts Act for Smart Wall projects.
- The successful Remain in Mexico policy was reinstated.
- The Trump Administration expanded third-country removal agreements with dozens of nations to expedite deportations, enabling the removal of more than 25,000 illegal aliens to countries other than their own.
- The failed Biden-era CBP One app was repurposed into a self-deportation tool.
- The Pentagon created National Defense Areas along the border in New Mexico and Texas, where illegal crossers can be charged with trespassing on a military installation.
- Visa processing was paused for 75 high-risk countries, visa interview waiver categories were tightened to require most applicants to attend in-person interviews, and a new visa integrity fee along with several other new fees was implemented to enhance the integrity of the visa application process and deter overstays.
- Temporary Protected Status was terminated for 13 countries, including Somalia, Venezuela, and Haiti.
- Refugee resettlement was immediately suspended and the number of refugees admitted was dramatically reduced.
- Illicit fentanyl and its core precursors were designated as Weapons of Mass Destruction, enabling harsher penalties, expanded seizure authorities, and treating this poison with the full force of national security tools.
- The de minimis loophole was closed, ending the flow of millions of uninspected packages that traffickers used to smuggle fentanyl precursors and finished product into the country.
- Migration through the Darién Gap collapsed by more than 99%, choking off a major transit route used under the prior administration.
Expanding Interior Enforcement and Accelerating Deportations
The Trump Administration has expanded enforcement capacity, accelerated removals, and targeted the criminal networks that exploit the border.
- Immigration court hearings have been accelerated while welcoming the largest-ever class of new immigration judges.
- The immigration enforcement workforce has been expanded, including more than doubling the number of ICE agents and record high Border Patrol staffing.
- Federal immigration detention capacity has been dramatically expanded, including opening the largest migrant detention facility in U.S. history.
- Deportation flights have been accelerated to record highs, and a record was set for the highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a month in August.
- More than 2,500 agreements have been secured with state and local law enforcement under Immigration and Nationality Act Section 287(g).
- President Trump signed the Laken Riley Act into law, requiring detention of illegal aliens charged with serious crimes.
- President Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act to expeditiously deport violent illegal alien gang members.
- Over ten Latin American cartels were designated as terrorist groups, including Tren de Aragua, MS-13, and Clan del Golfo.
- Major immigration enforcement operations were launched in cities around the country, including Metro Surge, Midway Blitz, and Catahoula Crunch.
- The Victims of Immigration Crime Engagement Office was re-launched to assist Americans harmed by immigrant crime after it was shuttered under Biden.
- The practice of conducting neighborhood investigations of potential new citizens was restored to verify their claims and ensure a full picture of their character.
- Enforcement of the federal requirement that illegal aliens register with the government was resumed, with criminal penalties for those who refuse.
- So-called sanctuary policies were terminated in Washington, D.C., while moving to strip federal funding from sanctuary jurisdictions.
- A stipend program and fine program were launched to incentivize self-deportation and reduce costs.
Tightening Legal Migration and Protecting American Workers
The Trump Administration has reformed legal immigration pathways, ended abuses of temporary programs, and restored priority for American workers and wages.
- Entry of H-1B aliens was restricted unless their petition is accompanied by a $100,000 payment, the random selection process for H-1B registrations was ended, and H-1B lottery registrations were driven down 38% for FY2027 under the new merit-based system, with no second selection planned.
- Bonds of up to $15,000 were implemented for visa applications from citizens of high-risk countries, and student visa applicants are required to make their social media public for screening.
- The practice of granting automatic extensions of employment authorization documents was ended.
- Access to immigrant work permits was restricted, prioritizing U.S. workers and tightening security.
- Employers’ ability to pay substandard wages to foreign workers in certain visa programs was ended to protect American workers.
- A fixed time period of program completion or four years, whichever is shorter, was established for foreign students and exchange visitors.
- The data schools must provide on students studying in the U.S. was significantly expanded, including information on programs of study, funding sources, graduation dates, and more.
- The $1 million Trump Gold Card was launched as a path to residency for vetted, high-value applicants.
- A new policy was established that generally requires aliens in the U.S. temporarily to return to their home countries to apply for a green card.
- The citizenship test was reformed to better assess aliens’ understanding of American history, government, and values, and to better ensure aliens meet all eligibility requirements.
- Naturalization fees were raised so American taxpayers are no longer subsidizing the process.
- An unprecedented denaturalization effort was launched targeting those who fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship.
- President Trump signed an Executive Order ending birth tourism and launched a dedicated Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force that has already revoked thousands of visas.
Protecting Taxpayers, Communities, and the Rule of Law
The Trump Administration has closed access to taxpayer benefits for illegal aliens, strengthened verification systems, and secured legal authority to enforce immigration law.
- Illegal aliens were banned from more than a dozen taxpayer-funded healthcare programs.
- Foreign nationals — including green card holders — were banned from accessing Small Business Administration loans intended for American entrepreneurs.
- Government-backed mortgage financing for illegal aliens and H-1B visa holders was ended.
- The human trafficking hotline was upgraded.
- Use of federal assistance and grant funding to provide services to illegal aliens was prohibited.
- Illegal aliens were blocked from accessing federal funds for higher education programming.
- Illegal aliens were barred from abusing refundable individual income tax credit benefits.
- Data sharing programs on illegal aliens receiving taxpayer-funded health insurance benefits were commenced.
- The financial system was secured against illegal aliens by urging financial institutions to detect and report illicit activity.
- A new remittance tax was implemented on money sent out of the country by illegal aliens.
- More than 206 million benefits eligibility checks were conducted in 2025.
- The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program was enhanced to ensure noncitizens cannot vote in U.S. elections while moving to purge tens of thousands of illegal aliens from states’ voter rolls.
- Strict English proficiency and residency requirements were implemented for commercial driver’s license holders. The emergency removal of 110 commercial driver’s license schools associated with more than 5,000 drivers who failed English language proficiency tests was ordered, and more than 20,000 truckers who failed to meet enhanced English proficiency standards were removed from U.S. roads. As a result, traffic fatalities fell to record lows in 2025.
- An aggressive crackdown on asylum fraud was launched.
- A new visa restriction policy was implemented for family members and associates of individuals sanctioned over ties to fentanyl trafficking.
- The Supreme Court affirmed the Trump Administration’s authority to remove green card holders who threaten American communities, upheld the policy to swiftly turn back illegal aliens seeking asylum before they set foot on U.S. soil, affirmed full discretion over Temporary Protected Status designations and terminations, allowed the Safe Third Country deportation program to continue, and allowed the Administration to end the Biden-era Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans (CHNV) parole scheme.
- A federal appeals court affirmed the Trump Administration’s expedited removal policy, accelerating deportations of illegal aliens.
- President Trump signed the Secure America Act into law, delivering $70 billion in vital homeland security funding for ICE and CBP.
- President Trump signed the Working Families Tax Cuts into law, providing a record $165 billion for border security — including funding for border wall construction, expanded state and local law enforcement partnerships, reimbursements to states that suffered under the Biden-era crisis, and much more.
- President Trump signed the Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026, into law, providing more than $18 billion for CBP, $10 billion for ICE, and $123 million for Citizenship and Immigration Services, and signed the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025, providing a $485 million budget increase for ICE.
- President Trump signed the HALT Fentanyl Act into law, permanently classifying fentanyl analogs as Schedule I drugs and closing chemical loopholes traffickers had exploited for years.
title: How President Trump Ended the Border Invasion and Restored American Sovereignty

VICENZA, Italy — Members of the Vicenza military community gathered for a public safety outreach demonstration Oct. 16, 2026, providing military spouses and children an opportunity to view local security operations.
The 525th Military Working Dog Detachment conducted a series of capability demonstrations. U.S. Army Staff Sgt. Payton May, a military working dog handler, introduced local families to Sawyer, a 4-year-old German Shepherd, and demonstrated the canine's physical drive and agility with a game of tug-of-war.
Staff Sgt. May also demonstrated Sawyer’s daily training routines and allowed children to meet the working dog. The children not only got to pet Sawyer, they were also able to watch him perform his duties with his handler.
"This event was important to the unit," May said. "This is a way to show the community the confidence of the military working dogs and how they are invaluable assets."
Along with the canine demonstrations, Soldiers assigned to the 529th Military Police Company displayed tools and vehicles used for installation safety. Military police Soldiers introduced local families to standard patrol vehicles, allowing children to sit inside and operate the buttons, sounds, lights, and public address systems MPs use daily.
"Getting children in front of military police, knowing that these are trusted people that are there to protect them, is important,” said U.S. Army Lt. Col. Jonathan Kuhn, U.S. Army Garrison Italy provost marshal. “It’s a partnership with the community, and that was the whole point of what we were trying to underscore.”
U.S. Army Staff Sgt. Taran Carter distributed stickers to children and families during the event, which highlighted the partnership between installation protective forces and military families.
The Directorate of Emergency Services hosts engagements like this on a regular basis to support the community.
title: K9s and kids connect in the Vicenza Military Community

Pensacola, Florida – Deshawn I. Donson, 23, of Pensacola, Florida, was convicted in federal court on charges related to fourteen armed robberies of gas stations and convenience stores in Escambia County. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the verdict.

US Attorney Heekin said: “For years, this violent criminal terrorized our community with a string of armed robberies, but the excellent investigative work by our state and federal law enforcement partners built a strong case that enabled my office to deliver this successful prosecution at trial. President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche have directed the full might of the Department of Justice toward protecting our communities from the predations of violent thugs, like this defendant, and my team of aggressive prosecutors continues to deliver on that promise with trial wins like this one.”

During the federal trial in Pensacola, the jury received evidence regarding Donson’s yearslong crime spree of robbing convenience store and gas station clerks at gunpoint. In fourteen separate instances between 2022 and 2025, Donson wore a hooded sweatshirt and a mask to conceal his identity and entered these stores with his semiautomatic pistol. He then pointed the pistol directly at the victims and demanded money from the businesses.

The jury heard from all of the victims, who testified about the terror they felt being robbed at gunpoint by the defendant while trying desperately to empty the cash register. Law enforcement was able to identify Donson as the suspect through electronic geolocation information that tied him to multiple armed robberies. Acting on this information, law enforcement caught Donson in his final armed robbery on May 18, 2025, as he fled the scene of his crime, leading to a high-speed chase at more than 100mph through the streets of Escambia County. The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office, supported by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, was able to capture Donson after the car chase and seized valuable evidence from his vehicle that confirmed he was the armed robber. In addition, Donson is a convicted felon who had previously been to state prison, so he was legally prohibited from possessing the firearm used to commit these robberies.

Sheriff Simmons said: “No one should have to wonder whether they will make it home safely at the end of their shift, especially because someone else made the decision to pick up a gun and commit a crime. This conviction reinforces a simple principle: your choices have consequences, and in Escambia County, we will make sure you are held accountable for them.”

Donson faces up to life imprisonment when he is sentenced in January 2027.

The case is being jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives; the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office; the Pensacola Police Department; and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys David L. Goldberg and Thomas Geeker.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

Congressman Menefee Backs Legislation to Protect Domestic Violence Survivors
HOUSTON, TX — Today, Congressman Christian D. Menefee (TX-18) announced his support of the Family Violence Prevention and Services Improvement Act of 2026 and the National Domestic Violence Awareness Month Resolution in recognition of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Both measures support efforts to protect survivors, prevent domestic violence, and keep families safe.
“We need to do everything in our power to improve safety around survivors and their families, and stop this violence from ever happening in the first place,” said Rep. Menefee. “That means investing in early prevention, making sure a survivor has a safe place to turn the moment they ask for help, and ensuring our communities have the resources to break the cycle of abuse before someone gets killed. These bills will help make that happen.”
According to the Texas Council on Family Violence (TCFV), more than half of the survivors in Texas who sought emergency shelter were denied solely due to a lack of space.
The Family Violence Prevention and Services Improvement Act of 2026, led by Representative Lucy McBath (GA-06), would support trauma-informed shelter and support services, strengthen the National Domestic Violence Hotline, and expand community-based prevention programs.
Domestic violence is a public health crisis. Last year alone, 160 Texans lost their lives to domestic violence, leaving 223 children without one or both parents. Harris County recorded the highest number of intimate partner homicides of any county in Texas, underscoring the devastating toll this crisis continues to take on our communities.
The National Domestic Violence Awareness Month Resolution, led by Representative Al Green (TX-09), supports the goals and ideals of National Domestic Violence Awareness Month and calls on Congress to keep raising awareness of domestic violence and supporting programs to end it.
Congressman Menefee remains committed to supporting the organizations and advocates working on the front lines to protect survivors, prevent domestic violence, and ensure that no one has to face abuse alone. As a member of the House Gun Violence Prevention Task Force, Congressman Menefee also supports federal policies aimed at addressing the dangerous intersection of domestic violence and gun violence, including efforts to keep firearms out of the hands of domestic abusers and protect families from further harm.
If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, help is available. Call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), text START to 88788, or visit thehotline.org.

title: Congressman Menefee Backs Legislation to Protect Domestic Violence Survivors

There’s no question as to the intent of the XM1180 Cannon-Delivered Area Effects Munition (C-DAEM) Armor’s Hit-to-kill (HTK) concept: the name says it all.
Yuma Test Center personnel along with teams from Project Manager Combat Ammunition Systems (PM-CAS), DEVCOM-Armaments Center (AC), Raytheon, and other organizations tested the technology for the C-DAEM Armor Program on three 155-mm XM1180 HTK prototype munitions, which they gun-launched from a 39-caliber cannon.
PM-CAS Col. Alicia Johnson and her leadership team traveled to Yuma Proving Ground to see the testing of the munitions’ capabilities. In this case, that location was in the middle of the Arizona desert.
The test is the second part of the Guided Test Vehicle (GTV) series and is intended to show the target-seeking capabilities explained Lovjoat Singh a Test and Evaluation Engineer with DEVCOM-AC based in Picatinny Arsenal, who was responsible for overall test planning and execution.
“It will be an open loop test then following a closed loop test. Open-loop test means the seeker is going to be seeking a target but not actually acting upon it. Then closed loop is actually using the seeker to guide to a target.”
Using a tank as a target, the test team fired three rounds at various configurations, each firing to evaluate its performance.
Casey Scharenbroich, an evaluator with Operational Evaluation Command, was on site to assess the technology maturation of the projectile.
“It’s a cool new technology that basically creates (an) image of the target area and it’s able to find the target in that area. It should be able to use the image to guide to target.”
While the C-DAEM Armor is an older program, a newer program, XM1230 is on the horizon that intends to use the same seeker technology. Scharenbroich will assess how that might apply to the newer program.
Scharenbroich explained the need for this type of technology saying, “It would be a huge advantage on the battlefield for commanders, allowing them to engage targets that have moved or are on the move with this munition.”
Adding it minimizes collateral damage, YTC Test Officer Ashley Lochetto discusses what’s next for the seeker technology, “our intent is to conduct GPS denied testing of the (seeker) along with integrating it into the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile.”
The C-DAEM Armor GTV series will continue through FY27 and the XM1230 testing will also be conducted in the next few months at Yuma Test Center.
title: Hit to kill: Guided munition tested at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground

text:
FORT SILL, Okla. — Christina “Chris” Smith spent much of her life finding value in things other people might overlook.
At the Fort Sill Recycle Center, that might mean a stack of moving boxes sturdy enough to help another military family make its next move, a ball gown set aside so a young Soldier or spouse could attend a unit formal without the added expense, or a discarded stuffed animal cleaned and given to law enforcement officers to comfort a frightened child.
But Smith’s greatest gift may have been seeing value in people, knowing the members of her team, understanding what they carried beyond the workplace and standing beside them when life became difficult.
After more than four decades as a Fort Sill civilian employee, and a connection to the installation that began with her own Army service in 1973, Smith retired in September 2026 as Fort Sill’s Qualified Recycle Program manager.
Her philosophy after all those years can be summed up simply.
“My team was my family,” Smith said.
It is easy to call that leadership. Smith lived it.
When one of her employees was dying of cancer after working until just days before his death, Smith and others across the Directorate of Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation worked with human resources to move his retirement paperwork through the system. He officially retired the day before he died, helping ensure his wife would receive an annuity rather than a one-time payment.
The Recycle team then helped arrange his funeral with military honors. When Department of Veterans Affairs benefits did not cover the full cost, members of the team helped pay the remaining expenses themselves.
When another worker assigned to the Recycle Center was found deceased at home, the team spent weeks searching for his next of kin in Pennsylvania. Once they located a family member, they helped with what came next, from clearing the home to coordinating access for the funeral home.
Those moments had nothing to do with recycling cardboard.
They had everything to do with Smith’s understanding of leadership.
“I prided myself in knowing each of my team,” she said. “Helping when needed, rearranging schedules for those who had military family members, allowing them the space and time that they needed to function.”
For Smith, taking care of the mission began with taking care of the people who accomplished it.
From Soldier to Fort Sill civilian
Smith’s Fort Sill story began more than half a century ago.
She enlisted in the Army in 1973 as an engineer illustrator, entering through the Women’s Army Corps during a period of significant change for women in military service. Assigned to Fort Sill, she eventually became a sergeant.
As the Women’s Army Corps was disbanded and women were integrated into the regular Army, Smith found herself helping others navigate a transition she was experiencing herself.
Serving in a career field then dominated by men gave her an early education in adapting, proving herself and leading through change, lessons that would follow her throughout her career.
After leaving active duty, Smith attended ROTC at Cameron University before leaving the program when she married an enlisted Soldier. The Army eventually brought the couple back to Fort Sill in 1982.
By then, Smith had earned a Bachelor of Science degree in animal science with a minor in chemistry.
Her civilian Fort Sill career began that same year at the Artillery Hunt, the installation’s stables. Initially operated as a private organization, the stables became part of Morale, Welfare and Recreation programming about a year later.
It was another transition and another opportunity to learn.
Smith worked with commanders and senior leaders throughout those years, observing different approaches to leadership and developing her own understanding of what it meant to lead.
She also learned something fundamental about MWR.
Its work was personal.
“I was in recreation for half of my career,” Smith said. “This is where you really work for Soldiers and their Families.”
Sometimes that meant building a beach, refurbishing a neighborhood swimming pool or planning community events. After the stables closed, Smith joined an engineering team during the early design phase of a major recreation project, helping move it from plans on paper to construction and, ultimately, a ribbon cutting.
There was always another challenge.
That was one reason she stayed.
“Somebody was always throwing me a challenge,” Smith said, “and I could catch it or hit it out of the park.”
An assignment she didn’t want and a program she came to love
One of those challenges arrived in August 2004.
Management reassigned Smith to the Fort Sill Recycle Center.
She freely admits she was not enthusiastic about the move.
Some members of her new workforce were not particularly enthusiastic about having her as their boss, either.
Smith entered an operation she initially viewed as primarily engineering- and machinery-driven. Some employees had reservations about working for a female manager. The adjustment took time.
“But we grew over the years and got past that,” Smith said.
Along the way, Smith began to rethink what the Recycle Program could be.
She already knew recreation was about serving Soldiers and families. She began asking why recycling could not do the same.
“I challenged myself and my team to program for Soldier and Family involvement,” she said. “We looked to see what services we could provide.”
That question helped shape the next 22 years.
As Army recycling requirements evolved and Fort Sill operated its Qualified Recycling Program, Smith worked with garrison, Defense Logistics Agency and DFMWR officials to meet regulatory requirements while preserving the program’s connection to MWR and the Fort Sill community.
At the same time, Smith and her team listened to the people they served.
The former Cash for Trash program evolved into the Sustainability Partnership. Active-duty units and other qualifying organizations could turn in recyclable material and earn recreation credits for eligible MWR activities at facilities such as Lake Elmer Thomas Recreation Area, the Patriot Club, Fort Sill Golf Course, Twin Oaks Bowling Center and the Outdoor Adventure Center.
Over time, participation expanded to include directorates and other eligible organizations, creating a broader partnership centered on reducing waste while returning benefits to the Fort Sill community.
For Smith, it represented what recycling could accomplish at its best: material diverted from the landfill, organizations encouraged to participate and benefits returned to the Soldiers, families and employees who make up the installation.
“A win-win for all,” she said.
The financial impact was substantial.
During the final decade of Smith’s tenure, the Recycle Program provided nearly $900,000 to DFMWR for programs, concerts and other Soldier and family activities. Another $175,000 supported refurbishment of the water plant at LETRA.
Many of the people enjoying those activities probably never knew recycling helped make them possible.
Smith never needed them to.
“When people attend events or go camping at LETRA and they’re having a good time with their families,” she said in an earlier interview, “that’s all that matters.”
Finding a second life for more than recyclables
Some of the center’s most memorable programs did not begin with formal studies or elaborate plans. They began with someone on the team noticing a need and asking what they could do about it.
Smith saw Soldiers buying moving boxes at retail stores while perfectly usable boxes were already passing through Fort Sill.
To her, the solution was obvious.
Families arriving at Fort Sill could bring their reusable boxes and packing paper to the center. Families preparing for their next move could pick up what they needed at no cost.
“No Soldier should ever have to buy a box if they don’t need to,” Smith said.
Then there was clothing.
For years, employees saw usable clothing discarded in collection areas. The need became especially clear after team members helped a man who had become trapped overnight in a dumpster while trying to retrieve a coat.
Afterward, the team began setting aside jackets and stuffed animals instead of letting usable items go to waste. Smith would take them home, wash them and return them to the warehouse so they could be given to people who needed them.
For a time, the program also provided cleaned stuffed animals to military police and local law enforcement officers to carry when responding to situations involving children who might need comfort.
Eventually, the center found a textile vendor that could accept clothing while also generating revenue for the program.
Another idea came directly from an employee.
When staff began noticing formal gowns among the donated textiles, Smith’s operations assistant suggested saving them.
The gowns could be cleaned and offered free to military families, a potentially significant savings for a junior enlisted Soldier or spouse preparing to attend a military ball.
“Recycle ideas are a team effort,” Smith said.
The statement says as much about her leadership as it does about recycling.
Good ideas did not have to come from the boss.
A Christmas tree and a family that needed one
Few programs captured the spirit of the Recycle team better than Trees for Troops.
Fort Sill has participated in the program for more than 18 years, helping provide live Christmas trees to military families.
The event began outdoors before eventually moving into one of the Recycle warehouses. Smith and her employees transformed the space with holiday decorations that had themselves been given a second life after being replaced at Lawton’s former Central Mall.
What could have been an ordinary warehouse became a place filled with Christmas trees, decorations and families. For many, selecting a tree became part of their Fort Sill holiday tradition.
One Christmas Eve, during a period of heavy deployments, Smith received a call from a chaplain.
A young family with a newborn had just learned their Soldier would be coming home unexpectedly on Christmas Day.
There was little time to prepare.
The chaplain asked whether Recycle could help.
For Smith and her team, there was really only one answer.
“Of course,” she recalled.
Team members delivered a Christmas tree to the family’s home, along with lights and decorations, and helped set everything up before the Soldier arrived.
No tonnage report could measure what that tree was worth to that family.
Watching generations grow
Over the decades, Smith had the rare opportunity to watch young people who once worked or learned under her grow into professionals and leaders of their own.
Teenagers who began in seasonal MWR jobs went on to positions of greater responsibility. Former riding students became Army colonels. A former lifeguard became a physician. Other MWR employees left Fort Sill and carried what they had learned to other Army installations.
“One of the most outstanding things for me was watching young people grow up over the years,” Smith said.
She had spent years learning from leaders around her. Somewhere along the way, she became one of the leaders others learned from.
Her leadership was never defined solely by position or hierarchy.
It was visible at lunches at the Patriot Club, holiday dinners, birthday celebrations and retirements. It showed in the schedules she rearranged when employees needed to care for military family members. It showed during illness, grief and the ordinary difficult days that rarely appear in performance reports.
Eventually, that care came back to her.
When Smith’s husband died unexpectedly, the people she had spent years looking after became the people she leaned on.
“My team was my family,” she said. “When my husband passed away unexpectedly, they were who I relied on for support.”
That bond made the decision to retire difficult.
Smith said one reason she remained as long as she did was because she wanted to know the people on her team would be taken care of.
She also had to imagine leaving a military community that had been part of nearly her entire adult life.
Watching another MWR leader accept a difficult new challenge eventually helped Smith look at retirement differently. She realized retirement did not have to be something she feared.
It was simply another challenge to take on.
“Learning to the end,” she said.
One unfinished fight
Smith does leave with one regret.
She wanted to see her Recycle team fully settled into its new site.
For years, employees worked in aging facilities that lacked many of the basic features Smith wanted for them. Finding and securing a better location required years of advocacy spanning multiple garrison commanders, and others have continued that effort.
The new site offers what Smith spent years seeking for her employees: better ventilation, heat, restrooms, improved lighting, personal workspace, a break area and ample yard space for operations.
To Smith, those things were never simply facility improvements.
They were another way to take care of people.
It is fitting that the unfinished business she thinks about as she leaves Fort Sill is not something she wanted for herself.
It is something she wanted for her team.
Team first
Smith’s Fort Sill story spans the Women’s Army Corps, horseback rides across the installation, decades of MWR recreation, the evolution of the Recycle Program and generations of Soldiers, family members and civilian employees.
There is very little of Fort Sill, she said, that she has not traveled on horseback. She remains passionate about the installation’s history, both the well-known stories and the smaller ones that can disappear unless someone takes the time to preserve them.
Her own story is now part of that history.
She first came to Fort Sill as a young Soldier in 1973. She returned as an Army spouse and civilian employee in 1982. Over the decades that followed, she helped build recreation opportunities, solve problems, find new purposes for discarded materials and demonstrate that a recycling program could serve people just as meaningfully as it served the environment.
When asked what she hopes people remember years from now, however, Smith does not point to dollars generated, tons diverted from landfills or programs created.
She points to her people.
“That my TEAM came first and I wasn’t afraid of being accused of ‘falling on my sword’ if necessary and that I believed in the need for DFMWR and its mission for Soldiers and their Families,” Smith said.
After more than four decades of civilian service, that may be the clearest measure of Chris Smith’s legacy.
She left Fort Sill cleaner. She helped make its MWR programs stronger. She found ways to save Soldiers and families money, turn discarded materials into opportunities and make life a little better for the people around her.
But perhaps most importantly, the people who worked for Chris Smith knew they mattered.
And that is leadership.
title: Team First: Chris Smith Leaves a Legacy of Leadership and Service at Fort Sill

ICYMI: Congressman Everton Blair Introduces the Newton County Water Infrastructure Improvement Act, Authorizing $23.9 Million for Vital Water Infrastructure
Media Contact:
Allison Phipps, Allison.Phipps@mail.house.gov; Amya Enlow, Amya.Enlow@mail.house.gov
WASHINGTON, D.C. — In an ongoing push to prioritize local needs and deliver tangible results for Georgia’s 13th Congressional District, Congressman Everton Blair Jr. (GA-13) introduced H.R. 10533, the Newton County Water Infrastructure Improvement Act, on September 24, 2026.
The legislation would extend the existing U.S. Army Corps of Engineers authorization to deliver on vital stormwater and wastewater infrastructure projects in Newton County. These long-overdue investments will improve the county's quality of life by repairing wastewater and stormwater infrastructure, restoring essential pumping facilities and expanding access to local drinking water.
"Delivering clean, reliable drinking water and functional public infrastructure is fundamental for the health and future of our communities." said Congressman Blair. "Newton County is seeing remarkable growth, and we must ensure our infrastructure keeps up with the needs of our people. The Newton County Water Infrastructure Improvement Act puts our community first by securing the federal resources required to expand water capacity, protect public health, and position Newton County for long-term strength and stability.".
The Newton County Water Infrastructure Improvement Act keeps the health, safety, and dignity of working people and local neighborhoods at the center of our federal policy agenda. As part of Congressman Blair’s continued efforts to modernize local infrastructure and deliver vital public resources across the district, this legislation takes immediate action to protect the local drinking water supply and improve critical public works, ensuring Newton County and communities across Georgia’s 13th District have the resilient infrastructure needed to thrive for generations to come.

Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026
The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.
In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered. FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations. Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.
“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”
“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.
“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”
“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."
Examples of cases charged during this period include:
In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses. Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted. In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.
In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.
In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.
In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo. His case is pending trial.
Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.
In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.
FBI’s Operation Steadfast Promise
Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.
This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.
During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.
Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.
The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.
The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at www.tips.fbi.gov.

Oct. 20, 2026
Ballots Are Being Delivered Securely and On Time
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Postal Service recently held a briefing on its Election Mail processes and procedures to reiterate its commitment to the secure and timely delivery of ballots.
“The Postal Service is confident and ready to deliver a successful Election Mail season,” said Postmaster General David Steiner. “[W]e share a common goal: instilling confidence in all Americans that their Election Mail will be handled securely – and delivered reliably.”
Adrienne Marshall, director of Election and Government Mail Services at the Postal Service added, “Our Postal Service employees are diligently working to process and deliver ballots on time, and we ask that voters do their part and mail early.” The organization’s long-standing recommendation is that domestic non-military voters mail their completed ballots BEFORE Election Day, and AT LEAST ONE WEEK before they must be received by their election office.
The nation’s postal network is currently operating without any major reported disruptions, and service performance across the nation is strong. Through October 9, ballot mail delivery performance scores are high: 97.98 percent of ballot mail was delivered on time when compared with the Postal Service’s service standard.
“The Postal Service has a long and strong record of successfully delivering Election Mail,” said the Postal Service Board of Governor’s Chair Amber McReynolds. “That record is not accidental, and it reflects extensive planning, close coordination with scores of stakeholders, and the training and commitment of hundreds of thousands of postal employees who understand the importance of this responsibility.”
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service partners with the Postal Service to ensure a successful election season.
“In this election cycle, and every election cycle, the Postal Inspection Service is committed to ensuring the safe and secure delivery of Election Mail, the integrity of our elections, and the protection of election officials and election offices from threatening and dangerous mail.” said Brendan Donahue, the organization’s deputy chief inspector. “With more than 170 million delivery points nationwide, upholding the security of Election Mail, and all mail, is a team effort.”
“Our processes and procedures for this year will be consistent with previous election cycles,” Marshall said. The Postal Service is not implementing or enforcing the Ballot Mail for Federal Elections rule for the 2026 General Election.
In the briefing, Postal Service officials addressed the following:
Proven  Track Record of Delivering the Nation’s Election Mail
For  the 2024 General Election, the Postal Service delivered 99.6% of ballots  from voters to election officials within three days, as reported  in this 2024 Post-Election  Analysis. 
Post-election analyses of the Postal Service’s performance can be found in reports on 2022 and 2024.
Extraordinary Measures Start Oct. 24
The Postal Service deploys specific Election Mail processes and procedures all year long. In the final weeks of the election season, USPS also implements extraordinary measures to swiftly move ballot mail that is entered close to when it must be received by the local election office.
This year, extraordinary measures begin Saturday, Oct. 24, and will continue through the last day in each state that their boards of elections will accept completed mail-in ballots as timely.
The extraordinary measures are designed to accelerate and enhance the delivery of ballot mail, when the Postal Service is able to identify the mailpiece as a ballot. The Postal Service’s extraordinary measures include but are not limited to:
These measures are consistent with the Postal Service’s efforts in past elections.
Ongoing Engagement with Election Officials to Quickly Address Any Issues
The Postal Service meets regularly with stakeholders across the Election Mail landscape to educate them on postal procedures and guidance, including local, state and federal election officials; postal unions and management associations; federal agencies and Congress, the mailing industry; and non-governmental organizations.
USPS provides recommendations regarding mailpiece design, including barcodes and other visibility tools, and best practices for using the mail. USPS also issues an Official Election Mail Guide for election officials and regularly updates the Election Mail pages on usps.com with detailed information for voters and the general public.
In addition, local USPS Customer Relations teams nationwide meet regularly with state and municipal election administrators to understand individual jurisdictions’ plans, share guidance from the Postal Service on effective mailing practices, and address local issues that arise.
Postmarking
The Postal Service has instructed employees throughout the country about the organization’s ballot postmarking processes and procedures and reviewed the standard operating procedures for ballot postmarking.
USPS has not changed its postmarking practices, but adjustments to transportation operations result in some mailpieces not arriving at originating processing facilities on the same day that they are mailed. Because postmarks are generally applied at those facilities, the date on the postmarks may not necessarily match the date that the mailpiece was collected by a letter carrier, dropped off at a retail location, or placed in a collection box. The transportation adjustments are designed to eliminate inefficiencies and ensure a reliable integrated mail and package network for customers well into the future.
Voters can ensure that their completed ballot-return envelope receives a postmark, and that the date on the postmark aligns with the date of mailing, by bringing the ballot to a Postal Service retail location and requesting a manual postmark at the retail counter when dropping it off. Manual postmarks are applied free of charge.
Protecting the Security and Integrity of Election Mail
The Postal Inspection Service works with the U.S. departments of Justice and Homeland Security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI and the USPS Office of Inspector General, as well as state and local law enforcement, to secure Election Mail.
Postal Inspection Service personnel will physically observe Election Mail processing and delivery operations. They will review the physical security of Election Mail and the workplace and report their findings to Inspection Service and Postal Service leadership so that corrective action may be taken for any concerns that are identified.
The Postal Inspection Service asks the public to report suspicious mail and Election Mail-related security or criminal incidents by calling the Postal Inspection Service national hotline at 877-876-2455, or reporting it online at www.USPIS.gov/report. Those who want to learn more about the Postal Inspection Service and Election Mail security can visit https://www.uspis.gov/election-mail-security.

title: Civil Rights Division and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Secure $5,000,000 Joint Settlement with Instacart for Discriminating Against U.S. Workers

text:
Scott, Takano Condemn EEOC Abandoning Workers Facing Discrimination
“One might reasonably conclude that this settlement appears to be an attempt to collude with a private organization to exempt the employer…from facing charges regarding unlawful discrimination.”
WASHINGTON – Today, Committee on Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and Equality Caucus Chair Mark Takano (CA-39) condemned the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) settlement with Christian Employers Alliance (CEA).
Under the settlement, the EEOC agreed not to bring charges against the CEA, a membership organization made up of businesses that identify as Christian and vow as a condition of membership to adhere to certain principles, over certain gender-identity discrimination. The CEA’s lawsuit claimed that the EEOC’s harassment guidance on gender identity and transgender status violated the religious freedom of Christian business owners. Specifically, CEA argued that the guidance forces Christian employers to use an employee’s stated pronouns over the employers’ religious beliefs; to allow employees to dress in ways that conform to a gender not assigned at birth; and to permit transgender employees to use sex-specific facilities in line with their gender identity.
Under this agreement, the EEOC is also prevented from acting against current and future CEA members who are alleged to have discriminated against transgender applicants or employees as described in the agreement. This raises serious constitutional questions and contradicts long-standing Department of Justice policy preventing the government from entering into agreements that limit the executive authority and discretion of future Administrations. It also hampers the EEOC’s ability to carry out its mission of combating discrimination now and in the future.
“The EEOC – charged with employment nondiscrimination laws – took an unprecedented step with this settlement by covering future members of the Christian Employers Alliance and preemptively agreeing to never bring certain charges against the organization and its members in perpetuity,” wrote the Members. “We strongly question the legal authority this settlement presumes—that the EEOC can bind the hands of the EEOC in perpetuity, including under future Presidents and Commissioners, to not bring charges against certain organizations for certain unlawful practices.
“One might reasonably conclude that this settlement appears to be an attempt to collude with a private organization to exempt the employer, including future employers who join the Christian Employers Alliance, from facing charges regarding unlawful discrimination,” the Members concluded.
To read the full letter, click here.
Background:
On February 15, 2025, CEC Chair Takano called on Acting EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas and Acting General Counsel Andrew Rogers to resign after the EEOC began filing motions to dismiss court cases the agency brought against businesses accused of discriminating against transgender and nonbinary employees.
On June 13, 2025, Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03), Mark Takano (CA-39), and CEC Vice Chair Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), led 70 members in sending a letter urging Andrea Lucas, Acting Chair of the EEOC, to uphold her obligations under federal law and address discrimination against transgender and nonbinary workers.
On November 24, 2025, Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) expressed his opposition to the EEOC’s proposed Harassment Guidance rescission and urged the EEOC not to abandon its mission to fully protect workers from discrimination.
On January 23, 2026, Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) called into question moves by the EEOC that would narrow its mission to only protect white men.
On June 17, 2026, Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and House Workforce Protections Subcommittee Ranking Member Ilhan Omar (MN-05) called for an immediate, long-overdue oversight hearing with the EEOC leadership to examine the EEOC’s budget request and Republicans’ deregulation agenda.
