Pensacola, Florida – Willie Curtis Slack Jr., 50, of Milton, Florida, was sentenced to fifteen years in federal prison after having previously pleaded guilty to two counts of possession of firearms and ammunition by a convicted felon. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Keeping firearms out of the hands of dangerous criminals, like this serial felon, is imperative if we hope to succeed in keeping our communities safe. Thanks to this successful prosecution by my office we can rest assured this thug can’t continue to terrorize our community. President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche have committed the full might of the Department of Justice toward incapacitating the perpetrators of violent crime, and my office will continue to aggressively prosecute those offenders to deliver the safe, crime-free streets that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that during a traffic stop in October 2023, law enforcement officers found and seized a loaded pistol and marijuana from the defendant’s waistband. Then, in December 2024, law enforcement seized two additional firearms and matching bulk ammunition that the defendant had knowingly possessed earlier that year. Prior to these incidents, the defendant had been convicted of numerous felonies, including batteries, resisting officer with violence, aggravated assault by threat, and multiple drug sale and trafficking convictions. As a result, he was subject to enhanced minimum mandatory penalties under the Armed Career Criminal Act in this case.

The sentence was the result of investigations by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Santa Rosa County Sheriff’s Office, with assistance from the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Alicia Forbes.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

text:
Illinois Laboratory Owner Charged in $66M COVID-19 Testing Fraud Scheme
A federal grand jury in the Northern District of Illinois returned an indictment yesterday charging Rajesh “Raj” Patel, 52, of Schaumburg, Illinois, with a $66.2 million fraud scheme in which Patel allegedly billed for hundreds of thousands of COVID-19 tests that were never performed.
“This defendant allegedly exploited a global crisis for personal gain, fabricating hundreds of thousands of COVID-19 tests – then billing the taxpayer for it,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s Fraud Division. “Every dollar taken from a federal health care program is a dollar taken from the American people. The Fraud Division will find those who steal from taxpayers, and we will prosecute them.”
“Fighting financial fraud and holding accountable those who unlawfully obtain federal assistance for personal profit remains a top priority for the FBI,” said FBI Chicago Special Agent in Charge Ryan Whalen. “Pandemic assistance programs were designed to provide a lifeline to vulnerable members of society. Those who are entrusted with federal healthcare dollars have a responsibility to bill honestly and accurately, and the FBI and our partners will stop at nothing to ensure that those who deceive and steal taxpayer dollars for their own purposes face full justice.”
“The COVID-19 pandemic required an unprecedented investment of public resources to protect the health and well-being of our communities. As alleged, this scheme exploited a federally funded program created to ensure uninsured individuals had access to critical testing services during a national emergency,” said Special Agent in Charge Thomas Ethridge of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “HHS-OIG is committed to holding accountable those who seek to profit through fraud and abuse of government health care programs. We will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect taxpayer dollars and safeguard the integrity of programs designed to serve the public.”
According to court documents, Patel was the co-owner and Chief Operating Officer of a clinical laboratory located in Hillside, Illinois, that processed polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests during the COVID-19 pandemic. In around March 2021, Patel’s laboratory entered into an agreement with Meridian Medical Staffing Inc. (Meridian). The laboratory paid Meridian tens of millions of dollars for collecting test specimens and providing the laboratory with the specimens and biological information of the purported patients. In reality, many of these patients never existed or never provided test specimens to Meridian.
Between May 2021 and April 2022, Patel allegedly created fake “negative” test results for at least 380,000 PCR tests on specimens provided by Meridian. The laboratory never actually performed these tests. Patel allegedly created the fake “negative” test results so that the laboratory could fraudulently bill the U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) Uninsured Program, a federally funded program that covered the costs of COVID-19 tests for individuals without health insurance coverage. Patel’s laboratory submitted approximately $66.2 million in fraudulent claims to HRSA as a result of Patel’s scheme, and HRSA paid the laboratory approximately $44.1 million due to these fraudulent claims. Patel personally obtained approximately $28 million in proceeds from the scheme.
Patel is charged with five counts of wire fraud. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on each count.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division); Special Agent in Charge Ryan Whalen of the FBI Chicago Field Office; and Special Agent in Charge Thomas Ethridge of the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) made the announcement.
The FBI Chicago Field Office and HHS-OIG investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Claire Sobczak Pacelli of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section is prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Illinois Laboratory Owner Charged in $66M COVID-19 Testing Fraud Scheme

Coast Guard repatriates 63 aliens to Dominican Republic following unlawful voyage vessel interdiction
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — The crew of Coast Guard Cutter Winslow Griesser repatriated 63 of 66 alien migrants to two Dominican Republic Navy vessels, Saturday, following the interdiction of an unlawful migration vessel voyage in Mona Passage waters, Friday.
Three of the interdicted aliens remain in federal custody facing further investigation and charges of illegal attempted reentry to the United States under 8 U.S.C 1326.
During a routine patrol Friday afternoon, the aircrew of a Coast Guard HC-144 Ocean Sentry aircraft detected a 30-foot grossly overloaded makeshift vessel, approximately 70 nautical miles northwest of Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. Coast Guard watchstanders at Sector San Juan diverted cutter Winslow Griesser to interdict the suspect vessel and directed the launch of an MH-60T Jayhawk helicopter crew from Air Station Borinquen to provide overhead rescue support.
Due to safety of life at sea concerns, the cutter crew safely embarked all the migrants from the makeshift vessel, including 55 men and four women who claimed to be Dominican Republic nationals, and six men and a woman who claimed to be Haitian nationals.
“I’m proud of my crew and the Coast Guard aircrews for stopping what could have been a treacherous journey for all onboard an overloaded migrant vessel Friday night,” said Lt. Alex Kearney, Coast Guard Cutter Winslow Griesser commanding officer. “They saved 66 people from a dangerously overloaded vessel attempting to transit across a vast ocean with little to no safety equipment and no regard to safety of human life at sea. These voyages are extremely dangerous, and anyone conducting illegal smuggling migrant ventures may be subject to prosecution and imprisonment.”
Following the interdiction, cutter Winslow Griesser rendezvoused with Dominican Republic Navy vessels Bellatrix and Acrux in the Mona Passage and completed the repatriation of 63 migrants.
Migrants interdicted at sea or apprehended ashore will not be allowed to stay in the United States or a U.S. territory. Furthermore, individuals who arrive unlawfully may be declared ineligible for legal immigration parole options and face repatriation to their country of origin or return to their country of departure.
The Coast Guard, along with its Operation Vigilant Sentry and Operation Bahamas, Turks and Caicos partners, maintains a continual presence with air, land and sea assets in the Florida Straits, Windward Passage, Mona Passage and Caribbean Sea in support of OVS. This multiagency and multilayered approach is designed to protect the safety of life at sea while preventing unlawful maritime entry to the United States and its territories.
This interdiction is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

Criminal alien from Mexico passes away in ICE custody in Texas
LAREDO, Texas – Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old criminal alien from Mexico, passed away in ICE custody Oct. 17, 2026. His criminal history includes an arrest for theft of property July 27, 2004.
On Oct. 17, at approximately 9:48 a.m. CST, Andrade was found unresponsive in his assigned bed at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas. Security staff declared a medical emergency and immediately began life saving measures. The Laredo Fire Department Emergency Medical Service was called and despite life-saving efforts, at 10:10 a.m. Andrade was declared deceased. The cause of death is unknown. An autopsy will determine the official cause of death.
While in custody, Andrade received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals. He had a documented medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and anxiety.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection arrested Andrade on June 26, 2026, while attempting to enter the U.S. at the Juarez-Lincoln Bridge in Laredo, Texas. Andrade, a lawful permanent resident, was determined to have obtained status through fraudulent means by failing to disclose his previous arrest during the review process. He was processed and transferred to ICE custody pending removal proceedings before an immigration judge. He was receiving due process.
Consistent with ICE policy, Enforcement and Removal Operations notified the Department of Homeland Security, the ICE Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility via the Joint Intake Operation Center. The Consulate of Mexico was notified.
ICE makes official notifications to Congress, nongovernmental organization stakeholders, and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.
ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure, and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental, and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility, access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.

text:
Massachusetts Man Pleads Guilty to Wire Fraud and the Fraudulent Use of Government Seals
OCALA, Fla. – Mario Cesar Dos Santos, Jr., 50, of Massachusetts, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud and one count of fraudulent use of government seals. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida made the announcement. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services assisted in the investigation.
According to court documents, Dos Santos was the president of Chaplain Emergency Management Agency, Inc. (CEMA), an organization he falsely represented as a government agency endorsed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Dos Santos fraudulently used the seals of FEMA, the Department of Homeland Security, and the FBI to fraudulently portray CEMA as a federal government agency and charge individuals to attend chaplaincy training courses in Florida, other states, and abroad. Dos Santos and CEMA did not have authorization to use the seals of DHS, FEMA, or FBI, nor are they affiliated with these agencies or any other federal government department or agency.
Dos Santos organized numerous CEMA chaplaincy training courses and lied to attendees that CEMA partnered with FEMA and that CEMA and its courses were endorsed by FEMA. The courses were free to attend, but Dos Santos charged attendees approximately $400 to $450 for a chaplaincy certificate. After attendees completed the course and paid the associated fees, Dos Santos provided them with identification cards, law enforcement badges, and course completion certificates containing the seals of various U.S. departments and agencies. Dos Santos told attendees that the ID cards and badges authorized them to support law enforcement during emergency situations and take control of emergency situations until law enforcement arrived. He also told them that their status as CEMA chaplains would give them a level of immunity from immigration enforcement and protection from deportation. These claims were false.
As shown in the images below, the identification cards displayed a CEMA logo that modified the DHS seal to read, “U.S. Department of Homeland Chaplain.” The back of the cards displayed the DHS/FEMA seal. The certificates displayed the FBI seal and a slightly different version of the CEMA logo that modified an older version of the FEMA seal to read, “U.S. Department of Homeland Chaplain.”
Dos Santos also offered CEMA merchandise for sale, including polo shirts, bumper stickers, jackets, badges, and badge holders, all bearing either the DHS or FEMA seal. During an undercover operation conducted at a training held on Sept. 27, 2025, a confidential informant purchased merchandise items pictured below. Approximately 30 to 45 individuals attended the training.
As part of the undercover operation, the confidential informant also obtained access to a CEMA group chat that had more than 750 members when the investigation began in August 2025. Dos Santos used the group chat to promote upcoming courses, including sending digital flyers of such courses.
CEMA’s website and social media accounts all displayed the CEMA logo, which incorporated an altered version of the DHS seal, and falsely identified CEMA as a government organization or federal agency. The website also falsely claimed that CEMA was “fully accredited by the International Association for Continuing Education and Training (IACET) and the American Council on Education (ACE).”
Dos Santos was arrested Feb. 19 at the Orlando International Airport, after he traveled from Boston to Orlando for a CEMA training that was scheduled for Feb. 21. At the time of his arrest, Dos Santos was wearing a CEMA polo shirt with the DHS seal on the sleeve and chest.
Dos Santos is a Brazilian alien who came to the United States in 2016. He has overstayed his visa and is undergoing deportation proceedings.
If you believe you have been a victim of this fraudulent scheme, please contact the FBI via email at CEMAPotentialVictims@fbi.gov no later than Oct. 30.
This case was investigated by the DHS Office of Inspector General and the FBI, with assistance from FEMA, USCIS’ Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, and the Federal Air Marshal Service.

text:
- For Immediate Release:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency.
“Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.”
The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users.
The guidance identifies two categories of companion software:
- Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used.
- Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising.
“This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.”
“Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology. “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.”
This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on.
The final guidance is available here.
###
The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.
title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software

Brad D. Schimel, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, Special Agent in Charge Todd C. Smith of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Chicago Field Division, and Assistant Special Agent in Charge John McGarry of the DEA Milwaukee District Office announced the extradition of three Mexican nationals, who were crew members of a U.S.-flagged vessel, to face maritime narcotics trafficking charges.

Miguel Ángel Campos-Barragán, Giovanni Vidrio-López, and Eustaquio Espinosa-Hernández, all Mexican citizens, were extradited from Costa Rica after being indicted in the Eastern District of Wisconsin in May 2025 for alleged violations of the Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act (MDLEA). On Oct. 19, the defendants made their initial appearance and arraignment before U.S. Magistrate Judge Nancy Joseph in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Judge Joseph ordered that they be held in pre-trial detention.

According to count one of the indictment, from approximately January 2024 until on or about April 15, 2025, the Campos-Barragán, Vidrio-López, and Espinosa-Hernández allegedly conspired together and with others to possess with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine while on board a vessel of the United States. Count two of the indictment alleges that on April 15, 2025, the defendants possessed with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine while on board a vessel of the United States.

On April 15, 2025, Costa Rican authorities interdicted the My Lisa Too , a U.S.-flagged vessel, near Quepos, Costa Rica. Law enforcement seized approximately 840 kilograms of cocaine concealed within the vessel, and arrested Campos-Barragán, Vidrio-López, and Espinosa-Hernández, who were the vessel’s crew.

“This case is noteworthy for several reasons,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Brad Schimel. “First, this is one of the largest drug seizures ever charged in the Eastern District of Wisconsin. Second, it is an unusual case because an enormous quantity of drugs was intercepted before it ever entered the United States. This case demonstrates the incredible capabilities of U.S. authorities working in partnership with our counterparts in Central and South America.”

“The extradition of these individuals reinforces our commitment to relentlessly pursuing those who traffic dangerous illicit drugs into our communities,” said Todd C. Smith, Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Chicago Field Division. “We are grateful for our partnerships with the Homeland Security Task Force, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, and our state and local law enforcement partners, as well as our foreign partners in Costa Rica, in holding those affiliated with Foreign Terrorist Organizations like the Sinaloa Cartel accountable.”

“The FBI and our Homeland Security Task Force partners are working together every day to crush violent crime to include cartels,” said FBI Milwaukee Special Agent in Charge Alan Karr. “The FBI along with our local, state, federal and international partners are committed to disrupting and dismantling drug trafficking networks through collaborative investigations to protect the American people.”

An indictment is merely an allegation, and a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

The DEA Milwaukee Field Office and the DEA San Jose, Costa Rica Country Office investigated this case, with support and assistance from the FBI’s Milwaukee Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs and the Costa Rican government, including the Policía de Control de Drogas (PCD) and the Grupo de Operaciones Policiales Especiales del Servicio Nacional de Guardacostas (GOPES SNG), secured the arrests and extraditions from Costa Rica. The U.S. Marshals Service provided substantial assistance with returning the fugitives to the United States. Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert J. Brady, Jr. of the Eastern District of Wisconsin is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. — To the uninitiated, Aberdeen Proving Ground (APG) sounds like a singular military base located in Harford County, Maryland. But for those who work within the installation, the reality is a sprawling regional presence that reflects the diverse history of Army research and testing.
Rather than a single, interconnected landmass, APG is a non-contiguous regional footprint spanning over 100 miles across four Maryland counties. Operating under the U.S. Army Installation Management Command, the U.S. Army Garrison (USAG) Aberdeen Proving Ground coordinates services and support across this multi-county network, balancing historic legacies, high-tech testing demands, and localized municipal partnerships.
The full scope of APG’s modern mission is distributed across eight distinct geographical areas, each carrying its own specialized role and history.
The first and largest of these is Aberdeen. Comprising approximately 30,508 acres of land in Harford County, this northern portion of the base serves as a major hub for military testing, research, and development, and it houses Phillips Army Airfield. APG North also encompasses Spesutie Island, a 1,800-acre area situated in the Chesapeake Bay immediately adjacent to Aberdeen that was acquired in 1945 to expand range and testing capabilities.
The second area is the Edgewood, which spans roughly 10,126 acres in Harford County. Formerly the independent Edgewood Arsenal, this southern sector now serves as the U.S. Army's premier chemical research, development, and engineering center.
The third area is the Churchville Test Area, a non-contiguous 221-acre vehicle testing facility located in northern Harford County, about 10 miles north of the main base. It features steep natural grades and tight curves used by the Aberdeen Test Center to stress-test tracked and wheeled military vehicles.
The fourth component is the Adelphi Laboratory Center, a 207-acre installation located just north of Washington, D.C., in suburban Prince George's County. This facility serves as the headquarters of the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Army Research Laboratory (DEVCOM ARL).
The fifth and sixth areas are located in neighboring Baltimore County. Carroll Island is a non-contiguous 855-acre island situated across the Gunpowder River that was historically used for open-air testing and is currently utilized for environmental and wetland mitigation. Nearby, Graces Quarters is a non-contiguous 309-acre peninsula historically tied to Edgewood chemical testing that now hosts specialized defense projects at the Robotics Research Collaborative Campus.
The final two areas extend into the waterways and southern regions of Maryland. Pooles Island is a 206-acre island in the Chesapeake Bay that historically served as an artillery impact area and features a historic lighthouse. Lastly, the Blossom Point Research Facility comprises approximately 1,600 acres of land on Cedar Point Neck in Southern Maryland's Charles County, operating as a vital proving ground and testing facility along the Potomac River.
This unique layout is a direct reflection of how the Army's testing needs have evolved over more than a century. Longtime USAG APG employee Ed Heasley notes that the physical separation of these properties means the garrison naturally operates across a wider regional footprint than most standard installations.
This geographical distribution includes satellite sites like the Adelphi Laboratory Center and Blossom Point in Southern Maryland, which operate alongside other regional military installations while remaining administratively connected to APG. Heasley points out that because these remote locations are situated further from the main Harford County campus, APG represents a statewide geographical footprint.
Even between the primary hubs of Aberdeen and Edgewood personnel travel daily between gates via public access points. While navigating local highway traffic between Aberdeen and Edgewood is a routine part of the day, Heasley notes that travel time, traffic accidents, and general highway congestion remain a practical part of moving between the two main sectors.
Because APG's testing areas are integrated into the regional landscape, maintaining strong relationships with surrounding civilian communities has been a long-standing practice. This is particularly true for sites like the Churchville Test Area, which was established by the Ordnance Department in 1942 to test iconic combat vehicles from the M-4 Sherman to the modern M1 Abrams and M2 Bradley.
To protect Churchville from urban encroachment—and to preserve the quiet of nearby residents from the noise of round-the-clock testing—the Army partnered with Harford County and the Harford Land Trust in 2007 to establish a protective agricultural buffer, including a historic family farm.
Similarly, islands and peninsulas like Carroll Island, Graces Quarters, and Pooles Island are managed with an eye toward safety and environmental conservation. Carroll Island was originally acquired by the Army to create a coastal buffer zone and weapons development area, and today it serves as a safe zone between testing activities and the surrounding community.
Graces Quarters, a 476-acre peninsula acquired in 1918 to serve as a coastal buffer and weapons development area, completed a formal Record of Decision in 2004. While strict environmental protocols remain active, chemical testing there has terminated, and the land now hosts the Robotics Research Collaborative Campus.
Pooles Island, which is on the National Register of Historic Places, served as an artillery impact area until the early 1970s. Except for a seven-acre area around the historic lighthouse, the island remains restricted due to the historical presence of unexploded ordnance.
Providing safety and emergency services across this fragmented footprint relies on close coordination with local civilian authorities. The garrison maintains emergency services tailored to the needs of both Aberdeen and Edgewood, and Heasley emphasizes that these services are built on mutual aid and community integration.
If an emergency arises, mutual assistance between the garrison and surrounding civilian agencies is a standard practice to support family housing and outlying testing spaces. These partnerships ensure a seamless safety net across county lines.
Operating an installation with such distinct geographic identities also means navigating its historical workforce cultures. The historical roots of the "Aberdeen side" and the "Edgewood side" date back to when they were entirely separate entities, a distinction that still lives in the memory of the long-term workforce and the surrounding civilian population.
Heasley notes that maintaining balanced communication across both major areas remains a standard approach to keeping the workforce connected. For those working within the garrison, leveraging the deep institutional knowledge of the civilian workforce has historically played an important role in supporting the installation's diverse missions.
title: One Garrison, Eight Frontiers: Inside the 100-Mile Footprint of Aberdeen Proving Ground

FORT POLK, La. — For eligible Bayne-Jones Army Community Hospital patients, taking the next step in colorectal cancer screening may begin by simply opening the mail.
Through the Defense Health Agency’s mailed fecal immunochemical test program, also known as FIT, June Lyons, BJACH’s population health nurse, identifies eligible patients and coordinates orders for at-home screening kits with step-by-step instructions and prepaid return packaging.
Lyons said mailings began in September, following a pause during the summer’s extreme heat. Kits continue to go out weekly, and BJACH received 26 screening results during the first month of mailings.
The program offers a convenient option for patients who might otherwise postpone screening.
Capt. Addison Bray, a physician and chief of primary care at BJACH, said concerns about colonoscopy and transportation issues can cause patients to delay screening.
“FIT testing helps to alleviate these concerns since it is done at home,” Bray said.
Screening options available to BJACH patients include FIT, stool DNA testing such as Cologuard, and colonoscopy. Bray said the appropriate choice depends on the individual patient.
FIT checks for hidden blood in a small stool sample and is repeated annually. Cologuard checks for hidden blood and certain DNA changes and is generally repeated every three years. Both are completed at home. Colonoscopy allows a provider to examine the colon directly and remove polyps when appropriate.
Patients who have already completed colorectal cancer screening should contact their care team to confirm when they are next due before completing a newly received kit.
For patients using FIT, no bowel-cleansing preparation is required.
“Patients do not make any changes to diet before they complete this stool test,” Lyons said.
Patients collect a small sample at home, label and package it according to the enclosed instructions, and return it promptly for laboratory testing. Keeping mailing addresses current helps ensure kits reach the right destination.
A positive result from either at-home screening option does not mean a patient has cancer. It means further evaluation with a colonoscopy is needed.
Results become part of the patient’s electronic health record. An abnormal result alerts the care team, who contacts the patient and coordinates the next steps. Bray said colonoscopy referrals are routed through TRICARE to community providers.
Patients experiencing symptoms should contact their provider rather than wait for routine screening.
“Screening tests are designed for asymptomatic, average risk patients,” Bray said.
Patients with symptoms need an evaluation to determine the appropriate testing and care. Medical and family history also help providers recommend an individualized screening plan.
Lyons encourages patients to discuss screening needs with their primary care team, even when they feel well.
“We are here to walk alongside you on your healthcare journey, not just to perform a procedure,” she said.
To ask about colorectal cancer screening or a mailed FIT kit, message your care team through the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal or to schedule a primary care appointment, call 726-780-2175.
Editor’s note: This is the second in a three-part series highlighting cervical, colorectal and breast cancer screening at BJACH.
title: Due for colorectal cancer screening? BJACH brings an option to your doorstep

text:
The Internal Revenue Service's (IRS's) Free File Program (FFP) is a public-private partnership between the IRS and Free File, Inc. (FFI), a group of tax software companies. The FFP allows certain taxpayers to electronically file (e-file) their federal income tax return free of charge using guided software provided by participating tax preparation companies. According to a 2023 FFP memorandum of understanding (MOU), the objective of the program is to increase e-filing of tax returns, especially for economically disadvantaged populations, through collaboration between the IRS and member companies.
In general, expanding e-filing options was originally intended to save taxpayers and the government time and money. According to a 2002 press release from the Department of the Treasury (Treasury), e-filing benefits include quicker refunds, lower taxpayer filing errors, and lower government processing costs.
This In Focus summarizes the FFP's origin and evolution, taxpayer participation and experience, and policy issues.
The IRS developed the FFP to comply with provisions in law. The IRS Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998 (RRA; P.L. 105-206) directed the IRS to increase the share of e-filed individual returns from 23% in 1998 to 80% by 2007, with input from the private sector. This goal was prioritized by President George W. Bush's E-Government Initiative. A 2001 directive from the Office of Management and Budget's Quicksilver Task Force identified the EZ Tax Filing Initiative as one of 24 projects to achieve the E-Government Initiative's main objectives. The EZ Tax Filing Initiative was intended to help the IRS reach the individual e-filing goal established in the RRA. The IRS first achieved the 2007 e-filing goal in 2012, when 83% of federal individual income tax returns were e-filed. In FY2025, e-filing was the most predominant filing method, with over 93% of federal individual income tax returns filed online.
Initially, the IRS tried to accomplish the aims of the EZ Tax Filing Initiative by developing free digitized versions of Form 1040 and related instructions; however, in January 2002, the Treasury asked the IRS to establish a partnership with tax software companies to develop a free online filing system that would be managed by the IRS for low-income taxpayers, who were most likely to file paper returns. The Treasury asserted that a public-private partnership was the best way to encourage growth in e-filing because it allowed the IRS to leverage the expertise of established companies in the field rather than requiring the IRS to develop its own software.
The FFP originated later that year, in October 2002, when the IRS signed an agreement with the 17 original FFI member companies.
The October 2002 agreement provided a division of authority and responsibility between the IRS and the member companies. It required the companies to provide their tax preparation and filing services through IRS.gov at no cost to the bottom 60% of individual taxpayers, ranked by adjusted gross income (AGI).
The companies, not the IRS, set the eligibility requirements for free filing based on a taxpayer's age, income, and state of residence. To participate in the FFP, a company had to prove that it could serve at least 10% of individual filers.
A controversial element of the agreement was a commitment by the IRS to not compete in the market for tax filing and preparation. Preventing the IRS from becoming a competitor was a major incentive for tax software companies to participate in the FFP. Other incentives for member companies included marketing benefits or the potential for retaining FFP participants as paid customers if they later became ineligible for the FFP.
The IRS and FFI have extended and revised the original agreement several times. The second (2005) agreement reduced the free services a member company could offer to eligible taxpayers, barred member companies from providing free filing to more than 50% of eligible taxpayers, and increased the share of taxpayers eligible for the FFP to the bottom 70% of individuals ranked by AGI. The third (2009) agreement expanded the FFP—by making free fillable individual income tax forms available to any taxpayer, regardless of income—and required FFI companies to embed a link to IRS.gov in their FFP online pages.
These subsequent agreements are linked to various MOUs intended to implement the revised agreements. The first MOU was signed in 2006. The current MOU was signed in 2023 and has been extended to October 31, 2029. It includes provisions intended to raise taxpayer awareness of the FFP, encourage eligible taxpayers to regularly use it, and prevent participating companies from excluding their Free File pages from internet searches. In a departure from previous rules, the MOU contains no commitment from the IRS to not develop its own free direct e-filing system.
The number of companies participating in the FFP has decreased from the 17 original members in 2002 to 8 members in 2026. According to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), two of the largest companies—H&R Block and Intuit—left the program at the end of the 2020 and 2021 tax filing seasons, respectively. These two companies combined had served approximately 70% of FFP participants.
The FFP provides eligible taxpayers with access to member companies' free online guided tax preparation and filing software tools. These tools use a self-directed tax preparation method, in which taxpayers input information about their tax situations that member companies use to complete and e-file the tax returns. The FFP is focused on covering taxpayers that are least able to afford e-filing, and it is currently available to taxpayers with an AGI of $89,000 or less.
Since the FFP's inception, participation among eligible taxpayers has averaged 3% each year. Participation peaked at roughly 6% (5.1 million taxpayers) in 2004, while the lowest participation rates were 2% each year from 2016 through 2018 (2.5 million to 2.6 million taxpayers). In FY2025, roughly 3% of taxpayers eligible for the FFP (3.2 million taxpayers) used the FFP, including both free fillable forms and guided tax preparation software. In tax year 2019, 44% of taxpayers who used the FFP had an AGI of $17,000 or less. Most users were single filers, under the age of 35, and did not claim dependents.
Most FFP-eligible taxpayers used other options for filing their tax return that likely would have required a fee. While a lack of awareness of the FFP may explain some of the low take-up for the program, there is also evidence that many first-time FFP users do not maintain usage in future years, even if they are still eligible for the program. A 2020 Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) evaluation found that reasons contributing to low program participation were "complexity, confusion, and lack of taxpayer awareness about the operation and requirements of the [FFP]." GAO estimated that roughly 40% of FFP users opted to use other filing options for the following year's tax return.
GAO reported that despite efforts to improve the taxpayer experience, opportunities remained to better align taxpayer experiences with existing guidelines for federal digital services. These opportunities could include optimizing the FFP for mobile devices, increasing access for taxpayers with disabilities, and providing the software in more languages.
Some concerns about the FFP's performance surfaced in 2019 during congressional consideration of a bill to reform certain aspects of IRS's taxpayer service. In April of that year, the House passed a bill (the Taxpayer First Act) that supporters intended to strengthen and codify taxpayer rights and further transform the IRS into a customer-friendly agency. One provision would have codified the existing FFP and permanently banned the IRS from providing its own direct e-file service.
The prospect of a statutory ban on an IRS direct-file tool triggered debate over the potential advantages and disadvantages of the FFP. The enacted bill (P.L. 116-25) did not include a provision to codify the FFP. The amended Free File MOU adopted in 2019 removed the provision banning the IRS from developing its own direct-file tool.
The IRS developed its own free tax preparation tool in a pilot program called Direct File (DF). The law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) provided the IRS with $15 million to create a DF task force to explore the feasibility of an IRS-run DF program; the IRS launched DF for use by eligible taxpayers in 2024.
Similar to software provided in the FFP, DF provided taxpayers with a free guided tax preparation and filing tool. Although DF was available to taxpayers regardless of income, the tool was only able to support taxpayers with relatively simple tax returns in a limited number of participating states.
DF was offered in the 2024 and 2025 filing seasons but was suspended for the 2026 filing season. In October 2025, the Treasury announced that it was suspending the DF program "due to the program's high costs, limited participation, and the [IRS's] need to focus resources on other priorities."
FFP proponents, including FFI companies, argue that the program should be retained because of its significant cost savings. According to one estimate, FFP filing saved taxpayers $1.5 billion in tax preparation and filing fees and saved the IRS millions of dollars in processing costs from 2003 to 2018.
Another potential advantage of the FFP cited by proponents is that it has the current technology to support a broad population. Although most tax returns filed through the FFP were simple returns, the tax preparation software available to taxpayers can support complex tax returns. Some participating members also offer free state tax returns for certain taxpayers, even though the FFP MOU does not require free state tax filing.
FFP critics say the FFP should be replaced by an IRS DF tool open to all taxpayers, regardless of income. Among the problems cited by critics are the following: (1) member company web pages for FFP filing are confusing and, in some cases, misleading; (2) the participation rate remains low; and (3) there are concerns relating to taxpayer privacy and security.
Critics also say that the program allows FFI companies to divert FFP-eligible taxpayers to using their paid filing services. In its 2020 report, TIGTA found that over 34.5 million FFP-eligible taxpayers e-filed their returns using member company paid services in FY2019. Other reporting found that FFI companies consistently discouraged interest in FFP alternatives.
Another potential policy option could include retaining the FFP, with additional investments in promoting the FFP among eligible taxpayers and in monitoring MOU compliance.
There is continued congressional interest in assessing free e-file options available to taxpayers, particularly the DF program and its potential impact on the FFP. In the 119th Congress, bills have been introduced to restore the DF program (S. 3948/H.R. 7806), while other bills have been introduced to prohibit the IRS from preparing tax returns through the DF program (S. 96/H.R. 451).
In a 2025 report, the Treasury highlighted various planned efforts to improve the FFP including enhancing awareness of the program, evaluating user experience, and strengthening program oversight. Additional evaluations of the FFP by GAO are also planned and may be helpful in assessing FFP performance.
title: The IRS Free File Program: An Overview

TRENTON, N.J. – A Somerset County woman who is an alien who immigrated to the United States from Jamaica admitted to illegally voting in a federal election, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced today.

Gaye Tyndale-Simpson, a resident of Bridgewater, New Jersey, who is not a citizen of the United States, pleaded guilty to one count of voting by an alien in a federal election before U.S. Magistrate Rukhsanah L. Singh in Trenton federal court.

According to documents filed in the case and statements made in court, Tyndale-Simpson, 55, is a citizen of Jamaica and has never been a citizen of the United States. In November 2024, Tyndale-Simpson voted in the General election that was held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of the President.

The voting by an alien charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 6 months in prison and a $100,000 fine. Sentencing is scheduled before Judge Singh on February 24, 2027.

U.S. Attorney Frazer credited special agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy, Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Michael McCarthy, U.S. Department of State, Diplomatic Security Service, New York Field Office, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Brian Wood, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, with the investigation.

This case was brought under the United States Attorney’s Office’s Election Integrity Task Force, a coalition of federal law enforcement partners focused on preserving and protecting the integrity of elections conducted in the District of New Jersey.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin D. Bleiberg of the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Criminal Division.

title: Alien Admits to Illegally Voting in Federal Election

First Lady Melania Trump Champions New U.S. Women’s Health Initiative
First Lady Melania Trump advanced a landmark program to improve women’s health through a new executive order that strengthens research, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for girls and women throughout every stage of life.
“Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest,” The First Lady said from the White House.
The Executive Order establishes a White House Women’s Health Task Force and establishes a new Women’s Health Division within the National Institutes of Health to accelerate scientific discoveries to improve women’s health outcomes.
First Lady Melania Trump highlighted her “First Lady’s Five Pillars of Women’s Health Innovation:”
- Direct research funding towards finding cures that affect women in a unique way.
- Use super intelligence to enhance our insight of female biology and speed up medical discoveries.
- Accelerate the process of getting promising therapeutics from laboratories to female patients, while maintaining strict safety standards.
- Ensure that medical breakthroughs are accessible and affordable to women, regardless of their financial circumstances.
- Replace generations of silence with open conversation, education, and compassion.
The Executive Order on Advancing Women’s Health to Improve Outcomes in All Phases of Life also recognizes the importance of collaboration with the private sector in advancing new technologies and solutions for women’s health. Through these efforts, the Trump Administration will work to ensure American women have access to the highest-quality, scientifically supported medical information and care while advancing new treatments, therapies, and cures.
To learn more about the Executive Order, read the fact sheet released by the White House.
First Lady Melania Trump’s full remarks, as prepared for delivery, are below.
Five Pillars of Women’s Health Innovation
Cabinet members, doctors, directors, administrators, and all in attendance today … thank you for standing behind this important issue.
Now is the time. This is the time.
This is a transformative moment for women in America. Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health.
Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.
The Advancing Women’s Health to Improve Outcomes in All Phases of Life Executive Order establishes a new standard for women’s health in America.
We now possess extraordinary scientific capabilities, such as super intelligence, advanced biotechnology, and groundbreaking therapies. At the same time, social norms are changing, and topics that were once taboo are becoming open, well-informed, and necessary.
Together, these developments present a unique chance to reinvent women’s healthcare.
We will move our hopes into action, beginning with the distinguished individuals and great minds present here today.
This afternoon, the first task force working session will convene. As you embark on this important work, I ask you to keep in mind the priorities that form my “First Lady’s Five Pillars of Women’s Health Innovation.”
Start by directing research funding towards finding cures for diseases that affect women in a unique way.
Second, use super intelligence to enhance our understanding of female biology and speed up medical discoveries- all to the benefit of women.
Third, accelerate the process of getting promising therapies from laboratories to female patients, while still keeping strict safety standards.
Fourth, ensure that medical breakthroughs are accessible and affordable to women, regardless of their financial circumstances.
And fifth, replace generations of silence with open conversation, education, and compassion.
Our mission must serve women at every stage of life, from young girls just starting out to mothers dealing with a complex range of responsibilities, to mature women who deserve to have vitality, dignity, and independence.
In 2026, medical advances can do more than just prolong life. It should give women the freedom to live life to its fullest- to pursue our dreams, experience love, discover, create, travel, and lead.
Today, we establish a new ambition: transforming hardship and pain into scientific discovery, effective treatments, and lasting cures.
We Are Women. We are resilient, capable, and deserving of lives defined not by the burdens we carry, but by the possibilities before us.
Our health should never limit the fullness of our lives.
I would like to thank the President for his support and for signing this very important Executive Order.
Thank you.
title: First Lady Melania Trump Champions New U.S. Women’s Health Initiative

The Federal Trade Commission issued its latest report to Congress on protecting older adults, which highlights key trends based on fraud reports submitted by older adults and the FTC’s efforts to combat the problem.
The report, Protecting Older Consumers 2025-2026, details the FTC’s efforts to stop unfair or deceptive acts or practices that impact older Americans through law enforcement actions, consumer education campaigns and outreach, and coordination with partners. It also highlights data analysis of consumer reports on fraud targeting older adults, including estimates that the overall cost of fraud to older adults in 2025 could be as high as $119.5 billion,
“The FTC is committed to protecting older Americans from scams, including by taking every action necessary to shut down fraud operations,” said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “This latest report showcases our enforcement actions, outreach efforts and other initiatives the FTC has undertaken to defend older adults from fraudulent enterprises and educate Americans on how best to protect themselves from scams.”
Older Adult Fraud Reporting Findings
The report outlines key findings from reports submitted in 2025 to the Consumer Sentinel Network, which collects reports from consumers about fraud and other consumer problems. Key findings include:
- Total fraud losses reported by older adults (ages 60 and over) increased about fivefold from 2020 to 2025, skyrocketing from about $600 million in 2020 to approximately $3 billion in 2025. This increase was driven largely by growing reports of extraordinarily large individual losses.
- Total reported fraud losses by older adults to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025 to over $1 billion, with consumers reporting that scammers often reach them on social media.
- In 2025, older adults continued to report much higher median individual dollar losses than younger adults. The disparity remained particularly large among people 80 and over, whose median reported loss was $2,000.
- Older adults continued to report losing money to fraud at lower rates than younger adults and filed no-loss fraud reports at much higher rates.
- Older adults continued to be more likely than younger adults to report losing money on tech support scams; prize, sweepstakes and lottery scams; romance scams; government impersonation scams; and scams impersonating friends or family members.
The report also details the FTC’s law enforcement actions that had an impact on older adults, which included matters involving debt relief services, health insurance fraud, government and business impersonation schemes, money-making opportunities and tech support scams.
The report also details the FTC’s outreach and education efforts through such programs as the Never Ever campaign, a public-private coordinated consumer education effort to raise awareness about government and business imposter scams. The report highlights the FTC’s collaboration with key partners, including government, academia and a wide array of partners from the nonprofit, financial services, retail and technology sectors. It also highlights the FTC’s efforts to coordinate with our criminal law enforcement partners to provide support and resources to older adults harmed by fraud, including referring older adults who suffered significant fraud losses to the DOJ’s National Elder Fraud Hotline for extra assistance.
The Commission vote authorizing the issuance of the report to Congress was 2-0.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: FTC Issues Annual Report to Congress on Agency’s Actions to Protect Older Adults

FinCEN Refers Findings to Federal Investigators to Combat Fraud and Protect Taxpayer Dollars
WASHINGTON - The U.S. Department of the Treasury announced today that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has identified approximately $270 million in suspicious financial activity potentially linked to fraud against federal student aid programs. FinCEN has referred these findings to federal investigators to pursue potential fraud schemes targeting federal student aid programs and help ensure those responsible are held accountable. These referrals underscore the Trump Administration’s commitment to eliminating fraud, protecting taxpayers, and safeguarding the integrity of federal student aid programs.
“Federal student aid is intended to expand educational opportunities, not line the pockets of fraudsters who steal from students pursuing their education and hardworking taxpayers,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “The Trump Administration will not tolerate criminals who exploit government programs for personal gain. Treasury is working with financial institutions and law enforcement to identify these fraud schemes, recover stolen funds, and hold those responsible accountable.”
“Federal student aid is meant to support students, not fraudsters. That is exactly why we introduced the new FAFSA fraud detection tool earlier this year, which stops fraud at the start of the federal student aid process,” said Education Secretary Linda McMahon. “We are proud to partner with the White House Task Force to combat fraud, waste, and abuse across these critical programs – already saving American taxpayers more than $2 billion in less than 2 years!”
In a July 2026 Alert, FinCEN warned financial institutions about student aid fraud and asked them to report suspicious activity. That Alert explained that schools or their payment contractors often send aid refunds by electronic bank transfer and that the payment description often includes the word “refund” along with the school’s name or initials. The Alert also noted that fraudsters often move stolen aid through money mules, shell companies, and fake accounts to hide the source of the money. These red flags help financial institutions spot suspicious payments and report them to FinCEN in suspicious activity reports, as required by the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA).
Financial institutions have filed nearly 100 suspicious activity reports since the July Alert. FinCEN’s review of these reports identified more than 20,000 potentially suspicious transactions since February 2026. These reports reflect suspicious activity that has been identified and reported by financial institutions and, therefore, should not be considered a complete representation of the scope of any particular type of suspicious activity. Accordingly, FinCEN has referred this information to law enforcement as tip-and-lead information for further investigation.
Federal student aid fraud schemes often involve fraudulent enrollments designed to divert financial assistance away from legitimate students. In “ghost student” schemes, criminals steal personal information, such as names and Social Security numbers, and use it to enroll fake students in classes under a victim’s identity. Fraudsters may also use super intelligence to produce fake documents that blend stolen information with invented details, which creates what are known as synthetic identities that can pass identity checks. Victims, including minors, often do not know that someone has received student aid in their name.
In “straw student” schemes, fraud rings pay real people for their personal information, enroll those people at a school, and then keep the aid refunds issued to them. Corrupt school employees sometimes help these rings by recruiting straw students and altering their school records. Student aid fraud drains taxpayer funds, and in some cases, keeps real students out of classes that fake enrollees have filled.
Student aid fraud has real consequences for students and American taxpayers. It drains finite grant resources from deserving students, potentially prevents legitimate students from enrolling in classes occupied by fraudulent enrollees, and can leave identity theft victims responsible for debts they never incurred.
As part of the Trump Administration’s efforts to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse across the federal government, Treasury is working with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, led by Vice President Vance, and encouraging whistleblowers to report credible information involving fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations, and tax-law violations. Whistleblower tips, combined with financial institutions’ reporting under the Bank Secrecy Act, help Treasury and its law enforcement partners uncover criminal networks, recover taxpayer funds, and hold bad actors accountable.
Treasury will continue to leverage financial intelligence, strengthen coordination across government, and pursue those who seek to profit by defrauding American taxpayers and harming legitimate students.
###
title: U.S. Treasury Identifies $270 Million in Suspicious Activity Linked to Federal Student Aid Fraud

WILLIAMSPORT — Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood, announced U.S Attorney Brian Miller. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller, Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today's sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia’s Capital Area Resident Agency.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

###
title: Canadian Man Sentenced to 50 Years in Prison for Committing an ISIS-Inspired Assault While in Prison for Plotting Terrorist Attack on New York City

US Department of Labor awards more than $10.5M in grants to support mine safety, health training across the nation
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor announced today that its Mine Safety and Health Administration has awarded more than $10.5 million in grants to reduce mining accidents, injuries, and illnesses by supporting training and education programs.
The agency is awarding these grants to support the delivery of federally mandated training for new and experienced miners at surface and underground coal and metal and nonmetal mines. MSHA is awarding grants in 45 states, the Navajo Nation, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership we’re investing billions of dollars into critical mining projects and resources for mining education,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Today’s grant announcement furthers the Department’s goal to expand mining across the United States to support this Administration’s goals to provide critical resources to the workers industries that continue to expand in America.”
States and territories apply for grant funding, which is then awarded to state mine inspectors’ offices, state departments of labor, and state-supported colleges and universities. Training and education programs are tailored locally to address conditions and hazards miners may experience.
“A strong and thriving America relies on a mining industry that safely produces the minerals essential to our economy,” said Assistant Secretary for Mine Safety and Health Wayne Palmer. “These grants will promote safe and healthful workplaces for over 300,000 miners across 47 states, territories, and tribal lands.”

Senior Air Force leaders, defense industry representatives and civic stakeholders gathered in Abilene, Texas, Oct. 8, for a B-21 summit focused on preparing Dyess Air Force Base for its future mission and strengthening the military-community partnerships essential to the next generation of long-range strike.
Hosted by the Abilene Chamber of Commerce’s Military Affairs Council, the summit brought together military, government and industry leaders to discuss bomber modernization, installation infrastructure and community resources while emphasizing the importance of maintaining combat readiness throughout the transition.
"The Air Force has responsibilities inside the fence line, and our community partners have responsibilities outside it. But our military families experience both sides of that fence every single day," said retired Air Force Maj. Gen. John Nichols, vice president of the Abilene Military Affairs Council.
The B-21 Raider, the Air Force's next-generation stealth bomber, is a long-range, penetrating strike aircraft designed to operate in highly contested environments. The aircraft will strengthen conventional and nuclear deterrence while providing the joint force with advanced capabilities to counter emerging threats. As the B-21's designated third main operating base, Dyess AFB will play a critical role in the Air Force's future long-range strike mission.
During a panel discussion, Lt. Gen. Mark Pye, deputy director, Critical Major Weapon Systems for the Department of War, and Maj. Gen. Peter Bonetti, director, Air Force Global Strike Command Strategic Plans, Programs and Requirements, discussed the B-21's role in national defense and the coordination required to integrate the aircraft into the operational force.
Pye described the B-21 as a generational advancement in bomber capabilities, emphasizing its range, payload flexibility and survivability in contested environments. He also highlighted the importance of preparing the personnel, training systems and infrastructure necessary to employ and sustain the aircraft.
"Successfully fielding the B-21 will require relentless teamwork and ruthless prioritization for years to come," Pye said. "We must remain focused on the mission, align our efforts and sustain that momentum throughout the transition."
Bonetti emphasized that the transition will require highly specialized Airmen whose experience and expertise will be essential to sustaining the B-21 mission.
"The B-21 will require some of the most highly trained and specialized Airmen in our force," Bonetti said. "Retaining that expertise depends not only on the mission, but also on the quality of life and support our Airmen and their families receive from the surrounding community."
U.S. Rep. Jodey Arrington, representing Texas' 19th Congressional District, reinforced the importance of building upon the community's longstanding advocacy for Dyess AFB and translating that commitment into preparations for the future mission. Chris Adams, Northrop Grumman sector vice president and general manager of the B-21 program, provided an industry perspective on the aircraft's development and opportunities for continued workforce collaboration.
While the B-21 represents a significant advancement in military capability, Air Force leaders emphasized that modernization must occur alongside the bomber force's existing operational responsibilities.
Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman, Eighth Air Force and Joint-Global Strike Operations Center commander, highlighted the importance of sustaining combat readiness while preparing for future capabilities.
"We must remain ready to execute today's mission while preparing for tomorrow's capabilities," Neuman said. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of readiness, and taking care of our Airmen is essential to sustaining both."
During a discussion featuring leaders from Dyess AFB and Whiteman AFB, Missouri, Col. Tim Griffith, 509th Bomb Wing deputy commander, shared lessons from sustaining the B-2 Spirit mission, including the importance of experienced Airmen, technical expertise and operational security.
Col. Robert Sturgill, 7th Bomb Wing and installation commander, reinforced the importance of maintaining Dyess AFB's current combat capabilities while preparing the installation for its future mission.
"We can bring in the B-21, develop new weapons and build new facilities, but people are more important than hardware," Sturgill said. "Our most important responsibility is preparing Airmen to execute the mission while ensuring we're ready to fight today."
Sturgill also highlighted housing availability, construction capacity and community resources as priorities requiring continued coordination with local partners as the installation prepares for future growth.
William Beuschel, Dyess AFB B-21 Program Integration Office deputy chief, outlined approximately $2 billion in planned infrastructure investments to support the aircraft's arrival. The projects represent a significant transformation of the installation, requiring extensive coordination among the Air Force, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and industry partners. Beuschel highlighted construction timelines, workforce availability and regional infrastructure as key considerations in preparing Dyess AFB for its future mission.
Community leaders expanded on those discussions during an afternoon panel focused on housing, child care, health care, workforce development and infrastructure. Katie Alford, representing the Community Foundation of Abilene, and Will Dugger, chairman of the Abilene Chamber of Commerce board, emphasized collaboration among local government, businesses and community organizations to address shared challenges and support future growth.
Abilene Mayor Weldon Hurt closed the summit by reaffirming the city's commitment to Dyess AFB, emphasizing that preparing for the B-21 extends beyond infrastructure and economic development to the Airmen and families who serve at the installation.
"Dyess isn't just a military installation in Abilene. It's part of our family," Hurt said. "Our commitment is to ensure the Airmen and families who serve our nation know they have a community standing behind them."
As Dyess AFB prepares to welcome the B-21 Raider, the summit reinforced that the installation's future depends on more than advanced aircraft and new facilities. Sustained collaboration among the Air Force, defense industry and Abilene community will be essential to maintaining combat readiness, supporting Airmen and their families and ensuring Dyess AFB is prepared to deliver long-range strike capabilities for decades to come.
title: B-21 summit unites military, community leaders to prepare Dyess AFB for future mission
