MONROE – On October 8, 2026, United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty sentenced three defendants in separate federal firearms cases.

Robert Lee Rodgers , Jr., 57, of Monroe, was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

Phillip E. Kendrix , 54, of Monroe, was sentenced to 57 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

Ricky Antonio Patrick , Jr., 34, of Monroe, was sentenced to 24 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

Each of the three men was also sentenced to three years of supervised release after completing their prison sentences. Rodgers, Kendrix, and Patrick all previously pled guilty to the charges on June 18, 2026.

RODGERS According to court documents, on August 7, 2024, officers with the Monroe Police Department (MPD) responded to a 911 call reporting that Rodgers had pointed a firearm at another individual. Upon the officers’ arrival, Rodgers initially refused to exit his residence, but officers later entered and encountered him inside. Rodgers denied pointing a firearm but admitted to possessing an unloaded .22 revolver. Officers located the revolver locked in a cabinet. Rodgers is a convicted felon prohibited from possessing firearms.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) and MPD investigated the case. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Samuel S. Crichton with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Emily Favrot.

KENDRIX According to court records, on October 24, 2024, law enforcement stopped Kendrix while he was driving in Ouachita Parish. A K-9 alerted to his vehicle, leading to a police search that revealed small amounts of methamphetamine and cocaine on his person, along with a loaded Kel Tec PMR 30 pistol in the center console. Kendrix admitted to acquiring the pistol by trading crack cocaine. He was also aware he was prohibited from possessing a firearm due to a previous felony conviction.

ATF and Ouachita Parish Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Cheyenne Y. Wilson with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

PATRICK According to court records, on February 2, 2026, ATF and MPD received information from the Texas Department of Public Safety regarding a federal arrest warrant for Patrick on a Texas firearm offense. On February 5, 2026, Monroe police officers located Patrick at a residence in Monroe. After Patrick exited the residence and entered a GMC Acadia, a traffic stop was conducted. Officers then executed a search warrant on the vehicle and located a loaded Beretta PX4 pistol beneath the front passenger seat. Patrick admitted possessing the firearm and is prohibited from doing so due to a previous felony conviction.

ATF, MPD, and the Texas Department of Public Safety investigated the case. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Aaron Crawford with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

These cases were prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents may be found at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer under the following case numbers: Rodgers – 3:26-00092 Kendrix – 3:25-cr-00249 Patrick – 3:26-cr-00074

CHEYENNE, Wyo. — Aaron Michael Underwood, 40, of Arapahoe, Wyoming, was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, for being a felon in possession of a firearm. U.S. District Court Judge Alan B. Johnson imposed the sentence on Oct. 13, 2026.

According to court documents, the Bureau of Indian Affairs responded on March 22, 2026, to a 911 call reporting a disturbance and shots fired in Riverton. Active gunfire was audible on the emergency dispatch call. Responding officers learned that an earlier family argument escalated when Underwood, who resided in an adjacent modular home on the property, discharged a firearm. Witnesses also documented a pattern of ongoing threats and prior firearm brandishing.

When law enforcement arrived, officers found the modular home door barricaded from the inside before detaining Underwood. An FBI special agent subsequently obtained and executed a search warrant, recovering a 9mm Beretta handgun and a 9mm Hi-Point/Beemiller carbine. While secured in a patrol vehicle, Underwood directed verbal intimidation toward witnesses.

The case was investigated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation, the Wyoming Highway Patrol and the Fremont County Sheriff's Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jesse Naiman prosecuted the crime.

Case No. 26-CR-00049.

This case was part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) , a collaborative initiative uniting federal, state, local, and Tribal law enforcement with community leaders to combat gun violence and gang activity.

DURHAM, NC (October 19, 2026) — Today, Congresswoman Valerie Foushee (NC-04) introduced a resolution designating the third week of October as National Hunter Syndrome Awareness Week, to reaffirm the commitment to increasing awareness and funding for research and treatments for Hunter syndrome.
“As Hunter syndrome continues to affect thousands of people across the globe, it is critical that Congress reaffirms our commitment to researching treatments for this disease which still has no cure,” said Congresswoman Valerie Foushee (NC-04). “As modern medicine continues to develop, Congress has an opportunity to take steps towards advancing lifesaving treatment options for those suffering from this disease. I am proud to introduce this resolution recognizing National Hunter Syndrome Awareness Week to reaffirm our commitment to supporting those living with Hunter syndrome across the globe.”
Hunter syndrome is a rare genetic disorder which prevents the body from properly breaking down sugar molecules, causing progressive, irreversible damage to organs and muscle tissue. This disease affects approximately 500 boys in the United States alone, and nearly 2,000 worldwide.
The full text of the resolution can be found here.

Rep. Vasquez Demands Answers From Forest Service on Trail Maintenance and Wildfire Preparedness
USFS trail maintenance operations have been significantly delayed by layoffs, hiring restrictions, and budget cuts, resulting in declining trail quality and heightened wildfire risk
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02), joined by 12 colleagues, sent a letter to U.S. Forest Service (USFS) leadership demanding answers on the agency’s efforts to maintain trails on public lands, which would ensure access to recreation and protect local communities from heightened fire risk. The letter follows up on an earlier letter raising concerns that USFS actions dramatically reduced the agency’s ability to adequately maintain public trails. That request followed a concerning report detailing a “trail maintenance crisis” with “impassable trails” and “unsafe bridges” due to staffing and budget cuts implemented by the Administration, leading to heightened wildfire risk.
“In April, I demanded answers from the Forest Service after concerning reports of our trails falling into disarray,” said Vasquez. “This is an urgent issue – my constituents know that overgrown brush increases wildfire risk, and the more there is this season, the more dangerous it becomes next season. This is a completely unnecessary risk – we have the tools to protect our communities, and I am calling on the Forest Service to use them.”
Read the full letter HERE.
Vasquez has fought to promote outdoor recreation, protect New Mexico’s public lands and reduce wildfire risks for rural communities throughout his time in Congress, including:
- Supporting the bipartisan Fix Our Forests Act: Vasquez cosponsored and voted to pass legislation to improve forest management, reduce hazardous vegetation that fuels catastrophic wildfires, strengthen wildfire prevention and protect communities from devastating fires.
- Holding USDA Accountable for Forest Service Staffing Cuts: Vasquez pressed USDA Secretary Rollins on how cuts to USFS personnel threaten wildfire preparedness, trail maintenance and public safety, emphasizing the critical role Forest Service crews play in maintaining trails, supporting firefighters and protecting rural communities.
- Opposing the Administration’s USFS Restructuring: Vasquez pushed back against the Administration’s plans to close 57 Forest Service research stations and slash the agency’s workforce, warning that these cuts would undermine wildfire prevention, weaken forest management and threaten outdoor recreation opportunities across New Mexico.
The letter asks USFS to respond by October 30 and to provide updated information on the following:
- Seasonal hiring: How many of the “up to 2,000” promised non-fire seasonal employees were hired and onboarded before the field season, where they were assigned, how many were primarily focused on trail work, and how many miles of trail they maintained.
- Staff vacancies: How many trail maintenance positions are currently vacant, how the agency addressed the “critical field level vacancies” it identified, and which forests and ranger districts are most affected, following a 2025 internal report indicating some forest units had lost their entire trails staff.
- Funding: Whether the agency can determine what it spends on staff and expenses for its trail program, and how that level has changed over the last two decades in inflation-adjusted dollars.
- Volunteers and partners: How many people participated in the adopt-a-trail program this season, how many miles they maintained, how administrative burdens were reduced for partners, and how the agency is ensuring volunteers are trained and operating safely.
- The backlog: How many miles of trail are in the maintenance backlog, and what federal funding would be needed to address it.
- The proposed cut: Why the Forest Service’s budget justification proposes cutting the Capital Improvement and Maintenance, Trails line from $22 million in the FY26 enacted level to $8 million in the White House’s FY27 budget, a reduction of roughly two-thirds.
- The ten-year goal: Whether the agency is on track to meet the objectives of its Ten-Year Trail Stewardship Challenge by 2030, and what barriers stand in the way.
###
title: Rep. Vasquez Demands Answers From Forest Service on Trail Maintenance and Wildfire Preparedness

Boise – United States Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed John Shirts as United States Attorney for the District of Idaho, effective October 18, 2026. Shirts was sworn in as U.S. Attorney yesterday by U.S. Chief District Judge Amanda K. Brailsford in a private ceremony.

“I am honored to serve as Idaho’s next U.S. Attorney,” said Shirts. “Our office will remain focused on upholding the rule of law and protecting the rights of citizens by prosecuting terrorism, drug trafficking, violent crime, human trafficking, illegal immigration offenses, and fraud. The safety of Idahoans and their communities is paramount. Those who commit federal crimes in our state will be held accountable and brought to justice.”

Shirts is a fifth-generation Idahoan who grew up in Weiser, Idaho. He most recently served as a State Representative in the Idaho Legislature, representing District 9. He served as the vice chair of the Agricultural Affairs Committee, and as a member of the Judiciary, Rules, and Administration Committee, and on the Revenue and Taxation Committee. From 2018 to 2024, Shirts served as an Assistant United States Attorney for the District of Idaho, prosecuting criminal cases in both the Pocatello and Boise offices. Shirts is married to Mercedes Shirts, a high school teacher.

Shirts was raised working on his family’s ranch. His great-great-grandfather homesteaded in Washington County in the 1880s. He attended Weiser High School and worked his way through the University of Idaho. After college, he graduated from the University of Colorado Law School. Shirts then clerked for the Honorable Jonathan P. Brody, an Idaho District Court judge in Rupert.

Following his clerkship, Shirts earned a commission in the U.S. Air Force as a JAG officer. During his active-duty service, he served in Korea as an adviser to the 51st Fighter Wing on Osan Air Base. Later appointed to the Air Force’s Special Victims Unit (SVU), he prosecuted sexual assault cases at thirty Air Force bases around the world, from Germany to Hawaii. His military decorations include the Air Force Commendation Medal and the Korean Defense Service Medal. After leaving active service to join the U.S. Attorney’s Office as an AUSA, he continued to serve as a prosecutor in the U.S. Air Force Reserve.

As U.S. Attorney, Shirts serves as the top-ranking federal law enforcement official in the state of Idaho, having prosecutorial responsibility over 44 counties in Idaho, encompassing more than 83,000 square miles and a population of nearly 1.5 million people. He leads three staffed offices located in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Pocatello with 65 employees, including 33 attorneys. The office is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in the district, including crimes related to immigration, terrorism, public corruption, child exploitation, firearms, and narcotics. The office also defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States.

###
title: John Shirts Appointed as United States Attorney for the District of Idaho

Fort Myers, Florida – John P. Skubinski (55, Naples) and Melvin A. Slawik, Jr. (68, Naples) have each been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Sheri Polster Chappell to 15 months in federal prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud. Both pleaded guilty on April 30, 2026. As part of their sentence, the court also entered an order of forfeiture in the amount of $536,200, the proceeds of the wire fraud. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court documents, in July 2020, Skubinski and Slawik participated in a scheme to obtain money from a victim by using false representations and promises. In 2020, Skubinski and Slawik owned and operated a business called Blue Hill Buffalo Consulting, LLC, located in Collier County.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, the victim was searching for a vender to supply nitrile gloves to the Cleveland Clinic. Skubinski and Slawik falsely represented that Blue Hill Buffalo had the nitrile gloves in a warehouse and could fulfill the order as soon as the money was paid. Skubinski and Slawik knew that they did not have the gloves to ship, but they drafted a contract to induce the victim to pay. On July 29, 2020, the signed contract falsely represented that Blue Hill Buffalo would deliver 38,300 boxes (200 per box) of nitrile exam gloves to the Cleveland Clinic, in Cleveland, Ohio, after the victim paid $536,200. On July 30, 2020, the victim wired the funds to the bank account of Blue Hill Buffalo.

Skubinski and Slawik never provided the medical gloves that the victim paid for. Instead, they offered false excuses concerning delays when they knew that they did not have the gloves as promised.

Bank records revealed that Skubinski and Slawik used the money that they received from the victim to fund their own lifestyle and to pay their expenses.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Yolande G. Viacava. The forfeiture is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney Julie A. Simonsen.
title: Two Collier County Men Sentenced to 15 Months in Federal Prison for Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud and Wire Fraud

Ranking Members Lofgren and Amo Demand Answers After GAO Report Reveals Trump-Inflicted Damage to America’s Future Weather Satellites
(Washington, DC) – Today, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) and Environment Subcommittee Ranking Member Gabe Amo (D-RI) sent a letterto National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Administrator Neil Jacobs regarding NOAA’s GeoXO satellite program. GeoXO is the future fleet of the nation’s weather satellites scheduled to replace the current satellites in the 2030’s and collect life-saving data to support weather forecasting. In early 2025, the Trump administration demanded that NOAA cut the GeoXO program by 50% and exclusively focus on the Agency’s “weather data needs,” disguising blatant climate denialism as an effort to cut costs. GAO released its report on Friday, October 16, 2026, and found that the Trump administration’s actions “put vital observations at risk.”
“Two fewer satellites and three fewer scientific instruments are not line items in a budget,” Ranking Members Lofgren and Amo write in their letter.“They represent a concrete, tangible weakening of America’s ability to understand the weather, the climate, and the world around us.”
The Members continue: “We now confront the real possibility that America’s next generation of weather satellites will be no better – or even worse – than the generation in orbit today. As GAO concludes in its report, ‘it is unclear whether GeoXO will improve, or even continue, the functionality available in the current generation of satellites.’ That is an unacceptable notion, and we are determined to return this program to its proper path."
In closing, the Members focus in on the hypocrisy of the administration’s claims that these cancellations are to save costs, pointing to the war in Iran: “In exchange for a less advanced, less capable next generation of weather satellites, the only meager rationale the Trump Administration can muster is $6.6 billion in reduced lifecycle costs. At a time when the war in Iran has cost the country an estimated $38 billion and counting while President Trump proposes to spend another $1.2 trillion on checks intended to lessen the political fallout of that war, it is hard to think of a more foolish, self-defeating way to save money than by stripping capabilities from a weather satellite program of vital long-term national significance. The Trump Administration has the wrong priorities, but NOAA must get GeoXO right. We expect nothing less.”
Read the letter here.
Find the GAO report here.
title: Ranking Members Lofgren and Amo Demand Answers After GAO Report Reveals Trump-Inflicted Damage to America’s Future Weather Satellites

DeLauro Responds to First Lady Melania Trump’s Women’s Health Initiative
WASHINGTON – Earlier today, First Lady Melania Trump posted a list of her “5 Pillars of Women’s Health Innovation” on social media. This post followed President Trump’s signing of an Executive Order that the White House claims will “advance women’s health.” House Appropriations Committee and Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies Subcommittee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro (D-CT-03) issued the following statement in response to the First Lady:
“I could not agree more with the First Lady, but her husband’s policies tell a different story. President Trump and his budget director, Russ Vought, have proposed slashing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding for programs that support women’s health. They have sought the elimination of entire agencies under the Department of Health and Human Services that conduct the very research into women’s health they are now claiming they want to increase.
“The President’s budget for fiscal year 2027 proposed only $43 billion for research funded under the National Institutes of Health (NIH), a cut of $6 billion (12%) below the fiscal year 2026 enacted level. I am all for supporting the First Lady’s initiative to increase resources for women’s health research and for making sure the treatments this research produces are accessible to all women who need them. Unfortunately, her husband’s choices are working against these goals.
“I would be glad to work with the First Lady to make the five pillars she lays out a reality. Since I first became chair of the Labor-HHS-Education subcommittee in 2019, we have tripled funding for NIH’s Office of Research on Women’s Health. I am eager to build on that progress, but that will mean reversing many of the policies this White House is pursuing.”
Ranking Member DeLauro was responsible for establishing a specific line-item in funding legislation for the Office of Research on Women’s Health, when before their funding had been at the discretion of the NIH director. She also led the effort to provide the Office of Research on Women’s Health the power to issue grants, directly supporting women’s health research across the country.
A full summary of House Republicans fiscal year 2027 Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and Related Agencies bill that details some of their proposed cuts can be found here. A fact sheet on this bill can be found here.
House Republicans advanced this bill out of the full committee in June.

October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, an annual reminder that protecting digital information is a shared responsibility. This year’s theme, “Securing the Next 250,” highlights the importance of keeping the nation’s information and technology secure as the country looks toward its future.
Sean Hannan, Tobyhanna Army Depot’s Cyber Security Enterprise Branch chief, highlighted a message from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency that reinforces the importance of staying vigilant.
“For over 20 years, this awareness campaign has highlighted the importance of taking regular action to reduce risks when online and using connected devices,” the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency states. The agency’s 2026 theme, “Securing the Next 250,” emphasizes the need to act now as cyber threats become faster and more sophisticated, including attempts powered by artificial intelligence to identify and exploit vulnerabilities.
At Tobyhanna Army Depot, cybersecurity is an important part of mission readiness. The depot provides C5ISR support to the joint warfighter, and protecting the systems and information behind that work helps ensure the mission can continue without interruption.
Employees can help protect Army networks by following a few basic cybersecurity practices throughout the year.
Keep software updated. Software updates often address security vulnerabilities that could otherwise leave devices exposed to threats. Install updates promptly and check Software Center or Company Portal regularly for available updates.
Use strong passwords and multifactor authentication. Avoid reusing passwords across accounts, and consider an approved password manager to keep credentials organized. Multifactor authentication (MFA) provides an additional layer of protection, even if a password is compromised. Never approve an authentication request you did not initiate.
Think before clicking. Phishing emails can look legitimate and may attempt to trick users into opening attachments, clicking links or sharing sensitive information. Watch for unexpected messages, unusual requests and language designed to create urgency. If an email seems suspicious, do not forward it. Contact the appropriate cybersecurity personnel for instructions.
Protect important information. Follow established procedures when storing, sharing and transmitting government information. Only use approved systems and share information with authorized individuals. Employees should also follow applicable requirements for backing up data and encrypting information or devices.
Know how to report a potential incident. If you suspect a cybersecurity incident involving government-furnished equipment, contact the CSEB Incident Response Team at extension X5-0252 or email AMC-CECOM-TYADCyberSecurityIncidents@army.mil. Contact the team directly for guidance rather than forwarding suspicious emails.
Employees can find additional information in the Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026 slides and other resources available on the CSEB SharePoint page.
Cybersecurity takes more than technical safeguards. Staying alert, following established procedures and reporting suspicious activity can help protect the information and systems Tobyhanna relies on every day.
Tobyhanna Army Depot is designated as the Center of Industrial and Technical Excellence for Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance, electronics, avionics, and missile guidance and control. TYAD provides cradle-to-grave lifecycle support through depot-level repair, systems integration, software and cyber engineering, and field support.
A key enabler of operational readiness for joint and allied forces globally, TYAD leverages new and emerging technologies to further expand the Department of War’s organic capabilities for microelectronics, secure communications infrastructure, unmanned aerial systems, joint all-domain command and control, integrated air and missile defense and the Army’s Next Generation Combat Systems.
TYAD’s ability to rapidly surge production, deploy field support teams and scale for contingency or theater-level operations makes it a vital contributor to strategic readiness and operational reach.
title: Cybersecurity Awareness Month Highlights Shared Responsibility

ROANOKE, Va. -- To resolve allegations that Negril Incorporated and its owners violated the False Claims Act and the Virginia Fraud Against Taxpayers Act by causing false claims to be submitted to the Virginia Medicaid Program, the company has agreed to a $1,817,910.60 civil settlement.

The Government alleged that, from January 2021 through May 2022, Negril billed Virginia Medicaid for certain mental health skill‑building services under its National Provider Identification (NPI) number. However, the company that actually provided those services to Virginia Medicaid beneficiaries did not have its own NPI, was not credentialed through the Virginia Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Services and was not enrolled as a Medicaid provider. Under the parties’ billing arrangement, Negril submitted the claims to Virginia Medicaid, remitted 75 percent of the Medicaid reimbursement to the other company, and retained the remaining 25 percent.

The Government filed its civil complaint on June 12, 2026, in United States et al. v. Negril Incorporated et al., Docket No. 6:26‑cv‑00066 (W.D. Va.).

The settlement was the result of a coordinated effort among the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Virginia, the Office of Inspector General and the Office of Counsel to the Inspector General for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit of the Virginia Attorney General’s Office.

First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci and Special Agent in Charge Maureen Dixon of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced the resolution.

The matter was handled by Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew G. Howells and Assistant Attorney General Kimberly M. Bolton of the Virginia Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.

The claims resolved by this settlement are allegations only; there has been no admission of wrongdoing and no determination of liability.
title: Negril Agrees to Settle Allegations of Improper Medicaid Billing

ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot
Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.
“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”
“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”
“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”
Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.
The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.
At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.
An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.
This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.
title: ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot

text:
Justice Department Notifies the District of Columbia of Investigation into Whether Conditions in the D.C. Department of Corrections Correctional Facilities Violate the Constitution
Today, the Justice Department notified District of Columbia (D.C.) Mayor Muriel Bowser of the initiation of a federal investigation into D.C. Department of Corrections (D.C. DOC) correctional facilities. The Justice Department will investigate whether D.C. DOC engages in a pattern or practice of violating prisoners’ and detainees’ constitutional rights.
“The Constitution protects the rights of every incarcerated American, including those held in custody in our nation’s capital,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “We are committed to upholding our federal civil rights laws so that no inmate is confined in unconstitutional conditions or subject to unconstitutional mistreatment at the District of Columbia Department of Corrections.”
The Department has received numerous allegations regarding conditions in D.C. DOC facilities, including a report from the District of Columbia’s own Auditor. Allegations include failing to protect them from use of excessive force, failing to provide adequate medical care, failing to provide safe and sanitary physical conditions of confinement, and failing to provide adequate nutrition. The Department will investigate the D.C. DOC pursuant to its authority to enforce the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (CRIPA). The Department has not reached any conclusions regarding allegations in this matter.
Under CRIPA, the Department has the authority to investigate violations of prisoners’ constitutional rights that result from a “pattern or practice of resistance to the full enjoyment of such rights.” The Department has conducted CRIPA investigations of many correctional systems, and where violations have been found, the resulting settlement agreements have led to important reforms.
Individuals with relevant information are encouraged to contact the Department via civilrights.justice.gov/report/. Additional information about the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department is available on its website at www.justice.gov/crt.
title: Justice Department Notifies the District of Columbia of Investigation into Whether Conditions in the D.C. Department of Corrections Correctional Facilities Violate the Constitution

text:
The federal crop insurance program (FCIP) offers insurance coverage for crops and livestock to help mitigate potential financial consequences of adverse growing and market conditions. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) regulates the policies offered and subsidizes the premiums that farmers pay in order to encourage farmer participation in the program. Premium subsidies were approximately $15 billion in 2026, which accounted for about 66% of the total premium on average for all policies sold in 2026. Since its inception in 1938, the FCIP has grown from an ancillary program with low participation to a central pillar of federal farm support. In the 10-year period from 2017 to 2026, the program grew from insuring more than 311 million acres to more than 572 million acres (84% increase) and from insuring more than $106 billion to more than $209 billion in crop and livestock value (96% increase in nominal terms, 48% in inflation-adjusted terms) (Figure 1).
By law, the FCIP operates as a public-private partnership. Farmers purchase FCIP policies from private sector companies—Approved Insurance Providers (AIPs)—who sell and service FCIP policies under contracts with USDA. USDA provides administrative and operating (A&O) subsidies to compensate AIPs for the cost of selling and servicing FCIP policies. USDA also provides insurance for the AIPs (i.e., reinsurance) for most policies sold and shares the gains and losses from reinsurance with the AIPs as per the terms of the contracts.
The FCIP is permanently authorized under the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 (P.L. 75-430, 52 Stat. 72) and the Federal Crop Insurance Act of 1980 (P.L. 96-365, 7 U.S.C. §§1501 et seq.), as amended. The FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21) made changes to increase premium subsidies, expand certain coverage offerings, allow farmers to purchase certain FCIP policies when enrolled in the Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) commodity support program, and increase compensation for AIPs in years of relatively large losses, among other changes. Title XI of the House-passed and Senate committee-reported drafts of the 2026 farm bill (H.R. 7567 and S. 5526, respectively) would make further changes with implications for policyholders and how the program is administered.
The Federal Crop Insurance Corporation—the agency that finances FCIP operations—receives mandatory appropriations of "such sums as necessary." Annual federal program outlays averaged $12.1 billion for FY2016-FY2025, in inflation-adjusted 2026 dollars (Figure 2). Outlays tend to increase with the number of policies sold, increases in commodity prices, and increases in natural disasters and adverse weather events. Between 2016 and 2025, premium subsidies for corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton—the top four crops in terms of acreage planted in the United States each year—averaged 74% of all premium subsidies paid.
The FCIP offers insurance for most field crops, a wide variety of specialty crops, certain types of livestock and animal products, and grazing lands. FCIP coverage is available for purchase in all U.S. counties, although coverage for some crops may be limited in certain areas. To receive coverage, farmers must purchase policies by specific deadlines that vary by commodity but are before planting usually begins. Farmers can choose among many types of policies and policy options to customize coverage to their farm businesses' specific needs. Farmers receive premium subsidies based on the coverage purchased. USDA fully subsidizes premiums for catastrophic-only (CAT) coverage; farmers pay only an administrative fee. Farmers pay an increasing share of premiums for higher levels of coverage, up to a maximum of 59% of the total premium for farm-level coverage. For certain county-level coverages, farmers pay 20% of the total premium.
FCIP policies insure against losses of expected yield or revenue due to unavoidable natural events. Covered perils or "causes of loss" include adverse weather conditions (e.g., hail, frost, drought, flooding); failure of irrigation water supply; fire; plant diseases; and insect and wildlife damage. Certain policies also insure against losses from seasonal market price declines. Farmers are required to follow USDA's guidance on good farm management practices in order to maintain coverage eligibility.
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law made changes to the FCIP. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that these changes would increase the program cost by about $6 billion for FY2025-FY2034.
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law increased premium subsidies for farm-level coverage, the first increase since 2002. For farm-level coverage levels of 55%-75% of expected yield or revenue, the law increased premium subsidies by 5%. For 80% and 85% coverage levels, the law increased premium subsidies by 3%. The law made no changes to premium subsidies for other farm-level coverage levels. The law also increased the additional premium subsidies available for beginning farmers and ranchers.
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law expanded the maximum coverage levels for Whole Farm Revenue Protection policies, a type of farm-level coverage, from 85% to 90% of expected revenue and for Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) policies, a type of county-level coverage, from 86% to 90%. The law also increased premium subsidies for SCO policies and removed the prohibition on purchasing SCO for acres enrolled in the ARC commodity support program.
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law required USDA to modify the terms of the contracts with AIPs to increase A&O subsidies paid to AIPs in years of relatively large losses. The law also increased A&O subsidies for specialty crop policies in certain years, required USDA to annually adjust caps on A&O subsidies for certain policies, and increased funds available for program compliance and integrity, among other changes.
The House-passed and Senate committee-reported versions of the farm bill would make other changes to the FCIP, with differences between some provisions. Both bills address subsidies for veteran farmers and ranchers, address compliance procedures for AIPs, freeze A&O subsidy rates for existing policies, establish a specialty crop advisory committee, modify the rules for private sector submissions for new FCIP policies, and require USDA to conduct certain research and development and pilot activities, among other changes proposed.
The FCIP is a central component of the federal farm safety net, a collection of programs that provide risk protection and financial support to farmers in times of low farm prices and natural disasters. In the last three farm bills and in the FY2025 budget reconciliation law, Congress expanded the FCIP to cover more commodities and more types of risks. Farmers tend to purchase FCIP coverage for all planted acres every year for many commodity crops. Some stakeholders favor further expanding the program, noting that opportunities exist to increase coverage, especially for specialty crops, livestock, and animal products.
Other stakeholders have proposed reducing the cost of the FCIP by capping AIPs' underwriting gains, reducing and/or capping premium subsidies for producers, and introducing a means test for premium subsidies, among other proposals. Congress could consider whether existing authorities and contracts between USDA and the AIPs are sufficient to achieve desired cost control aims for the program.
All FCIP policies include a deductible—losses that a policyholder absorbs before indemnities are triggered—to incentivize policyholders to guard against crop production risks. SCO indemnities and ARC payments may defray a portion of the deductible for farm-level coverage. SCO and ARC are both triggered by declines in county revenue compared with recent historical averages and thus may compensate for some of the same loss events. Farmers pay 20% of the cost of SCO premiums; enrollment in ARC is free. Congress could consider if a different combination of SCO coverage and ARC support would more adequately incentivize farmers to avoid risk, support farm incomes, and address concerns about government spending.
Some environmental stakeholders assert that improved soil health reduces crop production risk and propose to enhance the FCIP's role in promoting conservation and improving soil health. Congress may consider the potential environmental benefits of these proposals and what their effects might be on program performance. Statute requires USDA to operate the program such that, on average for the program as a whole, the sum of farmer-paid premiums and premium subsides should equal or exceed indemnities paid.
The number of private-sector insurers participating in the FCIP has decreased over time, largely due to consolidation in the insurance industry. Congress may choose to examine the drivers of this consolidation, as well as any implications of consolidation on outreach to producers in underserved areas, insurers' willingness to market new and existing policies, program efficiency, the number of AIPs in the industry, and the profitability of the remaining AIPs.
title: Farm Bill Primer: Federal Crop Insurance Program

DAVENPORT, Iowa – An Ottumwa, Iowa man was sentenced on October 19, 2026, to 135 months in federal prison for conspiracy to distribute cocaine, marijuana, and 50 grams or more of methamphetamine.

According to public court documents and evidence presented at sentencing, Robert Joe VanDyke, 53, was found in possession of nearly 300 grams of methamphetamine, 26.78 grams of cocaine, 16.17 grams of marijuana, $7,186, a digital scale, syringes, and a drug ledger in his vehicle in September 2025. VanDyke estimated that over four months he had received around 30 pounds of methamphetamine from his Monmouth, Illinois drug source.

After completing his term of imprisonment, VanDyke will be required to serve a five-year term of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system.

United States Attorney David C. Waterman of the Southern District of Iowa the announcement. The Southeast Iowa Narcotics Task Force and Burlington Police Department investigated the case.
title: Ottumwa Man Sentenced to 135 Months in Federal Prison for Drug Charges

National Veterinary Technician Week is celebrated every year in the third week of October by the National Association of Veterinary Technicians in America and the American Veterinary Medical Association, to recognize the work that veterinary technicians provide.
For Army Medicine that means recognizing their Army Animal Care Specialists.
These specialists provide skilled, compassionate care that supports the health, welfare, and readiness of military working animals worldwide. Their technical expertise and adaptability are essential across clinics, training environments, and deployed settings in support of the Joint Force and interagency partners.
From routine wellness care to surgical support and providing emergency care for military working animals, these 68Ts (the military occupational specialty designation) work alongside their veterinarian counterparts, animal handlers, and joint partners to care for military working dogs, equids, and other animal species entrusted to the Department of War.
Sgt. Clara Maia, a clinic noncommissioned officer in charge at Camp Bondsteel, Kosovo, said she entered the field to advocate for military working animals.
“I chose this profession because I believe military working animals deserve a strong advocate,” Maia said. “They serve alongside our Soldiers, support the mission and help save lives.”
Maia recently organized a training day for 32 medics and NATO partners at Camp Bondsteel to prepare participants to respond when a military working dog requires urgent medical evacuation. The event built practical skills and confidence for emergency situations.
In Japan, Staff Sgt. Derek Amsden serves as a branch NCOIC and has spent seven years as a 68T after first serving five years as an infantryman. He has helped demonstrate canine tactical combat casualty care alongside Air Force military working dog handlers during joint training.
Amsden said the most rewarding part of the work is seeing patients recover. “We often see patients when they are at the worst,” he said, “so being a part of the treatment plan and seeing them fully recovered … is always a good experience.”
At Joint Base San Antonio-Fort Sam Houston, Texas, Sgt. Megan Juan-Tomas serves as a clinic NCO. She said becoming an Animal Care Specialist allowed her to work with animals while pursuing a path toward veterinary school.
Her advice to Soldiers considering the career field is to “be flexible and take initiative.” Juan-Tomas encouraged Soldiers to volunteer and step forward when work needs to be done.
At Patrick Space Force Base, Florida, Sgt. Carlos D. Vergas Medina serves as a clinic NCOIC. His experience includes providing care for military working animals and supporting joint veterinary care.
“Resiliency and self-discipline are what keep me moving forward,” Vergas Medina said. “Knowing that the care we provide makes a difference for both the animal and the person on the other side of that leash gives purpose to what I do.”
These Soldiers exemplify the care, compassion, and competence of Army Animal Care Specialists. Their work strengthens the teams supporting Soldiers, installations and missions worldwide. Army Medicine is proud to recognize and celebrate these Soldier professionals.
title: Army Medicine Celebrates Army Animal Care Specialists

text:
- For Immediate Release:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life.
Patients with locally advanced rectal cancer often receive chemotherapy and radiation prior to surgery, which can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility. Surgery also carries risks of serious, sometimes life-threatening complications, including poor healing and leaks where the bowel is reconnected, and in some patients, permanent colostomy.
“The FDA is committed to closing the gap between scientific progress and patient access, and that commitment has to show up not just in policy, but in the pace of our work,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “American patients deserve timely access to innovative treatments, and the Trump Administration is making that a reality. Completing this review nearly 4 months ahead of schedule means some patients who might otherwise be preparing for surgery, radiation or chemotherapy may now have a different conversation with their doctor.”
Today’s approval is for Jemperli used alone in adults with previously untreated stage II or stage III locally advanced rectal cancer. At these stages, the cancer has grown into nearby tissue or reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. To be eligible, patients’ tumors must be mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), as determined by an FDA-authorized test. Published estimates suggest that approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR or MSI-H.
Both terms describe a defect in the way cancer cells correct errors when copying their DNA. Normally, a built-in repair system catches and fixes these mistakes. When the system does not work properly, errors accumulate and create proteins the immune system can recognize, making these tumors particularly vulnerable to immunotherapy.
Jemperli works by blocking a signal that cancer cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. Specifically, it targets a protein called PD-1 on immune cells.
“Standard treatment for rectal cancer has major life-changing effects. For certain types of rectal cancer, this approval represents a groundbreaking option that avoids surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. This represents a significant benefit for patients and their families,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “The FDA is acting on emerging evidence to bring new approaches to patients sooner, while requiring further studies to confirm that these treatments provide lasting benefits.”
The FDA based its decision on interim results from AZUR-1 (NCT05723562), a phase 2 study evaluating Jemperli alone in 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. In the study, patients received up to nine doses of Jemperli, given every 3 weeks over 6 months. After a median follow-up of more than 2 years — meaning at least half of patients had been monitored for that long — almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Longer follow-up is needed to understand the duration of response and how often the cancer returns.
An earlier study at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (NCT04165772) evaluated Jemperli alone in 50 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. None of the patients had detectable signs of cancer after Jemperli treatment, and nearly all patients (93%) maintained that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. Of the 27 patients followed for at least 3 years, only one had their cancer return, and it recurred in the same area.
Jemperli can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs and tissues. These reactions can be severe or fatal. The most common side effects, reported in at least 15% of patients treated for this type of rectal cancer, were fatigue, rash, diarrhea and itching.
The FDA granted Priority Review to the application and Breakthrough Therapy designation to Jemperli for the treatment of dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. This action marks the 11th approval of a drug reviewed under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program, which aims to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities. Because this is an accelerated approval based on interim trial results, the sponsor must continue following patients to show these responses create lasting clinical benefit.
The approval was granted to GSK.
Additional Resources
The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.
###
title: October 19, 2026 - FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery

Lofgren Requests Answers to Outstanding Oversight Requests, Demands Compliance from Secretaries Lutnick and Wright
(Washington, DC) – On Friday, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) sent letters to Department of Commerce (DOC) Secretary Howard Lutnick and Department of Energy (DOE) Secretary Chris Wright demanding that they comply with outstanding congressional oversight requests from the Committee.
“Rather than providing the requested information in a comprehensive and timely manner, DOC has failed to produce a single responsive document, communication, or record,” writes Ranking Member Lofgren in her letter to DOC. “In fact, the Department has not even formally replied to any of my oversight requests in nearly two years, let alone provided responsive answers to my questions. This is unacceptable. Such disregard for the role of Congress was never appropriate and becomes less tolerable with each passing month.”
“DOE’s non-responsiveness to Committee oversight during the 119th Congress has been unacceptable,” writes Ranking Member Lofgren in her letter to DOE. “We remain determined to obtain the information we need to perform our duties on behalf of the American people. DOE should understand that a lack of cooperation will not frustrate the Committee’s oversight permanently. It will merely strengthen our commitment to employing all the tools at our disposal to hold the Department accountable.”
In her letters, Ranking Member Lofgren requires a response from DOC and DOE to the Committee’s outstanding oversight requests by no later than 5:00 pm Friday, November 6th, 2026.

text:
Coast Guard suspends search for missing individuals 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico
U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Public Affairs: (206) 815-6689
SAN DIEGO — The Coast Guard suspended its search Sunday evening for an estimated 11 people missing approximately 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico, after rescuing 16 people from the water Friday.
The Coast Guard, alongside Mexico and the U.S. Navy, searched more than 2,441 square miles for a combined 89 hours.
Search efforts began after Coast Guard Sector San Diego command center watchstanders received multiple distress broadcasts at approximately 1 a.m. Friday reporting a vessel taking on water with 27 people reported aboard. On-scene assets located vessel debris in the water, and an Air Station Ventura aircrew rescued 16 people who were transferred to various hospitals in San Diego for medical assessment and care.
“We are grateful for the exceptional coordination and assistance from Mexico and the U.S. Navy throughout this challenging operation,” said Capt. Joseph Meuse, chief of staff, Coast Guard Southwest District. “Suspending a search is never easy, and this was an exceptionally dynamic case, far offshore, in rough weather. We can say with confidence that human traffickers have zero regard for human life and routinely put the lives of illegal aliens and the lives of rescue crews at risk.”
This incident is currently the subject of a federal investigation.
Involved in the search:
Coast Guard Southwest District
Coast Guard Sector San Diego
Coast Guard Air Station Ventura
Coast Guard Air Station Sacramento
Coast Guard Cutter Active (WMEC 618)
USS Kingsville (LCS 36)
U.S. Navy helicopter with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 23
ARM Mariano Matamoros – Armada de Mexico Uribe-class offshore patrol vessel
MLB-101 – Armada de Mexico 50-foot Motor Lifeboat
Sagittarius – Mexico’s Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transport 35-metre buoy tender vessel
-USCG-
title: Coast Guard suspends search for missing individuals 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico

text:
Federal appeals courts disagree as to whether the federal ban on individuals convicted of felonies from possessing firearms—located at 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) and commonly known as the "felon-in-possession" prohibition—violates the Second Amendment. The Department of Justice (DOJ) had asked the Supreme Court to review a case on one side of divide: United States v. Hembree, in which the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (circuits are hereinafter referenced by their jurisdiction, such as "Fifth Circuit") held that § 922(g)(1) is unconstitutional as applied to a defendant whose underlying felony was deemed nonviolent, here the possession of methamphetamine. At the start of its October 2026 Term, the Supreme Court denied DOJ's petition for a writ of certiorari in Hembree, leaving the circuit split unresolved and leaving open the possibility that the Court may accept a future case on whether § 922(g)(1) complies with the Second Amendment.
This Sidebar summarizes this constitutional question. The Sidebar begins by providing an overview of the Supreme Court's modern Second Amendment jurisprudence, including decisions on other class-based firearms restrictions. The Sidebar then outlines the three divergent positions taken by federal appeals courts as to the constitutionality of the felon-in-possession prohibition: (1) that § 922(g)(1) is categorically constitutional because, as a threshold matter, individuals convicted of felonies fall outside of the protections of the Second Amendment; (2) that § 922(g)(1) is categorically constitutional because, as a historical matter, § 922(g)(1) is consistent with the nation's tradition of firearms regulation; and (3) that, as a historical matter, § 922(g)(1) may be unconstitutional as applied to individuals convicted of nonviolent felonies, such as the drug-possession conviction of the defendant in Hembree. The Sidebar closes with considerations for Congress.
The Second Amendment provides, "A well-regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed." In 2008, more than two hundred years after the Second Amendment's adoption, the Supreme Court in District of Columbia v. Heller engaged in its "first thorough" examination of the meaning of the amendment. The Supreme Court in Heller held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess an operable firearm for certain purposes, particularly self-defense in the home. Whatever the full extent of the Second Amendment right, the Court wrote, it "surely" includes "the right of law-abiding, responsible citizens to use arms in defense of hearth and home." In its discussion, the Court cautioned that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on longstanding prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons" and others. In a footnote, the Court clarified that these prohibitions are "presumptively lawful regulatory measures." In 2010, in McDonald v. City of Chicago, the Court recognized that, by virtue of the Fourteenth Amendment, firearms laws and regulations enacted at the state and local levels, as well as at the federal level, must comply with the Second Amendment.
In a 2022 decision, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen, the Court announced a history-centric test for courts to apply in evaluating Second Amendment challenges to firearms laws and regulations: "when the Second Amendment's plain text covers an individual's conduct, the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct"; the government may overcome this presumption by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." The Court also made clear that the Second Amendment right applies outside of the home, to nonsensitive public spaces where "confrontation" may occur.
Federal law generally prohibits nine classes of individuals from possessing firearms. In 2024, in United States v. Rahimi, the Supreme Court rejected a "facial" challenge to one such prohibition, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which bars individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders from possessing a firearm. (A "facial" challenge argues that a statute is unconstitutional in all applications, in contrast with an "as applied" challenge, which argues that a statute is unconstitutional in specific circumstances.) The Supreme Court explained that, at step two of the Bruen framework, sufficient historical support existed for the principle that "[w]hen an individual poses a clear threat of physical violence to another, the threatening individual may be disarmed" temporarily. In its discussion, the Court quoted Heller's language that the felon-in-possession prohibition, among others, is "presumptively lawful," language that Justice Thomas in dissent characterized as "dicta" (i.e., extraneous, nonbinding commentary).
In 2026, in United States v. Hemani, the Supreme Court examined the constitutionality of another categorical prohibition, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which forbids any person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" from possessing a firearm or ammunition. In the words of the Court, the federal government argued that § 922(g)(3) "automatically disarms anyone who regularly uses any amount of any controlled substance for anything other than its 'prescribed purpose,'" regardless of individualized circumstances, including "whether [the defendant's] drug use has ever made him a danger to himself or others." In Hemani, the Court determined that, at Bruen's second step, the government presented insufficient historical support for this broad interpretation of § 922(g)(3) and, in doing so, the Court ruled that the prosecution of the defendant solely because he used marijuana "a few times a week"—without proof of relevant individual circumstances—violated the Second Amendment. In a footnote, the Court repeated Heller's disclaimer that the opinion should not be construed to "cast doubt" on the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1).
In applying Bruen to Second Amendment challenges to § 922(g)(1), the Fourth and Eleventh Circuits hold that, as a threshold matter, felons are not among those protected by the Second Amendment and that the Second Amendment inquiry comes to an end at step one of the Bruen framework. The Fourth Circuit determined that "conviction of a felony necessarily removes one from the class of 'law-abiding, responsible citizens' for the purposes of the Second Amendment," with the "narrow exceptions" of pardoned convictions or felonies that are found to be "unconstitutional or otherwise unlawful." The Eleventh Circuit interpreted Heller as "clearly excluding" felons from the universe of "law-abiding and qualified individuals" who are entitled to the Second Amendment right.
The Second, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits have reached the same result as the Fourth and Eleventh Circuits, although through different legal reasoning. These courts have held that, at step two of the Bruen inquiry, violent felons and nonviolent felons alike may be categorially disarmed under the Second Amendment. For instance, the Second Circuit has proclaimed that, at the first step of the Bruen analysis, felons belong to "the people" protected by the Second Amendment. As support, the court quoted Heller for the proposition that "'the people' . . . 'unambiguously refers to all members of the political community, not an unspecified subset.'" The Second Circuit went on to find at step two of the Bruen framework, however, that felons may be categorically barred from possessing firearms due to a historical record showing that "legislatures could disarm people as long as they belonged to an identity group that the legislature perceived as dangerous," and in the context of § 922(g)(1) "Congress perceives [felons], broadly, as dangerous." Felons, including those who have committed nonviolent offenses, have violated the "basic terms of the social contract" and thus indicated that they do not possess the character to be entrusted with firearms, the court added. The court wrote that "the Second Amendment does not bar Congress from passing laws that disarm convicted felons, regardless of whether the crime of conviction is nonviolent," and Congress may disarm felons as a class. The court warned that to make such distinctions would usurp the role of the legislature's class-based judgment and would present administrability concerns, as "embark[ing] on a line-drawing process . . . would raise endless questions with which the courts have had difficulty in other contexts."
The Eighth Circuit has ruled against challengers at both steps of the Bruen framework, concluding that a felon "is not a law-abiding citizen, and history supports the authority of Congress to [categorically] prohibit possession of firearms by persons who have demonstrated disrespect for legal norms of society." In the case of felons, the court held that historical analogues supported disarming classes presenting a risk of dangerousness and that individualized determinations of such risk were not historically necessary for purposes of disarmament.
The Third, Fifth, Sixth, and D.C. Circuits have held that the Second Amendment prohibits nonviolent felons from being dispossessed of their firearms. The Third Circuit took this position in a case involving a defendant who was convicted of making false statements to obtain food stamps in violation of Pennsylvania law, which qualified as a felony under § 922(g)(1). The Third Circuit first determined that the defendant was one of "the people" protected by the Second Amendment. While the government argued that the Amendment covers only "law-abiding, responsible citizens," the court found, among other things, that the government's conception of this phrase was too restrictive and logically could mean that "every American who gets a traffic ticket is no longer among 'the people' protected by the Second Amendment." The court decided that the plain text of the Second Amendment implicates the felon-in-possession ban, which would preclude the defendant from exercising his right to bear arms. The court then held that the government did not carry its burden at Bruen step two. The court concluded that the historical analogues offered by the government fell short, as the government did not show that the defendant belonged to a specific class of historically disarmed individuals, that historical punishments for nonviolent felonies entailed lifetime disarmament, or that historical laws disarming individuals who used firearms in the commission of their offenses would have applied to the defendant (who did not use a firearm to commit his fraud offense). The court thus ruled that § 922(g)(1) could not constitutionally be applied to the defendant, stressing that its decision was a "narrow" one applicable only to the defendant based on his particular offense. The United States filed a petition for review with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the Third Circuit after deciding Rahimi, and a panel of the Third Circuit again held that § 922(g)(1) could not be constitutionally applied to the defendant.
The Fifth Circuit similarly has taken a case-by-case approach to evaluating the constitutional validity of § 922(g)(1) as to specific defendants. On one hand, the court has upheld the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1) in cases in which a defendant was convicted of an offense that was inherently violent or associated with violence, such as drug trafficking; drug distribution; possession with intent to distribute cocaine; aggravated battery, burglary, and robbery; evading arrest or detention with a vehicle; aggravated assault and manslaughter; aggravated battery; felony assault of family member; aggravated assault with a firearm and possession of a firearm while on probation; illegal possession of a controlled substance and burglary; and bank robbery. On the other hand, the Fifth Circuit has held that the statute cannot be constitutionally applied where the predicate felony is the possession of methamphetamine (as in Hembree, which the Supreme Court declined to review) or failure to pay child support. In 2026, a majority of the active judges on the Fifth Circuit agreed to a full circuit review of whether § 922(g)(1) is facially consistent with the Commerce Clause. The majority accepted a reframed petition for review of a three-judge panel decision finding § 922(g)(1) constitutional as applied to a defendant convicted of drug trafficking.
The Sixth Circuit has also examined the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1) in light of the particular circumstances of the defendant's offense of conviction and criminal history. The court has recognized three categories of criminal offenses: (1) "crimes against the person," which include "murder, rape, assault, and robbery"; (2) crimes that "do not always involve an immediate and direct threat of violence against a particular person" and that "may nonetheless pose a significant threat of danger," including drug trafficking and burglary; and (3) crimes that often "cause no physical harm to another person or the community." The court declared that a defendant who has committed an offense in one of the first two categories "will have a very difficult time, to say the least, of showing he is not dangerous." The circuit has not, as of this writing, found § 922(g)(1) to be unconstitutional under any of these categories.
These three circuits have split further as to what courts may consider in a § 922(g)(1) challenge. The Fifth Circuit determined that, in making these case-by-case assessments of the danger to others posed by the felon, the court should consider only the felony convictions and not any offense conduct that was "unproven." The court contrasted its approach with that employed by the Third and Sixth Circuits, which appear to permit consideration of broader information indicative of dangerousness in a § 922(g)(1) challenge, particularly relevant offense conduct that may not have resulted in a conviction.
The D.C. Circuit has concluded that "felons are not protected by the Second Amendment" and are thus excluded from the constitutional right. The court engaged in a historical analysis to conclude that, at the founding, the right to bear arms was limited to the class of "virtuous" or "law abiding, responsible" citizens, which did not include felons—regardless of whether the predicate offense was violent or indicative of dangerousness. That said, the D.C. Circuit left open the possibility that a felon could "show that his crime was so minor or regulatory that he did not forfeit his right to bear arms by committing it."
In upholding the facial constitutionality § 922(g)(1), the Seventh Circuit reserved the question as to whether certain as-applied challenges may be viable, explaining that "in this circuit the issue is open." The court subsequently held that an individual convicted of violent offenses, including drug distribution, may be disarmed. The court added, however, that it "reserve[s] ruling" on as-applied challenges where the "predicate felony offense is not 'dangerous.'" The First Circuit has not made a de novo ruling on the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1), but on plain error review, the First Circuit rejected a Second Amendment challenge to § 922(g)(1), pointing to the absence of Supreme Court precedent on the constitutionality of the statute; language in Supreme Court opinions suggesting that the statute is "presumptively lawful"; and the defendant's criminal history, which included a conviction for drug trafficking. The court subsequently "assumed" that an as-applied challenge to the statute could be entertained, but held that the defendant "failed to show any error" in the district court's rejection of his challenge.
As previously mentioned, the Supreme Court denied the government's petition in Hembree, but the denial does not preclude the possibility that the Court in the future will grant a petition raising whether and to what extent § 922(g)(1) comports with the Second Amendment. Congress retains the authority to amend § 922(g)(1) either in response to, or in anticipation of, an eventual Supreme Court ruling. Congress's options include amending § 922(g)(1) to conform to one of the positions taken by the circuit courts; Congress also may take no action and leave further constitutional developments to the courts.
title: Circuit Split on Constitutionality of Federal Felon-in-Possession Prohibition Persists After Supreme Court Denies Review

News Release
Consent judgment orders California-based home appliance company to pay $800K to 339 employees denied overtime pay
LOS ANGELES – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a home appliance company to pay $800,000 in back wages and damages to 339 employees after an investigation found the company violated federal wage laws.
The judgment comes after the department’s Wage and Hour Division investigated Coway USA Inc. and found that the employer paid employees on a piece-rate basis and failed to pay employees for time spent attending mandatory meetings, picking up and loading supplies, and performing work before and after their shifts, in violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Investigators also found that Coway did not include nondiscretionary incentives, bonuses, and commissions in overtime pay calculations and frequently reduced the number of hours employees recorded working on their timecards.
Entered in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Sept. 9, the consent judgment requires Coway to record all hours the implicated employees worked, including time they spend picking up supplies, attending mandatory training, and communicating with customers before and after appointments. Coway is also required to give employees pay statements that show their hours worked, services provided to customers, and the rate Coway paid for the hours and services.
The consent judgment orders Coway USA Inc. to pay $400,000 in unpaid overtime wages and an equal amount in damages to 339 employees working in the greater metro areas of Los Angeles, New York City, and Washington, D.C. The company also agreed to pay $10,000 in penalties for willful violations.
Coway USA Inc. is a subsidiary of Coway Co. Ltd., a multinational company specializing in home appliances. The company installs and maintains various appliances, including water and air filtration products throughout the U.S.
Employers and employees can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division.
The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the Fair Labor Standards Act, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.
title: Consent judgment orders California-based home appliance company to pay $800K to 339 employees denied overtime pay
