text:
States, territories, and the District of Columbia (DC) administer federal elections. Each of these jurisdictions has its own process for counting votes and declaring election winners, though all follow similar steps. These processes have drawn renewed congressional and public attention during recent election cycles.
The results that voters see reported on election night are the culmination of several steps in the election administration process, but are not the end of that process. Finalizing federal election results typically occurs days or weeks after election day. Among other steps, state, territorial, and local election officials canvass votes to ensure that ballots are valid and counted correctly. Election observers, audits, and other measures are designed to help ensure transparency and accuracy.
This updated report addresses frequently asked questions on these and related subjects. The discussion emphasizes the period between the time a voter casts a ballot and when states, territories, and DC finalize or certify the results.
The results voters see reported on election night are the culmination of several steps in the election administration process, but are not the end of the process. States, territories, and the District of Columbia administer federal elections. Each of these jurisdictions has its own process for counting votes and declaring winners, but all follow similar steps. Election administrators, political officials, and members of the public continue working after election night to finalize official results. This process typically takes several days or even weeks. State- or territorial-level federal election results in the United States are never official on election night.
Events in recent election cycles have generated renewed interest among some Members of Congress, other public officials, and voters about how election officials count votes and determine election results. This report provides brief answers to frequently asked questions about the processes for counting, documenting, and ensuring transparency after votes are cast. It addresses federal elections, although the discussion herein also generally applies to elections for state or local offices.
Professional election administrators manage most or all of the ballot-counting process.1 Members of the public, the media, or credentialed observers typically monitor most or all of the ballot-counting process.2 Election officials have developed standard practices to document the chain of custody for ballots, ensure transparency, and generate accurate results, but specific practices and requirements vary by jurisdiction.
The frequently asked questions below are designed to provide a resource for Members of Congress and congressional staff as they conduct oversight and consider legislation related to federal elections. This report is intentionally brief in scope, though references to other resources on other related topics are provided throughout.
The discussion in this report emphasizes the period between when voters cast ballots for federal elections and when election officials finalize election results. Because states, territories, and localities administer federal elections, this report contains general discussion of law, policy, and practice in those jurisdictions, but does not attempt to do so comprehensively.3 This report briefly discusses recounts and contested elections, but those topics are largely beyond the scope of this report. Other CRS products provide information on related topics concerning contested U.S. House elections,4 the electoral college,5 the congressional role in verifying and counting presidential election results, and election workers.6
This report does not discuss legislation or identify specific requirements and processes in individual jurisdictions. As such, the general information presented in this report does not assess any election jurisdiction's processes for or performance at administering elections. Similarly, this report does not provide specific compliance information, legal analysis, or policy analysis about critical infrastructure issues. Other CRS reports provide additional information about elections policy issues generally.7 Similarly, other CRS products discuss developments in the 2026 election cycle and related implications for the states. Some of those developments, as of this writing, may be unresolved due to litigation or other factors.8
Federal election results at the state or territorial levels are never official in the United States until after election day. Results that appear in media reports or that election jurisdictions publish on election night are unofficial and preliminary. These initially reported (either by the media or election officials) totals do not necessarily include all ballots submitted in the jurisdiction, have not been subject to the canvassing process, and could change. Consequently, it is normal and expected that final election totals differ from those announced on election night. It is also common that the candidates in various races can trade leads throughout election night and after, as additional ballots are counted.10 Typically, it takes several days or weeks to finalize election results through the canvass (and audits, where applicable) and certify a winner. State or territorial law sets deadlines for how and when these processes occur.
Although individual procedures vary by state, finalizing election results typically involves two major steps, the canvass and certification. The canvass involves assembling and verifying all validly cast ballots so that they can be aggregated into the final official election results (generally called certified results).11 As a U.S. Election Assistance Commission publication explains,
The canvass is a post-election process that aggregates and confirms that all valid ballots cast in the election are accurately counted and included in the final election results. Through the canvass, election officials determine whether to count provisional ballots, resolve ballot marking errors, adjudicate voter intent, and reconcile the number of ballots cast with the number of people who voted. The process allows election officials to verify that staff and poll workers followed procedures (e.g., confirming voter eligibility and documenting chain of custody) throughout early, absentee, by mail, and Election Day voting.12
Depending on jurisdiction, groups of professional election officials, appointed canvassing boards, or both conduct the canvass.
Typical steps in the canvass include reconciling any discrepancies in the number of ballots issued versus those cast; duplicating damaged ballots that scanners cannot read, documenting that duplication process, and counting the duplicated ballots; if applicable, addressing discrepancies in signatures or cast ballots (e.g., questions about voter intent based on ballot markings); and reconciling the number of ballots cast with the number of voters who voted in person at the polling place.13 These processes may be repeated multiple times as precincts and vote centers compile their results and balloting information is consolidated at subsequently higher levels of election administration (e.g., precinct, county, and state).
In some jurisdictions, statistical data and written reports accompany the certified results and provide additional information about the canvassing process and how discrepancies were addressed. Similarly, in some cases, the certification is the final step in the canvassing process. In others, the governor or chief state election official (e.g., secretary of state) issues certified results based on information provided in the canvassing authority's final report or meeting.14
In some states, very close election margins during the canvass trigger recounts, discussed at the end of this report. Many jurisdictions also conduct post-election audits, which are intended to check the accuracy of the election outcomes reported by the voting system.15 These audits involve comparing the results generated by the voting system against a sample of paper records of votes.16
Election officials work to ensure that the election results they report are generally perceived to be fair, accurate, and legitimate. One way they do so is by having consistent, reliable, and transparent ballot collection and canvass procedures, which are typically established well before the election. To ensure that voters can cast their ballots privately and securely and that ballots are handled and counted correctly, vote-collecting and -counting processes generally involve multiple election workers and/or observers, representing multiple political parties.17
Policies about who can serve as an election observer, which stages of the election process they can observe, and what accreditation, if any, they must have are typically set by the states.18 Common categories of election observers include the general public, academics, and representatives of political parties or nonpartisan civic or legal organizations.19 An important role observers play in some states is monitoring in-person voting on election day for technological problems, administrative issues, or indications of voter fraud, coercion, or intimidation.20
States and localities that provide drop boxes for mail ballots often have video surveillance or trained election staff monitoring drop box sites and mechanisms in place to secure ballot retrieval and chain of custody,21 such as assigning two election workers to collect ballots from each drop box.22 Other parts of the election process, including signature verification for mail ballots, typically also involve multiple people.23
Many states include individuals who were not directly involved in the administration of the election on their canvassing boards or in canvassing processes, in order to help ensure impartial review.24 Most states also offer election observers or members of the media access to certain post-election procedures,25 such as counting mail ballots or conducting post-election audits or logic and accuracy tests.26 Some jurisdictions also livestream their canvasses, enabling the public to watch the process online, or use an independent board rather than state or local administrators to conduct post-election audits.27
State and local election officials use various mechanisms to ensure that only eligible voters cast ballots and that each voter only votes once in an election. The specific processes used to verify voter identity vary by state and can further vary based on the type of ballot cast (e.g., in-person or by mail).
Election officials primarily use voter registration data to determine whether an individual is eligible to vote in a given election, regardless of whether the individual chooses to vote in person or via a mail ballot.28 Election officials use state-level voter registration requirements and procedures,29 as well as verification requirements under the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (HAVA),30 to confirm a registrant's identity and eligibility to vote, often by comparing information on voter registration applications with other government agency records.
Once a voter is on a state's list of eligible voters, this information is used by election officials to monitor how, and if, voters have received a ballot, to ensure that each eligible voter can cast a vote and that no voter casts multiple ballots in the same election.31 When voting in person, poll books, or lists of eligible voters, are used by local election administrators to confirm that individuals are currently registered voters and are at the correct voting location for their precinct or election district. Electronic poll (or e-poll) books are commonly used today and may be able to provide more recently updated voter information or some voter data in real time.32 In jurisdictions that use centralized vote centers, e-poll books can help election administrators verify that a voter has not previously voted at another location. In addition to identifying voters from poll book records, 36 states had some form of voter identification law in effect for in-person voting as of September 2026.33
In circumstances where voters can vote by mail, some jurisdictions automatically send ballots to all active registered voters and others require voters to request a mail ballot.34 States that automatically send ballots or ballot request forms to voters generally rely upon address information on file in state voter registration records.35 In the voter records, election administrators typically note which persons have requested and cast mail ballots. Ballot tracking measures often allow an individual voter to check the status of his or her mail ballot, following it from the time it is sent out by election administrators to when it is returned and processed.36 These mail ballot tracking measures, in conjunction with in-person voting records, also help election officials to ensure that only a single ballot is counted for each voter; for example, election officials can void a mail ballot if it has not yet been cast by a voter who decides to vote in person instead or if officials receive a mail ballot from a voter after he or she has voted in person.37
States employ a number of measures to verify that a mail ballot is completed by the intended voter.38 Many jurisdictions require voter signatures on the ballot envelope for completed mail ballots. The voter's signature often accompanies a legal attestation, asserting the voter's identity and eligibility. Election officials, computer software, or both may be used to match the signature(s) submitted by the voter to a known signature on file from the voter's registration records or other government agency records, if applicable, via a process known as signature verification.39 If there is a missing, mismatched, or ambiguous signature, some states contact the voter and may provide an opportunity for the voter to correct the issue through processes known as signature curing, which may include an affidavit, a copy of additional identification, or both.40 States may also have requirements for witness signatures or notarization of mail ballots, and voters may need to submit a copy of their photo identification with a mail ballot in certain circumstances.41 Election officials may also check to ensure that the return address on a mail ballot matches that of the voter.42 Some states require that a voter return his or her own ballot or limit who can return a mail ballot on a voter's behalf.43
The timeline for counting votes can vary, depending on when states and localities allow voters to cast their ballots44 and when election officials are allowed to begin processing and counting them. The window for casting ballots differs by state, as jurisdictions have different polling place hours on election day and different policies about whether or when to offer mail voting or early in-person voting.45 The date election officials could start sending voters mail ballots varied from 60 days before election day to 18 days as of September 2026, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), and early in-person voting periods ranged from 3 to 46 days as of August 2026.46 Depending on state law, early voting might continue until election day or end several days earlier, and mail ballots might be accepted as long as they are postmarked on or before election day or only if they are received by the close of polls.47
In many states, election officials can begin processing early or mail ballots before election day. Exactly what counts as "processing" varies by state, but it might include conducting signature verification, removing mail ballots from their envelopes, or running ballots through scanners in preparation for generating a tally. Some states also allow early or mail ballots to be counted on or before election day, while others prohibit counting until after the polls close.48
Depending on the state, localities may have anywhere from days to weeks after an election to certify their election results to the state. According to NCSL, deadlines for state certification of results can range from specific hours like 5 p.m. the 17th day after the election to more general timeframes like, "Upon completion of the state ballot counting review."49 In presidential elections, federal law requires governors to issue certificates of ascertainment naming electors at least six days before the electoral college convenes.50
Different terminology applies to various scenarios surrounding disputed election results. The term recount refers to retabulating ballots to ensure that the certified count was accurate (although, in some jurisdictions, recounts might occur before certification).51 Election officials generally conduct recounts when elections result in very close margins of victory to confirm that the certified results are accurate, or if there is evidence that counting equipment malfunctioned.52 There are two kinds of recounts: automatic and requested. A narrow margin of victory in an individual race (e.g., less than one-half percent in some states) can trigger an automatic recount in many states. Candidates or voters may also request recounts (sometimes called initiated recounts) in most states, often at their expense and under processes specified in state statutes.53 Relevant state, territorial, or local election statutes specify which recount options are available in particular jurisdictions, if any, and under what circumstances.
States or other election jurisdictions conduct recounts either by rescanning ballots or by hand counting, depending on circumstances and relevant requirements. Recounts may include all or part of the certified results. They also may involve a recanvass—in some states a separate process—to reexamine the validity of the ballots included in the certified results. Election officials, recount boards, or both may conduct recounts.
Although timing varies by state, statutes typically limit the period during which recounts may occur. Election officials can face particularly tight deadlines for conducting recounts if recounts occur shortly before officeholders-elect are to be sworn in.
Election contests focus on the circumstances surrounding the conduct of the election. As with recounts, contests follow processes addressed in relevant state law. Generally, contests are resolved through litigation that is beyond the scope of this report. The Federal Contested Election Act (FCEA) provides procedures for resolving contested U.S. House elections.54 Ultimately, Article I, Section 5 of the U.S. Constitution specifies that each chamber of Congress "shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members." Other CRS products provide information on related topics concerning contested U.S. House elections,55 the electoral college,56 and the congressional role in verifying and counting presidential election results.57
Tyler Wolanin, former Research Assistant at the Congressional Research Service, and Jane Wright, current Research Assistant at CRS, contributed to this report.

text:
Interview

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Thomas Jefferson Room

Washington, D.C.

October 19, 2026

QUESTION: All right. So, Mr. Secretary, I really want to thank you for taking the time to do this with us here. We’re here in the Thomas Jefferson Room at the State Department. I think no better place than – to talk about Western civilization —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Right.

QUESTION: — and protecting it than, frankly, the – one of the most important founders of our great country. You just gave a massive speech at the Acropolis in Greece – in Athens, Greece. Talk to us about that message that you had about defending the West.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think the message is at the core of a lot of what we’re trying to instill in our foreign policy. I think people sometimes forget – like, look around our system of government, our culture, our values, the things we believe as a country are important. They’re not just words on paper. They are backed up by thousands of years of civilization. We are the heirs, we inherited from Greece and from Rome, and ultimately through Europe, many of the values that today are in our country. A lot of people view that as an attack on other cultures, but it’s not. I’m just saying every culture should be proud of themselves. The only culture, the only civilization in the world today who seems apologetic about its history and its achievements is the West. And it’s having a dramatic impact on foreign policy.

It is important for us to remind ourselves that we, too, are heirs to a great civilization that has done great things for humanity and for the world; that many of the things we take for granted in our everyday life, whether it’s the size and wealth of our country, whether it’s our democracy and our republic, whether it’s all of these things – they didn’t come from nowhere. They came from a shared history that we need to rediscover and embrace. We’re doing that here in this country under President Trump. We want more Western leaders to do the same.

QUESTION: So this is a message that you delivered as well, as well as the Vice President, at the Munich Security Conference the last couple of years. We – I think we’ve started seeing – I’ve had a lot of conversations with European leaders, particularly in Greece. I’ve interviewed the prime minister there twice, and several of their ministers. They do, slowly but surely, seem to be coming the United States’s way, following the lead of the Trump Administration on things like security and migration and other policies as well. Are you noticing a shift worldwide, particularly around the West, in Europe and elsewhere, our way?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I think I’ve noticed receptivity, that they’re receptive to what we’re saying. And even privately, I think a lot of leaders will tell you that was a great speech, we agree with you. Obviously, it takes time for that to translate into policy.

I also think there is still – and I think this is true even in our country, but certainly in Europe and in other parts of the world – they’re still worried that signing up for this thing – well, signing up for this point of view and speaking the way we have will open them up to criticisms from their far left, from their media, from their academia, from their entrenched bureaucracy. Because we’ve allowed this point of view to be stigmatized as something that’s evil, when in fact it should embraced as – embraced as something that is good.

So the answer is yes, I sense more receptivity. And I think where you’re really going to start seeing it play out is in elections; as more and more leaders are willing to say these things and then get elected, that is ultimately what’s going to shift the way other countries respond to our shared interests.

QUESTION: One of the reasons why I think we really hit it off with the Greeks – and again, like I said, I’ve been there five times in the last year or so; I’ve interviewed the prime minister twice and a number of their ministers, including their energy minister – is that – is energy, right? Like, they are – unlike some other places in maybe Western Europe, they’re actually going out there and seeking to do – explore their energy and get it, like we’re doing here in the United States, getting their natural gas and oil. I know that major American energy companies are working over there. I think you met with the prime minister when you were there in Greece. Can you talk to us about that? And maybe there were some discussion about refineries and some big deals that happened while —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, if you noticed, I mean, there was a lot of silliness around the world for the last 10 years about how energy – trying to de-emphasize energy; in fact, bragging about how expensive energy needed to become, fossil fuels, in order to get rid of them. No one’s talking about that anymore, right? Everyone now – unfortunately, global crises remind us that at the core of anything we want to do, whether it’s powering our everyday lives, our industries, or our defenses, it requires energy.

I think Greece is in a very unique place, both geographically and politically. Politically, they are open to energy exploration. In fact, they are encouraged by it and excited about it, and their population seems to support it as well, so that’s good. And then geographically, they’re located in a very key place as a transit corridor to build pipelines and ways to transmit energy. Energy is only as good as your ability to move it, whether it’s oil or gas or the generation of electricity. And they’re in a very important place because they are in the perfect place. They’ve always been the connector between Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. They’re in a very key place, where in addition to generating energy, they can actually help transport it – north into Europe; south into Israel, the Middle East, broader – these are – it’s – they’re a very advantageous position geographically now for energy, as they have been for trade and so many other industries throughout history.

QUESTION: Is the hope that other countries follow their lead? Right, like the Italians, the British, right, like the Germans, et cetera, elsewhere around the world, that they go in and get their energy too. Why should we have to be dependent on the Middle East or the Russians or elsewhere for energy? Obviously, we would like them to take American energy, but should they all go and explore? I think natural gas is everywhere, right?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah.

QUESTION: Like, so should the rest of them be doing the same thing?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Absolutely. I remember, I was in the Senate at the time when President Trump, in his first term, said that the Germans had left themselves vulnerable to Russian energy as a tool of blackmail in case of conflict. And they laughed. They mocked him. Our media mocked the President for saying that, and our media celebrated European leaders that laughed at the President. Well, guess what? That’s exactly what happened. Their dependence on Russian energy is one of the reasons why Putin went into Ukraine, because he thought he could, because he believed Europe wasn’t going to do anything about it.

So I hope they’ve learned that lesson. It seems like they now are, but it takes time now to reverse-engineer 20 years of both this green hyperbole in terms of believing they’re going to go completely green, and their belief that they could somehow not develop any domestic sources of energy and in fact just be overly reliant on one method.

So the answer is I hope they are, because Europe’s future depends on it. Right now their economy faces, unfortunately, real stagnation in most of these countries, because their fuel costs, both for electricity and transport, are incredibly high. They were already higher than they should’ve been even before the recent conflicts.

QUESTION: So another big part of defending Western civilization is the Western Hemisphere. Obviously, President Trump and you have made a major focus on this throughout – there’s been a major focus on Latin America in particular. Obviously, the Greenland deal that we have seen – now seen come together, and there’s some big energy components with that as well. Can you talk to us a little bit about the shift back to focusing on our own backyard that we hadn’t maybe seen from the last several administrations of either political party?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. I think the – technology has allowed us to connect with the world so that today you can instantaneously talk to someone halfway around the world, and in some ways it causes us to forget that despite that, geography is still real. When it comes to people, geography is still real. Anything bad that happens in the Western Hemisphere is going to impact us faster than if something bad is happening in Africa, or in the Middle East, or in Asia – or anywhere, for that matter. So we need to care about it just from our national interest.

Understand that America’s foreign policy, at its core, has to deal with what’s in the national interest of the United States. It is in the national interest of the United States to live in a region in which we have as many not just partners, but allies, who are stable and secure as possible. And that’s what we’re hoping to achieve. You see that now. Now, the people in these countries are making this choice through their elections. But we have seen country after country choose pro-Western, pro-American, anti-drug-cartel candidates in place after place after place. And it’s created a historically unique opportunity which, frankly, hasn’t gotten the coverage it deserves, and President Trump hasn’t gotten the credit he deserves for the fact that today, if I put a map of the Western Hemisphere in front of you and we said red were pro-American, blue for anti-American, the red has continued to grow and the blue continues to diminish to just a handful of places. This is an extraordinary, historic achievement, one that we need to build upon, and that we are very focused on.

QUESTION: Yeah, so we’ve seen countries – as you’re mentioning there, Colombia, Peru – swinging the pro-American way in their recent elections. We have a big election upcoming in Brazil; we’ll see what happens there. The – it really is remarkable just how fast this has happened across the Western Hemisphere. Why is it happening this quickly? I’ve seen some people out there suggesting, oh, it’s USAID is gone – (laughter) – so they’re not funding the NGOs and they’re not funding the left.

SECRETARY RUBIO: No, it’s —

QUESTION: I don’t know if that’s why, but maybe it’s – that’s part of it, but what do you think?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t think it’s a coincidence, to some extent, that the pulling foreign aid into the State Department and away from the sort of independent, do whatever they want organization, which was USAID, has had a direct impact on what’s happening in the region. Absolutely. There are groups in that region that are clearly aligned with the anti-America left. Now, they may be dressed up as an environmental NGO, or a group that works with the indigenous population in these countries, but the reality of it is they are part of this anti-American global network of NGOs. And we were funding many of them. We were funding many of them.

Now our foreign aid, it’s still – we’re still the most generous country in the world in foreign aid. The difference is our foreign aid is now designed specifically to further the national interest. We are not going to pay for things that are bad for America. We are not going to give money to people, organizations that hate America. And that’s why – that’s – now, whether or not I can prove to you that’s had a direct impact on these elections, I’m not sure we’ve studied it. But I don’t think it’s a coincidence, in my personal view.

I think the other thing that’s happened – understand these are not puppet presidents; these are elected by their populations. They’re going to make decisions – as they should – that are in the national interests of their respective countries. But what they are is they are not leaders that hate America; they are leaders that would prefer to partner with us than any other country in the world, and who share our same priorities. They want to dismantle these narcoterrorist organizations that are operating in the region. They want more American investment in their countries. They want to be supportive of what we’re doing on the global stage.

I think this an extraordinary achievement of President Trump and one that I just don’t think has gotten enough coverage yet. But that’s okay. History and the next few months and years will, I think, begin to give him the credit he deserves.

QUESTION: Well, we’re going to give a lot of coverage —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Good. Good, good, good. (Laughter.)

QUESTION: — at Breitbart, Mr. Secretary. So the – now another thing about – so we’ve seen several major crises that you guys have responded to in the Western Hemisphere, that the State Department has directly led the aid in – after the shutdown of USAID. The latest is the earthquake in Panama —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Right.

QUESTION: — but we’ve seen in earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia, as well as the hurricane in Jamica. Talk to us about the efforts that you guys have had on this. And we’re going to talk to the Ambassador to Panama Kevin Cabrera this weekend.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Great ambassador.

QUESTION: Yeah. So – and we’re going to have him on radio this weekend. But talk to us a little bit about the efforts in – what’s changed and how it’s different.

SECRETARY RUBIO: So when it comes to foreign assistance, there are two things that people – there’s three, really: security assistance; there is foreign aid, like helping them deal with health issues and economic development issues; and then there’s the humanitarian response – hurricane, earthquake, natural disasters. Without a doubt, the foreign aid has gotten way better in terms of direct aid, and it’s getting better, but there’s work still to be done. We’re improving it, and it’s an adjustment process.

The one that is unequivocally better right now – I mean, by far, just night and day – is humanitarian response. It is faster; it is more effective; it gets to the target way faster than ever before. We were able to deploy, for example, search and rescue teams substantially faster than the old model. And even those first responders are admitting it and telling us that. So every case is – Venezuela was a disaster. And we had to go in there and basically, like, run their airport, because their airport was shut down; you couldn’t get aid in without that. But just the amount of assistance that went there was extraordinary and historic.

Jamaica was the first test of our system – worked excellent there. Panama – different than Venezuela, not as bad, not – appears to be no significant or any loss of life per se, but they had the destruction. And what you’re seeing is media coverage – and Ambassador Cabrera will tell you this – the media coverage in Panama is recognizing it. They are seeing America was there fast and first. We’re not doing more than we need to. We are doing everything we need to, and we’re doing it based on what they’re telling us they need, not what we tell them they need. And it’s worked extraordinarily well. So all is very different. By the way, it’s not just there. We’ve been able to help with that mudslide out in Asia. We’ve been able to help in other places. But we rely on those countries to tell us: this is what we need; this is what we desire. And then we try to fill that gap available to us.

But it’s – no doubt, it’s harder. It’s – one of the things is this. If you’re going to be a pro-America leader in a democracy, you have to go to voters and say, “Guys, we are friends with the United States and here are the benefits of being a friend of the United States.” And I think the people of Panama are seeing that right now, and I think they saw it in Jamaica, and I think they’ve seen it in Venezuela. So there’s a – for a long time, we demanded countries be friendly to us, but we didn’t reward them. There was no, like, reward for being nice to the U.S. And oftentimes we seemed to pay more attention to our adversaries than we did to our friends. That has changed under President Trump, and I think, in many ways, is at the core of not just the change you’ve seen in the hemisphere but what I hope we’ll make it permanent and enduring.

QUESTION: Okay. So I want to get to some of the other major global crises in a second. But on the – after your big speech at the Acropolis, a lot of people were – I got a new 2028 question, right? But a lot of people were wondering: Should Secretary Rubio run for president? There’s a – I know you previously said that if the Vice President runs, JD Vance runs, you wouldn’t run against him. I don’t know if that position has changed. Where do you come down on this? Have you changed your mind on that? Are you considering running in 2028 or —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I’m not – I’ve said everything. I’ve already said things. Like, it doesn’t matter how many times you say it. So at this point, I’m just not answering anymore 2028 questions. Not anything against you.

QUESTION: Yeah, yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO: It’s the first time we’ve talked.

QUESTION: I know. (Laughter.)

SECRETARY RUBIO: But some of these reporters – that’s all they ever ask me about. I’m just done with it. I’m doing my job. I have two jobs, and I’m focused on them. They take, like, every hour of the day. Sometimes I don’t have enough hours in the day, depending on the day, to deal with my job. I just don’t have time anymore for those questions.

As far as the speech is concerned, what am I supposed to be doing? I mean, I’m the Secretary of State. I’m supposed to be representing this country on the international stage. I think people liked the speech. I think they should be happy and pleased that their Secretary of State is delivering an important message on the global stage. I’m just doing my job.

Everybody here is doing their job. The Vice President right now is out there campaigning for candidates to keep us – he’s doing his job. The Secretary of Treasury is crushing Iran with sanctions. He’s doing his job. Everyone’s doing their job, and I think we’re all part of the same team. And I think we should all be encouraged when members of the team are doing their job and are doing it well – and I hope I’m doing it well in my roles. And – but that’s kind of where it’s at.

QUESTION: Okay. So now on the – one last question on Greece, too, and then I want to talk about Russia, Ukraine, and China – and Iran. We’ll try to pack it all in. But just on Greece, we just saw the U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle was relieved by the President. The – I know a lot of people in Greece are going to watch this interview. They want to know what’s next for Greece. Like, can you talk to us a little bit about what is coming down the pike? Where do – what can we expect for – when can we expect a new ambassador to be there? What are we going to be looking for in that? What’s next for the relationship?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, Greece is an important country, very important. They’re a great ally of the United States. They’ve been – helped us in so many different ways and they’re important for our future. They’re at the cornerstone of so much of what we care about, whether it’s energy independence, whether it’s regional stability, whether it’s NATO and the role they play in NATO. So Greece deserves a strong and good ambassador that has access and the confidence – access to and confidence of the President.

And so obviously. we’re in early stages. This interview is 48 hours after all this happened, so there will be a process to identify the right person, and obviously they have to go through the whole confirmation process.

In the meantime, we’ll make sure we have a good team of people there on the ground. In no way should any of this be viewed as sort of a de-emphasizing of the Greek relationship. On the contrary, I think it’s so important to us that it is important that the person that’s there have the complete support and confidence of the President. So, we’ll have to take time to identify who the right person is, because we want to get at least the kind of ambassador that deserves the merit and that rises to the level of the relationship and how important it is.

QUESTION: Okay. So now let’s talk about Russia and Ukraine.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah.

QUESTION: The President really would like to end that thing. So I’m curious, the latest development is that the President did the deal with the Russians over the diesel, and has pushed both sides to not attack energy infrastructure. Both sides are apparently not following that. So first off, just meta, big picture here, how do we actually end this war between the Russians and the Ukrainians? I guarantee it never would have happened if President Trump was in the White House. But that being said, it’s still going on. How do we end this thing? And talk to us a little bit about the latest stuff with the energy infrastructure.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. So let me break this out into two buckets because they’re both very important. Let me start with the most important one, and that is ultimately, the job of the President of the United States and all of us who work for him is to make sure that the national interest of the United States is foremost, before anything else, okay? Before what is good for another country, before what is good for another continent, it’s what’s good for America. It has to be, because if we’re not looking out for our national interest, nobody else is going to.

And by the way, I expect every country to do things that way. Like, I expect the Colombian Government to put as their priority the national interest of Colombia. So, we have to put our national interest as the number one priority, above everything else. That doesn’t mean we’re deliberately looking for things that are bad for other countries, and hopefully what’s in our national interest is in their national interest. But if it comes down to a conflict between what’s good for them and what’s good for us, we always have to be for what’s good for us.

Right now, this economy, given what’s going on around the world, needs a bigger diesel supply in the global economy. We’ve already done this once before, and the President chose to do it again, which is a 30-day moratorium on sanctions to allow more Russian delivery of diesel into the global marketplace. That’ll impact and help the United States. It’ll help other countries as well. And that’s a decision he made not because it’s bad for Ukraine or good for Russia, but because it’s good for America and it’s important for America.

Now let’s talk about that conflict between Russia – the war between Russia and Ukraine. Here’s the reality of it. This war is honestly about one part of Ukraine called Donetsk. The Russians occupy all but about 11 percent of that area. In that province, Donetsk or in that region of Donetsk, the Ukrainians have a defensive line that they’ve embedded themselves in. They argue – the military strategists say, and I think it’s true – that it is the last defensible line; that if they give that up, there is nothing to defend Kyiv. From there it’s a straight shot into Kyiv.

The core of this conflict is that Russia demands all of Donetsk, including that defensive line, as part of their territory. That’s what they have defined as victory. And Ukraine has said we can’t give up that 11 percent that’s remaining of Donetsk because that defensive line is our last defensible line. Hence, that is at the core of this conflict.

Now, there are a lot of other issues going on, but ultimately that is really what they’re fighting over. How are they fighting over it? The Russians have not been able to advance in the battlefield and take that region, so what they are doing is they are applying extraordinary pain on the people of Ukraine through drone strikes and ballistic missile strikes, trying to destroy their energy infrastructure, their electricity, the ability of Ukraine to generate electricity, especially with winter coming up.

How does Ukraine respond to this? They have responded by going after Russian oil and gas refineries, which is at the core of how their economy funds itself, and bringing the war home. For the first time, Russians are seeing explosions going on in Moscow, in St. Petersburg, deep into their territory. It’s no longer a faraway war.

Hence, this is the situation we find ourselves in – not an easy one to negotiate and not an easy one to fix. The United States remains willing, able, and prepared to play a mediating role if one – if the opportunity presents itself to end this war through a negotiated settlement, which is how we think this war will ultimately end. But it has not been easy, not for lack of trying, because Jared and Steve and others have invested a lot of time into it, but because of the dynamics I’ve just described to you seem deeply entrenched right now. And – but we’re going to keep trying as much as we can to see what we can do. We’d like for the war to end. But ultimately, we also have other priorities around the world we’re focused on as well.

QUESTION: So Mr. Secretary, on the Russia-Ukraine war, so not to say – Putin’s not a great guy. But at the same time, it does seem like there’s some frustration now from the President with President Zelenskyy, and we’ve seen this bubble up at different moments. We’re more than two and a half years, I believe, since the regularly scheduled elections that they were going to have in Ukraine. Is it time to have an election in Ukraine? I know that their constitution allows them, with the declaration of martial law, to suspend elections, which is what they’ve done during the war here. But is it time to maybe have an election, see a new president?

SECRETARY RUBIO: See, but look, the election issue comes up and I’m not saying it’s irrelevant, but that’s not at the core of why there’s still a war going on.

QUESTION: Sure.

SECRETARY RUBIO: What I would say is the frustration more than anything else – and we’ve talked about this publicly. For example, months ago we have seen strikes on energy vessels in the Black Sea, and there have been complaints lodged because we have American companies calling us and saying hey, that was our oil on that ship that was hit by Ukraine. Now, I don’t believe Ukraine intentionally targeted them, but those ships got hit. And we already have a world that is facing an energy crisis because of what’s happening in Hormuz, what’s happening in the Red Sea, what’s happening in different places. We don’t need any exacerbating situations, and there’s been frustration despite these asks. That has happened.

So that’s bubbled to the surface. That doesn’t mean we don’t have frustrations with the Russian side either. The President does not like to see this image of a ballistic missile hitting an apartment building in Kyiv and innocent civilians being wiped out as a result of it. He doesn’t like that either. That’s why this has been so frustrating to try to get a resolution to it.

QUESTION: Okay, so I want to talk about Iran now. So, with regard to the war in Iran, I think people around the country ahead of this midterm election, they want to see this thing wrapped up. At the same time, it does look like the President has achieved the original military objective, which is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. Address both of those points for us. How do we end this thing, a similar type of a thing for the – I think people want to see the war is over. How do we end this thing, but also what have we accomplished there so far?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, it’s important to remind people why it started in the first place. Iran wanted to build a conventional shield of tens and tens of thousands of missiles and drones that once they got to that point, they would be able to say to the world, guys, we’re now going to build a nuclear weapon and there’s nothing you can do about it because we have many – so many drones and so many missiles that we will destroy the entire region, so you can’t touch us; we are immune.

The President was not going to allow them to build a nuclear weapon hiding behind the conventional weapon shield that they were trying to achieve. So he destroyed their navy. He destroyed their air force. He destroyed their factories that make the missiles. Now, they still have them, but they can’t make as many as they used to, far less able to make them the way they used to because he’s destroyed their factories for drones and missiles. They don’t have an air force, they don’t have a navy, and they’ve lost a lot of air defenses as well. Large portions of their country are deeply vulnerable to future strikes, if necessary. So he’s achieved that objective. They can no longer hide behind a conventional shield to build a nuclear weapon.

The second objective is they chose to take the straits hostage. They would have done it anyway. Imagine if Iran had a nuclear weapon. At that point they could say: And by the way, we own the Straits of Hormuz and you guys can’t do anything about it because we won’t just hit ships. We’ll use a nuclear weapon against you if you try to do anything about it. They are trying to control the Straits of Hormuz. They lost control of the straits. Today, on average over the last 10 days and certainly over the last 30, about 13 to 14 million barrels of oil are going through the Straits of Hormuz out to the global market, and some days it’s actually equivalent to what it was pre-conflict. And the U.S. military is involved in escorting and defending these ships from these strikes. Iran is still shooting at these, but by and large we’ve been able to get that flow going.

And at the same time, because Iran continues to fire at these ships, we have imposed crippling additional sanctions – Scott Bessent has been doing a great job on it – and a blockade. The only country in the world that cannot get a single barrel of oil through the Straits of Hormuz is Iran. They’re the only ones, and we’re inflicting tremendous pain on them. In addition, these sanctions are costing them money, which means that’s money they don’t have. Every dollar you deny them in sanctions is a dollar they don’t have for Hizballah, a dollar they don’t have for Hamas, a dollar they don’t have for the terrorist militias inside of Iraq, and a dollar they don’t have for their own military or their own nuclear ambitions.

So I understand people’s frustration, because we all want it to be wrapped up. In some ways it is, and right now we are basically in the Strait of Hormuz as a defense posture and doing an excellent job of crippling their economy in the process.

QUESTION: So Mr. Secretary, another big thing. This is actually similar to the successes that we’ve seen around Latin America and the Western Hemisphere. Across the broader Middle East, I think when we look back on what President Trump has done, both in his first term here and in the second term, what you guys have been able to do here at the State Department, it’s going to – it’s – the Middle East looks very different than it did before. And there are still major conflicts and different things going on in different places, but the pathway to – I mean, look, peace in the Middle East used to be a bumper sticker slogan. It wasn’t a serious thing, right? And now it’s like a serious thing. We have a pathway to real peace in the Middle East and prosperity in the region, and that’s because of many of the changes that President Trump has brought to the Middle East. Talk to us about that broader vision here, because I think when we look back on it, it’s going to be a really historic thing.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. So look, I think, traditionally, the American political class thought that peace in the Middle East, a core central issue is the Palestinian question. It’s an important issue. It’s not irrelevant. I’m not saying that it’s irrelevant. But I think what President Trump has exposed is that the number one driver of instability and war and conflict, and the number one obstacle to peace in the Middle East, is the Islamic regime in Tehran. And I think the evidence bears it out.

In Lebanon, why is Lebanon a country that’s used as an attack point against Israel and other interests? Who sponsors Hizballah? Hizballah is 100 percent an agent of Iran. In Iraq, why does that country still have terrorist militias that operate from their territory and launch missiles against Saudi Arabia, against Israel? Who sponsors them? They are Shia militias sponsored by Iran, which is the only country in the region that has launched not simply proxy attacks but direct attacks. Direct attacks against Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan – I’m probably leaving somebody out. Who’s launched them? The only country in the region that’s done that: Iran – direct attacks, in addition to what their proxies have done. By the way, with the Houthis now and Saudi Arabia, who is the number one sponsor of the Houthis? Iran.

So if you look at all the things that are going on in that region and all the flash points that exist there, they all track back to the Islamic Republic of Iran, to the clerical – radical clerics that run Iran from Tehran. They are the central problem in that region. If there was no Islamic clerics, these radical Shia clerics in Iran, if they didn’t exist, if that wasn’t there, none of these problems would exist. You may still have the Palestinian issue. I would argue that issue would be easier to deal with if Iran didn’t exist. So, they’re at the core of all of these problems, and I think correctly identifying who it is that’s driving instability and war in the Middle East is important in order to solve it. And that issue has to be confronted, and I think what’s happened in the last few months has revealed it for the world to see.

QUESTION: Okay. The last thing I really want to ask you about here is the President’s address to the UN General Assembly. He talked about the use of American power to achieve the American objective. Can you lay out that America First foreign policy for us? What is that America First foreign policy? How do we do what the President talked about in that address to achieve that American First – America First objectives? How do we use that American power?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Look, first of all, I know that, like, people in the media – not this media but other media – like to criticize the term America First as sort of evil thing. Let me ask you, how many candidates would be elected if they went out and told the American people, my job is to put America second, or America third, or America last? If they don’t like America First, they should have the guts to go out there and tell people, I am running for office on the belief that our foreign policy should be driven by America second or America third. No one ever does that because I think, at its core, everyone understands that our foreign policy, which is what I can speak about, has to be about what is good for America. I think every country should do that for their own countries, and foreign relations is how you untangle the differences.

So I think the President is basically saying common sense, which is, our foreign policy, what we do around the world, is going to be driven by what’s good for America. Now, we would argue that what is good for America is probably also good for many of our allies as well. And in those instances in which what’s good for us and what’s good for someone we like are not exactly aligned, then we’ll work on it with diplomacy and try to manage all of that. But in the end, America First is common sense. It’s what it is.

And I think what the President is saying is that we as a country, we’re the largest economy in the world, the most powerful military in the world, the most influential culture in the world. We are going to use all the elements of American power to further the interests of the United States, which we believe also furthers the interests of our allies and the broader world. So – but America First, I mean, we’re going to always do what’s right for America before anything else. We’re going to put it before the UN. We’re going to put it before the global commons or whatever you want to call it, the global order that people worshipped around here for a very long time. We’re not against of those things. We’re just not going to put them ahead of American interests anymore.

That’s what the President is doing. And it offends a lot of people in these think tanks and editorial writers. But if we had listened to them, I mean, at this point America would be a middle power.

title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio With Matthew Boyle of Breitbart News

EPA to Hold Public Meeting on Modification of Remedy at New Bedford Harbor Superfund Site on October 28, 2026
BOSTON, MASS (Oct. 19, 2026) — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is hosting a virtual public meeting on October 28, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. via Microsoft Teams to present the draft eighth Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD) proposing to modify the upper and lower harbor remedy for the New Bedford Harbor Superfund Site.
Under the ESD, EPA would remove soil in areas where polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) contamination is higher than 1 part per million. The contaminated soil would be excavated to a depth of three feet and replaced with clean soil. The plan would also include land use controls for the property. These controls would allow the City of New Bedford to pursue residential development on the site, but would require a soil management plan to make sure any PCB-contaminated soil located deeper than three feet would be handled safely, if it were to be disturbed in the future.
"The City of New Bedford has been a key partner during EPA's implementation of the Superfund remedy, allowing EPA to perform remedy support work at the City's Sawyer Street property since the 1980s," said EPA Regional Administrator Mark Sanborn. "This proposed work is an important step as we near completion of the New Bedford Harbor Superfund Site cleanup."
EPA is seeking public input on the draft ESD during the 30-day public comment period starting on October 30, 2026, and ending on November 28, 2026. Beginning on October 30, 2026, the draft ESD Administrative Record can be reviewed and comments submitted via https://www.regulations.gov (Docket ID No. EPA-R01-SFUND-2026-6304). All comments are reviewed and responded to in writing by EPA prior to selecting a final alternative for the ESD, if necessary.
Meeting materials and link to join October 28th meeting at 6:00 p.m. will be posted prior to the meeting on https://www.epa.gov/new-bedford-harbor.
title: EPA to Hold Public Meeting on Modification of Remedy at New Bedford Harbor Superfund Site on October 28, 2026

text:
Grijalva, Stanton, and Ansari Statement on Suspicious Letters Sent to Arizona Offices
    Monday, October 19, 2026
  
Tucson, AZ –- Today, Congresswoman Adelita S. Grijalva, along with U.S. Representatives Greg Stanton (AZ-04) and Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), released the following joint statement after being notified by the FBI Phoenix Field Office and the Arizona Department of Homeland Security that suspicious letters had been sent to their offices.
“This weekend, the FBI Phoenix Field Office and the Arizona Department of Homeland Security informed us that suspicious letters had been sent to our offices. Similar letters, many containing unknown substances, have been mailed to elected officials across the country.
The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating. We’re grateful to law enforcement for acting quickly and keeping our staff and communities safe. We will not be intimidated, and we’ll keep doing the work that Arizonans elected us to do.”
The letters addressed to Representatives Grijalva and Ansari were sent to former office addresses. The letter addressed to Representative Stanton’s Mesa office was intercepted before delivery.
###
title: Grijalva, Stanton, and Ansari Statement on Suspicious Letters Sent to Arizona Offices

Pensacola, Florida – Dominique J. Stanberry, 33, of Pensacola, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to two counts of wire fraud involving Small Business Administration (SBA) Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan funds. This prosecution was part of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud launched by President Donald J. Trump, a whole-of-government effort to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “We saw unprecedented levels of fraud during the COVID-19 pandemic by scammers, like this defendant, who sought to enrich themselves by ripping off the American taxpayer, but my office will tirelessly pursue those fraudsters to make them pay for their crimes. Anyone in the Northern District of Florida who abuses or defrauds a Federal benefit program should be on notice: my office is coming for you.”

Court documents reflect that in 2021, the defendant, while working full time as a United States Postal Service employee, caused to be submitted a fraudulent online application for a PPP loan that falsely claimed she was self-employed with a business that lost income due to the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result of her fraud, the defendant received $20,833 in PPP loan funds to which she was not entitled.

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Stanberry faces up to 20 years’ imprisonment on each count. As part of her plea agreement, Stanberry has agreed to forfeit any forfeitable assets and to pay restitution.

Sentencing is scheduled for December 3, 2026, at 9 a.m. at the United States Courthouse in Pensacola before United States District Judge T. Kent Wetherell, II.

The case was investigated by the United States Postal Service-Office of Inspector General with assistance from the United States Postal Inspection Service. Assistant United States Attorneys Alicia H. Forbes and Thomas S.P. Geeker are prosecuting the case.

The Fraud Section leads the Criminal Division's prosecution of fraud schemes that exploit the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP). Since the inception of the CARES Act, the Fraud Section has prosecuted over 150 defendants in more than 95 criminal cases and has seized over $75 million in cash proceeds derived from fraudulently obtained PPP funds, as well as numerous real estate properties and luxury items purchased with such proceeds. More information can be found at Justice.gov/OPA/pr/justice-department-takes-action-against-covid-19-fraud .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access available public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: National Fraud Enforcement Division Obtains Guilty Plea of Pensacola Postal Worker for PPP Loan Fraud

VA Home Loan Servicer Village Capital to Pay Over $500,000 for Violating Servicemembers’ Rights
The Justice Department today announced that Village Capital & Investment LLC, a servicer of home loans guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs, will pay over $500,000 to resolve allegations that it failed to properly apply Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA) interest rate benefits to at least 41 servicemembers’ mortgages and retaliated against servicemembers who requested interest rate benefits.
“When lenders refuse to honor the benefits guaranteed under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act — or worse, retaliate against those who assert their rights — they not only violate federal law, but undermine the trust that military families place in financial institutions,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “Today’s action makes clear that such conduct will not be tolerated. We will continue to enforce the law to ensure servicemembers receive the protections they have earned.”
“Protecting our nation’s heroes from unlawful lending practices is a fundamental duty, not an option,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “By failing to apply the interest rate cap correctly and misrepresenting mortgage terms, Village Capital & Investment LLC breached the trust of servicemembers. This settlement serves as a clear directive to VA home loan servicers everywhere: illegal lending practices that harm servicemembers will be met with swift accountability and strict enforcement.”
Under this settlement, Village Capital will pay at least $425,000 to affected servicemembers. The company will also be required to pay a $79,380 civil penalty, which is the maximum penalty for a first violation of the SCRA. The agreement also requires Village Capital to revise its policies and procedures to prevent future SCRA violations and provide SCRA training to its employees.
The Department alleges that Village Capital violated the SCRA by failing to reduce the interest rate on servicemembers’ pre-service debts to 6% retroactively to the date they received their military orders and by failing to reduce the monthly mortgage payments by the amount of interest forgiven. Village Capital also allegedly misled servicemember borrowers regarding the interest rates on their mortgages, telling them that their interest rate was already below 6% when the rate was in fact above 6%. The Department also alleges that Village Capital violated the SCRA by retaliating against servicemembers who requested interest rate benefits by accelerating the payment of principal on their loans and falsely reporting their mortgages as delinquent to the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The Department’s enforcement of the SCRA is conducted by the Civil Rights Division’s Housing and Civil Enforcement Section in partnership with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country. Since 2011, the Department has obtained over $490 million in monetary relief for over 153,000 servicemembers through its enforcement of the SCRA. For more information about the Department’s SCRA enforcement efforts, please visit www.servicemembers.gov.
Servicemembers and their dependents who believe that their rights under the SCRA may have been violated should contact the nearest Armed Forces Legal Assistance Program Office. Office locations can be found at legalassistance.law.af.mil.
Note: Read the executed settlement here.
title: VA Home Loan Servicer Village Capital to Pay Over $500,000 for Violating Servicemembers’ Rights

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, announced that CHUKWUEMEKA VICTOR AMACHUKWU, a/k/a “Chukwuemeka Victor Eletuo,” a/k/a “So Kwan Leung,” was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Paul G. Gardephe to eight years in prison for his role in multiple fraud, hacking, and identity theft offenses. AMACHUKWU previously pled guilty to conspiracy to commit computer intrusions and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

“Chukwuemeka Amachukwu believed he was operating safely offshore when he targeted his victims, but he has now been held to account and now faces a serious sentence for his crimes,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into U.S. businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud. These crimes imposed significant harm on the victims and the public, and so it is only appropriate that the crimes also come with a significant sentence for the defendant.”

According to the Superseding Indictments, public court filings, and statements made in court:

Beginning in at least in or about 2019, AMACHUKWU, his co-conspirator Kinglsey Uchelue Utulu, and other Nigeria-based conspirators took part in a scheme to hack into U.S-based tax preparation businesses. The conspirators utilized spearphishing emails to obtain access to these business’s electronic systems. Once they had obtained access, the conspirators stole the tax and other identifying information for at least approximately 800 of the business’ customers. The conspirators hacked into several U.S. based tax businesses, located in New York, Texas, and other states.

The conspirators obtained the stolen identity information of thousands of individuals. They used this information to file fraudulent tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service and state tax authorities. The conspirators sought fraudulent refunds of at least approximately $8.4 million, of which they successfully obtained at least approximately $2.5 million.

In addition to filing fraudulent tax returns, the conspirators used the stolen identities to file fraudulent claims with the Small Business Administration’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program. The conspirators were able to obtain at least an additional approximately $819,000 in fraudulent payouts.

In addition, AMACHUKWU took part in a fraud scheme in which he offered U.S. victims investments in purportedly valuable standby letters of credit. In the course of this scheme, AMACHUKWU impersonated a wealthy overseas financier in order to fool his victims. In reality, these investments did not exist, and AMACHUKWU and his co-conspirators were able to pocket more than $7 million in fraudulent proceeds.

* * *

In addition to the prison term, AMACHUKWU, 40, of Nigeria, was sentenced to one year of supervised release and ordered to pay restitution in an amount of $3,647,629.39 and forfeiture in the amount of $10,846,634.39.

Mr. McDonald thanked the Federal Bureau of Investigation for its outstanding work.

This case is being handled by the Office’s Complex Frauds and Cybercrime Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel G. Nessim is in charge of the prosecution.
title: Nigerian Man Sentenced To Eight Years For Hacking, Fraud, And Identity Theft Schemes

HOUSTON – Two Houston-area residents have been indicted for allegedly submitting fraudulent financial documents to multiple mortgage lenders.

Tammi Hunnicutt, 64, made her initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Dena Palermo on October 2. Taylor Dickson, 33, pictured, made her initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Peter Bray on Oct. 15.

According to the now-unsealed 11-count indictment, Hunnicutt and Dickson allegedly participated in a scheme to defraud mortgage lenders from approximately October 2019 through September 2023. The indictment alleges they submitted loan applications supported by falsified pay stubs, W-2 forms and bank statements to misrepresent borrowers’ employment and income and help them qualify for mortgage loans.

“Mortgage fraud undermines the integrity of our financial system and puts lenders, taxpayers, and legitimate homebuyers at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron F. Reitz. “The defendants allegedly created fraudulent financial documents to help borrowers obtain loans they might not otherwise qualify for. Our office will aggressively pursue those who exploit the mortgage lending process for financial gain and work with our law enforcement partners to hold them accountable.”

“Mortgage fraud undermines the integrity of our financial system and puts lenders, taxpayers, and legitimate homebuyers at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron F. Reitz. “The defendants allegedly created fraudulent financial documents to help borrowers obtain loans they might not otherwise qualify for. Our office will aggressively pursue those who exploit the mortgage lending process for financial gain and work with our law enforcement partners to hold them accountable.”

“The Federal Housing Finance Agency Office of Inspector General vigorously investigates schemes to commit mortgage fraud, particularly those involving loan officers and other industry insiders who have a duty to conduct honest business,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher Lane of the FHFA-OIG Central Region. “We are committed to working with the Department of Justice and our investigative partners to hold accountable participants in these schemes and are grateful to the United States Attorney’s Office for their support.”

“Tammi Hunnicutt and Taylor Dickson allegedly facilitated a scheme to help borrowers obtain FHA and conventional loans by creating false financial documents, including pay stubs, bank statements, and W2 forms. By misrepresenting borrowers’ financial qualifications, their actions exposed the FHA insurance program to approximately $5,890,112.30 in potential losses,” said Special Agent in Charge Grant Permenter of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development-Office of Inspector General. “HUD-OIG remains committed to protecting the integrity of HUD programs and will continue working closely with the U.S. Attorney’s Office and our law enforcement partners to hold accountable those who use fraud and deception to circumvent federal housing requirements.”

If convicted, each faces up to 20 years in prison and a possible maximum $250,000 fine for conspiracy to commit wire fraud or wire fraud. They also face up to 30 years in prison and a possible $1 million maximum fine for making false statements to a mortgage lending business.

FBI, FHFA-OIG, and HUD-OIG conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Rodolfo Ramirez and Special Assistant United States Attorney Shalimar Addy are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law.
title: Two charged in mortgage fraud scheme involving falsified financial documents

FORT DRUM, New York – Senior leaders from the Guthrie Army Health Clinic and Veterans Affairs Syracuse Healthcare System officially marked the opening of the Fort Drum VA Clinic with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Oct. 16, 2026.
Held in the shared lobby of Guthrie’s specialty care clinic and the VA’s new location, the ceremony brought together attendees from Fort Drum, local veteran service organizations, healthcare partner agencies, and others from the North Country community. The event concluded with senior representatives from both Guthrie AHC and the Syracuse VA Healthcare System cutting the ceremonial ribbon in front of both organizations’ flags.
“(The ceremony is) about far more than just opening clinic doors,” said Col. Elizabeth Duque, Guthrie AHC’s commander, during her remarks. “It marks an exciting new chapter in a partnership that has been actually forged over decades of service to those who wear or have worn the uniforms of our forces.”
The ceremony marks the formal relocation of VA specialty medical services from Watertown, New York, to Fort Drum. Under a facility-sharing agreement, the VA is co-locating its specialty clinic inside dedicated space within Guthrie AHC to share resources and streamline infrastructure usage across agencies.
“When we bring together our people and strategic resources around the needs of our veterans, we can serve them better and serve our nation better,” said Michael DelDuca, executive director of the VA Syracuse Healthcare System. “Today, as we cut this ribbon, we are doing more than opening a clinic. We are strengthening access to care, building strong partnerships, and reaffirming our commitment to the veterans of the North Country.”
The arrival of the VA Specialty Care Clinic builds on a long-standing history of resource sharing between the two healthcare systems. Guthrie AHC already hosts VA physical therapists and benefits coordinators alongside its medical team, and the VA previously operated a clinic on Fort Drum during the 1990s.
“Bringing the VA specialty services here from the CANI Building in Watertown is a natural evolution of that bond for our veterans who work, live, and raise families across the North Country,” Duque said. “Accessing care in this modern, state-of-the-art facility on an installation woven deeply into their military roots honors their service in the way it should be honored.”
While the primary focus of the relocation is delivering specialty care to enrolled VA patients, leaders view the agreement as a foundation for broader inter-agency collaboration. Future efforts aim to deepen integration between the VA and the Department of War, expand regional healthcare access, and create a more seamless experience for beneficiaries across both healthcare systems.
“As proud as we are of this ribbon cutting, we don’t see this moment as a finish line,” Duque said. “This is a launching pad. Having the Syracuse VA inside Guthrie’s footprint lays the groundwork for even tighter relationships and cooperation down the road, sharing specialized services and enhancing clinical cooperation.”
title: Ribbon cutting marks official opening of new Fort Drum VA Clinic

FBI Raleigh Durham Safe Streets Task Force Dismantles Durham Drug Trafficking Ring
A yearlong joint investigation by the FBI Raleigh Durham Safe Streets Task Force and the Durham County Sheriff’s Office resulted in ten defendants sentenced to a combined 738 months in federal prison. The defendants were sentenced in separate court appearances between December 17, 2025, to July 8, 2026, after being convicted as part of a cocaine and fentanyl drug trafficking operation in Durham. The undercover investigation seized a totaling of 24.5 kilograms of cocaine and 2.5 kilograms of fentanyl, including one tractor trailer intercepted in New Mexico.
- Khuram Choudhry: Sentenced to 204 months on June 29, 2026
- Matt Morton: Sentenced to 7 months on December 17, 2025
- Jerrell Green: Sentenced to 30 months on March 18, 2026
- Shazad Khan: Sentenced to 120 months on March 2, 2026
- Jason Chase: Sentenced to 32 months on March 3, 2026
- Shance Bostic: Sentenced to 36 months on February 25, 2026
- Wendy Rizo-Bodden: Sentenced to 24 months on February 20, 2026
- Kevin Johnson: Sentenced to 204 months on February 23, 2026
- Jamaal Robertson: Sentenced to 66 months on February 19, 2026
- Dwight Chandler: Sentenced to 51 months on July 8, 2026
“This investigation demonstrates the unwavering resolve of the FBI and our partners to dismantle the criminal networks flooding our communities with deadly narcotics. Over the course of a year, the FBI Raleigh Durham Safe Streets Task Force executed a coordinated, resource-intensive operation that removed significant quantities of fentanyl and cocaine from the pipeline and brought ten offenders to justice. These sentences underscore a simple truth: if you traffic drugs in our communities, the FBI will find you, we will dismantle your operation, and you will be held fully accountable," said Reid Davis, the FBI special agent in charge in North Carolina.
“This joint operation demonstrates the power of federal and local law enforcement standing shoulder-to-shoulder,” said Durham County Sheriff Clarence F. Birkhead. “I’m proud of the work our investigators do every day in conjunction with the FBI’s Safe Streets Task Force. Taking 10 dangerous drug traffickers off our streets—including repeat violent offenders who put law enforcement lives at risk—makes Durham County safer. Collectively, these defendants received more than six decades of federal prison time, which demonstrates our unwavering commitment to addressing drug trafficking and violent crime to protect everyone in our community.”
The investigation was conducted by the FBI Raleigh Durham Safe Streets Task Force, Durham County Sheriff’s Office, Chapel Hill Police Department, Durham Police Department, North Carolina Department of Adult Corrections Special Operations and Intelligence Unit, North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation, Wake County Sheriff’s Office, and Homeland Security Investigations.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of North Carolina prosecuted the cases.
title: FBI Raleigh Durham Safe Streets Task Force Dismantles Durham Drug Trafficking Ring
