The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulates wells used for underground injection of carbon dioxide, known as Class VI wells. The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), administered by EPA, prohibits underground injection of fluids without a permit, including underground injection of carbon dioxide for geologic sequestration. Under SDWA, EPA is authorized to delegate primary enforcement authority, or primacy, for underground injection control (UIC) programs to individual states that meet minimum UIC program requirements. As the number of carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) projects using deep well injection has increased in the United States in recent years, Class VI permitting and state program primacy have been topics of interest to Congress.
EPA has established minimum permitting requirements for Class VI injection wells and for state UIC programs. Requirements are specified for well siting and construction, operation and maintenance, monitoring and testing, reporting and recordkeeping, site closure, financial responsibility, and post-injection site care. The minimum contents of a permit are established in regulation, but each Class VI permit is developed and approved based on the site-specific characteristics of the injection well project and is designed to address potential leakage or endangerment of underground sources of drinking water.
Currently, there are at least 8 federal EPA-permitted Class VI projects with at least 13 permitted wells operating in 5 U.S. states. According to EPA, 142 Class VI permit applications are currently pending review by the agency. Additional permits are under review by states with delegated authority for state Class VI UIC programs.
Class VI permits are required to include information about the project and underground formations, demonstrate site suitability, and provide financial assurances. Permits must also include six required plans that provide detail on how the owner or operator will conduct injection well activities throughout the project lifecycle of the project. When reviewing permit applications, the permitting authority (either EPA or a state) typically conducts five stages of review: completion review, technical review, draft permit, public comment, and final permit. The technical review, which involves evaluation of information and plans in the application package, is the longest and most complex step in the permitting process. Once the permit is in place, the permitting authority is responsible for ensuring the permit requirements continue to be met.
EPA has approved UIC Class VI program primacy for six states: Arizona, Louisiana, North Dakota, Texas, West Virginia, and Wyoming. When granted primacy for a class of UIC wells, a state administers that UIC program through enforcement of state laws and regulations in lieu of EPA regulations. EPA retains oversight authority over all state UIC programs under federal law. EPA UIC regulations set out the specific requirements for state programs in permitting, compliance evaluation, enforcement, and information sharing. A state must demonstrate that it has the legal authorities and processes in place to administer the Class VI program. A memorandum of agreement between a state and EPA, which is submitted along with other required documents, typically serves as the foundation of a state's specific responsibilities and commitments in administering the Class VI program.
Congress has appropriated funding in recent years to EPA for implementation of federal and state Class VI programs. On top of regular annual appropriations in several fiscal years for Class VI activities, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58) provided $50 million in supplemental appropriations to EPA for grants to states that have or are working toward Class VI primacy and $25 million to EPA for Class VI program administration. As Congress continues to debate policy on Class VI well permitting and state primacy, several issues may arise regarding Class VI wells, including EPA appropriations, legislation, and EPA oversight. These issues may include
Several industries in the United States are expanding the process of injecting captured carbon dioxide (CO2) through deep wells into underground geologic formations with the objective of reducing CO2 levels in the atmosphere. As one option for mitigating the potential impacts of climate change, this carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) process could reduce the amount of CO2—a greenhouse gas—emitted from power plants and other large industrial facilities. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issues permits for CO2 injection wells, known as Class VI wells, used for injection and geologic sequestration of CO2. In some cases, EPA delegates authority to states, known as program primacy, to administer underground injection programs and issue Class VI permits.
In recent years, Class VI permitting and state program delegation has been a topic of interest to Congress. In 2022, in response to a directive in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (P.L. 116-260) directing EPA to provide recommendations to "improve Class VI permitting procedures," EPA provided a report to Congress on Class VI permitting.1 For FY2026, Congress provided targeted appropriations for Class VI well activities in the Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-74). Some Members have continued to express interest in Class VI well permitting and primacy issues, including the status of applications, EPA review processes, public participation in applications, and options for increasing the numbers of approved well permits and state program primacy applications.
This report discusses the statutory and regulatory framework for permitting Class VI wells; describes Class VI permit application requirements and the permit review process; describes state primacy requirements and the primacy review process; and highlights selected policy issues for Congress.
Other environmental regulations and permit requirements may apply to projects injecting CO2, depending on the scope and purpose of the project, such as requirements under the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act administered by EPA. EPA also regulates injection of CO2 for oil production (in a process known as enhanced oil recovery) through Class II Underground Injection Control (UIC) wells.2 These regulations and permits are beyond the scope of this report. For more information on CO2 injection and sequestration, including the federal statutory and regulatory framework, and general policy issues, see CRS Report R46192, Injection and Geologic Sequestration of Carbon Dioxide: Federal Role and Issues for Congress, by Angela C. Jones.
As part of the CCS process, CO2 is first captured from a stationary source, such as a coal-fired power plant or chemical production facility. The CO2 is then injected into subsurface geologic formations for geologic sequestration, the long-term containment of a fluid (including a gas, liquid, or supercritical CO2 stream) in subsurface geologic formations.3
The CO2 is injected through Class VI wells, typically injecting fluid a half mile or more below the earth's surface. Geologic formations used for injecting CO2 include, for example, large deep saline reservoirs (underground basins containing salty fluids) and oil and gas reservoirs no longer in production.
The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), administered by EPA, provides authorities for regulating the underground injection of fluids.4 SDWA prohibits any underground injection activity, except when authorized by a permit or rule, to prevent endangerment of underground sources of drinking water (USDWs).5 As part of EPA's UIC program, the agency has promulgated regulations and established minimum federal requirements for injection wells, including for Class VI wells for the purpose of long-term geologic sequestration.6
SDWA also authorizes EPA to delegate primary enforcement authority—the aforementioned primacy—for UIC programs to states (see "7 EPA has delegated primacy for state UIC Class VI programs to six states to date.
Federal requirements for injection well permits, including Class VI well permits, are codified in UIC regulations at 40 C.F.R. §§144-146. Class VI permits are issued by EPA, or in certain cases, states that have been granted authority for the Class VI well program (discussed in detail later in this report). Minimum requirements are specified for well siting and construction, operation and maintenance, monitoring and testing, reporting and recordkeeping, site closure, financial responsibility, and post-injection site care. The well owner or operator must seek a permit for each individual Class VI well.8
Each UIC Class VI permit is specific to the characteristics of the individual injection site and operation. Site-specific permitting is necessary to address the risks of CO2 injection at high pressures, such as leaks into the atmosphere, underground leaks, or movement of formation water into USDWs that could affect drinking water quality.
Class VI permit requirements and standards are generally more stringent than requirements for other well classes. EPA based the regulation and permitting requirements of Class VI wells on several risk factors specific to this type of injection activity. These risk factors include the large volumes of CO2 expected to be injected through wells, the mobility of CO2 within subsurface formations, and the corrosive properties of CO2 in the presence of water that can affect well materials.9
To assist states and owners/operators with the permitting process, EPA has issued 11 technical guidance documents on Class VI wells.10 These documents are not legally enforceable, but they provide additional information on site characterization, area of review, construction, reporting and recordkeeping, site closure, financial responsibility, and other permit elements.
During the Class VI well permit application process, the owner or operator works with the permitting authority, either EPA or a state, that has primacy for the Class VI UIC program. EPA identifies four phases of permitting for a Class VI project:11
Class VI permits extend for the operating life of the facility and a 50-year post-injection site care period.12 The duration of a Class VI well injection project varies depending on the amount of CO2 captured for storage and the capacity of the underground formation, but current projects estimate a 10- to 15-year timeframe for injection. Permitting authorities are required to review Class VI permits at least once every five years.13
For EPA-issued Class VI permits, 40 C.F.R. Parts 144 and 146 set out specific requirements for the permit application and approval process. While the minimum contents of a permit are established in federal regulation, the site-specific permit conditions, technical standards, and other requirements in each permit are based on the permitting authority's evaluation of the potential risks to USDWs and the necessary conditions and standards required for the project to prevent and manage potential endangerment of USDWs. Permits are updated based on site or project circumstances. States must have equivalent requirements if administering their own UIC Class VI programs and issuing Class VI permits (see "State UIC Class VI Program Primacy").
Class VI permit applicants are required to include general project information and to meet the permit conditions applicable to all UIC permits, as well as Class VI-specific permit criteria and standards.14 Injection project information includes
Class VI permit applications are also required to
For more information on Class VI well standards and permitting requirements, see CRS Report R46192, Injection and Geologic Sequestration of Carbon Dioxide: Federal Role and Issues for Congress, Appendix C.
Class VI regulations require that permit application packages include several plans that provide detailed information on how the owner or operator will conduct injection well activities from construction through closure.18 These plans are finalized and approved by the permitting authority as part of the permitting process. The following plans are required in a permit application:
By regulation, Class VI wells are defined as wells that are used for the geologic sequestration of CO2 "beneath the lowermost formation containing a USDW" (emphasis added).19 In some cases, the USDWs may be deep in the formation. In these cases, during the permitting process, well owners or operators may seek a waiver to allow injection into non-USDWs above or between USDWs. Class VI regulations include specific requirements for approval of a depth waiver, such as the information to be provided to the state or EPA, consultations with state Public Water System Directors and tribes, public notice, and approval or concurrence by the EPA Regional Administrator.20
Class VI permit regulations require that an owner or operator submitting a permit application package meet specific requirements and follow certain processes. Once an applicant submits a permit application to EPA, that application is reviewed by staff in the EPA regional office covering that state. While EPA has stated that its objective is to complete the permit review process within two years, review times may vary due to differences in the initial completeness of the application, timing of revisions by the applicant, the public comment process, agency review capacity, and other factors.21
EPA's Class VI permit application review process includes five steps, listed below.22
Once construction and testing are completed and approved, the final phase includes an authorization from EPA to inject. At this point, the operator is permitted to begin injecting CO2.
The technical review is the longest and most complex step in the permitting process. During this step, EPA reviews the detailed siting, construction, operation, injection, and closure information submitted, as well as each of the draft plans required in the application package.
During the review and drafting steps, EPA typically works with the applicant to seek clarification on permit elements and identify additional information required. The permitting authority may issue a formal Request for Additional Information (RAI). Applicants are expected to respond to an RAI within 30 days or provide an alternative timeline for a response.
Once the permit is in place, the permitting authority is responsible for ensuring that the owner or operator continues to meet the permit conditions and requirements. The permitting authority reviews testing, monitoring, and verification data reported by the owner and operator to evaluate compliance and enforce permit conditions in place to prevent endangerment of USDWs. The permitting authority may also conduct on-site inspections to observe well testing and operation, review records, or evaluate procedures being taken to bring the facility into compliance, among other purposes. Potential permit violations that may lead to compliance or enforcement actions from the permitting authority include, among others, a loss of a well's mechanical integrity; failure to follow monitoring, testing, or reporting requirements; or movement of CO2 or formation fluids out of the designated injection zone.
Class VI permit application review processes are subject to the general public participation requirements under SDWA.23 These regulations apply to EPA issuance of UIC permits. They outline minimum requirements for public information, public notice, and public consultation. Public participation activities may include providing notice in the media, holding hearings, responding to public comments, and involving stakeholders.
While the above general public participation requirements exist, EPA has not issued specific regulatory requirements for public participation for the Class VI permit application process. EPA guidance on public participation in Class VI permitting, issued in 2010, anticipated "high levels" of public interest in geologic sequestration.24 The guidance encouraged UIC programs and owners and operators to provide information on Class VI permits early in the process and to involve a broad range of stakeholders.25
In its 2022 report to Congress on Class VI well permitting, EPA identified several stakeholder concerns regarding environmental justice in the permitting process, including concerns about project siting and public involvement. EPA stated that the agency intended to expand the amount of information available to the public about Class VI well permit applications and "explore additional ways in which EPA Class VI permitting can consider the specific needs of any EJ communities located near a proposed Class VI project."26
In August 2023, EPA issued a memorandum and accompanying guidance that outlined expectations for how agency staff should consider environmental justice in permitting and review of state applications for UIC Class VI program authority. EPA rescinded the guidance in August 2026, as part of a larger review of Office of Water guidance documents.27
As of September 2026, EPA had issued at least 23 Class VI individual well permits for injection of CO2, including permits for wells that were never constructed and permits initially issued by EPA and subsequently transferred to state authority.28 Currently, at least 13 EPA-permitted Class VI wells are in operation at 8 projects in California, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, and Kansas.29
In addition to EPA-permitted wells, some states with Class VI permitting authority have issued their own permits. For example, North Dakota has issued at least eight Class VI permits for three facilities for injection of CO2. Wyoming has issued at least three Class VI permits, including the Frontier Carbon Solutions project for a storage hub that would store CO2 from various capture projects.30 Louisiana has issued at least one Class VI permit.31
According to EPA, as of September 2026, Class VI permit applications were pending for 44 projects (including 142 individual wells).32 See Figure 1 for details on EPA permit applications and Class VI well locations.
SDWA authorizes EPA to delegate primary enforcement authority for UIC programs, known as primacy, to individual states.34 EPA grants a state primacy through a federal rulemaking process for one or more classes of wells. To be delegated Class VI program primacy, states must adopt laws and regulations at least as stringent as EPA regulations and must meet other statutory and regulatory requirements. UIC regulations allow states to apply for primacy either for the Class VI program only, or for multiple UIC well programs at once.
If granted primacy for a UIC program, such as a Class VI well program, a state administers the program through enforcement of state laws and regulations in lieu of EPA regulations. The state administers the UIC program and is responsible for day-to-day program responsibilities, including issuing permits and enforcing permit requirements and standards. Under SDWA, EPA retains oversight of states with primacy to ensure that the state programs comply with federal regulatory requirements.
EPA has delegated primacy for Class VI wells to six states: North Dakota (in 2018), Wyoming (2020), Louisiana (2023), West Virginia (2025), Arizona (2025), and Texas (2025).35 In 2025, Louisiana paused all new permit approvals as the state considered various environmental and legal issues, as well as a lack of resources to process the more than 30 applications that were pending in the state.36 In addition, Alaska, Colorado, and Utah are in the process of applying for primacy or revising their underground injection program applications to include Class VI authority.37 See Figure 2 for a map of states that have been granted UIC Class VI program primacy or are in the application process. As Class VI wells require specific types of geologic conditions and underground formations to receive and store injected CO2, some states may not have suitable sites for Class VI wells. These states would not apply for Class VI program primacy.
As directed in Section 1421 of SDWA, EPA has established minimum requirements for state UIC programs. If a state seeks primacy for its UIC program, Section 1422 of SDWA requires the state to submit an application "showing satisfactorily" to EPA that, after reasonable notice and public hearings, the state will implement a program that meets the minimum requirements of Section 1421.
EPA UIC regulations promulgated at 40 C.F.R. Part 145 set out the specific requirements for state programs for permitting, compliance evaluation, enforcement, and information sharing. The regulations set out the process and requirements for state applications to EPA for primacy, as well as the procedures EPA follows in evaluating primacy applications.
Class VI regulations require the state to demonstrate that it has the authorities and processes in place to administer the Class VI program, including
States seeking primacy are required to submit a detailed description of their UIC program that includes information on
A state seeking primacy must submit copies of its UIC statutes and regulations to EPA and must demonstrate that these laws and regulations are at least as stringent as federal UIC requirements.
Other documents required to be included in a primacy application package include
The MOA typically serves as the foundation of the state's specific responsibilities and commitments in administering the UIC program.
Once a state submits a Class VI primacy application, EPA assesses the completeness of the application and evaluates the contents of the application against federal regulatory requirements. Specifically, EPA examines the stringency and equivalency of the state's regulations in protection of USDWs. According to EPA, the agency maintains a goal of completing the review in 30 days.41
In reviewing applications, EPA seeks to ensure that the state's UIC Class VI regulations are at least as strict as federal regulations and that they contain the same necessary requirements for well permitting, construction, operation, recordkeeping, site closure, and other requirements established in federal Class VI regulations. The typical UIC primacy application process involves a series of communications and discussions among state agencies and the relevant EPA regional office during review and evaluation. During the review process, EPA may request additional information or clarification from the state.
Class VI regulations require that, once EPA determines that a new Class VI primacy application is complete, the agency must hold a public hearing announced through notice in the Federal Register and provide information on the availability of the application to the public for review and comment.42
Once the application is approved, EPA promulgates a rulemaking finalizing the decision to award primacy to the state for the UIC program. The regulations require that EPA must approve, disapprove, or approve in part the UIC program through a rule published in the Federal Register.43 The six approved state Class VI primacy rules are available in the Federal Register and codified in 40 C.F.R. Part 147.44
The timing from EPA receiving a complete primacy application package to approval has varied. For example, with the first state to apply, North Dakota, the review process took four years. EPA approved Wyoming's primacy in eight months.45
Once granted primacy, the state is responsible for the day-to-day administration of the program, such as issuing permits, monitoring compliance with state regulations, and leading enforcement actions in the event of violations. Under SDWA, however, EPA retains oversight and enforcement authority over all delegated UIC programs. The MOA between the state and EPA typically includes provisions specifying that EPA will conduct periodic performance evaluations of the state program to ensure that minimum federal requirements are being met.
In recent years, Congress has appropriated funding for EPA to provide grants to states for implementation of new and existing UIC programs, including Class VI programs. For example, for FY2026, Congress appropriated $12.3 million for UIC grants (including all well classes).46 Congress has provided specific funding for Class VI grants—in 2021, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58) directed EPA to establish a specific UIC Class VI grant program for states. Division J of the act provided $50 million in supplemental appropriations to EPA for grants to states that have or are working toward Class VI primacy. States may use these funds for Class VI primacy applications, program revisions, or existing Class VI program implementation activities.47 Twenty-three states and two tribes submitted letters of intent to participate in the grant program. EPA allocated $1.93 million to each of these states and tribes, for a total of $48.25 million.48
UIC regulations at 40 C.F.R. Section 145 establish requirements for public participation in the state primacy application process. During EPA's primacy application review, requirements include public notice of a state's intent to adopt a UIC program, a public comment period, and a public hearing, among other requirements.49 The regulations also require that a state with primacy provides for public participation in the state enforcement process.50
EPA has addressed public participation and environmental justice during the rulemaking process for state UIC Class VI program approval, including for Louisiana and West Virginia. In the final 2024 rule granting Louisiana Class VI primacy, EPA stated that it worked with the state to incorporate the Class VI environmental justice guidance into Louisiana's permitting process and program description, including public participation and environmental justice considerations in environmental review.51 As noted earlier, however, EPA has since rescinded that guidance. Without this guidance, states with Class VI primacy may differ in considering public participation and environmental justice issues not specifically required in regulation when applying for primacy and implementation of Class VI programs. States may choose to go beyond federal minimum requirements.
In the 119th Congress, some Members have demonstrated interest in Class VI permitting and primacy by introducing legislation specific to Class VI programs, providing targeted appropriations to EPA, and discussing Class VI well issues in hearings.52 For example, the Primacy Certainty Act of 2025 (H.R. 4880/S. 2505) would amend SDWA to require EPA to issue a determination on a state's Class VI primacy application within 180 days, among other provisions. More recently, in the Joint Explanatory Statement accompanying the Consolidated Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-74), Division C, Title II, Congress provided $5 million for FY2026 for EPA to "help develop expertise and capacity at the Agency … to expeditiously review and process Class VI permits and primacy applications from States and Tribes."53
As Congress continues debate on Class VI well permitting and state primacy, Members could consider several policy issues related to EPA appropriations, legislation, and oversight. While the issues outlined below focus on policies specifically related to Class VI wells, policy support for CCS project deployment, such as research funding and federal tax credits, are part of broader climate change policy discussions in Congress. For more information on policy considerations for Class VI wells and CCS as a climate change mitigation option, see CRS Report R44902, Carbon Capture and Sequestration (CCS) in the United States.
As discussed earlier in this report, for the past several fiscal years, Congress has supported state UIC well programs through regular annual appropriations to EPA for grants to states to be used for UIC program implementation and for EPA Class VI permit activities. Congress has also provided targeted appropriations for state grants and EPA programs to support Class VI permit and primacy activities. EPA is currently reviewing at least 142 Class VI permit applications. Congress may consider how the level of EPA UIC Class VI program resources aligns with some Members' interest in increasing the number and duration of Class VI permit and primacy approvals, as part of supporting CCS projects generally.
As noted earlier in this report, six states currently have Class VI primacy. In 2023, in response to a request from EPA, 23 states and 2 tribes communicated an intent to pursue Class VI primacy, including four states that have been granted primacy since that time. Some Members argue that EPA would need sufficient staffing and resources at the headquarters and regional office level to manage the significant increase in primacy applications for review. For example, in the Joint Explanatory Statement accompanying P.L. 119-74, the Appropriations Committees noted the need for additional EPA resources and capacity to conduct Class VI permitting and primacy activities.54 Congress also appropriated $1.8 million for FY2026 for Class VI regulation education and training.55
If more states were to be granted primacy, there could be a long-term decrease in the number of Class VI permit applications under federal EPA review as these delegated states took on permitting and enforcement responsibility. One consideration for Congress, however, is potential limits on states that would be able to be granted primacy and thus be able to review and enforce Class VI permits. States differ in their capacity and expertise to administer all the elements of a Class VI program. For example, some states have regulated deep oil and natural-gas-related wells for decades, while other states with smaller numbers or different types of UIC wells have relied on EPA to administer programs. States without experience regulating wells for oil and gas production or complex wells may need additional time and resources to establish state regulations and develop all the program elements needed to administer a state UIC program, or may not develop the capacity to manage the program without EPA assistance. Even some experienced oil and gas states with primacy have faced barriers to implementing Class VI programs. For example, Louisiana, a state with a relatively high number of potential Class VI projects, has been unable to process the large volume of applications and paused permit reviews.56
Another consideration for policymakers involves potential amendments to the 2010 Class VI rule that established specific regulations and standards for Class VI wells and permitting. For example, Congress could consider whether to direct EPA to amend the 2010 Class VI rule based on new information available since it was promulgated. Some stakeholders support EPA promulgating revisions to the rule. They note that the rule has been in place for over a decade and that requirements such as monitoring standards, modeling the area subject to the injection permit requirements, financial assurances, and individual well permits should be revised to reflect more recent technology and conditions.57
In the preamble to the 2010 rule, EPA stated its intention to review the rule every six years.58 In its 2022 report to Congress, however, EPA stated that it would need additional data from more projects before amending the Class VI rule.59 As the first permits for an operating facility were issued in 2017, and injection is expected to continue for approximately 10 years for that facility, no Class VI well project has completed its permit cycle from construction and injection through post-injection site care, which occurs once injection and well closure is complete.
As described earlier in this report, some stakeholders have raised concerns about the environmental and community impacts of carbon capture and sequestration projects in general and with specific Class VI well projects. Congress may consider exploring these concerns, particularly in the context of other policy objectives related to climate change or energy policy.
Although there are a limited number of active Class VI wells permitted by EPA, fluid migration within underground formations near well sites has led EPA to take compliance actions and has increased concern among some local communities. In September 2024, Archer Daniels Midland Company (ADM) paused injection at its Decatur, IL, Class VI well site when fluid migration was detected.60 In 2025, EPA issued an administrative order to ADM for violating the monitoring requirements of a well permit.61 At the site, fluid had migrated into an unauthorized zone of the underground formation, associated with the location and condition of the site monitoring wells.62 The order directs ADM to undertake compliance actions, such as implementing response plans for failure of well integrity, evaluating fluid migration, and reporting and documentation.63 ADM resumed injection in August 2025.64
As discussed earlier in this report, EPA has promulgated regulations on public participation and issued guidance (now rescinded) on consideration of environmental justice in Class VI permitting and primacy processes. In earlier state program primacy application processes, some community groups had raised objections to Class VI projects as well as the UIC public participation process.65 With the rescission of the 2023 Class VI environmental justice guidance and implementation of other Trump Administration policies, the current role of public participation and environmental justice considerations in Class VI well permitting and state programs is less clear. Further, in 2025, President Trump issued multiple executive orders (EOs) that revoked prior environmental-justice-related EOs and changed direction to EPA and other executive branch agencies regarding consideration of environmental justice in agency activities and programs, including elimination of programs focused on environmental justice or diversity, equity, and inclusion.66
Congress could choose to take no action on these issues. Alternatively, Congress could consider oversight actions related to how EPA is implementing relevant public participation regulations and guidance, including actions detailed in the agency's 2022 report to Congress on Class VI permitting. Congress also could consider legislation that would direct EPA to develop programs or regulatory actions related to the public health and environmental concerns expressed by stakeholders or codify actions that had been included in EPA's 2023 environmental justice guidance for Class VI wells.
Other issues associated with Class VI permits and state primacy have been the subject of ongoing legal action that may affect future permitting and primacy decisions, such as the legal standing of environmental groups challenging permit and primacy approvals and whether state liability laws for well owners and operators meet federal minimum Class VI program standards. Analysis of these legal issues is beyond the scope of this report.67
title: Class VI Carbon Sequestration Wells: Permitting and State Program Primacy

HOUSTON – Another 204 people, including 182 illegal aliens have been charged with immigration-and border security-related crimes from Oct. 9-15.

A total of 161 criminal complaints were filed for felony reentry after prior removal, while another 16 people face charges of illegal entry. Most of those illegal aliens have prior felonies such as narcotics, violent crime, immigration crimes, and more. In addition, 22 people have been charged with human smuggling which includes six illegal aliens themselves. The remaining four cases charged this week relate to other immigration crimes and firearms charges.

One of those charged is Enrique Roel Pena-Soto, a Mexican national whom law enforcement allegedly discovered unlawfully in the McAllen area despite his Aug. 22, 2022, removal. According to the criminal complaint, he has a prior conviction for carjacking and possession with the intent to distribute more than 100 kilograms of marijuana. If convicted of illegal reentry, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison.

In addition to the new cases, a Needville resident was sentenced in Corpus Christi to 21 months in federal prison for transporting 10 illegal aliens concealed in a tractor-trailer. Robert Martinez Jr. approached the Border Patrol checkpoint near Sarita, where authorities discovered the illegal aliens hidden in the truck’s sleeping compartments. Two were trapped beneath four others and unable to escape. In imposing the sentence, the court noted the dangerous conditions and Martinez’s prior felony drug convictions.

The cases are referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations, ICE - Enforcement and Removal Operations, Border Patrol, Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, U.S. Marshals Service, as well as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives with additional assistance from state and local law enforcement partners.

The cases are part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigrants, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Under current leadership, public safety and a secure border are the top priorities for the Southern District. Enhanced enforcement both at the border and in the interior of the district have yielded aliens engaged in unlawful activity or with serious criminal histories, including convictions for human trafficking, sexual assault, and violence against children.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas remains one of the busiest in the nation. It represents 43 counties and more than 10 million people covering 44,000 square miles. Assistant U.S. Attorneys from all seven divisions including Houston, Galveston, Victoria, Corpus Christi, Brownsville, McAllen, and Laredo work directly with our law enforcement partners on the federal, state, and local levels to prosecute the suspected offenders of these and other federal crimes.

An indictment or criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law.
title: Southern District border-enforcement efforts continue with 203 more cases filed

Congress has expressed concern about the military threat posed by Russia and China. The Army believes to address this threat, it must be able to operate in a multi-domain (air, land, water, space, cyber, information) environment, requiring new operational concepts, technologies, weapons, and units. The MDTF is the Army's self-described organization centerpiece of this effort. The Army's Chief of Staff Paper #1: Army Multi-Domain Transformation Ready to Win in Competition and Conflict describes the MDTF as "theater-level maneuver elements designed to synchronize precision effects and precision fires in all domains against adversary anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) networks in all domains, enabling joint forces to execute their operational plan (OPLAN)-directed roles."
Figure 1 depicts a generic MDTF.
MDTFs are to be tailored to Combatant Commander requirements, so it is possible the generic MDTF in Figure 1 may contain more, fewer, or other types of units depending on the requirements of its assigned theater of operations.
The Army originally planned to build five MDTFs: two aligned to the Indo-Pacific region; one aligned to Europe; one stationed in the Arctic region and oriented on multiple threats; and a fifth MDTF aligned for global response.
The 1st MDTF was activated on September 16, 2020, and is headquartered at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, WA, and aligned to the U.S. Army Pacific.
On April 13, 2021, the Army announced it would station its 2nd MDTF in Germany. The Germany-based MDTF is to support U.S. Army Europe and Africa. On September 16, 2021, the Army activated the 2nd MDTF at Clay Kaserne in Wiesbaden.
On December 13, 2023, Senator Charles Schumer and Representative Elise Stefanik announced in 2025 Fort Drum, NY, would become the home of 1,495 soldiers and personnel from the 2nd MDTF's Long-Range Fires Battalion (LRFB), Brigade Support Battalion (BSB), and Air Defense (IFPC) Battalion. The 2nd MDTF's Headquarters and Effects Battalions, activated in 2021, would remain in Germany.
The Army activated the 3rd MDTF at Schofield Barracks, HI, in September 2022. The 3rd MDTF is to support the U.S. Army Pacific as a component of U.S. Pacific Command (USPACOM).
On February 27, 2024, the Army released a white paper, Army Force Structure Transformation, outlining plans to transform the force. The white paper noted the Army intended to "complete the build out of the Army's five MDTFSs" and that
Three task forces will be assigned to U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC); one will be assigned to U.S. Army Europe-Africa (USAREUR-AF); and another will be service-retained with a likely focus on the CENTCOM area of responsibility.
According to an April 2024 Defense News article, the Army updated MDTF pre-decisional plans. The Army reportedly plans to consolidate Mid-Range Capability and Long-Range Hypersonic batteries under an LRFB and complete programming of the remaining Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) battalions over the next five years. The Army also plans to convert all brigade support companies to battalions. In terms of specific MDTFs
Reportedly, based on a May 1, 2026, Administration decision to remove 5,000 U.S. troops from Germany:
one full brigade will leave Germany and a long-range fires battalion that was due to be deployed later this year will be cancelled.
While specific units were not identified, the 2nd MDTF's LRFB had previously been designated by the Army as European-aligned.
Reportedly, the Army plans to move "hundreds of multidomain troops from Germany to South Korea within the year," although this was not confirmed by the Pentagon. The report suggests that the 2nd MDTF's MDEB "would join U.S. Forces Korea to strengthen capabilities against North Korea while bolstering deterrence against China."
In January 2026, the Army created Multi Domain Command Europe (MDC-E) by merging the 56th Artillery Command with the 2nd MDTF. According to the Army, MDC-E "plans, integrates, executes, and assesses long-range precision fires and multi-domain effects for U.S. Army Europe and Africa to destroy enemy A2/AD capabilities and disrupt ground forces."
According to U.S. Army Pacific, the 1st MDTF is to merge with the 7th Infantry Division (ID) to form Multi Domain Command Pacific (MDC-PAC). U.S. Army Pacific further noted the following: "The new command merges the 7th Infantry Division's two Stryker infantry brigades with the multidomain fires, cyber, space, electronic warfare and intelligence capabilities developed by the 1st MDTF."
On October 8, 2026, the Army activated the 4th MDTF at Fort Carson, CO. The 4th MDTF, consisting of almost 2,100 soldiers, along with the 1st MDTF "reports to the 7th Infantry Division, designated as the multi-domain operational headquarters."
On October 7, 2026, the Vice Chief of Staff of the Army published How the Army Fights. This new operational warfighting guidance
builds on the Army's multidomain operations doctrine by explaining how the force employs land power at the operational level of war. The guidance aligns how the Army organizes, trains, equips and sustains its formations for contested, high-intensity conflict.
Neither the MDTF's nor MDC's operational or doctrinal roles are specifically discussed in How the Army Fights, except in a hypothetical vignette on pages 32 and 33.

Trump Administration Announces $8 Billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program
(Washington, D.C., October 19, 2026) – Today, President Donald J. Trump, alongside U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins, announced the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) will make $8 billion available for one-time payments to American farmers this harvest season to provide relief during temporary market disruptions and increased input costs.
“President Trump is the most pro-farmer president of my lifetime and he is continuing to put Farmers First every day,” said Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins. “Today, I am proud to announce alongside President Trump more targeted relief is coming to our farmers through the Harvest Fuel Relief program. This $8 billion dollar investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation.”
Similar to the Farmer Bridge Assistance (FBA) program, the Harvest Fuel Relief (HFR) program will provide simple, proportional support to producers using a uniform formula to cover a portion of modeled losses during the 2026 crop year. This national loss average will be based on FSA reported planted acres, Economic Research Service cost of production estimates, and World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates yields and prices.
The $8 billion in payments provided through the Harvest Fuel Relief program are authorized under the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) Charter Act and will be administered by the Farm Service Agency (FSA).
Commodity-specific payment rates for Title I commodities will be released in November. Payment methodology for other eligible commodities will be announced at a later date. Crop insurance linkage will not be required for participation in the Harvest Fuel Relief program; however, USDA strongly urges producers to take advantage of the enhanced risk management tools included in the Working Families Tax Cuts Act to best protect against price risk and volatility in the future.
Producers of non-Title I commodities, including specialty crop growers and fishermen, are encouraged to provide data related to increased fuel costs to HarvestFuel@usda.gov for USDA’s consideration when determining payment rates.
Eligible producers are encouraged to create a Login.gov account in advance of the application period announcement. Pre-filled applications will be available online to producers with a Login.gov account linked to USDA.
The Harvest Fuel Relief program builds upon the Trump administration’s unprecedented support for America’s farmers. Earlier this year, the Farmer Bridge Assistance program delivered $12 billion in one-time bridge payments over 560,000 farmers across the country. Just two weeks ago, nearly $14 billion in gross payments were provided to producers through the Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs through The Working Families Tax Cuts Act – an approximate $8 billion increase over what farmers would have received without the historic bill.
To see more of how the Trump Administration putting farmers first please visit: https://www.usda.gov/farmers-first
###
title: Trump Administration Announces $8 Billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program

The National Labor Relations Board is an independent federal agency that protects the rights of private sector employees to join together, with or without a union, to improve their wages and working conditions.

Federal law gives you the right to form, join or assist a union; choose representatives to bargain with your employer on your behalf; act together with other employees for your benefit and protection; and choose not to engage in any of these protected activities.

The law we enforce gives employees the right to act together to try to improve their pay and working conditions, with or without a union.

The National Labor Relations Act forbids employers from interfering with, restraining, or coercing employees in the exercise of their rights.

OAKLAND, Calif. — With El Niño conditions strengthening ahead of winter, FEMA encourages everyone to take steps now to prepare for possible heavy rain, flooding and other storm impacts.
El Niño can influence seasonal weather patterns, and conditions will vary by location. Everyone should follow National Weather Service forecasts and guidance from their state, territorial, tribal and local officials as storms develop. You can also download the free FEMA App which allows you to receive real-time weather alerts, locate emergency shelters in your area, prepare for common hazards, and more.
“Readiness does not have to happen all at once,” said FEMA Region 9 Regional Administrator Robert J. Fenton. “Start by making a plan with the people in your household, checking your insurance coverage and gathering the things you would need if you had to leave quickly.”
FEMA encourages households to:
- Don’t wait for a storm to review your flood insurance. Most standard homeowners and renters policies do not cover flood damage. Because National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) policies typically have a 30-day waiting period before taking effect, it is vital to secure coverage early. Visit www.floodsmart.gov/policy-quote to get a personalized quote and connect with local providers to purchase your policy.
- Make an evacuation plan. Know where you can stay, how you will get there and how family members will reconnect if separated. Include pets and anyone who needs help evacuating in your plan.
- Prepare a go-bag with medications, chargers, a flashlight, a battery-powered radio and essential supplies. Keep important documents in a waterproof container and secure copies you can access if you leave home.
- Stay informed. Sign up for local alerts and follow instructions from local officials. Never drive or walk through floodwater.
Visit Ready.gov/floods for preparedness tips and FloodSmart.gov to learn about flood insurance.
To download a flyer with more information, visit https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/graphics/fema_r9_el-nino-flyer.jpg.
title: FEMA Region 9 Encourages Households to Prepare Ahead of El Niño Winter Storms

Remarks

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Registan Square

Samarkand, Uzbekistan

October 19, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO: Ready?

QUESTION: Yes. Mr. Secretary —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Hold on one second. Let me say a few words.

QUESTION: Yes, okay. Sorry, sorry.

SECRETARY RUBIO: First of all, I want to thank the Head of the Presidential Administration for joining us here. She’s fantastic. She is an incredible leader and also an incredible spokesperson for the country. We had a chance to interact now numerous times, and thank you. I told you I would come and here I am.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Both in this beautiful spot, the historic – this is for centuries a crossroads of trade and commerce. Global trade and commerce came right through here. And this is why we’re here now because American companies – many of them are joining us here today not just to visit here but also as part of the C5+1 Forum that we think is so important. The United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia, obviously rooted in this country but also all the neighboring countries who want to do more business and trade with us.

We have an incredible delegation, almost 300 American businesses that are here with us, and the opportunity to sign over, when it’s all said and done, billions of dollars of agreements that will both enrich the countries in the region but also benefit the United States economically. So it’s an honor to be here and an honor to be a part of it. Thank you for welcoming us.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Thank you. Thank you very much.

SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m so happy to be with you.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Thank you for choosing Uzbekistan.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Of course.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you for welcoming us and allowing us to see this incredible place.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Yes, thank you very much for being with us here. Thank you. It’s important for us.

SECRETARY RUBIO: It’s an honor.

Okay.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, I was going to ask you about your impressions here, but you just gave them. So it’s an extraordinary place, I have to say. So straight to substance. What does – China is making big inroads in Central Asia, and including in Uzbekistan. What does the U.S. have to offer specifically to the countries of the C5?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, look, it’s competition, right? We have products, we have companies; they make things. And we just want fair competition and an opportunity. There’s no part of the world in which we feel like America and American business should not be – have a fair shot to compete, and that’s what we seek to do.

This is not about coming here to say stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country. That’s not about that. This is about ensuring that in every part of the world that is opening its doors to American business and American commerce that we’re available, that we’re showing up, and that we’re there. And that’s what this is all about.

I mean, if you look at for a long time people have understood the importance of Central Asia, all five countries, Uzbekistan in particular. You see it. You guys have gone through this. This is a beautiful country. It’s incredible what they have achieved in just the last decade in terms of economic growth and prosperity. And we just want to identify opportunities on things we can work together on, and we’re here to do that, and that’s what we want to do. And that’s not a negative action against any other country. That’s just – I mean, countries want to have as many relationships as possible.

Uzbekistan has been clear they want to be friends to everybody. They want to have a relationship with everybody. They want to have economic relations with everybody. And we are saying that we are interested, and that’s why we’ve come here with almost 300 American businesses joining us who are looking forward to seeing what opportunities exist, and in fact some of whom have already done agreements that we’ll be announcing a little later.

HEAD OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION MIRZIYOYEVA: Yeah.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, on that line, the decades of Cold War era restrictions —

SECRETARY RUBIO: The what?

QUESTION: The decades of Cold War era restrictions, Jackson-Vanik is still in place. Why is it not repealed yet?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, you’ll have to ask Congress. We are in favor of repealing it. There are a number of strong voices in Congress that are in favor of repealing it. I was actually asked that during my confirmation hearing in the Senate, and I said that I was in favor of repealing it, and the administration has asked for that to be done. Congress just hasn’t gotten around to it, but we hope that they will.

QUESTION: Secretary, in terms of geopolitics and the part of the world that we’re in, President Vladimir Putin reportedly has proposed a meeting with President Trump.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Saida, did you leave? (Laughter.) She’s left. She’s got to go work. I understand. Okay, sorry.

QUESTION: President Putin of Russia has reportedly, according to The Wall Street Journal , proposed a meeting with President Trump and with Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. Is that something you can comment on at all? Is that accurate or is being discussed?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know. I mean, I think there’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know anything’s been finalized. But the President has been clear he’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end. He wants that war to end. He has said that when he was a candidate. He said it never would have happened if he’d been president at the time, but it did happen. And now we’ve done everything we can and will continue to do everything we can to help facilitate the end of that war.

No one is winning that war. People are dying every day. Things are being blown up every day. Things are being destroyed every day. And he’s talked about it. He’s talked about the death toll. If you listen to the President, he repeatedly cites the 25,000 people a month dying in these wars, the amount of destruction that’s occurred, the amount of economic damage that’s occurring.

So as you have seen, we have engaged repeatedly over the last almost two years now to try to bring about or facilitate an end to this war, and I think the President is open to anything that he can do to help bring the war to an end if it’s possible. And we’ll continue to look for opportunities to do that.

So far, obviously, we haven’t made the kind of progress we would like to have made, but it’s not for lack of trying, and the President remains very committed to it. You saw his post overnight, or overnight our time at some point on the East Coast in the United States, where he once again reiterated why it is that he has done the things he’s done with suspending the sanctions for 60 days. It’s because he wants to see if there’s an opportunity for the talks that are going on right now with both Ukraine and Russia to lead to something positive and avoid another disastrous year of war and conflict.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what evidence do you actually have that President Putin is open to peace talks, to coming to the negotiating table? Because his —

SECRETARY RUBIO: What evidence?

QUESTION: Yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, this is – I mean, I don’t know. This is not a criminal case. I mean, what this is is about diplomacy, and in diplomacy you continue to try. And sometimes, unfortunately, when these conflicts are the kinds that we’re talking about now, these are complicated, they’re entrenched, in some cases a deadlock, sort of a stagnated conflict in which neither side is making clear victories but both sides are inflicting tremendous damage. We’re just going to keep trying to the extent we can to see if we can facilitate an end to it. We’ll keep testing every opportunity that presents itself.

In the end, the evidence will be whether a deal gets done or not, whether both sides are willing to give in order to end this war. But you just have to keep trying to do it. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, but that’s the nature of diplomacy.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, Ukraine says last night —

SECRETARY RUBIO: The what?

QUESTION: Ukraine says it did not receive early warning last night before Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv. Can you please enlighten us what happened there? And as the nation’s top —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I can’t – I don’t – if it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system that I know CENTCOM – sorry, I know that EUCOM had been involved in looking at, and that’s the report they gave us back. I can’t comment on what happened last night.

QUESTION: But as the nation’s top diplomat, Mr. Secretary, are you concerned that Americans diplomats, Americans in Kyiv, also are at risk?

SECRETARY RUBIO: That what?

QUESTION: Americans are also at risk.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we’re concerned about Americans at risk anywhere in the world. We have a diplomatic presence there and we do – we do meetings on a weekly basis in all of our posts, especially those that are in conflict zones, to determine whether or not we can continue to maintain people there. As of now, we’ve not changed our posture or our footprint in Kyiv. We have our presence there, but of course we’re concerned. We’re always concerned about the safety and security of our diplomats and our facilities.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary —

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Go ahead.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, welcome to Uzbekistan, first of all.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you.

QUESTION: How do you assess Uzbekistan’s role in the current developments of Central Asia?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think it’s key and a cornerstone. I mean, it’s the most populous country. And you see the – I mean, we’ve seen – I’ve never been here before. I just arrived. But just the incredible – reading up on the incredible economic development, a growth rate now of GDP of almost 8 percent a year. It’s phenomenal and we want – encourage for that trend to continue.

So I think you have tremendous opportunity here. If you can have another decade like you had in the last decade, I think you’ll be in an incredible place. You already are. And I was stunned by the number of tourists that come – stunned meaning surprised that the numbers were that high. I know I inquired about direct flights from the United States. There’s actually talks underway potentially for a direct flight from Miami. I know that there’s one already from different other places.

So we’re always encouraged coming to places like that and seeing a country that emerged, like all of its neighbors, from the Soviet era to where they are today in such a short period of time and the incredible opportunities they have to really build on that and transform the country in an incredibly positive way. And that’s why we’re here. We just want to be a positive part of it, and that’s why we’ve brought all these businesses with us as well, because they want to be a part of it.

QUESTION: Secretary Rubio, what should people in Uzbekistan expect from this visit and also from the delegation of 200 American companies traveling with you?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think we’ll have some concrete deals to announce, meaning companies that are going to be doing business here that are being welcomed here and that are excited about doing business here. So we’ll have those announcements at the end of the forum. I think that’s very positive for both countries.

And I also think that’s just the foundation that we intend to build on. We want to do more. This is not the end. This is the beginning. And so we’re excited about it. This is a part of the world that frankly has not gotten a tremendous – Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policy makers over the last 20 years that it deserves, but that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now. That’s why we had the meeting with the leaders and the President last year, and that’s why I encourage more congressional delegations to come and visit, and ultimately why I hope to be able to come back as well, and why we wanted to do the C5+1 here in addition to the bilateral visit.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what are the key issues —

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, in terms of the relationship with Ukraine —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Hold on. What?

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what are the key issues of today’s topic with your colleague and when the President of United States is planning to visit Central Asia and especially Uzbekistan?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I can’t comment on the President’s future travel plans. I think – I think we would love to see that happen, and we’ve got to work on that in the year to come and see what dates are possible, because I think he would like to come if he can. He has said so. So obviously – but I’m not – I can’t speak about the presidential schedule.

About today it’s the point that I made earlier, and that is we have a lot of bilateral issues to talk about. But ultimately – because I think like every country in the world – Uzbekistan is concerned and looking at what’s going on in other parts of the world and the impact it’s having economically on the global economy. But there is so much positive going on in our bilateral relationship, and really at the cornerstone of it is, if you think about it, it’s a relationship that’s defined not by challenges, not by conflicts, but by opportunity.

CARLISLE BARRACKS, Pa. — Lt. Gen. Joe E. Hilbert spoke with U.S. Army War College students Oct. 16, 2026, about Eighth Army’s role in supporting U.S. Forces Korea and contributing to deterrence across Northeast Asia.
Hilbert described the region as strategically important because of its geography, security environment and network of allies. He outlined how Eighth Army supports the joint force as an Army operational-level command on the Korean Peninsula.
“We live in a strategic region—strategic because of its geography, our adversaries and our allies,” Hilbert said. “Eighth Army supports U.S. Forces Korea and enables the joint force to deter forward.”
During the visit, Hilbert discussed Eighth Army’s support to the joint force through convergence, strike, close battle and theater sustainment. He also emphasized the importance of integration with U.S., Republic of Korea and regional partners.
The engagement provided U.S. Army War College students an opportunity to learn more about Eighth Army’s mission and its role in maintaining readiness and supporting security on the Korean Peninsula. Hilbert is a 2015 graduate of the U.S. Army War College.
title: Lt. Gen. Hilbert discusses Eighth Army’s role in Northeast Asia

We need actual diplomats working to achieve actual peace."

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. — Modern warfare is now defined by software, where milliseconds in code execution can determine mission success and survivability. To examine how artificial intelligence is transforming software development, the U.S. Army Communications-Electronics Command Army Software & Innovation Center hosted its first technical panel on Sept. 15, 2026.
The event took place at Myer Auditorium and was broadcast to defense networks worldwide. Over 600 virtual and in-person attendees from the APG community participated. The CECOM ASIC APG-Wide Technical Panel “Vibe Coding” focused on how quickly AI-assisted software is being used. Ike Faddis moderated a panel that included experts: Kriss Knopp, High Side Administration, Infrastructure, CECOM ASIC; Tom Cummings, Chief Software Architect for the Chief Automation and Data Integration Office, CADIO, ASA(ALT); Chief Warrant Officer 3 Victor Fernandez III, DevSecOps Lead, U.S. Army AI Integration Center; David Arty, Chief, Data Security Branch, Combat Capabilities Development Command, Command, Control, Computers, Communications, Cyber, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance Center; and Maluki Montgomery, Chief Architect, Software & Support Services, CECOM ASIC. Erin Hayner and Gene Thompson from CECOM ASIC provided panel support.
The panel focused on vibe coding. This industry trend involves giving generative large language models, or LLMs, a high-level mission goal, and the models quickly produce working code. While the term started in commercial tech, the panelists pointed out that the military is now using this approach too.
"We have chosen to focus on this because as we all work and support the warfighter, AI is 100 percent a part of our daily lives," Hayner said in her opening remarks. "It is not just proofreading our emails anymore. For some of us, it is generating code. The question before us is: who should be doing it, what are the guardrails, and how do we harness it for the force?"
The strategic priority behind the technology is tactical lethality and sensor-to-shooter velocity. Historically, military software development has been bound to extensive requirements gathering and protracted contracting cycles that can take months or years to deliver minor field modifications. In contrast, peer adversaries iterate on electronic warfare scripts and digital countermeasures in days. Putting AI-assisted development tools in the hands of Soldiers and defense civilians lets units rapidly script custom solutions — whether automating fires data feeds, writing translation parsers for electronic signals, or developing maintenance tools to keep weapons platforms operational.
To connect fast prototyping with the need for reliable, long-lasting software, Maluki Montgomery shared the "pirate and the architect" idea. He based this on lessons from the Army's AI-Assisted Maintenance project.
"You need the pirate and the architect," Montgomery said. "The pirates are the domain experts, the frontline personnel and maintainers who understand the exact tactical problem, move fast, and rapidly iterate on prototypes. But they must partner with the architect, who steps back to ensure the foundation is scalable, modular, secure, and ready for deployment across the wider enterprise."
Cummings, who helped bring generative models to Army platforms, pointed out that while AI speeds up delivery, it does not replace the need for solid engineering.
"When I have my hands on the tools, I am able to produce hundreds or thousands of lines of production-ready code daily," said Cummings. "It changes the 'make or buy' calculus entirely. But rapid integration does not automatically mean good software. What makes it good is not a given — it takes genuine engineering discipline to make sure what you create is an enduring, sustained capability rather than just a quick fix."
However, the fast pace of AI-generated code brings serious cybersecurity risks. In a discussion with the audience, Arty said, "You cannot just trust that it is giving you the right answer. How are you validating and verifying that the harness is not executing code locally or injecting vulnerabilities?"
Chief Warrant Officer 3 Victor Fernandez III responded to the security concerns by warning that machine-generated scripts are not automatically safe. He mentioned platforms like Caravan and Expedition 0, which use strict rules to keep infrastructure secure.
"You can never delegate understanding," Fernandez said. "AI is good at presenting the illusion of correctness. However, you must always be suspicious of what you are having the model execute on your behalf. Whether using low-code platforms, commercial LLMs, or agent harnesses, blind trust will get you into trouble. Version control tools like Git and automated DevSecOps pipelines are mandatory to audit and roll back changes when things break."
Arty, who reviews both traditional and AI-generated software for network approval, explained the standard for managing operational risks.
"From a cybersecurity perspective, you, the human developer, still own the code at the end of the day," Arty said. "Before you deploy, you have to understand the blast radius if something goes wrong. If you are vibe-coding a basic administrative tool where human eyes verify every output, the blast radius is small. But if you are generating code that directly serves warfighter communications or weapon system functions, the risk is severe. You are responsible for making that assessment up front."
Arty and Fernandez both highlighted that AI-generated software intended for Army networks must pass through the certified Community-Secured DevSecOps pipeline to generate verified software bills of materials and undergo strict static and dynamic application security testing before deployment.
Thompson concluded the event by highlighting how teamwork will shape the Army's future software innovation.
"Our mission today was to promote a collaborative environment, and the depth of the discussions we engaged in has certainly achieved that," Thompson told attendees. "This cooperation does not end here. The recording and session materials will remain available across defense channels for the next 180 days as we continue improving our policies, training pathways, and harness security standards to ensure our developers deliver the most lethal, secure software possible to the warfighter.”
title: Transforming code into combat power: CECOM hosts its first panel on 'Vibe Coding'

INDIANAPOLIS – Residents in Carroll, Cass, Dearborn, Decatur, Delaware, Fayette, Franklin, Hamilton, Hancock, Henry, Lake, LaPorte, Madison, Marion, Morgan, Pike, Porter, Pulaski, Putnam, Randolph, Rush, Tipton, Union and Wayne counties who have been affected by the August 11 – 24, 2026 storms, tornadoes and flooding have less than one week left to apply for FEMA assistance. The application deadline is Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.
Financial assistance is available for eligible survivors who need help covering uninsured costs for things like home repairs, personal property, vehicle damage, medical expenses including accessibility items, moving and storage and reimbursement for temporary housing.
How to apply for FEMA Assistance:
Apply online at DisasterAssistance.gov or call the FEMA Helpline at 800-621-3362. If you use a relay service give FEMA your number for that service.
For video assistance:
What to Expect Before Applying for FEMA Assistance | ASL | Spanish
Next Steps After Applying for FEMA Assistance | ASL | Spanish
To apply for a low-interest disaster loan from the U.S. Small Business Administration Office of Disaster Recovery (SBA) apply online at MySBA Loan Portal or sba.gov/disaster or call the Customer Service Center at 800-659-2955. People who are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability may dial 711 to access telecommunications relay services. For more information or assistance in-person visit Appointment.sba.gov to find a location nearest you. The application deadline to apply for an SBA physical disaster loan is also Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, with a deadline to apply for the SBA economic injury disaster loan on May 25, 2027.
After You Apply, FEMA Help Remains Available
Stay in touch. Let FEMA know of any changes in your circumstances or contact information, including the status of your insurance settlement. Ask FEMA any questions you may have about your recovery, including any unmet needs.
You can create an account on DisasterAssistance.gov where you can submit paperwork and check your status tracker for updates. For in-person assistance visit a support site. To find a location near you visit: on.in.gov/August2026Disaster.
Learn more about the disaster recovery operation in Indiana at www.fema.gov/disaster/4933.
Disaster survivors who feel they have been discriminated against based on race, color, nationality, sex, religion, age, disability, English proficiency, or economic status have the right to file a complaint by contacting FEMA at FEMA-CR-Intake@fema.dhs.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362.
###
FEMA’s mission is helping people before, during, and after disasters.
title: Less than One Week Remains to Apply for FEMA Assistance
