LOS ANGELES – Federal law enforcement throughout California today arrested 11 foreign nationals living in the United States who are charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in U.S. elections, electoral contests in which most of them cast illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots.

Today’s arrests are part of “Operation Protect the Vote” – a coordinated effort among all four California-based United States Attorney’s Offices to combat and root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity.

All 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or “green card” holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not U.S. citizens and are not permitted to vote in U.S. elections.

The criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application and some of the defendants also are charged with fraudulent voter registration. Both charges are felonies that carry a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison.

The defendants arrested today are expected to make their initial appearances this afternoon in U.S. District Court. No pleas will be taken today.

On October 13, the federal government provided a list of these individuals to California to ensure that their vote-by-mail ballots were set aside until these individuals’ citizenship status could be confirmed. California declined to assist the federal government in setting aside their ballots, prompting a lawsuit by the United States that seeks a court order to prevent the unlawful dilution of American citizens’ votes and to uphold the integrity of our elections.

“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today's charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk. California must verify the citizenship of those more than 20,000 registrants before mail-in ballots are counted.”

“Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.”

“Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is committed to protecting the integrity of our nation’s electoral process by investigating allegations of criminal conduct that undermine public confidence in our elections,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Working with our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners, we will continue to pursue those who knowingly violate federal law, while ensuring that every investigation is conducted fairly, thoroughly, and consistent with due process.”

According to court documents, the defendants knowingly and willfully lied under oath in their voter registration applications that they were U.S. citizens to be permitted to vote in California. Their fraudulent voter registration applications were approved, and, in many cases, the defendants illegally voted in recent U.S. elections. They subsequently lied in their paperwork to become naturalized U.S. citizens that they had never claimed U.S. citizenship, nor had they registered to vote or voted in U.S. elections.

Broken down by jurisdiction, the following defendants are charged in today’s takedown:

Central District of California

All the following defendants below in this jurisdiction face felony charges,

including false statements in a naturalization application:

Omar Alexander Muñoz, 72, a Belizean national living in Commerce, fraudulently registered to vote in September 2019, claiming his was a U.S. citizen, then voted in U.S. elections in 2020, twice in 2022, and in 2024. He also lied on his application to become a naturalized U.S. citizen when he falsely stated under oath to have never claimed to be a U.S. citizen.

Amandeep Kaur, 30, an Indian national living in Rancho Palos Verdes and who is seeking to become a U.S. citizen, fraudulently registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 U.S. election.

Ana Domínguez, 60, a Salvadoran national living in Long Beach, fraudulently registered to vote in July 2006 and lied in her naturalization paperwork in March 2026.

Axel Giovani Prera García, 46, a Guatemalan national and Pico Rivera resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2002 and 2005, and lied in his naturalization paperwork in June 2025.

Flavio Alejandro Zúñiga, 43, a Mexico national and La Puente resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2003 and lied in his naturalization paperwork in February 2026.

Butleng Taing, 43, a Cambodian national living in Long Beach, fraudulently registered to vote in July 2021, voted in the 2022 and 2024 U.S. elections, and lied on his naturalization paperwork in August 2025.

Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54, a Honduran national and West Covina resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2012 and 2016, then lied in his naturalization paperwork in September 2018.

Ernest Gutiérrez Ruvalcaba, 57, a Mexican national living in Wilmington, fraudulently registered to vote in February 2024 and voted one month later.

Jesús Narez-Madrigal, 52, a Mexican national living in Carson, fraudulently registered to vote in 2014, voted in the 2024 U.S. general election, and lied in his naturalization paperwork in June 2024.

José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, a Mexican national and West Adams resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2007 and lied on his naturalization paperwork in March 2025.

Muhammad Khan, 50, a Pakistani national and Anaheim resident, submitted a provisional ballot in 2020 and lied on his naturalization paperwork five years later.

Rouzbeh Seyamaknejad, 63, a Canadian national and Rancho Palos Verdes resident, fraudulently registered to vote in December 2018, lied in his naturalization application in January 2024, and voted in the November 2024 U.S. election.

Sulema de León, 35, a Mexican national and Long Beach resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2013, lied on her naturalization application in 2019, and voted in the November 2020 U.S. general election.

Eastern District of California

The following defendants are charged with voting by an alien in a federal election, a misdemeanor that carries a statutory maximum sentence of one year in federal prison:

Maricela Nazarín González, 43, a Mexican national living in Clovis, registered to vote in 2020, indicating that she was a U.S. citizen, and voted in elections in 2022, twice in 2024, and 2025.

Rony de Jesús Sicaja, 38, a Guatemalan national living in Fresno, fraudulently registered to vote in 2017, and voted in the June 2022 primary election and the November 2024 general election in the United States.

Camino Giles Jiménez, 51, a Mexican national living in Kerman, knowingly voted in three U.S. elections despite knowing he is a noncitizen, the most recent election being the June 2026 primary.

Juan Antonio Rivas García, 46, a Mexican national and Sacramento resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2018 and 2020, both times falsely asserting under oath that he was a U.S. citizen. Rivas voted in the 2022 and 2024 U.S. elections.

Giezell Viduya Adawag, 41, a Philippines national and Vacaville resident, fraudulently registered to vote the day of the November 2024 general election, falsely certified that she was a U.S. citizen, and voted in the election that day.

Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, an Indian national living in Sacramento, fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and voted that day. He is charged via information.

Northern District of California

The following defendants are charged with attempted procurement of naturalization contrary to law, false statement under oath in any matter relating to naturalization or citizenship, and voting by an alien:

Verónica Bullene, 43, a.k.a. “Verónica Hernández Martínez,” a Mexican national living in Petaluma, made false statements on her naturalization application that she had never claimed to be a U.S. citizen when, in fact, she did so under penalty of perjury to register to vote in 2022 and 2023 then voted in 2024.

David Shapiro, 41, a Georgian national living in San Jose, fraudulently registered to vote in 2024 and later voted in a U.S. election, and made false statements on his naturalization application that he had never claimed to be a U.S. citizen.

Moe Thida Lwin, 57, a Myanmar national and Daly City resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2024 and then proceeded to illegally vote in a U.S. citizen. She made false statements on her naturalization paperwork as well.

Manakotau Mataele Finau, 61, a Tongan national and Hayward resident, fraudulently registered to vote in the 2024 election then vote, then lied about it in naturalization paperwork.

Maribel del Carmen Garcés Barriga, 62, an Ecuadoran national and San Francisco resident, made false statements in her naturalization paperwork that she never claimed U.S. citizenship and had never voted in a U.S. election or had registered to vote. In fact, Garcés fraudulently registered to vote in 2024 and proceeded to vote in a U.S. election.

Southern District of California

The following defendants are charged with false claim to citizenship to vote, unlawful attempted procurement of naturalization, and false statement under oath in matter relating to naturalization or citizenship:

José Probitsado Amaro, 51, a citizen of the Philippines living in National City, fraudulently registered to vote by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. He then cast a ballot in the November 2024 general election and made false statements during his naturalization interview, denying that he had ever claimed U.S. citizenship and misrepresenting his voting history.

Jennifer Jung, 31, a Canadian national living in San Diego, fraudulently registered to vote by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. She then cast a ballot in the November 2024 general election and made false statements during her naturalization interview, denying that she had ever claimed U.S. citizenship and misrepresenting her voting history.

Erick Ronaldo Soto Mendizábal, 64, a citizen of Guatemala and former Oceanside resident now living in Moreno Valley, fraudulently registered to vote by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. He then cast a ballot in the November 2024 general election and made false statements in his naturalization application, denying that he had ever claimed U.S. citizenship and misrepresenting his voting history.

Pamele Arbués Line, 56, a citizen of the Philippines living in Escondido, registered to vote, cast a ballot in the November 2024 general election, and made false statements in her naturalization interview, denying that she had ever claimed U.S. citizenship and misrepresenting her voting history.

Criminal complaints and informations merely contain allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is investigating these matters in the Central District of California. HSI and the FBI are investigating these matters in the Eastern and Northern Districts of California. HSI, the FBI, and United States Citizenship and Immigration Services are investigating the matters in the Southern District of California.

Assistant United States Attorneys Michael Wheat and Minjae Kim of the Orange County Office are prosecuting the Central District of California cases. Assistant United States Attorneys Kevin Khasigian and Joshua Banister are prosecuting the Eastern District of California cases. Special Assistant United States Attorney Roger Dinh is prosecuting the Northern District of California cases.
title: 11 Foreign Nationals Arrested in California on Federal Charges Alleging They Illegally Registered and Voted in U.S. Elections

Rep. Tlaib introduces bill to restore temporary protected status for Yemen
Rep. Tlaib’s district in Michigan is home to a large Yemeni population
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) introduced a bill to restore temporary protected status for Yemen, which the Trump administration officially terminated in July, following a legal battle. Conditions in countries designated for TPS are too dangerous for people to return safely. Those who qualify for TPS are allowed to remain in the U.S. temporarily.
Yemen is facing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises amid an ongoing civil war and foreign siege and military intervention, including the Trump administration’s bombing of the country last year. The Department of State has placed Yemen under a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory, citing violence, kidnapping, landmines and unexploded ordinances, as well as the re-emergence of diseases like cholera, polio, and measles.
Michigan, especially Rep. Tlaib’s district, is home to large Yemeni communities.
“The Trump administration is threatening our Yemeni neighbors, and I will not stand for it. DHS unjustly terminated temporary protected status for Yemen without care for the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe and escalating armed conflict facing the country,” said Rep. Tlaib. “The Trump administration was bombing civilians in Yemen as recently as last year and is currently trying to give the Saudi monarchy billions of dollars in bombs and jets to continue the devastation. The State Department explicitly warns against any travel to Yemen, and yet, this president wants to send our neighbors back as part of his racist mass deportation agenda. I am proud to represent one of the most Yemeni districts in the country. These are our family members, coworkers, friends, and neighbors. They belong here, and I will not turn my back on them.”
In April, Rep. Tlaib led 23 Members of Congress in urging the Trump administration to halt its planned termination of TPS for Yemen. Conditions in the country have only deteriorated since then.
The Yemen TPS Act is cosponsored by 14 Members of Congress: U.S. Reps. André Carson (IN-07), Jim Costa (CA-21), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Jonathan L. Jackson (IL-01), Henry C. “Hank” Johnson, Jr. (GA-04), Timothy Kennedy (NY-26), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-at large), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), and Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12).
The bill is also endorsed by 50 organizations: Adhikaar For Human Rights and Social Justice, African Communities Together (ACT), American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), Arab America, Arab American Family Support Center, Arab American Heritage Council (AAHC), Arab American Institute (AAI), Arkansas Community Organizations, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund, Center for Constitutional Rights, Center for Gender & Refugee Studies, Center for Nonviolent Solutions, Climate Refugees, Council on American-Islamic Relations, Democratic Progressive Caucus of Florida, Families For Freedom, Flint Alliance for Immigrant Rights, Grantmakers Concerned with Immigrants and Refugees (GCIR), Hindus for Human Rights Action, Houston Immigration Legal Services Collaborative, Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef), Immigration Justice Action Team, Indivisible Mass Coalition, Justice Is Global, Kino Border Initiative, MADRE, Majdal: Arab Community Center of San Diego, Migrant Roots Media, Migrant Support Collective, Muslim Advocates, Muslims for Just Futures, National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum, National Network for Arab American Communities (NNAAC), National Partnership for New Americans, Never Again Action, Nicaraguan American Legal Defense and Education Fund (NALDEF), NM CAFe (Comunidades en Accion y de Fe), No Concentration Camps US, No Detention Centers in Michigan, NorCal Resist, North Shore Sides With Love, Northern Indivisible, Oasis Legal Services, ReThinking Foreign Policy, RootsAction, Syrian Community Network, United We Dream Network, We are CASA, Yemen Relief and Reconstruction Foundation.
title: Rep. Tlaib introduces bill to restore temporary protected status for Yemen

FORT CARSON, Colo. — The Fort Carson Police and Provost Marshal Division (P/PMD) announced Oct. 16. 2026, the launch of the Blue Envelope Program, a new community policing initiative designed to foster safer interactions between first responders and individuals with specific communication or sensory processing needs.
The program is a dedicated resource available exclusively to Department of Defense Common Access Card (CAC) holders and their dependents. It is specifically designed to support individuals with autism spectrum disorder, dementia, anxiety, PTSD and other conditions that may impact verbal communication or social interaction during high-stress encounters.
“Our goal is to ensure every member of the Mountain Post community is treated with the specialized care and patience they deserve,” said Fort Carson Chief of Police Brandon Graber. “By utilizing the Blue Envelope, we can help reduce anxiety and prevent misunderstandings before they begin, creating a safer environment for both the citizen and the responder.”
How the program works
The Blue Envelope Program utilizes a high-visibility identification system to alert responders to an individual's needs before a verbal interaction even begins. Each set consists of three primary components:
- The Blue Envelope: A high-visibility carrier for a driver’s license, vehicle registration and insurance documents. Handing this to an officer during a traffic stop immediately signals the need for specialized communication techniques.
- The information card: A fillable document where individuals can list specific limitations, triggers and emergency contact information to assist responders in providing the best possible care.
- The blue sticker: A decal for vehicle windows or residential entrances to alert first responders to the presence of an individual with specialized needs before they approach the vehicle or home.
Obtaining a Blue Envelope set
The Blue Envelope Program is voluntary, self-managed and confidential. A valid DoD CAC or dependent ID card is required to receive a kit. Eligible individuals may obtain a set through the following methods:
- Provost Marshal Division desk: Sets are available 24/7 at the front desk of Building 2700, 7227 Christy Street. Desk personnel are available to provide the kit and offer instructions on the proper use and placement of materials.
- Patrol distribution: Fort Carson Police officers maintain these kits in their patrol vehicles and are authorized to distribute them to eligible Families during field contacts and calls for service.
“This initiative reinforces the Fort Carson Police Department’s commitment to proactive, inclusive community policing and the safety of the Mountain Post Family,” Graber said.
For more information regarding the Blue Envelope Program, contact the Police/Provost Marshal Division desk at 719-526-6991.
title: PPMD launches Blue Envelope Program to enhance community safety

FORT KNOX, Ky. — For some Veterans, recognition for their service comes decades after they leave the Army. An award earned years earlier may finally be approved, giving the Veteran the recognition they have long deserved.
Helping make those moments possible is Staff Sgt. Yesenia Saldivar, the noncommissioned officer in charge for the Army Human Resources Command Awards and Decorations Branch.
“Having a Veteran recognized for something they did is important to me,” Saldivar said. “I also think it’s important to create memories for the family, especially in situations where the Veteran receives a posthumous award.”
Much of Saldivar’s work happens behind the scenes. She reviews award cases, verifies names and orders medals and certificates. She also coordinates with units and family members to help ensure awards are presented to recipients in a meaningful way.
When an award is approved, Saldivar contacts the Veteran or family member to ask whether they would like a formal presentation. The awards may include the Bronze Star, Purple Heart or Silver Star.
“Her mission-driven focus is perfectly balanced by an unwavering empathy for people,” said Chief Warrant Officer 3 Veronica Fallon, the Awards and Decorations Branch policy chief and Saldivar’s supervisor. “She treats every inquiry as a commitment to a Veteran, retiree or next of kin who sacrificed for their country or loved someone who did.”
Saldivar recently helped coordinate the presentation of the Bronze Star Medal with “V” Device to former Spc. 5 David L. Wright for heroism in connection with ground operations against a hostile force in the Republic of Vietnam in 1970.
Working with Wright’s family and Army unit contacts, Saldivar ensured the presentation was meaningful and memorable for the Veteran. Following the ceremony, the branch received a message commending Saldivar for her assistance.
“She was so responsive and worked hard to ensure that the family had representatives from the Army present for the ceremony,” Fallon said.
Saldivar routinely reaches out to units across the Army and Department of War to help Veterans and their families receive personalized presentations.
“I recently contacted someone at the Pentagon, for example, who was able to assist me with a ceremony at a family member’s request,” she said.
While some of the awards Saldivar works with recognize service from decades ago, including the Vietnam War, others are more recent.
“I think having those memories and ceremony photos is very significant,” she said. “It’s rewarding to be part of coordinating that process. I really enjoy working with Veterans and their families.”
From New York to Kentucky
Saldivar’s desire to help others is rooted in her upbringing.
Born in New York and raised in Queens, she moved to the Bronx when she was 15. She grew up in a blended family with seven siblings, three on her mother’s side and four on her father’s side.
Her close-knit family emphasized helping and supporting one another, values her parents instilled in all their children.
Initially, Saldivar planned to pursue a civilian career. After high school, she earned an associate degree in medical assisting but eventually began considering another path.
“I said, ‘You know what? Let me just explore the whole military thing,’” she said. “I loved to travel, and I felt like I had been stuck in New York my whole life. I wanted to try something new.”
In 2009, Saldivar joined the New York National Guard. She deployed to Guantanamo Bay in 2015. After returning in 2016, she entered the Individual Ready Reserve, but her separation from military life did not last long.
“Five months went by, and I missed going to drill. I missed the camaraderie,” she said.
Saldivar joined the Army Reserve later that year and deployed to Egypt, where she supported postal missions.
“I feel like that deployment was an eye-opener for me,” Saldivar said. “I realized I wanted a full career in the military.”
That realization, combined with a conversation with an Army leader, eventually led Saldivar to accept an assignment at HRC as an Active Guard Reserve Soldier.
“My supervisor at the time, Master Sgt. Xiomara Rosadosantos, really encouraged me to take a position at HRC if the opportunity arose,” Saldivar said. “For the AGR community, there are a lot of great opportunities at HRC that I feel are unique. I’ve learned a lot, even in just one year here, and have really enjoyed my work.”
As she works toward becoming a senior Army leader, Saldivar believes leaders should take time to know the Soldiers with whom they work.
“To establish that human connection and to know my Soldiers and their families, I feel that’s very important,” she said.
She also tries to support Soldiers as they pursue their own goals.
“I always try to cheer them on and be supportive when they are going to school or achieve something with their career,” she said. “I like to encourage them to learn new things and take advantage of new experiences that might come their way.”
That emphasis on supporting others stems from Saldivar’s own family values.
Her mother has supported her throughout her military service, including during periods when Saldivar was both at home and away from New York.
“My mom’s support has always been a constant for me, despite the distance,” she said.
The two remain close, and Saldivar calls her mother regularly.
“When I don’t call her, she’s like, ‘OK, why haven’t you called me?’” Saldivar said with a laugh.
Focus on the Future
Saldivar’s time at HRC has given her a closer look at one part of the Army’s human resources enterprise, and she hopes to continue expanding her experience in Army HR.
“I would love to work for a higher headquarters one day,” she said. “I also have the goal of being stationed somewhere in Europe so my fiancé and I can experience living in a different country.”
For now, Saldivar remains committed to her work in the Awards and Decorations Branch and to helping Veterans and their families preserve lasting memories of military service.
“I love working with Soldiers, and now I’m working with Veterans,” she said. “I hope the ceremonies and awards presentations we coordinate are something that Veterans and their families can value all their lives.”
title: Honoring their service: Soldier helps veterans receive overdue recognition

text:
Wild Horses in Peril: BLM’s Delayed Emergency Operations Begin on Riddle Mountain
Organization:
Media Contact:
BURNS, Ore.—The Bureau of Land Management plans to begin an emergency operation tomorrow, Oct. 20, to rescue up to 140 wild horses from the Riddle Mountain Herd Management Area in southeast Oregon. BLM originally intended to gather a larger number of horses due to the Bald Mountain Wildfire, which burned almost half of the area, severely depleting forage for the winter and threatening the herd’s health and survival.
“Our priority is to protect as many of these horses as we’re allowed,” said Don Rotell, Burns District Manager. “We need to act before late fall rain limits access.”
The original plan to rescue horses was delayed last month by a temporary restraining order. The United States District Court for the District of Oregon issued a preliminary injunction last week preventing the BLM from conducting the full gather as planned. However, the court is allowing the BLM to rescue approximately one-third of the horses, leaving 278 on the landscape, as specified in the injunction.
The Bald Mountain Fire burned across the Riddle Mountain Herd Management Area, and the BLM estimates that about half of the herd management area lost forage due to the fire. These losses compounded already existing shortages caused by ongoing drought.
Gathering roughly one third of the horses from the affected area will support the post-fire emergency stabilization and rehabilitation efforts by relieving some grazing pressure on the fragile landscape. While this is a step in the right direction, BLM plans to continue its efforts to protect the herd and sustain other uses by ensuring that the number of wild horses on the range aligns with the amount of forage available. BLM managers have also worked with the permittee to pause cattle grazing in the area to allow the land to recover. Severe wildfire can destroy vegetation and alter soil structure, leaving the landscape vulnerable to erosion and invasive plants. Resting the burned rangeland allows newly planted grasses to take root, facilitating ecosystem recovery so it can continue to provide habitat for wild horses and other wildlife, as well as support additional land uses, into the future.
Media and the public may observe operations, as long as observation does not disrupt operations or jeopardize the safety of the animals or staff. BLM staff will escort participants to observation sites on public lands. Observation is available by reservation only and is limited to 10–15 people per viewing day. More information on how to make a reservation is available on the 2026 Riddle Mountain Emergency Wild Horse Gather webpage.
The BLM will transport the rescued horses to off-range holding facilities, where they will receive veterinary evaluations, appropriate care, high-quality feed, and continuous access to fresh water. The facilities provide ample space that meets established agency standards. Once they have been evaluated and are ready, some of the horses may be available for adoption through the BLM Online Corral. The BLM will post updates on the operation’s progress, public viewing opportunities and adoption opportunities on the 2026 Riddle Mountain gather webpage.
VIDEO: BLM video of the herd traveling through the scorched rangeland is available on YouTube.
The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.
title: Wild Horses in Peril: BLM’s Delayed Emergency Operations Begin on Riddle Mountain

WASHINGTON, DC — This month, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Chemical Safety Board Accountability Act, to ensure open board seats on the U.S. Chemical Safety Board (CSB) are filled in a timely manner by qualified candidates who have experience working in mills or other trades settings. The CSB is an independent watchdog tasked with investigating chemical incidents, including the incident at Nippon Dynawave Packaging Company in Longview that killed 11 men, and making recommendations for safety improvements. 
The Clean Air Act (CAA) states that the CSB’s governing body shall consist of five members, including a chairperson nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Currently, the board only has two members, and there is no indication of a plan to fill the empty seats. With two board members, the CSB can continue to carry out its statutory responsibilities, but a reduction to a single member could constrain the board’s ability to fulfill its mission.  Under the CAA, there is no mechanism requiring empty board seats be filled and new board members are only required to be “technically and professionally qualified.” The bill introduced by Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez would amend the CAA to ensure board seats are filled quickly and by members with real experience working in the trades.
Specifically, this legislation would:
- Amend the CAA to ensure that at least one Board member of the Chemical Safety Board has substantial experience in the trades.
- Require that the President must fill vacancies within 90 days if a vacancy arises or a term expires.
- Ensure that if the President fails to nominate someone within 90 days, they must submit a report to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works that includes the reasons why the President did not submit a nomination and a plan to submit a nomination within the next 90 days. They must repeat this until they submit a nomination.
“When it comes to worker safety, we need a system that prioritizes people with actual skin in the game. Lab conditions aren’t mill conditions and ensuring that people investigating incidents and making recommendations on rules changes have real experience in the trades will help increase confidence in findings and usefulness of the recommendations,” said Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez. “Since coming to Congress, ensuring working people have a seat at the table when rules are made has been a priority for me–and this is a step in the right direction.”
“Workers deserve a voice in the decisions that affect their safety, including the investigations that follow when something goes terribly wrong. People who have operated and maintained these facilities bring firsthand knowledge of the equipment, working conditions, and warning signs that must inform both an investigation and the recommendations that come out of it,” said Josh Estes, spokesperson for the Association of Western Pulp and Paper Workers. “The loss of 11 men at Nippon Dynawave makes this responsibility deeply personal for our union. We support Congresswoman Gluesenkamp Perez’s proposal to embed practical trades experience in the Chemical Safety Board’s leadership and ensure vacancies receive timely action. Families deserve answers, and workers deserve a fully functioning, independent board equipped to turn those answers into changes that save lives.”
Through her work on the House Appropriations Committee, Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez has fought to ensure that the CSB has the resources needed to perform their oversight and investigative work. In a major win this June, she was able to secure full funding for the CSB after the President’s budget proposed defunding the Board completely. In August of this year, the CSB released a report with initial findings on the Nippon Dynawave incident. In a statement that week, the Congresswoman highlighted the significant value of the Board and the dire need to ensure seats are filled with experienced trades workers.
####
title: Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez Introduces Legislation to Require Trades Experience on Board Investigating Nippon Dynawave Incident

Mathew Christopher Jacoby , 58, of Cheyenne, was sentenced on October 15, 2026, by U.S. District Judge Scott W. Skavdahl to 100 months in federal prison followed by 4 years of supervised release for possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine. According to court documents, a Wyoming Highway Patrol Trooper pulled over Jacoby's silver Saab for driving 95 mph in a 75 mph zone. During the roadside investigation, the trooper noticed a suspicious, cylindrical package protruding from under Jacoby’s right hip. When questioned, Jacoby insisted the object was simply a burrito. The trooper deployed a narcotics detection K-9, which gave a positive alert on the vehicle. A subsequent search revealed the concealed package contained 446 grams of methamphetamine, rather than food. Troopers also seized 14 grams of cocaine from the vehicle. The crime was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jesse Naiman following a joint investigation by the Wyoming Highway Patrol and the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation. Case No. 26-CR-00055.

Michael Scott Hopper , 59, of Nevada, was sentenced to 30 months’ imprisonment with three years of supervised release for being a felon in possession of firearms. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives investigated the case with substantial assistance from the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation and the Wyoming Highway Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy W. Gist prosecuted the case. Michael Scott Hopper was indicted May 20 and pleaded guilty July 15. U.S. District Judge Alan B. Johnson imposed the sentence Sept. 18 in Cheyenne under Case No. 26-CR-00050-ABJ.

Le’Andray Steven Thompson , 33, of Phoenix, was sentenced to 27 months in prison and 3 years of supervised release for Bank Fraud. He was also ordered to pay $160,248.54 in restitution. Chief U.S. District Judge Kelly H. Rankin imposed the sentence on Oct. 7, 2026. According to court documents, on Jan. 9, 2023, Thompson traveled with others from Arizona to Wyoming where he opened a fictitious bank account at a financial institution in Casper, Wyoming, and falsely endorsed and deposited a stolen check into the account. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service in Fort Wayne, Indiana investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Margaret Vierbuchen of the District of Wyoming prosecuted the crime, with assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Dawn Ransom of the Northern District of Indiana. Case No. 26-CR-00073.

Dennison Jay Antelope , 35, of Riverton, was sentenced Tuesday to 21 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release for being a felon in possession of a firearm. According to court records, a Wyoming Highway Patrol trooper initiated a traffic stop on a white Chevrolet S-10 pickup truck with an expired registration at about 10:43 p.m. Jan. 11. The vehicle was traveling south on North Smith Road outside Riverton. Antelope, who was riding as a passenger, was found to have an outstanding Fremont County arrest warrant. A subsequent search of the vehicle uncovered drug paraphernalia in the driver's seat, a marijuana pipe on the floorboard where Antelope had been sitting, and a black Taurus 9mm pistol in a back-seat laundry basket located between the front seats. Antelope stated he’d found the firearm and was intending to sell it. Antelope is prohibited from possessing firearms due to a 2020 felony conviction for strangulation. The case was investigated by the Wyoming Highway Patrol, the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy W. Gist prosecuted the case, and U.S. District Court Judge Alan B. Johnson imposed the sentence in Cheyenne. Case No. 26-00054.

The United States Attorney’s Office is responsible for representing the federal government in virtually all litigation involving the United States in the District of Wyoming, including all criminal prosecutions for violations of federal law, civil lawsuits brought by or against the government, and actions to collect judgments and restitution on behalf of victims and taxpayers. The Office is involved in several programs designed to make our communities safer. They include:

Operation Take Back America is a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. It also streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN).

White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section plays a unique and essential role in the Department's fight against sophisticated economic crime and other forms of complex misconduct that endanger public health and safety. The Section investigates and prosecutes these complex cases throughout the country.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) program that unites federal, state, local, and Tribal law enforcement with community leaders to target and reduce violent crime, with a primary focus on gun violence and gang activity.

Victim Witness Program for the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Wyoming is dedicated to ensuring victims of federal crimes and their family members are treated with compassion, fairness, and respect.

TOLEDO, Ohio – A Texas man has been sentenced to federal prison for his role in sexually abusing minors in Ohio.

Christopher Hagerman, 50, of McDade, Texas, has been sentenced to 360 months (30 years) in prison by U.S. District Judge Jeffrey J. Helmick, after pleading guilty in June to:

• Conspiracy to Produce Child Pornography • Sexual Exploitation of a Minor

Hagerman was also ordered to serve lifetime supervised release after imprisonment and pay $5,000 toward the Justice for Victims of Trafficking Act, which was established in 2015 to provide justice for victims of trafficking.

Two co-defendants were previously sentenced for their roles in the abuse: Chaz Jacob, 36, of Toledo, and Hagerman’s wife Amy Fountain, 51, also of McDade, Texas. Jacob was sentenced to 420 months (35 years) in prison for Conspiracy to Produce Child Pornography, two counts of Sexual Exploitation of a Minor, and Receipt and Distribution of Child Pornography. He was also ordered to serve a lifetime of supervised release and pay a combined $75,000 in restitution to 25 victims.

Fountain was sentenced to 262 months (21.83 years) in prison for Conspiracy to Produce Child Pornography and Sexual Exploitation of a Minor. She was ordered to serve three years of supervised release after imprisonment.

According to court documents, federal agents were investigating the suspected sexual abuse of a minor victim in Toledo and Jacob was subsequently identified. During a search warrant executed at his residence, several of his electronic devices were seized. Forensic analysis of these electronic devices revealed videos that Jacob recorded of himself while he sexually abused several minors. Other videos found on the devices depicted Hagerman and his wife sexually abusing two minors under the age of 12 at Jacob’s residence.

The investigation leading to the indictment was led by Homeland Security Investigations and the Ohio Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force.

Assistant United States Attorneys Sara Al-Sorghali and Frank Spryszak led the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. The initiative is led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, visit justice.gov/PSC .

To report child exploitation, please visit cybertipline.org , or call 1-800-843-5678, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
title: Texas Man Sentenced to 30 Years in Prison for Sexually Abusing and Exploiting Children

Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud
CLEVELAND — U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services assisted with the investigation that resulted in charges against Jingming Chen, 31 of Quincy, Massachusetts, for conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and immigration document fraud. A federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Chen for his role in a conspiracy where he allegedly agreed to be paid to enter into a sham marriage so that a co-conspirator could illegally obtain lawful permanent resident status, commonly known as a Green Card. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio made the announcement.
According to court documents, Chen, a U.S. citizen, was paid by a Chinese alien co-conspirator residing in Aurora, Ohio, to enter into a sham marriage and commit immigration document fraud by fabricating evidence intended to support the false claim that their marriage was legitimate.
Chen and the co-conspirator submitted false statements to USCIS to obtain a Green Card and other immigration benefits for the co-conspirator. Chen allegedly agreed to receive partial payment at each step of the Green Card process. Chen and the co-conspirator discussed creating a false account of an online romance and long-distance relationship, including how they met and who introduced them. They also discussed obtaining a prenuptial agreement and opening joint accounts for banking, cellular service, insurance, and a discount store membership.
Chen and the co-conspirator filed a notice of intention of marriage in Quincy, and Chen directed the co-conspirator to buy a cheap, fake diamond ring to use for the wedding ceremony. After they married, Chen directed a preparer to submit a Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative, to document Chen’s claimed marital relationship with the alien. This would pave the way for the co-conspirator to obtain a Green Card.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations in Cleveland and the USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate in Boston conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian M. McDonough is leading the prosecution.
If convicted, the defendant faces up to five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
An indictment is merely an allegation. A defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
To report suspected immigration benefit fraud or abuse to USCIS, please use the USCIS Tip Form.
For more information on USCIS and its programs, please visit uscis.gov or follow us on X, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.
title: Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud

Trump Administration Announces More Than $16 Million for Rural Healthcare Workforce Training and Retention Across Maryland
This federal investment will prepare Marylanders for healthcare careers and help rural communities recruit and retain nurses, physicians, dentists, and other providers
Today, the Trump Administration announced $16.4 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to address critical healthcare workforce shortages and improve access to care. This investment will support projects ready for rapid deployment that train new healthcare workers, expand apprenticeships, and help rural communities recruit and retain skilled professionals across Maryland.
This $16.4 million investment will train Marylanders for healthcare jobs, expand registered apprenticeships, and reduce financial barriers to training and certification. Funding will also help rural communities recruit and retain nurses, physician assistants, physicians, dentists, and other healthcare professionals. Additional investments will help current workers build skills, prepare middle and high school students for healthcare careers, and train dental assistants with support for tuition, transportation, and uniforms.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is expanding access to quality healthcare, regardless of a patient’s zip code, and equipping rural health systems with the workforce and infrastructure needed to deliver timely care. This funding will make critical investments to strengthen rural healthcare, expand access to lifesaving services, and bring modern technology to communities across Maryland.
“President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”
“President Trump made a historic commitment to rural America, and these investments are turning that commitment into better care for patients in communities across Maryland,” said Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “This is what rural health transformation should look like: federal investment that is putting patients first, driving lasting improvements and expanding healthcare for the hardworking Americans who call these communities home.”
Today’s investment was made possible through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act — passed by Republicans in Congress and unanimously opposed by Democrats — delivering a historic $50 billion investment to help states transform the way healthcare is delivered in America.
“As the sole member of the Maryland delegation to vote to create the Rural Health Transformation Program, I applaud CMS for investing $16.4 million to strengthen Maryland’s rural healthcare workforce. For patients in Maryland’s First District, recruiting and keeping doctors and nurses means more than filling vacancies—it means having someone nearby to turn to for care. This funding will help rural Maryland recruit those providers and train the next generation of healthcare professionals,” said Rep. Andy Harris.
Today’s announcement is one part of the larger overall funding amount awarded to Maryland for fiscal year 2026.
Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:
- Building the rural healthcare workforce: Supporting recruitment, training, and retention strategies to strengthen the pipeline of healthcare professionals serving rural communities.
- Strengthening rural facilities and access: Supporting partnerships, operational improvements, and care-delivery changes that help rural providers maintain essential services and improve access.
- Advancing innovative care and payment models: Supporting new approaches to delivery and financing designed to improve quality, strengthen primary care, and support sustainable rural healthcare.
- Expanding community-based and preventive care: Investing in school-based care, mobile services, and other community strategies that improve prevention, address chronic disease, and expand access to care.
- Modernizing rural healthcare technology: Expanding remote care and data-driven tools to improve coordination and extend healthcare services to rural communities.
The Trump Administration is delivering on its commitment to strengthen rural America by investing in solutions that modernize technology to promote health and well-being for rural communities. Led by CMS, the RHTP is moving beyond the failed one-size-fits-all approach and giving rural communities the tools to build stronger, more innovative, and more sustainable health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes for the Americans they serve.
For more information about the RHTP, visit: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health.

title: Trump Administration Announces More Than $16 Million for Rural Healthcare Workforce Training and Retention Across Maryland

Illegal Alien Admits to Illegally Voting in Federal Election in New Jersey
An illegal alien from Jamaica admitted to illegally voting in a federal election, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer for the District of New Jersey announced today.
Gaye Tyndale-Simpson, an illegal alien from Jamaica, pleaded guilty to one count of voting by an alien in a federal election before U.S. Magistrate Rukhsanah L. Singh in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey.
According to documents filed in the case and statements made in court, Tyndale-Simpson, 55, is a citizen of Jamaica and has never been a citizen of the United States. In November 2024, Tyndale-Simpson voted in the general election that was held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of the President.
The voting by an alien charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 6 months in prison and a $100,000 fine. Sentencing is scheduled before Judge Singh on Feb. 24, 2027.
U.S. Attorney Frazer credited special agents of the FBI, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy, Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Michael McCarthy, U.S. Department of State, Diplomatic Security Service, New York Field Office, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Brian Wood, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, with the investigation.
This case was brought under the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Election Integrity Task Force, a coalition of federal law enforcement partners focused on preserving and protecting the integrity of elections conducted in the District of New Jersey.
The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin D. Bleiberg of the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Criminal Division.
title: Illegal Alien Admits to Illegally Voting in Federal Election in New Jersey

OAKLAND, Calif. – The FEMA Region 9 Regional Administrator has authorized the use of federal funds to assist the State of California in combating the Norte Fire burning in Orange County.
On October 16, the State of California submitted a request for a Fire Management Assistance Grant (FMAG) for the Norte Fire. At the time of the request, the fire was threatening approximately 4,000 homes in and around San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano. The fire began on October 16 and had already burned more than 465 acres at the time of the request.
FMAGs provide federal funding for up to 75 percent of eligible firefighting costs. FMAGs are approved through FEMA to assist in fighting fires that threaten to become major disasters.
Eligible costs covered by FMAGs can include expenses for field camps, equipment use, materials, supplies and mobilization, and demobilization activities attributed to fighting the fire. For more information on FMAGs, visit fema.gov/assistance/public/fire-management-assistance.
title: FEMA Approves Fire Management Assistance Grant for Norte Fire in Orange County

Media Note

Office of the Spokesman

October 19, 2026

The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan on the occasion of the C5+1 Ministerial in Samarkand.

Begin Text

We, the Foreign Ministers of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, and the United States Secretary of State, on the occasion of the October 19, 2026, C5+1 Ministerial in Samarkand, share a vision for enduring U.S.-Central Asian partnership.

We envision the United States and Central Asia as enduring partners of choice.

More than ten years ago, the first C5+1 Ministerial took place, marking an important step in the development of a diplomatic platform grounded in our shared respect for the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of all nations.

This year, as Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan celebrate 35 years of independence, and the United States commemorates a remarkable 250 years of independence, we are looking forward to many more generations of enduring partnership.

As C5+1 governments affirm the importance of friendship among sovereign nations, we honor our countries’ historical contributions, seize opportunities of the present, and strive for a more peaceful and prosperous future for the citizens of each of our nations. We look forward to nurturing the peaceful resolutions of disputes, leading to ever-strengthening dialogue and cooperation among our countries.

We envision ever-strengthening connections between the United States and Central Asia.

It is here, at the crossroads of connectivity, where we reflect on the historic connections that bind the United States and Central Asia and find innovative ways to strengthen them. Where distance once limited our citizens’ dreams to experience each other’s remarkable destinations, we are creating new and modern transportation links. Along the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, we are strengthening mutually beneficial partnerships and investing in infrastructure to smooth the way. We are forging digital connections and community, including through English language training and education, for the purpose of bridging geographical divides and bringing the people of C5+1 countries ever closer together.

We envision a Central Asia central to the global economy.

We will strive for a Central Asia that returns to the center of the global economy. Our shared efforts to further develop the Trans-Caspian Trade Route will catalyze unprecedented two-way trade and investment between Central Asia and the United States and unlock opportunities in high-growth markets.

As we support greater regional economic integration in Central Asia, including through the expansion of intraregional trade, improved transport connectivity, harmonized customs procedures, and stronger industrial cooperation, we are creating a competitive regional market connected with the United States.

A thriving B5+1 platform will continue to create new mutually beneficial commercial opportunities for American companies operating in Central Asia. At the same time, our governments envision expanded opportunities for Central Asian enterprises to invest in, and operate within, the U.S. market. By leveraging secure and trusted technology, American technological excellence, and the growing technology sectors of Central Asia, we seek to foster a region where e-commerce flourishes, innovative solutions abound, and talented entrepreneurs thrive.

We envision cooperation that energizes the future.

We recognize that strengthening U.S.-Central Asian energy cooperation will galvanize efforts to develop integrated, high-value supply chains that yield sustained economic growth and energy resilience. Each of our countries has a unique collection of untapped natural resources; we will combine our strengths to be a collective, powerful driver of regional energy sector development. Data is gold; as such, we intend to exchange expertise and best practices on managing geological data. We envision expanded opportunities for mineral extraction and processing that maximize benefits for our respective countries. We also envision Central Asia realizing its export potential by developing innovative ways to increase value-added products within the region and creating pathways to introduce these products to the international market.

We envision a secure future for all C5+1 countries.

The people of the United States and Central Asia will benefit from strengthened C5+1 security cooperation. Our governments will place particular importance on countering terrorism and transnational organized crime and enhancing border security. Our efforts will strengthen security, including through cooperation to counter illegal immigration, human trafficking, illicit drug trafficking, and arms trafficking. In turn, our cooperation will strengthen customs and trade facilitation, thereby enabling economic growth that benefits all C5+1 countries. A modern approach that focuses on mitigating threats of the digital era, including through enhanced C5+1 cyber security cooperation, will strengthen our ability to successfully counter cyber threats and cybercrime.

We welcome the longstanding cooperation between the United States and the countries of Central Asia in securing nuclear materials and recognize joint contributions to strengthening nuclear security expertise and capacity in the region. Building on the Central Asian Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone, we will deepen practical cooperation on nuclear security, safeguards, the physical protection of nuclear material, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

We envision a future that honors the past.

As we seize opportunities within cutting edge industries of the modern era, we reaffirm our commitment to preserve the rich cultural legacies of all C5+1 countries.

As we recall the remarkable contributions our peoples have made throughout history, we intend to create new avenues for cultural heritage cooperation and strategic connections among our populations. We will pursue greater cooperation between law enforcement and cultural institutions to promote and protect the unique histories of C5+1 countries. Together, we seek to expand professional, cultural, and educational exchanges; capitalize on new technologies to preserve and protect antiquities; integrate cultural heritage protection with law enforcement efforts; and professionalize a talented workforce ready to lead on the global stage.

As we enhance our business ties in cultural sectors such as tourism and the creative economy, we will create the jobs of the future while we embrace the past. With the lessons from our collective experience, we will forge a more prosperous future together.

We envision C5+1 cooperation that continues to deliver regional solutions to global challenges.

End Text

Tags
title: C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future

Press Statement

Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Spokesman Office of the Spokesman

October 19, 2026

Today, the Department of State is sanctioning five entities connected to People’s Republic of China national Linwei Ding under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA) in connection with theft of trade secrets from U.S. persons. The United States has long been a leader in developing emerging technology. This theft of trade secrets is a serious threat to U.S. economic, foreign policy, and national security interests.

Today’s designations follow an investigation of Ding by the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation. On January 29, 2026, a U.S. federal jury convicted Ding of seven counts of theft of trade secrets. Ding was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information containing Google’s trade secrets related to super intelligence (SI) technology to benefit himself and China-based tech companies.

Theft of trade secrets related to sensitive and emerging technologies harms U.S. jobs, companies, and investments, and costs U.S. industry billions of dollars each year. The Trump Administration remains committed to protecting American innovation and safeguarding Americans from intellectual property theft.

Today’s action is being taken pursuant to the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (50 U.S.C. 1709). For more information on today’s action, please see the Department of State’s Fact Sheet .

FBI Detroit Announces Michigan Results of Operation Summer Heat 2.0
The FBI Detroit Field Office and its law enforcement partners announced Michigan results from Operation Summer Heat 2.0, a four-month nationwide initiative focused on combating violent crime, apprehending fugitives, disrupting criminal organizations, and identifying and locating child victims.
From June 1 through September 20, 2026, all 56 FBI field offices worked with law enforcement partners to focus investigative resources on violent crime and public safety. According to the FBI’s national announcement, the operation produced the following results nationwide:
- 8,927 arrests, including more than 5,900 under the FBI’s violent crime and gang program
- 5,013 illegally possessed weapons recovered
- 687 kilograms of fentanyl seized
- 27,512 kilograms of cocaine seized
- 1,410 child victims identified or located
In Michigan, FBI Detroit reported the following results during the initiative:
- 177 arrests
- 66 weapons recovered
- 77.2 kilograms of drugs seized
- 21 children located
"Our partnerships across Michigan are vital to reducing violent crime and keeping communities safe. Through the coordinated efforts of our FBI personnel and law enforcement partners, Operation Summer Heat 2.0 resulted in 177 arrests, 66 weapons recovered, more than 77 kilograms of drugs seized, and 21 children located," said Jennifer Runyan, special agent in charge of the FBI Detroit Field Office. "These results demonstrate what we can accomplish when local, state, federal, and international partners work together toward a shared mission. While this operation has concluded, our commitment to protecting Michigan families, holding violent offenders accountable, and safeguarding communities across our state continues."
The initiative brought together FBI agents, intelligence analysts, task force officers, and law enforcement partners to execute federal warrants, investigate violent offenders and criminal networks, and locate vulnerable children. FBI Detroit’s work to combat violent crime continues beyond the conclusion of the nationwide operation. Anyone with information about violent criminal activity can contact local law enforcement or submit a tip to the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324) or tips.fbi.gov. For more information on the nationwide results, visit: https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/fbi-operation-summer-heat-20-nets-thousands-of-violent-crime-arrests
An accompanying graphic summarizes FBI Detroit’s Michigan results.

OPM Finalizes Rule Removing Governmentwide Time-in-Grade Barrier to Promotions
Qualified employees can be considered for covered promotions without first completing 52 weeks at a lower grade; agencies retain authority to set job-related requirements
WASHINGTON, DC – The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has finalized a rule removing the governmentwide time-in-grade restriction for advancement to covered competitive-service General Schedule positions at GS-6 and above. The restriction generally required employees to spend 52 weeks at a lower grade before they could be considered for promotion, even if they met the qualifications for higher-level work.
“The old rule made the calendar a gatekeeper. If someone is qualified and ready to take on more responsibility, the government shouldn’t make them wait another year just because the clock says so,” said OPM Director Scott Kupor. “This rule allows agencies to reward demonstrated merit over tenure. Employees still have to meet the standards for the job, and promotions still have to follow merit procedures.”
The final rule removes the time-in-grade restriction from OPM regulations. It does not guarantee a promotion, waive qualification standards, or change the competitive procedures agencies use to evaluate and select candidates. Agencies may continue to establish job-related promotion prerequisites, including a period of service in grade, through their written merit-promotion plans, provided those requirements are consistently applied.
The rule takes effect January 14, 2027. It also makes related changes to regulations governing student appointments, training, and other personnel matters.
OPM said eliminating the governmentwide waiting period supports its effort to make federal service more competitive for early-career talent. The agency’s Early Careers Initiative and U.S. Tech Force recruit emerging talent for public-service careers.
title: OPM Finalizes Rule Removing Governmentwide Time-in-Grade Barrier to Promotions

Coast Guard rescues 4 people from capsized vessel near Boot Key Harbor
Southeast Public Affairs - Southeastpublicaffairs@uscg.mil
MIAMI — A U.S. Coast Guard Station Marathon boat crew rescued four people, Sunday, after their 26-foot catamaran capsized approximately 5 miles south of Boot Key Harbor.
No injuries or pollution concerns were reported.
Coast Guard Sector Key West watchstanders received a mayday call on VHF-FM Channel 16 and coordinated response efforts. The Station Marathon boat crew arrived on scene, located all four people aboard the capsized catamaran, and brought them safely aboard the boat.
“Having a marine radio onboard allowed the boaters to call for help, and our crew was able to respond quickly and bring all four people to safety,” said Petty Officer 3rd Class Jackson Boggs, the Station Marathon coxswain during the case. “With a small craft advisory in effect, this case is a reminder to check marine weather forecasts before getting underway and carry the proper safety equipment, including a marine radio.”
The Coast Guard reminds mariners to check weather conditions before getting underway and use VHF-FM Channel 16 to call for help in an emergency.
For more boating safety tips, click here: https://www.uscgboating.org/
Visit our Newsroom for Coast Guard Southeast District press releases. Visit our DVIDS account for Coast Guard Southeast District imagery.
For breaking news, follow us on X. For additional information, find us on Facebook and follow us on Instagram.

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-FORT SAM HOUSTON, Texas — Six Soldier-athletes from the U.S. Army World Class Athlete Program will carry Army pride and medal ambitions on to wrestling’s biggest international stage.
Four Greco-Roman wrestlers and two women’s freestyle wrestlers will compete as part of Team USA on Oct. 24-Nov. 1 at the 2026 United World Wrestling Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan.
Army WCAP accounts for 20 percent of Team USA’s 30-person roster, underscoring the program’s significant contribution to the nation’s international wrestling success.
“It’s always an honor to go out there and represent the World Class Athlete Program, the Army, and the United States on the global stage,” said Sgt. 1st Class Spenser Mango, U.S. Army Greco-Roman wrestling coach and two-time Olympian who is participating in his 14th world championships as a competitor and coach. “It doesn’t get better than that.”
Here are the Soldier-athletes competing in the world championships:
Sgt. Kamal Bey, 82 kilograms
This is the fifth world championships for Bey, who finished 10th at 77kg in last year’s world championships in Zagreb, Croatia.
Moving up to 82kg was more of a health decision to prepare his body before cutting down to 77kg for the Olympic push, he said, but he’s not giving up anything moving up a weight class.
“It definitely feels good,” said Bey, a 2024 Olympian whose military occupational specialty is culinary specialist.
“I’m filling out the weight class. I got in the weight room, worked with the coaches, and I’m getting bigger, stronger, faster, and most importantly, I’m healing up. I’m not giving up anything by moving up to 82kg, I’ll tell you that.”
Bey’s experience makes him an important resource to his teammates competing on the world stage, some for the first time.
“He’s been doing this for a while,” said Spc. Timothy Young, who will represent Team USA at 97kg and like Bey is an Illinois native. “I’m always taking whatever I can from him because he’s done this a few times.”
For Bey, there’s no better feeling than representing the United States on all fronts, not only as a citizen but as a U.S. Army Soldier.
“When WCAP and All-Army post about us and share what we’re doing, I know it gives fellow Soldiers something to be proud of,” Bey said. “It shows that somebody just like them is out there accomplishing amazing things. It also shows civilians ther are different avenues within the Army to achieve success. I don’t think there’s any other country in the world I’d rather represent.”
Sgt. Dalton Roberts, 60 kilograms
This will be the third world championships for Roberts, a motor transport operator who relishes being one of Army WCAP and Team USA’s senior competitors.
“I’d say the team cohesion is really high,” Roberts said. “In Greco-Roman wrestling, there’s always been a strong brotherhood, so that’s nothing new, but something feels different this year. We all get along well, we push each other, and we hold each other accountable.”
Working with new sports psychologists, new strength and training coaches, and more international travel has boosted the team’s confidence going into the world championships, Roberts said, and has boosted his own confidence.
“I believe I can accomplish what I want; I just have to put it all together on the day of competition,” he said. “I believe this year is the time to do it.”
Representing the Army and the United States on the world stage is a privilege Roberts doesn’t take for granted.
“It’s a beautiful thing, and it’s an honor,” Roberts said. “I carry a great deal of pride on my shoulders when I get these opportunities. It’s awesome.”
Staff Sgt. Xavier Johnson, 63 kilograms
Johnson, a motor transport operator, returns to the world championships after making his senior-level debut in Belgrade, Serbia, in 2023.
The difference this time is perspective.
Johnson admitted he was initially caught up in the magnitude of his first World Championships. Three years later, he views himself as a seasoned competitor who belongs among the world’s best.
“It’s not a mistake that I got here,” Johnson said. “It was supposed to happen the way it happened.”
He has also approached his weight management more scientifically. Although cutting to 63kg remains demanding, Johnson said this cycle has been easier than previous attempts because he began managing his weight earlier and more deliberately.
Johnson believes WCAP’s qualifiers are carrying teammates who could not compete because of injuries or military requirements. That collective responsibility – and the emergence of strong domestic Greco-Roman programs – has given the Army wrestlers added motivation.
“This is bigger than just myself,” Johnson said. “It’s for the people behind me as well.”
Spc. Timothy Young, 97 kilograms
Young, a unit supply specialist, made his first world championships by turning a difficult moment at the U.S. Open in Las Vegas in April into a defining tournament.
After losing his second match in the best-of-3 final, Young recognized that nobody would give him a place on the world team. He responded by increasing his aggression.
“This isn’t going to be just given to me,” Young said. “I have to go out there and take it if I really want this.”
Traveling to a previous world championships as a teammate’s training partner made the goal feel attainable.
Former world champion and WCAP coach Dremiel Byers, a member of the National Wrestling Hall of Fame, told Young the experience would leave him hungrier.
Young said Byers was right.
“Ever since I’ve been at WCAP, he’s the one coach where I’m like, ‘This is the guy I want in my corner,’ ” Young said. “He’s definitely one person I can trust.”
A tall wrestler for his class, Young intends to maximize his leverage from the top position, securing his lock quickly and lifting opponents before they can defend.
“I get really excited when I get my chance on top. I'm like, ‘This is it right here,’ ” Young said. “My coach tells me, ‘Tim, get right to your lock, get them up, and send them. Don't waste any time. Just lock it and get it up.’ ”
Competing in his first world championships fulfills Young’s four core principles.
“I get to go out there and represent God, family, country, and wrestling,” Young said. “It just feels really good. I get to honor all of them every time I step on the mat.”
Spc. Abby Nette, 59 kilograms
Nette, a culinary specialist, returns to the world championships for the first time since placing 10th in 2022, carrying sharper execution and a clearer competitive identity.
She attributes much of her renewed purpose to her father, who died in 2025. Before his death, he urged her to keep moving forward and told her how proud he was.
“Now I do it for both of us,” Nette said.
Nette said she has finally learned to trust the complete wrestler she has become, and she understands how her individual strengths work together.
“For the first time ever, I know exactly who I am,” she said.
She also draws confidence from WCAP’s institutional support. Nette said she never has to enter competition questioning whether her unit and the Army stand behind her.
“That's something beautiful about WCAP,” Nette said. “It's also a privilege to represent the United States of America and the U.S. Army. As a U.S. Soldier, that's really cool to say.”
Spc. Aduago Nwachukwu, 62 kilograms
Nwachukwu, who earned a silver medal on Oct. 16 at the Under-23 World Championships in Las Vegas, begins her second senior world championships campaign after placing seventh in 2025.
Her preparation has centered on disciplined weight management while transitioning from the U-23 world championships to the senior tournament. Instead of regaining substantial weight between events, she remained close to 62 kilograms, expecting the controlled cut to improve her performance.
Nwachukwu’s confidence comes from results. She has defeated wrestlers who later competed for senior world medals, convincing her that she can reach the podium – and the top step.
“I’m on that level where I know I can be a world champion,” Nwachukwu said.
For Nwachukwu, competing as a member of Army WCAP also represents a rare union of service and sport.
“Serving your country while doing the thing you love most is a blessing and a privilege,” she said. “I always tell people it’s the best thing you could ever do.”
title: Six Soldier-athletes to represent Army WCAP at United World Wrestling Championships in Kazakhstan

The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) announced today an $80 million conditional loan commitment with Antheia, Inc. to scale the company's domestic production of key starting materials (KSM) and active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) for generic pharmaceutical drugs. The OSC investment, alongside additional private capital, is intended to support Antheia's domestic biomanufacturing efforts to secure critical medicine supply chains.
Today, the vast majority of KSMs and APIs are manufactured outside the United States. OSC's conditional loan commitment to Antheia would help address this reliance on foreign production while directly advancing President Donald J. Trump's Executive Order 13944, Ensuring Essential Medicines, Medical Countermeasures, and Critical Inputs Are Made in the United States. Antheia specializes in using bioengineered yeast to convert sugar directly into KSMs and APIs in a one-step fermentation process. The company's U.S. manufacturing operations would onshore production of essential medicines and enable the rapid repurposing of manufacturing capacity to address sudden changes in demand.
"Antheia's biosynthesis platform represents an innovative method to establish cost-effective domestic supply chains which enable to the United States to compete globally. We are pleased to support Antheia's domestic biomanufacturing, which would represent an important step in strengthening the essential medicines supply chain in the United States," said David A. Lorch, Director of the Office of Strategic Capital and Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg.
Due to a lack of available and adequate domestic manufacturing capacity, Antheia currently produces its pipeline of KSMs and APIs with contract manufacturing partners abroad. OSC's conditional financing would enable Antheia to establish its U.S. manufacturing operations, onshore essential medicine supply chains, and ultimately reduce the risk of essential medicine shortages.
"OSC's investment in Antheia represents an exciting opportunity to establish domestic supply chains for the production of KSMs and APIs that are critical to our most important pharmaceuticals," said Akshaya Trivedi, Managing Director (Investments) with OSC.
The conditional loan commitment specifies additional steps Antheia must complete before financial close, including satisfying various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements.
"I applaud the Office of Strategic Capital on this important conditional investment which advances the onshoring of pharmaceutical supply chains. Biomanufacturing is one of the Department of War's six critical technology areas, making domestic production an imperative," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
title: Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital Signs $80 Million Conditional Loan Commitment With Antheia, Inc.
