Senior Chaplain Corps leaders from across Air Education and Training Command gathered Oct. 14–15 for the 2026 AETC Senior Religious Support Team Symposium to prepare teams to support Airmen, families and commanders at home station and in deployed environments.
The symposium took place as the Department of the Air Force implements Secretary of War-directed Chaplain Corps reforms that place greater emphasis on chaplains’ core ministry functions, including religious services, pastoral care, commander advisement and operational religious support.
Chaplain (Col.) Chris Conklin, AETC command chaplain, and Chief Master Sgt. Jonathan Torres, AETC religious affairs functional manager, led wing chaplains and senior enlisted religious affairs leaders in discussions on planning, resourcing and professional development.
“A Bold and Ready Force for Good begins with deliberate preparation,” Conklin said. “This symposium gives our leaders an opportunity to turn broad guidance into practical plans, strengthen partnerships and take a clearer understanding of the mission back to their installations.”
The opening AETC Chaplain Corps vision and mission brief set the strategic direction for the symposium, framing how the Chaplain Corps can translate its core responsibilities into support for Airmen, families and commanders across the command.
Lt. Gen. Clark Quinn, commander of Air Education and Training Command, and Chief Master Sgt. Chad Bickley, AETC command chief, emphasized senior-leader support for the Chaplain Corps and highlighted the connection between character, resilience and mission effectiveness during a leadership brief.
“The Department of War and Department of the Air Force are taking deliberate steps to strengthen the Chaplain Corps and make its support more accessible across our force,” Quinn said. “At AETC, that support helps forge Airmen of character who can meet training demands and further develop into combat-effective Airmen.”
At the installation level, those priorities take shape through Annual Ministry Plans. Installation Chaplain Corps teams use the plans to forecast ministry programs, manpower and funding needs for the upcoming fiscal year, providing a foundation for deliberate stewardship and support to the base community.
“Our Ministry Plans are more than a calendar and funding request,” Conklin said. “They help our teams anticipate where Airmen and families may need support most, make deliberate choices about limited resources and remain aligned with the commander’s priorities throughout the year.”
That deliberate planning extends beyond home station. The symposium examined how the Chaplain Corps can build and sustain cohesive teams for deployed operations, beginning with a deployment-pairing approach designed to keep chaplains and religious affairs Airmen from the same or nearby installations together when possible.
The approach builds on established team cohesion and improves synchronization in deployed environments.
“Readiness is built long before a team deploys,” Torres said. “When chaplains and religious affairs Airmen train together, understand each other’s strengths and have a clear picture of the resources available, they can spend less time building a team after arrival and more time caring for Airmen and advising commanders.”
To make informed sourcing and deployment decisions, leaders also need an accurate picture of available personnel, qualifications and resources. The AETC Chaplain Corps uses the Envision readiness reporting tool to help leaders identify available personnel, specialized training and on-hand resources.
A readiness update from the Air Force Installation and Mission Support Center addressed potential FY28 changes to how Chaplain Corps personnel are sourced for deployment, as well as recent updates to deployment qualification requirements. The changes may affect how leaders assess personnel availability, maintain readiness and schedule training.
Training discussions addressed the development of religious affairs Airmen from initial skills instruction through advanced professional development. A planned force protection and weapons familiarization initiative provided one example of how the Chaplain Corps is preparing teams to operate safely alongside warfighters in deployed environments.
Sustaining Chaplain Corps capability also depends on recruiting, retraining and developing religious affairs Airmen. Recent changes to accession standards, along with retraining opportunities and career-development pathways, support HQ AETC Chaplain Corps efforts to build and retain the enlisted force that enables religious support across the force.
By integrating religious support throughout accession, training and education, AETC helps Airmen carry character, resilience and spiritual readiness into the operational force.
title: AETC symposium prepares religious support teams for future fight

WASHINGTON -- Today, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) made $250 million available to states and territories through a new Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS) Grant Program funding opportunity. This funding will empower state and territorial governments to enhance their capabilities to aggressively combat the unlawful use of unmanned aircraft systems—also known as “drones.”
“Unlawful drones are not a future threat. They are a real and growing danger to our communities, critical infrastructure, and major public events,” said FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton. “Through this grant program, FEMA is enabling states and territories to build the capabilities they need to detect, identify, track and monitor drone threats before they can cause harm.”
In recent years, criminals, terrorists and hostile foreign actors have intensified their use of unmanned aircraft systems to endanger the American people, threaten the integrity of our communities and jeopardize the protection of critical infrastructure and vital institutions. With the support of the White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026, the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) have coordinated federal efforts to address unlawful drone threats and protect communities, critical infrastructure and large-scale public events. FEMA designed its C-UAS Grant Program to address this evolving threat by empowering state and territorial governments to build the capabilities they need to effectively detect, identify, track and monitor this technology. This program aligns with President Trump’s broader initiative to protect the public from hostile drones, as outlined in the Executive Order on Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty.
The C-UAS Grant Program was established under the Working Families Tax Cut Act and signed into law by President Donald J. Trump in July 2025. This legislation directed DHS to provide $500 million in federal funding to enhance state and local capabilities to combat unmanned aircraft systems. Last year, FEMA awarded $250 million specifically to states hosting FIFA World Cup matches and to the National Capital Region, which hosted national events celebrating America’s 250th anniversary. This year, the remaining $250 million will be distributed to all 50 states, five territories and the District of Columbia, enabling robust detection and response capabilities in communities nationwide. This design demonstrates that the Trump Administration is working to keep Americans secure as they attend historic events across the nation while also building long-term protections against drone threats.
The Fiscal Year 2027 C-UAS Grant Program funding opportunity is published on Grants.gov. This is a noncompetitive grant program. State Administrative Agencies are the only eligible applicants for this funding opportunity. All applications must be submitted in FEMA Grants Outcomes (FEMA GO), the grants management system of record. The application period opens on October 16, 2026, and will close on November 16, 2026.
title: Trump Administration Announces Another $250 Million in Federal Funds to Secure America from Unlawful Drones

NORFOLK, Va. – A Portsmouth man was sentenced today to 35 years in prison for production of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), coercion and enticement of a minor, receipt of CSAM, and possession of CSAM.

Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. text:
Fast Facts
Critical minerals—such as lithium, copper, and zinc—are essential to the nation's economic and national security.
The U.S. relies on imports for many of these minerals. But those supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions. Amid efforts to increase domestic mineral production, concerns have been raised about foreign influence in domestic supply chains.
Mining companies aren't required to disclose foreign ownership of mines on federal land. So, the full extent of foreign ownership is unclear. But we found companies operating critical mineral mines that were subsidiaries of foreign companies, some of which had investment from Chinese entities.
Copper Mine on Federal Lands
A terraced open pit mine.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The U.S critical mineral supply chain faces numerous constraints, including the need for substantial capital investment and limited domestic processing capacity. The U.S. exports large quantities of domestically extracted ore to Canada, Mexico, and China, among other countries.
Copper Mine on Federal Lands
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the Forest Service oversee hardrock mines on federal land. As of February 2026, there were 632 approved hardrock mining plans of operation on federal land. The 1872 Mining Law generally requires mining claimants to be U.S. citizens or business entities incorporated in the U.S. Foreign businesses can meet this requirement by having a U.S. subsidiary serve as the claimant. While there is limited available information on the full extent of foreign investment in mining on federal lands and parent-subsidiary relationships, GAO reviewed ownership information of 43 claimants and operators associated with critical mineral mines on federal lands. GAO determined ownership for 32 of those companies and found that 14 were subsidiaries of foreign entities. GAO found that none of the 14 had Chinese-owned parent companies, but in at least two cases, Chinese entities had financial interest in the foreign parent companies.
The 1872 Mining Law does not contain a provision requiring BLM or Forest Service to collect information on foreign parent companies nor does it require claimants or operators to submit information regarding foreign ownership. However, other federal agencies have some authorities and processes to identify foreign investment in mining. For example, the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, chaired by the Department of the Treasury, can review foreign investment in mining as it relates to potential national security concerns.
Why GAO Did This Study
Critical minerals are essential to the economic and national security of the United States. These minerals, including copper, lithium, and zinc, are key components in advanced technologies and have vulnerable supply chains.
As demand for these minerals increases, U.S. access to critical minerals has become a key topic in domestic policymaking and international relations. Recently, the administration and Congressional entities have expressed concerns over U.S. dependence on imports and the role of potential adversary nations, such as the People’s Republic of China (China), in the U.S. supply chain of critical minerals.
Most critical minerals that can be mined in the U.S. are obtained through hardrock mining, some of which occurs on federal lands. However, policymakers have raised questions about the full amount and extent of foreign investment in those mines.
This report provides information on hardrock mining that occurs on federal lands, foreign investment in mining on federal lands, and steps federal agencies take to identify foreign investment. It also provides information on the amount of extracted critical minerals exported from the U.S. from 2019 through 2025. GAO reviewed ownership information using a variety of sources for 43 claimants and operators associated with critical mineral mines, analyzed federal laws, and interviewed officials. In a related report (GAO-27-108196), GAO reports on BLM’s role in collecting citizenship information from mining claimants.
For more information, contact Dr. Nagla'a El-Hodiri at elhodirin@gao.gov.
title: Critical Minerals: Limited Available Information on the Full Extent of Foreign Investment in Mining on Federal Lands

CHARLOTTE, N.C. – U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson, U.S. Marshal Terry Burgin, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff Garry McFadden today announced a new agreement between the Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) and the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) to relocate federal detainees from detention facilities outside of North Carolina to facilities in Mecklenburg County.

“Housing federal detainees in Mecklenburg County whose cases are pending in this district not only brings millions of federal dollars to North Carolina that otherwise went to other states, it benefits the federal justice system. It means defendants are closer to their attorneys—making it easier to prepare their defense and thus move cases faster—and closer to their families, which makes rehabilitation and reentry to society more likely to be successful. It also means shorter, quicker, and cheaper transportation to court, which makes it easier to schedule hearings and trials,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “I am so thankful to Sheriff Garry McFadden and Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge for making this partnership possible.”

“The U.S. Marshals Service is excited to once again house federal detainees with the Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office. The MCSO and the USMS have a long-standing partnership. The reopening of Mecklenburg County Detention Center North will allow for the continued due process of federal detainees and ensure the federal judicial system operates efficiently,” said Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge.

“When law enforcement and criminal justice agencies work together through transparent collaboration, open communication, and an unwavering commitment to public safety, we reinforce accountability and the integrity of the justice system while demonstrating the unity and professionalism our communities expect and deserve. Today stands as a clear example of that commitment by bringing federal detainees back to the Sheriff’s Office’s North facility. I commend U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson and Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge for their leadership and partnership in supporting the Sheriff’s Office throughout this process,” said Sheriff Garry McFadden.

Because of the new agreement, federal detainees in the custody of the USMS with pending federal cases in the Western District of North Carolina currently housed in detention facilities in other states in the region will be relocated to detention facilities in Mecklenburg County, including Mecklenburg County Jail Central (Jail Central) and the newly reopened Mecklenburg County Detention Center North (Jail North).

Jail North, a former detention facility closed in 2022, was recently reopened under the direction of Sheriff McFadden. MCSO transferred more than 200 state detainees to Jail North in September, and now the federal funds paid to house federal inmates will contribute to the operation of the facility.

The U.S. Marshals Service is responsible for the custody, care, and transportation of individuals held on federal charges, from the time they are ordered detained by a federal judge until the case concludes. The agency relies on partnerships with state and local governments to house federal detainees.

In 2023, federal detainees were transferred out of detention facilities in Mecklenburg County following the end of the previous arrangement between MCSO and USMS. Since then, federal pretrial detainees have been held in as many as 14 different facilities in a number of different states, such as Georgia, Virginia, South Carolina, and Kentucky, with some facilities as far as six hours away. The renewed agreement brings federal detention operations back to Charlotte.

For federal prosecutors and defense attorneys, easier access to federal detainees is an important part of the federal criminal justice process. Bringing federal detainees to Mecklenburg County means defense attorneys will more easily meet with their clients to review documents and make critical case decisions, and federal prosecutors will have easier access to detainees serving as witnesses in other federal cases. For the most part, detainees will also be closer to their families and loved ones, which is key for rehabilitation and successful reentry into society as productive members without a criminal future. Moreover, closer proximity to the federal courthouse expedites court proceedings while reducing logistical challenges associated with transporting federal detainees over long distances.

“This renewed arrangement between the Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office and the U.S. Marshals Service makes the federal justice system work more efficiently, while returning federal resources to North Carolina,” said U.S. Attorney Ferguson. “When federal detainees can be housed closer to their attorneys, their families, and the courthouse, the whole system is smoother and more efficient.”

The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecutes federal criminal cases across the western district’s 32 counties in partnership with federal, state and local law enforcement agencies. The United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina operates through divisions in Charlotte, Asheville, and Statesville. The main courthouse, which serves as the primary headquarters for the Western District, is located uptown Charlotte.
title: Federal Detainees to Be Relocated to Detention Facilities in Mecklenburg County; Partnership Between the U.S. Attorney’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office Brings Federal Resources to North Carolina

text:
Fast Facts
Geostationary weather satellites provide critical information on atmospheric conditions, including severe storms and hurricanes. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is working on acquiring the next generation of these satellites, called GeoXO.
Starting in 2025, NOAA restructured the GeoXO program. It reduced the number of satellites and cut costs from $19.6 billion to $13 billion.
But this program needs to document its new cost estimates. It also needs to fully incorporate lessons learned from prior programs—including contingency planning to address gaps in satellite weather data.
Our recommendations address these issues.
Satellite in space orbiting Earth
Highlights
What GAO Found
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) initially planned for the Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) program to be a series of six satellites with a projected lifecycle cost of $19.6 billion. In August 2025, Commerce directed the GeoXO program office to implement a major restructuring to reduce lifecycle costs, and in April 2026 Commerce approved the program’s new baseline. This new baseline reduces the number of satellites from six to four, decreases the number of instruments from five to two (see figure), and is expected to reduce the program’s lifecycle cost to $13 billion.
Instrument Changes for the Geostationary Extended Observations Program, as of April 2026
If the first GeoXO satellite launches as expected in 2032, there is a risk of a gap in the continuity of satellite data. NOAA’s policy requires at least two operational satellites and one operational spare to be available to ensure the continuity of data. The current spare satellite is projected to meet the end of its life in October 2032, several months before the first GeoXO satellite is fully operational. There may be a period of several months when NOAA does not have an operational spare satellite. If either of the two operational satellites were impaired during that time, there would be a gap in geostationary weather data (see figure).
Potential Gap in Data Continuity Without Operational Spare Satellite
The effects of the rebaseline add uncertainty to the program’s cost, schedule, and instrument configuration. For example, the program office has yet to complete an independent cost estimate for its updated cost baseline, so it is unclear whether the $13 billion estimate for the restructuring is reasonable.
GeoXO’s prior lifecycle cost estimate of $19.6 billion from 2022 partially met three and substantially met one of the best practices associated with a well-documented estimate. The gaps were due, in part, to the program’s lack of a separate narrative document that summarized the estimate and the methodology used. These gaps will make it difficult for GeoXO to replicate calculations and detect possible errors in the estimate and its ongoing revisions, and can undermine the ability to use the information to improve future cost estimates.
The GeoXO program fully incorporated selected leading practices related to requirements management in its policies and procedures, which was a lesson learned from previous weather satellite programs. However, the program did not fully incorporate leading practices for other lessons learned:
- Contingency planning: NOAA partially incorporated leading practices for contingency planning into its plans to address potential satellite availability gaps. Specifically, the plan was missing key elements, such as an impact analysis for potential failure scenarios and specific actions needed to implement all contingency strategies. Until NOAA incorporates the missing key elements, it may not be sufficiently prepared to mitigate potential gaps in geostationary weather satellite data, which would diminish its ability to track and monitor hazardous weather.
- Technology readiness: NOAA and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) did not incorporate leading practices related to documenting the results of its process to assess the readiness of key new technologies. Specifically, the GeoXO program did not document its assessment of the readiness of key technologies for three new instruments and did not develop a comprehensive report with the results of this assessment, which is required by NASA guidance. Thus, whether the program has enough information to determine if a technology is sufficiently mature is unclear, which increases the risk of delay and cost overruns.
Why GAO Did This Study
Geostationary environmental satellites play a critical role in the nation’s weather forecasting. These satellites provide information on atmospheric conditions for monitoring Earth’s weather, including severe storms and hurricanes.
NOAA, a component of the Department of Commerce, through collaboration with NASA, is procuring the next generation of geostationary weather satellites, called GeoXO. GeoXO satellites are intended to replace the current series of geostationary environmental satellites as they reach the end of their useful lives. The GeoXO mission was planned to continue the vital observations provided by the existing operational geostationary satellites and bring new and improved capabilities.
GAO was asked to review the GeoXO program. This report addresses (1) the status of the GeoXO program, (2) the extent to which NOAA and NASA have implemented relevant best practices to establish cost estimates, and (3) the extent to which NOAA and NASA incorporated leading practices related to selected lessons learned from previous weather satellite programs into the development and organization of GeoXO program.
GAO analyzed agency documents, including program office plans, management reports, documentation supporting the program’s December 2022 cost estimate, contingency plans, requirements policies and procedures, and documentation that provided the results of the technical readiness assessments. GAO then compared this documentation against leading practices and interviewed agency officials.
Recommendations
GAO is making three recommendations to Commerce to ensure that the GeoXO cost estimate incorporates best practices, contingency plans address weather data gaps and impacts of failure scenarios, and a complete technology readiness report is developed for each instrument. NOAA concurred with the recommendations.
title: Geostationary Weather Satellites: Next Generation Program Challenges Put Vital Observations at Risk

text:
Fast Facts
U.S. national security and economic interests depend on technological innovation and advantage. This Q&A looks at people who collect sensitive information for other countries. This group may include university students and researchers. The FBI calls these people "non-traditional intelligence collectors" and says they pose an insider threat to the U.S.
The FBI works with academic institutions and industry to identify and address such threats, but its relationships with academia vary. According to FBI officials, good relationships can help institutions come forward with tips and requests for help.
We recommended strengthening these relationships.
Picture of the FBI's seal on a wall outside of an office.
Highlights
What GAO Found
According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), non-traditional intelligence collectors (NTCs) are individuals whose primary profession is not intelligence collection, but who actively or passively collect sensitive U.S. information on behalf of foreign entities. For example, researchers and students at universities may act as NTCs if they collect non-public research on behalf of a foreign entity. According to the FBI, unlike intelligence officers, NTCs function independently of established intelligence organizations.
FBI officials and representatives from academic associations identified several challenges in addressing threats posed by NTCs. For example, FBI officials said that it is difficult to identify and investigate NTCs because their activities may not constitute a violation of the law until information is transferred to foreign entities. Also, there are cultural differences between the FBI and academia that may impede communication, as academic institutions promote the free exchange of information, and, according to FBI officials, may not want to be perceived as “turning over” their students.
FBI offices involved in mitigating and investigating threats posed by NTCs are the Office of Private Sector, which leads information-sharing and engagement with the private sector, and the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. The FBI also uses the National Counterintelligence Task Force and field office-based Counterintelligence Task Forces to coordinate with partner agencies.
Interplay Between FBI’s Headquarters and Field Offices in Mitigating Threats Posed by NTCs
According to FBI officials, building relationships between field offices and academic institutions is important, so academic institutions come to the FBI for assistance in addressing NTCs. FBI officials also said they rely on tips from academia to identify potential NTCs. Publicly, FBI officials have stated that relationships with academic institutions need strengthening to address research security issues. Academic association representatives similarly have said the FBI could improve outreach efforts and that relationships between the FBI and universities are stronger at some universities than others. However, the FBI did not identify a plan for strengthening partnerships with academic institutions. Without strong partnerships, the FBI’s ability to counter NTC threats and protect U.S. research, intellectual property, and technological advantage is hindered.
Why GAO Did This Study
U.S. national security and economic interests are heavily dependent on technological innovation and advantage. According to FBI officials, NTCs pose a significant insider threat to U.S. information, intellectual property, and technological advantage.
GAO was asked to review the FBI’s efforts to investigate and address threats posed by NTCs. This report provides information on the challenges posed by NTCs, the FBI offices involved in mitigating and investigating threats posed by NTCs, and the relationships between the FBI and academic institutions relative to NTC threats, among other things.
To conduct this work, GAO reviewed laws and statutes related to the FBI’s authorities to investigate federal crimes and national security threats, analyzed documentary evidence to understand how key offices interact and coordinate with each other, and reviewed the mechanisms the FBI uses to coordinate its efforts with other federal agencies, academia, and the private sector. GAO also interviewed FBI officials and representatives from academic associations and private industry, selected based on their experiences in addressing NTC activities in academia and the private sector.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that the FBI develop and implement a plan to strengthen the FBI’s partnerships with academic institutions to better facilitate the exchange of information and to help address threats posed by NTCs. The FBI concurred with our recommendation.
title: National Security: FBI Should Strengthen Partnerships to Combat Non-Traditional Intelligence Collectors

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.
“Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman. “Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line. As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter. I am also grateful to Rae Ann Meyer for the leadership she has provided to Marshall during this transition and for her continued service to NASA.”
“Leading a NASA center requires a commitment to its people and to the technical capabilities entrusted to them,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Steve understands that the jewel of Marshall is its workforce and that engineering excellence is sustained by giving talented people the opportunity to design, build, test, and learn through hands-on work. As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.”
As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities. Marshall plays a critical role in NASA’s Artemis program, including the development of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, management of the Human Landing System Program, as well as other capabilities supporting sustained exploration of the Moon and future missions to Mars. Further, Marshall plays a key role in the advancement of nuclear power and propulsion, an area of focus that is expected to grow as NASA works towards sending the first humans to Mars.
“It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash. “I am humbled to stand alongside the brilliant minds here as we continue to turn the impossible into everyday history.”
Cash began his NASA career at Marshall in 1982 and spent 34 years with the agency, holding senior engineering and management positions supporting some of the nation’s most significant human spaceflight programs.
During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions. He later served as director of Marshall’s Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate from 2011 until his retirement in 2016, providing leadership in safety, reliability, and quality engineering to support mission success across the center.
Following his retirement from NASA, Cash continued his work in the aerospace industry, including serving as vice president for advanced space systems at Axient, supporting the development and execution of major spaceflight programs. In 2024, he was inducted into the Alabama Engineering Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to engineering and the nation’s space program.
Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025. Meyer, who previously served as Marshall’s deputy center director and associate director, has provided leadership and continuity across the center’s programs and operations during her tenure as acting director. Meyer will return to her role as Deputy Center Director.
Established in 1960, Marshall has played a central role in American space exploration for more than six decades, from developing the Saturn rockets that carried astronauts to the Moon during Apollo to advancing the propulsion systems, infrastructure, and technologies supporting the next era of human spaceflight.

Rep. Gillen and House Minority Whip Clark Hold Fireside Chat on Impacts of Rising Healthcare Costs on Long Island
More than 63,000 Long Islanders have lost health insurance following historic federal cuts to Medicaid and the expiration of ACA tax credits
Watch the full conversation HERE.
GARDEN CITY, NY — Today, Congresswoman Laura Gillen (NY-04) and Whip Katherine Clark (MA-05) hosted a fireside chat with Nassau County residents and leaders at Harmony Health in Garden City to discuss how rising healthcare costs are affecting Long Island and the country. Both lawmakers discussed a path in Congress to lower healthcare costs, extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits and reverse the $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
"Long Island’s hardworking families, care workers and providers are being crushed by rising healthcare costs and the GOP majority’s $1 trillion cut to Americans’ coverage,” said Rep. Gillen. “Alongside Whip Clark, we’re fighting to pass bipartisan solutions to reverse these cuts, restore the ACA tax credits, lower costs and protect the people who care for us. Together in Congress, we will continue working to ensure that quality healthcare is more affordable for all Americans.”
“Congresswoman Laura Gillen is fighting every day for the quality, affordable healthcare that Long Island families deserve," said Democratic Whip Katherine Clark. “It was a privilege to join her in the 4th District of New York and discuss House Democrats’ agenda to deliver for working families. In the 120th Congress, we will reverse this administration’s harmful cuts and pass legislation to ensure everyone can get the medical care they need, when they need it.”
“Congresswoman Gillen has been a strong and consistent advocate for healthcare and for the needs of the communities we serve, and we are deeply grateful for her continued support” said David Nemiroff, Chief Executive Officer of Harmony Healthcare Long Island. “We also extend our sincere thanks to Whip Clark for coming to Long Island and lending her voice and leadership to this critical issue. At a time when access to affordable, high-quality healthcare is more important than ever for our patients and families, this level of advocacy and engagement makes a meaningful difference. We appreciate their partnership and unwavering commitment to the health and well-being of our communities.”
During the conversation, Whip Clark expanded on House Democrats’ plan to restore expired federal ACA tax credits, which lowered health insurance premiums by thousands of dollars for some Nassau County residents. In January, Clark and Gillen helped pass a bipartisan three-year extension of the tax credits in the House, which now awaits passage in the Senate.

She has fought against cuts to Medicaid and SNAP in the OBBBA, led and signed bipartisan letters opposing policies that would increase healthcare costs or jeopardize cancer research and safety-net hospitals and called on congressional leadership to protect Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid.

Tampa, Florida – David Sartin, Jr. (40, St. Petersburg) has been charged by criminal complaint with two counts of bank robbery. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each count. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court documents, on August 24, 2026, Sartin robbed a bank in Largo. On September 15, 2026, he robbed a bank in St. Petersburg. During both robberies, Sartin entered the bank wearing a prosthetic “old man” mask, approached the teller counter and demanded money, and instructed the teller not to include dye packs.

The investigation revealed that Sartin had arrived at a nearby gas station shortly before the first robbery, then drove through the surrounding area before parking, switching to a bicycle, and approaching the bank. After the robbery, Sartin fled on the bicycle, retrieved the staged vehicle, and drove away. The vehicle was later seen on multiple nearby roadways heading in the direction of his residence.

Video surveillance captured a vehicle leaving Sartin’s home before the second robbery and returning afterwards. When the vehicle returned to the residence, a white male resembling Sartin was seen unloading a bicycle from the vehicle and rolling it toward the residence. The next day, investigators observed Sartin spray paint the vehicle’s white roof black, making the entire vehicle appear black in color.

A search of Sartin’s residence uncovered a bicycle, a blue suit, and a black bag, all similar to the items used during the first robbery. A black suit similar to the one used during the second robbery was also recovered. Investigators also seized materials covered in black spray paint and a receipt for clothing purchased the day before the second robbery.

A search of Sartin’s storage unit revealed a backpack and laptop bag containing disguise items matching those seen in the surveillance footage from the robberies, including the old‑man mask with grey facial hair, dark‑framed glasses, and work gloves with black paint on them. The bags also contained a fake handgun and clothing consistent with the disguise worn during the second robbery, including a white dress shirt with black studs, a pinstriped sports coat, a dark blue flat cap, and black dress shoes and pants.

Agents also searched another residence where Sartin occasionally stayed. There, they found several items, including a prosthetic mask different from the one used in the robberies and a journal titled, “God’s Best friend is a Bank Robber! Uncle Henry Cops and Robbers the world through the eyes of a Bank Robber.” The journal was dated “Jan 1, 2021,” and was “written by: David Sartin.” One of the pages had a drawing of a character holding up a mask along with the handwritten phrase, “My face holding up uncle Henry, looking at it, Face to Face.”

At the time of the robberies, Sartin was on supervised release for a 2018 federal conviction stemming from five bank robberies he had committed in Texas in 2016. During these robberies, he wore a similar mask and used the same vehicle he used during the robberies he is charged with now. Sartin was sentenced to 10 years and 1 month in federal prison. Prior to that, in 2008, Sartin was convicted in federal court of attempted bank robbery after he and a co-conspirator had tried robbing a bank wearing Halloween masks and disguises.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Largo Police Department, and the St. Petersburg Police Department. It will be prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Belkis H. Callaos.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: Previously Convicted Bank Robber Charged Again for Robbing Banks Wearing “Old Man” Mask

SAN DIEGO – Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of California filed 111 border-related cases this week, including charges of bringing in aliens for financial gain, reentering the U.S. after deportation, and importation of controlled substances.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California is the fourth-busiest federal district, largely due to a high volume of border-related crimes. This district, encompassing San Diego and Imperial counties, shares a 140-mile border with Mexico. It includes the San Ysidro Port of Entry, the world’s busiest land border crossing, connecting San Diego (America’s eighth largest city) and Tijuana (Mexico’s second largest city).

In addition to reactive border-related crimes, the Southern District of California also prosecutes a significant number of proactive cases related to terrorism, organized crime, drugs, white-collar fraud, violent crime, cybercrime, human trafficking and national security. Recent developments in those and other significant areas of prosecution can be found here .

A sample of border-related arrests this week:

On October 11, Rafael Perez Rosario, a Mexican national, was arrested and charged with Deported Alien Found in the United States. According to a complaint, U.S. Border Patrol agents discovered Perez Rosario hiding in a bush in a remote area near the U.S.-Mexico border, approximately two miles east of the Otay Mesa Port of Entry. He was apprehended after a foot chase. Perez Rosario was previously being deported to Mexico on August 5, 2026.

On October 12, Lemuel Muniz-Valle, a United States citizen, was arrested and charged with Importation of a Controlled Substance. According to a complaint, Customs and Border Protection officers discovered approximately 115 pounds of methamphetamine concealed inside the doors, dashboard and fuel tank of the 2016 Honda Accord he was driving as he applied for entry to the U.S. at the San Ysidro Port of Entry.

On October 14, Summer Smith, a United States citizen, was arrested and charged with Importation of a Controlled Substance. According to a complaint, Smith had 139 grams of fentanyl hidden under clothing as she attempted to cross the border at the San Ysidro Port of Entry pedestrian lanes.

The immigration cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE ERO), Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), with the support and assistance of state and local law enforcement partners.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

DALLAS — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that a federal grand jury in Dallas, Texas returned an indictment on Sept. 22, 2026, charging four Texas residents with conspiracy to defraud the United States and other crimes for promoting an illegal tax shelter.

According to the indictment, Texas residents Duncan John MacDonald, Sarah Duren, Richard Ronald Cayce and Thomas Weickgenant promoted and sold a fraudulent trust scheme that was used to shelter more than $1.5 billion of income, causing an estimated tax loss to the IRS of more than $200 million. The defendants allegedly sold clients the tax shelter for fees that often exceeded $100,000 by fraudulently telling clients that they could assign their income to sham trusts to defer paying taxes in perpetuity, all while continuing to enjoy the benefit and control over their assets and income. The defendants also allegedly encouraged some clients to backdate their trusts and file amended income tax returns claiming refunds for prior years’ taxes.

The indictment also alleges that Weickgenant, who allegedly filed false tax returns for tax shelter clients, obstructed IRS efforts to audit those clients. Weickgenant’s alleged obstruction included instructing clients not to speak with the IRS and encouraging at least one client not to comply with a U.S. District Court order to enforce an IRS summons.

The indictment further alleges that MacDonald and Duren, common-law spouses, evaded income taxes on the millions they received in fees from selling the tax shelter. To do so, the couple allegedly concealed MacDonald’s ownership of the tax shelter business and lied to federal investigators. They also allegedly filed false tax returns, used trusts to conceal their receipt of income, and paid personal living expenses through trusts and nominee accounts held in the names of third parties. Allegedly, Cayce, who owned the distributorship licensing the trust tax shelter, likewise received millions of dollars in fees, which he failed to report on his income tax returns.

Additionally, according to the allegations, MacDonald fraudulently solicited $2 million from investors to purportedly purchase shares in a business promoting the tax shelter by allegedly developing digital trusts. Instead, MacDonald allegedly used the $2 million to purchase luxury goods for himself, including a Rolls Royce Ghost (pictured below top with MacDonald) and the downpayment for a yacht (pictured below bottom). At the time he received funds from investors, MacDonald allegedly was under a court-ordered injunction prohibiting him from selling securities not registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

DOT, DoW, DHS Join Forces to Protect Southern Border Airspace
Temporary flight restriction will prohibit unauthorized drone operations within one nautical mile of the U.S.-Mexico border, from the surface to 400 feet
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), Department of War (DoW) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) today announced a new, coordinated effort to strengthen airspace security along the southern U.S. border through a temporary flight restriction (TFR) for drones. The TFR – effective today – will bar any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet above ground level and extend one nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border.
The move builds on the Trump Administration’s successful efforts to secure the southern border and defend the homeland from national security threats – including illicit cartel activity. The new measure will reduce risks to ongoing border security operations, protect federal personnel, facilities and the Homeland, and enhance enforcement against those who violate the restrictions.
“President Trump promised to secure the Southern Border, and he did. Now we’re doubling down on that promise by protecting our skies from cartel drone threats and other illicit activities,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “I appreciate the close collaboration with our partners at DHS and DoW as we work together to defend our airspace and keep the American people safe.”
“The United States government will maintain 100% operational control of our border: land, air, and sea,” said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. “For too long, cartels have taken advantage of gaps along our southern border. Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, those days are over. By restricting unauthorized drone activity, we are giving commanders greater awareness, greater decision space, and more options to defend the Homeland. Equipped with cutting-edge technology—including Directed Energy Weapons—our warfighters will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America’s sovereignty.”
“DHS will not stop building on the historic progress made to secure the southern border,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “This action will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border. President Trump promised to secure the border, and we are delivering on that promise through continued action and strong partnership with Department of Transportation and the Department of War.”
Additional Information:
The FAA will publish a NOTAM which will include links to the Domestic Notice and the FAA's UAS Data Delivery System.
Drone operators are responsible for reviewing all applicable NOTAMs and restrictions before operating and must comply with the requirements in effect for their planned operations.
title: DOT, DoW, DHS Join Forces to Protect Southern Border Airspace

IR-2026-123, Oct. 16, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service has already begun issuing refunds to more than 50,000 taxpayers who benefited from the adoption tax credit carryforward and expects the refund process for most eligible taxpayers to be complete by the end of the year.
The Treasury Department clarified its interpretation of the Working Families Tax Cuts affecting the adoption tax credit. Under the new interpretation, for tax year 2025 only, adoption tax credit carryforwards from prior tax years (2020-2024) can increase the amount of the adoption tax credit that is refundable in 2025, subject to the $5,000 per qualifying child limitation.
“By issuing refunds without requiring eligible families to file an amended return, the IRS is helping reduce the financial burden on those who decided to adopt a child into their family,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano. “This administrative change will help families access the tax benefits they are entitled to as quickly and simply as possible.”
IRS will adjust affected taxpayers’ accounts to reflect this change and issue any resulting refunds, notifying taxpayers of any changes made to their accounts. Taxpayers should not need to file an amended return to receive the additional credit. This approach offers immediate relief to affected taxpayers, lessening the burden and reducing the necessity to file amended returns.
Taxpayers will receive notices from the IRS, generally within 30 days of the adjustment, informing them of the amount and whether the adjustment resulted in a refund or was applied towards another tax or non-tax debt. Taxpayers should review the notice carefully, compare it with their 2025 tax return, and keep it with their tax records.
Refunds and adjustments began in late September and will continue until complete. Affected taxpayers generally do not need to take action. Taxpayers who filed their 2025 return before April 15, 2026, will generally receive any applicable adjustment automatically. Taxpayers who filed their returns under an extension or whose accounts have identity theft indicators, freezes, dependency conflicts or other issues will be reviewed later in 2026 after the return is processed or the account issue is resolved. For more information, visit IRS.gov/AdoptionCredit.
The IRS encourages all taxpayers to create an IRS Individual Online Account to access their tax account information securely online. An IRS Online Individual Account enables taxpayers to view their tax records, check refund status, view notices and make payments without the need to call or mail the IRS.
title: IRS has begun issuing automatic refunds to individuals who claimed Adoption Tax Credit carryforward from prior years

Fort Myers, Florida – Olivier Emanuel Fevrier-Sildor (27, North Fort Myers) has pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute cocaine, possession with intent to distribute cocaine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, and three counts of distribution of cocaine. He faces up to life imprisonment, a mandatory minimum term of 5 years, consecutive to any other sentence, as well as a $1,000,000 fine. Fevrier-Sildor remains detained pending sentencing. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court records, Fevrier-Sildor was arrested on March 31, 2026, in North Fort Myers, while possessing a distributable quantity of cocaine along with a firearm. Fevrier-Sildor has a prior felony conviction for robbery by sudden snatching. Therefore, he is prohibited from possessing a firearm under federal law. After his arrest and while incarcerated, Fevrier-Sildor recruited Ramiro Jimenez-Flores (20, North Fort Myers) to utilize Fevrier-Sildor’s cell phones and continue to distribute cocaine on his behalf. Law enforcement subsequently conducted three controlled buys of approximately 112 grams of cocaine from Jimenez-Flores on April 10, April 17, and April 29. During the April 29 controlled buy, law enforcement conducted surveillance on Jimenez-Flores as he met up with his source of supply, Christopher Antonio Sierra Lopez (26, Lehigh Acres), and obtained approximately 56 grams of cocaine, which he then sold to an undercover agent.

Jimenez-Flores pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute cocaine on July 28, 2026.

Sierra Lopez pleaded guilty to distribution of cocaine on August 18, 2026.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Lee County Sheriff’s Office. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Matthew Redavid.
title: North Fort Myers Man Pleads Guilty to Illegally Possessing a Gun and Drug Offenses

WASHINGTON —The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low- interest federal disaster loans for Indiana businesses, private nonprofits, and residents affected by severe storms, tornadoes, straight-line winds, and flash flooding occurring June 6 – 26. The SBA issued a disaster declaration in response to an Oct. 9 request received from Governor Mike Braun.
The declaration covers the Indiana counties of Clark, Crawford, Dubois, Elkhart, Floyd, Gibson, Harrison, Jasper, Jefferson, Jennings, Knox, Kosciusko, Lagrange, Lake, Marshall, Newton, Noble, Pike, Porter, Posey, Ripley, Scott, Spencer, St. Joseph, Switzerland, Vanderburgh, Warrick, and Washington, the Illinois counties of Cook, Kankakee, Wabash, White, and Will, the Kentucky counties of Carroll, Daviess, Hardin, Henderson, Jefferson, Meade, and Trimble, as well as the Michigan counties of Cass and St. Joseph, which are eligible for both physical damage loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA.
Businesses and private nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against high wind damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “At these centers, our specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofits — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for private nonprofits, and 3.00% for homeowners and renters, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
Beginning today, Oct. 16, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the Disaster Loan Outreach Centers in Harrison, Gibson, Jefferson, and Elkhart counties to answer questions about SBA’s disaster loan program, explain the application process, and help individuals complete their application. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an in-person appointment in advance at appointment.sba.gov.

BLM to Begin North Complex Wild Horse Gather in Nevada to Prevent Suffering in Winter
Organization:
Media Contact:
CARSON CITY, Nev. – The Bureau of Land Management will begin a wild horse gather tomorrow, Oct. 17, in and around the North Complex Herd Management Areas in northwest Nevada, to protect the health of the herd as late season forage declines and winter approaches. The gather, the first since January 2012, will help to reduce the risks wild horses face when the range can no longer support the current population.
The North Complex includes the Dogskin Mountains, Flanigan, and Granite Peak Herd Management Areas. Horses may appear healthy at the start of the fall, but forage and water resources are limited, especially in areas affected by the Bug Fire. With far more wild horses on the landscape than the range can sustain, competition intensifies, creating conditions that can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, and long-distance travel in search of food and water as winter sets in.
The North Complex’s healthy, sustainable herd size is 101-157 wild horses, but the 2026 population estimated nearly 424 wild horses within and just outside the Complex; more than three times what the land can support. Removing approximately 320 excess horses is necessary to relieve pressure on limited food and water resources, support long-term herd stability, and prevent winter suffering. The decline in forage has been further intensified in the Dogskin Mountains and Granite Peak Herd Management Areas following the 2026 Bug Fire.
With seasonal change already underway, lowering herd numbers now ensures the remaining horses have access to the food and water they need to make it through winter safely. A balanced herd size also helps protect sensitive wildlife species such as sage grouse, pronghorn antelope, and mule deer and supports progress toward the “Standards for Rangeland Health” identified by the Sierra Front–Northern Great Basin Resource Advisory Council.
The BLM’s Sierra Front Field Office will manage the gather. BLM staff and contractors will follow the Comprehensive Animal Welfare Program, which uses proven, science-based practices to ensure humane care. Crews maintain a controlled approach that keeps horses moving at a steady pace. All gathered animals will be transported to the Litchfield Wild Horse and Burro Corrals to receive veterinary evaluation and care and then prepared for placement through the BLM’s Adoption and Sales Program.
The public lands within a five-mile radius surrounding drive trap sites and temporary holding facilities will be temporarily closed to all forms of public access in accordance with 43 C.F.R. § 8364.1 to ensure that the gather is effective and safe for wild horses, BLM employees and contractors, and members of the public.
However, the BLM will provide public observation opportunities during the gather. Members of the public are welcome to view the gather operations provided that doing so does not jeopardize the safety of the animals, staff and observers, or disrupt gather operations. The BLM will escort the public to gather observation sites located on public lands. Those wanting to view the gather operations must RSVP by calling 775-885-6150 no later than 5 p.m. the day before they want to observe gather operations. Callers will be contacted with specific instructions on each day’s meeting location and time by 9 p.m. the evening before.
The gather plan documents can be viewed on the BLM National NEPA Registry. Daily gather reports and additional information will be posted on the gather website.
The BLM’s Wild Horse and Burro Program is grounded in science, law, and humane‑care standards and adheres completely to the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act and other federal laws. The BLM does not send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and no loophole exists that would legally allow people who adopt or buy wild horses to ever sell animals directly or to middlemen for slaughter.
Information on how to adopt or purchase a wild horse or burro can be found on the BLM Wild Horse and Burro Program webpage.
The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.
title: BLM to Begin North Complex Wild Horse Gather in Nevada to Prevent Suffering in Winter

Fast Facts
The National Nuclear Security Administration currently has its largest workload since the Cold War. It's overseeing a $200 billion, two-decade-long effort to modernize nuclear weapons and infrastructure.
We previously found that NNSA faced challenges recruiting and retaining skilled federal staff to meet its mission. In 2024, NNSA committed to rebuilding its workforce.
But in this Q&A, we reported that NNSA—in response to presidential directives in FY 2025—halted workforce planning and limited hiring. At the same time, employee separations increased significantly.
Consequently, NNSA has seen a 12% decrease in its federal staff since FY 2025.
Close-up of a person cutting the word jobs on paper with scissors
Highlights
What GAO Found
The National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) oversees a $25 billion annual budget and approximately 70,000 management and operating contractor personnel to maintain the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile and nuclear nonproliferation efforts. NNSA took steps to build its federal workforce to meet mission needs in 2024, with its workforce peaking at 1,991 early in fiscal year 2025. However, since then through the second quarter of fiscal year 2026, NNSA has reduced its federal workforce by 236 employees—or 11.9 percent. These reductions have impacted NNSA’s mission critical workforce, including occupations like nuclear engineers and contract specialists.
Number of National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) Federal Employees and Annual Appropriations, Fiscal Year (FY) 2023–FY 2026 Quarter (Q) 2
Note: The Federal Salaries and Expenses appropriation account funds the salaries, benefits, and other related expenses for most of NNSA’s federal workforce.
The reduction of NNSA’s workforce occurred because of two primary reasons: (1) very limited hiring and (2) employee separations—primarily employees choosing to retire or resign. Hiring was limited during the second quarter of fiscal year 2025 through the first quarter of fiscal year 2026.
Why GAO Did This Study
NNSA—a separately organized agency within the Department of Energy (DOE)—has a current workload that is at its highest level since the Cold War as the agency oversees a $200 billion, 2-decades-long effort to modernize nuclear weapons and related infrastructure.
In May 2024 (GAO-24-106167), GAO found NNSA continued to face challenges recruiting and retaining federal staff to meet the agency's mission needs, even though a statutory cap limiting the number of its federal employees was eliminated in fiscal year 2023. NNSA committed to developing a workforce planning process intended to inform future budget requests in response to its increased workload, the elimination of the cap, and consistent with GAO’s May 2024 report. The agency began building its workforce to meet mission needs in 2024. However, in response to presidential directives in early 2025, NNSA reduced the size of its federal workforce.
GAO was asked to examine NNSA’s retirements, resignations, terminations, and other voluntary or involuntary workforce reductions since January 2025. This report describes changes to NNSA’s federal workforce from the beginning of fiscal year 2023 through the second quarter of fiscal year 2026. GAO analyzed relevant NNSA data for workforce and personnel actions, including hires and separations, by program, office, and location. GAO also reviewed NNSA budget information and interviewed NNSA officials.
For more information, contact John Bumgarner at BumgarnerJ@gao.gov.
title: National Nuclear Security Administration: Reductions to Federal Workforce

text:
Fast Facts
The federal government spends billions of dollars every year to operate and maintain federal space—whether or not the space is being fully used.
A 2025 law requires agencies to collect and report data on the extent to which office space is being used. Many agencies said they were using or planning to use the data to dispose of unneeded space, which could save millions of dollars.
But the data doesn't offer a complete picture because it excludes some spaces that are vacant. And some agencies' collection and reporting of data isn't consistent with guidelines.
We recommended ways to improve future reporting to address this High Risk area.
Office area with empty cubicles.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Under the Utilizing Space Efficiently and Improving Technologies (USE IT) Act, enacted in January 2025, federal agencies are now required to collect and report occupancy data. This data is used to calculate utilization rates for agencies’ office space in federally owned buildings and leased locations. While 20 of the 23 agencies that responded to GAO’s survey reported using existing badging systems for this purpose, 16 of these 20 agencies reported supplementing that information with data from other sources such as daily check-in surveys. Nearly all agencies surveyed noted the importance of having easy to implement, cost-effective data collection approaches that they could put in place by the act’s July 2025 implementation deadline. Most agencies reported minimal costs associated with collecting and reporting USE IT Act data—collectively $16 million across 23 agencies in 2025.
Agencies’ Use of Approaches to Collect Occupancy Data, as of September 2025
Many agencies told GAO they are either using or plan to use their USE IT Act data to identify and dispose of unneeded real property. Some agency officials told GAO that they have already made decisions to consolidate or dispose of underutilized spaces, informed in part by USE IT Act data, and that they expect to save millions of dollars annually as a result.
However, the USE IT Act data submitted to Congress and the public in March 2026 does not have important context—including on GSA-controlled vacant space—needed to fully reflect office space utilization. Without this information, Congress and the public may have an inaccurate impression of the extent to which owned and leased office spaces are being utilized, including some locations that are likely being utilized at lower or higher rates than reported.
While surveyed agencies generally agreed that USE IT Act data are helpful, about one-third expressed concerns about how GSA data collection and reporting guidelines affect their utilization rate calculations. Further, some agencies described approaches to collecting and reporting their occupancy data that are inconsistent with GSA guidelines, resulting in data that are incomplete. For example, one agency reported the number of employees that are assigned to each location rather than measuring the extent to which employees were present in those spaces. By coordinating with agencies to improve the consistency and completeness of their occupancy data, GSA could better position agencies to make informed decisions about which underused spaces to prioritize for disposal, potentially leading to tens of millions of dollars in financial savings.
Why GAO Did This Study
Chronic underutilization of federal buildings is one of the main reasons that the management of federal real property has been on GAO’s High Risk list for more than 20 years. The USE IT Act requires the 24 Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Act agencies to collect and report occupancy data on the number of employees working in certain owned and leased spaces. It also contains a provision for GAO to review the costs to these agencies of this requirement to measure the occupancy and utilization rates of their spaces.
This report examines 1) the approaches CFO Act agencies reported using to collect the occupancy data required by the USE IT Act and their associated costs; 2) how agencies are using USE IT Act data to inform real property decisions and what additional information, if any, may help Congress and the public better understand federal office space utilization; and 3) agencies’ concerns about USE IT Act data collection and reporting and GSA’s actions to address these concerns.
GAO surveyed the CFO Act agencies about their data collection approaches, associated costs, and any limitations to their data or selected approaches. GAO also reviewed GSA guidelines for USE IT Act data collection, analyzed GSA data on vacant spaces, and conducted in-depth interviews with five agencies selected based on the variety of approaches to collecting occupancy data and the size of their real property portfolios.
Recommendations
GAO is making four recommendations to GSA to improve future office space utilization reporting, including that it provide data on vacant space to help fully reflect utilization. GSA did not agree or disagree but stated it would consider these recommendations.
title: Federal Real Property: New Occupancy Data Help Agencies Shed Unneeded Office Space But Gaps Limit the Full Picture

HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Sean Sakaida, 44, of Honolulu, Hawaii, was indicted on October 15, 2026, and charged with four counts of production of child pornography, four counts of distribution of child pornography, one count of receipt of child pornography, four counts of possession of child pornography, and one count of child sex trafficking. He was previously arrested and taken into custody on September 24, 2026, after being charged by criminal complaint.

According to court records, Sakaida, a former coach of the girls’ wrestling team at Moanalua High School, frequently communicated with a minor victim using the messaging application WhatsApp between 2025 and 2026. In these communications, Sakaida received multiple sexually explicit photographs of the minor victim. As charged in the indictment, he also produced and distributed multiple videos of himself engaged in sexual acts with the minor victim. Sakaida was also charged with enticing a second minor victim into engaging in a commercial sex act.

If convicted, Sakaida faces at least 15 years and up to 30 years in prison on each production count, at least 5 years and up to 20 years in prison on each distribution and receipt count, up to 10 years in prison on each possession count, up to life in prison on the sex trafficking count, a fine of up to $250,000, plus a term of supervised release.

The charges in the indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. In the case of conviction, any sentence would be imposed by a United States District Judge based on the statutory sentencing factors and the advisory United States Sentencing Guidelines.

The FBI is investigating the case.

Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Heidi Turner is prosecuting the case.

The FBI’s Honolulu Field Office is seeking to identify potential victims of Sean Sakaida. If you and/or your minor dependent(s) were victimized by Sean Sakaida or have information relevant to this investigation, please fill out this short form: https://forms.fbi.gov/victims/SakaidaVictims/view If you know of someone else who has possibly been victimized by Sean Sakaida, please encourage them to complete the form themselves.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .
title: Oahu Girls’ Wrestling Coach Indicted for Production, Distribution, Receipt, and Possession of Child Pornography and Child Sex Trafficking

COLUMBIA, S.C. — Four South Carolina law enforcement officers were honored for their achievements today at the 43 rd annual Strom Thurmond Awards for Excellence in Law Enforcement Luncheon. “In South Carolina, we proudly stand with the men and women of law enforcement who work every day to keep our communities safe,” said U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling. “These awards reflect our deep appreciation for their dedication and sacrifice. We’re grateful to partner with the South Carolina Law Enforcement Officers Association and the Strom Thurmond Foundation to recognize these outstanding public servants.” State, local, and federal law enforcement officials from across South Carolina attended the awards luncheon to celebrate these officers. The awards are presented by the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Law Enforcement Coordinating Committee, along with the South Carolina Law Enforcement Officers Association (SCLEOA) and the Strom Thurmond Foundation. The 2026 honorees are: City – Chief Chris Watts, Rock Hill Police Department

County – Sheriff Hobart Lewis, Greenville County Sheriff’s Office

State – Major Mayrant Jones Gamble, South Carolina Highway Patrol

Federal – Special Agent Craig Januchowski, FBI Columbia Field Office The Strom Thurmond Awards for Excellence in Law Enforcement were established by then Senator Strom Thurmond in 1983 to recognize law enforcement officers whose performances demonstrate the highest ideals of excellence in professional law enforcement. An annual award is given in each of the four categories: (1) city/municipal; (2) county; (3) state; and (4) federal. An awards committee composed of representatives from the U.S. Attorney's Office, the Strom Thurmond Foundation, the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, the South Carolina Sheriffs’ Association, the South Carolina Police Chiefs’ Association, SCLEOA, and past recipients selects the winners from nominations received from across the state.
