WASHINGTON — U.S. Army Pacific strengthens deterrence by positioning ready forces forward, training alongside allies and partners, and building the interoperability needed to operate together before a crisis begins, Gen. Ronald P. Clark said during a panel at the Association of the United States Army’s 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition Oct. 12.
Speaking during the Contemporary Military Forum, “Decisive Landpower: Deterrence and Partner Integration Against the Pacing Threat,” Clark emphasized that the distances across the Pacific make forward posture and sustained partner engagement essential to delivering combat-ready forces when and where they are needed.
“Our responsibility to deliver warfighting capability at the place and time of our choosing is really tied to posture,” Clark said, “The only way that we've been successful in the business of deterrence is to provide those forces at scale.”
Clark highlighted Operation Pathways, USARPAC’s exercise program, as a key way to strengthen readiness and relationships with regional allies and partners. He said the program includes 54 exercises over the course of a year, providing opportunities to train alongside partner forces on their own territory.
Those exercises help build the readiness needed to deter conflict and, if necessary, fight and win, Clark said.
He identified USARPAC’s priorities as “people, partnerships, and then our efforts to prevail in competition, crisis, and conflict,” underscoring the role of relationships and interoperability in the command’s approach to deterrence.
Training together also allows forces to develop trust, align procedures and improve the ability of their systems to work together. Clark stressed that these relationships must be built before a crisis, when forces may need to respond together under pressure.
Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command and U.S. Forces Korea, reinforced the importance of posture, protection and sustainment in maintaining a credible presence. He explained that the ability to remain effective in a location over time depends on having the right capabilities, protection and sustainment in place.
“If you can have the right posture, if you can be protected in the place where you are, if you can sustain yourself in that place, you've achieved endurance,” Brunson said.
Clark also highlighted the importance of developing people and strengthening interoperability across partner forces, including through noncommissioned officer development. He described NCOs as not only the backbone but also “the muscle of our formations,” emphasizing their role in building capable, integrated forces.
Together, forward posture, realistic training and enduring partnerships help USARPAC provide landpower that supports the joint force and strengthens deterrence across the Pacific.
title: USARPAC integrates allies and partners to strengthen deterrence, deliver decisive landpower

BANGOR, Maine: A Brazilian national was sentenced today in U.S. District Court in Bangor for reentering the United States after a prior removal.

U.S. District Judge John A. Woodcock, Jr. sentenced Jose Carlos Ferreria , 50, to time served (59 days). Ferreira pleaded guilty on September 4, 2026.

According to court records, on August 15, 2026, U.S. Border Patrol Agents in Franklin County observed a car registered to an alien who had been ordered removed from the United States. During a subsequent roadside immigration inspection, agents determined that the car’s three occupants were, in fact, illegal aliens without lawful authority to be in the country. They were transported for processing to the Rangeley Border Patrol Station, where agents determined that Ferreira had been ordered removed in 2005, and subsequently removed from the U.S. twice in 2010.

The U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case.

Operation Take Back America : This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

###

Reps Grijalva, Clarke Lead 63 Members of Congress in Urging USCIS to Address Processing Backlog Costing Lawfully-Present Immigrants Their Healthcare
    Friday, October 16, 2026
  
Tucson, AZ — Congresswoman Adelita S. Grijalva and Congresswoman Yvette Clarke, alongside 61 Members of Congress, sent a letter urging U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to immediately expedite pending green card applications for immigrants who have lost or are at risk of losing Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicare, and Affordable Care Act premium credits  as a result of new eligibility restrictions under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) that went into effect on October 1st.
The lawmakers warn that thousands of lawfully-present immigrants, including refugees, asylum recipients, and survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking, could lose access to critical healthcare while waiting for USCIS to process their green card applications providing permanent residency. More than 281,000 lawfully present immigrants across nine states and Washington, D.C., were identified as facing the loss of Medicaid coverage beginning October 1. Nationwide, the Congressional Budget Office estimates that 1.4 million lawfully present immigrants will become uninsured by 2034 under Republicans’ healthcare eligibility restrictions.
The letter highlights the case of an Arizona woman with stage four metastatic breast cancer who lost her Medicaid coverage on October 1. Although she is lawfully present in the United States, delays in processing her green card application have left her without coverage for the chemotherapy she depends on to survive.
The lawmakers argue that eligible applicants should not lose access to healthcare because their immigration applications are caught in processing backlogs.
“Because Lawful Permanent Residents (LPRs), that have already waited any required time, retain federal eligibility under health law, these individuals are losing their health insurance simply because they are trapped in a bureaucratic bottleneck. This is a backlog crisis that lies within the administrative capabilities of USCIS to resolve and the agency cannot allow its own administrative delays to cause catastrophic gaps in their healthcare,” the letter wrote.
They also warn that these delays could increase healthcare costs for federal and state governments by forcing patients to forgo preventive treatment until their conditions become more severe.
In their letter, the lawmakers call on USCIS to take three immediate steps:
- Establish an emergency expedited processing pathway for Form I-485 adjustment of status applications for individuals who face the imminent loss of healthcare coverage because their applications remain pending.
- Clarify expedited processing criteria to explicitly recognize the imminent loss of federal or state healthcare coverage as grounds for expedited processing under severe financial loss or humanitarian considerations.
- Coordinate with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and state agencies to provide guidance on delaying coverage terminations for individuals with pending adjustment of status applications.
“In Arizona, more than 20,000 lawfully present refugees and immigrants are at risk of losing their healthcare due to USCIS processing bottlenecks, including a woman with stage-four breast cancer and a nine-year-old boy with epilepsy who depends on Medicaid to attend school,” said Rep Grijalva. “These cuts, thanks to Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill, are forcing Arizona families to choose between their health and their financial security. USCIS needs to act with urgency so that their bureaucratic delays do not cost people their lives.”
"Needless red tape should never be the determinant between life and death,” said Congresswoman Yvette D. Clarke. “While thousands of immigrant American families remain stuck in a bureaucratic backlog that risks ripping their healthcare out from under them, USCIS has a moral obligation to ensure all those caught in its processing bottleneck do not suffer due to circumstances beyond their control. Government inefficiencies are not the fault of immigrant communities, and they deserve better than to suffer the consequences of them."
###
title: Reps Grijalva, Clarke Lead 63 Members of Congress in Urging USCIS to Address Processing Backlog Costing Lawfully-Present Immigrants Their Healthcare

MOBILE, AL – A Mobile man was sentenced to 63 months in federal prison for participating in a conspiracy to traffic cocaine and crack cocaine.

According to court documents, Rodney Antwaine Davis, 42, was arrested on November 9, 2023, after leading police officers on a high-speed chase through a residential neighborhood in Mobile. Davis crashed into a ditch and attempted to flee on foot but was apprehended by officers. During the arrest, officers seized $6,145 in cash and a plastic bag containing crack cocaine from Davis’s underwear. A chemist confirmed that the crack cocaine weighed 52.69 grams.

On March 20, 2025, federal agents obtained a warrant to search a package mailed from Houston, Texas, to an address on Johnston Street in Mobile under a fictitious name. The package contained more than two kilograms of vacuum-sealed powder cocaine and a bottle containing 300 alprazolam pills, as confirmed by laboratory testing. The following day, an undercover agent delivered the package to the residence on Johnston Street. Davis arrived and retrieved the package. Agents moved in to arrest him, but Davis fled into the house before being apprehended in a bedroom. At the time of his arrest, Davis had $5,734 in cash in his pocket. Agents also discovered a small amount of methamphetamine on a bed near where Davis was arrested and three bottles of promethazine syrup in Davis’s car, which was parked outside the residence. Agents seized and searched Davis’s cell phone, which contained messages and other data related to his drug-trafficking conspiracy.

U.S. District Judge Kristi K. DuBose sentenced Davis to a total of 63 months in prison, with his sentence adjusted to account for the 19 months he has spent in custody since March 2025. Upon his release from prison, Davis will serve four years of supervised release, during which he will be subject to drug testing. The ordered Davis to pay $100 in special assessments.

U.S. Attorney Sean P. Costello of the Southern District of Alabama made the announcement.

Homeland Security Investigations, the United States Postal Inspection Service, the Mobile Police Department, and the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Justin Roller prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States.
title: Mobile Man Sentenced to More Than Five Years in Prison for a Cocaine and Crack Cocaine-Trafficking Conspiracy

Spokane, Washington – First Assistant United States Attorney Pete Serrano announced that on October 14, 2026, United States District Court Judge Rebecca L. Pennell sentenced Nicholas Howard to five years in custody, to be followed by a life term of federal supervised release. Judge Pennell also ordered Howard to pay $31,000 in restitution to his victims and a $5,000 special assessment under the Amy, Vicky, and Andy Child Pornography Assistance Act of 2018. The United States argued for a term of imprisonment of 210 months, while Howard’s attorney, Bevan Maxey, requested the 60-month term ultimately imposed by the Court.

As reflected in court documents and public proceedings, Howard had a long history of viewing child pornography and hid his sexual interest in minors from friends and family for 20 years. On the Dark Web, Howard was a “senior member” of a website dedicated to child sex abuse and images memorializing that abuse. The Federal Bureau of Investigation reviewed 179 posts by Howard, where he communicated with other users and traded images and videos of child sex abuse material. Howard wrote in his posts of his attraction to children aged “7–14 years old” and said that that he “understood the appeal of being sexually active with a minor female” and that he “fantasized about this for decades.” Howard also shared that he “became sexually aroused” when explaining sex to his nine-year old daughter, that he “masturbated to minor females he knows or comes across in real life,” and that he “followed multiple minor aged females on Instagram to whom he masturbates to.” Howard wrote that “he would engage in sexual intercourse with his [11-year-old] daughter’s friend if he could” and appreciated that the website was “truly full of [his] people.”

The FBI executed a search warrant at Howard’s residence and seized a number of Howard’s devices. On Howard’s phone, the FBI discovered 223 images and 23 videos of child sex abuse material, including depictions of minors as young as toddlers. The footage included sadistic abuse of young, prepubescent girls. Howard also possessed videos of Nazi ideology and violent footage of adult women being hung and strangled. Howard’s phone further revealed that he had been viewing child sex abuse material just minutes before picking up his young daughters on the day of his arrest and used anti-forensic software to help delete and conceal evidence of his crime. AUSA Wick relied upon these aggravated facts to support the recommended sentence of 210 months.

“This defendant posed a significant risk to the community,” stated Serrano. “Without the extraordinary investigative efforts of the FBI and my office, Howard would have continued to engage in this egregious conduct, trafficking in images and videos depicting the sexual abuse of children on the Dark Web. This office remains committed to protecting the public and ensuring that individuals who engage in these offenses are brought to justice.”

“For decades, even leading up to right before his arrest, Mr. Howard repeatedly and incessantly harmed dozens of victims by accessing child abuse material,” said W. Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Seattle field office. “This digital media is impossible to erase from the internet and depicts these young people at the worst moments of their lives. The FBI and our partners will continue to hold child predators accountable.”

This case is being brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the U.S. Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals, who sexually exploit children, as well as to identify and rescue victims.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation Spokane Office and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Ann Wick.

News Release
US Department of Labor awards $81.5M in grants to support industry-driven job training programs in rural communities
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today announced the award of $81.5 million in funding to address the critical workforce needs of employers in high-growth and emerging industries across the Appalachian, Delta, and Northern Border regions.
Administered by the department’s Employment and Training Administration, the seventh round of Workforce Opportunity for Rural Communities program funding supports 13 projects across 11 states to stimulate employment and wage growth, as well as economic mobility, self-sufficiency, and increased labor force participation. The demonstration grants support the workforce needs of regional employers in predominantly rural areas to enable them to better compete economically and enable residents of the regions to obtain or retain family-sustaining employment opportunities so they can remain and thrive in their communities.
“These grants ensure those in our rural communities have a pathway to the training they need for in-demand jobs that feed a family and strengthen our supply chains,” said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “They help us advance President Trump’s goal of building the workforce for the Golden Age and enable more people to pursue the American Dream.”
The WORC Initiative is made available in partnership with the Appalachian Regional Commission, the Delta Regional Authority, and the Northern Border Regional Commission.
The grants will help provide industry-driven training, including Registered Apprenticeships, for new and dislocated workers, and those already in the workforce who need to learn new skills. These programs will focus on high-growth and emerging industry sectors such as skilled trades and construction, healthcare, information technology, manufacturing, domestic energy production, and business and professional services.

GRAND RAPIDS, MICHIGAN – U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Michigan Timothy VerHey today announced that Sefton Olivair Stewart, also known as “Powa,” age 41 of Montego Bay, Jamaica, was sentenced to 72 months in federal prison for his role in a nationwide scheme that fraudulently obtained $3.4 million from 28 victims, including a victim who resides in West Michigan. Stewart was sentenced by the Honorable Paul Maloney, United States District Judge. Stewart will be removed from the United States after he serves his prison sentence.

In July 2026, after being extradited from Jamaica to Grand Rapids by the U.S. Marshals Service, Stewart pleaded guilty to participating in a conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. Between October 2019 and September 2024, Stewart, co-conspirator Danielle Diarbakerly, and others participated in a scheme to defraud people in the United States by falsely telling the victims that they had won large prizes (cash and luxury vehicles) in a multistate lottery. To claim the prizes, the conspirators told the victims that they first had to pay taxes and fees associated with their winnings. All of this was false and the conspirators used fake bank and U.S. government documents to convince some victims to believe the fraudulent representations and promises. Diarbakerly, a Florida resident, previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and was sentenced to 37 months in federal prison for her role in the scheme.

U.S. Attorney Timothy VerHey said, “There are people out there, like Stewart and Diarbakerly, who have decided to make a career out of defrauding U.S. citizens. We are doing everything we can to send the message that such careers have no future. If you engage in fraud, we will find you no matter where you are, charge you, convict you and persuade a judge to put you in prison. Stewart got that message today. Other con artists out there need to get the message that it’s time to change careers.”

“Fraudsters who prey on victims with false promises of life-changing prizes will be held accountable, regardless of where they operate,” said HSI Detroit acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski. “HSI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to pursue transnational fraud schemes, bring offenders to justice, and protect communities from financial exploitation.”

“Fraud schemes like this leave real victims with significant financial and emotional losses,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Todd Strom, IRS Criminal Investigation’s Detroit Field Office. "Stewart and his co-conspirators used deception, fake documents, and false promises of large cash prizes and luxury vehicles to steal millions of dollars from victims across the country. IRS Criminal Investigation and our law enforcement partners remain committed to finding, investigating, and bringing to justice those who engage in fraud schemes that exploit the public. Those who believe they can hide behind international borders while defrauding Americans should know we will pursue them and hold them accountable."

The Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Grand Rapids office and IRS Criminal Investigation jointly investigated this case, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Chris O’Connor prosecuted it.

###
title: Jamaican Fraudster Extradited To Michigan Sentenced To Prison For His Role In Nationwide Fraud Scheme

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-FORT SAM HOUSTON, Texas—Mission and Installation Contracting Command contracting professionals are expanding the Army’s ability to address minor construction, repair and modernization requirements across seven installations through a regional contracting solution designed to increase agility, competition and responsiveness.
The National Capital Region Multiple Award Task Order Contract, or NCR MATOC, establishes a pool of 42 eligible contract holders that can compete for individual task orders supporting sustainment, renovation and modernization requirements, including minor construction, repairs and demolition.
With a ceiling value of around $1 billion and a maximum task order limit of $4 million, the 42 indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity (IDIQ) awards under the MATOC were released and effective on Sep. 14. The IDIQ awards include a 5-year ordering period plus two, one-year renewal options, supporting U.S. Army Garrisons at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Fort Belvoir, Fort Detrick, Fort Meade, Fort AP Hill, Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall and Arlington National Cemetery.
While MATOCs are not new contracting vehicles, this marks the first time MICC has developed this type of regional vehicle encompassing seven installations for this type of work, according to Lucy Lopez, director of the MICC Theater Support Center.
“This effort represents an initiative in which a new contract solution was sought to provide a multiple award, regional contract vehicle for minor construction and repairs,” Lopez said.
Danette Wilson, a TSC contracting officer, and Amy Hahka, a TSC contract specialist, led the team that awarded the MATOC. Wilson said the requirement presented an opportunity to apply a contracting approach not typically implemented by the TSC.
“In this instance, a MATOC was an outstanding solution in resolving a mission partner’s request that dates back to 2022 in which seven Army installations have similar sustainment, renovation and modernization requirements, including minor construction, repairs and demolition,” Wilson said.
The overarching statement of work allows the participating installations to use the regional vehicle for requirements within its scope while competing individual requirements at the task-order level. Wilson said the vetted pool of contractors encourages competition that can help deliver cost savings on mission partner requirements.
“There are 42 MATOC Holders on this vehicle which will foster healthy competition with each Request for Task Order Proposal, encouraging cost benefits to the Government and the American taxpayer,” Wilson explained.
This MATOC grew from an open Installation Management Command requirement dating back to 2022. MICC contracting professionals worked alongside IMCOM through several fiscal years to develop the solution for similar requirements across multiple installations.
“Across several fiscal years, we worked persistently and shoulder to shoulder with IMCOM to achieve this outcome,” Wilson said. “This was due to the efforts of an entire village with a common goal.”
The NCR MATOC is one example of MICC’s broader effort to match acquisition strategies to mission requirements. David Markelz, deputy director of MICC Contracting Operations, explained why MICC strived to use a broader range of acquisition authorities starting in fiscal year 2025, including Other Transactions Authorities (OTAs), Small Business Innovation Research Phase (SBIR) III and Multiple Award Task Orders (MATOCs) to address complex, multilayered regional requirements and expand opportunities for collaboration with industry.
“New legislation and updated Department of War guidance have enabled MICC to directly support construction and modernization requirements historically managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers,” Markelz said.
“By employing a broader array of acquisition authorities, the MICC is better positioned than ever to meet the evolving needs of the Army and deliver timely, mission‑focused results.”
Although each acquisition approach serves different requirements, they reflect MICC’s focus on developing responsive contracting solutions that support mission partners and Soldiers while promoting competition, flexibility and responsible stewardship of resources.
Wilson said the success of the NCR MATOC will likely renew interest in this type of contract vehicle when fair competition across multiple installations is a high priority.
“Should a future requirement present with the same or similar indicators as the NCR MATOC, and a MATOC vehicle appears to be a viable solution, we will absolutely entertain the use of a MATOC for future procurements,” Wilson said.
The NCR MATOC ultimately gives the MICC another way to turn sustainment, repair and modernization requirements into contracting actions for participating installations while demonstrating MICC’s commitment to delivering agile contracting solutions across the Army.
About the MICC
Headquartered at Joint Base San Antonio-Fort Sam Houston, Texas, the Mission and Installation Contracting Command consists of about 1,500 military and civilian members who are responsible for contracting goods and services in support of Soldiers as well as readying trained contracting units for the operating force and contingency environment when called upon. A subordinate command of the Army Contracting Command and the Army Materiel Command, MICC contracts are vital in feeding more than 200,000 Soldiers every day, providing many daily base operations support services at installations, facilitate training in the preparation of more than 100,000 conventional force members annually, training more than 500,000 students each year, and maintaining more than 14.4 million acres of land and 170,000 structures. See also the fiscal year 2027 MICC Fact Sheet.
title: MICC delivers regional contracting solution for seven Army installations

MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that Jeffrey Allen Petersen, 68, of Minnetonka, Minnesota, was found guilty on 10 counts of threatening to murder U.S. judges and elected officials, and 10 counts of interstate transmission of threats to injure.

A federal jury found Petersen guilty of all 20 counts on October 15, 2026, after a trial before U.S. District Judge Patrick J. Schiltz. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled by the Court at a date yet to be determined.

“My office has no tolerance for political violence and threats of political violence,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “We will prosecute—to the fullest extent of the law—those who intimidate or threaten public servants who are just doing their jobs.”

“Threats against federal judges and lawmakers strike at the heart of our judicial system and our democracy,” said FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson. “The FBI Minneapolis Joint Terrorism Task Force will investigate and disrupt individuals who attempt to intimidate or harm public officials. At a time when Minnesota communities are especially mindful of political violence, this conviction on all 20 counts reflects the strength of our partnerships and our unwavering commitment to protecting those who serve the public.”

According to court documents and evidence introduced at trial, in July 2025, the U.S. Marshals Service for the District of Maryland received a report from their judicial security intelligence unit regarding threatening comments posted to an article on a website referencing a federal judge in that District. On at least one website, Petersen used the username, “Adam Lanza,” the mass murderer who shot and killed 26 people, 20 of whom were school children between the ages of six and seven years old, at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012.

Image 1: Online post from Petersen

Image 2: Online post from Petersen

The U.S. Marshals Service investigated the post and found it was made with an IP address assigned to Petersen with a service address in Minnetonka, Minnesota. The U.S. Marshals Service then referred the matter to the FBI.

During the investigation, law enforcement received additional reports concerning similar threatening comments posted on other sites toward federal judges and various elected officials throughout the United States. The username of some of the posts was “Behring.a,” and the full registered account name was, “Anders Breivik Behring.” Breivik is the name of the mass murderer who shot and killed 77 people in 2011 at a summer camp in Norway in “support of white supremacy.” The username for some of the other posts was “james holmes,” the 2012 Aurora Colorado theater mass murderer who killed 12 people and injured 62 others during a mass shooting event. The investigation revealed that the IP address of these usernames also traced back to Petersen in Minnesota.

Image 3: Online post from Petersen

Image 4: Online post from Petersen

After learning that Petersen was the registered user for the accounts making the threatening posts on various platforms, federal law enforcement agents obtained and executed a federal search warrant at Petersen’s Minnetonka residence and recovered several electronic devices, which were later forensically examined. The forensic examinations showed that Petersen used the associated email addresses that were used to make the threatening posts on various online platforms. Law enforcement additionally found a June 2025 web search history on one of Petersen’s devices with terms including, “MN senators shot,” “adam lanza,” “anders brevik,” and “james holmes.” In total, Petersen’s posts threatened to murder eight federal judges, including an Associate Supreme Court Justice, and at least four elected United States Officials.

This case was the result of an investigation by the U.S. Marshals Service and the FBI, with assistance from other federal and local law enforcement partners.

Assistant United States Attorneys Albania Concepcion, Michael Blackburn, and Benjamin Bejar are prosecuting this case.
title: Federal Jury Finds Minnetonka Man Guilty on All Counts for Threatening to Murder Federal Judges and Elected Officials

FORT WAINWRIGHT, Alaska — Army Community Service staff at Fort Wainwright are highlighting support resources and raising awareness across the installation during Domestic Violence Awareness Month this October.
The ACS Family Advocacy Program team - including program specialist Eldotha Fields and domestic abuse victim advocates Susan Hesser and Toney Price - are engaging the community through an outreach booth at the post’s Exchange main entrance hall.
"This year, as in any other year, we'd like to spotlight those survivors," Fields said. "We'd like to spotlight those people that we might have lost to domestic violence. We also want to encourage people to support those folks and to reach out to us at Army Community Service if they need any resources."
The Fort Wainwright ACS team stresses that domestic abuse extends beyond physical violence to include emotional manipulation, financial control, digital abuse and threats involving pets. Advocates help individuals recognize concerns, connect with confidential resources and make informed decisions about their next steps.
Being in rural Alaska brings unique challenges; by working together and strengthening ties with off-post community partners, such as the Interior Alaska Women's Center and the Fairbanks Native Association, the Fort Wainwright team can extend the availability of resources and the understanding of local needs on and off the installation.
"Our main goal is to make sure that we can provide the resources that they need, so they can make their own decisions," Price said.
ACS offers 24/7 advocate support via its victim advocacy hotline at (907) 799-9770. Community members can also visit the Family Advocacy Program office on the second floor of the Fort Wainwright Welcome Center, Building 3401 on Santiago Ave.
Community members looking to connect with advocates can visit the ACS outreach booth at the Main Exchange on Oct. 23 and Oct. 30 from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Whether you need support or want to help someone you care about, ACS is here for you. Safe, respectful relationships strengthen our community, and we all have a role in preventing abuse.
title: Fort Wainwright Family Advocacy Team spotlights outreach, awareness

FORT DETRICK, Md. – A single unit of blood on the battlefield can be the difference between life and death for an injured Soldier.
Recognizing that reality, personnel across Fort Detrick joined together Oct. 2 to donate 30 units of blood during a U.S. Army Medical Logistics Command-hosted blood drive.
The drive, coordinated in partnership with the Armed Services Blood Program, or ASBP, produced enough blood products to support up to 90 service members, veterans, military families and civilians worldwide.
Every whole-blood donation collected can be separated into three essential components – red blood cells, platelets and plasma – directly supporting trauma care, surgical operations and critical clinical needs in both deployment environments and military medical treatment facilities.
Beyond its lifesaving potential, the effort also saved the military medical system more than $8,000 in blood procurement costs, according to ASBP estimates.
For AMLC, the event served as a direct operationalization of the command’s core priorities of people, mission and partnerships.
“Through the collection of 30 units of blood, AMLC and our mission partners demonstrated how unified effort saves lives, sustains medical capability and strengthens resilience of the joint force,” said Col. Deon Maxwell, AMLC commander.
The donor pool reflected a broad joint and interagency community footprint across Fort Detrick. Personnel participated from AMLC, the 6th Medical Logistics Management Center, Defense Health Agency, Defense Logistics Agency, U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command, U.S. Navy and Air Force.
“The event reinforced the critical importance of partnerships,” AMLC Command Sgt. Maj. Andrew DeCola said. “Collaboration among AMLC, the Armed Services Blood Program and the many tenant organizations represented in Building 693 enabled the command to make an immediate, measurable contribution to force health protection and readiness.”
Organizers noted that events like this give personnel an immediate way to embody selfless service, while directly reinforcing joint force health protection.
Headquartered at Fort Detrick, AMLC, a major subordinate command to U.S. Army Communications-Electronics Command, serves as the Army’s Class VIII medical materiel command, delivering integrated medical logistics that enables Army and Joint Forces readiness from the strategic support area to the tactical edge.
title: AMLC hosts Fort Detrick blood drive, supports warfighter readiness

text:
Fast Facts
The National Institutes of Health is the largest public funder of biomedical research. Foreign entities' efforts to misappropriate or gain unauthorized access to this research could undermine U.S. national security and economic competitiveness.
NIH relies heavily on disclosures from researchers and institutions to identify and manage foreign interference risks. But foreign interference often involves undisclosed conflicts of interest or commitments. Therefore, it's important for NIH to determine when additional controls, such as verifying disclosures, may be needed.
We recommended ways that NIH could better manage foreign interference risks.
Front entrance of a National Institutes of Health building.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) funds extramural research through awards to universities and other institutions. Implementation of federal research security requirements helps safeguard this research from foreign interference, including misappropriation and unauthorized access by foreign countries and entities.
NIH implemented 14 of the 15 federal research security requirements GAO reviewed that address: (1) disclosure, (2) malign foreign talent recruitment programs, (3) research security training and programs, and (4) collaboration and information sharing. These requirements apply across federal research agencies and include actions NIH must take, as well as requirements it must impose on grant applicants, recipients, and specified individuals. For the remaining requirement concerning certification by certain recipient institutions that they have established and operate research security programs, NIH is working with an interagency group to implement the requirement.
NIH relies heavily on self-reported information disclosed by researchers and institutions to identify and manage foreign interference risks and generally does not verify such disclosures using sources outside those required during pre-award risk assessments unless it receives a foreign interference allegation. Additionally, NIH does not require disclosure of all past affiliations, and foreign component disclosures are only required when the collaboration involves the performance of a significant element or segment of the NIH-funded project outside of the United States. As a result, NIH may not identify risks when relevant information is not required to be disclosed or is left out.
From 2017 through 2025, NIH received 697 allegations of potential foreign interference involving personnel on NIH awards. NIH identified disclosure violations in 264 cases, and NIH or recipient institutions took one or more actions in most of those cases, such as prohibiting individuals from participating on awards.
NIH Allegations of Potential Foreign Interference and Outcomes, 2017–2025
Source: GAO analysis of National Institutes of Health data. | GAO-27-107848
In seven nongeneralizable case studies, GAO used outside sources to identify publicly available information about foreign affiliations and coauthored publications that did not appear in the award documentation. These cases do not establish the prevalence of undisclosed information or foreign interference across NIH awards but illustrate potential limitations of NIH’s disclosure-based process.
NIH’s risk management program is fully aligned with GAO’s enterprise risk management practices but not fully aligned with GAO’s Fraud Risk Framework. Although NIH’s annual risk inventory considers fraud, it is not a documented extramural-program-specific assessment of fraud schemes, controls, and residual risks. Without such an assessment, NIH lacks a documented basis for determining whether its controls and monitoring activities address the most significant fraud risks and are adjusted as those risks evolve.
Why GAO Did This Study
The U.S. has long promoted an open and collaborative research environment, but policymakers have raised concerns that foreign countries and entities may exploit the openness of the federally funded research enterprise to undermine national security and economic competitiveness. In fiscal year 2025 alone, NIH awarded about $35 billion in extramural funding.
GAO was asked to review NIH’s efforts to safeguard extramural research from foreign interference and related ethical concerns. This report examines, among other things: (1) NIH’s implementation of selected federal research security requirements, (2) the extent to which NIH identifies and manages foreign interference risks in its extramural research program, and (3) the alignment of NIH’s risk management policies and practices with GAO risk management practices.
GAO reviewed relevant legal authorities, policies, and NIH documentation; analyzed NIH foreign interference allegation data from 2017 through 2025; conducted seven nongeneralizable case studies of NIH awards selected based on their potential for heightened foreign interference risk; compared NIH practices with GAO risk management frameworks; and interviewed NIH and Department of Health and Human Services officials.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that NIH regularly conduct and document a fraud risk assessment tailored to NIH’s extramural research program that considers foreign interference risks. NIH concurred with the recommendation.
title: Research Security: NIH Action Needed to Strengthen Foreign Interference Risk Management

text:
Any non-citizen who illegally votes in American elections will be arrested and held accountable
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, a non-citizen, for knowingly making a false claim of United States citizenship to vote in the 2024 general election.
On September 10, a federal grand jury in the District of Minnesota returned the two-count indictment charging Chaudhari with allegedly making the false citizenship claim. According to the indictment, on or about November 5, 2024, Chaudhari signed the voter signature certificate required by Minnesota law to vote in the general election. The certificate required him to swear or affirm that he was a citizen of the United States. The indictment alleges Chaudhari was not a U.S. citizen and knowingly made the false citizenship statement in order to vote.
Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari
“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration will never allow the votes of American citizens to be cancelled out by non-citizens illegally voting in our elections. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.”
“Voting is reserved for U.S. citizens, and falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot is a serious crime,” said HSI St. Paul Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard. “HSI has the experience and authority to investigate these cases, and we take that responsibility seriously. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect the integrity of our election systems.”
Chaudhari is charged with one count of false information in voting and one count of making a false claim of citizenship in order to register to vote or vote. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on each count.
# # #
title: ICE HSI Arrests Non-Citizen for Illegally Voting in the 2024 Election

RIVERSIDE, California – A twice-deported illegal immigrant from Mexico has been arrested on a federal criminal complaint charging him with possessing approximately 360 kilograms (793.7 pounds) of cocaine in his San Bernardino County apartment, the Justice Department announced today.

José María Mena Rosales, 38, of Fontana, was arrested on Wednesday and is charged with possession with intent to distribute cocaine.

Rosales made his initial appearance on Thursday in United States District Court in Riverside. United States Magistrate Judge David T. Bristow ordered Rosales released on $50,000 bond. No plea was taken. Rosales’s arraignment is scheduled for November 10.

According to an affidavit filed with the complaint, in February 2026, law enforcement investigating a Mexico-based drug trafficking organization learned that a large quantity of cocaine was to be delivered in four suitcases to Rosales at a public parking lot in Fontana. Rosales later retrieved the cocaine from the parking lot and drove to his apartment, where he unloaded the suitcases of narcotics into a garage.

Law enforcement executed a search warrant at Rosales’s garage and apartment and seized approximately 360 kilograms of cocaine spread across 17 cardboard boxes. The four empty suitcases were found in the garage. Law enforcement officers confirmed Rosales’s identity with his California driver’s license and found several cell phones that contained text messages between Rosales and the individual who arranged the cocaine delivery.

According to court documents, Rosales was deported from the United States in May 2014 and June 2014.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

If convicted, Mena would face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in federal prison and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison.

The FBI is investigating this matter with assistance from the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department.

Assistant United States Attorney Courtney N. Williams of the Transnational Organized Crime Section is prosecuting this case.
title: Twice-Deported Illegal Alien from Mexico Arrested on Federal Complaint Charging Him with Possessing 360 Kilograms of Cocaine

WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury today released Treasury International Capital (TIC) data for August 2026. The next release, which will report on data for September 2026, is scheduled for November 18, 2026.
The sum total in August of all net foreign acquisitions of long-term securities, short-term U.S. securities, and banking flows was a net TIC inflow of $199.8 billion. Of this, net foreign private inflows were $178.5 billion, and net foreign official inflows were $21.3 billion.
Foreign residents increased their holdings of long-term U.S. securities in August; their net purchases were $300.7 billion. Net purchases by private foreign investors were $257.8 billion, and net purchases by foreign official institutions were $42.9 billion.
U.S. residents increased their holdings of long-term foreign securities, with net purchases of $21.6 billion.
After including adjustments, such as estimated foreign portfolio acquisitions of U.S. stocks through stock swaps, overall net foreign purchases of long-term securities are estimated to have been $279.2 billion in August.
Foreign residents decreased their holdings of U.S. Treasury bills by $47.8 billion. Foreign resident holdings of all dollar-denominated short-term U.S. securities and other custody liabilities decreased by $37.8 billion.
Banks’ own net dollar-denominated liabilities to foreign residents decreased by $41.6 billion.
Complete data are available on the Treasury website here.
###
About TIC Data
The monthly data on holdings of long-term securities, as well as the monthly table on Major Foreign Holders of Treasury Securities, reflect foreign holdings of U.S. securities collected primarily on the basis of custodial data. These data help provide a window into foreign ownership of U.S. securities, but they cannot attribute holdings of U.S. securities with complete accuracy. For example, if a U.S. Treasury security purchased by a foreign resident is held in a custodial account in a third country, the true ownership of the security will not be reflected in the data. The custodial data will also not properly attribute U.S. Treasury securities managed by foreign private portfolio managers who invest on behalf of residents of other countries. In addition, foreign countries may hold dollars and other U.S. assets that are not captured in the TIC data. For these reasons, it is difficult to draw precise conclusions from TIC data about changes in the foreign holdings of U.S. financial assets by individual countries.
title: Treasury International Capital Data for August 2026

ATF and law enforcement partners conclude Operation Show Me Justice
435 dangerous offenders arrested, 166 illegal firearms seized, 81 kg illicit drugs off the streets in St. Louis
WASHINGTON — The Department of Justice, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, U.S. Marshals Service, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Missouri, and others today announced the conclusion of Operation Show Me Justice, an ATF-led high‑impact violent crime enforcement surge in St. Louis.
The DOJ-sponsored operation was a whole‑of‑government initiative led by ATF and carried out in close coordination with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Missouri and in partnership with the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, United States Marshals Service, Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, and other federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies.
“Operation Show Me Justice demonstrates exactly what happens when federal, state, and local partners unite behind a single mission: protecting communities from violent criminals,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “The results speak for themselves. Dangerous criminals are off the streets, their weapons are out of circulation, and families in St. Louis are safer today than they were before.”
“Operation Show Me Justice delivered the kind of decisive action the public should expect from ATF,” said ATF Director Rob Cekada. “We removed violent offenders from the street, cut off their access to firearms, and dealt a significant blow to the criminal networks endangering this community.”
“By removing these dangerous firearms from St Louis, together, we have achieved unprecedented results, not just for the partners who participated in Operation Show Me Justice, but for all the residents, commuters, students, and visitors to the Gateway City,” said Director Gadyaces S. Serralta of the U.S. Marshals Service.
“We in St. Louis are very grateful for the women and men of ATF who left home, came to our community, and faced daily danger to assist in this enforcement effort,” said U.S. Attorney Thomas C. Albus for the Eastern District of Missouri. “Just as important, we are grateful to all local, state, and federal law enforcement and prosecutors who fight violent crime every day and who will remain. We are in this for the long haul and want so much to help continue to drive down violence for the health and safety of our city that we love.”
“Driving down violent crime takes relentless follow-through, and our partnership with ATF and our other law enforcement partners helps us turn local intelligence into cases that hold violent offenders accountable,” said St. Louis Metropolitan Police Chief Robert J. Tracy. “Operation Show Me Justice builds on that daily collaboration and our commitment to lasting progress — so every neighborhood can experience a safer St. Louis.”
Photo of law enforcement as part of Operation Show Me Justice.
The operation focused on violent criminal conduct and the illegal supply of firearms to violent offenders. During the operation, ATF and its partners arrested more than 435 violent offenders, including individuals with histories of possessing machine guns illegally, carrying stolen firearms, resisting arrest, violating felon‑in‑possession laws, engaging in straw purchasing, and committing other serious weapons-related offenses.
Agents, officers, analysts, and prosecutors combined local intelligence with ballistic leads from the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network (NIBIN) and insights from crime‑gun tracing to drive investigations forward. This coordinated approach enabled investigators to connect shootings, link firearms to multiple crime scenes, identify gun and drug trafficking patterns, and develop leads that otherwise would remain isolated across jurisdictions.
Photo of illegal guns, ammunition, and narcotics seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
Photo of an illegal gun seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
NIBIN compares ballistic evidence from crime scenes with test‑fired shell casings from recovered firearms, generating actionable leads. Crime‑gun tracing tracks a firearm’s commercial history, from the manufacturer or importer to its first retail sale. When paired with traditional investigative work, these tools help investigators identify shooters, associates, firearms traffickers, and sources of crime guns fueling violence.
Operation Show Me Justice has delivered significant enforcement results in St. Louis, with 435 criminal arrests and 166 firearms seized to date. Participating agencies have cleared 412 warrants, including the execution of 32 search warrants, and seized 81 kilograms of drugs, six machine gun conversion devices, and more than $1.25 million in currency related to suspected illegal firearms and drug transactions.
Photo of individual arrested during Operation Show Me Justice.
Photo of illegal guns seized as a result of Operation Show Me Justice.
###
ATF protects American communities from violent crime driven by the illegal use of firearms, explosives, and acts of arson. Through crime gun intelligence, forensic analysis, and relentless investigation, we identify and arrest violent offenders and gang members, dismantle trafficking networks, and sever the supply chains arming cartels, prohibited persons, and terrorist organizations. We defend the rights of law-abiding citizens by safeguarding lawful commerce and upholding the Constitution of the United States. Learn more about what ATF is doing to reduce violent crime in your community by following us on X @ATFHQ, Instagram @ATFHQ, LinkedIn @ATF, and Facebook @HQATF, or on the web at www.atf.gov.
title: ATF and law enforcement partners conclude Operation Show Me Justice

CHIÈVRES AIR BASE, Belgium – For military installations, energy resilience means more than simply reducing energy consumption, it means ensuring critical operations can continue even when the primary power supply is disrupted. U.S. Army Garrison (USAG) Benelux partnered with USA Girl Scouts Overseas (UGSO) to introduce young learners to renewable energy, energy resilience and the importance of maintaining a reliable power supply at military installations, on Oct. 10, 2026, at Chièvres Air Base (CAB), Belgium.
The Girl Scouts explored the operational solar field on CAB to learn about renewable energy, grid reliability, and science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).
Mélanie Chaballe, USAG Benelux Directorate of Public Works energy manager, brought the science to life with hands-on displays and guided the scouts through an energy roadmap.
“We are trying to raise awareness to the community about what the garrison does in regard to energy security and resilience,” said Chaballe. “If we have an electric power outage, we want to make sure we have some resilient ways to sustain and maintain power to keep the mission running.”
CAB currently harnesses solar arrays to generate electricity during peak daylight hours. By diversifying the power sources with renewable generation, backup generators and upcoming battery-storage capabilities, the garrison actively reduces vulnerability to disruptions and sharpens operational readiness.
For the visiting Girl Scouts, those industrial solar panels served as the backdrop for discovery. Equipped with questions designed to turn them into field investigators, the participants examined how photovoltaic cells capture sunlight before putting the principles to work by designing and racing miniature solar-powered cars.
The collaborative event also marked a milestone for the broader scout community, coinciding with the launch of a worldwide science, technology, engineering and science (STEM) initiative.
"We are launching a new energy patch that will be available to girls all over the world," said Erin Twamley, USA Girl Scouts Overseas STEM program partner. "We wanted to coordinate with our military bases on energy resiliency, so we reached out to the Directorate of Public Works to ask if we could partner with USAG Benelux and explore the solar field that helps power Chièvres Air Base."
By combining high-level military readiness with accessible, hands-on experiments, the collaboration showcased how military installations can bridge the gap between classroom theory and real-world technology.
Understanding energy resilience does not require an engineering degree, it begins with curiosity, a little sunlight and the opportunity to test what is possible. For USAG Benelux, the afternoon was an investment in both present readiness and future capability, securing today's power grid while inspiring the next generation of engineers who may one day design it.
title: Operational energy meets hands-on discovery

Fast Facts
Service Member Records: DOD Needs to Address Improper and Delayed Releasing of Personnel and Health Information.
The Department of Defense is a primary recordkeeper of the personnel and health records that service members accrue during their military careers. DOD must safeguard and process them in a timely manner.
But the military services reported almost 50 improper releases of records affecting more than 1,000 service members from fiscal years 2021-25. It also saw the volume and complexity of requests for personnel records increase amidst staffing challenges.
And as we previously reported, DOD's use of multiple data systems for its health records has complicated its records release process.
We made several recommendations to address these issues.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Service members can accrue a large volume of personnel and health records during their military careers. The custodians of these records are the Department of Defense (DOD) and the Department of Veterans Affairs. DOD and the military services developed policies and procedures to properly adhere to federal laws for safeguarding records and timely processing records requests. However, the risk of breaches and delays exists. For example, GAO covertly tested 26 requests for records from DOD; of the 18 processed requests, one was improperly released and did not redact personally identifiable information.
Examples of Breaches of Military Records Among Record Custodians
Personnel records. The military services have procedures intended to safeguard records, such as redacting personally identifiable information. However, of the thousands of requests received during fiscal years 2021 through 2025, the services reported 49 breaches. The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requires agencies to respond to requests within 20 business days, and Privacy Act requests are generally processed within 20 business days. According to military service officials, staffing limitations across the military services contribute to challenges with the proper and timely processing of records requests. For example, during the time of GAO’s review, the Navy had one employee processing FOIA requests, which officials stated contributed to an increased average processing time from 1.6 to 55.5 days. With a clearer understanding of the staffing levels needed to manage the volume and complexity of FOIA and Privacy Act requests, DOD and the services would be better prepared to improve response time, reduce the improper release of information, and minimize exposure to litigation costs.
Health records. GAO found that the Defense Health Agency (DHA) relies on a complex record processing system to access service member health records, which leads to challenges in processing requests. Request processors identify health records among multiple data systems and review them to redact personally identifiable information. DHA officials stated that system issues and complex workflows challenged request processing. Multiple officials stated that the redaction process can be the most cumbersome part of fulfilling requests, particularly if the record is large or contains scanned documents. GAO previously reported that DOD determined the multiple legacy electronic health record systems that it implemented over the past 3 decades to manage patient health information required modernization, and that DOD sought to replace these legacy systems with a comprehensive electronic health record system. However, DOD has not assessed the current framework and systems for processing health records requests to identify opportunities to streamline them.
Why GAO Did This Study
Accessing military service records can be complex, due partly to the number of entities involved in creating, retrieving, and maintaining this information. FOIA entitles the public to request access to federal agency records, while the Privacy Act of 1974 governs how personally identifiable information is released. The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) establishes national standards for safeguarding protected health information.
House Report 118-125, accompanying a bill for the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, includes a provision for GAO to review DOD’s release of service member records pursuant to FOIA or other requests. This report examines the extent to which DOD has established policies and procedures and has taken steps to address any challenges in the proper and timely release of service members’ personnel and health records.
GAO reviewed relevant laws and DOD policies and processes governing the release of service member records. GAO also reviewed data on records requests and breaches; interviewed relevant officials; visited all four military services’ personnel centers and selected military medical treatment facilities; and conducted a covert test of internal controls to protect personnel records for 26 records requests.
Recommendations
GAO is making five recommendations, including that DOD conduct a workforce planning analysis to ensure staffing levels align with current and projected requests for processing personnel records, and identify opportunities to streamline systems used for processing health record requests. DOD generally concurred with the recommendations.
title: Service Member Records: DOD Needs to Address Improper and Delayed Releasing of Personnel and Health Information

The Department of the Air Force executed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A Collaborative Combat Aircraft from an F-22 Raptor earlier this month, advancing efforts to rapidly develop, evaluate and deliver mission-autonomy capabilities to the warfighter.
During the demonstration, an F-22 pilot served as an airborne “quarterback,” issuing high-level tactical directives to a single YFQ-44A. The aircraft’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed those directives in real time, conducting dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.
“This achievement demonstrates what is possible when we are aligned with industry on a shared imperative: delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. “We are driving urgency into every part of acquisition from rapid integration and flight learning to disciplined assessment, so we can turn promising technology into combat capability at the pace the threat demands.”
The event brought together personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group, Experimental Operations Unit, F-22 System Program Office and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch.
The Department will use data from this test milestone to inform continued software integration, developmental testing and the Air Force’s future CCA concepts.
“This flight shows the power of crewed-uncrewed teaming and the advantage it provides our warfighters,” said Gen. Ken Wilsbach, Chief of Staff of the Air Force. “We must test often, learn fast and give commanders what they need, when they need it.”
The CCA program is part of a broader Department of the Air Force effort to deliver affordable, adaptable and combat-ready capability at speed. The Air Force intends to have 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet size of 1000 that will extend reach, awareness and survivability of American airpower in contested environments.
title: F-22 directs Collaborative Combat Aircraft in airborne tactical-control demonstration

LAKEWOOD – Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen (CO-07) today announced her effort demanding answers from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) about new Trump Administration guidance that could jeopardize addiction treatment and other essential services funded through state Medicaid programs. In Colorado, those programs support residential and inpatient treatment, in large part because of Pettersen’s work as a state legislator.
 
Last year, Donald Trump and Congressional Republicans made a historic, nearly $1 trillion cut to Medicaid in their One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), provisions which Pettersen has introduced legislation to repeal. But now, Trump’s Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has released guidance expressing the Administration’s intent to “reduce federal [Medicaid] outlays,” ringing alarm bells that the Administration is attempting to further cut Medicaid after devastating cuts could leave over 7 million people without health care. With changes potentially taking effect as early as January 1, 2027, Pettersen led eight other members in pressing CMS to preserve existing services and state flexibility—and provide clarification within 10 days of receiving their letter.
 
“Like so many Americans, my mom was overprescribed opioids when she hurt her back when I was just 6 years old, which led to a decades-long addiction. When she was cut off from her prescription opioids without access to treatment, my mom turned to heroin and fentanyl to avoid withdrawal. I watched her being turned in and out of the ICU from overdoses while begging for help with nowhere to go. In my fight to save my mom’s life, I saw firsthand how broken our healthcare system was,” said Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen.
 
Pettersen continued, “Medicaid did not cover treatment for those who were struggling with addiction, so I fought to change that —drawing down hundreds of millions of dollars a year for the critical care people desperately need. But everything we have done to address the opioid epidemic in this state is being dismantled by Trump and Republicans. That’s why I’m demanding answers and fighting back.”
 
This recent guidance from CMS is described as “early notice” ahead of forthcoming rulemaking, leaving states to prepare for potentially significant changes without these final requirements. States must navigate that uncertainty while implementing the broader Medicaid changes in H.R. 1. Pettersen and her colleagues are pressing CMS to explain its expectations before disrupted funding becomes disrupted care.
 
For more than six decades, Section 1115 Medicaid waivers have allowed states to test new approaches, expand benefits, and improve access to care. Colorado uses this flexibility to cover inpatient and residential substance use disorder treatment. Access to that care helps people recover while reducing costly emergency care and hospitalizations.
As a state legislator, Pettersen passed legislation directing Colorado to seek a waiver covering residential and inpatient addiction treatment. That waiver took effect in 2021. Today, up to an estimated 20,000 people annually access licensed residential and intensive substance use disorder services, with nearly 50,000 Coloradans receiving support across the continuum of care each year.
Over the program’s first five years, Colorado expanded its residential treatment provider network, integrated medication-assisted treatment and naloxone into emergency departments, primary care settings, and community health clinics, and expanded inpatient mental health coverage. Colorado has also reported a 35% decline in fentanyl-related deaths, highlighting the importance of sustaining efforts to prevent overdoses and connect people with treatment.
 
Nearly one-third of all Medicaid spending flows through these Section 1115 demonstration projects. Changes to their financing could affect care nationwide, including long-standing programs that patients and providers already depend on.
Inspired by her mom’s struggle, Congresswoman Pettersen has fought to expand access to treatment to help people like her mother receive the care they need. Pettersen is also a co-chair of the Bipartisan Mental Health and Substance Use Task Force, a coalition of over 100 members from both parties that work together to advance evidence-based policies that address the root causes and impacts of the mental health and addiction crises. 
See the full text of the letter HERE and below.
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
We write today in response to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) June 11th,  2026 State Medicaid Director letter (SMDL) sent regarding “Budget Neutrality and Certification by the Chief Actuary of CMS for Section 1115 Medicaid Demonstration Projects.” This guidance was issued to implement a provision of H.R. 1 that requires the CMS Chief Actuary to certify that section 1115 demonstration projects are budget neutral – a standard all section 1115 demonstration projects have been required to meet. Concerningly, however, the guidance clearly states an intent to “reduce federal outlays” – in other words, proposing additional federal cuts to Medicaid beyond the nearly trillion dollars cut through H.R. 1.
 
Section 1115 demonstration projects are the backbone of many state Medicaid programs, and states have long been required to ensure that they are budget neutral. For over six decades, demonstration projects have ensured that states have the flexibility to be innovative and meet the needs of their residents. For example, states rely on these demonstration projects to provide enhanced benefits to enrollees, expand coverage, and improve delivery systems to ensure people are able to access the quality care they need and deserve, among other priorities. CMS’s June 11thSMDL and forthcoming rulemaking stand to undermine these initiatives by setting forth a framework for upending long-standing budget neutrality requirements, and leaving states with more questions than answers about what standards they will need to imminently conform to.
 
Given the unique nature of each state demonstration project and each state’s Medicaid population, regular collaboration between the states and CMS have always been pivotal to ensuring states’ continued adherence to budget neutrality requirements. Instead of allowing states to foster creative solutions to meet the needs of their unique Medicaid population, CMS’ new framework threatens to reduce state flexibility, limit innovation, and narrow the approval pathway for certain health care initiatives.
 
Additionally, this guidance prompts numerous questions notwithstanding an incredibly compressed implementation timeline. Now, while working to operationalize massive changes to Medicaid programs as established by H.R. 1, states will also be required to interpret this complicated new framework and evaluate the implications for their own existing or proposed demonstration projects—even without final, robust guidance from CMS. In addition to the complexities of this new proposal, CMS indicated that the SMDL would only serve as “early notice” to inform changes expected from CMS’ imminent notice of proposed rulemaking. Given the changes taking effect as early as January 1, 2027, this timeline imposes a severe administrative burden on states, and leaves them in an operational limbo. Nearly one-third of all Medicaid spending flows through section 1115 demonstration projects and changes to disrupt the financing of these programs will have a direct impact on the health care that Medicaid beneficiaries across the country may receive. 
 
Section 1115 demonstration projects have had a profound impact on our local communities nationwide. Given the importance of these programs, we ask that CMS carefully consider the implications of this guidance on states and their Medicaid beneficiaries. We have concerns that this new blanket framework will limit states’ ability to innovate and threaten existing services. Considering our concerns, we ask that the agency keep beneficiaries at the forefront, by preserving state flexibility to utilize section 1115 demonstration projects to best serve their residents. We also that the agency provide states with further clarification on the expectations of the June 11th guidance within 10 days of [receiving this letter]. 
 
We appreciate your attention to this matter.
 
Sincerely, 
 
U.S Representatives Brittany Pettersen (CO-07), Ritchie Torres (NY-15), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Joe Neguse (CO-02), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), and Yvette Clarke (NY-1)

﻿Final rule restores longstanding framework, respects state wildlife management authority and local participation, while maintaining federal subsistence priority and NPS conservation responsibilities

Interior_Press@ios.doi.gov

WASHINGTON — The Department of the Interior and the National Park Service today announced a final rule restoring the longstanding Alaska-specific regulatory framework governing wildlife harvest, subsistence-related activities and certain public access procedures in national parks and preserves across Alaska.

The rule restores much of the regulatory framework developed under the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980 that guided management of Alaska national parks and preserves for more than three decades. The action advances President Donald J. Trump’s direction under Executive Order 14153, Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential, and Secretary’s Order 3422 of the same name, issued by Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum.

“For more than three decades, Alaska’s national parks and preserves were managed under a framework that recognized Alaska’s unique circumstances, respected the State’s role in managing fish and wildlife, protected subsistence uses and conserved these remarkable lands and resources,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “This final rule restores that commonsense framework and gives Alaskans a stronger voice in decisions affecting the lands, wildlife and traditions they know best, while ensuring the National Park Service continues to protect park resources for future generations.”

ANILCA established a management framework for Alaska that differs in important ways from much of the National Park System. The law provides for subsistence uses in certain Alaska park areas and allows sport hunting and trapping in national preserves under applicable state and federal law. The framework also recognizes distinct but complementary responsibilities among the State of Alaska, the Federal Subsistence Management Program and the National Park Service and provides opportunities for local participation in decisions affecting subsistence and other authorized uses.

“ANILCA recognizes that managing national parks and preserves in Alaska requires an approach tailored to the state’s unique landscapes, communities and traditions,” said Don Striker, Alaska regional director for the National Park Service. “This rule restores a longstanding framework that strengthens local participation and recognizes the State’s role in wildlife management while maintaining the National Park Service’s responsibility to conserve these extraordinary places for future generations.”

The final rule rescinds regulatory changes adopted in 2015, 2017 and 2024 and restores key elements of the longstanding Alaska-specific framework that preceded them. Among other changes, the rule:

Restores public hearing requirements for certain closures and restrictions affecting fish and wildlife harvest and locally focused notification procedures, including newspaper, radio and post office notices and publicly available maps.﻿ ﻿

Removes certain restrictions added after 2015 affecting subsistence activities, including requirements associated with the collection of nonedible animal parts for handicrafts and methods used for subsistence bear harvest. ﻿ ﻿

Restores the application of state-authorized wildlife harvest methods in national preserves where consistent with applicable federal law.

The rule does not amend ANILCA or change the federal subsistence priority established under Title VIII. Under ANILCA, qualified rural Alaska residents receive a priority for subsistence uses of fish and wildlife on federal public lands when resources are limited. The Federal Subsistence Management Program continues to administer that priority. The rule also does not diminish National Park Service authority or responsibility to conserve park resources and protect visitors.

The rule maintains distinct but complementary management responsibilities. The State of Alaska continues to manage fish and wildlife except where federal law provides otherwise; the Federal Subsistence Management Program administers the federal subsistence priority on federal public lands; and the National Park Service continues to conserve park resources, protect visitors and manage Alaska park areas consistent with ANILCA and other applicable federal laws.

The National Park Service completed an Environmental Assessment and Finding of No Significant Impact in accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act. The analysis determined that implementation of the rule will not result in significant impacts to the human environment.

The final rule will publish in the Federal Register on Oct. 19, 2026 and will take effect 30 days after publication. To view the final rule once published, visit www.federalregister.gov and search for document #2026-21299.
