Man Convicted at Trial for His Role in North American Drug Trafficking Organization That Transited Through Los Angeles
A member of a Canadian-based drug trafficking organization that moved large amounts of narcotics throughout North America was convicted at trial on the afternoon of October 16, 2026, in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles.
David Joner, 58, a known trafficker from Fall City, Washington, was found guilty on October 16, 2026, of one count of conspiracy with intent to distribute and possess with intent to distribute cocaine, and one count of conspiracy to export cocaine.
Joner was one of 16 defendants indicted by a federal grand jury in 2019 as part of Operation “Dying Declaration,” a joint FBI and Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) investigation which targeted a large drug trafficking organization (DTO) which was based in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.
According to the indictment, the DTO, which was led by defendant Tenny Guon Lim, a convicted Canadian drug trafficker also known as “The Goat” and “Max Power,” sent multi-kilogram quantities of Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA), also known as “ecstasy” or “molly,” to the United States in exchange for multi-kilogram quantities of cocaine, which was obtained by U.S.-based associates in Mexico. Lim is currently in Canada pending extradition to the U.S. Through the investigation, agents learned that the DTO used encrypted digital devices to communicate.
The cocaine obtained in Mexico was exchanged for MDMA in the Los Angeles area. The cocaine and MDMA were transported between Los Angeles and Canada either directly or through Washington state, with the help of Washington-based associates of the DTO. The DTO transported cocaine and methamphetamine from the Los Angeles area to Canada for resale in exchange for bulk quantities of MDMA or for currency. Joner worked for the Washington cell of the DTO and trafficked numerous multi-kilogram sized loads of cocaine from the Los Angeles area to Canada.
Seven defendants charged in the case have been convicted. Nine defendants are pending prosecution.
This case was investigated by the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, and the LAPD. It was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California.
title: Man Convicted at Trial for His Role in North American Drug Trafficking Organization That Transited Through Los Angeles

Gas and grocery prices continue to soar under Trump, costing New Mexican families $3,400 more
WASHINGTON, D.C. – On October 16, 2026, U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) released a new report detailing how much prices have spiked under the Trump Administration, costing New Mexicans $3,400 on average.
"This report confirms what New Mexicans already know: this Administration is squeezing them for everything they’ve got,” said Vasquez. "New Mexicans can’t afford the consequences of Trump’s economy – while the rich get richer, New Mexicans struggle more and more, and it’s only getting worse. My Affordability Agenda would help get us out of this mess and focus the work of Congress on supporting our working families – not billionaires.”
Read the full report HERE.
In addition to this report, Rep. Vasquez released a report in April detailing how much energy prices have spiked since the Administration took control in January 2025:
- Annual energy bills went up by an average of $70 per New Mexico family in 2025 compared to 2024.
- New Mexico has consistently ranked among the top states nationally for highest gas price jumps since the war started.
Since introducing his Affordability Agenda to lower the high cost of living in New Mexico, the Congressman has:
- Introduced the Tax Relief from Tariffs and High Costs Act to offer a fully refundable 10% tax credit to households making under $100,000 to offset rising prices — under this bill, a New Mexican making $70,000 could expect around $700 back in their pocket to offset higher prices caused by tariffs.
- Cosponsored the Capping Prescription Costs Act, which caps annual prescription drug costs at $2,000 for individuals and $4,000 for families with private health insurance plans.
- Cosponsored two bills — the Bipartisan Families First Housing Act and the Stop Wall Street Landlords Act — to address New Mexico’s housing affordability crisis by cracking down on greedy, corporate landlords to ensure hardworking New Mexicans have a fair shot at homeownership.
- Has introduced legislation to roll back harmful cuts to food assistance enacted under the Republican tax law, fighting to feed our veterans, seniors, children, and hardworking families.
- Introduced the Energy Bills Relief Act to bring down utility bills for hardworking New Mexicans by cutting red tape, speeding up permitting processes to get more energy projects online, expanding the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program and more.
- Supported the Tipped Income Protection and Support (TIPS) Act to permanently end tax on tips for those making under $112,500.
- Introduced the Boost the Middle Class Act to increase eligibility for the Earned Income Tax Credit, allowing more working New Mexican families to receive higher tax refunds each year.
- Pushed for the passage of his Keep Mobile Homes Affordable Act, which would crack down on rent price gouging and utilities neglect by predatory investors who have purchased 2,500 or more manufactured housing units since 2015.

text:
Fast Facts
The Department of Energy cleans up nuclear waste at contaminated sites. To make cleanup decisions, DOE—together with state and federal regulators—considers health risks to people who may use the land in the future for residential, industrial, or conservation purposes.
We looked at how DOE considers future land use when making cleanup decisions.
Future residential land has stricter cleanup standards and usually costs more
DOE has transferred or leased cleaned-up land at 5 sites for industrial use
Transferring land to communities or private entities can have benefits, such as economic growth; and drawbacks, including potential recontamination
Cranes and construction equipment demolishing a building
Highlights
What GAO Found
The Department of Energy (DOE) created initial future land use plans in coordination with local communities as early as 1992 at six cleanup sites GAO selected for review. These plans inform but do not bind assumptions about future land use that DOE and regulators make when selecting a cleanup remedy at a site. The remedy selected during the cleanup process has lasting consequences for how a parcel of land can be used, even after DOE transfers or leases it to another federal agency, a state or local government, or a private party. For example, any future use that would increase exposure to residual contamination above the contemplated level could undermine the protectiveness of the remedy. Accordingly, assumptions about future land use provide a framework for the range of uses that are safely available for a given parcel after cleanup.
The Department of Energy’s (DOE) General Process for Identifying Future Land Use and Subsequent Cleanup and Transfer Decisions at Selected Cleanup Sites
At the Oak Ridge, Paducah, Portsmouth, and Savannah River sites, DOE and regulators established cleanup levels that aligned with DOE’s initial future land use plans for these sites. DOE agreed to clean up most of the contaminated areas at these sites to support industrial use. For nearly a third of the Hanford site and most of the contaminated areas of the Idaho site, DOE and regulators set more stringent cleanup standards than needed to meet DOE’s anticipated conservation, preservation, or industrial uses for the land. However, while they agreed to cleanup standards based on residential use, future residential use is unlikely. They said it would be difficult to go back and calculate the cost difference between cleaning up to support residential and the other uses, but others noted cleaning up to support residential use is typically more costly.
DOE has transferred or leased a small amount of land to the community or private entities for industrial use at five of the sites. DOE recently announced new initiatives for energy development, integrated hubs for nuclear fuel cycle activities, or co-located data centers to support artificial intelligence infrastructure. Some community stakeholders have expressed interest in more land transfers, and they generally expressed support for industrial reuse. DOE officials and stakeholders cited some potential benefits, such as economic growth, high-quality jobs, or local tax revenue. They also cited potential drawbacks, such as taking focus and resources away from cleanup, pollution and site recontamination risks, and future DOE liabilities.
Why GAO Did This Study
DOE is responsible for cleaning up sites contaminated from decades of nuclear weapons production and research. DOE estimates cleaning up 15 remaining sites will cost between $641 billion and $840 billion and be completed in 2100. When making cleanup decisions, DOE and its regulators assess risk to people who may use the land in the future—such as for industrial or residential purposes—to inform its approach and set cleanup standards.
Senate Report 118-188 includes a provision for GAO to report on DOE’s future land use planning at cleanup sites. This report describes (1) DOE’s role in future land use determinations, (2) how cleanup decisions align with initial land use plans, and (3) what land DOE has transferred or leased to local communities.
GAO reviewed laws, regulations, policies, and agency documents at six sites selected to represent a range of regulatory frameworks, stages of cleanup, and future land uses. GAO visited two of the sites and interviewed DOE officials, regulators, tribal officials, and community stakeholders.
Recommendations
In a related October 2026 report on defense nuclear waste (GAO-27-107791), GAO recommended that Congress consider clarifying DOE’s and regulators’ roles and decision-making authority in determining future land uses. GAO also recommended, among other things, that DOE direct cleanup sites to evaluate cleanup costs and schedule based on multiple potential future land uses as part of its cleanup decisions. Implementing these recommendations would help DOE link future land use assumptions with cleanup decisions in more transparent and cost-effective ways.
title: Nuclear Waste: Future Land Use Planning at Selected DOE Cleanup Sites

Congressman Al Green Secures $900,000 in Federal Funding for Houston Fire Department’s New Mobile Stroke Unit Launch
(Houston, Texas) — On Monday, October 19, 2026, Congressman Al Greenwill join Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher, the City of Houston, the Houston Fire Department (HFD), and Memorial Hermann for a press conference celebrating the launch of HFD’s new Mobile Stroke Unit (MSU) service. In 2022, Congressman Green secured $900,000 in federal funding to support the purchase of the new unit for the Houston Fire Department.
Through a partnership with Memorial Hermann, the unit will expand access to lifesaving emergency stroke care and bring Houston closer to achieving comprehensive Mobile Stroke Unit coverage.
“When someone has a stroke, every minute matters,” said Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher. “Mobile Stroke Units (MSU) bring diagnosis and treatment directly to patients, and they work. Research that began here in Houston in 2014 found that for every 100 patients an MSU treats, 27 have less lasting disability, and 11 recover with no disability at all. The $900,000 I secured for the Houston Health Department’s Mobile Stroke Unit is already helping patients, and with this new Houston Fire Department unit, made possible by Congressman Al Green’s work, more Houstonians will get faster care when it counts. I am grateful to Mayor Whitmire and the City of Houston for their commitment to expanding this life-saving service across our city, and I will continue working to make innovative treatments like this more accessible to people across our community.”
Congressman Al Green stated, “I am proud to have secured $900,000 in federal funding to help bring this life-saving initiative to fruition through our partnership with the City of Houston, the Houston Fire Department, and Memorial Hermann. This is more than an investment in emergency medical services; it is an investment in saving lives, preventing lifelong disabilities, and protecting the well-being of our communities. No person should suffer preventable, permanent disability because critical medical care could not reach them in time. We must continue to make health care a priority for all and ensure that federal resources serve the people who need them most.”
title: Congressman Al Green Secures $900,000 in Federal Funding for Houston Fire Department’s New Mobile Stroke Unit Launch

Office of the Spokesman

October 16, 2026

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau will travel to Asunción, Paraguay, and Buenos Aires, Argentina, from October 19 to 26. Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura will join the Deputy Secretary.

In Asunción, the Deputy Secretary will lead a trade delegation of U.S. companies to explore investment opportunities in Paraguay. Deputy Secretary Landau will also meet with senior Paraguayan government officials to reaffirm the historic U.S.-Paraguay strategic partnership. They will discuss ways to expand trade and investment, deepen cooperation on regional security, and combat transnational crime.

In Buenos Aires, the Deputy Secretary will meet with senior Argentine government officials and private sector leaders to build on the momentum of the U.S.-Argentina launch of the Andes-Atlantic Corridor during the UN General Assembly High-Level Week. The Deputy Secretary’s travel reflects the Trump Administration’s commitment to a safe, secure, and prosperous Western Hemisphere.

FORT KNOX, Ky. — Finances are like a football game.
The goal is to win, so you need a solid defense, a vibrant offense, and a smart strategy that moves the ball toward the endzone.
With persistent high prices and elevated interest rates burdening today’s economy, understanding the differences between saving and investing has never been more important. The line between capital preservation and wealth accumulation is the cornerstone of any sound financial plan.
A simple rule of thumb is: “Saving protects your present; investing profits your future.”
Saving is your financial defense.
The main purpose of saving is to preserve capital as well as provide liquidity, meaning your money is easy to access for emergencies and short-term needs. It is designed to guarantee stability.
If you expect to need your money within the next three years for a home or car down payment, upcoming taxes, college expenses and more, you should save up for them. The rationale is simple; you do not want to risk losing principal right before you need to use funds.
Common places to hold savings might include high-yield savings accounts (HYSA), certificate of deposits (CDs), money market accounts and Treasury bills (T-Bills).
These options are conservative, cash-equivalent instruments ideal for low-risk, interest-bearing storage. They carry very little risk of principal loss, especially because the accounts are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per institution. They also provide strong liquidity, being able to provide funds either immediately or within a few business days.
Maintaining three to six months of liquid emergency reserves is one of the best ways to avoid being forced into debt when unexpected expenses arise.
Investing is your financial offense.
Investing requires accepting market volatility in exchange for the opportunity to earn returns that outpace inflation – the silent wealth destroyer – and build long-term wealth through compounding.
If your time horizon is five years or more, such as planning for retirement or creating a long-term family legacy, investing is an important path. Certainly, the risk of inflation eroding your purchasing power is far more dangerous than short-term ups and downs in the stock market.
The goal of investing is long-term growth by accumulating funds for the future. Investment assets might include index funds – a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund ETF that mimics the performance of the market index, like the S&P 500 or Dow Jones – stocks, bonds and workplace retirement plans, like the Thrift Savings Plan, 401(k)s and real estate.
The primary risks are market volatility and fluctuations in principal value. However, investments can also act as a natural hedge against inflation since businesses may raise prices over time, which can help preserve long-term purchasing power.
Historically, long-term investing has produced average annual returns in the range of 6-10%. The trade-off is reduced liquidity and, in some cases, heavy taxes or penalties that may apply for early withdrawal. Also, selling during market dips can lock in losses.
Understanding when to play defense and when to deploy offense is the cornerstone of sustainable financial health.
So, how do saving and investing perform in current market pressures?
For savers, higher interest rates have created opportunities to earn more money than in recent years. However, money left in low-yield savings or standard checking accounts may still lose purchasing power if inflation exceeds the interest earned.
Debt: a gamechanger.
If you carry credit card balances or high-rate personal loans, especially with an APR higher than 8%, paying them off should be your top priority. Eliminating high-interest debt that can charge 22% or higher is a rate that neither a savings account nor the stock market can compete with.
Avoid draining your liquid cash to pay off debt. It is still wise to build a “rainy day” account and maintain a modest emergency cushion while paying down high APRs. It is just as important to invest as much as you can to gain benefit from compound interest over time.
Securing your present and mobilizing your future must work together to produce a winning strategy. Determine your financial goals to ensure the future you envision is fully funded.
For financial questions, make an appointment with an Army Community Services financial counselor in-person or by calling 502-624-5989.
Visit Fort Knox News at www.army.mil/knox for Central Kentucky's latest military news and information.
title: Save, invest, and tackle debt: Don’t let personal finances, fickle economy fumble your future

CLEVELAND – A 31-year-old man has been charged for his role in a conspiracy where he allegedly agreed to be paid to enter into a sham marriage to allow a co-conspirator to illegally obtain a green card.

A federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Jingming Chen, 31, of Quincy, Massachusetts, with Conspiracy to Commit Marriage Fraud and Immigration Document Fraud.

According to allegations in the indictment, Chen, a U.S. citizen, was paid by a Chinese national co-conspirator residing in Aurora, Ohio, to enter into a sham marriage and commit immigration document fraud by fabricating evidence to support the false claim that their marriage was legitimate.

They submitted false statements to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS) to obtain lawful permanent resident status—commonly known as a Green Card—and other immigration benefits for the co-conspirator. To carry out the conspiracy, Chen allegedly agreed to receive partial payment at each step of the green card process as they were completed. Chen and the co-conspirator discussed creating a false backstory of their online romance and long-distance relationship, including how they met and who introduced them. They also went so far as to discuss obtaining a prenuptial agreement and opening various joint accounts for banking, cellphone service, insurance, and a discount store membership card.

Eventually, the two filed an intent to get married in Quincy, Massachusetts, and Chen directed the co-conspirator to buy a cheap, fake diamond ring to use for the wedding ceremony. After they married, Chen directed a preparer to submit his USCIS Form I-130, “Petition for Alien Relative,” to document his relationship with a foreign national which would pave the way for the co-conspirator to obtain a green card.

The Homeland Security Investigations Cleveland office and the USCIS-Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate in Boston conducted the investigation preceding the indictment.

Assistant United States Attorney Brian M. McDonough is leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

If convicted, the defendant faces up to five years in prison. The court will determine the sentence after reviewing the factors unique to this case, including the defendant’s prior criminal record, if any, the defendant’s role in the offenses, and the characteristics of the violations.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division investigates and prosecutes those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An indictment is merely an allegation. A defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud

Justice Department Reaches Settlement Agreement with City of Lexington, Mississippi, Regarding Lexington Police Department’s Unlawful Police Practices
The Justice Department announced today that it has obtained an out-of-court settlement agreement with the City of Lexington, Mississippi, to remedy certain violations described in the Department’s Sept. 26, 2024, findings report. Specifically, the Department found that the Lexington Police Department (LPD) engages in a pattern or practice of civil rights violations.
“The Department of Justice supports local law enforcement” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights division. “We are very pleased that the City of Lexington and the Lexington Police Department reached an agreement to enhance the lawful and essential activities of the police department and its officers as they continue to protect and serve the citizens of Lexington and its surrounding areas.”
“Today’s agreement reflects a shared commitment to meaningful and sustainable change” said U.S. Attorney J.E. Baxter Kruger for the Southern District of Mississippi. “Through these reforms, we seek not only to address the concerns identified in our investigation, but also to strengthen public trust and promote practices that respect the rights and dignity of every person.”
As part of the agreement, the City and LPD will amend policies and practices regarding fines and fees, bail and release criteria, and potential conflict of interests. LPD will also revise its policies and practices regarding stops, searches, arrests, and use of force policies and update its reporting and review of such activities by officers.
The Department looks forward to working cooperatively with the City and LPD to ensure that they remedy the alleged violations.
The Civil Rights Division’s Special Litigation Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Mississippi initiated the investigation in March 2023 under 34 U.S.C. 12601 which authorizes the Department to take action to remedy a pattern or practice of deprivation of constitutional rights by state or local law enforcement agencies.
Additional information about the Civil Rights Division’s work regarding the conduct of law enforcement agencies is available on its website at: www.justice.gov/crt/conduct-law-enforcement-agencies.
title: Justice Department Reaches Settlement Agreement with City of Lexington, Mississippi, Regarding Lexington Police Department’s Unlawful Police Practices

WASHINGTON — The Army is rewriting the playbook on how it partners with the private sector. At a contemporary military forum on the Strategic Capital Initiative during the Association of the United States Army 2026 Annual Meeting, senior Army leaders and commercial executives sent a clear, unified message: the Army is doing business differently than ever before.
The panel explored how SCI is bridging the gap between national defense and private capital focused on six strategic pillars. Panelists highlighted how the Army is cutting through red tape and rigid acquisition rules by actively leveraging Commercial Solutions Openings (CSOs), public-private partnerships and enhanced use leases (EULs) to work at the speed of trust and capital.
Panel members echoed Acting Secretary of the Army Adam R. Telle opening remarks that the service “needs to build adaptable and symbiotic relationships with both industry and service partners to maintain a strategic advantage over the nation’s adversaries.”
Lt. Gen. Gavin Lawrence, deputy commanding general and acting commander of Army Materiel Command, emphasized that AMC is leaning heavily into these innovative, particularly across the Army’s 23 Organic Industrial Base sites.
“The government defines a problem, we send it out to commercial industry, and we let commercial industry do what they do best – innovate and bring solutions,” said Lawrence. “We're not bounding commercial industry by our constraints. We give them the clearly defined problem, what it is important, and then let American ingenuity go to work.”
Lawrence outlined four critical lessons the Army and private industry must embrace to make these CSOs successful.
First, he noted that the Army has a responsibility to clearly define its requirements and problem sets, but conversely, industry must feel empowered to speak up if there is a lack of understanding. Ensuring clear conversations and a shared vision upfront prevents costly misalignments down the road.
Second, he highlighted the importance of understanding statutory guardrails and respecting the legal boundaries that distinguish government operations from the private sector. He said for example, within the OIB, certain core functions are inherently governmental, and operations must comply with statutory regulations like the 50-50 rule, which dictates the balance of military and commercial depot maintenance work.
Third, Lawrence called for a clear, mutual understanding of the value proposition on both sides from the very beginning. He said, while the Army is focused on increasing production capacity, lowering acquisition costs, and accelerating capability delivery to the warfighter, the military must also recognize that commercial partners have obligations to their stakeholders, including expectations for return on investment and profit.
Fourth, he emphasized the need to balance these guardrails without binding or inhibiting the innovation that commercial industry brings. He explained that the government must establish boundaries without over-constraining its partners.
‘We need to be working at the speed of trust, and trust is based on communication and understanding each other,” said Lawrence. “Speed absolutely matters, so if there is something we are not thinking about, help us get to the right place.”
Under the SCI framework, the Army is already utilizing CSOs to implement advanced manufacturing flexible lines to resolve parts obsolescence and enhance readiness. At Red River Army Depot, a partnership with Hadrian is establishing a flexible line for battery production to support drone dominance and manufacture tactical wheeled vehicle repair parts. Additionally, Anniston Army Depot is collaborating with Siemens to onshore manufacturing capabilities for small Unmanned Aircraft System stator systems and produce parts for heavy armored fleets.
Industry panelists echoed the enthusiasm for this collaborative evolution. Chip Chattelier, Vice President, Business and Technology Strategy, FedEx Dataworks, commended the Army's willingness to lean in.
“The single most effective way to accelerate private investment is to bring industry in earlier, even before putting pen to paper, to understand the ground truth of the mission,” said Chattelier. “By doing so, partners can move past reactive, static dashboards and implement ‘predictive logistics intelligence’ to anticipate supply chain disruptions and prevent readiness impacts before they happen.”
title: American ingenuity at work: The Army’s Strategic Capital Initiative

October 16, 2026
WATCH: Pressley Slams Trump, Duffy for Unlawful Cancellation of $20M Grant for Roxbury Transit Improvements
“The people of Roxbury have made their priorities clear. They have shown up, spoken up, and helped envision what a safer, healthier, more connected neighborhood can look like. Our responsibility now is to make sure that vision does not get taken away from them. Roxbury has waited long enough.”
Last Month, Pressley, Wu Announced a Lawsuit Against the Trump Admin. to Protect Critical Investment in Roxbury Street Infrastructure
ROXBURY – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) joined Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and local leaders at a press conference to condemn the Trump Administration’s unlawful withdrawal of a $20 million federal grant for critical street infrastructure improvements along three major corridors in Roxbury. In her remarks, Congresswoman Pressley underscored the transformative nature of this project and robust community input from Roxbury residents, who deserve to see this project move forward after decades of divestment and underinvestment in their community.
Last month, Congresswoman Pressley and Mayor Wu announced that the City of Boston is filing a lawsuit challenging the Administration’s illegal withdrawal of the funds, which Rep. Pressley helped deliver to fund safety, transit, accessibility, and traffic flow improvements to essential roadways in Roxbury. The grant, awarded to the City in 2022 under the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity (RAISE) Grant Program, would fund the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project, including state of good repair, safety, transit, accessibility, and traffic flow improvements to Melnea Cass Boulevard, Malcolm X Boulevard, and Warren Street.
A transcript of Congresswoman Pressley’s remarks is available below and the video is available here. For video of the full press conference, click here.
Transcript: Pressley Slams Trump, Duffy for Unlawful Cancellation of $20M Grant for Roxbury Transit Improvements
October 15, 2026
Boston, MA
Well, it is always good to be home, to be in the Massachusetts 7th, to be in the City of Boston, and certainly to be in the historic neighborhood that is Roxbury.
I only wish that I was here for a celebration and not to report a crime. This is theft.
The grant that was awarded after a competitive process was exactly that: awarded.
It was not charity. It was an investment long overdue, and one that was consistent with the visioning of community about what is needed here.
So it feels good to be home. I wish we were coming together for a different reason.
Under this 2.0 version of the Trump Administration, I decided early on that our strategy to combat the lawlessness of this administration would be to combat it with the rule of law, and that we would use litigation, we would use legislation, we would use agitation, we would use organization, we would use mobilization.
And that is what is necessary to resist and do everything we can to ensure that these funds that are owed are reinstated. I am grateful to our mayor for being exhaustive in defense of this federal investment.
I want to underscore the investment part. Every disparate outcome in the Massachusetts Seventh, including and especially where Black folks are concerned, is not naturally occurring.
It is the result of policy choices and federal divestment, and that is why this fight matters.
When we talk about transportation, we are talking about much more than just how to get from point A to point B. What does it matter if we do the work collectively of making a city more affordable, more livable, if you can’t navigate it?
This is about whether or not a parent can get their child to school safely. This is about whether or not an elder can get to a doctor. This is about whether or not a worker can get to their job without spending hours in transit. This is about whether or not people can breathe clean air and safely move through their own neighborhood.
There is a statistic that has been ingrained in my mind from my early work on transit justice, beginning on the Boston City Council, and it’s why I founded the Future of Transportation Caucus in Washington to fight for federal investment in transportation that centers equity, accessibility, connectivity, and sustainability. But the statistic that stays in my mind is from Livable Streets, and their report that said the average Black Boston bus rider was riding, waiting, transferring an additional 60 hours a year.
Now that might sound nominal, but that means that people are not experiencing a quality of life because they are in limbo. They are riding, waiting, transferring to get to work, to get to healthcare, to get to childcare, to get to church, or any place else they would like to.
And that is exactly why I advocated alongside community and our mayor to secure a $20 million federal investment for the Roxbury Resiliency Corridors project. Transit justice has always gone hand in hand with racial, economic, and environmental justice, and Roxbury knows that history all too well.
Melnea Cass Boulevard, Malcolm X Boulevard, Warren Street–these are some of the most important corridors in the heart of historic Roxbury. But for generations, they have reflected a transportation system that too often only prioritized cars and did not prioritize people enough, which is why you need investments in multimodal infrastructure.
Roxbury has lived with the consequences: unsafe infrastructure, unreliable transit, poor air quality, some of the highest asthma rates in the Commonwealth, and the scars of urban renewal and disinvestment.
So when we secured this funding, what we saw was an opportunity to do something different, to create dedicated bus corridors, safer bicycle facilities, better intersections, and more green infrastructure, more resilient streets.
Pastor Bodrick, Mayor Wu, when you were referencing this unlawful action by Secretary Duffy, you might have indicated that they didn’t give a reason. They gave a reason. It’s just an unacceptable one.
The reason was because there was anything in here having to do with electric vehicles and electrification because they don’t believe in climate change, and they did not want anything that had to do with the Inflation Reduction Act or the Green New Deal, and just because of that addition, they took an unlawful and rogue action to rescind this investment.
But again, at the end of the day, this is about people, not concrete and asphalt. It’s about making everyday life safer and more accessible for the people who live and work in Roxbury. And again, the community helped to shape that vision.
So after the federal government had awarded that Boston $20 million, this administration again canceled the funding and left the community to once again contend with the consequences.
So, Roxbury should not have to keep waiting. Roxbury has been waiting. So I stand with Mayor Wu and the City as they challenge the cancelation of this RAISE grant.
We secured these dollars because Roxbury deserves a transportation that works for the people who depend on it. Because communities that have experienced generations of disinvestment should not be the first to sacrifice when resources are on the line.
The people of Roxbury have made their priorities clear. They have shown up, spoken up, and helped envision what a safer, healthier, more connected neighborhood can look like.
Our responsibility now is to make sure that vision does not get taken away from them. Roxbury has waited long enough.
—
Rep. Pressley has been advocating for federal funding to support the Roxbury Resiliency Corridors Project and submitted a letter of support for the project to DOT in April 2022. In September 2025, Rep. Pressley vehemently condemned the Trump administration’s cancellation of this essential federal grant.
More information about the Roxbury Resiliency Corridors Project and the benefits it would bring is available here.
In July 2025, Congresswoman Pressley and Senator Markey re-introduced the Freedom to Move Act, their legislation to support state and local efforts to establish public transportation as a public good through fare-free services. In August 2025, Rep. Pressley, Sen. Markey, and Mayor Wu announced their continued efforts to implement fare-free public transportation in Boston and across the Commonwealth.
In August 2026, Rep. Pressley and Sen. Markey released a new report, Making Transit Free, Frequent, and Reliable: Massachusetts shows the need for federal investment in fare-free transit, detailing the need for increased federal investments in fare-free transit.
In December 2025, Rep. Pressley led 14 colleagues in sending a letter to House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chair Sam Graves and Ranking Member Rick Larsen urging they prioritize affordability, accessibility, and sustainability in crafting the Surface Transportation Reauthorization bill—including by investing in fare-free transit. These priorities reflect the mission of the Future of Transportation Caucus, which reimagines America’s transportation systems to center equity, access, and sustainability.
In October 2019, Rep. Pressley founded the Future of Transportation Caucus, a Congressional caucus focused on centering equity, access, and sustainability in our transportation systems. Rep. Pressley also co-chairs the Congressional Bike Caucus.

Three People Charged in Conspiracy to Commit Sex Trafficking of Minors and Related Charges
An indictment was unsealed today in the District of Delaware charging Jamar Geeter, 39, of San Francisco, California, Kalvin Carter Jr., 44, of Waldorf, Maryland, and Jada Hasty, 29, of Coatesville, Pennsylvania, with conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of a minor by force, fraud, and coercion, sex trafficking, and coercion and enticement of a minor. Geeter and Hasty are also charged with producing child sexual abuse material (CSAM).
“These three individuals are alleged to have exploited and abused four victims — including three children — for their financial gain,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Human trafficking is a serious crime that strips people of their dignity and safety. Anyone who engages in this heinous conduct will be investigated and prosecuted.”
“Human-trafficking schemes don’t stop at state lines, and neither does our work to investigate them,” said U.S. Attorney Benjamin L. Wallace for the District of Delaware. “Alongside the Criminal Division and the FBI, my office will pursue anyone charged with exploiting minors in Delaware, no matter where the perpetrators reside.”
“According to court documents, Jamar Geeter, already a convicted sex trafficker, continued directing abuse from behind bars with Jada Hasty and Kalvin Carter Jr. as his willing accomplices,” said Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul of FBI Baltimore. “I am proud of the work done by our agents, analysts and victim specialists who handled this case with urgency and care. Their investigation spanned coast- to-coast, rescuing three children and one woman from the clutches of human trafficking and guaranteeing their alleged abusers will feel the full weight of the federal justice system.”
According to court documents, Geeter is currently serving a 97-year sentence in California for unrelated state sex trafficking convictions. It is alleged that Geeter used contraband cell phones to engage in some of the alleged criminal conduct while incarcerated.
It is also alleged that the defendants conspired to compel three minors and one adult to engage in commercial sex acts in Delaware and elsewhere. Geeter and Hasty recruited, enticed, harbored, transported, provided, obtained, and maintained two minors knowing or in reckless disregard of the fact that they were under the age of 18 and would be caused to engage in commercial sex acts. Geeter and Hasty also used facilities of interstate commerce, including cell phones and the internet, to induce and entice three minors to engage in prostitution. Geeter and Hasty produced CSAM images of two of the minor victims as well. The defendants involved in the scheme used force, threats of force, fraud, or coercion to compel the victims to engage in commercial sex acts.
All three defendants are charged with conspiracy to traffic a minor and by force, fraud, and coercion and sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion. Geeter and Hasty are also charged with sex trafficking of a minor and by force, fraud, or coercion, coercion and enticement of a minor, and production of CSAM materials. Geeter is charged with additional counts of production and receipt of CSAM materials. If convicted, all three defendants face a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison and a maximum penalty of life in prison on the sex trafficking by force, fraud, and coercion charges.
In addition, Geeter and Hasty face a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison and a maximum penalty of life in prison for sex trafficking of a minor charges and coercion and enticement of a minor. Geeter faces a minimum penalty of 25 years in prison and a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison while Hasty faces a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison and a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison on the CSAM charges.
The FBI’s Delaware Violent Crime and Safe Streets Task Force and Delaware State Police are investigating the case.
Trial Attorney Nicole Raspa of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Claudia Pare for the District of Delaware are prosecuting the case.
Anyone who has information about human trafficking should report that information to the National Human Trafficking Hotline toll-free at 1-888-373-7888, which is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For more information about human trafficking, please visit www.humantraffickinghotline.org. Information on the Department of Justice’s efforts to combat human trafficking can be found at www.justice.gov/humantrafficking.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Three People Charged in Conspiracy to Commit Sex Trafficking of Minors and Related Charges

Congresswoman Scholten Statement on Threatening Letter She Received at Grand Rapids Office
GRAND RAPIDS, MI – Today, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03) received a threatening letter at her Grand Rapids, Michigan office that contained unidentified white powder. The letter, which claimed to be from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), made a direct and specific reference to an impending “civil war” beginning after the election. The letter sent to Congresswoman Scholten is similar to those received at other congressional offices across the country. The DSA has not yet addressed the attacks, either to condemn them or to take or deny responsibility. The Grand Rapids Police Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) responded immediately.
The Congresswoman released the below statement on the incident.
“My first thoughts today are with my staff who opened the mail and the first responders on the scene. Everyone is safe. The people who work in congressional offices are public servants. They work every day to help constituents and serve their communities. No one should ever feel unsafe doing that work. I’m thankful to law enforcement for their professionalism, and I’m proud of my team for staying calm and looking out for one another.
“Even as law enforcement works to verify the authenticity of these letters sent to congressional offices, it is the responsibility of the DSA to condemn these threats done in its name—and to refute responsibility if there is none. Unfortunately, this is another instance where the DSA has excused or ignored extremism. Extremists resort to threats, intimidation, violence, and terrorism when they fail to convince others of their ideas on the merits. That is a sign of a weak mind and weak character. The DSA has allowed extremists in its movement who not only allow but justify violence as a viable means to achieve political ends.
“Regardless of party or origin, extremism must be rejected, condemned, and removed from our political discourse. Far too many leaders and civilians are looking the other way right now, and innocent people are being put in harm’s way. I won’t ever stop standing up to the bullies—on the right or the left. The American people deserve no less. My team and I will keep serving the people of West Michigan.”
###
title: Congresswoman Scholten Statement on Threatening Letter She Received at Grand Rapids Office

Trump Administration Announces More Than $11 Million to Strengthen Rural EMS and Expand Mobile Healthcare Across New Hampshire
This federal investment will create and expand mobile health programs, connect EMS agencies with rural hospitals, and bring more care directly to patients across New Hampshire
Today, the Trump Administration announced more than $11 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to strengthen emergency medical services and expand Mobile Integrated Health across rural New Hampshire. This investment will support Mobile Integrated Health programs that bring healthcare services directly into rural communities, while helping EMS agencies respond to rising demand and workforce pressures.
This transformational funding will support rural municipalities, EMS agencies, and health systems facing rising call volumes, workforce shortages, and financial pressures. Funding will create and expand mobile healthcare programs across rural New Hampshire, giving communities new ways to deliver care outside traditional healthcare settings and bring care closer to home. The investment will also support partnerships among municipalities, EMS agencies, and rural hospitals to improve coordination, expand access to services, and help build a more reliable and sustainable rural emergency medical system.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is expanding access to quality healthcare, regardless of a patient’s zip code, and equipping first responders with the lifesaving resources they need when every second counts. This funding will make critical investments to strengthen rural healthcare, expand access to lifesaving services, and bring modern technology to communities across New Hampshire.
“President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”
“President Trump made a historic commitment to rural America, and these investments are turning that commitment into better care for patients in communities across New Hampshire,” said Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “This is what rural health transformation should look like: federal investment that is putting patients first, driving lasting improvements and expanding healthcare for the hardworking Americans who call these communities home.”
Today’s investment was made possible through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act — passed by Republicans in Congress and unanimously opposed by Democrats — delivering a historic $50 billion investment to help states transform the way healthcare is delivered in America.
“I’m proud to announce more than $11 million in grants through GO-NORTH to strengthen emergency medical services and expand access to Mobile Integrated Health programs across our state. With this funding, we will ensure our rural EMS system is strong, reliable, and sustainable while developing new ways to reach patients through Mobile Integrated Health. Through our efforts with GO-NORTH, the largest rural health transformation award in New England, we will continue pushing to make healthcare and critical services like our EMS system more innovative, affordable, and accessible for all of New Hampshire,” said Gov. Kelly Ayotte.
Today’s announcement is one part of the larger overall funding amount awarded to New Hampshire for fiscal year 2026.
Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:
- Building the rural healthcare workforce: Supporting recruitment, training, and retention strategies to strengthen the pipeline of healthcare professionals serving rural communities.
- Strengthening rural facilities and access: Supporting partnerships, operational improvements, and care-delivery changes that help rural providers maintain essential services and improve access.
- Advancing innovative care and payment models: Supporting new approaches to delivery and financing designed to improve quality, strengthen primary care, and support sustainable rural healthcare.
- Expanding community-based and preventive care: Investing in school-based care, mobile services,and other community strategies that improve prevention, address chronic disease, and expand access to care.
- Modernizing rural healthcare technology: Expanding remote care and data-driven tools to improve coordination and extend healthcare services to rural communities.
The Trump Administration is delivering on its commitment to strengthen rural America by investing in solutions that modernize technology to promote health and well-being for rural communities. Led by CMS, the RHTP is moving beyond the failed one-size-fits-all approach and giving rural communities the tools to build stronger, more innovative, and more sustainable health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes for the Americans they serve.
For more information about the RHTP, visit: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health.

NASHVILLE – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee announced charges as part of nationwide enforcement actions led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee was a key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and today, federal prosecutors across the country facilitated fraud enforcement actions spanning over 76 criminal defendants reaching more than $490,000,000 in intended loss to American taxpayers .

According to court records, Thomas William Jones, 59 years old, of Brentwood, Tennessee, pleaded guilty last month to one count of failing to collect and pay taxes to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), announced United States Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee Braden H. Boucek.

Jones was the owner and operator of Alternative Solutions Consulting Corporation (“ASCC”), a software consulting company in Franklin, Tennessee, where he employed others and maintained the ASCC’s finances. Jones controlled ASCC’s bank account and paid his employees from this account. As an employer, Jones had a duty to truthfully account for and pay the required federal income and employment taxes.

Between 2014 and 2023, Jones failed to file the appropriate forms with the IRS for ASCC to report his employees’ wages. Jones also did not make payments to the IRS for federal income and Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) tax withholdings which were required to be taken from his employees’ paychecks. In addition, Jones did not make payments to the IRS for the matching portion of the FICA taxes ( i.e ., the employer contributions to Social Security and Medicare) that he was required to make. The total amount of taxes Jones failed to collect and pay is not more than $1,975,964.24.

Jones was charged by an Information on July 7, 2026. He pled guilty on September 1, 2026. He faces up to five years in federal prison. U.S. District Court Judge Eli J. Richardson scheduled Jones’s sentencing for January 15, 2027.

***

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The IRS and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) investigated the case. Criminal Chief Ahmed A. Safeeullah is prosecuting the case.

title: The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing Tax Fraud

Fast Facts
Multiple companies may sell health insurance in a given market, but only a small number of these insurers will have the most enrollees, as we previously reported. Known as market concentration, this can leave enrollees with fewer choices of insurers and higher premiums because of less competition in the market.
Market concentration generally increased from 2011 through 2024, with three or fewer insurers holding at least 80% market share for the individual and employer group markets in at least 36 states. However, concentration in the markets for individuals peaked in 2019 and has become slightly less concentrated since.
Map of the United States on a tablet, with some states colored in various shades of blue. It says HEALTH INSURANCE above the map.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Since 2014, GAO has reported that enrollment in private health insurance plans has been concentrated, meaning a small number of issuers, such as health insurers, enrolled most of the people in a given market. Specifically, GAO considers a market concentrated in a state if three or fewer issuers hold at least 80 percent of the market share of enrollment.
For this report, GAO examined the individual (coverage primarily sold to individuals who lack access to group coverage), small-group (coverage offered by small employers), and large-group (coverage offered by large employers) health insurance markets from 2011 through 2024 across states. GAO found that the number of states with concentrated markets generally increased, with recent decreases in the individual market (see figure).
Number of States, Including the District of Columbia, Where the Three Largest Issuers Had at Least 80 Percent of Enrollment, 2011 Through 2024
Note: The most recent years in GAO’s series on market concentration, 2023 and 2024, are highlighted in this figure.
GAO also examined concentration across the individual insurance exchanges, which are part of the overall individual market. Individual exchanges, which are marketplaces where consumers can compare and select among insurance plans offered by participating issuers, were established by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA). Similar to the overall individual insurance market, the individual exchanges became more concentrated from 2015 through 2020 and then generally less concentrated through 2024. The number of states where the individual exchanges were concentrated increased from 47 states in 2015 to a peak of 51 states in 2020 and then decreased to 49 states in 2024.
Why GAO Did This Study
Private health insurance is the most common source of health insurance coverage in the United States. Individuals have various options for obtaining private health insurance, including through the individual, small-group, and large-group markets. A concentrated health insurance market may indicate less issuer competition and could affect consumers’ choices of issuers and the premiums they pay for insurance.
PPACA includes a provision for GAO to periodically study health insurance market concentration. This report, the seventh in this series, describes changes in the concentration of enrollment among issuers in the overall individual, small-group, and large-group health insurance markets and in the individual insurance exchanges.
GAO determined market share in each of the three overall markets and the individual insurance exchanges using enrollment data from 2011 through 2024 that issuers report to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and enrollment data that GAO collected from individual states from 2015 to 2017. GAO used the most recent two years of data available at the time of its review and presented this information alongside its prior analyses beginning in 2011.
GAO provided a draft of this report to the Department of Health and Human Services. The department provided technical comments that we incorporated as appropriate.
For more information, contact John Dicken at DickenJ@gao.gov.
title: Private Health Insurance: Market Concentration in 2024 Was Generally Higher Than in 2011

Quigley, Costa Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Strengthen U.S. Defense Innovation Through Partnership with Ukraine
Today, Chicago Congressman Mike Quigley (IL-05), Representative Jim Costa (CA-21), and members of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus introduced the bipartisan H.R. 10772 Frontline Innovation Act. This legislation will authorize the Department of Defense’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) to evaluate and invest in Ukrainian defense technologies, allowing the United States to benefit directly from innovations developed and refined on the battlefield in Ukraine.
"When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the entire world expected Kyiv to fall within days. Instead, the strength, resilience, and innovation of Ukrainians and the Ukrainian military have kept the capital free for over four years. The United States should learn from Ukraine's battlefield innovation to strengthen and modernize our own military to ensure our forces are prepared for a new generation of threats," said Representative Mike Quigley, a Co-Chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus. "The Frontline Innovation Act would enable the U.S. military to accelerate defense innovation while continuing to support Ukraine as a critical ally."
Ukraine has emerged as a leader in developing modern defense technologies as it continues to defend itself against Russia’s invasion. Ukrainian companies are developing advanced drones, unmanned systems, and electronic warfare tools that are being tested and improved under real combat conditions against a determined adversary. These innovations offer valuable opportunities to strengthen U.S. defense capabilities while supporting Ukraine’s ongoing efforts to defend its sovereignty.
However, existing U.S. defense cooperation agreements have not kept pace with these technological advancements. The last U.S.-Ukraine agreement on exchanging military research and development information dates back to 2001. Although the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) has worked with the Ukrainian government and firms since 2023, legal barriers currently limit its ability to expand these partnerships and invest directly in Ukrainian defense technologies
“Ukraine has demonstrated extraordinary resilience in the face of Russia’s aggression, and Ukrainians are innovating and developing new defense technologies under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable,” said Congressman Costa. “This bipartisan bill will help strengthen our national security by investing in technologies that have been tested on the battlefield, while continuing to support Ukraine’s fight to defend its sovereignty."
“Ukraine is fighting for its survival against Putin’s illegal invasion, and its forces have been forced to innovate at an extraordinary pace,” said Rep. Bacon. “They are proving new drones, unmanned systems and electronic warfare capabilities against Russia in real combat, and our military should be learning from that experience. I’m joining Rep. Costa in introducing the bipartisan Frontline Innovation Act to help bring battlefield-proven technologies into our own defense innovation system and strengthen our military while continuing to support Ukraine’s fight for freedom.”
"Standing with Ukraine is in America’s own interest, and the Frontline Innovation Act is a smart, practical way to do it. Every day, Ukrainian forces are developing and testing new technologies on the battlefield, providing valuable lessons that can help make our own service members safer and prepared for the challenges of tomorrow,” said Rep. Bell. "As a member of the House Armed Services Committee, I know our military must have the best tools and technology, and after my recent trip to Ukraine, I can see how much Ukrainian battlefield innovation has to offer. I’m proud to cosponsor this bipartisan legislation to learn from our partners’ battlefield experience and help them continue defending their freedom.”
The Frontline Innovation Act would:
- Expand defense cooperation by authorizing the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) to evaluate and invest in Ukrainian defense technologies, notwithstanding any other provision of law.
- Strengthen U.S. defense capabilities by directing DIU to ensure the United States benefits from technologies developed and refined through Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s invasion.
- Allow technology proven in combat to reach the U.S. military faster while creating new opportunities for the American defense industrial base to gain new partners and a larger market.
- Support Ukraine through increased investment and cooperation, allowing both countries to collaborate on developing the next generation of defense capabilities.
title: Quigley, Costa Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Strengthen U.S. Defense Innovation Through Partnership with Ukraine

text:
After a heart-pounding finish that saw the Black Knights score 10 points in the final seven minutes, including a game-winning 25-yard field goal by junior kicker Dawson Jones, to defeat Tulane 20-17 last weekend, the Army West Point Football team (3-2) faces American Conference opponent Florida Atlantic at noon on Oct. 17 at West Point’s Michie Stadium.
The Black Knights take the field this week against the Owls, honoring the 82nd Airborne Division with division patches on the back of their helmets. The recognition highlights the history, accomplishments and continued service of Army divisions as part of the Honored Division theme featured throughout the 2026 football season.
The 82nd Airborne Division represents Soldiers and units stationed at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.
History of the 82nd Airborne Division
The 82nd Infantry Division was activated at Camp Gordon, Georgia, in August 1917 for the Great War. It was the second of eight divisions to deploy and fight in France. During this period, divisions were generally constituted from Soldiers drawn from a certain region, but the 82nd incorporated Soldiers from all 48 states, earning the moniker, “All-American Division.”
The first 82nd Division commander was Maj. Gen. Eben Swift, U.S. Military Academy Class of 1876 graduate. During World War I, the division fielded two infantry brigades, each containing two infantry regiments and a machine gun battalion. Of the division’s infantry regiments, only the 325th and 327th Infantry still serve on active duty. The division also boasted a field artillery brigade of two regiments and a trench mortar battery.
In May 1918, the division deployed to France, gaining combat experience along the Somme and Woëvre fronts before participating in the Saint-Mihiel and Meuse-Argonne offensives. On Oct. 3, Maj. Gen. George Duncan, USMA Class of 1886 graduate, assumed command of the division. During the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, the division broke through the Hindenburg Line, and Sgt. Alvin York of C Company, 328th Infantry, earned the Medal of Honor for his actions near Hill 223.
Following the war, the 82nd returned to the United States and was deactivated in May 1919 before being reconstituted into the Organized Reserve in 1921.
In March 1942, the division resumed active service at Camp Claiborne, Louisiana, under Maj. Gen. Omar Bradley, USMA Class of 1915 graduate. During this period, Matthew Ridgway, USMA Class of 1917 graduate; James Gavin, USMA Class of 1929 graduate; and Maxwell Taylor, USMA Class of 1922 graduate, also joined the division.
In August 1942, Ridgway took command of the division, which was redesignated as an Airborne Division, the first airborne division in the U.S. Army.
During its training, the division underwent several organizational changes, including the addition of the 504th and 505th Parachute Infantry Regiments. In April 1943, the 82nd Airborne Division deployed to the Mediterranean Theater, landing in North Africa.
In July 1943, elements of the division jumped into Sicily, and in September 1943 they jumped into Salerno. During the Italian campaign, elements also conducted amphibious landings during Operations Avalanche and Shingle. At Anzio, the 504th earned the nickname “Devils in Baggy Pants,” reportedly from an entry in a German officer's diary.
Following the Italian campaigns, the division trained in England before participating in the Normandy invasion on June 6, 1944. In the subsequent 33 days of combat, Ridgway noted that the division operated “without relief, without replacements. Every mission accomplished. No ground gained was ever relinquished.”
Once the division was pulled out of Normandy, they returned to England to prepare for their next mission, Operation Market Garden in the Netherlands. On Sept. 17, 1944, the division jumped into the Netherlands to capture the bridges at Grave and Nijmegen to facilitate the advance of the British XXX Corps.
Following Market Garden, the 82nd refitted in France, but in December 1944, they were rushed to Elsenborn Ridge to stop the German offensive at the Battle of the Bulge. In January 1945, the 82nd launched a counterattack, capturing over 2,400 German prisoners. At the end of the war, the 82nd Airborne Division occupied Berlin from August until November 1945. During World War II, the division suffered more than 9,000 casualties, and four Soldiers — John R. Towle, Charles N. DeGlopper, Leonard A. Funk Jr. and Joe Gandara — earned the Medal of Honor.
During the Cold War, the 82nd was stationed at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and was designated as the nation’s strategic reserve. Elements of the division deployed to both the Dominican Republic (Operation Power Pack) and to Vietnam in response to the Tet Offensive, serving 22 months in Vietnam.
In the 1980s, elements of the 82nd Airborne Division took part in the invasion of Grenada, Operation Urgent Fury (October 1983), Operation Golden Pheasant in Honduras (March 1988), and Operation Just Cause in Panama (December 1989). In August 1990, following the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, the 82nd deployed to Saudi Arabia for Operation Desert Shield, followed in January 1991 by Operation Desert Storm.
In August 1992, the 82nd conducted humanitarian operations in response to Hurricane Andrew in southern Florida. For the remainder of the 1990s, elements of the division served in Haiti, guarded Cuban refugees in Panama, and deployed to Bosnia and Kosovo. During the Global War on Terrorism, the division deployed multiple times to both Iraq and Afghanistan.
From the 82nd Airborne Division to West Point
Before making the jump to the U.S. Military Academy, Class of 2027 Cadet Deklan Wilk began his military career as an 11 Bravo (Infantryman) in the 82nd Airborne Division, primarily as a squad automatic weapon (SAW) gunner and, during his final six months, a team leader. The USMA senior majoring in Defense and Strategic Studies (DSS) achieved the rank of Specialist (E-4) while serving in the division from 2021-23.
Wilk truly felt it was an “honor” to the serve in and wear the 82nd Airborne Division patch for two years.
“The 82nd has an incredible history and reputation, and being able to wear the AA patch and serve alongside the Soldiers in the division was something I will be always proud of,” Wilk stated.
He said one of his fondest memories and “easily” his favorite part of the job at the 82nd were airborne jumps.
“There is nothing quite like standing in the door of a C-130 staring into the pitch-black night and then jumping out,” Wilk described.
Equally memorable were the relationships he formed with fellow Soldiers, many of whom he still keeps in touch with.
Within the first month with his unit and within a year of being in the Army, he earned his Expert Infantryman Badge (EIB).
“Earning the EIB significantly improved my confidence and showed me that I was capable of more than I initially believed,” Wilk explained. “My experiences in the infantry, especially being given increased responsibilities as I progressed into a team leader role, helped me realize that I wanted to continue serving and pursue a commission.”
The mentor who pushed Wilk to improve as a Soldier and helped him realize his potential was Sgt. 1st Class Josh Harris, who is now a first lieutenant.
“His mentorship played a significant role in encouraging me to pursue West Point and continue my Army career,” Wilk said. “He was the driving force in my decision to become an officer as he was also working toward becoming an officer. I would regard him as one of the best leaders I’ve ever had.”
Lt. Col. Ryan Boeka, a 2005 USMA graduate and Academy professor, currently serves as the International Affairs Program director in the Department of Social Sciences, leading 16 military and civilian faculty members and a program with more than 120 cadet majors.
Boeka served in the 82nd Airborne Division from 2010-13 as a company commander. He returned in 2023 as a lieutenant colonel commanding 3rd Squadron, 73rd Cavalry Regiment in the 1st Brigade Combat Team and also served as the division G-5 until June 2025.
For Boeka, wearing the All-American patch and maroon beret meant serving alongside “some of the finest NCOs, officers and paratroopers in our Army.”
“I set a goal as a cadet to serve in the 82nd, and I’m grateful I had the chance to do so multiple times and in several different roles,” Boeka said. “Each time I left the division, it was hard to take off the maroon beret, not knowing whether I would have a chance to wear it again,”
His best memories of working in the division were doing the hard things alongside incredible leaders during deployments, combat training center rotations and long field problems.
“There is nothing like jumping into a multi-day exercise with nothing but your rucksack, seizing an airfield and then leading your paratroopers on follow-on missions,” Boeka explained. “The level of planning and detail that goes into those operations is intense, and it prepared me for every assignment that followed. Everything else seemed easy in comparison.”
Boeka expressed that confidence is something that comes from not just doing the hard things but “keeping pace with the talented people around you, and the 82nd offers plenty of opportunities for both.”
Boeka also credited several exceptional leaders with shaping his career, including retired Col. Eric Baus, Col. Jason Schuerger, Maj. Gen. Pat Work and the division's deputy commanding generals, who invested in his development and held him “to the highest standard.”
“However, most importantly, I grew because of the NCOs I served with, from my platoon sergeants to first sergeants to my operations sergeant major and command sergeant major,” Boeka said. “Command Sgts. Maj. Alan Sutton and Jay Barber enabled me to command my squadron and made me better every day as I tried to keep up with them.”
Capt. Matthew Moser currently serves as the tactical officer for India Company, Second Regiment (I-2), where he mentors cadets and oversees their development outside the classroom.
A 2016 Virginia Tech graduate, Moser served in the 82nd Airborne Division from 2022-25. He began as a logistics planner in the 1st Brigade Combat Team before commanding Golf Forward Support Company, 1st Battalion, 504th Parachute Infantry Regiment. He later served as a logistics planner at the division level.
“Having the opportunity to serve and command paratroopers in the 82nd was a privilege that I’ll never forget and will undoubtedly be one of the greatest highlights of my Army career,” Moser stated. “The division’s duty as the nation’s Immediate Response Force means that paratroopers in the 82nd are constantly staring down the world’s toughest problems and greatest threats.
“As a result, I found myself surrounded by the greatest Soldiers, NCOs and officers the Army has to offer, and each day felt like a test to confirm that I deserved to serve with them,” he added. “The pride, grit and tenacity of paratroopers in the 82nd Airborne Division is unique and inspiring, and leading them is something that every West Point cadet should strive to do at least once in his or her career.”
Moser's fondest memories include airborne operations and Joint Readiness Training Center (JRTC) rotations, where shared challenges helped strengthen relationships within the unit.
“Helping young paratroopers overcome their fear of jumping, inspecting the parachutes of your subordinates and sharing a meal in the field are all opportunities to build trust and create memories with your paratroopers,” Moser said.
Becoming a jumpmaster and competing alongside his Soldiers also strengthened Moser's confidence as a leader. “Every day in the 82nd is a test, as you’re constantly surrounded by the highest caliber of Soldier the Army has to offer,” Moser exclaimed. “Competing with and against my paratroopers, whether it be at morning PT, during E3B training, or during the AFT, it always made me confident that I had earned my spot in the division.”
More than a Patch on Gameday
As Army Football takes the field Saturday, players will wear the 82nd Airborne Division's All-American patch on their helmets, honoring the division's legacy and the Soldiers who have served in its ranks.
For Wilk, honoring the 82nd recognizes both division’s history and the modern Army that the Corps of Cadets is preparing to join.
“For me, wearing the AA patch was more than just wearing the insignia of my unit,” Wilk said. “It represented the Soldiers I served with, the standards I was held to, and the experiences that shaped me as a Soldier and leader.
“Being recognized at the Army Football game also gives the Corps of Cadets an opportunity to see the connection between their time at West Point and the Soldiers and units they will eventually serve alongside,” he added. “As someone who came to West Point after serving in the 82nd, I have experienced both sides of that connection, and I think it is especially meaningful to be able to represent my former division here.”
Moser feels that honoring the 82nd Airborne Division this weekend serves as a way “to thank those paratroopers who have worn the patch in the past, while simultaneously showing support to those who are currently answering the call to defend our nation.”
“Also, as Army takes the field Saturday, there will likely be family members watching who have a loved one forward deployed to serve as a deterrence to our enemies,” Moser stated. “Seeing the 82nd patch on the Army’s helmets reminds them that their paratrooper has our respect, admiration and support.”
For cadets, Moser said the recognition also serves as a reminder of the responsibilities they may one day assume.
“Cadets must understand that serving in the 82nd means they may be asked to lead paratroopers through the hardest days of their lives,” Moser replied. “They must be confident that West Point has prepared them to succeed when that time comes.”
Boeka echoed that sentiment, emphasizing how serving alongside the Soldiers and leaders of the 82nd shaped him as an officer.
“Excellence breeds excellence, and there is no better unit for West Point and the Army team to be associated with,” Boeka explained. “For cadets, seeing the All-American patch should serve as a reminder that the standards they are held to here are the standards they will be expected to uphold in units like the 82nd, where paratroopers will be counting on them to lead.”
(Editor’s note: 82nd Airborne Division historical knowledge was provided by Dave Siry, the Director for the Center of Oral History at the U.S. Military Academy.)
title: Honored Division Week #6: Black Knights at home versus Florida Atlantic, honor 82nd Airborne Division with gameday patch
