U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Kweisi Mfume (D-MD-07), and Wesley Bell (D-MO-01) introduced the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act and the Department of Defense Renaming Integrity and Ethics (DORIE) Act. These two pieces of legislation would honor the legacy of Mess Attendant Third Class Doris “Dorie” Miller and ensure that the Navy aircraft carrier currently under construction retains his name.
The U.S.S. Doris Miller Act would express the sense of Congress regarding the naming of a naval aircraft carrier in Miller’s honor. Miller famously manned an anti-aircraft gun during the attack on Pearl Harbor in World War II, despite having never been trained to operate the weapon, and helped carry wounded soldiers to safety even after being ordered to abandon ship. He was the first Black service member to receive the Navy Cross, the Navy’s second-highest award for valor.
The Department of Defense Renaming Integrity and Ethics (DORIE) Act would prohibit the naming of Department of Defense assets, including military bases, ships, and other military installations, after sitting presidents. The DORIE Act would amend Title 10 of the United States Code, which is the section of federal law that outlines the legal framework, roles, missions, and organization of the U.S. Armed Forces and the Department of Defense. This comes after an unprecedented proposal by Navy leadership to rename the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Doris Miller in honor of President Donald Trump.
“Doris Miller represented courage, sacrifice, and the essential role African Americans have played in defending this country,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “Naming this carrier after him is more than honoring one extraordinary sailor—it recognizes that African Americans are an essential part of American history. No sitting president has ever been able to, nor should they be able to, name a vessel after themselves. I am proud to support the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act to ensure American heroes are honored for their sacrifice.”
“Black history is American history, and you cannot tell the story of the Second World War without the story of Doris (Dorie) Miller,” said Congressman Kweisi Mfume. “Doris Miller’s life was one of extraordinary bravery and patriotism, and I will continue to fight against any and all efforts to minimize or denigrate that history. The aircraft carrier that was scheduled to be named in his honor represents a fitting tribute to the estimable legacy of Dorie Miller. It is the very least that we owe to this great American hero who like so many before him, laid down his life for his country. Taking his name off that ship to instead name it for President Trump while he is still in office would be a disgrace. That has never been the practice of our government, nor should it be now. No sitting President, of any party, should have a ship, a base, or any other military asset named after them while in office. That is just one of the many reasons why I am proud and honored to support the DORIE Act. It's the right thing to do.”
“Doris Miller put himself in harm’s way to save his fellow sailors, and he did it at a time when segregation limited what Black servicemembers were allowed to do. His courage deserves to be celebrated, not forgotten,” said Congressman Bell. “As a member of the House Armed Services Committee, I will continue working to ensure our sailors are honored for their service, and that their legacy is never erased. Our warships should carry the names of those who gave something to this country, and few gave more than Dorie Miller. That’s why I’m proud to champion these bills.”
Bill text for the DORIE Act can be found HERE.
Bill text for the U.S.S. Doris Miller Act can be found HERE.
title: Dingell, Colleagues Introduce Legislation Honoring Doris Miller and Prohibiting Renaming of Naval Vessels After Sitting Presidents

Rep. Gillen Statement on Suspicious Letter to Congressional Office
GARDEN CITY, NY — Today, Congresswoman Laura Gillen (NY-04) issued the following statement in response to a suspicious letter sent to her congressional office.
"Today, my office received a suspicious envelope, similar to those sent to other congressional offices. My staff and I are safe, and law enforcement was notified and intervened right away. Thank you to our law enforcement for their rapid response and commitment to our safety everyday.
“There is no excuse for acts of violence or intimidation against elected officials in our country. We have to lower the temperature and rise above the hatred, vitriol and extremism that is seeping into our politics. It prevents us from solving the biggest issues affecting all Americans, regardless of party. My office will continue to serve Nassau County families and not allow this threat to get in the way of that work.”
Letters containing unknown substances have been mailed to congressional and election officials across the country. The incidents have prompted notifications to law enforcement at both local and federal levels.
title: Rep. Gillen Statement on Suspicious Letter to Congressional Office

text:
Many federal laws are subject to time limits known as statutes of limitations or statutes of repose, which generally bar enforcement of the law after a certain amount of time has passed. Congress can set or modify statutes of limitations and repose via legislation, subject to some constitutional limits. This In Focus provides a brief overview of the law related to statutes of limitations and repose with a focus on time limits that apply to civil litigation. (CRS Report RL31253 provides more information on criminal statutes of limitations.) The In Focus then discusses selected considerations for Congress regarding legislation that imposes time limits on enforcing the law.
Statutes of limitations and statutes of repose both impose time limits on when a law can be enforced, but they function somewhat differently. In CTS Corp. v. Waldburger, 573 U.S. 1 (2014), the Supreme Court distinguished between the purposes and functions of the two types of laws. The Court explained that statutes of limitations "require plaintiffs to pursue diligent prosecution of known claims" and "promote justice by preventing surprises through [plaintiffs'] revival of claims that have been allowed to slumber until evidence has been lost, memories have faded, and witnesses have disappeared" (internal quotation marks and citations are omitted from all quotes in this In Focus). While statutes of repose "also encourage plaintiffs to bring actions in a timely manner, and for many of the same reasons," the Court explained that "the rationale has a different emphasis. Statutes of repose effect a legislative judgment that a defendant should be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time," and "embod[y] the idea that at some point a defendant should be able to put past events behind him."
In light of these differing rationales, the Court explained, "the time periods specified are measured from different points." A statute of limitations "creates a time limit for suing in a civil case, based on the date when the claim accrued," usually meaning "when the injury occurred or was discovered." By contrast, a statute of repose "puts an outer limit on the right to bring a civil action. That limit is measured not from the date on which the claim accrues but instead from the date of the last culpable act or omission of the defendant." A statute of repose thus bars all suits brought after the specified amount of time has elapsed, "even if this period ends before the plaintiff has suffered a resulting injury" or discovered that a legal violation or injury has occurred.
In Rotkiske v. Klemm, 589 U.S. 8 (2019), the Supreme Court explained, "When interpreting limitations provisions, as always, we begin by analyzing the statutory language." When the statutory language is unambiguous, that ends the inquiry. If there are two plausible constructions of a limitations provision, the Court will generally
adopt the construction that starts the time limit running when the cause of action … accrues because Congress legislates against the standard rule that the limitations period commences when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action.
The question of when a cause of action accrues can give rise to litigation. For instance, in Corner Post, Inc. v. Board of Governors of Federal Reserve System, 603 U.S. 799 (2024), the Supreme Court held that a facial claim under the Administrative Procedure Act accrues when a plaintiff is injured by final agency action, even if the injury occurs after the statute of limitations would run from the time of the challenged action.
Federal statutes set default statutes of limitations for both civil and criminal cases. For civil cases, 28 U.S.C. § 1658(a) establishes a default four-year limitations period for most federal statutes enacted after 1990 that do not contain explicit limitations provisions. 28 U.S.C. § 2401 sets a default six-year limit for civil suits against the U.S. government. As discussed in CRS Report RL31253, the default statute of limitations for criminal cases is five years, but specific offenses may be subject to other limitations periods or no limitations period.
Multiple questions may arise when lawmakers consider whether and how to impose time limits on enforcement of a law. Statutes and court decisions impose certain default rules with respect to such time limits, but Congress has significant authority to depart from those default rules via legislation. These considerations relate to statutes of limitations and repose in federal laws. When courts apply state law, including in federal court cases based on diversity of citizenship, they apply state statutes of limitations.
The first question Members of Congress may consider in this area is whether enforcement of a law should be time-limited. As noted, federal statutes lay out default statutes of limitations for civil and criminal cases. Thus, if a piece of legislation does not expressly address time limits on enforcement, courts interpreting the law may apply a default time limit. The equitable doctrine of laches may also bar claims that are unreasonably delayed.
If Congress does not want enforcement of a statute to be time-limited, it should expressly state that in the legislation. Some existing federal laws are not subject to a statute of limitations or statute of repose. For instance, 38 U.S.C. § 4327(b) provides that "there shall be no limit on the period for filing" a lawsuit alleging a violation of the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994.
If Congress imposes a time limit on enforcement of a statute, it may consider whether to do so via a statute of limitations or a statute of repose. A statute of limitations may allow more flexibility for plaintiffs who are delayed in discovering or addressing their injuries by circumstances beyond their control, while a statute of repose may provide greater legal certainty for potential defendants. Statutes of limitations are more commonly used in federal law than statutes of repose.
There are several possible events that may start the clock on a statute of limitations or repose. Statutes of repose run from when a violation of the law occurred, regardless of whether the plaintiff was injured or discovered the injury within the limitations period. Statutes of limitations often run from the time when a plaintiff is injured, regardless of whether the plaintiff is aware of the injury. As noted above, the Court in Rotskiske stated that if Congress does not specify when a statute of limitations begins running, courts will generally default to starting the clock when a plaintiff's claim accrues, that is, when the plaintiff is injured and thus has a right to bring the claim in court. Congress may also choose to apply a rule known as the discovery rule, meaning that the clock runs from when the plaintiff discovered their injury, or when a reasonably diligent plaintiff would have discovered it. The discovery rule may increase legal uncertainty by extending the statute of limitations, potentially indefinitely, but may also protect the rights of plaintiffs who could not discover an injury promptly despite reasonable diligence. Courts sometimes read statutes to implicitly include the discovery rule and sometimes decline to do so. Congress can reduce uncertainty by expressly stating whether the discovery rule applies.
Congress may also consider how long the limitations period should be. On one hand, a longer limitations period gives plaintiffs more time to discover and bring their claims, preventing potentially meritorious claims from being time-barred. This may enhance the deterrent effect of the law if defendants know they are less likely to escape liability. On the other hand, a shorter limitations period may mitigate concerns about evidence being lost or witnesses' memories fading over time, and may provide greater legal certainty for potential defendants. Congress has applied short statutes of repose, such as 60 days, to challenges to certain agency actions to "impart[ ] finality into the administrative process, thereby conserving administrative resources and protecting the reliance interests of regulatees who conform their conduct to the regulations."
Another question Congress may consider is whether exceptions should apply to the statute of limitations. The Supreme Court has recognized certain default exceptions that apply to statutes of limitations, but not statutes of repose, if Congress is silent on the matter. The first of these is equitable tolling. In CTS Corp., the Court explained that this difference between statutes of limitations and repose "underscores their differing purposes":
Statutes of limitations … are subject to equitable tolling, a doctrine that pauses the running of, or "tolls," a statute of limitations when a litigant has pursued his rights diligently but some extraordinary circumstance prevents him from bringing a timely action. Statutes of repose, on the other hand, generally may not be tolled, even in cases of extraordinary circumstances beyond a plaintiff's control.
Second, some Supreme Court decisions have applied an equitable "fraud discovery rule," holding that when a defendant's fraudulent actions prevent the plaintiff from discovering an injury, the limitations period begins when the plaintiff discovers the fraud.
Congress can specify in legislation that these exceptions do not apply, or it can expressly provide for exceptions. For instance, a prior version of the Fair Credit Reporting Act's statute of limitations provided that the plaintiff ordinarily had two years from the date liability arose to file suit, but if the defendant materially and willfully misrepresented certain information to the plaintiff, the two-year limitations period would instead run from the date the plaintiff discovered the misrepresentation. The Supreme Court has suggested that when Congress enumerates specific exceptions to a statute of limitations in statutory text, courts should not read additional, implicit exceptions into the statute. Thus, when drafting a statute of limitations, Congress may consider whether explicitly creating particular exceptions may foreclose judicial recognition of others.
Members of Congress may also consider whether to add a statute of limitations or repose to an existing law or remove or modify an existing time limit. Congress's authority in this area is subject to one firm constitutional limit, which relates to criminal law: The Supreme Court has held that the Constitution's Ex Post Facto Clause, which forbids retroactively imposing or increasing criminal punishment, prohibits reviving a criminal statute of limitations after the limitations period has run. Congress can, however, extend a criminal statute of limitations that has not lapsed.
Changes to civil statutes of limitations are sometimes challenged on due process grounds. Review of such claims may be fact-dependent. Courts have at times invalidated changes to statutes of limitations that were found to deprive people of vested rights in property. For instance, in Stewart v. Keyes, 295 U.S. 403 (1935), the Supreme Court held that where the statute of limitations has run on an action to recover real or personal property, a later attempt "to repeal or remove the bar after it became complete" violates "constitutional provisions forbidding a deprivation of property without due process of law."
Generally, however, due process review of statutes of limitations is deferential, and legislation will usually be upheld as long as it serves a rational purpose and does not impose undue hardships on parties. In the analogous context of due process review of state statutes of limitations, the Supreme Court has held that reviving a lapsed civil statute of limitations is not inherently unconstitutional. The Court has also stated:
It is well settled that a statute shortening the period of limitation is within the constitutional power of the legislature, provided a reasonable time, taking into consideration the nature of the case, is allowed for bringing an action after the passage of the statute, and before the bar takes effect.
title: When a Case Can Be Filed: Statutes of Limitations and Statutes of Repose

On Oct. 16, 1942, the Army's Military Intelligence Service (MIS) published its fifth special study—"The Development of German Defensive Tactics in Cyrenaica—1941." The study concluded that German desert defense was not designed as an immovable barrier; instead, it was an integrated system organized in depth to absorb and wear down an enemy assault before launching a decisive armored counterattack.
The MIS developed its assessment through the systematic evaluation of captured German military documents. Rather than depending on wartime estimates or enemy propaganda, American intelligence analysts translated and evaluated captured German unit war diaries, operational orders, after-action battle reports, and defensive sketches. The study largely reviewed the defensive tactics developed by the Afrika Korps’ three divisional commanders: Maj. Gen. Johann von Ravenstein of the 21st Panzer Division; Maj. Gen. Walter Neumann‑Silkow of the 15th Panzer Division, and Maj. Gen. Max Summermann of the 90th Light Motorized Division. The study also looked at how the battalion and company officers executed the trio’s tactical concepts on the ground through captured documentation on tactical trials, successes, and failures in the field.
The study concentrated on the defensive lessons German forces learned through hard experience. German officers initially relied on rigid, linear defense lines that were thinly spread and vulnerable to artillery and armor breakthroughs. Early in the campaign, one German major criticized this lack of defensive preparation, writing that “our people know next to nothing about the construction of defenses” and pointing out that “positional infantry warfare is 60 percent with the spade, 30 percent with the field glasses, and only 10 percent with the gun.”
In response, the Germans abandoned continuous front lines in favor of self-contained, mutually supporting strongpoints known as Stützpunkte. These fortified centers featured all-around defense, deep minefields of antipersonnel and antitank mines, antitank ditches, and dummy positions designed to deceive Allied reconnaissance. At the tactical level, the Germans mastered the “trefoil” formation, arranging squads and platoons into triangular clusters that provided overlapping fields of fire. Furthermore, commanders established strict fire discipline; heavy weapons and antitank guns were hidden and ordered to hold their fire until enemy forces reached close ranges to ensure surprise and maximize lethal effect.
The study pointed to the paramount importance of the German 88-mm dual-purpose gun in holding these positions. Standard 37-mm and 50-mm antitank guns often proved ineffective against heavily armored British tanks, leaving the high-velocity 88-mm antiaircraft gun as the core antitank weapon. The report noted the “terrific antitank performance of the twelve 88-mm guns” during fighting on the Egyptian frontier, asserting that “the 88-mm gun, the 5th Tank Regiment, and the solid defenses of Halfaya and Point 208 won the battle for the Axis.” During critical moments, such as the defense of Capuzzo, single 88-mm guns manned by makeshift crews halted entire armor columns. As the study concluded, “without the 88-mm gun, however, none of the positions could have repulsed the British drive,” making it “the most outstanding single element in German defenses.”
"The Development of German Defensive Tactics in Cyrenaica" provided an in-depth examination of how Field Marshal Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps, originally trained almost exclusively in rapid offensive warfare, adapted to static desert defense in early 1941. Facing unique desert logistics and terrain, German commanders had to rapidly invent and refine new defensive practices. Consequently, in addition to laying out German defensive tactics, this study showed American military leaders that the German Army was highly adaptable, rapidly transforming its tactical doctrine to master defensive position warfare in the desert.
***
Article by Michael E. Bigelow, INSCOM Command Historian. New issues of This Week in MI History are published each week. To report story errors, ask questions, request previous articles, or be added to our distribution list, please contact: TR-ICoE-Command-Historian@army.mil.
title: Assessing German Adaptation in World War II (16 OCT 1942)

Coast Guard, partners rescue missing diver near Catalina Island
U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Public Affairs: (206) 815-6689
LOS ANGELES — The Coast Guard and partner agencies rescued a missing diver Wednesday near Little Harbor on the western side of Catalina Island.
At about 6 p.m., watchstanders at Coast Guard Sector Los Angeles-Long Beach received a report that a 22-year-old man was missing in the vicinity of Shark Harbor. Friends reported he was freediving and spearfishing in the area and was not seen since about 5:30 p.m.
Sector launched a Coast Guard Station Los Angeles-Long Beach 45-foot Response Boat–Medium crew, diverted Coast Guard Cutter Narwhal (WPB 87335), and requested air support from Coast Guard Air Station Ventura. The Los Angeles County Fire Department Lifeguard Division also responded and provided a response boatcrew with rescue divers and two air assets.
At about 7:45 p.m., the Coast Guard boatcrew heard someone calling for help from rocky terrain approximately one mile north of Little Harbor. The crew members directed Narwhal and the LA County Lifeguard boatcrew toward the location.
A rescue swimmer from LA County Lifeguards deployed to assist the diver. At about 8:30 p.m., a Narwhal boatcrew recovered the diver and rescue swimmer and transferred them to the LA County Lifeguard boat, who reunited the diver with his group.
“We are grateful for the swift response and continued partnership with the Los Angeles County Lifeguards,” said Capt. Stacey Crecy, commander of Coast Guard Sector Los Angeles-Long Beach. “This rescue highlights the importance of notifying someone of your plans before heading out on the water. Early notification gives rescue crews valuable time to respond when every minute counts.”
-USCG-
title: Coast Guard, partners rescue missing diver near Catalina Island

SCHNEIDER STATEMENT ON SUSPICIOUS MAIL IN LINCOLNSHIRE OFFICE
LINCOLNSHIRE, IL - Today, Congressman Brad Schneider (IL-10) released the following statement after his Lincolnshire office received one of many suspicious letters sent to Congressional offices across the country.
"Yesterday, we saw the first reports of threatening mail with suspicious substances being sent to Congressional offices in the U. S. Capitol and across the country. Today, more offices, including mine, received these letters. Following protocol, we open all mail under a mail hood. Upon reviewing the threatening letter, we contacted the U.S. Capitol Police followed by the Lincolnshire Police Department. Lincolnshire Police and Fire, including a hazmat team, came to the office with specialized equipment from Lake Forest. They tested the letter and confirmed it did not contain any harmful substances. The space was deemed ‘all clear’ after a couple of hours. I am very grateful for the swift response of local law enforcement and fire department personnel and thankful that my team and the building is safe."
"The FBI is leading the investigations of these mailings nationwide. It is imperative that they follow all leads to apprehend and prosecute those responsible."
"Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken."
###

BUFFALO, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that James R. Muench Jr., 47, of Depew, NY, who was convicted of entering aircraft or aircraft area, was sentenced to serve five years’ probation and ordered to pay a $5,000 fine by U.S. Magistrate Judge H. Kenneth Schroeder, Jr.

On May 20, 2025, Muench drove his vehicle up to a closed security gate outside the Buffalo Niagara International Airport. He initially stopped at the gate, but then repeatedly rammed his vehicle into the gate, eventually bending the metal gate. Muench then drove his vehicle through the damaged and partially open gate and continued onto the aircraft operational area of the airport. Muench drove through various secure parts of the airport including the inner airfield roads, aircraft taxiways, the commercial passenger aircraft ramp area, and the active airport runways, where aircraft take off and land.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Franz M. Wright. The sentencing is the result of an investigation by the Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority Police, under the direction of Chief Brian Patterson and the FBI, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II.

# # # #
title: Depew man sentenced for entering secure area at the Buffalo Niagara International Airport

DOT, DoW, DHS Join Forces to Protect Southern Border Airspace
Temporary flight restriction will prohibit unauthorized drone operations within one nautical mile of the U.S.-Mexico border, from the surface to 400 feet
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), Department of War (DoW) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) today announced a new, coordinated effort to strengthen airspace security along the southern U.S. border through a temporary flight restriction (TFR) for drones. The TFR – effective today – will bar any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet above ground level and extend one nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border.
The move builds on the Trump Administration’s successful efforts to secure the southern border and defend the homeland from national security threats – including illicit cartel activity. The new measure will reduce risks to ongoing border security operations, protect federal personnel, facilities and the Homeland, and enhance enforcement against those who violate the restrictions.
“President Trump promised to secure the Southern Border, and he did. Now we’re doubling down on that promise by protecting our skies from cartel drone threats and other illicit activities,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “I appreciate the close collaboration with our partners at DHS and DoW as we work together to defend our airspace and keep the American people safe.”
“The United States government will maintain 100% operational control of our border: land, air, and sea,” said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. “For too long, cartels have taken advantage of gaps along our southern border. Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, those days are over. By restricting unauthorized drone activity, we are giving commanders greater awareness, greater decision space, and more options to defend the Homeland. Equipped with cutting-edge technology—including Directed Energy Weapons—our warfighters will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America’s sovereignty.”
“DHS will not stop building on the historic progress made to secure the southern border,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “This action will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border. President Trump promised to secure the border, and we are delivering on that promise through continued action and strong partnership with Department of Transportation and the Department of War.”
Additional Information:
The FAA will publish a NOTAM which will include links to the Domestic Notice and the FAA's UAS Data Delivery System.
Drone operators are responsible for reviewing all applicable NOTAMs and restrictions before operating and must comply with the requirements in effect for their planned operations.
###
title: DOT, DoW, DHS Join Forces to Protect Southern Border Airspace

text:
"Most" modern federal criminal laws are predicated on Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce. Federal firearms offenses are no different in this respect. For example, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), which prohibits felons from possessing firearms "in or affecting commerce," stems from Congress's Commerce Clause power. The Supreme Court has interpreted the statutory precursor to § 922(g)(1) to require that the government prove that the firearm has a "requisite nexus" with interstate commerce. Federal appeals courts have uniformly held what was perhaps "implicit" in the Court's cases: that the felon-in-possession prohibition is a valid exercise of Congress's authority under the Commerce Clause.
Justice Thomas, federal judges, and scholars have expressed serious doubt, however, as to the soundness of these and similar constitutional conclusions, suggesting that the felon-in-possession ban and other federal restrictions on firearms possession exceed Congress's authority under the Commerce Clause. On July 21, 2026, in Squire v. United States, a majority of the active judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (Fifth Circuit) agreed that the full court would decide whether the Commerce Clause is a proper source of authority for § 922(g)(1). One judge dissented from the order granting a rehearing, warning that to invalidate § 922(g)(1) as unconstitutional would by logical extension "imperil much of the United States Code" that rests on the Commerce Clause and "would mark the start of a new, severely contracted Commerce Clause era."
This Sidebar describes the relationship between the Commerce Clause and federal firearms laws to aid in an understanding of the constitutional issues to be considered by the Fifth Circuit in the Squire case. The Sidebar begins with an overview of the Supreme Court's Commerce Clause jurisprudence. It then addresses the Commerce Clause in the context of federal firearms laws, paying specific attention to judicial concerns with the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 922(o), the federal prohibition on the possession of machineguns. The Sidebar closes with considerations for Congress.
The Supreme Court has stressed that every law enacted by Congress must be traced to a power in the Constitution. The same is true of federal criminal laws; the Court has recognized that Congress "cannot punish felonies generally" but instead "may enact only those criminal laws that are connected to one of its constitutionally enumerated powers, such as the authority to regulate interstate commerce." Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 of the Constitution, referred to as the "the Commerce Clause," grants Congress the power "to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes." Federal courts have observed that the Commerce Clause is the constitutional source of authority for "most" federal offenses. Such is the case for federal firearms offenses: The primary federal "criminal" statute applicable to firearms, the Gun Control Act (GCA), is predicated on the Commerce Clause.
The scope of the Commerce Clause power has "evolved over time" to include three general areas. In 1995, the Supreme Court in United States v. Lopez recognized that Congress may invoke the Commerce Clause to regulate "three broad categories of activity": (1) the "channels of interstate commerce," or what interstate commerce moves through (e.g., highways, railroads, navigable waterways, or airspace); (2) the "instrumentalities of interstate commerce, or persons or things in interstate commerce," or what travels on the channels of interstate commerce (e.g., airplanes, trucks, or trains, as well as people or objects); and (3) "activities that substantially affect interstate commerce," that is, intrastate activities that, when taken in the aggregate, would substantially affect interstate commerce (e.g., limiting the intrastate, personal production of a good to stabilize national prices for that good). Applying the stated scope of the Commerce Clause, the Court in Lopez struck down a federal law that prohibited the possession of a gun in a school zone, reasoning that the law regulated a purely local, noneconomic activity. In its discussion, the Court appears to have "relied heavily" on the economic/noneconomic distinction, observing that under the third category the Court has upheld "regulations of activities that arise out of or are connected with a commercial transaction," further recounting that the Court has "upheld a wide variety of congressional Acts regulating intrastate economic activity where [it has] concluded that the activity substantially affected interstate commerce." The Court said the "pattern is clear": "Where economic activity substantially affects interstate commerce, legislation regulating that activity will be sustained." As to the federal law in question, the Court explained that the third category does not extend to "a criminal statute that by its terms has nothing to do with commerce or any sort of economic enterprise," or to a statute that is "not an essential part of a larger regulation of economic activity, in which the regulatory scheme could be undercut unless the intrastate activity were regulated."
Similarly, in 2000, in United States v. Morrison, the Court invalidated a provision of the Violence Against Women Act that created a federal civil remedy for victims of gender-motivated violence, as the Court found that such violence is not an economic activity. The Court in Morrison compiled four factors that may help draw the distinction between economic/noneconomic activities, including (1) whether the regulated "actor" or the regulated "conduct" "has a commercial character," or whether the statutory "purpose" has an "evident commercial nexus"; (2) the existence of a jurisdictional hook; (3) congressional findings; and (4) the link between the activity and interstate commerce. Quoting Lopez, Morrison also explained that federalism undergirds the inquiry into the economic nature of the regulated activity: "Were the Federal Government to take over the regulation of entire areas of traditional state concern, areas having nothing to do with the regulation of commercial activities, the boundaries between the spheres of federal and state authority would blur."
In 2005, in Gonzalez v. Raich, the Court upheld the application of the federal Controlled Substances Act to growing marijuana for personal, intrastate use because Congress had a "rational basis" for concluding that such cultivation and consumption would impact the supply and demand in the national market for cannabis. According to the Court, the regulated market's federal illegality did not matter for purposes of the statute's constitutionality.
In 2012, concluding that the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate could not be upheld pursuant to the Commerce Clause, in National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) v. Sebelius, the Court determined that Congress cannot compel individuals to engage in an economic activity (i.e., to purchase health insurance or face a fine) and thereby bring these individuals within the ambit of the Commerce Clause. Similarly, the Court explained that Congress cannot regulate inactivity, even if the individual choice to not do something (i.e., to not purchase health insurance) has economic consequences (i.e., externalized and increased health care costs).
Federal law, at 18 U.S.C. § 922(g), prohibits nine classes of individuals, including felons, from possessing firearms "in or affecting commerce." The Supreme Court has recognized that this "in or affecting commerce" language and similar formulations, referred to as a "jurisdictional hook," "signal Congress' intent to invoke its full authority under the Commerce Clause."
In 1971, in United States v. Bass, the Supreme Court rejected a Commerce Clause challenge to the predecessor statute to § 922(g)(1), which subjected any felon who "receives, possesses, or transports" a firearm "in commerce or affecting commerce" to criminal punishment. The Court read the "in commerce or affecting commerce" language to apply to all three elements of the offense, including possession and receipt, to alleviate federalism concerns. The Court interpreted the language to mean that the government must prove that the firearm "previously traveled in interstate commerce." In 1977, the Court in Scarborough v. United States clarified that, in enacting this clause, there is "no indication that Congress intended to require any more than the minimal nexus that the firearm have [sic] been, at some time, in interstate commerce." According to these cases, the interstate movement of the firearm need not be contemporaneous with the defendant's possession of the firearm.
Some federal appeals court judges have opined that there is a "tension" and a "fundamental and irreconcilable conflict" between Scarborough—allowing Congress to regulate any firearm that has "at some time" traveled between states—and Lopez and its progeny—which insist that the regulation fit within at least one of three categories of activities. Federal courts also have noticed that some circuits adhere to Scarborough, while others apply Lopez. Courts using the former approach observe that the Supreme Court has not overruled Scarborough. For instance, Lopez did not cite Scarborough, let alone place Scarborough in a negative light. Moreover, these courts have explained that Scarborough is the appropriate case to use when the statute at issue has an express jurisdictional hook, as the statute under review in Scarborough had such language and the law examined in Lopez did not. Courts following Scarborough in other contexts have stated that a statute would necessarily be read with the Commerce Clause in mind and resultingly construed to fall within its constitutional boundaries.
At the same time, some judges in concurring and dissenting opinions have questioned the vitality of Scarborough. One question arises out of the temporal separation between when the firearm may have crossed state lines and when the firearm was possessed. On this score, a judge raised the concern that Scarborough would enable Congress to criminalize firearm possession if the "firearm had, perhaps decades previously before the charged possessor was even born, fortuitously traveled in interstate commerce." As an example, a circuit upheld a § 922(g)(1) prosecution where the firearm had "crossed into [the state] after its manufacture at some indeterminate moment in time—possibly years before it was discovered in [the defendant's] possession." Some have suggested that Scarborough may disturb the federal-state balance by permitting Congress to assume state police powers: As one judge put it, under Scarborough's logic, Congress could "enact a federal law requiring students in private schools to read their homework assignments, so long as the government establishes that the textbooks were published in another state." In addition, some Justices have argued that Scarborough turned on statutory interpretation and thus should not govern a constitutional Commerce Clause analysis. Still other judges have reasoned that to use Scarborough is to render the Lopez framework "superfluous" and to reduce the constitutional inquiry to a simple check for a jurisdictional hook.
For courts that analyze § 922(g)(1) under Lopez, the statute may fall within the case's first category on the theory that Congress sought to keep the channels of interstate commerce "clear of firearms" possessed by felons. Critics have resisted this proposition for at least three reasons. First, they argue that Lopez rejected the argument that a federal statute prohibiting firearm possession in a school zone could be justified under the first category, finding the statute "is not a regulation of the use of the channels of interstate commerce, nor is it an attempt to prohibit the interstate transportation of a commodity through the channels of commerce." Judges upholding § 922(g)(1) have found the first category to be "not relevant" in its constitutional analysis. Second, Justice Thomas has expressed concern with the potential temporal gap between when the firearm traversed a channel of interstate commerce and when the defendant has possessed that firearm; as that gap grows, the interstate character of the regulation and the justification for federal involvement lessen. Third, a circuit court has observed that a federal statute prohibiting felons from possessing body armor "in" commerce did not, under Lopez, regulate a channel of interstate commerce because the statute "is not directed at the movement of body armor through the channels" and instead "prohibits the stationary and entirely intrastate act of possession of body armor." Some judges have found this analysis to be persuasive in the context of § 922(g)(1).
With § 922(g)(1) expressly prohibiting felons from possessing a firearm "in" commerce, some courts have posited that the second category of Lopez—authorizing Congress to regulate goods or things in interstate commerce—is the applicable source of constitutional authority for the statute. Others disagree, pressing arguments related to the intrastate character of firearm possession, costs to federalism, and the specialized meaning of an "instrumentality" of interstate commerce. First, some argue that the firearm's existence "in" interstate commerce could occur many years prior to the firearm possession, yet the harm addressed by § 922(g)(1) is possession of the firearm by a felon and therefore § 922(g)(1) at bottom criminalizes an intrastate act—an argument made by Justice Thomas with respect to § 922(g)(1) and judges in other federal criminal contexts. Second, according to an expert on firearm manufacturing and distribution, 95% of firearms cross state lines; put differently, "few" firearms stay within a state. These individuals argue that the "in" interstate commerce requirement—if read only to ensure that a firearm has crossed state lines at some point—would not meaningfully limit the scope of congressional power under the Commerce Clause, at the expense of state rights. Third, § 922(g)(1) may not involve an instrumentality as that term is understood by some courts. In a case on the constitutionality of a federal carjacking offense, a circuit court held that Congress can regulate intrastate instrumentalities of interstate commerce where the instrumentalities have the capability of "transporting goods and people across state lines," but a firearm, unlike a vehicle, train, or plane, does not have an "inherently mobile" character. In addition, according to Justice Thomas, a regulation of an instrumentality of interstate commerce requires proof that the possession poses a "risk to interstate buying, selling, shipping, or transportation"; § 922(g)(1) does not require this showing. In the body armor case, the circuit court determined that the second Lopez category only permits Congress to regulate activities that "threaten" instrumentalities of commerce and "things actually being moved in interstate commerce, not all people and things that have ever moved across state lines"—reasoning that concurring judges favorably cited in a § 922(g)(1) case.
With respect to whether § 922(g)(1) fits the Lopez third category, on one hand, Lopez held that "[t]he possession of a gun in a local school zone is in no sense an economic activity," such as purchasing, selling, transporting, producing, or consuming a thing. The same logic may apply to firearm possession generally. It may especially apply to the defendant in Squire, who possessed a firearm in his home, the defense of which lies at the core of the right to keep and bear arms. A finding that possession is not economic may end the constitutional inquiry; a circuit court argued that aggregation of economic effects is appropriate only when the underlying activity is economic. The Lopez Court also cautioned against stacking inferences to find that an activity substantially affects interstate commerce, and here possession may be seen as a step removed from production, an economic exchange, or other commercial conduct.
On the other hand, courts have found that "[p]rohibiting possession by felons limits the market for firearms, and discourages shipping, transporting, and receiving firearms in or from interstate commerce," adding that firearms possession facilitates interstate firearms trafficking, "a clearly commercial activity." Likewise, a circuit court upheld the constitutionality of a federal law prohibiting juveniles from possessing a handgun on similar grounds, writing that the ban "is an essential part of a regulatory scheme . . . that directly and substantially regulates interstate handgun markets by excluding juveniles from them." Further, the Supreme Court has emphasized that, under the third category, Congress need only have a rational basis to believe the regulated activity will substantially affect interstate commerce—a "modest" bar for congressional action. It remains to be seen how the Fifth Circuit will respond to these and other prospective arguments.
Federal law, at 18 U.S.C. § 922(o), prohibits the possession of machineguns. Unlike § 922(g)(1), § 922(o) lacks a jurisdictional hook. Every circuit to have confronted the issue has found that § 922(o) is an appropriate exercise of the Commerce Clause. Several Fifth Circuit judges in dissent have argued, however, that § 922(o) exceeds this source of authority. They have stated that § 922(o) is a "clone" of the statute invalidated in Lopez and that § 922(o) should suffer the same constitutional fate. In contending that § 922(o) falls short under Lopez, these judges have added that § 922(o) extends to intrastate possession of machineguns and thereby "intrudes upon the traditional police powers of the states." Private possession is not economic and "does not involve a market activity," they have argued. Finally, they lamented the absence of a limiting principle to the market regulation approach: Criminalizing possession to impact "the demand side of the market can be applied to the possession of anything."
The Fifth Circuit's Squire case could impact the constitutionality of many federal firearms laws, and its reasoning could apply to other federal statutes criminalizing possession and other federal statutes grounded in the Commerce Clause power. Congress may, in anticipation of or as a result of Squire, add or strengthen the jurisdictional hook in federal firearms statutes. Congress also may seek to await two pending consolidated Supreme Court cases on whether certain assault-weapon bans comply with the Second Amendment; while these cases involve another constitutional provision, the Court may offer insight into its impressions of the constitutional basis for federal firearms regulations.
title: The Commerce Clause and Federal Firearms Prohibitions

HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Shalom Tuimalealiifano, 44, of Honolulu, Hawaii, was indicted on October 15, 2026 with possessing with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking, and unlawful possession of ammunition as a convicted felon.

According to court records, Tuimalealiifano possessed methamphetamine with the intent to distribute it to others, as well as a loaded pistol with a 31-round extended magazine, which he used in furtherance of his drug trafficking. Tuimalealiifano, who has a prior felony conviction for drug trafficking, was also charged with unlawfully possessing ammunition, including 39 rounds in a separate drum magazine.

If convicted, Tuimalealiifano faces at least 20 years and up to life in prison, a fine of up to $20,000,000, plus a term of supervised release.

The charges in the indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. In the case of conviction, any sentence would be imposed by a United States District Judge based on the statutory sentencing factors and the advisory United States Sentencing Guidelines.

The FBI is investigating the case.

Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Heidi Turner is prosecuting the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Force, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

CONCORD – Nashua resident Mario Monserrate Morgan, age 41, pleaded guilty today to unarmed bank robbery, U.S. Attorney Erin Creegan announces.

According to court documents and statements, on the afternoon of June 9, 2026, Morgan entered the Citizens Bank located at 238 Main Street in Nashua carrying a black backpack. After waiting in line for a few minutes, Morgan approached the teller station, leaned over the counter with his backpack, and told the teller, “Put the money in the bag and don’t press any buttons.”

The teller placed $645 into Morgan’s backpack and he left the bank. Nashua Police responded to the scene and were able to apprehend Morgan a short distance from the bank approximately 10 minutes after the robbery. Inside Morgan’s backpack was the cash from the bank.

Sentencing is set for January 26, 2027. Morgan faces up to 20 years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and up to three years of supervised release following incarceration. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

The Nashua Police Department led the investigation with valuable assistance provided by the FBI. Assistant U.S. Attorney Mike Shannon is prosecuting the case.
title: Nashua Man Pleads Guilty to Bank Robbery

PLANO, Texas – A Palm Bay, Florida man has been sentenced to federal prison for a money laundering scheme in the Eastern District of Texas, announced U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs.

Joshua Thomas Jackson, 41, pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced to 51 months in federal prison by U.S. District Judge Sean D. Jordan on October 15, 2026.

According to information presented in court, Jackson engaged in a scheme to defraud individuals using false representations and statements. To facilitate the scheme, Jackson created business entities and marketed opportunities to invest in real estate development, purchases, and rehabilitation schemes. As Jackson carried out his scheme, he falsely represented that funds investors provided would be used to purchase real property or distressed residential properties, that the investors funds were secure and would be repaid within a defined period of time, and that his business activities and the victims’ investments were secure and profitable. During the period of his scheme Jackson received over $3 million from investors and caused losses to investors exceeding $2.8 million.

“Investor fraud is a destructive crime and causes significant losses across our nation,” said U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs. “Together, with our partners at the FBI, we will continue to investigate and prosecute this type of fraud in the Eastern District of Texas, bring justice to these perpetrators, and seek restitution for victims.”

This case was investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys in the Plano office.

###
title: Floridian sentenced to federal prison, ordered to pay $2.8M in restitution for money laundering scheme in the Eastern District of Texas

Press Releases
October 16, 2026
Washington D.C. — Today, U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell (AL-07) announced a $27 million Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grant award to improve rail infrastructure and boost job creation in the Black Belt and Gulf Coast region.
Watch Rep. Sewell's video message here.
"I am thrilled to announce that we have secured $27 million in federal funding to modernize the Alabama & Gulf Coast Railway," said Rep. Sewell. "That means safer, more efficient rail service and more job opportunities for communities across the Black Belt. This investment builds on the $15.8 million in rail grants that we secured for the Black Belt in 2023, and it will be especially beneficial for Monroeville, Pine Hill, Linden, Demopolis, Boligee, and Pickensville."
"The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law continues to deliver for Alabama!" continued Sewell. "I was proud to vote for this transformational legislation, and I will keep fighting to bring more opportunities home to our district."
The proposed project was selected for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction and includes track rehabilitation and improvement on the Alabama & Gulf Coast Railway and the Eastern Alabama Railway in Alabama and Mississippi. The project will replace rail, ties, turnouts, and ballast, surface the track, modernize signals and communications, rehabilitate 34 at-grade crossings, and install trespassing signage.
The purpose of the CRISI Program is to invest in a wide range of projects within the United States to improve railroad safety, efficiency, and reliability; mitigate congestion at both intercity passenger and freight rail chokepoints to support the more efficient movement of both people and goods; enhance multi-modal connections; and lead to new or substantially improved intercity passenger rail transportation corridors.
The CRISI Program is authorized by 49 U.S.C. § 22907, and funds were made available by Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025, Div. A Tit. XIII, Pub. L. No. 119-4 (2025 Appropriation); the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, Div. D Tit. I Pub. L. No. 119-75 (2026 Appropriation); and Division J, Title II of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), Pub. L. No. 117-58 (2021).

Pappas Joins Bipartisan Letter Raising Concerns About Meta’s Use of Research Tax Credit for Data Centers
Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01) joined a bipartisan letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressing concerns about reports that Meta is seeking to use the federal research tax credit for its data center buildout. The bipartisan letter emphasized that any claims by Meta for the federal tax credit must meet the clearly defined requirements for qualified research and experimentation.
Congress established the research tax credit in 1981 amid concerns about declining private-sector research investment and U.S. technological competitiveness. By reducing the cost of qualifying research, the credit is meant to encourage businesses to pursue projects involving technical uncertainty and experimentation, rather than simply purchasing and deploying proven technology.
“We are concerned by Meta’s apparent position that expenditures associated with its massive data-center buildout qualify for the research credit,” wrote the lawmakers. “The purchase and deployment of commercially available servers, networking equipment, electrical infrastructure, cooling equipment, and other proven technologies cannot be transformed into qualified research merely because they are installed at unprecedented scale or in new configurations.”
To qualify for the credit, research must meet a four-part test, including being technological in nature, addressing technical uncertainty, seeking to develop or improve a product or process, and involving a process of experimentation. Certain activities, including research conducted after commercial production begins and duplication of an existing product or process, are excluded. The lawmakers emphasized that the scale or configuration of a data center does not, by itself, establish that its construction and equipment costs qualify.
“Allowing ordinary data-center construction and deployment costs to qualify would significantly expand the research credit beyond its intended purpose and risk converting an incentive for technological experimentation into a subsidy for capital expenditures that companies would undertake in the ordinary course of business,” continued the lawmakers.
“The research credit is an important tool for promoting American innovation. Protecting its integrity requires ensuring that it rewards genuine research and experimentation rather than subsidizing routine capital investment,” concluded the lawmakers.
The full text of the letter is available here.
Background:
Pappas helped introduce the Reverse Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act, which would rein in tax giveaways for data center development that was included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Specifically, the bill would prohibit data centers from taking the 100% bonus depreciation tax deduction, and from being eligible for Opportunity Zone tax benefits. Pappas voted to pass the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which would protect American families from the costs of energy and grid upgrades required for new data centers by requiring state public utility commissions consider strategies to make data centers pay their own way, instead of passing costs onto consumers.
title: Pappas Joins Bipartisan Letter Raising Concerns About Meta’s Use of Research Tax Credit for Data Centers

Crow Demands Trump Administration Explain Disruptions to Starshield
AURORA — Congressman Jason Crow (D-CO), a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who serves on the House Armed Services Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, is demanding President Donald Trump explain why Ukrainian forces’ access to SpaceX’s Starshield was reportedly restricted earlier this week. This decision disrupted their military operations, crippling their air defense and putting Ukrainians at further risk to deadly Russian aerial bombardments.
According to SpaceX, any limits on speed or usage of Starshield is decided by the U.S. military and the President. The Trump administration has not publicly stated who authorized these changes, when authorization was given, and what the intended purpose was.
Joining Crow on this letter are Ranking Member of the Armed Services Committee Adam Smith (D-WA), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Jim Himes (D-CT), and member of the House Armed Services Committee Congressman George Whitesides (D-CA).
“The President’s failed policies and reckless war with Iran has raised prices. As his popularity plummets at home, he’s shamefully abandoning our allies and once again cozying up to dictators,” said Congressman Crow. “We need to stand with the people of Ukraine as Russia continues its war of aggression, not fund Putin’s war machine that is killing civilians.”
Crow and his colleagues wrote: “According to SpaceX, any limits on speed or usage of Starshield are decided by the U.S. military and the President. To date, your Administration has refused to respond to Congressional inquiries on who directed these changes to Ukraine’s Starshield services.”
They continued: “In this context there are two possibilities – either SpaceX independently made the decision to restrict Ukrainian Starshield service, or the U.S. Government directed them to do so. If a private company can unilaterally restrict a critical operational service governed by a signed contract with the Department of Defense during an active conflict, it raises serious concerns about public accountability and the outsized influence of private actors over U.S. national security matters. If, on the other hand, the direction was given by your Administration, it raises serious questions about U.S. defense policy regarding Russia and Ukraine. Either way, the American people, our allies, and Ukraine deserve to know why this decision with life-threatening consequences was made.”
Congressman Crow has been a strong supporter of the Ukrainian people. He recently introduced a bill to protect Ukrainian nationals already in the U.S. against the threat of deportation by extending their Temporary Protected Status (TPS). When Putin’s invasion began, Crow immediately called for the U.S. to send military and humanitarian support to Ukraine, for international sanctions against Russia, and for a stronger NATO alliance to meet these new security threats. Weeks later, as Ukrainians fled their homes, Congressman Crow and other members advocated for an expedited immigration status for Ukrainians to the U.S. Crow has visited Ukraine several times since Russia’s invasion.
The Congressman has been one of the earliest and strongest supporters of military, development, and humanitarian assistance for Ukraine. He voted for, and strongly advocated for, every supplemental package provided to Ukraine.
A PDF of the letter can be found here, with full text appearing below:
President Trump,
On October 14, 2026, Ukrainian forces reported that unexpected restrictions on their SpaceX Starshield satellite communications services severely disrupted their military operations, crippling their air defense and putting Ukrainians at further risk to deadly Russian aerial bombardments. These restrictions came as officials in your Administration were actively pressuring Ukraine to limit strikes on Russia, particularly on oil refineries. The reported goal of your Administration’s pressure campaign was to pump more Russian diesel into global markets, amidst high fuel prices caused by your war with Iran.
According to SpaceX, any limits on speed or usage of Starshield are decided by the U.S. military and the President. To date, your Administration has refused to respond to Congressional inquiries on who directed these changes to Ukraine’s Starshield services.
In this context there are two possibilities – either SpaceX independently made the decision to restrict Ukrainian Starshield service, or the U.S. Government directed them to do so. If a private company can unilaterally restrict a critical operational service governed by a signed contract with the Department of Defense during an active conflict, it raises serious concerns about public accountability and the outsized influence of private actors over U.S. national security matters. If, on the other hand, the direction was given by your Administration, it raises serious questions about U.S. defense policy regarding Russia and Ukraine. Either way, the American people, our allies, and Ukraine deserve to know why this decision with life-threatening consequences was made.
Please provide responses to the following questions by October 30, 2026:
- Who authorized the speed restrictions on Starshield services provided to Ukraine? a. Was this an independent SpaceX decision, a U.S. Government directive, or a coordinated effort between SpaceX and the U.S. Government? b. What was the intent of the speed restrictions when authorized?
- Was there any communication between the White House, the Pentagon, or other parts of the U.S. Government and SpaceX on the decision to implement speed restrictions?
- Was there any communication between the White House, the Pentagon, or other parts of the U.S. Government and Russia on a decision to restrict Starshield services for Ukraine prior to any directive to SpaceX to implement such speed limitations?
- Were the operational consequences of restricting Starshield services for Ukraine assessed before the decision took effect, including potential impacts on Ukrainian forces and/or their air defense capabilities?
- Why were Ukrainian forces not given advanced notice of this restriction?
We will not allow your Administration to abandon our commitment to Ukraine by siding with Putin over the Ukrainian people and undermining their fundamental right to defend their sovereignty and freedom.
###
title: Crow Demands Trump Administration Explain Disruptions to Starshield

ANCHORAGE, Alaska – A federal grand jury in Alaska returned an indictment charging a doctor with five counts of attempting to evade and defeat taxes.

According to court documents, between January 2018 and May 2024, John Michael Koller, 66, of Kodiak, Alaska, willfully attempted to evade and defeat income tax owed to the United States. During this time, Dr. Koller was the owner and manager of Kodiak Island Ambulatory Care Clinic (KIACC).

The indictment alleges that in attempting to evade taxes, Dr. Koller submitted fraudulent corporate and individual income tax returns to the IRS, maintained falsified accounting records, provided tax preparers with incomplete and inaccurate financial information, and made false statements to investigators. Dr. Koller also concealed cash income generated by KIACC by directing employees to record the cash income in separate places, destroying cash receipts and cash deposit slips, and not depositing cash income into bank accounts.

Dr. Koller’s initial appearance was held on October 9, 2026, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Kyle F. Reardon of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman of the District of Alaska; and Special Agent in Charge Adam Jobes of the IRS Criminal Investigation, Seattle Field Office made the announcement.

The IRS Criminal Investigation, Seattle Field Office is investigating the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Ainsley McNerney is prosecuting the case.

This press release details one way in which this office has contributed to ensuring that all Americans pay their fair share. To see the successes of other offices, please see this press release: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/dojs-fraud-division-irs-and-irs-ci-expose-more-490m-tax-fraud-national-tax-enforcement-surge .

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

###
title: The District of Alaska Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing Over $490 Million in Tax Fraud

The information contained in these summaries is originally written by Italian news sources and does not reflect the opinion of U.S. Army Garrison Italy or any of its tenant commands. Direct any questions about the Italian news to the garrison public affairs office.*
Italian News from Camp Darby – October 16, 2026
- Livorno to demolish historic waterfront kiosks in 2027
