Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Answers from USPS About Mail Delivery Problems on Oregon Coast
WASHINGTON, DC [10/16/26] – Representative Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01) and Oregon Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley demanded answers from the United States Postal Service (USPS) about significant ongoing mail delivery issues in Astoria and surrounding areas.
The lawmakers noted that the city government, county government, and several downtown businesses are within a few blocks of the Astoria Post Office, but they have not been receiving mail regularly, and some are not receiving mail at all.
“The Astoria Post Office will not hold mail for city officials to pick up, which has caused major disruptions in local commerce and governance,” the Members of Congress wrote. “Payments sent through the mail to the city are being delivered late or not being delivered at all and downtown businesses are experiencing sporadic delivery. We are hearing concerning anecdotes indicating that Amazon packages, which are delivered via USPS in Astoria, are still regularly arriving on time. It’s unacceptable that mail from a billion-dollar retailer is successfully delivered to its destination on time, but mail to and from local small businesses is unreliable.”
The Members of Congress demanded answers to a series of oversight questions and requested that USPS set a time to meet with local elected officials in Clatsop and Columbia counties. They also requested USPS hold an informational session within the next 60 days for residents to discuss the agency's plans to address these issues.
“Timely, reliable mail delivery is essential infrastructure. Businesses, residents, and local governments rely on USPS for commerce, communication, medications, and more,” the Members of Congress wrote. “This is not an exhaustive list of issues with USPS brought to our attention.”
On October 15, 2026, Representative Bonamici visited the Astoria Post Office in person and asked to speak with the Postmaster to try to find a solution to the late and missing mail. The Postmaster denied the request.
The full letter can be read here and below:
Dear Postmaster General Steiner:
We write with significant concerns about the state of operations of the United States Postal Service (USPS) in northwest Oregon. Many community members from across the region are alarmed about inconsistent and unacceptable USPS delivery.
In Astoria, the city government, county government, and several downtown businesses have not been receiving mail regularly, and some are not receiving mail at all. This is happening despite the Astoria Post Office’s central location, just minutes away from Astoria City Hall and the county government building. Additionally, the Astoria Post Office will not hold mail for city officials to pick up which has caused major disruptions in local commerce and governance. Payments sent through the mail to the city are being delivered late or not being delivered at all and downtown businesses are experiencing sporadic delivery. We are hearing concerning anecdotes indicating that Amazon packages, which are delivered via USPS in Astoria, are still regularly arriving on time. It’s unacceptable that mail from a billion-dollar retailer is successfully delivered to its destination on time, but mail to and from local small businesses is unreliable.
The city had scheduled a meeting with the Astoria Postmaster to work to resolve the issue, but the Postmaster did not attend, and the meeting has not been rescheduled.
In Warrenton, USPS has been looking for a new post office location for several years. When the city of Warrenton has asked USPS about location options, USPS directs inquiries to a third-party contractor. This contractor directs all inquiries back to the USPS, resulting in a frustrating cycle where constituents are no closer to getting answers to their questions.
In Gearhart, roughly half the residents in town must travel to the Seaside post office to get their mail which is an unacceptable inconvenience for Gearhart residents. We have been advised that one possible solution involves the placement of a 950-unit cluster box which is exceedingly difficult for a town this size. It is unacceptable that residents of Gearhart cannot receive home delivery or at least have cluster boxes installed at several points throughout the community. The USPS must find a reasonable solution. Furthermore, there are concerning reports that mail pickup is inaccessible on Saturdays to Gearhart residents.
Recently, residents in Gearhart have heard rumors that the Seaside Post office will be remodeled to accommodate permanent mail pick up for Gearhart residents. Though Gearhart residents want a permanent solution to the problems they experience receiving mail, travelling to Seaside is not a practical or acceptable long-term or permanent solution.
Similar issues of concern also exist in Columbia County. In Rainier, roughly a third of the town is not included in the mail route and must use a PO Box. If mail is addressed to a home that is ineligible for home delivery instead of to their PO Box, the mail is not held – it is returned to sender. In a world where people often shop online, many online retailers don’t offer a format for a PO Box address, resulting in orders never reaching their intended addresses. Finally, it is concerning that not every residence is eligible for home delivery in Rainier, considering the small size of the town and well-maintained streets.
Timely, reliable mail delivery is essential infrastructure. Businesses, residents, and local governments rely on USPS for commerce, communication, medications, and more. This is not an exhaustive list of issues with USPS brought to our attention.
We ask that you respond to us in writing within 14 days of receipt of this letter outlining how the USPS will address the issues described and answer the following questions:
- When will Astoria downtown businesses, city government, and county government receive regular mail services?
- When will USPS announce a new location for the Warrenton post office? What is the current status of the search? Please provide the name and contact information for a specific person who can provide updates to the city.
- Why are so many Gearhart residents unable to receive mail at their doors?
- What is the plan to deliver mail to residents in Gearhart and/or provide additional PO boxes in Gearhart?
- Why are some residents of Rainier, who live within city limits, unable to receive mail at home?
- If these issues are caused by post offices being understaffed, what is USPS doing to remedy this?
In light of the volume and gravity of these concerns, we respectfully request that USPS set a time to meet with local elected officials in Clatsop and Columbia counties. We also ask that USPS hold an informational session within the next 60 days for residents to discuss the agency's plans to address these issues.
Our offices will gladly work with USPS and community leaders to find mutually agreeable times and locations for these meetings.
Sincerely,
###
title: Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Answers from USPS About Mail Delivery Problems on Oregon Coast

Temporary flight restriction will prohibit unauthorized drone operations within one nautical mile of the U.S.-Mexico border, from the surface to 400 feet
The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), Department of War (DoW) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) today announced a new, coordinated effort to strengthen airspace security along the southern U.S. border through a temporary flight restriction (TFR) for drones. The TFR — effective today — will bar any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet above ground level and extend one nautical mile north of the U.S.-Mexico border.
The move builds on the Trump Administration's successful efforts to secure the southern border and defend the homeland from national security threats — including illicit cartel activity. The new measure will reduce risks to ongoing border security operations, protect federal personnel, facilities and the Homeland, and enhance enforcement against those who violate the restrictions.
"President Trump promised to secure the Southern Border, and he did. Now we're doubling down on that promise by protecting our skies from cartel drone threats and other illicit activities," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. "I appreciate the close collaboration with our partners at DHS and DoW as we work together to defend our airspace and keep the American people safe."
"The United States government will maintain 100% operational control of our border: land, air, and sea," said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. "For too long, cartels have taken advantage of gaps along our southern border. Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, those days are over. By restricting unauthorized drone activity, we are giving commanders greater awareness, greater decision space, and more options to defend the Homeland. Equipped with cutting-edge technology — including Directed Energy Weapons — our warfighters will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America's sovereignty."
"DHS will not stop building on the historic progress made to secure the southern border," said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. "This action will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border. President Trump promised to secure the border, and we are delivering on that promise through continued action and strong partnership with Department of Transportation and the Department of War."
Drone operators are responsible for reviewing all applicable NOTAMs and restrictions before operating and must comply with the requirements in effect for their planned operations.
title: DOT, DoW, DHS Join Forces to Protect Southern Border Airspace

STEVEN MURPHY, M.D. and his practices, MURPHY MEDICAL ASSOCIATES, LLC and DIAGNOSTIC AND MEDICAL SPECIALISTS OF GREENWICH, LLC, located in Stamford, have entered into a civil settlement agreement with the federal and state governments in which they will pay $866,539 to settle allegations of COVID-19 related fraud and health care fraud. As part of the settlement, Murphy and his practices agreed to be excluded from all federal health care programs for a period of three years.

The government alleges that Murphy and his practices submitted false and fraudulent claims to the Health Resources Services Administration (HRSA), which is a sub-agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, to reimburse Murphy for “uninsured” patients treated during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government also alleges that Murphy submitted false claims to Medicaid and Medicare for blood testing “panels” allegedly performed by Murphy’s in-house lab.

COVID-19 Uninsured Program Fraud

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress passed a series of bills to provide funds to health care providers for COVID-19 testing and treatment for uninsured individuals (the “Uninsured Program”). The Uninsured Program reimbursed eligible health care providers for COVID-19 testing, treatment, and vaccine administration provided to uninsured individuals. HRSA was selected to provide oversight and management of the Uninsured Program.

An uninsured individual was defined as someone who was “not enrolled” in a government or private health insurance program as of the date of service in question. Prior to seeking reimbursement from the Uninsured Program, health care providers were required to attest to the government that they had confirmed that the patients for whom they were seeking reimbursement were uninsured.

Murphy and his practices participated in the Uninsured Program, attested that the patients for whom they sought payment were uninsured, and received reimbursement from the Uninsured Program for those patients. The government alleges that Murphy and his practices had information, including copies of insurance cards and other documents, in their files indicating that certain patients for which they made attestations and submitted claims for reimbursement to the Uninsured Program were, in fact, enrolled in government or private health insurance programs. In addition, Murphy and his practices changed the patient’s insurance identifying information to “Covid19 HRSA Uninsured” in their internal electronic medical records system and then submitted claims and received reimbursement from the Uninsured Program for those patients.

Blood Testing Fraud

Murphy had an in-house lab that performed blood tests on patients. The lab performed blood tests on patients who had possible exposure to COVID-19 or were presenting with COVID-19 symptoms, and also performed blood tests on non-COVID patients, including those who were having an annual physical exam.

Murphy and his practices utilized blood testing panels in their in-house lab. The blood testing panels were not billed and paid at one price per panel. Each blood test that made up the panel was billed separately to Medicare or Medicaid.

Reagents were used to run the specific blood tests that made up the panel, but there were times when Murphy and his practices failed to purchase certain reagents or otherwise did not have certain reagents, so they could not run the complete blood testing panel. The government alleges that Murphy and his practices billed Medicare and Medicaid for specific blood tests that were part of their standard panel, but which were never actually performed, because they did not have the reagents necessary to perform the specific blood tests that were billed.

To resolve the governments’ federal and state False Claims Act allegations, Murphy and his practices have agreed to pay $866,539, which covers the time-period from September 2019 through April 2022. Murphy and his practices also agreed to be excluded from all federal health care programs for a period of three years.

This matter was investigated by the Office of Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The matter was handled by Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard M. Molot, with the assistance of Auditor Susan Spiegel, and by Deputy Associate Attorney General Gregory O’Connell of the Connecticut Office of the Attorney General.

People who suspect health care fraud are encouraged to report it by calling 1-800-HHS-TIPS or the Health Care Fraud Task Force at (203) 777-6311.
title: Connecticut Physician and His Practices Pay More Than $860K to Settle False Claims Act Allegations

Coast Guard responds to vessel taking on water 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico
U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Public Affairs: (206) 815-6689
SAN DIEGO — The Coast Guard is responding to a report of 27 people in the water approximately 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico, Friday.
At approximately 1 a.m., watchstanders at Coast Guard Sector San Diego received a radio distress call reporting a vessel taking on water.
Sector San Diego is coordinating search and rescue efforts and has deployed crews from Air Station Ventura, Air Station Sacramento, and Coast Guard Cutter Active (WMEC-618) to search the area. The USS Kingsville (LCS-36) and a U.S. Navy helicopter with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 23 are also providing search and rescue assistance. Assets located vessel debris while searching.
Sixteen people have been rescued and transported to Coast Guard Sector San Diego, where emergency medical services personnel transferred them to local hospitals for further medical evaluation. Two of the sixteen individuals rescued were confirmed to be Mexican nationals.
“This case highlights the extreme dangers of taking to the sea,” said Capt. Robert Tucker, commander, Coast Guard Sector San Diego. “The vessel had a large number of people onboard and was following a route normally used in illegal maritime smuggling operations. Offshore conditions are unforgivable and can quickly result in death.”
The search and rescue operation remains ongoing.
More information will be released as it becomes available.
-USCG-
title: Coast Guard responds to vessel taking on water 140 miles west of Ensenada, Mexico

JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The next chapter in the transformation of 11th Airborne Division was officially started on Oct. 16, 2026, with the activation of the 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic), along with its subordinate battalions and companies.
While still the “youngest” division in the active Army after being re-activated in 2022, 11th Airborne Division is also growing faster than any comparable unit. In addition to its two Infantry Brigade Combat Teams, the 11th Airborne Division is now strengthened by a sustainment brigade that will aid its many complex and challenging arctic missions.
“Today’s uncasing ceremony represents much more than the unfurling of our unit colors,” said Col. George Plys, commander, 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic). “It symbolizes the beginning of a new chapter, the commitment to a mission, and the readiness of our Soldiers to answer the call wherever and whenever our nation needs them.”
Plys also noted how his brigade helps give Arctic Angel Soldiers the endurance to accomplish their missions. With the Army’s recent release of foundational doctrine “How the Army Fights,” the service highlighted “endurance” as one of the four interdependent operational elements, along with convergence, strike and close battle.
This link between endurance, sustainment and warfighting was also highlighted at the ceremony by Maj. Gen. John Cogbill, commanding general, 11th Airborne Division.
“Our ability to endure and sustain ourselves in the crucible of large-scale combat operations is impossible without the formations you see in front of you today,” said Cogbill.
The activation ceremony also highlighted the re-activation and re-designation of multiple subordinate battalions to the Division Sustainment Brigade. 106th Intelligence and Electronic Warfare Battalion was re-activated, while the 17th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion was re-designated as 17th Division Sustainment Support Battalion.
“While these two battalions have distinct missions, both are essential to our Army’s ability to fight and win,” said Plyls. “One sustains the force; the other provides the intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities that help commanders understand the battlefield and make informed decisions.”
Also activated was 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Troops Battalion.
title: Division Sustainment Brigade activates to strengthen ‘endurance’ of Arctic Angels

85% of Granite State households cannot afford the median home. Goodlander’s bipartisan Build More Homes Act, co-led with Republican Congressman Jefferson Shreve, would put pre-approved home designs that save builders time and money under the microscope, so more communities can use what works
Concord, N.H. — Today, Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (NH-02) introduced the bipartisan Build More Homes Act to attack one of the most expensive and least visible obstacles to building a home in New Hampshire: the months a homebuilder is often forced to spend drawing up plans and waiting for them to be reviewed before a single shovel goes in the ground.
The bill, which Goodlander is leading with Congressman Jefferson Shreve (R-IN-06), directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to conduct the first nationwide review of housing “pattern books” — catalogs of pre-reviewed, permit-ready home designs that let builders skip costly custom design work and get approved faster, while giving towns and cities homes that fit the character of their neighborhoods.
This bill takes aim at some of the most preventable costs in homebuilding: architecture, review, and delay.
“New Hampshire is in a full-blown housing crisis: 85% of households across our state are priced out of this cornerstone of the American Dream,” said Congresswoman Goodlander. “Nurses, teachers, firefighters, electricians, and hardworking people of all ages are being pushed out of the communities they love and the communities that depend on them. I’m using every tool I have to lower the sky-high housing costs New Hampshire families face and make it cheaper and faster to build the homes we urgently need. Our bipartisan Build More Homes Act is about cutting costs and red tape, and learning from communities like Lebanon that are already showing us what works.”
A Full-Blown Housing Crisis
New Hampshire’s housing crisis has never been worse. According to Housing is New Hampshire’s Future, the report New Hampshire Housing released last month:
- The median single-family home hit a record $575,000 in June 2026. A family needs to earn about $189,000 a year to afford it, and only 15% of New Hampshire households — and just 4% of renters — earn that much.
- The median rent statewide is $2,011 a month. A worker needs to earn $38.67 an hour to afford it, while the typical Granite Stater earns about $26 an hour.
- Prices across the Northeast have risen about 28% — gasoline 67%, food 31% — while median household income has grown only about 4% after inflation since February 2020.
- New Hampshire added 25,872 homes from 2020 through 2025, just 39% of what the state needs by 2030. The state is building about 5,174 homes a year; it needs more than 8,100 a year to catch up.
What Builders Are Up Against
New Hampshire’s homebuilders face rising costs at every step. President Trump’s tariffs have jacked up the price of lumber, and builders estimate recent tariffs add roughly $10,900 to the cost of a typical new home. His war in Iran has driven up the price of the diesel that hauls materials to every job site. Moreover, government regulation now accounts for $131,734 — more than 1 in every 4 dollars (26.4%) — of the average price of a new single-family home, according to a June 2026 study by the National Association of Home Builders. That’s up from $93,870 in 2021, the biggest jump NAHB has ever recorded between its studies. And 94% of developers say complying with regulations delays their projects, by about 7 months on average — exactly the kind of delay pre-approved designs are built to cut.
Goodlander’s Build More Homes Act
Pre-approved designs go straight at the “soft costs” of architecture, review, and delay. Communities with these programs most often report savings of $5,000 to $10,000 per homeand approvals that come weeks to months faster, according to a May 2026 Pew report that identified more than 40 jurisdictions using them. But the Congressional Research Service has found that there has been little systematic research into the impacts of these designs. Goodlander’s Build More Homes Act closes that gap, so towns, builders, and Congress know what saves the most money and gets homes built fastest.
In Lebanon, New Hampshire, the city’s Pattern Zones initiative pairs pre-approved, code-compliant designs for duplexes, triplexes, and small apartment buildings with rules tailored to existing neighborhoods, making room for new homes on underused lots while preserving neighborhood character. Next door, Vermont’s 802 Homes initiative is building a statewide catalog of small-home and multi-unit designs for both traditional and off-site construction; Maine enacted legislation requiring the preparation of pre-approved building types for municipalities to adopt; and Bangor already offers pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units, triplexes, and fourplexes. Repeatable designs also open the door for factory-built homes, connecting housing production to the region’s manufacturing economy and to pioneering New Hampshire companies that already build homes off-site.
The bill builds on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which Goodlander helped get across the finish line this summer and which created a Pattern Book Grant Program based on a provision she cosponsored. That program’s required research is limited to the communities that receive grants. The Build More Homes Act broadens the lens to programs nationwide, helping policymakers and communities measure how these designs affect the time and cost of building housing.
Fighting to Lower Housing Costs for New Hampshire
“I came to Congress to lower costs, and housing is where families feel it most,” said Goodlander. “I helped get the ROAD to Housing Act into law. I’m taking on the corporate landlords using algorithms to rig rents, because I did that work at the Justice Department. And I’m working with Republicans and Democrats to clear away every rule that makes it slower and more expensive to build a home in New Hampshire. I won’t stop until every Granite Stater has a fair shot at a home they can afford.”
The Build More Homes Act is the latest step in Goodlander’s fight to bring down housing costs:
- Got the biggest housing law in years across the finish line. Goodlander helped passthe bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act through the House, sent it to the President’s desk, and saw it become law in July 2026 — including 6 provisions she cosponsored to speed up homebuilding with pre-approved designs, cut red tape for rural housing, expand modular and manufactured homes, support resident-owned communities, help veterans use their home-loan benefits, and clarify Build America, Buy America rules for the HOME program.
- Cutting costly delays for affordable housing. With Republican Rep. Mike Flood, Goodlander introduced the Build Housing Affordably Act to study and temporarily pause federal sourcing rules that are delaying affordable housing projects, and to force faster waiver decisions. The bill is backed by more than 30 national housing organizations, including the National Council of State Housing Agencies, the National Association of Home Builders, and Habitat for Humanity International.
- Taking on corporate landlords rigging rents. Goodlander leads the End Rent Fixing Act to outlaw the algorithmic price-fixing tools that cost renters at least $3.8 billion in 2023 — the same practices she took on at the Justice Department.
- Cutting red tape on manufactured homes. Goodlander joined Republicans to pass the bipartisan Affordable HOMES Act to remove federal rules that drive up the cost of manufactured housing for first-time buyers, young families, and seniors.
- Financing more homes. Goodlander helped introduce the bipartisan SUPPLY Act to help homeowners finance accessory dwelling units, and is an original cosponsor of the Affordable Housing Credit Improvement Act to expand the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, which has helped NeighborWorks Southern New Hampshire alone build 550 apartments. She also cosponsored the Empty Lots to Housing Act to turn surplus public land into homes.
- Protecting Granite Staters at risk of losing their homes. Goodlander helped deliver more than $14 million to New Hampshire organizations fighting homelessness, pressed HUD to prevent 170,000 people from losing their homes in the dead of winter, and joined the delegation last month in urging HUD to release overdue housing funds.
- Bringing New Hampshire’s voices to Washington. Goodlander convened builders, lenders, and housing advocates at a Concord housing roundtable, launched the Lowering Costs Caucus, welcomed $500,000 to create workforce housing for health care staff at Speare Memorial Hospital in Plymouth, and called on the President to cut tariffs on building materials and act on the housing crisis.
###
title: As New Hampshire Home Prices Hit a Record $575,000, Goodlander Introduces Bipartisan Bill to Cut the Delays Driving Up the Cost of Building a Home

Today, Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), founder of the Slow Fashion Caucus and Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, and Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee, released a new Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on developing a textile circular economy in the United States. The report, requested by Pingree and DeLauro, builds on GAO’s December 2024 report on textile waste and lays out how policymakers can take federal action to address textile waste as momentum grows in states and other countries.
“GAO’s 2024 report made clear that the growing textile waste crisis demands federal leadership. Now, as states and other countries take action, this new report gives Congress an important resource to build on that momentum,” said Pingree. “Keeping textiles in use longer can cut pollution and create opportunities for American businesses that repair, reuse, and recycle them. I recently introduced the Textile Waste Reduction Act to lay the foundation for a coordinated national response. This report strengthens the case for that effort and outlines options for how Congress can seize this opportunity to reduce waste, support American businesses, and protect our environment.”
“States and countries around the world are already figuring out how to keep clothing out of landfills, and this report shows the United States does not have to be left behind,” said DeLauro. “A healthier textile economy means jobs in repair, resale, and recycling. It means less pollution in our soil and water. And it means lower costs for communities running out of landfill space. GAO found that what is holding us back is a lack of infrastructure, funding, and reliable data. Congress can fix all three. It is time to build a new kind of textile industry here at home – for the economy, for the environment, and for workers.”
GAO’s December 2024 report documented the environmental harms of textile waste and found that federal efforts to address it were fragmented and given a lower priority than other goals. GAO recommended that Congress consider directing and expressly authorizing federal entities to take coordinated action to reduce textile waste and advance textile recycling.
The new report broadens that work to examine a textile circular economy: a system that keeps clothing and other textiles in circulation through durable design, reuse, repair, and recycling. Drawing on research, site visits, and interviews with 49 stakeholders, GAO identifies potential benefits including new jobs and markets in secondhand retail, repair, recycling, and infrastructure development; reduced pollution and demand for raw materials; and changes in how consumers purchase and dispose of textiles.
GAO also identifies barriers to realizing those benefits, including limited domestic infrastructure and funding, gaps in comprehensive data, and a lack of common terminology and standards.
The report documents policies being proposed, enacted, or implemented in U.S. states and abroad, including textile producer responsibility programs in California, France, and the Netherlands, and the European Union. These efforts offer U.S. policymakers lessons as they consider how to support textile circularity nationwide.
GAO’s menu of policy options ranges from maintaining the federal status quo to expanding industry responsibilities, providing incentives such as tax credits, restricting textile disposal in landfills, improving data collection, and educating consumers. The report describes opportunities and considerations associated with these approaches without endorsing a particular option.
Pingree’s Textile Waste Reduction Act would establish a coordinated federal framework to advance textile circularity. The legislation would require a comprehensive National Textile Circularity Strategy, create an Interagency Working Group and stakeholder advisory board to coordinate and inform federal activities, improve textile waste data collection, and make existing federal funding opportunities easier to identify. These steps would help provide the foundation for policymakers to evaluate and pursue the opportunities outlined in GAO’s new report.
Textile waste is now one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the United States, with millions of tons of textiles discarded each year and the vast majority ending up in landfills. These discarded materials may leach contaminants including PFAS and microplastics into water and soil and increase costs on communities grappling with capacity shortages at landfills. 
Despite the harmful impacts of this fast fashion-driven increase in textile waste, there has been no coordinated effort at the federal level to tackle this problem and support a more circular textiles economy.  
In addition, over the past several decades, hundreds of thousands of fiber and textile jobs that once sustained communities across America have shifted overseas, harming American farmers and communities in the process.  
Pingree founded and launched the Congressional Slow Fashion Caucus in June 2024 to create climate-smart policies to reduce, repair, rewear, and recycle textiles. The caucus has garnered widespread support, including from American Circular Textiles, the Garment Worker Center, Al Gore’s Climate Reality Project, Patagonia, ThredUp, fashion designer and slow fashion influencer Kelly Dempsey, and more. 
###
title: Pingree, DeLauro: New GAO Report Builds Case for Congressional Action on Textile Waste

Lawmakers Reject Kirkland’s Excuses for Stonewalling Investigation and Demand Immediate Compliance
Washington, D.C. (October 16, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee; Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations; and Sen. Adam Schiff wrote to the Chairman of the law firm Kirkland & Ellis Jon Ballis, rejecting the firm’s bogus legal justifications for refusing to cooperate with the Committees’ investigation into Kirkland’s decision to provide President Trump with $125 million in free legal services that align with his political agenda.
“To date, Kirkland has not cooperated with our legitimate oversight requests. Your firm has failed to produce a single responsive document and has refused to meet with Congressional staff. Instead, Kirkland has devoted its time to compiling a laundry list of legally specious claims of privilege. Notwithstanding Kirkland’s lack of cooperation, we will use every tool at our disposal to pursue this investigation—in this Congress and the next,” wrote the lawmakers.
Kirkland has failed to produce any written agreement memorializing its $125 million deal with the Trump Administration beyond President Trump’s Truth Social posts. Absent another written agreement, Trump appears to be the sole arbiter of Kirkland’s legal obligations under the deal. As the lawmakers point out, Kirkland’s professional judgment is necessarily compromised when it is under constant threat of being deemed in violation of its personal agreement with the famously vindictive President.
To resist congressional oversight, Kirkland has provided a litany of vague, contradictory and legally unsound privilege claims that are not supported by legal precedent. The lawmakers reject each of these sham claims in detail. Requests for client identities, hours worked and the value of services do not implicate attorney-client privilege. The firm’s attempt to extend executive privilege to dealings with Trump’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, is unsupported by legal precedent. Its settlement privilege claim is similarly flawed; Kirkland faced no executive order when it entered negotiations, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) acknowledged in federal court that its requests constituted informal information gathering, not an investigation.
The lawmakers are renewing their demands for records and answers concerning Kirkland’s negotiations with the Administration, communications with the President’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, free legal work for federal agencies, potential conflicts with existing clients and efforts to poach attorneys and clients from Paul Weiss while it faced Trump’s retaliatory executive order. They also seek an itemized response to outstanding questions, a detailed log supporting any privilege claims and written confirmation that Kirkland is preserving relevant records, including encrypted or disappearing-message communications.
The inquiry continues an investigation Raskin and Blumenthal launched in April 2025 into Trump’s coercion of major law firms and the deals firms struck to avoid retaliation. Joined by Schiff, they subsequently scrutinized firms’ free legal work for the Commerce Department, sought records of Epshteyn’s role in Kirkland’s deal and pressed Skadden over potential conflicts involving its work for Intel and the Commerce Department.
Click here to read the letter.
title: Raskin, Blumenthal and Schiff Rebuke Kirkland & Ellis for Withholding Details of $125 Million Trump DealLawmakers Reject Kirkland’s Excuses for Stonewalling Investigation and Demand Immediate Compliance

Proposed rule would allow qualifying Anaktuvuk Pass residents to use off-road vehicles for lawful subsistence activities, opens 60-day public comment period

NewsMedia@nps.gov

FAIRBANKS, Alaska — The Department of the Interior and the National Park Service today announced a proposed rule that would allow qualifying rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass to use off-road vehicles for lawful subsistence activities in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve. The proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days.

The proposed rule advances Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum’s direction to recognize off-road vehicles as a traditional means of transportation used by Anaktuvuk Pass residents for subsistence purposes under the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act.

“For generations, the people of Anaktuvuk Pass have relied on access to Alaska’s lands and wildlife to sustain their families and way of life,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “President Trump’s administration is committed to respecting Alaska’s unique traditions and ensuring rural communities have reasonable access for lawful subsistence activities. This proposal recognizes the importance of traditional transportation methods while maintaining protections for the extraordinary natural resources of Gates of the Arctic.”

Anaktuvuk Pass is a remote community inside Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve and is not connected to the state road system. Residents used off-road vehicles for subsistence activities before Congress established the park. The Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to ensure people have reasonable access to subsistence resources.

“Honoring traditional subsistence practices and ensuring rural communities have reasonable access to park resources are central to the National Park Service’s mission,” said Jessica Bowron, Comptroller Exercising the Delegated Authority of the Director of the National Park Service . “Under Secretary Burgum’s leadership, we are working to help local residents get the access they need while also protecting the special places and culture of Gates of the Arctic.”

The proposed rule would allow eligible local rural residents of Anaktuvuk Pass to use off-road vehicles for lawful subsistence activities in the park. It would also allow the superintendent to address harmful impacts from off-road vehicles when necessary to protect park resources and values. The proposed rule applies only to qualifying subsistence use and does not authorize recreational off-road vehicles.

“This proposed rule provides a clear framework for subsistence-based use of off-road vehicles in Gates of the Arctic,” said Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve Superintendent Mark Dowdle. “We look forward to hearing from Anaktuvuk Pass residents and the public as we move through the rulemaking process.”

NPS will accept public comments on the proposed rule for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. Comments may be submitted online at Regulations.gov by searching for RIN 1024-AF12 or mailed to Superintendent, Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve, 101 Dunkel St., Suite 110, Fairbanks, AK 99701.

Comments must be received by 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Dec. 18, 2026.

The proposed rule will publish in the Federal Register on Oct. 19, 2026. To view the proposed rule once published, visit www.federalregister.gov and search for document #2026-21300.

Trump’s Transportation Department, Air Traffic Controller Union Announce 2.8% Pay Increase Deal
Pay raise comes with new workforce reforms to track controllers’ time, align staffing with demand, & improve the controller reassignment process
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy announced today that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) have reached a deal to provide air traffic controllers with a 2.8% pay increase following key workforce reforms.
In the Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act of 2026, Congress directed to FAA to tie a pay increase to measurable improvements in operational efficiency.
Improvements include:
- Timecard Tracking: Most federal employees are required to “badge in” and “badge out” at their place of work. This approach will now be applied to air traffic facilities to ensure managers have the data they need to better track training and safety needs.
- Align Staffing with Demand: Local managers and union representatives will develop shift guidelines based on forecasted workload and operational requirements. This will ensure more productive controller schedules that maximize coverage during peak traffic hours.
- Improved Reassignment Process: Controller reassignments will now focus on where the staffing needs are the most severe. Past changes to the controller reassignment process resulted in significantly more controllers transferring to locations with minimal shortages.
Together, these changes will improve controller quality of life, strengthen coordination between managers and frontline employees, make better use of the FAA’s existing workforce, and improve operational efficiency to keep America’s skies safe.
“President Trump has made clear that we must modernize our skies and deliver results for the flying public,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “That means taking a hard look at how we operate, fixing outdated staffing practices, and growing our air traffic control workforce. We are making these changes to better support the men and women who keep our skies safe, get controllers where they are needed most, and improve how we utilize the airspace. I appreciate the collaboration with NATCA and the thousands of hard-working controllers they represent to reach this deal so we can build a stronger system for the future.”
“Air traffic controllers perform critical work every day to keep the National Airspace System safe,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “By improving how we track work, schedule shifts and allocate personnel, we can make better use of our workforce and respond more effectively to operational demands. Our work with NATCA is helping us put practical changes in place that support our controllers and improve the way the system operates.”
“This increase reflects the vital role these dedicated professionals play in keeping our nation’s skies safe and efficient,” said NATCA President Nick Daniels. “Fair compensation and better working conditions are essential to sustaining a strong, experienced air traffic controller workforce.”
The pay increase takes effect Oct. 18 and is retroactive to the beginning of the year.
title: Trump’s Transportation Department, Air Traffic Controller Union Announce 2.8% Pay Increase Deal

text:
Fast Facts
The Department of Energy oversees nuclear waste cleanup at U.S. sites—which could last until the year 2100 and cost up to $840 billion.
DOE, the Environmental Protection Agency, and state regulators make cleanup decisions. But a complex legal and regulatory framework has led to inconsistent approaches, regulator disputes, and unachievable requirements. As a result, cleanup efforts are taking longer and costing more.
Clarified roles and better decision making, with input from independent experts, can help by potentially addressing risks decades sooner and avoiding billions in additional costs.
Our recommendations address these issues and more.
Workers at the Department of Energy's Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico
Two workers walk in an underground salt mine.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The Department of Energy’s (DOE) nuclear waste cleanup is proceeding largely under three laws that set cleanup and waste management requirements. Each law has different requirements, applications, and regulators.
Selected Cleanup and Waste Management Laws and Regulators for the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Nuclear Waste Cleanup
GAO and experts GAO convened with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identified several legal and regulatory factors that affect the cost and schedule of DOE’s nuclear waste cleanup.
Certain state regulatory actions may exceed state authority. According to experts who participated in GAO’s National Academies meetings, some states are taking legal and regulatory actions that address the radiological aspects of nuclear waste at DOE’s cleanup sites, which are generally regulated by DOE under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended. Such actions may exceed a state’s authority to regulate hazardous waste under authorizations from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) pursuant to the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976, as amended (RCRA). These state actions have led to disagreements between DOE and states on requirements for the radiological portion of DOE’s waste, longer cleanup schedules, and billions in higher costs for the federal government, according to experts.
Courts have recognized that DOE’s authority to manage and regulate its nuclear waste under the Atomic Energy Act preempts certain state regulatory actions that impact DOE’s management of nuclear waste during its cleanup efforts. However, based on GAO’s analysis, statutes and case law are unclear on what kinds of state actions that affect DOE’s management and cleanup of radioactive waste are appropriate under the law, in part because of the prevalence of mixed waste at DOE cleanup sites. According to experts, because states are often taking such actions under state programs that are authorized by EPA to implement a federal law (RCRA), EPA could play a more active role in addressing instances where states may be improperly seeking to regulate radioactive materials covered by the Atomic Energy Act. EPA officials told us they currently do not have authority to challenge such state actions, as long as those actions are at least as stringent as federal requirements. If Congress clarifies the scope of the Atomic Energy Act’s preemption—and creates a mechanism that allows for DOE to appeal to EPA to evaluate state actions that may infringe on federal authority over nuclear waste covered by the Atomic Energy Act—costly and resource-intensive legal disputes could be reduced and decision-making could be accelerated.
Assumptions about anticipated future land and groundwater use are sometimes unrealistic and can unnecessarily increase costs and schedules. Under the applicable laws and regulations, DOE’s cleanup of its sites is based, in part, on the anticipated future uses of land and groundwater for an area. According to experts at GAO’s meetings, DOE is cleaning up some areas based on unrealistic assumptions about those future uses. For example, DOE has agreed with state regulators and EPA to clean up large portions of some sites to allow for future residential use, even though there are no plans for such use. DOE did not evaluate the costs associated with cleaning up to less stringent standards associated with different land uses in those cases.
By comparison, realistic decisions about future land use have been critical to the successful cleanup of other DOE sites, such as at Rocky Flats in Colorado. After Congress designated that site as a national wildlife refuge in 2001, cleanup costs decreased from an estimated $23 billion for residential use to about $10 billion.
Historical Disposal (left) and Its Cleanup (right) at Idaho National Laboratory
According to experts, a better framework for making realistic assumptions about future land use at DOE’s cleanup sites is needed. For example, DOE could assess benefits and costs associated with cleanup based on a range of potential future land uses. Clarification from Congress, and additional guidance from EPA and DOE, on incorporating future land use assumptions into the cleanup process would better position DOE to select appropriate cleanup approaches that are realistic, cost-effective, and aligned with congressional expectations.
The legal framework often requires DOE to clean up contaminated groundwater to meet drinking water standards, but, according to experts, the assumption that groundwater beneath contaminated sites will be used for drinking water in the future is sometimes unrealistic. Further, according to experts, standards for certain contaminants that can apply to groundwater are based on outdated information from the 1960s and may affect the feasibility of cleanup. By accounting for current scientific information, DOE may be able to achieve cleanup that is both protective and avoids unnecessary expenditures.
Other aspects of the legal and regulatory framework for DOE’s nuclear cleanup are sources of conflict and affect costs and schedule. For example, DOE entered into various cleanup agreements with EPA and states in the 1990s before the extent of contamination was fully known. These agreements include hundreds of milestones that DOE has sometimes struggled to meet.
In a poll, all experts at GAO’s meetings recommended that DOE and EPA create an interagency task force of experts to review high-priority cleanup decisions and areas of legal and regulatory disagreement for opportunities to make DOE’s cleanup approach more risk-informed and cost-effective. Having an independent task force provide recommendations to DOE and EPA—such as when disagreements occur over revising cleanup agreements—may help to allow for cleanup approaches that more efficiently complete DOE’s cleanup mission.
Why GAO Did This Study
DOE is cleaning up nuclear sites across the country, the majority of which were created during World War II and the Cold War to research and produce nuclear weapons. DOE has estimated it could take until 2100 and cost $641 billion to $840 billion dollars to complete its nuclear waste cleanup mission. Much of the waste at DOE sites is mixed waste, meaning that it includes both radiological and hazardous constituents. Radioactive waste emits radiation, sometimes for thousands of years. Hazardous waste may be toxic, corrosive, ignitable, or reactive.
Under a complex legal and regulatory framework, DOE and regulators (EPA and states) make decisions that affect the cost and schedule of DOE’s nuclear cleanup efforts. For years, organizations have reported on the ways in which this framework has affected DOE’s ability to complete its nuclear waste cleanup mission, such as through inconsistent decision-making processes for similar risks across sites.
GAO was asked to review the impact of the legal and regulatory framework on DOE’s nuclear waste cleanup mission. This report examines (1) how state legal and regulatory actions affect DOE’s ability to manage the radiological portions of nuclear waste at its cleanup sites, (2) how DOE’s cleanup efforts are affected by assumptions about future land and groundwater use under the applicable legal framework, and (3) other aspects of the legal and regulatory framework that can contribute to higher cleanup costs and longer schedules.
GAO convened a series of expert meetings with the National Academies; conducted legal research, a literature review, and four case studies across six DOE cleanup sites; and interviewed DOE, EPA, and state officials.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that Congress consider (1) clarifying the preemptive scope of the Atomic Energy Act with respect to DOE nuclear waste cleanup and related activities, (2) creating a mechanism whereby DOE can appeal to EPA to evaluate state actions that may infringe on certain federal authorities over nuclear materials, and (3) providing more specific direction about incorporating potential future land use assumptions in the process for DOE nuclear waste cleanup.
GAO is also making six recommendations to DOE and EPA, including (1) that EPA take action to clarify guidance on making assumptions regarding future land use during the cleanup process, and (2) that DOE evaluate and document the expected costs and schedule associated with cleanup of a particular area based on multiple potential future land use assumptions when substantial cost or schedule benefits are possible. GAO is further recommending that DOE and EPA work together to (1) develop options to address certain outdated standards that can apply to groundwater cleanup; and (2) establish an interagency task force of experts to review cleanup decisions, processes, and areas of disagreement driving higher costs and longer schedules.
DOE concurred with two recommendations and did not concur with one related to evaluating multiple future land use assumptions. EPA also concurred with two recommendations and did not concur with one related to developing options to address certain outdated standards that can apply to groundwater cleanups. GAO continues to believe that taking action on these recommendations will help DOE achieve cleanup in a more risk-informed, cost-effective manner.
title: Nuclear Waste: Addressing Legal and Regulatory Barriers Could Accelerate Cleanup and Reduce Costs

WASHINGTON — The Army continues to make big strides in modernizing how it feeds Soldiers across its installations.
Army leaders outlined the Army food ecosystem at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting during a panel on warfighter performance optimization, detailing how initiatives like Campus Style Dining Venues (CSDV), Flexible Eating and Expanded Dining (FEED) and partnerships are bringing generational change.
"We are evolving the Army's food program from a 20th century chow hall to a modern 21st century network that’s part of a larger food ecosystem on all of our installations," said Jay Condrey, acting Army Materiel Command G-4. "It’s not just something we are doing out of convenience. It’s about quality of life. It’s about community, and at the end of the day, most importantly, it’s about warfighter readiness."
Central to this effort is a deliberate shift to separate garrison dining operations from tactical field feeding, ensuring Soldiers receive balanced nutrition while military culinary specialists sharpen their combat readiness. What makes this shift possible is the ability for the Army to partner with commercial food service providers.
"Bringing in a commercial partner to focus solely on garrison feeding absolutely reduces that burden of Tactical Field Feeding Specialist redundancies inside of a brick-and-mortar facility," said Sgt. Maj. Damarco Wyatt, AMC G-4 sergeant major. "Now what you have is more opportunity for field feeding proficiency and concentration on equipment as we prepare for large-scale combat operations."
One example of partnering with industry is the CSDV initiative. CSDVs feature varied daily menus curated by professional chefs, a registered dietitian, grab-and-go choices, lounge areas with couches, Ping-Pong and foosball tables, mounted flat-screen televisions and free Wi-Fi. Compass Group USA currently manages the first wave of campus-style dining facilities, located at Forts Hood, Carson, Drum and Bragg, with Fort Stewart coming in 2027 with additional expansions at these sites in the works.
The venues allow meal-card holders to swipe their Common Access Cards and use meal entitlements. While Soldiers on meal cards is a primary audience, families and other patrons are welcome to purchase meals à la carte.
"For the past 29 years, we’ve never seen a highchair inside of a dining facility," said Wyatt. "That captures that moment where we're allowing family members to actually come inside of the facility. They can eat with their Soldiers. That’s where the community comes back, because first impressions are long-lasting."
This approach has driven a sharp rise in meal service. For example, looking at the same facilities a year apart, Fort Hood has seen an increase of more than 312% meals served. Fort Carson and Fort Drum are seeing increases of 385% and 534% respectively.
"Soldiers are voting with their feet," said Sydney Smith, director of supply policy for the Department of the Army G-4. "The contractors are innovating because they want the foot traffic. They only get paid when our Soldiers go there to eat. It incentivizes them to make sure that it’s well done."
While the CSDV initiative is the Army’s flagship effort, the service is providing Soldiers with even more options. Starting with Fort Stewart, Georgia, the Army launched the FEED program which enables meal-card holders on essential station messing to use their meal entitlements at select Army & Air Force Exchange Service restaurants, including Qdoba, Starbucks and Subway, with plans to expand to Morale Welfare and Recreation and Defense Commissary Agency locations.
To safeguard nutritional standards, Army dietitians work directly with vendors to configure menus based on the military’s traffic-light nutritional framework. Participating eateries are limited to "green" and "amber" categorized foods, such as lean, high-protein options, fresh produce and whole grains. "Red" designated items are excluded from entitlement purchases.
"About a third of the Soldiers at Fort Stewart are using the AAFES locations for their meals or at least a portion of their meals now," Smith said. "Overall, the feedback has been great, plus we know they’re getting nutritious food."
With these new efforts, Army leaders acknowledged that broad implementation faces logistical hurdles, including infrastructure reinvestment for aging facilities, flexible contracting mechanisms and sustained funding.
The Army is also coordinating with the Office of the Secretary of War to establish cross-service guidelines and IT interoperability, enabling service members from the Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard to use dining entitlements interchangeably at joint installations.
"As we begin to roll out the CSDVs, everybody's asking, 'Hey, when can I have one?'" Wyatt said. "We'll ensure that we have a deliberate plan to roll these out accordingly."
title: Generational food changes optimize warfighter performance

Sedrick Skinner, age 37, of Tickfaw, Louisiana, was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison following his conviction for possession with the intent to distribute methamphetamine. U.S. District Judge Brian A. Jackson further sentenced Skinner to serve five years of supervised release following his term of imprisonment.

According to admissions made as part of his guilty plea, on January 22, 2026, a Livingston Parish Sheriff’s Office Criminal Patrol K-9 Deputy conducted a traffic stop on a white 2024 Hyundai Tucson near Juban Road in Denham Springs, Louisiana.

Skinner, identified as the driver, had difficulty producing a vehicle registration or proof of insurance. The deputy then observed marijuana gleanings and Skinner voluntarily admitted that he and a guest passenger had smoked marijuana while traveling.

During a search of the vehicle, a clear sandwich bag that contained suspected marijuana was found in the glove compartment. In the rear cargo trunk area was a dog kennel containing a small pitbull. Under the kennel, within the spare tire compartment, a large, shrink-wrapped bundle of methamphetamine was hidden which contained over two pounds of methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney Kurt L. Wall stated, “I am thankful that Judge Jackson imposed this 10-year sentence. Those who try to profit from those battling addictions deserve every minute of their sentence.” Wall also praised the work of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security – Homeland Security Investigations and Livingston Parish Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Lyman E. Thornton III led the prosecution.
title: TICKFAW MAN SENTENCED TO 120 MONTHS IN FEDERAL PRISON FOR POSSESSING METHAMPHETAMINE WITH THE INTENT TO DISTRIBUTE

PITTSBURGH, Pa. – An electrician convicted of joining in a scheme to defraud Primary Health Network, a non-profit medical organization headquartered in Sharon, Pennsylvania, has been sentenced in federal court to 24 months in prison on three counts of wire fraud, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.

United States District Judge J. Nicholas Ranjan imposed the sentence on John O’Brien, 63, of Masury, Ohio. As part of the sentencing, the Court found that O’Brien had provided false testimony at the trial in the matter.

Three individuals were previously sentenced in the case: PHN’s former CEOs Drew Pierce and Jack Laeng were both sentenced in April 2026, with Pierce sentenced to 40 months of imprisonment and Laeng to 24 months of imprisonment (read the news release on those sentencings here ), and Mark Marriott, a former facilities manager at PHN, was sentenced to 30 months of imprisonment.

According to information presented to the Court, O’Brien controlled a company called Keystone Tele-Data, which performed electrical work on a construction project in Lewistown for which PHN was to be the master tenant. O’Brien joined in a scheme to defraud PHN by submitting fraudulently inflated invoices to TopCoat, a company inserted by Pierce, Laeng, and Marriott between PHN and the company’s vendors. Keystone Tele-Data submitted fraudulently inflated invoices to TopCoat, which passed along the costs and further fraudulent charges to PHN, despite TopCoat’s providing no services for PHN. Keystone Tele-Data used the funds in part to pay kickbacks to Marriott.

Assistant United States Attorney William B. Guappone prosecuted this case on behalf of the government.

United States Attorney Rivetti commended the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Internal Revenue Service–Criminal Investigation for the investigation leading to the successful prosecution of O’Brien.
title: Ohio Electrician Sentenced to 24 Months in Prison for Role in Defrauding Non-Profit Medical Organization

On October 13 and 14, 2026, Vikki Bradt, age 51, a British National, of Ballston Spa, NY, Samantha Merkle, age 55, a British National of Glens Falls, NY, Suad Sasic, age 30, a Bosnian National of Clifton Park, NY, Jacques Patry, age 64, a Canadian National of Tupper Lake, NY, and Paula Stitt, age 57, a Canadian National of Albany, NY, appeared on charges of voting by aliens. All defendants are lawful permanent residents. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Anthony Patrone, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) made the announcement.

The complaints against all five defendants allege that they are aliens, who knew they were not United States citizens and that they knowingly voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the United States Senate, or Member of the United States House of Representatives.

These charges carry a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000. A defendant’s sentence is imposed by a judge based on the particular statute(s) the defendant is convicted of violating, the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines, and other factors.

First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III stated, “the law is clear that only U.S. citizens can vote in elections that have candidates running for federal office. When non-citizens vote, the public loses confidence in the integrity of the election process and its outcome. Our office, working with our federal law enforcement partners, will work tirelessly to prosecute those who should not have voted, but did. Just this week, our office filed charges against five individuals, all of whom were non-citizens and unlawfully voted in federal elections within the last few years.”

"The integrity of lawful voting and government processes is essential to maintaining public confidence in our institutions," said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Buffalo Acting Special Agent in Charge Anthony J. Patrone." From the North Country to the Capital Region, residents expect that the systems affecting their communities, including the electoral process, operate fairly, lawfully, and with accountability. Today’s charges reflect that coordinated effort and HSI's commitment to investigate alleged voter fraud and protect the integrity of government processes that communities in this region rely upon."

The charges in the complaints are merely accusations. The defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Richard Belliss and Benjamin Loefke are prosecuting the case.
title: Five Non-Citizens Arrested for Voter Fraud Across the Northern District

INDIANAPOLIS- Gregory Vernon Dupree, 38, of Muncie, has been charged in a federal indictment with eight counts of filing false COVID-19 claims,including claims for the Employee Retention Credit (ERC) and COVID‑related Sick and Family Leave credits. These charges were brought as part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

According to the indictment, between January 2021 and January 2022, Dupree allegedly filed eight Forms 941 (Employer’s Quarterly Federal Tax Return) with the Internal Revenue Service. Through these filings, Dupree made claims against the United States requesting refunds totaling over $1 million, knowing those claims to be false.

The Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigations investigated this case. U.S. Attorney Wheeler thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Eakman, who is prosecuting this case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An indictment or criminal complaint are merely allegations, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Fort Thompson, South Dakota, woman convicted of Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury. The sentencing took place on October 5, 2026.

Rosilee Grey Owl, 30, was sentenced to five years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Grey Owl was indicted by a federal grand jury in November 2025. She pleaded guilty on July 1, 2026.

On the evening of September 2, 2025, Grey Owl was involved in an argument with the victim, an adult male, at his residence in Fort Thompson, SD, within the Crow Creek Sioux Indian Reservation. Grey Owl became irate and swung a shovel at the victim, striking him in the head and causing a deep laceration to the back of his head. The victim was seen by an ambulance crew but refused additional medical help and went back to his room. The next morning, the victim was found deceased.

This matter is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to State court.

This case is part of the Department of Justice’s Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons (MMIP) Regional Outreach Program, which aims to aid in the prevention and response to missing or murdered Indigenous people through the resolution of MMIP cases and communication, coordination, and collaboration with federal, Tribal, state, and local partners. The Department views this work as a priority for its law enforcement components. Through the MMIP Regional Outreach Program, a broad spectrum of stakeholders work together to identify MMIP cases and issues in Tribal communities and develop comprehensive solutions to address them. This prosecution upholds the Department’s mission to the unwavering pursuit of justice on behalf of victims and their families despite the passage of time.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs-Office of Justice Services. Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Great Plains Troy R. Morley prosecuted the case.

Grey Owl was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. — Soldiers and civilians with the U.S. military’s premier all-hazards formation celebrated more than two decades of safeguarding the nation against chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive threats.
The 20th CBRNE Command, headquartered at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, officially reached the 22nd anniversary milestone on Oct. 16.
Activated in 2004 under U.S. Army Forces Command, which has since been renamed U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, the Army consolidated the military's specialized assets under a single operational headquarters to streamline global responses to weapons of mass destruction and explosive hazards.
Retired Vice Chief of Staff of the Army Gen. Richard Cody drafted the memo that charted the course for the establishment of 20th CBRNE Command when he served as the deputy chief of staff of the Army for operations and plans.
Originally established as the 20th Support Command (CBRNE) following the post-9/11 restructuring of Army technical capabilities, the unit was redesignated as the 20th CBRNE Command in 2013 to more accurately reflect its specialized mission.
Today, the formation includes approximately 3,500 soldiers and 220 civilians stationed across 17 states and 20 different installations. The command routinely operates in support of domestic civil authorities, joint forces, special operations and international allies to counter evolving global CBRNE threats.
The 20th CBRNE Command is home to 75 percent of the Active-Duty Army’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) and Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear (CBRN) units, as well as the 1st Global Field Medical Laboratory, CBRNE Analytical and Remediation Activity, Weapons of Mass Destruction Coordination Teams and Nuclear Infrastructure Exploitation Teams.
“The Soldiers and civilians of this organization and its major subordinate commands are some of the most innovative, creative and bravest warriors in a long line of experts,” said Command Sgt. Major Dennis R. Kirk, the command’s senior enlisted leader.
“While the entire country sleeps, they work tirelessly to confront and defeat the world’s most dangerous CBRNE hazards,” Kirk said. “They run towards hazards that most people run away from.”
Over its 22-year history, the command routinely demonstrates its CBRNE defense readiness, integrating into decisive action training rotations at major combat training centers and supporting critical overseas missions, including rotational deployments in support of U.S. Pacific Command, U.S. Central Command, and U.S. Africa Command.
The command marked the occasion with anniversary events at its headquarters compound, celebrating its legacy of defending liberty while continuing to adapt to evolving multi-domain threats.
“Twenty-two years ago, this command was established and it has endured because the threats will continue to evolve, technology will change and our adversaries will adapt,” said Brig. Gen. W Bochat, commanding general of the 20th CBRNE Command and a career chemical officer.
“We must continue our persistent stare and leverage emerging technologies to strengthen our overall readiness - Liberty we defend!”
title: Premier CBRNE command celebrates 22 years of readiness

SAN FRANCISCO – Mario Robinson pleaded guilty in federal court today to robbing a Pleasanton CVS in July 2024 and possessing a fully-automatic handgun and ammunition as a convicted felon in San Francisco in February 2026.

Robinson, 35, of Richmond, California, was indicted by a federal grand jury on April 23, 2026. Under the plea agreement, Robinson pleaded guilty to Robbery Affecting Interstate Commerce, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1951(a), Illegal Possession of a Machinegun, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(o)(1), and Felon in Possession of a Firearm and Ammunition, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1).

In pleading guilty, Robinson admitted that: on or about July 9, 2024, he entered a Pleasanton, California CVS pharmacy wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, black sweatpants, and a black ski mask, and carrying a garbage bag. He approached a CVS employee from behind and took out a paintball gun that appeared to be an AR-style rifle. He followed the employee behind the counter and pointed the AR-style paintball gun at her while she opened one of the store’s cash registers. He took the entire cash drawer, which contained approximately $247.22, and put it in his bag.

He then fled the store and got on a BART train. Pleasanton Police were able to track his movements by a GPS tracker hidden in the cash drawer, and he got off at a nearby train station, having changed clothes and carrying a duffel bag. Robinson fled from police, who ultimately apprehended him and recovered the duffel bag where he had abandoned it along his flight path. The bag contained the clothes Robinson had been wearing during the robbery, the cash drawer, and the AR-style paintball gun.

Robinson further admitted that: on or about February 25, 2026, he approached a group standing outside a convenience store in the Tenderloin neighborhood of San Francisco, wearing a black hooded sweatshirt and black pants. He began firing at the group with a Glock model 22 .40 caliber handgun fitted with a machinegun conversion device commonly referred to as a “switch”. Robinson fired a single shot multiple times; the gun failed to cycle properly and he manually racked the slide of the gun between each shot. After doing this multiple times, he successfully fired an automatic multiple-round burst. The group fled, and Robinson put the gun in his waistband and walked away. San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) officers responded to the scene, and Robinson began running. He fled into a nearby parking lot and discarded the gun under a parked car. Officers then apprehended him.

SFPD recovered the handgun from beneath the car, as well as seven spent shell casings, three unfired cartridges, and a bullet fragment from in front of the convenience store. Subsequent testing revealed gunshot residue on Robinson’s hands and his DNA on the grip of the gun. Prior to the February 2026 incident, Robinson had been convicted of multiple felonies, including robberies in California and Louisiana.

United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian and FBI Special Agent in Charge Scott Schelble made the announcement.

Robinson is currently in federal custody. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for January 7, 2027, at 1:30 p.m. before U.S. District Judge William H. Orrick III. The defendant faces maximum statutory penalties of 20 years imprisonment and a $250,000 fine for Count One, 10 years imprisonment and a $250,000 fine for Count Two, and 15 years imprisonment and a $250,000 fine for Count Three. Any sentence will be imposed by the court after consideration of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and the federal statute governing the imposition of a sentence, 18 U.S.C. § 3553.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Eli J. Cohen is prosecuting the case with the assistance of Tina Rosenbaum. The prosecution is the result of an investigation by the FBI, with the assistance of the ATF, the Pleasanton Police Department, the San Francisco Police Department, the San Francisco District Attorney’s Office, and the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office.
title: Serial Robber Pleads Guilty To Robbing East Bay CVS With Imitation AR-Style Rifle And Possessing Machine Gun And Ammunition

David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, and P.J. O’Brien, Special Agent in Charge of the New Haven Division of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, today announced that a federal grand jury in New Haven has returned an indictment charging VASHAWN RAY, 38, of East Hartford, with drug distribution and firearm possession offenses.

The indictment was returned on October 13, 2026, and Ray was arrested yesterday. He appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert A. Richardson in Hartford and was ordered detained

As alleged in court documents and statements made in court, on October 25, 2025, Ray and a companion drove a Mercedes SUV to the Westfarms Mall in West Hartford. While they were inside the mall, a tow truck operator took the vehicle as part of a repossession. After arriving at the impoundment lot, the tow truck operator found narcotics and a bag containing a firearm in the SUV, and contacted police. Responding police arrived and recovered approximately 160 wax folds of fentanyl, a quantity of crack cocaine, and a loaded 9mm handgun. The bag that contained that firearm also contained Ray’s wallet, identification, and credit cards.

The indictment alleges that Ray’s criminal history includes state felony convictions for robbery and drug offenses, and a federal conviction in 2013 for a crack cocaine trafficking offense.

The indictment charges Ray with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and cocaine, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of 20 years, and unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of 15 years.

U.S. Attorney Sullivan stressed that an indictment is not evidence of guilt. Charges are only allegations, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

This investigation is being conducted by the FBI’s Northern Connecticut Gang Task Force with the assistance of the Newington and Bloomfield Police Departments. The Task Force includes members from the Connecticut State Police, the Connecticut Department of Correction, and the East Hartford, Hartford, Manchester, Naugatuck, New Britain, Newington, Waterbury, West Hartford, and Wethersfield Police Departments. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Christopher Lembo and Daniel Makofsky.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.
