REP. HOYLE JOINS REP. ZINKE AND REP SCHRIER TO INTRODUCE BIPARTISAN NORTHWEST WETLANDS VIP ACT
Eugene, OR – This week, during National Wildlife Refuge Week, Representative Val Hoyle, Rep. Ryan Zinke (MT-01) and Rep. Kim Schrier (WA-08) joined conservation partners in the Pacific Northwest to introduce the bipartisan Northwest Wetlands Voluntary Incentives Program (VIP) Act.
“Conservation is a team effort, and everyone needs to play their part,” said Rep. Hoyle. “Our bipartisan bill supports habitat restoration and active management of invasive species across Northwest wetlands that support Tribes, farmers and other local economies. This work will strengthen our climate resilience, supporting these lands for the next generation.”
“Good conservation starts by bringing everyone to the table,” said Rep. Zinke. “The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act gives farmers, ranchers, Tribes, sportsmen and local communities a way to work together on voluntary projects that restore wetlands and keep working lands working. That’s how we protect habitat and water for the next generation. I'm proud to support this legislation.”
“Farmers, Tribes, and local communities across our region rely on wetlands and the species they protect,” said Congresswoman Schrier. “I am proud that this bipartisan bill will take a meaningful step to make sure Washingtonians continue to benefit from these important habitats that are a critical part of our ecosystem.”
The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would create a new grant program under the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to provide critical water infrastructure and on-the-ground habitat needs for birds in the Columbia River Basin and along the Washington and Oregon coasts. 
This legislation is supported by a host of nonpartisan, regional conservation organizations, including. Ducks Unlimited the Coalition of Oregon Land Trusts (COLT), Montana Wildlife Federation, Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership (TRCP), Pacific Birds Habitat Joint Venture (Pacific Birds), Trout Unlimited, Oregon Agricultural Trust, Washington State Audubon, and more. 
“We’re thankful to Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for introducing the Northwest Wetlands VIP Act in the House of Representatives. The future of conservation is on private working lands. This important legislation will bring much-needed resources for landowners to more effectively provide multi-benefits for people, wildlife, agriculture, and wetlands in the Northwest and the Columbia River Basin.” said Jeff McCreary, Ducks Unlimited Director of Operations for the Western Region.
"The Columbia River?Basin holds critical habitat for migratory birds and other wetland-dependent species,” said Joe Buttafuoco, COLT Executive Director. “COLT and our members are thrilled about the bipartisan NW?Wetlands VIP?Act. This bill would offer grants that land trusts, Tribes, private landowners, and nonprofits can use to improve habitat, manage invasive species, and restore floodplain connectivity. Thank you to Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for advancing this important legislation." 
“Wetlands on the coast of Oregon and Washington and within the Columbia River Basin are vital for millions of waterbirds and wetland-dependent species. Support for durable ecosystems, strong partnerships, and natural and working landscapes will deliver real benefits for wildlife, communities, and the economy of the Pacific Northwest. The NW Wetlands VIP Act emphasizes collaboration — consistent with Pacific Birds’ partnership-driven approach. This bill will provide resources for the installation, maintenance, and replacement of critical infrastructure, which aligns with Pacific Birds’ goal to support long-term habitat management while emphasizing multi-species benefits and multi-benefit projects, and empowering collaborative on the ground action,” said Glenn Lamb, Vice Chair of the Pacific Birds Habitat Joint Venture Management Board.  
“The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would bring critical infrastructure dollars to Pacific Northwest farmers and ranchers. These water management projects not only enhance and restore wetland habitat for migratory birds, but also help producers improve agricultural production on parts of their properties. The Act also provides funding to support conservation easements, which protect farms and ranches for agriculture and associated habitat,” said Nellie McAdams, Executive Director of Oregon Agricultural Trust.  
“Montana’s waterfowl hunters and anglers depend on healthy, connected wetlands, and the birds we chase each fall rely on habitat across the entire Columbia River Basin. The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act gives ranchers, farmers, and Tribes a voluntary way to restore that habitat while keeping working lands working, so our kids and grandkids still have ducks in our skies and fish in our rivers,” said Frank Szollosi, Executive Director of the Montana Wildlife Federation.  
"TRCP appreciates Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier introducing the NW Wetlands VIP Act,” said Michael O’Casey, Director of Public Lands for the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership. “As someone who learned to hunt and fish among the many wetlands and sloughs at the mouth of the mighty Columbia River, and who has seen firsthand the impact of development and fragmentation, this legislation would provide a healthy boost to wetland conservation for both private landowners and the public.” 
“The Association of Northwest Steelheaders strongly supports S.1615 and the continued commitment to policies that protect and strengthen the future of our fisheries, waterways, and outdoor heritage," said James Adkins, Executive Director, Association of Northwest Steelheaders. "Healthy rivers and responsible stewardship are essential to sustaining wild fish populations, supporting local communities, and preserving opportunities for future generations of anglers. Prime habitat for migrating waterfowl also provides critical rearing habitat for juvenile salmon, steelhead and other endangered aquatic species of the Pacific Northwest. We appreciate congressional leadership in advancing this important legislation.” 
“The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act recognizes the importance of investing in wetland infrastructure and habitat restoration projects that benefit both working lands and wild places,” said Christopher Borgatti, Policy & Conservation Manager for Backcountry Hunters & Anglers. “BHA applauds Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for championing this commonsense investment in the future of wetlands, waterfowl, and public access throughout the Columbia River Basin and coastal wetlands.” 
“Healthy wetlands provide a critical foundation for healthy rivers,” said Lindsay Slater, Trout Unlimited Vice President of Government Affairs. “By incentivizing voluntary restoration and conservation, the bipartisan Northwest Wetlands VIP Act will improve water quality, sustain coldwater fisheries, and benefit the communities that depend on them. Trout Unlimited supports this collaborative approach that helps landowners, sportsmen, and conservation partners work together in the Columbia River Basin and along the coast of Oregon and Washington to restore habitat while keeping working lands working.” 
“Healthy wetlands are essential to birds, coastal ecosystems, and the people and communities who help care for these landscapes,” said Amanda Kaplan, vice president for the National Audubon Society’s Washington state office. “The Northwest Wetlands Voluntary Incentives Program Act would give landowners, Tribes and conservation partners resources to restore and improve wetland habitat that shorebirds and waterfowl depend on across the Columbia River Basin and the Pacific Northwest coast. By supporting voluntary conservation efforts, this legislation would also strengthen Audubon’s work with ranchers and other landowners to improve habitat on working lands throughout the region. We thank Reps. Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for introducing this bipartisan bill.” 
“Healthy wetlands are essential to healthy river systems, supporting fish, waterfowl, and other bird species while helping ensure clean drinking water,” said Liz Hamilton, Policy Director for the Northwest Sportfishing Industry Association. “We thank Representatives Hoyle, Zinke, and Schrier for working with Ducks Unlimited to advance this important legislation. These projects will create jobs during implementation and support long-term employment across the region through the outdoor recreation economy.”
"Healthy wetlands are foundational to Washington’s economy, ecosystems, and communities,” said Washington Association of Land Trusts (WALT) Executive Director Erik Kingfisher. “The Northwest Wetlands VIP Act would provide much needed investments in enhancing, maintaining and restoring these vital lands across the Columbia River Basin, Washington coastal zone, and throughout the Puget Sound. As land trusts with the skills to make these projects happen across our beautiful state, we support this bipartisan legislation that would empower landowners through a voluntary, partnership-based approach to establish an open space legacy and enable the care and restoration of these lands to sustain them for future generations."

text:
Fast Facts
People use and throw away textiles, like clothes, more than ever before. Increases in textile waste raise concerns globally about consumption and environmental effects.
Some U.S. states and other countries are implementing policies to develop a textile circular economy where reuse, repair, and recycling keep textiles in use longer. This could create new jobs but currently doesn't have much funding or infrastructure.
Our report looks at policy options to support this, such as:
Requiring industry to be responsible for managing textile waste
Removing sales tax on secondhand apparel
Using tax credits to incentivize industry involvement
Textile Repair Company for Outdoor Gear in the U.S.
People repairing outdoor textile apparel at tables with sewing machines, fabric, work lights, and various hand tools.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Developing a textile circular economy includes repairing, reusing, and recycling textiles and making them last longer.
Example of a Circular Economy for Textiles
In the U.S., a textile circular economy may create potential benefits and involve challenges, according to reports by federal agencies and organizations and stakeholder interviews. Potential benefits could include creating new jobs and markets related to textile repair and recycling, reducing environmental harm, and changing consumer practices. Challenges could include limited funding and domestic infrastructure for nationwide textile collection and recycling efforts.
GAO identified a number of policy options—based on relevant literature, site visits, and interviews with 49 stakeholders in the public and private sectors—that federal and state policymakers can consider if the U.S. chooses to develop a textile circular economy. Two of the options are:
- Developing a textile extended producer responsibility program: makes companies responsible for what happens to their products after use, along with other requirements.
- Creating tax credits related to a textile circular economy: reduces or offsets the amount of taxes paid by businesses when they contribute to textile circularity efforts, such as reusing textiles or reducing textile waste.
Some U.S. states and other countries are proposing, enacting, or implementing most of the identified policy options that can help develop a textile circular economy. For example, U.S. states, the European Union, and others have proposed or enacted legislation to develop textile extended producer responsibility programs. When discussing policy options, stakeholders shared key observations. For example, several stakeholders, including industry groups, told GAO they prefer a federal approach to develop a textile circular economy. A federal approach may provide for coordination, compliance, and consistent implementation across U.S. states or other countries’ legal requirements, among other reasons, according to these stakeholders. However, this would require additional federal coordination and resources and depend on the government’s legal authority to implement a federal approach.
Why GAO Did This Study
The textile industry is part of a massive, global economic sector—including fiber sourcing, yarn production, and textile manufacturing. Textiles include apparel and other products, such as carpets, footwear, and towels. In response to global increases in the amount of textile consumption and waste, certain U.S. states and other countries have begun to consider and implement policies that can help develop a textile circular economy.
GAO was asked to review aspects of developing a textile circular economy. This report continues GAO’s previous work from December 2024 on federal efforts to address textile waste. This report describes (1) the potential benefits and challenges with developing a textile circular economy in the U.S.; (2) the options that policymakers could consider to develop a textile circular economy; and (3) identified proposed, enacted, or implemented policies, both domestically and internationally, and stakeholders’ key observations.
GAO reviewed legislation, regulations, federal agency documents, and academic reports. GAO also interviewed a range of stakeholder groups, including government entities (international, federal, and state), industry, academia, and other nonfederal stakeholders, such as representatives from nonprofit organizations. These stakeholders were selected because they have, or will have, a role in ongoing or planned efforts related to a textile circular economy or were recommended by knowledgeable officials. GAO also conducted site visits to the states of Washington and Oregon, as well as France and the Netherlands to meet with private sector organizations involved with various aspects of developing a textile circular economy.
For more information, contact J. Alfredo Gómez at gomezj@gao.gov.
title: Textile Circular Economy: Policy Options for the U.S.

FORT LEE, Va.—Halloween trick-or-treat hours this year will be Oct. 31, 6 to 8 p.m. in the Fort Lee residential areas.
Participation is restricted to on-post residents, Department of Defense ID cardholders and their guests.
The Fort Lee Provost Marshal Office reminds residents, families and visitors to use extra caution during trick-or-treat activities. Increased pedestrian traffic, reduced visibility, costumes and distracted driving can create additional safety risks in residential areas.
“The PMO will support a safe Halloween by monitoring traffic and pedestrian activity, enforcing posted speed limits and traffic regulations,” said Louis P. Ostmann, Jr., Fort Lee police chief. “Safety is a shared responsibility and parents, residents and drivers all play an important role in ensuring children can enjoy Halloween safely. We ask everyone to remain alert, follow installation rules and look out for one another.”
Residents who welcome trick-or-treaters should turn on exterior lights and keep sidewalks, stairs, driveways, and walkways clear. Decorations, hoses, toys and other objects should be removed from areas where children may walk. Residents should also keep pets secured indoors and avoid decorations that could create a safety hazard.
Parents and guardians are encouraged to accompany young children and supervise older children, according to the PMO. Children should use sidewalks, carry flashlights or glow sticks, and wear costumes that fit properly and do not restrict their vision or movement. Parents should inspect all treats before children eat them and remind children never to enter an unfamiliar home or vehicle without permission.
Parents and guardians are also advised to walk with their children instead of following them in a vehicle. Extra vehicles on residential streets can create congestion, reduce visibility and increase risks for children and other pedestrians. Walking together helps keep roadways clear, improves safety and preserves access for emergency responders.
“Drivers should use extreme caution throughout trick-or-treat hours,” Ostmann said. “They should slow down, keep headlights on, avoid distractions, yield to pedestrians and expect children to cross unexpectedly between parked vehicles. Drivers should use additional care when entering or leaving driveways and parking areas.”
The PMO and Army Sustainment University volunteers will be working together to ensure everyone’s safety with the volunteers patrolling on foot and wearing reflective vests.
The phone number for the non-emergency Military Police Desk is 804-734-7400. For an emergency, dial 911.
title: Provost Marshal Office announces trick-or-treat hours, safety measures

ST. LOUIS – A registered sex offender on Friday admitted viewing child sexual abuse material that he found online.

Corey Adam Oliver, 53, pleaded guilty Friday in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of possession of child pornography. In December of 2024, a Cyber Tipline report to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children indicated that Oliver had uploaded child sexual abuse material (CSAM) to Bing’s image search application. On January 14, 2025, the Missouri State Highway Patrol obtained a search warrant for Oliver’s home near Bismarck, in St. Francois County. In an interview with law enforcement, Oliver initially denied viewing or receiving CSAM. After he failed a consensual polygraph examination, he admitted using a tablet to do so.

Oliver was required to register as a sex offender after having been convicted in Louisiana in 2000 of the felony offenses of molestation of a juvenile and carnal knowledge of a juvenile and in Georgia in 2007 of the felony offenses of enticing a child for indecent purposes and interference with child custody.

Oliver is scheduled to be sentenced in January. The U.S. Attorney’s office will recommend 15 years in prison, followed by a lifetime on supervised release.

The Missouri State Highway Patrol investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jillian Anderson prosecuted the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Department of Justice Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .
title: Missouri Sex Offender Admits Possessing Child Sexual Abuse Material

text:
The motion to recommit in the House of Representatives proposes to send legislation under consideration on the floor back to committee. A Member may move to recommit a measure prior to a vote on final passage of a bill, providing a late-stage opportunity for a vote in relation to the legislation. Priority in recognition to offer the motion is given to an opponent of the measure, and the motion is considered to be a minority party right.
The motion to recommit is one of the most common roll call votes taken on the House floor, as House rules guarantee the opportunity to offer the motion during initial consideration of a bill or joint resolution under the terms of a special rule. Specifically, the Committee on Rules cannot report a special rule that precludes the minority leader or a designee from moving to recommit the underlying legislation.
Historically, a motion to recommit could include "instructions" that proposed to immediately amend a measure on the House floor. Oftentimes, the minority party would use such a motion to obtain a vote in connection to a favored policy. Since the 117th Congress, however, Members may no longer use a recommittal motion to directly propose changes to a legislative text. Nevertheless, minority Members often connect the vote on the motion to recommit to a policy proposal during general debate on the bill. They sometimes present an amendment they would like to have offered, if allowed, or that they would like the committee to consider if the motion to recommit is successful.
The rules and procedures of the House of Representatives are designed to allow a numerical majority to work its will on the floor. Major legislation is considered under special orders of business—more often called rules or special rules—which determine the text that will be brought before the full House for consideration and what changes, if any, may be proposed from the floor.1 Special rules, if they are approved on the House floor after being reported by the Committee on Rules, allow a voting majority to control the floor agenda, with few limits on the parameters they may set.
Some standing rules of the House, however, protect the ability of members of the minority party to participate in the legislative process. Perhaps most significantly, prior to final passage of a bill, members opposed to the measure have an opportunity to propose that it be sent to committee. They do this by offering a motion to recommit—or, if the measure has not yet been sent to committee, a motion to commit.2 This motion is permitted whenever the House is considering a measure under the terms of a special rule, even a special rule that precludes all other motions and amendments. In recent Congresses, Members have used the motion in approximately half of the circumstances during which it was available, making the vote on the motion to recommit one of the most common roll call votes taken in the House.
This report describes the rules and precedents governing the motion to recommit, the potential effects of the motion, and the minority Member practice of connecting the motion to recommit to specific policy proposals during debate on the bill.
House Rule XIX, clause 2, permits a motion to recommit prior to a vote on final passage or adoption of a measure. More precisely, it allows the motion even if the previous question has been ordered or proposed on a measure.3 The previous question is used to bring the House to an immediate vote on the main question under consideration. If the House votes to order the previous question on a measure, it prevents further debate, amendment, and motions—except that clause 2 of Rule XIX allows a single motion to recommit. In current practice, it is almost always the case that during floor consideration when this motion to recommit would be permitted, the House is considering legislation under the terms of a special rule reported by the Rules Committee.4
Clause 2 of Rule XIX directs the Speaker to give priority in recognition for this form of a motion to recommit to a Member opposed to the measure. Preference in recognition among those opposed is given first to the minority leader or a Member designated by the minority leader, then to minority party members of the committee that reported the measure (in order of seniority), then to other minority party Members, and, finally to majority party Members.5 In practice, the minority leader arranges in advance of floor consideration which Member of the minority party will offer the motion.6
Since the start of the 117th Congress (2021-2022), the motion to recommit offered pursuant to House Rule XIX cannot include "instructions" to the committee and is not subject to debate. As discussed below, previous forms of House Rule XIX allowed for instructions as well as 10 minutes of debate.7
House Rule XIII, clause 6(c), prohibits the Rules Committee from reporting a special rule for the consideration of a bill or joint resolution that precludes the minority leader or a designee from offering the motion to recommit permitted by House Rule XIX, clause 2.8 There is an exception, however, if the House has agreed to an amendment to a Senate-passed bill or joint resolution that substitutes the text of a House-passed measure. In that case, Members would have had a chance to offer the motion to recommit when the House-passed measure was initially considered.
Rule XIII does not protect the motion to recommit during consideration of simple and concurrent resolutions. For example, a special rule precluding a recommittal motion on a congressional budget resolution (concurrent resolution) or a "sense of the House" resolution (simple resolution) would not violate House rules.
Further, House Rule XIII does not protect the motion to recommit during consideration of Senate amendments, as the protection applies only to initial passage.9 For instance, a special rule may make in order a motion to concur in a Senate amendment with an amendment consisting of language the House has not previously considered. House rules would not require such a special rule to guarantee the minority a motion to recommit, even though the special rule was providing for action on what is effectively a new proposal.10
Simply stated, the motion to recommit proposes to send the measure under consideration back to committee. Although a successful motion does not preclude future procedural action on the legislation, it may effectively kill a measure or prompt significant modification. Motions to recommit almost always fail, typically along party lines.
Oftentimes, a Member requests that the question of adopting a motion to recommit be decided by roll call vote, wherein Members cast their votes on the floor by electronic device, establishing a record of how each Member voted. In such cases, the Speaker may put the vote to the House immediately but has authority to postpone the vote within two additional legislative days.11
House approval of a motion to recommit could send a bill back to the committee from which it was reported for further work on the measure. Members often discuss desired modifications during general debate on the bill, which may provide the committee with a nonbinding understanding of how to improve the legislation if it chooses to take additional action. If the underlying legislation was not reported by a committee—either because it was never referred to committee or because a committee was discharged from further consideration of the bill—the minority might try to use the motion to provide for a markup process. A motion to recommit can also send a measure to a different committee than the one that reported it, perhaps to facilitate the inclusion of provisions outside the original committee's jurisdiction.
Proponents of a measure sometimes argue that a successful motion to recommit effectively disposes of the underlying measure because a committee is not required to take further action on a recommitted measure. In some political contexts, a committee may interpret a vote to remove a bill from the floor as a rejection of the legislation altogether.
The motion to recommit has existed since the First Congress, although its form and function have evolved.12 Oftentimes, modifications of procedure have reflected attempts to balance the minority's right to have its positions considered with the majority's need to control floor action.13 Previous iterations of the motion to recommit shape the manner in which the motion is understood and characterized today, particularly with regard to its effect on policy outcomes.
Most notably in recent history, the rules package adopted at the start of the 117th Congress (2021-2022) contained several revisions to House Rule XIX that affected the motion to recommit.14 The rule prior to the 117th Congress provided for 10 minutes of debate on the motion and the option of making a motion to recommit with instructions "in the form of a direction to report an amendment or amendments back to the House forthwith."15 Such a motion would direct the committee of referral to immediately report the bill back to the House with any amendment(s) contained within the instructions. If successful, a motion to recommit with instructions effectively provided the minority an opportunity to offer an amendment before final passage. For instance, the House adopted a motion to recommit H.R. 2102 in the 110th Congress (see Figure 1).
Immediately after the motion's approval, the chair of the Committee on the Judiciary reported the bill back to the House with the specified amendment, and the House agreed to the amendment by voice vote.
Since the 117th Congress, both the 10 minutes of debate on the motion to recommit and the option to include instructions have been eliminated. To date, only one motion to recommit offered after the rules change of the 117th Congress has succeeded.16
As House rules exist now, the motion to recommit may not include instructions and therefore cannot directly propose modifications to a legislative text. However, since the 117th Congress, and regardless of which political party controls the House, members of the minority party have often characterized the motion to recommit vote as a vote on a policy position.
During general debate, Members may discuss amendments they would have offered using a motion to recommit with instructions to report back "forthwith," if it were allowed. For example, during floor consideration of H.R. 140 in the 118th Congress, a minority party Member made such a statement (see Figure 2).
The Member then provided the amendment he would have offered as text inserted in the Congressional Record at the conclusion of his remarks (see Figure 3).
Minority Members sometimes ask unanimous consent to include the text of an amendment they would like to have offered in the Congressional Record immediately prior to the vote on the motion to recommit.17 Oftentimes, this text will have been drafted as a motion to recommit with instructions.
For example, during floor consideration of H.R. 4468 in the 118th Congress, a minority party Member made the following request:
Ms. STEVENS. Madam Speaker, I ask unanimous consent to insert the text of my amendment in the Record immediately prior to the vote on the motion to recommit.
At the appropriate time, the Member moved to recommit the bill without instructions. Text describing a motion to recommit with instructions was then inserted into Congressional Record directly after (see Figure 4).
Although the text inserted into the Congressional Record appears in the form of a motion, the Member inserting the text into the Congressional Record is not offering a motion to recommit the bill with instructions, as House rules do not permit such a motion. Rather, such insertions highlight a policy change the proponent could have offered under the previous version of Rule XIX. During general debate, the proponents of such motions sometimes indicate they would like the committee to consider the proposed changes if the motion to recommit were successful.
This report was written by Sarah Solomon, former CRS Analyst on Congress and the Legislative Process. The CRS Analysts listed below are available to answer questions on the topic. CRS Visual Information Specialist Amber Wilhelm assisted in creating the graphics in this report.
title: The Motion to Recommit in the House

ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man was sentenced to 20 years in prison for fatally stabbing a man in broad daylight near a community grocery store in Shiprock, New Mexico.

According to publicly available court documents, on the afternoon of July 25, 2024, officers with the Navajo Nation Police Department responded to a fight in progress near a high-traffic Navajo Nation shopping center in Shiprock, New Mexico. Upon arrival, they found a man lying on the ground with wounds to his face and chest. Witnesses reported that Edison Brady , 57, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, had stabbed the man in the chest after the man was already badly beaten, hardly conscious, lying on the ground, and bleeding from the head. According to multiple witnesses, Brady attacked the victim without provocation, repeatedly punching and kicking him as he remained on the ground and attempted to shield his face. Brady then walked away, retrieved a long kitchen knife from his nearby bag, and returned to stab the victim in the chest as the victim lay bleeding and barely conscious. The victim died from his injuries shortly after arriving at the Northern Navajo Medical Center. Officers recovered the knife, which was covered in the victim’s blood, from Brady ’s bag minutes after the attack.

Brady pleaded guilty without a plea agreement to an indictment charging him with one count of second-degree murder. Upon his release from prison, Brady will be subject to five years of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system.

Brady must also compensate the New Mexico Crime Victim Reparations Commission for the $6,000.00 it expended paying for the victim’s funeral expenses.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Nation Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant United States Attorneys Jena Ritchey and Zachary C. Jones are prosecuting this case.
title: Shiprock Man Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison for Second-Degree Murder

El representante Tran emite un comunicado sobre el acuerdo extrajudicial de 125 millones de dólares de GKN
Condado de Orange, California – El representante Derek Tran (CA-45) ha emitido la siguiente declaración en respuesta al anuncio de la Fiscalía del Condado de Orange de que ha alcanzado un acuerdo de 125 millones de dólares con GKN Aerospace tras la emergencia relacionada con un depósito de sustancias químicas tóxicas en mayo de 2026, que provocó la evacuación de 50000 residentes y negocios:
“Me tranquiliza ver que el Condado de Orange y GKN han llegado a un acuerdo que da prioridad a las necesidades de los residentes y los propietarios de pequeñas empresas que se vieron afectados por la evacuación forzosa de mayo”, dijo el representante Tran. “Espero que este acuerdo pueda superar rápidamente el proceso de aprobación judicial, para que podamos poner en marcha el proceso de reclamaciones y gestionar la ayuda económica y los reembolsos que tanto necesitan los afectados. Seguiré vigilando de cerca la situación para garantizar que las familias, las empresas y los socios comunitarios reciban una indemnización adecuada.’’
“Todos los californianos merecen sentirse seguros en su propio hogar, sin temor a ser desalojados ni a sufrir trastornos. Como su representante en el Congreso, supervisaré de primera mano la aplicación del plan de seguridad integral de GKN a medida que avancen en sus operaciones de fabricación.”
El acuerdo extrajudicial, presentado por la Fiscalía del Condado de Orange el lunes 12 de octubre, está pendiente de aprobación por parte del Tribunal Superior del Condado de Orange.
En respuesta a la evacuación de mayo de 2026, el representante Tran presentó la Ley de Transparencia sobre Materiales Peligrosos, que obligaría a instalaciones como GKN a informar adecuadamente a las comunidades en las que operan sobre las medidas de seguridad establecidas para proteger a los residentes y a las pequeñas empresas.

WASHINGTON, DC – Representative Josh Riley (NY-19) is demanding the federal government get heating assistance to Upstate families on time as energy costs rise and colder weather approaches. Riley joined a bipartisan group of 116 lawmakers calling on the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to release Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) funding to states as soon as possible, and no later than November 1, 2026.
“Upstate New Yorkers shouldn’t have to choose between staying warm or buying groceries. But while utility monopolies keep raising prices on working families, Washington bureaucracy is threatening to leave people out in the cold,” Riley said. “With winter right around the corner, the government needs to do its job, cut through the delays, and get this relief directly into the hands of the families who need it.”
Riley’s letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. highlights concerns about LIHEAP’s capacity to operate without dedicated staff following mass firings in April 2025. The letter urges Secretary Kennedy to ensure that the necessary personnel and resources are in place to make sure families receive assistance on schedule.
In addition to today’s actions, Riley has also signed onto a bipartisan letter urging the House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in emergency funding for LIHEAP to ensure that every family who qualifies for the program can receive the assistance they need. Across the nation, LIHEAP helps nearly 6 million households afford their energy bills, including nearly 1.3 million households in New York; however, five out of six families who qualify for LIHEAP receive no financial assistance because of budget shortfalls.
You can read Riley’s letter to HHS HERE and his letter to the House Appropriations Committee HERE.

title: RILEY DEMANDS HOME HEATING AID BE DELIVERED ON TIME FOR UPSTATE FAMILIES

TOPEKA, KAN. – Two defendants received prison sentences following an $897,405 health care scheme where they used their pharmaceutical service to bill Medicare for thousands of unnecessary and illegal prescriptions.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

According to court documents, the following defendants pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, mail fraud, and wire fraud:

Steven Anthony Churchill, 39, of Boca Raton, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison;

Samson Kollelil Solomon, 28, of Pompano Beach, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison; and

Fawn Lickteig, 46, of Lawrence, Kansas, will be sentenced on November 10, 2026.

In March 2020, Steven Churchill bought Free State Pharmacy (FSP) in Lawrence, Kansas, but under the name of a now deceased, accused coconspirator. FSP operated as a mail-order pharmacy despite representing itself to Medicare as a retail pharmacy. FSP contracted with Fawn Lickteig’s company, Pharmacy Consulting, to complete and submit its applications to Medicare and other health care related government entities.

As part of the scheme, FSP acquired information from telemedicine companies, including names and addresses of patients. FSP employees then filled and shipped medications to these people even though the doctors who wrote the prescriptions had not physically examined or conducted proper telemedicine visits with the patients. FSP received calls from patients unexpectedly receiving medical products, and some patients returned the products to FSP.

FSP prioritized the filling of prescriptions based on the amount of profit Medicare would ultimately pay the pharmacy. The majority of the medications prescribed were high-dollar dermatological products. Although FSP was based in Kansas, most of the beneficiaries were Floridians, with 948 claims for Florida residents and 381 claims for Kansas residents.

Of the 40 prescribing physicians who worked with FSP, 15 were under investigation at the time for referring medically unnecessary services. Between September 2020 and February 2021, Churchill, Solomon, and Lickteig submitted 2,699 false claims causing Medicare to make fraudulent payments to FSP totaling $897,405.

“Medicare exists to help senior citizens obtain the medical services and supplies they need,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “Those who pillage government programs for their own enrichment will pay a heavy price when brought to justice. The agency Inspectors General under this administration are hard at work rooting out this type of fraud, and the Department of Justice stands ready to prosecute when it is found.”

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (OIG) investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sara Walton and Lindsey Debenham prosecuted the case.

###
title: Two Florida defendants sentenced to prison for nearly $900,000 health care scam

text:
Fast Facts
Critical minerals–like copper and lithium–are vital to the U.S. economy and national security. The U.S. relies on imported critical minerals to meet its needs, raising concerns that have prompted the President to call for expanding mining on federal lands.
To extract minerals from federal lands, individuals must generally be U.S. citizens and companies must be incorporated in the U.S. However, the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees mines on federal lands, rarely collects information to know if these requirements are being met.
We recommended that BLM do so to help ensure that only those qualified can extract minerals from federal lands.
Photo of a copper mine on federal lands.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management (BLM) administers mining claims that grant the exclusive right to extract critical and other hardrock minerals from most federal lands. U.S. mining laws include citizenship requirements for individuals and business entities holding such claims, known as mining claimants. Under these laws, mining claimants generally must be U.S. citizens, which can include individuals as well as business entities incorporated in a U.S. state or territory. Foreign entities are not qualified to be claimants, but their subsidiaries can hold claims if they are incorporated in the U.S. Mining claimants are not required to disclose to BLM if they are a subsidiary of another entity, foreign or domestic, and they do not have to provide information on any foreign investment they may receive.
Under BLM’s regulations and guidance, the agency collects basic identifying information from individuals and business entities holding mining claims. However, BLM generally does not collect citizenship information and does not document if mining claimants meet the U.S. citizenship requirements. In addition, BLM officials said the agency rarely verifies the citizenship of mining claimants. As a result, BLM generally does not know whether mining claimants are qualified to hold mining claims.
Information the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Collects from Mining Claimants
GAO analyzed a nongeneralizable sample of 15 mining claimants that appeared to be business entities and could not find evidence that seven of the claimants were incorporated in the U.S., as required. BLM was unable to help determine if these entities met the requirement to be incorporated in the U.S. because it did not have the necessary information to do so. Until BLM directs staff to collect citizenship information and document that mining claimants meet the U.S. citizenship requirements, BLM lacks reasonable assurance that only qualified individuals and business entities hold mining claims that allow them to extract and profit from the minerals produced on federal lands.
Australia and Canada—examples of top mineral-producing countries—collect detailed information on foreign investors in businesses in their countries. They can use this information to restrict foreign investments in mining and other sectors by prohibiting certain investments or imposing conditions, as each country has done in some cases in recent years. In addition, both countries limit the ability of foreign state-owned enterprises and other foreign investors to acquire control of businesses involving critical minerals.
Why GAO Did This Study
Critical minerals are vital to the U.S. economy and national security. Federal lands are a significant source of hardrock minerals and include some mining operations supported by foreign investments, according to BLM officials. The administration and Congress have expressed concern about U.S. reliance on foreign sources for critical minerals, and the President has called for expanding mineral production from federal lands.
GAO was asked to review issues related to foreign entities’ involvement in mining on federal lands. This report examines (1) the extent to which BLM collects, documents, and reviews mining claimants’ citizenship information and (2) how selected mineral-producing countries address foreign investments in mining. GAO was also asked to report on the extent of foreign investment in mining on federal lands (see GAO-27-108094).
GAO reviewed U.S. laws and regulations; analyzed a nongeneralizable sample of mining claimants to assess if they appear to meet citizenship requirements; examined BLM documents; visited three BLM state offices; and interviewed officials and representatives from BLM and other federal and nonfederal entities. GAO also reviewed Australian and Canadian laws, guidance, reports, and written responses to questions.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that BLM direct staff to collect citizenship information from mining claimants and document that they meet the citizenship requirements to hold mining claims. Interior did not provide comments on this report.
title: Critical Minerals: BLM Should Ensure Individuals and Businesses Meet Citizenship Requirements for Hardrock Mining Claims

text:
ICYMI: Director Kupor Discusses Responsible SI Leadership on CNBC’s Squawk Box
WASHINGTON, DC – US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director Scott Kupor, Vice Chair of the Super Intelligence Task Force, joined CNBC’s Squawk Box to discuss the task force’s work, technology companies’ responsibilities, government oversight, the impact of data centers, and the need to advance super intelligence responsibly.
On the task force’s goals:
“Thanks, Joe. You’re exactly right. The goal is to make sure that we continue to win, which we are winning, and ensure that we do so responsibly. I think what you’re going to see from us are a couple things. One is—and I just saw the last segment you guys did—there’s a lot of work on behalf of the industry that needs to happen.”
On industry responsibility:
“We’ve been very clear from the beginning, and you’ll see us continue to follow up. The industry bears a lot of responsibility here to make sure that when they release things, they’re safe, they’re appropriately vetted, and when things go wrong, you’re going to see us make sure that there’s a very appropriate ongoing notification program so that the government has all the information they need.”
“We’re also going to make sure that all the major players outside of technology—critical infrastructure, financial services, energy, oil and gas, all these companies—have the appropriate information they need to make sure that they’ve got plans in place and that we’ve got coordination across things.”
“There’s a whole set of laws that the President has mentioned—product liability laws, principal-agent laws, all these things that really govern corporate responsibility in these areas. I think you’re going to see a much greater articulation of that and an indication among the companies that the government has a very clear expectation of their responsibility here.”
On enforcement and oversight:
“You’re right. That was with a pact that was signed, I guess, a week ago Tuesday with the various players. These are independent auditors. They will report to the board, and all the traditional fiduciary duties and corporate responsibilities will attach to that.”
“But there’s also got to be a mechanism whereby the government actually has insight into that and appropriate oversight. We’re not just going to sit around and wait for the companies to tell us they’ve done their work. I think you should expect that the government should have a role in making sure that what the companies say they do, they do, and that there’s an appropriate mechanism for enforcement on our end.”
On data center energy and water use:
“Water and energy—we’ve seen this already, even in the data that’s come out. There’s no question that whatever concerns there traditionally were about energy usage and water use, all those are going in the right direction, meaning the technology continues to improve and will reduce those.”
“To be completely honest, I think this is the easiest part of the problem to solve. The players in this space should just go into those local communities and say, ‘Look, we don’t need to debate whether water is going to get better or energy is going to get better. We should just take care of that.’”
“If you’re concerned about rate rises, we’ll take care of those. If you’re concerned about electricity, we can either bring our own or, again, we can take care of those rates. We don’t need to debate these topics. I imagine no average American is going to read the studies on water usage. So let’s just take these things off the table.”
“We’ve been very clear with the industry on this as well. We think this is a much easier problem to solve. They should just go in and resolve these issues. Yes, absolutely, the technology will take care of these problems over time, but in the meantime, there’s a much simpler way to do this: companies should make sure those concerns are taken right off the table.”
On harnessing SI innovation:
“I think you can do both things. You’re absolutely right: The power of this will be that, over time, the recursive nature of the idea—that it can learn from mistakes—will continue to evolve the technology.”
“You’ve been around a long time, as you probably know. Many technology industries develop in this area. In the early stages of these companies, there are lots of challenges that need to be dealt with. For every challenge out there, I can tell you there’s somebody on Sand Hill Road trying to start a company to address it.”
“The technology will evolve not just in terms of the benefits, but also around security control and all these other areas. Nvidia put out, about a week and a half ago, an open-source piece of software that would prevent things like the jailbreaks that happened in the Hugging Face case. The industry is going to have to—and I’m very confident it will—continue to release products that deal with these issues as they come up.”
“In the short term, obviously, we do need to make sure that we’ve got the appropriate level of government oversight, that there is a notification scheme, an information scheme, and the government has all the information required to make sure that public safety remains a number one concern.”
On industry views and the risk of slowing down:
“I’m not going to ascribe motivations or try to discern those for those individuals. Those are extremely smart people who, as you know, probably have lots of—”
“I think that’s a fair point, and I get that. What’s really important for these players to understand is a couple things. Number one, if Dario and others really honestly believe that they are putting products out that they are fundamentally unable to control and that actually are going to cause harm to people, there is a very strong existing set of laws and regulations that should prohibit that behavior, and those companies need to understand that.”
“If he’s got questions and concerns, the issue is: Can we evolve the technology and make sure that we can address those? I think that’s a totally different story, and I think there is a role for the government to play here to make sure that they stand by those ideas.”
“I think everybody’s going to have different motivations on this. At the end of the day, the fundamental question the President has asked us is this idea of a pause or a slowdown. What is the impact of that?”
“There is no magical kill switch somewhere where, if we decide to slow this down, that doesn’t mean other adversaries won’t continue to advance the technology. That’s not a good place for us to be. What’s critical is that we allow the technology to develop, but we’ve got to do so in a responsible way.”
“Different players in this area have different views on it. Part of our job, which is why we’re here, is we’ve got to coalesce those views and make sure we have a plan that protects the American people.”
title: ICYMI: Director Kupor Discusses Responsible SI Leadership on CNBC’s Squawk Box

CHOICE in Action: Ohio Employers Explore New Approach to Health Benefits
Federal leaders spotlight CHOICE Arrangement to aid Ohio small businesses in delivering flexible and affordable healthcare to workers
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the Small Business Administration (SBA), and Take Command, the first provider of Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangements (ICHRAs) in the country, partnered to bring together policymakers, industry experts, and Ohio businesses for a meaningful conversation about the future of employer-sponsored health coverage at CHOICE in Action: Ohio.
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator for CMS, along with Bill Briggs, Deputy Administrator for SBA, heard directly from Ohio employers and workers about how the new approach to employer-sponsored healthcare is helping small businesses tackle rising group insurance costs. Key members of the CHOICE ecosystem were in attendance, including carriers, brokers, and members of the HRA Council.
Established during President Trump’s first Administration, ICHRAs expanded employers' options by enabling them to make tax-favored contributions toward qualifying individual health insurance or Medicare coverage instead of offering a traditional group health plan.
Recently renamed from ICHRA, CHOICE Arrangements let employers provide employees with a tax-advantaged contribution toward individual health coverage instead of a traditional group health plan. Employees can use the contribution toward qualifying individual coverage based on their own healthcare needs and preferences.
“Ohio’s small businesses deserve healthcare options that prioritize affordability, expand access to coverage, and give both employers and employees greater flexibility,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “CHOICE Arrangements offer a practical alternative to traditional group health insurance, helping Ohio employers better manage healthcare costs while empowering workers to choose coverage that meets their individual needs. The experiences that Ohio businesses shared today demonstrate the real-world impact of CHOICE.”
"For too long, small businesses have had to choose between costly group plans and offering no health benefits at all," said SBA Deputy Administrator Bill Briggs. "CHOICE Arrangements give Ohio's job creators another option. Under CHOICE Arrangements, small business owners control their costs, compete for talent, and their workers get to choose their own coverage."
“Businesses in Cleveland and beyond are facing rising healthcare costs that make it difficult to offer competitive benefits while managing their budgets,” said Jack Hooper, CEO of Take Command. “CHOICE Arrangements give employers greater control over their health benefit costs while giving employees the freedom to choose coverage that best fits their individual needs. By expanding options on both sides, CHOICE helps Ohio businesses offer quality health benefits at a price point both they and their employees can afford.”
To learn more about CHOICE Arrangements for Ohio businesses, visit https://www.takecommandhealth.com/blog/ohio-ichra and www.cms.gov/choicearrangements.

CMS Proposes Reforms to Strengthen Transparency and Affordability in Medicare Advantage and Part D
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) today issued a proposed rule that would improve the accuracy of provider directories for Medicare Advantage plans, establish transparency and compensation requirements for Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs), and deliver enhanced cost-saving protections for low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
“CMS has been working to improve data connectivity and accuracy in provider directories across the healthcare system,” said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz. “The actions we are proposing today will give Medicare Advantage and Part D enrollees more reliable information, stronger financial protections, and greater confidence in both programs.”
To ensure beneficiaries have reliable and up-to-date information, CMS is proposing to make improvements to Medicare Advantage provider directories. This proposal establishes a clear framework to significantly improve the accuracy of provider directories for Medicare Advantage plans. Under the proposed rule, plans would be required to verify and update their provider directory information at least every 90 days and report an accuracy score to CMS. These scores would also be prominently displayed on the plans’ public-facing directories, empowering beneficiaries to choose plans with confidence.
This proposal protects beneficiaries from unexpected costs and care disruptions that can occur when they rely on inaccurate directory information to find an in-network provider. By codifying these standards, CMS is strengthening enrollee protections and increasing transparency across the Medicare Advantage program. In addition, CMS is proposing that enrollees who rely on inaccurate directory listings that led them to receive care by an out-of-network provider would pay no more than their in-network cost-sharing amount. These changes are part of a broader effort to modernize provider directories and ensure beneficiaries can easily find and access the care they need.
CMS is also proposing transparency and reporting requirements for PBMs aimed at curbing practices that drive up drug costs. PBMs would have to report their compensation and cost performance to plan sponsors and CMS on an annual basis. The rule would also require PBM payments to reflect fair market value for services provided, rather than drug costs.
The proposed changes for Contract Year (CY) 2028 for Medicare Advantage and Part D to implement these key sections of the CAA will be open for public comment for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register here: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/current. CMS anticipates releasing another proposed rule consisting of policy and technical changes for Parts C and D later this fall.
For more information, please view the fact sheet at: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicare-program-implementation-sections-6219-6220-6224-consolidated-appropriations-act-2026-cms.

text:
Lofgren Demands Answers to Outstanding Oversight Requests, Warns EPA that Lack of Cooperation is Unacceptable
(Washington, DC) - On Tuesday, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) sent a letter to Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin demanding that he comply with outstanding congressional oversight requests from the Committee.
“Since January 2025, I have sent a number of formal oversight letters to EPA requesting agency records, documents, and communications regarding various policies and activities,” writes Ranking Member Lofgren in her letter. “However, rather than providing the requested information in a comprehensive and timely manner, EPA has failed to produce a single responsive document, communication, or record.”
In closing, she writes: “EPA’s non-responsiveness to Committee oversight during the 119th Congress has been unacceptable. The agency must respect congressional prerogatives. We remain determined to obtain the information we need to perform our duties on behalf of the American people. EPA should understand that a lack of cooperation will not frustrate the Committee’s oversight permanently. It will merely strengthen our commitment to employing all the tools at our disposal to hold the agency accountable.”
In her letter, Ranking Member Lofgren requires a response from EPA to the Committee’s outstanding oversight requests by no later than 5:00 pm Friday, November 6th, 2026.
Access the letter here and below.
Dear Administrator Zeldin,
Agencies are required to comply with congressional oversight. It is an obligation, not a choice. But under your leadership, the EPA appears to have forgotten that basic principle. Since President Trump took office in January 2025, I have made multiple requests to the agency for internal records, documents, and communications related to various topics. These oversight requests are crucial to my ability to properly carry out my oversight duties as the Ranking Member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, which possesses jurisdiction over environmental research and development programs at EPA. However, rather than providing the requested information in a comprehensive and timely manner, EPA has failed to produce a single responsive document, communication, or record. Instead, the agency has merely responded with letters that deflect questions rather than answering them. That was never acceptable. It becomes less tolerable with each passing month. I am writing to you to reaffirm my prior oversight requests from the 119th Congress, and to formally notify the agency that they remain outstanding. I expect EPA to promptly comply.
Since your confirmation as the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on January 29th, 2025, roughly 20% of the agency’s workforce has quit, retired, or been fired. Irreplaceable laboratory facilities have been shut down. The independent Office of Research and Development (ORD) has been wiped out. Scientific capacity has been gutted, scientific integrity is compromised, industry capture is widespread, and climate denialism is ascendant. In short, EPA’s basic mission to use the best available science to protect human health and the environment has been damaged under your leadership.
To take just one of countless examples, I have learned that the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR), acting under direct orders from former Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo, has refused to grant the Office of Applied Sciences and Environmental Solutions (OASES) permission to conduct or publish virtually any air pollution research without prior approval from OAR political leadership. OASES is the ostensible successor to ORD, which was a global scientific leader in air quality and air pollution research. It is my understanding that OAR has categorically denied OASES the authority to conduct and publish its own air-related research without OAR political approval, except for narrow circumstances in which technical support from OASES cannot be avoided for OAR to meet certain statutory obligations. Indeed, OASES cannot even independently initiate air-related research without approval from OAR political appointees. OAR can only assert this control because of the agency’s new “no surprises” policy for OASES, which appallingly requires that OASES research “must be supported by appropriate political leadership” before it can proceed. The policy is a clear violation of scientific integrity, and the notion that EPA’s primary science office cannot even study air pollution without getting permission from the political appointees of a different office would be laughable if it was not so dangerous.
In my role as the Ranking Member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (“the Committee”), I have attempted to conduct oversight of these types of actions. There are many reasons for this oversight: to document the damage done to the agency and its workforce; to understand the scientific capabilities that have been lost and the implications of those losses for human health and the American people; to identify violations of scientific integrity and administrative procedure; and to comprehend why all of this happened in order to inform legislative efforts to reverse it and prevent it from ever happening again. Since January 2025, I have sent a number of formal oversight letters to EPA requesting agency records, documents, and communications regarding various policies and activities. The agency has been non-responsive to my requests and has utterly failed to comply. I am now reaffirming these oversight requests to provide the agency with a second opportunity to demonstrate the appropriate degree of deference and respect for congressional prerogatives. I expect EPA’s full and prompt responsiveness to each of the requests detailed below, which are long overdue:
1. Agency RIF and Reorganization Plans (ARRPs)
On March 26th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with several other Democratic Committee Members requesting that the agency “provide the Committee with your Agency RIF and Reorganization Plan immediately upon transmitting it to OMB and the Office of Personnel Management (OPM).” The context for this request was the revelation that EPA’s ARRP proposed to “eliminate the Office of Research and Development as an EPA National Program Office” while pushing “a majority (50-75%)” of ORD’s employees out of the agency. Of course, that is exactly what happened. But EPA never provided its Phase One and Phase Two ARRPs to the Committee, which has hindered the Committee’s ability to understand the motivations and decisions that led to the elimination of ORD. For instance, information revealed last year in a lawsuit related to agency ARRPs appeared to suggest that disagreements may have existed between EPA and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) regarding the elimination of ORD. Without reviewing the ARRPs themselves, the Committee cannot properly assess the agency’s position towards ORD and the bureaucratic actions that contributed to its demise.
2. Laboratory Budget and Staffing Levels
On May 27th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with Environment Subcommittee Ranking Member Gabe Amo requesting that the agency “share the projected post-reorganization budget and staffing levels for each of the facilities that will remain open.” The “facilities” in this case referred specifically to the ten field laboratory and research facilities managed by ORD. These research laboratories are a crown jewel of EPA science, and the agency’s intention to eliminate ORD had raised the alarming prospect that the laboratories might be shut down as well. EPA has not subsequently acted to do so, and the laboratories appear to be continuing under the management of different program offices. But while I am relieved that they continue to operate, I remain concerned that staffing shortages and reduced scientific capabilities at the former ORD laboratories could undermine their ability to appropriately study environmental hazards. EPA’s unwillingness to provide basic budgetary and personnel information for its research laboratories impedes the Committee’s ability to evaluate whether they remain capable of supporting core agency activities.
3. Endangerment Finding Repeal Documents and Communications
On August 18th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with Environment Subcommittee Ranking Member Amo requesting that the agency provide “all documents and communications” exchanged between EPA and OMB, the Department of Energy (DOE), and the Trump Vance 2025 Transition Team, regarding “the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.” I also requested “all documents and communications” exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the report developed by DOE’s Climate Working Group, and “all documents and communications” within EPA regarding “the agency’s review of the scientific basis for the proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding.” These oversight requests relate to the repeal of the 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding, which the agency proposed in July 2025 and finalized in February 2026. I continue to have concerns about potential violations of administrative law in the agency’s rulemaking process to repeal the Endangerment Finding. The documents and communications that I requested are central to the Committee’s ability to conduct oversight of the agency’s actions. EPA’s refusal to provide them only strengthens my belief that these records remain highly material to my review and must be disclosed without delay.
4. Status of PFNA IRIS Assessment
Dr. Maureen Gwinn, the EPA Deputy Associate Administrator for Science, testified before the Science Committee’s Subcommittee on Environment on June 4th, 2026. The subject of her testimony was OASES and the general status of environmental research and development at the agency after the elimination of ORD. During that hearing, I questioned Dr. Gwinn about the agency’s decision earlier in 2026 to disavow chemical assessments conducted by the Integrated Risk Information System (IRIS). In particular, I asked about the status of the IRIS assessment for PFNA, which press reports indicate has been fully completed for more than a year but which the agency refuses to finalize and publish. In response, Dr. Gwinn told me that she was “not sure of the details on that” and said that she would “have to get back to you.” She also stated that she would “go back and confirm” the status of the PFNA assessment. While that hearing took place over four months ago, the agency has not provided any subsequent information regarding the PFNA assessment and whether it ever intends to finalize and publish the assessment, nor has it offered any scientific justification for refusing to do so. I continue to seek clarity on whether the IRIS assessment for PFNA, a dangerous and highly toxic PFAS chemical, will ever see the light of day under this administration.
5. Administration Delays of Environmental Research
At the same June 4th Environment Subcommittee hearing with Dr. Gwinn, one of my colleagues, Representative Suzanne Bonamici, questioned Dr. Gwinn about whether the agency under its current leadership had sought to delay or suppress any environmental research due to its perceived lack of alignment with administration priorities. Specifically, Representative Bonamici asked whether “any proposed research products, even one, [had] been delayed, modified, or declined because they did not align with the priorities set by political appointees?” In response, Dr. Gwinn acknowledged that “there have been delays” due to the agency’s review of whether certain research products complied with President Trump’s various Executive Orders. But when Representative Bonamici followed up and directly asked “what was the topic of the research,” pertaining to research that had been halted, Dr. Gwinn could only respond that she would “have to get back to you on that.” The agency has not provided any further information regarding which specific research topics were “delayed, modified, or declined” due to the political directives of agency leadership. This information is highly material to the Committee’s ability to understand the current state of scientific integrity at EPA, as well as the role played by political appointees in influencing the environmental research being conducted by the agency.
In summary, the following oversight requests remain outstanding and require compliance on the part of the agency. Please produce the requested records no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, November 6th, 2026:
1. Please provide to the Committee the EPA’s Agency RIF and Reorganization Plans (ARRPs) transmitted to OMB and OPM pursuant to OMB Director Russ Vought’s February 2025 memo.
2. Please provide to the Committee the post-reorganization budget and staffing levels for each of the agency’s field laboratory and research facilities that remain open.
3. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and OMB regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.
4. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.
5. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and the Trump Vance 2025 Transition Team regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.
6. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the report titled, “A Critical Review of Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions on the U.S. Climate.”
7. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) within EPA regarding the agency’s review of the scientific basis for the proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding.
8. Please provide to the Committee a written update regarding the status of the IRIS assessment for PFNA, including whether any scientific work remains ongoing for the assessment and the date by which the agency intends to finalize and publish the assessment.
9. Please provide to the Committee a list of all research products that have been delayed, modified, or declined since January 20th, 2025, due to the agency’s review or conclusions regarding the alignment of scientific research with administration priorities, including the topics of the research products.
EPA’s non-responsiveness to Committee oversight during the 119th Congress has been unacceptable. The agency must respect congressional prerogatives. We remain determined to obtain the information we need to perform our duties on behalf of the American people. EPA should understand that a lack of cooperation will not frustrate the Committee’s oversight permanently. It will merely strengthen our commitment to employing all the tools at our disposal to hold the agency accountable.
Pursuant to Rule X of the House of Representatives, the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology “shall review and study on a continuing basis laws, programs, and Government activities relating to nonmilitary research and development.” The Committee possesses jurisdiction over environmental research and development.
title: Lofgren Demands Answers to Outstanding Oversight Requests, Warns EPA that Lack of Cooperation is Unacceptable
