DETROIT – The United States Attorney’s Office today announced charges in two separate fraud schemes totaling over $6 million as part of a nationwide enforcement action led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Eastern District of Michigan was a key participant in this surge effort.

Since early September, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490,000,000.

“Fraud is not a crime committed in the heat of the moment. It takes a deliberate and repeated choice to steal from the American people. We are committed to prosecuting these bad actors and cutting off crime at its source,” U.S. Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr. stated.

“Every dollar stolen through tax fraud is a dollar taken from the American people,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “What we uncovered during this concentrated surge is only the tip of the iceberg. The Department of Justice is committed to expanding our investigations and exposing schemes designed to evade accountability, because there is no safe haven for fraudsters.”

“The Fraud Division is resolved to protect American taxpayers from criminal actors on every frontier of fraud, including tax fraudsters seeking to steal the wealth of America,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “Over six weeks, the Fraud Division’s Tax Section, 35 U.S. Attorneys' Offices, and IRS Criminal Investigation took action against over 70 defendants

who sought more than $490 million from the Treasury. Today’s results send a clear message to fraudsters: those who intentionally lie to steal the money of the American people should expect to answer for their conduct in federal court.”

“This enforcement surge delivered results for taxpayers,” said IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are working across government to go after fraud, hold bad actors accountable, and protect the integrity of our nation’s tax system.”

“If there was ever any question whether criminal tax enforcement remains a priority, today’s actions should dispel all doubt. These cases send an unmistakable message that individuals and businesses who deliberately cheat the tax system will be held accountable,” said Jarod Koopman, Chief of IRS Criminal Investigation and Chief Tax Compliance Officer. “The investigations announced today involve hundreds of millions in identified tax losses to the United States, funds that should have supported the programs and services Americans depend on every day. When taxpayers evade their legal obligations, the burden does not disappear, it is shifted to law-abiding Americans.”

U.S. Attorney Gorgon Jr. announced the following cases in the Eastern District of Michigan:

US v. DePriest

Defendant Delilah DePriest, 43, of Detroit, was charged in an indictment that alleged that, as a tax preparer, DePriest prepared false Schedule C's reflecting large "business losses" to generate substantial tax refunds for her clients. She then took a cut of the refunds as her fee. DePriest was charged with nine counts of Aiding and Assisting in the Preparation of False Presentment of False Tax Returns, 26 U.S.C. § 7206(2). The alleged loss amount is $415,000 and maximum penalties are up to 3 years’ imprisonment for each count and a fine of up to $100,000.

US v. Davis

Defendants James Davis, 49, of Northville, MI and Claudia Moore, 55, of West Bloomfield, were charged by information with one count each of Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud and Conspiracy to Defraud the Government with Respect to Claims. The information alleges dual conspiracies: (1) to obtain PPP loans to which various business entities were not entitled, and (2) to obtain or attempt to obtain Sick and Family Leave credits and Employee Retention Credits to which individuals and businesses were not entitled. The information alleges that Davis is a business owner and client-recruiter who found individuals willing to provide PII in exchange for a cut of false PPP loan proceeds and/or false tax credits and Moore is a tax preparer who created false Forms 941, 7202, and 7200, and Schedules C for numerous “clients.” Both took a cut of the proceeds. The alleged loss amount is $5,535,050.64. Maximum penalties include up to 20 years’ imprisonment, a fine up to the greater of $250,000 or twice the pecuniary gain or loss, or both, for the conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge and up to 10 years imprisonment, a fine up to the greater of $250,000 or twice the pecuniary gain or loss, or both, for the conspiracy to defraud the government with respect to claims charge.

An indictment, information, or complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

This press release details one way in which this office has contributed to ensuring that all Americans pay their fair share. To see the successes of other offices, please see this press release: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/dojs-fraud-division-irs-and-irs-ci-expose-more-490m-tax-fraud-national-tax-enforcement-surge

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: The Eastern District of Michigan Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing Two Defendants Involved in Tax Fraud

LOS ANGELES – A South Los Angeles man was arraigned today on a four-count federal indictment charging him with violently sex trafficking two teenage girls on the Figueroa Corridor, plying at least one of them with narcotics, and with attempting to kidnap a woman at a mobile phone store after she escaped his apartment while he was physically attacking her.

Derrick Harrison Enrico Brooks, Jr., 31, of Baldwin Village, is charged with two counts of sex trafficking of children by force, fraud, or coercion, one count of distribution of controlled substances to a person under 21, and one count of attempted kidnapping.

Brooks pleaded not guilty to all charges at his arraignment today in United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles. His trial is scheduled for December 1.

Last month a federal magistrate judge ordered him detained without bond.

According to the complaint, indictment, and other court documents, in November 2025, Brooks sex trafficked a 15-year-old girl – identified in court documents as “Minor Victim 1.” Brooks and this victim traveled from California to Colorado in his green limousine for commercial sex work. Brooks demanded that she earn $1,000 per day, physically assaulted her several times, and at one point, caused the victim to think she was going to die from his physical violence.

Brooks posted an advertisement of her on the Craigslist website.

Minor Victim 1 returned to Los Angeles and escaped from Brooks while working on the Figueroa Corridor, a 3.5-mile stretch of Figueroa Street in South Los Angeles that is notorious for prostitution activity.

In January and February of 2026, Brooks trafficked a 17-year-old girl, identified in court documents as “Minor Victim 2,” who also worked on the Figueroa Corridor. Brooks physically assaulted this victim as well and knowingly distributed Ecstasy to her.

In August 2026, Brooks assaulted and attempted to kidnap a woman – identified in the indictment as “Victim 3” – in a mobile phone store in Baldwin Village. Victim 3 had fled Brooks’s nearby apartment after he choked her and punched her in the face.

Two weeks after the attempted kidnapping, law enforcement arrested Brooks in connection with that incident.

An indictment merely contains allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

If convicted of all charges, Brooks would face a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years in federal prison and a statutory maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

The FBI is investigating this matter with assistance from the Los Angeles Police Department, Pomona Police Department, and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office.

Assistant United States Attorneys Chelsea Norell and Mirelle Raza of the Major Crimes Section are prosecuting this case.
title: South L.A. Man Arraigned on Federal Charges that He Sex Trafficked Minors on Figueroa Corridor and Attempted to Kidnap Woman at Phone Store

text:
LYNCHBURG, Va. – A Danville man, who sexually exploited minor females using social media, and in some cases threatened the minors with the distribution of their nude images to their friends, family, and churches, was sentenced this week to 19 years in federal prison to be followed by 20 years of supervised release.

Jesus Diaz, 25, pled guilty in July 2026 to one count of making extortive threats to injure the reputation of another and four counts of enticement of a minor.

“This defendant targeted and sexually exploited children, then tried to silence them through fear and intimidation,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert N. Tracci said. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Virginia will utilize every available tool to hold online sexual predators accountable for their crimes. I appreciate the outstanding work of DHS Homeland Security Investigations in this matter.”

“Diaz used deception and threats to exploit children as young as 13. He coerced kids into providing compromising photos of themselves, then used those photos to extort his victims for years, causing immeasurable pain and distress,” said Homeland Security Investigations Washington, D.C. Acting Special Agent in Charge Kai Wah Chan. “The courage of the victims who reported Diaz and cooperated with investigators was essential to this outcome. HSI remains committed to pursuing those who exploit children and holding them accountable.”

According to court documents, between July 2019 and November 2021, Diaz used social media platforms to entice Minor 1 (M1) to send him nude and sexually explicit photos and videos of herself. At the time, M1 was approximately 13 to 14 years old.

After years of having no contact with M1, Diaz contacted her again on February 28, 2024, via social media. Diaz sent M1 nude and sexually explicit images and videos, along with other non-nude images, that M1 had sent to Diaz years before and demanded that M1 add him as a friend on another social media platform “or else I start sending these out.” Diaz then started a countdown: “25” “20” “15.” M1 added Diaz on the social media platform as demanded.

From February 2024 through April 2024, Diaz repeatedly contacted M1. Diaz told M1 he was in love with her, despite having never met her. He threatened to expose M1 to her high school, her family, her ex-boyfriend, and her church. Diaz accused M1 of “playing with [his] strings” and blamed her for “hurting [him] like this.” He also sought more nude and sexually explicit images.

For weeks, Diaz created new accounts and continued to contact M1, despite her blocking him on social media. Diaz sent her multiple friend requests, direct messages threatening to send her nude images to her ex-boyfriend or her best friend and left a comment on a social media post she made.

M1 reported the threats to state authorities in Idaho, who quickly worked to identify Diaz as a suspect. Subsequent investigation by the Homeland Security Investigations, revealed a pattern of similar behavior.

Between August 2022 and April 2024, Diaz used social media platforms to entice Minor 2 (M2) to take nude and sexually explicit photos and to record nude and sexually explicit videos of herself. Diaz also called M2 using FaceTime and recorded M2. M2 periodically felt uncomfortable and blocked Diaz on social media. In order to contact M2, Diaz created different social media accounts using names M2 did not recognize.

In 2024, following an extended period of no contact, Diaz messaged M2 from a social media account she did not recognize and sent M2 a video of herself showering and threatened to send it to her high school if she didn’t answer him. Diaz demanded a new shower video every day for the next six months. M2 pleaded with Diaz to not publish her images. Ultimately, she agreed to send Diaz one final video, which she sent in April 2024. M2 then blocked Diaz and cut off contact with him. During the relevant period, M2 was between 15 and 17 years old.

Between May 2024 and October 2024, Diaz used social media platforms to entice Minor 3 (M3) to take nude and sexually explicit photos and to record nude and sexually explicit videos of herself. Diaz also called M3 using FaceTime and recorded M3. At the time, M3 was 15 years old.

Between August 2024 and November 2024, Diaz used social media platforms to entice Minor 4 (M4) to take nude and sexually explicit photos and to record nude and sexually explicit videos of herself. When M4 expressed discomfort, Diaz threatened to leak M4’s pictures. Ultimately, M4 blocked Diaz when she believed it was safe to do so. At the time, M4 was 16 and 17 years old.

Homeland Security Investigations Washington, D.C. is investigating the case, with assistance from the Homeland Security Investigations Albuquerque, NM office, which played a key role in the apprehension of Diaz. Valuable investigative support was also provided by the Idaho Office of the Attorney General, Criminal Division; the City of Danville Police Department; U.S. Customs and Border Protection; the United States Postal Inspection Service; and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Lee Brett is prosecuting the case.

The case is brought as part of Project Safe Childhood. In 2006, the Department of Justice created Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative designed to protect children from exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identity and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov/ .

San Diego Man Pleads Guilty to Tax Evasion
A California man pleaded guilty yesterday to tax evasion.
According to court documents and statements made in court, Peter L. Roper, of San Diego, operated various La Jolla-based businesses that marketed and sold purported federal tax credits throughout the United States. Between 2010 through 2021, Roper and his businesses received nearly $19 million in income, on which he owed more than $6.7 million in federal income taxes. Roper and his businesses, however, did not report any of this income on tax returns or pay taxes to the IRS. Throughout this period, Roper used his businesses’ bank accounts to pay personal expenses and concealed assets by titling them in the names of others. Instead of paying taxes, Roper spent $187,432.34 on a 2015 McLaren 650S Spider and another $277,698.50 on a 2021 Aston Martin DBX, among other things.
Roper pleaded guilty to one count of tax evasion. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 8 and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case.
Trial Attorneys John C. Gerardi and Charles A. O’Reilly of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathan Brooks for the Southern District of California are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Washington, D.C. (October 15, 2026) – The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) today issued its new Strategic Plan for 2027 to 2032, which charts a course to meet the rapidly changing needs and priorities of Congress. The new plan outlines how the agency will help Congress address emerging opportunities and challenges, including the rise of artificial intelligence, mounting fiscal pressures, and growing national security threats. The plan’s goals advance GAO’s mission to improve federal accountability and performance for the benefit of the American people.
“Congress needs answers at the speed of today’s challenges, and this plan positions GAO to deliver them,” said Orice W. Brown, Acting Comptroller General of the United States and head of GAO. “We will continue meeting our mission in providing rigorous, nonpartisan, fact-based work while enhancing how we deliver it, so it reaches Congress when and how it’s most useful.”
The Strategic Plan is built around three cross-cutting goals that strengthen GAO’s oversight mission and its ability to respond quickly to congressional needs. The first two goals focus on identifying savings in federal programs, addressing fraud, waste, and abuse across government, strengthening accountability, and improving the safety and security of the American people. The third goal centers on strengthening GAO’s workforce and modernizing its technology, sharing knowledge, and developing innovative tools to meet Congress’s needs today and in the future.
The plan also places new emphasis on how federal agencies are adjusting to emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. By anticipating new science and technology trends, opportunities, and risks, GAO will help Congress and federal agencies use these advancements to carry out their missions.
As a legislative branch agency, GAO has a longstanding history of providing independent, nonpartisan oversight to assist Congress with complex decisions. Since 2002, its work has provided more than $1.51 trillion in financial benefits and 30,800 program and operational improvements. The new Strategic Plan is designed to build on that record and keep delivering results for Congress and the American people.
“Taxpayers expect their government to work effectively and be accountable for how it uses public resources,” added Ms. Brown. “This plan outlines how we will support Congress to advance those goals in the years ahead.”
The Strategic Plan is available online. For more information, contact Sarah Kaczmarek, Managing Director of Public Affairs, at media@gao.gov.
#####
The Government Accountability Office, known as the investigative arm of Congress, is an independent, nonpartisan agency that exists to support Congress in meeting its constitutional responsibilities. GAO also works to improve the performance of the federal government and ensure its accountability to the American people. The agency examines the use of public funds; evaluates federal programs and policies; and provides analyses, recommendations, and other assistance to help Congress make informed oversight, policy, and funding decisions. GAO provides Congress with timely information that is objective, fact-based, nonideological, fair, and balanced. GAO’s commitment to good government is reflected in its core values of accountability, integrity, and reliability.
title: Oct 15, 2026 GAO Unveils New Strategic Plan Focused on the Nation's Emerging Challenges and Opportunities

Routine emergency-response training and rapid coordination between Emergency Department and Labor and Delivery staff helped ensure the safe transfer and care of a mother and newborn after an unexpected delivery in the family car enroute to the Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center in the early morning of Oct. 7.
Hearing a cry of “Help! My wife is having a baby!” shocked Patrizia Brown into action just outside the CRDAMC parking garage around 7 a.m. Brown, a certified nursing assistant assigned to the Women’s Health Clinic, immediately rendered assistance to the distraught new father, directing him to the emergency room entrance.
Brown alerted emergency department staff where registered nurse Debra Woods activated the response team to assess the mother and baby. While alerting staff, the father, Spc. Matthew Perez, an automated logistics specialist, close behind Brown into the department said, “correction she had the baby”.
“Since he said she had already delivered, I put on gloves went to the care and assessed the baby and mom,” Woods said. “I made sure the baby had good coloring, was breathing, and that mom was okay and holding the baby securely.”
Woods instructed the mother to stimulate the newborn by stroking the baby’s back while additional emergency staff arrived. Recognizing the need to safely move both patients, Woods directed the team to bring a stretcher and warm blankets.
Doctors, nurses, medics and the emergency department charge nurse worked together to transfer the mother and newborn from the vehicle to a stretcher, protect them from the morning temperatures and begin immediate care.
Spc. Colin Evans, a combat medic, and Sgt. 1st Class Justin Harper, the emergency room noncommissioned officer in charge, assisted in meeting the immediate needs of the new family.
Both are parents and for Harper, it was particularly thrilling to be a part of the care team because it was his own daughter’s birthday that day.
“It was a super feeling,” said Evans. “I remember what it was like to have my kid, so being there to actually experience that and help somebody else was exciting.”
The mother and newborn were transported to labor and delivery, where the obstetric and pediatric teams completed the delivery process, stabilized the mother and continued newborn care.
Capt. Demetria Miller, an OB-GYN senior resident, said the real-life situation reinforced the value of medical readiness and team coordination.
“Our senior resident selects an education and training topic each day, and that morning we happened to choose infant resuscitation and childbirth,” Miller said. “When we heard the call for a delivery outside, the team immediately responded with the stretcher, blankets and necessary support.”
“That is exactly why we train,” Miller said. “We must be prepared for unexpected emergencies and ready to respond quickly. In this case, the teams worked together, and mother and baby received the care they needed.”
Emmanuel Diaz-Perez, an OB-GYN assigned to Labor and Delivery, said vehicle deliveries at the medical center are uncommon, making preparation and teamwork especially important.
“I’ve been here since 2017, and this is only the third time it’s happened,” Diaz-Perez said.
Both parents, Perez and mom Jedhrynn Manalo, were grateful for the fast actions of the staff.
Manalo said the delivery progressed rapidly during the family’s drive to the medical center. Initially she was concerned when she did not hear her daughter cry immediately after birth, but she said the responding staff quickly assessed the situation and reassured the family.
“The team did really good,” Manalo said. “They checked both of us, and everything was OK.”
Perez said his priority was getting his wife and daughter to medical care as quickly as possible. He credited the staff with providing attentive care while keeping him involved throughout the response.
“My whole thing was making sure my wife and baby were taken care of, and they were very attentive to that,” Perez said. “They worked around me so I could stay with them.”
Amina Lee, weighing 7 pounds and 14 inches long, will have an unusual birth story to share.
For CRDAMC staff, the response demonstrated how regular training, clear communication and coordinated emergency care support medical readiness and ensure the health of military families during unexpected events.
title: Emergency, Labor and Delivery teams’ readiness ensures safe care for mother and newborn

Staffing Business Owner and Son Indicted for Employment Tax and Wire Fraud Schemes
A federal grand jury in the District of Minnesota returned an indictment today charging Ku Kelvin Vue and his son, Travis Vue, with willfully failing to collect, account for and pay over employment taxes to the IRS on behalf of the staffing business they operated, and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ku Kelvin Vue was also charged with willfully failing to file corporate tax returns, and Travis Vue was charged with filing a false individual tax return and willfully failing to file individual tax returns.
The following is according to the indictment: Ku Kelvin Vue was the owner and president of UniSelect Services Inc., a temporary staffing agency that provided temporary workers to client companies in the manufacturing industry and other industries. Travis Vue helped run the company as early as 2014. Both men were allegedly responsible for withholding Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from UniSelect’s employees’ wages and paying those withholdings over to the IRS, as well as filing quarterly tax returns with the IRS documenting those withholdings. According to the indictment, however, from the third quarter of 2020 through the second quarter of 2022, neither Ku Kelvin Vue nor Travis Vue collected those taxes or paid them over to the IRS, nor filed quarterly tax returns with the IRS.
The indictment also alleges that Ku Kelvin Vue willfully failed to file corporate tax returns on behalf of UniSelect for the years 2020 through 2022. It is alleged that Travis Vue willfully failed to file individual tax returns for the years 2021 through 2023. Travis Vue also allegedly filed a false tax return for 2020 reporting zero wages or income, even though he received substantially greater wages and income during that year and was required to file a tax return.
In addition to their tax crimes, the indictment also charges Ku Kelvin Vue and Travis Vue with one count each of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. According to the indictment, the Vues conspired to secure business for UniSelect by falsely assuring clients the company maintained active workers’ compensation insurance coverage for all UniSelect employees furnished to the clients as temporary workers. In reality, UniSelect allegedly did not maintain workers’ compensation insurance coverage on behalf of its workers. Instead, Kelvin Vue and Travis Vue allegedly conspired to create false and fraudulent workers’ compensation insurance policy certificates, which they provided to clients to deceive them into believing UniSelect maintained insurance coverage.
Both defendants face maximum penalties of 20 years in prison for the wire fraud conspiracy count, five years in prison for each count of willful failure to collect, account for and pay over employment taxes and one year in prison for each count of willful failure to file a tax return. Travis Vue also faces a maximum penalty of three years in prison for filing a false tax return.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen for the District of Minnesota made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case.
Assistant Deputy Chief Eric B. Powers and Trial Attorney Megan E. Wessel of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Staffing Business Owner and Son Indicted for Employment Tax and Wire Fraud Schemes

COLUMBIA, S.C. — Desmond Levon Brown, 30, of Orangeburg, has been sentenced to five years in federal prison for animal crushing, which includes burning, under the Preventing Animal Cruelty and Torture Act (PACT Act). This was the first PACT ACT case prosecuted in the District of South Carolina. On Dec. 18, 2024, the Orangeburg County Sheriff’s Office received reports of a Facebook Live video showing Brown throwing a puppy into a fire that day. Deputies discovered the deceased puppy in a wooded area near the incident location. Federal law enforcement obtained the Facebook video, which showed Brown holding the puppy above the fire, dropping it into the fire, and repeatedly kicking the puppy into the fire every time it tried to escape, burning it alive. After his arrest, Brown was recorded on jail calls admitting to burning the puppy. “Brown’s actions were cruel, heinous and depraved,” said U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling for the District of South Carolina. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office is committed to working with law enforcement to investigate and prosecute animal cruelty in South Carolina.” “This was an awful act of animal cruelty that deserves accountability,” said ATF Special Agent in Charge Alicia Jones. “No animal should ever have to experience such terrible abuse, and those who commit reprehensible acts of violence like this will be brought to justice.” “This puppy could neither fend for itself nor find a way out of this horrific torture because it was thrown into the fire over and over," Orangeburg County Sheriff Leroy Ravenell said. "Hopefully, this sentence will give Brown enough time to realize what he has done, and it weighs on his heart for the rest of his days.” United States District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis sentenced Brown to 60 months’ imprisonment, to be followed by a three-year term of court-ordered supervision. As a condition of his supervised release, Brown is prohibited from owning or possessing any animal. There is no parole in the federal system. This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Orangeburg County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Elle E. Klein prosecuted the case. Citizens can report suspected animal abuse to local law enforcement, the Department of Justice or the U.S. Department of Agriculture .

title: Orangeburg Man Sentenced to 5 Years in Federal Prison for Burning Puppy Alive in S.C.’s First PACT Act Prosecution

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. – Safety teams from the U.S. Army Communications-Electronics Command, CECOM Integrated Logistics Support Center, CECOM Army Software & Innovation Center, and Army Contracting Command staged the 4th annual APG Safety Day, organizing this robust event with the assistance of community partners on Sept. 16.
Along with printed materials and in-booth presentations to inform the workforce, vendors also provided multiple demonstrations related to safety training and best practices, especially when it comes to the workplace. Most notable among the new offerings this year, a military K-9 demonstration displayed advanced tactics that uniformed personnel can employ in the interest of public safety.
CECOM ILSC Acting Executive Director Abel Salgado, who also serves as the ILSC Safety Champion, presented opening remarks for the day. “I ask you all to consider that ‘Safety starts with me.’ Taking personal responsibility is an important first step for safety. Don’t get complacent, and always be mindful,” he said. Following Salgado’s remarks, attendees walked the APG C5ISR-M courtyard, visiting booths dedicated to topics like ladder safety, fall protection, electrical safety, hearing conservation, bicycle safety, and much more. Other vendors offered demos such as portable fire extinguisher training and materials aimed at mental health awareness and suicide prevention.
Jurgen Williams, a safety and occupational health specialist at CECOM ILSC whose Logistics, Operations, Technology, Intelligence & Safety Branch played an integral role in the planning and execution of APG Safety Day, praised the group effort and the impact it had. “Our Employee Safety Committee and volunteers’ commitment to excellence provided a positive safety culture to make this a successful day. They worked tirelessly with the vendors to ensure that all requirements were met and accomplished,” he said. “Effective communication is the bridge between the planning of an event and its real world impact, and today it ensured that participants understand, engage with, and apply safety messages going forward.”
The most popular feature of the day proved to be the hazard identification room, which was first introduced at this event last year. This was a controlled, interactive environment for members of the APG workforce, who were given three minutes to study a room that had been previously staged by Safety experts to identify as many safety hazards as possible within that timeframe. Hazards ranged from broken chairs to cluttered walkways to daisy-chained extension cords and missing ceiling tiles. Safety organizers staged these hazards in an effort to familiarize employees with different threats in the workplace, reinforcing the need to make hazard recognition a natural part of daily work habits.
Representatives from local emergency medical services were on site, and APG Safety Day also showcased a thermal imaging technology trailer that impressed eventgoers. Linnea Tober, CECOM ILSC wellness coordinator, held a gentle yoga session. She believes the self-care benefits behind the session fit perfectly into the overall spirit and mentality of the day, saying “The weather was perfect, and these employees enjoyed some much needed de-stressing and relaxation.”
Safety is something to always be mindful about, and the Safety teams at APG work every day to keep the workforce informed and prepared. The annual Safety Day event is the centerpiece of their efforts, and APG partner organizations extend our gratitude to these subject matter experts for their commitment and continued dedication to this critical area.
title: Aberdeen Proving Ground Safety Day brings knowledge and awareness to the installation workforce

CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas – A 51-year-old Needville, TX man will serve federal prison time after authorities discovered 10 illegal aliens concealed inside his tractor-trailer.

Robert Martinez Jr. pleaded guilty May 20.

U.S. District Judge Nelva Gonzales Ramos ordered Martinez to serve 21 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by three years of supervised release. At the hearing, the court heard additional information regarding his prior felony convictions for possession of a controlled substance. In handing down the sentence, the court considered the dangerous conditions in which Martinez transported the illegal aliens. Two were concealed inside a storage compartment beneath four others, making it impossible for them to escape.

On March 9, Martinez drove a tractor-trailer to a Border Patrol checkpoint near Sarita, TX. During the inspection, law enforcement questioned Martinez about his cargo. He claimed he was transporting onions and agreed to a scan of the vehicle. The scan revealed anomalies in the tractor cab.

Upon further inspection, law enforcement discovered 10 illegal aliens concealed on the top bunk, beneath a blanket on the lower bunk, and inside a storage compartment underneath it. Authorities observed that those found inside the compartment were sweating and had flushed faces.

The illegal aliens identified Martinez as the driver of the tractor-trailer.

Martinez has been and will remain in custody pending transfer to a Federal Bureau of Prisons facility to be determined in the near future.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation with the assistance of Border Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney Izaak Bruce prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigrants, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

DAYTON, Ohio – Marcus Gullatte, Sr., 38, of Dayton, was sentenced in U.S. District Court today to 264 months in prison for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl and methamphetamine.

Gullatte is a career offender and a prolific drug trafficker. He has engaged in an escalating pattern of drug trafficking over the past decade and has multiple drug convictions.

According to court documents in this case, throughout the summer of 2024, Gullatte acquired bulk amounts of fentanyl and methamphetamine from a source of supply in the Dayton area and then resold the drugs for cash.

Gullatte was on supervised release when he engaged in the drug transactions in this instant case. He has two prior federal drug trafficking convictions for which he was sentenced to 36 months and 60 months in prison respectively.

Gullatte was indicted by a federal grand jury in November 2024 and pleaded guilty in June.

Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio, and Jason Cromartie, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cincinnati Division, announced the sentence imposed today by Senior U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Rose. Deputy Criminal Chief Tabacchi is representing the United States in this case.

NEWARK, N.J. – A man formerly of Gwinnett County, Georgia and currently residing in Chicago, Illinois admitted to furnishing false U.S. passport cards through the mail, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced.

Juma Wajid, a/k/a “Jay Khan” and “Jamal Anthony,” 38, of Chicago, IL, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Court Judge Susan D. Wigenton in Newark federal court today to an Information charging him with furnishing a false, forged, and counterfeit passport.

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court:

Wajid used an online account to send mailings that contained six or more fake U.S. passport cards and other identification documents that he created. In August 2024, law enforcement purchased five false U.S. Passport cards, as well as additional documents, from Wajid, who believed that the false documents that he created were going to be used to commit bank fraud. Wajid created the documents and mailed them to an address in New Jersey in exchange for payment in cryptocurrency.

The charge of furnishing a false passport to another person carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a fine of $250,000, or twice the amount of money involved in the offense, whichever is greater.

U.S. Attorney Frazer credited special agents of the U.S. Department of State, Diplomatic Security Service, New York Field Office, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Brian Wood; postal inspectors of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, under the direction of Inspector in Charge Christopher A. Nielsen; and officers of the New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness, under the direction of Director Thomas Hauck, with the investigation leading to the guilty plea.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Trevor A. Chenoweth of the Cybercrime Unit in Newark.

Agency delivers major deregulatory action under President Trump's agenda, eliminating costly requirements without weakening consumer safety protections
WASHINGTON, D.C. – The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) today announced a major deregulatory action eliminating unnecessary federal requirements for fuel additives, saving American businesses up to an estimated $10.7 billion over 30 years while preserving existing consumer safety protections.
The action clarifies that fuel additives used to clean engines, improve performance, extend engine life, prevent weather-related effects, or stabilize fuel are not “flammable liquid fuels” under the Portable Fuel Container Safety Act. As a result, manufacturers will not be required to equip containers for these products with costly flame mitigation devices intended for gasoline cans and other portable fuel containers.
The action eliminates an estimated $545.7 million in annual regulatory costs and protects small businesses from disproportionate regulatory burdens. CPSC's economic analysis found that smaller manufacturers, many of which depend heavily on fuel additive sales, would have faced substantial packaging costs if they had to comply with requirements never intended for their products. The action also protects American consumers from unnecessary price increases and preserves access to widely used engine maintenance products.
“This is what meaningful deregulation looks like: eliminating billions of dollars in unnecessary costs while keeping consumer safety protections firmly in place,” said Acting Chairman Peter A. Feldman. “Congress imposed these requirements on fuel containers, not products designed to clean and maintain engines. Washington should not force American businesses to spend billions complying with regulations that were never intended to apply to their products in the first place.”
“President Trump has directed federal agencies to eliminate unnecessary regulatory burdens, and CPSC is delivering. The Supreme Court made clear in Loper Bright that agencies must follow the best reading of the law, not interpretations that expand their regulatory authority. A federal court has already recognized that these additives are not fuel. Today, we're putting that principle into practice, restoring regulatory clarity, and making clear that CPSC will not impose requirements beyond those authorized by Congress.”
The action advances President Trump's Executive Order 14192, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” and reinforces CPSC's commitment to ensuring that federal regulations are grounded in statutory authority, impose no unnecessary costs, and provide clear, predictable requirements for American businesses.
Existing flame mitigation requirements for gasoline cans and other covered portable fuel containers remain unchanged. CPSC has identified no reported flame-jetting incidents involving the fuel additives in containers covered by this action.
About the U.S. CPSC
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is charged with protecting the public from unreasonable risk of injury associated with the use of thousands of types of consumer products. Deaths, injuries, and property damage from consumer product-related incidents cost the nation more than $1 trillion annually. Since the CPSC was established more than 50 years ago, it has worked to ensure the safety of consumer products, which has contributed to a decline in injuries associated with these products. 
Federal law prohibits any person from selling products subject to a Commission ordered recall or a voluntary recall undertaken in consultation with the CPSC.

- Report a dangerous product or a product-related injury on www.SaferProducts.gov.
- Call CPSC’s Hotline at 800-638-2772 (TTY 800-638-8270).

WASHINGTON — TheU.S. Small Business Administration announced low-interest federal disaster loans are now available to small businesses and private nonprofit organizations in Arizona to offset economic losses caused by flash flooding at the Grand Canyon National Park occurring Aug. 29 – Sept. 3. The SBA issued a disaster declaration in response to a request received from Governor Katie Hobbs on Oct. 8.
The disaster declaration covers the Arizona counties of Coconino, Gila, Mohave, Navajo, and Yavapai, as well as the Utah counties of Kane and San Juan.
Under this declaration, SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith-based organizations — with financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Economic Injury Disaster Loans are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
“SBA loans help eligible small businesses and private nonprofits cover operating expenses after a disaster, which is crucial for their recovery,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “These loans not only help business owners get back on their feet but also play a key role in sustaining local economies in the aftermath of a disaster.”
The loan amount can be up to $2 million with interest rates as low as 4% for businesses and 3.625% for private nonprofits, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The deadline to return economic injury applications to SBA is July 13, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Offers Relief to Arizona Small Businesses, Private Nonprofits Affected by Flash Flooding at Grand Canyon National Park

WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) announced the first federal small-business classification guidance specifically recognizing qualifying content creators within the SBA’s lending and contracting framework. Following SBA’s recent small business size standards proposal, the agency clarified that the nation’s 27 million creator-led businesses are classified under NAICS 5121 — Motion Picture and Video Industries — for purposes of SBA program eligibility. The clarification reflects the robust growth and evolving business models of America’s creator economy.
“American’s creators are entrepreneurs who build businesses from original ideas, unique audiences, and content into thriving small businesses that create jobs,” said SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler. “For the first time, the SBA is recognizing these enterprising content creators within our small-business framework. This historic guidance cuts through outdated classifications and gives qualifying creators greater clarity as they build businesses, create jobs, and compete and build for the future.”
“Content creators are small businesses, and always have been,” said Daniel Abas, Founder and President of the Creators Guild of America. “Thanks to the vision of the SBA and its leadership, the federal government has unequivocally affirmed this status, and millions of creators stand to benefit. We look forward to our members taking full advantage of the access to capital that the SBA’s guidance provides, and are proud that the professional infrastructure established by the CGA has contributed to this outcome. Committed creators like Shira Lazar, founder of Creators 4 Mental Health and a member of our Advisory Board, and Avi Gandhi, CGA’s Chair of Government Advocacy, played instrumental roles in advancing this effort. This breakthrough is both a testament to their hard work, and a major step forward in the CGA’s mission to help creators.”
"With more than 8.5 million American small businesses on TikTok U.S., millions of people turn to our platform every day to discover new experiences, support local favorites, and connect with thriving entrepreneurs, said Nicole Nason, Head of Public Policy at TikTok U.S. “This historic guidance places the SBA at the forefront of the creator economy and establishes clear pathways for modern entrepreneurs to expand their reach, create jobs, and fuel local economies.”
Content creator businesses have long been eligible for SBA support when they meet applicable program requirements, but creators previously lacked clear guidance on the NAICS code that best reflects their integrated business models. Because today’s creators often produce, edit, distribute, market, and monetize original audiovisual content across multiple platforms and revenue streams, SBA is providing clearer guidance to help them identify the industry group most appropriate for SBA program-eligibility purposes.
The SBA’s proposed size standards adopt revisions to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) to simplify the size standards for related motion-picture, video-production, post-production, and distribution activities under NAICS 5121 — Motion Picture and Video Industries. Creator-led businesses whose principal activity falls within this umbrella—including filmmakers, video producers, podcasters, streamers, gamers, digital publishers, social-media entrepreneurs, creative agencies, and other businesses that produce and distribute original audiovisual content—should begin with NAICS 5121 and identify the applicable six-digit NAICS code within that industry group that best matches their primary business activity.
The SBA also received comments on its proposed size standards rule requesting the issuance of an industry exception for content creators, which would permanently house creator-led businesses. The agency will consider those comments, along with all public feedback submitted on the proposed rule, after the public comment period closes on November 20th.
The SBA is helping qualifying creator-led businesses determine their small-business status and navigate opportunities for SBA-backed financing and other agency resources. The action advances the Trump Administration’s commitment to reducing unnecessary regulatory complexity, modernizing government, and ensuring federal programs reflect the evolving needs of America’s entrepreneurs.

The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of entrepreneurship. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Issues Historic Guidance to Recognize America’s Content Creator Economy

There were roughly 50 checkpoints on the map given to competitors. Each had numeral markers in the legend and plain descriptions such as “Top of a Small Hill” or “Dried, Gnarled Pine.” The final point on the map was listed simply as “110 – Dark Rock.”
These were the coordinates, or unmanned points, using the military grid reference system that teams of four had to plot and navigate to earn points during a recent reconnaissance competition in southern Estonia.
The competition, called Walk in the Hills or Day in the Life of a Forest Brother, is hosted annually by the Estonian Defence League. This year’s event took place near the small village of Rouge in Võru County, Estonia. The origins of the event can be traced back more than 80 years.
During World War II and the decades that followed, armed fighters who resisted Soviet occupation in Estonia sought refuge in the forest to escape capture and disrupt enemy operations. These fighters learned to survive and remain elusive in harsh terrain and conditions. They became known as the Forest Brothers. That lineage continues today, and the EDL invites its NATO partners to share in the team building and camaraderie.
"The main purpose of this competition is the camaraderie between the competitors," said Cpt. Tõnis Kask, the event organizer, Võrumaa District, EDL. "They can come here and have a challenging exercise and test their orienteering skills on the ground. Test the tough Southern Estonian Trail and see how they manage our weather as it is different every year.”
The event is open to all EDL subunits, the Women’s Voluntary Defence Organization, Estonian youth scout organizations, and security and rescue authorities. Military service members from NATO allies are welcome to participate. Of the dozen or so teams, most were EDL representatives, along with a Latvian group and three U.S. Army teams.
One U.S. team was from the 6th Squadron, 1st Cavalry Regiment. The remaining two teams hailed from the 734th Regional Support Group, Iowa Army National Guard. All U.S. Soldiers who competed are in Central Europe and the Baltic States in support of Operation Atlantic Resolve under V Corps’ forward-deployed headquarters and pivotal role in the defense of NATO’s eastern flank.
Many of the U.S. Soldiers traveled from forward operating sites throughout the V Corps area of operation. A few traveled nearly 1,000 kilometers for the chance to compete in the austere reconnaissance challenge, which lasted through the night and totaled about 30 hours. Competitors were provided a map with checkpoints. No backpacks or rucks were allowed, and participants could only use what they could carry in their pockets.
Items of necessity for most teams included a canteen, protein bar, compass, protractor and extra socks. Add in creature comforts like gum, caffeine or snacks and that was it. Many brought lighters, which proved useful as fires were allowed in certain neutral areas and helped teams survive overnight in the chilly autumn forest.
Teams could also navigate to another neutral “safehouse” in a barn, where they were safe from the notional enemy and were provided food, water and heat. Medical aid was stationed there and could be dispersed anywhere in the competition area if needed.
Those creature comforts and the safehouse provided a much‑needed reprieve while traversing over 100 square kilometers of bogs, dense forest and uneven terrain — not to mention a notional enemy or opposing force. Points were deducted each time a team member was captured by OPFOR, which used drones and patrolled roads by foot and vehicle. Each team member had five lives until they were eliminated from the competition.
In addition to the grid points, there were six manned checkpoints where teams had to complete tasks and were graded on their performance. Near a large climbing tower was the Tower of Tires checkpoint, a brain teaser.
"Essentially, there were five tires," said Spc. Franklin Mandein, a signal operations support specialist, 734th RSG, IAARNG. "Each with varying sizes, one being the smallest, five being the biggest. And they were on one pole. There were three other poles in the ground and your goal was to get all five of those tires in the exact same order, from 1 to 5 on the third pole without having any of the bigger tires on top of the smaller tires."
Other manned checkpoints included mortar, driving, communication, medical and NATO identification lanes. In the NATO ID lane, participants had to identify which NATO country the gear or clothing items belonged to — useful information since a core part of what the 734th RSG and V Corps are doing in Central Europe and the Baltic States is working alongside NATO and host nations to maintain and grow military partnerships. Events like these improve partner convergence and interoperability throughout the area of operation.
The Walk in the Hills competition took place near one of the 734th RSG’s forward operating sites in Estonia, where one of the U.S. participants, Sgt. Patrick Bennett, a military police officer with the 734th RSG, IARNG, works in the mayor cell assisting U.S. regional aligned forces as well as host nation counterparts and other allies.
"My favorite part about working with the Estonian military is being able to see the shared brotherhood across borders with one of our NATO partners," said Bennett. "The hospitality that they shared towards U.S. forces is comparable to the hospitality we receive from other U.S. Soldiers. They shared their food, their experience, and their training as if we were one of their own."
Cpt. Kask echoed that sentiment, saying, "I'm really glad that I can do this kind of an event with our allies and we can provide them an opportunity to enjoy the southern Estonian beautiful nature that we have over here."
The Estonian FOS is one of many 734th RSG‑managed forward operating sites in Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. The purpose of these sites is to offer base operation support‑integrator functions to rotational units and partner countries. BOS‑I functions include managing life support, which can encompass housing, food, water, maintenance, contracting and force protection.
Spc. Mandein, who serves in the mayor cell at a FOS in Latvia, said he learned a few things about himself and what it takes to keep going in a challenging reconnaissance event where fatigue is ever present. "Towards the end of it, there were some points where you were running on such little sleep that you kind of misread the map," said Mandein. "I couldn't function at my best. So getting enough rest was really something big for me."
Another important factor, besides incorporating proper rest cycles into the plan, is teamwork. "My advice for the competitors is keep a cool head,” said Rusk. “Listen to your teammates and cooperate. Because cooperation is key in all the tasks that we have prepared for them.”
That cooperation — nurtured at the smallest team or squad level and cultivated upward to the highest echelon — is integral to the V Corps mission of strengthening relationships and improving partnership along the Eastern Forward Defense Initiative.
title: ‘Walk in the Hills’ Puts U.S. Soldiers Through SERE‑Style Recon Challenge

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low‑interest federal disaster loans to Colorado businesses, private nonprofits, and residents to offset physical and economic losses caused by the Aspen Acres Fire occurring June 29 and continuing.
The declaration covers the Colorado counties of Crowley, Custer, El Paso, Fremont, Huerfano, Las Animas, Lincoln, Otero, Pueblo, and Saguache.
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against high wind damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith‑based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Economic Injury Disaster Loans are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the small business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “At these centers, our SBA specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”

LITTLE ROCK—Aaron Hatfield will spend the next 168 months in federal prison for possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and being a felon in possession of firearms. Jonathan D. Ross, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, announced the sentence, which was handed down today, by United States District Judge Brian S. Miller.

On August 5, 2025, a federal grand jury returned a six-count Indictment charging Hatfield, 46, of England, with one count of being a felon in possession of firearms, two counts of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and one count of possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. Hatfield’s co-defendant, Terry Wright, 36, also of England, was charged with two counts of trafficking firearms. Wright pleaded guilty on April 28, 2026, to one count of trafficking firearms. On August 27, 2026, Judge Miller sentenced Wright to serve five years in federal prison followed by three years’ supervised release.

Hatfield pleaded guilty on April 1, 2026, to being a felon in possession of firearms and possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine. In addition to the 168-month sentence, Judge Miller also sentenced Hatfield to three years’ supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system.

Upon learning Wright was selling firearms to known felons in December 2024, law enforcement officials opened an investigation. While conducting a review of Wright’s cell phone, investigators determined Wright sold at least two guns to Hatfield, a convicted felon. Investigators reviewed text messages between Wright and Hatfield that indicated drug use and distribution of drugs. After obtaining a search warrant, investigators searched Hatfield’s residence on February 13, 2025. During a search of Hatfield’s residence, investigators located 19 grams of methamphetamine and three firearms, a Walther, model PK380, .380 caliber firearm; a Norinco, model SKS 7.62x39 rifle; and, an American Tactical, model Mil-Sport, multi-caliber rifle. After being advised of his Miranda rights, Hatfield admitted to investigators that he sold drugs to Wright and that he purchased guns from Wright.

Because Hatfield has at least three prior convictions for a violent felony or serious drug offense, he is classified as a career offender. Hatfield’s criminal history includes felony convictions for commercial burglary and theft of property, possession of drug paraphernalia, manufacture of methamphetamine, possession of drug paraphernalia with intent to manufacture methamphetamine, use or possession of drug paraphernalia, possession of drug paraphernalia with intent to manufacture methamphetamine or cocaine, possession of ephedrine with intent to manufacture methamphetamine, and possession of ephedrine.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

The investigation was conducted by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, with assistance from the England Police Department. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Bart Dickinson.

San Antonio Felon Sentenced to Over 16 Years for Dealing Fentanyl in Schertz
SAN ANTONIO – A San Antonio man was sentenced in federal court to 200 months in prison for possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, announced Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Special Agent in Charge of the San Antonio Division Miguel C. Madrigal and U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.
According to court documents, in 2025, the Guadalupe County Sheriff’s Office began investigating Daniel Mendoza Jr., 44. Throughout the investigation, Mendoza advertised “cocaine, bars, and perk 30s” on social media and completed multiple sales of illicit pills laced with fentanyl and fluorofentanyl in Schertz. Mendoza was arrested on Jan. 14, 2026. A search of his residence revealed Mendoza stored additional fentanyl, cocaine, and alprazolam in his kitchen.
In his bedside table, Mendoza, a convicted felon with an extensive criminal history, stored a .40 caliber pistol and a magazine loaded with 10 rounds. Mendoza was indicted on Jan. 7 for two counts of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and two counts of possession with intent to distribute fluorofentanyl.
A superseding indictment on March 4 added a third count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and one count of felon in possession of a firearm. Mendoza pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl on May 28. The Drug Enforcement Administration and Guadalupe County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Amy Marie Walker prosecuted the case.

INDIANAPOLIS – Between 2003 and 2023, 99% of counties in the United States experienced a flood event. Flood insurance can protect your home from damage during a flooding event— so you can recover faster.
Even if you don’t live near water, your home can still be at risk of flooding from changing conditions such as construction projects, surface erosion or natural events. From 2014 to 2024, almost one-third of National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) claims came from areas located in low- to moderate-risk flood zones.
Flood insurance covers the cost of damage to your property and belongings after a flood event and is available to anyone in an NFIP participating community. You do not need a presidential disaster declaration to receive payment from your flood insurance policy. In comparison, federal disaster assistance requires a presidential disaster declaration and only comes in the form of financial or direct assistance from FEMA and low-interest disaster loans from the U.S. Small Business Administration Office of Disaster Recovery (SBA).
Get a quote to see how you can protect the life you’ve built at floodsmart.gov/policy-quote.
Contact FEMA Mapping and Insurance eXchange (FMIX) Customer Call Center for general flood insurance and flood mapping questions. Go to msc.fema.gov/fmix to chat live with a specialist from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET Monday-Friday, email FEMA-FMIX@fema.dhs.gov or call (877) 336-2627.
With flood insurance from the NFIP, you’re covered.
A policy can cover up to:
- $250,000 for your residential property.
- $100,000 for your personal belongings. This is available to homeowners and renters.
- $500,000 for your commercial property.
- $500,000 for your commercial property contents.
For more information regarding floodplain-related issues, contact your local floodplain administrator, the National Flood Insurance Program at 877-336-2627, or visit FloodSmart.gov.

FEMA’s mission is helping people before, during, and after disasters.

KANSAS CITY, Mo. – A Lee’s Summit, Mo. man pleaded guilty in federal court today for operating an ongoing investment scheme that defrauded millions of dollars from victims.

Trevor Uhls, 29, pleaded guilty before United States District Judge Stephen R. Bough to one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. This is one of many federal fraud cases pursued under the leadership of President Donald Trump and through the establishment of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

According to court documents, Uhls operated a Ponzi scheme that fraudulently obtained more than $3.8 million from at least 60 individual investors through false and misleading representations. Investor funds were misappropriated for Uhls’ personal benefit.

An indictment was returned on Aug. 26, 2026, charging the defendant with one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. The indictment alleges that on or about June 12, 2025, Uhls text messaged an Independence, Mo., investor claiming the investor could earn 8.5% interest by pooling his money with others for a storage unit investment. The investor wired money to Uhls’ checking account. According to the complaint, the storage unit investment Uhls offered the victim was part of a fraudulent scheme and Uhls made false statements to solicit funds to further the scheme. A review of Uhls’ financial records found no evidence he invested the victim’s money in storage units, according to the complaint.

Under federal statutes, Uhls is subject to a sentence of up to 20 years in federal prison without parole for the wire fraud charge, up to three years supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the money laundering charge, Uhls is subject to a sentence of up to 10 years in federal prison without parole, three years supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000 The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as any sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Dave Ketchmark. It was investigated by Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigations.

National Fraud Enforcement Division

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Lee’s Summit Man Pleads Guilty to Defrauding Millions of Dollars from Investors Through Ponzi Scheme

Congresswoman Nikema Williams Introduces Resolution Commemorating National Nonviolence Week
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congresswoman Nikema Williams (GA-05) introduced a resolution commemorating National Nonviolence Week, which occurs annually during the first week of October. Congresswoman Williams introduced a similar resolution in 2021 and 2022 during National Nonviolence Week. Congressman John Lewis historically introduced resolutions to mark National Nonviolence Week during his time in Congress.
The resolution raises awareness of youth violence, the need to become a more peaceful society, and the important role Georgia’s Fifth Congressional District played in America’s history of nonviolent social change.
Congresswoman Nikema Williams (GA-05) said:
“Violence in every form is far too pervasive in our country. However, the work of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and my friend and predecessor, John Lewis, both of whom were champions of nonviolence, can inspire us to create a more peaceful country. I am proud to build on their legacy every day in Congress, but especially during National Nonviolence Week, as we continue advancing nonviolent social action in the Fighting Fifth and across our nation in pursuit of a more equal and equitable world.”
The resolution reads in part:
“Whereas the principle of nonviolence has been a core philosophy of many successful social change movements: Now, therefore, be it Resolved, That the House of Representatives—supports the goals and ideals of ‘‘National Nonviolence Week’’ to raise awareness of youth violence in the United States and the benefits of practicing nonviolence principles; and encourages the people of the United States, State and local officials, middle schools and high schools, law enforcement agencies, and other interested groups to observe ‘‘National Nonviolence Week’’ with appropriate programs and activities that promote awareness and prevention of youth violence.”
Read the full resolution here.
Read a one-pager on the resolution here.
title: Congresswoman Nikema Williams Introduces Resolution Commemorating National Nonviolence Week

text:
Final rule modernizes Denali Park Road regulations and supports expanded access

NewsMedia@nps.gov

WASHINGTON — The Department of the Interior and the National Park Service today announced a final rule updating vehicle use regulations on the Denali National Park Road to expand visitor access and bring the regulations in line with the park’s longstanding management plan. The action supports President Trump’s Executive Order 14314, “Making America Beautiful Again by Improving Our National Parks,” which calls for expanding opportunities for Americans to enjoy the nation’s public lands.

The final rule brings the vehicle limit on the restricted section of the Denali Park Road in line with the park’s 2012 Vehicle Management Plan. The plan was developed with public input and established standards for protecting park resources and maintaining a high-quality visitor experience.

“America’s national parks belong to the American people, and we should be looking for every responsible opportunity to make these incredible places more accessible,” said Secretary Doug Burgum. “At Denali, we’re cutting red tape, honoring a management plan shaped by years of public input, and expanding access while protecting the extraordinary landscape that makes this park so special.”

Under the final rule, up to 160 vehicles may travel each day on the restricted section of the park road (from mile 15 to mile 90) during the park’s visitor season as long as standards for desired resources conditions and visitor experience are met. The season runs from the Saturday before Memorial Day through the second Thursday after Labor Day. The new daily limit replaces the current seasonal limit of 10,512 vehicle permits.

“This commonsense update will improve opportunities for more Americans to experience Denali National Park and Preserve,” said Jessica Bowron, Comptroller Exercising the Delegated Authority of the Director of the National Park Service. “By modernizing these regulations, we are improving visitor access while continuing to protect the extraordinary resources that make Denali one of our nation’s most iconic national parks.”

The final rule also removes regulatory language that could end the visitor season on Sept. 15 when that date occurs before the second Thursday after Labor Day. Under the revised regulation, the season will always end on the second Thursday after Labor Day, providing additional opportunities for recreation and visitor access in years when the season otherwise would have ended earlier.

“Updating the Denali Road vehicle limit allows the NPS to meet visitor demand while maintaining a high-quality experience,” said Denali National Park Superintendent Brooke Merrell . “It will make the extraordinary landscapes and wildlife of Denali more accessible, while preserving its natural and cultural resources for future generations."

The regulatory update comes as the NPS prepares to restore public bus access to the west end of Denali Park Road in 2027. In September, the NPS and Federal Highway Administration announced completion of the Pretty Rocks Bridge , which reconnects the eastern and western portions of the road following the 2021 landslide and road closure.

Built over 16 years, from 1922 to 1938, the 92-mile Denali Park Road is the primary means of access into the park and one of the best places in the world to observe large northern mammals in their natural habitat. Visitors traveling the road may see Dall sheep, caribou, wolves, grizzly bears, moose and foxes, along with smaller mammals and birds, some of which are rarely seen elsewhere in North America. The road also offers views of Alaska Range features, including glacially carved mountains, Mount McKinley and dynamic alpine landscapes, and provides opportunities for wilderness recreation, discovery, adventure and connection with nature.

To view the final rule, please visit www.federalregister.gov and search for document #2026-21222.
