text:
EPA Spotlights a Leaner, Stronger Agency Delivering More for Taxpayers
New webpage and video detail billions in savings, a reorganization that puts scientists at the center
WASHINGTON — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) today launched a new webpage and video highlighting the agency's reform, reorganization, and savings, showing how EPA is delivering its core mission faster while returning taxpayer dollars.
“For too long, EPA’s budget grew while the agency fell behind on its core statutory work. Since President Trump was sworn back into office, we have flipped that,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. “We’re delivering clean air, land, and water faster than ever and returning billions to the taxpayers who fund this agency. That’s what accountability looks like.”
Prior to the Trump administration taking office, EPA spending climbed while core statutory work fell behind, leaving backlogs across the agency. Since January 2025, EPA has cut costs across grants, contracts, staffing, real estate, technology, and travel, including $30 billion in canceled grants, roughly $825 million a year in reduced contracting obligations, and about $750 million a year from staffing efficiencies and reorganization.
At the same time, EPA reorganized to put scientists at the center of the agency, standing up the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions (OASES), adding more than 130 scientific and technical experts to clear chemical and pesticide review backlogs, and creating a one-stop Office of Finance and Administration. Looking ahead, the agency's Superfund Solutions initiative, launched in May 2026, is focused on getting contaminated sites to the finish line faster.
title: EPA Spotlights a Leaner, Stronger Agency Delivering More for Taxpayers

text:
The joint federal-state Unemployment Insurance (UI) system provides temporary and partial wage replacement to involuntarily unemployed workers and stabilizes the economy during recessions. Two permanent law unemployment benefits—Unemployment Compensation (UC) and Extended Benefits (EB)—are countercyclical, with spending and weekly benefit payments that increase automatically during a recession. States administer unemployment benefits under their state laws, with U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) oversight, resulting in 53 different UC programs operated in the states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF) in the U.S. Treasury accounts for transactions related to UC and EB. The UTF is a single trust fund with 59 accounts: the Employment Security Administration Account (ESAA); the Extended Unemployment Compensation Account (EUCA); the Federal Unemployment Account (FUA); 53 state accounts (including the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands); the Federal Employees Compensation Account (FECA); and two accounts related to the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB).
Congress has shown interest in the operations of the UTF as part of its oversight of the UI system. For example, at a June 2024 hearing on "Reforming Unemployment Insurance to Support American Workers and Businesses," the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare of the House Committee on Ways and Means discussed several reform issues, including the reconsideration of the method through which funding for state administration is collected and distributed via the UTF.
This report provides a figure that displays FY2026 flows of funding through the UTF. Specifically, this figure includes projections from DOL related to the income, outlays, and end-of-year balances of the UTF as well as relevant FY2026 annual appropriations data, which are enacted amounts under P.L. 119-75, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026. This report also describes, including relevant statutory authorities, UTF sources of revenue, accounts, statutory transfers, federal loans to states, UC appropriations out of ESAA, and outlays on unemployment benefits.
For a broad overview of the UC program, see CRS In Focus IF10336, The Fundamentals of Unemployment Compensation. For additional information on how UC benefits are funded through the UTF, see CRS Report RS22077, Unemployment Compensation (UC) and the Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF): Funding UC Benefits.
The Unemployment Insurance (UI) system is constructed as a joint federal-state partnership of which the Unemployment Compensation (UC) program is the foundation. Created under the Social Security Act of 1935 (SSA; P.L. 74-271), the UC program provides income support through weekly benefit payments to involuntarily unemployed workers. Although there are broad requirements under federal law regarding UC benefits and financing, the specific parameters are set out under each state's laws. States administer UC benefits with U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) oversight, resulting in 53 different UC programs operated in the states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.1
The Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970 (P.L. 91-373)2 established the Extended Benefits (EB) program to provide additional weeks of unemployment benefits if high unemployment exists within a state. After UC benefits are exhausted, the EB program, also administered by states, may provide up to an additional 13 or 20 weeks of benefits, depending on worker eligibility, state law, and economic conditions in the state. Under permanent law, the EB program is funded 50% by the federal government and 50% by the states.3
Designated as a trust fund for federal accounting purposes, the Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF) in the U.S. Treasury accounts for UC and EB financial transactions. The UTF's structure, which involves 59 separate accounts, and complexity, which includes four types of statutory transfers between key UTF accounts, present challenges in tracking the annual flow of UI income and outlays. Congress may be interested in understanding how federal unemployment tax revenue moves through UTF accounts. In particular, there may be interest in which UTF flows are based on statute and statutory thresholds and which flows require annual appropriations. Additionally, Congress has expressed interest in reconsidering the method through which funding for state UI administration is collected and distributed via the UTF.4
This report illustrates the operations of the UTF using FY2026 projections from DOL on UI income, outlays, and end-of-year balances as well as relevant FY2026 annual appropriations data, which are enacted amounts under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75). Included is a description of sources of revenue, UTF accounts, statutory transfers, federal loans to states, UC appropriations out of the relevant UTF account, and outlays on UI benefits. Relevant statutory authorities are also provided throughout. The Appendix provides a glossary of acronyms used in this report.
The UTF's authority and structure are set out under Title IX of SSA.5 The UTF is a single trust fund with 59 accounts: the Employment Security Administration Account (ESAA); the Extended Unemployment Compensation Account (EUCA); the Federal Unemployment Account (FUA); 53 state accounts (including the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands); the Federal Employees Compensation Account (FECA); and two accounts related to the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB).
The UI system is financed by federal payroll taxes under the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA)6 and by state payroll taxes commonly referred to as the State Unemployment Tax Acts (SUTA). All federal and state UI tax receipts and outlays for benefits and administration flow through the U.S. Treasury and thus affect federal revenue, outlays, and the overall financial position (deficit or surplus) of the federal government. The trust fund designation is used to accumulate legal spending authority that is available automatically when needed. The revenue and the outlays of the UI system are counted in the federal budget.7
For additional information on the UTF, see CRS Report RS22077, Unemployment Compensation (UC) and the Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF): Funding UC Benefits.
Figure 1 displays FY2026 flows of funding through the UTF, which are explained in detail below.
Sources of UTF revenue are depicted in Figure 1 as gray ovals.
The federal-state UI program is financed by federal payroll taxes under FUTA and by state payroll taxes under SUTA.9
FUTA is set out under Title 26, Sections 3301-3311, of the U.S. Code and establishes a federal payroll tax that employers pay to fund both federal and state administrative costs as well as the federal share of the EB program (50%), loans to insolvent state UC accounts, and state employment services. If a state UC program complies with all federal requirements, the net FUTA tax rate for employers is 0.6% on the first $7,000 of each worker's annual earnings. Federal law defines which jobs a state UC program must cover for the state's employers to avoid paying the maximum FUTA tax rate (6.0%) on the first $7,000 of each employee's annual pay.10
FUTA revenues are deposited in the U.S. Treasury and credited to ESAA within the UTF (see "ESAA" section).
In FY2026, income from FUTA was projected to be $7.30 billion.11
For additional information on FUTA, see CRS Report R44527, Unemployment Compensation: The Fundamentals of the Federal Unemployment Tax (FUTA).
States levy their own payroll taxes on employers to fund regular UC benefits and the state share of the EB program (50%). The SUTA tax rate on an employer is, in most states, based on the amount of UC benefits paid to former employees. Generally, the more UC benefits paid to its former employees, the higher the tax rate of the employer, up to a maximum established by state law.12
SUTA revenues are deposited into the relevant state account (see "State Unemployment Accounts" section) in the UTF and, under Title 26, Section 3304(a)(4), of the U.S. Code, may be used only to pay for the state's UC benefits and the state's portion of EB payments.
In FY2026, income from SUTA was projected to be $44.59 billion.
UTF accounts are depicted in Figure 1 as light blue boxes.
Although the UTF is a single trust fund, it has 59 accounts: ESAA; EUCA; FUA; 53 state accounts (including the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands); FECA; and two accounts related to the RRB. The FECA and the two RRB accounts are not depicted in Figure 1 to simplify the graphical presentation of UTF flows.13
ESAA is authorized under SSA, Section 901.14
All FUTA revenue is credited to ESAA. Under SSA, Section 901(c),15 funds from ESAA are made available through the annual federal appropriations process,16 which designates these funds to be used by DOL for the costs of administering the state UC programs as well as other expenditures, including the federal share of EB (50%), loans to insolvent states, and some other purposes described in the "UC Appropriations out of ESAA" section.
Under SSA, Section 901(d)(1),17 any additional FUTA revenue paid by employers because the state has an outstanding, unpaid loan from FUA (see "FUA" section) is transferred from ESAA to FUA and reduces the state's outstanding loan balance (not shown in Figure 1; for more information, see CRS Report RS22954, The Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF): State Insolvency and Federal Loans to States). Additionally, under SSA, Section 905(b)(1),18 each month 20% of the FUTA deposits into ESAA are transferred to EUCA, which funds the federal share of EB (see "Monthly 20% ESAA to EUCA Transfer" section). Under SSA, Section 901(f),19 at the close of the fiscal year, the ESAA balance is limited to 40% of the amount of the total appropriation for the fiscal year (for FY2026, DOL estimated the ESAA balance to be $1.46 billion), with the excess to be deposited into EUCA at the beginning of the next fiscal year (see "End-of-Fiscal-Year Transfer Above Ceiling from ESAA to EUCA" section).
For additional information on the role of ESAA in funding state administration of UC benefits, see CRS In Focus IF10838, Funding the State Administration of Unemployment Compensation (UC) Benefits.
EUCA is authorized under SSA, Section 905.20
If a state has an active EB program,21 EUCA distributions are made for the federal portion (50%) of EB payments. There was no EB projected to be payable in states in FY2026 due to low rates of projected unemployment; therefore, there was no transfer from EUCA to any state unemployment account.
Under SSA, Section 905(b)(2),22 the EUCA balance is limited to 0.5% of covered wages. For FY2026, the limit was $48.84 billion.23 If the EUCA balance exceeds the limitation, the excess is distributed to FUA (see "End-of-Fiscal-Year Transfer Above Ceiling from EUCA to FUA" section).
Although EUCA was projected to have $1.61 billion in cash at the end of FY2026, the net end-of-year balance for EUCA was projected to be negative (-$4.88 billion). EUCA's negative balance was due to borrowing attributable to (1) the Great Recession (December 2007-June 2009) and (2) the COVID-19 recession (February-April 2020). Under SSA, Section 905(d),24 EUCA has the authority to borrow funds from the General Fund of the U.S. Treasury without fiscal year limitations.
In FY2026, EUCA was projected to have two large outstanding debts. First, EUCA was projected to have approximately $4.00 billion in debt to the General Fund because of debt incurred from paying the statutorily obligated EB during the COVID-19 recession. Second, EUCA was projected to owe an additional $2.49 billion via an inter-account transfer loan from FUA, which was incurred paying for statutorily obligated EB during the Great Recession.25
FUA is authorized under SSA, Section 902.26
Under SSA, Section 901(d)(1),27 FUA is credited with the additional taxes paid by employers when the state has an outstanding unpaid loan from FUA.28
FUA funds are distributed as loans to states through the state unemployment accounts (see "Federal Loans to States" section). Under SSA, Section 902(a),29 the FUA balance is limited to 0.5% of covered wages.30 For FY2026, the limit was $48.84 billion. When this FUA balance ceiling is met and the same ceiling is met for EUCA, then Reed Act distributions are made (see "Reed Act Distributions" section).
In FY2026, the end-of-year balance for FUA was projected to be $13.94 billion.
Under SSA, Section 904,31 SUTA revenues are deposited into the relevant state accounts in the UTF.
In FY2026, the end-of-year balance for the state unemployment accounts was projected to be $84.69 billion. In addition to this balance, the state unemployment accounts were projected to owe $19.77 billion in federal loans in FY2026 (see "Federal Loans to States" section).
Statutory transfers are depicted in Figure 1 as lines with arrows. These lines are either solid (see "Monthly 20% ESAA to EUCA Transfer" section) or dotted (see "End-of-Fiscal-Year Transfer Above Ceiling from ESAA to EUCA," "End-of-Fiscal-Year Transfer Above Ceiling from EUCA to FUA," and "Reed Act Distributions" sections), depending on whether the transfer is automatic (solid) or certain conditions must be met for the transfer to occur (dotted).
The following statutory transfers among accounts in the UTF are presented in Figure 1.32
Under SSA, Section 901(f),33 any funds in excess of the amount equal to 40% of the total appropriation from ESAA are taken out of ESAA at the end of the fiscal year. The excess funds are deposited into EUCA at the beginning of the next fiscal year. The net FY2025 end-of-year balance for ESAA was $1.78 billion, which was above the 40% ESAA balance limit for FY2025 ($1.73 billion). This resulted in $.05 billion being deposited into EUCA at the beginning of FY2026. The FY2026 projected net ESAA end-of-year balance was $3.61 billion, which was above the ESAA FY2026 balance limit of $1.51 billion. The projected $2.10 billion from ESAA would be deposited into EUCA in FY2027.
Under SSA, Section 901(f),34 each month, ESAA distributes 20% of the net monthly activity to EUCA.35
In FY2026, the sum of monthly transfers from ESAA to EUCA was projected to be $1.46 billion.
Under SSA, Section 905(b),36 the EUCA balance was limited to $48.84 billion for FY2026. If the EUCA balance exceeds the limitation, the excess is distributed to FUA.
In FY2026, there was no projected statutory transfer from EUCA to FUA, as the account balance (-$4.88 billion) was projected to be under the applicable ceiling for FY2026 of $48.84 billion.
As explained above, at the end of the fiscal year, there is a limitation on the balance in ESAA—the account balance cannot exceed 40% of the prior fiscal year's congressional appropriation (SSA, §901(f)). 37 If the balance in ESAA exceeds this limitation, the excess is distributed to EUCA. After the distribution, if the balance in EUCA exceeds the applicable EUCA limitation,38 the excess is distributed to FUA. If after the distribution from EUCA, the FUA balance exceeds the limitation,39 the excess is distributed as a Reed Act distribution to the states under SSA, Section 903.40
In FY2026, there were no projected Reed Act distributions, as the account balances for EUCA 
(-$4.88 billion) and FUA ($13.94 billion) were both under the FY2026 ceilings of $48.84 billion.
For additional information on Reed Act distributions, see CRS Report RS22006, The Unemployment Trust Fund and Reed Act Distributions.
Federal loans to states are depicted in Figure 1 as a solid line with an arrow between FUA and the state unemployment accounts.
If states do not have enough funding in their state accounts, Title XII of SSA41 allows the states to borrow funds from FUA within the UTF. States may borrow from other sources, although some states are prohibited from doing so under state laws.42 The issuing of a loan to the state would require that FUA redeem securities. This redemption would decrease the federal debt. If FUA is insolvent and the other federal accounts within the UTF do not have sufficient balances to lend the funds that states need (as occurred in FY2010-FY2015 and began again in May 2020), Title XII of SSA allows FUA to borrow funds from the U.S. Treasury. If Treasury were to issue new securities in order to lend funds to FUA, this would increase the federal debt. When a state pays back the loan from FUA, FUA then uses those funds to repay its debt to Treasury, and the federal debt decreases.
In FY2026, there was a projected $5.38 billion in income to FUA, which included interest earnings ($0.17 billion), state repayments and reduced credits ($2.69 billion and $1.84 billion, respectively), and state interest payments ($0.67 billion).43 States were projected to have a cumulative $19.77 billion in outstanding loans at the end of FY2026.
For additional information on federal loans to states, including timelines on repayment, see CRS Report RS22954, The Unemployment Trust Fund (UTF): State Insolvency and Federal Loans to States.
UC appropriations out of ESAA are depicted in Figure 1 as green lines with arrows ending with large "$" symbols. Appropriated amounts, along with their descriptions, are displayed as green boxes with rounded corners.44
Each fiscal year, funds are made available through the appropriations process to make distributions of FUTA revenue for state administration, the federal costs of administration, and other purposes—for example, the Employment Service (ES), Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS).45 Most of these UC appropriations are accounted for through DOL's Employment and Training Administration's State Unemployment Insurance and Employment Service Operations (SUIESO) funding.46
SSA, Section 901(c)(1)(A)(I),47 authorizes administrative grants to the states (subject to appropriations limits) from ESAA. The discretionary annual appropriations to DOL for administrative expenses are not based on the size of FUTA collections. Instead, each year, DOL assesses state budgetary requirements,48 which are provided within budget justification documents for considerations by appropriators. The subsequent appropriations customarily include a base level of funding as well as an additional contingent appropriation. The appropriations language also customarily provides a baseline estimate of national unemployment as measured by the volume of UC claims expected to be filed per week—the average weekly insured unemployment (AWIU). Additionally, the contingent funding includes a trigger based on the average volume of weekly UC claims exceeding the AWIU baseline. For example, under P.L. 119-75, for every 100,000 increase in the total AWIU above the 3,075,000 baseline, an additional $28.6 million in state administrative funding would have been available.
Once the AWIU is above the contingent appropriation threshold, DOL notifies the Office of Management and Budget, which then releases funds from the contingent appropriation. If the need for contingency funds exceeds the base appropriation, but the national AWIU is less than the contingent appropriation threshold, then either Congress must enact a supplemental appropriation or states must reduce administrative expenses or provide additional state funding from different revenue streams or state general funds (as SUTA funds may pay only for UC and EB).49
As shown in Figure 1, in FY2026, P.L. 119-75 provided $3.23 billion to be appropriated for state administrative grants.
For additional information on funding state UI administration, see CRS In Focus IF10838, Funding the State Administration of Unemployment Compensation (UC) Benefits.
SSA, Section 901(c)(1)(B),50 authorizes expenditures out of ESAA (subject to appropriations) to support the necessary expenses of DOL for the performance of its functions as required by UC law (i.e., under SSA and FUTA), VETS, and any federal UC law. In FY2026, P.L. 119-75 appropriated $18 million for federal UI administration from ESAA.
SSA, Section 901(c)(1)(A)(ii),52 authorizes expenditures out of ESAA (subject to appropriations) for the establishment and maintenance of public employment offices (ES)53 on the basis of the share of the workforce that is in covered employment (see SSA, §901(c)(4)).54 The proportion of ES funding provided from ESAA ranged from 85% in 1973 to 97% in 1980 (as UC program coverage increased) and has remained at 97% through the present.55
Similarly, SSA, Section 901(c)(1)(A)(iii),56 authorizes expenditures for carrying out the activities of VETS.57
While there is no similar authorizing language for expenditures out of ESAA to BLS within Title IX of SSA, DOL's FY2027 budget justification provides information on how BLS activities support the ES and UC programs. For example,
[p]rograms in this area help fulfill many requirements of the Wagner-Peyser Act as amended by the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) of 2014, including requirements that the Secretary of Labor "develop and maintain the elements of the workforce and labor market information system" as well as develop and maintain national projections of employment opportunities by occupation and industry. This legislation requires the development of information on jobs in demand to support states' efforts to better train for the hiring needs of businesses.58
Additionally,
[t]he BLS operates the CES [Current Employment Statistics], Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS), and LAUS [Local Area Unemployment Statistics] programs in cooperation with the states and territories. As noted within their respective descriptions, these programs compose the BLS Labor Market Information (LMI) Cooperative Statistical Program, which is conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Wagner-Peyser Act as amended by WIOA. The BLS uses cooperative agreements to fund the states for these programs. BLS regional staff, under the direction of the Office of Field Operations in the national office, negotiate and monitor LMI cooperative agreements.59
In FY2026, P.L. 119-75 appropriated $17.5 million for ES using funds within ESAA. Similarly, the FY2026 appropriations funded by ESAA were $68.0 million for BLS and $269.8 million for VETS.
Finally, three additional appropriations out of ESAA fund the Employment and Training Program Administration,60 DOL Management,61 and the DOL Office of Inspector General (OIG).62 Similar to BLS funding out of ESAA, although there is no specific authorizing language in SSA for expenditures out of ESAA for these purposes, all such expenditures support federal administration or oversight related to UI programs and activities. In FY2026, P.L. 119-75 appropriated $53.9 million for the Employment and Training Program Administration, $0.3 million for DOL Management, and $5.8 million for the DOL OIG, all using funds within ESAA.
Outlays for UC, UCFE, UCX, and EB benefits are depicted in Figure 1 with a dark blue box.
Titles III, IX, and XII of SSA authorize the joint federal-state UC program to provide unemployment benefits. Most states provide up to a maximum of 26 weeks of UC benefits. Former federal workers may be eligible for unemployment benefits through the UCFE program. Former U.S. military servicemembers may be eligible for unemployment benefits through the UCX program. The Emergency Unemployment Compensation Act of 1991 (P.L. 102-164) provides that ex-servicemembers be treated the same as other unemployed workers with respect to benefit levels, the waiting period for benefits, and benefit duration.
The EB program was established by the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970 (P.L. 91-373).63 P.L. 91-373 extends the duration (i.e., number of weeks) of unemployment benefits (extended benefits) at the state level if certain economic conditions exist within the state.
In FY2026, outlays on UC, UCFE, and UCX benefits were projected to be $41.21 billion. No EB was projected to be payable in FY2026.
For more on UC, UCFE, UCX, and EB benefits, see CRS Report R46687, Unemployment Insurance (UI) Benefits: Permanent-Law Programs and the COVID-19 Pandemic Response.
title: The Unemployment Trust Fund: FY2026 Income, Outlays, and End-of-Year Balances

HAMMOND- Angel Antonio Penaloza-Rojo, 33 years old, a Mexican national, was sentenced by United States District Court Judge Gretchen S. Lund after pleading guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute Fentanyl, announced United States Attorney Adam L. Mildred.

Penaloza-Rojo was sentenced to 70 months in prison followed by 3 years of supervised release.

According to documents in the case, on August 11, 2024, Penaloza-Rojo brought approximately 3 kilograms of a substance containing Fentanyl to East Chicago, Indiana, where he was delivering it to members of law enforcement operating undercover.

"Today’s sentence holds Angel-Antonio Penaloza-Rojo fully accountable for his malicious disregard for American laws and the lives of Hoosiers. The defendant, an undocumented immigrant, deliberately entered the United States illegally for the sole purpose of trafficking deadly fentanyl from Mexico directly into the Northern District of Indiana. Penaloza-Rojo and his co-conspirators operated a transnational drug pipeline, profiting from addiction and building wealth at the direct expense of our residents' lives and our community’s safety. Fentanyl is an absolute poison, and those who smuggle it across our borders to prey on our neighborhoods will find no safe haven here. This successful prosecution is a direct result of strong interagency partnerships. By combining the specialized resources of federal, state, and local law enforcement, we successfully dismantled this network from the street level up to its international roots. As in this case, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s North Central Laboratory, AUSA Michael J. Toth, and the United States Attorney’s Office remain relentless in our collaborative mission to protect the Northern District of Indiana," said United States Attorney Adam L. Mildred.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives Indiana, through the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area Fire Task Force, with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations/Enforcement and Removal Operations, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s North Central Laboratory, and the Indiana State Police. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael J. Toth.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

title: Mexican National Sentenced to 70 Months in Prison for Drug Offense

The H-2A visa program allows for the temporary admission of foreign workers to the United States to perform agricultural labor or services of a seasonal or temporary nature. (See CRS Report R44849, H-2A and H-2B Temporary Worker Visas: Policy and Related Issues for a discussion of the H-2A visa program.)
The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes the H-2A program and requires that prospective H-2A employers apply to the Department of Labor (DOL) for labor certification. Per 8 U.S.C. §1188(a)(1), before approving a labor certification application, DOL must determine that
The INA does not specify a method for the Secretary of Labor to make these two determinations. To ensure there are not sufficient U.S. workers who are qualified and available to perform the work, DOL requires employers to advertise and engage in positive recruitment of U.S. workers for the H-2A job opportunity, and to offer U.S. workers terms and working conditions that are not less favorable than those offered to H-2A workers. To guard against adverse effects on similarly employed U.S. workers, DOL also requires employers to offer wages at or above the highest of five wages levels: (1) the adverse effect wage rate (AEWR), (2) the applicable prevailing wage rate, (3) an agreed-upon collective bargaining wage rate, (4) the federal minimum wage rate, or (5) the applicable state minimum wage rate. DOL regulations govern the offered wage rate and provide the methodologies for determining AEWRs and prevailing wage rates.
For most H-2A workers, the applicable AEWR is a state-level hourly rate based on average wage estimates. However, a national-level monthly AEWR is used for certain positions—referred to as range occupations—that involve the herding or production of livestock on the range, under certain working conditions. For the purpose of H-2A labor certification, agricultural positions that do not meet these requirements are referred to as non-range occupations.
DOL calculates a monthly AEWR for range occupations. For H-2A program purposes, range occupations involve the herding or production of livestock, performed on the range for more than 50% of the workdays in the work contract period, and generally require workers to be on-call 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. DOL provides a monthly AEWR for such positions given their unique nature, which makes recording work hours difficult.
The monthly rate for these positions was initially calculated in 2016 as $7.25 per hour (i.e., the federal minimum wage) multiplied by 48 hours per week and 4.333 weeks per month. Since 2017, the monthly AEWR for range occupations has been adjusted annually based on growth in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Employment Cost Index (ECI) for private sector wages and salaries over the preceding September-to-September (12-month) period. Effective February 3, 2026, it is $2,132.41 per month.
On October 2, 2025, DOL released an interim final rule (IFR) with a new methodology for calculating hourly AEWRs for non-range occupations (This IFR is in effect, but a court has ordered DOL to replace it by December 30, 2026). The AEWR methodology in the 2025 IFR provides AEWRs at two experience/skill levels within each non-range occupation in each state or territory. These are based on estimates of hourly wages from the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) program for each state or territory, with a deduction for the estimated value of employer-provided housing.
"Entry-level" (Skill Level I) wage rates are determined as the average hourly wage paid to the lowest-paid third of workers in the occupation in the state or territory (roughly the 17th percentile of the wage distribution). "Experienced" (Skill Level II) wage rates are determined as the average hourly wage rate paid to all workers in the occupation in the state or territory.
DOL groups five agricultural occupations together as "Field and Livestock Workers (Combined)," with AEWRs specified for these occupations as a group. All other non-range occupations have occupation-specific AEWRs.
Per 8 U.S.C. §1188(c)(4), employers must provide H-2A workers with housing. The 2025 IFR includes a new housing cost adjustment in the AEWR. This adjustment is based on the weighted average of Fair Market Rents for four-bedroom housing units in the state or territory, as published by the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This monthly rent is then divided by eight (assuming eight workers per housing unit) and spread over an assumed 173.9 hours worked per month. The housing adjustment may not exceed 30% of the hourly AEWR. These adjustments in 2026 range from -$.71 (Puerto Rico) to -$3.20 (Hawaii).
DOL states "the vast majority of certified H-2A job opportunities are concentrated in the five field and livestock worker (combined) occupation[s]." These five occupations have the following Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) codes and titles:
Per the 2025 IFR methodology, AEWRs for non-range occupations in the Field and Livestock Workers (Combined) group ranged from $7.93 per hour (Guam) to $15.33 (District of Columbia [DC]) in entry-level positions and from $8.82 per hour (Guam) to $21.90 (DC) in experienced positions. Among states, entry-level AEWRs for these occupations ranged from $8.84 (Mississippi) to $14.91 (Nebraska), and experienced AEWRs ranged from $13.41 (Florida) to $19.22 (Nebraska).
Farm supervisors or managers, heavy truck drivers, and logging workers are examples of agricultural occupations not included in the Field and Livestock Workers (Combined) category. For these occupations, the AEWR is based on the state- or territory-wide OEWS wage estimate for the individual occupation at the appropriate experience/skill level. If the OEWS program does not publish state or territory-wide wage estimates for the occupation, the AEWR is based on national OEWS wages for the occupation at the appropriate experience/skill level.
As part of labor certification, employers identify the tasks, duties, and requirements associated with work to be performed by H-2A workers. DOL uses this information to determine the occupation or occupations and the experience/skill level for each H-2A job. Descriptions of the definitions, skill requirements, and tasks typically performed by workers in each occupation are available from the Occupational Information Network (O*NET) website at https://www.onetonline.org/
Some H-2A jobs cannot be classified within a single occupation. If the DOL-assigned occupations have different AEWRs, then the wage rate applies for the occupation in which the worker spends the majority of their workdays.
The OEWS program collects wage data from all states, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. OEWS does not collect data from—and consequently AEWRs are not available for—American Samoa or the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. DOL publishes notices of AEWR adjustments in the Federal Register on or about July 1 each year.
DOL's previous final rule on the methodology for determining hourly AEWRs for non-range agricultural occupations took effect March 30, 2023. It used the Farm Labor Survey (FLS) of the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) to determine the AEWR for field and livestock occupations and the OEWS to determine the AEWR for other occupations and for geographic areas without FLS data. It set the AEWR for positions spanning multiple occupations using the highest applicable AEWR.
Multiple groups of agricultural employers sued to block the 2023 AEWR final rule. On August 25, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana vacated the 2023 rule. This meant AEWRs were set according to a 2010 rule that relied only on the FLS data. On August 28, 2025, NASS announced it was cancelling the FLS, leaving a regulatory gap. DOL issued the 2025 IFR a few weeks later on an emergency basis, bypassing usual procedures.
On November 21, 2025, United Farm Workers and multiple farm workers sued to block the 2025 IFR, arguing it was unlawful. On August 26, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California held the challenged portions of the IFR were procedurally defective and arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and therefore unlawful. The court ordered DOL to "promptly produce a new methodology" and provide notice to H-2A employers that they may be required to pay back wages. On October 2, 2026, the court further ordered DOL to issue a new IFR by December 30, 2026.
title: New Adverse Effect Wage Rate Methodology for Temporary Employment of H-2A Nonimmigrants in the United States

Presiding over the ceremony was U.S. Air Force Gen. Gregory Guillot, commander, North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command. Gen. Shawn N. Bratton, vice chief of space operations, provided additional remarks.
“We’re in the business of providing manpower, expertise and systems to operate in space, gain and maintain space superiority, deny our adversary space capabilities, and through our combatant commands, protect the joint force and our homeland from space-enabled attack,” Bratton said. “Space Forces-Northern is the critical space-based link to NORTHCOM’s defense of our nation; Space Forces-Northern provides the NORTHCOM team with a critical edge in combating all adversary threats.”
Guillot lauded the command’s contribution to joint operations, highlighting space superiority as essential to homeland defense.
“Modern homeland defense cannot succeed without uncompromised superiority in the space domain,” Guillot said. “Space Forces-Northern rapidly transformed from a conceptual blueprint into an indispensable warfighting organization.”
During the ceremony, Guillot presented Schreiner with the Legion of Merit for exceptionally meritorious service as Space Forces-Northern commander from Aug. 23, 2025, to Oct. 13. The award citation credited Schreiner’s leadership with delivering initial operating capability for the U.S. Space Force component command in five months, activating the unit four years ahead of schedule.
Schreiner established critical command-and-control structures, synchronized joint operational planning, and secured essential manpower and resources. He also integrated Air Force Reserve interservice transfers with active-duty personnel, strengthened space support for continental defense and civil-support missions, and built relationships across the joint force, civilian agencies, and regional allies and partners.
“When we activated Space Forces-Northern, we proudly unfurled our new flag and immediately got to work standing up a team of Guardians with a singular focus: to support U.S. Northern Command and integrate space power in the defense of our homeland,” Schreiner said in his farewell remarks to the Guardians of Space Forces-Northern. “The culture you fostered, the excellence you demonstrated and the partnerships you built will echo across the combatant command for years to come.”
Reflecting on the foundation established by the command’s Guardians and partners, Verroco outlined his approach to sustaining that momentum in an evolving operational environment.
“We will stay up to date with the changing operational environment. We’ll modify our approach as needed to make sure that we stay in line with the commander’s intent, but the path to operate, integrate and mature is well chosen,” Verroco said. “The line ‘standing guard both night and day’ harmonizes well with the motto, ‘We have the watch.’”
With Verroco assuming command, U.S. Space Forces-Northern will continue integrating space capabilities into joint operations, strengthening strategic partnerships, and supporting homeland defense missions.
title: Space Forces-Northern changes command at Peterson SFB

FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Servicemembers, civilians, families and community members gathered Oct. 15 at the installation Community Club to honor three retirees whose decades of service strengthened the Army’s mission in the Caribbean and left a lasting impact on Fort Buchanan.
During the ceremony, leaders, coworkers and loved ones came together to celebrate the careers of Staff Sgt. Alexis Montañez, an Army recruiter; Ms. Maria “Angie” Lopez, director of the Directorate of Public Works; and Joel Pérez Vega, a Fort Buchanan firefighter, each recognized for their devoted service to the nation and the community they supported for so many years.
Garrison Manager Ulises Marrero opened the event by reflecting on the significance of their service. “Today is not just a celebration of retirement, it is a celebration of impact, legacy, and lives changed,” he said. He also thanked the families whose support made their careers possible. “You gave strength when they were tired, encouragement when challenges mounted, and love that made it possible for them to serve at such an exceptional level.”
Command Sgt. Maj. Everett B. Sikes echoed that appreciation. “Behind every successful mission, there are dedicated people who often work quietly, without recognition, making that readiness possible. You are three of those people,” he said. “Your service mattered. Your sacrifices mattered. And the difference you made will remain long after you leave.”
Each retiree received traditional Army retirement honors.
Montañez was presented a Certificate of Retirement, Certificates of Appreciation for both his service and his spouse’s support, a U.S. flag, and an Army retirement pin. Bouquets of red roses were also given to his spouse and mother in recognition of their sacrifices.
“After more than 24 years in the Army, there are a lot of people I want to thank, because I definitely didn’t get here by myself,” Montañez said. He reflected proudly on his recruiting career, adding, “Today, I can proudly say that 137 Soldiers joined the Army through my efforts… many of them from my own community.”
Ms. Lopez received a Retirement Certificate, a Department of the Army Certificate of Retirement, a Certificate of Appreciation, and a U.S. flag. Her sisters received white roses honoring their support throughout her 28-year civilian career.
“Projects eventually end. Buildings and infrastructure may change. But the people are what remain in our hearts and in our memories,” Lopez said. “Today, I leave with a full heart… but most of all, I take with me my Fort Buchanan DPW family.”
After 35 years of service, Joel Pérez Vega was honored with a Retirement Certificate, a Department of the Army Certificate of Retirement, a Certificate of Appreciation and a U.S. flag. For Pérez Vega, the ceremony marked the closing chapter of a lifetime of service — but not the end of his bond with Fort Buchanan.
“This community became part of my life, and I’m really going to miss this place,” Pérez Vega said. “I just want to thank everybody for the experience and for letting me be part of this great community.”
As the ceremony concluded, Marrero offered a final message on behalf of the installation. “You leave behind footprints of service that will not fade,” he said. “We celebrate your achievements, honor your sacrifices, and recognize the families who supported you every step of the way.”
The retirees formed a receiving line as attendees expressed congratulations to the three professionals whose careers helped shape the readiness and resilience of Fort Buchanan—now and for generations to come.
Fort Buchanan supports approximately 15,000 military personnel, including active-duty Soldiers, Army Reserve, Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve and Navy Reserve members. The installation’s mission is to enable readiness and facilitate the deployment of forces anytime, anywhere.
title: Army, Families Celebrate Legacy of Service at Fort Buchanan Retirement Ceremony

Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia Joins Field Hearing in Austin to Examine ICE Shootings Across Texas
AUSTIN, T.X. — Today, Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia (D-TX-29) joined Democratic Members of Congress for a field hearing in Austin to examine shootings involving federal immigration agents across Texas and demand greater transparency and accountability from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The hearing was led by Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX-35), Congressman Bennie G. Thompson (D-MS-02), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, and Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal (D-WA-07), Ranking Member of the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement.
Also participating were Representatives Troy A. Carter, Sr. (D-LA-02), Lou Correa (D-CA-46), Lizzie Fletcher (D-TX-07), and Al Green (D-TX-09).
The hearing examined incidents involving federal immigration agents, including the July 7 killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, the killing of Ruben Ray Martinez, and the recent shooting of Wilber Garcés-Pérez in Austin.
The Members of Congress were joined by witnesses Ms. Rachel Reyes, mother of Ruben Ray Martinez, Kristin Etter, Director of Policy & Legal Services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, Carolina Rivera Nelson, Attorney at the ACLU of Texas, and Danny Woodward, Policy Attorney with Texas Civil Rights Project.
"Trump promised to go after the worst of the worst. But judging by what we're seeing across Texas and the country, that sounds more like ICE's recruitment strategy. People are being shot, injured, and killed by federal agents operating without basic law enforcement standards or accountability," said Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia. "In Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed on his way to work. One hundred days later, his family still has no answers. Instead, they've been met with stonewalling and excuses. These families deserve the truth and justice, and we will not stop fighting until they get both."
Video of the full hearing can be viewed HERE.
title: Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia Joins Field Hearing in Austin to Examine ICE Shootings Across Texas

FORT KNOX, Ky. — In its zenith in 2014, 19th Engineer Battalion was considered the largest battalion in the U.S. Army, commanding about 1,000 troops based at Fort Knox.
At the deactivation ceremony in the General George Patton Museum of Leadership on Oct. 14, a little over 100 Soldiers remained, along with about a dozen alumni from as far back in the unit’s history as the Vietnam War. They stood together to sing the Engineer Regiment Song:
“Pin the castle on my collar, I’ve done my training for the team. You can call me an engineer Soldier; the warrior spirit has been my dream …”
“The 19th Engineer Battalion is among the most well-known stand-alone battalions in the world,” said Maj. Elizabeth Likins-Smith, commander of the battalion. “These colors have lived the engineer motto of Essayons – or “Let Us Try” – having met every mission asked of us, performing sometimes as infantrymen and logisticians for nearly a hundred years across this world.”
At the front of the auditorium stood a wooden red and white “Stand Tall” castle with crossed US and battalion colors hoisted behind it. On the left corner tower hung a bridle and reins – an artifact linked to the unit’s World War II “little seahorse” lore.
“Seven independently deployable companies [lived] inside one battalion – sappers, mappers, firefighters, construction assets, bridging,” said Likins-Smith. “No one had a broader task list in our regiment and in our Army than the 19th Engineer Battalion.”
Acutum Acumen – Sharp Ingenuity
The battalion became the last of Fort Knox’s major operational units after 3rd Battalion, 1st Infantry Division inactivated and cased its colors on May 21, 2014. A 19th Engineer Vietnam War alumnus at the ceremony noted the significance of the 19th deactivation, which typically carries more permanence than an inactivation.
Veterans of the unit lauded its unit motto Acutum Acumen as a fitting tribute to its legacy.
“It’s kind of sad seeing the unit deactivated,” said Tom Fox, who lives in North Carolina. “It was inactivated in ’70, which I never even knew about, so I figured I would show up to this one. We thought it was going to be another inactivation; turns out it was a deactivation.”
Fresh out of basic training, Fox was assigned to the unit during the Vietnam War and said he considers it one of the best in the Army.
“I could have been sent anywhere when I arrived in Vietnam, but I was sent to the 19th,” said Fox. “I stayed at the battalion headquarters and worked comms and operations. There were a lot of great people there.”
The 19th has inactivated and reactivated numerous times, according to its history. It originally stood up at Plattsburg Barracks in June 1941 as 3rd Battalion, 36th Engineer Combat Regiment.
The unit’s original mission was more amphibious. Engineer Soldiers conducted five amphibious landings across North Africa, Sicily, Italy and France during World War II and fought the German army in Germany and Austria, earning 10 campaign streamers, seven Silver Stars and 13 Bronze Stars.
The unit’s valorous history was read aloud during the ceremony.
“Continuously geographically separated from our headquarters and at times from our supporting companies,” Likins-Smith said, “the 19th has shown its sharp ingenuity time and time again under the harshest of conditions.”
In its most recent history, various companies of the unit have deployed in support of operations Iraqi and Enduring Freedom, Hurricane Sandy in October 2012, Operation Faithful Patriot in 2018, Atlantic Resolve to Bulgaria in 2021, as well as two key training operations in Europe the same year.
‘Seahorse Battalion’ bridle and reins
The unit is not without its share of mystery and lore. Few stories are told more than that of its seahorse artifact that has been passed down from commander to commander over the decades.
As the story goes, from https://ww2combatengineers.com, a commander of the unit in World War II, Lt. Col. Larson – no first name given and who ironically doesn’t show up on the official list of unit commanders -- was leading a Ranger Task Force in a landing craft toward Anzio, Italy on Jan. 22, 1944, when he was blown off the craft and into the water.
While struggling to not drown, he grabbed hold of what he thought was a rope, only to find out later that it was a horse’s bridle, bit and reins. Legend says he thought it was from a seahorse and dockworkers later claimed they had never seen such a bridle before.
Likins-Smith said the bridle and reins, along with other artifacts will be donated to the Patton Museum.
Stand Tall
Fort Knox leaders acknowledge that the unit’s significance to the post over the past several years has been unmatched.
“The 19th has had a significant impact on Fort Knox,” said Fort Knox Garrison Command Sgt. Maj. Alex Licea. “They’ve been involved in so many improvements, everything from range towers and steel and concrete bunkers to Castle Lake and its gazebo as kind of a farewell gift to us.
“It’s a bittersweet loss; it’ll be different around here without them, but we support them and their Families.”
Ken Boeglen, previously acting as Garrison deputy commander and now executive officer, said he agreed.
“Units come and go, but these folks have left gifts to the community, like Castle Lake, the gazebo and the demo range at Crum for others to use long after they’re gone,” said Boeglen. “They also have done work at the airfield for us. They’ve been a phenomenal support for the installation.”
Prior to the deactivation, the battalion lost companies to other locations and units over the past year or so, starting with 42nd Clearance Company casing its colors at Fort Knox and moving to Fort Campbell, Kentucky in July 2021. In the latest round of changes, 15th Engineer Construction Company and 502nd Multirole Bridge Company merged with 46th Engineer Battalion at Fort Polk, Louisiana.
“It’s a good thing that they’re keeping the company legacies intact,” said Licea. “Some of the Soldiers of 19th Engineer Battalion will move down there, some will naturally ETS or PCS from here, and some will stay on.”
At the ceremony, Col. Jefferson Burges, the unit’s higher headquarters commander of 20th Engineer Brigade out of Fort Bragg, North Carolina, watched as Likins-Smith extended the colors and assisted Command Sgt. Dustin French in rolling them up. French slid the case over the colors and watched as a Soldier marched out of the auditorium.
“Today we case the colors of the Seahorse Battalion,” said Burges. “While the ceremony marks the conclusion of this chapter of service, let us be clear: we are not here to mourn the ending of this battalion’s history.
“We’re here to celebrate a legacy unmatched in excellence, a history of sacrifice, a reputation of solving the toughest problems in the most hostile environments.”
Burges suggested the unit might still have a future:
“I’m convinced that there will come a day when the Army and the Nation will call upon the Seahorse Battalion yet again.”
At the conclusion of the ceremony, halls of the museum echoed with the voices of the final 19th Engineer Soldiers who stood tall and sang the last lines of the Engineer Regiment Song one final time ...
“Essayons, whether in war or peace, we will bear our red and white. Essayons. We serve America, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Essayons! Essayons!”
title: ‘Let us try:’ 19th Engineer Battalion cases colors during Patton Museum ceremony

text:
Fort Stewart employees visited its Recycling Center Oct. 7 during a Meet Your Directorate event. This is the second event of its kind put on by the Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield U.S. Army Garrison Workforce Development Office.
“We found that a lot of civilians who have been working with Fort Stewart have been in the same directorate or agency, and the intent is trying to get them out to see what actually happens within the garrison outside of their working area,” said Adam Harris, Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield Workforce Development specialist. “That way they have better familiarization with what’s going on in the garrison and what it means as far as installation support.”
The Directorate of Public Works Environmental Branch was highlighted this quarter. DPW Environmental has three components: Prevention and Compliance, Forestry, and Fish & Wildlife.
The recycling program, which falls under prevention and compliance, started in 2004 through a directive from U.S. Army Installation Management Command. Last year, over 23,500 tons were diverted from the landfill.
“Diversion rate is what we don’t put in our landfill,” said Nolan Fields, environmental protection specialist. “That means our landfill has increased space time for 11 years, so it doesn’t close until 2045.”
The small but mighty team clears over 750 dumpsters spilt between Fort Stewart and Hunter Army Airfield every week. Currently, the recycling plant processes plastic, metal cans, aluminum, glass and cardboard. They cannot accept scrap metal as it is an entirely different process.
Fields wishes more people knew tires and furniture cannot be processed or disposed of in the installation’s landfill because it does not meet the necessary standards. Those items must be taken off post.
One participant asked if they accept off post recycling from their home and the answer is yes.
“If you ever recycle materials off the installation, please bring them and put them in any blue dumpster,” Fields said.
Fort Stewart doesn’t have a designated drop-off center due to illicit dumping in the past, but Hunter Army Airfield has a convenient drop-off location by the main post exchange.
title: Fort Stewart host Meet Your Directorate event

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, Special Agent in Charge of the New York Task Force Division of the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), Christopher Roberts, and Commissioner of the New York City Police Department (“NYPD”) Jessica S. Tisch, announced today the unsealing of a three-count superseding Indictment charging MOISES FREIRE and BRIAN PERALTA CABRERA with participating in a fentanyl distribution conspiracy that resulted in the fatal poisoning of one college student (“Victim-1”) and the near-fatal poisoning of another college student (“Victim-2”) in a college residence hall in Manhattan, New York this past March. The Indictment further alleges that after rendering both women unconscious through fentanyl exposure, FREIRE raped Victim-1, who never regained consciousness and later died. FREIRE is also charged with distributing fentanyl with the intent to commit a violent crime, specifically, rape.

“This case alleges not only the deadly distribution of fentanyl to two young women but also the sexual assault of a victim rendered defenseless by that poisoning,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “This Office remains committed to protecting college communities against the extraordinary danger posed by those who weaponize narcotics to exploit vulnerable victims. We will work tirelessly to hold accountable those who endanger young people living and learning on our campuses.”

“The allegations in this case are beyond disturbing and include a cruel deception and unimaginable assault. Two young college students, with their entire futures ahead of them, were allegedly deceived into taking fentanyl disguised as cocaine, leaving one dead and the other fighting for her life,” said DEA New York Task Force Division Special Agent in Charge Christopher Roberts. “Even more horrifying is the allegation that one of these young women was sexually assaulted while unconscious and defenseless. College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability. Every student deserves to feel safe, whether walking across campus, sitting in a classroom, or inside their own dorm room. The DEA New York Task Force Division, alongside the NYPD, and our prosecutorial partners, will not stand idle while individuals’ prey on young people, poison our communities, and attempt to escape accountability. Those days are over.”

“Moises Freire and Brian Peralta Cabrera’s actions were truly unconscionable,” said NYPD Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch. “As alleged in the indictment, the two defendants supplied the fentanyl that killed one young woman and nearly killed another. Rather than immediately seek help, Freire allegedly first raped the incapacitated victim who died and then lied to first responders. These actions are as sick and twisted as they come, and I thank our investigators, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, and law enforcement partners for their work to hold these predators accountable.”

As alleged in the Indictment and statements made in Court:

From at least February 2026 through March 2026, FREIRE and PERALTA CABRERA conspired to distribute fentanyl. After FREIRE told PERALTA CABRERA that FREIRE wanted to distribute narcotics to the Victims that would “last the entire night,” and that if PERALTA CABRERA could provide drugs that were strong enough, the Victims would get addicted, FREIRE went on to describe that scenario as a “win win situation.” Knowing that FREIRE intended to distribute the drugs to at least the Victims, PERALTA CABRERA subsequently provided fentanyl to FREIRE.

On March 18, 2026, FREIRE brought that fentanyl to the undergraduate residence hall where the Victims were living while attending college in Manhattan. FREIRE falsely claimed that the drug did not contain fentanyl and was “pure cocaine,” even though he had previously described the substance as “fake” and “poison.”

After FREIRE encouraged the victims to ingest the substance, both women lost consciousness almost immediately. FREIRE himself did not ingest the drug that night. While the victims were incapacitated, FREIRE allegedly raped Victim‑1 in the victims’ dorm room.

Rather than immediately seeking help, FREIRE waited approximately 45 minutes, during which he sent photos of the victims to others. When he finally approached campus security, he initially falsely claimed that the victims had simply consumed too much alcohol.

Campus security responded and administered emergency aid, including Narcan. Both victims were transported to hospitals in Manhattan. Toxicology results later confirmed that both women had ingested fentanyl and no cocaine.

Victim‑2 regained consciousness after life‑saving treatment. Victim‑1 remained in critical condition and eventually died from complications of acute fentanyl intoxication.

* * *

FREIRE, 19, of the Bronx, New York and PERALTA, 18, of Queens, New York, are both charged with one count of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death and serious bodily injury, which carries a mandatory minimum sentence of 20 years in prison and a maximum sentence of life in prison. FREIRE is also charged with distribution of a controlled substance resulting in death and serious bodily injury, which carries a mandatory minimum sentence of 20 years in prison and a maximum sentence of life in prison, as well as distribution of a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding investigative work of the DEA, the NYPD, as well as the Special Agents, Task Force Officers, the Digital Forensic Unit, and the Complex Analytics and Social Media Enhancement Team at the New York / New Jersey High Intensity Drug Trafficking from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

The case is being handled by the Office’s Narcotics Unit. Assistant United States Attorney Ariana L. Bloom is in charge of the prosecution.

The charges contained in the Indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

National Fraud Enforcement Division and the Department of Health and Human Services Announce Self-Disclosure Protocol for Criminal Health Care Fraud
The Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division) and the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) today issued a policy that clarifies that companies seeking to voluntarily self-disclose potential criminal conduct related to health care need only to disclose to the Fraud Division to receive the benefit of both the Department’s Corporate Enforcement Policy and HHS-OIG’s Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (SDP). HHS-OIG separately updated the SDP to clarify that criminal health care matters should be disclosed to the Department of Justice.
“Companies that discover fraud within their own operations should not have to navigate a maze of agencies before reporting it,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “Today, together with our partners at HHS-OIG, we are eliminating unnecessary bureaucratic barriers that have caused confusion about whether companies must make multiple disclosures of potentially criminal conduct. There is now one clear point of contact: DOJ’s Fraud Division. If a company comes forward, cooperates fully, and remedies the misconduct, the benefits are clear and predictable. If a company conceals what it knows, it should expect a very different conversation.”
“We encourage companies to come forward and disclose criminal conduct to the Justice Department, and we are committed to extending the benefits of the HHS-OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol to those who do.” said Department of Health and Human Services Inspector General T. March Bell. “The OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol is a critical tool for promoting accountability, transparency, and integrity across the health care system, providing organizations with a clear pathway to voluntarily report potential misconduct and address compliance concerns. This process helps strengthen trust in federally funded health care programs by encouraging timely corrective action, reducing future risk, and demonstrating a commitment to ethical conduct.”
The Policy announced today is designed to eliminate obstacles that may slow disclosures. A single arrangement - an illegal kickback, a scheme to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary services, a scheme concealing an excluded provider - routinely may result in potential criminal, civil, or administrative consequences. Companies facing that overlap have had to decide not only whether to come forward, but also where to make that disclosure. Under the Policy announced today, a company that voluntarily self-discloses criminal conduct affecting a federal health care program to the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section will receive the benefits of HHS-OIG’s SDP - automatically, with no additional direct submission necessary through the HHS-OIG portal.
HHS-OIG separately updated the SDP today to settle the reverse question. The SDP covers conduct that may violate civil or administrative law, and the SDP was updated today to clarify that criminal conduct should be disclosed to the Department of Justice. A company that discloses only to HHS-OIG generally will not have made a voluntary self-disclosure to the Department and generally will not qualify for a declination on that basis. Companies seeking the benefits of both programs should bring potentially criminal conduct to the Fraud Division first.
The policy announced today may be found here. HHS-OIG’s updated protocol may be found here. Self-disclosures may be reported to the Fraud Division at: corporate.enforcement@usdoj.gov.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
title: National Fraud Enforcement Division and the Department of Health and Human Services Announce Self-Disclosure Protocol for Criminal Health Care Fraud

Press Statement

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

October 15, 2026

President Trump has been absolutely clear: under his administration, the United States will not tolerate terrorism, organized crime or extra-hemispheric forces spreading anti-American influence in our region. For too long, Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups – including the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s number one state sponsor of terrorism – to target the United States.

Cuba’s BANCO INTERNACIONAL DE COMERCIO S.A. (BICSA) has provided services to the designated Iran’s Karafarin Bank since at least 2022. The Department of the Treasury sanctioned Karafarin Bank pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902 in 2020. Today, in concert with a Department of the Treasury action on Iranian financial actors, I am sanctioning the Cuban state-owned BICSA pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy.

Let me be clear: the Trump Administration will not tolerate a rogue state hosting hostile foreign military, intelligence and terror operations less than a hundred miles from the American homeland. We will continue to aggressively identify and eliminate the Cuban regime’s financial and security interconnections with Iran and other dangerous and hostile states and actors.

The Department’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 14404, which authorizes sweeping sanctions on Cuba, including against persons who support the Cuban regime’s security apparatus and those responsible for repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security. These actions also further both E.O. 14380, “ Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Cuba ” and National Security Presidential Memorandum 5 , which directs the Executive Branch to improve human rights, encourage the rule of law, foster free markets and free enterprise, and promote democracy in Cuba.

Sanctions Implications

As a result of today’s sanctions actions, and in accordance with E.O. 14404 of May 1, 2026, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy,” all property and interests in property of the designated person described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Additionally, all entities that are owned individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.

Any transaction or dealing by U.S. persons or persons subject to the jurisdiction of the United States in property or interests of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized or exempt. These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Foreign persons that engage in transactions with persons designated pursuant to E.O. 14404—or that operate or have operated in the energy, defense and related materiel, metals and mining, financial services, or security sector of the Cuban economy, as identified in E.O. 14404—are themselves at risk of sanctions. Non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, should proceed with caution in any dealings with a party sanctioned under this authority. Actions to return assets to a sanctioned party or transfer them to another jurisdiction for potential use by the target expose non-U.S. persons to significant sanctions risk. All property and interests in property of persons that are blocked pursuant to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) are blocked. The CACR prohibits persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction from dealing in property in which Cuba or a Cuban national has an interest, unless authorized or exempt.

The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the List of Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN List), but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law. The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.

Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be routed through OFAC’s Reconsiderations Portal . Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page.

Between Oct. 15 and Nov. 28, 1990, the XVIII Airborne Corps conducted a defensive deception operation as part of Operation DESERT SHIELD in Saudi Arabia. This was an informative precursor to a larger offensive deception operation coalition forces unleashed during the ground campaign of Operation DESERT STORM three months later.
Within days of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait on Aug. 2, 1990, the U.S. launched Operation DESERT SHIELD to defend Saudi Arabia from further Iraqi expansion. By Aug. 9, Lt. Gen. Gary Luck’s XVIII Airborne Corps assault command post touched down at Dhahran Airport. The Corps’ presence in the Persian Gulf grew over the following two months, as did the number of Iraqi divisions in Kuwait. Saddam Hussein’s intentions to invade Saudia Arabia were unknown, but intelligence analysts concluded he had the capability to do so. The U.S. needed time to deploy enough air and ground forces to deter any attempts to seize Saudi oil fields, ports, and airfields.
Even before the deployment of the XVIII Airborne Corps, its Deception Element began planning for the unit’s deception operations. In 1990, deception was considered something of a “lost art” in the U.S. Army. Attempts to revitalize the capability began with the 1988 publication of FM 90-2 "Battlefield Deception" (BAT-D) and the implementation of associated training. FM 90-2 and the 1989 FM 100-15 "Corps Operations" called for twelve-member BAT-D cells working with the corps G-3 planners and similar cells in the divisional MI battalions to execute deception plans.
Maj. Gary P. Melton, a West Point graduate who had received his commission as an infantry officer in 1975, led the XVIII Airborne Corps Deception Element. On Aug. 27, 1990, he led an initial planning and administrative group to Saudi Arabia. Once there, they continued “the corps planning cycle we began back at Fort Bragg and put the first deception equipment package on the ground.” The remaining six members of Melton’s team followed over the next two months, along with additional communication emulators and camouflage decoys on loan from the deception equipment office at Fort Belvoir.
As planning for the offensive campaign continued, the G-3 planners considered ways to deter further Iraqi expansion. In lockstep, Major Melton’s Deception Element provided courses of action that dovetailed with the G-3’s operational plans. Hussein’s forces seemed to be positioned to invade along the coastal roads into Saudi Arabia with the Trans-Arabian Pipeline (TAPLine) Road as their first strategic objective. Thus, the deception plan, according to Major Melton, was
to portray our corps establishing a defense in a sector along the TAPLine Road [near al-Jubayl in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province]. We tried to portray the sparse Pan-Arab forces as the only covering force forward of TAPLine Road, when, in fact, a large U.S. covering force was there. . . If believed, this deception would have confused Iraqi command and control when they ran into a formidable U.S. covering force before they expected.
Initially, Melton’s team conducted the deception, but later in the six-week operation, the 101st Airborne, 24th Infantry, and 1st Cavalry divisions began complementary operations. The deception operation utilized a wide variety of elements to enhance its credibility. This included planting decoy tracked and wheeled vehicles and forward arming and refueling points; posting unit signage; transmitting real, high frequency, radioteletype traffic in deception mode; running vehicle convoys; moving troops in and around local towns; and conducting psychological operations.
Whether this early deception effort succeeded was unclear because the Iraqis did not attack into Saudi Arabia. Yet, it was educational for Melton’s team, who confirmed the deception equipment, including signal emulators, worked in the desert environment. The operation also led Melton to recommend consolidating division and corps deception cells to ensure sufficient resources to enhance the deception’s credibility. Ultimately, the team’s operations helped inform the successful deception operations the coalition undertook as part of the DESERT STORM ground offensive that kicked off the following February.
Article by Lori S. Stewart, USAICoE Command Historian. New issues of This Week in MI History are published each week. To report story errors, ask questions, request previous articles, or be added to our distribution list, please contact: TR-ICoE-Command-Historian@army.mil.
title: XVIII Airborne Corps Deception on Kuwaiti Border (15 OCT 1990)
