Item C-1 | Docket No. RM26-2-001 | News Release
Good morning, Chairman and Commissioners.
Item C-1 is a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (or NOPR) that establishes a blanket program for authorizing activities at liquefied natural gas (or LNG) plants without the need for case-specific authorization orders under sections 3 or 7 of the Natural Gas Act. The proposed rule aims to streamline LNG infrastructure development while maintaining safety and environmental protections.
The Commission regulates the siting, construction, expansion, and operation of LNG plants pursuant to sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act.
Broadly, there are two types of LNG plants subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction. First, LNG import and export terminals, which the Commission regulates under section 3 of the Natural Gas Act. And second, LNG plants that receive LNG or natural gas from a pipeline and liquefy it, store it as LNG, and regasify it for delivery in interstate commerce, which the Commission regulates under section 7. The latter are often called peak shavers because they typically receive natural gas to liquefy during low demand periods and then regasify and deliver it during peak demand periods. Both types of LNG plants are composed of two categories of facilities: LNG facilities and auxiliary systems. LNG facilities receive, load and unload, store, transport, gasify, liquefy, or process natural gas, and auxiliary systems are those necessary to support safe and reliable operation of the plant.
Currently, LNG operators may make modifications to LNG plants that are already-authorized or operating, but the operator may need to file a case-specific application on which the Commission must make a public interest determination. The Commission previously determined that LNG activities were not appropriate for a blanket authorization program, based on its assessment in 1982 that they “may have a significant impact on ratepayers” and, in 2006, that such activities were not sufficiently routine or well-understood to exempt from case-specific engineering and environmental review. However, the Commission no longer regulates rates under section 3 of the Natural Gas Act and, since 2006, the Commission and the LNG industry have gained substantial experience with LNG plant engineering, safety, and environmental effects. More recently, the U.S. has become the largest exporter of LNG. Given this experience, it is appropriate to build on the longstanding success of the Commission’s section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program and provide a similar streamlined review of certain activities at LNG plants. This would more quickly facilitate the implementation of improvements to increase the safety, reliability, efficiency, and capability of LNG plants, while maintaining safety and environmental protections.
Thus, on November 20, 2025, the Commission issued a notice of inquiry in this proceeding, soliciting stakeholder comment on whether, and if so how, to revise its regulations toestablish procedures for authorizing activities at LNG plants without the need for case-specific authorization orders. In response, the Commission received 18 comments from the LNG industry, public interest organizations, and states. The comments addressed a variety of issues, including the scope of a blanket program, stakeholder notification, safety and environmental impacts, and the suitability of blanket authorization for LNG activities.
After reviewing the comments, the Commission proposes to promulgate regulations to establish an LNG blanket program. To the extent practicable, the proposed LNG blanket program is modeled after the Commission’s existing section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program. Specifically, the NOPR proposes to adopt a tiered blanket authorization program with three categories of blanket projects:
- automatic authorization projects that may proceed automatically after landowner and community notification;
- prior notice projects that require a 60-day notice period and an opportunity for Commission staff or stakeholders to protest; and
- prior notice projects that require a 90-day notice and protest period.
Unlike the section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program, LNG blanket projects would not be subject to cost limits. Instead, the NOPR establishes defined categories of activities, eligible for one of the previously mentioned tiers, based on the extent of their effects.
In general, activities eligible for automatic authorization include the construction, replacement, or abandonment of components of LNG facilities or auxiliary systems provided the activity would not:
- increase the authorized capacity of the LNG plant;
- expand the authorized vertical or horizontal extents within the footprint of the LNG plant; or
- result in changes outside of the design limits of the new or existing equipment.
Activities eligible for 60-day prior notice authorization are similar to those allowed under automatic authorization. However, 60-day prior notice projects may increase the authorized capacity of the LNG plant, provided that the activities would:
- be located within the LNG plant footprint;
- not significantly adversely impact reliability or risks to public safety; and
- not result in changes outside the design limits of the new or existing equipment.
Activities eligible for 90-day prior notice authorization are those that would involve the construction of new LNG facilities, such as liquefaction trains, LNG tanks, and marine berths. Such activities may extend outside of the plant footprint provided that they would:
- permanently occupy no more than 25 acres of previously disturbed or developed land or waterways located within industrial zones or areas without zoning; and
- be designed using the same in-kind or upgraded LNG facilities and auxiliary systems previously evaluated and authorized at the LNG terminal or plant.
The NOPR would apply to both section 3 LNG terminals and section 7 LNG plants, with the same activities eligible for automatic and 60- and 90-day prior notice authorization. However, only section 7 LNG blanket projects would be subject to the same rate treatment requirements as under the section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program, as proposed to be revised in the Commission’s May 21, 2026 NOPR.
As with the section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program, the NOPR proposes to adopt standard filing requirements and environmental and engineering design conditions to address effects and to ensure compliance with applicable law. The NOPR explains that Commission staff will prepare an environmental document under the National Environmental Policy Act (or NEPA) to address the environmental effects of automatic authorization and the rulemaking. Prior notice projects will undergo project-specific NEPA analyses or have a categorical exclusion applied, as occurs under the section 7 pipeline blanket certificate program.
The NOPR also proposes, among other requirements, that blanket authorization holders must obtain a Letter of Determination from the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline and Hazardous Material Safety Administration or a determination that a Letter of Determination is not required.
In addition, to comply with the interagency consultation requirements of section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, the NOPR proposes to require that blanket authorization holders obtain for section 3 blanket projects concurrence from the U.S. Department of War using the department’s Clearinghouse process. The NOPR also proposes, among other requirements, that blanket authorization holders must obtain for prior notice projects at section 3 LNG terminals:
- a new or updated Letter of Recommendation from the U.S. Coast Guard or a determination that a new Letter of Intent, Waterway Suitability Assessment, or Letter of Recommendation is not required;
- a letter from the state designated agency that the project does not raise any state or local safety concerns or evidence that the agency has been notified; and
- letters from all relevant state and local emergency response organizations and emergency responders that the project is consistent with the terminal’s Emergency Response Plan or evidence that the organizations have been notified.
The NOPR would waive the Commission’s pre-filing regulations, as LNG blanket projects would not involve significant state and local safety considerations that have not been previously addressed.
The NOPR seeks comment on the proposed changes and specifically on the following discrete issues:
- whether 25 acres beyond the existing plant footprint is an appropriate acreage limit for 90-day prior notice expansions;
- whether the Commission should consider any additional limits or criteria for expansions that extend beyond the existing plant footprint; and
- whether the Commission should establish eligibility criteria concerning who may protest a prior notice project.
We would like to acknowledge and thank the numerous staff from the Office of Energy Projects and the Office of the General Counsel who worked on the proposed rule.
This concludes our presentation. We are happy to answer any questions.
title: Presentation | Authorizations for Certain Activities at Liquefied Natural Gas Plants

Serbian National Sentenced to 17 years in Federal Prison as Part of Homeland Security Task Force Investigation into International Cocaine Trafficking Conspiracy
PLANO, TEXAS – A Serbian national has been sentenced to federal prison as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation into cocaine trafficking in the Eastern District of Texas.
Milan Tanovic, 59, also known as Marco, a Serbian national living in Spain, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute cocaine while aboard a vessel subject to the jurisdiction of the United States and was sentenced to 204 months in federal prison by U.S. District Judge Sean D. Jordan on October 15, 2026.
“This sentence sends a clear message that any drug trafficker who profits from the sale of drugs at the expense of American victims will not be tolerated,” said DEA Dallas Special Agent in Charge Joseph B. Tucker. “DEA’s reach goes beyond the borders of the US, and we will pursue drug traffickers anywhere to ensure they are held accountable for the damage they inflict on our communities, just as we did with Mr. Tanovic. They cannot hide and will ultimately be extradited and prosecuted in a U.S. courtroom.”
According to information presented in court, Tanovic was identified as a large-scale cocaine trafficker who worked with other drug traffickers based in Serbia and Albania to ship ton amounts of cocaine from South America to Europe, using container vessels. Tanovic was connected to multiple drug shipment seizures through analysis of multiple chats on an encrypted messaging platform.
This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Dallas comprises agents and officers from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Dallas Field Office; U.S. Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations - Dallas (ICE-HSI); Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Dallas Field Division; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Dallas Field Division; Internal Revenue Service, Criminal Investigations (IRS-CD; United States Postal Service, United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS); Transportation Security Administration, Federal Air Marshal Service (FAMS); United States Secret Service (USSS); Department of State, Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DSS); TEXOMA HIDTA; DEA Country Offices in Rome (Italy), Brasilia (Brazil), Santa Domingo (Dominican Republic), Madrid (Spain), Vienna (Austria), Zagreb (Croatia), and Bogota (Colombia); EUROPOL; and U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) Eastern District of Texas with the prosecution being led by Eastern District of Texas Assistant U.S. Attorney Wes Wynne.
title: Serbian National Sentenced to 17 years in Federal Prison as Part of Homeland Security Task Force Investigation into International Cocaine Trafficking Conspiracy

text:
Krishnamoorthi Responds to Attempted Mass Shooting at His Family’s Hindu Temple in Aurora, Warns of Surging Anti-Indian Hate
SCHAUMBURG — Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) issued the following statement after authorities arrested a 19-year-old man accused of attempting to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. According to prosecutors, the suspect, who espoused white supremacist and neo-Nazi beliefs, allegedly attempted to open fire Sunday before his rifle jammed. After he told coworkers what happened and shared plans to try again, they alerted police, who arrested him before he could return.
“I am horrified that a white supremacist attempted to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at the Hindu temple in Aurora where my family worships. My family and I were there when the attack was attempted last Sunday. The threat of such violence shows how dangerous anti-Indian hatred and white supremacy have become, and we cannot wait until innocent people are killed to take these threats seriously. I am grateful to the suspect’s coworkers who alerted police and commend the law enforcement officers who intervened. Every American deserves to live and worship without fear, and we must stand together against hatred in all its forms.”

WASHINGTON – Christian Rodriguez, 21, of Hyattsville, Maryland, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 84 months in federal prison for his role in a spree of armed carjackings, vehicle thefts, and thefts from vehicles committed across the metropolitan region between December 2023 and August 2024, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“The era of unchecked violence in the District is over. We are taking violent criminals off our streets, and our communities are safer because of it,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “District residents deserve to feel safe in their neighborhoods, and we will never back down from that fight. Those who terrorize our residents with guns and violence should know exactly where that road leads: federal prison. Rodriguez is headed where he belongs.”

“The era of unchecked violence in the District is over. We are taking violent criminals off our streets, and our communities are safer because of it,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “District residents deserve to feel safe in their neighborhoods, and we will never back down from that fight. Those who terrorize our residents with guns and violence should know exactly where that road leads: federal prison. Rodriguez is headed where he belongs.”

Rodriguez pleaded guilty on April 16, 2025, before U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras to possessing a firearm in furtherance of a crime of violence and aiding and abetting. In addition to the 84-month prison term, Judge Contreras ordered Rodriguez to serve three years of supervised release.

According to court documents, Rodriguez was an active participant in a brazen carjacking conspiracy responsible for a series of violent and coordinated vehicle-related offenses. On January 24, 2024, Rodriguez and his co-conspirators carried out a targeted armed carjacking in Northwest Washington during which two masked, armed assailants approached a Dodge Challenger, punched the victim, and held him at gunpoint with a firearm equipped with a green laser sight before fleeing with the vehicle and the victim’s belongings.

Two days later, on January 26, 2024, Rodriguez and other co-conspirators attempted to conceal evidence after the arrest of another participant. Rodriguez directed a co-conspirator via text message to remove incriminating items from a residence, leading to law enforcement observing the transfer of a trash bag containing evidence linked to the conspiracy.

The criminal spree continued into August 2024. On August 6, Rodriguez helped steal a 2021 Infiniti Q50 in Silver Spring, Maryland, which contained the victim’s identity documents and bank cards. The items were later recovered from Rodriguez’s residence. The following day, Rodriguez participated in two more vehicle break-ins, including the theft of a Corvette in Alexandria, Virginia, using an electronic device designed to bypass vehicle security.

During a court authorized search of Rodriguez’s residence on Aug. 9, 2024, law enforcement recovered a stockpile of weapons, ammunition, firearm components, multiple loaded extended magazines, in addition to license plates, and stolen identification cards and bank cards belonging to victims of the August thefts. Investigators also found a firearm equipped with a “switch” that converted the semiautomatic handgun into a fully automatic weapon.

The investigation was conducted by the Metropolitan Police Department, Prince George’s County Police Department, Baltimore County Police Department, Alexandria City Police Department, and the FBI Washington Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Caelainn Carney prosecuted the case.

Firearms recovered from Rodriguez’s residence.

Houston Felon Convicted of Trafficking Methamphetamine and Possessing Firearm
HOUSTON – A 46-year-old man has been convicted of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.
A federal jury deliberated for approximately two hours before convicting Eduardo Nevares Oct. 8 following a two-day trial.At trial, the jury heard that law enforcement attempted to stop Nevares for an expired vehicle registration. Nevares refused to pull over and led authorities on a chase that ended when he crashed through two chain-link fences and his vehicle stalled on a baseball field at an Alief, Texas public school. He then attempted to flee on foot before authorities apprehended him.
Law enforcement discovered a .45-caliber pistol on the driver’s seat and methamphetamine and cocaine in his pocket.
A subsequent search of the vehicle revealed more than a pound of methamphetamine with a purity level of 96%, along with baggies, a scale, and loaded pistol magazines.
The defense argued Nevares was unaware of the methamphetamine inside a black duffle bag in the back seat. However, the jury rejected that argument and found him guilty as charged. U.S. District Judge David Hittner presided over the trial and set sentencing for Dec. 29. At that time, Nevares faces up to life in prison and a possible maximum $10 million fine.
Nevares has been and will remain in custody pending sentencing.
The Bureau for Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, and Houston Police Department conducted the investigation with the assistance of the Drug Enforcement Administration South Central Laboratory. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Charles Hagerman and Tanja Titre are prosecuting the case.
title: Houston Felon Convicted of Trafficking Methamphetamine and Possessing Firearm

Tallahassee, Florida – Omarion Laparis Rashad, 21, of Tallahassee, Florida, was sentenced to federal prison for illegal possession of machinegun. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution is another win for the safety of our communities. The Homeland Security Task Force continues to deliver on the promise that, by unifying our federal law enforcement agencies toward a common goal of eliminating the influence of criminal cartels, foreign gangs, and transnational criminal organizations in our communities, we will achieve the safe, crime-free streets that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect the Tallahassee Police Department executed a search warrant at the defendant’s residence on November 25, 2025. Officers found marijuana, synthetic cathinone, and ammunition, along with a Glock .40 caliber pistol that had been converted to fire as a machinegun. A second machinegun conversion device was found in a commercial marijuana bag. The defendant gave a voluntary statement acknowledging his possession of the pistol with the “switch” and acknowledged knowing the switch made it a machine gun.

The defendant was a first-time offender and received 6 months in prison followed by 3 years of supervised release.

“This case reflects the importance of coordinated law enforcement efforts to address the illegal possession of machineguns and conversion devices,” said Homeland Security Investigations Tampa acting Special Agent in Charge Nicholas Ingegno. “The Homeland Security Task Force aligns federal, state, and local partners toward a common goal of protecting our communities and holding offenders accountable. We remain committed to working together to promote public safety throughout North Florida.”

The case involved a joint investigation by the Tallahassee Police Department and Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney James A. McCain.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF comprises agents and officers from multiple agencies with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Federal Prison for Illegal Possession of a Machinegun

MSTF Arrests 29 Wednesday on Multiple Felonies, Including Homicide, 1st-Degree Murder; Recovers 7 Guns
For immediate release
Office of Public Affairs
Usms.mediadesk@usdoj.gov
MEMPHIS - The Memphis Safe Task Force (MSTF) on Wednesday executed 29 arrests, including one woman on a homicide charge and a man on a first-degree murder charge, and recovered seven illegal firearms.
Of note:
Tamela Taylor, 23, was arrested at a residence in the 180 block of Woods Road in Humboldt on multiple warrants for a vehicular homicide-- vehicular homicide (intoxication), vehicular assault/aggravated assault (reckless), and vehicular homicide (reckless). Taylor was transported to Shelby County jail.
Taeveon Smith, 19, was arrested in the 100 block of Village Road in Covington on multiple felony warrants including first-degree murder, criminal attempt first-degree murder, aggravated assault and use of a firearm in commission of a felony stemming from a March 29 shooting incident in the 30 block of West Shelby Drive that left one man dead and two others injured. As part of their investigation into the first-degree murder, MSTF developed an address for Smith in Covington and, with assistance from the Covington Police Department, arrested Smith without incident.
Justin Thomas, 32, is being charged with vehicular manslaughter, possession of controlled substances, speeding, and fleeing law enforcement after he led officers on a pursuit that ended in a crash, killing the passenger in his vehicle and injuring himself and two other motorists. MSTF conducted surveillance in the 800 block of Red Leaf Lane on a matte black Cadillac, previously reported as having fled from MSTF during a traffic stop attempt. During surveillance, Thomas was seen getting into the driver’s seat of the Cadillac, with a woman (identified later as Renisha Thompson) as the passenger. After departing the residence, Thomas is alleged to have initiated several evasive maneuvers (multiple U-turns) in the residential area attempting to disrupt MSTF's mobile vehicle surveillance. Thomas then turned onto West Shelby Drive where Tennessee Highway Patrol attempted a traffic stop near the intersection of South Third Street. Thomas fled from THP, resulting in a vehicle pursuit on South Third Street that ended just before the West Levi Road intersection. The Cadillac struck four vehicles causing Thompson’s ejection from the Cadillac, serious injuries to Thomas and minor injuries to two other motorists. Thomas was transported to the hospital in critical condition. Thomas had an active warrant for a weapons charge prior to this incident.
Lavelle Moore, 54, was arrested in the 2800 block of East Hickory Bluff on a warrant for theft of merchandise $2,500-$10,000. As MSTF arrived at the residence, Moore fled to the backyard where he was arrested. A subsequent search of the residence yielded six firearms. Moore was also charged with felon in possession of a firearm.
Niquavious Hargrow, 20, was arrested at an apartment in the 3500 block of Bellbranch Drive for aggravated assault, unlawful possession and criminal trespass. MSTF was patrolling near an apartment complex in the 3600 block of Kingsgate Drive when two female security guards signaled for assistance. Prior to MSTF's arrival on scene, the security guards had been patrolling on Millbranch Road when they saw a woman (later identified as Synique Malone, 20) holding money next to a man (later identified as Hargrow). The security guards made a comment to the pair, after which Hargrow is alleged to have brandished an AR-style black rifle/pistol, pointing it at the security guards and verbally threatening them before walking toward the apartments. Upon arrival at the apartment, MSTF seized a Palmetto PA-15 multi-caliber rifle (round chambered) w/loaded magazine and a second loaded magazine from Hargrow. Malone and Hargrow were arrested at the apartment. Malone was charged with simple assault and criminal trespass.
Since the launch of the Memphis Safe Task Force initiative, officers have made 13,598 arrests, including 144 for homicide, 1,464 for controlled substances, 1,336 for firearms violations, and 126 for sex offenses. Of those arrested, 433 were juveniles and 1,523 were known gang members. The task force has seized 2,290 illegal firearms. These enforcement actions reflect a sustained commitment to reducing violent crime and removing dangerous weapons from Memphis neighborhoods.
The Memphis Safe Task Force is a multi-agency initiative established via a Presidential Memorandum signed by President Donald Trump on Sept. 15, 2025. Aimed at addressing violent street crime, the task force coordinates federal, state, and local law enforcement and includes mobilized members of the Tennessee National Guard. The MSTF is focused on arresting violent criminals, clearing warrants, seizing firearms, and locating missing children. Since the operation began, the MSTF has located 196 missing children.
This operation reflects the MSTF’s commitment to coordinated enforcement efforts and its mission to identify, apprehend, and hold accountable those who pose a threat to public safety.
title: MSTF Arrests 29 Wednesday on Multiple Felonies, Including Homicide, 1st-Degree Murder; Recovers 7 Guns | U.S. Marshals Service

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A Hickory County, Missouri man was charged by criminal complaint with distribution of child pornography.

Kenneth S. Ratliff, 51, appeared in federal court on a criminal complaint signed by Chief United States Magistrate Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. According to the complaint, Ratliff was in a group chat used for trading Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) when he encountered undercover agents. While chatting with the undercover agents, Ratliff sent a CSAM video depicting a prepubescent child. Ratliff currently substitute teaches at Mack’s Creek School and is the head cross country coach.

The charges contained in this indictment are simply accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty is to determine guilt or innocence.

Under federal statutes, Ratliff is subject to a sentence of up to 20 years in federal prison without parole. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled after the completion of a presentence investigation by the United States Probation Office.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Ashley S. Turner It was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigations

Project Safe Childhood

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.usdoj.gov/psc . For more information about Internet safety education, please visit www.usdoj.gov/psc and click on the tab "resources."

CLEVELAND – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced several enforcement actions as part of a nationwide effort led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service (IRS), and the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) Division targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Northern District of Ohio (NDOH) was a key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and Oct. 14, 2026, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorney’s Offices across the country participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490,000,000.

“There are always those who try and cheat the system and think they are exempt from complying with tax laws,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “Dishonest individuals who deceive and choose to engage in unlawful business practices will be held accountable. You can try and hide yourself and your unlawful actions, but as seen in our case with the fugitive on the run for 11 years and hiding overseas, we’ll find you and hold you accountable for violating federal laws.”

“There are always those who try and cheat the system and think they are exempt from complying with tax laws,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “Dishonest individuals who deceive and choose to engage in unlawful business practices will be held accountable. You can try and hide yourself and your unlawful actions, but as seen in our case with the fugitive on the run for 11 years and hiding overseas, we’ll find you and hold you accountable for violating federal laws.”

“Tax fraud undermines the system every American taxpayer relies on, and IRS Criminal Investigation is committed to finding those who cheat it,” said Todd Strom, Acting Special Agent in Charge, Detroit Field Office, IRS-CI . “Our special agents are among the best financial investigators in federal law enforcement, with the training and expertise to uncover even the most complex schemes. Working side by side with our law enforcement and prosecutorial partners, we will continue to pursue tax cheats and protect the integrity of our nation’s tax system.”

“Individuals who allegedly abuse positions of trust to defraud an employer, falsify financial records, and conceal income cause real harm to businesses and the hardworking people who depend on them,” said Brad Porcella, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Secret Service Cleveland Field Office. “This investigation reflects the persistence and expertise of our Cleveland Field Office’s Money Laundering Task Force, working alongside our partners at IRS Criminal Investigation and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio. My office will continue to investigate and bring to justice criminal actors who seek to exploit the hardworking men and women of Ohio.”

NDOH Notable Cases and Intended Loss Figures

United States v. Sherita Booker (Information) – $11,806,165

On Sept. 30, 2026, Sherita Booker, 47, of Cleveland, was charged with five counts of submitting and aiding or assisting in the preparation of false and fraudulent federal income tax returns. She allegedly filed hundreds of fraudulent tax returns for clients and herself, submitting hundreds of claims seeking at least $11.8 million in fraudulent refunds, resulting in the IRS paying out over $3.9 million in refunds. She filed these fraudulent claims primarily by fabricating information to claim three different refundable credits: (1) Covid sick leave credits for non-existent businesses and employees; (2) Refunds of purported fuel taxes paid for off-road (farm) use; and (3) Claims for refunds of taxes purportedly over-paid in previous years. She was also charged with possessing a firearm and ammunition as a convicted felon. If convicted, she faces up to three years in prison per tax fraud count, and up to 15 years in prison for illegally possessing a firearm.

The investigation was conducted by IRS-CI, with Assistant United States Attorneys Brenna Fasko and Elliot Morrison leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

United States v. Glen Zucker (Plea) - $2,947,752

On Sept. 17, 2026, Glen L. Zucker, 67, of New Washington, Ohio, pleaded guilty to not paying employment taxes. As the owner of OneIT, a technology consulting company, he was ultimately responsible for all business functions including filing and paying employment taxes. Although he withheld trust fund taxes for the company’s employees, he did not file or pay over employment taxes from 2019-2023. Sentencing is set for Jan. 19, 2027. He faces up to five years in prison.

The investigation was conducted by IRS-CI, with Assistant United States Attorney Michael L. Collyer leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

United States v. John Siefert (Information) - $1,507,951

John Siefert, 64, of Highland Heights, was charged by way of Information on Oct. 14, 2026, with wire fraud and filing false tax returns. Siefert was the CEO of a local branch of a plumbing supply company who allegedly stole more than $5 million from his employer. Siefert’s methods included submitting more than $4.3 million in fraudulent invoices to his employer from a realty company he controlled and obtaining more than $880,000 in fraudulent bonuses by falsifying sales figures that determined his compensation. At times, when his employer sold customers products, he had the customer provide him and his family members with over $25,000 in services instead of paying his employer. Finally, he failed to disclose the income obtained by fraud on his personal tax returns, thus failing to pay over $1.5 million to the IRS for years 2021 to 2024. He faces up to 20 years in prison per wire fraud count and up to three years for filing a false tax return if convicted.

The investigation was conducted by the United States Secret Service Cleveland Field Office-Money Laundering Task Force and IRS-CI. Assistant United States Attorney Michael L. Collyer is leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

United States v. Cesare Noce (Information) - $316,141

Cesare Noce, 67, of Chardon, Ohio, was charged by way of Information on Oct. 5, 2026, with willfully failing to file tax returns. For years 2014 through 2020, he managed a construction company and made substantial wage income and also received side payments for extra jobs, all while not filing any tax returns. By not filing taxes, Noce avoided paying more than $316,000 in income taxes. If convicted, he faces up to 12 months in prison.

The investigation was conducted by IRS-CI, with Assistant United States Attorney Elliot Morrison leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

United States v. Thomas Armour II (Plea) - $1,247,888

On Sept. 17, 2026, Thomas Armour II, 60, of Akron, pleaded guilty to not paying employment taxes. He was the owner and operator of American Made Bags, a promotional goods supply company. The U.S. Department of Labor previously investigated Armour’s company Fair Labor Standards Act violations, but the matters were settled in 2014. Later, investigators learned that Armour failed to file the required quarterly forms and pay over employment taxes from 2017-2020. Sentencing is set for Jan. 11, 2027. He faces up to five years in prison.

The investigation was conducted by IRS-CI, the U.S. Department of Labor Office of Inspector General, and the Social Security Administration Office of Inspector General, with Assistant United States Attorney Megan R. Miller leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

United States v. Sbeih Sbeih (Sentencing) - $422,345

On Sept. 17, 2026, Sbeih Sbeih, 57, previously of North Olmstead, was sentenced to 24 months in prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy to defraud the IRS. Sbeih was arrested this past February, in the country of Georgia, after being a fugitive for 11 years. Sbeih was the co-owner of several pharmacies in Ohio that conspired to divert proceeds into personal, non-business bank accounts to conceal income from their accountant and the IRS. The failure to report gross receipts on their corporate tax filings resulted in underreporting of income on their personal tax returns. After he was indicted, while attempting to contest forfeiture proceedings related to seized accounts, Sbeih claimed to be unable to leave Israel. But he was arrested in early 2026 vacationing in Georgia and extradited.

The investigation was conducted by IRS-CI, the DEA, FBI Cleveland Division, Ohio Board of Pharmacy, Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigations, Akron Police Department, Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Office, Lake County Drug Task Force, Summit County Sheriff’s Office, Lorain County Drug Task Force, Strongsville Police Department, MEDWAY Drug Enforcement Agency, and the Cleveland Heights Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Michael L. Collyer led the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.

For a list of similar enforcement actions across the country, please visit

https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/dojs-fraud-division-irs-and-irs-ci-expose-more-490m-tax-fraud-national-tax-enforcement-surge .

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud—a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance—to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An information is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: U.S. Attorney’s Office for Northern Ohio Joins DOJ Fraud Division and IRS Partners in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing Millions in Tax Fraud

ARLINGTON, Va. — As floodwaters surged near an Interstate 10 off-ramp outside Tallahassee, a Florida National Guard convoy spotted a pickup truck beginning to sink. Inside, a family was trapped. The Soldiers stopped, helped the occupants escape, called 911 and remained at the scene until law enforcement, fire and emergency medical personnel arrived.
The rescue was among more than 100 missions completed by Florida Guard members during the ongoing Hurricane Isaias response that began Oct. 6.
Florida and Alabama National Guard members supported response and recovery operations across the region, clearing roads, removing debris, delivering emergency supplies and assisting storm-affected communities. At the height of the response, more than 5,000 Guard members were activated to support communities across the affected region. The storm left approximately 800,000 residents without power.
“Our Soldiers and Airmen live and work in the communities they serve,” said Senior Enlisted Advisor John Raines, senior enlisted advisor to the chief of the National Guard Bureau. “When those communities face their toughest moments, our Guard members bring their training, experience, and commitment to service to help protect lives and support recovery.”
Within 36 hours of the storm’s impact, the Florida National Guard moved thousands of Soldiers and Airmen to the Florida Panhandle, positioning personnel and equipment to support response operations across 16 affected counties. They also assisted isolated residents as flooding worsened near the Shoal River.
“Speed to need is our mantra,” said U.S. Army Col. Blake Heidelberg, joint director of military support for the Florida National Guard. “We alert, mobilize and deploy to ensure our forces are staged in or near communities before the full impact of the hurricane.”
Those missions included nearly 5,000 Florida Guard members clearing 4,000 miles of essential roadways, removing more than 12,500 cubic yards of debris and restoring access to storm-affected communities. Aircrews flying four UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters supported damage assessments and transported response teams to areas inaccessible by standard vehicles.
“Beyond the statistics, you’ve made a meaningful impact on the lives of Floridians. Behind every cleared road and delivery of supplies were Guardsmen dedicated to helping their neighbors,” said Maj. Gen. John Haas, the adjutant general of Florida, in a message to Florida Guard members.
In Alabama, the National Guard activated approximately 500 Soldiers and positioned them across southern Alabama to support storm preparations in coordination with local emergency management agencies. Most Soldiers remained on standby, while others assisted with debris clearance.
Although Alabama experienced less severe weather than anticipated, prepositioning personnel and equipment enabled the Guard to respond quickly if conditions worsened.
Should additional out-of-state support be required, emergency management officials can use the Emergency Management Assistance Compact, or EMAC. This state-to-state mutual aid system allows governors to share personnel, equipment, commodities and services during governor-declared emergencies or disasters. EMAC provides a framework for states to request, coordinate and reimburse assistance across state lines.
“Our primary mission is to support the state’s overall effort, which is coordinated out of the State Emergency Operations Center,” Heidelberg said. “While we are always in a supporting role to local authorities, we provide aviation support for search and rescue and damage assessment, tactical vehicles for ground transportation and search and rescue, and debris removal and road clearance capabilities.”
Guard members also coordinated with other Department of War organizations supporting storm preparedness. The Air Force Reserve’s 403rd Wing relocated aircraft and continued weather reconnaissance flights, while the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Nashville District managed Cumberland River Basin reservoirs and monitored flood risks.
“When disaster strikes, our National Guard members are among the first to answer the call. They step forward because the people in need are their neighbors, friends, and family,” Raines added.
title: Florida, Alabama National Guard mobilize for hurricane response

SAVANNAH, Georgia: Multiple defendants have been indicted by the October term of the federal Grand Jury in the Southern District of Georgia for Re-entry after Removal or Deportation, a charge applied to an illegal alien present in the United States after at least one prior removal.

Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia, announced the indictments. Those facing federal charges include:

Gerardo Bautista-Ramirez , 50, a citizen of Mexico, illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Bulloch County.

Samuel Orozco Lopez , 37, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Tattnall County.

Victor Lozano-Mota , 51, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Chatham County.

Leonardo Arriaga Mendoza , 43, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Chatham County.

Rubicil Perez-Valle , 37, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Effingham County.

Ernesto Ramirez-Sierra , 34, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Appling County.

Reentry after Removal or Deportation charges carry statutory penalties of up to two years in prison, followed by referral to immigration authorities for deportation. If a defendant’s removal is subsequent to a felony or aggravated felony, statutory penalties can be significantly more severe.

Criminal indictments contain only charges; defendants are considered innocent unless and until proven guilty.

These cases are being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and local law enforcement agencies and are being prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Joshua Kyle Davis, Lyle J. Burnham II, L. Alexander Hamner, Kendall S. Huennekens, and Special Assistance U.S. Attorney Lauren C. Olsen.
title: Multiple defendants indicted for immigration violations

FORT LEONARD WOOD, Mo. — As autumn leaves begin to turn and the nights grow cooler, Fort Leonard Wood is preparing a full lineup of seasonal events to celebrate the Halloween season.
The Piney Valley Golf Couse is scheduled to host Harvest Fest from 3:30 to 9 p.m., Oct. 24, 2026. The event is set to offer the Better Opportunities for Single Soldiers Haunted House, zombie paintball, rock climbing wall, bounce houses, a hayride, pumpkin patch and pumpkin decorating.
“Harvest Fest is our ultimate fall celebration,” said Caitlyn Marler, Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation marketing specialist. “We invite the community to join us at PVGC for an evening of fun.”
Marler said the cost for Harvest Fest is $5 per individual or $20 per family, and the cost for Harvest Fest and the haunted house is $10 per individual or $25 per family. Family pricing includes up to six members, she added.
According to Marler, a shuttle service to PVGC from the Pershing Community Center parking lot is set to begin at 3 p.m.
Marler wanted to let everyone know about another event MWR is planning for that evening.
“Don’t forget to also swing by Pershing Community Center for the Harvest Fest Dance Party beginning at 4 p.m.,” Marler said. “Enjoy dancing, socializing and a costume contest at 5 p.m.”
The Halloween StoryWalk is scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m., Oct. 28 at the Bruce C. Clarke Library.
Participants can show up wearing their costumes and take a walk around the library while reading "How to Scare a Ghost" by Jean Reagan page-by-page. Following the walk, the library staff is organizing trick-or-treating and other fun activities.
A trunk-or-treat is slated for 4 to 6 p.m., Friday, Oct. 30, at the parking lot of Fort Leonard Wood’s Main Post Exchange.
Also, that evening, a Costume Karaoke Craze is scheduled for 7 p.m., Oct. 30 at Morelli Heights Bar and Grill.
Daugherty Bowling Center is planning to host X-tremely Spooktacular Bowling from 6 to 10 p.m., Oct. 31 where customers in costume can enjoy lights-out bowling for $2 per game. A costume contest is planned, and the winners are set to be announced at 9 p.m.
A costume dance party is scheduled for 7 p.m., Oct. 31 at Ozark Tavern.
The main event of the spooky season will be trick-or-treating from 6 to 8 p.m., Saturday, Oct. 31, around Fort Leonard Wood’s housing areas — if the porch light is on, then the house is ready to receive candy hunters.
Christian Marsh, Directorate of Emergency Services chief of police, said the community can expect to see additional law enforcement officers throughout housing areas during trick-or-treat hours.
“The Maneuver Support Center of Excellence Noncommissioned Officer’s Academy is providing personnel again this year,” Marsh said.
As in years past, Soldiers will be wearing vests to identify them as security and will assist law enforcement officials with walking patrols throughout the housing areas, he added.
title: Harvest Fest, sweet autumn treats to thrill this frightful season

Pappas Leads Bipartisan Call to Increase Home Heating Assistance Funding
Today Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01) led a bipartisan group of 73 members in calling on the House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental appropriations for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) for Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27).
In the letter, the members wrote, “As the war with Iran remains unresolved, energy prices are expected to keep rising, with heating oil up 60% since February. LIHEAP’s $4 billion in funding for the last fiscal year would fall significantly short in meeting the needs of American families this fiscal year.”
“LIHEAP is a critical lifeline for low- and moderate-income individuals, but even if your household qualifies, LIHEAP does not provide guaranteed security. Five out of six families who qualify for LIHEAP receive no financial assistance due to the program’s woefully underfunded status. When adjusting for inflation, LIHEAP funding is lower now than it was in 1981 when the program was first created. If LIHEAP was funded at the same level as it was 45 years ago, the program would have received nearly $7 billion in FY27,” they continued.
“Emergency LIHEAP assistance is urgently needed as winter weather approaches and colder temperatures have already begun. Families should not have to choose between staying warm and purchasing other essential items like food, medication, or rent. Congress must act and not leave families in the cold,” they concluded.
LIHEAP helps low-income individuals and families pay for heating and cooling and mitigates the impacts of rising energy costs and extreme weather events. Across the nation, LIHEAP helps nearly 6 million households afford their energy bills, including nearly 30,000 households in New Hampshire, but Secretary Kennedy’s decision last year to fire all LIHEAP staff last year and President Trump’s repeated demand to cut all funding for the program has put this assistance at risk. In response, Pappas led 89 of his Congressional colleagues in calling for the protection of LIHEAP and the rehiring of all HHS staff who manage the LIHEAP program that were fired in April 2025. Pappas also led a bipartisan letter in November 2025 calling for immediate distribution of funds following delays in LIHEAP allocations to states. In April of this year, Pappas again led his colleagues in a bipartisan letter following additional LIHEAP delays from HHS.
Last month Pappas led a group of 116 bipartisan members in calling on HHS to take all necessary steps to ensure that LIHEAP funds are distributed to the states as soon as possible and no later than November 1, 2026. Pappas also recently introduced the American Homes First Act which would redirect $1 billion from President Trump’s ‘Board of Peace’ slush to LIHEAP.
title: Pappas Leads Bipartisan Call to Increase Home Heating Assistance Funding

Justice Department Files Complaints Against the Cities of St. Paul and Portland Challenging Mask Ban and Identification Requirements for Federal Officers
Today, the Department of Justice filed two lawsuits against the Cities of St. Paul, Minnesota and Portland, Oregon, challenging their unconstitutional attempts to regulate federal law enforcement officers by prohibiting federal officers from wearing masks and requiring them to provide identification in the manner prescribed by Code of Ordinances of the City of Saint Paul, Minnesota §§ 268A–268B and P.C.C. §§ 23.30.030, 23.30.100.
Not only are these laws illegal attempts to regulate the Federal Government, but, as alleged in the complaints, the laws threaten the safety of federal officers who have faced an unprecedent wave of harassment, doxxing, and even violence. Threatening officers with prosecution for simply protecting their identities and their families also chills the enforcement of federal law and compromises sensitive law enforcement operations.
“Under the Supremacy Clause of our Nation’s Constitution, states and localities cannot regulate the Federal Government and its law enforcement officers,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. “And they certainly cannot enact laws that place the safety of federal law enforcement at risk and undermine federal operations authorized by Congress. This Department of Justice will never tolerate the doxxing or harassment of federal officers, or any law like those in St. Paul and Portland that enables violent behavior against federal law enforcement officers and their families.”
“These St. Paul and Portland local laws are a direct regulation of federal law enforcement operations and threaten severe consequences for officers and public safety alike,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “The Federal Government, not state and local governments, gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties.”
“Aside from being unconstitutional, laws like these impede federal law enforcement’s ability to keep Oregonians safe and endanger the brave men and women of federal law enforcement,” said U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford for the District of Oregon. “They live in our communities. Their kids go to school in our communities. They care about our communities. They are part of our communities. It is unfair and improper to vilify them for political purposes.”
Attorney General Blanche has instructed the Department’s Civil Division to identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal laws or impede lawful federal operations. Today’s lawsuits are the latest in a series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division targeting illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country, including in New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, California, Maryland, Philadelphia, Denver, and Milwaukee. Through these filings, the Department reaffirms that federal law enforcement operations cannot be compromised by state or local measures that violate federal law.
Note: Read the lawsuit against St. Paul here and Portland here.
Press Release Number: 26-1209
title: Justice Department Files Complaints Against the Cities of St. Paul and Portland Challenging Mask Ban and Identification Requirements for Federal Officers

text:
FORT RUCKER, Ala. -- A mighty team of Fort Rucker Soldiers, civilians and contractors worked together to prepare for and recover from Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of 105 mph. The storm continued north, bringing heavy rain and damaging wind gusts across southern Alabama and the Wiregrass region.
To prepare for the potential storm, installation leaders and weather personnel held planning meetings and daily command update briefs to ensure the safety of those who live and work on Fort Rucker, as well as protect buildings, aircraft and equipment. All key leaders remained engaged throughout the process, while the Directorate of Public Works had a contractor team on standby to respond during the storm and coordinated with Alabama Power to support power outages and recovery operations once conditions were safe.
According to Matthew Patton, chief of the plans, operations, mobilization and security division, a trained battle captain staffed the Installation Operations Center before and during the height of the storm to support coordination and situational awareness.
“Aircraft and equipment were secured,” Patton said, “and personnel were directed to depart at 1 p.m., based on mission requirements, using administrative leave and weather and safety guidance.”
Following the storm, Soldiers, civilians and contractors began cleanup and recovery efforts across the installation to address infrastructure damage and restore safe conditions for the Fort Rucker community.
Keeping an Army installation safe takes a team effort. From the planning that took place before the storm, to communication during, and the hands-on work required during recovery, the Rucker team played an important role in protecting the community and operations.
Garrison leaders said they are grateful to have weathered the storm together and to everyone who stepped up, worked hard and continue to get Fort Rucker back on their feet.
Command Sgt. Maj. Castro, Fort Rucker garrison command sergeant major, said the team on Fort Rucker is well prepared to respond to emergencies.
“Fort Rucker stakeholders are well rehearsed and postured to respond to incidents like this,” Castro said. “Through continuous rehearsals and process preparation, it almost feels like clockwork. The responsiveness, professionalism, pride and passion for this community are felt and seen as Fort Rucker returns to normal operations.”
Col. Jeffrey Paulus, Fort Rucker garrison commander, said he was grateful to everyone who stepped up to support the recovery effort.
“The community response to the storm and its aftermath has been phenomenal,” he said.
Paulus said Maj. Gen. Phillip Baker, commanding general of Fort Rucker and the Army Aviation Center of Excellence remained focused on the safety and welfare of families throughout the response.
“The entire AVCOE and garrison team, through coordinated efforts with our community partners, including Alabama Power and Corvias, executed storm recovery operations effectively and efficiently,” Paulus said. “Because of the team effort, most facilities and operations were back online within about 12 hours.”
title: Fort Rucker Weathers the Storm Together

BOSTON – A Lynn man has been charged in connection with an alleged scheme to fraudulently obtain Massachusetts Commercial Learners Permits.

Rudy Nolasco, 42, is charged with fraudulently producing an identification document. He made an initial appearance in federal court in Boston on Oct. 13, 2026 and was released by the court on conditions.

According to charging documents, in November 2021 Nolasco allegedly arranged to sneak a Bluetooth earpiece into his Massachusetts Commercial Learners Permit examination, allowing co-conspirator, Frank Castro, to provide Nolasco with the answers to the exam. It is alleged that Nolasco had previously taken the examination and failed. During a meeting with an undercover agent wearing a recording device, Nolasco allegedly explained the scheme, including how to pay his co-conspirator and how the agent could cheat the commercial permit exam using a Bluetooth device.

Frank Castro was convicted of similar charges following a jury trial in January 2026 . In May 2026 , Castro was sentenced to time served (approximately 23 months in prison).

The charge of unlawfully producing an identification document provides for a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; and Brian C. Gallagher, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Transportation - Office of Inspector General, Northeast Region made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney David Tobin of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Lynn Man Charged for Role in Fraudulent CDL Scheme

CAMP HENRY, South Korea – The 403rd Army Field Support Brigade and the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon successfully concluded series of engagements here, Oct. 7.
The program brought together KAAY cadets and 403rd AFSB Soldiers and Department of the Army civilians for professional mentorship, English-language practice and cultural exchange. The engagements were designed to build the cadets’ confidence in communicating in English and help prepare them for their future responsibilities as Republic of Korea Army officers.
Nine mentors from the 403rd AFSB visited KAAY on Sept. 22 and 28. During the visits, each mentor was paired with a group of English major cadets. The cadets guided the mentors through academy facilities and queried them about their military careers, training experiences and the skills required to accomplish their missions.
“Cadets from the academy’s English department partnered with leaders from the 403rd AFSB to exchange cultural perspectives and leadership lessons. These future ROK Army leaders had the opportunity to engage with and seek advice from experienced U.S. Army leaders,” said Lt. Col. Curtis A. Gibbs, executive officer, 403rd AFSB. “The mentorship relationships established through these engagements will continue to benefit the ROK-U.S. Alliance for years to come.”
The mentors also provided feedback on the cadets’ use of English and shared their professional and personal experiences. Drawing on their extensive experience with the Army, the U.S. mentors shared the values, leadership lessons and practical knowledge essential for junior officers. These discussions not only allowed the cadets to practice English in a real-world setting but also provided a strong foundation for their development into capable and effective Army officers.
As part of the reciprocal engagement, KAAY cadets and faculty members visited Camp Henry. The visit started with a briefing on Contested Logistics presented by Col. Jason P. Book, commander, 403rd AFSB. The event also included lunch with mentors at the Sustainer Grill Warrior Restaurant, and tours of Camp Henry facilities and the brigade headquarters. The visit gave the cadets an opportunity to observe a U.S. Army installation, learn about the U.S. forces’ role on the Korean Peninsula and reconnect with the mentors they had met at KAAY.
“The engagement with the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon cadets marked another important step in strengthening the alliance between the Republic of Korea Army and the U.S. Army,” said Staff Sgt. Courtney B. Roberts, S3 maintenance noncommissioned officer, 403rd AFSB.
“These future leaders were highly inquisitive, professional and are well prepared to meet the challenges they will face as ROK Army officers,” Roberts said. “Their questions and perspectives demonstrated a strong commitment to learning, teamwork and leading Soldiers. Based on my experience with them, I believe these cadets represent some of the Republic of Korea’s brightest young leaders and have tremendous potential to serve with distinction. Opportunities like this allow us to learn from one another and reinforce the enduring strength of our alliance.”
The engagements provided the cadets with valuable academic, military and cultural experiences while giving 403rd AFSB personnel an opportunity to contribute directly to the development of future ROK Army officers. The program also enhanced the U.S. participants’ understanding of their role in South Korea and reinforced the importance of person-to-person relationships in maintaining the ROK-U.S. Alliance.
“I am a U.S. Army officer, and these cadets will soon become Republic of Korea Army officers. Together, we will be brothers and sisters in arms, standing shoulder to shoulder to strengthen the ironclad alliance between the United States and the Republic of Korea.” said Lt. Col. Jung Y. Schorr, commander, Army Field Support Battalion–Northeast Asia. “I was once a brand-new second lieutenant, and I still remember what one of my company commanders told me, ‘Your time as a lieutenant is the closest you will ever be to your Soldiers. It is the time to master the fundamentals of the Army and truly learn how to train and lead Soldiers.’”
“Spending these two days with the cadets at the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon reminded me exactly why I serve,” Schorr said. “Sharing my experiences and hearing about the officers they aspire to become was deeply inspiring. Being an officer begins with being a good Soldier, but it also means leading these outstanding young men and women as they carry forward our proud Army traditions and values. Together, we are building a better, safer world where our children can grow up believing they can ‘Be All They Can Be.’”
The 403rd AFSB and KAAY plan to continue engagements as a recurring program. The brigade has also been invited to participate in the KAAY Cadet Festival in November, and mentors may have an opportunity to attend the cadets’ commissioning ceremony in February 2027.
Through continued mentorship and professional exchange, the two organizations seek to strengthen their partnership, support the development of future Army leaders and further reinforce the enduring ROK-U.S. Alliance.
title: 403rd AFSB and KAAY forge future ROK officers together

FORT HUACHUCA, Ariz. - For military veterans, the transition to civilian life often marks the closure of a public service chapter. For Phillip McCluskey, it simply meant changing the uniform.
McCluskey, a former U.S. Army Criminal Investigation Division investigator and current team member at the U.S. Army Electronic Proving Ground (EPG), received the Veteran Servant Leader Award on Oct. 14 in recognition of his extensive volunteer service with the Cochise County Sheriff’s Office.
The award, presented by U.S. Rep. Juan Ciscomani, recognizes military veterans who continue to demonstrate exceptional leadership, selflessness, and dedication in their local communities after leaving active duty.
For McCluskey, the call back to badge and duty came after reading a troubling headline.
"The Lord gave me a pretty strong dose of justice, protection, and a desire to help others in my nature," McCluskey said. "Around 2022, I saw a news article about a drug cartel putting out a bounty on one of the sheriff’s deputies, and I wanted to do something to help."
McCluskey contacted Cochise County Sheriff Mark Dannels, outlining his military investigative background and offering to assist in any capacity needed. Dannels directed him to John Black, commander of the Sheriff’s Assist Team (SAT). After learning about the volunteer unit's mission, McCluskey applied and was sworn in.
"I saw a lot of ways I could help—way more than I have time to be able to do," McCluskey said. "Any amount of help I could provide; I was and am willing to do."
Colleagues at the Electronic Proving Ground say his dedication carries over into his daily civilian work supporting the installation’s test and evaluation mission.
“Beyond his daily duties at the Electronic Proving Ground, Mr. McCluskey’s volunteer work resonates deeply across our entire team,” said Chris Lawrence, EPG engagement liaison officer. “His service sets a standard of trust, dedication, and genuine commitment to our mission.”
While receiving recognition from a member of Congress is an honor, McCluskey emphasized that the award belongs just as much to his family and fellow volunteers.
"It’s really an honor to be recognized by a sitting congressional representative," he said. "My wife and kids have been really supportive of the mission of the SAT and allowing me to take the time to go out and help with the various activities."
He noted that volunteers on the team are motivated by duty rather than public accolades.
"The work we do is great, but I don’t think any of us on the SAT are out there to promote ourselves or to seek some kind of self-promotion," McCluskey said. "While it is a little awkward to receive an award, I think it is also nice that others appreciate what we are doing, and my family thinks it’s cool that I am getting this award."
title: From CID to Cochise County: Army veteran earns Veteran Servant Leader Award

ICE turns over criminal illegal alien charged in newlyweds’ deaths to Oregon state officials for prosecution after county ignored detainer
BEND, Or. — ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Seattle transferred Rajinder Kumar, a 32-year-old criminal illegal alien from India to Oregon state custody to face prosecution in connection with the deaths of two newlywed Americans.
Kumar has been indicted in Deschutes County, Oregon, on two counts of first-degree manslaughter and three counts of recklessly endangering another person. The charges stem from a November 2025 tractor-trailer accident and remain pending in Oregon state court.
“Two Americans lost their lives, and their families deserve accountability. ICE worked closely with law-enforcement partners to ensure Kumar is returned to state custody to answer for the serious charges against him,” said ICE ERO Seattle acting Field Office Director Julio S. Hernandez. “This coordinated action protects the public, supports the victims’ families, and ensures that an individual accused of these crimes does not evade justice. ICE will continue using every lawful tool available to protect the American people from criminal activity committed by illegal aliens.”
U.S. Border Patrol apprehended Kumar near Lukeville, Arizona, on Nov. 28, 2022, after he illegally entered the United States from Mexico. He was placed in removal proceedings. A pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.
Following his indictment on the manslaughter and reckless-endangerment charges, ICE lodged an immigration detainer with the Deschutes County Jail. In April 2026, Deschutes County released Kumar from custody without honoring ICE’s detainer.
ICE officers subsequently located and arrested Kumar on April 22, 2026.
Following the conclusion of state criminal proceedings, ICE will pursue Kumar’s immigration case consistent with federal law.
Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s public-safety priorities, ICE remains focused on enforcing immigration law, supporting victims of crime, and protecting the American people.
title: ICE turns over criminal illegal alien charged in newlyweds’ deaths to Oregon state officials for prosecution after county ignored detainer

Jacksonville, Florida – Tyler Bruce McClure (25, Jacksonville) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Jordan E. Pratt to 12 and 7 months in federal prison for using social media apps to distribute videos depicting toddler-aged children being sexually abused over the internet. McClure was also ordered to serve a 13-year term of supervised release, pay $16,000 in restitution to child victims, and register as a sex offender. On November 17, 2025, McClure was arrested in Jacksonville and has been in custody since that time. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

McClure pleaded guilty on June 17, 2026.

According to court documents, in June 2025, the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office received information from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) regarding child sexual abuse material (CSAM) being uploaded to a particular online application (“app”) by a particular app user known as “Ava_Tree_.” The company that owns the app reported that child-pornographic files were uploaded between May 23, 2025, and June 9, 2025. A review of the multimedia files contained in the account used by app user “Ava_Tree_,” who was subsequently identified as Tyler Bruce McClure, revealed several videos that depicted minors engaging in sexually explicit conduct.

There were also text message conversations between McClure and other app users. For example, in one such conversation, McClure negotiated with another app user to purchase videos depicting children being sexually abused using a popular online payment app. Further investigation revealed that an internet protocol (IP) address used to upload the CSAM was linked to a residence in Jacksonville where McClure resided.

On October 7, 2025, JSO detectives, Clay County Sheriff’s Office detectives, and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents executed a federal search warrant at the residence where McClure had been living. The agents seized an electronic tablet device belonging to McClure, but he was not present at the residence. Later that day, agents made contact with McClure at a local construction site and seized his Samsung cell phone. A subsequent forensic review of McClure’s cell phone and his electronic tablet device seized at his residence revealed that together these two devices contained at least 47 videos and 7 photos depicting minors engaging in sexually explicit conduct, including toddlers and other prepubescent children in bondage. This review also showed that on September 26, 2025, McClure used a social media app to distribute a video depicting several young children being sexually abused.

This case was investigated by the Northeast Florida INTERCEPT Task Force, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Jacksonville, the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office, the St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office, the Clay County Sheriff’s Office, and the Columbia County Sheriff’s Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney D. Rodney Brown.

It is another case brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify, rescue, and seek justice for child victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.usdoj.gov/psc. For more information about internet safety education, please visit www.usdoj.gov/psc and click on the tab “resources.”
title: Jacksonville Man Sentenced to Over 12 Years for Distributing Child Sexual Abuse Material Using Social Media Apps

MISSOULA – A Missoula woman who was trafficking meth into Montana was sentenced Wednesday to 10 years in prison, followed by five years of supervised release, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Steger Smith said.

Jennifer Lynn Stephens, 45, pleaded guilty in June 2026 to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime.

U.S. District Judge William W. Mercer presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Stephens was a known meth dealer in Missoula. Law enforcement had learned from multiple sources that Stephens was making two trips a week to Washington where her connection supplied her with 7 to 10 pounds of meth per trip.

Agents began tracking Stephens’s movements, and in February 2026, as she was returning from Washington, they pulled her over near Arlee. In the vehicle, law enforcement found several pounds of meth and a handgun. They searched Stephens’s house and, in a safe, found bags of meth, currency from the U.S. and Russia, gold coins and bars, and a 9mm pistol. Agents found another 9mm pistol in a safe in her bedroom and found a 30-30 rifle behind her bedroom door.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case. The FBI’s Montana Regional Violent Crime Task Force conducted the investigation.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: Missoula woman sentenced to 10 years in prison on meth trafficking, firearm charges
