PITTSBURGH, Pa. - After deliberating for just under two hours, a federal jury in Pittsburgh on October 14, 2026, found Seth Allen Aikens II guilty of 17 counts of wire fraud, seven counts of mail fraud, and six counts of money laundering, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.

Aikens, 29, of Crown, Pennsylvania, was tried before United States District Judge W. Scott Hardy.

The evidence presented during the week-and-a-half trial established that, between 2016 and 2020, Aikens carried out a scheme to defraud customers by making false representations about software design, production, and other services he would perform for those customers through several purported businesses he owned and operated in Clarion County. This scheme included, for example, false claims from Aikens of possessing expertise and capabilities to provide services in those areas; the defendant producing and providing to prospective clients fictitious documents showing business relationships with well-known reputable companies and bank statements falsely reflecting account balances in the millions of dollars earned from past projects; Aikens demanding additional money from clients for various fees; and the defendant making various lulling statements to deceive clients on the status of their projects, along with numerous other false representations.

The evidence further established that customers paid Aikens for the promised services using interstate wires, the U.S. mail, and/or private carrier services. Further, Aikens used customers’ money to purchase personal vehicles and equipment, including a number of items in excess of $10,000.

Judge Hardy scheduled Aikens’s sentencing for February 17, 2027. The law provides for a maximum total sentence of up to 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed is based on the seriousness of the offenses and the prior criminal history, if any, of the defendant.

Assistant United States Attorneys Barbara K. Doolittle and Eleni F. Skezas prosecuted this case on behalf of the government.

The United States Postal Inspection Service and Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation that led to the prosecution of Aikens.
title: Federal Jury Finds Clarion County Man Guilty on 30 Counts of Money Laundering and Wire and Mail Fraud

text:
Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez Introduces Legislation to Target Scammers who Prey on Older Americans
WASHINGTON, DC — This week, Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Tom Barrett (MI-07) introduced the One Front Door for Elder Fraud Act, a piece of legislation designed to streamline the reporting process for elder fraud. This bill will create an inter-agency framework to give law enforcement and prosecutors better information to fight fraud.
Reporting fraud is the first step to recovering stolen funds or preventing other would-be victims from falling prey to the same scam. Right now, there are ten federal agencies, most with their own separate intake channels, and a poorly coordinated set of federal reporting sites, plus 50+ state portals, with no single number to call and no designated first-click destination. As a result, fraud reporting is an overly complicated process that handicaps law enforcement efforts to quickly respond and, in some cases, recover stolen funds. This legislation will address these barriers.
Specifically, this legislation would:
- Designate a single front door for elder-fraud reporting, reachable two ways, by phone and on the web, to route each request to the federal agency whose mandate fits.
- The hotline should answer 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
- The website should also include digital resources for combatting the most common types of scams.
The new reporting framework would be similar to VSAFE, introduced by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs in 2024 to create a single number and website specifically for veterans to report fraud, scams, and predatory practices.
“People who steal from seniors and retirees are the lowest of the low. No one should have to navigate impenetrable government websites or spend hours stuck on hold trying to report these scams,” said Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez. “ My bill makes it simple, you call one number or go to one site and your report goes directly to the investigator you need. When we give law enforcement the tools to fight back, they can respond immediately and take on these predatory scammers.”
“Fraudsters are constantly targeting seniors to cheat them out of their hard-earned retirement. These sophisticated scammers pose as federal agencies, banks, and even loved ones, while artificial intelligence is making impersonation easier than ever,” said Congressman Tom Barrett (MI-07). “Families need resources to recognize and quickly report suspected fraud. By establishing a 24/7, one-stop shop for addressing elder fraud, this bipartisan bill will protect vulnerable seniors and empower law enforcement to crack down on these criminals.”
“When an older American falls victim to fraud, every minute counts. Yet victims and families are often left navigating a fragmented reporting system when they need help the most. No one should have to figure out which government agency to call while their life savings are at risk. By establishing a single national entry point, available around the clock, the One Front Door for Elder Fraud Act of 2026 represents an important step toward protecting older Americans.”
- Yuksel Aydin, Director of the anti-scam website seniors.hcsk.org
“Reporting a scam should be as simple as one click or one call. But today, older adults who’ve been scammed face a maze of reporting options, leaving them unsure where to turn and often not reporting at all. Combating fraud requires a system that makes it easy for people to report scams and for authorities to track them. By creating one front door, a single website, and hotline, the One Front Door for Elder Fraud Act would give the growing number of older adults targeted by scammers the help they deserve.”
- Ramsey Alwin, President and CEO, National Council on Aging
During the appropriations process this year, Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez advanced multiple provisions targeting scammers and helping working families keep their hard-earned money. This included encouraging the Department of Justice to pursue further action against crypto scams targeting older Americans and instructing law enforcement to work across jurisdictions to combat fraud and scams.
The legislation is supported by the National Council on Aging and seniors.hsck.org.
####
title: Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez Introduces Legislation to Target Scammers who Prey on Older Americans

Castro Nominates 25 Latino Recordings for Preservation in the Library of Congress
SAN ANTONIO, TX— To close out Hispanic Heritage Month, today, Congressman Joaquin Castro (TX-20) released his annual list of Latino songs, albums, and broadcasts nominated for preservation in the National Recording Registry at the Library of Congress, established in 2000 to preserve recordings with cultural, historic, or aesthetic significance to American life. The Library of Congress adds 25 recordings each year and now holds 700 titles. Yet Latino artists account for fewer than 5 percent of the registry, despite Latinos making up nearly 20 percent of the U.S. population.
This year’s list was shaped by suggestions from the public and adds new nominations from Maná, Julio Iglesias, Los Lobos, Jon Secada, Mazz, and The Royal Jesters. It also renews Rep. Castro’s nomination of the first full-time Spanish-language radio broadcast in the United States, which aired on KCOR in San Antonio in 1946. Congressman Castro is also submitting a separate list of nominations honoring Texas artists.
"It is essential to continue to appropriately include and celebrate the contributions of Latino artists who are part of the American story," Congressman Castro wrote in his nomination letter. "The National Recording Registry’s existence speaks to the importance of preserving music and audio in American culture and society. Latino music’s influence sparks innovation and sways trends across the music industry."
Since Congressman Castro began submitting nominations in 2022, the Library of Congress has inducted 10 titles from his lists. These include Juan Gabriel’s “Amor Eterno,” Héctor Lavoe’s “El Cantante,” Irene Cara’s “Flashdance…What A Feeling,” Daddy Yankee’s “Gasolina,” Vicente Fernández’s “El Rey,” Freddy Fender’s “Before the Next Teardrop Falls,” Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “Hamilton,” and most recently Pérez Prado’s “Mambo No. 5” and José Feliciano’s “Feliz Navidad,” both selected in 2026.
Congressman Castro’s Full List of Nominations to the National Recording Registry:
- First Full Time Spanish-Language Radio Station Broadcast in the United States based in San Antonio, TX (formerly KCOR-TV and later known as KWEX-TV) (1946) (Broadcast)
- Diamonds and Rust – Joan Baez (1975) (Album)
- Suavemente – Elvis Crespo (1999) (Song)

PORTLAND, Ore.— A federal grand jury in Portland has returned an eight‑count indictment charging Rosa Cazares , Chief Executive Officer of La Mota, LLC, and 503 Staffing LLC, with willfully failing to collect, account for, and pay over federal payroll taxes, announced Scott E. Bradford, United States Attorney for the District of Oregon.

According to the indictment, Cazares—who resided in Portland and oversaw the financial affairs of both La Mota, a cannabis business, and 503 Staffing, a payroll processing company—was responsible for withholding federal income taxes and Social Security and Medicare taxes from employee wages and remitting those funds to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Employers are required to deposit these withheld “trust fund” taxes, as well as their own matching contributions, on a quarterly basis and to file a Form 941 federal employment tax return.

The indictment alleges that between March 2020 and December 2021, Cazares failed to collect, truthfully account for, or pay over required trust fund taxes for La Mota and 503 Staffing. Across eight calendar quarters, the unpaid trust fund taxes totaled $1,542,413 . Each quarter of nonpayment constitutes a separate criminal count under 26 U.S.C. § 7202 , which prohibits willful failure to collect or pay over taxes.

If convicted, Cazares faces up to five years in federal prison, fines, and restitution for each count.

An indictment is only an allegation of criminal conduct. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith D.M. Bateman.

For additional information, please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Oregon.

___________________________________________________________________________

This is one of several major fraud cases being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Oregon in conjunction with the Department of Justice’s national fraud enforcement efforts. Additional matters are pending. Please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for more information.
title: Federal Prosecutors Uncover Over $1.5 Million in Tax Fraud as Additional Cases Move Forward

FORT LEE, Va. — Soldiers, families, and distinguished guests of the 59th Ordnance Brigade gathered to honor a significant leadership transition as Command Sgt. Maj. Pearl Reeder-Hensley relinquished responsibility to Command Sgt. Maj. Edgar Lopez during a Change of Responsibility ceremony.
The event celebrated Reeder-Hensley's dedicated service to the brigade while formally welcoming Lopez, who arrives from the 6th Ordnance Battalion in South Korea, to assume responsibility as the brigade's senior enlisted leader.
Presiding over the ceremony, Col. Joel Machak, commander, 59th Ordnance Brigade, praised Reeder-Hensley's contributions to the organization and her unwavering commitment to Soldiers and families.
"The scope of what you [Reeder-Hensley] steered is breathtaking," said Machak. "Under your watch, this brigade has worked tirelessly to provide the Army's operating force with more than 21,000 new professional Ordnance Soldiers each year…across 23 Military Occupational Specialties."
During her tenure, Reeder-Hensley helped guide the brigade through critical training missions and professional development initiatives, ensuring the brigade continued to develop technically proficient and combat-ready ordnance Soldiers for the Army.
As she reflected on her time with the brigade, Reeder-Hensley expressed gratitude for the Soldiers, noncommissioned officers, officers, civilians, and family members who contributed to the unit's success.
"Serving as the brigade command sergeant major has been one of the greatest honors," Reeder-Hensley said. "This responsibility was never mine alone. It was carried by commanders, first sergeants, drill sergeants, instructors, staff, mentors, family and friends. So, I want to say thank you to the people who helped make this journey possible."
Following the ceremony, Reeder-Hensley will report to her next assignment as the Army Sustainment Command support operations sergeant major at Rock Island Arsenal, Illinois.
As the ceremonial passing of the colors transferred responsibility to the incoming senior enlisted leader, Lopez pledged to build upon the strong foundation established by his predecessor.
"I'm truly honored and excited to serve as your next 59th Ordnance Brigade command sergeant major," Lopez said. "I will be present. You'll see me in your formations, at your training, and where you work. I'm here to listen, support you, and help this team succeed."
Machak expressed confidence in Lopez's ability to lead the brigade's enlisted force, citing his extensive experience and proven leadership at multiple levels across the Army.
"Command Sgt. Maj. Lopez is no stranger to this brigade, having served here previously as a senior AIT platoon sergeant, chief Munitions NCO, and first sergeant," Machak said. "Today, you inherit an important mission, a proud brigade, and a team of Soldiers, civilians, and leaders who understand that their work matters. You also inherit the trust of the people we serve."
The change of responsibility ceremony, a time-honored Army tradition, symbolizes the transfer of responsibility, authority, and accountability from one senior enlisted leader to another. As the brigade bid farewell to Reeder-Hensley and welcomed Lopez, Soldiers gathered to recognize both leaders and reaffirm the organization's commitment to mission accomplishment and leader development.
With a new chapter underway, the 59th Ordnance Brigade continues its mission of developing adaptive, disciplined, and technically proficient ordnance professionals, guided by the leadership and experience of its incoming command sergeant major while carrying forward the legacy of excellence established by those who have served before.
title: 59th Ord. Bde. Welcomes New CSM During Change of Responsibility Ceremony

NEWARK, N.J. – An Essex County, New Jersey, man was sentenced in connection with his online enticement and exploitation of minors, United States Attorney Robert Frazer announced.

Nabeen Leigh Singha, 39, of West Orange, New Jersey, was sentenced on October 13, 2026, to 600 months’ imprisonment followed by 10 years’ supervised release before U.S. District Court Chief Judge Renée M. Bumb in Camden federal court on charges of production, receipt, and possession of child pornography.

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court:

From July 2021 through March 2022, Singha exchanged sexually explicit messages with two minor victims and paid them to create sexually explicit videos and images of themselves to send to Singha over the internet.

During that time-period, Singha also communicated with an intermediary and paid that intermediary to send sexually explicit videos and images of four additional minor victims.

Law enforcement searched and seized Singha’s phone and found nearly 5,000 images and 620 videos depicting child pornography. These materials included depictions of prepubescent minors under 12 years old.

United States Attorney Frazer credited special agents and members of the Child Exploitation Group of Homeland Security Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Michael S. McCarthy, with the investigation.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) in the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit: https://www.justice.gov/psc .

U.S. Attorney Frazer has announced proactive steps to connect with New Jersey’s families and communities, bringing training opportunities and resources through direct outreach. Organizations and community members interested in arranging prevention programming or learning more about available resources can contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey at USANJ.CommunityOutreach@usdoj.gov . Moreover, prevention resources are available through the Department of Justice's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section Prevention webpage and the Department of Homeland Security’s Know2Protect Campaign.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jake A. Nasar of the Health Care Fraud and Opioid Enforcement Unit in Newark.

###

Defense counsel: Jonathan F. Marshall, Esq., Freehold, NJ
title: Essex County Man Sentenced to 50 Years for Online Enticement of Minors and Child Pornography Crimes

DETROIT – A former U.S. Postal Service (USPS) employee has been sentenced to 20 months in prison by United States District Judge Susan K. DeClercq for fraudulently obtaining unemployment insurance benefits, U.S. Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon announced today.

Gorgon was joined in the announcement by Tammy Hull, Inspector General, United States Postal Service, Felicia George, Detroit Division Inspector, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and Anthony P. D’Esposito, Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor Office of Inspector General.

Christopher Powell, 37, of Detroit, worked as a letter carrier with the USPS and previously pleaded guilty to two counts of wire fraud. At the time of his guilty plea, Powell admitted that from July 2020 through January 2024, he submitted fraudulent unemployment insurance (UI) claims in multiple states using his own personal identifying information and made false certifications to obtain and maintain such benefits.

Powell also admitted that he directed mail related to at least one fraudulent claim to an address on his mail route. In July 2023, after spending the stolen benefits associated with one false claim, Powell falsely reported to his bank that he never received the UI funds, prompting the bank to issue him even more money he was not entitled to.

In addition to the prison term, Judge DeClercq imposed three years of supervised release and ordered Powell to pay restitution in the amount of $166,366.53 and a forfeiture money judgment in the same amount.

This case was investigated by the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and U.S. Department of Labor Office of Inspector General. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Kelly Fasbinder.
title: Former Postal Employee Sentenced to 20 Months in Prison for Fraud in Connection with Unemployment Insurance Benefits

FORT LEE, Va. – Singapore Armed Forces Army Logistics Training Institute leadership visited U.S. Army Combined Arms Support Command Oct. 7-8, 2006, to discuss and observe Army logistics training.
Singapore Army Lt. Col. Yixian Ong, commander of the training institute, met with CASCOM Commanding General, Maj. Gen. Sean Davis, and CASCOM Command Sergeant Major, Command Sgt. Maj. James Lafratta.
They visited and received briefings from U.S. Army Transportation School, U.S. Army Logistics School and U.S. Army Ordnance School.
After the briefing from the U.S. Army Quartermaster School, the Singaporeans visited the Aerial Delivery and Field Services, Logistics Training Department, and the Petroleum, Water, and Energy Department.
The visit enhanced mutual learning between the U.S. Army and Singapore Armed Forces which strengthens strategic readiness, interoperability, and coalition effectiveness, ensuring both sides can “stage, move, and fight together” more efficiently.
title: Singapore Army Logistics Training Institute visits CASCOM

text:
Administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), the Impact Aid program is one of the oldest federal education programs, dating from 1950. Impact Aid, authorized under Title VII of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA, P.L. 89-10, as amended), compensates local educational agencies (LEAs) for the financial burden resulting from certain federal activities carried out in their areas. These activities include federal ownership of certain lands, as well as the enrollments in LEAs of children of parents who work or live on federal land (e.g., children of parents in the uniformed services and children living on Indian lands). The federal government provides compensation because these activities deprive LEAs of the ability to collect property or other taxes from these individuals (e.g., members of the uniformed services living on military bases) or their employers, even though the LEAs are obligated to provide free public education to their children. Impact Aid also provides support for certain students with disabilities and for school construction.
The largest Impact Aid component, Section 7003(b) payments (also known as Basic Support Payments), compensates LEAs for enrolling "federally connected" children. For FY2026, Section 7003(b) accounted for $1.477 billion, 90.6% of all funds appropriated for the Impact Aid program. As Section 7003(b) payments account for the majority of all Impact Aid funding, this report primarily focuses on these payments.
All Impact Aid payments are funded through the Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (L-HHS-ED) annual appropriations act. Funds are provided through "budget year appropriations," meaning the funds would be available for the budget year beginning on the first day of the fiscal year (e.g., October 1, 2025, for the FY2026 L-HHS-ED appropriations act), unless otherwise specified. This availability generally is retroactive to October 1 if annual appropriations are enacted after the fiscal year has begun. The Impact Aid program is also authorized to receive appropriations through advance appropriations and forward funding. In current practice, advance appropriations become available one fiscal year after the budget year covered by a given appropriations act (e.g., appropriations provided for FY2027 in an FY2026 appropriations act). Forward funding becomes available during the last quarter of the budget year (e.g., starting July 1, 2026, for the FY2026 appropriations act) but remains available through at least the following fiscal year (e.g., available from July 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027).
Without advance appropriations or forward funding, when full-year appropriations are not provided prior to the beginning of the budget year, LEAs are generally unable to receive their full Section 7003(b) payments until sometime after October 1. This can create financial difficulties for LEAs, particularly those that are heavily dependent on Impact Aid funding. Providing funds for Section 7003(b) payments through advance appropriations or forward funding has the potential to ease some of these difficulties, but either change has budget enforcement implications that may complicate any attempt to transition to an alternative funding schedule.
This report considers three different appropriations scenarios for Impact Aid Section 7003(b) payments that are an alternative to budget year appropriations: (1) providing forward funding for Section 7003(b) payments, (2) providing advance appropriations for Section 7003(b) payments, or (3) using both forward funding and advance appropriations to provide Section 7003(b) payments, as is done for other federal education programs such as Title I-A Grants to Local Educational Agencies authorized by the ESEA or Grants to States authorized under Part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Each of these scenarios has budget implications that may require at least a one-time increase in discretionary appropriations, a change in the limit set on advance appropriations (if applicable), or some combination of both.
Administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), the Impact Aid program is one of the oldest federal education programs, dating from 1950. Impact Aid, authorized under Title VII of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA, P.L. 89-10, as amended), compensates local educational agencies (LEAs) for the financial burden resulting from certain federal activities carried out in their areas.1 These activities include federal ownership of certain lands, as well as the enrollments in LEAs of children of parents who work or live on federal land (e.g., children of parents in the uniformed services and children living on Indian lands). The federal government provides compensation because these activities deprive LEAs of the ability to collect property or other taxes from these individuals (e.g., members of the uniformed services living on military bases) or their employers, even though the LEAs are obligated to provide free public education to their children. Impact Aid also provides support for certain students with disabilities and for school construction.
The largest Impact Aid component, Section 7003(b) payments (also known as Basic Support Payments), compensates LEAs for enrolling "federally connected" children. These are children who reside with a parent who is a member of the uniformed services living on or off federal property; reside with a parent who is an accredited foreign military officer living on federal property; reside on Indian lands; reside in low-rent public housing; or reside with a parent who is a civilian working or living on federal land. For FY2026, Section 7003(b) payments accounted for $1.477 billion, 90.6% of all funds appropriated for the Impact Aid program. As Section 7003(b) payments account for the majority of all Impact Aid funding, this report primarily focuses on them. The Appendix provides a brief description of other payments made under the Impact Aid program.
The purpose of this report is to describe options for adjusting the timing of when Impact Aid appropriations become available for obligation to carry out Section 7003(b).2 The Section 7003(b) payments represent the largest federal elementary and secondary education program administered by ED that is funded in annual appropriations acts using "budget year appropriations," meaning funding for a school year does not become available until the first day of the fiscal year (October 1), which occurs after the school year has begun. The use of budget year appropriations to fund Section 7003(b) payments can create some complexities for the LEAs that receive these funds. For example, the current timing of enactment and availability of federal funds provided through Impact Aid may make it difficult for LEAs to include these funds in their budget planning process. In addition, the allocation of funds to LEAs is delayed in instances where the federal government is operating under a temporary continuing resolution (CR) at the beginning of the fiscal year until regular appropriations bills or a full-year CR is enacted. Thus, LEAs may experience delays in receiving their funds. Other funding approaches used in annual appropriations acts could be applied to the Section 7003(b) payments to address these issues.
This report begins by explaining how Section 7003(b) activities are currently funded through "budget year appropriations" and the effect that period of availability has on those activities. It then discusses alternatives to providing funding through budget year appropriations, including forward funding and advance appropriations. The final section analyzes the way in which adopting an alternative period of availability such as forward funding, advance appropriations, or a combination approach (forward funding and advance appropriations) would affect the appropriations process. More specifically, it discusses the appropriations actions required to make these changes and the ways in which this would affect the annual appropriations process, both once the alternative period of availability was fully implemented and in the transition fiscal year.3
Section 7003(b) of the ESEA authorizes payments (often referred to as Basic Support Payments) to LEAs to compensate them for the cost of serving certain groups of federally connected children. Federally connected children include
The presence of these children can increase the number of children an LEA must serve without a commensurate increase in the taxes that otherwise could be collected to support public education. To be eligible for Section 7003(b) payments, an LEA must have at least 400 federally connected children, or such children must represent at least 3% of an LEA's average daily attendance (ADA). Of the more than 17,000 LEAs nationwide,4 932 LEAs were eligible for a Basic Support Payment in FY2025.5 Thus, fewer than 10% of all LEAs qualify for Section 7003(b) payments.
For FY2026, $1.477 billion was appropriated for Section 7003(b) payments. These payments accounted for 90.6% of the $1.630 billion provided overall for the Impact Aid program. Section 7003(b) payments differ from funds provided by most other federal elementary and secondary education programs in that they are not limited to specified uses (such as improving the educational achievement of disadvantaged students). Section 7003(b) payments are considered general aid to the recipient LEA. The funds may be used for any purpose selected by the LEA in accordance with state and local requirements. Funds are often used for current expenditures (e.g., teacher salaries, purchasing instructional materials, tutoring) but may also be used for other purposes such as capital expenditures.6 In addition, funds need not be spent only on federally connected children. Finally, because Impact Aid payments are not aimed at specific educational goals, accountability requirements for the use of funds or for specific outcomes are minimal.
The federal government's fiscal year starts on October 1 of one calendar year and ends on September 30 of the following calendar year.7 A federal fiscal year is identified by the calendar year in which it ends.8 For example, FY2025 began on October 1, 2024, and ended on September 30, 2025. Funding for federal programs provided through the annual appropriations process typically becomes available for obligation by a federal agency on the first day of the fiscal year for which the act makes appropriations, unless otherwise specified. For example, acts making appropriations for FY2026 typically provided funds that first became available to federal agencies for obligation on the first day of FY2026, October 1, 2025.9 This period of availability is also referred to as the budget year. For the purposes of this report, such periods of availability are referred to as "budget year appropriations."
The Impact Aid program is funded using budget year appropriations provided in the Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (L-HHS-ED) appropriations act. Since school years typically begin in the months preceding the October start of a new fiscal year, this means that funds become available for use during a school year after that school year has started. Of the elementary and secondary education programs administered by ED that received $1 billion or more in annual appropriations in FY2026, only Impact Aid Section 7003(b) received budget year appropriations.10
The use of budget year appropriations to fund Section 7003(b) payments can create some complexities for the LEAs that receive these funds. For example, because of the timing of the school year, substantial planning and preparation for the upcoming year by LEAs tends to occur during the spring and summer months. However, the current timing of enactment and availability of federal funds provided through Impact Aid may make it difficult for LEAs to include these funds in their budget planning process. In addition, the allocation of funds to LEAs is delayed in instances where the federal government is operating under a temporary CR at the beginning of the fiscal year until regular appropriations bills or a full-year CR is enacted. In the case of a CR, LEAs that must have an initial Basic Support Payment in the first quarter of the fiscal year to meet current operating costs are able to request an early payment from ED.11 However, payments provided by ED in such instances are partial Basic Support Payments.
LEAs dependent on Impact Aid funding also are affected more quickly by any decrease (or increase) in funding than LEAs receiving funds under other federal elementary and secondary education formula grant programs. For example, as a result of the FY2013 sequester, Impact Aid funding was reduced immediately during the 2012-2013 school year, while the decrease in funding for federal education programs receiving forward funding or advance appropriations did not affect LEAs until the following school year (2013-2014). The uncertainty related to the provision of budget year appropriations due to CRs or other situations such as sequestration or government shutdowns can create financial difficulties for LEAs, particularly those that are heavily dependent on Impact Aid funding.12
Rather than providing appropriations for Impact Aid after a school year is underway, program funding could be provided prior to the start of the school year, as is done with several other education grant programs. In general, this alternative approach would provide appropriations months in advance of when they would become available with budget year appropriations (i.e., prior to the start of the school year in which they would be used). Such a process would presumably allow LEAs to incorporate funding with more certainty in their planning process for the upcoming school year. In addition, if appropriations acts were delayed in any given fiscal year, LEAs presumably would be less likely to be adversely affected for the purposes of the upcoming school year.
While appropriations could be made available at any time, as specified in the appropriations act in which they are enacted, two such conventions have been used for certain other ED programs to accommodate the disconnect between the federal fiscal year and the school year—advance appropriations and forward funding.13 For example, programs administered by ED that received total annual appropriations for a fiscal year of at least $1 billion in FY2026 and received both advance appropriations and forward funding include the following: (1) Title I-Grants to Local Educational Agencies (ESEA Title I-A), (2) Improving Teacher Quality (ESEA Title II-A), (3) Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) Part B Grants to States, and (4) Career and Technical Education State Grants (Carl. D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act of 2006, Title I). Additionally, the following programs received appropriations in excess of $1 billion through forward funding only: the Student Support and Academic Enrichment (SSAE) program (ESEA Title IV-A) and the 21st Century Community Learning Centers program (ESEA Title IV-B). Impact Aid Section 7003(b) is the only ED-administered elementary and secondary education program receiving at least $1 billion annually that is not funded through advance appropriations, forward funding, or a combination of the two.
Although the Impact Aid programs have generally been authorized to receive funding in appropriations acts on either of these bases since 1968, through Title IV, Section 420 (a), of the General Education Provisions Act (see below), no such appropriations are currently being provided with such timing:
To the end of affording the responsible Federal, State, and local officers adequate notice of available Federal financial assistance for carrying out ongoing education activities and projects, appropriations for grants, contracts, or other payments under any applicable program are authorized to be included in the appropriations Act for the fiscal year preceding the fiscal year during which such activities and projects shall be carried out.14
While funding for any or all of the Impact Aid payments could be provided through forward funding or advance appropriations (as discussed below), for the purposes of this report it is assumed that any change in appropriations would affect only Section 7003(b) payments.
Advance appropriations are enacted one or more fiscal years prior to when they become available.15 For example, in an appropriations act for FY2027, funds would generally become available for obligation at the start of the fiscal year—October 1, 2026. Advance appropriations included in this FY2027 act, however, would not become available until the start of FY2028—October 1, 2027—or later.16
Advance appropriations have been provided for a variety of programs besides the education programs mentioned above, particularly those that provide payments or services directly to individuals or states, such as the Veterans Health Administration (Department of Veterans Affairs) and the Tenant-Based and Project-Based Rental Assistance Programs (Department of Housing and Urban Development). The reasons such appropriations have been advocated include avoiding funding gaps or relying on CRs for funding at the beginning of the fiscal year, as well as the belief that such appropriations enable better advanced planning for those programs because they are typically enacted many months prior to the beginning of the fiscal year in which they become available. Others have argued, however, that the ability to make such commitments may be limited by the extent to which programmatic needs can be forecasted in advance, and that providing alternative periods of availability for some programs makes their budgetary levels difficult to compare to programs that receive budget year appropriations.17
Forward funds are also enacted in advance but become available during the last quarter of the budget year as opposed to a future fiscal year.18 For example, in an appropriations act for FY2027, budget authority that is forward funded would not become available until the last quarter of FY2027 (i.e., July 1, 2027, or later) and would remain available through at least part of the following fiscal year.19
Forward funding is provided for many elementary and secondary education programs to allow additional time for school officials to develop budgets in advance of the beginning of the school year and to better align federal appropriations with the fiscal year used by many school districts, which runs from July 1 to June 30.20 Forward funding is similar to advance appropriations in that it is enacted in advance of the school year for which it is provided. In the context of education, the distinction between the two is that forward funding becomes available during the summer months to provide for program costs that largely occur during the following fiscal year, whereas advance appropriations first become available in the fall during that following fiscal year. For example, in an FY2027 appropriations act, forward funding for the 2027-2028 school year would become available on July 1, 2027, whereas advance appropriations for that same school year would become available on October 1, 2027.
At the program level, there may be little difference between providing funds in July or October, as most expenditures for a standard school year (e.g., for salaries and expenses) occur throughout the year. Using forward funding or advance appropriations, however, may have budget enforcement implications, and the choice of one approach over the other may be determined, to some extent, by those implications.
Congress has historically used various methods to set total discretionary funding levels for a fiscal year, as well as the discretionary funding that is to be allocated for the L-HHS-ED appropriations bill. These methods have included statutory limits on the applicable spending and procedural limits on such spending.21 Statutory limits on defense and nondefense discretionary spending have not been in effect since FY2025, although they were intermittently in effect for many years prior to that time pursuant to the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 (BBEDCA; P.L. 99-177, as amended).22 When in effect, statutory spending limits are enforceable through sequestration (i.e., largely across-the-board reductions to eliminate excess spending), as well as points of order during floor consideration.23 For procedural enforcement, the Congressional Budget Act of 197424 provides for allocations of budget authority under the jurisdiction of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, referred to as a "302(a) allocation," as well as the suballocation of that spending to each of the 12 appropriations subcommittees, referred to as a "302(b) allocation."25 Both the 302(a) and 302(b) allocations are enforceable during floor consideration through points of order that may be raised against any measure, including amendments, that would cause these limits to be exceeded.26
The amount provided in an appropriations act for a given fiscal year, for budget enforcement purposes, is determined by its period of availability. That is, the amount provided is "scored" in the fiscal year in which it first becomes available for obligation.27 Forward funding becomes available during the latter part of the budget year and so is scored against the budget year of the bill in which it is enacted. In contrast, advance appropriations are scored against the limits on appropriations that apply the first fiscal year that they are available for obligation (typically the following fiscal year) and not the budget year of the bill in which they are enacted.28 Consequently, budget enforcement for advance appropriations would typically occur that following fiscal year in combination with the new discretionary appropriations for that year. That is, in the following fiscal year, the appropriations process begins with a "charge" against the appropriations limits for the budget year, even before the appropriations acts for that fiscal year have been drafted.
Given that budget enforcement rules generally limit discretionary spending to a single fiscal year at a time, providing appropriations in advance may allow them to be considered outside the context of the spending decisions for the upcoming year. In response to concerns about the potential to avoid the budget year limits when considering advance appropriations, various House and Senate procedural limits on the amount of advance appropriations that may be provided have been imposed through the congressional budget resolution and other associated procedural mechanisms for most fiscal years since FY2001. These limits have typically specified the accounts for which advance appropriations may be provided and have capped the amounts for certain advance appropriations.29
This section considers three different appropriations scenarios for Impact Aid Section 7003(b) payments that are an alternative to regular budget year appropriations: (1) providing forward funding for Section 7003(b) payments, (2) providing advance appropriations for Section 7003(b) payments, or (3) using both forward funding and advance appropriations to provide Section 7003(b) funding, as is done for other federal education programs such as Title I-A Grants to Local Educational Agencies authorized by the ESEA or Grants to States authorized under Part B of the IDEA. This section considers each of these scenarios in terms of how they might affect the annual appropriations process once they were fully implemented, the appropriations actions required in the transition fiscal year, and various potential budget process issues that might arise during that transition.30 For discussion purposes, it is assumed under each scenario that appropriations will be enacted in an FY2027 appropriations act (as well as in an FY2028 appropriations act, in some discussion) and that the Section 7003(b) program will remain level funded at its FY2026 appropriations level of $1.477 billion. For the sake of this illustrative example, it is also assumed that budget year appropriations in the FY2027 appropriations act would be enacted by October 1 of the fiscal year corresponding to the appropriations bill,31 forward funding would be available on July 1 of the year corresponding to the appropriations bill, and advance appropriations would be available on the first day of the succeeding fiscal year. As previously discussed, the ESEA would not have to be amended to permit the Section 7003(b) payments to receive forward funding or advance appropriations, as both funding mechanisms are already authorized for the Impact Aid account.
As noted previously, Impact Aid is currently funded using regular budget year appropriations that first become available about one month after the start of the school year (i.e., October 1). If Section 7003(b) payments were to be forward funded, however, funds would shift from being available in October to support the current school year to being available in July to support the upcoming school year. For example, if Section 7003(b) continued to be funded through budget year appropriations for FY2027, the funds would be available as of October 1, 2026, and be used to support activities during the 2026-2027 school year. If appropriations for Section 7003(b) were forwarded funded in FY2027, funds would become available on July 1, 2027, and be used to support school activities during the 2027-2028 school year. More specifically, such funds would typically be made available for the next 15 months, through September 30, 2028. Likewise, the following fiscal year, if all Section 7003(b) appropriations were forward funded, funds to support activities during the 2028-2029 school year would be provided by the FY2028 appropriations act to become available on July 1, 2028.
To change the Impact Aid program to be solely forward funded starting in FY2027 without reducing the funding available each fiscal year would essentially require double funding the program in the transition year through the following appropriations actions. First, the FY2027 appropriations would need to include the regular budget year appropriation that the program has historically received to fund activities in the 2026-2027 school year. These would be available for obligation as of October 1, 2026. Otherwise, under the switch to forward funding, the program would be without an appropriation until July 1, 2027, leaving little to no funding for the 2026-2027 school year. Second, funds for the 2027-2028 school year would need to be forward funded to become available in the final months of FY2027. If the intent is to completely forward fund the Section 7003(b) payment, then the full amount required to level fund the payment would need to be appropriated using a forward funding period of availability. That is, for the FY2027 appropriations process, the Section 7003(b) payment would need to be funded through both regular budget year appropriations and forward funding appropriations, a scenario that was arguably contemplated in Title IV, Section 420(b) of the General Education Provisions Act:
In order to effect a transition to the timing of appropriation action authorized by subsection (a) of this section, the application of this section may result in the enactment, in a fiscal year, of separate appropriations for an applicable program (whether in the same appropriations Act or otherwise) for two consecutive fiscal years.
The following scenario illustrates this potential transition. For FY2026, the Section 7003(b) payments were funded at $1.477 billion. Assuming the program continues to be funded at this level, $2.954 billion would need to be provided for the program in FY2027 under this funding scenario ($1.477 for regular budget year appropriations and $1.477 billion for forward funding). In subsequent fiscal years, however, assuming the program remained forward funded (and level-funded), the annual appropriation provided solely through forward funding would be $1.477 billion. The increase in discretionary appropriations required to forward fund the Section 7003(b) payments in FY2027 would be counted against any statutory or procedural limits on discretionary spending applicable to that fiscal year. In effect, this might require that the additional appropriations to forward fund the Section 7003(b) payments during this transition period be offset by reductions to another discretionary program. Alternatively, this transition period could be addressed by enacting a provision specifying that a certain amount, such as the additional funding technically needed to effectuate a switch to the forward funding schedule for future years, is not to be counted for the purposes of budget enforcement.
In contrast to the regular budget year appropriations that are enacted to fund education activities for a school year that is already underway, advance appropriations are enacted prior to when that school year starts. For example, budget year appropriations to fund the 2026-2027 school year would be enacted in the FY2027 appropriations act and become available as of October 1, 2026. Advance appropriations to fund the 2027-2028 school year, however, would be enacted one year in advance—in the appropriations act for the fiscal year starting October 1, 2026 (FY2027)—but not become available until October 1, 2027, one full fiscal year after the budget year. The following fiscal year, advance appropriations for the 2028-2029 school year would be enacted in the FY2028 appropriations act but not become available until October 1, 2028.
Changing appropriations for payments for federally connected children from regular budget year appropriations to advance appropriations without reducing the funding available each fiscal year requires a different set of appropriations actions, with a different set of costs, for a given fiscal year. First, to change the Section 7003(b) payment to receive advance appropriations during the FY2027 appropriations process, the FY2027 L-HHS-ED appropriations act would need to include the budget year appropriation that the program has historically received to cover program needs for the 2026-2027 school year. Funds for the 2026-2027 school year would be available for obligation as of October 1, 2026, once enacted. A switch to advance appropriations without also providing these budget year appropriations would leave the program without an appropriation until October 1, 2027, resulting in little to no funding for the 2026-2027 school year. Second, advance appropriations for the 2027-2028 school year would also need to be provided in the FY2027 L-HHS-ED appropriations act, to become available on October 1, 2027. If the intent is to completely fund needs for the 2027-2028 school year through advance appropriations, then the full appropriation for that program year would need to be provided in this way.
The budget process implications for a switch to advance appropriations also differ from those for forward funding. The funding for advance appropriations for FY2028 included in the FY2027 appropriations bill would not count against any limits on FY2027 discretionary spending and would not require any additional funding of Section 7003(b) payments in a single fiscal year. Such spending would count against the FY2028 limits, however, if provided on the schedule considered in this scenario. It would also require that any procedural limit on advance appropriations, which if in effect would generally be imposed via a congressional budget resolution adopted prior to that fiscal year, allows such appropriations for the Impact Aid account and be set at a level sufficient to accommodate appropriations for the Section 7003(b) payments.
Appropriations for Section 7003(b) payments could also be made using a combination of forward funding and advance appropriations, as has been the practice for other federal education programs such as ESEA Title I-A and IDEA Part B. Under this approach, only the portion of funding needed during the summer months would be forward funded, while the rest would be advance appropriated to become available after the start of the following fiscal year. For example, for the 2027-2028 school year, in the FY2027 appropriations act, a portion (e.g., 25%) of the Section 7003(b) payments would be forward funded and become available on July 1, 2027, while the rest (e.g., 75%) would be advance appropriated and become available three months later, on October 1, 2027. This combination of advance appropriations and forward funding would be appropriated each fiscal year to fund payments for the upcoming school year.
If this change were made during the FY2027 appropriations process without reducing the funding available each fiscal year, appropriations subject to the applicable FY2027 limits would be needed to fund both the 2026-2027 school year through budget year appropriations, as well as whatever percentage of the 2027-2028 school year was determined to be necessary through forward funding. The amount provided through forward funding could be set at any appropriate percentage of the total payment (e.g., 25%, 50%, 75%), with the remainder for the 2027-2028 school year being provided through advance appropriations. For example, if 25% of the funds were provided through forward funding and 75% were provided through advance appropriations, $1.846 billion would need to be provided in total appropriations for FY2027—$1.477 billion in budget year appropriations to support activities during the 2026-2027 school year and $369 million (25% of the budget year appropriations amount) for forward funding—and an additional $1.108 billion would need to be included as advance appropriations for FY2028 to support activities during the 2027-2028 school year.
This combination approach involves, to a lesser degree, the same budget process implications that apply to forward funding and advance appropriations. A combination approach would entail a one-time increase over the typical amount appropriated subject to the applicable limits but only for the portion of the funding for Section 7003(b) payments that was forward funded. Because that forward funded portion would be counted against any statutory or procedural limits on discretionary spending in the budget year, those additional appropriations during this transition period might need to be effectively offset by reductions elsewhere. In subsequent fiscal years, only the forward funding amount would need to be appropriated in the budget year, and the remainder could be advance appropriated. At the same time, any limits on advance appropriations established through a budget resolution would need to be altered to accommodate advance appropriations for the portion of Section 7003(b) payments funded in this way. As was previously mentioned, this transition period could also be addressed by enacting a provision specifying that a certain amount, such as the additional funding to effectuate that transition, is not to be counted for the purposes of budget enforcement.
Table 1 summarizes the key elements of current law and transitions to each of the three approaches discussed above. It is assumed that the alternative funding approaches would be applied in an annual FY2027 appropriations act. The table details how much discretionary funding would be needed in FY2027 and the level of advance appropriations for FY2028 that would need to be included in the FY2027 appropriations act, assuming the Section 7003(b) payment remains level funded at the FY2026 level. It is also assumed that regardless of the approach taken, the FY2027 appropriations act would provide level funding for Section 7003(b) payments for the 2026-2027 school year, as well as the 2027-2028 school year. For the combination approach, it assumes a distribution of 25% forward funding and 75% advance appropriations.

Title VII of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA, P.L. 89-10, as amended) authorizes several types of Impact Aid payments. These include payments made under Section 7002, Section 7003, Section 7007, and Section 7008. Each of these types of payments is discussed briefly below. In FY2026, a total of $1.630 billion was appropriated for Impact Aid.
Section 7002
Section 7002 compensates local educational agencies (LEAs) for the federal ownership of certain property. To qualify for compensation, the federal government must have acquired the property, in general, after 1938, and the assessed value of the land at the time it was acquired must have represented at least 10% of the assessed value of all of the LEA's real property. In FY2025, $79.0 million was appropriated for 200 LEAs, and payments ranged from $1,200 to $6.3 million.32 Payments are usually used by LEAs for general operating expenses (e.g., teacher salaries, books, supplies, and utilities), but funds may also be used for other expenses such as capital expenditures.33 For FY2026, appropriations were $80.0 million.
Section 7003
Section 7003 compensates LEAs for enrolling "federally connected" children. These are children who reside with a parent who is a member of the uniformed services living on or off federal property; reside with a parent who is an accredited foreign military officer living on federal property; reside on Indian lands; reside in low-rent public housing; or reside with a parent who is a civilian working or living on federal land.
Two payments are made under Section 7003. Section 7003(b) authorizes "Basic Support Payments" for federally connected children.34 In FY2025, $1.474 billion was appropriated for Section 7003(b). These funds were awarded to 932 LEAs, serving about 598,000 federally connected students.35 Payments ranged from $365 to $67.3 million. In FY2026, $1.477 billion was appropriated for Section 7003(b) payments.
Section 7003(d) authorizes additional payments to LEAs based on the number of certain federally connected children with disabilities who are eligible to receive services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). More specifically, payments are limited to certain IDEA-eligible children—those whose parents are members of the uniformed services (residing on or off federal property) and those residing on Indian lands. In FY2025, $48.3 million was appropriated for Section 7003(d) payments. Grants were made to 766 LEAs to serve about 49,000 eligible children. Grant amounts ranged from $567 to $1.3 million.36 Appropriations for FY2026 were $49.3 million.

CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Ronnie Lorenzo Robinson, Jr., 56, of Charlotte, appeared in federal court today and pleaded guilty to health care fraud for defrauding the North Carolina Medicaid out of hundreds of thousands of dollars by submitting claims for psychotherapy services that were never provided to recipients.

“Medicaid is for those who need medical care and cannot afford it, it is not a free pot of money to be exploited,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “We are working diligently with state and federal partners to aggressively pursue those who steal from the American taxpayer.”

“Healthcare fraud schemes drain taxpayer-funded government programs designed to help those in need and raise healthcare costs for all Americans. The FBI and our partners work diligently to hold criminals accountable who defraud the government and to protect the integrity of the programs for those who truly need them,” said FBI Charlotte Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis.

“After this defendant stole hundreds of thousands of Medicaid dollars, our Medicaid Investigations Division worked closely with U.S. Attorney Ferguson and other state and federal partners to get this guilty plea. We are going to go after every single instance of fraud and taxpayer theft,” said North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson.

According to plea documents, Robinson was the beneficial owner of a company called The Fisher of Men Project, LLC. As Robinson admitted in court today, he concealed his ownership of the company because he had previously been excluded from Medicaid and instead held out another individual as the owner of the company. During the scheme, Robinson obtained the personal identifying information of medical professionals and Medicaid recipients, then used that information to submit to Medicaid approximately $735,000 in false reimbursement claims for psychotherapy services, without the knowledge, authorization, or approval of those medical professionals or the Medicaid recipients. Court documents show that Robinson’s company received approximately $440,000 as payment from Medicaid as a result of the fraudulent reimbursement claims.

Robinson has been released on bond. The maximum penalty for the health care fraud offense is 10 years in prison. A sentencing date has not been set.

The FBI and the North Carolina Medicaid Investigations Division investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine Armstrong and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Kristina Fleisch of the Western District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Charlotte Man Pleads Guilty to Health Care Fraud for Stealing Hundreds of Thousands from the North Carolina Medicaid Program

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Ramon Emilio Sanchez, Jr., age 57, of Reading, PA, was indicted by a federal grand jury on bank robbery and attempted bank robbery charges.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, the indictment alleges that Sanchez attempted to rob the Mid Penn Bank located in Harrisburg, PA, on July 13, 2026. On that same date, it is alleged that Sanchez robbed the M & T Bank also in Harrisburg, PA.

The FBI Philadelphia’s Capital Area Resident Agency, Swatara Township Police Department, and the Harrisburg Street Crimes Unit investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Stephen W. Dukes is prosecuting the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

The maximum penalty under federal law for these offenses is 20 years of imprisonment, a term of supervised release following imprisonment, and a fine. A sentence following the finding of guilt is imposed by the Judge after consideration of the applicable federal sentencing statutes and the Federal Sentencing Guidelines.

Indictments are only allegations. All persons charged are presumed to be innocent unless and until found guilty in court.

CONGRESSMAN JOE MORELLE HONORS ROCHESTER STUDENT AZALEA DIETZ WITH CONGRESSIONAL AWARD GOLD MEDAL
Dietz receives Congress' highest honor for young civilians in recognition of her commitment to community service, personal growth, and achievement
(Rochester, N.Y.)—Today, Congressman Joe Morelle recognized Rochester student Azalea Dietz with the Congressional Award Gold Medal, the highest honor bestowed by the United States Congress upon young civilians. The prestigious award recognizes Dietz's exceptional dedication to community service, personal development, physical fitness, and exploration.
“Azalea represents the very best of the next generation of leaders in our community,” said Congressman Joe Morelle. “I am proud to recognize her achievements with this prestigious honor, and I hope her example inspires other young people across our community to get involved, pursue their passions, and discover the difference they can make.”
A student at Rochester's School of the Arts, Dietz has demonstrated a wide-ranging commitment to service and personal achievement. She volunteered at a local music and arts center, where she worked with children, assisted with summer camp activities, and supported the center's operations and photography needs. Her service also extended internationally to Portugal, where she volunteered at an animal rescue center caring for puppies and at a food bank packaging essential supplies for families in need. As part of her Congressional Award journey, Dietz planned and completed a five-day hiking expedition through the Adirondack Mountains alongside her mother and brother, tackling trails on Whiteface Mountain, Mount Jo, and Ampersand Mountain.
Established by Congress in 1979, the Congressional Award is a nonpartisan, voluntary, and noncompetitive program designed to encourage young Americans to set goals, challenge themselves, and make meaningful contributions to their communities. The program recognizes achievement in four areas: Voluntary Public Service, Personal Development, Physical Fitness, and Expedition/Exploration.
Young people interested in participating in the Congressional Award program are encouraged to contact Congressman Morelle's office to learn more about the program, eligibility requirements, and how to get started.

HOHENFELS, Germany – Markt Hohenfels hosted U.S. Army Garrison Bavaria, Joint Multinational Readiness Center, and other organization leadership and leaders from local communities for the Community Connector Oct. 8, 2026 at Markt Hohenfels, Germany.
The recurring event was a forum for exchanging information about the installation and military activities taking place thereon; the event was also an opportunity for the host nation and military leaders to get to know each other better.
The event took place in the town’s culture center, the windows of which look out over Hohenfels and the high cliffs of its namesake.
Christian Graf, mayor of Markt Hohenfels, welcomed the guests, telling them it was good to meet since there were so many new leaders present. This was the first community connector to take place since both the German elections in March and the summer permanent change of station season.
After he spoke, Graf introduced the deputy garrison manager for Hohenfels Angela Lane.
“Your presence highlights our shared commitment to strengthening bonds between our communities,” Lane said. “Our daily cooperation is a foundation of our strong partnership and cultural ties. True partnership rises from open communication. If any concerns or misunderstandings arise, please bring them to our attention immediately so we can address and resolve them together.”
Col. Adam Latham, commander of the operations group for JMRC, followed Lane during the opening remarks.
“I look forward to this opportunity to get to know you a little better, to understand our relationship,” he said.
Latham also offered the local leaders a glimpse into the busy training schedule JMRC has in the coming seasons. He also detailed the warfighting innovations JMRC was implementing as part of its thorough training program.
“Part of our responsibility is preparing both U.S. forces and members of the Alliance to win in the first fight of their next war,” Latham said. “It’s important that we leverage cutting-edge technology.”
The mayors received briefings on construction projects, housing occupation rates, upcoming events of interest to the community leaders, and information on the airspace boundaries.
Following the presentation and a question-and-answer session, Lane thanked the attendees.
“I just truly appreciate the attendance and the dialogue that we have, which keeps our communications transparent and our partnerships strong,” she said.
Graf, in a point to emphasize the decades of partnership between the cities and the training area, invited the attendees to take part in an exhibition and photographic lecture series about the long history of the training area. For more on that and other Markt Hohenfels events, visit the page here (external link, no endorsement implied, auf Deutsch).
The group assembled for a photograph outside and returned indoors to share lunch.
title: Community connector brings mayors, military leaders to Hohenfels

Rep. Costa Leads Bipartisan Push for Full Implementation of Graham Russia Sanctions Law
WASHINGTON – Today, Congressman Jim Costa (CA-21), a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, joined Co-Chairs of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus Representatives Mike Quigley (IL-05), Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01), and Joe Wilson (SC-02) in leading a bipartisan letter urging President Trump to fully implement the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
“As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war,” the lawmakers wrote. “Utilizing the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously.”
In the letter, the lawmakers urged the Administration to:
- Fully enforce mandatory sanctions against Russian officials, oligarchs, banks, state enterprises, and foreign entities helping Russia evade existing restrictions.
- Impose secondary tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy, targeting revenue from oil and gas sales that continues to finance Russia’s war.
- Crack down on sanctions evasion, including foreign financial institutions, shadow fleet operators, and intermediaries facilitating Russian energy transactions.
- Protect U.S. allies by applying exceptions and tariff adjustments for countries actively reducing their dependence on Russian energy.
- Strengthen congressional oversight by providing implementation details, tariff justifications, and measurable benchmarks to assess the effectiveness of sanctions.
The lawmakers emphasized that Russia continues to rely heavily on oil and gas exports to finance its military operations, while intensifying attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Black Sea, threatening global food security. The letter also calls on the Administration to reverse course in issuing general licenses that could reopen Russian energy transactions and restore revenue to the Kremlin. The lawmakers requested answers ahead of the October 18 deadline on which sanctions and tariffs will be implemented, whether any provisions will be delayed or waived, and how the Administration will measure their effectiveness.
The letter was signed by Don Bacon; Sanford Bishop; Salud Carbajal; Ed Case; Steve Cohen; Jim Costa; Danny Davis; Madeleine Dean; Brian Fitzpatrick; Jared Golden; Josh Gottheimer; Steny Hoyer; Marcy Kaptur; John Mannion; Michael McCaul; Robert Menendez; Dan Newhouse; Mike Quigley; Melanie Stansbury; Dina Titus; Jill Tokuda; and Joe Wilson.
The full text of the letter can be found HERE.
title: Rep. Costa Leads Bipartisan Push for Full Implementation of Graham Russia Sanctions Law

text:
MATSUI, LEADER SCHUMER, MARKEY, MENENDEZ, MENG LEAD COLLEAGES IN DEMANDING TRUMP FCC WITHDRAW PROPOSAL TO UNDERMINE E-RATE PROGRAM
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Doris Matsui (D-CA), Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), and Representatives Rob Menendez (D-NJ) and Grace Meng (D-NY), led nearly the entire Senate Democratic Caucus and more than 60 members of the House Democratic Caucus in urging Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr to withdraw the Commission’s damaging proposal to eliminate or limit the E-Rate program. In June, the Carr FCC voted to open a rulemaking examining E-Rate, which helps schools and libraries across the country afford reliable internet access.
For nearly 30 years, E-Rate has helped close the digital divide by ensuring that students and library patrons can access the internet regardless of their income or ZIP code. In 2025, E-Rate helped more than 158,000 schools and libraries pay recurring broadband bills, increase bandwidth, maintain secure internal Wi-Fi networks, and replace aging infrastructure. Ending or sharply curtailing E-Rate would impose severe costs on schools and libraries while weakening economic growth, undermining American technological leadership, and jeopardizing national security.
The E-Rate program has invested more than $69 billion to connect schools and libraries to the internet across the country. Massachusetts schools and libraries have received more than $950 million from the E-Rate program and another $97 million from the Emergency Connectivity Fund, a $7 billion program that Senator Markey created within the American Rescue Plan to provide devices and connectivity for students and educators at home.
In the letter, the lawmakers wrote, “Schools and libraries help develop the next generation of engineers, scientists, and cybersecurity professionals, including in communities that have historically lacked access to those opportunities. Cutting E-Rate would narrow that talent pipeline. Maintaining connectivity in every school and library is therefore an investment in America’s technological leadership, economic competitiveness, and national security.
The lawmakers continued, “We strongly support measures to protect children online and address concerns around excessive screen time. But cutting E-Rate is not a child-safety measure. E-Rate funds broadband connectivity — not laptops, tablets, applications, or online content — and recipients must already comply with the Children’s Internet Protection Act, including by using filtering and blocking tools, adopting internet-safety policies, and educating students about appropriate online behavior. States and local communities, meanwhile, are developing targeted policies governing when and how students use devices in schools — an appropriate way to address screen-time concerns, rather than cutting broadband support. The Commission should not use child safety as a pretext to dismantle the secure, managed broadband infrastructure that schools and libraries need to educate students and help them navigate the digital world safely.”

DENTON, Texas – Preliminary Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs) are available for review by residents and business owners in the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma and in portions of the towns of Camargo, Leedey, Oakwood, Seiling, Taloga and Vici and the unincorporated areas of Dewey County, Oklahoma.
Property owners are encouraged to review the latest information to learn about local flood risks and potential future flood insurance requirements. Community residents can identify any concerns or questions about the information provided and participate in the appeal and comment periods for the maps.
This is Dewey County’s first complete set of digital FIRMs. These maps serve multiple purposes, including defining Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs). SFHAs are areas at high risk for flooding. Communities and residents can use the information to make informed decisions about building, development and flood insurance.
FEMA stresses that flooding can and does happen outside of the most vulnerable areas.
Review the preliminary flood maps by visiting the local floodplain administrator (FPA). A FEMA Map Specialist can help identify community FPAs. Specialists are available by telephone at 877-FEMA-MAP (877-336-2627) or by email at FEMA-FMIX@fema.dhs.gov.
The preliminary maps may also be viewed online:
- The Flood Map Changes Viewer at http://msc.fema.gov/fmcv
- FEMA Map Service Center at http://msc.fema.gov/portal
- The Base Level Engineering-to-FIRM Viewer at https://webapps.usgs.gov/fema/ble_firm
For more information about the flood maps:
- Use a live chat service about flood maps at floodmaps.fema.gov/fhm/fmx_main.html (just click on the “Live Chat Open” icon).
- Contact a FEMA Map Specialist by telephone at 877-FEMA-MAP (877-336-2627) or by email at FEMA-FMIX@fema.dhs.gov.
There are cost-saving options available for those newly mapped into a high-risk flood zone. Learn more about your flood insurance options by talking with your insurance agent or visiting floodsmart.gov.
title: Preliminary Flood Maps for Dewey County, Oklahoma Ready for Public View
