The order sustains the Commission’s May 21, 2026, order dismissing McKenzie Electric Cooperative, Inc.’s complaint alleging that Basin Electric Power Cooperative engaged in a loan transaction with the Rural Utilities Service in a manner inconsistent with the Federal Power Act. 
E-2 | North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Docket No. RR26-3-000
ORDER ACCEPTING 2027 BUSINESS PLANS AND BUDGETS
The order accepts the 2027 business plans and budgets for NERC, the six Regional Entities, and WIRAB and authorizes the issuance of billing invoices to fund their fiscal year 2027 operations. The order also grants limited waivers of the NERC Rules of Procedure to permit specified deposits into, withdrawals from, assessment stabilization reserves and approves WECC’s use of Peak Reliability Donation Reserves to fund a gas-electric interface study, AI projects, and data management projects. 
E-3 | IGS CTS, LLC, Docket Nos. EL26-84-000 and QF26-1177-001
ORDER GRANTING REQUEST FOR PARTIAL WAIVER
The order grants IGTS CTS, LLC’s request for partial waiver from the filing requirement in section 292.303(a)(3) of the Commission’s regulations applicable to small power production qualifying facilities during a non-compliance period, starting December 3, 2025, the date the facility began operations, and ending June 17, 2026, the date Petitioner filed a Form No. 556 for QF certification.
E-4 | FirstLight Power Management LLC, et al., Docket No. EC26-110-000
ORDER AUTHORIZING DISPOSITION OF JURISDICTIONAL FACILITIES AND ACQUISITION OF SECURITIES
The order finds the proposed transaction between FirstLight Power Management LLC, FirstLight CT Housatonic LLC, FirstLight MA Hydro LLC, and Northfield Mountain LLC and Hull Street Energy, LLC is consistent with the public interest. 
E-5 | PJM Interconnection LLC., Docket No. ER24-2045-005
ORDER ACCEPTING COMPLIANCE IN PART AND DIRECTING FURTHER COMPLIANCE
The order accepts in part, and rejects in part, the proposed revisions submitted by PJM to its Open Access Transmission Tariff to comply with the requirements of Order Nos. 2023 and 2023-A and the Commission’s order on compliance issued April 2026. The order also directs PJM to submit further compliance filings. 
E-6 | Mammoth Central LLC, Docket Nos.  ER26-2932-000 and TS26-6-000
ORDER ON REQUEST FOR WAIVERS
The order accepts in part, and dismisses in part, the request for temporary waivers of the Commission’s requirements to file an Open Access Transmission Tariff, to establish and maintain an Open Access Same-Time Information System, and to comply with the Commission’s Standards of Conduct. 
E-7 | Mammoth South LLC., Docket Nos. ER26-2949-000 and TS26-6-000
ORDER ON REQUEST FOR WAIVERS
The order accepts in part, and dismisses in part, the request for temporary waivers of the Commission’s requirements to file an Open Access Transmission Tariff, to establish and maintain an Open Access Same-Time Information System, and to comply with the Commission’s Standards of Conduct. 
E-8 | Lost Island Wind Energy, LLC, Docket No. ER26-3431-000
ORDER GRANTING WAIVER REQUEST
The order grants Lost Island Wind Energy, LLC’s (Lost Island) waiver request to allow a 24-month extension of the commercial operation deadline for its wind generating facility. Specifically, the order grants waiver of (1) section 4.4.4 of Attachment X of Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (MISO) Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff; and (2) Article 2.3.1 of the Generator Interconnection Agreement among Lost Island as interconnection customer, MidAmerican Energy Company as transmission owner, and MISO as transmission provider. 
E-9 | Deseret Generation & Transmission Coop., Inc., Docket No. ER26-3333-000
ORDER CONDITIONALLY ACCEPTING NOTICE OF CHANGE IN STATUS AND TARIFF REVISIONS
The order accepts Deseret Generation & Transmission Co-operative, Inc.’s (Deseret) notice of change in status and conditionally accepts its market-based rate tariff revisions. Deseret is authorized to participate in SPP West and EDAM at market-based rates on the condition that it: (1) offers its units that are participating in SPP West at or below each unit’s mitigated energy offer; (2) offer its units that are participating in EDAM into EDAM at or below each unit’s Default Energy Bid as defined in the California Independent System Operator Corporation tariff; and (3) submits compliance filings within 12 months of beginning participation in SPP West and nine months of beginning participation in EDAM. 
E-10 | Stony Creek Wind Farm, LLC, Docket No. ER23-2595-001 et al.
ORDER ON CONTESTED SETTLEMENT
The order approves Stony Creek Wind Farm, LLC’s settlement offer for Reactive Supply and Voltage Control from Generation Sources Service as that service is defined in Schedule 2 of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Open Access Transmission Tariff. 
E-11 | Conyers Renewable Power, LLC, Docket Nos. EL26-80-000 and QF14-355-003
ORDER GRANTING REQUEST FOR PARTIAL WAIVER AND ACCEPTING REFUND REPORT
The order grants Conyers Renewable Power, (Petitioner) a partial waiver from the filing requirements in section 292.303(a)(3) of the Commission’s regulations applicable to small power production qualifying facilities during a non-compliance period starting when a change in upstream ownership of the facility owned by Petitioner occurred on April 10, 2020, and ending when Petitioner filed a self-recertification of QF status for the facility on March 16, 2026. The order also accepts the Petitioner’s filed refund report.  
G-1 | Revisions to Oil Pipeline Regulations Pursuant to the Energy Policy Act of 1992, Docket No. RM93-11-004; Five-Year Review of the Oil Pipeline Index, Docket No. RM20-14-005
ORDER ON CLARIFICATION AND MOTION FOR STAY
The order clarifies the Commission’s November 20, 2025, order that granted certain oil pipelines remedial relief for the period from March 1, 2022, to September 17, 2024, following the reinstatement of the index level of Producer Price Index for Finished Goods (PPI-FG) plus 0.78% pursuant to Liquid Energy Pipeline Association v. FERC, 109 F.4th 543 (D.C. Cir. 2024). The order also denies a motion to stay the November 20, 2025, order pending judicial review. 
C-3 | Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC, Docket No. CP26-11-000
ORDER ISSUING CERTIFICATES
The order grants Columbia Gulf’s request for a certificate of public convenience and necessity authorizing it to construct and operate new natural gas pipeline facilities in Lincoln and Pulaski Counties, Kentucky. The project is designed to provide 260,000 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of firm transportation service to meet the needs of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.
C-4 | Louisiana LNG Infrastructure LLC and Driftwood Pipeline LLC, Docket Nos. CP26-537-000 and CP17-118-000 
ORDER AMENDING AUTHORIZATION AND VACATING IN PART CERTIFICATE OF PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY
The order grants Louisiana LNG Infrastructure LLC’s (Louisiana LNG) and Driftwood Pipeline LLC’s (Driftwood) June 1, 2026, request to  vacate the Commission’s Natural Gas Act (NGA) section 7 certificate authorizing Driftwood to construct and operate certain facilities and amend Louisiana LNG’s NGA section 3 authorization to include those same facilities as part of the company’s liquefied natural gas export facilities. The facilities consist of an interconnect and receipt meter station that would interconnect the Louisiana LNG facility with the Kinder Morgan Louisiana Pipeline LLC interstate natural gas pipeline system.

AUSTIN, TEXAS – On Thursday, October 15th, Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas), alongside Representatives Bennie G. Thompson (D-Miss.), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and five other members of Congress held a field hearing to investigate the numerous ICE shootings across Texas, including the recent shooting of Wilber Garcés-Pérez.

Representatives Greg Casar, Bennie G. Thompson, and Pramila Jayapal were joined by Representatives Troy A. Carter, Sr. (LA-02), Lou Correa (CA-46), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), and Al Green (TX-09).

The Members of Congress were joined by witnesses Ms. Rachel Reyes, mother of Ruben Ray Martinez, Kristin Etter, Director of Policy & Legal Services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, Carolina Rivera Nelson, Attorney at the ACLU of Texas, and Danny Woodward, Policy Attorney with Texas Civil Rights Project.

“Texas has become the epicenter of Trump’s deadly deportation machine, so we brought Members of Congress from across the country to Austin to see it firsthand,” said Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas). “ICE shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez, a DoorDash driver and a father, in the back then denied him medical care. They even tried to deport him so he could never speak the truth. Donald Trump’s ICE isn’t going after the worst of the worst — it’s gone after people like Wilber, who have no criminal record. We will fight to hold the perpetrators in this administration accountable, and not provide another dime in funding to this rogue agency.”

“Democrats came to Austin today to demand justice and accountability for Wilber Garcés-Pérez and the others that have been shot by immigration agents in Texas. If Republicans refuse to conduct any oversight of the Trump administration, we must do so in their place,” added Congressman Bennie G. Thompson. “What we heard today was powerful and informative. Make no mistake: we will do everything possible to hold this administration accountable for what it is doing. This violence, lawlessness, and chaos in our communities must end.”

“Twenty-five days ago, ICE agents in Austin, Texas shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez in the back. Instead of taking him to the hospital, they locked him up in a detention center and did not allow him to have surgery for 11 days. This is not the most recent shooting by ICE, and is one of nearly a dozen that we know of since Trump returned to office,” said Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal. “ICE is a lawless, rogue agency that is causing generational trauma in communities across the country. House Democrats today are doing the oversight work that Republicans refuse to do — and we will continue to do everything possible to protect our communities from Trump’s mass deportation agenda.”

“The shooting and medical neglect of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez follows the many other cases that have become synonymous with cities being swarmed with masked, armed federal agents and the nation’s dangerous descent into tyranny: Renée Nicole Good, Alex Pretti, Johan Sebastian Guerrero, and too many others. No life is meaningless, and each individual assaulted or killed by our immigration system is someone’s child, someone’s sibling, someone’s parent, and they all still belong here with us,” said Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. “Unless you’re Native American, we all come from somewhere else. The Trump immigration system is structured and staffed as a deportation machine that violates individuals’ constitutional rights. Democrats will fight for an immigration system that honors our history and sets forth a reasonable, compassionate path to citizenship.”

“President Trump got elected on the promise to go after the “worst of the worst.” Instead, since January, federal immigration agents have detained over 500 U.S. citizens and killed at least three. ICE is arresting people with no criminal record to hit political quotas while cutting training and lowering hiring standards,” said Congressman Lou Correa. “There is an urgent need for major reforms to keep our communities safe from violence. DHS was created to defend Americans against foreign terrorists. Instead, we have permanent residents and American citizens being shot by ICE agents in our streets.”

“In Texas, we have witnessed at least three ICE shootings since this administration began its aggressive, unprecedented enforcement actions,” said Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher. “People across our community in Houston are still reeling from the shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Just last weekend, ICE agents ran over and gravely injured Miguel Parra Hernandez while pursuing someone else. ICE’s reckless and brutal actions are not only unprecedented, they’re unconstitutional. They are making us less safe, creating fear and danger for immigrants and citizens alike. This Republican-led Congress that has enabled this lawlessness has utterly failed Wilber Garcés-Pérez, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Ruben Ray Martinez, and so many others. All Americans deserve better from our government, and that is why I joined Congressman Casar, Ranking Member Thompson, Congresswoman Jayapal, and my Democratic colleagues in Austin today to hear from some of the many people impacted, learn more, and demonstrate our commitment to bringing justice, accountability, and change.”

“Trump promised to go after the worst of the worst. But judging by what we’re seeing across Texas and the country, that sounds more like ICE’s recruitment strategy. People are being shot, injured, and killed by federal agents operating without basic law enforcement standards or accountability,” said Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia. “In Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed on his way to work. One hundred days later, his family still has no answers. Instead they’ve been met with stonewalling and excuses. These families deserve the truth and justice, and we will not stop fighting until they get both.

“No President is above the law, and no federal agency should be allowed to serve as judge, jury, prosecutor, and executioner while operating with impunity,” said Congressman Al Green. “Under President Trump, ICE has been emboldened to use deadly force against people in our communities while the administration evades transparency and accountability, engaging in a cover-up. These shootings are not isolated incidents. They are part of a deeply troubling pattern of conduct that threatens the constitutional rights and lives of people in this country.”

The Members of Congress’ full remarks can be found here.
title: Members of Congress Hold Hearing in Austin to Investigate ICE Shootings Across Texas

The Federal Trade Commission is sending payments totaling more than $9.8 million to consumers harmed by Walmart’s alleged failure to stop scammers that took hundreds of millions of dollars from U.S. consumers using the company’s wire transfer services.
In June 2025, Walmart settled FTC charges that the company failed to implement effective anti-fraud policies and procedures, did not properly train its employees and failed to warn customers about potential fraud related to money transfers, according to the complaint.
Under the settlement terms, Walmart is required to take appropriate actions to effectively detect and prevent fraud-induced money transfers.
The FTC is sending checks to 65,022 affected consumers. Recipients should cash their checks within 90 days, as indicated on the check.
Consumers who have questions about their payment should contact the refund administrator, Rust Consulting Inc., at 1-833-472-1990, or visit the FTC website to view frequently asked questions about the redress process. The Commission never requires people to pay money or provide account information to get a payment.
The Commission’s interactive dashboards for redress data provide by state-by-state breakdown of redress in FTC cases. In 2025, FTC actions led to more than $435 million in redress to consumers across the country.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: FTC Sends More than $9.8 Million to Consumers Harmed by Walmart’s Failure to Stop Scammers that Used its Wire Transfer Services to Take Millions from Customers

COLUMBUS, Ohio – An illegal alien from Mexico pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court today to illegally reentering the United States after previously being convicted of a felony crime.

Jamie Cruz-Bobadilla, 42, was previously convicted of cocaine trafficking crimes.

According to court documents, Columbus police officers encountered Cruz-Bobadilla in February 2025 during a traffic stop. The defendant provided officers a false identity, but his true identity was confirmed via fingerprints and immigration photos.

Cruz-Bobadilla was in the United States illegally after being deported in 2012 following a prison term. In spring 2012, Cruz-Bobadilla was convicted in Wake County, North Carolina, of four felonies related to cocaine trafficking.

Illegally reentering the United States after being convicted of a felony is a federal crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the Court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors at a future hearing.

Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio; Jeremy Pierczynski, Acting Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit; and Columbus Police Chief Elaine Bryant announced the guilty plea entered before U.S. District Judge Michael H. Watson. Assistant United States Attorney Kevin W. Kelley is representing the United States in this case.

# # #
title: Mexican illegal alien with prior cocaine trafficking convictions pleads guilty to illegally reentering United States

FORT CUSTER TRAINING CENTER, Mich. — Three Illinois Army National Guard Soldiers earned prestigious Army expert skill badges (ESB) Oct. 9 during a demanding multistate assessment at Fort Custer Training Center, demonstrating the technical proficiency, discipline and determination required to meet the Army’s rigorous individual performance standards.
The Soldiers were among 26 candidates who successfully completed the assessment out of 169 participants, an overall success rate of approximately 15%. Hosted by the Michigan National Guard, the event marked the first time a National Guard state hosted all three Army expert badge assessments simultaneously.
Command Sgt. Maj. Michael Kelly, state command sergeant major of the Illinois Army National Guard, said the assessment reinforced the importance of mastering fundamental Soldier skills and maintaining the technical and tactical proficiency required for battlefield success.
“We often talk about the importance of being brilliant at the basics, and the E3B competition is a true demonstration of what that means,” Kelly said. “Whether Soldiers are pursuing the Expert Infantryman Badge, Expert Soldier Badge, or Expert Field Medical Badge, this event challenges them to demonstrate their proficiency in the fundamental skills that are essential to success on the battlefield.”
Known collectively as E3B, the Expert Infantryman Badge, Expert Soldier Badge and Expert Field Medical Badge assessments evaluate Soldiers on essential military tasks, including weapons proficiency, land navigation, medical procedures and physical endurance. Candidates must complete a series of demanding events while maintaining accuracy and attention to detail under strict performance standards.
Brig. Gen. Lenny Williams, assistant adjutant general – Army, Illinois National Guard, said the assessment gave Soldiers a chance to challenge themselves personally and professionally, whether they ultimately earned a badge.
“It’s about striving for excellence,” Williams said. “Whether they made it or didn’t make it, the training they got here was exceptional.”
Of the 22 Illinois Army National Guard Soldiers who participated, three earned their respective badges. Williams said those who did not successfully complete the assessment still gained valuable training and experience they could bring back to their home units.
“What I told all of them is, go back home and pay that forward,” Williams said.
Sgt. Maj. Christopher Winling, Illinois Army National Guard operations, plans and training sergeant major, helped lead the assessment and said the event highlighted the importance of returning to fundamental Soldier skills, regardless of rank or years of military service.
“It is harder for those that have been in the military longer because we have bad habits and we get away from the basics,” Winling said.
Winling recalled failing his first attempt to earn the Expert Infantryman Badge early in his military career before returning and successfully earning it as a private first class.
“So it took me two tries,” Winling said.
He said the experience helped shape his military career and reinforced the importance of perseverance, attention to detail and maintaining proficiency in fundamental military tasks.
Kelly emphasized that the value of the assessment extends beyond earning a badge, particularly as the Army prepares Soldiers for increasingly complex operational environments.
“These assessments go beyond earning a badge,” Kelly said. “They reinforce the importance of mastering individual Soldier skills, building confidence, and developing the technical and tactical proficiency necessary to operate effectively in a large-scale combat operations environment.”
The three Illinois Soldiers who successfully completed the assessment were Maj. Jonathan Logeman of Rockford, Illinois, who earned the Expert Infantryman Badge; Staff Sgt. Elijah Harlan of Marion, Illinois, who earned the Expert Soldier Badge; and Staff Sgt. Bill Warszewik of Elk Grove Village, Illinois, who earned the Expert Field Medical Badge.
For Logeman, an infantry officer assigned to the 1st Battalion, 178th Infantry Regiment, the opportunity represented a challenge unlike anything he had encountered in more than a decade of military service.
A civilian high school teacher, Logeman said participating required stepping away from his family and civilian responsibilities for two weeks. Despite those challenges, he recognized the assessment as a rare opportunity to test himself against the Army’s expert standards.
“For me, 90% of the time I was here, I thought I was going to fail,” Logeman said.
Logeman said the assessment proved considerably more demanding than he anticipated, requiring candidates to demonstrate technical proficiency and maintain attention to detail while completing complex tasks under strict time constraints.
“You’re not going to grow unless you challenge yourself,” Logeman said.
He emphasized that while earning an expert badge requires individual performance, the encouragement and support of fellow Soldiers played an important role in helping candidates succeed.
“It’s definitely a team event,” Logeman said. “But you have to accomplish all the events individually.”
Harlan, a chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear specialist assigned to the 445th Chemical Company in Shiloh, Illinois, shared a similar perspective.
Harlan said the assessment required Soldiers to perform approximately 30 individual tasks, often involving complex procedures that had to be executed in the correct sequence and within demanding time limits.
“It was definitely brutal,” Harlan said.
He identified call-for-fire procedures, the Mk 19 grenade launcher and the nine-line medical evacuation request as some of the most challenging tasks because of their technical requirements and strict time constraints.
Despite the individual nature of the assessment, Harlan credited his fellow Soldiers with helping him prepare and ultimately succeed.
“I didn’t get through this by myself,” Harlan said.
Harlan said several of the Soldiers who helped him study and practice did not earn their badges, but their encouragement and willingness to share knowledge contributed to his success.
Warszewik, assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Company, 766th Engineer Battalion, based in Decatur, Illinois, said the assessment challenged him to revisit fundamental Soldier skills and perform them according to precise Army standards.
A nine-year military veteran and civilian police officer who has deployed to Afghanistan and Somalia, Warszewik described the experience as a demanding test of his military knowledge and experience.
“I told General Williams ... for me, it was like a midcareer gut check,” Warszewik said.
Warszewik identified land navigation and tactical combat casualty care as particularly challenging, along with the volume of information candidates were required to learn and retain throughout the assessment.
He said instructors repeatedly encouraged candidates to focus on the next task rather than becoming overwhelmed by the number of remaining events.
For Williams, the experiences of Soldiers such as Logeman, Harlan and Warszewik illustrate why the Illinois Army National Guard intends to continue encouraging participation in demanding professional development opportunities.
Williams said many Soldiers who did not earn their badges were eliminated because of relatively minor mistakes, despite demonstrating considerable skill and determination throughout the assessment.
He said those Soldiers remain motivated to return and attempt the assessment again, and the Illinois Army National Guard intends to support their efforts.
“They’ll be back and we’re going to support them,” Williams said.
Winling echoed that commitment, emphasizing the success of the partnership between the Michigan and Illinois National Guards in executing the combined assessment.
Michigan’s established training facilities and the experience gained by participating cadre provide a foundation for future events, he said.
“Illinois will continue to help resource and participate through cadre and board members and candidates in Michigan,” Winling said.
The training also provides benefits beyond earning a badge, particularly as Soldiers return to their home units with improved technical skills and firsthand experience performing tasks under pressure.
Logeman said he would welcome the opportunity to return as an experienced badge holder and help other Illinois Soldiers prepare for future assessments.
“Any Soldier who makes it through this is a much better Soldier today than they were two weeks ago,” Logeman said.
Kelly praised the Illinois Soldiers who volunteered to participate and the Michigan National Guard for hosting the event.
“I’m extremely proud of our Illinois Army National Guard Soldiers who stepped forward to challenge themselves and compete at this level,” Kelly said. “Their willingness to test their abilities against such demanding standards speaks volumes about their commitment to excellence and readiness.”
Williams said the physical and mental challenges of E3B help prepare Soldiers for the pressures they may encounter during real-world military operations.
“These Soldiers are going to be way better and more prepared if they have to go do their job for real,” Williams said.
As the Illinois Army National Guard looks toward future opportunities to participate in E3B, senior leaders hope this year’s candidates' experiences will encourage more Soldiers to challenge themselves, strengthen their individual proficiency and pursue excellence throughout their military careers.
title: Three Illinois Guard Soldiers earn Army expert skill badges

CHARLOTTE, N.C. – A Statesville, N.C., man appeared in federal court today and pleaded guilty to federal charges for breeding, advertising, and selling pit bulls for illegal dog fighting and related offenses, announced Russ Ferguson, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of North Carolina. Juelz Christopher Daniels, 19, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Animal Welfare Act, possession, training, and sale of fighting dogs, and advertising fighting dogs for sale on Facebook.

According to plea documents, from January 2021 to May 2026, Daniels and his co-defendant, Reginald Lionel Goodson, bred, trained and sold pit bull-type dogs intended for dog fights and operated one or more dog kennels for the purpose of raising pit bull-type dogs for dog fighting. Daniels also posted advertisements for various pit bull-type dogs he bred and sold on multiple Facebook Groups dedicated to illegal dog fighting and to various individuals via Facebook Messenger, knowing that at least some of the purchasers were using the animals to participate in dog fights. Law enforcement executed search warrants at three residences associated with Daniels and Goodson, where they rescued and seized 25 pit bull-type dogs, including puppies, as well as other items, tools, and paraphernalia associated with breeding and training animals for dog fighting.

Daniels is in federal custody. A sentencing date has not been set. The charges against Goodson are still pending.

In making today’s announcement, U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson credited the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Office of Inspector General, the Iredell County Sheriff’s Office, the Burke County Sheriff’s Office, the Catawba County Sheriff’s Office, the Caldwell County Sheriff’s Office, and the Hickory Police Department for their investigation and assistance in this case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine Armstrong of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Charlotte is prosecuting the case.

To report animal fighting crimes, please contact your local law enforcement or the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Office of Inspector General complaint hotline at 1-800-424-9121 or online at https://usdaoig.oversight.gov/hotline .
title: Statesville Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Dog Fighting Charges

The Federal Trade Commission sued REPS & Company Inc., alleging the ticket broker illegally circumvents measures designed to limit the number of tickets that can be purchased for a single event, purchasing millions of tickets to high-demand events that it later resells at a significant profit.
The complaint, filed by the Department of Justice upon notification and referral from the FTC, alleges REPS, along with its CEO Ryan Pancheri, President Brian Archibald and Chief Operating Officer Nicholas Totagrande, violated the Better Online Ticket Sales Act. The law makes it illegal to “circumvent a security measure, access control system or other technological control or measure on an Internet website or online service that is used by the ticket issuer to enforce posted event ticket limits or to maintain the integrity of posted online ticket purchasing order rules.”
The complaint alleges that, since 2022, REPS and its operators used a variety of unlawful tactics to bypass security measures from ticket issuers in order to exceed ticket limits set by ticket issuers. REPS purchased more than eight tickets for at least 83,500 events—many of which were high demand and likely to sell out. REPS spent more than $1.3 billion to amass more than 18.5 million tickets for these events, generating at least $120.8 million in profit by reselling these tickets on the secondary marketplace. For example, REPS generated $833,000 in profit by using 1,300 accounts to purchase 7,624 tickets to just one Beyonce Renaissance tour concert in Kansas City, Mo., in 2023, according to the complaint.
“REPS’ entire business model is focused on trying to game the ticket-purchasing system in order to obtain as many tickets as possible to resell at inflated prices to consumers,” said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Companies that seek to profit by driving up prices or depriving ordinary fans of access to reasonably priced tickets to their favorite shows or events should be on notice that we are watching and will take action to stop this unlawful conduct.”
Ticket issuers such as Ticketmaster and AXS have put in place measures to block resellers from violating ticket-purchasing limits to popular events. These security measures include ticket quantity selectors capped at the ticket-purchasing limit and monitoring whether purchases are associated with verifiable accounts and unique credit cards, email addresses, phone numbers and IP addresses, according to the complaint.
The complaint alleges that REPS uses a team of employees, most of whom are based in the Philippines, who use unlawful methods to bypass Ticketmaster and other ticket-issuer account security measures. These unlawful methods include using thousands of ticket-purchasing accounts created with names, addresses or phone numbers belonging to someone other than the ticket purchaser and virtual credit card accounts and phone numbers controlled by REPS. In addition, they also used IP proxy services and multi-session browsers that mask the identity and location of the account user, the complaint alleges.
For example, REPS has agreements with its employees and third-party partners authorizing the company to use their names and addresses to establish accounts with ticket issuers to create multiple accounts that are used to help purchase tickets, according to the complaint.
When ticket issuers detect attempts to bypass ticket limits, the issuers often block or cancel the ticket purchase. In response, REPS has developed strategies to help its employees work around these ticket limit controls, such as making slight changes to an account holder’s address or name, the complaint alleges. In fact, internal company documents show that REPS officials discussed tactics to ensure their accounts won’t be blocked by ticket issuers.
The Commission vote to refer the complaint to the DOJ for filing was 2-0. The Department of Justice filed the complaint on behalf of the Commission in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California.
NOTE: The Commission refers a complaint for civil penalties to the DOJ for filing when it has “reason to believe” that the named defendants are violating or are about to violate the law and that a proceeding is in the public interest. The case will be decided by the court.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: FTC Sues Ticket Broker Over Unlawful Tactics Used to Buy Millions of Tickets to Popular Live Events

Sánchez, Sewell lead 55 Democrats in opposing U.S. Withdrawal from International Labor Organization
ILO withdrawal would weaken international labor standards, undercut American workers
WASHINGTON – Ways and Means Trade Subcommittee Ranking Member Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.) and Oversight Subcommittee Ranking Member Terri Sewell (D-Ala.) today led 55 of their House Democratic colleagues in calling on the Trump administration to maintain United States participation in the International Labor Organization (ILO), which brings together governments, workers and employers to establish international labor standards. Those standards help protect American workers from being undercut by other countries with weaker labor standards.
Reports that the administration is considering withdrawal come amid a severe budget crisis at the ILO, driven largely by the Trump administration’s failure to pay approximately $300 million in outstanding U.S. membership dues.
“At the same time that the Administration has called on countries to improve labor standards, it is reportedly considering a withdrawal from the very institution that develops those standards and helps governments implement them,” the members wrote. “Notably, USTR relied on ILO data in conducting [its Section 301] investigations, underscoring the organization’s value to U.S. efforts to identify and combat forced labor.
“If the Administration believes that weak labor standards distort trade and disadvantage American workers and firms, withdrawing from an institution whose standards, research, and expertise it relies upon to address those concerns runs counter to American interests.”
In addition to Sánchez and Sewell, the letter was signed by Representatives Gabe Amo (D-R.I.), Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.), Donald Beyer (D-Va.), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), Danny Davis (D-Ill.), Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.), Christopher Deluzio (D-Pa.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), Dwight Evans (D-Pa.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Val Hoyle (D-Ore.), Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), William Keating (D-Mass.), Robin Kelly (D-Ill.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Greg Landsman (D-Ohio), John Larson (D-Conn.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), John Mannion (D-N.Y.), Morgan McGarvey (D-Ky.), James McGovern (D-Mass.), Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), Gwen Moore (D-Wis.), Richard Neal (D-Mass.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), Stacey Plaskett (D-V.I.), Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), Nellie Pou (D-N.J.), Emily Randall (D-Wash.), Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.), Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.), Robert Scott (D-Va.), Terri Sewell (D-Ala.), Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.), Thomas Suozzi (D-N.Y.), Mike Thompson (D-Calif.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.), Norma Torres (D-Calif.), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) and Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.).
The full text of the letter is available HERE and follows:
October 15, 2026
Secretary Rubio
U.S. Department of State
2201 C Street NW
Washington, D.C. 20520
Dear Secretary Rubio:
We write to express our deep concern regarding reports that the Administration is preparing to withdraw the United States from the International Labor Organization (ILO). Such a decision would undermine the organization’s core mission of establishing and promoting international labor standards in the global economy and would be difficult to reconcile with the Administration’s stated pro-worker trade agenda. These reports come amid a severe budget crisis at the ILO, which is largely due to the Administration’s failure to pay approximately $300 million in outstanding U.S. membership dues. Unlike most international organizations, the ILO’s unique tripartite structure gives governments, workers, and employers the central role of developing international labor standards to combat the global “race to the bottom” that has undermined wages and working conditions here in the United States and around the globe.
The labor standards developed and articulated by the constituents of the ILO underpin the labor provisions in U.S. trade agreements, which require trading partners to adopt, maintain, and effectively enforce labor laws related to eliminating forced labor, child labor, and employment discrimination, while also protecting workers’ fundamental right to organize unions and bargain collectively. Such obligations are vital to levelling the playing field by preventing other countries from gaining an unfair advantage through common forms of labor exploitation. But negotiated commitments are only as effective as the institutions that implement them. For decades, the ILO has helped governments put these commitments into practice through technical assistance, training, advisory services, reporting, investigations, and capacity-building support to labor inspectorates.
Several U.S. trading partners have reportedly sought ILO assistance in response to the Administration’s recent imposition of Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to impose or effectively enforce prohibitions on imports produced with forced labor. Other partners have sought to extend ILO programming that is a key U.S. trade condition for access to the U.S. market. Yet, at the same time that the Administration has called on countries to improve labor standards, it is reportedly considering a withdrawal from the very institution that develops those standards and helps governments implement them. Notably, USTR relied on ILO data in conducting these investigations, underscoring the organization’s value to U.S. efforts to identify and combat forced labor. If the Administration believes that weak labor standards distort trade and disadvantage American workers and firms, withdrawing from an institution whose standards, research, and expertise it relies upon to address those concerns runs counter to American interests.
The ILO’s value extends beyond government enforcement and directly benefits American companies operating in global supply chains. Through programs such as Better Work, a joint initiative of the ILO and the International Finance Corporation, factories receive auditing, training, and support to improve compliance with national laws and international labor standards. Improved transparency at the factory level enables companies to identify risks in their supply chains, address problems before they become more serious, and avoid reputational damage through responsible sourcing practices. The American Apparel & Footwear Association and other U.S. business organizations recently highlighted the important role of the ILO in strengthening labor enforcement in sourcing countries, addressing forced labor, and maintaining a competitive environment for American companies and workers.
The ILO’s role in advancing U.S. trade policy is well illustrated in Haiti, where U.S. law ties preferential market access to labor law compliance and integrates the ILO into that statutory framework. In September, Congress reauthorized the Haitian Hemispheric Opportunity through Partnership Encouragement Act (HOPE) and the Haiti Economic Lift Program Act (HELP). Under these programs, Haiti is mandated to work with the ILO to implement the Technical Assistance Improvement and Compliance Needs Assessment and Remediation (TAICNAR) program. The ILO’s Better Work program in Haiti operates the core compliance component of TAICNAR, conducting factory assessments, supporting remediation, and providing technical assistance to strengthen industrial relations and labor law enforcement. If the ILO is unable to continue performing these functions, Haiti will be unable to meet the labor compliance requirements Congress established as a condition of these trade preferences—programs that continue to enjoy strong bipartisan support.
Finally, the United States withdrawal from the ILO will only serve to expand China’s influence at the organization and deprive us of a key forum for holding them accountable for systemic labor rights violations. For example, in 2022 the United States delegation to the ILO’s annual conference played a decisive role in rallying support from governments, workers, and employers to condemn China’s use of forced labor camps to “re-educate” Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR). A U.S. withdrawal will not halt the development of international labor standards; rather, it will strip American policymakers, workers, and employers of their ability to shape their creation and implementation in a manner that reflects our values. Walking away cedes strategic leverage to a major economic competitor over the very rules that govern fair competition in the global marketplace. This exposure is particularly critical as the ILO facilitates the development of standards for emerging issues, including the platform economy, artificial intelligence, and workplace health and safety. American workers and companies will ultimately be impacted by these international standards, regardless of whether the United States chooses to participate in their creation.
Accordingly, we urge the Administration to maintain full United States membership in the ILO and utilize appropriated Contributions to International Organizations (CIO) funds to expeditiously pay the approximately $300 million in arrears. Abandoning the ILO does not protect American interests. Instead, it diminishes our ability to enforce trade agreements, taints our supply chains, and hands a strategic victory to our economic competitors. The United States must maintain its seat at the table to ensure that global labor standards are driven by American values, interests, and priorities.
To assist Congress in monitoring the implementation of U.S. trade policy and funding mandates, please provide comprehensive responses to the following questions by October 30, 2026:
- Given the Administration’s extensive reliance on ILO data to execute recent Section 301 tariff enforcement actions, what concrete steps is the Department of State taking to ensure the ILO remains fully funded and operationally viable so that U.S. trade enforcement mechanisms are not compromised?
- Because Congress has explicitly tied preferential market access for Haiti to the execution of the TAICNAR program, what immediate actions is the Department taking to ensure that the U.S. remains fully engaged in the ILO framework so as not to jeopardize the legal compliance of these congressional trade preferences?
- In alignment with the 2025 National Security Strategy’s mandate to protect American workers from foreign economic distortion, what is the Department’s explicit plan to utilize the United States' permanent seat on the ILO Governing Body to actively counter China's expanding influence over global standard-setting?
- Out of funds appropriated by Congress under the CIO account for Fiscal Years 2024, 2025, and 2026, what is the exact timeline for the Department to release the necessary funds to clear the outstanding $300 million in arrears and stabilize U.S. standing and voting rights within the organization?
###
title: Sánchez, Sewell lead 55 Democrats in opposing U.S. Withdrawal from International Labor Organization

KANSAS CITY, KAN. — The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Kansas (USAO-KS) is proud to join the U.S. Department of Justice, the Office on Violence Against Women (OVW), and communities across the country in observing Domestic Violence Awareness Month (DVAM) this October. We reaffirm our dedication to using every available resource and building strategic partnerships with local law enforcement, fellow prosecutors, and victim service organizations to ensure justice, safety, and healing for victims.

“As a society, we must rid ourselves of the dangerous belief that domestic violence is a private family matter. These volatile situations threaten not only victims but also relatives, friends, neighbors, and the law enforcement officers who respond,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “According to the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, in 2025 alone, 97 Kansas police officers were injured and two were killed while responding to domestic violence calls. These tragedies underscore the profound impact this crime has on our entire community.”

Each year, DVAM gives us an opportunity to focus on our collective responsibility to address domestic violence and emphasize the importance of collective action.

Domestic violence-focused collaborations with local organizations, including law enforcement, prosecutors, victim service providers, healthcare providers, etc.

OVW grant funding to local organizations, including Tribes and law enforcement–reach out to Erica Lacy for assistance, if needed.

U.S. Attorney’s role in enforcing federal laws related to domestic violence, including federal firearm prohibitions protecting victims of domestic violence.

USAO-KS employees donned purple clothing during the month of October. Purple symbolizes survivors who were hurt by physical and emotional abuse but still go on to thrive and live a life free of violence. By raising awareness about domestic violence during DVAM, we can bring everyone together to end the abuse. We encourage all who live in our jurisdiction to learn more about domestic violence and take meaningful action to support friends, family, co-workers, and neighbors who may be affected. Victims deserve safety, dignity, and justice. By understanding the signs of abuse and connecting victims to resources, we can all play a role in creating safer communities.

We are committed to prosecuting those who violate federal laws, collaborating with local law enforcement and prosecutors, and ensuring victims have access to the resources they need. Together, we can bring hope to those in need and build a future free from domestic violence. For more information on domestic violence or to access resources, please visit the OVW webpage on Domestic Violence .

The Department of Justice funds essential victim services through its grantmaking. Grantees of OVW and the Department’s Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) run programs that support victims in the aftermath of domestic violence. There is help available, including the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), and the Strong Hearts Native Helpline, 1-844-7NATIVE (762-8483). In addition, OVW’s Resources for Victims and Survivors webpage lists national hotlines as well as state, territorial, and Tribal domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions that provide resources and support.

###
title: USAO-KS wears purple for Domestic Violence Awareness Month

EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater
EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater
GAINESVILLE, Florida (Oct. 15, 2026) – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will hold an open house on Wednesday, Oct. 21 from 5 – 7 p.m. at the Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, 200 NW 23rd Avenue in Gainesville, Florida, to share an update on cleanup activities, including installation of a 5,300-foot wall extending 65 feet below ground to help prevent contaminated groundwater and soil from spreading.
Additional actions, planned in coordination with local, state, and federal partners, include:
- Replacing existing stormwater ditch with a new piping system configured to avoid the groundwater cut-off wall.
- Removing contaminated soil piles, surface soil, and ditch sediments from former Municipal Storage Yard and relocating them inside the cut-off wall.
Background
The Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site encompasses 140 acres in Gainesville, Florida. The Cabot portion of the site operated as a pine-tar products facility from 1910 until 1967 and has been redeveloped into commercial properties. Cleanup on this portion is mostly complete and includes a separate cut-off wall to prevent contaminated water and soil from leaking out. The Koppers site operated as a wood treatment facility from 1916 until 2009. This site is owned by Beazer East, Inc. and is undergoing cleanup. Under a consent decree with EPA, Beazer East has certain cleanup responsibilities for a portion of the site.
###
title: EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater

Congresswoman Dina Titus introduced legislation today to require the Department of Transportation to examine whether it can strengthen fuel efficiency requirements to counter high gas prices and reinstate penalties for automakers that fail to produce fuel-efficient vehicles.
“With gas prices skyrocketing because of President Trump’s prolonged and illegal war, we must take immediate steps to give American consumers some relief,” Congresswoman Titus said. “In May 2026, gas prices rose at a rate ten times higher than the rate of inflation. In Nevada, they now average $5.45 per gallon. Coupled with higher prices on groceries and other goods because of the Trump tariffs, families are struggling to make ends meet.”
Congresswoman Titus, a member of the House Transportation Committee. and co-sponsor Doris Matsui, (CA-7), a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the Gas Money Saved Act to review Corporate Fuel Economy (CAFÉ) standards and reinstate fuel-efficiency requirements that were stripped away by Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill in 2025. Companion legislation has been introduced in the Senate by Senator Ed Markey (D-MA).
“These giveaways to Big Oil and automakers worsened the pain at the pump and should not stand,” Congresswoman Titus said. 
“Fuel economy standards help American drivers get around without breaking the bank while gas prices are high, but Trump and the Republicans gutted these standards as part of their crusade to put Big Oil above American families,” said Senator Markey. “Auto innovation should give consumers better choices, not cut corners at their expense. The Gas Money Saved Act would make sure American drivers have fuel-efficient vehicle options that are cheaper to fill up and hold automakers to account—a cost-saving measure that is especially critical as the Trump Administration would rather spend billions on an illegal war than keep costs low for Americans.”
“Across the country, Americans are being squeezed by high gas prices, rising grocery bills, and everyday costs that keep stretching family budgets thinner,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “The Gas Money Saved Act meets people where they are by strengthening fuel efficiency standards that help drivers spend less on gas for years to come. This is a practical step to lower everyday costs, give families more breathing room, and build a cleaner, more efficient transportation future.”
The Gas Money Saved Act would:
    - Require DOT to reevaluate Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE)standards if gas prices rise at a rate five times faster than inflation over a six-month period, and;
- Restore and increase financial penalties on automakers if their car and truck fleet does not meet fuel efficiency standards.
###
title: Rep. Dina Titus Introduces Legislation to Protect Americans from High Costs at the Pump

ROCK ISLAND ARSENAL, Ill. — Excellence, discipline, and commitment to continuous improvement are qualities that define First Army's mission and its people. For First Army civilian Devin Daniels, those qualities propelled him onto the international stage.
Daniels, a First Army logistician, earned a runner-up finish in the heavyweight division at the Static Monsters World Championships in Phoenix on Sept. 20. Competing against some of the world's strongest athletes, Daniels placed second in his category with a combined total of 1,162 pounds in the log clean-and-press and 18-inch axle deadlift events. Among hundreds of athletes who entered preliminary online qualifying rounds, Daniels was one of only 10 competitors whose qualified for the championship finals.
His performance culminated with receiving the runner-up trophy from Mitchell Hooper, the reigning World's Strongest Man.
The achievement was the product of nearly 14 years of dedication to the sport.
"I got into strongman in 2012 in Las Vegas," Daniels said. "I started lifting pretty seriously. I was benching over 500 pounds. My strength came pretty quick. I didn't have anyone coaching me. I was just lifting."
After returning to eastern Iowa a few years later, Daniels became involved with a local community of strongman competitors and began regularly participating in events. Surrounded by experienced athletes, he developed a deeper appreciation for the sport and a more structured approach to training.
To prepare for competition, Daniels follows the conjugate method, a strength-training system that rotates exercises and varies training intensity to build overall power. While physical strength is essential, Daniels believes success in strongman competition depends just as much on developing the nervous system's ability to generate force.
"A 200-pound powerlifter might be stronger than a 350-pound bodybuilder," Daniels explained. "The bodybuilder is training higher reps and isolating muscles. The powerlifter is training for maximum strength and force production."
Daniels compares strength development to learning any demanding profession. Over time, the body adapts to repeated challenges, becoming stronger and more efficient through consistent effort and disciplined practice.
That mindset extends beyond competition. Daniels continues to train multiple times each week, carefully evaluating performance, adjusting techniques, and looking for opportunities to improve.
"I just get as strong as possible and let my natural athleticism and quick feet do their job," he said. "I'm very methodical and analytical with my training. I look at what I did right, what I did wrong, and every little detail I can improve."
While strongman athletes are often stereotyped as relying solely on physical ability, Daniels says success at the highest levels requires significant technical knowledge and critical thinking. Many competitors possess advanced academic and professional backgrounds and apply their understanding of anatomy, physiology, and kinesiology to refine their training and performance.
Balancing a demanding career, family responsibilities, farm work, and training can be challenging, but Daniels credits the strongman community for helping sustain his commitment to the sport.
"Strongman has been the greatest lifting group I've been with," Daniels said. "There's almost no ego. I've never been to a competition where your opponents weren't there cheering you on."
For First Army, Daniels' accomplishment reflects the same qualities that underpin the organization's mission: Commitment, resilience, teamwork, and the pursuit of excellence. Whether supporting readiness as a logistician or competing on the world stage, Daniels embodies the professionalism and dedication that strengthens First Army and contributes to a culture of excellence across the Total Force.
Partnership is our method. Readiness is our mission. People are our greatest strength. Daniels' achievement serves as a reminder that exceptional outcomes are built through discipline, continuous improvement, and a commitment to being stronger than yesterday.
title: First Army Strong: Civilian earns runner-up finish at international competition

Florida Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Opioid Distribution Conspiracy
A Miami, Florida man pleaded guilty yesterday for his role in a conspiracy to distribute over 87,000 oxycodone 30mg pills.
According to court documents and statements made in court, Jose Llerena, 49, of Miami, Florida, conspired with others, including Olushola Yusuf—a pharmacist and pharmacy owner convicted at trial earlier this year for illegally dispensing over 300,000 oxycodone 30mg pills—to illegally distribute oxycodone to individuals who had no medical need for the drug. Llerena was a “patient recruiter” who paid individuals to pose as patients and obtain illegal and unnecessary oxycodone prescriptions from South Florida clinics and doctors. Llerena then took his recruits and their illegal prescriptions to Yusuf’s pharmacies in order to get the pills. Yusuf kept a list of Llerena’s recruits at her pharmacy. Llerena paid Yusuf cash for the drug at above market value.
List Seized by Law Enforcement from Yusuf’s Pharmacy of Purported “Patients” Llerena Recruited to Illegally Obtain Oxycodone Pills
Llerena then paid his recruits, usually via Zelle, for the oxycodone pills before reselling the pills on the street. Llerena was personally responsible for distributing 3,735 oxycodone pills.
Llerena pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance. A sentencing date has not been set. Llerena faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; United States Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida; Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda Bennett; DEA Special Agent in Charge Miles Aley, Miami Field Division; and FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles made the announcement.
HHS-OIG, DEA, and FBI investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Angela Benoit of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Jacqueline DerOvanesian for the Southern District of Florida are prosecuting the case.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Item C-1 | Docket No. RM26-2-001 | Presentation
In a historic, unanimous vote, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) proposed accelerating liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure development through a landmark blanket authorization program. The proposal would streamline permitting, speed energy infrastructure development, and deliver unprecedented regulatory certainty for project developers.
In a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NOPR), FERC proposes to establish an LNG blanket authorization program to allow eligible activities at LNG facilities to proceed without case-specific authorization orders under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act. The program is modeled on the Commission’s successful 40-year blanket certificate program for interstate natural gas pipelines.
“American energy dominance requires us to build and maintain the energy infrastructure our country needs without unnecessary delay. I am immensely proud of FERC’s historic proposal. It shows what can be possible when we combine regulatory excellence, robust safeguards, and a firm commitment to the nation’s energy future. Consumers benefit when more energy infrastructure is online, dependable, and affordable, and FERC is helping make that future a reality.”—FERC Chairman Laura V. Swett
FERC is proposing a three-tiered authorization framework under which certain activities could proceed automatically, with periodic reporting, while others would require advance notice to the Commission. The proposed categories are as follows:
- Automatic authorization: Activities that would not increase an LNG plant’s authorized capacity, expand the authorized vertical or horizontal extents within the plant’s footprint, or cause flows, levels, volumes, pressures, temperatures, compositions, or loads to exceed applicable design limits.
- 60-day prior notice: Activities that may increase the plant’s authorized capacity but remain within the plant’s footprint and do not cause operating conditions to exceed the design limits of the affected or remaining facilities.
- 90-day prior notice: Construction of new LNG facilities—such as liquefaction trains, LNG tanks, and marine berths—and related auxiliary systems, including those located outside the plant’s footprint, subject to limitations on facility type, location, and size.
FERC’s NOPR also proposes standard environmental and engineering design conditions to address the potential impacts of projects approved under the blanket authorization program, as well as other requirements to ensure compliance with all applicable laws.
Interested parties will have 60 days after the NOPR is published in the Federal Register to submit comments.

title: FERC Takes Historic Action Launching First LNG Authorization Program

WASHINGTON — Marshall Morgan, 42, a previously convicted felon residing in the District of Columbia, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 34 months in prison in connection with illegally possessing a loaded Ruger P85 pistol while driving through the city accompanied by an infant and a four-year-old child in his car, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Morgan pleaded guilty on March 3, 2026, before Judge Carl J. Nichols to possession of a firearm and ammunition by felon. In addition to the 34-month prison sentence, Judge Nichols ordered Morgan to serve three years of supervised release. Federal prosecutors had requested a 52-month prison term.

According to court documents, at about 1:30 a.m. on Aug. 12, 2025, Metropolitan Police Department officers stopped a car for heavily tinted windows. Morgan, who was driving, did not have a valid driver's license. A woman with Morgan sat in the front passenger seat, and an infant and a four-year-old child sat in the back.

After arresting Morgan for driving without a license, officers searched the car and found a loaded Ruger P85 pistol under the driver's seat. The gun was loaded with one round in the chamber and 15 rounds in the magazine. Investigators found Morgan's DNA on both the pistol and the magazine. Officers also found about three grams of powder cocaine in Morgan's pocket.

Morgan was previously convicted in 2006 in Prince William County, Virginia, on a weapons count stemming from an armed bank robbery in Manassas. For that offense, he served eight years in prison. He also was convicted in 2017 in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, of possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance.

While released pending trial in this case, Morgan repeatedly violated his conditions of release. He missed curfews, tested positive for illicit substances, and traveled out of state without permission. In April 2026, the court revoked his release and he has been detained since then.

The Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Washington Field Office investigated the case.

The matter was prosecuted under the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful initiative by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Joshua Satter and Lauren Ibanez.

Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful is a law enforcement initiative in support of President Trump's Executive Order to crack down on gun violence, prioritize federal firearms violations, pursue tougher penalties, and seek detention for federal firearms violators.

Police found the Ruger P85 pistol under the driver's seat, with a round in the chamber and 15 rounds in the magazine. Morgan's DNA was later found on both the firearm and the magazine.

Bahamian charged with illegally voting in 2024 election
OCALA, Fla. — Bahamian national and U.S. lawful permanent resident, Terrance Patrick Evans, 37, has been charged by information with one count of voting by an alien. This charge was brought following an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tampa, the Florida Department of State’s Office of Election Crimes, and the Citrus County Supervisor of Elections.
President Trump and Secretary Mullin have made a promise to the American people that they will restore integrity to our elections. Election security is national security. The votes of American citizens should not be diluted by non-citizens illegally voting in U.S. elections. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.
The charge in this case is the result of the hard work of the men and women of ICE and its federal partners.
The investigation showed that Evans voted in the 2024 federal general election, despite knowing that he was not a citizen of the United States. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of up to one year in federal prison.
An information is merely a formal charge that a defendant has committed one or more violations of federal criminal law, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.
The case is being prosecuted by Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Jerry M. Harre.
title: Bahamian charged with illegally voting in 2024 election

Today, Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) and a bipartisan group of 73 members called on the House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental appropriations for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) for Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27). 
 
In the letter, led by New Hampshire Congressman Chris Pappas, the members wrote, “As the war with Iran remains unresolved, energy prices are expected to keep rising, with heating oil up 60% since February. LIHEAP’s $4 billion in funding for the last fiscal year would fall significantly short in meeting the needs of American families this fiscal year.”
 
“LIHEAP is a critical lifeline for low- and moderate-income individuals, but even if your household qualifies, LIHEAP does not provide guaranteed security. Five out of six families who qualify for LIHEAP receive no financial assistance due to the program’s woefully underfunded status. When adjusting for inflation, LIHEAP funding is lower now than it was in 1981 when the program was first created. If LIHEAP was funded at the same level as it was 45 years ago, the program would have received nearly $7 billion in FY27,” they continued.
 
“Emergency LIHEAP assistance is urgently needed as winter weather approaches and colder temperatures have already begun. Families should not have to choose between staying warm and purchasing other essential items like food, medication, or rent. Congress must act and not leave families in the cold,” they concluded. 
 
LIHEAP helps low-income individuals and families pay for heating and cooling and mitigates the impacts of rising energy costs and extreme weather events. Across the nation, LIHEAP helps nearly 6 million households afford their energy bills,including more than 45,000 households in Maine, but Secretary Kennedy’s decision last year to fire all LIHEAP staff last year and President Trump’s repeated demand to cut all funding for the program has put this assistance at risk. In response, Pingree and 89 of her Congressional colleagues in called for the protection of LIHEAP and the rehiring of all HHS staff who manage the LIHEAP program that were fired in April 2025. 
 
Last week, Pingree and a group of 24 Members of Congress representing Northeastern states pressed the Department of Energy (DOE) to take immediate action to address the rapidly rising cost of heating oil, which has surged around 60 percent since the start of President Trump’s war in Iran.
 
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed crude oil from $72 to over $100 a barrel, causing a massive increase in heating oil costs in the United States. American families that rely on heating oil are projected to pay about $600 more to keep their homes warm this winter than last year. In Maine, which uses more residential heating oil per capita than any other U.S. state, the statewide average price of heating oil recently hit a record $6.02 a gallon—marking an 80% increase over last year.
 
Pingree is a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee and has long fought to protect and fully fund LIHEAP. 
 
 
###
title: Pingree Joins Bipartisan Call to Increase Home Heating Assistance Funding

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — U.S. Army officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will host a public open house on Oct. 15th, to address upcoming safety operations to dispose of lead azide via controlled detonation on the installation in November.
The open house will take place from 4:30 to 6:30 p.m. CST at the Army Reserve Center in Middletown.
During a routine stockpile surveillance operation at the plant, technicians discovered a quantity of degraded lead azide, a highly sensitive primary explosive, that has potentially become unstable. Because transporting the material off-site poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, the Army determined that the safest course of action is to neutralize the material on-site via an intentional, controlled detonation. Specialized explosive ordnance disposal personnel will execute the operation in compliance with the regulations set by the Environmental Protection Agency.
"Our absolute top priority is the safety of the surrounding community and our workforce," said Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, IAAAP installation commander. "By taking proactive, deliberate action to neutralize this material in place, we are permanently eliminating a critical hazard under the most stringent and highly monitored safety conditions possible."
Comprehensive Environmental and Blast Mitigations
The Army is establishing rigorous safety protocols to monitor and minimize the environmental and physical impacts of the planned detonation:
Environmental Monitoring: Specialized teams will conduct air and soil testing before, during, and after the detonation.
Groundwater: After the hazard is neutralized, environmental teams will assess the area and take action according to environmental regulations.
Atmospheric Controls: The detonation will occur strictly during daylight hours under favorable weather conditions. Operations will be delayed if there is low cloud cover to prevent magnification of acoustic or physical shockwaves.
Localized Community Impact and Precautionary Measures
While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise and ground vibrations.
Residents in Middletown will hear loud noises and feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations. Due to the potential for localized window damage, or other potential damage, the U.S. Army recommends that residents in the Middletown City Park neighborhood temporarily vacate the area during the detonations out of an abundance of caution.
Open House Structure
The open house on Oct. 15th is designed to provide maximum transparency and address specific residents’ questions.
Rather than a formal presentation, the event will feature an informational walk-through. Residents can arrive at their convenience to view maps of the expected blast radius, review safety precautions, and speak one-on-one with EOD technicians, environmental scientists and installation leadership.
Open house details:
Date: Oct. 15th
Time: 4:30 to 6:30 p.m. CST
Location: Army Reserve Center, 17879 Highway 79, Middletown, Iowa

ST. LOUIS – Two drug dealers on Thursday admitted shooting an 18-year-old at a gas station in 2023.

Christopher “Face” Hall, 25, and Bryant “BJ” Pirtle, 23, pleaded guilty in separate hearings in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of discharge of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime resulting in death. According to their plea agreements, in the late evening of Jan. 28, 2023, Pirtle and Hall cruised around St. Louis City and County in a 2017 Honda Accord, selling marijuana. Around 3 a.m. on January 29, they stopped at a gas station in the 1700 block of South Florissant Road. Inside the station, Pirtle offered the victim marijuana and told him to meet him at the waiting Honda outside. The victim left the store and walked to the Honda with $20. After some discussion, the victim turned and walked away. Hall then got out of the driver’s seat of the Accord and the duo simultaneously opened fire, fatally wounding the victim. While fleeing the station, Hall ran the victim over and later bragged about doing so in text messages.

During an unrelated arrest later, police seized Pirtle’s iPhone and gray Lacoste backpack, which matched the phone and backpack seen on gas station surveillance camera video the night of the murder.

On March 10, 2023, Hall, Pirtle and several others were arrested in an apartment in St. Louis County with five guns, a significant amount of marijuana and three scales. Police also conducted a court-approved search of Hall’s house and found marijuana, plastic baggies and firearm accessories.

On March 22, 2023, St. Louis County Anti-Gang Unit detectives arrested Pirtle with a black AM-15 semiautomatic rifle loaded with 32 rounds and distribution quantities of marijuana. Along with drug paraphernalia and two scales, Pirtle had $4,543 in the glove box.

The 9mm Beretta handgun that Hall used to shoot the victim was seized by the St. Louis County Police Department in an unrelated stop on July 9, 2024.

Both men are scheduled to be sentenced on January 20. The charge carries a penalty of up to life in prison.

The case was investigated by the FBI, the St. Louis County Police Department and the Normandy Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Nino Przulj and Jen Szczucinski are prosecuting the case.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: Duo Admits Cool Valley Murder
