FORT BRAGG, N.C. — A U.S. Army Soldier assigned to the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command was recognized Thursday for his immediate actions in providing lifesaving medical care to a wounded civilian off post.
Pfc. Stephen Bradley, a Spanish Town, Jamaica native, and a motor transport for 126th Composite Truck Company, 264th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion,3rd Corps Sustainment Command, was off duty at his residence in nearby Spring Lake, when he heard multiple gunshots nearby. Upon investigating, Bradley discovered an injured man in urgent need of medical assistance.
“I heard several shots and immediately went out to see what happened,” said Bradley. “When I saw someone was wounded, my training immediately took over. All that mattered was getting to him and keeping him stable.”
Bradley coordinated with an off-duty law enforcement officer on the scene, identified himself as an Army combat lifesaver-qualified soldier, and retrieved his emergency medical kit. Bradley applied a tourniquet to the victim’s arm along with a pressure dressing and chest seal to treat additional wounds, stabilizing the patient until local emergency medical services arrived.
Local first responders commended the Soldier's rapid intervention, noting that the immediate application of medical aid proved critical before paramedics could transfer the patient to a dedicated medical facility.
During an awards ceremony on Thursday, Brig. Gen. Raphael S. Heflin, commanding general of the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, presented Bradley with the Army Commendation Medal for his decisive actions and selfless service.
“This is a clear testament to why combat lifesaver qualification is so vital across our entire formation,” said Heflin. “When seconds count, that training saves lives—whether in combat or right here in our local communities. Pfc. Bradley is exactly the kind of Soldier you want standing beside you as your battle buddy, because when an emergency happened, he didn’t hesitate to act.”
Civilian law enforcement officials are handling all inquiries regarding the criminal investigation.
title: 3rd Corps Sustainment Command Soldier receives Army Commendation Medal after aiding wounded civilian

United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods announced that Jeremy Sherman, 54, of Lincoln, Nebraska, was sentenced on October 9, 2026, in federal court in Lincoln for one count of possession with intent to distribute 50 grams of methamphetamine actual and 400 grams of a mixture containing fentanyl. United States District Judge Susan M. Bazis sentenced Sherman to a total of 188 months’ imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system. After Sherman’s release from prison, he will begin a 5-year term of supervised release.

On September 16, 2025, law enforcement conducted a traffic stop for a vehicle traveling on Interstate 80 in Seward County, Nebraska. Sherman was identified as a passenger in the rear seat of the vehicle. After contacting the vehicle, a Seward County deputy saw an open bottle of Smirnoff in one of the rear doors. All three occupants of the vehicle were removed, and a probable cause search was conducted. A pat search of Sherman was conducted and investigators felt something that was consistent to feeling like a large baggie full of narcotics in Sherman’s pants pocket.

Sherman was asked what was in his pocket, and he responded that it was methamphetamine. The contents were removed and it was a gallon-sized Ziploc baggie that contained approximately 140 grams of methamphetamine, a glass pipe, and a smaller baggie of approximately 3.5 grams of methamphetamine. Investigators also found a black backpack in the rear seat next to where Sherman had been sitting. This backpack contained a Ziploc baggie with more than 4,000 M30 fentanyl pills.

The methamphetamine and fentanyl were both sent to the Nebraska State Patrol crime laboratory to be tested. The methamphetamine was confirmed to be at least 120 grams of methamphetamine actual with a purity of 98.8% and the suspected M30 fentanyl pills weighed a total of 451 grams and did in fact contain fentanyl.

This case was investigated by the Lincoln/Lancaster County Narcotics Task Force and the Seward County Sheriff’s Office.
title: Lincoln Man Sentenced to More Than 15 Years for Possession with Intent to Distribute Methamphetamine and Fentanyl

text:
On this day, we mark the 136th birthday of President Dwight David Eisenhower—a visionary leader, respected warrior, distinguished statesman, and noble public servant. In command of great armies and in the White House, he met every trial with steadiness, courage, and resolve, earning the enduring trust of the American People and the lasting gratitude of the free world.
Born in Denison, Texas, and raised in Abilene, Kansas, President Eisenhower began his legendary life of service to our great Nation as a graduate of West Point. His stellar military career spanned nearly four decades and included appointments such as the Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force during World War II, during which he orchestrated the historic D-Day Invasion of Normandy, and as NATO’s first Supreme Allied Commander Europe. In his first bid for the Presidency in 1952, the celebrated general and political outsider was elected in a landslide victory. After four years, Americans still liked “Ike” and handed him another decisive win in the 1956 election.
Eisenhower’s tenure in the White House was marked by peace, growth, economic prosperity, and a remarkable record of foreign and domestic accomplishments. He negotiated an armistice in the Korean War, signed the Civil Rights Act of 1957, created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Small Business Administration, and championed the Interstate Highway System, which connected communities across our country and boosted American commerce. Eisenhower’s commitment to military might and the preservation of our birthright of freedom is reflected in the cautionary words from his 1953 Inaugural Address: “History does not long entrust the care of freedom to the weak or the timid.”
My Administration is proudly advancing the ideals that shaped Eisenhower’s Presidency, including economic prosperity, a strong national defense, secure borders, an unwavering commitment to peace through strength, and the tireless pursuit of American exceptionalism. Like President Eisenhower, I believe lasting peace is secured only through unquestioned American strength, and my Administration is rebuilding our military into the most powerful fighting force on Earth. We are upholding the law and order he championed, making our streets and communities safe again, igniting an economic boom unlike anything our country has ever seen, and renewing the strength and spirit of American life at every turn. More than seven decades later, Eisenhower’s example continues to guide our Nation as we restore the peace, prosperity, and confidence that defined his era and usher in a new Golden Age for the American People.
As we commemorate the birthday of our 34th Commander in Chief, we honor the extraordinary life and legacy of this patriot, hero, and American icon, whose devotion to duty and country will inspire Americans for generations to come.
Happy Birthday, President Eisenhower!
title: Presidential Message on the Birthday of President Dwight D. Eisenhower

text:
Justice Department Sues State of California over Voter List
Note: view complaint here.
The Justice Department, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), today filed a complaint against the State of California over its voter list after determining that more than 20,000 people who are likely aliens are registered to vote in California. Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot. It is unlawful for aliens to vote in federal elections.
“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation’s representative system of government. The Department of Justice will continue working to uncover cases of voter fraud, hold fraudsters accountable, and restore trust in American elections.”
“It is unlawful for noncitizens to vote in federal elections,” said Secretary Markwayne Mullin of DHS. “The Department of Homeland Security and our federal partners reviewed publicly available California voter-registration files and compared relevant records with federal immigration data to identify alien registrants. This preliminary analysis has identified a significant number of individuals in California who are likely noncitizens and appear to be registered to vote; the analysis and review remain ongoing. This is completely unacceptable — as even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen and undermines our elections. DHS is committed to identifying unlawful voting, protecting the integrity of federal elections, and ensuring that only eligible American citizens elect America’s leaders.”
“The law is clear, aliens in the United States cannot vote in federal elections,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “What our complaint alleges is that California is facilitating unlawful voting by knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. This needs to stop.”
“California election officials were given an opportunity to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls and to sequester ballots returned from suspected ineligible voters. They refused,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “We are taking California to federal court to demand that the votes of American citizens not be diluted by noncitizens.”
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), in coordination with federal partners, analyzed publicly available voter-registration records to identify potential indicators that aliens may have registered to vote, cast ballots, or received election-related mail. The Department of Justice has filed a complaint against the State of California alleging that these individuals, who are likely noncitizens, registered to vote and/or voted in a federal election. HSI and its federal partners used multiple data-enrichment and verification methods to assess whether the individuals identified were likely aliens.
title: Justice Department Sues State of California over Voter List

The Eastern Pennsylvania Violent Crimes Fugitive Task Force is a team of law enforcement officers led by U.S. Marshals in Philadelphia and the surrounding counties. text:
Read my Op-Ed in The Portland Press Herald
Between the mountains of snow, the waves of bitter cold and the occasional Nor’easter, we Mainers are no strangers to harsh winters.
This winter could be one of the hardest in recent memory. And not because of the weather. The statewide average price of heating oil just hit a record $6.02 a gallon. As of Sept. 28, it was still averaging $5.96 — up nearly 79% from the same week last year. At today’s price, a 250-gallon fill-up costs about $1,490 — an expense many Maine families will face more than once this winter.
Meanwhile, gas prices are hovering around $4.40 per gallon as of Sept. 25, according to Maine Public.
As if all this wasn’t awful enough, the number of Mainers receiving assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by 13% — 13,000 people in all, including 7,000 children. Another 31,000 Mainers are projected to lose MaineCare coverage over the next year.
Add it all up and this winter is going to put an enormous strain on Maine families — especially those who can least afford it.
This looming crisis is the result of choices President Trump and congressional Republicans made. Choices they continue to defend.
Let’s back up to July 4, 2025, when the president signed his hallmark legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, into law.
The “Big Ugly Bill” is a more accurate name. It slashed Medicaid by $1.2 trillion and SNAP by $211 billion over the next decade, all while handing hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations.
Far from offsetting those devastating cuts, the Big Ugly Bill’s ludicrous tax breaks are projected to increase federal deficits by $4.6 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also handed $175 billion to the Department of Homeland Security, helping turbocharge the Trump administration’s cruel immigration enforcement agenda and bringing chaos and violence to communities across the country. That includes Maine, where an ICE agent shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13.
The young father was not the target of ICE’s operation that morning. He had no criminal history, and we don’t have body camera footage of the shooting. His family has still not been contacted by the federal government and is still waiting for a full accounting of what happened. 
This bill will go down as one of the most irresponsible, destructive, and costly pieces of legislation in American history. Not just in terms of its fiscal recklessness, but its human toll as well: nearly 13 million fewer people enrolled in Medicaid by 2034 and roughly 2.4 million fewer people receiving SNAP in an average month, according to CBO estimates. Its consequences will reach every community in America, in shuttered rural hospitals, overwhelmed food banks and increased costs for state and local governments.
The Big Ugly Bill alone would have been devastating enough for Maine. Then Trump’s reckless, unauthorized war of choice in Iran has kicked every one of these crises into overdrive. In the nearly eight months since the war began — a conflict Trump insisted wouldn’t last more than a few weeks — the global economy has been thrown into turmoil.
The on-again, off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, has sent energy prices skyrocketing — and disrupted the flow of goods around the world. When the world’s energy supply gets squeezed, everyone pays more. In a state like Maine, where a colder-than-average winter can mean the difference between keeping the heat on and putting on extra layers just to stay warm, the potential consequences are catastrophic.
None of this had to happen. These crises have been created or made worse by Trump’s policies — and by congressional Republicans’ refusal to push back on the president and stand up for their constituents.
And now, with Americans staring down record energy costs, Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early for a seven-week campaign recess. Rather than staying to work on the many challenges facing our nation, Republicans tucked tail and left.
Republicans could’ve chosen to help you. They chose to help the already-rich get even richer — and to give an army of masked, heavily armed and utterly unaccountable ICE agents virtually unlimited resources to terrorize our communities.
My Democratic colleagues and I have been fighting them every step of the way. We’ve voted against these devastating cuts. We’ve introduced legislation to protect healthcare and food assistance. We’ve demanded accountability for an administration that continues to put its deeply unpopular agenda ahead of the people it’s supposed to serve.
And we are demanding action on the heating crisis: end the war in Iran, protect the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, reverse changes to the Home Owner Managing Energy Savings Rebates and High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate programs and reinstate the energy efficiency tax credits Republicans eliminated. Speaker Johnson should call the House back to Washington so Congress can get to work.
We will keep fighting — at every turn, and for as long as it takes. Because Mainers deserve better. They deserve a government that makes their lives more affordable — not one that cuts their healthcare and food assistance, sends energy prices through the roof and hands massive tax breaks to the people who need them least.
Mainers have survived plenty of hard winters. But the hardships coming this winter are the result of decisions made by Republicans in Washington, who would rather leave town than fix the problems they created.
title: Op-Ed: Mainers are in for a harsh winter— thanks to Republicans

text:
CONCORD – Haverhill, Massachusetts resident Ozeias Guilherme, age 40, was sentenced yesterday to 121 months in prison for attempting to sex traffic a 12-year-old at a Manchester hotel, United States Attorney Erin Creegan announces. After a four-day trial in April of 2026, Guilherme was convicted of one count of attempted sex trafficking of a minor and one count of travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct. United States District Court Judge Steven McAuliffe presided over the trial and announced the sentence, which also included a 5-year term of supervised release.

On November 14 and November 15, 2024, in a proactive law enforcement operation, agents posted and monitored an advertisement on a website commonly used to advertise commercial sex. The advertisement contained images of what appeared to be two minor females, and a contact phone number. Law enforcement agents monitored this line and used it to communicate with potential sex buyers, including Guilherme. During a text conversation between an undercover agent and Guilherme, the agent stated that she had a 12-year-old girl available to perform sex acts in exchange for money. The agent then provided Guilherme with the address of a hotel in Manchester. Once at the hotel, the defendant met with an undercover agent and showed her $100 cash, the amount agreed upon to pay for the commercial sex act.

“This defendant preyed on children, ready to pay money to sexually assault a little girl, and will now be spending significant time behind bars as a result,” said Erin Creegan, U.S. Attorney for the District of New Hampshire. “Our office is committed to working with all our partners to combat child sexual exploitation to the maximum extent the law allows.”

“Ozeias Guilherme actively sought out a 12-year-old child to sexually abuse. He planned, he negotiated, and he travelled to New Hampshire to meet a little girl who he was fully prepared to assault for cash. Thankfully, he never had the opportunity to follow through on his plan and, after today’s sentence, he will be spending the next decade in prison,” said Homeland Security Investigations New England Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeffrey Grimming. “This case was only made possible through the coordination and commitment of our local law enforcement partners and the New Hampshire Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force. Together, we are working to protect children and bringing predators like Guilherme to justice.”

Homeland Security Investigations led the investigation. Manchester Police Department, the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office, and the New Hampshire Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force provided valuable assistance. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Matthew Hunter and Matthew Vicinanzo prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .
title: Massachusetts Man Sentenced to More Than 10 Years in Prison for Attempting to Sex Traffic a Minor at a Manchester Hotel

text:
Alexander Suvorov, age 52, a Russian national residing in Sweden, has been charged by a criminal complaint with three counts related to the unlawful exporting of micro-electronic components from the United States to Russia via a front company based in Hong Kong.

Suvorov was extradited from Sweden to the Northern District of New York on October 15, 2026, and is expected to have his initial appearance on Friday, October 16, 2026, at 1:30 p.m. in Albany before United States Magistrate Judge Paul J. Evangelista. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III, Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Jonathan Carson, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security, New York Field Office, made the announcement.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III said, “Those, like the defendant, as alleged, who seek to enrich themselves by evading economic sanctions on Russia, must understand that their actions carry serious consequences and will not be tolerated. My office, working together with the FBI and the Department of Commerce, will continue to aggressively prosecute these types of cases and hold offenders accountable to the fullest extent of the law. This historic extradition shows that we will fly over 3,800 miles to locate and bring to justice those who threaten national security.”

The complaint filed against Suvorov alleges that between about March, 2022 and April, 2023, Suvorov led an illicit procurement network responsible for unlawfully exporting U.S. electronic components out of the United States to Russia. One of the procurement network’s main goals was to fraudulently obtain dual-use electronic components – that is, electronic components with both civilian and military applications – from U.S. companies for shipment to Russia. As alleged in the complaint, Suvorov’s primary role in the procurement network was to maintain front companies based in Hong Kong, including GS Group Limited, which the procurement network used to order electronic components from U.S. companies in an effort to conceal that the end users of the components were in Russia, and to then transship, via Hong Kong, the components from the U.S. companies to the end users in Russia. Suvorov and his companies are also alleged to have sent multiple wires to various U.S. companies to pay for the electronic components. Some of the components unlawfully purchased and exported to Russia by Suvorov and his procurement network can be used in military communication and radar systems, as well as precision location systems.

“As alleged, Mr. Suvorov tried to hide his criminal actions by conducting them in a foreign country, but he couldn’t hide from the FBI,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albany Field Office. “Thanks to our partners from the United States Attorney’s Office Northern District of New York, Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and our international partners, he’s now here to face American justice. This investigation represents an important step forward in the FBI’s ongoing efforts to protect our national security, safeguard American innovation, and defend the integrity of our supply chains.”

U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security, New York Field Office Special Agent in Charge Jonathan Carson said, “The Bureau of Industry and Security is committed to strong enforcement. Working closely with out law enforcement partners, we will continue to uncover and disrupt illicit procurement and diversion networks wherever they operate.”

Count One of the complaint alleges Conspiracy to Commit International Promotional Money Laundering and carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $500,000, and a term of supervised release of up to three years. Count Two of the complaint alleges Conspiracy to Commit Outbound Smuggling and carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, and a term of supervised release of up to three years. Count Three of the complaint alleges Conspiracy to Violate the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA) and carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $1,000,000, and a term of supervised release of up to three years. A defendant’s sentence is imposed by a judge based on the particular statutes the defendant is convicted of violating, the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other factors.

The charges in the complaint are merely accusations. The defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

The FBI and Department of Commerce are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Belliss and National Security Division Trial Attorney Garrett Coyle are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs secured the extradition of Suvorov with the assistance of the Swedish authorities.

text:
SAN ANTONIO – A San Antonio man was sentenced in federal court to 200 months in prison for possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, in 2025, the Guadalupe County Sheriff’s Office began investigating Daniel Mendoza Jr., 44. Throughout the investigation, Mendoza advertised “cocaine, bars, and perk 30s” on social media and completed multiple sales of illicit pills laced with fentanyl and fluorofentanyl in Schertz.

Mendoza was arrested on Jan. 14, 2026. A search of his residence revealed Mendoza stored additional fentanyl, cocaine, and alprazolam in his kitchen. In his bedside table, Mendoza, a convicted felon with an extensive criminal history, stored a .40 caliber pistol and a magazine loaded with 10 rounds.

Mendoza was indicted on Jan. 7 for two counts of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and two counts of possession with intent to distribute fluorofentanyl. A superseding indictment on March 4 added a third count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and one count of felon in possession of a firearm. Mendoza pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl on May 28.

The Drug Enforcement Administration and Guadalupe County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Amy Marie Walker prosecuted the case.

title: San Antonio Felon Sentenced to Over 16 Years for Dealing Fentanyl in Schertz

text:
Hattiesburg, MS – A former gymnastics coach was sentenced today in federal court to 90 years in prison for secretly videoing young gymnasts in the bathroom of a gym where he coached.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Sean Gardner, 39, of West Des Moines, Iowa, used his access to children as a gymnastics coach in Purvis, Mississippi to surreptitiously record minors changing clothes and using the bathroom. The investigation began after reports were made to the U.S. Center for SafeSport alleging that Gardner, while working as a gymnastics coach, engaged in inappropriate conduct involving minor athletes. SafeSport forwarded the allegations to law enforcement, which led to a joint investigation by local and federal authorities.

During the execution of a search warrant at Gardner’s Iowa residence, law enforcement seized multiple electronic devices. A forensic examination revealed numerous images and videos depicting minor children – some under the age of 12 – in states of undress that appeared to have been recorded using a concealed camera. Investigators determined that several of the recordings were made in a restroom at a gym in Purvis, Mississippi, where Gardner previously worked. The evidence included multiple files dated as early as 2017 and 2018, and investigators identified several of the minors depicted as former gymnastics students.

If you are a parent of a child that has at any point been under the instruction of Gardner, the FBI has set up a website to provide you with resources and further information about this case: https://forms.fbi.gov/seeking-victim-information-in-sean-michael-gardner-investigation.

“Today’s sentence sends an undeniable message: those who prey on our children will be found, prosecuted, and held accountable to the fullest extent of the law,” said United States Attorney J.E. Baxter Kruger. “Today’s sentence ensures that Gardner will spend the rest of his life paying the price for the devastating harm he caused.”

"Sean Gardner committed horrific and unforgivable acts, manipulating and abusing children while betraying the profound trust their families placed in him. Today marks a decisive moment: justice has been delivered. His victims can take solace in knowing he will never again have the opportunity to harm another child. When any child is exploited, the FBI—working alongside our law enforcement partners—will marshal every resource, pursue every lead, and relentlessly ensure that predators are identified, stopped, and held fully accountable," said Special Agent in Charge Robert A. Eikhoff of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

This case is the result of an investigation conducted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the West Des Moines Police Department.

Assistant United States Attorneys Kimberly Purdie and Lee Smith prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc.
title: Former Gymnastics Coach Sentenced to 90 Years in Federal Prison for Production of Child Sexual Abuse Material

text:
The National Park Service (NPS) has a multibillion-dollar backlog of deferred maintenance—maintenance that was not performed as scheduled or as needed and was put off to a future time. NPS's deferred maintenance, also known as deferred maintenance and repairs or the maintenance backlog, was estimated for FY2025 at $24.237 billion. Other federal land management agencies also have deferred maintenance, but NPS's backlog is the largest and has drawn the most congressional attention.
During the past decade (FY2016-FY2025), NPS deferred maintenance grew by $12.906 billion (+114%) in nominal dollars and $7.263 billion (+43%) in inflation-adjusted dollars. Many factors might contribute to the growth or reduction of deferred maintenance, including the aging of NPS assets, availability of funding for maintenance activities, acquisition of new assets, agency management of the backlog, completion of individual projects, changes in construction and related costs, and alterations in the methods used to estimate deferred maintenance. NPS reported that a 60% nominal-dollar increase in the backlog between FY2020 and FY2021 was due in part to changes in how the agency estimates deferred maintenance. NPS's deferred maintenance is distributed unevenly among states and territories, with California, the District of Columbia, Arizona, and Wyoming having the largest amounts. The amounts also vary among individual park units. Among the various types of assets that NPS maintains, deferred maintenance is highest for the agency's paved roads and buildings.
Sources of funding to address NPS deferred maintenance have included discretionary and mandatory appropriations, allocations from the Department of Transportation, park entrance and concessions fees, and donations, among others. Often it is not possible to determine the total amount of funding from these sources that NPS has allocated each year to address deferred maintenance, because NPS does not aggregate these amounts in its budget reporting. In 2020, the Great American Outdoors Act (GAOA; P.L. 116-152) provided a major new source of mandatory funding to address deferred maintenance of NPS and other federal land management agencies. The GAOA's National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund (LRF) received $1.9 billion annually for five years (FY2021-FY2025), with 70% of the funds—approximately $1.3 billion annually—going to NPS. In the 119th Congress, H.R. 9250 and S. 1547 would reauthorize deposits to the fund for FY2027-FY2031. For more information, see CRS Insight IN12729, Legacy Restoration Fund for Deferred Maintenance: 119th Congress Reauthorization Bills.
Congressional attention in the 118th and 119th Congresses has focused on NPS's use of the LRF funding provided under the GAOA, including the agency's project selection priorities, the funds' impact in addressing the backlog, the reasons for changes in NPS's deferred maintenance estimates, and proposals to reauthorize deposits to the LRF. Separately from the LRF, Congress also has debated the sufficiency of ongoing annual appropriations for NPS deferred maintenance, as well as appropriations for preventive maintenance that could keep assets from deteriorating to the point that deferred maintenance is accrued. Some in Congress also have expressed interest in potential actions to reduce the backlog without additional funding, such as through public-private partnerships or disposal of unneeded assets.
The National Park Service's (NPS's) backlog of deferred maintenance (DM)—maintenance that was not performed as scheduled or as needed—is of ongoing interest to Congress. The agency estimated its DM needs for FY2025 at $24.237 billion.1 Although other federal land management agencies also have DM backlogs, NPS's backlog is the largest.2 Because unmet maintenance needs may damage park resources, adversely affect visitors' enjoyment of the parks, and jeopardize safety, NPS DM has been a topic of concern for Congress and for nonfederal stakeholders. Potential issues for Congress include, among others, how to weigh NPS's maintenance needs against other financial demands within and outside the agency, how to prioritize limited DM funding among multiple parks and types of infrastructure, and how to ensure that NPS is efficiently and successfully managing funds to reduce the backlog. This report provides an overview and discussion of issues related to NPS DM. The report begins with general background and then contains more detailed sections on estimates of NPS DM, agency funding to address DM, and issues under consideration in the 119th Congress.
The Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB) defines deferred maintenance and repairs (DM&R) as "maintenance and repairs that were not performed when they should have been or were scheduled to be and which are put off or delayed for a future period."3 Federal agencies and Members of Congress also refer to DM&R as deferred maintenance (DM, the term used in this report) or as the maintenance backlog.4 The term DM encompasses both maintenance and repair needs.
As suggested by the above definition, DM does not include all maintenance and repairs, only those that were not accomplished when scheduled or needed and were put off to a future time. Another type of maintenance is cyclic maintenance—that is, maintenance performed at regular intervals to prevent asset deterioration, such as to replace a roof or upgrade an electrical system at a scheduled or needed time.5 Although NPS considers cyclic maintenance separately from DM for budgeting purposes, NPS has emphasized the importance of cyclic maintenance for preventing accrual of DM.6 NPS also performs routine, day-to-day maintenance as part of its facility operations activities; such activities include, for example, mowing and weeding landscapes and trails, conducting custodial and janitorial functions, and removing litter.7
NPS estimated its total DM for FY2025 (the most recent year available) at $24.237 billion (Table 1).8 Although all four major federal land management agencies—NPS, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), and the U.S. Forest Service (FS)—have DM backlogs, NPS's backlog is the largest. For FY2025, NPS's DM was more than twice that reported by FS, more than three times that reported by BLM, and nearly seven times that reported by FWS.9 One factor in the difference may be that NPS has more infrastructure assets (over 70,000 assets) than the other land management agencies.10 DM for the four agencies and agency asset comparisons are discussed further in CRS Report R43997, Deferred Maintenance of Federal Land Management Agencies: FY2013-FY2022 Estimates and Issues.
Sources: NPS, Budget Justifications and Performance Information, Fiscal Year 2027, pp. 179-180.
Notes: DM = deferred maintenance. Totals may not sum precisely due to rounding. "Paved Roads" includes paved roadways, bridges, and tunnels. "All Others" includes utility systems, dams, constructed waterways, marinas, aviation systems, railroads, ships, monuments, fortifications, towers, interpretive media, and amphitheaters. Separately, NPS's FY2027 budget justification contains an alternate method of asset categorization, created by the Department of the Interior (DOI) for common reporting across DOI bureaus. For a breakdown according to this alternate categorization method, see p. 180 of the budget justification.
NPS's DM estimates have increased over the past decade (FY2016-FY2025) in both nominal and inflation-adjusted dollars. Figure 1 and Table 2 show a growth in NPS DM of $12.906 billion (+114%) in nominal dollars and $7.263 billion (+43%) in inflation-adjusted dollars over the decade. In particular, NPS's DM estimate rose by 60% in nominal dollars (51% in inflation-adjusted dollars) in a single year (FY2020-FY2021), which NPS attributed in part to changes in its methods for estimating DM (see discussion below, "Estimating NPS Deferred Maintenance").
Table 2. NPS Deferred Maintenance Estimates, FY2016-FY2025
($ in billions; nominal and inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars)
Sources for Figure 1 and Table 2: Nominal-dollar estimates for FY2016-FY2018 were archived by CRS from the NPS website. Nominal-dollar estimates for FY2019-FY2022 are from CRS communication with NPS Office of Legislative and Congressional Affairs, July 27, 2023. Nominal dollar estimates for FY2023-FY2025 are from NPS, "Infrastructure: By the Numbers," https://www.nps.gov/subjects/infrastructure/deferred-maintenance.htm; and CRS communication with NPS Office of Legislative and Congressional Affairs, September 11, 2026. Adjustments for inflation (2025 dollars) use Bureau of Economic Analysis Table 3.9.4, "Price Indexes for Government Consumption Expenditures and Gross Investment," nondefense structures, annual indexes, https://apps.bea.gov/itable/?reqid=19&step=2&isuri=1&categories=survey. Totals may not sum precisely due to rounding.
Notes for Figure 1 and Table 2: Through FY2022, NPS's estimates of its own deferred maintenance (DM) differed from estimates of NPS DM made by the Department of the Interior (DOI) for annual departmental financial reports; see the section on "Estimating NPS Deferred Maintenance," below, for discussion. The FY2016-FY2022 DM estimates shown here are NPS's own estimates. For the estimates used in DOI financial reports during this time, see CRS Report R43997, Deferred Maintenance of Federal Land Management Agencies: FY2013-FY2022 Estimates and Issues, by Carol Hardy Vincent. For FY2023-FY2025, NPS's estimates of its DM are the same as DOI's estimates.
Multiple factors may contribute to growth or reduction of NPS DM. One key driver of growth in NPS maintenance needs has been the increasing age of agency infrastructure. Many NPS assets—such as visitor centers, roads, and other assets—were constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s or as part of NPS's Mission 66 infrastructure initiative in the 1950s and 1960s.11 As these structures have reached or exceeded the end of their anticipated life spans, unfunded costs of repair or replacement have contributed to the DM backlog. Further, observers point out that as time goes by and needed repairs are not made, the rate at which such assets deteriorate accelerates, potentially leading to higher maintenance costs.12
A related key factor is the amount of funding available to NPS to address DM. The sources and amounts of agency funding for DM have fluctuated over time and are discussed in greater detail below, in the section on "Funding for NPS Deferred Maintenance." In addition to funding for DM specifically, funding for routine and cyclic maintenance can affect DM, if a lack of available funds results in scheduled maintenance being deferred.
Some observers have expressed concern that growth in NPS DM may be at least partly due to inefficiencies in the agency's asset management strategies and/or the implementation of these strategies. NPS has taken steps over the past decade to improve its asset management systems and strategies. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the Department of the Interior's (DOI's) Office of Inspector General (OIG) have recommended further improvements.13 Some aspects of NPS management of the DM backlog are discussed further in the report sections below.
Another issue is that the methods used by NPS to estimate DM have changed over time. NPS's methods are discussed in the section on "Estimating NPS Deferred Maintenance." In particular, NPS attributed a large jump in estimated DM between FY2020 and FY2021 partly to changes in its estimation methods, and additional changes have been implemented in other years. Also, NPS has worked to build and maintain a complete and accurate data set during the past decade.14 What portion of the overall change in NPS DM over the decade may be attributable to changes in methodology or data completeness, rather than to other factors, remains unclear.
From year to year, the completion of individual projects, changes in construction and repair costs, and similar factors play a role in the growth or reduction of NPS DM. The DM amounts reported by NPS for each fiscal year represent a snapshot of the backlog on the applicable date. The amount of DM changes frequently as NPS managers and staff complete or cancel maintenance work, recalculate costs, and record new maintenance and repair needs.
NPS and DOI report DM estimates by individual park and by state and territory on their respective websites.15 The 20 states and territories with the highest FY2025 NPS DM are shown in Table 3.
The states and territories with the highest NPS DM are not necessarily those with the most park acreage. For example, Alaska contains almost two-thirds of the total acreage in the National Park System but accounts for 1% of the agency's DM backlog. Instead, the amount, type, and condition of infrastructure in the NPS units, along with other factors, combine to determine the NPS DM in each state or territory. For example, paved roads are a major component of NPS DM, and the states and territories with NPS-administered parkways—such as the George Washington Memorial Parkway (Virginia, Maryland, and Washington, DC), the Natchez Trace Parkway (mainly in Mississippi and Tennessee), and the Blue Ridge Parkway (North Carolina and Virginia)—are all among the 20 states and territories with the highest DM.
Table 4 shows the 20 individual park units with the highest amounts of DM. Various factors may contribute to the relatively high DM estimates for these park units as compared with others. For example, some units, such as Yellowstone National Park and Grand Canyon National Park, are older parks whose infrastructure was largely built in the mid-20th century. Some units, such as Gateway National Recreation Area, Golden Gate National Recreation Area, and the National Mall and Memorial Parks, are located in or near urban areas and may contain more developed infrastructure than some more remotely located parks. The costs of labor and materials to execute DM projects also may be higher in these urban areas. Three of the units with the highest estimated DM are national parkways, consistent with the relatively high portion of NPS's overall DM that is related to road needs.
Source: CRS, using data from NPS, "Infrastructure: By the Numbers," https://www.nps.gov/subjects/infrastructure/deferred-maintenance.htm. DM = deferred maintenance.
a. NPS reports DM for the National Mall and Memorial Parks as a rounded number of $1.3 billion (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/infrastructure/upload/National-Mall-and-Memorial-Parks-Deferred-Maintenance-and-Repairs-Factsheet.pdf). The National Mall and Memorial Parks unit consists of 14 individual memorials, monuments, and other park units (e.g., Vietnam Veterans Memorial).
b. The George Washington Memorial Parkway also includes Arlington House; Clara Barton National Historic Site; LBJ Memorial Grove on the Potomac; Potomac Heritage National Scenic Trail; and Theodore Roosevelt Island.
c. The Natchez Trace Parkway also includes Natchez Trace National Scenic Trail and Tupelo National Battlefield.
d. National Capital Parks—East includes the Baltimore-Washington Parkway, Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site, Fort Washington Park, Greenbelt Park, Mary McLeod Bethune Council House National Historic Site, Piscataway Park, and Frederick Douglass National Historic Site.
NPS estimates the DM needs of park assets through a multi-step process. Park staff record data about the condition of individual assets in a software system, which generates estimates of each asset's maintenance and repair needs.16 Over the years, NPS has evolved its methods for estimating DM.17 The changes have included, among others, redefining the set of assets for which DM is tracked and changing the inputs and formulas that generate financial estimates of DM needs. NPS has stated that such changes aim to bring estimation methods into line with industry standards and provide "a more comprehensive understanding of facility conditions."18 In a September 2023 report, the DOI OIG found that despite the changes, the data in NPS's software system remained "inaccurate and unreliable ... possibly underestimating the figures in some cases and overestimating in others."19 NPS has taken several steps in response to the DOI OIG report.20
In recent years, several methodological changes have affected the agency's DM estimates. According to NPS and the DOI OIG, such changes include the following:
It can be difficult to determine to what extent methodological changes such as these have been responsible for variations in NPS's estimated DM over the years. The DOI OIG found that of the approximately $8.8 billion increase in NPS DM between FY2020 and FY2021, approximately $3.7 billion was attributable to the new 35% markup for non-transportation assets.32 NPS stated that other factors in the FY2020-FY2021 increase included insufficient funding for annual maintenance needs (thus creating more DM) and increased construction and maintenance costs due to inflation.33
In other cases, such as with the shift to estimating DM through condition assessments rather than work orders, the effects of the change on DM estimates are unclear. Also unclear are the impacts, if any, of the FY2023 change in the portfolio of assets NPS tracks, as compared with the set of assets tracked in FY2022 and previous years. To the extent that NPS is tracking DM for fewer assets than it previously did, this could lower estimated DM compared with earlier years, although any such effects would be difficult to measure given other factors also affecting DM.
In general, the DOI OIG found that NPS "does not have a monitoring mechanism to ensure the accuracy and completeness of its … data" and that "without reliable data, the NPS cannot make informed decisions on how to manage its deferred maintenance, improve program effectiveness and accountability, and potentially enhance decision making."34 However, the OIG noted steps NPS has taken to improve data quality and monitoring, such as directing park staff to rectify data anomalies and to annually review the accuracy of condition assessment scoring.35
NPS has used discretionary and mandatory appropriations, allocations from the Department of Transportation, park entrance and recreation fees, donations, and other funding sources to address the DM backlog. Often it is not possible to determine the total amount of funding from these sources that NPS has allocated each year to address DM, because NPS does not specifically aggregate these amounts in its budget reporting.36 From FY2021 to FY2025, NPS received a notable increase in its financial resources to address DM through the National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund (Legacy Restoration Fund, or LRF; 54 U.S.C. §§200401-200402), a five-year fund for DM of multiple land management agencies.
In 2020, the Great American Outdoors Act (GAOA) established the LRF to address DM of five agencies (NPS, FS, BLM, FWS, and the Bureau of Indian Education).37 The fund received annual deposits over five years (FY2021-FY2025) of amounts equal to 50% of all federal energy development revenues—from oil, gas, coal, or renewable energy—that were credited in the preceding fiscal year as miscellaneous receipts to the Treasury, up to a cap of $1.900 billion annually. NPS received a 70% share, with the remainder going to the other agencies at specified percentages. The LRF received the maximum allowable deposit of $1.900 billion each year, with 70% of this total ($1.330 billion annually) going to NPS, for a cumulative total of $6.650 billion for DM over the five-year period. Bills in the 119th Congress would reauthorize deposits to the LRF for FY2027-FY2031 and make other changes; for discussion, see CRS Insight IN12729, Legacy Restoration Fund for Deferred Maintenance: 119th Congress Reauthorization Bills.
The GAOA contained provisions for allocating LRF funding to individual DM projects. The GAOA directed the President to submit lists of projects to be addressed with LRF funds in agencies' annual budget submissions to Congress.38 Congress, in appropriations acts, could accept the President's proposals or provide alternate allocations (while adhering to the overall funding percentages defined for each agency).39 For FY2021-FY2025, appropriators generally, but not always, allocated the NPS funds as proposed by NPS.
The GAOA required that NPS and other agencies use the LRF funding for "priority deferred maintenance projects," and that at least 65% of each agency's monies over the term of the fund be used for non-transportation projects.40 DOI and NPS developed additional selection criteria for GAOA projects.41 In early 2024, GAO examined the land management agencies' processes for selecting LRF projects and found that the agencies, including NPS, "generally followed leading practices for managing deferred maintenance in their processes for selecting projects for LRF funding."42
Outside of the LRF, much of the funding used to address NPS DM has come from annual appropriations, primarily through the agency's Operation of the National Park System (ONPS) and Construction accounts. Because both accounts fund other activities in addition to DM, it is unclear how much funding under these programs has gone directly to address the DM backlog.
Within the ONPS account, annual appropriations reports have identified funding for NPS "maintenance, repair, or rehabilitation projects," and NPS uses these amounts for both DM and other types of maintenance.43 NPS has historically used this funding for projects with anticipated costs of less than $2 million each.44 For FY2026, Congress provided $157.2 million for maintenance, repair, or rehabilitation projects.45
Within the Construction account, NPS has historically used funding in the Line-Item Construction program for DM projects (among other projects) expected to cost $2 million or more.46 For FY2026, Congress did not provide funding for Line-Item Construction projects, except for one project designated as community project funding/congressionally directed spending. The joint explanatory statement for P.L. 119-74 stated that this activity was not funded because NPS did not submit a list of line-item project funding requests.47
Portions of other NPS discretionary budget activities and accounts also are sometimes used for DM. These include other programs within the ONPS and Construction accounts as well as NPS's Centennial Challenge account (discussed below under "Other NPS Funding for Deferred Maintenance").
Combined discretionary appropriations for maintenance, repair, or rehabilitation projects within the ONPS account and Line-Item Construction within the Construction account—the two primary sources of annual appropriations for NPS DM—declined after the LRF funding became available. Comparing FY2020 combined funding for the two programs (prior to establishment of the LRF) with FY2026 combined funding, the appropriations decreased by 62% in nominal dollars.48
Like other federal land management agencies, NPS receives mandatory appropriations from the Highway Trust Fund to address transportation needs, including transportation-related DM.49 As with discretionary appropriations, NPS uses these funds for both DM and other work on transportation assets (e.g., preventive maintenance), and does not record the portion of funding that is used specifically to address DM.50
Funds are provided to NPS by FHWA, primarily through the Federal Lands Transportation Program (FLTP), which was most recently reauthorized by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA).51 Under the IIJA, NPS's annual FLTP allocation grew from $332.4 million in FY2022 to $360.0 million in FY2026. Through related federal highway programs in the IIJA, such as the Federal Lands Access Program and others, NPS could receive additional funding.52
In FY2023 (the most recent year reported), the federal highway programs funded more than half of NPS's spending on transportation maintenance and improvements.53 NPS has noted, however, that its transportation projects may often require greater investments than can be supported by the available funding from the FLTP and related programs.54 NPS has stated that the cost of major transportation projects can range from $25 million to nearly $1 billion, with the costs of some individual projects exceeding NPS's entire FLTP allocation for a given year.55 Mandatory appropriations from the LRF—the GAOA's DM fund—also were available for transportation projects for FY2021-FY2025, although the GAOA funding for transportation projects was capped at no more than 35% of NPS's total LRF allotment over the five-year life of the fund.56
Park entrance and recreation fees collected under the Federal Lands Recreation Enhancement Act may be used for DM, among other purposes.57 The fees are available for use without further appropriation, and most are retained at the collecting parks.58 Fee collections may be used for purposes benefiting visitors, including facility maintenance and repair, interpretation and visitor services, law enforcement, and others. NPS policies require parks to obligate at least 55% of the collections to "deferred and preventive facility maintenance projects."59 In its FY2027 budget justification, NPS estimated FY2026 entrance and recreation fee collections at $596.0 million.60
NPS collects concessions franchise fees from park concessioners that provide services such as lodging and dining at park units. The fees, collected under the National Park Service Concessions Management Improvement Act of 1998, are typically set as a percentage of a concessioner's gross receipts.61 The fees are available for use without further appropriation and are mainly retained at the collecting parks.62 They may be used to reduce DM (including concessions-related DM) and are also used for other NPS concessions-related activities, such as contract development and payment of leasehold surrender interest (an amount owed to concessioners that have invested in improvements to NPS infrastructure).63 In its FY2027 budget justification, NPS estimated concessions fee collections of $206.1 million for FY2026.64
The National Park Service Centennial Act (Centennial Act) established the NPS Centennial Challenge Fund.65 The fund provides a federal match to private-sector donations for NPS projects and programs that "further the mission of the Service and … enhance the visitor experience in System units."66 The fund receives both discretionary appropriations and offsetting collections made up of certain amounts from sales of entrance passes to seniors.67 In selecting projects and programs to receive the funding, the Secretary of the Interior is to prioritize DM, physical improvements to visitor service facilities, and trail maintenance.68 The FY2026 appropriation for the Centennial Challenge Fund in P.L. 119-74 was $5.0 million.69 NPS estimated that senior pass sales would provide $8.5 million for the fund in FY2026.70
The Centennial Act also established the NPS Second Century Endowment and directed that the endowment receive revenues from senior pass sales totaling $10 million annually.71 In addition, the endowment is authorized to receive gifts, devises, and bequests from donors. The funds may be used for projects approved by the Secretary of the Interior that further the mission and purposes of NPS, including projects on the maintenance backlog. For FY2025 (the most recent year available), the National Park Foundation, which administers the endowment, reported spending $1.0 million from the endowment on unspecified projects.72
Other NPS mandatory appropriations also have been partially used for DM. These include donations, monies collected under the Park Building Lease and Maintenance Fund, transportation fees collected under the Transportation Systems Fund, and rents and payroll deductions for the use and occupancy of government quarters, among others. NPS estimated varying amounts for these mandatory appropriations for FY2026.73
In the 119th Congress, debate about NPS DM has focused on potential reauthorization of deposits to the LRF, the DM fund established by the GAOA. H.R. 9250, as ordered reported by the House Committee on Natural Resources, and S. 1547, as reported by the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, would reauthorize deposits to the fund for FY2027-FY2031 and make other changes related to the distribution and use of monies, streamlining project implementation, and ensuring the accuracy of DM data, among other matters. For further discussion, see CRS Insight IN12729, Legacy Restoration Fund for Deferred Maintenance: 119th Congress Reauthorization Bills.
Congressional oversight of the LRF after its 2020 establishment raised multiple issues that have informed legislation in the 119th Congress. Some Members questioned whether the fund was an effective tool for NPS, given that the NPS backlog grew rather than decreased after FY2020 (Figure 1). NPS has emphasized that despite factors leading to growth in the DM estimates—changes in DM estimation methods, inflation in the costs to execute projects, and new maintenance needs—the LRF has played a major role in addressing the backlog. NPS estimated in August 2025 that the FY2021-FY2025 LRF funding would address $4.7 billion in DM upon completion of the funded projects.74 GAO has stated that another positive impact of the LRF is that it has "fostered a cultural change [at the land management agencies] toward maintaining better data on deferred maintenance."75 Nonetheless, GAO still noted issues with unclear reporting by NPS and other DOI agencies on reasons for changes in DM estimates, which have compromised the availability of information Congress may need for its decisionmaking.76 GAO stated that, "in the absence of additional information on agencies' DM&R estimates, Congress and the public are limited in their ability to determine the true impact of DM&R on agency operations or the actual amount of funding needed to address the DM&R backlog."77 H.R. 9250, as ordered reported, and S. 1547, as reported, would require NPS and other agencies to establish "clear, quantifiable, and standardized metrics" for calculating DM and to meet other data criteria.
Some Members also questioned the geographic distribution of NPS's LRF projects, expressing concern about uneven distribution of the funding across states and regions.78 NPS's criteria for LRF project selection did not explicitly include geographic distribution; in contrast, FS's criteria for choosing LRF projects included a requirement that 40% of LRF funding go to "regional priority projects" across the FS regions.79 A related concern for some was the distribution of LRF funds among large versus small parks and urban versus rural parks.80 H.R. 9250, as ordered reported, and S. 1547, as reported, would require NPS and other agencies to achieve a "reasonable balance" between projects at higher- and lower-visitation units.81
Outside of debates about the LRF, some Members of Congress have advocated for prioritizing annual discretionary appropriations for NPS deferred and cyclic maintenance, especially in light of declines in this annual funding since enactment of the LRF (see section on "Annual Appropriations for NPS Deferred Maintenance").82 Some emphasize the importance of annual appropriations for preventing further growth of the backlog and point out that the GAOA stated that no amounts in the LRF were to be used to "supplant discretionary funding made available for annually recurring facility operations, maintenance, and construction needs."83 In contrast, some other Members of Congress, as well as NPS officials on some occasions, have expressed that the availability of LRF funding could allow annual appropriations to be used for NPS priorities other than maintenance (such as facility improvements), given limitations on overall funding for NPS and other DOI agencies.84
Some stakeholders have proposed additional options to increase funding for NPS infrastructure maintenance, beyond annual appropriations and the LRF. Options could include increasing the revenues that NPS collects, such as by raising park fees or introducing tolling on park highways that are used as commuter routes (e.g., in the region around Washington, DC).85 In FY2026, pursuant to Executive Order 14314, NPS introduced a $100 surcharge for international visitors to 11 national parks, and the land management agencies also raised the price of their multiagency pass for international visitors.86 H.R. 9250, as ordered reported, and S. 1547, as reported, would codify international visitor fee increases and would deposit revenues from the increases in the LRF.87 Some also have proposed funding NPS DM through monies from the Land and Water Conservation Fund, income tax overpayments and contributions, taxes on outdoor recreation gear, motor fuel taxes, DOI land sales, or revenues from coin and postage stamp sales.88 Others have opposed such proposals as diverting federal funds from other valued uses or imposing unnecessary fees on the public.
Various proposals have focused on ways NPS could reduce DM without the use of additional funds. Some have suggested that this could be accomplished by increasing the role of nonfederal partners in park management (e.g., by leasing more historic buildings to private businesses or transitioning NPS-operated campgrounds to concessioner management); by promoting volunteer assistance (e.g., through conservations service corps); by expanding the role of friends-of-the-park groups and similar nonprofits in NPS maintenance and construction projects; by disposing of unneeded structures in poor repair; or by transferring some NPS assets (e.g., commuter roads) out of federal ownership.89 NPS and other stakeholders have identified challenges in considering some of these options, including challenges related to the costs and procedures for disposing of unneeded assets,90 limitations to authorities for federal-nonfederal partnerships for infrastructure project management,91 and regulatory and market obstacles to expanded use of leasing authority.92 Debate continues on the optimal strategies for reducing NPS deferred maintenance and the extent to which this should be a priority for NPS and for Congress.
title: National Park Service Deferred Maintenance: Overview and Issues

text:
Congress oversees the Farm Credit Administration (FCA), which is the federal financial regulator responsible for ensuring the safety and soundness of Farm Credit System (FCS) institutions and the Federal Agricultural Mortgage Corporation (Farmer Mac). FCA is directed by a three-member board of directors nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate (12 U.S.C. §2242). Currently, two positions are vacant, and one board member is serving beyond the end of his term.
Congressional oversight is provided by the House Committee on Agriculture and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. The most recent oversight hearings with board members as witnesses were in the Senate on May 19, 2016, and in the House on November 19, 2019. The Senate committee most recently held a nomination hearing for an FCA board member in 2022.
FCA sets the policies, regulations, charters, and examinations of FCS and Farmer Mac entities. This includes compliance with laws concerning eligibility and regulations protecting the rights of borrowers. FCA is an independent agency with about 300 employees. It is located in McLean, VA, and conducts examinations from several field offices. FCA reports to Congress on the financial condition of FCS. Statutory authority for FCA is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2241 et seq.), as amended, notably by the Agricultural Credit Act of 1987. Regulations are at 12 C.F.R. Part 600.
FCA's operating expenses are paid through assessments on FCS banks and associations, not by congressional appropriations. However, annual Agriculture Appropriations Acts place limits on FCA's expenses ($106.5 million in FY2026).
FCS is a privately owned, federally chartered, nationwide financial cooperative that lends to full- and part-time farmers, farming-related businesses, rural homeowners, farmer-owned cooperatives, and certain rural utilities. Borrowers must meet creditworthiness requirements. FCS is not a lender of last resort.
Established in 1916 as a government-sponsored enterprise (GSE), FCS has a statutory mandate—and limitation—to serve agriculture. FCS is the only direct lender among the GSEs. It receives tax benefits, but FCS operates without any direct federal appropriations. Statutory authority for FCS is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2001 et seq.), as amended.
FCS is composed of 4 regional banks that provide funds and support services to 55 smaller credit associations that in turn provide loans to eligible borrowers. FCS associations are owned by their borrowers, who are required to purchase stock as part of their loans. FCS banks and associations do not take deposits like commercial banks. It obtains funds by selling bonds on capital markets through the Federal Farm Credit Banks Funding Corporation. FCS banks are jointly and severally liable for the debt, meaning they stand collectively behind the obligations to repay bonds. The Farm Credit System Insurance Corporation ensures timely payment of principal and interest on bonds.
As of December 31, 2025, FCS had $457 billion in total loans outstanding to agriculture, agribusiness, rural utility, and other borrowers. Agricultural loans are the largest portion ($289 billion). FCS provided 46% of loans on the sector-wide farm balance sheet at the end of 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Farmer Mac is a secondary market for agricultural mortgages. It purchases loans from originating lenders and provides other risk management tools. Farmer Mac was created by Congress in 1987 as a privately funded GSE. It is an investor-owned corporation that is financially and corporately separate from FCS. Statutory authority for Farmer Mac is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2279aa et seq.).
As of December 31, 2025, Farmer Mac's total business volume (a measure similar to assets) was $33 billion.
As a regulator, FCA is directed by a three-member board of directors nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate (12 U.S.C. §2242).
Terms for board members are six years in length, fixed when they begin, and staggered so that one term begins every two years regardless of whether a new member has been confirmed. Board members may not be reappointed after serving a full term or more than three years of an unexpired term. A board member may continue to serve beyond the end of his/her term until a replacement has been confirmed. This helps maintain continuity on the board if confirmation of successors is delayed. Not more than two members of the board may be from the same political party. Board member qualifications are to include some background in agricultural economics, financial reporting, finance, law, or financial regulation.
The President designates one member as chairman—not subject to further confirmation—who has often held that role until the end of his/her term. The chairman is also the chief executive officer (CEO) of FCA (12 U.S.C. §2244).
The current FCA board has one member serving in an expired term. Two seats are vacant (Table 1). This leaves the board without the necessary quorum to conduct business (12 U.S.C. §2242(c)).
On January 20, 2025, President Trump designated Jeffery S. Hall, board member since 2015, as chairman and CEO of FCA.
Hall replaced Vincent Logan, board member and chairman from 2022 to 2025, as chairman. Logan resigned from the FCA board on March 31, 2025, creating a vacancy. Subsequently, Glen R. Smith, board member since 2017 and chairman from 2019 to 2022, left the board after he was confirmed as USDA Under Secretary for Rural Development on August 7, 2026 (Figure 1).
On September 28, 2026, President Trump nominated three individuals for the FCA board: Carl Bednarski (PN1365-1, for a vacancy set to expire in 2034), John Grunewald II (PN1365-2, for the vacancy set to expire in 2032), and James Russell Middleton (PN1365-3, for the seat held by Hall set to expire in 2030). The nomination for Bednarski includes a prospective term that would begin in 2028. Their nominations have been referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry.
President Trump may nominate people for all three positions, given that there are two vacancies and the incumbent is serving beyond his original term. Bednarski and Grunewald are Republicans and Middleton is a Democrat, consistent with the requirement that not more than two members are from the same political party. The most recent time a President nominated someone outside his party was in 2015, when President Obama nominated Hall (PN40/114th Congress). President Obama also made a prospective reappointment; Kenneth A. Spearman was confirmed in 2009 to complete a term ending in 2010 with a simultaneous reappointment for a term ending in 2016 (PN817 and PN818/111th Congress).
Figure 1 is a timeline showing the service by board members since 2015. The timeline shows that terms are fixed, six years in length, and staggered (gray lines). A board member's service depends on Senate confirmation and may extend beyond the end of a term (blue lines) until a successor is confirmed. Service as chairman is by presidential appointment (gold lines).
Historically, a full board occurred when board members typically served until their successors were confirmed. FCA last had a single board member for about 11 months in 1989. Since 2015, FCA has operated three times with a two-member board: twice following deaths and once following a resignation. Hall's 10 years of service, with continuation after the end of his term in 2018, makes him the longest-serving board member in FCA history.
title: Farm Credit Administration and Its Board Members

After You Apply
▪You will receive a nine-digit FEMA application number. Keep this number in a safe place and refer to it whenever you contact FEMA.
▪Your application will be reviewed. FEMA may contact you by phone, text, email, mail, or through your online account if more information is needed.
If you haven’t applied yet, the fastest way to do so is online at DisasterAssistance.gov or the Spanish language DisasterAssistance.gov/es. You can also call the FEMA Helpline at 800-621-3362.
A Home Inspection
Within ten days of applying for assistance, you may be contacted by an inspector to schedule an appointment at the address where damage was reported.
Here’s what to expect:
▪A FEMA inspector will contact you using the phone number you provided. The contact may come from an unfamiliar or restricted number. Be sure to answer or call back so your application can move forward.
▪When the FEMA inspector contacts you, write down their name, date of contact, date and time of appointment and the inspector’s phone number.
▪Inspectors will show official FEMA photo identification when they arrive at your home. You should always ask to see identification.
▪There is no cost for a FEMA inspection. Inspectors will never ask for money, banking information, or payment of any kind.
▪During the inspection, you or your co-applicant should be present to:
Confirm your identity, home ownership (if applicable) and occupancy,
Provide a list of household occupants living in the home at the time of disaster,
Supply any insurance documents requested by the inspector,
Walk the inspector through the damaged areas or show documentation of damage, and
Describe your losses.
▪If you are unable to meet with the inspector, you can designate someone else to meet with the inspector on your behalf. You must provide FEMA with a copy of this written designation.
▪If you have already started repairs, photos and receipts can help show the damage that occurred.
After the Home Inspection
Information gathered during the inspection is only one of several criteria used by FEMA to determine eligibility for assistance. If you have questions after your inspection, please call FEMA’s Helpline at 800-621-3362.
You will receive information explaining FEMA's eligibility decision within 10 days after the inspector's visit. To receive updates and notifications faster, create an online DisasterAssistance.gov account after applying for FEMA assistance.
Learn more about FEMA’s inspection process by visiting the Home Inspections page.
###
FEMA’s mission is helping people before, during and after disasters.
title: What to Expect After you Apply for FEMA Assistance

text:
Norcross, local officials break ground on long-awaited third lane for Atlantic City Expressway
GLOUCESTER TOWNSHIP – Congressman Donald Norcross (NJ-01) yesterday joined local and state officials to break ground on the construction of a third lane for the Atlantic City Expressway (ACE) in Gloucester and Camden counties. Upon completion, it will be the culmination of a broader highway widening project that began in 2008.
“Safer roads and less waiting in traffic are goals everyone can get behind, regardless of their political stripes,” Norcross said. “The Atlantic City Expressway is one of the most heavily used roads for residents and visitors of South Jersey alike. I’ve suffered through its congestion my whole life, and have been advocating for its widening since my days in the state legislature. I’m extremely excited to see this long-needed improvement project finally break ground.”
The Atlantic City Expressway runs between Washington Township and Atlantic City, connecting the Philadelphia metro area with the Southern Jersey Shore. Despite serving as the primary roadway for an average of 45,000 daily residents and visitors alike, the highway suffers the second lowest “level of service” grade possible from the New Jersey Department of Transportation and sees a significant number of crashes annually – particularly around the Route 42 interchange.
To relieve congestion and make the ACE safer, the state constructed a third lane in the section closest to Atlantic City between 2008 and 2014. Planning for the northern section to be widened began in 2022, and is expected to be completed in three phases between 2029 and 2031 at the cost of roughly $400 million.
Benefits of the new lane will include fewer accidents due to the freer flow of traffic, reduced air and noise pollution, and faster travel times across the region.
Norcross’ advocacy for road safety dates back to his service in the state legislature. In addition to his longstanding calls for the northern portion of the ACE to be widened, in 2011, he introduced legislation that would raise fines on drivers who created unsafe traffic patterns by failing to return to the right lane of the highway after passing another driver. Norcross’ bill was signed into law in 2013.
title: Norcross, local officials break ground on long-awaited third lane for Atlantic City Expressway
