text: St. Thomas, USVI – U.S. Attorney Adam F. Sleeper announced today that Chief U.S. District Court Judge Robert A. Molloy sentenced Carlos Cruz Resto, 40, of Puerto Rico, to 87 months’ imprisonment for possession with intent to distribute cocaine, pursuant to 21 U.S.C. §§ 841(a)(1) and (b)(1)(A). Cruz Resto was also placed on five years of supervised release and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment. According to court documents, on July 21, 2025, Cruz Resto was the captain of a vessel traveling in the waters near Savanah Island, just west of St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands. At approximately 3:00 a.m., U.S. Customs and Boarder Protection Air and Marine (AMO) detected the vessel operating without navigation lights and traveling towards St. Thomas from Culebra, Puerto Rico. AMO launched a vessel to investigate and located the lights-out vessel west of Savanah Island, headed towards Culebra. Cruz Resto fled from the AMO vessel at a high rate of speed while his companion threw duffle bags overboard. Cruz Resto stopped the vessel only after AMO agents fired warnings flares in front of the fleeing boat. Once the boat was stopped, and the defendant and another male were arrested, AMO agents searched the area and recovered two duffle bags that were thrown overboard. The duffel bags contained 65 packages. A Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Laboratory analyst confirmed that the 65 packages contained approximately 65 kilograms of cocaine. This case was investigated jointly by AMO and the DEA. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Erik Tate and Criminal Chief Kyle Payne.
title: Puerto Rican Man Sentenced for Trafficking 65 Kilograms of Cocaine During Boat Chase West of Savanah Island

Rep. Summer Lee Celebrates $850,000 in Federal Funding for New West Mifflin Community Recreation and Wellness Center
PITTSBURGH, PA – OCTOBER 15, 2026 — Yesterday, Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) joined West Mifflin Borough officials and community leaders for a ceremonial groundbreaking and check presentation celebrating $850,000 in federal funding she secured for the planned West Mifflin Community Recreation and Wellness Center.
The funding, secured through the federal Community Project Funding process, will support the development of a new community facility at 371 Camp Hollow Road, creating a dedicated space for recreation, wellness, youth activities, senior programming, and community gatherings.
“I’m proud to have secured $850,000 in federal funding to help make the new West Mifflin Community Recreation and Wellness Center a reality,” said Rep. Lee. “Folks in West Mifflin deserve a space where kids can grow, seniors can stay active, and families have somewhere to come together—right in their own backyards. I'm grateful to our borough leaders and state partners for helping bring us this far and look forward to seeing how this space transforms generations to come.”
"The Borough of West Mifflin extends its sincere thanks to Congresswoman Summer Lee for helping secure this funding. This project represents an important investment in West Mifflin’s future, creating opportunities for recreation, community programs, senior services, and activities for residents of all ages. This project will be a valuable asset to our community and region for generations to come,” said Michael Moses, Council President.
The project will transform an undeveloped site into a community destination designed to serve residents of all ages. Plans for the facility include indoor athletic and recreational spaces, public meeting rooms, youth activities, senior programming, and spaces for civic and community services.
Alongside the $850,000 in federal funding secured by Rep. Lee, the project has received an additional $425,000 through Pennsylvania's Statewide Local Share Account program, bringing combined federal and state funding commitments to $1.275 million.

These projects are part of more than $24.9 million in Community Project Funding secured during her time in Congress. Rep. Lee’s office has consistently directed federal dollars to historically overlooked communities to ensure equitable access to opportunities and long-term regional growth and stability.

Congresswoman Summer Lee serves on the House Committee on Judiciary and the Committee on Education and Workforce. Since taking office in January 2023, she has delivered historic levels of federal investment totaling over $2.7 Billion brought back to Western PA, including over $580 million for infrastructure, over $110 million for affordable transit, over $500 million to keep clean energy manufacturing at home in Pennsylvania, and over $55 million on clean energy efforts in and around schools to help keep our kids and communities safe. These investments will help improve Western Pennsylvania’s infrastructure and transit, ensure cleaner air and drinking water, lower housing costs, fund research institutions, fuel clean manufacturing, fund STEM innovation and entrepreneurship, boost workforce development, and create thousands of good paying union jobs. WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09) reintroduced the REAL Political Ads Act, legislation to strengthen transparency and accountability in political advertising by requiring disclosure when generative artificial intelligence (AI) is used to create images or videos in political advertisements.
A recent Quinnipiac poll found that 55 percent of Americans are concerned about the growing risks associated with artificial intelligence, and a recent Blue Rose Research poll found that 74 percent of voters believe AI-generated voices should be prohibited in political calls to protect transparency. Those concerns are compounded in the context of the Federal Communications Commission’s proposal to waive the federal ban on unsolicited AI-generated political robocalls, as well as in the widespread use of AI by the Trump Administration and across the political spectrum to attack political opponents and spread disinformation.
“As generative AI technologies continue to evolve, clear disclosure standards to preserve transparency are essential to civic engagement. Unfortunately, Congress has failed to keep up the pace with this rapidly advancing technology, leaving voters vulnerable to AI-generated misinformation and disinformation,” said Congresswoman Yvette D. Clarke. “This legislation would ensure voters know when political ads use AI-generated images and videos. If AI content can manipulate and deceive people on a large scale, it can be a serious threat to our democracy and have devastating consequences for our national and election security.”
“Voters deserve to know that the election information that we read, watch, and listen to is honest. AI makes it far too easy for campaigns to create convincing content intended to mislead voters, and too often it’s at the expense of voters of color and other communities historically pushed to the margins. Congresswoman Clarke’s REAL Political Advertisements Act would help ensure that every voter can make informed decisions based on the facts,” said Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, Vice President of The Leadership Conference’s Center for Civil Rights and Technology.
This legislation is co-sponsored by: Reps. Debbie Dingell (MI-06), Jim Costa (CA-21), Valerie Foushee (NC-04), and Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07).
The full bill text can be found here.

title: CLARKE REINTRODUCES REAL POLITICAL ADS ACT TO STRENGTHEN TRANSPARENCY IN AI-GENERATED POLITICAL ADVERTISING

NEWPORT NEWS, Va. – A Newport News man was sentenced today to 38 years and six months in prison following his conviction at trial for series of armed bank robberies.

According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Tyrone K. Jefferson, 38, worked for a rental car company where he had access to rental cars and license plates owned by the company. Jefferson stole several license plates and a sedan from the company. From Feb. 4 to Feb. 26, 2025, Jefferson used the sedan to rob a credit union and two banks. In each robbery, Jefferson threw a bag to tellers and demanded that it be filled with money, with no dye or trackers. Jefferson brandished a firearm during two of the robberies. He also used the stolen vehicle to visit a Portsmouth casino after the robberies.

On Feb. 27, 2025, Newport News Police attempted to stop the stolen sedan, but Jefferson fled at a high rate of speed, abandoned the vehicle, and escaped on foot. Police located mail, court documents and other paperwork addressed to Jefferson in the vehicle.

On March 1, 2025, Jefferson robbed another credit union by brandishing a firearm and demanding that two tellers fill a bag with money. Jefferson then fled on foot.

On March 27, 2025, police traced Jefferson to the same Portsmouth casino, to which he traveled in a rented vehicle. During a search of the vehicle, police recovered rental paperwork in Jefferson’s name, a stolen handgun, an extended magazine, a black balaclava mask, traffic safety vest, and stolen license plates used in the earlier robberies.

Jefferson has five previous felony convictions, including for assault of a federal employee (2018 for macing a Navy police officer); possession of stolen property and hit and run (2008); grand larceny of a motor vehicle (2012); and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and eluding police (2006). As a convicted felon, Jefferson cannot legally possess firearms or ammunition.

A federal jury convicted Jefferson on April 24 on charges of bank robbery, bank robbery with a dangerous weapon, brandishing a firearm in furtherance of a violent crime, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Ian Kaufmann, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Richmond Field Office, made the announcement after sentencing by Senior U.S. District Judge Raymond A. Jackson. The York-Poquoson Sheriff’s Office, Smithfield Police Department, Henrico County Police Division, and Newport News Police Department assisted in the investigation.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mack Coleman and Alyson C. Yates prosecuted the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 4:25-cr-53.
title: Newport News man sentenced to over 38 years in prison for armed bank robberies

PHOTO RELEASE: Gottheimer Visits Ukrainian Community in Ramsey, Slams Appeasement of Dictator Putin, Calls for TPS Extension to Keep Ukrainian Families Safe
Calls for TPS Extension and Continued U.S. Commitment to Ukraine
Above: Gottheimer Visits St. Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church in Ramsey.
RAMSEY, NJ — Today, Thursday, October 15, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) visited St. Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church in Ramsey, where he met with parishioners and faith leaders from North Jersey’s Ukrainian community. He discussed his support for Ukrainian families in the Fifth District, the urgent need to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Ukrainians living in the United States, and America’s continued commitment to standing with Ukraine in its war with Russia.He also slammed the Trump Administration’s appeasement of dictator Vladimir Putin, including its new deal to import Russian diesel.
“North Jersey’s Ukrainian community has shown incredible strength, faith, and generosity, and they have my full support. We must extend TPS so Ukrainian families here are not sent back into a war zone, and we must keep standing with Ukraine as it fights for freedom against Putin’s brutal invasion. America’s commitment to Ukraine cannot waver,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5).
TPS for Ukrainians is currently set to expire on Monday, October 19, 2026, which puts at risk neighbors, workers, and students who fled amid Russia’s invasion and have since built lives here. Congressman Gottheimer called on the Administration to extend TPS protections so these families are not forced to return to an active war zone.
Gottheimer also criticized the Trump Administration’s new deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. It comes just weeks after the President signed the bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Gottheimer supported, that Congress passed to choke off the energy revenues that fund Putin’s war. Gottheimer argued that the deal breaks our own laws and hands Putin’s war machine a lifeline funded by American taxpayers.
The Congressman also reaffirmed his support for Ukraine abroad. He stressed that the United States must continue to back Ukraine’s defense against Russian aggression and stand firmly with its people.
Gottheimer was joined by Maria Keniuk, Church Trustee; Irene and Victor Hurlinsky; Jed Sunden, Director of the American Ukraine Committee and the American Ukraine PAC; Jackie Colgan, American Association for Ukraine; Oleksandr Tran, President of Svitanok; Anna Move, President and Co-Founder of the Leonid Foundation; and Tanya Khapko, Mike and Oksana Dyakiv, Ivan Durbak, and Nadiya Dovhan, members of St. Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church.

MOBILE, AL – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama today announced sentencings as part of a nationwide enforcement actions led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama was key participant in this surge effort. Several defendants were sentenced for defrauding the United States of millions of dollars intended for businesses impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Between early September and today, federal prosecutors across the country facilitated fraud enforcement actions spanning over 76 criminal defendants, whose alleged crimes resulted in over $490,000,000 in intended loss to American taxpayers.

Earlier this month, Echandza Maxie (Echandza), 43, and her husband, Glennie McGee (McGee), 42, both of Mobile, were sentenced to 20 years in federal prison for their roles in a scheme to defraud the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) by illegally obtaining more than $1.5 million in COVID-19-related tax credits intended to provide relief to legitimate businesses and individuals during the pandemic. Three additional defendants were convicted and sentenced for their roles in a related scheme to defraud the Small Business Administration (SBA) through fraudulent applications for COVID-19 relief loans. A sixth defendant was separately sentenced for his role in the tax fraud scheme. In total, the defendants were ordered to pay over $2.4 Million in restitution to the IRS and SBA for their crimes.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic impact, Congress authorized refundable tax credits for paid sick and family leave to reimburse eligible employers and self-employed individuals for qualifying leave related to COVID-19. Congress also established the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) and Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program to provide emergency financial assistance to legitimate businesses suffering economic losses during the pandemic.

During a cocaine-trafficking investigation involving a court-authorized wiretap of a telephone belonging to John David Clarke of Mobile, Alabama, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), working with IRS-CI, uncovered a large-scale tax fraud scheme.

Federal agents determined that Echandza, her husband, McGee, Echandza’s sister, Edeszann Maxie (Edeszann), Tiveria Populus (Populus), Jamael Nettles (Nettles), John David Clarke (Clarke), and others participated in schemes to fraudulently obtain COVID-19-related tax credits and SBA loans.

According to court documents, Echandza owned and operated a Mobile tax-preparation business known as “Self Made Taxes,” which was purportedly co-located with a clothing store, an eyelash business, and other businesses. Edeszann, who also worked as a tax preparer, worked with Echandza, McGee, and others to obtain the personal identifying information of prospective taxpayers and use that information to file fraudulent tax returns in their names.

The defendants enlisted recruiters who were paid finder’s fees to obtain names, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers belonging to prospective taxpayers. Echandza, Edeszann, and McGee generally required only that the prospective taxpayer had not yet filed a tax return and did not owe child support. They did not obtain information necessary to determine whether the taxpayer actually operated a business or otherwise qualified for the COVID-19 tax credits.

Using the personal identifying information they obtained, Echandza and Edeszann fabricated fictitious self-employed businesses, frequently claiming that the taxpayers operated landscaping or hairstyling businesses. The fraudulent tax returns routinely claimed that the taxpayers had taken the maximum amount of COVID-19-related sick and family leave and sought the maximum available credit of approximately $30,000 per return. Echandza and Edeszann also fabricated business revenues for the 2021 tax year.

Many of the fraudulent refunds were directed to bank accounts controlled by the defendants. Although the IRS identified and rejected a significant number of fraudulent returns after placing identity-theft holds on them, the scheme nevertheless generated more than $1.5 million in fraudulent tax refunds.

Some individuals whose information was used in the scheme believed they were legitimately eligible to receive COVID-19 relief and trusted the defendants to prepare accurate tax returns on their behalf. Some individuals unfamiliar with the tax-filing process paid between $10,000 and $15,000 to have their returns prepared, believing the payments were legitimate tax-preparation fees.

FBI and IRS-CI special agents identified dozens of individuals whose personal information had been used to file fraudulent tax returns. Many had no knowledge that a return had been filed in their names. Others were unaware that their returns contained false information, including claims that they operated businesses they did not own or operate.

In some instances, the defendants filed fraudulent returns as “self-prepared,” even though the returns had been prepared and submitted by Echandza or Edeszann. Investigators identified the fraud through contact and banking information on the returns that belonged to the defendants, demonstrating that the named taxpayers had no knowledge of the refunds generated using their personal information. In other cases, individuals learned that fraudulent returns had been filed in their names after receiving notice from the Social Security Administration that their disability benefits could be affected by purported business income reported to the IRS.

Fraudulent SBA Loans

The defendants, except for Nettles, also fraudulently applied for and obtained dozens of PPP and EIDL loans administered by the SBA in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The PPP provided eligible businesses with potentially forgivable loans guaranteed by the SBA, while the EIDL program provided low-interest loans to help eligible small businesses maintain operations during the pandemic. The programs were intended to provide financial assistance for legitimate business expenses, including payroll, rent, and utilities.

With assistance from special agents with the SBA Office of Inspector General, investigators determined that Echandza, McGee, Edeszann, Clarke, and Populus each submitted fraudulent SBA loan applications. The applications contained material misrepresentations that the defendants operated legitimate businesses before the pandemic and that those businesses generated substantial revenue.

For businesses that had some evidence of operation before 2020, investigators determined that the defendants fabricated revenue figures and the number of employees to obtain larger loan proceeds. In total, the defendants obtained more than $885,000 in SBA loans to which they were not entitled.

Each defendant pleaded guilty to charges arising from his or her participation in the fraud schemes. United States District Court Judge Terry F. Moorer imposed the sentences.

Sentences

Echandza Maxie was sentenced to 20 years in prison, followed by a mandatory two-year consecutive sentence for aggravated identity theft. She was ordered to pay $1,576,358.88 in restitution to the IRS and $257,413.93 to the SBA. Her 20-year sentence, excluding the mandatory consecutive sentence for aggravated identity theft, was ordered to run concurrently with her life sentence stemming from a multi-million-dollar cocaine and fentanyl trafficking organization related convictions. If released from prison, she will be subject to three years of supervised release. She was also ordered to pay a $300 special assessment and forfeit approximately $85,000 in fraud proceeds seized by the FBI during the investigation.

Glennie McGee was sentenced to 20 years in prison, followed by a mandatory two-year consecutive sentence for aggravated identity theft. McGee was ordered to pay $672,219 in restitution to the IRS and $340,910.16 to the SBA. His 20-year sentence, excluding the mandatory consecutive sentence for aggravated identity theft, was ordered to run concurrently with his life sentence stemming from his multi-million-dollar cocaine and fentanyl trafficking organization. If released from prison, he will be subject to three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay a $300 special assessment.

Edeszann Maxie was sentenced to 135 months in prison, followed by a mandatory two-year consecutive sentence for aggravated identity theft. She was ordered to pay $187,301 in restitution to the IRS and $298,667.70 to the SBA. Upon release from prison, she will be subject to three years of supervised release. She was also ordered to pay a $300 special assessment.

John David Clarke was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay $28,764.10 in restitution to the IRS and $55,167 to the SBA. His sentence was ordered to run concurrently with his separately imposed 20-year-sentence stemming from his convictions related to a large-scale cocaine trafficking conspiracy . Upon release from prison, Clarke will be subject to three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay a $200 special assessment.

Tiveria Populus was sentenced to time served and ordered to pay $28,764.10 in restitution to the IRS and $46,206.29 to the SBA. Populus will be subject to five years of supervised release and was ordered to pay a $200 special assessment.

Jamael Nettles, in a separate case, was sentenced to five days in prison and ordered to pay $29,339 in restitution to the IRS. Nettles will be subject to three years of supervised release and was ordered to pay a $100 special assessment.

“The defendants exploited programs created to provide relief to businesses and individuals during an unprecedented national crisis, stealing millions of dollars through fraudulent tax returns and applications for pandemic relief,” said U.S. Attorney Sean P. Costello. “Fraud of this kind does more than steal money from the government—it undermines the integrity of our tax system and diverts resources away from the people and businesses who were entitled to receive them. I commend IRS Criminal Investigation and our other law enforcement partners for following the financial trail, uncovering this scheme, and holding fraudsters responsible.”

“The defendants carried out a coordinated scheme to defraud the government by filing fraudulent tax returns, misusing personal identities, and submitting false pandemic relief loan applications,” said Special Agent in Charge Demetrius Hardeman, IRS Criminal Investigation, Atlanta Field Office. “IRS Criminal Investigation special agents, working closely with our federal partners, traced the movement of illicit proceeds and uncovered the financial trails that revealed the full extent of the conspiracy. Their efforts ensured that those responsible were identified and held accountable.”

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, IRS Criminal Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations, the Small Business Administration Office of Inspector General, and the Social Security Administration, with assistance from multiple state and local law enforcement agencies, including the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office and Mobile Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kasee S. Heisterhagen and Justin Kopf prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States.

In addition to its outstanding financial impact, this prosecution was also a part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership focused on investigating and prosecuting criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking organizations operating in the United States and abroad. Through interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs federal law enforcement resources toward investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by these organizations. HSTF Mobile includes agents and officers from, among others, Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, with prosecutions led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division investigates and prosecutes individuals and organizations that commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s efforts to combat fraud support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to address fraud, waste, and abuse involving federal benefit programs.

This press release details one way in which this office has contributed to ensuring that all Americans pay their fair share. To see the successes of other offices, please see this press release .

If you believe you are a victim of identity theft or suspect a paid tax return preparer is engaged in fraud or misconduct, you may report it to the IRS and make a complaint about a tax return preparer online .

Individuals with information about allegations of fraud involving COVID-19 are encouraged to report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form .
title: United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing over $490 Million in Tax Fraud

Larson Statement on the 2027 Social Security COLA Announcement
Washington, D.C. - Today, House Social Security Subcommittee Ranking Member John B. Larson (CT-01) released the following statement after the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6 percent Social Security Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for 2027.
“Today’s announcement demonstrates just how hard President Trump’s affordability crisis has hit our seniors," said Larson. “As Americans struggle to make ends meet, a small bump in benefits is always welcome news—but for many seniors living on fixed incomes, it won’t be enough to keep pace with rising costs. With insolvency looming, we are only a few years away from automatic benefit cuts for everyone on Social Security if Congress does not act. Rather than come to the table with solutions, this administration and their allies in Congress have been laser-focused on breaking the system from within, so they can privatize Social Security. They have slashed staff and services at the Social Security Administration, making it harder for seniors to get their benefits in full and on time, and Speaker Johnson has even teased a plan to cut benefits if Republicans hold their majorities in the House and Senate. We cannot let that happen. Americans are depending on their Congress to enhance benefits—not cut them—and Democrats are ready to act. Our plan will stop these automatic cuts, boost benefits across the board, and ensure no one can retire into poverty after a lifetime of work, all by finally making the ultra-wealthy pay their fair share. It is time for a vote.”
The annual Social Security Trustees Report released this summer confirmed that Congress must act and that failed Trump policies, including the Big, Ugly Bill, mean that Social Security’s insolvency is closer than ever. Inaction will lead to the average senior losing about $500/month in Social Security benefits in 2032.
Ranking Member Larson’s Social Security 2100 Act would enhance Social Security benefits to help beneficiaries dealing with rising costs and extend the program’s solvency by eliminating the FICA cap and imposing a net investment income tax on income over $400,000.
title: Larson Statement on the 2027 Social Security COLA Announcement

MISSOULA – A Missoula man who had stored tens of thousands of images and hundreds of videos of Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) was sentenced today to 15 years in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Steger Smith said.

Jamie T. Felde, 47, pleaded guilty in June 2026 to receiving child pornography.

U.S. District Judge William W. Mercer presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Felde had uploaded several files of Child Sexual Abuse Material online between 2021 and 2023. Cybertips from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children indicated someone was uploading CSAM files to Microsoft’s Bing Image. Investigators eventually narrowed the activity to Missoula County and identified Felde as the source.

Using a warrant, law enforcement searched Felde’s home and seized several phones, USB drives, external hard drives, and computer towers. A forensic analysis of the electronics showed that Felde had received and possessed 23,716 images and 643 videos of minors engaged in sexually explicit conduct.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Lowney prosecuted the case. The Missoula Police Department and Montana Division of Criminal Investigation conducted the investigation.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOs, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .
title: Missoula man sentenced to 15 years in prison for receiving thousands of images and videos of Child Sex Abuse Material

Greenbelt , Maryland – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maryland announced, today, that a Maryland man is facing indictment as part of a nationwide enforcement action led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service - Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses.

Between early September and today, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section, and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country, participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490 million.

In the District of Maryland, Martin Herrera Navarrete, 66, of Glenn Dale, is charged with willful failure to collect, account, and pay over taxes, and willful failure to file tax returns. The charges stem from Navarrete failing to account for and pay over trust fund taxes owed to the IRS on behalf of Navarrete’s employees. This prosecution is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the indictment with Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, DOJ Fraud Division; Frank Bisignano, Chief Executive Officer, Internal Revenue Service; and Chief Jared Koopman, Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI).

“This prosecution sends a clear and strong message that we will root out fraudsters, charge cheaters, and bring justice to those who think our tax laws don’t apply to them,” Hayes said. “Tax fraud not only harms the federal government, but also adversely affects every American who plays by the rules. We’re committed to continuing to work with our law-enforcement partners to apply these laws, which is essential to maintaining fairness, accountability, and public confidence.”

According to the indictment, Navarrete, who served as sole owner and sole corporate officer of Navarrete Brothers Construction, Inc. (NBC), exercised significant control and authority over NBC’s finances. Among his responsibilities, he was supposed to collect trust-fund taxes, account for employment taxes by filing Forms 941 with the IRS, and pay the IRS the trust fund taxes for NBC’s employees.

However, from September 2020 through December 2025, Navarrete allegedly willfully failed to truthfully account for and pay over the taxes owed to the IRS on behalf of NBC’s employees, which were withheld from employees in trust for the U.S. Treasury. The indictment further alleges that Navarrete willfully failed to file U.S. Corporate Income Tax Return and Individual Tax Return forms for calendar years 2020-2024.

An indictment is not a finding of guilt. Individuals charged by indictment are presumed innocent until proven guilty at a later criminal proceeding. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

If convicted, Navarrete faces a maximum of five years in federal prison for willful failure to collect, account, and pay over taxes, and a maximum of one year for willful failure to file tax returns.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes commended the IRS-CI for its work in the investigation. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Rosenthal and Fraud Division Trial Attorney Catriona Coppler who are prosecuting this federal case.

For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to report fraud, please visit justice.gov/usao-md and justice.gov/usao-md/report-fraud .

The Federal Water Pollution Control Act, commonly referred to as the Clean Water Act (CWA), is the principal federal law in the United States governing water pollution. To help achieve its goals, the statute prohibits the discharge of pollutants from any point source (e.g., a discrete conveyance such as a pipe) to waters of the United States (WOTUS) without a permit. The CWA also establishes two permitting programs that may be used to authorize certain discharges. These include the Section 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitting program and the Section 404 permitting program for dredged or fill material.
NPDES permits are issued by states and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for discharges of pollutants from point sources, such as municipal and industrial sources. These sources include wastewater treatment facilities, municipal stormwater collection systems, and a wide variety of industrial dischargers. Section 404 permits are issued primarily by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and two states (Michigan and New Jersey) for discharges of dredged or fill material. Activities that may require a Section 404 permit include pipeline projects, water resource projects, mining projects, transmission line projects, or other development projects. Separate from, but related to permitting, CWA Section 401 requires a type of approval, called a water quality certification, for any federal permit or license that may result in a discharge to WOTUS. Although Section 401 water quality certifications are not permits, they are a type of approval required for some projects to move forward and have implications for issuance of some federal permits and licenses. Examples of activities that may require a CWA Section 401 water quality certification include activities requiring a USACE-issued CWA Section 404 permit, projects requiring USACE Rivers and Harbors Act permits, hydropower projects licensed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), and certificates of public convenience and necessity issued by FERC.
The second Trump Administration has issued proposed regulations that, if finalized, would affect some aspects of CWA permitting and 401 certifications. EPA and USACE have issued a proposed rule and a proposed supplemental rule to update the definition of WOTUS. If finalized, the rule would likely narrow the scope of waters and wetlands considered WOTUS, and therefore subject to the CWA's permitting programs and water quality certification requirements. EPA has also issued a proposed rule to update the Section 401 implementing regulations, which, if finalized, would likely narrow the scope of what states may consider in issuing water quality certifications, among other changes. These changes could have implications for the issuance of certain federal licenses and permits, including Section 404 permits.
Many Members have shown interest in policy issues pertaining to CWA permitting—especially permitting reform—in recent Congresses. Congressional committees have held hearings that have included discussions of CWA permitting, and some Members have introduced legislation that either focuses specifically on CWA permitting or would amend CWA permitting within broader permitting reform bills. Of the over 50 bills introduced during the 119th Congress that propose to address some aspect of CWA permitting, more than half include changes to NPDES permitting, more than half include changes to Section 404 permitting, and over a quarter would make changes to Section 401 certification. A few of these bills propose changes to the scope of WOTUS.
Congress's interest in CWA permitting, as demonstrated through hearings and legislative efforts, can be grouped under a few broader policy areas: the balance of federal versus state authority for permitting-related programs and decisions; regulatory certainty; and timelines for permit issuance, particularly for certain energy, mineral, and other projects identified as being of national importance. Congress may consider proposing or supporting legislation that addresses these issues, may consider overseeing the Administration's ongoing regulatory efforts; may consider oversight of existing permitting processes generally, or specific to certain industries or project types; or may opt not to act and leave implementation of these issues to EPA, USACE, and states.
The Federal Water Pollution Control Act, commonly referred to as the Clean Water Act (CWA), is the principal federal law in the United States governing water pollution.1 Congress passed major amendments to the statute in 1972, which significantly reorganized and expanded it to establish a new framework for controlling water pollution.2 Among the many revisions, the amendments set ambitious goals for water quality and established the basic structure for regulating pollutant discharges into the nation's surface waters.
The CWA's objective, as stated in the 1972 amendments, is "to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation's waters."3 The CWA also established two goals: to eliminate the discharge of pollutants into navigable waters by 1985; and as an interim goal, wherever attainable, to achieve water quality that is "fishable" and "swimmable" by July 1, 1983.4 Although much progress has been made, those goals have not been met fully in many places. While those dates have long passed, the goals remain, and efforts to attain them continue.
To help achieve the CWA's objective and goals, the statute prohibits the discharge of pollutants from any point source (e.g., a discrete conveyance such as a pipe) to waters of the United States (WOTUS) without a permit.5 The CWA also establishes two permitting programs that may be used to authorize certain discharges. These are the Section 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitting program and the Section 404 permitting program for dredged or fill material.6 NPDES permits are issued by 47 states and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for discharges of pollutants from point sources, such as municipal and industrial sources. These sources include wastewater treatment facilities, municipal stormwater collection systems, and a wide variety of industrial dischargers. Section 404 permits are issued primarily by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and two states (Michigan and New Jersey) for discharges of dredged or fill material. Activities that may require a Section 404 permit include pipeline projects, water resource projects, mining projects, transmission line projects, or other development projects.
In recent Congresses, some Members have shown interest in a wide range of policy issues pertaining to CWA permitting and reform. One issue of interest has been the definition of waters of the United States (WOTUS), which determines the scope of waters subject to the CWA's permitting provisions. Some Members have also sought to find ways to streamline the CWA permitting process to help expedite the approval of certain projects—including linear infrastructure and other projects that they assert are critical to national interests. Other policy topics related to CWA permitting that some Members have sought to address include permit term lengths; permit requirements for emerging contaminants such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); permit requirements for aerial discharges including pesticides and fire suppressants; EPA's authority to "veto" Section 404 permits approved by USACE; and state authority under CWA Section 401 to issue water quality certifications, which has implications for the issuance of some CWA permits.7 The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, each held hearings at the start of the 119th Congress that focused on permitting, including CWA permitting.8
This report provides an overview of CWA permitting, including the scope of CWA permitting and a summary of each of the CWA permitting programs. The report also summarizes congressional interest in CWA permitting, including a summary of the hearings and legislation in recent Congresses on this topic, and discusses policy options in this area.
Several CWA provisions and definitions establish the scope of discharges that require a permit under the statute. Broadly, CWA Section 301 specifies that the discharge of any pollutant by any person is unlawful without a permit.9 CWA Section 502, the statute's definitions provision, defines several terms pertinent to the scope of this prohibition:
Taken together, the scope of the prohibition on discharges without a permit pertains to discharges of pollutants (defined broadly) from point sources (i.e., discrete conveyances) to WOTUS. The prohibition extends to the contiguous zone and the ocean for point sources other than vessels or other floating craft. Examples of such point sources include wastewater facilities with deep ocean outfalls, certain aquaculture operations, and certain offshore oil- and gas-development-related facilities.
As introduced above, the CWA establishes two permitting programs that may be used to authorize discharges. These are the Section 402 NPDES permitting program and the Section 404 permitting program for dredged or fill material. Each of these programs has their own specific scope of applicability.
The scope of waters included in the definition of WOTUS has been, and continues to be, a matter of debate. Because the CWA does not define WOTUS, USACE and EPA—the two agencies that administer the statute—have defined the term in regulations. For much of the past several decades, regulations promulgated by USACE and EPA in the 1980s have been in effect. However, Supreme Court rulings, stakeholder interest, and congressional interest prompted the last three presidential Administrations (the Obama Administration, the first Trump Administration, and the Biden Administration) to promulgate revised definitions of WOTUS. Each of these regulatory efforts prompted reactions from a variety of stakeholders with numerous groups filing lawsuits to challenge the rules. In addition, in 2023, the Supreme Court issued a decision construing WOTUS more narrowly than previous regulatory interpretations.22 EPA and USACE have since attempted to align the regulatory definition of WOTUS with the Court's ruling.
In March 2025, the Trump Administration announced its intent to revise the definition of WOTUS again through new rulemaking.23 On November 20, 2025, EPA and USACE published a proposed rule to revise the definition of WOTUS for public comment.24 On September 9, 2026, EPA and USACE issued a supplemental proposed rule, which supplements the initial proposed rule with additional regulatory options on certain aspects of the proposed rule.25 If finalized, the updated regulations would likely result in a narrower scope for WOTUS compared to the existing regulations, meaning that fewer waters and wetlands would be subject to CWA permitting requirements.26
Given that the scope of WOTUS determines which waters are subject to CWA permitting requirements, the definition continues to be a key policy issue in the CWA permitting space. For more information on this issue, see CRS Report R47408, Waters of the United States (WOTUS): Frequently Asked Questions About the Scope of the Clean Water Act, by Kate R. Bowers and Laura Gatz.
One of the two permitting programs authorized by the CWA is the NPDES permitting program. Under the CWA, one of the primary mechanisms to protect or improve surface water quality is to limit or prohibit discharges of pollutants in NPDES permits.27 The following sections detail who needs an NPDES permit, who administers NPDES permits, how pollutant limitations in the permits are established, the types of NPDES permits and term lengths, permitting time frames, and information on monitoring and enforcement.
Any person who discharges a pollutant from a point source to WOTUS needs an NPDES permit unless the activity is specifically exempt under Section 402.28 This includes a wide range of potential dischargers—typically the owners or operators of a facility or activity subject to regulation under the NPDES program.29 These facilities/activities include publicly owned treatment works (i.e., municipal wastewater treatment facilities), municipal separate storm sewer collection systems (MS4s), a wide range of industrial facilities that discharge wastewater and/or stormwater, construction activities that discharge stormwater, certain pesticide applications, and certain fire-retardant applications.30 Any owner or operator of a point source other than a vessel or floating craft that discharges a pollutant into the contiguous zone or the ocean also needs an NPDES permit. The CWA identifies specific activities that do not require NPDES permits in Section 402(l).31
The CWA authorizes both EPA and delegated states to administer NPDES permits.32 States, territories, and tribes may administer their own NPDES permits if they seek and receive approval from EPA to assume the program.33 Most states (47 states) and one territory (the U.S. Virgin Islands) are authorized to administer their own NPDES permits.34 EPA administers NPDES permits in Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, the District of Columbia, the remaining territories, on Indian lands, and on Lands of Exclusive Federal Jurisdiction.35 EPA may also issue some NPDES permits in states that are authorized to administer NPDES permits, but do not have authorization for all NPDES program components. For example, some states do not have authorization to regulate federal facilities (e.g., military bases, national parks, federal lands) or do not have an authorized biosolids (e.g., sewage sludge) program.36 In such cases, EPA retains NPDES permitting authority for those program components.
As discussed above, delegated states issue NPDES permits for discharges to WOTUS in their states (including the territorial seas for coastal states). EPA may issue NPDES permits for discharges to WOTUS, as well as for certain discharges to the contiguous zone and the ocean.
Once a state assumes administration of its NPDES permitting program, the state is responsible for issuing permits as well as for monitoring and enforcement, although EPA also retains an oversight and enforcement role.37 These aspects are discussed in more detail below.
When a state or EPA establishes effluent (i.e., discharge) limitations in a permit, it must consider limitations based on both the technology available to control the pollutants (i.e., technology-based effluent limitations) and what is needed to attain or maintain the water quality standards of the receiving waterbody (i.e., water-quality-based effluent limitations). The permitting authority must also consider antibacksliding requirements that aim to prohibit the renewal, reissuance, or modification of an existing NPDES permit that contains effluent limitations, permit conditions, or standards less stringent than those established in the previous permit.38
TBELs are specific numerical limits (i.e., maximum allowable levels of specific pollutants), or in some cases, best management practices, that represent the minimum level of control that must be established in a permit.39 The CWA requires EPA to establish TBELs for various categories of point sources/dischargers.40 Technology-based requirements consider the performance of specific technologies as well as economic achievability. These limits do not specify what technologies must be employed; rather, they establish the levels of specific pollutants that are allowable in the discharge based on the performance of technologies identified as representing specified levels of control (e.g., best available technology economically achievable, best conventional pollutant control technology). The CWA prescribes levels of control for various dischargers, as described below.
EPA broadly classifies NPDES permittees as either (1) publicly owned treatment works (POTWs)41 or (2) non-POTWs, which include all other point sources and are also often called nonmunicipal facilities or industrial facilities.42
The CWA requires POTWs to meet secondary treatment standards as determined by EPA.43 Secondary treatment standards are based on performance data for POTWs that use physical and biological treatment to remove or control conventional pollutants.44
As shown in Figure 1, the CWA requires industrial dischargers to achieve specified levels of control based on (1) whether a discharger directly or indirectly discharges into WOTUS (an indirect discharger discharges to a POTW for treatment prior to discharge into WOTUS), (2) whether the discharger is a new or existing source, and (3) the category of pollutant (conventional, toxic,45 or nonconventional46).47
The CWA requires EPA to publish national regulations for industrial dischargers—called Effluent Limitation Guidelines and Standards (ELGs)—which set minimum standards for specific pollutants in industrial wastewater discharges based on the specified levels of control.48 Since 1972, EPA has developed ELGs for 59 industrial categories.49 For direct dischargers, states or EPA incorporate the limits established in ELGs into the NPDES permits they issue. For indirect dischargers, pretreatment standards established in ELGs to prevent pass through and interference at the POTW apply.50
In cases where technology-based effluent limitations are not adequate to meet applicable water quality standards, permits also incorporate water-quality-based effluent limitations.51 Water-quality-based effluent limitations are specific limits established in a permit (numeric or narrative) that, if not exceeded in the discharge, allow for attainment of water quality standards in the receiving water.52 Water quality standards—established by states, territories, tribes, and EPA—define the desired condition or level of protection of a water body and what is needed to achieve or protect that condition.53
A 2025 Supreme Court decision—City and County of San Francisco, California v. EPA—ruled that the CWA does not authorize EPA (or states) to impose what the Court called "end-result" provisions in NPDES permits.54 Such "end-result" requirements condition a permittee's compliance on the quality of the receiving water rather than on adherence to specific effluent limitations. Examples include certain narrative conditions added to permits to prohibit the permittee from creating nuisance conditions or causing or contributing to a violation of water quality standards in the receiving water body. Prior to the Supreme Court ruling, such provisions were commonly used by permit writers.55 As a result of the ruling, permit writers will need to specify specific, measurable discharge limits, or will need to include specific actions a permittee must take to comply with its permit.
There are two main types of NPDES permits: individual permits and general permits. While both types include the same minimum components, these permits are used under different circumstances.56 The CWA identifies some of the elements that must be included in NPDES permits and directed EPA to promulgate regulations establishing the minimum procedural requirements and elements of state NPDES programs.57 EPA's regulations outlining the NPDES permitting processes are codified at 40 C.F.R. Part 122. State-issued laws and regulations also identify the process and requirements for NPDES permits issued by each state.
The processes for developing and issuing individual permits and general permits are similar, but there are some differences, as shown in Figure 2. The CWA limits NPDES permit terms for both individual and general permits to five years.58
EPA or states issue individual permits for a single discharger (or in rare cases to multiple co-permittees) to reflect site-specific conditions based on the discharger's operations and unique information provided in the permit application.59 These individual permits are specifically tailored to an individual facility.60
EPA or states issue general permits for one or more categories or subcategories of dischargers with similar operations and types of discharges that can provide coverage to multiple dischargers.61 According to EPA, "when a large number of similar facilities require permits, a general permit allows the permitting authority to allocate resources in a more efficient manner and to provide more timely permit coverage than issuing an individual permit to each facility. In addition, using a general permit ensures consistent permit conditions for comparable facilities."62 Once a general permit is issued, a discharger typically submits a Notice of Intent (NOI) to request coverage under the permit.63 Some general permits, however, automatically cover some discharges without submission of a NOI.
EPA recognizes the importance of timely issuance and reissuance of NPDES permits, noting that timeliness provides greater regulatory certainty to the business community and ensures that permits improve environmental protection by reflecting the most recent scientific information.64 However, EPA and some states have permitting "backlogs" for both individual and general permits. EPA notes that it "continuously works to increase efficiencies in permitting processes to decrease the NPDES permit backlog and encourages authorized NPDES permit programs to do the same."65
EPA regulations require any person proposing a new discharge to apply for a permit at least 180 days before the discharge is to commence.66 EPA considers applications for new EPA-issued permits that are not issued or denied within 365 days of receipt of the application to be backlogged.67
Permittees that want to renew their permit must submit a complete application for permit renewal at least 180 days prior to their permit expiration date.68 If the permitting authority receives the complete application but fails to reissue the permit prior to the expiration date, the permit is "administratively continued" and operates under the same terms and conditions until the new permit is issued.69 EPA considers permits that are administratively continued for 180 days or more to be backlogged.70
EPA tracks the NPDES permit backlog for both EPA-issued and state-issued permits, including individual and general permits.71 Table 1 provides a summary of the NPDES permit backlog for individual existing permits as of October 1, 2025.72 EPA data also indicate that as of the same date, EPA had a backlog for new individual permits—10 for permits on Tribal land and 14 for other EPA-issued permits.73 EPA's NPDES backlog data do not provide information on the backlog for new state-issued individual permits. Table 2 provides a summary of the NPDES permit backlog for general permits as of October 1, 2025, including data on the estimated number of facilities covered by the backlogged permits.

States, permitted entities, and EPA have roles in ensuring NPDES permit compliance. Monitoring to ensure compliance with NPDES permits includes both monitoring performed by the permittee as well as monitoring performed by the permitting authority (either the state or EPA) during inspections. Authorized states and EPA also cooperatively enforce NPDES permitting requirements.
NPDES permits specify the monitoring requirements the permittee must conduct to demonstrate compliance with permit limitations.74 EPA's regulations require that NPDES permits specify the required monitoring including the type, intervals, and frequency sufficient to yield data representative of the monitored activity, and may include continuous monitoring when appropriate.75 EPA regulations also require NPDES permits to specify reporting requirements, which are established on a case-by-case basis with a frequency dependent upon the nature and effect of the discharge. In most cases, permittees must report their monitoring results at least annually.76 NPDES permits also include standard conditions that require the permittee to notify the permitting authority regarding any instances of noncompliance.77 In 2015, EPA promulgated a regulation to require electronic reporting and sharing of NPDES information.78 Since that time, EPA has worked with states to phase-in electronic reporting.79
The CWA also authorizes EPA or states to enter premises with permitted effluents, access records, inspect monitoring equipment, and sample effluents subject to CWA monitoring requirements.80 EPA inspects NPDES-permitted facilities in states where the agency is the permitting authority as well as on Tribal lands.81 In states that administer their own NPDES permitting programs, the states take the lead on inspections. EPA retains inspection authority in states with NPDES program authorization and sometimes conducts inspections at the request of states (to support the state's own inspection efforts) and to respond to tips or complaints.82
The CWA authorizes EPA and delegated states to use a range of enforcement tools—administrative, civil judicial, and criminal actions—to address noncompliance with NPDES requirements.84 EPA retains enforcement authority in delegated states, although such states generally take the lead on enforcement.85 EPA and states will sometimes undertake joint enforcement proceedings where violations of both federal and state law are alleged. EPA and states may seek voluntary compliance with violations or may use a range of tools authorized under CWA Sections 309 and 402. The CWA authorizes EPA and states to issue administrative compliance orders (e.g., to correct violations, comply with permit conditions or limitations) and assess administrative penalties.86 The statute also provides judicial enforcement tools. EPA and states may seek civil judicial enforcement actions and penalties, as well as criminal judicial enforcement actions (e.g., fines, imprisonment, or both) for knowing or negligent violations.87
The other permitting program authorized under the CWA is the CWA Section 404 permitting program for the discharge of dredged or fill material into WOTUS.88 Dredged material includes material dredged or excavated from waterbodies, such as coastal waters, lakes, rivers, and stream beds.89 These materials can contain pollutants that may affect water quality when discharged into receiving waters or wetlands. Regardless of the presence of pollutants in the dredged material, when it is used to fill wetlands or other receiving waters for purposes of development, the discharge can negatively affect aquatic ecosystems and the functionality of wetlands, among other outcomes. Fill material—including rock, sand, soil, construction debris—may have similar consequences when used to fill wetlands or other receiving waters.90
The following sections detail who needs a Section 404 permit, who administers Section 404 permits, the types of Section 404 permits and term lengths, the 404 permitting process, permitting time frames, and monitoring and enforcement.
Any person who discharges dredged or fill material into WOTUS needs a Section 404 permit, unless the activity is specifically exempt under Section 404(f).91 Examples of activities that may require a Section 404 permit include infrastructure development (e.g., highways, pipelines, utility lines), water resource projects (e.g., dams and levees), mining projects, or residential or commercial development.
The CWA authorizes both the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and states to administer Section 404 permits.92 States, territories, and tribes may administer their own Section 404 permits if they seek and receive approval from EPA to assume the program.93 In states that assume administration of their Section 404 permits, USACE retains authority over certain waters—generally those that are currently used, or capable of being used, for interstate or foreign commerce, as well as those subject to tidal ebb and flow and their adjacent wetlands.94 Currently, two states—Michigan and New Jersey—are authorized to administer their own Section 404 permits.95 Florida also previously had authority to administer its own program, which EPA approved in 2020.96 However, a U.S. District Court vacated the approval in February 2024 on Endangered Species Act grounds.97 A U.S. Court of Appeals upheld the vacatur in March 2026.98 USACE administers Section 404 permits in the remaining states and territories and on Indian lands, as well as for activities in retained waters in Michigan and New Jersey.99
The CWA also establishes distinct responsibilities for EPA in implementing Section 404. EPA is responsible for developing and interpreting policy, guidance, and environmental criteria to be used in evaluating permit applications.100 Section 404(b) requires USACE to evaluate permit applications using guidelines developed by EPA, in conjunction with the USACE—commonly referred to as 404(b)(1) guidelines.101 EPA also reviews and comments on individual permits and can elevate specific cases (i.e., request a higher level of review) using authority under Section 404(q) when the agencies do not agree.102 In addition, EPA has authority under Section 404(c) to prohibit, deny, restrict, or withdraw the use of a specified area as a disposal site for dredged or fill material whenever the Administrator determines that the discharge will have an unacceptable adverse effect on municipal water supplies, shellfish beds and fishery areas, wildlife, or recreational areas.103 This authority is commonly referred to as EPA "veto" authority. To date, EPA has issued final determinations under its 404(c) authority 14 times.104
Similar to NPDES permits, there are two main types of Section 404 permits: individual permits and general permits. However, in contrast to NPDES permits, there are multiple types of individual and general permits under Section 404, which have different permit terms. Section 404 establishes requirements for some aspects of the permits, and USACE and EPA have promulgated regulations to implement these requirements.105 States with delegated authority also have their own state laws and regulations that apply to the permits they issue.106
USACE or states issue individual permits for individual projects or applicants, typically when the project's discharge may cause more than minimal individual or cumulative impacts.107 There are two types of individual permits: standard individual permits and letters of permission (LOPs). The term lengths for individual permits issued by USACE vary based on the project. If the discharge is of a more permanent nature, the permit may include timelines for completing the work or activity or may specify a date by which the work must be started.108 If the discharge is of a temporary nature, the permit would include an expiration date.109 The CWA limits permit terms for state-issued individual permits to five years.110
Standard individual permits authorize discharges following a comprehensive case-specific review, including a public notice period, public interest review, an option for a public hearing, activity-specific environmental documentation, and a 404(b)(1) guidelines analysis.111 See Figure 3 for a general overview of the procedure USACE uses to evaluate a standard individual permit application.
If USACE is the permitting authority, the district engineer must comply with environmental procedures and documentation required under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).112 A decision on the permit application requires either an environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement unless the permitted activity is included within a categorical exclusion.113
Public interest reviews evaluate the probable impacts of the proposed activity to determine whether the activity is in the public interest. The review includes a careful weighing of a wide range of factors relevant to a particular permit application. These potential factors include conservation, economics, aesthetics, general environmental concerns, wetlands, historic properties, fish and wildlife values, flood hazards, floodplain values, land use, navigation, shore erosion and accretion, recreation, water supply and conservation, water quality, energy needs, safety, food and fiber production, mineral needs, considerations of property ownership, and the needs and welfare of people.114
USACE and states also conduct 404(b)(1) guidelines evaluations when considering whether to issue a standard individual permit. The fundamental principle of the criteria within the guidelines is that dredged or fill material should not be discharged into WOTUS unless it can be demonstrated that the discharge will not have unacceptable adverse impacts on those waters. The 404(b)(1) guidelines require the following determinations for permit issuance: (1) the project is the least environmentally damaging practicable alternative; (2) the project will not cause or contribute to the violation of applicable state or federal laws, such as water quality standards or the Endangered Species Act; (3) the project will not cause or contribute to significant degradation of WOTUS; and (4) any appropriate and practicable steps have been taken to minimize the adverse impacts of the project on wetlands and other waters.115
The 404(b)(1) guidelines aim to ensure that all appropriate and practicable steps are taken to avoid and minimize impacts to aquatic resources. For unavoidable impacts, the guidelines require compensatory mitigation to replace the loss of wetland, stream, and/or other aquatic resource functions.116 USACE (or the approved state authority) is responsible for determining the appropriate form and amount of required compensatory mitigation. Mitigation may include aquatic resource restoration, enhancement, establishment, and in certain circumstances, preservation.117 The 404(b)(1) guidelines specify what the USACE district engineer (or state authority) should consider when determining the required compensatory mitigation as well as the general requirements for compensatory mitigation.118
LOPs are a type of individual permit issued by USACE under a more expedited process when a USACE district determines that the proposed work is minor, would not have significant individual or cumulative impacts on the environment, and is unlikely to face substantial opposition.119 Applications that qualify for authorization under a letter of permission do not require USACE to publish an individual public notice and are categorically excluded from NEPA (so do not require an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement).120 However, USACE still must conduct a public interest evaluation and comply with other laws. USACE issues LOPs in the form of a letter, which includes details such as the permittee's information, project location, authorized work, time limits, general conditions, and any specific limitations or conditions applicable to the project.121
USACE (and authorized states) may issue general permits for proposed activities that are similar in nature and will result in only minimal individual and cumulative adverse environmental effects.122 These permits, authorized under CWA Section 404(e), are issued on a nationwide, regional, or state basis for particular categories of activities.123 The CWA limits general permit terms to no more than five years.124
General permits are a key means by which USACE streamlines the requirements of its permitting process: they essentially preauthorize categories of activities USACE has identified as being similar in nature and causing only minimal environmental impacts. The issuance process for a general permit closely parallels the issuance process for individual permits, with a public notice, opportunity for a public hearing, and detailed decision documentation.125 Once a general permit is issued, activities that qualify for the general permit may proceed, provided the terms and conditions of the general permit are met, without the project proponent having to obtain an individual, site-specific permit.
Many general permits require a NOI to seek coverage under the general permit (sometimes called a preconstruction notification, or PCN), USACE review of the proposed work, and USACE's written verification of compliance with the general permit before the project can commence.126 However, in some cases, activities that qualify for a general permit can proceed without USACE's written confirmation if the permit applicants adhere to the terms and conditions of the permit.127
Nationwide permits (NWPs) are general permits that authorize categories of similar activities on a nationwide basis.128 USACE issues NWPs (along with general conditions and definitions for the NWPs) through rulemaking, typically every five years. In January 2026, USACE reissued 56 existing NWPs (with some modifications) and issued one new NWP.129 These NWPs went into effect on March 15, 2026. Examples of activities covered under NWPs, if they meet terms and conditions of the permit, are oil and natural gas pipeline activities, linear transportation projects, utility line activities, residential developments, commercial and institutional developments, agricultural activities, mining activities, and wetland and stream restoration activities.130
To qualify for a NWP, a proposed activity must satisfy its terms and conditions.131 These aim to ensure the activity will not result in greater than minimal individual or cumulative adverse impacts. Some NWPs limit the acreage of WOTUS that may be impacted (e.g., no greater than ½ acre of impacts) or may limit discharges to only certain types of wetlands (e.g., allowing discharges only to nontidal wetlands).132 USACE has established 32 general conditions that apply to the NWPs. These conditions address a wide range of issues, including endangered species, water supply intakes, historic properties, tribal rights, coastal z
title: Clean Water Act Permitting: Overview and Policy Issues

text:
News Release 2026-90 | October 14, 2026

Share This Page:

WASHINGTON—The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released a report of its findings from its supervisory review of debanking activities at the nine largest national banks it supervises: JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank.

The OCC conducted its supervisory review in accordance with the President’s Executive Order , “Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans,” to determine whether these banks’ policies or practices may have required, encouraged, or otherwise influenced banks to deny or limit access to financial services to Americans because of their political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The OCC’s findings show that, between 2020 and September 2025, all nine banks had such policies.

“Today’s report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation’s largest banks have denied, debanked and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses,” said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould. “Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra—it is a mandate. The Trump Administration is committed to ending the weaponization of finance against hardworking Americans, once and for all.”

In the report, the OCC found that broad reputation risk policies—which lacked clear standards and objective, risk-based criteria—disadvantaged certain Americans based on their political, religious, or social views or based on their lawful business activities. The OCC also found that banks maintained public and nonpublic policies restricting certain industry sectors’ access to financial services, including those in oil and gas exploration, coal mining or coal-powered plants, firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution, construction or operation of detention facilities, the manufacturing, distribution or online retail of tobacco or e-cigarettes, and digital asset activities.

In preparing the report, the OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints to OCC-regulated institutions and received approximately 50,000 documents consisting of approximately 420,000 pages from these banks regarding their policies, procedures, practices, and individual customer decisions.

The OCC first announced this review of its nine largest banks by asset size in September 2025 and issued preliminary findings in December 2025. Today’s report is the latest action by the OCC to address debanking and promote fair access. Other OCC actions include eliminating considerations of reputation risk in bank examinations, clarifying the OCC’s consideration of improper debanking in assessing licensing applications and during certain examinations, and improving the OCC’s complaint intake and review processes.

The OCC’s broader work to promote fair access to financial services and advance objective and risk-based banking decisions remains ongoing. The OCC is considering actions to prevent banks from discriminating against customers or prospective customers on the basis of their political or religious beliefs and to address the problematic role of reputation risk in bank decision-making.

"Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," Comptroller Gould said. "Accordingly, the OCC will be assessing further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework applicable to the largest banks to reduce the likelihood of these harmful practices recurring in the future.”
