text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection announces the extension of the compliance date for new informal entry procedures for international mail from Oct. 22, 2026, to Jan. 20, 2027. The 90-day extension provides importers, brokers, and logistics providers additional time to update their processes while helping avoid disruptions to certain international postal shipments destined for the United States.
As previously announced in the June 24, Interim Final Rule, “Indefinite Suspension of the De Minimis Exemption for Mail Shipments and New Postal Informal Entry Process” and the Federal Register Notice, “Test of the New Electronic Entry Process for Mail,” all international postal shipments that are subject to Section 201, 232, or 301 duty or are the jurisdiction of a Partner Government Agency will be required to be filed electronically in the Automated Commercial Environment through the new Entry Type 13 process for purposes of informal entry (otherwise, formal entry is required).
To allow more time for filers to adjust to the new electronic requirements for informal entry, CBP extends the timeline for mandatory use of Entry Type 13 for these shipments to Jan. 20, 2027. There are no changes to international mail entry procedures before Jan. 20, 2027. Beginning on that date, CBP requires the use of the new Entry Type 13 process for the informal entry of international postal shipments subject to Section 201, 232 or 301 duties or the jurisdiction of a PGA.
“CBP is focused on securing our borders and using advance data to identify threats in international mail before they reach American communities,” said CBP Office of Trade Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas. “These requirements will close gaps that have been exploited by criminals to smuggle contraband sent through international mail.”
CBP has proposed requiring the new entry and data requirements for the informal entry of all international mail packages, except for letters and flats, in the Oct. 8 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking “Low-Value Shipments.” The agency is committed to bringing international mail entry procedures into parity with informal entry procedures across all other cargo modes while setting a global standard for modern customs controls in the international mail environment.
“These requirements will help create a more secure international mail stream, strengthening both our economic and national security,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino of CBP’s Office of Field Operations. “Advance electronic data will help CBP identify and stop illegal and unsafe shipments before they enter the United States.”
While the mandatory implementation date is being extended, CBP encourages filers to begin using the optional Entry Type 13 process for the informal entry of international mail shipments during this transition period to ensure readiness in advance of the new mandatory deadline. CBP will continue providing guidance, resources, and direct support to help the trade community prepare for and comply with the new international mail entry requirements. Additional information is available on CBP’s e-Commerce page.
Follow the CBP Office of Trade on X@CBPTradeGov, Instagram@cbpofficeoftrade and Linkedin@cbpofficeoftrade, and CBP's Office of Field Operations (Office of Cargo and Conveyance Security) on Instagram@cbptradesecure for breaking news and current events.
title: International Mail Entry Type 13 mandatory implementation date extended to Jan. 20, 2027

Washington, D.C. — Today, Rep. Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, reiterated he will continue his investigation demanding answers from Kimberly Guilfoyle, former United States Ambassador to Greece who resigned in disgrace. Guilfoyle’s resignation followed alarming allegations that, while in office, Guilfoyle engaged in a pay-to-play scheme with a Republican donor, demanding $100,000 in exchange for access to senior Trump Administration officials at the White House.
“Kimberly Guilfoyle is a fraud, and if she thinks she’s escaping accountability just because she resigned, she’s sorely mistaken. Our investigation is just getting started,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.
In the letter to former Ambassador Guilfoyle, Ranking Member Robert Garcia wrote, “Although your tenure as the United States Ambassador to Greece is coming to an end, Oversight Democrats’ inquiry will continue… Notwithstanding your announced resignation as ambassador yesterday morning, our requests for detailed information about your financial records, personal communications, and your communications with senior Administration officials on behalf of your benefactors still stand.”
In October 2026, Ranking Member Robert Garcia demanded answers from Kimberly Guilfoyle, then-United States Ambassador to Greece, following reports that Guilfoyle engaged in a corrupt pay-to-play scheme with a Republican donor.
###
title: Ranking Member Robert Garcia Advances Investigation into Now Private Citizen Kimberly Guilfoyle Following Resignation

text:
This year’s Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank provide an important opportunity to engage on current global economic challenges as well as our work with partners and the international financial institutions to support a pro-growth agenda, macroeconomic and financial stability, and poverty reduction. We thank Thailand for hosting us for the Annual Meetings.
In the United States, President Trump’s America First Investment Policy is promoting robust economic growth and prosperity, fiscal prudence, energy abundance, and regulatory modernization. Internationally, we are getting back to basics by forging a broad consensus on the need to promote growth as the key condition on which durable prosperity depends. As G20 President, the United States is focused on promoting strong economic growth, and has prioritized increasing productivity, addressing global imbalances, engaging with the private sector, advancing financial literacy, improving the sovereign debt architecture, and promoting financial sector innovation and regulatory modernization. When focused on their core missions, the IMF and World Bank are well-placed to help advance these important objectives.
The IMF is making progress at getting back to basics. Through recent policy reviews, the IMF is upgrading its policy toolkit for surveillance and lending and restoring its focus on its core responsibilities. This includes the external sector issues at the heart of the IMF’s mandate, strengthening surveillance of debt vulnerabilities in low-income countries, and making the financial sector surveillance more risk-based. Moreover, the IMF has rightly focused on strengthening program design to enhance the effectiveness of IMF-supported reform programs to durably address balance of payments challenges and restore external viability.
One area where this refocus must go further is in the IMF’s work on global imbalances. This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances. Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment. The IMF was founded to prevent these kinds of distortive policies and negative spillovers, and must exercise its voice on this critical issue or risk being sidelined.
With recent major policy reviews complete, the hard work of implementation begins. The United States will hold the IMF accountable for translating these reforms into stronger surveillance, more effective lending, and more robust assessment of debt sustainability. Successfully delivering on the IMF’s core mandate will require commitment from IMF management to be an unflinching truth-teller through surveillance and to hold borrowers accountable in IMF-supported programs. That same commitment is required of the authorities undertaking painful but necessary macroeconomic adjustments and structural reforms.
The IMF must continue to prioritize its work and focus its resources on its core mandate. New and emerging issues warrant IMF engagement only where they are clearly macrocritical and within the Fund’s mandate, and adding new priorities should require reducing lower-value work, rather than continually expanding the Fund’s agenda such as financing provided through the Resilience and Sustainability Trust that lacks a clear linkage to balance of payments pressures and veers into development-policy lending.
The IMF has sufficient resources to accomplish its mission. The United States remains committed to a strong, quota-based, and adequately resourced IMF, and we continue to work to secure congressional approval for the 16th General Review of Quotas. Future quota reviews should be based on resource adequacy needs, as reflected in the recently approved Diriyah Guiding Principles on IMF Quota and Governance Reforms. Any future quota realignment should reflect members’ relative position in the world economy and be based on a new quota formula.
After years of mission creep, the World Bank is beginning to refocus on its core mission of reducing poverty and raising economic growth. Over the last year, the Bank has strengthened its development agenda by further implementing its jobs initiative, removing inefficient and distortionary climate finance targets, beginning to phase out lending to certain advanced client countries that have not needed Bank support for years, taking steps to better implement its graduation policy, and devising a strategy for supporting a more diversified minerals value chain.
These are necessary steps in returning the Bank to its core mission, but significantly more is needed. The Bank must promote country self-reliance by deploying resources where they are most needed and impactful, graduating more advanced countries from Bank support, delivering better access to reliable, affordable, and abundant energy, and increasing competition and quality in Bank-financed procurement to improve development outcomes. And, in doing these things, the Bank must be more efficient and selective, pursuing operations with the greatest development impact, rather than simply pushing as much money as possible out the door.
We expect the Bank to phase out sovereign lending to countries that have long since met the graduation policy criteria so that the Bank can refocus its resources where they are most needed and impactful. Despite being long overdue, the planned phase outs of lending to China and Poland represent an important milestone for both countries. As the Bank continues to implement the graduation policy, we expect to see Graduation Progress Notes that meaningfully assess where graduation-eligible countries fall short of meeting the graduation criteria, and associated Country Partnership Frameworks focusing Bank programming on addressing those shortcomings. As the Bank enters the longest period in its history without a country graduating from lending eligibility, World Bank Management should take concrete steps to ensure that graduations resume.
Similarly, the International Development Association (IDA) must facilitate graduation so that it can focus its resources on the poorest countries where its investments in foundational infrastructure, as well as in reforms that promote debt sustainability and transparency, enhanced domestic resource mobilization, and strong public financial management, help countries develop and stand up to coercive and opaque lending terms from some creditors. As we discuss IDA’s resources over the next 15 months, IDA must clearly identify its accomplishments in boosting growth, and reducing poverty. We also support extending the deadline for low-income countries to subscribe to the shares allocated under the 2018 capital increases, helping them preserve and strengthen their representation and voice in the institution.
Contributing to country self-reliance also requires the Bank to focus more on the sectors most critical to development and industrialization, chief among them reliable and affordable energy. Energy abundance sparks economic abundance. We continue to support the World Bank and African Development Bank goal to extend energy access to 300 million more people in Africa. Achieving this goal will require the Bank to take a technology-neutral approach rather than restricting borrower choice, including by removing constraints on its support for natural gas and positively responding to borrower demand for gas projects. Accordingly, the World Bank Group should formally retire its prohibition on financing upstream gas and oil. The Bank cannot credibly invoke country ownership while categorically excluding upstream projects before their development merits are even assessed.
We welcome the recent approval of an IDA project to secure near-term gas supply, prepare mid-and downstream investments, and develop gas strategies in West Africa. Ultimately, success must be measured by whether countries gain the energy access needed to drive growth, create jobs, and reduce poverty. We therefore welcome the move to focus on outcomes rather than on arbitrary targets. To further support energy abundance, the United States is also making an initial contribution to the Nuclear Energy Assistance Trust Fund, which will help countries lay the groundwork for future nuclear energy investments.
Critical minerals are foundational inputs to growth and economic security. We welcome the Bank’s recently approved Metals and Minerals Implementation Plan. The Bank has an important role to play through policy and regulatory reform, investing in enabling infrastructure and local processing capacity, project finance and de-risking, and strengthening natural resource management. This includes deep-sea mining, where the Bank can play a catalytic role by providing knowledge and guidance in a nascent sector.
Directing resources to countries most in need is not enough; the Bank must position those resources to deliver value. Procurement policies that reward distortive industrial policies, encourage subsidies, and incentivize corruption and collusion ultimately undermine development, stifle the private sector, and result in higher long-term costs. The Bank must pursue procurement reforms that result in greater competition and quality. We recognize recent efforts to expand the use of quality-based procurement approaches, boost the use of local labor, and improve industry outreach, but much of this was necessary just to move closer to the value-for-money objective embodied in the Procurement Framework adopted over a decade ago. The Bank needs to assess where its current procurement framework, policies, and implementation are still not delivering competition and quality needed for long-term development and adopt further reforms and capacity-building measures to address those shortcomings. The Bank’s peer institutions are implementing a robust procurement reform agenda. We expect the World Bank to lead on these efforts rather than fall behind.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC) can play an important role in mobilizing private capital to support economic growth and private sector development. But higher mobilization levels are not a substitute for the harder work of creating markets and crowding in truly private investment in poorer, less creditworthy countries. We call on the IFC to redouble efforts to meet its 2018 capital increase pledge to make 40 percent of new commitments in the poorest and most fragile countries. The IFC’s rate of progress towards this commitment has fallen unacceptably short, underscoring the need to align the institution more closely with its core mission.
Finally, the IMF and World Bank are ultimately taxpayer-funded public institutions whose budgets should reflect the narrower set of operations that comes with refocusing on their core missions. We appreciate the flat real administrative budget growth being pursued at both institutions this fiscal year, and expect to see this same approach in future years. Both institutions and their Governors can and should go further, including by indefinitely freezing – and even reducing – Executive Board budgets and salaries, which now have a combined annual cost over $200 million. The reduction in the IMF Board’s core budget this year is an important first step in this direction. The Boards are significantly more expensive, both in overall and per-capita terms, than at other international financial institutions. Every unnecessary dollar spent on the Boards is a dollar that cannot be used to reduce poverty, promote macroeconomic stability, or foster growth. The Bank, Fund, and their members must do more to restrain these inexcusably bloated budgets. We also call on the IMF to divest from the Bretton Woods Recreation Center and the Concordia Hotel.
Streamlining policy priorities will allow both the World Bank and IMF to focus limited public resources on effectively fulfilling their core mandates while responding to crises. We look forward to working with Management, staff, and other shareholders, to accomplish this task.

NASA will provide an update on its plans to return American astronauts to the surface of the Moon by 2028 at 2 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 23, at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
Learn where to watch online:
Participants in the briefing include:
- NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman
- NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya
- Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager
The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and how plans to return American astronauts to the Moon by 2028 are progressing.
U.S. media interested in attending in person must apply online by 12 p.m., Friday, Oct. 16. To ask questions remotely, media must request the dial-in number from the Kennedy newsroom no later than one hour prior to the start of the update by emailing: ksc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov. NASA’s media accreditation policy is online.
As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

Op-Ed: Violent Crime Down Across U.S., FBI Pivots to Emerging Threats
Numbers are telling the story of key crime rates falling throughout the United States from 2024 to 2025 based on data reported to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program.
Overall, in the United States, key crime rates dropped to include violent crime (-9.3%), murder (-18.1%), robbery (-18.5%), and property crime (-12.4%). Wisconsin followed the national trend and also saw a drop in crime rates in all categories above. These are historic decreases, representing the largest year-to-year decrease in the violent crime rate and the murder and non-negligent manslaughter rate since the FBI began estimations of crime rates in 1936. In addition, the murder rate is tied with the 1955 and 1956 rates (4.1 murders per 100,000 people).
These promising trends continue into 2026. From January to June of this year, preliminary estimates continue to show a decrease across the four key categories of crime.
These favorable numbers are no doubt tied to the collective efforts of law enforcement. Over the last 18 months, the FBI has leaned into becoming a nimbler and more flexible organization with a renewed focus on combating violent crime. The organization has implemented over 60 changes, and we are seeing positive results in our ability to quickly pivot to emerging threats. We know criminals and criminal organizations never stop innovating new ways to commit crimes and conceal their illegal actions. As law enforcement we must continue to be just as nimble and innovative in our ways to detect, investigate, and counter criminal activity within the Constitution of the United States and the law.
Collaboration with other law enforcement agencies paying off
In addition to our efforts as an organization, we work collaboratively with our federal, state, local, and tribal partners to identify criminal organizations and those responsible for acts of violence. Cooperation takes many forms and includes everything from basic technical assistance on specific cases to participation in joint task forces.
This year, our joint task forces have had significant successes, and several large cases have come to a resolution. Some recent examples include rooting out a neighborhood-based gang operating in Milwaukee and the targeting of an individual responsible for multiple robberies.
Over the course of multiple years, 30 members of a neighborhood-based gang were convicted. Members of the gang funded their criminal activity by stealing from the American taxpayer. As part of their scheme, they submitted false applications for benefits from the United States government. The conspirators fraudulently received over $10 million in federal unemployment benefits which they then used to purchase firearms, controlled substances, vacations, and jewelry. In one instance, members of the gang solicited a murder for hire. Gang members Lawrence Turner and Ronnell Bowman were sentenced to life in prison for their role in paying $10,000 each to have someone murdered. The murder victim was ambushed and killed because he was a friend of someone against whom Bowman wanted revenge. In addition to the murder, this gang was responsible for violations of federal firearms laws to include possession of machine guns, transferring firearms to felons, and illegally possessing firearms.
The Milwaukee Area Violent Crime Task Force worked collaboratively with other law enforcement agencies which led to the sentencing of Jeremiah Tyler. Tyler was sentenced to 16½ years in prison for committing seven robberies and attempting to commit another two. During his approximately month-long crime spree he brandished a firearm in the commission of his crimes and in one robbery he discharged the firearms.
Milwaukee FBI Field Office committed to reducing crime in neighborhoods
My goal for the FBI Milwaukee Field Office is to continue our focus on disrupting and dismantling criminal organizations. Further, we are committed to working with our law enforcement partners to continue the reduction of crime in our neighborhoods.
Law enforcement cannot do this work alone; we need your help. I ask you to remain vigilant.
If you see an emergency situation, immediately notify local police via 911 or your local emergency number. The FBI is always ready to intake complaints and information on criminal and national security threats. Tips can be reported online at tips.fbi.gov or via telephone at 1-800-CALL-FBI.
title: Op-Ed: Violent Crime Down Across U.S., FBI Pivots to Emerging Threats

Louisville, KY – On August 19, 2026, a federal grand jury in Louisville returned a second superseding indictment charging 13 men and women with drug trafficking and money laundering offenses. Two of the defendants were previously charged with conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine.

United States Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner stated, “A seizure of over 250 pounds of methamphetamine is enormous for Louisville, Kentucky. Methamphetamine is an incredibly addictive drug that has ruined countless lives. I’m very proud of the important work being done by Louisville’s Homeland Security Task Force.”

U.S. Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson of the FBI Louisville Field Office, acting Special Agent in Charge Dennis M. Fetting of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Nashville, acting Special Agent in Charge Todd Strom of the IRS Criminal Investigation Detroit Field Office, Special Agent in Charge Robert J. Scott of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), U.S. Postal Inspector in Charge Lesley Allison of the Pittsburgh Division, Special Agent in Charge John Nokes of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Louisville Field Division, U.S. Marshal Gary B. Burman of the of the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) for the Western District of Kentucky, and Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. of the Kentucky State Police (KSP) made the announcement.

According to the second superseding indictment, Zelos Rashon Fields , 55, of California, Chauncey Lavelle Ransom , 62, of California, Charles Taylor , 53, of California, and Austin Redd , 29, of Louisville, were all charged with one count of conspiring together and with others to possess with the intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine from May 2025 through March 13, 2026, in Jefferson County, Kentucky, and elsewhere.

Additionally, Redd was charged with three counts of distributing methamphetamine, one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and one count of money laundering conspiracy. Fields was charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and having a prior serious violent felony conviction, and one count of money laundering conspiracy. Ransom was charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and having a prior serious drug felony conviction, and three counts of money laundering conspiracy.

Meshaun Swan , 26, of Louisville, was charged with one count of distribution of methamphetamine. Charles Taylor , Demond Jackson , 54, of California, Dariecea Brock , 28, of Louisville, Iecia Taylor , 28, of Louisville, Raeshonda Presley , 33, of Louisville, Ebony Manson , 44, of California, Laquisha Beals , 32, of Louisville, Lajean Guess , 56, of California, and Kimberly Sowells , 45, of California, are all charged with money laundering conspiracy.

This indictment supersedes an indictment returned April 8, 2026, charging Fields with one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine, and a superseding indictment returned on May 20, 2026, charging Fields and Ransom with one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute over 500 grams of methamphetamine.

Prior to the indictments, criminal complaints were issued for Fields and Ransom . The complaints alleged that in March 2026, law enforcement identified Ransom , along with Fields , as two individuals involved in the transport of methamphetamine to Louisville for distribution. On March 13, 2026, law enforcement executed search warrants pertaining to this investigation and recovered approximately 257 pounds of methamphetamine, which had been sent to Louisville by Ransom and Fields for distribution.

Fields and Ransom previously appeared before a U.S. Magistrate Judges of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Kentucky on the underlying drug trafficking charges and were ordered detained.

If convicted of the offenses alleged in the second superseding indictment, Fields and Ransom face a potential minimum penalty of 15 years in prison. Charles Taylor , Redd , and Swan all face a potential minimum penalty of 10 years in prison. Jackson , Brock , Iecia Taylor , Presley , Manson , Beals , Guess , and Sowells all face a potential maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

There is no parole in the federal system.

This case is being investigated by the FBI, HSI, IRS-CI, DEA, ATF, USPIS, USMS and KSP, with assistance from the St. Matthews Police Department, Los Angeles Police Department, Joint Regional Intelligence Center, Shively Police Department, and the Floyd County Sheriff’s Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alicia P. Gomez and Corinne Keel are prosecuting the case with assistance from paralegal Adela Alec.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Louisville comprises agents and officers from FBI, HSI, DEA, ATF, and IRS-CI, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Kentucky.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
New Jersey Brothers Plead Guilty to Stealing More Than $2.6 Million, Collectively, in Tax Refunds
Two New Jersey brothers pleaded guilty in September to stealing more than $978,126 and $1,643,172, respectively, in tax refunds.
According to court documents and statements made in court, in early 2023, Ronald Chrichlow, of Somerset, and Gordon Chrichlow, formerly of Carteret, each filed a false 2022 Form 1041, U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts, on behalf of their trusts. These Forms 1041 falsely reported that the trusts made tax payments to the IRS when they had not and claimed refunds of $978,126 and $1,643,172, respectively. Pursuant to these false filings, in March 2023, the IRS issued Ronald Chrichlow a U.S. Treasury check for $978,126 and Gordon Chrichlow a U.S. Treasury check for $1,643,172. With his proceeds, Gordon Chrichlow purchased a Porsche Taycan for approximately $117,364 and bought a house for approximately $686,258.
In August 2023, the IRS assigned a revenue officer to collect the fraudulently obtained refunds. In response to IRS collection efforts, the Chrichlow brothers mailed to the IRS amended 2022 Forms 1041 for their trusts that removed the originally claimed tax payments. They also mailed 2022 Forms 1040-NR, U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return, on which they falsely claimed not to be residents of the United States and falsely claimed that their 2022 income was tax exempt pursuant to a tax treaty.
The Chrichlow brothers also willfully failed to file their personal income tax returns in some years, despite earning income. Ronald Chrichlow earned $960,000 in income between 2021 and 2024, but did not file income tax returns between 2022 and 2024. For 2021, he filed a false tax return falsely reporting tax payments he did not make in order to claim a tax refund of $93,228 to which he was not entitled. Gordon Chrichlow willfully failed to file his 2021 through 2024 tax returns, despite earning more than $1.4 million in gross income in those years.
The Chrichlow brothers also filed false COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loan applications on behalf of their business entities in 2020 that reported false numbers of employees and false gross receipts, in order to receive loans and grants to which they were not entitled.
Ronald and Gordon Chrichlow each pleaded guilty to one count of theft of government funds. Ronald Chrichlow is scheduled to be sentenced on January 12, 2027, and Gordon Chrichlow is scheduled to be sentenced on January 27, 2027. They each face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the cases.
Trial Attorneys Melissa Siskind and Likhitha Butchireddygari of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section are prosecuting the cases.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: New Jersey Brothers Plead Guilty to Stealing More Than $2.6 Million, Collectively, in Tax Refunds

More than 30 U.S. Attorney’s Offices joined the Fraud Division in bringing enforcement actions against alleged fraudsters

Milwaukee, Wisconsin - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin today announced the sentencing of Edward Kuhn as part of a nationwide enforcement action led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Eastern District of Wisconsin was a key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and today, federal prosecutors across the country facilitated fraud enforcement actions against 76 criminal defendants, including approximately 31 newly charged defendants, reaching approximately 490 million dollars in intended loss to American taxpayers.

As part of this enforcement action, Brad D. Schimel, First Assistant United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, announced that on September 18, 2026, United States District Judge Byron C. Conway sentenced Edward Kuhn (age 62) of Hilbert, Wisconsin, to 13 months’ imprisonment for willfully failing to pay taxes.

According to court records, Mr. Kuhn was the owner and operator of Kuhn Salvage and Demolition based in Stockbridge, Wisconsin. Between 2020 and 2023, Mr. Kuhn withheld $194,403.56 from employees’ paychecks and did not turn that money over to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). In total, from 2009 to 2023, Mr. Kuhn willfully failed to pay $868,175.95 in taxes he owed to the IRS.

At sentencing, Judge Conway noted that Mr. Kuhn had numerous pro-social characteristics, but that a sentence of imprisonment was necessary because of Mr. Kuhn’s repeated failure to pay the payroll taxes he collected and the other taxes owed to the IRS.

“This defendant stole from his own employees, but also from every honest taxpayer,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Brad Schimel. “Anyone who does so should expect to go to prison.”

“IRS Criminal Investigation recognizes the serious consequences of employment tax evasion, from the lost tax revenue to the United States government and to the loss of future Social Security or Medicare benefits for the employees,” stated Robert Kuszynski Special Agent in Charge of the Chicago Field Office. “Business owners are responsible for withholding and remitting those taxes, and failing to do so is a serious offense. IRS Criminal Investigation continues to vigorously pursue anyone who collects taxes and fails to timely remit those taxes.”

This case is one example in which this office has contributed to ensuring that all Americans pay their fair share. To see the successes of other offices, please see this press release [link] .

Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation investigated the case, which Assistant U.S. Attorney Zachary J. Corey prosecuted.

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

###

For further information contact: Public Affairs Officer Steve Caballero (414) 297-1700 Follow us on X
title: The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge

EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces American Farmer First Policy During Three-Day Swing in Iowa and Wisconsin
WASHINGTON – Earlier this week, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin traveled across Iowa and into Wisconsin for a number of meetings and engagements with farmers, industry leaders, veterans, and local officials where he highlighted the Trump EPA’s efforts to support American farmers, advance right-to-repair efforts, strengthen domestic energy production, and improve water infrastructure.
During his swing through Iowa, Administrator Zeldin announced EPA’s proposal to reallocate 100% of additional 2025 small refinery exemption volumes under the Renewable Fuel Standard at the Dubuque County Farm Bureau in Iowa. The proposal keeps the agency’s promise to propose 100% reallocation by the end of October and furthers the Trump Administration’s commitment to open stable markets for American farmers to sell their crops. If finalized as proposed, the 100% reallocation will ensure that farmers in Iowa and across the country do not lose the demand for their crops, while also unleashing American energy.
The announcement came on the heels of Administrator Zeldin and U.S. Representative Ashley Hinson’s (R-IA-02) tour of Big River United Energy ethanol facility in Dyersville, Iowa. The visit highlighted the role of American biofuels, which will benefit from EPA’s proposal if finalized, in supporting farmers, rural economies, and domestic energy production.
On Sunday, October 11, Administrator Zeldin visited Summit Products, a member of the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA), in Altoona, Iowa. While there he discussed EPA’s implementation of its February Right to Repair guidance and President Trump’s Freedom to Fix memo. The President’s memo directed EPA to deliver two things: ensure every American has the Freedom to Fix their vehicle and reduce the reliance on California’s emission certification process for aftermarket vehicle products. He highlighted EPA’s work to ensure farmers and equipment operators have the right to repair their own equipment instead of being forced to take it to a dealer, which is often more expensive. Administrator Zeldin touted EPA’s July decision to recognize SEMA as a certification authority for aftermarket vehicle parts.
To celebrate National Farmer’s Day on Monday, October 12, Administrator Zeldin participated in a farmers’ roundtable at Savor the Barn in Monticello, Iowa. Administrator Zeldin met with representatives from the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa Soybean Association, Iowa Corn Growers Association, and local agricultural producers to discuss EPA actions to grow the agriculture economy while maintaining strong environmental protections including EPA’s work on to end deratements caused by Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) system failures, the agency’s E15 waivers, EPA’s Waters of the United States (WOTUS) proposal, and more.
Later in the day, Administrator Zeldin and Representative Hinson spent time with local veterans at the Veterans Freedom Center in Dubuque, Iowa. During the visit they heard powerful stories about veterans helping veterans as they transition back home. The pair ended the day by touring Dubuque’s Water & Resource Recovery Center, where a $2 million federally funded project is planned to support upgrades to the facility’s capacity to treat high-strength waste. The improvements are intended to help the facility better serve local residents and businesses.
Administrator Zeldin ended his 3-day Midwest swing by meeting up with Representative Derrick Van Orden (R-WI-03) in Cuba City, Wisconsin where they toured the sixth generation Tranel Family Farms. The Trump EPA’s work reversing DEF deratements, restoring the Right to Repair, and applying common sense to environmental regulations were major topics throughout the visit.
title: EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces American Farmer First Policy During Three-Day Swing in Iowa and Wisconsin

text:
Dingell, Colleagues Introduce Legislation to Delay 340B Rebate Model, Protect Access to Affordable Medicine
  
  
    
      Washington, D.C. ,
      October 14, 2026
    
    
    
    
  
  
  
  
  
  
    
      U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Rob Bresnahan, Jr. (R-PA-08), Tracey Mann (R-KS-01), and Lois Frankel (D-FL-22) introduced the 340B Rebate Model Delay Act, bipartisan legislation to delay implementation of the federal government’s 340B rebate model, citing concerns that the new system could create significant financial and administrative risks for healthcare providers and patients.
“Families in Michigan are already struggling to pay for healthcare,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “Safety-net providers are not in the financial position to front this money, especially in light of Medicaid cuts, and will either have to hike up prices for patients or stop offering lifesaving drugs. This bill would delay the implementation of this rebate model so we can ensure people’s lives are not put at risk.”
Under the rebate model, participating providers would pay the full price of certain prescription drugs upfront and receive the 340B discount later through rebates. This could create cash-flow pressures, increase administrative burdens, and make it more difficult for community health centers, hospitals, and other safety-net providers to maintain access to affordable medications.
“Patients and providers should not have to bear the risks of an untested change to a program that helps deliver affordable medicines to communities across the country,” said Congressman Bresnahan. “Congress needs more time to evaluate the potential financial and administrative consequences of the rebate model and ensure that any changes to 340B protect patients and the providers who serve them.”
“Rural hospitals and health care providers across the Big First District rely on the 340B program to stretch limited resources and continue providing quality care close to home,” said Congressman Mann. “The new rebate model would force these providers to pay higher upfront costs and wait to be reimbursed, putting unnecessary financial strain on facilities that already operate on tight margins. This legislation provides certainty for our rural health care providers by stopping the rebate model through 2028 and protecting their ability to serve patients in rural communities.”
“Safety-net hospitals and community health centers are lifelines for low-income families, seniors, and people without health insurance,” said Congresswoman Lois Frankel. “Our bipartisan bill stops a new requirement forcing these providers to pay full price for prescription drugs and then wait for rebates. Their limited resources should go toward caring for patients, not waiting for drug companies to pay them back. We should be making it easier for people to get the medicine they need, not putting more financial strain on the hospitals and clinics they depend on.”
The 340B Drug Pricing Program allows eligible healthcare providers serving underserved communities to purchase covered outpatient drugs at discounted prices and stretch limited resources to provide care.
Bill text can be found HERE.
title: Dingell, Colleagues Introduce Legislation to Delay 340B Rebate Model, Protect Access to Affordable Medicine

Guardians,
In my first public speech as CSO, I made it clear that Guardians must always be prepared to fight and win our nation’s wars by achieving and maintaining space superiority – and I outlined the three Lines of Effort (LOEs) that will define our priorities during my time as CSO: Forging the Guardian Ethos, Arming and Growing the Guardian Force, and Integrating Guardian Power at Scale.
Forging the Guardian Ethos is our first and most foundational priority because ethos underpins how we act, how we fight, and the character of our service. It is the reason why Character is the first of our Guardian core values. You are a Guardian first, a member of our nation’s military uniquely and specifically trained, educated, and equipped to deliver unparalleled warfighting advantage in, from, and to the space domain. Every Guardian – regardless of specialty or position – has a vital role in our achieving success. This Guardian mindset not only grounds us in how we bring our unique space-centric methods of warfare but also informs our approach to force design, development, generation, and employment. As General Washington reminds us, “If we desire to secure peace… it must be known, that we are at all times ready for war.”
Second, to meet future challenges, we will continue Arming and Growing the Guardian Force. As members of our nation’s Armed Forces, we must continue to arm and grow our service to defend the Joint Force from space-enabled attack while simultaneously providing space capabilities to enable Joint Force combat power. We must do our part to make the Joint Force lethal, while defending our domain, which includes operating on-orbit weapons. This means we acquire and deliver the right technology while ensuring we Guardians train the way we will fight, all to guarantee we deliver mission success for our Nation. Guardians must make decisions at all levels, using Mission Command to communicate with transparency and clarity. This is our no-fail mission and we will get it done.
Third, we must deliver capability and capacity to combatant commands by Integrating Guardian Power at Scale. We have proven that spacepower produces battlefield success. This means providing effective and well-equipped space forces, in the right quantities, to combatant commands on the front lines, staying ahead of threats through rapid acquisitions, and bringing space expertise directly to the fight no matter where it is. The Space Force needs to continue refining how we generate, embed, and sustain combat-effective Guardians and capabilities across the Joint Force. Likewise, the Joint Force must have enough Guardians in key positions to achieve space superiority and drive combat success.
Looking ahead, we must build a sustained pipeline of Guardian talent, tailored with the appropriate training, and equipped with the most advanced capabilities, to ensure the Joint Force is fully powered by space expertise. Working together, as Guardians, we must Build the Force our Nation Needs today, tomorrow, and every time our nation calls.
Semper Supra!
Gen. Douglas Schiess
Chief of Space Operations
title: CSO Notice to Guardians: Lines of Effort for the Force

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, announced today that OSCAR MATA LEMUS was sentenced to 16 years in prison by United States District Judge Cathy Seibel for his enticement of three minors to engage in sexual activity. Judge Seibel also imposed a 15-year term of supervised release to follow the prison term. The sentencing today followed MATA LEMUS’s guilty plea on November 25, 2025.

“Oscar Mata Lemus’s conduct is the nightmare of any parent,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Today’s sentencing illustrates that we will continue to use every tool available to law enforcement to prosecute and punish those who sexually exploit children.”

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in related court proceedings:

On or about April 20, 2024, Oscar Mata Lemus, who was 23 years old at the time, communicated online with a 14-year-old minor (“Victim-1”). Mata Lemus told her he was 16 years old and persuaded Victim-1 to meet him in person to engage in sexual activity. On or about April 23, 2024, Mata Lemus went to Victim-1’s home in Rockland County, New York, entered her bedroom through a window, and engaged in sexual activity with her.

A federal investigation revealed that that, prior to his abuse of Victim-1, Mata Lemus abused at least two other minors. In or about January 2024, Mata Lemus met Victim-2, a 14-year-old, via social media. As with Victim-1, Mata Lemus told Victim-2 that he was 16 years old. Mata Lemus met Victim-2 in the Bronx on numerous occasions between January 2024 and April 2024, and they engaged in sexual activity. Mata Lemus took photos and videos of the sexual activity, some of which were recovered from his phone in connection with the investigation.

In addition, in or about June 2023, Mata Lemus met Victim-3, a 15-year-old in Mississippi, via social media. Mata Lemus told Victim-3 that he was 17 years old. At MATA LEMUS’s direction, Victim-3 sent him sexually explicit images of herself. She also engaged in numerous live video sessions, during which Mata Lemus requested that Victim-3 engage in sexual acts for him on camera.

On November 25, 2025, Oscar Mata Lemus entered a guilty plea to an Information, charging him with three counts of enticement, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 2422(b).

* * *

In addition to the prison term, OSCAR MATA LEMUS, 26, of Haverstraw, was sentenced to 15 years of supervised release.

Mr. McDonald praised the efforts of the FBI, Town of Ramapo Police Department, Westchester County Safe Streets Task Force, which is comprised of special agents and task force officers from the FBI, U.S. Probation, New York State Police, New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, Putnam County Sheriff's Office, Westchester County DAs Office, Rockland County DAs Office, NYPD, Westchester County PD, and the Yonkers, New Rochelle, Mount Vernon, Greenburgh, White Plains, Peekskill, Ramapo, Clarkstown Police Departments, in connection with this investigation.

The prosecution is being handled by the Office’s White Plains Division. Assistant United States Attorney Marcia S. Cohen is in charge of the prosecution.
title: Haverstraw Man Sentenced To 16 Years In Prison For Enticing Multiple Minors To Engage In Sexual Activity

BUFFALO, N.Y.- U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Ping Ye, 35, of Amherst, NY, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge John L. Sinatra, Jr. to conspiracy to transport aliens within the United States for financial gain, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, and a fine of $250,000.

Ye is the owner of the Sushi Queen restaurant on Delaware Avenue in Tonawanda. On February 5, 2025, North Tonawanda Police officers conducted a traffic stop of a minivan registered to Ye. Co-conspirator Wenjie Xu was driving the minivan, which contained five passengers. During the traffic stop, Xu, who did not speak English, called Ye, who spoke with law enforcement officers, falsely stating that that the five passengers were friends of his visiting from New York City for a few days, and that they did not work for him. However, the five passengers had actually been in Western New York between several months and over a year, during which time they were working at Sushi Queen. Ye further stated that the five passengers were staying at his house on Ganson Street. At the request of North Tonawanda Police, Border Patrol agents responded and took both Xu and the five passengers into custody. Agents subsequently determined that Xu was a Chinese national who was present in the United States illegally, and the five passengers were Guatemalan nationals who were likewise present in the United States illegally.

On February 7, 2025, Border Patrol agents conducted surveillance at the Ganson Street residence and subsequently arrested two more individuals, also Guatemalan nationals present in the United States illegally. On March 25, 2025, investigators executed a search warrant at the Sushi Queen restaurant, seizing various employee personnel records. No employee personnel records were found for the seven Guatemalan nationals illegally present in the United States.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Douglas A. C. Penrose. The plea is the result of an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Acting Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone, and U.S. Border Patrol, under the direction of Acting Chief Patrol Agent James D’Amato.

Sentencing will be scheduled at a later date.

title: Tonawanda restaurant owner pleads guilty to conspiracy to transport aliens

PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a man from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, convicted of Failure to Register as a Sex Offender. The sentencing took place on October 6, 2026.

Joseph Paul Marshall, age 47, was sentenced to two years and four months in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Marshall was indicted by a federal grand jury in November 2025. He pleaded guilty on July 8, 2026.

Marshall was required to register as a sex offender and update his registration within three business days of changing his residence due to a prior federal sex offense conviction. After updating his registration to an address in Sioux Falls, SD, on January 27, 2025, Marshall moved from his registered address in March 2025 and failed to update his registration. Marshall failed to update his registration until his arrest on August 20, 2025.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .

This case was investigated by the U.S. Marshals Service. Assistant U.S. Attorney Wayne Venhuizen prosecuted the case.

Marshall was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.
title: Sioux Falls Man Sentenced to More Than Two Years in Federal Prison for Failure to Register as a Sex Offender

Crystalline Silicon Photovoltaic Cells, Whether or Not Assembled Into Modules, from India, Indonesia, and Laos Injure U.S. Industry, Says USITC [UPDATED]
The United States International Trade Commission (USITC) today determined that a U.S. industry is materially injured by reason of imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells, whether or not assembled into modules, from India, Indonesia, and Laos that the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) has determined are sold in the United States at less than fair value and subsidized by the governments of India, Indonesia, and Laos.
Chairman Brett W. Doyle and Commissioners Jason E. Kearns, Peter-Anthony Pappas, Bart Thanhauser, and David Foley Jr. voted in the affirmative. Commissioner Samuel T. Negatu did not participate in the vote.
As a result of the USITC’s affirmative determinations, Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders on imports of these products from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The USITC also made negative critical circumstances determinations with respect to certain imports from India and Laos for which Commerce had made final affirmative critical circumstances findings in its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations, and made affirmative critical circumstances determinations with respect to certain imports from Indonesia for which Commerce had made final affirmative critical circumstances findings in its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations.*
The USITC’s public report, Crystalline Silicon Photovoltaic Cells, Whether or Not Assembled Into Modules, from India, Indonesia, and Laos(Inv. Nos. 701-TA-772-774 and 731-TA-1756-1758 (Final), USITC Publication 5804, October 2026), will contain the views of the USITC and information developed during the investigations.
The report will be available on the USITC website by November 23, 2026.
Status of proceedings, links to relevant documents, and more information about the investigations can be found at the USITC’s Investigations Database System (IDS).

text:
Expected impacts include warmer North, wetter South and East 
    
NOAA’s U.S. Winter Outlook, released today, shows how El Nino will likely influence the upcoming winter months (December 2026 to February 2027), with warmer-than-average temperatures expected across the northern U.S.; wetter-than-average conditions likely across the southern U.S., from California to Florida, and along the Eastern Seaboard; and drought improving for the majority of the country, including areas in the East, Southern Great Plains and Southwest.
“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” said Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service. “While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.”
Temperature Outlook
- Warmer-than-average temperatures are favored for northern California, the Pacific Northwest, Midwest, Mississippi Valley, much of the East, Alaska and for Puerto Rico / U.S. Virgin Islands.
- Near-normal temperatures are most likely for parts of the Southeast including Florida.
- Hawaii and much of the Southwest have equal chances of below-average, near-average or above-average seasonal mean temperatures.
Precipitation Outlook
- Wetter-than-average conditions are most likely across the southern tier, from the Southwest to the Southeast, and along the East Coast.
- Elevated odds for drier-than-average conditions for Hawaii, much of Alaska, the northern Mountain West, some areas in the Great Lakes and the western Pacific Islands.
- Areas in the Intermountain West, northern Plains, Ohio Valley and Puerto Rico / U.S. Virgin Islands have equal chances of below-average, near-average or above-average seasonal total precipitation amounts.
Drought Outlook
- Drought conditions are forecast to improve or end in the Southwest, Southern Great Plains, Southeast and parts of the East Coast.
- Drought conditions are favored to develop or worsen across parts of the northern Rockies, along with northeastern Oregon and eastern Washington.
Winter forecasting tools: What’s new this year
NOAA has also implemented upgrades to many of its winter weather products for the 2026-27 winter season:
- The National Weather Service’s Probabilistic Precipitation Portal is now operational. This platform enables users to view the low-end, expected, and high-end amounts of snow, ice and rain, as well as the probabilities of precipitation exceeding specific thresholds. Data are accessible through an interactive map, tables and graphics to assist local partners and emergency managers with decision support. Local graphics and probabilistic snow resources can be found online.
- The National Weather Service will implement the use of “Particularly Dangerous Situation” wording in select Blizzard Warnings and Ice Storm Warnings this season. This language will help forecasters alert partners and the public about high-confidence blizzards or ice storms of historic severity. These rare events typically pose exceptional threats by posing imminent danger to life and unprecedented disruptions to emergency services.
About NOAA's seasonal outlooks
NOAA’s seasonal outlooks provide the likelihood that temperatures and total precipitation amounts will be above-, near- or below-average, and how drought conditions are anticipated to change in the months ahead. The outlook does not project seasonal snowfall accumulations as snow forecasts are generally not predictable more than a week in advance. NOAA’s Weather Prediction Center updates its three-month outlook monthly. The next update will be available on November 19.
Stay current on winter weather risks in your area with the latest official watches and warnings at weather.gov. Visit weather.gov/safety for important winter preparedness information.
title: El Nino looms large over U.S. Winter Outlook

USDA Makes Historic $3.3B Loan to Build Electric Generation Facility in Georgia
(Washington, D.C., October 14, 2026) – Today, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins announced a historic $3.3 billion loan to Oglethorpe Power Corporation to help finance its Smarr Combined-Cycle electric generating facility in Monroe County, Georgia, during a visit to the construction site. This new facility will deliver dependable, affordable power for generations while helping meet America’s growing energy needs.
This loan is the largest ever delivered in the history of USDA Rural Development’s Rural Utilities Service and comes at a critical time for investing in American energy. As stated by President Trump, the United States is experiencing a surge in electricity demand from rapid technological advancements. This project strengthens the nation’s electrical grid, and lower-cost financing will help keep electricity affordable for Georgia families.
"Historic times call for historic actions, and this tremendous investment in America’s electric power grid is evidence of President Trump’s focus on powering our nation forward," said Secretary Brooke L. Rollins. "Great things are happening with our rural electric cooperatives nationwide, and Oglethorpe Power is one example in Georgia through this project, which will generate reliable electricity, create jobs, and bring significant investment to rural America."
"We are proud to partner with Oglethorpe on this significant investment in America's rural energy infrastructure," said USDA Under Secretary for Rural Development Glen Smith. "As we celebrate National Cooperative Month, this announcement highlights the vital role rural electric cooperatives play in powering our communities, supporting local economies, and strengthening American energy independence. President Trump and Secretary Rollins are doubling down on investments in our power grid to ensure rural America remains a driving force behind our nation's economic prosperity."
“This historic loan will allow us to build the reliable generation Georgia families, farms and businesses need at a lower cost, helping our member cooperatives keep electricity affordable for the communities they serve,” said Annalisa Bloodworth, President and CEO of Oglethorpe Power. “We are grateful to USDA and RUS for their longstanding partnership and for providing the lower-cost financing that helps electric cooperatives make critical investments in reliable, affordable power.”
Oglethorpe Power is a generation cooperative owned by 38 electric distribution cooperatives that serve nearly 5 million people across Georgia. It supplies wholesale power through a diverse energy portfolio that includes natural gas, coal, nuclear, and hydroelectric resources, helping its member cooperatives provide reliable, affordable electricity to the Georgians they serve.
For more information on USDA Rural Development investments in rural America, visit the Rural Data Gateway. The Rural Data Gateway is an online tool that strengthens USDA Rural Development partnerships with rural people, entrepreneurs, government officials and Congress by making agency investment data accessible to the public.

MIAMI – Two Miami men have been sentenced to more than 10 years in federal prison for their roles in a drug trafficking conspiracy that distributed fentanyl, fentanyl analogues, and cocaine throughout Miami-Dade County.

U.S. District Judge Jose E. Martinez sentenced Jose Rodriguez Jr., 27, of Miami, to 121 months in prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy to distribute 10 grams or more of fentanyl analogues and 40 grams or more of fentanyl.

Juan Carlos Nunez, 27, of Miami, was also sentenced to 131 months in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to conspiracy to distribute 10 grams or more of fentanyl analogues and 40 grams or more of fentanyl, distribution of fentanyl, and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime.

“Fentanyl trafficking is deadly, and those who profit from spreading this poison through our communities will face serious consequences,” said U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida. “Rodriguez will spend more than 10 years in federal prison, and Nunez nearly 11 years, for their roles in distributing fentanyl throughout Miami-Dade County. Nunez also carried a loaded firearm while trafficking these deadly drugs. Their sentences reflect the seriousness of these crimes and our commitment to aggressively prosecute fentanyl traffickers in South Florida.”

According to court records, between January 2024 through May 2025, Rodriguez led a drug trafficking organization that distributed fentanyl, fentanyl analogues, and cocaine throughout Miami-Dade County. Rodriguez negotiated drug transactions with undercover law enforcement officers, set prices and quantities, and directed co-conspirators, including Nunez, to complete drug transactions on his behalf. Rodriguez received a sentencing enhancement for his leadership role in the conspiracy.

Nunez served as a distributor for Rodriguez, selling hundreds of fentanyl pills to undercover officers. In May 2025, Nunez delivered 300 fentanyl pills to an undercover officer while carrying a Glock handgun in his waistband.

U.S. Attorney Reding Quiñones and Special Agent in Charge José R. Figueroa of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Miami made the announcement.

HSI Miami investigated the case, with assistance from the Miami Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Almas Abdulla prosecuted the case.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Southern District of Florida at www.flsd.uscourts.gov or at http://pacer.flsd.uscourts.gov , under case number 25-cr-20274.

title: Two Miami Men Sentenced to Federal Prison for Roles in Fentanyl Trafficking Conspiracy

Rep. Panetta Leads Call for Transparency, Accountability in the Administration’s Global Health Strategy
Monterey, CA – United States Representative Jimmy Panetta (CA-19) wrote a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio requesting greater transparency and stronger oversight of the Trump Administration’s “America First Global Health Strategy.” Rep. Panetta led 34 other lawmakers in calling for the public release of global health agreements and detailed answers about how the Administration will measure results, monitor spending, and respond to the misuse of U.S. taxpayer dollars.
Following the dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and the transfer of foreign assistance responsibilities to the U.S. Department of State, the Administration announced roughly $16 billion in bilateral assistance programs for 36 countries. Under the new model, assistance goes directly to foreign governments. However, only a handful of the agreements have been made publicly available, and the lawmakers raised concerns that many participating governments have a history of corruption involving foreign assistance.
“While we applaud efforts to build up global health mechanisms that fight HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, Ebola and other infectious diseases, this new model raises significant concerns about the efficient and transparent use of U.S. taxpayer dollars,” wrote Rep. Panetta and his colleagues. “Given that the Administration’s dismantling of USAID was triggered by alleged wasteful spending, we want to ensure this new foreign assistance model is free of waste, fraud and abuse.”
The lawmakers highlighted the multiple layers of oversight USAID used to monitor funding provided to nongovernmental organizations and other implementing partners, including contracting officers, program officials, technical experts, and the USAID Office of Inspector General. They cited testimony from the U.S. Government Accountability Office and the USAID Office of Inspector General indicating limited ability to track or audit funds sent directly to foreign governments. While acknowledging the need to modernize foreign assistance, the lawmakers warned that shifting to government-to-government assistance requires clear safeguards to protect taxpayer dollars.
“Failure to implement these programs thoughtfully, while ensuring accountability to the taxpayer, jeopardizes American leadership in the global health space, which is second to none. It also encourages nations to seek partnerships with our adversaries, while making America less safe, less strong and less prosperous,” continued the lawmakers.
The lawmakers requested written responses explaining how the Administration will define success and monitor whether the health agreements meet their objectives, who will oversee that work, and what staffing, technical expertise, and funding will support it. They also asked the State Department to identify the systems and safeguards it will use to track and audit spending and explain how it will respond to allegations or evidence of misuse, including whether it will immediately suspend assistance.
To ensure taxpayers can review these commitments, the lawmakers called for all existing and future global health agreements to be made publicly available. They requested a detailed explanation if the State Department cannot release the agreements.
The letter was also signed by Reps. Joyce Beatty (OH-03), Sanford Bishop (GA-02), Julia Brownley (CA-26), Gil Cisneros (CA-31), Yvette Clarke (NY-09), Jim Costa (CA-21), Madeleine Dean (PA-04), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Jared Golden (ME-02), Josh Gottheimer (NJ-05), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Hank Johnson (GA-04), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), Bill Keating (MA-09), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Ted Lieu (CA-36), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), Jennifer McClellan (VA-04), Dave Min (CA-47), Kevin Mullin (CA-15), Johnny Olszewski (MD-02), Nancy Pelosi (CA-11), Chellie Pingree (ME-01), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Jamie Raskin (MD-08), Brad Schneider (IL-10), Terri Sewell (AL-07), Melanie Stansbury (NM-01), Marilyn Strickland (WA-10), Tom Suozzi (NY-03), Dina Titus (NV-01), James Walkinshaw (VA-11), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25).
The full text of the letter is available here and below:
Dear Secretary Rubio,
We write to express concerns about transparency and oversight of the Administration’s new bilateral international assistance model, which grants money directly to foreign governments. Following the dissolution of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and the transfer of foreign assistance to the U.S. Department of State, the Administration announced roughly $16 billion in bi-lateral assistance programs for 36 countries and launched the America First Global Health Strategy. While we applaud efforts to build up global health mechanisms that fight HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, Ebola and other infectious diseases, this new model raises significant concerns about the efficient and transparent use of U.S. taxpayer dollars.
Since the bi-lateral international assistance agreements were signed with host countries, only a handful have been made available to the U.S. public for review. Furthermore, many of the foreign governments that have signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the State Department have a history of corruption with respect to foreign assistance.
USAID had several layers of accountability mechanisms built to help monitor funds sent to nongovernmental organizations (NGO) and other implementing partners, including country-based contracting officers, programmatic officials and U.S.-based technical officials, as well as the USAID Office of Inspector General (OIG). Testimony from the U.S. Government Accountability Office and the USAID OIG indicate that there is limited ability to track or audit U.S. taxpayer dollars sent directly to foreign governments. While many development stakeholders agree that a foreign assistance model based primarily on international NGOs needs improvement and modernization, the wholesale adoption of government-to-government assistance without accountability or transparency raises serious questions.
Given that the Administration’s dismantling of USAID was triggered by alleged wasteful spending, we want to ensure this new foreign assistance model is free of waste, fraud and abuse. We therefore request written responses to the following questions:
1) Please detail how the Administration will monitor and evaluate these health agreements to ensure they meet their objectives. How will success be defined?
2) Who will be charged with monitoring and evaluating these bi-lateral assistance agreements? What resources, including staffing, technical capacity, and financial support, are being deployed to support these efforts?
3) How will the State Department respond to allegations or evidence of improper use of U.S. taxpayer dollars used in foreign assistance? Do you plan to immediately cut off all aid if U.S. taxpayer money is not used for its intended purpose? If not, please explain why.
4) Please detail how the Administration plans to track and audit U.S. taxpayer dollars sent to foreign governments to ensure they are used for their purposes of supporting global health programs. What systems, tools, and safeguards are in place to ensure adequate monitoring and evaluation?
5) We request that all previously signed, as well as all future, global health agreements be made publicly available. If you are unable to do so, please provide a detailed explanation of why you can’t make these agreements publicly available for review to U.S. taxpayers.
Failure to implement these programs thoughtfully, while ensuring accountability to the taxpayer, jeopardizes American leadership in the global health space, which is second to none. It also encourages nations to seek partnerships with our adversaries, while making America less safe, less strong and less prosperous.
Thank you for your attention to these questions as we work toward a shared goal of ensuring quality oversight of a critical tool in our national security apparatus.
Sincerely,
###
title: Rep. Panetta Leads Call for Transparency, Accountability in the Administration’s Global Health Strategy
