SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Puerto Rico, Héctor Ramírez-Carbó, Acting United States Attorney, in conjunction with our partner agencies in the Homeland Security Task Force (“HSTF”) announce the following prosecutorial results for the week of October 5 through October 9, 2026. The HSTF is a permanent, interagency law enforcement task force created by executive order to combat transnational criminal organizations—including cartels, trafficking networks, and foreign terrorist organizations.

Convictions through Guilty Pleas:

On October 6, 2026, Gregory Vega-De Jesús pleaded guilty to transportation of illegal aliens, in Criminal Case 26-317 (MAJ). According to the indictment, the defendant was charged with conspiring to bring illegal aliens to the United States for financial gain, aiding and assisting entry of an aggravated felon into the United States, and transporting illegal aliens within the United States. Defendant was arrested on July 22, 2026. The court set defendant’s sentencing date for January 21, 2027. AUSA Steven Liong-Rodríguez is in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 8, 2026, Roberto Crispín Padilla pleaded guilty to Count One in Criminal Case number 25-272 (SCC). According to the indictment, the defendant was charged with conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute controlled substances and possession of firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking. Defendant was arrested on July 10, 2025. The court set defendant’s sentencing date for January 20, 2027. AUSAs Laura Díaz-González and Andrés Orr are in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 8, 2026, Ángel Luis Álvarez Torres pleaded guilty to Counts One and Seven in Criminal Case number 25-272 (SCC). According to the indictment, the defendant was charged with conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute controlled substances and possession of firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking. Defendant was arrested on July 10, 2025. The court set defendant’s sentencing date for January 20, 2027. AUSAs Laura Díaz-González and Andrés Orr are in charge of the prosecution of the case.

Sentencings:

On October 5, 2026, Eli Y. Couvertier-Pollock, a.k.a. “Tata/Maike/Maike Casiano” was sentenced by United States District Court Judge Camille Vélez-Rivé to fifteen (15) years of imprisonment to be followed by ten (10) years of supervised release for his participation in a violent drug trafficking organization that worked out of various Public Housing Projects in the Carolina and San Juan areas, principally the Sabana Abajo Public Housing Project. According to court documents, defendant was indicted on December 5, 2024, in Criminal Case 24-453 (MAJ), and pleaded guilty on June 16, 2026. AUSAs Laura Díaz González and Joseph Russell are in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 6, 2026, Alejandro Veliz was sentenced by United States District Court Chief Judge Raúl Arias Marxuach to 24 months of imprisonment and 4 years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute and distribution of more than five grams of methamphetamine. According to court documents, defendant was indicted on April 24, 2026, in Criminal Case 25-203 (RAM), and pleaded guilty on December 9, 2025. AUSA Camille García Jiménez was in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 7, 2026, Joshua E. Bula-Cartagena, a.k.a. “Inquilino/El Corista” was sentenced by United States District Court Judge María Antiongiorgi-Jordán to ten (10) years of imprisonment to be followed by eight (8) years of supervised release for his participation in a violent drug trafficking organization that worked out of various Public Housing Projects in the Carolina and San Juan areas, principally the Sabana Abajo Public Housing Project. According to court documents, defendant was indicted on December 5, 2024, in Criminal Case 24-453 (MAJ), and pleaded guilty on July 9, 2026. AUSAs Laura Díaz González and Joseph Russell are in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 8, 2026, Ángel M. Franqui-González, a.k.a. “Blanquito” was sentenced by United States District Court Judge María Antiongiorgi-Jordán to six (6) years of imprisonment to be followed by six (6) years of supervised release for his participation in a violent drug trafficking organization that worked out of various Public Housing Projects in the Carolina and San Juan areas, principally the Sabana Abajo Public Housing Project. According to court documents, defendant was indicted on December 5, 2024, in Criminal Case 24-453 (MAJ), and pleaded guilty on June 11, 2026. AUSAs Laura Díaz González and Joseph Russell are in charge of the prosecution of the case.

On October 9, 2026, Melvis Marcano González was sentenced by United States District Court Judge Pedro Delgado to 70 months of imprisonment and 3 years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute 225 kilograms of cocaine aboard a vessel subject to the jurisdiction of the United States. According to court documents, defendant was indicted on April 12, 2022, in Criminal Case 21-317 (PAD), and pleaded guilty on July 14, 2026. AUSA Camille García Jiménez was in charge of the prosecution of the case.

These prosecutions are part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

HSTF San Juan comprises agents and officers from the following federal partners: FBI, ICE-HSI, CBP (OFO, AMO and Border Patrol), the U.S. Marshals Service for Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, DEA, ATF, IRS, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the Department of State, and the U.S. Secret Service, the Puerto Rico/U.S. Virgin Islands HIDTA, TSA, FAA, and the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Districts of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The HSTF also has the following state and local law enforcement partners as participating agencies: the Puerto Rico Police Department; the San Juan, Carolina, Guaynabo, Barceloneta, and Ponce Municipal Police Departments, the Puerto Rico National Guard – Counter Drug Program; the Puerto Rico Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation; the Puerto Rico Internal Revenue Service (Hacienda); the Puerto Rico Port Authority; and the Virgin Islands Police Department.

Today, President Donald J. Trump returns to the Grand Canyon State for a visit to Bullhead City. He arrives with a clear record of America First results that put Arizona workers, families, seniors, and communities first — delivering tax relief, unleashing major private investment, ending the Biden-era border crisis, driving down violent crime, and securing Arizona’s critical water resources.
Delivering Tax Relief for Hardworking Arizonans
President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts are delivering direct relief to Arizona workers, families, and seniors.
- No Tax on Social Security: Approximately 1.3 million Arizona seniors benefit from the new senior deduction.
- Bigger Refunds: Arizona taxpayers saw average refunds of $3,659 in 2026.
- Rural Health Investments: Arizona secured $167 million in first-year Rural Health Transformation Program funding.
- Protecting Jobs and Wages: The Working Families Tax Cuts safeguarded 119,000 Arizona jobs, $22 billion in state GDP, and $11 billion in workers’ wages.
Unleashing an Investment Boom in Arizona
President Trump’s agenda of tax cuts, energy dominance, secure borders, and pro-growth policies has attracted major private capital and high-quality jobs to Arizona.
- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is expanding advanced semiconductor manufacturing at its Phoenix facility with a $200 billion investment.
- EVelution Energy is building an $850 million cobalt processing facility in Yuma County, creating 3,300 jobs.
- Amkor Technology is constructing a $2 billion semiconductor packaging and test facility in Peoria, creating 2,200 jobs.
- Hadrian is establishing a $200 million large-scale manufacturing and software hub in Mesa, creating 350 jobs.
- Cyclic Materials is developing its first $20 million commercial facility in Mesa.
Securing the Southern Border
President Trump ended the Biden-era border crisis and restored control at the southern border.
- The Trump Administration has not released a single illegal alien into the country at the border for 16 consecutive months.
- Southern border apprehensions in August were 94% lower than the monthly average under Biden.
- Refugee admissions in the first ten months of this fiscal year are down almost 90% from 2024.
- The Working Families Tax Cuts allocated $46.5 billion to complete the border wall.
- Fentanyl and other drug trafficking are down, with CBP seizing 73% more drugs this fiscal year through August than in the same period of FY 2024, and 61% more than the average for the same period over the prior four years.
- The Trump Administration transferred 285 acres of public land in Yuma County along the U.S.-Mexico border to the Department of the Navy to establish a National Defense Area in direct support of border security operations.
Making Safer Streets Across Arizona
Violent crime is falling as President Trump’s law-and-order agenda delivers real results for Arizona communities.
- Violent crime fell 13% statewide last year, including a 13% drop in homicides, an 11% drop in aggravated assaults, a 24% drop in robberies, and a 10% drop in sexual assaults.
- In Mesa, homicides fell 33% and rapes fell 15% in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year.
- In Phoenix, homicides fell 22% and robberies fell 19% in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year.
- In Tucson, homicides fell 24% and robberies fell 10% in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year.
Protecting Arizona’s Water Resources
The Trump Administration is making targeted investments to strengthen Arizona’s water supply and long-term resilience.
- In July 2025, the Bureau of Reclamation announced a $179 million investment to design and construct the North Gateway Advanced Water Purification Facility in Phoenix.
- In May 2025, the Trump Administration finalized 18 short-term System Conservation Implementation agreements with water entitlement holders in Arizona and California to increase conservation of Colorado River System water.
President Trump and Republicans are delivering America First policies that put Arizona first: lower taxes, major private investment, a secure border, safer communities, and critical water infrastructure. Arizonans face a clear choice between continuing this progress, or returning to the higher taxes, energy restrictions, and open borders policies of the past.

Today, President Donald J. Trump heads to Montana for a stop in Kalispell. He arrives with a proven record of America First policies that put Montana workers, families, seniors, and communities first — delivering historic tax relief, unleashing private investment and job growth, securing energy dominance, building critical minerals independence, and protecting public lands and rural communities.
Delivering Tax Relief for Hardworking Montanans
President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts are putting money back in the pockets of Montana workers, families, and seniors.
- No Tax on Social Security: Approximately 200,000 Montana seniors benefit from the new senior deduction, with the average senior expected to pay zero federal taxes on Social Security benefits.
- Bigger Refunds: Montana taxpayers saw average refunds of $3,304 in 2026.
- Protecting Jobs and Wages: The Working Families Tax Cuts safeguarded 20,000 Montana jobs, $4 billion in state GDP, and $2 billion in workers’ wages.
Strengthening Rural Healthcare
President Trump is bolstering access to care in Montana’s rural and frontier communities.
- Rural Health Investments: Montana secured $233 million in first-year Rural Health Transformation Program funding from the Working Families Tax Cuts — the fourth-highest award among all states.
- Rural EMS: The Trump Administration announced $8.7 million in September 2026 from the Rural Health Transformation Program for new ambulances and lifesaving equipment at 79 rural Montana EMS agencies, including three tribal governments.
- Behavioral Health: Montana secured federal approval in May 2026 to stand up certified community behavioral health clinics at roughly 20 sites statewide, replacing short-term grants with permanent funding.
Growing Montana’s Manufacturing Base
President Trump’s pro-growth agenda is driving private investment and job creation across the state.
- Janicki Industries selected Great Falls for an $800 million advanced manufacturing campus, creating more than 1,000 jobs within five years and more than 2,000 jobs at completion.
- Montana ranked ninth in the nation for job growth during the first year of President Trump’s second term.
- Under Republican leadership, Montana’s unemployment rate stood at 3.2% in August — well below the national average and ranking among the lowest in the country.
Driving American Energy Dominance
President Trump’s energy dominance agenda has reversed the previous Administration’s restrictions and unlocked major coal development that supports high-paying jobs and reliable power.
- Spring Creek Mine (Big Horn County): In March 2025, the Department of the Interior approved an expansion that extends the mine’s operating life by 16 years, enables production of 39.9 million tons of coal, and supports hundreds of jobs.
- Rosebud Mine (Rosebud and Treasure counties): Interior approved an expansion that recovers 33.75 million tons of federal coal, extends operations through 2039, supports more than 300 high-paying jobs, and supplies the Colstrip and Rosebud power plants, which together generate 1,500 megawatts of electricity.
- Bull Mountains Mine: Interior approved a mining plan modification that authorizes 22.8 million tons of federal coal and 34.5 million tons of adjacent non-federal coal, extends the mine by up to nine years, supports more than 250 jobs, and enables significant exports to U.S. allies.
Building America’s Critical Minerals Supply Chain
President Trump is restoring domestic production of critical minerals and ending reliance on foreign adversaries.
- United States Antimony Corporation (USAC) has earned millions in Department of War grant milestones for its Thompson Falls smelter expansion under a $27 million Defense Production Act award.
- USAC resumed mining at Stibnite Hill and is processing ore at its newly acquired Radersburg mill, restoring domestic antimony production for the first time in decades.
- Montana antimony is refilling the National Defense Stockpile under a five-year, $245 million contract with the Defense Logistics Agency.
Returning Control of Lands and Water to Montanans
President Trump is putting decision-making back in the hands of Montanans while delivering critical infrastructure.
- Grizzly Bears: The Fish and Wildlife Service proposed a rule in July 2026 giving Montana and other Western states greater flexibility to manage grizzlies in the Yellowstone ecosystem and other recovery areas where populations have met or exceeded recovery benchmarks, while maintaining Endangered Species Act protections.
- Fort Peck Water: President Trump signed the Fort Peck rural water reauthorization in September 2026, keeping clean water construction on schedule for the Fort Peck Reservation and Roosevelt, Sheridan, Valley, and Daniels counties.
- Crow Tribe Water Rights: Congress passed the Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act in September 2026 and sent it to President Trump’s desk, giving the tribe flexibility to finish its water system and hydropower project.
Rebuilding America’s Nuclear Deterrent at Malmstrom AFB
President Trump is modernizing the land-based leg of the nuclear triad in Montana.
- The Air Force and Army Corps of Engineers broke ground in May 2026 on a $26 million commercial entrance facility that clears the way for nearly $1 billion in Sentinel construction work at Malmstrom.
- Work is advancing on surveying and preparing sites across central Montana’s missile fields to replace the aging Minuteman III with the new Sentinel ICBM.
President Trump and Republicans are delivering America First policies that put Montana first: lower taxes, major private investment, energy dominance, a secure critical minerals supply chain, safer communities, and critical infrastructure. Montanans face a clear choice between continuing this progress or returning to the higher taxes, energy restrictions, and failed policies of the past.

SEC Small Business Advisory Committee to Discuss IPO Modernization and Regulation Crowdfunding
Washington D.C., Oct. 14, 2026 —
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s Small Business Capital Formation Advisory Committee announced that it will hold a meeting on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, at 10 a.m. to continue discussing IPO modernization and explore potential policy changes to Regulation Crowdfunding.
The meeting will be open to the public and held at the SEC’s headquarters at 100 F Street, N.E, Washington D.C. The discussion will also be streamed live on SEC.gov.
Building upon ideas generated during prior committee meetings, the morning session will focus on ways to encourage more companies to go public. The committee will consider ways to modernize the IPO process and potential regulatory reforms to improve the offering process, IPO communication rules, and analyst coverage and support.
During the afternoon session, the committee will consider Regulation Crowdfunding (Reg CF), including the current regulatory framework, successes to-date, challenges, and whether there are potential policy changes to Reg CF that could improve the exemption in order to further expand access to early-stage capital raising. To facilitate the discussion and deepen the committee’s understanding of the Reg CF landscape, members will hear from several experienced professionals in the crowdfunding space.
The Small Business Capital Formation Advisory Committee provides advice and recommendations to the SEC on rules, regulations, and policy matters relating to small businesses.
View the full agenda for meeting details.

WASHINGTON -- Sequan Collier, 29, a previously convicted felon residing in the District, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 29 months in federal prison in connection with his illegal possession of a loaded Glock pistol when police encountered him parked illegally with two additional armed men while he was on supervised release for a previous firearms offense, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Collier pleaded guilty on June 29 before Judge Timothy J. Kelly to unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition by a felon. In addition to the 29‑month prison term, Judge Kelly ordered Collier to serve three years of supervised release.

According to court documents, on March 16, 2025, at approximately 1:42 a.m., officers with the Metropolitan Police Department approached a black Audi A6 illegally parked in a no parking zone in the Logan Circle neighborhood. Collier was in the driver’s seat, accompanied by three other men, two of whom were also armed.

After Collier stepped out of the vehicle, officers recovered a Glock Model 29, 10mm handgun from his waistband. The firearm was loaded with 15 rounds—14 in the magazine and one in the chamber.

At the time, Collier had three prior felony convictions in D.C. Superior Court for offenses punishable by more than one year of imprisonment and was on supervised release for a 2023 firearms conviction involving another loaded Glock recovered from his pants. Collier had served 22 months in prison for that offense yet reoffended just six weeks after his release. As a convicted felon, Collier was prohibited from possessing any firearm.

This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Washington Field Division.

The matter was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Kate Naseef under the president’s Make DC Safe and Beautiful Again initiative. The initiative targets violent crime by prioritizing federal prosecution of armed repeat offenders and removing illegal firearms from District neighborhoods.

Memphis, TN – The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee today announced tax fraud cases as part of nationwide enforcement actions led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Western District of Tennessee was a key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and today, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants, whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490,000,000.

United States Attorney D. Michael Dunavant, of the Western District of Tennessee, said, “Income tax fraud schemes strike at the very heart of our federal government’s financial ability to provide services and protection for our citizens, and we will use all available resources to punish and deter such dishonest criminal behavior. The outcomes of these cases send a clear message: there will always be a consequence, a reckoning, for stealing from the American taxpayer.”

According to court documents and in-court statements:

Lynnette Hogue, 45 , of Memphis, pleaded guilty on October 13, 2026 to preparing false tax returns for others and failing to file her own tax returns. Hogue prepared and filed with the IRS false and fraudulent income tax returns for clients of the tax preparation business where she worked. These tax returns contained false and fraudulent items, which generated refunds the clients were not entitled to receive. Hogue also willfully failed to file her own tax returns, even though she earned substantial income from her tax return preparation business and was required to file by law. Hogue’s fraudulent conduct caused a loss to the IRS of $4.1 million. Hogue pleaded guilty to one count of willfully aiding and assisting in the preparation and presentation of a false tax return and one count of willfully failing to file a tax return. She is scheduled to be sentenced on January 15, 2027 and faces a maximum penalty of four years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Trial Attorneys Isaiah Boyd III and Matthew C. Hicks of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Carroll L. André III for the Western District of Tennessee are prosecuting the case.

Rebecca Gilley, 41 , of Memphis, was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison on October 8, 2026 for filing false tax returns on behalf of clients of her tax preparation business. Gilley, who also went by the names Rebecca Green and Rebecca Maxwell, owned and operated a tax preparation business in Memphis. Gilley prepared tax returns for clients for the years 2018 through 2022 that included false education credits and sick and family leave credits. As a result of these and other false items, Gilley caused her clients to receive fraudulently inflated tax refunds they were not entitled to receive. For the years 2020 and 2021, Gilley filed more than 1,000 tax returns seeking more than $9.25 million in fraudulent sick and family leave credits. She often added these false items to her clients’ returns without their knowledge and rarely reviewed the final returns with the clients. In total, Gilley’s scheme caused a loss to the United States exceeding $350,000. Gilley was also sentenced to one year of supervised release and ordered to pay $289,908 in restitution to the IRS. She will also permanently be enjoined from operating as a tax return preparer. Trial Attorneys Caroline Pearson and Max Willner-Giwerc of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section prosecuted the case.

Frank Jason Cole , 49 , of Memphis, pleaded guilty on September 14, 2026 to wire fraud for preparing and submitting false tax returns. Cole was developed as a lead after Internal Revenue Service (IRS) investigative analysts analyzed tax filings associated with Cole that showed unusual filing activity of Form 944, Employer’s Annual Federal Tax Return, to include unprecedented refund requests. The Forms 944, filed in 2022 and 2023, made false claims for the Employee Retention Credit or “ERC.” Cole prepared and filed false business tax returns for 52 individuals, requesting more than $24 million in false refunds, of which over $19 million were paid out. United States District Judge Thomas L. Parker is scheduled to sentence Cole on January 21, 2027. Cole faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in federal prison, a three-year period of supervised release, restitution, and monetary penalties. Assistant United States Attorney William Bateman prosecuted the case on behalf of the government.

"These investigations reflect the outgoing efforts of IRS Criminal Investigation to combat tax-related crimes and protect the integrity of the federal tax system,” said Special Agent in Charge Donald “Trey” Eakins, Charlotte Field Office, IRS Criminal Investigation. "We will continue to work with our law enforcement partners and the U.S. Attorney’s Office to pursue those who attempt to defraud the government and ensure that individuals are held accountable for their actions."

This press release details one way in which this office has contributed to ensuring that all Americans pay their fair share. To see the successes of other offices, click here .

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An indictment, information, or complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

title: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing More Than $490M in Tax Fraud

WASHINGTON – Representative Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03) celebrated the recent signing into law of her bipartisan Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, legislation to increase transparency and accountability for taxpayer-funded federal projects that are significantly over budget or behind schedule. President Donald Trump signed the bill into law following its passage in both chambers of Congress.
“The American people deserve transparency and accountability for how their tax dollars are spent, especially as families struggle with the rising costs of everyday essentials,” said Rep. Ansari. “While the level of corruption across the federal government right now is stunning and unprecedented, this is a truly longstanding, bipartisan issue. Taxpayers deserve this transparency. And now they’ll have a great deal more.”
Text of Rep. Ansari’s Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act HERE.
The Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act requires the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to compile and submit an annual report to Congress identifying qualifying taxpayer-funded projects and detailing changes to their scope, estimated costs, and projected completion dates. The reporting requirement will give the public greater insight into federal projects experiencing significant delays or cost overruns.
The House of Representatives originally passed the legislation in July 2026. The Senate approved the bill in September, sending it to the President for his signature and final enactment into law.
Follow @RepYassAnsari on all social media platforms and visit Ansari.House.govto learn more.

LAS VEGAS – A Las Vegas man who admitted to using a firearm and Molotov cocktails to destroy and damage vehicles and property at a Tesla-branded repair facility in March 2025, was sentenced today by United States District Judge Jennifer A. Dorsey to 60 months in prison, followed by 3 years of supervised release. The government recommended a sentence of 240 months in prison.

“The Department of Justice has been clear: anyone who participates in domestic terrorism will suffer severe legal consequences,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “There is no place for violence as a means of resolving political differences in our democracy. We will continue to work with our federal and local partners to prevent, disrupt, and deter unlawful acts of violence, whatever their motive remains.”

“Today’s sentencing highlights the undeniable power of task force partnerships,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Field Office. “Keeping our streets safe requires unified action across local, state, and federal lines. Our badges may be different, but we stand completely united against crime.”

“Threats to public safety will be taken seriously,” said Special Agent in Charge John Wester, San Francisco Field Division, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives (ATF). “Crimes of this nature will not be tolerated. ATF deployed our experts in arson related crimes in response to this incident. Those experts included members of our Arson Task Force. The Arson Task Force is a collaboration between ATF and the Clark County Fire Department. Utilized at the scene were a certified fire investigator, bomb technician, certified explosive specialist, an accelerant detection K9, as well as special agents from our local field office that also responded to the incident. We are pleased with today’s sentencing. Combatting violent crime is at the forefront of our mission. ATF is committed to working alongside our partners to ensure crimes of this nature are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and statements made in court, in the early morning hours on March 18, 2025, Paul Hyon Kim shot out two exterior security cameras at the Tesla Collision Center Las Vegas with a .300 Blackout AR-platform semiautomatic rifle. He spray-painted the word “RESIST” in large capital letters on the double entrance doors. Kim then fired several shots into Tesla vehicles parked in front of the repair facility. Next, Kim threw three Molotov cocktails into three vehicles; two exploded and erupted into flames, and a third did not detonate. In total, five vehicles were destroyed beyond repair. Kim fled on foot to his car, then drove away.

Upper Left Photo of defendant spray painting business entrance doors, Upper Right Photo of Molotov cocktail inside a damaged vehicle, and Bottom Photo of two Teslas ablaze, U.S. v. Paul Hyon Kim, Case No: 2:25-mj-00261-EJY

In February 2026, Kim pleaded guilty to two counts of arson of property used in interstate commerce; one count of attempted arson of property used in interstate commerce; and one count of unlawful possession of an unregistered firearm (destructive device).

First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada, Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Division, and Special Agent in Charge John Wester for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives (ATF) San Francisco Field Division made the announcement.

The FBI, ATF, and Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department investigated the case with significant assistance from the Clark County Fire Department. Assistant United States Attorneys Jake Operskalski and Dan Cowhig prosecuted the case.

text:
The Congressional Review Act (CRA, 5 U.S.C. §§801-808) provides Congress with a mechanism to review federal agency actions that meet the CRA's definition of rule. Enacted in 1996, the CRA requires agencies to report the issuance of rules to Congress and provides Congress with special fast-track procedures under which to consider legislation that overturns a rule. A joint resolution of disapproval will become effective once both houses of Congress pass a joint resolution and either it is signed by the President or Congress overrides the President's veto.
The category of rules the CRA covers is broader than the category of rules that are subject to the Administrative Procedure Act's (APA's) notice-and-comment requirements for federal rulemaking (at 5 U.S.C. §553). For instance, the CRA can apply to agency actions such as guidance documents that are not generally subject to notice-and-comment requirements.
Even if an agency action falls under the CRA's definition of rule, however, the CRA's fast-track procedures for considering legislation to overturn the rule become available only after Congress has received the rule. In practice, agencies appear to be fairly consistent in submitting rules to Congress that have undergone notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures and have been published in the Federal Register. Agencies are less consistent in submitting actions to Congress that did not go through notice-and-comment procedures but nonetheless fall under the broad scope of the CRA's definition of rule. Thus, questions have arisen as to how Members can avail themselves of the CRA's special procedures if the agency has not submitted the action.
This In Focus describes what types of agency actions are subject to the CRA by providing an overview of the statutory definition of rule. It then explains how Congress can use the CRA to review covered rules that agencies did not submit to Congress.
For an agency action to be eligible for review under the CRA, it must qualify as a rule as defined in Title 5, Section 804(3), of the U.S. Code. The CRA adopts the broad definition of rule contained in the APA but creates three exceptions. The APA defines a rule as "the whole or a part of an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy" (5 U.S.C. §551(4)). This definition includes regulations that are subject to the APA's notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures. It also covers interpretive rules and general statements of policy, and it can encompass agency actions referred to as guidance documents.
The CRA excludes three categories of actions from its broad definition of rule (5 U.S.C. §804(3)):
(A) any rule of particular applicability, including a rule that approves or prescribes for the future rates, wages, prices, services, or allowances therefor, corporate or financial structures, reorganizations, mergers, or acquisitions thereof, or accounting practices or disclosures bearing on any of the foregoing;
(B) any rule relating to agency management or personnel; or
(C) any rule of agency organization, procedure, or practice that does not substantially affect the rights or obligations of non-agency parties.
Thus, determining whether a particular agency action is a rule subject to the CRA entails a two-part inquiry: first, whether the statement qualifies as a rule under the APA Section 551 definition and, second, whether the statement falls within any of the CRA's three exceptions (Figure 1).
Following judicial precedent interpreting the APA, the CRA applies only to final agency action (see CRS In Focus IF12386, Defining Final Agency Action for APA and CRA Review, by Valerie C. Brannon (2026)). Accordingly, the CRA does not cover actions of the President, such as executive orders and presidential proclamations.
The CRA requires agencies to submit a report containing a copy of each covered rule and information on the rule to Congress and to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) before the rule may take effect (5 U.S.C. §801(a)). Once the rule is received, Members may introduce and take action on a joint resolution of disapproval, provided they do so within certain time periods specified in the CRA.
Under the text of the CRA, the fast-track procedures become available only after Congress has received the rule. Because Congress's ability to access the CRA's special procedures hinges on the rule having been received, an agency's failure to submit a rule to Congress could frustrate Congress's ability to review rules under the act. Furthermore, the CRA states that "no determination, finding, action, or omission under this chapter shall be subject to judicial review" (5 U.S.C. §805). Most courts to consider this provision have interpreted it to prohibit judicial review of claims that an agency violated the CRA by failing to submit a rule. In a September 2026 decision, one trial court concluded that even though an agency's decision to classify its action as a rule under the APA was reviewable, its decision to submit that rule to Congress under the CRA was not.
To avoid being denied its opportunity to review rules under the CRA, Congress has developed a practice to enable the law's review mechanism even when an agency has not submitted a rule for review. That practice has involved seeking an opinion from GAO on whether an agency action should have been submitted under the CRA (i.e., whether the action is covered by the CRA's definition of rule).
If a Member requests a GAO opinion and GAO concludes that an action should have been submitted, under current practice, Congress can then proceed with consideration of a joint resolution of disapproval under the CRA's special procedures. While the House and Senate Parliamentarians are the sole definitive arbiters of procedural matters under the CRA—including the determination of whether a joint resolution of disapproval is privileged under the CRA—it appears that the chamber Parliamentarians have generally deferred to GAO's opinions on whether an agency action is covered.
Some Members of Congress have sought such opinions from GAO since the CRA was enacted in 1996. Those opinions are available on GAO's website. GAO describes the process for requesting a legal opinion in its publication GAO's Protocols for Legal Decisions and Opinions.
The Senate appears to consider the publication in the Congressional Record of a GAO opinion concluding that an agency action should have been submitted under the CRA as the trigger date for the CRA's fast-track disapproval procedures. When agencies submit rules to Congress under the CRA as required under Title 5, Section 801(a), a record of each rule's receipt is published in the Executive Communications portion of the Congressional Record. The publication of the GAO opinion in the Congressional Record fulfills this same purpose: notifying Congress that a rule is now available for review under the CRA.
The 115th Congress (2017-2018) was the first to enact a CRA joint resolution of disapproval overturning an agency guidance document that had been neither promulgated through the APA's notice-and-comment procedures nor submitted to Congress under the CRA. In that case, Congress allowed a GAO opinion to trigger the CRA's fast-track procedures and overturned a guidance document issued by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The 119th Congress (2025-2026) has employed this process as well, overturning several actions taken by the Bureau of Land Management relating to the management of public lands.
If a joint resolution of disapproval is introduced, both houses pass the resolution within the CRA-specified deadlines, and the President signs it (or if Congress overrides the President's veto), the CRA states that the "rule shall not take effect (or continue)" (5 U.S.C. §801(b)(1)). If the rule already went into effect, it must be treated as though it "had never taken effect" (5 U.S.C. §801(f)). A CRA joint resolution of disapproval thus is retroactive. In addition, the CRA provides that after a joint resolution of disapproval is enacted, an agency may not issue the rule in "substantially the same form" as the disapproved rule unless a subsequent law specifically authorizes the reissued rule (5 U.S.C. §801(b)(2)).
For an in-depth discussion of the issues discussed in this In Focus, see CRS Report R45248, The Congressional Review Act: Determining Which "Rules" Must Be Submitted to Congress, by Valerie C. Brannon and Maeve P. Carey (2024).
For a broad overview of the CRA, including an explanation of the CRA's fast-track procedures and associated timelines, as well as court opinions interpreting the CRA's bar on judicial review, see CRS Report R43992, The Congressional Review Act (CRA): Frequently Asked Questions, by Maeve P. Carey and Christopher M. Davis (2021). For a shorter overview, see CRS In Focus IF10023, The Congressional Review Act (CRA): A Brief Overview, by Maeve P. Carey and Christopher M. Davis (2026).
title: The Congressional Review Act: Defining a “Rule” and Overturning a Rule an Agency Did Not Submit to Congress

The federal government divided up tribal lands in the Southwest during the 19th and 20th centuries, triggering long-standing land disputes between the Navajo Nation and the Hopi Tribe (both federally recognized Tribes). In 1868, the United States entered into a treaty with the Navajo Nation that, among other things, established the Tribe's 3.5 million acre reservation, initially in northern Arizona and New Mexico. In 1882, an executive order set aside about 2.5 million acres in Arizona for the Hopi Tribe. In 1934, Congress expanded the Navajo reservation so that it surrounded the Hopi reservation (P.L. 73-352). These federal actions led to some citizens of each Tribe living on, or using, land arguably set aside for the other Tribe. Both the 1882 executive order and the 1934 act allowed "other Indians" besides those belonging to the designated Tribe to reside on the specified lands; however, the Tribes have since disputed ownership and occupancy. This In Focus provides an overview of federal actions to address these tribal land disputes, including the Office of Navajo and Hopi Indian Relocation, and potential issues for Congress.
The federal government attempted to settle these tribal land disputes throughout the 20th century. In 1958, Congress authorized the Tribes to file lawsuits to settle ownership (quiet title) to the 1882 reservation (P.L. 85-547). In 1962, a federal district court in Arizona ruled that (1) the Hopi had exclusive rights to about 631,000 acres of the 1882 reservation (District Six) and (2) the Tribes had "joint, undivided, and equal interests" to about 1.9 million acres of the rest of the reservation—the Joint Use Area (JUA) (Healing v. Jones, 210 F.Supp. 125, D.Ariz. 1962).
In 1966, the Hopi Tribe filed a lawsuit claiming about 1.5 million acres of Navajo lands within the 1934 reservation. That year, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs at the Department of the Interior (DOI), Robert Bennett, restricted construction on those disputed lands until the conflict was resolved (absent approval from both Tribes). This Bennett Freeze was intended to stop either Tribe from taking advantage of the other while the dispute was being settled.
Despite these developments, litigation continued over both the 1882 and the 1934 reservations, leading Congress to enact the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act of 1974 (Settlement Act, P.L. 93-531). The act authorized the Tribes to settle the 1882 reservation dispute using a federal mediator. The negotiation was unsuccessful, and in 1977, a court ordered the partition of the JUA into two equal land areas—Hopi Partitioned Lands (HPL) and Navajo Partitioned Lands (NPL). The act also authorized either Tribe to initiate or defend a court action on land claims related to the 1934 reservation.
The Settlement Act also established the Navajo and Hopi Indian Relocation Commission to relocate tribal households on the newly partitioned lands stemming from the resolution of the 1882 reservation dispute. In 1988, the commission was restructured and renamed the Office of Navajo and Hopi Indian Relocation (ONHIR) (P.L. 100-666). ONHIR's mission is to relocate Navajo and Hopi tribal households and to provide related benefits and assistance. The Settlement Act also required relocation sites to include "housing and related community facilities and services, such as water, sewers, roads, schools, and health facilities." Navajo and Hopi households must apply to ONHIR and demonstrate that they meet certain criteria to become certified for relocation benefits. If denied, applicants may appeal.
ONHIR's relocation process was originally scheduled to end in July 1986 but has been delayed for various reasons. Some Navajo households refused to relocate during the first application period, which eventually led to a negotiated settlement agreement between the Tribes (ratified by P.L. 104-301). Under that agreement, the Hopi Tribe was authorized to acquire additional lands and the Hopi Tribe agreed to allow Navajo residents to remain on HPL under 75-year leases. Those residents who did not obtain leases could apply to relocate during ONHIR's second round of applications (1997-2000). ONHIR opened a third round of applications in 2005 to provide another opportunity for relocation. In 2008, ONHIR opened up a fourth round in response to a federal court decision. As of December 2017, ONHIR had relocated more than 3,600 Navajo and Hopi families, consisting of about 16,700 individuals (see this 2018 Government Accountability Office [GAO] report).
The Settlement Act, as amended, authorized the federal government to take 400,000 acres into trust for the Navajo Nation to relocate (P.L. 96-305). According to a 2023 DOI Office of Inspector General (OIG) report, 387,000 acres have been acquired pursuant to the act, including 352,000 acres of land in Arizona that ONHIR refers to as the New Lands. On the New Lands, ONHIR issues leases and rights-of-way for housing and related facilities and manages the Padres Mesa Demonstration Ranch (P.L. 99-190). The ranch was established to teach sustainable cattle ranching and livestock marketing to the Navajo relocatees.
Funding for ONHIR
Congress may continue to consider whether, and if so how much, funding is necessary for ONHIR or a successor agency to complete its mission. Funding for ONHIR generally has been provided in annual appropriations laws for DOI. These laws typically have funded relocation benefits and office operations. Annual appropriations over roughly the past five fiscal years have fluctuated. In FY2022-FY2024, Congress made available funding from unobligated (carryover) balances but provided no new funding. For FY2025, Congress provided $1.7 million for ONHIR, and for FY2026, no funding. The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) also receives annual appropriations that have been used to support the Tribes (i.e., BIA's Navajo-Hopi Settlement Program), which helps manage agriculture and rangeland on HPL and NPL.
In addition to annual appropriations, the 1988 amendments to the Settlement Act established the Navajo Rehabilitation Trust Fund in the U.S. Treasury. The trust fund consists of appropriations and income derived from leases of Navajo Nation lands and minerals. According to a 2023 DOI OIG report, Congress authorized up to $60 million for the fund over a six-year period; as of 2023, $16 million had been appropriated. The 1988 amendments required the Navajo Nation to repay the federal government for any appropriations, but the Tribe has asked Congress to eliminate that requirement.
Whether and how ONHIR might cease operations is another issue. In September 2025, ONHIR and DOI signed a memorandum of understanding that, among other provisions, transferred the functions and responsibilities of ONHIR to the Office of the Secretary. The MOU further stated, "ONHIR anticipates that it shall cease to exist as of September 30, 2026." However, the Settlement Act states that ONHIR "shall cease to exist when the President determines that its functions have been fully discharged" and ONHIR has not publicly stated whether it has asked for a presidential determination around closure.
Although a presidential determination has not been made, Congress has nevertheless expressed interest in closing ONHIR. For example, the explanatory statement accompanying P.L. 119-74, Division C, the Department of the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026, stated that Congress remained "committed to the orderly and timely closure" of ONHIR. To that end, Congress did not fund ONHIR but instead provided $7.0 million to DOI's Office of the Secretary to work with stakeholders and the Department of Justice to address "all outstanding administrative duties, fiduciary responsibilities, land management and livestock obligations of ONHIR that are necessary to support its final closure." The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (P.L. 119-103, Division A, Section 140) allows funding provided to DOI's Office of the Secretary to be available to assume the functions performed by ONHIR.
The two Tribes have different views on next steps for ONHIR. In the past, the Hopi Tribe has supported the completion of relocation activities and ONHIR's subsequent closure. On the other hand, the Navajo Nation has generally opposed closure. Nevertheless, the Navajo Nation acknowledged the 2025 MOU transferring ONHIR's responsibilities to DOI (BIA). The Navajo Nation emphasized that BIA is now responsible for various issues, including resolving the remaining relocation cases; addressing ongoing housing construction and infrastructure repairs; land and range management; and continued Navajo land selections estimated at approximately 13,000 acres.
Since 1966, BIA modified the Bennett Freeze several times, and Congress eventually codified it in 1980 (P.L. 96-305). Court actions in the 1990s lifted, and then reinstated, the freeze. In 2006, the Tribes entered into an intergovernmental compact that lifted the freeze. In 2009, Congress repealed the freeze (P.L. 111-18). (See Figure 1.)
Although the Bennett Freeze was formally repealed in 2009, concerns remain about its ongoing impacts. In 2022, the Navajo Nation reported that 24% of the area's houses are habitable, with almost 60% lacking electricity and most lacking potable water. Congress has considered legislation to support economic development in the former Bennett Freeze area; for example, H.R. 6141 from the 117th Congress proposed establishing a Former Bennett Freeze Area Rehabilitation Trust Fund. That bill and others have proposed creating Navajo Sovereignty Empowerment Zones, where certain laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act, would be waived to promote economic development.

BOSTON – A Dominican national unlawfully residing in Lawrence, Mass. pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston for unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation.

Eddy Antonio Perdomo, 32, pleaded guilty to one count of unlawful reentry of a deported alien. U.S. District Court Judge Angel Kelley scheduled sentencing for Nov. 13, 2026. Perdomo was charged in August 2026 .

Perdomo previously pleaded guilty to one count of unlawful reentry of a deported alien in July 2025 . He was subsequently sentenced to time served (approximately four months in prison) on Sept. 5, 2025 and removed from the United States on Sept. 15, 2025. It is alleged that sometime after his September 2025 removal, Perdomo illegally reentered the United States without permission.

The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.
title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty To Illegal Reentry

PHOENIX, Ariz. –Mohammed Maio, 44, of Phoenix, was sentenced yesterday by United States District Judge Michael T. Liburdi to 10 years in prison. Maio previously pleaded guilty to Conspiracy to Commit Wire and Bank Fraud, Conspiracy to Commit Money Laundering, Bank Fraud, Felon in Possession of a Firearm, and Materially False Statement During the Acquisition of a Firearm.

“Maio’s actions resulted in significant financial loss to the U.S. government and exploited a program intended to provide relief to small businesses during a national crisis,” said U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine. “Fraud of this nature weakens the effectiveness of federal assistance programs and places an additional burden on taxpayers who ultimately bear the cost of these crimes.”

“While business owners and families were struggling during the COVID pandemic, Maio was scheming to defraud the government relief programs for personal gain,” said Scott Brown, Acting Special Agent in Charge, IRS CI Phoenix Field Office. “This case demonstrates IRS CI’s ongoing commitment to pursuing individuals who abused these pandemic relief programs and ensuring they are held accountable.”

“This significant sentence is part of a multi-agency effort to hold those who took advantage of COVID-era programs accountable,” said A.J. Gibes, Special Agent in Charge for the ATF Phoenix Field Division. “Not only did Mr. Maio commit fraud against the United States government, he illegally armed himself to protect his multi-million-dollar scheme. We are proud to work with our IRS partners to bring those who would defraud the American people to justice.”

According to court documents, between May 2020 and March 2024, Maio conspired to fraudulently obtain and misuse multiple Paycheck Protection Program and Economic Injury Disaster Loan relief loans. He submitted false information to secure nearly $2.2 million in loans for multiple businesses that had no employees, and the funds were used for personal enrichment, including the purchase of multiple properties, rather than legitimate business purposes.

In addition to the fraud charges, Maio, a convicted felon, arranged for his mother to purchase a firearm on his behalf in May 2021. Mohammed Maio admitted that he caused his mother to falsely state on the purchase application that the firearm was for her use, rather than his, and that he later illegally possessed the firearm she purchased.

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives conducted the investigation in this case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin M. Rapp, District of Arizona, Phoenix, handled the prosecution.

PLANO, Texas –The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Texas today announced results as part of a nationwide enforcement action led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Eastern District of Texas was a key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and now, federal prosecutors across the country facilitated fraud enforcement actions against 76 defendants and more than $90 million in intended loss to American taxpayers.

“Tax fraud is not fraud against the federal government or the IRS,” said U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs. “Tax fraud is fraud against the American people. Federal income tax is used to fund programs that support American children, families, veterans, the disabled, and the elderly, and tax fraud directly impacts those programs.”

“Tax fraud is a crime that comes with a litany of victims. Criminal return preparers often steal the identities of the taxpayers that hire them, steal large chunks of the fraudulent refunds, and target the communities that can least afford it. Employment tax fraud steals from your personal contributions to Social Security, Medicare and other programs you thought you were paying into. Tax evaders simply want to enjoy their lives by having you and I pay for it,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher J. Altemus Jr., of IRS-CI's Texas Field Office. “We are taking back what they stole and taking away their freedom to deter them from stealing again, but that won’t stop every criminal. If you don’t want to be a victim, select your return preparer carefully, avoid the temptation for a fraudulent better refund and report suspected fraud on IRS.Gov.”

In the Eastern District of Texas, U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs announced that five defendants have pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing for tax fraud.

On September 23, 2026, Antwon Pierre Sadler , 41, and Raegan Samone Hagler, 29, both of Longview, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to aid or assist in tax fraud. According to information presented in court, Sadler and Hagler worked at a tax preparer business owned by Marneitha Scott and operated under the name of F.A.S.T. Financial Firm (“FAST”) with two locations in Longview. Scott, Hagler, and Sadler devised a scheme to defraud the United States by creating and instructing other tax preparers to create fraudulent entries on client tax returns, including claims for business losses when the client had no business. The tax returns were filed by Scott, Hagler, and Sadler or other employees and the tax preparation business was paid a fee by the clients for preparing and filing the returns. Their conduct resulted in a known tax loss for tax years 2019 – 2022 of at least $400,000.00 and an estimated tax loss of at least $5 million. Scott pleaded guilty to the same offense on February 18, 2026. All three defendants are awaiting sentencing.

On October 1, 2026, Jerome Theodore Powell, Jr., 51, of Horn Lake, Mississippi, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to file false claims. According to information presented in court, Powell was involved in a conspiracy which involved filing fraudulent tax returns for fictitious businesses and trusts that were created for the sole purpose of obtaining tax refunds. The scheme resulted in a tax loss of $4,192,028 and an attempted loss of approximately $17 million. Powell is awaiting sentencing.

On October 6, 2026, Joy Nicole Murphy, 36, of Mabank, Texas, pleaded guilty to aiding or assisting in tax fraud. According to information presented in court, Murphy operated a tax return preparer business in Gun Barrel City. She executed a scheme to file returns on behalf of her clients containing false and fraudulent information to ensure larger refunds. The scheme resulted in a tax loss of more than $350,000. Murphy is awaiting sentencing.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire temporary foreign workers for specialty occupation positions (i.e., positions that require specialized knowledge and a college degree). To date in 2026 the Trump Administration has announced several policy changes aimed at addressing perceived abuses of the program, such as replacing U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign workers. These executive actions come on the heels of policy changes announced in 2025.
In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) implemented a weighted (instead of random) selection process for the H-1B lottery to "favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid" workers. The first affected lottery was for H-1B employment starting in October 2026.
In March 2026, the Department of Labor (DOL) published a proposed rule to increase H-1B prevailing wage requirements. DOL asserted that under the current regulation, "employers were permitted to hire alien workers at wage levels below those that similarly employed U.S. workers were paid, resulting in adverse effects to the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers." H-1B prevailing wage requirements differ by skill level (See Table 1), specialty occupation, and Metropolitan Statistical Area.
Source: CRS Presentation of 91 Federal Register 15454.
DOL estimated these proposed wage requirements would increase H-1B employer costs by approximately $1.46 billion in the first year.
In August 2026, DHS issued a proposed rule to establish a new $103,265 fee to "generate dedicated revenue to support the costs of administering the lawful immigration system." The new fee would apply to each cap-subject petition submitted by employers for H-1B workers. This is separate from the $100,000 fee the Administration imposed in September 2025 on U.S. employers petitioning for new H-1B workers from abroad (which was in effect for most of the past year but is currently temporarily blocked due to ongoing litigation).
In August 2026, DHS issued a final rule that applies an existing $4,000 "9-11 Biometric Fee" to petitions filed by certain employers on behalf of H-1B or L-1 workers (within-company transfers to the United States) who are extending their status. Before this rule, DHS had interpreted the 9-11 Biometric Fee passed by Congress in 2015 to apply only to petitions for new workers or those changing employers. Employers subject to this fee—before and after the change—are those with more than 50 employees in the United States, of whom more than 50 percent are in H-1B or L-1 status. The 9-11 Biometric Fee is scheduled to sunset on September 30, 2027.
In July 2026, the DOL Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation and intensified enforcement efforts "to combat fraud and human trafficking" in the H-1B program, focusing on fraudulent applications and coercive wage-kickbacks. This initiative includes a nationwide awareness program encouraging workers to report concerns to DOL. It builds on the 2025 launch of "Project Firewall," an initiative to strengthen labor enforcement of the H-1B program by "prioritizing investigations where there are signs of displacements, inadequate recruitment of U.S. workers, or other abuses." Data on DOL H-1B compliance enforcement actions in FY2026 are not yet available.
In September 2026, President Trump issued an executive order, requiring more coordination between agencies to "ensure the compliance … with statutory requirements" and requires them to "take into account in any labor condition application, petition, visa, and entry of aliens entering or attempting to enter the United States as H-1B nonimmigrants … whether the employer sponsor directly or indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year or plans future layoffs." Current law does not bar employers with recent layoffs of U.S. workers from employing H-1B workers. DHS is also considering "revising eligibility for cap exemptions, providing greater scrutiny for employers that have violated program requirements, and increasing oversight over third party placements."
In October 2026, DHS proposed removing a policy of deferring to prior approvals when employers petition to extend H-1B workers' employment. Removing "prior deference" would increase scrutiny of extension requests when the circumstances of H-1B employment are unchanged.
In September 2026, DHS proposed eliminating a grace period (implemented in 2017), which allows H-1B and certain other temporary workers to remain in the United States for up to 60 days after their employment ends. In October, DHS eliminated automatic extensions of work authorization for spouses of H-1B workers and is considering removing their eligibility for work authorization altogether.
Some employers sponsor their H-1B workers for permanent labor certification (known as PERM). If approved, these workers may become LPRs, which allows them to more easily change employers (and to eventually become U.S. citizens). The administration has initiated rulemaking "improving the minimum standards for recruiting qualified U.S. workers, strengthening safeguards for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs, and enhancing employer compliance with program requirements related to non-discriminatory recruitment and hiring practices." Such changes could result in fewer H-1B workers being approved for PERM.
There are indications that employers are filing fewer petitions for H-1B workers coming from abroad. DHS data show reduced petition filings from both cap-subject and cap-exempt employers following the implementation of the $100,000 fee in 2025. For example, during the first eight months that the fee was in effect, the number of initial H-1B petitions that DHS received for consular processing from cap-exempt employers dropped 91% from the same period the year before. Similarly, cap-subject companies that typically had high numbers of H-1B employees coming from abroad submitted significantly fewer entries to the FY2027 H-1B lottery. Among the highest lottery entrants in FY2026 were Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata, which submitted 100%, 91%, and 95% fewer registrations in FY2027, respectively.

HHS Issues Final Demand to Medical Organizations to Answer for Sex-Rejecting Procedures for Minors
WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 14, 2026—The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) today sent letters to leading medical organizations requesting that they state clearly whether they continue to support sex-rejecting procedures for minors and account for the evidence-base and HHS reports showing the harms these interventions inflict on minors in their guidance and position statements.
The letters were sent to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH), the American Medical Association, American Psychiatric Association, American Psychological Association, Endocrine Society, and others.
“When medical organizations set standards that shape the care of children, they have a responsibility to explain the evidence behind those standards,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “HHS has asked these organizations for clear answers about their current positions, the evidence supporting their guidance, and whether they intend to change it. Parents and clinicians deserve transparency, and we expect these organizations to provide it.”
HHS previously requested a substantive response from these organizations regarding their positions on sex-rejecting procedures for children and any planned updates to their guidance or position statements.
The Department is now requesting a clear statement of the current position of these organizations on sex-rejecting procedures for minors, identification of any planned revisions to their respective guidance, and a timeline for those changes. HHS expects a written response within 10 business days.
Today’s action is the latest step in the Trump Administration’s sustained effort to protect children from sex-rejecting procedures and bring transparency and accountability to so-called “gender medicine” in pediatric care. HHS has moved to bar hospitals participating in Medicare and Medicaid from performing these procedures on children and prohibit federal Medicaid and CHIP funding for them; exposed potentially fraudulent insurance coding associated with sex-rejecting procedures on minors; and released research examining ideological influences associated with support for these clinical practices.
Organizations that set standards of care and medical guidelines for children and shape accepted medical practice have a responsibility to answer for the consequences of their guidance. The Trump Administration will make sure they do.

PITTSBURGH, Pa. - A resident of Sewickley, Pennsylvania, has been sentenced in federal court to two months of imprisonment, to be followed by two years of supervised release, on her conviction of bank fraud, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.

Senior United States District Judge Nora Barry Fischer imposed the sentence on Judith A. Hetzell, 64, on October 13, 2026, also ordering the defendant to pay $80,966 in restitution to her former employer.

According to information presented to the Court, between November 2023 and February 2025, Hetzell, the former business manager for a non-profit guardianship agency based in the Western District of Pennsylvania, fraudulently drafted checks against individuals’ bank accounts to which the agency had access as a provider of guardianship and other fiduciary services to the victims. The checks were drafted to cash and to Hetzell’s mother and deposited into two personal bank accounts that Hetzell controlled.

Prior to imposing the sentence, Judge Fischer stated that, while Hetzell had otherwise lived a law-abiding life, her criminal conduct was quite serious in that she stole funds from the accounts of vulnerable individuals who, for various physical and mental health reasons, required the services of a guardianship agency. Judge Fischer also observed that Hetzell’s conduct risked the viability of the agency for whom she worked.

First Assistant United States Attorney Carolyn J. Bloch prosecuted this case on behalf of the government.

United States Attorney Rivetti commended the United States Postal Inspection Service for the investigation leading to the successful prosecution of Hetzell.
title: Sewickley Woman Sentenced for Bank Fraud Involving Guardianship Agency Funds

HUD Makes It Easier to Build More Housing
Updated FHA policy encourages new housing supply by removing outdated restrictions for Multifamily Build to Rent communities.
October 14, 2026
WASHINGTON - HUD today announced that its Federal Housing Administration (FHA) is expanding access to quality rental housing by allowing Build to Rent communities to qualify for FHA-insured financing under two of its Multifamily mortgage insurance programs. Effective immediately, this update makes it easier to finance new rental homes and helps increase the supply of rental housing, particularly in light of manufactured housing innovation.
“America needs more affordable housing,” said Secretary Scott Turner. “We’re eliminating barriers to spur development, expand rental options, and improve housing affordability for hardworking American families.”
Build to Rent communities are multifamily rental properties that consist of single-family homes, duplexes, or triplexes, including both site-built and manufactured homes. These properties will now be treated under the same terms and conditions as traditional multifamily rental developments, subject to the specific requirements outlined in today’s Mortgagee Letter.
“Expanding housing supply, including new rental housing, is essential to improving affordability,” said Joe Gormley, currently overseeing the FHA and Office of Housing. “Combined with other initiatives we are working on at HUD, including chassis removal in our manufactured housing programs, we are unshackling the market to deliver housing where it’s needed most.”
FHA’s updated policy reflects growing demand for single-family, duplex, and triplex rental housing, as well as the expanding presence of professionally managed Build to Rent developments. The policy applies to FHA's Section 221(d)(4) program for new construction and Section 223(f) program for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities.
This change supports President Trump's efforts to remove barriers to housing and aligns with Executive Order 14376, Stopping Wall Street from Competing with Main Street Homebuyers.
Follow @SecretaryTurner on X, FB, and Instagram.
title: HUD Makes It Easier to Build More Housing

Sherman Joins House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats in Condemning Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal
Washington, D.C. – Congressman Brad Sherman (CA-32), a senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, joined Ranking Member Gregory W. Meeks and fellow Committee Democrats in condemning President Trump’s decision to authorize purchases of Russian diesel, warning that the move would enrich Vladimir Putin and undermine U.S. support for Ukraine:
“President Trump is blaming Ukraine for rising fuel costs to distract from the real cause: his war of choice in Iran. The American people are paying the price for this president’s decisions, and now he is filling the Kremlin’s war chest. It is a shameful betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies, and everything the United States stands for.
“We welcome the bipartisan condemnation of this deal. But condemnation alone is not enough. When Republicans have had the chance to do more, most have refused.
“In April, HFAC Democrats introduced the End Russian Oil Windfalls Act, legislation that would bar the administration from issuing the very licenses Trump is now using to enrich Putin. Republicans declined to cosponsor it and Republican leadership has not moved it since.
"If Republicans are genuinely outraged by this deal they should join us, pass this legislation, and put a check on a president who is more interested in appeasing Putin and enriching himself and his inner circle than defending American interests or our commitments to Ukraine. Congress has the power to act.” 
Sherman and his Democratic colleagues also renewed calls for passage of the End Russian Oil Windfalls Act (H.R. 8222), legislation introduced in April to prevent the administration from issuing such licenses.

DALLAS — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould today announced several legal proceedings as part of a nationwide enforcement actions led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Internal Revenue Service and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation targeting tax fraud and related offenses. The Northern District of Texas was key participant in this surge effort.

Between early September and today, federal prosecutors across the country facilitated fraud enforcement actions spanning over 70 criminal defendants, including approximately 31 newly charged defendants, reaching approximately490 million dollars in intended loss to American taxpayers.

“Every dollar lost to tax fraud is a dollar stolen from the American public,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “These enforcement actions make one thing unmistakably clear: fraudsters who cheat the tax system will be held accountable. By working in close partnership with the Fraud Division, IRS and IRSCI, we are restoring trust in the system and ensuring that those who attempt to evade their obligations are brought to justice. This surge reflects our shared commitment to fairness, integrity, and protecting hardworking taxpayers.”

“Every dollar lost to tax fraud is a dollar stolen from the American public,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “These enforcement actions make one thing unmistakably clear: fraudsters who cheat the tax system will be held accountable. By working in close partnership with the Fraud Division, IRS and IRSCI, we are restoring trust in the system and ensuring that those who attempt to evade their obligations are brought to justice. This surge reflects our shared commitment to fairness, integrity, and protecting hardworking taxpayers.”

“Tax fraud is a crime that comes with a litany of victims,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher J. Altemus Jr., of IRS-CI's Texas Field Office. “Criminal return preparers often steal the identities of the taxpayers that hire them, steal large chunks of the fraudulent refunds and target the communities that can least afford it. Employment tax fraud steals from your personal contributions to Social Security, Medicare and other programs you thought you were paying into. Tax evaders simply want to enjoy their lives by having you and I pay for it “We are taking back what they stole and taking away their freedom to deter them from stealing again, but that won’t stop every criminal. If you don’t want to be a victim, select your return preparer carefully, avoid the temptation for a fraudulent better refund and report suspected fraud on IRS.Gov.”

Notable cases

United States v. Duncan John MacDonald a.k.a. Duncan John a.k.a. DJ, Sarah Duren, Richard Ronald Cayce a.k.a. Richard Ronald and Thomas Weickgenant (Indictment)

On Sept. 22, a federal grand jury returned a 24-count indictment against MacDonald, Duren, Cayce and Weickgenant (collectively, the "Defendants") for allegedly engaging in a scheme to defraud the United States through the promotion, sale and facilitation of a fraudulent tax shelter.

According to the indictment, the Defendants encouraged high-income individuals to illegally evade income taxes by selling those clients so-called copyrighted, irrevocable, complex, non-grantor, discretionary, spendthrift trusts (the "Abusive Trusts"). At the Defendants' direction, clients used the Abusive Trusts to unlawfully shield approximately 90%o of their income from taxation

In total, the Abusive Trust scheme illegally sheltered more than $ 1.5 billion of clients' income from taxation and caused an estimated loss to the United States Treasury exceeding $200 million. In sum, the Defendants collectively earned millions of dollars in fees selling these Abusive Trusts.

The defendants are charged with the following offenses and, if convicted, face the following maximum prison sentences:
