LAS VEGAS – An illegal alien has been arrested and charged in a federal criminal complaint alleging he possessed with intent to distribute fentanyl and methamphetamine after law enforcement officers discovered approximately 14 kilograms (30 pounds) of suspected fentanyl and more than 307 kilograms (677 pounds) of suspected methamphetamine during a traffic stop in Lincoln County, Nevada.

“Anyone who plans to release a deadly drug like fentanyl onto American streets will be prosecuted,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the diligent work of federal and local law enforcement, the lethal drugs allegedly possessed by this illegal alien are no longer endangering the lives of countless Americans. The Department of Justice will continue rooting out illegal drug trafficking networks and keeping American neighborhoods safe.”

“Under the leadership of President Trump, DHS and HSI are laser-focused on hunting down fentanyl traffickers and smugglers to get this poison off our streets,” said Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “I commend the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office for their work with HSI to remove a lethal amount of fentanyl and methamphetamine from American communities. We will continue to work with our Homeland Security Task Force partners to disrupt criminal networks and prosecute these drug traffickers to the fullest extent of the law.”

“The massive scale of this seizure underscores the staggering volume of illicit narcotics flowing into our communities from transnational criminal organizations,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “ Fourteen kilograms of fentanyl alone represents approximately seven million potentially lethal two-milligram doses—enough to kill more than twice the population of Nevada—and, when combined with over 650 pounds of methamphetamine, represents an estimated street value of approximately $2 million. These staggering quantities reflect a blatant disregard for human life, driven purely by profit. I commend the outstanding work of our federal partners at Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office. Our office will continue working tirelessly to dismantle these dangerous criminal networks, secure our borders, and ensure that those who traffic these deadly substances face the maximum penalties allowed under the law.”

“HSI is committed to disrupting the criminal networks responsible for moving deadly narcotics into and through our communities,” said John A. Condon, Executive Associate Director of Homeland Security Investigations. “The suspected fentanyl and methamphetamine seized in this case represent an extraordinary threat to public safety. Through close coordination with the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, the U.S. Attorney’s Office, and our Homeland Security Task Force partners, HSI will continue to identify, investigate and hold accountable those who profit from poisoning Americans and endangering our communities.”

“The allegations in this case underscore the serious threat illicit narcotics pose to rural communities and the traveling public,” Lincoln County Sheriff Derek Foremaster said. “I am proud of the vigilance and professionalism demonstrated by our deputies, whose proactive traffic enforcement and trained K-9 deployment led to the identification of suspected narcotics and a coordinated response with Homeland Security Investigations. We greatly value our partnership with HSI and the Homeland Security Task Force. That collaboration strengthens our ability to protect Lincoln County, disrupt drug trafficking and support thorough, criminal investigations.”

According to allegations in the criminal complaint, on October 13, 2026, a deputy with the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office conducted a traffic stop of a pickup truck driven by Francisco Joel Garcia Farias, 26, on U.S. Highway 93 near Ash Springs, Nevada, after observing the vehicle traveling above the posted speed limit. During the stop, a trained narcotics detection K-9 alerted to the presence of suspected controlled substances in the vehicle.

A subsequent search of the pickup truck revealed 13 large storage totes containing numerous vacuum-sealed packages of suspected narcotics. Law enforcement officers recovered approximately 187 packages containing a white crystalline substance weighing a total of approximately 307.22 kilograms, along with 13 brick-shaped packages weighing approximately 14 kilograms. Field testing of selected samples returned positive results for methamphetamine and fentanyl, respectively.

File photo and photos of totes of methamphetamine and fentanyl powder, U.S. v. Francisco Joel Garcia Farias, Case 2:26-mj-00773-MDC

Garcia Farias is charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute 400 grams or more of a mixture containing fentanyl and one count of possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine.

If convicted, Garcia Farias faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in prison and a maximum sentence of life imprisonment on each count, followed by five years of supervised release.

This case is led by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) in partnership with the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office as part of the Homeland Security Task Force Core Region 8. Assistant United States Attorney Steven J. Rose is prosecuting the case.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

This alien entered the country illegally, and was then granted Lawful Permanent Resident status by the Obama Administration
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after an investigation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) led to the arrest of an alien for illegally voting in multiple prior elections in Missouri.
On October 6, HSI Kansas City arrested Andres Garcia, a Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR) from Cuba, after he was charged with TWO counts of voting by an alien for voting in the November 2022 and November 2024 elections.
Andres Garcia during his arrest by HSI Kansas City
Even before receiving his LPR status, Garcia allegedly registered to vote in Cass County, Missouri, in 2004. He has voted regularly for the last 20 years in at least 15 elections, including at least 13 federal elections. Despite knowing he was not a United States citizen, Garcia claimed to be one when registering to vote in 2004, and did so again in 2013.
“This alien from Cuba has been arrested and charged with illegally voting in multiple elections,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “He illegally entered the country in 1969 and was then granted legal status by the Obama Administration. Now, thanks to the hardworking men and women of HSI and our partners at the Department of Justice, this alien will have to answer for repeatedly interfering in our elections. Let this be a message to any non-citizens out there who are thinking about voting in our elections: If you illegally vote, we will arrest you and you will be charged. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.”
“Election integrity is nonnegotiable. Individuals who knowingly violate federal voting laws undermine public trust in the democratic process and will be held accountable,” said HSI Kansas City Acting Special Agent in Charge Rick Sabatini. “HSI will continue working with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and stop those who illegally interfere with the integrity of our elections.”
“When an individual who is not legally permitted to vote casts a ballot, it undermines the public’s confidence in our elections,” said R. Matthew Price, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Missouri. “Free and fair elections depend on the integrity of our voting process and compliance with the law. Our office will aggressively enforce federal election laws and hold accountable anyone who interferes with the integrity of the electoral process.”
Garcia illegally entered the United States through Florida in September 1969. He then applied for LPR status in February 2009, which was approved in July 2009 by the Obama Administration and backdated to August 2006.
This case is being prosecuted by Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael J. Nichols.
# # #
title: ICE HSI Arrests Cuban Alien for Illegally Voting in Past Elections in Missouri

Silicosis Prevention and Treatment Act would fund education, screening, and care for workers exposed to silica
ANAHEIM, Calif. – Representatives Lou Correa (CA-46) and Maxine Dexter (OR-3) introduced the Silicosis Prevention and Treatment Act, which would create a federal grant program to help healthcare facilities educate the public about silicosis and provide prevention and treatment measures for those affected.
Silicosis is entirely preventable by stopping silica dust from entering the lungs. Because there is no cure or way to reverse the lung damage it causes, prevention is vital.
"No worker should lose their ability to breathe because of the job they do to support their family," said Congressman Lou Correa. "In Anaheim's Tile Mile, workers who cut manufactured stone countertops are being diagnosed with silicosis at alarming rates. Silicosis is preventable, and early detection can save lives. This bill puts resources into the hands of the clinics and hospitals that treat these workers, so they get the care they need before it's too late."
"A paycheck should never come at the cost of your ability to breathe,” said Congresswoman Maxine Dexter, M.D. “As a pulmonologist, I know the devastating impacts of lung disease. As cases rapidly increase, it is critical that we are educating those that are most at risk for this irreversible disease. The Silicosis Prevention and Treatment Act will create funding for healthcare facilities to disseminate information and raise awareness about this progressive lung disease. We must protect the people whose hard work builds our communities."
The Silicosis Prevention and Treatment Act creates a grant program to award healthcare providers with federal funding to:
- 
Conduct outreach and education to increase awareness of silicosis
- 
Provide screening, diagnosis, and treatment of silicosis
- 
Education programs for patients, family members, and workers in industries heavily impacted by silicosis
- 
Pulmonary rehabilitation and other patient care and coordination
Background
Silica is a common mineral found in sand, quartz, and other types of rock. Exposure can cause silicosis, a disease that scars the lungs, makes breathing difficult, and can lead to irreversible complications. Approximately 2.3 million people are exposed to silica on the job, including in construction and mining.
Correa's district is home to the Tile Mile in Anaheim, where many workers cut and fabricate manufactured stone countertops, a process that releases silica dust. Orange County alone accounts for 135+ of California’s 662+ confirmed silicosis cases.
There is no cure for silicosis, but awareness and early treatment can help people identify symptoms sooner and prevent or manage lung damage.
title: CORREA INTRODUCES BILL TO PREVENT AND TREAT SILICOSIS, PROTECT WORKERS IN ORANGE COUNTY

Amo Visits Solid State Power to Highlight Ocean State Manufacturing on Blue Economy Tour
Solid State Power designs, assembles, and ships high-performance solid-state battery systems for defense, commercial, and recreational marine applications.
Pawtucket, RI – TODAY, Congressman Gabe Amo (D-RI) continued his Blue Economy tour with a stop at Solid State Power’s manufacturing facility in Pawtucket to highlight the importance of new battery technology to maritime innovation.
“Rhode Island manufacturers, like Solid State Power, are developing cutting-edge battery technology, creating good-paying jobs, and propelling our state’s Blue Economy into the future,” said Congressman Gabe Amo (D-RI). “It was an honor to meet with Solid State’s team and tour their newly expanded facility in Pawtucket. Whether making our marinas cleaner or powering submersibles exploring the deepest wells of our oceans, their team of engineers and technicians are making discovery possible and maritime battery power a sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. I will keep supporting their innovative work in Congress and fighting for federal policies so Rhode Islanders can keep building the technology fueling our Blue Economy.”
“Advanced energy systems are quickly becoming critical infrastructure for our Navy, our commercial fleets, and the autonomous platforms reshaping maritime operations. Rhode Island has the engineering talent and ocean heritage to lead in this space, and Solid State Power is proud to be building that capability in Pawtucket,” said Tom Calef, President and CEO of Solid State Power. “We appreciate Congressman Amo's leadership in making sure companies like ours have the support to grow and hire here at home.”
Background
Congressman Amo kicked off his 2026 Blue Economy Tour with a visit to REGENT Craft, where he helped cut the ribbon on their new electric Seaglider factory. Next, Amo visited Roger Williams University’s shellfish farm and research facilities. Then, Congressman Amo toured Hinckley Yachts’ expanded Portsmouth facility, highlighting the research, skilled workers, and businesses driving Rhode Island’s maritime economy.
Rhode Island’s Blue Economy directly employs 36,000 Rhode Islanders and contributes over $5 billion to the state’s gross domestic product every year.
In 2024, Congressman Amo toured Rhode Island’s First Congressional District to highlight the Ocean State’s leadership in the Blue Economy across labor, education, business, and defense.

text:
Under Section 18 of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, as amended (OCSLA; 43 U.S.C. §1344), the Secretary of the Interior must prepare and maintain forward-looking plans—typically referred to as national programs or five-year programs—that indicate proposed public oil and gas lease sales in U.S. waters. In doing so, the Secretary must balance national interests in energy supply and environmental protection. The lead agency within the Department of the Interior (DOI or Interior) responsible for the program has been the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM). Under a July 2026 order issued by the Secretary, BOEM and a sister agency are being merged into a new agency within DOI to be called the Marine Minerals Administration.
BOEM's development of a five-year program typically has taken place over two or three years, during which successive drafts of the program are published for review and comment. At the end of the process, the Secretary must submit each program to the President and to Congress for a period of at least 60 days, after which the proposal may be approved by the Secretary and may take effect with no further regulatory or legislative action. In the past, BOEM also developed a programmatic environmental impact statement (PEIS) for the leasing program under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA; 42 U.S.C. §4321). The PEIS examined the potential environmental impacts from oil and gas exploration and development on the U.S. outer continental shelf and considered a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed plan.
Congress typically has been actively involved during the planning phases of BOEM's five-year leasing programs. For example, some Members of Congress have conveyed their views on BOEM's proposals by submitting public comments on draft versions of programs during formal comment periods. Congress also has evaluated programs in committee oversight hearings. Further, although Congress does not play a direct role under the OCSLA in the approval or disapproval of a leasing program, Congress has sometimes influenced the terms of five-year programs through legislation, such as legislation to mandate or prohibit lease sales in certain offshore areas. For example, in the 119th Congress, P.L. 119-21 mandated 12 lease sales (9 for the Gulf of America region and 3 for the Alaska region) in the 2024-2029 period, in addition to the 3 sales already scheduled by the Biden Administration in its 2024-2029 leasing program.
Since 1980, 10 distinct five-year programs and a revised version of one program have been submitted to Congress. The five-year programs have reflected the offshore oil and gas leasing policies of different presidential Administrations, along with input from states, Members of Congress, and other stakeholders. Most recently, in September 2023, DOI submitted BOEM's offshore oil and gas leasing program for 2024-2029, and then-Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland issued a record of decision approving the program in December 2023. In November 2025, under the second Trump Administration, BOEM published a draft proposed program for 2026-2031 that would replace some years in the current 2024-2029 program. BOEM stated that it would not prepare a PEIS in conjunction with this program. For discussion of recent activities and issues for Congress, see CRS Report R44692, Five-Year Offshore Oil and Gas Leasing Program: Status and Issues in Brief.
Under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA), as amended,1 the Department of the Interior (DOI or Interior) must prepare and maintain forward-looking five-year plans—referred to by DOI as national programs or five-year programs—that indicate proposed public oil and gas lease sales on the U.S. outer continental shelf (OCS) over a five-year period.2 In preparing each program, DOI must balance national interests in energy supply and environmental protection.3 Since 2011, the lead agency within DOI responsible for the program has been the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM).4 In July 2026, the Secretary of the Interior directed the merger of BOEM and a sister agency, the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), in a new agency within DOI to be called the Marine Minerals Administration, which will administer offshore energy leasing along with safety and enforcement functions.5
The development of a five-year program typically takes place over two or three years, during which successive drafts of the program are published for review and comment.6 All available leasing areas are initially examined,7 and the selection may then be narrowed based on economic and environmental analysis to arrive at a final leasing schedule. At the end of the process, the Secretary of the Interior must submit each program to the President and to Congress for a period of at least 60 days, after which the proposal may be approved by the Secretary and may take effect with no further regulatory or legislative action.8
The planning process has typically included preparation of a programmatic environmental impact statement (PEIS) under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).9 The PEIS examines the potential environmental impacts from oil and gas exploration and development on the OCS and considers a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed plan. Public comments from stakeholders, including state governors, companies, individuals, and public interest organizations, are addressed in both the PEIS and the five-year program itself. For the five-year program currently in preparation—a program for the years 2026-2031 that would replace some years in the most recent (2024-2029) program—BOEM announced that the program process would not include NEPA analysis, based on judicial rulings "that found that NEPA was unripe at the National OCS Program stage."10
Because of the stages of review and comment required under the OCSLA, BOEM generally could not revise a finalized program—for example, to add new sales—without restarting the program development process.11 However, scheduled sales could potentially be cancelled (but not added) during implementation of the program, based on requirements for environmental review that are associated with each individual sale.
The leasing decisions in BOEM's five-year programs may affect the economy and environment of individual coastal states and of the nation as a whole. Accordingly, Congress often has been involved in the planning process for the five-year programs. Under the OCSLA, Congress's review of BOEM's final program does not include approval or disapproval of the program. However, Members of Congress may influence the program in other ways. Members may convey their views on the Administration's proposals by submitting public comments on draft versions of the program during formal comment periods, and they may evaluate the program in committee oversight hearings.12 More directly, Members may introduce legislation to set or alter a program's terms, such as by prohibiting or mandating specific sales. For example, in the 119th Congress, P.L. 119-21 mandated 12 lease sales (9 for the Gulf of America region and 3 for the Alaska region) in the 2024-2029 period in addition to the 3 lease sales already scheduled by the Biden Administration in its 2024-2029 leasing program.13
This report discusses the history and legal framework for DOI's five-year leasing programs, outlines the program development process, summarizes previous programs, and discusses the role of Congress. The five-year program currently in force, which was prepared during the Biden Administration and covers the years 2024-2029, was approved by then-Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland in December 2023.14 This program scheduled three lease sales for the 2024-2029 period, located in specified planning areas of the Gulf of Mexico region of the OCS. (BOEM renamed this region as the Gulf of America region in 2025, pursuant to Executive Order 14172.)15 Prior to the December 2023 approval of the 2024-2029 program, a gap occurred between leasing programs, the first prolonged gap since publication of the programs began in 1980.16 In November 2025, under the second Trump Administration, BOEM published a draft proposed program for 2026-2031.17 For further discussion of the 2026-2031 program, recent actions, and issues for Congress, see CRS Report R44692, Five-Year Offshore Oil and Gas Leasing Program: Status and Issues in Brief.
In 1953, Congress enacted two laws that addressed jurisdiction and rights off the coasts of the United States, including rights to regulation of subsurface oil and natural gas exploration and production. The first of these acts, the Submerged Lands Act,19 provides that coastal states are generally entitled to an area extending 3 geographical miles20 from their officially recognized coasts (or baselines).21 The second, the OCSLA, defined the OCS as "all submerged lands lying seaward and outside of" state coastal waters that are subject to the jurisdiction and control of the United States.22 The OCSLA has as its primary purpose "expeditious and orderly development [of OCS resources], subject to environmental safeguards, in a manner which is consistent with the maintenance of competition and other national needs."23
As offshore activities expanded in the years following adoption of the OCSLA, Congress sought a means by which to allow for expedited exploration and production in order to achieve national energy goals while also providing for environmental protection, opportunities for state and local governments affected by offshore activity to have their voices heard, and a competitive bidding and leasing process.24 The product was the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act Amendments of 1978.25 This legislation added a number of new provisions to the OCSLA, including Section 18, which mandates the creation and maintenance of an OCS leasing program to "best meet national energy needs for the five-year period following its approval or reapproval."26 These five-year programs, which include schedules for lease auctions, have provided the framework for OCS oil and gas exploration and production since the first one was adopted by DOI in 1980.
Although the 1978 amendments were the last major overhaul to the OCSLA, Congress has taken other actions since that time that have altered the scope of offshore oil and gas exploration and production. For example, the Deep Water Royalty Relief Act of 1995 attempted to encourage exploration and production in deep water by providing relief from otherwise applicable royalty payment requirements for some deepwater oil and natural gas production.27 The Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006 directed the leasing of certain regions of the Gulf of Mexico for oil and gas exploration and production and placed a moratorium on leasing in other regions.28 It also created a mechanism for sharing revenues from leasing in the region with Gulf states and the Land and Water Conservation Fund.29 Also, starting in 2008, Congress removed language from annual Interior appropriations legislation that had been in place to bar leasing and related activities in certain OCS regions.30 These legislative actions helped to shape subsequent five-year programs.
The statutory framework governing development of a five-year offshore oil and gas leasing program includes the OCSLA as well as other federal statutes, particularly NEPA and the Coastal Zone Management Act (CZMA).32
Section 18 of the OCSLA provides:
The Secretary [of the Interior] ... shall prepare and periodically revise, and maintain an oil and gas leasing program to implement the policies of this subchapter. The leasing program shall consist of a schedule of proposed lease sales indicating, as precisely as possible, the size, timing, and location of leasing activity which he determines will best meet national energy needs for the five-year period following its approval or reapproval.33
Section 18 further provides that the OCS is to be managed in a manner "which considers economic, social, and environmental values" of the resources of the OCS as well as the potential impact of oil and gas exploration on the marine, coastal, and human environments.34
Specifically, Section 18 directs the Secretary of the Interior to schedule the timing and location of oil and gas exploration and production among the regions of the OCS based on consideration of a variety of factors, including existing geographical, geological, and ecological characteristics of the regions; relative environmental and other natural resource considerations of the regions; the relative interest of oil and natural gas producers in the regions; and the laws, goals, and policies of the states that would be affected by offshore exploration and production in the region. In addition to striking this balance, leasing under the five-year program must "be conducted to assure receipt of fair market value for the lands leased and the rights conveyed by the Federal Government."35 The OCSLA also requires that the five-year program include estimates on appropriations and staffing needs.36
The OCSLA also imposes a number of consultation requirements. During preparation of the five-year program, the Secretary of the Interior must "invite and consider suggestions for such program from any interested Federal agency, including the Attorney General, in consultation with the Federal Trade Commission, and from the Governor of any State which may become an affected State under such proposed program."37 In addition to these mandatory consultation requirements, the Secretary may choose to consult with local government officials in affected states.38
Once the Secretary has satisfied these consultation and other requirements and prepared a proposed program, that program must be submitted to the governor of each affected state for further comments at least 60 days prior to publication of the proposed program in the Federal Register.39 The OCSLA also authorizes the Attorney General, in coordination with the Federal Trade Commission, to submit comments regarding potential effects of the proposed program on competition.40 At least 60 days prior to the program's approval, the Secretary must submit the proposed program to Congress and the President, along with an explanation as to why any specific recommendation of the Attorney General or a state or local government was not accepted.41 Once these steps have been completed, the Secretary is free to approve a final five-year program. The OCSLA also authorizes the Secretary to revise the five-year program at any time pursuant to a mandated review, but any revision that is "significant" must go through the process for the initial five-year program described above.42
DOI regulations applicable to preparation of the five-year program include details regarding these consultation requirements. For example, DOI is required to send letters to governors of affected states requesting that they identify specific laws, goals, and policies that they would like DOI to consider during preparation of the five-year program.43 The regulations also outline requirements for publication of the proposed program in the Federal Register.
While the OCSLA and the applicable regulations guide the five-year planning process, other federal statutes also play a role in the program's formation. Two federal statutes that have played a prominent role in the preparation of the five-year program are NEPA and the CZMA.
NEPA generally requires federal agencies to consider the environmental impacts (i.e., through an environmental review) of their actions prior to finalizing certain decisions.44 How a federal agency demonstrates compliance with NEPA depends on the level of the proposed action's impacts.45 A proposed action that has a "reasonably foreseeable significant effect on the human environment" typically requires the preparation of an environmental impact statement (EIS).46 If the proposed action does not have a reasonably foreseeable significant effect on the quality of the human environment, or if the significance of the effects is unknown, an agency typically prepares an environmental assessment (EA).47 BOEM follows DOI regulations and departmental guidance to carry out the NEPA environmental review process.48
Historically, BOEM has prepared a PEIS49 concurrently with preparation of the five-year program. However, when it published the most recent draft proposed program for 2026-2031, BOEM noted that it would not be preparing a PEIS for the program.50 The agency described past reviews as "discretionary," and cited recent judicial decisions that it described as concluding that the five-year program "does not constitute an irreversible and irretrievable commitment of resources" and that "the obligation to fully comply with NEPA does not mature until the lease sale stage."51 The agency stated that it would, instead, prepare "an environmental analysis outside of the NEPA framework to provide the relevant environmental and predictive information for different areas of the OCS as required by Section 18" of the OCSLA, as discussed above.52
Under the CZMA,54 states are encouraged to enact coastal zone management plans to coordinate protection of habitats and resources in coastal waters.55 The CZMA establishes a policy of preservation alongside sustainable use and development compatible with resource protection.56 State coastal zone management programs that are approved by the Secretary of Commerce are eligible to receive federal monetary and technical assistance. State programs must designate conservation measures and permissible uses for land and water resources,57 and must address various sources of water pollution.58
The CZMA also requires that the federal government and federally permitted activities comply with these state programs.59 To that end, the regulations governing the five-year program provide that "[i]n development of the leasing program, consideration shall be given to the coastal zone management program being developed or administered by an affected coastal State."60 The regulations require DOI to request information concerning the relationship between a state's coastal zone management program and OCS oil and gas activity from the governors of affected coastal states and the Secretary of Commerce prior to development of the leasing program.61
The development of a five-year program typically takes place over two or three years, during which three successive versions of the program proposal are published for review. The process can sometimes take longer; for the 2024-2029 program, program development spanned a six-year period over two presidential Administrations.63 Conversely, BOEM projected a shorter development period for its proposed 2026-2031 program, with an initial request for information for the program published in April 2025 and the first lease sales projected in 2026.64 The program drafts are submitted to state governors and federal agencies and, in the final stage, to Congress and the President (see discussion of consultation requirements in the "Legal Framework" section, above). The second and final program proposals have typically been released concurrently with draft and final versions of the PEIS prepared under NEPA, which also are opened to public comments (although, as described previously, BOEM is not preparing a PEIS for the 2026-2031 program). After the program takes effect, individual lease sales also undergo NEPA compliance, as do companies' exploration and development plans on leased tracts.65 Figure 1 outlines the steps from development of the five-year program to actual oil and gas production in an individual well.
Because of the analysis and review undertaken at each stage of drafting the five-year program, the successive drafts represent a winnowing process. The initial draft proposed program (DPP) examines all of the agency's available planning areas for oil and gas leasing,66 analyzing them according to factors in Section 18 of the OCSLA and considering public input, to develop an initial schedule of proposed lease sales. In subsequent versions of the program, BOEM might remove proposed sales on the basis of further analysis, but could not add new sales without reverting to an earlier stage of the process and undertaking new environmental reviews.
The steps of the process are discussed in greater detail below, with examples from the 2024-2029 program, the most recent five-year program to complete the development process. This summary refers to BOEM because it was the DOI agency that published the 2024-2029 program, but as discussed above, as of July 2026, DOI is merging BOEM and its sister agency BSEE into a new Marine Minerals Administration.
When the DPP is published, BOEM also typically has issued a notice of intent (NOI) to publish a PEIS for the proposed lease areas and has sought public input (through a scoping process) on the issues that should be analyzed in the PEIS. The NOI to prepare a PEIS for what became the 2024-2029 program (at that time planned as a 2019-2024 program) was published on January 8, 2018, along with the DPP.72 As discussed, for its proposed 2026-2031 program, BOEM announced its intent not to prepare a PEIS.73
The PP has typically been accompanied by a draft PEIS analyzing the OCS areas that were identified for leasing at the DPP stage (although BOEM has stated that the 2026-2031 program will not include a PEIS). The draft PEIS for what became the 2024-2029 program (at that time covering the 2023-2028 period) was released along with the PP, with a comment period that closed on October 6, 2022.76 BOEM received more than 750,000 comments on the PP and draft PEIS.77
Along with the PFP, BOEM typically has published a final PEIS that concludes the analysis of the areas proposed for leasing (although BOEM has stated that the 2026-2031 program will not include a PEIS). The final PEIS is submitted to the President and Congress along with the PFP. BOEM released the final PEIS for the 2017-2022 program on September 29, 2023, along with the PFP.79
Since 1980, 10 distinct five-year programs and a revised version of one program have been submitted to Congress.83 Following the 60-day review period required by the OCSLA, each of these five-year programs has taken effect as an approved program. Table 1 shows the previous submissions, dating back to 1980. The five-year programs have reflected the offshore oil and gas leasing policies of different presidential Administrations, along with input from states, Members of Congress, and other stakeholders.
Source: CRS.
Notes: OCSLA = Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
a. Acreage leased is shown in BOEM, Outer Continental Shelf Lease Sale Statistics, "All Lease Offerings," https://www.boem.gov/oil-gas-energy/leasing/outer-continental-shelf-lease-sale-statistics.
b. Lease Sale 262 for the Gulf of America, the first scheduled lease sale in the 2024-2029 program, was planned for December 10, 2025. However, after enactment of P.L. 119-21, which required semiannual lease sales for the Gulf of America in addition to those in the five-year program, BOEM deferred Lease Sale 262 and instead held the first lease sale under P.L. 119-21, titled Lease Sale BBG1, on December 10, 2025. See BOEM, "Lease Sale 262," https://www.boem.gov/oil-gas-energy/leasing/lease-sale-262. BOEM also held a second Gulf lease sale under P.L. 119-21, Lease Sale BBG2, on March 11, 2026, and a third sale, Lease Sale BBG3, on August 12, 2026, as well as a sale for Alaska's Cook Inlet under P.L. 119-21, Lease Sale BBC1, beginning on February 2, 2026 (the Cook Inlet sale was extended through March 4, 2026, but received no bids).
c. Eight sales were held under the 2017-2022 program prior to its June 30, 2022, expiration. Lease Sale 257 was vacated by a judicial order (Friends of the Earth v. Haaland,—F. 3d.—, 2022 WL 254526 (D.D.C. 2022)), and leases were not issued. Subsequent to the program's expiration, P.L. 117-169 was enacted, requiring BOEM to conduct the remaining lease sales despite the program's expiration and to issue the leases from the vacated Lease Sale 257. BOEM subsequently held the remaining three lease sales from the program in December 2022, March 2023, and December 2023.
d. The George W. Bush Administration developed the original program for 2007-2012 and submitted it to the 110th Congress with a lease schedule containing 21 sales. Following a court order in 2009, the Department of the Interior revised the program under the Obama Administration and resubmitted it to the 111th Congress with a revised lease schedule containing 16 sales.
e. This program was originally referred to as the Comprehensive Program 1980-1985, but the covered years were changed to 1980-1982 due mainly to judicial activity. California v. Watt, 688 F.2d 1290 (D.C. Cir. 1981).
Congress can influence the Administration's development of a five-year program in a number of ways. Members of Congress may convey their views on the Administration's proposals by submitting public comments on program drafts during the formal comment periods, and they may evaluate the program in committee oversight hearings. More directly, Members may introduce legislation to set or alter a program's terms. Congress also has a role under the OCSLA of reviewing each five-year program once it is finalized, but as discussed above, the OCSLA does not require that Congress directly approve the final program in order for it to be implemented.
As examples of these types of participation, this section summarizes congressional action on the 2024-2029 program, the most recent completed program. For developments related to the upcoming 2026-2031 program, see CRS Report R44692, Five-Year Offshore Oil and Gas Leasing Program: Status and Issues in Brief.
Members of Congress, along with other stakeholders such as state governors, interested agencies and organizations, and members of the public, may submit comments on draft versions of five-year programs. For the 2024-2029 program, BOEM received 12 comments from Members of Congress on its initial RFI, 49 comments from Members on the DPP, and 3 comments from Members on the PP. Some of these comments came from one or a few Members, and others had many signers (in some cases, 130 Members or more).84 Some comments opposed the inclusion of certain regions in the program, whereas others supported the proposed lease sales or sought an expansion of lease areas and a higher number of sales.85 The comments also addressed related issues such as seismic testing in the Atlantic.86
DOI takes the public comments into account when developing successive drafts of a five-year program. Each draft contains an appendix summarizing the substantive comments received on the previous version, including those from Members of Congress, and explaining the agency's response to each.87 The agency may revise the program to partially or fully adopt a suggestion, or may explain why it declined to do so.
The House or Senate may hold oversight hearings to evaluate a proposed five-year oil and gas leasing program. Such hearings help to inform Members in their legislative decisionmaking concerning the program and provide an opportunity for agency officials to hear Members' views. For example, during development of the 2024-2029 program, committees in both chambers held hearings on the program and the offshore oil and gas strategies of both the Biden and Trump Administrations.88 Members and witnesses addressed issues such as the Biden Administration's temporary pause on development of the leasing program, the optimal number of sales for the program, and economic and environmental impacts of offshore oil and gas development.
Under the OCSLA, the final version of each five-year program must be submitted to Congress for a period of 60 days before the Secretary of the Interior can approve and implement the program.89 During or outside the 60-day period, Congress could consider legislation to alter the program. Legislation could, for example, remove scheduled lease sales, add new lease sales, or make broader changes to the program. The 118th and 119th Congresses both considered legislation to alter the 2024-2029 program, and one enacted measure, P.L. 119-21, mandated 12 lease sales in the 2024-2029 period in addition to the program's 3 scheduled lease sales. Other bills in the 119th Congress include measures to change the terms of program development or to prohibit leasing consideration for certain areas.90

Mexican Citizens Charged in a Fraudulent Tax Scheme
An indictment was unsealed today in the Northern District of Georgia charging two brothers and a third man with conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud, mail fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, all arising out of a $74 million scheme to defraud the IRS through the filing of fraudulent tax returns.
The following is according to the indictment: from 2019 to the present, Gustavo Rojano Salazar, Gabriel Rojano Salazar and Andres Huerta Rendon, who all resided in the Atlanta area and were Mexican citizens, obtained Mexican identification documents in the names of third parties. They used these identification documents to obtain Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITIN) with the IRS. An ITIN was a number issued by the IRS to an individual who was required to file a federal tax return, but who did not have or was not eligible to receive a Social Security number. The three co-conspirators directed the IRS to mail the ITIN letters to post office boxes they controlled. In total, the co-conspirators obtained a significant number of Mexican Identification cards and ITIN letters, as depicted in the photo below:
Mexican Identification cards and ITIN letters
After receiving the ITIN information, the co-conspirators prepared and filed fraudulent tax returns in the names of the Mexican ITIN holders that included fabricated Forms W-2 reporting certain income and withholdings. Each of these returns resulted in refunds, which the co-conspirators directed to be mailed to the post office boxes they controlled. The co-conspirators then collected the resulting U.S. Treasury refund checks issued in the names of the Mexican ITIN holders and cashed them using a check cashing company. In total, the three co-conspirators and others cashed more than 16,000 U.S. Treasury tax refund checks worth over $74 million. Below is a photograph of cash from a photograph taken by one of the defendants:
Image of cash from a photograph taken by one of the defendants
Gustavo Rojano Salazar and Gabriel Rojano Salazar are also charged with knowingly making false statements on immigration forms submitted under penalties of perjury.
All three defendants face maximum penalties of 20 years in prison for each count of conspiracy to commit mail fraud, mail fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Gustavo Rojano Salazar and Gabriel Rojano Salazar also face a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison for each count of making false statements on immigration forms.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and United States Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg of the Northern District of Georgia made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and Homeland Security Investigations are investigating the case.
Senior Litigation Counsel Michael C. Boteler of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Kelly K. Connors of the Northern District of Georgia are prosecuting the case.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Mexican Citizens Charged in a Fraudulent Tax Scheme

text:
Today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Maliek Miller, a leader of the Ninedee Gang, a violent criminal enterprise operating out of the Louis H. Pink Houses (Pink Houses) in East New York, Brooklyn, was sentenced by United States District Judge LaShann DeArcy Hall to a mandatory sentence of life in prison. Miller was convicted in June 2024 following a jury trial of murder in-aid-of-racketeering for the murder of former federal witness Shatavia Walls in July 2020 and related crimes, including racketeering, conspiracy to commit murder in-aid-of racketeering, unlawful use and possession of firearms, being a felon in possession of ammunition and conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana.

Joseph Nocella, Jr., United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, James C. Barnacle, Jr., Assistant Director in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation, New York Field Office (FBI), and Jessica S. Tisch, Commissioner, New York City Police Department (NYPD), announced the sentence.

“It is our hope that today’s sentence brings some solace to the family of Shatavia Walls for her senseless murder,” stated United States Attorney Nocella. “For his brutal crimes of conviction, Miller will spend the rest of his life in a federal prison.”

“Today’s sentence is the product of close collaboration between the Metro Safe Streets Task Force and our partners at the NYPD and the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York to hold violent offenders accountable. While nothing can undo the loss of Shatavia Wells, this outcome ensures Miller is held fully accountable for his crimes. Dismantling violent gangs remains a priority for the FBI as we work to safeguard communities from their ruthless violence,” stated FBI Assistant Director in Charge Barnacle.

“Maliek Miller, a leader of the Ninedee Gang, orchestrated the murder of Shatavia Walls for daring to cross him,” said NYPD Commissioner Tisch. “With today’s life sentence, this defendant will never again threaten our communities, and the streets of East New York are safer because of it. I thank our investigators, partners at the FBI, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York for their work to hold this criminal. The NYPD will continue to break up violent gangs, take guns off our streets, and keep our communities safe, and cases like this are a reminder of the significance of that work.”

As proved at trial, Miller was a leader of Ninedee Gang, a violent gang affiliated with the “5” and “6” Pink Houses apartment buildings that engaged in ongoing gang-related violence within and outside of the New York City Housing Authority complex. The Ninedee Gang’s main rivalry, dating back over a decade, was against a rival gang operating in the “7” and “8” buildings in the Pink Houses. Ninedee Gang protected its turf from rival gang members through violence and sought to silence anyone perceived to be working with law enforcement. Miller and other Ninedee Gang members planned the murder of Shatavia Walls because she had previously testified at a federal criminal trial against a Ninedee member in the Eastern District of New York .

In June 2019, Walls testified for the government during United States v. Boykins , 18-CR-338 (ERK), a federal criminal trial in the Eastern District of New York. Shakeem Boykins, the defendant in that trial, was a Ninedee gang member charged with being a felon in passion of a firearm in connection with shooting Walls at the Pink Houses in 2017. Boykins was convicted at trial and sentenced to 110 months’ imprisonment. Prior to Boykins’s trial, posters were placed around the Pink Houses that stated: “Shatavia Been a Rat And She Still Ratting.” After the trial, Walls became a high-value target for the Ninedee Gang, as they held her responsible for Boykins’ incarceration.

On July 4, 2020, Walls and others were involved in a physical altercation with members of Ninedee, including Miller’s cousin, for lighting fireworks around young children. Miller went to the scene of the altercation, called Walls a “snitch,” fought with Walls and fired a shot in the air. Following the altercation, Miller agreed with other Ninedee Gang members to kill Walls and set a plan to do so in motion.

On July 7, 2020, Walls was spotted by a Ninedee Gang hit team, who chased her down a path at the Pink Houses. She was shot numerous times by Ninedee Gang members Quintin Green and Joe Santana. Ninedee Gang member Shakur Bey destroyed the clothing that Green and Santana wore during the shooting by throwing the items down an incinerator chute. Ninedee Gang member Kevin Wint, who was not present at the murder, rented a hotel room at a Best Western Hotel near John F. Kennedy International Airport to provide a place where the shooters could hide out overnight. Walls died of her injuries ten days later. After Walls died, Miller and Wint texted each other about celebrating with champagne.

Miller’s co-defendants pleaded guilty for their roles in the murder and were sentenced to terms of incarceration as follows: Green was sentenced to 420 months imprisonment; Santana was sentenced to 264 months’ imprisonment; Wint was sentenced to 110 months’ imprisonment; and Bey was sentenced to 60 months’ imprisonment.

The government’s case is being handled by Office’s Organized Crime and Gangs Section. Assistant United States Attorneys Emily J. Dean and Irisa Chen are in charge of the prosecution with the assistance of Intelligence Analyst Eungee Hwang and Intelligence Specialist Ashley Hinkson. Former Paralegal Specialist Elizabeth Reed also provided assistance with the case.

Maine Tax Preparer Pleads Guilty to Filing False Returns for Clients
A Maine man pleaded guilty on October 7, 2026, to filing false tax returns for himself and others and defrauding clients by diverting a portion of their refunds to himself without their authorization.
According to court filings and statements made in court, Thierry Musese operated a tax preparation business out of an Auburn, Maine barbershop. For the 2021 and 2022 tax years, Musese prepared tax returns for clients that reported fabricated business losses, false fuel tax credits, and improper residential energy credits. These false items generated inflated refunds that the taxpayers were not entitled to receive. Additionally, Musese defrauded clients by diverting a portion of his clients’ tax refunds to himself without their knowledge or authorization. Musese continued preparing false returns even after the IRS revoked his electronic filing credentials. During this same period, Musese also filed false personal tax returns for himself.
Musese pleaded guilty to one count of aiding and assisting in the preparation of a false tax return, one count of filing a false tax return and one count of wire fraud. Musese faces up to three years in prison for each count of aiding and assisting in the preparation of a false tax return and filing a false tax return and up to twenty years in prison for the count of wire fraud. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Andrew B. Benson for the District of Maine made the announcement. Trial Attorney Likhitha Butchireddygari of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Sean Green for the District of Maine are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Maine Tax Preparer Pleads Guilty to Filing False Returns for Clients

Tallahassee, Florida – Willard Lawrence Gibson, 48 of Seattle, Washington, was sentenced in federal court to 30 years in federal prison for one count of attempted sexual exploitation of children, one count of attempted enticement of a minor, one count of attempted transfer of obscene material to a minor, and one count of distribution of child pornography. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution and substantial prison sentence were made possible thanks to the outstanding investigative work of our state and federal law enforcement partners who are zealously pursuing sexual predators, like this defendant, wherever they lurk to keep our kids safe from exploitation and victimization. My office is firmly committed to aggressively prosecuting these horrific crimes to ensure our kids are safe both online and in our communities.”

Court documents reflect that in July 2025, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Leon County Sheriff’s Office, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations, and other state and federal law enforcement agencies conducted an undercover operation focused on identifying individuals using the internet to sexually exploit children. During that operation, the defendant began communicating through a social media platform with an undercover officer posing as a child, and the conversation later moved to text messaging. During their interactions, the defendant sent the undercover officer two images of child sexual abuse material. Further, court records show that, on multiple occasions, the defendant asked the undercover officer to produce child pornography images and send them to him. When the defendant was arrested in Seattle, his cell phone was seized as evidence and a subsequent search of the device revealed multiple child sexual abuse material images and videos. The defendant’s phone also contained other evidence confirming that he communicated with the undercover officer.

After serving his term of 30 years’ imprisonment, Gibson will have to register as a sexual offender and be on supervised release for the remainder of his life.

“Predators who use sexually explicit material to groom, manipulate, or prey on a child is committing a calculated and unforgivable abuse of that child’s trust and vulnerability,” said Homeland Security Investigations Tampa Acting Special Agent in Charge Nicholas Ingegno. “HSI and our law enforcement partners will pursue those who seek to groom, coerce, or exploit children online, bring every available investigative resource to bear, and we will work to ensure they face the full consequences of their crimes.”

This case was a joint investigation by the Leon County Sheriff’s Office, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office and Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the Seattle Police Department and the King County, Washington, Sheriff’s Office. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Eric W. Welch.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Seattle Man Sentenced to 30 Years in Federal Prison for Child Sexual Exploitation Offenses

text:
Randall, Jayapal Lead PNW Members in Demanding Answers on NWDC Contract
SEATTLE, W.A. — U.S. Representatives Emily Randall (WA-06) and Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) led Members from Washington and Oregon in demanding answers and transparency into ongoing efforts by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to purchase existing immigration detention centers currently owned and operated by private prison companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic. Currently, the GEO Group contract with the Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) is set to expire in October 2026.
Earlier this summer, ICE purchased two CoreCivic detention centers in California for $1.5 billion and facilities in Kansas and Minnesota for $734 million. Despite these facilities having been purchased by ICE, CoreCivic will continue managing operations. In October, ICE purchased three detention facilities in Adelanto, California, from GEO Group for $950 million. Similarly, GEO will continue running the facilities and says ICE is considering buying 10 facilities or more from the company.
“We are deeply concerned about the potential purchase of these facilities, as it appears to be an attempt to circumvent oversight and accountability at detention facilities. Both GEO Group and DHS have stated that acquiring these facilities is aimed, at least in part, at circumventing attempts by states to conduct oversight at immigration detention centers located within their borders,” wrote the Members.
Any attempt to dodge oversight is particularly troubling at the NWDC, as Washington State recently had to go to court to ensure access to the facility for state Department of Health officials. There is serious cause for concern if this purchase is being made to shield ICE and GEO from oversight efforts by putting the facility under federal ownership.
There are also troubling financial incentives. Under the Trump administration, GEO and CoreCivic have reaped enormous financial benefits. In 2025, both companies received an additional $2 billion in profit each, a 13 percent increase in revenue, and there has been a revolving door between the Trump administration and these companies — including border czar Tom Homan and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, who were previously employed by GEO.
“As of March 2026, the Washington State Department of Health received over 3,500 complaints about [NWDC]. Individuals have reported being sexually assaulted by an officer in their unit; unsanitary conditions, including unclean drinking water, worms, hair, and metal in food, and black mold in showers; and insufficient medical care. State oversight is an essential way to help ensure that the people detained in these facilities at U.S. taxpayer expense are being treated with dignity. Attempting to circumvent such oversight by purchasing substandard detention facilities and continuing to allow such inhumane conditions to persist is unacceptable,” continued the Members.
The full text of the letter can be found here.
The letter was also signed by Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Janelle S. Bynum (OR-05), Suzan DelBene (WA-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03), Rick Larsen (WA-02), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Kim Schrier (WA-08), Adam Smith (WA-09), and Marilyn Strickland (WA-10).
Rep. Randall recently sent a letter to U.S. Forest Chief Tom Schultz demanding transparency regarding immigration enforcement activities on U.S. Forest Service (USFS) lands. She returned to the Tacoma NW ICE Detention Center to follow up on several cases her office is assisting with, including Julián Palacios Obregon, a human and civil rights activist from Colombia who’s been held in detention since presenting himself for asylum at the Sumas, WA port of entry in December 2024. This was Randall’s 11th oversight visit to the Tacoma NW ICE Detention Center since being elected to Congress.
title: Randall, Jayapal Lead PNW Members in Demanding Answers on NWDC Contract

California Man Pleads Guilty to Sex Trafficking a Minor
Keynin McGee, 27, of Oakland, California, pleaded guilty to sex trafficking a minor in the Eastern District of California.
According to court documents, McGee met the minor victim in 2021 through Instagram. After months of speaking with her, McGee bought the victim a bus ticket for her to travel to meet him in person. When she arrived, McGee picked the victim up at the bus station, bought her clothing, and took her to a hotel. He then posted photographs of the victim online on a website commonly used to buy and sell sex. McGee then drove the victim to outdoor areas in Oakland and San Francisco known for commercial sex work and instructed her to solicit sex buyers in passing cars. Because of his conduct, the minor victim engaged in commercial sex acts with multiple buyers.
“Exploiting a child for financial gain is reprehensible and heinous,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Yesterday’s guilty plea of Keynin McGee to sex trafficking of a minor, who he lured to meet him in person then trafficked her for commercial sex in the Oakland and San Francisco areas, reflects our commitment to protecting children from the scourge of sex trafficking. The Criminal Division will continue to pursue and prosecute vile individuals who victimize and traffic minors.”
“This guilty plea illustrates the dedicated work of our law enforcement partners and prosecutors to investigate and stamp out sex trafficking and to hold traffickers accountable,” said U.S. Attorney Eric Grant for the Eastern District of California. “Protecting vulnerable victims requires sustained collaboration, thorough investigations, and a commitment to prosecute to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue working together to identify and support victims and bring to justice those who exploit them.”
“Keynin McGee reduced his young victim to a commodity to be bought and sold for his own gain,” said Special Agent in Charge Brian Tosh of FBI Sacramento. “Anyone who seeks to exploit children will face relentless pursuit from the FBI and our law enforcement partners. We will hold traffickers fully accountable for the harm they inflict. Together, we can protect the vulnerable and create a safer future for every child.”
McGee pleaded guilty to sex trafficking of a minor. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 19, 2027, and faces a minimum penalty of 10 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
The FBI is investigating the case with assistance from the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.
Deputy Chief Leah Branch of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney David Gappa for the Eastern District of California are prosecuting the case.
Anyone who has information about human trafficking should report that information to the National Human Trafficking Hotline toll-free at 1-888-373-7888, which is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For more information about human trafficking, please visit www.humantraffickinghotline.org. Information on the Justice Department’s efforts to combat human trafficking can be found at www.justice.gov/humantrafficking.
title: California Man Pleads Guilty to Sex Trafficking a Minor

TOPEKA, KAN. – Five people have been sentenced to prison after engaging in a fraudulent scheme that stole over three-quarters of a million dollars from a company that provides cash access services to casinos and online sports betting operators.

According to court documents, the following defendants pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and were sentenced to:

Jeremy Cushing, 53, of Topeka was sentenced to 95 months in prison;

Rachael Matoian, 36, of Topeka was sentenced to 38 months in prison;

Cassandra Williams, 39, of Spring Valley, California was sentenced to 12 months in prison;

Abraham Ruiz, 44, of Joplin, Missouri was sentenced to 34 months in prison; and

Leroy Noll, 46, of Newton was sentenced to 12 months in prison.

Starting approximately July 2021 and continuing until March 2024, Cushing, Williams, Ruiz, Matoian, and Noll participated in a scheme to defraud a casino and online gaming services company. After identifying customers, the members of the conspiracy would obtain personal identifying information of the customers and use it to create fake driver’s licenses. The co-conspirators would then withdraw funds from customers’ accounts. The defendants repeated this numerous times at various casinos throughout the United States.

“This case underscores how criminals can exploit stolen personal information for financial gain,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “We urge the public to safeguard their identifying information and to immediately report any unusual account activity. Working together, we can disrupt schemes like this and protect our communities from financial exploitation.”

“In a world where technology and advancement has made it easier for people to participate in gaming activities - traditional methods of fraud are still being used. This scheme used a method of fabricating official identity documents to commit wire fraud. This sentencing should be a healthy reminder to all: no matter who you try to defraud or how you try to do it, the FBI will bear all resources to seek justice and to bring closure for victims,” said Chris Ormerod, FBI Kansas City Special Agent in Charge.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Prairie Band Potawatomi Tribal Police Department, and Jackson County, Missouri Sheriff’s Office investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Lindsey Debenham prosecuted the case.

SCHNEIDER, MURPHY INTRODUCE BIPARTISAN LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE ACCESS TO MEDICAL SUPPLIES
LINCOLNSHIRE, IL — Congressman Brad Schneider (IL-10) and Congressman Greg Murphy, M.D., (NC-03) introduced the bipartisan Access to Medical Supplies Act, which would exclude urological and ostomy supplies from Medicare’s Competitive Acquisition Program for five years to protect Medicare beneficiaries who rely on them.
“Everyone deserves access to the medical supplies that will improve their quality of life and improve their well-being. Unfortunately, the new rule from CMS making ostomy and urological medical supplies part of a competitive bidding program undermines this goal,” said Schneider. “These are highly specialized prosthetics, and a sweeping rule like this should never be put in place without patient, provider, and supplier feedback. I’m proud to work with my Ways and Means colleague Dr. Murphy to introduce the bipartisan Access to Medical Supplies Act to pause this rule and ensure patients continue to receive the medical supplies they need.”
“Patients who rely on urological and ostomy supplies should not be forced to sacrifice the products that work best for them,” said Murphy. “As a physician, I know that every patient has different medical needs, and access to the right supplies can make a meaningful difference in their health and quality of life. This legislation will give patients, physicians, and policymakers time to evaluate competitive bidding and ensure that any future program protects access to the supplies patients need.”
The Access to Medical Supplies Act would:
- Exclude urological and ostomy supplies from Medicare’s Competitive Acquisition Program for five years, from January 1, 2028, through December 31, 2032.
- Establish a technical expert panel of patients, caregivers, clinicians, suppliers, manufacturers, and other stakeholders to evaluate the impact of competitive bidding and recommend changes.
- Establish a demonstration project to assess the impact of competitive bidding on patient access and health outcomes before broader implementation.
View the full bill text here.
title: SCHNEIDER, MURPHY INTRODUCE BIPARTISAN LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE ACCESS TO MEDICAL SUPPLIES

Effective Oct. 7, SPACEFOR-SOC was activated as a component field command of the U.S. Space Force. While space capabilities are already integrated into USSOCOM missions, this activation institutionalizes how the Space Force organizes, trains, equips and presents forces for the special operations enterprise, placing SPACEFOR-SOC alongside sister service SOF components: U.S. Army Special Operations Command, Naval Special Warfare Command, Air Force Special Operations Command and Marine Forces Special Operations Command.
This is the newest service component under USSOCOM, establishing a headquarters at MacDill AFB to be commanded by U.S. Space Force Col. Peter Norsky. The Space Force has previously established service components to U.S. Space Command, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, U.S. Central Command, U.S. Forces Korea, U.S. European Command and U.S. Africa Command, U.S. Forces Japan, U.S. Northern Command and U.S. Southern Command.
SPACEFOR-SOC’s presence at MacDill AFB marks another milestone in the Department of War’s ongoing effort to establish Space Force service components within combatant commands, ensuring space effects are fully operationalized across every domain of modern warfighting.
title: Space Force activates SPACEFOR-SOC as service component command to Special Operations Command

text:
Stakeholders Are Encouraged to Review Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and Submit Comments
Alexandria, VA (October 14, 2026) ― The National Credit Union Administration today announced the twelfth round of proposed regulatory changes associated with NCUA’s Deregulation Project. The project is an ongoing review of NCUA’s regulations to ensure regulations are focused on credit unions’ safety, soundness, and resilience.
With today’s announcement, NCUA is requesting comments on three proposals that would eliminate obsolete regulations, as well as unduly burdensome requirements in the Code of Federal Regulations.
The proposals include:
The Board proposes to amend 12 CFR 704 and 12 CFR 713 to simplify fidelity bond requirements for FICUs and corporate credit unions. The proposal would remove or modify certain requirements related to fidelity bond purchases and renewals, approved bond forms, and guidance on bond coverage levels.
The proposed rule would continue to require credit unions to maintain adequate fidelity bond coverage and would preserve NCUA oversight of approved bond forms. The Board believes these changes would reduce unnecessary regulatory burden while maintaining protection against fraud, dishonesty, theft, and other covered losses.
The Board proposes to clarify that FCUs may apply directly to the Board for approval of an activity that is not already recognized as an authorized incidental power. While FCUs may still seek guidance from the NCUA Office of General Counsel, the Board notes that obtaining an advisory opinion has always been optional. The proposed rule would remove language that has caused confusion about whether an advisory opinion is required before submitting an application to the Board.
The Board proposes to update 12 CFR 725 by incorporating certain regulatory changes adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic, removing outdated provisions, and simplifying CLF membership and reporting requirements. The proposal would also provide additional flexibility for capital stock subscription adjustments and make technical updates to improve clarity and consistency.
The Board believes these changes would reduce regulatory burden and modernize the CLF regulations while maintaining the CLF's role as a contingent liquidity source for credit unions.
Find a detailed summary for each proposal at https://ncua.gov/news/deregulation-project/.
To submit comments, type or paste the docket numbers into the search on the Federal Rulemaking Portal.
title: NCUA Announces Twelfth Round of Deregulation Proposals

David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that ISMAEL ROMAN, also known as “Poochie, ” 47, of Hartford, was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Sarah F. Russell in New Haven to 60 months of imprisonment and four years of supervised release for a cocaine trafficking offense and for violating the conditions of his supervised release from a prior federal conviction.

According to court documents and statements made in court, in January and February 2026, an investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Hartford Task Force revealed that Jose Colon, also known of “Uncle Benny,” was attempting to purchase several kilograms of cocaine and was in possession of a large amount of cash to complete a purchase. Investigators arranged a meeting with Colon at his residence on Pearl Street in Hartford on February 19, 2026. Prior to the meeting, investigators observed Roman, who was carrying a backpack, and an associate enter Colon’s apartment. Colon, Roman, and their associate were arrested a short time later after a court-authorized search of the residence revealed approximately $52,000 in cash, which had been concealed in a small cooler within the backpack.

Roman has been detained since his arrest. On June 1, 2026, he pleaded guilty to attempting to possess with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of cocaine.

In October 2022, Roman was sentenced in Hartford federal court to 41 months of imprisonment for a cocaine trafficking offense and he was on federal supervised release at the time of his arrest in this case.

Colon pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.

This investigation is being conducted by the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Hartford Task Force, which includes personnel from the DEA Hartford Resident Office, the Connecticut State Police, and the Bristol, Hartford, East Hartford, Enfield, Manchester, New Britain, Rocky Hill, Wethersfield, and Windsor Locks Police Departments. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Reed Durham.

Support Grows For Stop The Settlements Act, Bill To Impose Sanctions On Drivers Of Settlement Expansion
WASHINGTON, DC — Support continues to grow for Reps. Joaquin Castro’s (TX-20), Stop the Settlements Act. Castro introduced the legislation with Reps. Madeleine Dean (PA-04), Don Beyer (VA-08), Greg Casar (TX-35), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), and Veronica Escobar (TX-16). The bill now has 53 co-sponsors since its introduction on October 1, with the addition of Hank Johnson (GA-04), Everton Blair (GA-13), Maxine Waters (CA-43), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Nikema Williams (GA-05), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-AL), LaMonica McIver (NJ-10), Bill Foster (IL-11), James Walkinshaw (VA-11), and Valerie P. Foushee (NC-04).
“The Stop the Settlements Act would sanction anyone looking to take Palestinian land in the West Bank or Gaza,” said Congressman Castro. “And support keeps growing. Since I introduced the bill alongside Reps. Dean, Beyer, Casar, Jacobs, and Escobar, over 50 members have now co-sponsored. Settlement expansion pushes Palestinians off their land and makes peace harder to achieve. It’s time to use tools like sanctions to stop it.”
The Stop the Settlements Act would halt the construction of new settlements and the expansion of existing Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza through sanctions and a prohibition on importing goods made in these settlements and outposts. Ending settlement construction and expansion would protect Palestinians from the dispossession of their land and help create a pathway to peace, where both Israelis and Palestinians are able to fully exercise their right to self-determination. To learn more about the bill, click here.
