MACON, Ga. – A defendant who helped obtain and distribute large amounts of methamphetamine from Atlanta for distribution in Milledgeville, Georgia, was sentenced to prison following an Operation Take Back America investigation led by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Baldwin County Sheriff’s Office.

“This drug trafficking organization funneled methamphetamine into Milledgeville, endangering people and undermining the safety of the entire community,” said U.S. Attorney William R. “Will” Keyes. “We are grateful to our law enforcement partners for their tireless efforts and dedication to protecting our neighborhoods.”

“This case demonstrates what can be accomplished when law enforcement agencies work together toward a common goal,” said Michael J. Connolly, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Atlanta Field Division. “Through collaboration, information sharing, and a coordinated investigative approach, we can identify those responsible for distributing dangerous drugs and dismantle the networks that threaten our communities. These partnerships remain essential to our mission of disrupting drug trafficking and holding offenders accountable.”

Cory Wilson, 41, of Milledgeville, was sentenced to serve 120 months in prison followed by five years of supervised release on October 14, after he previously pleaded guilty to one count of distribution of methamphetamine on July 20.

The following codefendants previously pleaded guilty, and most have been sentenced:

Ruby Fogg, 39, of Austell, Georgia, was sentenced to serve 324 months in prison followed by 10 years of supervised release on June 10, after she previously pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute methamphetamine on January 21.

Robert Matthew Wood, 43, of Marietta, Georgia, was sentenced to serve 262 months in prison followed by 10 years of supervised release on June 10, after he previously pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine on Dec. 17, 2025.

Desmond Glenn, 35, of Milledgeville, was sentenced to serve 260 months in prison followed by 10 years of supervised release on August 12, after he previously pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute methamphetamine and one count of possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime on February 17.

Tony Baker, 39, of Macon, was sentenced to serve 92 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release on June 10, after he previously pleaded guilty to one count of convicted felon in possession of a firearm on Dec. 17, 2025.

Katherine Short-Barcenas, 36, of Milledgeville, was sentenced to serve 48 months in prison followed by five years of supervised release on August 12, after she previously pleaded guilty to one count of distribution of methamphetamine on Dec. 17, 2025.

Rodney May, 38, of Milledgeville, Georgia, pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine on Dec. 17, 2025, and faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years in prison up to a maximum of life in prison followed by 10 years of supervised release and a maximum $20 million fine. Sentencing is scheduled for May 12, 2027.

U.S. District Judge Marc T. Treadwell is presiding over the case. There is no parole in the federal system.

According to court documents and statements made in court, federal agents began investigating a group of individuals distributing methamphetamine in the Baldwin County, Georgia, area in early 2023. Between April 25, 2023, and July 31, 2023, agents conducted four separate controlled purchases from Glenn totaling approximately 162 grams of methamphetamine. Under surveillance, Glenn was recorded selling methamphetamine and other controlled substances to people in Baldwin County as well as obtaining large amounts of methamphetamine from several sources of supply, including Fogg, who was the leader of the criminal network. Short-Barcenas and Wilson, members of this drug trafficking ring, sold methamphetamine twice to a confidential source in early March 2023, as part of this investigation.

Fogg was working closely with Wood to obtain and distribute large amounts of methamphetamine. Fogg and Wood often rented hotel rooms in Atlanta where they stored and sold narcotics. On Nov. 14, 2023, Fogg directed Glenn to pick up methamphetamine from Wood at an Atlanta area hotel, while she was traveling to deliver drug proceeds to Jackson, Georgia. May and Baker traveled with Glenn to the Atlanta hotel; on the return trip, their vehicle was stopped by law enforcement, and nearly one kilo of methamphetamine was found in a bag, along with a smaller amount on the floorboard. Officers also found a firearm tucked between Glenn’s seat and the center console, and another firearm in the backseat. A search warrant was executed at Glenn’s Milledgeville home, where officers found an additional 64.68 grams of methamphetamine and five firearms in his bedroom. Glenn was previously convicted of robbery by force in Baldwin County, Georgia. It is illegal for a convicted felon to possess a firearm.

Two days later, on Nov. 16, 2023, Fogg and Wood were arrested; the hotel they were renting was searched, and an additional 154.97 grams of methamphetamine was located, along with drug paraphernalia. Fogg has three prior criminal felony methamphetamine distribution convictions in Douglas County, Georgia, Superior Court.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. The DEA and the Baldwin County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Howard is prosecuting the case for the Government.
title: Member of Milledgeville Methamphetamine Trafficking Organization Sentenced

Congresswoman Scholten Introduces Legislation to Expand Conservation Efforts, Federal Funding Opportunities for Great Lakes Region
WASHINGTON, DC – This week, Representatives Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03), Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Tim Walberg (R-MI-05), Marcy Kaptur (D-OH-09), Bill Huizenga (R-MI-04), David Joyce (R-OH-14), Haley Stevens (D-MI-11) and Tom Barrett (R-MI-07) introduced the Regional Great Lakes Partnership Act. The bipartisan, bicameral bill would expand access to federal support for the Great Lakes region, including for conservation research and programs.
“As the largest freshwater system in the world, the Great Lakes are one of Michigan’s greatest assets,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “I’m proud to join my colleagues on both sides of the aisle in supporting the Regional Great Lakes Partnership Act. This commonsense bill will strengthen the research and coordination that keeps the Great Lakes region healthy. Investing in our Great Lakes is investing in our future, and it’s crucial that we conserve this resource for the next generation.”
“The Great Lakes and their connected waterways are invaluable resources for Michigan and the United States,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “As a Co-Chair of the Congressional Great Lakes Task Force, I am proud to help introduce this bipartisan bill to strengthen federal support for Great Lakes research and conservation for future generations to enjoy these national treasures.”
“Michigan is the Great Lakes state, period. Jobs, recreation, and tourism across the Midwest depend on a healthy and flourishing Great Lakes ecosystem,” said Congresswoman Stevens. “I’m proud to work alongside my colleagues of both parties to ensure that Michigan receives our fair share of federal investment that will protect and preserve our Lakes for generations to come.”
“The Great Lakes are a critical resource for the economies and communities that surround them,” said Congressman Joyce. “As Co-Chair of the Congressional Great Lakes Task Force, I am proud to be an original co-sponsor of this bipartisan legislation, which will strengthen federal partnerships and expand funding opportunities to advance the research, coordination, and conservation efforts needed to protect the Great Lakes — ensuring they remain a resource our communities can rely on for generations to come.”
“As the largest freshwater system in the world, the Great Lakes are central to Michigan’s economy, identity, and long‑term prosperity,” said Congressman Walberg. “The bipartisan Regional Great Lakes Partnership Act ensures the region receives its fair share of federal support, strengthening the research and conservation work needed to protect this indispensable resource. We must equip our partners with the tools necessary to safeguard the waters and communities that rely on a healthy Great Lakes ecosystem.”
“As a Co-Chair of the bipartisan Congressional Great Lakes Task Force, I helped introduce this legislation to close a gap in a national program that benefits only coastal ocean states. The bill continues our work together to ensure the federal government levels the playing field to commit equivalent, well‑deserved resources to our Great Lakes region,” said Congresswoman Kaptur. “The Great Lakes are central and essential to Northwest Ohio’s livelihood and economic well-being, and enabling the Great Lakes Commission to participate in this NOAA program will strengthen data sharing, enhance information access, and improve management of our coastal and ecosystem resources. In Lake Erie’s Western Basin, home to the shallowest and southernmost shoreline in the Great Lakes system, we face these challenges in real ways and will continue to lead in advancing research and information exchange for the benefit of our entire region.”
“As Co-Chair of the bipartisan Congressional Great Lakes Task Force, I have made it my mission to have the federal government recognize the Great Lakes as a national priority,” said Congressman Huizenga. “The Regional Great Lakes Partnership Act furthers this objective by enhancing the Great Lakes Commission’s steadfast work to protect and conserve Michigan’s most valuable natural resource.”
“Protecting the Great Lakes means protecting our water, wildlife, and communities throughout the region,” said Congressman Barrett. “This bipartisan legislation will help bring federal resources to the table and strengthen the partnerships already working to preserve our state’s natural resources. I’m proud to work with colleagues from across the region to ensure our Great Lakes remain healthy for generations to come.”
This legislation would designate the Great Lakes Commission (GLC) as the official regional Great Lakes Partnership within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Regional Ocean Partnerships Program. This designation would expand opportunities for the Great Lakes region to access existing federal funding, supporting the Great Lakes Commission’s longstanding work to coordinate research, conservation, and restoration efforts across the region.
The Great Lakes Commission (GLC) brings together eight U.S. states and two Canadian provinces to protect the Great Lakes and promote economic growth in the Great Lakes basin. The GLC is composed of the states of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin.
NOAA’s Regional Ocean Partnerships (ROPs) coordinate interstate ocean and coastal resource management efforts and create opportunities for increased efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Although NOAA administers four Regional Ocean Partnerships (ROPs) across the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Gulf, and West Coast, the Great Lakes currently lack an ROP. Designating the GLC as the region’s ROP will ensure the Great Lakes region receives its fair share of program funding.
Companion legislation, introduced in the Senate by U.S. Senators Gary Peters (D-MI) and Bernie Moreno (R-OH), has been advanced by the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
Read the full text of the billhere.

text:
On February 27, 2026, President Trump directed federal agencies to stop using technology from U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, and Secretary of Defense Hegseth announced that he was directing the Department of Defense (DOD) to designate Anthropic a "Supply-Chain Risk to National Security." (DOD and the Secretary are now using "Department of War" and "Secretary of War" as "secondary" designations per Executive Order 14347.) These actions followed a reported months-long dispute between DOD and Anthropic regarding certain uses of its AI technologies. On June 12, 2026, the Department of Commerce (DOC) reportedly imposed export controls on certain AI models—Mythos 5 and Fable 5—from Anthropic's Claude family of models. The export controls were lifted on June 30, 2026. The risk designation, use prohibitions, and export control restrictions may have implications for AI innovation and competition, including at Anthropic and other domestic AI companies. This In Focus provides information on the AI models under debate, U.S. government (USG) actions and their potential implications, and considerations for Congress.
Frontier AI models are the most advanced foundation models—general-purpose AI models pretrained on large datasets that can be used for many applications. Anthropic's Claude models, including several frontier models, have reportedly been deployed across DOD and national security agencies for such applications as intelligence analysis, operational planning, and cyber operations. In June 2024, Anthropic stated that it was the first AI company to deploy frontier models in classified USG networks. In July 2025, four U.S. AI companies, including Anthropic, entered into contracts of up to $200 million each with DOD to "accelerate [DOD] adoption of advanced AI capabilities to address critical national security challenges." In classified DOD systems, the Pentagon agreed to the use of AI models and services from xAI, Google, and six other tech companies as of May 1, 2026. Anthropic was not included.
In February 2026, Anthropic claimed that it requested two use exceptions for its Claude models during contract negotiations with DOD. First, Anthropic stated that it "do[es] not believe that today's frontier AI models are reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons. Allowing current models to be used in this way would endanger America's warfighters and civilians." Second, Anthropic asserted that "mass domestic surveillance of Americans constitutes a violation of fundamental rights."
Anthropic's requested use exceptions highlight a broader debate over frontier AI model capabilities and limitations. Though frontier AI models demonstrate powerful capabilities, as measured by publicly available benchmarks and assessments, some studies have described their potential limitations, particularly regarding safety risks. A December 2025 Frontier AI Trends Report by the UK's AI Security Institute reported that, in its evaluations of frontier AI systems across domains critical to national security and public safety, model safeguards are improving, but the institute found "vulnerabilities in every system [it] tested."
Anthropic released Mythos Preview to about 50 partners in April 2026 through a collaborative called Project Glasswing. Per Anthropic, the company limited availability because of the model's advanced capability to find and exploit software vulnerabilities. On June 9, 2026, Anthropic released Mythos 5 for "a small group of cyberdefenders and infrastructure providers" via Project Glasswing, "in collaboration with the [USG]," and Fable 5, a "Mythos-class model … made safe for general use," to the public. As mentioned, DOC subsequently imposed and lifted export control restrictions on these products in June 2026.
On February 27, 2026, President Trump directed federal agencies to "IMMEDIATELY CEASE all use of Anthropic's technology" and outlined a six-month "phase out period for Agencies like [DOD] who are using Anthropic's products, at various levels." That same day, Secretary Hegseth announced the designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk to national security, stating, "no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic." DOD made designations under two distinct statutes: 10 U.S.C. §3252 and 41 U.S.C. §4713. Federal agencies took actions to stop using Anthropic's models. For example, the General Services Administration (GSA) announced that it was removing Anthropic from USAi.gov and its multiple award schedule (i.e., long-term government-wide contracts with commercial firms).
On June 12, 2026, DOC required Anthropic to restrict Mythos 5 and Fable 5 access to "any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States." In response, Anthropic disabled access to both models for all customers. This followed Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026, which directed the establishment of a voluntary framework to facilitate USG-industry evaluation of frontier AI models. On June 30, 2026, DOC lifted export control restrictions, and Anthropic then redeployed Mythos 5 and Fable 5.
Some information suggests that USG actions might not have a significant financial effect on Anthropic. The $200 million awarded by DOD and an $18,960 award from the Department of State in 2026 (the only government contract with Anthropic on USAspending.gov) are relatively small compared to the company's run-rate revenue (i.e., annual revenue estimate based on its current financial performance). On February 12, 2026, Anthropic stated that its run-rate revenue had reached $14 billion, and on May 28, 2026, Anthropic announced that its run-rate revenue had surpassed $47 billion earlier in the month. On June 1, 2026, Anthropic filed documents for a proposed initial public offering.
Anthropic has stated that USG actions are "harming Anthropic irreparably." If Anthropic were to lose a significant share of its revenue or funding from investors, it might have difficulty continuing to develop its AI models, potentially affecting its ability to compete and innovate. The effect of USG actions on Anthropic may partially depend on the response of its clients. For example, after Secretary Hegseth's February 27, 2026, actions, some initial reporting indicated that a subset of defense contractors stopped using Anthropic's AI models, while others were waiting to see how the conflict resolved. Anthropic has argued that DOD's designation of it as a supply chain risk is illegal and that DOD should not prohibit contractor use of Claude outside of DOD contracts.
On March 9, 2026, Anthropic filed two federal lawsuits against the USG. In one, filed in a federal district court in California, Anthropic argues that the government's actions, including DOD's supply chain risk designation under 10 U.S.C. §3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and the First and Fifth Amendments. The second lawsuit, filed with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (D.C. Circuit), challenges the legality of DOD's designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk under 41 U.S.C. §4713 and order to remove all Anthropic products from DOD's systems. On March 26, 2026, a federal judge in the first suit granted Anthropic's motion for a preliminary injunction and temporarily blocked the implementation of this designation and the President's directive ordering federal agencies to stop using Claude. In response, GSA restored Anthropic on USAi.gov and its multiple award schedule. On August 27, 2026, the same judge vacated and permanently enjoined enforcement of the Section 3252 designation and Secretary Hegseth's directive that other defense contractors stop doing business with Anthropic on the grounds that DOD violated Anthropic's First and Fifth Amendment rights and the APA. In the second suit, on September 25, 2026, the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic's challenge, upholding DOD's supply chain risk designation under Section 4713. As a result, DOD may continue to enforce its directive to remove all Anthropic products from DOD systems, barring additional court action.
USG actions against Anthropic might have broader effects on AI markets and competition. For example, if USG actions negatively impact Anthropic's revenues and thereby its ability to develop frontier models, that would reduce the number of innovative AI models that other companies could use to create AI products. However, USG actions also appear to have contributed to a boost in public adoption of Claude, which became the most popular app on Apple's top free apps in the United States on February 28, 2026. Separately, OpenAI's decision to strike a deal with the Pentagon reportedly resulted in public backlash as users uninstalled ChatGPT.
USG actions against Anthropic have also raised concerns about potential effects on innovation and U.S. competitiveness. Some trade groups reportedly raised concerns that designating an American technology company as a national security risk would "have a chilling effect on U.S. innovation." A letter reportedly sent by former defense officials, academics, and tech policy leaders to congressional committees asserted that "blacklisting an American company weakens U.S. competitiveness" and warned that "this is 'not a marketplace any serious entrepreneur or investor can build around.'" The sudden inability to use Mythos 5 and Fable 5 reportedly renewed efforts in other countries to lessen their reliance on American technology. Further, while some analysts have noted that the DOC export controls were aimed at preventing national security risks from possible access to Mythos by the Chinese government, others have voiced concern that the process leading to DOC's reversal of the restrictions was opaque and "will not lend itself well to a stable, investable, trustworthy industry over time."
Federal policies and actions may influence competition among AI companies and potentially encourage or stifle innovation. Congress may conduct oversight on the extent of DOD's authority to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk to national security and how such actions may affect private sector innovation. Congress may also consider legislation to clarify safety and security considerations around the use of AI technologies for sensitive applications, such as public surveillance, and to establish an AI regulatory approach that balances safety, national security, and innovation. Alternatively, Congress may wait to see if the USG and Anthropic reach an agreement or if there is additional legal action. In weighing these options, among others, Congress might consider a range of questions, including these:
title: Federal Government and Anthropic: Considerations for AI Innovation and Competition

Seattle – A 30-year-old Bellingham, Washington resident, James Cody Bryant, was indicted today by a grand jury sitting in the Western District of Washington for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country for Bryant’s role in a February 10, 2026, school shooting in British Columbia, Canada. Bryant was in frequent communication with Tumbler Ridge school shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar in the six months leading up to the school shooting that killed six people and seriously injured others. Bryant is scheduled for arraignment on October 22, 2026.

The indictment details several overt acts that Bryant took to further the school shooting conspiracy:

As early as August 2025 Bryant agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet;

In August 2025, Bryant tested the quality of the live stream and confirmed it looked “solid;”

At various times Bryant offered the shooter advice on where to attack and what weapons to carry.

In January 2026, Bryant again tested the livestream and told Van Rootselaar it worked;

In late January Bryant sent Van Rootselaar money via pay pal to purchase a lighter for use in an improvised explosive device;

On the day of the murders Bryant confirmed the livestream was visible, and later that the livestream had gone down.

On various occasions Bryant made clear the planning of the attack was illegal, discussing ways they should conceal their communications or the source of the livestream.

According to the RCMP, Van Rootselaar was born a male. Van Rootselaar had been transitioning and identified as female on official government identification and on law enforcement reports.

On February 10, 2026, Jesse Van Rootselaar killed two relatives and then drove to the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where Van Rootselaar shot and killed five children ages 12 and 13 and killed an educational assistant. Van Rootselaar used an improvised explosive device to damage the school and tried to get into other classrooms by firing through locked doors. Van Rootselaar exchanged gunfire with police and ultimately committed suicide.

According to records filed in the case, shortly after the shooting, law enforcement learned Van Rootselaar had been in frequent communication with someone via the platform Discord. That person was identified as Bryant. Law enforcement has obtained and reviewed thousands of communications between the two.

Conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country is punishable by up to life in prison.

The charges contained in the indictment are only allegations. A person is presumed innocent unless and until he or she is proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

The case is being investigated by the FBI with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Todd Greenberg with assistance from the Justice Department’s National Security Division.
title: Bellingham, Washington, resident indicted for conspiracy to murder people in a foreign country for role in BC school shooting

DOJ’s Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI Expose More than $490M in Tax Fraud in National Tax Enforcement Surge
The Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division), along with the Internal Revenue Service, Criminal Investigation, today announced a nationwide series of enforcement actions targeting tax fraud.
Between early September and today, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490,000,000.
“Every dollar stolen through tax fraud is a dollar taken from the American people,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “What we uncovered during this concentrated surge is only the tip of the iceberg. The Department of Justice is committed to expanding our investigations and exposing schemes designed to evade accountability, because there is no safe haven for fraudsters.”
“The Fraud Division is resolved to protect American taxpayers from criminal actors on every frontier of fraud, including tax fraudsters seeking to steal the wealth of America,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “Over six weeks, the Fraud Division’s Tax Section, 35 U.S. Attorneys' Offices, and IRS Criminal Investigation took action against over 70 defendants who sought more than $490 million from the Treasury. Today’s results send a clear message to fraudsters: those who intentionally lie to steal the money of the American people should expect to answer for their conduct in federal court.”
“This enforcement surge delivered results for taxpayers,” said IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are working across government to go after fraud, hold bad actors accountable, and protect the integrity of our nation’s tax system.”
“If there was ever any question whether criminal tax enforcement remains a priority, today’s actions should dispel all doubt. These cases send an unmistakable message that individuals and businesses who deliberately cheat the tax system will be held accountable,” said Jarod Koopman, Chief of IRS Criminal Investigation and Chief Tax Compliance Officer. “The investigations announced today involve hundreds of millions in identified tax losses to the United States, funds that should have supported the programs and services Americans depend on every day. When taxpayers evade their legal obligations, the burden does not disappear, it is shifted to law-abiding Americans.”
The Department’s prosecutors returned 23 actions with new charges against 31 defendants. The estimated intended loss to the public fisc arising from the allegations against these defendants exceeds approximately $350,000,000. In addition to returning these new charges, the Fraud Division’s Tax Section and the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices partook in around 39 other enforcement actions — trials, guilty pleas, and sentencings. These events affected another 45 defendants whose actions produced an estimated intended loss of nearly $140,000,000.
National Tax Enforcement Surge Map
Notable Cases
1) United States v. Martin Navarrete (Indictment) – $2,800,000 – District of Maryland
According to the indictment, Navarrete, who served as sole owner and sole corporate officer of Navarrete Brothers Construction Inc. (NBC), exercised significant control and authority over NBC’s finances. Among his responsibilities, Navarrete was tasked with collecting trust-fund taxes, accounting for employment taxes by filing Forms 941 with the IRS and paying the IRS the trust-fund taxes for NBC’s employees.
From September 2020 through December 2025, Navarrete allegedly willfully failed to truthfully account for and pay over the trust-fund taxes owed to the IRS on behalf of NBC’s employees. Additionally, Navarrete willfully failed to file U.S. Corporate Income Tax Return and Individual Tax Return forms for calendar years 2020–2024.
2) United States v. Sherita Booker (Information) – $11,806,165 – Northern District of Ohio
On Sept. 30, Sherita Booker, of Cleveland, was charged with aiding or assisting in the preparation of false and fraudulent federal income tax returns. She allegedly prepared false returns and obtained large, fraudulent refunds for hundreds of clients, primarily using three programs: (1) COVID-19 sick leave credits for non-existent businesses and employees; (2) Refunds of purported fuel taxes paid for off-road (farm) use; and (3) Claims for refunds of taxes purportedly overpaid in previous years.
3) United States v. Marty Allen Linville (Sentencing) – $2,595,679 – Western District of Arkansas
Since at least 2010, Marty Allen Linville, age 58, owned and operated Malco Inc., a trucking business located in De Queen, Arkansas, where he had employees and paid them wages. Linville provided his employees with Forms W-2 that reported withholdings paid to the IRS on their behalf. However, Linville did not separately file the Forms W-2 with the Social Security Administration or make the required tax deposits. More than one employee reported to Linville that their tax return refunds were frozen because no Form W-2 was on file with the IRS. Linville pled guilty to 2 counts of Willful Failure to Account for and Pay Over Trust Fund Taxes. Linville was sentenced to 20 months imprisonment and ordered to pay restitution, including penalties and interest, in the amount of $3.8 million.
4) United States vs. Duncan John MacDonald, Sarah Duren, Richard Ronald Cayce, and Thomas Weickgenant (Indictment) – $200,000,000 – Northern District of Texas
Four Texas residents charged with conspiracy to defraud the United States and other crimes for promoting an illegal tax shelter. According to the indictment, the defendants promoted and sold a fraudulent trust scheme that was used to shelter more than $1.5 billion of income, causing an estimated tax loss to the IRS of more than $200 million. The defendants allegedly sold clients the tax shelter for fees that often exceeded $100,000 by fraudulently telling clients that they could assign their income to sham trusts to defer paying taxes in perpetuity, all while continuing to enjoy the benefit and control over their assets and income. The defendants also allegedly encouraged some clients to backdate their trusts and file amended income tax returns claiming refunds for prior years’ taxes.
5) United States v. Ephantus Mwangi (Sentencing) – $1,500,000 – District of Kansas
A Kenyan national and Missouri businessman was sentenced to 51 months in prison for willfully failing to pay over employment taxes to the IRS on behalf of the credit-card processing services companies he owned and operated. During this time, he spent more than $200,000 on loan payments for various luxury vehicles, including a Hummer H2, a Cadillac Escalade, two Range Rovers, two Mercedes, and a Lexus. He also willfully failed to file individual income tax returns for the years 2017 and 2020, and he filed 2018 and 2019 individual income tax returns after the deadline had passed.
6) United States v. Nelai Mitchell (Sentencing) – $13,800,000 – Eastern District of North Carolina
Nejlai Mitchell, an owner of a North Carolina tax return preparation business was sentenced to 60 months in prison for conspiring to prepare false returns claiming fraudulent refunds based on COVID-19 tax credits. From approximately April 2022 through May 2023, Mitchell and seven employees filed false tax returns seeking fraudulent refunds based on the paid sick and family leave credit, a credit passed by Congress to aid struggling businesses during the COVID-19 global pandemic. The conspiracy resulted in a total of approximately $23.9 million in fraudulent tax refund claims. The IRS paid out approximately $13,890,697 of that amount.
Five other return preparers were sentenced for their roles in the scheme. On Sept. 3, Tiffany Moody was sentenced to 26 months in prison. On July 8, Shaneen Ray was sentenced to 18 months in prison, Eyoubo McBurney was sentenced to 18 months in prison, and Sylvia Swindell was sentenced to 16 months in prison. On July 9, Katrena Stanback was sentenced to six months in prison.
7) United States v. Gustavo Rojano Salazar, Gabriel Rojano Salazar, and Andres Huerta Rendon (Indictment) – $74,000,000 – Northern District of Georgia
Two brothers and a third man were charged with conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud, mail fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, all arising out of a $74 million scheme to defraud the IRS through the filing of fraudulent tax returns. According to the indictment, the three men, who are Mexican citizens, obtained Mexican identification documents in the names of third parties. They used these identification documents to obtain Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITIN) with the IRS used by an individual who was required to file a federal tax return, but who did not have or was not eligible to receive a Social Security number. After receiving the ITIN information, the co-conspirators prepared and filed fraudulent tax returns in the names of the Mexican ITIN holders. Each of these returns resulted in refunds, which the co-conspirators directed to be mailed to post office boxes they controlled. The co-conspirators then collected the resulting U.S. Treasury refund checks issued in the names of the Mexican ITIN holders and cashed them using a check cashing company. In total, the three co-conspirators and others cashed more than 16,000 U.S. Treasury tax refund checks worth over $74 million.
8) United States v. Pedro Cabrajal (Indictment) - $4,900,000 – District of New Jersey
New Jersey man charged with willful failure to account for and pay over employment taxes, tax evasion and willful failure to file income tax returns. According to the indictment, from 2012 to 2020, Pedro Carbajal, of Sparta, New Jersey, operated Option Staffing Services LLC, an employee-leasing business that was nominally owned by another individual. During this period, Carbajal allegedly did not file quarterly employment tax returns with the IRS or pay the required trust fund and unemployment taxes on behalf of his company’s employees. Carbajal allegedly failed to pay over a total of approximately $4.9 million in taxes to the IRS.
9) United States v. Jose Da Costa Gomez (Indictment) – No public loss announced – Southern District of Florida
Business owner charged with conspiracy to defraud the United States, filing false tax returns with the IRS, wire fraud conspiracy and wire fraud. According to the indictment, Da Costa Gomez was the owner of a series of businesses Da Costa Gomez and his family members allegedly used the companies’ funds to pay tens of millions of dollars of personal expenses and failed to report those payments as income to the Internal Revenue Service. Da Costa Gomez and others also allegedly evaded Florida sales and use taxes on purchases by having items shipped out of Florida and then surreptitiously bringing them back to the state or submitting false resale certificates to sellers.
10) United States v. John Labee (Indictment) – $6,900,000 – Western District of Texas
Defendant charged with conspiring to file false claims and filing false claims. From approximately October 2021 through July 2022, Labee and co-conspirator Andrea Dotson allegedly agreed to have Labee prepare and file false tax returns on behalf of Dotson’s business, Divine Grinde. Although Divine Grinde had minimal operations and no employees, Labee and Dotson allegedly conspired to file nine false tax returns that falsely claimed the Employee Retention Credit and the Sick and Family Leave Credit based on completely fabricated wage and tax figures. Dotson previously pleaded guilty on March 10, 2026, for her role in the offense. In total, Labee and Dotson’s fraudulent claims sought refunds of approximately $6.9 million, of which the IRS paid over $1.1 million. Dotson kept a portion of the tax refunds for herself and allegedly provided the remainder to Labee.
11) United States v. Pacifique Kashosi (Trial) – Loss to be determined at sentencing – District of Arizona
Phoenix tax preparer convicted at trial for aiding and assisting in the filing of false tax returns and filing false personal income tax returns. Kashosi prepared false tax returns for his clients that reported false Covid tax credits, false fuel credits and false business losses. The false tax returns claimed thousands of dollars in fraudulent refunds. In cases like this one, the intended loss is often millions of dollars and can result in significant prison time.
12) United States v. Marquis Al Bey (Guilty Plea) – $35,000,000 – District of Maryland
Marquis Al Bey, of Forney, Texas, pleaded guilty on Sept. 17, for his role in a tax refund fraud conspiracy that sought to obtain more than $35 million in fraudulent refunds through the filing of false tax returns. Bey prepared tax returns for clients, including clients located in Maryland, that sought large tax refunds that the individuals and entities listed on the returns were not entitled to receive. Bey charged clients for his tax return preparation services and, in some cases, required that clients agree to pay him a percentage of any resulting refund. As part of his plea, Bey admitted to preparing seven false returns between 2017 and 2021 for his co-defendant and another individual in Maryland that collectively sought more than $35 million from the Internal Revenue Service. Two of those returns resulted in the IRS issuing refunds totaling more than $10 million to Bey’s clients.
13) United States v. LaMar Dazjar Burgess and LaMar Javis Burgess (Guilty Pleas) – $9,200,000 – District of Minnesota
Father and son, LaMar Javis Burgess and son LaMar Dazjar Burgess, participated in a scheme to fraudulently obtain tax refunds by filing false income tax returns based primarily on COVID-related sick and family leave credits, fuel tax credits, and false withholdings. For tax years 2022 and 2023 Javis and his son prepared and/or filed at least 300 false income tax returns claiming at least $9.2 million in fraudulent refunds.
14) United States v. Ronald Chrichlow and Gordon Chrichlow (Guilty Pleas) – $978,126 and $1,643,172 – District of New Jersey
Two brothers plead guilty to stealing more than $978,126 and $1,643,172, respectively, in tax refunds. Ronald Chrichlow and Gordon Chrichlow both filed a false 2022 Form 1041, U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts, on behalf of their trusts. These Forms 1041 falsely reported that the trusts made tax payments to the IRS when they had not and claimed refunds as a result. In response to IRS collection efforts, the Chrichlow brothers mailed forms to the IRS on which they falsely claimed not to be residents of the United States and falsely claimed that their 2022 income was tax exempt pursuant to a tax treaty. The Chrichlow brothers also failed to file their personal income tax returns in some years, despite earning income and being legally obligated to file.
15) United States v. Lakeibia Fannin (Sentencing) – $1,400,000 – District of Nevada
Illinois woman sentenced to 13 months in prison for conspiring to defraud the United States by making false claims for refunds based on COVID-19 tax credits. Lakeibia Fannin conspired with others, including Candies Goode-McCoy, from June 2022 through November 2023 to file tax returns seeking fraudulent refunds based on false Employee Retention Credits and Sick and Family Leave Credits. Fannin and her businesses were not eligible to receive these refundable credits in the amounts claimed. In total, Fannin claimed more than $3.5 million in fraudulent refunds, of which more than $1.4 million were paid.
16) United States v. McDonald Preval (Sentencing) – $4,200,000 – Southern District of Florida
Florida man was sentenced to 36 months in prison for filing a false tax return on behalf of a trust he controlled as part of a $4.2 million refund fraud scheme.
McDonald Preval, of Miami, filed a number of false tax returns for himself and trusts he claimed to control. The trust tax returns reported that the trusts had earned significant income and made tax withholding payments to the IRS, purportedly entitling the trusts to large tax refunds. In fact, the trusts did not have the claimed income and did not make payments in the amounts claimed on the returns and therefore were not entitled to the refunds Preval claimed. He also filed tax returns for 2023 that did not include the income from his employment. The false tax returns Preval caused to be filed on behalf of purported trusts and himself collectively sought tax refunds totaling more than $4.2 million. Preval obtained more than $580,000 from his scheme, which he used to pay off the mortgage loan on his house and other personal expenses.

FBI Springfield Warns of Illicit Prescribing and Diversion of Controlled Substances
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is concerned about medical professionals unlawfully prescribing opioids and other prescription narcotics, contributing to the opioid epidemic.
The FBI has identified the following red flags as possible indicators of the illicit prescribing and diversion of controlled substances:
Prescriber red flags:
- frequently authorizing patients to fill their controlled substance prescriptions early
- writing prescriptions for large quantities of opioids
- writing prescriptions for multiple concurrent immediate-release opioids
- writing the same combination and quantity of controlled substance medications to multiple patients
Patient red flags:
- filling controlled substance prescriptions at multiple pharmacies
- prescription combinations of contraindicated substances (cocktails)
- receiving controlled substance prescriptions from multiple prescribers
- traveling far to visit the prescriber or fill the prescription
- forged or altered prescriptions
Report tips, complaints, and information to SI-opioid@fbi.gov.
title: FBI Springfield Warns of Illicit Prescribing and Diversion of Controlled Substances

RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced that a jury has convicted Brandon Brave Heart, age 42, of Kyle, South Dakota, of Assault by Striking, Beating, or Wounding and Simple Assault following a two-day jury trial in federal district court in Rapid City, South Dakota. The verdict was returned on October 8, 2026.

The charges carry a maximum penalty of one year in custody and/or a $100,000 fine, one year of supervised release, and a $25 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Brave Heart was indicted for Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury and Assault with a Dangerous Weapon by a federal grand jury in September 2024.

On July 23, 2024, shortly before 7:30 pm, the victim and his family were at the Common Cents convenience store located at Sharp’s Corner near Kyle, SD. The victim had his back to the door when Brave Heart entered the store. Brave Heart walked towards the victim from behind and struck him with a closed fist in the back of the head. The victim fell to the ground, and Brave Heart continued to strike the victim. During the assault, Brave Heart used fists to punch the victim and his tennis shoes to kick the victim twice in the face.

This matter is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in Federal court as opposed to State court.

This case was investigated by the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety Criminal Investigations Division. Assistant U.S. Attorney Abby VanDenBerg prosecuted the case.

A presentence investigation was ordered, and a sentencing date has yet to be set.
title: Kyle Man Found Guilty at Federal Trial for Assault in Pine Ridge Reservation

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low-interest federal disaster loans to small businesses and private nonprofit organizations in South Carolina to offset economic losses caused by the Walhalla Main Street Fire occurring Sept. 17. The SBA issued a disaster declaration in response to an Oct. 7 request received from Governor Henry Dargan McMaster.
The declaration covers the following South Carolina counties of Anderson, Oconee, and Pickens, and the Georgia counties of Franklin, Habersham, Hart, Rabun, and Stephen, as well as the North Carolina counties of Jackson, Macon, and Transylvania, which are eligible for Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA.
SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith‑based organizations — with financial losses directly related to the disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for small aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
“SBA loans help eligible small businesses and private nonprofits cover operating expenses after a disaster, which is crucial for their recovery,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “These loans not only help business owners get back on their feet but also play a key role in sustaining local economies in the aftermath of a disaster.”
The loan amount can be up to $2 million with interest rates as low as 4% for small businesses and 3.625% for private nonprofit organizations, with terms of up to 30 years. Interest does not accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. SBA sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
Beginning Thursday, Oct. 15, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the SBA Business Recovery Center in Oconee County to answer questions about SBA’s disaster loan program, explain the application process, and help individuals complete their application. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an in-person appointment in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The hours of operation are listed below:
OCONEE COUNTY
Business Recovery Center
City of Walhalla – The Earle House
Walhalla, SC 29691
Opens at noon, Thursday, Oct. 15
Hours: Monday – Friday, 8:30 a.m. – 5 p.m.
Permanently closing: Friday, Nov. 6, at 5 p.m.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return economic injury application is July 9, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.

ATLANTA – Dye’Shuan Green, who pressured girls as young as nine years old to send him sexually explicit photos and videos online, has been sentenced to nearly 17 years in federal prison for production of child sexual abuse material.

“The Court’s sentence holds a predator accountable for his reprehensible acts and ensures he won’t victimize another child for most of the next two decades,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg, “This case also serves as a reminder to parents and caretakers about the dangers deviant criminals like Green pose to young people online.”

“Posing as a child and then pressuring children, among the most vulnerable members of our society, to produce sexually explicit and harmful material is unconscionable,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “The FBI, alongside our local, state, and federal partners, will relentlessly work to bring justice to the victims and their families.”

According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the charges, and other information presented in court: In 2022, a mother in Columbus, Georgia reported to the Columbus Police Department that her daughter had been manipulated by a man, who was posing as a child online, to send nude images of herself. The FBI then conducted a multi-year investigation, which revealed that Green had preyed on young girls across the country.

The investigation established that Green targeted young girls on social media and gaming sites and pretended that he was a boy their age. Green befriended them, convinced them that he loved them and wanted a relationship with them, and discussed having sex with them. Green then relentlessly begged and threatened victims to produce sexually explicit photos of themselves to send him, and many girls sent nude images to him. A review of Green’s phone and social media accounts showed that he chatted online with hundreds of young girls as part of his scheme.

On October 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Sarah E. Geraghty sentenced Dye’Shuan Green, 23, of College Park, Georgia, to 16 years, 10 months in prison to be followed by 15 years of supervised release. Green pleaded guilty to one count of production of child sexual abuse material and four counts of enticement to create child sexual abuse material on June 29, 2026.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, with valuable assistance provided by the Columbus Police Department.

Assistant United States Attorneys Matthew R. LaGrone and Leanne M. Marek prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood. In February 2006, the Attorney General launched Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative designed to protect children from online exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorney’s Offices around the country, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov.

For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga .

DENVER – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado announces that Steve Randall Howe, 74, of Denver, Colorado, was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison, two years of supervised release, restitution in the amount of $1,253,691.84, and a fine of $15,000 after pleading guilty to one count of bank fraud, and one count of money laundering.

According to the plea agreement and facts established at the sentencing hearing, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Howe obtained $1,243,799.91 in emergency Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans based on false representations made to six different banks. In each PPP loan application, the defendant made false representations about the business listed on the application including as to the business’ number of employees and average monthly payroll. Most of the businesses had no employees or business function. He additionally submitted to the lenders fabricated payroll and tax documents which had not been filed with the Internal Revenue Service. Howe used a majority of the funds not on payroll, but on the lease and purchase of a home, retail purchases, monetary transfers to China, payment for legal services, travel expenses, subscriptions, and gym memberships. The loans were forgiven by the Small Business Administration before any of the defendant’s purported businesses made a single payment.

“This sentence continues to send a clear message that the District of Colorado will not tolerate theft from the American taxpayer,” said United States Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “We will always seek out criminals who abuse public funds for personal gain.”

“During the pandemic, financial assistance programs were created to keep businesses and employees afloat, not to line the pockets of greedy opportunists,” said FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski. “This case is a reminder that the FBI aggressively continues to pursue criminals who think they can defraud the federal government and American taxpayers.”

“Howe saw the COVID-19 pandemic as an opportunity to defraud the government, depriving small businesses and families of the support they needed,” said Scott Brown, Acting Special Agent in Charge, IRS Criminal Investigation Phoenix Field Office. “This case demonstrates our ongoing commitment to pursuing individuals who abused these pandemic relief programs and ensuring they are held accountable.”

United States District Judge Nina Y. Wang presided over the sentencing.

The investigation was handled by the FBI and IRS-Criminal Investigation Denver Field Offices.

Assistant United States Attorneys Craig Fansler and Taylor Glogiewicz handled the prosecution.

The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

ICYMI: Director Kupor Discusses Responsible SI Leadership on Fox News’ Saturday in America
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director Scott Kupor, Vice Chair of the Super Intelligence Task Force, joined Kayleigh McEnany on Fox News’ Saturday in America to discuss the task force’s work, the importance of U.S. leadership in SI, and the responsibility of technology companies to develop and release safe products.
On the task force’s dual mandate:
“We’ve got a dual mandate here. The President has been very clear that this is a race we are winning and need to win, and that it’s critical to Americans’ economic and national security for Americans. But he’s also said we have to do so responsibly. That’s a lot of what we’ve been discussing at the task force: How do we allow the technology to continue in and appropriate way while also protecting the best interests of the American people? I’m absolutely confident we can square those two goals.”
On addressing SI safety risks:
“Those very same people were also predicting a jobs apocalypse about 18 months ago. The opposite has happened: We’ve actually had a huge increase in jobs as a result of SI.
“Nonetheless, we take this seriously. The answer, though, is not to slow down or pause. That’s the absolute worst thing we can do. All that does is inure to the benefit of our adversaries, China foremost among them.
“We’ve been very clear with [model providers] that they have a key fundamental responsibility to put out safe products. If they deem a product isn’t safe, the answer is to slow its release, not put it out and just pray for good times.”
On company responsibility and incident response:
“Companies have a responsibility from a technology perspective to develop the security tools. Second, they have an obligation to respond and notify the government when these things happen. In cases like the Philadelphia one you mentioned, those are things that should have happened immediately. We’ve been very clear with those vendors that they need to do that and be an active part of remediation if something happens.
“A lot of this is about setting the right expectations with companies, making sure the government has all the information it needs, and making sure other critical infrastructure providers, like financial services companies, are fully in the loop if something happens.”
On the risk of falling behind:
“We believe this is the most important economic and national sovereignty tool that will govern international relationships for the next 30, 40, 50 years. If we lose this race to China, or suspend or slow down our efforts, all we do is encourage an adversary to have economic control over our future, as well as control over our national sovereignty and security control.
“I’m confident there’s a way to square these two problems: winning the race and doing so in a responsible way.”
title: ICYMI: Director Kupor Discusses Responsible SI Leadership on Fox News’ Saturday in America

New Orleans, Louisiana – Today, United States Attorney David I. Courcelle for the Eastern District of Louisiana, announced the sentencing of a local fraudster as part of a nationwide enforcement action led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, Internal Revenue Service, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation that targeted tax fraud and related offenses. The Eastern District of Louisiana was a key participant in this anti-fraud surge effort.

Between early September and today, the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country participated in the Department’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge. The surge of nationwide resources resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government of more than $490,000,000.

“Today’s coordinated surge effort highlights the commitment of the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Eastern District of Louisiana, the Department of Justice’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the IRS and the IRS Criminal Investigation Service, to uncover and prosecute tax fraud,” said U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. Today’s surge signals a day of reckoning for tax fraudsters nationwide.”

“Today’s coordinated surge effort highlights the commitment of the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Eastern District of Louisiana, the Department of Justice’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the IRS and the IRS Criminal Investigation Service, to uncover and prosecute tax fraud,” said U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. Today’s surge signals a day of reckoning for tax fraudsters nationwide.”

In the Eastern District of Louisiana, U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle announced that Amanda Wilkerson, age 57, of Marrero, was sentenced on September 22, 2026 to 13 months of imprisonment by U.S. District Judge Brandon S. Long for failing to pay payroll taxes, failing to file individual income tax returns, and providing false statements on a Cares Act Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”) loan application.

According to court documents, Wilkerson owned and operated a home healthcare business, Divine Purpose Home Care LLC (“Divine”). From 2017 through 2024, Wilkerson failed to properly report Divine’s payroll taxes due, and failed to pay to the IRS, the $1.1 million in payroll taxes Wilkerson had collected from her employees’ wages. In 2023, Wilkerson earned over $1.6 million in income but failed to file her 2023 individual income tax return. For years, Wilkerson failed to file tax returns and failed to pay the taxes due for the years she failed to file returns. Also in 2021, Wilkerson made false and fraudulent statements to the Small Business Administration on her PPP loan application. In her application, Wilkerson stated that a non-operational business she established had annual gross income of $75,639 in 2019. Wilkerson submitted with her PPP application, a fraudulent IRS tax return that falsely reported the business earned income. Wilkerson’s false PPP loan application resulted in Wilkerson receiving $19,907. Wilkerson was ordered to pay $2,367,686 in restitution to the IRS and $19,907 to the Small Business Administration. She was also ordered to serve three years of supervised release following the term of imprisonment.

In May 2026, Wilkerson pled guilty to a three-count bill of information charging her with one count of failure to pay over payroll/trust fund taxes, in violation of 26 U.S.C. § 7202, one count of failure to file her individual income tax return in violation of 26 U.S.C. § 7203, and one count of providing false statements on a government Cares Act Paycheck Protection Program (“PPP”) loan application in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

U.S. Attorney Courcelle praised the work of the Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigations who investigated the case. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Tiwana Wright, Financial Crimes Unit.

Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Navy Flies Drones Without GPS, Lands Autonomously on Moving Ships
NAVAL AIR WARFARE CENTER AIRCRAFT DIVISION, PATUXENT RIVER, Md. — The Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD) successfully proved an unmanned system can navigate missions and land aboard Navy ships without GPS or pilot control.
“In contested areas where satellites and communications are jammed, autonomy gives significant advantage to our sailors,” said NAWCAD Commander Rear Adm. Todd Evans. “Breakthroughs like this help us scale unmanned capability fast and affordably across a distributed fleet.”
The live-flight demonstration proved that a tactical drone can fly mission tasks and execute recoveries on a pitching vessel at sea – even when satellite navigation is jammed or unavailable – by using its own commercial-standard cameras, motion sensors, and electronics.
“In a high-end maritime conflict, GPS is the first operational link an adversary attempts to sever,” said NAWCAD aerospace engineer Peter Arslanian. “By developing a modular adaptable system and putting it directly onto a UAS, we expand where and how the fleet can deploy unmanned systems with a simple software upgrade rather than expensive modifications to space-constrained ships.”
Traditional UAS landings rely on multimillion-dollar radar systems, recovery gear for the flight deck, and ship modifications that can take months to install. NAWCAD’s software-driven approach replaces that hardware by pairing an unmanned system’s mission sensors such as cameras with advanced guidance, navigation, and control software developed by the warfare center’s Maritime Autonomous Guidance-Navigation-Control Intelligent Coupled Systems Lab.
In flight, the UAS uses its camera to recognize a ship’s shape and visual cues to guide its flight path like a human pilot, while its guidance and control algorithms predict the ship's rising and falling deck in real time so the aircraft can touch down smoothly. The software works with nearly any UAS computer hardware and can scale across unmanned systems of all sizes, from small tactical quadcopters to large, combat-class aircraft.
With initial flight demonstrations complete, the software is ready for operational testing on fleet platforms. NAWCAD plans to scale the technology to larger unmanned systems, including tactical resupply drones, and is working with program offices to transition the capability into acquisition pipelines at the Navy’s Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program, and DARPA’s EVADE project.
The project was funded through the Naval Innovative Science and Engineering Program and the Office of Naval Research.
NAWCAD employs military, civilian, and contract personnel to operate test ranges, laboratories, and aircraft in support of test, evaluation, research, development, and sustainment for all Navy and Marine Corps aviation platforms. Based in Patuxent River, Maryland, NAWCAD also has major sites in St. Inigoes, Maryland; Lakehurst, New Jersey; and Orlando, Florida.

WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Congressman Josh Riley (NY-19) introduced the Ad-Free Means Ad-Free Act, legislation to crack down on streaming companies that promise customers commercial-free viewing, then change the rules and force them to sit through advertisements.
Many digital streaming platforms that built massive user bases on promises of commercial-free viewing have later added advertisement to their default tiers for both live and on-demand programming. For example, RedZone – the NFL’s popular streaming service – recently announced it would broadcast advertisements for the first time in its 17-year history. Outraged fans viewed the change as a bait-and-switch that fundamentally breached the ad-free experience they had already purchased.
“If you pay for ad-free, you should get ad-free. It’s that simple,” Riley said. “For years, football fans were promised seven hours of commercial-free football. Now the big streaming companies are moving the goalposts to squeeze even more money out of hardworking people. Upstate New Yorkers are sick and tired of getting ripped off. My bill makes these companies honor their promises and gives fans what they paid for.”
RedZone is not alone in its change from an ad-free model. Across the industry, major streaming platforms are introducing commercials into previously ad-free tiers, often forcing users to pay an additional surcharge to restore the uninterrupted experience they originally signed up for. The Ad-Free Means Ad-Free Act would prohibit streaming services from adding commercials to paid subscriptions originally advertised or offered as commercial-free within one year or the length of the original contract.
The Ad-Free Means Ad-Free Act is endorsed by the Sports Fans Coalition.
“If sports fans pay extra to watch games without additional commercial interruptions, they should get what they pay for – no ads. We thank Congressman Josh Riley for throwing the flag on the bait-and-switch some streaming services are pulling on fans,” said David Goodfriend, Chair of the Sports Fans Coalition.
You can read the text of the legislation HERE.

title: RILEY TAKES ON STREAMING GIANTS WITH BILL TO END AD-FREE BAIT-AND-SWITCH

Congressmen Carter, Thompson Visit Nation’s Largest Permanent ICE Migrant Detention Facility
NATCHEZ, MS – Today, Rep. Bennie G. Thompson (D-MS), Ranking Member of the Committee on Homeland Security, and Rep. Troy Carter (D-LA), Committee Member, released the below statement on their surprise oversight visit yesterday to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility at Adams County Correctional Center (ACCC) in Mississippi, the nation’s largest migrant detention facility.
“One of Congress’ primary responsibilities is oversight of federal agencies, and we exercised that power – and legal right – in an unannounced visit to ACCC after a summer of crises, protests, and power outages. We wanted an unvarnished look at the institution to make sure that facility problems highlighted in correspondence our offices and in public inspection reports are being addressed, and that everyone in the facility has access to their constitutional due process rights. Regardless of a person’s station in life, they are still human and deserve safe shelter with adequate, sanitary food and water, and access to health care.
“We continue to have concerns that detainees aren’t able to obtain access to adequate mental health services, a full understanding of what crimes they are charged with, and transparency and accountability for when ACCC staff fail in upholding their constitutional rights. As the Trump administration continues to weaponize ICE against communities across the country, we will continue rigorous oversight of immigrant detention facilities so that the law is followed and immigrants have access to their full constitutional rights.”
Background
Adams County Correctional Center (ACCC), operated by the private prison company CoreCivic, is the largest permanent immigration detention facility in the U.S. and detains an average of 1,878 men daily.
In the past six months, ACCC and the men detained there have experienced multiple crises. In May 2026, ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight inspected ACCC and downgraded the facility from a “Superior” rating to “Acceptable/Adequate,” with only 24 of 28 standards met. In July, nearly 70 detainees submitted a petition to the warden demanding an end to the practice of placing three detainees in cells meant to hold two people. During the week of August 10, 2026, a lengthy power outage at ACCC left detainees without air conditioning for two days in nearly 100-degree heat. On August 22, 2026, around 100 male detainees started a protest over poor living conditions, spoiled food, and meager rations.
title: Congressmen Carter, Thompson Visit Nation’s Largest Permanent ICE Migrant Detention Facility

SEATTLE, W.A. — U.S. Representatives Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) and Emily Randall (WA-06) are leading Members from Washington and Oregon in demanding answers and transparency into ongoing efforts by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to purchase existing immigration detention centers currently owned and operated by private prison companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic. Currently, the GEO Group contract with the Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) is set to expire in October 2026.
Earlier this summer, ICE purchased two CoreCivic detention centers in California for $1.5 billion and facilities in Kansas and Minnesota for $734 million. Despite these facilities having been purchased by ICE, CoreCivic will continue managing operations. In October, ICE purchased three detention facilities in Adelanto, California, from GEO Group for $950 million. Similarly, GEO will continue running the facilities and says ICE is considering buying 10 facilities or more from the company.
“We are deeply concerned about the potential purchase of these facilities, as it appears to be an attempt to circumvent oversight and accountability at detention facilities. Both GEO Group and DHS have stated that acquiring these facilities is aimed, at least in part, at circumventing attempts by states to conduct oversight at immigration detention centers located within their borders,” wrote the Members.
Any attempt to dodge oversight is particularly troubling at the NWDC, as Washington State recently had to go to court to ensure access to the facility for state Department of Health officials. There is serious cause for concern if this purchase is being made to shield ICE and GEO from oversight efforts by putting the facility under federal ownership.
There are also troubling financial incentives. Under the Trump administration, GEO and CoreCivic have reaped enormous financial benefits. In 2025, both companies received an additional $2 billion in profit each, a 13 percent increase in revenue, and there has been a revolving door between the Trump administration and these companies — including border czar Tom Homan and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, who were previously employed by GEO.
“As of March 2026, the Washington State Department of Health received over 3,500 complaints about [NWDC]. Individuals have reported being sexually assaulted by an officer in their unit; unsanitary conditions, including unclean drinking water, worms, hair, and metal in food, and black mold in showers; and insufficient medical care. State oversight is an essential way to help ensure that the people detained in these facilities at U.S. taxpayer expense are being treated with dignity. Attempting to circumvent such oversight by purchasing substandard detention facilities and continuing to allow such inhumane conditions to persist is unacceptable,” continued the Members.
The full text of the letter can be found here.
The letter was also signed by Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Janelle S. Bynum (OR-05), Suzan DelBene (WA-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03), Rick Larsen (WA-02), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Kim Schrier (WA-08), Adam Smith (WA-09), and Marilyn Strickland (WA-10).
Issues: Immigration
title: Jayapal, Randall Lead PNW Members in Demanding Answers on NWDC Contract
