SEATTLE – The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, in collaboration with more than 4,300 law enforcement partners, will host the 31st National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on Saturday, October 24, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
The DEA Seattle Field Division is working with more than 90 law enforcement partners across the Pacific Northwest with collection sites in Washington (49), Oregon (18), Idaho (25), and Alaska (7).
More than 4,400 collection sites will be set up across the country to dispose of unneeded, expired, and unused prescription medications. This is a simple step that prevents diversion, reduces the risk of accidental poisonings, and helps protect communities.
“Since 2010, Take Back Day has helped Americans remove more than twenty million pounds of unneeded medications from their homes,” said DEA Administrator Terry Cole. “By participating in Take Back Day, you are preventing potentially addictive medications from falling into the wrong hands – a small step that can save lives. I am grateful to the thousands of law enforcement and community partners who make these events possible, and I urge everyone to take a few minutes on Saturday, October 24, to clean out your medicine cabinets.”
“Preventing prescription drug misuse starts at home. By safely disposing of unused and expired medications, we can prevent diversion and reduce the risk of accidental poisonings.” said Robert A. Saccone, Special Agent in Charge, DEA Seattle Field Division. “DEA and our more than 90 law enforcement partners across the Pacific Northwest are committed to protecting our communities, and we encourage everyone to take advantage of Take Back Day. Together, we can make a difference and save lives.”
What will be collected
- Tablets, capsules, patches, and other forms of prescription medications
- Liquid medications securely sealed in their original containers
What won’t be collected
- Syringes, sharps, and illicit drugs
Why it matters

- Removing unneeded medications from the home reduces the risk of misuse or accidental ingestion.

ALBUQUERQUE – An Arizona man has been indicted in connection with four alleged sexual assaults on a child that occurred over a three-year period on the Navajo Nation.

According to court documents, between June 2017 and June 2020, Roman B. Ortiz , 36, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, engaged in or attempted to engage in sex acts with a minor under 12 years old, doing so at a residence located within the exterior boundaries of the Navajo Nation.

Ortiz is charged with four counts of aggravated sexual abuse. Ortiz will remain in custody pending trial, which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted, Ortiz faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 30 years in prison per felony charge.

WAYCROSS, Georgia: Defendants in five separate cases were issued a total of 870 months’ worth of prison sentences, Oct. 7, 2026.

The sentences were imposed by U.S. District Judge Lisa Godbey Wood and announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.

The defendants and their sentences are as follows:

Christopher Hawkins , a/k/a “Rayshon Hawkins,” 31, of Douglas, was sentenced to 240 months in prison followed by five years of supervised release following his conviction at trial for one count of Conspiracy to Possess with Intent to Distribute, and to Distribute Cocaine, Marijuana, Oxycodone, and 500 grams or more of Methamphetamine, five counts of Distribution of Cocaine, six counts of Distribution of Methamphetamine, two counts of Possession with Intent to Distribute Cocaine, and one count of Possession of a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime.

Ernest Goodman , 44, of Waycross, was sentenced to 212 months in prison followed by four years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Conspiracy to Possess with Intent to Distribute, and to Distribute Cocaine, Marijuana, Oxycodone, and Methamphetamine and Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon. Goodman was subjected to enhanced penalties due to his designation as an Armed Career Criminal.

Aaron Kahn , 50, of Douglas, was sentenced to 138 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Conspiracy to Possess with Intent to Distribute, and to Distribute Cocaine, Marijuana, Oxycodone, and Methamphetamine.

As described in court documents and testimony, Hawkins, Goodman, and Kahn were members of a wide-ranging drug trafficking conspiracy spanning Coffee, Atkinson, Ware, and Bacon Counties. The defendants participated in a conspiracy to import and distribute large amounts of illegal drugs in the Douglas community and in surrounding counties during a roughly four-year period from early 2021 through the time of the indictment. Much of the conspiracy was directed from inside Georgia state prisons using contraband cell phones, and the investigation included the seizure of 21 illegally possessed firearms.

There were 33 additional defendants who were convicted after pleading guilty to various drug- and gun-related charges, with 17 of them sentenced to terms of up to 126 months in prison. An additional defendant, Marquan Jenkins , 32, an inmate in the Georgia Department of Corrections, was convicted at trial and awaits sentencing, one defendant passed away before adjudication, and another was acquitted at trial.

The case was investigated under the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), and the HSTF initiative was established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

The agencies responsible for conducting this investigation included the FBI, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Coffee County Sheriff’s Office Drug Unit, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation Southeast Regional Drug Enforcement Office, the Georgia State Patrol, the Georgia Department of Community Supervision, Ware County Sheriff’s Office, the Douglas Police Department, the Bacon County Sheriff’s Office, the Atkinson County Sheriff’s Office, the Waycross Police Department, the Marion County (Florida) Sheriff’s Office, and the Jacksonville (Florida) County Sheriff’s Office. The case has been prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Bradley R. Thompson and Joshua K. Davis.

Judge Wood also sentenced two additional defendants associated with separate cases; they include:

Guillermo Sanchez-Zuniga , a/k/a “G,” a/k/a “Kasper,” 28, of Pearson, Ga., was sentenced to 160 months in prison followed by four years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Distribution of more than 5 grams of Methamphetamine.

According to court documents and testimony, between November 2024 and May 2025, investigators with the FBI began an investigation in conjunction with the Atkinson County Sheriff’s Office into drug trafficking activities of the defendant. On multiple occasions, investigators determined that Sanchez-Zuniga had sold quantities of methamphetamine during controlled purchases to undercover agents.

This case was investigated by the FBI and the Atkinson County Sheriff’s Office and was prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorney Jennifer J. Kirkland.

Herlindo Perez-Barajas , a/k/a “Jose Flores Garcia,” a/k/a “Primo,” 50, an illegal alien living in Waycross, Ga., was sentenced to 120 months in prison followed by immediate deportation after pleading guilty to Possession with Intent to Distribute more than 50 grams of Methamphetamine.

According to court documents and testimony, during an October 2024 traffic stop by Georgia State Patrol, Perez-Barajas was discovered with more than 50 grams of methamphetamine. After the illegal narcotics were found, troopers referred the defendant to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement due to his illegal immigration status.

This case was investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration, Georgia State Patrol, Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and was prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Marcela C. Mateo and Bradley R. Thompson.

“Each of these cases are a testament to our law enforcement partners, and to the commitment of investigators across all levels of local, state and federal agencies providing extensive investigative material to the court,” said U.S. Attorney Heap. “These significant sentences send an unmistakable message: no matter where you attempt to direct criminal enterprise, law enforcement will find you, disrupt your network, and ensure you face justice.”

“These sentences reflect the impact of strong partnerships and coordinated investigations in dismantling drug trafficking networks,” said Brad Snider, Supervisory Senior Resident Agent of FBI Atlanta’s Brunswick office. “The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue targeting those who distribute dangerous drugs and use firearms to fuel criminal activity, ensuring they are held accountable for the harm they cause our communities.”

“These sentences reflect the serious harm drug trafficking operations and illegal firearms pose to our communities,” said ATF Assistant Special Agent in Charge Brian Graves. “ATF is committed to working alongside the FBI and our law enforcement partners to investigate and ensure those who threaten public safety are brought to justice.”

BRATTLEBORO, VT — Yesterday, U.S. Representatives Becca Balint (VT-AL) and Jim McGovern (MA-02) met with Vermont and Massachusetts business owners to discuss the economic consequences of Trump’s ongoing trade tensions with Canada. The roundtable, held in Brattleboro, included Canadian Consul General Bernadette Jordan and the Director of Economic Affairs from the Quebec Government Office in Boston, and gave business owners an opportunity to share how tariffs and unpredictable trade policy are negatively affecting their costs, customers, employees, and ability to plan for the future.  
The meeting also underscored the importance of maintaining strong relationships between communities on both sides of the border. Business owners and regional stakeholders emphasized that cross-border commerce supports jobs, sustains rural industries, and connects families and communities throughout Vermont, Massachusetts, and the New England region.
“Vermont and Canada have been neighbors, partners, and friends for generations,” said Congresswoman Becca Balint. “As a part of this conversation, we heard directly from business owners who are paying the price for this administration’s reckless trade war. They are facing higher costs, losing customers, and putting plans for growth on hold because they can’t count on the rules staying the same. That uncertainty hurts workers, families, farmers, and small businesses across Vermont and broader New England. I’m grateful to Rep. McGovern for joining us in standing up for our regional economy. We need a stable, predictable trade relationship with Canada, and I’ll keep working with him and our partners across the region to push for a trade policy that reflects our shared economic interests and gives our businesses the stability they need to succeed.”
“Trump’s trade war with Canada is destroying American businesses and livelihoods,” said Congressman Jim McGovern. “It was heartbreaking to hear from small business owners in Massachusetts and Vermont about how these tariffs are devastating their businesses. Let’s be clear: Canada isn’t paying Trump’s tariff tax. American workers, families, and small businesses are. Trump’s tariffs are wrecking our economy, killing jobs, driving businesses to the brink, and damaging our relationship with one of our closest trading partners. Congresswoman Balint and I will keep fighting to overturn these illegal tariffs, protect our small businesses, and put working people first.”  
New England’s regional economy is deeply connected to Canada through agriculture, forestry, manufacturing, tourism, and cross-border supply chains. Businesses participating in the discussion described additional costs ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, lost Canadian customers, delayed investments, and difficult decisions about staffing and production.
For many businesses, the uncertainty surrounding trade policy is compounding the financial strain. Companies are being forced to reconsider suppliers, absorb additional expenses, raise prices, delay investments and equipment upgrades, and devote significant staff time to navigating changing rules and pursuing tariff relief.
Representatives Balint and McGovern are committed to bringing the concerns raised during the discussion back to Washington and continuing to work toward a more stable U.S.-Canada trade relationship that supports New England’s workers and businesses.  
###
title: Balint, McGovern Meet with Vermont and Massachusetts Businesses on U.S.-Canada Trade Tensions

PITTSBURGH, Pa. — After less than two hours of deliberation, a federal jury in Pittsburgh convicted Justin Lee Plunk, 39, of Corinth, Mississippi, of conspiring to distribute and distributing child sexual abuse material for profit over multiple years on platforms including Instagram and Telegram.

The jury found Plunk guilty of the two counts on October 9, 2026, following a four-day trial before United States District Judge Robert J. Colville.

“Justin Plunk was an active participant in a conspiracy that, for years, preyed upon and sexually exploited children for profit through a variety of online platforms, including popular social media and children’s gaming apps and mobile payment services,” said United States Attorney Troy Rivetti of the Western District of Pennsylvania. “Although it can never undo the harm these victims experienced, this verdict holds Plunk responsible for his role in the recruitment and abuse of those minors, and is another example of our office’s commitment to working with our law enforcement partners at all levels to protect children from such crimes and to prosecute to the fullest extent of the law predators who exploit and conspire to exploit minors.”

“Justin Plunk exploited the most vulnerable members of our society to turn a profit,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva for the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “He operated a business that trafficked in horrific images of the sexual exploitation of children both in America and abroad. The verdict in this case sends a strong message that such horrific and depraved conduct will be met with accountability.”

“This verdict reflects the jury’s clear recognition of the harm caused by those who exploit children for their own profit,” said FBI Pittsburgh Special Agent in Charge Richard Evanchec. “Our children are precious, and their safety must remain our highest priority. We are grateful for the dedicated FBI employees who work every day to protect the most vulnerable among us and to ensure that those who prey on them are brought to justice.”

The evidence presented during the trial established that Plunk was part of a criminal conspiracy that operated online from at least 2021 to 2024 in which the conspirators recruited female minors, including as young as 10 years, in the Western District of Pennsylvania and elsewhere to create “packages” of 30 images and seven videos of child sexual exploitation material, as well as to participate in live video calls with customers. The conspiracy operated over social media and messaging platforms that included Instagram, Snapchat, and Telegram, with one female minor also introduced to the conspiracy on Roblox. In addition, the conspiracy used multiple payment methods, including payment services Cash App and Venmo as well as gift cards from Walmart and Roblox.

The evidence established that Plunk was involved in the conspiracy in numerous ways, including receiving more than $57,000 in proceeds from the conspiracy in the form of cash transfers and retail store gift cards. Plunk had previously been convicted of enticement of a child for sexual purposes in Mississippi in 2016.

Judge Colville scheduled Plunk’s sentencing for January 26, 2027. The law provides for a maximum sentence of up to 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both on each count. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed is based on the seriousness of the offenses and the prior criminal history of the defendant.

Assistant United States Attorney Heidi Grogan for the Western District of Pittsburgh and Trial Attorney Gwendelynn Bills of the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) prosecuted the case.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation-Pittsburgh and Mississippi Attorney General’s Office conducted the investigation that led to the prosecution of Plunk.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, including resources on Internet safety, please visit Justice.gov/psc .
title: Mississippi Man Convicted by Federal Jury of Participating in a Criminal Conspiracy to Exploit Children and to Distribute Child Sexual Abuse Material

FAIRFIELD, CA – Today, Rep John Garamendi (D-CA-08), a senior member of the House Armed Services, released the following statement on President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel:
“President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and reach an agreement with Vladimir Putin to bring more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel onto American and global markets is a terrible decision.
“This amount of fuel represents less than a single day of diesel consumption by the American transportation sector and will do little to meaningfully reduce the price Americans pay at the pump. More importantly, allowing Russia to sell this fuel undermines American national security and provides additional revenue to Putin as he continues his brutal war of aggression against Ukraine.
“The national security implications extend well beyond Ukraine. Russia is actively supporting Iran, a country currently at war with the United States. According to U.S. intelligence reporting, Russia has provided Iran with information that could help its military target American warships, aircraft, and other military assets throughout the Middle East. This intelligence assistance threatens the lives of American service members who are already facing Iranian attacks.
“At a time when Russia is helping Iran target American forces, President Trump is opening the door for hundreds of millions of dollars in additional Russian diesel sales. That revenue strengthens the Russian economy and undermines our efforts to pressure Putin to end his aggression.
“The United States has imposed strong economic sanctions on Russia for good reason. Those sanctions are intended to deny Putin the resources necessary to sustain his war against Ukraine and threaten American national security interests.
“We should not be easing economic pressure on a country that is helping our enemies target American troops. President Trump’s decision contradicts our national security objectives, undermines our support for Ukraine, and puts American interests at risk. He should reverse it immediately.
###
title: Garamendi Statement on Trump Lifting Russian Fuel Sanctions

Meets with Impacted Kentucky Coal and Firearm Industry Representatives

WASHINGTON—Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould today discussed findings of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s newly-released report on large banks’ debanking activities during a press conference held in Lexington, Kentucky, with U.S. Congressman Andy Barr.

During the event, representatives of local Kentucky coal and firearms industries provided insights about the specific impacts of the debanking practices to their businesses.

Excerpts from Comptroller Gould’s remarks are below. His full statement can be found here .

On Ensuring Fair Access to Financial Services for All Americans

The President directed federal banking regulators to examine whether financial institutions had denied Americans access to banking services because of their political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. Thanks to his leadership as well as that of U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent, we are continuing to take steps to ensure that all Americans have fair access to the financial services they need to finance mortgages, fund small businesses, and support their families.

On Report Findings

We found that all of these banks had adopted reputation risk policies at various levels which allowed political considerations, public opinion, and social pressures to influence who banks deemed not worthy to access financial services. Americans were denied banking services because of their political or religious affiliations and entire industries faced scrutiny due to the fact that their lawful business activities were considered "controversial" by some banks or their employees. What began as decisions made by executives to debank disfavored industries became institutionalized and opaque bureaucracies that empowered bank employees to cut off industries and persons from financial services or created procedural frictions that achieved the same result as a practical matter.

On Specific Impacts to Coal and Firearms Industries

Our review found that many of the banks maintained policies restricting financing for new or expanded coal mining operations and coal-fired power plants. Some went even further, restricting financial services to companies based on how much of their revenue is derived from coal. These decisions were not based on financial risk; instead, banks cited concerns about negative headlines, public protests, and the perceived reputational consequences of supporting the industry.

We found similar practices affecting the firearms industry. Several banks restricted financing for firearms manufacturers and retailers. In one instance, a bank denied a firearms business assistance with an initial public offering because the company's policies governing lawful firearms sales did not align with the bank's own standards. Banks should not be denying customers for activities protected by the constitution of the United States.

We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer. Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria.

On OCC Continuing Efforts to Eliminate Debanking

At the OCC, we have eliminated reputation risk from our supervisory framework. As our report makes clear, there is more work to do to ensure that Americans are not denied financial services simply because of their beliefs or that their businesses have fallen out of favor.

WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) announced $1.05 million in grants to five organizations for new entrepreneurial training programs focused on veteran business ownership and growth in sectors vital to America’s supply chains, industrial strength, and economic resilience. Operating through April 30, 2027, the programs will combine industry-specific instruction with practical support in corporate supply-chain procurement, business acquisition, procurement for specialized industries, and regenerative farming and ranching—equipping veteran entrepreneurs for new opportunities while strengthening America’s domestic capacity.
“Veterans are among our most effective entrepreneurs in critical sectors across our economy, and the Trump SBA is fighting for those who fought for our country by offering more resources to strengthen America’s production capacity,” said SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler. “By pairing specialized training with practical business support, our grant funding will position veteran entrepreneurs to become essential suppliers across industry and agriculture—building the domestic capacity America needs to compete and reducing reliance on foreign adversaries.”
The grant awards have been awarded to the following organizations:
- National Veteran-Owned Business Association (NaVOBA): $150,000 for training in Corporate Supply Chain Procurement.
- Owners in Honor & Vet to CEO: $200,000 each ($400,000 total) to provide training and technical assistance in Business Acquisition.
- National Veteran Small Business Coalition (NVSBC): $250,000 for Procurement Training for Specialized Industries.
- The Utah Veteran Business Resource Center at Salt Lake Community College (VBRC): $250,000 for Veteran Entrepreneurship Training in Regenerative Farming and Ranching.
The awards build on the SBA’s recent investments in veteran entrepreneurship, including a $3.75 million grant over five years for nationwide training that will prepare veteran-owned small businesses to compete for federal contracts, and nearly $4.9 million in grants over five years to establish new Veterans Business Outreach Centers.
These latest grants will bolster the SBA Office of Veterans Business Development’s efforts to provide specialized resources and training for veteran-owned small businesses across the country. Through its Entrepreneurship Training Programs, the Office of Veterans Business Development provides customized online and in-person training to help veteran entrepreneurs develop the skills, relationships, and business knowledge needed to start, manage, and sustain small businesses, including in federal contracting. The office also provides resources, counseling, and training opportunities for veterans, service members, National Guard and Reserve members, military spouses, and their families.
To find a Veterans Business Outreach Center (VBOC) near you, visit www.sba.gov/vboc. To learn more about SBA’s programs for veterans, visit www.sba.gov/veterans.
# # #
About the Office of Veterans Business Development
The SBA Office of Veterans Business Development (OVBD) works through SBA’s extensive resource partner network, including 51 Veterans Business Outreach Center (VBOC) locations throughout the nation. VBOCs are the leading partners in delivering the “Boots to Business (B2B),” “Boots to Business Reboot,” and “Military Spouse Pathway to Business” programs—entrepreneurship courses offered on military installations and in local communities. Since B2B’s inception in 2013, these programs have collectively trained and graduated nearly 260,000 service members, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and military spouses. OVBD’s broader resource partner network also includes Small Business Development Centers, the SCORE mentoring program, and Women’s Business Centers. For more information on the resources available for veteran entrepreneurs, visit sba.gov/veterans.
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of entrepreneurship. As the leading voice for small businesses within the federal government, the SBA empowers job creators with the resources and support they need to start, grow, and expand their businesses or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Announces $1.05 Million in Grant Awards for Specialized Veteran Entrepreneurship Training

Kansas Business Owner Sent to Prison for Employment Tax Crimes
A Kenyan national and Missouri businessman was sentenced on October 5, 2026, to 51 months in prison today for willfully failing to pay over employment taxes to the IRS on behalf of the company he owned and operated.
According to documents and statements made in court, Ephantus Mwangi, 48, a resident of Missouri, owned and operated True Payment Solutions, Inc., a Kansas-based business that sold credit-card processing services and card readers to merchants. Mwangi also owned True POS Solutions, Inc, a separate business that offered similar services.
True Payment Solutions typically employed between 20 and 30 people at a time. Because Mwangi was responsible for all financial matters at the business, Mwangi was required by law to withhold Social Security, Medicare and federal income taxes from the wages of his employees and then pay over those funds to the IRS each quarter, as well as file quarterly employment tax returns with the IRS. From at least the third quarter of 2017 through at least the fourth quarter of 2018, however, Mwangi withheld employment taxes from his employees’ wages, but he willfully failed to pay over these taxes to the IRS or file employment tax returns. In total, Mwangi withheld $331,404.33 in taxes from his employees’ wages that he did not pay over to the IRS.
Mwangi also willfully failed to pay over employment taxes due from True Payment Solutions. Instead, from 2016 to 2019, Mwangi transferred more than $1.5 million from the corporate bank accounts of True Payment Solutions and True POS Solutions Inc. to his personal bank accounts. During this time, he spent more than $200,000 on loan payments for various luxury vehicles, including a Hummer H2, a Cadillac Escalade, two Range Rovers, two Mercedes, and a Lexus. He also used these funds to rent an 11,000 sq. ft. mansion as a second home in San Antonio for $13,000 per month and to pay for private school tuition for his children. Additionally, between 2016 and 2019, Mwangi transferred a total of $763,000 in funds to “TRUE PAYMENT SOLUTIONS, EA LTD,” in Kenya, Africa. Mwangi also frequently visited a casino for 10 to 12 hours at a time.
Mwangi also willfully failed to file individual income tax returns for the years 2017 and 2020, and he filed 2018 and 2019 individual income tax returns after the deadline had passed. Mwangi did not file corporate income tax returns for Mwangi also willfully failed to file individual income tax returns for the years 2017 and 2020, and he filed 2018 and 2019 individual income tax returns after the deadline had passed. For the years 2017 through 2019, Mwangi did not file corporate income tax returns for True Payment Solutions or True POS Solutions, Inc.
In total, Mwangi caused a tax loss to the U.S. government exceeding $1.5 million.
Mwangi was previously scheduled to be sentenced on April 27, 2026. He failed to appear in court on this date and remained a fugitive from justice for approximately six weeks, until he was arrested during a traffic stop. During the stop, Mwangi falsely identified himself to law enforcement by providing a false name and birth date.
In addition to the term of imprisonment, U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ordered Mwangi to serve 3 years of supervised release and pay $1,597,835.24 in restitution to the United States.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser for the District of Kansas made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case with the assistance of the U.S. Marshals Service and the Texas State Police.
Trial Attorney J. Parker Gochenour of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Huschka of the District of Kansas prosecuted the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Kansas Business Owner Sent to Prison for Employment Tax Crimes

DEL RIO, Texas - U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at Del Rio Port of Entry recently seized more than $657,000 in narcotics.
“In just four days, exceptional target profiling and rigorous inspections led to these significant seizures,” said Acting Port Director Julian DeHoyos, Del Rio Port of Entry. “This string of successful actions underscores our absolute commitment to dismantling the networks trying to poison our communities.”
The first seizure occurred on Oct. 8 at the Del Rio International Bridge when a CBP officer referred a 2013 GMC Acadia driven by a 23-year-old male United States citizen for secondary inspection. CBP officers examined the vehicle using a nonintrusive inspection system. Upon physical examination, CBP officers discovered 16 packages containing a total of 23.68 pounds of alleged cocaine hidden within the frame of the vehicle. The cocaine has a combined estimated street value of $316,142.
CBP seized the narcotics. Homeland Security Investigations special agents made one arrest and have initiated a criminal investigation.
The second seizure occurred on Oct. 11 at the Del Rio International Bridge when a CBP officer referred a 2005 Ford Expedition driven by a 54-year-old male United States citizen for inspection. CBP officers conducted a secondary examination of the vehicle that included utilization of a nonintrusive inspection system. Upon physical examination, CBP officers discovered 30 packages containing a total of 37.08 pounds of alleged methamphetamine hidden within the spare tire of the vehicle. The methamphetamine has a combined estimated street value of $316,142.
Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the dedicated men and women of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, alongside our law enforcement partners, have arrested and removed thousands of criminal aliens from the country - including gang members, rapists, kidnappers, and drug traffickers - to make our communities safer.
CBP seized the narcotics. The Texas Department of Public Safety arrested the driver and initiated a criminal investigation into the seizure.
title: CBP officers seize more than $657K in narcotics over a four-day period at Del Rio Port of Entry

MOBILE, AL – Gregory Deon Hickenbottom was sentenced on October 8, 2026, by United States District Court Judge Terry F. Moorer to 181 months in prison for trafficking methamphetamine and possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime.

According to court documents, on July 8, 2025, a Mobile County Sheriff’s Office deputy stopped Hickenbottom for speeding. While speaking with Hickenbottom and obtaining his driver’s license, the deputy observed an open container of liquor and smelled marijuana coming from the vehicle. When the deputy and a backup unit approached the driver’s side to ask Hickenbottom to exit the vehicle, he sped away, prompting deputies to pursue him.

During the pursuit, a deputy saw a large, clear plastic bag being thrown from the passenger-side window. Deputies later recovered the bag from a ditch near the location where they had observed Hickenbottom discard it. The bag contained multiple one-ounce bags of methamphetamine packaged for distribution. Deputies also recovered a loaded 9mm handgun across the street from an elementary school. Although deputies did not see Hickenbottom discard the firearm because he had just rounded a turn at a high rate of speed, the weapon was found along his path of flight. The drugs were recovered a short distance away. Testing at the Drug Enforcement Laboratory in Miami, Florida, determined that the methamphetamine weighed 294 grams and was 99% pure.

Hickenbottom eluded deputies during the pursuit, driving recklessly at speeds exceeding 90 mph through a residential area. A short time later, deputies located his Mercedes sedan, abandoned at the Scenic Motel on Moffett Road. While deputies remained in the area to continue their investigation, a citizen reported seeing Hickenbottom get into a Ford Escape driven by a woman. Deputies located the Ford Escape near the area where the methamphetamine and firearm had been discarded. The woman later told deputies that Hickenbottom had admitted throwing drugs and a gun from his vehicle and needed a ride to recover them. Deputies found Hickenbottom hiding on the floorboard behind the front seats of the vehicle. When arrested, he possessed a small amount of cocaine and digital scales used to weigh drugs.

Deputies also encountered a man walking in the area where the methamphetamine and firearm had been discarded. The man told law enforcement that Hickenbottom had contacted him by phone and asked him to search the ditch for the gun and drugs. Hickenbottom later admitted to deputies that he had fled because he had so much “dope.”

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case.

U.S. Attorney Sean P. Costello commended the law enforcement officers who investigated the case, noting that the deputies’ persistence in remaining in the area until Hickenbottom and the drugs were located demonstrated their dedication to duty. Costello also emphasized that, although deputies did not see Hickenbottom discard the firearm, their thorough search along his path of flight prevented a potentially dangerous situation in which a child in the neighborhood could have encountered the loaded weapon.

Assistant U.S. Attorney George F. May prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Mobile comprises agents and officers from the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms and other federal and local agencies with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Alabama.
title: Mobile County Man Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison for Methamphetamine Trafficking and Firearm Offense

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Following an 11-day trial, a federal jury today returned a guilty verdict against Karla Montoya, 45, of Sacramento, the general manager of the Sacramento‑area grocery chain Viva Supermarkets, for her role in a long‑running scheme involving the hiring of undocumented workers, the use of false immigration documents, and obstruction of two U.S. Department of Labor proceedings, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced.

“Today’s verdict makes clear that employers who rely on false immigration documents, exploit their workers, and obstruct federal oversight will be held to account,” said U.S. Attorney Grant. “Our Office will not tolerate employers who deliberately engage in unlawful hiring practices. No one is above the law, and we will continue to safeguard the integrity of federal labor investigations and the rights of workers in our community.”

“This verdict sends a clear message that document fraud, labor exploitation and efforts to obstruct federal investigators are criminal acts and carry serious consequences,” said HSI Northern California Special Agent in Charge Jeff Brannigan. “HSI Northern California has broad authority to investigate a wide array of criminal enterprises and we bring that authority to bear in combatting fraud and ensuring the integrity of the American economy.”

“The jury’s verdict against Ms. Montoya reflects the consequences of enriching yourself at the expense of workers through fraudulent and unlawful business practices,” said IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) San Francisco Field Office Acting Special Agent in Charge David Lowe. “IRS-CI will continue working alongside our law enforcement partners to investigate and hold accountable those who seek unfair advantages over honest businesses by concealing wages, falsifying records, and obstructing investigators.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Montoya worked closely with Viva Supermarkets owner and former Sacramento City Councilmember Sean Loloee to employ undocumented workers throughout the chain’s Sacramento‑area stores. Montoya knowingly accepted false Permanent Resident cards and Social Security cards as part of the hiring process for numerous employees, as well as her own false immigration documents. She also helped facilitate a system of off‑the‑books payments and irregular pay practices, including depriving workers of overtime pay.

Montoya joined Loloee in obstructing two Department of Labor Wage and Hour Division investigations, including by hiding employees likely to provide unfavorable information and interfering with investigators on site. As a result of this obstruction, the earlier investigation significantly understated the true amount of back wages owed to workers.

This case is the product of an investigation by IRS Criminal Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Audrey B. Hemesath, Sam Stefanki, and Matthew Thuesen are prosecuting the case.

This case was investigated with the assistance of the Tax Recovery in the Underground Economy (TRUE) Task Force, which includes the California Department of Justice, the California Employment Development Department, the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration, the Franchise Tax Board, IRS CI and HSI. The TRUE Task Force was created to ensure multi-agency collaboration and to combat wage theft, tax evasion, and other crimes in the underground economy.

On April 23, 2026, Shahriar “Sean” Loloee, 55, of Granite Bay, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to obstruct a Department of Labor investigation, one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS, three counts of filing false tax returns, one count of wire fraud, and one count of money laundering. On Aug. 18, 2026, co-defendants Mirwais Shams and Ahmad Shams pleaded guilty to filing false tax returns. Sentencing for the three has been set for Nov. 19, 2026.

Montoya is scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge Troy L. Nunley on Jan. 7, 2027. Montoya faces a maximum statutory penalty of five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for the count of conspiracy, up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for each count of possession of false immigration documents and possession, acceptance and receipt of false immigration documents, and five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for obstruction of agency proceeding. The actual sentence, however, will be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables.
title: Viva Supermarkets manager found guilty of immigration document fraud, obstruction of 2 federal labor investigations and conspiracy

DEA Chicago Field Division Hosts National Prescription Drug Take Back Day
CHICAGO – The Drug Enforcement Administration, in collaboration with more than 4,300 law enforcement partners, will host the 31st National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on Saturday, Oct. 24, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Additionally, the DEA Chicago Field Division will be hosting Take Back Day collection sites on the following dates and locations throughout Chicago:
- Oct. 15, 10 a.m. – 2 p.m.: Mount Sinai Hospital Chicago (1500 S. Fairfield Ave.)
- Oct. 23, 10 a.m. – 2 p.m.: St. Michael Missionary Baptist Church (4106 W. Monroe St.)
- Oct. 24, 10 a.m. – 2 p.m.: Northwestern Medicine (Streeterville and Bronzeville locations)
More than 4,400 collection sites will be set up across the country to dispose of unneeded, expired, and unused prescription medications. This is a simple step that prevents diversion, reduces the risk of accidental poisonings, and helps protect communities.
“Since 2010, Take Back Day has helped Americans remove more than twenty million pounds of unneeded medications from their homes,” said DEA Administrator Terry Cole. “By participating in Take Back Day, you are preventing potentially addictive medications from falling into the wrong hands – a small step that can save lives. I am grateful to the thousands of law enforcement and community partners who make these events possible, and I urge everyone to take a few minutes on Saturday, October 24, to clean out your medicine cabinets.”
“National Prescription Drug Take Back Day is about more than collecting unused medications. It’s about protecting families, preventing prescription drug misuse, and making our communities safer,” said Todd Smith, Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Chicago Field Division. “We recognize that access to safe and convenient disposal options is not the same in every neighborhood. That’s why we’re working with our community partners to bring Take Back Day directly into more neighborhoods throughout Chicago, making it easier for residents to safely dispose of unwanted medications. Whether it’s at a hospital, a church, or another trusted community location, our goal is to expand access, and ensure every community has an opportunity to participate.”
What will be collected
- Tablets, capsules, patches, and other forms of prescription medications
- Liquid medications securely sealed in their original containers
What won’t be collected
- Syringes, sharps, and illicit drugs
Why it matters
- Prescription opioids, such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, and morphine, are among the most frequently misused prescription pain medications, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA).
- Removing unneeded medications from the home reduces the risk of misuse or accidental ingestion.
Visit www.DEATakeBack.com to find a registered Take Back location near you. If you are unable to participate in this fall’s National Prescription Drug Take Back Day, there are more than 15,300 pharmacies, hospitals, and businesses that offer safe medication disposal year-round. In addition, many police departments also provide permanent drop boxes to ensure Every Day is Take Back Day.
title: DEA Chicago Field Division Hosts National Prescription Drug Take Back Day

text:
On September 16, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued a proposal to rescind Rule 14a-8, which requires companies subject to the SEC's proxy rules to include qualifying shareholder proposals in their proxy materials. The SEC also proposed amendments to its proxy rules that would expand companies' ability to obtain discretionary voting authority for shareholder proposals submitted outside the Rule 14a-8 process. This Legal Sidebar discusses the SEC's proposed rule and related issues that may be of interest to Congress. The Sidebar begins by providing background information on Rule 14a-8. Much of this background is derived from CRS Report R48855, The Shareholder Proposal Rule (Feb. 11, 2026), which offers a more detailed overview of Rule 14a-8's history and current role in corporate governance.
Shareholders of public companies vote on a variety of corporate matters at annual shareholder meetings, including director elections, charter amendments, executive compensation plans, and (as relevant here) proposals from their fellow shareholders. The vast majority of shareholder proposals are nonbinding recommendations, which are often called "precatory" proposals; a much smaller percentage consists of binding amendments to corporate bylaws. Generally, shareholder proposals involve either corporate governance or environmental and social (E&S) issues raised by a company's operations. Common topics for governance proposals include the structure of a corporation's board of directors, voting standards for director elections, and takeover defenses. E&S proposals often involve issues such as climate change, diversity, corporate lobbying and political expenditures, and human rights practices.
The SEC has traditionally taken the view that state law provides shareholders with the right to present proposals at annual meetings. In the case of bylaw amendments, this right is explicit: Most state corporation statutes empower shareholders to amend a corporation's bylaws without board approval. Precatory proposals exist in a murkier legal landscape. Most state corporation statutes are silent on the question of whether shareholders may offer precatory proposals, and there is little case law addressing that issue. Nevertheless, for much of Rule 14a-8's history, the SEC has assumed that shareholders have a state law right to present precatory proposals.
The majority of voting shareholders do not attend annual meetings in person; instead, they vote by proxy. As part of this process, corporations distribute to shareholders a form of proxy (often called a proxy card or simply a proxy) by which shareholders can authorize a corporate official to vote their shares as instructed. In contested votes, shareholders may receive proxy cards from both incumbent management and a dissident shareholder running an alternative slate of director candidates or advocating for a proposal.
While shareholder voting rights are largely derived from state law, the SEC regulates the proxy solicitation process. Section 14(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the Exchange Act) makes it unlawful to solicit proxies in contravention of rules that the SEC may prescribe "as necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors." Using this authority, the SEC has adopted rules governing proxy solicitation, which apply to companies with securities registered under Section 12 of the Exchange Act—i.e., companies that are listed on a national securities exchange or that exceed certain asset and shareholder thresholds.
The proxy rules are principally concerned with ensuring that solicited shareholders receive adequate disclosures. To that end, the rules prohibit soliciting parties from transmitting a proxy card to shareholders unless the card is accompanied or preceded by a proxy statement containing specified disclosures. The proxy rules also include Rule 14a-8, commonly called the shareholder proposal rule, which requires companies to include qualifying shareholder proposals in their proxy materials. In imposing this requirement, Rule 14a-8 allows eligible proposal proponents to avoid the expenses that would accompany independent solicitations on behalf of their proposals.
The SEC adopted the predecessor to Rule 14a-8 in 1942 after a series of cases in which the agency took the position that it was materially misleading for companies to omit from their proxy materials shareholder proposals of which they had notice. The rule has changed considerably since then. Today, it includes 13 substantive grounds on which companies may exclude proposals from their proxy materials, ownership thresholds and holding-period requirements for proposal proponents, and procedural requirements for proponents and companies.
The procedural elements of Rule 14a-8 include a requirement that companies intending to omit a shareholder proposal from their proxy materials notify the SEC and explain the basis for the omission. As a matter of practice, companies have generally filed these notifications along with requests for "no-action" letters stating that SEC staff will not recommend an enforcement action if a company omits a proposal. While no-action letters are not legally binding on any party, for much of Rule 14a-8's history, the no-action process played a key practical role in determining which proposals proceeded to a shareholder vote.
The shareholder proposal rule has long been a source of debate. The rule's supporters tout it as a key instrument of corporate democracy and credit shareholder proposals with spurring valuable corporate governance reforms. Rule 14a-8's detractors argue that many proposals seek to advance social and political agendas unrelated to shareholder value, creating costly distractions for corporate management. Other criticisms focus on the SEC's role in the proposal process, with some commentators arguing that Rule 14a-8 makes the SEC the arbiter of matters that should be determined by state law and private ordering.
Speaking in his personal capacity, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins has expressed support for some of these critiques. During his tenure, the SEC has withdrawn from its traditional role in the proposal process. In November 2025, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance (Corp Fin) announced that it would not respond substantively to Rule 14a-8 no-action requests during the 2025-2026 proxy season, except for requests seeking to exclude proposals as improper subjects for shareholder action under governing state law (one of the 13 substantive exclusions mentioned earlier). In August 2026, Corp Fin expanded this policy and announced that it would discontinue responding to Rule 14a-8 no-action requests entirely.
The SEC's retreat from the Rule 14a-8 no-action process has coincided with discussion of whether states and companies can adopt restrictions on shareholder proposals beyond those in Rule 14a-8. In an October 2025 speech, Chairman Atkins said that Rule 14a-8's "procedural bases for exclusion" are default rules that apply only if states and companies decline to establish their own standards. Relying on similar premises, some commentators have argued that federal law permits states and companies to adopt substantive limits on shareholder proposals that are stricter than those in Rule 14a-8.
There is little case law addressing these issues. Texas—which allows public companies to opt into procedural requirements for shareholder proposals that are stricter than those in Rule 14a-8—is the only state to have adopted legislation addressing shareholder proposals. While some companies have opted into these requirements, the SEC says that it is unaware of any companies that have adopted their own proposal frameworks in their governing documents.
The SEC's proposed rule would rescind Rule 14a-8, leaving shareholder proposal issues to states and, if permitted by state law, companies. In its release, the SEC argues that Rule 14a-8 exceeds its statutory authority under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act and that independent policy reasons justify rescission.
In arguing that Rule 14a-8 exceeds its statutory authority, the SEC contends that Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act authorizes regulations of the manner in which proxy solicitation is conducted and the information that soliciting parties must disclose to shareholders—not the scope of shareholder voting rights, which are determined by state law. Rule 14a-8, the SEC says, has come to operate not as a procedural mechanism to facilitate shareholders' state law rights, but as "a substantive Federal overlay that improperly intrudes into matters of State law" by dictating when companies must include shareholder proposals in their proxy materials. In the SEC's view, this intrusion results in part from Rule 14a-8's substantive exclusions (some of which are not derived from state law) and the rule's presumption that precatory proposals are proper under state law despite an absence of explicit legal authority for that proposition. The SEC also argues that Rule 14a-8's "overall structure"—including its procedural and eligibility requirements, which are not grounded in state law—confirms the rule's function as "a de facto Federal standard for shareholder voting rights."
Setting aside the question of legal authority, the SEC adds that independent policy reasons justify rescinding Rule 14a-8. The SEC maintains that many of Rule 14a-8's original justifications have not been substantiated or are less compelling today. Those justifications included a belief that it was inexpensive for companies to include proposals in their proxy materials; that many proposals were already supported by management or had received meaningful shareholder support; that overall proposal volume was low; and that shareholders' state law proposal rights were reasonably clear. The SEC contends that reviewing and evaluating proposals imposes nontrivial costs on companies (which are ultimately borne by shareholders), that a small percentage of proposals receive majority support, that the volume of proposals has increased significantly, and that state law is often unclear or silent as to the scope of shareholders' proposal rights.
The SEC also argues that Rule 14a-8 has had negative unintended consequences. First, the SEC says that proponents sometimes submit proposals in an attempt to gain leverage in negotiations with company management or to secure private benefits from such negotiations—a practice that is inconsistent with Rule 14a-8's purpose. Second, the SEC contends that Rule 14a-8 places it in the position of making judgments about state law that are best left to state legislatures, state courts, and (where permissible) companies themselves. Third, the SEC maintains that Rule 14a-8 has inhibited the development of state law and private ordering by encouraging companies and shareholders to look to the SEC to resolve proposal disputes.
The SEC argues that retaining Rule 14a-8 in any form would be unwarranted and unlikely to avoid unintended consequences. Even a version of the rule that attempted to defer entirely to state law, the SEC reasons, would need to include a default rule addressing whether proposals must be included in company proxy materials and identify the necessary steps to opt out of that default. In the SEC's view, such a rule would necessarily advantage either proposal proponents or companies and continue to entangle the SEC in issues that should be resolved based on state law and private ordering.
While the SEC proposes rescission of Rule 14a-8, its notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) invites comments on reliance interests that may have developed around the rule and alternatives to complete rescission that would fall within the agency's authority.
As discussed, Rule 14a-8 requires companies subject to the SEC's proxy rules to include qualifying shareholder proposals in company proxy materials, allowing the proponents of such proposals to avoid the expenses that would accompany dissemination of their own proxy materials. While independent solicitations on behalf of shareholder proposals are much rarer than Rule 14a-8 submissions, they remain an option for proposal proponents. If the SEC rescinds Rule 14a-8, independent solicitations on behalf of shareholder proposals may become more common.
If a shareholder makes an independent solicitation for a proposal, a company can obtain voting authority with respect to the proposal from shareholders in two ways. One option is for the company to include the proposal in its proxy materials and receive instructions as to how to vote on the proposal from shareholders who return the company's proxy card. Alternatively, in limited circumstances, a company can omit the proposal from its proxy materials and seek discretionary voting authority if it includes a brief description of the nature of the proposal and how it intends to vote. Under Rule 14a-4(c)(2), however, a company cannot exercise discretionary voting authority for proposals submitted outside the Rule 14a-8 process if the proponent (1) timely provides the company with a statement that the proponent intends to deliver proxy materials to holders of at least the percentage of voting shares required to carry the proposal, (2) includes the same statement in its own proxy materials, and (3) provides evidence to the company that it has in fact solicited holders of at least the requisite percentage of voting shares.
In its NPRM, the SEC says that this framework may result in companies feeling compelled to include shareholder proposals in their proxy materials even when they are not required to do so. If a company cannot exercise discretionary voting authority because a proponent has complied with the conditions outlined above, the company would face a choice between (1) including the proposal in its proxy materials, and (2) not soliciting votes with respect to the proposal on its proxy card. If a company opts for the latter route, proponents may obtain sufficient votes to pass their proposals, particularly if the company employs a majority-of-votes-cast (as opposed to a majority-of-shares-outstanding) voting standard. Facing this possibility, companies may opt to include proposals in their proxy materials, allowing proponents to benefit from company solicitation efforts without relying on Rule 14a-8.
The SEC contends that the likelihood that companies will include such proposals in their proxy materials has increased following the agency's adoption of the universal proxy rules in 2021. The universal proxy rules allow shareholders conducting independent solicitations for proposals to include company director nominees on their proxy cards even if the shareholders do not present their own competing nominees. In these circumstances, if a company omits a proposal from its proxy materials, shareholders may be more likely to use the proponent's proxy card (which would allow them to vote on both the proposal and director nominees) than the company's card (which would not allow them to vote on the proposal). The company may thus include the proposal in its proxy materials to avoid this outcome. The SEC observes that there have been "at least three" of these "zero-slate" proxy contests since the adoption of the universal proxy rules and that, in each of those cases, the company included the shareholder proposals in its proxy materials.
To address the pressure that companies may feel to include shareholder proposals submitted outside Rule 14a-8 in their proxy materials, the SEC proposes expanding the circumstances in which companies may obtain discretionary voting authority with respect to such proposals. Under the SEC's proposed rule, a proponent's solicitation of a sufficient number of shares to carry a proposal would no longer preclude the company from obtaining discretionary voting authority with respect to the proposal. Instead, a company could exercise such authority if it (1) included in its proxy statement a brief description of the proposal and how the company intends to vote, (2) included on its proxy card a cross-reference to the location of this disclosure in its proxy statement, and (3) included on the proxy card a check box that, if checked by a shareholder, would prevent the company from exercising its discretion.
The SEC maintains that this proposed change is "aligned with" the agency's proposed rescission of Rule 14a-8 because retaining Rule 14a-4(c)(2) in its current form could effectively perpetuate the ability of proposal proponents to have their proposals included in company proxy materials even in the absence of Rule 14a-8. The NPRM also says that several of the considerations discussed above constitute independent justifications for the proposed amendments to Rule 14a-4(c) even if Rule 14a-8 is not rescinded.
The SEC's conclusion that Rule 14a-8 exceeds its legal authority raises difficult questions about the distinction between substantive regulations of corporate governance and regulations of the proxy solicitation process. In its 1990 decision in Business Roundtable v. SEC, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit relied on this distinction to hold that Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act did not empower the SEC to prohibit national securities exchanges from listing the stock of companies that reduced the per-share voting rights of existing shareholders. The court reasoned that Congress's "central concern" in enacting Section 14(a) was ensuring that solicited shareholders receive adequate disclosures. Based on this reading, the court held that Section 14(a) does not authorize the SEC to "step beyond control of voting procedure and into the distribution of voting power."
While Business Roundtable emphasized that Section 14(a) is principally concerned with disclosure, it cautioned that disclosure is not "necessarily the sole subject" of that provision. In offering this caveat, the D.C. Circuit acknowledged a provision in the proxy rules requiring proxies listing director nominees to provide a mechanism for shareholders to withhold authority to vote for each nominee individually. This provision, the court explained, "may lie in a murky area between substance and procedure" and "may be supportable as a control over management's power to set the voting agenda, or, slightly more broadly, voting procedures." Since Business Roundtable, the SEC has adopted other proxy regulations that may straddle the boundary between substance and procedure, including a rule prohibiting proxies from bundling separate matters and the universal proxy rules, which (subject to various conditions) require companies to list the director nominees of dissident shareholders on their proxy cards.
Rule 14a-8 may likewise be difficult to classify as substantive or procedural. At times, the SEC has appeared to characterize Rule 14a-8 as a regulation of disclosure and the proxy solicitation process that requires companies to include shareholder proposals in their proxy materials only if proponents have an independent state law right to present the proposals. Chairman Atkins offered a similar interpretation in an October 2025 speech, contending that "the notion that Rule 14a-8 gives shareholders the right to present precatory proposals . . . when state law does not" is not supported by the rule's text or history.
The SEC anticipates this objection in its NPRM. It responds by arguing that, with proxy voting replacing in-person voting as the "primary means of corporate suffrage," rules regarding the types of proposals that must be included in company proxy materials effectively amount to regulations of substantive voting rights. The SEC attempts to distinguish Rule 14a-8 from the universal proxy rules based on the explicit state law right of shareholders to elect directors. In contrast, the SEC contends, state law is far less clear on the issue of shareholder proposal rights, meaning Rule 14a-8 functions as a substantive regulation of voting rights in a way that the universal proxy rules do not. It is uncertain whether a court would agree that the relative clarity of state law on these issues is dispositive in applying the substance/procedure distinction.
Congress has the power to modify or clarify the SEC's authority with respect to shareholder proposals. Several bills have aimed to narrow the scope of Rule 14a-8; others would repeal it altogether. Alternatively, Congress could codify the rule and direct the SEC to resume its practice of responding to no-action requests involving shareholder proposals. Congress could also await the outcome of the SEC's rulemaking and, if Rule 14a-8 is rescinded, evaluate how states and companies respond.
title: SEC Proposes Rescission of the Shareholder Proposal Rule

NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects. With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role. I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.”
“Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions. Christina brings a unique combination of engineering expertise, operational experience, and proven leadership, both on the ground and in space. I am grateful to Katherine for her exceptional service and confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence that is essential to everything we do at NASA.”
Koch most recently served as a mission specialist aboard NASA’s Artemis II mission in April, helping carry out the first crewed flight around the Moon in more than 50 years. She previously spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, setting the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman and participating in the first all-female spacewalks.
Koch began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, developing scientific instruments for space missions. Before her selection as an astronaut in 2013, her experience also included scientific field engineering in Antarctica and the Arctic. She has since held leadership positions within NASA’s Astronaut Office and at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, bringing a combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and firsthand understanding of the demands of human spaceflight to her new role.
Van Hooser joined NASA in 1991 at the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, beginning a distinguished career in propulsion engineering and technical leadership. Her early work focused on liquid rocket engine turbomachinery before she became chief engineer for the space shuttle main engine, leading engineering efforts through the final 21 shuttle flights. She later served as the first chief engineer for the Space Launch System’s Liquid Engines Element, helping advance the propulsion systems supporting NASA’s Artemis missions.
As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs. Her steady guidance through complex engineering challenges and organizational transitions helped maintain continuity, strengthen collaboration, and keep mission readiness at the forefront of NASA’s work.

USS San Antonio (LPD 17) Returns to Norfolk from Deployment to U.S. 4th Fleet Area of Operations
NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Vir. – The first-in-class amphibious transport dock USS San Antonio (LPD 17) returned to Naval Station Norfolk, Oct. 13, 2026, concluding a dynamic deployment to the U.S. 4th Fleet area of operations.
The warship departed Norfolk on June 29, 2026, embarking Marines and loading critical relief supplies before heading south to conduct theater operations.
“I am in awe of the efforts San Antonio’s crew gave during two deployments across a little over fourteen months,” said Capt. Matt Gleason, commanding officer, USS San Antonio. “Captain Tom Uhl led this incredible team through most of this period, and I am honored to take over such a professional and lethal crew. Working alongside Marines from the 22nd Marine Expedition Expeditionary Unit and Littoral Combat Force 24, San Antonio proved the valuable combat power and flexibility that an amphibious warship provides to the Joint Force. My heartfelt thanks go out to the families and friends of this crew for supporting their dedicated loved ones.”
During the deployment, San Antonio provided disaster relief following two earthquakes in Venezuela. Operating near the epicenter in La Guaira, the warship served as the afloat command-and-control center for the U.S. Southern Command Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) element. The crew executed a mid-mission cross-deck of Littoral Combat Force 24 (LCF-24) from USS Fort Lauderdale (LPD 28) and delivered two Landing Craft Air Cushion (LCAC) loads of critical aid directly to the Venezuelan people, in coordination with the Department of State and non-governmental organizations. The warship also hosted senior military-to-military diplomatic talks aboard with Venezuelan defense leadership.
Following a brief logistics stop in Ponce, Puerto Rico, San Antonio sailed to the Pacific, marking a historic milestone as the first amphibious transport dock since 2018 to transit the Panama Canal, and the first of its class to pass through the expanded Neo-Panamax locks.
In the Eastern Pacific, the crew shifted to security and maritime interdiction operations under Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere. These actions systematically disrupted the supply networks of transnational narco-trafficking organizations, with all detained personnel safely transferred to the Ecuadorian Coast Guard.
Following its Eastern Pacific operations, San Antonio returned to the Caribbean via the Panama Canal, offloading LCF-24 Marines and equipment in Ponce.
USS San Antonio is a versatile, amphibious transport dock capable of embarking, transporting, and landing elements of a landing force. As the lead warship of her class of amphibious transport docks, equipped with an expansive well deck and flight facilities, San Antonio is designed to support expeditionary warfare, special operations, and humanitarian missions. By leveraging its landing craft and tilt-rotor aircraft capabilities, San Antonio can project power and deliver combat-ready Marines directly to shore in complex operational environments.
USS San Antonio (LPD 17) was commissioned on Jan. 14, 2006, and is named in honor of San Antonio, Texas, celebrating the city's rich military history and its enduring moniker as "Military City, USA." The naming further commemorates the historic 1836 Battle of the Alamo. Inspired by the resolute determination of Lt. Col. William B. Travis during the historic siege, the warship and her crew sail under the official command motto, “Never Retreat, Never Surrender,” carrying forward a legacy of unyielding courage and service to the nation.
Commander, Naval Surface Force Atlantic is responsible for manning, training, and equipping assigned surface forces and shore activities, ensuring a capable and combat-ready force to support U.S. national interests. The SURFLANT force consists of more than 66 warships and 34 shore commands.
For more information about SURFLANT, visit Facebook.com/SURFLANT or http://www.surflant.usff.navy.mil.

Texas Return Preparer Pleads Guilty to Conspiring to Defraud the United States
A Texas man pleaded guilty on September 17, 2026, for his role in a tax refund fraud conspiracy that sought to obtain more than $35 million in fraudulent refunds through the filing of false tax returns.
According to court documents, Marquis Al Bey, of Forney, Texas, owned and operated Creative Associates, Inc., a tax return preparation business that advertised that it was located in North Carolina. Through Creative Associates, Bey prepared tax returns for clients, including clients located in Maryland, that sought large tax refunds that the individuals and entities listed on the returns were not entitled to receive. Bey charged clients for his tax return preparation services and, in some cases, required that clients agree to pay him a percentage of any resulting refund.
As part of his plea, Bey admitted to preparing seven false returns between 2017 and 2021 for his co-defendant and another individual in Maryland that collectively sought more than $35 million from the Internal Revenue Service. Two of those returns resulted in the IRS issuing refunds totaling more than $10 million to Bey’s clients. Bey received a 10% share of these proceeds. Bey used a portion of these funds to purchase a home in Texas.
In December 2023, a grand jury in Maryland returned a superseding indictment charging Bey and his codefendant with multiple offenses related to their refund fraud scheme, including conspiracy to defraud the United States, aiding and assisting in the preparation of false tax returns, and theft of government funds.
Bey’s sentencing is set for January 22, 2027. Bey faces up to five years in prison, as well as a term of supervised release and monetary penalties.
A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. As part of his plea, Bey has agreed to pay restitution to the IRS in the amount of $3,145,598.21.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case.
Trial Attorneys Melissa Siskind and Emerson Gordon-Marvin of the National Fraud Enforcement Division are prosecuting this case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Texas Return Preparer Pleads Guilty to Conspiring to Defraud the United States
