Congress typically considers 12 distinct appropriations measures on an annual basis to fund federal programs and activities. Between FY2008 and FY2025, one of these measures was the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS) appropriations. Beginning in FY2026, Congress retitled this measure as the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs (NSRP) appropriations. The measure includes funding for U.S. diplomatic activities; cultural exchanges; development, security, and humanitarian assistance; and participation in multilateral organizations, among other international activities. For FY2027, the Trump Administration is requesting $37.79 billion in new budget authority for NSRP accounts. This funding level, if enacted, would be 26.8% less than what Congress provided for FY2026. When including proposed rescissions of certain prior-year balances, the FY2027 request totals $35.51 billion, a 29.1% decrease from the FY2026 enacted NSRP level.
As with previous budget requests and annual SFOPS/NSRP appropriations measures, the budget request is divided into two main components:
On July 15, 2026, the House passed a FY2027 NSRP bill, H.R. 8595. If enacted, the bill would provide $49.21 billion in new budget authority for NSRP accounts, or a net total of $47.37 billion when including rescissions of prior year budget authority.
On September 2, 2026, the President signed into law P.L. 119-103, a continuing resolution (CR) to fund federal government agencies in FY2027, largely at FY2026 levels, through December 11, 2026.
Table A-1 provides an account-by-account comparison of the FY2027 request and reported legislation with FY2026 and FY2025 enacted funding levels. Table A-2 offers a similar comparison focused specifically on the International Affairs budget (Function 150). Figure A-1 depicts the International Affairs budget account structure.
This report tracks NSRP budget requests and appropriations, comparing funding levels for component accounts and purposes. It does not provide extensive analysis of international affairs policy issues. For in-depth analysis and contextual information on international affairs issues, consult the wide range of CRS reports on specific subjects, such as human rights, diplomatic security, and U.S. participation in the United Nations. For more information on NSRP accounts, see CRS Report R48939, National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations: A Guide to Component Accounts.
Annual National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs (NSRP)—previously Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS)—appropriations support a range of U.S. activities around the world.1 These include the operation of U.S. embassies, diplomatic activities, foreign assistance, U.S. participation in multilateral organizations, and U.S. export promotion activities, among others. The NSRP appropriation closely aligns with the International Affairs budget function (150), which typically represents about 1% of the annual federal budget.2
For FY2027, the Trump Administration is requesting $37.79 billion for NSRP appropriations accounts, or $35.51 billion when including proposed rescissions (see Figure 1). When compared to enacted FY2026 NSRP appropriations, this total would represent a 29.1% decrease. As with its FY2026 proposal, the Administration is not requesting emergency funding for NSRP accounts.3
On July 15, 2026, the House passed a FY2027 NSRP bill, H.R. 8595. If enacted, the bill would provide $49.21 billion in new budget authority for NSRP accounts, or a net of $47.37 billion when including rescissions of prior year budget authority. This amount would be 5.4% lower than the FY2026 enacted total for NSRP and 33.4% higher than the President's proposal.
On September 2, 2026, the President signed into law P.L. 119-103, a continuing resolution (CR) to fund federal government agencies in FY2027, largely at FY2026 levels, through December 11, 2026. Members of Congress may still proceed with consideration of FY2027 NSRP appropriations in various ways. The Senate could introduce and move its version of an NSRP bill through committee and floor consideration, a conference committee could resolve differences between that and the House-passed measure, and the resulting legislation could then be considered and ultimately passed by both chambers before moving to the President for signature. It is also possible that the Senate could consider H.R. 8595; the two chambers then might exchange amendments until both pass the identical legislation before moving it to the President for signature.4 Alternatively, NSRP legislation may be added to an omnibus or minibus appropriations package negotiated outside of the Appropriations Committee process. Congress also may include NSRP in further CRs when the current one expires in December, to fund some or all federal agencies at FY2026 levels for a longer period, or all, of FY2027. Congress also may allow appropriations to lapse, leading to a full or partial government shutdown.
As Congress deliberates further action, it might consider the following:
The Department of State and Related Agency title includes appropriations accounts for the State Department's management functions and many non-foreign assistance programs. Such functions and programs include most Foreign Service and Civil Service personnel salaries, passport and visa services, diplomatic security and embassy construction, and U.S. assessed contributions (membership dues) to international organizations and international peacekeeping missions. Congress also funds the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM) in Title I through the International Broadcasting Operations (IBO) and Broadcasting Capital Improvements (BCI) accounts. For FY2027, the Trump Administration proposed a new Title I account, called International Communications Activities, to sustain USAGM statutory functions and language services while "consolidating and coordinating Federal international communications activities under the [State Department's] leadership."5 The Administration did not request any FY2027 funding for IBO or BCI.
The Trump Administration's FY2027 request for the Title I accounts totals $13.24 billion, or 20.4% less than the $16.63 billion Congress provided for these accounts in FY2026. Figure 2 provides additional detail regarding the Trump Administration's Title I funding priorities. For a full listing of the Title I accounts and recent proposed and enacted funding levels, see Table A-1.
House Legislation. If enacted, H.R. 8595 would provide $15.15 billion for the Title I appropriations accounts. This funding level is 8.9% less than the FY2026 enacted level and is 14.4% higher than the Administration's FY2027 request.
The Human Resources category of the Diplomatic Programs (DP) appropriation within Title 1 funds salaries for around two-thirds of State Department Foreign and Civil Service employees, the National Foreign Affairs Training Center (NFATC) tasked with training foreign affairs personnel across the U.S. government, and State Department Bureau of Human Resources operating costs.6 The Administration is requesting $3.71 billion for Human Resources funding for FY2027, which totals 6.9% less than the $3.99 billion Congress provided for this category in FY2026.7 The Administration notes that this request reflects the State Department's FY2025 reorganization, which resulted in the reduction of 1,680 DP-funded positions (1,506 Civil Service positions and 174 Foreign Service positions) through the Deferred Resignation Program and Reductions in Force, as well as approximately 400 new personnel hired in FY2025 to transition certain USAID functions to the State Department (see Table 1).8
Source: State Department (Biden Administration), Global Talent Management Fact Sheet As of 9/30/2024; State Department, FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification Appendix 1: U.S. Department of State Diplomatic Engagement, pp. 10-11.
Notes: CRS pulled the FY2025 Estimate data from a fact sheet the Biden Administration published that reflected onboard personnel as of September 30, 2024. According to the State Department's FY2027 congressional budget justification, FY2026 Estimate data reflect actual onboard personnel as of October 31, 2025.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595 includes $4.00 billion for the DP Human Resources funding category, which totals 0.4% more than the FY2026 enacted level and 7.8% more than the Administration's FY2027 request. The bill does not specify the number of Civil Service and Foreign Service positions this funding level would support.
Congress established the Consular and Border Security Programs (CBSP) account in 2017 and directed the State Department to deposit collected consular fees and surcharges into this account to expend on consular services, including passport and visa processing.9 While fees the State Department deposits into CBSP primarily fund the Bureau of Consular Affairs (CA), some fees are allocated to other bureaus that support CA's operations. The State Department is not authorized to expend passport application and execution fees (PAEF) unless Congress provides annual budget authority.10 For FY2027, the Administration is requesting authority to spend $533.0 million in PAEF collections.11 The State Department projects that it will spend a total of $5.62 billion in consular fees, most of which do not require annual budget authority, to support consular programs and services in FY2027, which totals 1.7% more than the estimated $5.52 billion in estimated expenditures for FY2026.12 Priorities the State Department intends to fund through fee expenditures include recruiting, training, and paying of salaries for the consular workforce; expanding passport services for U.S. citizens through the construction of six new passport agencies across the United States; and implementing the Administration's visa and passport fraud prevention policies.13
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide the State Department $533.0 million in budget authority to expend PAEF collections. This figure is identical to the Administration's request.
The Worldwide Security Protection (WSP) allocation within the DP account and the Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance (ESCM) account are also known as the NSRP "diplomatic security accounts." WSP is the primary operating appropriation for the Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DS), the State Department's federal law enforcement and security arm responsible for securing hundreds of U.S. diplomatic facilities around the world and protecting more than 70,000 U.S. government personnel from over 25 federal agencies operating overseas.14 WSP also funds security-related functions for nine other State Department bureaus.15 ESCM is the primary operating appropriation for the Bureau of Overseas Buildings Operations (OBO). OBO is responsible for the "planning, acquisition, design, construction, operations, maintenance, and disposal of U.S. governmental diplomatic and consular property overseas."16 Congress has long provided budget authority for both WSP and ESCM on either a multi-year or no-year basis. Such action allows the State Department to retain unobligated funds for several years after the fiscal year for which they were appropriated or, in the case of no-year appropriations, indefinitely. Therefore, the annual appropriation Congress provides for WSP and ESCM constitutes only a share of all available funding for these accounts at any point in time (see Figure 3).
For FY2027, the Trump Administration is requesting a combined $6.11 billion for the diplomatic security accounts, which totals 5.8% more than the funding Congress provided for these accounts in FY2026 (see Table 2). For WSP, the Administration's request reflects priorities such as modernizing DS's counterintelligence, insider risk, and facility security capabilities, along with establishing a permanent U.S. presence in both Syria and Libya.17 For ESCM, the request includes $1.03 billion in funding for the Capital Security Cost Sharing (CSCS) and Maintenance Cost Sharing (MCS) programs, which fund the construction, replacement, renovation, and maintenance of U.S. overseas posts. When accounting for further contributions from consular fees and other agencies with personnel assigned to U.S. embassies and other overseas posts, the Administration's total request for these programs is $2.22 billion.18 This request slightly exceeds the estimated $2.21 billion FY2026 funding level for CSCS/MCS.19
Table 2. Diplomatic Security and Embassy Construction Funding: FY2025-FY2027
(In millions of current U.S. dollars; includes emergency funds)
Sources: P.L. 118-47; P.L. 119-4; P.L. 119-75; State Department, FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification Appendix 1: U.S. Department of State Diplomatic Engagement; H.R. 8595, as passed by the House.
Notes: Figures exclude $224 million rescission provided for Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance in FY2025 pursuant to Section 7075(a) of P.L. 118-47, as carried forward by P.L. 119-4.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide $6.15 billion for the diplomatic security accounts, totaling 6.6% more than the FY2026 enacted level and 0.7% more than the Administration's FY2027 request. H.R. 8595 would make $1.04 billion of these funds available for the CSCS/MCS programs. When combined with additional funding from consular fees and anticipated program contributions from other agencies, available FY2027 resources for CSCS/MCS would total $2.23 billion.20 This figure is 0.6% more than the Administration's FY2027 request.
The Contributions to International Organizations (CIO) account traditionally has funded the United States' payments of its annual assessed contributions (membership dues) to over 40 international organizations (IOs). These include the United Nations (UN), UN specialized agencies (such as the Food and Agriculture Organization and World Health Organization), and regional entities (such as NATO).21 Separately, the United States has paid its assessed contributions to UN peacekeeping missions through the Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities (CIPA) account. The United States also has provided additional funding to IOs through various NSRP humanitarian and multilateral assistance accounts.
Like the FY2026 request, the FY2027 request seeks to eliminate funding for the UN regular budget; certain UN affiliated agencies; and all UN peacekeeping.22 For CIO, the Administration requested $292.42 million, which totals 78.9% less than the FY2026 funding level of $1.39 billion for this account. The request would eliminate funding for the CIPA account; Congress enacted $1.23 billion for CIPA for FY2026 (see CIO and CIPA in Table A-1).
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide a combined $799.7 million for CIO and CIPA, totaling a 69.5% reduction from the FY2026 funding level and a 173.5% increase from the FY2027 request. For CIO, the bill does not include any funding to the UN regular budget and would prohibit funds to the World Health Organization. With regard to CIPA, the bill would give the Secretary of State discretion to support missions that are aligned with U.S. national security interests, while withholding funds from missions "that are ineffective or associated with repeated cases of sexual abuse."23
Title II of the NSRP bill has undergone changes since FY2025, primarily related to the Trump Administration's dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).24 Through FY2025 appropriations, Title II was titled "U.S. Agency for International Development" and provided funding for USAID's administrative accounts, including the Operating Expenses (OE), Capital Investment Fund, and Office of Inspector General (OIG) accounts. For FY2026, Congress changed the title to "Administration of Assistance" and appropriated $112.0 million for the Operating Expenses account and $62.5 million for the Office of Inspector General. For FY2027, the Administration is not requesting funding for Title II accounts.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would rename Title II "Oversight of Diplomatic Engagement and Foreign Assistance" and provide nearly $186.1 million for the Offices of Inspector General. This would shift funding for the State Department's Office of Inspector General from Title I, where it has traditionally been, and instead combine it with that of the Inspector General responsible for overseeing foreign assistance programs.
The bilateral economic assistance title typically provides funding for bilateral foreign assistance programs (excluding security assistance), independent agencies, and select Department of the Treasury international programs. For FY2027, the Administration is requesting $15.75 billion in new budget authority for Title III accounts. If enacted, this level would be a reduction of 32.6% from the FY2026 enacted level.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide $22.45 billion for Title III accounts. This total is 42.5% higher than the President's request and 3.9% lower than the FY2026 enacted level.
The non-health economic and development assistance accounts in Title III typically provide funding for programs across sectors such as democracy and governance, agriculture and food security, basic and higher education, and energy and the environment, among others. For FY2026, Congress made changes to these accounts by (1) establishing the National Security Investment Programs (NSIP) account, which combined the authorities of the prior Development Assistance, Economic Support Fund, and Assistance for Europe, Eurasia, and Central Asia accounts; and (2) eliminating funding for the Transition Initiatives and Complex Crises Fund accounts.
For FY2027, the Administration is proposing $5.00 billion for an America First Opportunity Fund (A1OF), which would essentially hold the same authorities as NSIP. The Administration is not requesting funding for the Democracy Fund (DF) account, noting that "programs previously funded through this account could be funded through the America First Opportunity Fund" (see Figure 4).25
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would maintain the FY2026 accounts, providing $6.89 billion for NSIP and $205.2 million for DF. Consistent with the FY2026 NSRP Act, the House legislation includes a provision in the General Provisions that would make available up to $1.50 billion in certain Title III and Title IV funds for the A1OF.26 The report accompanying the bill directs $750.0 million in NSIP for the A1OF.27
Title III humanitarian assistance accounts provide for relief for disaster-struck nations, emergency food assistance, refugee assistance and protection activities, and resettlement of refugees, among other activities. For FY2026, in line with the President's request, Congress established the International Humanitarian Assistance (IHA) account, combining the authorities of the prior International Disaster Assistance (IDA) and Migration and Refugee Assistance (MRA) accounts, and provided funding for the Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance (ERMA) account. For FY2027, the Administration is requesting funds for those same two accounts: $4.00 billion for IHA and $500.0 million for ERMA (see Figure 5).
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide $5.00 billion for IHA and $100.0 million for ERMA.
The Global Health Programs (GHP) account typically funds a range of health assistance activities. Congress directs funds for specific health programs in a GHP subaccount allocation table in the joint explanatory statement or report(s) accompanying the legislation. For FY2027, the Administration is requesting $5.12 billion for GHP (see Table 3). The Administration does not include requests for subaccounts. The Administration asserts it would invest in programs that align with its America First Global Health Strategy and the bilateral Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) it is pursuing, and that "[t]he Request provides the Secretary with greater flexibility to program global health assistance based on outcomes of negotiations with partner governments and the specific needs of countries and their unique disease burdens."28
Sources: P.L. 118-47; P.L. 119-4; P.L. 119-28; P.L. 119-75; State Department, FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs; H.R. 8595; H.Rept. 119-631.
Notes: n.a. = not applicable; dash (-) indicates no funding or not specified.
a. The FY2027 request does not provide subaccount levels.
b. The report accompanying the House bill does not specify a funding level for Family Planning/Reproductive Health. Section 7058 of the bill would set a $461 million ceiling on funding for reproductive health and voluntary family planning programs funded by the act.
c. Includes funding for Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs).
d. The report accompanying the House bill does not provide a specific level for Global Health Security. It notes that, "The Committee supports continued efforts to promote global health security, address emerging health threats overseas, and prevent future pandemics, including support to strengthen laboratory and surveillance capabilities."
e. The rescission enacted in P.L. 119-28 did not indicate from which subaccounts unobligated balances would be rescinded.
f. Subaccount allocations provided in H.Rept. 119-631 do not sum to the total.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide a total of $8.88 billion for GHP. Consistent with prior years, the report accompanying the legislation includes allocations for subaccounts.
For FY2026, in addition to its appropriations for the four, long-standing independent agencies—the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), Peace Corps, Inter-American Foundation (IAF), and U.S. Africa Development Foundation (USADF)—Congress included an appropriation for the new U.S. Foundation for Natural Security and Counterterrorism. For FY2027, the Administration proposes funding for the MCC and Peace Corps, and seeks to eliminate funding for IAF, USADF, and U.S. Foundation for Natural Security and Counterterrorism. For Treasury accounts, the Administration requests funding at similar levels to the FY2026 appropriation. For account-level details, see Table A-1.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide level funding for the Millennium Challenge Corporation, Peace Corps, and U.S. Foundation for Natural Security and Counterterrorism when compared to FY2026. Consistent with the President's request, it would eliminate funding for IAF and USADF. For Treasury accounts, the House measure would eliminate funding for Debt Restructuring, noting that "The Committee includes transfer authority for such purpose under the Treasury International Assistance Programs account [in Title V]."29
The five security assistance accounts have remained consistent across recent budget cycles. For FY2027, however, the Administration has proposed renaming the Peacekeeping Operations (PKO) account to be the National Security Engagement Assistance (NSEA) account. The Administration also seeks to reduce funding for that account by 92.0% when compared to the FY2026 enacted level. This would represent the steepest proposed reduction to any of the Title IV accounts (see Figure 6).
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would rename PKO to be the Security Sector Programs (SSP) account and reduce its funding by 29.9% when compared to the FY2026 PKO enacted level. Funding amounts provided for the other four accounts would be level with, or higher than, FY2026 enacted amounts.
For Title V, the Trump Administration proposes $1.21 billion for FY2027 for contributions to various multilateral entities (for account-level details, see Table A-1). This total, if enacted, would be a reduction of 35.5% from FY2026 enacted levels. The Administration asserts that such a reduction seeks to "return the World Bank, International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the rest of the international financial institutions (IFIs) to their core missions to spur poverty reduction and economic growth, and build and preserve economic stability" while also maintaining American leadership at such institutions.30 When compared to the FY2026 NSRP law, a significant change proposed for FY2027 is the zeroing out of both the International Organizations and Programs (IO&P) and Global Environment Facility accounts.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595, if enacted, would provide 25.7% less than the Administration's request for Title V accounts. Like the request, it would eliminate funding for IO&P. However, while the bill would fund the Global Environment Facility, it would provide reduced funding, compared to the request, for the International Development Association, African Development Bank, and International Fund for Agricultural Development.
Title VI typically provides funding for three agencies: the Export-Import Bank of the United States (Ex-Im Bank), the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), and the U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA).31 For Ex-Im and DFC, offsetting collections are meant to reduce each agency's budgetary impact. For FY2027, the Administration is proposing $277.5 million for these agencies, inclusive of offsetting collections. When compared to FY2026 enacted appropriations, the Ex-Im operating budget would more than double under the request (from $153.9 million to $357.6 million), while DFC and USTDA's operating and program budgets would be reduced by 18.3% and 11.5%, respectively.
House Legislation. H.R. 8595 would provide a total of $887.3 million for the Title VI agencies, inclusive of offsetting collections. Olszewski and McBride Introduce ASSURE Act to Expand Voter Registration Opportunities
(Washington, DC) – Maryland Congressman Johnny Olszewski today introduced the ASSURE Act to expand opportunities for eligible Americans to register to vote ahead of this year’s midterm elections. The bill would embed voter registration into everyday interactions with the federal government. Delaware Congresswoman Sarah McBride joined Olszewski as an original co-sponsor of the legislation. 
With the midterm elections just weeks away, voter registration deadlines are fast approaching across the country. In Maryland, the deadline to register is today, October 13. 
“As a government teacher, I spent years teaching my students that democracy only works when people participate in it,” said Congressman Olszewski. “That participation requires something basic: making sure people can register to vote and have their voices heard. If someone is interacting with their government to access veterans benefits, Social Security, or another federal service, we should use that opportunity to make sure they know how to register to vote.”
“Access to the ballot box should be a basic promise of our democracy, not a privilege that depends on who occupies the White House,” said Congresswoman McBride. “The ASSURE Act puts that principle into practice by restoring voter registration opportunities that President Trump has rolled back and ensuring Americans have access to reliable election information. At a moment when this administration continues to undermine voting rights, particularly for Black Americans and communities of color, this work is more urgent than ever. I’m grateful to Rep. Olszewski for his leadership on this legislation, and I’ll keep fighting to ensure every eligible voter can make their voice heard.”
The ASSURE Act – short for the Agency Support for Secure and Universal Registration Enhancement Act – codifies a Biden-era executive order, later reversed by President Trump, that directed federal agencies to integrate voter registration opportunities into services Americans already use. It also restores a longstanding policy – also reversed by President Trump – that permits nonpartisan groups to provide voter registration assistance and civic participation information at naturalization ceremonies for new Americans.
Together, these measures would give eligible Americans more opportunities to register without having to seek out a separate government office, website, or registration event.
Olszewski has made expanding civic participation and strengthening democratic institutions a central focus of his work in Congress. He has also supported legislation to make Election Day a national holiday and require states to offer same-day voter registration.
“We should make it easier for eligible Americans to participate in our democracy – not put up unnecessary barriers,” Congressman Olszewski said. “The ASSURE Act is a simple idea: meet people where they are, make registration easier, and make our democracy more accessible to everyone who is eligible to participate.”
title: Olszewski and McBride Introduce ASSURE Act to Expand Voter Registration Opportunities

Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI
An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.
“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”
“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”
“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”
According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.
Recording Device 1
Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.
According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.
The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:
Image of Alfozan
Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.
The FBI is investigating the case.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker for the Northern District of California is prosecuting the case with valuable assistance from Trial Attorney Kate Tagert of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.
This prosecution is in support of National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) designed to support American superiority in super intelligence technology.
title: Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI

BOSTON – A Dominican national unlawfully residing in Salem, Mass. has been charged with illegally reentering the United States after deportation. The defendant was previously removed on two occasions.

Newton Persido Ortiz Santana, 41, was charged with one count of unlawful reentry of a deported alien. Ortiz Santana will be arraigned in federal court in Boston on Oct. 20, 2026.

According to the charging documents, Ortiz Santana, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, was first deported from San Antonio, Texas to the Dominican Republic in January 2010. In September 2021, Ortiz Santana was encountered by Border Patrol agents near Penitas, Texas. He subsequently pleaded guilty to unlawfully re-entering the United States and was again removed from the United States in December 2021.

It is alleged that, at an unknown place and time thereafter, Ortiz Santana re-entered the United States. On Nov. 8, 2024, Ortiz Santana was arrested and charged in Salem, Mass., with negligent operation of a vehicle and operating after suspension. Immigration authorities learned of Ortiz Santana’s unlawful presence in the United States later that day as the result of a biometric fingerprint match.

On March 20, 2025, federal immigration agents attempted to arrest Ortiz Santana. It is alleged that Ortiz Santana evaded capture by accelerating directly towards a law enforcement vehicle, driving through multiple stop signs and fleeing at a high rate of speed using the sidewalk. He was taken into custody on May 29, 2026.

The charge of illegal reentry provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director, Boston, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Massachusetts State Police. Assistant U.S. Attorney Craig Estes of the Criminal Division is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: Illegal Alien Charged with Unlawful Reentry

Neguse, Bennet, Hickenlooper Urge Federal Agencies to Restore Cell Service in Boulder County
Lafayette, CO — Following recent reports of unacceptable cellular service issues across Boulder County, Congressman Joe Neguse and Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper penned a letter to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) urging the agencies to meet with cellular carriers immediately and resolve the issues.
The three major cellular carriers apparently limited their Boulder County coverage earlier this year to comply with federal signal transmission rules surrounding the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone north of Boulder. These federal signal limits protect ongoing research at several government agencies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the U.S. Geological Survey.
“We write to urge your agencies to assist in resolving major reported cellular network outages in Boulder County, Colorado, following signal adjustments made to comply with National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) regulations protecting the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone,” wrote Neguse, Bennet, and Hickenlooper.
The lawmakers also pressed the NTIA and FCC to find a collaborative solution that will quickly address community concerns, particularly preserving access to cellular coverage as a vital public safety resource.
“Full cell phone coverage is indispensable to everyday life. When people leave their homes, they expect to be able to use their cell phones for navigation, payment, and communication with others. Cell phones are also vital for public safety in Boulder County, which is prone to rapidly escalating wildfires.”
They concluded with a call for swift solutions and asked that the FCC and NTIA keep congressional offices and local governments updated on the outcome of the requested meeting and progress toward restoring full connectivity.
“[W]e respectfully request that FCC and NTIA officials meet with carriers immediately in order to find a solution that will allow them to restore functional cellular service to their customers as soon as possible. We also request that you update our offices and local governments on the outcome of that meeting and report back to us on your progress as all parties work to restore full connectivity,” the lawmakers concluded.
Read the full letter HERE and below:
October 13, 2026
The Honorable Brendan Carr
Chairman
Federal Communications Commission
45 L Street NE
Washington, DC 20554
The Honorable Arielle Roth
Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information
Administrator, National Telecommunications and Information Administration
1401 Constitution Avenue NW
Washington, DC 20230
Dear Chairman Carr and Assistant Secretary Roth,
We write to urge your agencies to assist in resolving major reported cellular network outages in Boulder County, Colorado, following signal adjustments made to comply with National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) regulations protecting the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone.
As we understand it, in late 2024, the NTIA Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) notified three major cellular carriers that they needed to modify their signals received within the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone, the 50-mile radius where federal regulations limit radio transmission frequency that could otherwise interfere with the research of the ITS, National Institute of Standards and Technology, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and U.S. Geological Survey. The three major carriers have publicly stated that they have since adjusted their signals to comply with Table Mountain frequency limits.
However, these signal adjustments appear to have significantly downgraded cellular network coverage for Boulder County consumers. Our constituents in the nearby towns of Longmont and Niwot have filed more than 100 formal complaints with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) reporting that they cannot make phone calls or use data on their cell phones, even when their devices indicate full network coverage. While the three major carriers have publicly indicated they will further upgrade their networks to compensate for the necessary signal reductions, our constituents lack vital cell connectivity in the interim.
Full cell phone coverage is indispensable to everyday life. When people leave their homes, they expect to be able to use their cell phones for navigation, payment, and communication with others. Cell phones are also vital for public safety in Boulder County, which is prone to rapidly escalating wildfires. Our constituents use their cell phones to notify their families and friends that they are safe during wildfire season and to warn neighbors of unpredictable wildfire shifts. For example, the 2021 Marshall Fire, which killed two people and burned nearly 1,000 structures, progressed so rapidly that many residents would not have known to immediately evacuate had they not been alerted by a phone call or text from someone they knew.
Given all of the foregoing, we respectfully request that FCC and NTIA officials meet with carriers immediately in order to find a solution that will allow them to restore functional cellular service to their customers as soon as possible. We also request that you update our offices and local governments on the outcome of that meeting and report back to us on your progress as all parties work to restore full connectivity.
Sincerely,
###
title: Neguse, Bennet, Hickenlooper Urge Federal Agencies to Restore Cell Service in Boulder County

ASHLAND, Ky. – A Martha, Ky., man, Josh Ferguson, 42, was sentenced on Tuesday to 5 years’ probation, with 12 months of home detention and electronic monitoring, and a $20,000 fine by Chief U.S. District Judge David Bunning for knowingly discharging waste product into waters of the United States.

According to his plea agreement, in the fall of 2025, the Kentucky Department of Environmental Protection (“Kentucky DEP”) received a tip about the discharge of “brine water,” a waste product of oil production, into the Left Fork Blaine Creek in Lawrence County. On September 3, 2025, a Kentucky DEP inspector investigated the site where Ferguson owned two oil production wells. A hose connected to a metal brine tank ran through a field to the Left Fork Blaine Creek, where it was actively discharging waste product into the waterway. Downstream of the discharge, the water was orange with no signs of life, and water samples indicated extremely elevated chloride levels. When interviewed by the Kentucky DEP inspector, Ferguson admitted that he had been discharging brine water into the creek in order to save money, that he did not have a permit to do so, and that the conduct had been ongoing for two years. The Left Fork Blaine Creek is a water of the United States.

Jason Parman, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Kentucky and Anthony R. Hatton, Commissioner, Kentucky Department of Environmental Protection, jointly announced the sentence.

The investigation was conducted by SA Ryan Baker with the EPA-CID and Kentucky Department of Environmental Protection. Assistant U.S. Attorney Emily Greenfield prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States.

– END –
title: Lawrence County Man Sentenced for Water Pollution

text:
Ocasio-Cortez, McClain Delaney, Beyer, Mfume, Subramanyam, and Elfreth Lead Calls to Pause FAA’s AI Tool at Washington-Area Airports
Press Release
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), April McClain Delaney (MD-06), Don Beyer (VA-08), Kweisi Mfume (MD-07), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), and Sarah Elfreth (MD-03) are leading a congressional letter urging the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause use of its new artificial intelligence-enabled air traffic management tool until the agency answers questions about safety testing, implementation, and oversight.
The letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford raises concerns about the September 21 deployment of the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) tool at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport, and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport.
“Last month, the Federal Aviation Administration surprisingly launched an AI tool to help control air traffic over three major National Capital Region Airports, with plans to expand nationwide in the following 90 days. They did so without publishing a safety evaluation or sufficiently consulting air traffic controllers and safety experts. We are urging Transportation Secretary Duffy and FAA Administrator Bedford to stop the rollout until we have answers. This administration may treat Big Tech companies with impunity, but air traffic control leaves zero margin for error,” said Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
“When Maryland families board a plane, they deserve to know that every system guiding their flight has been thoroughly tested and that the people keeping them safe have the training they need,” said Congresswoman McClain Delaney. “After the devastating crash over DCA that took 67 lives, the FAA owes this region answers. I support modernizing our aviation systems, but passenger safety must come first. I’m calling on the FAA to pause this rollout, show us the safety testing, and explain who is accountable when something goes wrong.”
The FAA’s rush to deploy a system that could affect the lives of millions of Americans is especially concerning for residents of this region, who are still grappling with questions about air safety following last year’s fatal crash at DCA. Before deploying its AI-enabled SMART air traffic control tool, the FAA must demonstrate, through air traffic controller feedback and independently verified testing, that this technology is safe and reliable, and it must clearly communicate those findings to the public,” said Congressman Don Beyer.
"Families across Baltimore count on BWI to get them where they’re going safely. Yet the Trump Administration recklessly rolled out an untested AI air traffic tool there without publishing a safety evaluation or adequately consulting the air traffic controllers who keep us safe. There is no room for error in our skies. I am proud to co-lead this letter calling for public transparency and answers from Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford on how this system was tested, who was consulted, and how it will be evaluated. Until they provide answers that ensure that this technology is safe, the FAA must pause its use," said Congressman Kweisi Mfume.
“The airspace in the DC region is incredibly complicated and demands the highest standard of safety and reliability from Air Traffic Control. We need to be extremely cautious about implementing AI tools into the systems responsible for the safety of our skies. I urge the FAA to prove that the system does not pose a risk to the public before allowing its use," said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam.
“Every day, our airports and their staff ensure tens of thousands of worldwide travelers are safe and secure – including here at the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport in Maryland’s Third District. While we fully recognize the need to modernize our air traffic control systems, we cannot pursue modernization at the expense of public safety, especially when it comes to implementing new technologies like AI,” said Congresswoman Elfreth. “As AI safety concerns are top of mind for our neighbors, this is another instance where we cannot afford to miss the moment on regulating this technology. I also am determined to continue to work with my colleagues to ensure our hardworking air traffic controllers have every resource they need to do their jobs and ensure the safety of our passengers.”
At a time when AI safety concerns are sky high, the lawmakers warn that the FAA has not provided sufficient transparency around its decision-making process prior to deployment, nor the functioning of SMART’s underlying AI systems. Congress, and the public, deserve to know how AI systems were tested and how they will influence decisions before being deployed in safety critical systems.
The letter also raises concerns about reports that frontline aviation safety workers received only days of notice, or no notice at all, before deployment. With air traffic controllers already facing staffing pressures, the lawmakers stress that new technology must be introduced with adequate training and clear procedures for human oversight.
The lawmakers request answers in three areas:
- Safety testing: What evaluations were completed before deployment, how the system performs during severe weather or outages, and whether any safety review requirements were waived during the contracting process.
- Consultation and training: What input the FAA sought from airport authorities, air safety workers, and airlines; what training personnel received; and how the tool should influence decision-making.
- Evaluation and accountability: How the FAA will measure performance during the initial 90-day evaluation, what standards must be met before nationwide expansion, and who is responsible if a recommendation contributes to a safety incident.
The letter calls for a pause until lawmakers can better understand the FAA’s decision-making, rollout process, and evaluation plan. The co-leads emphasize that modernizing air traffic control must prioritize safety, transparency, and the expertise of the people responsible for keeping our skies safe.
###
title: Ocasio-Cortez, McClain Delaney, Beyer, Mfume, Subramanyam, and Elfreth Lead Calls to Pause FAA’s AI Tool at Washington-Area Airports

Sánchez, House Democratic colleagues oppose rule denying legal immigrants tax credits
WASHINGTON – Congresswoman Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.) led her House Democratic colleagues today in calling on the Trump administration to withdraw a proposed IRS rule that would strip certain legal immigrants of refundable tax credits.
The rule would reclassify these credits as “Federal public benefits” under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA), imposing strict citizenship requirements on recipients. It is similar to a failed attempt by the Department of Health and Human Services last year to block certain legal immigrants from health services, an effort the courts struck down.
“The rules regarding the eligibility criteria for refundable tax credits are clearly defined by Congress in the Internal Revenue Code, and PRWORA was clearly never intended to separately address them,” the members wrote. “Yet, this proposed regulation would strip hundreds of thousands of people of their deserved tax refunds by redefining refundable tax credits as ‘Federal public benefits’ under PRWORA, harming our constituents, their families, and our communities.”
The members continued, “The administration’s apparent desire to change the law to attack immigrant communities does not change Congress’s intent when it passed PRWORA, nor does it change the law.”
In addition to Sánchez, the letter was signed by Representatives Mike Thompson (D-Calif.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), Gwen Moore (D-Wis.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.), Danny Davis (D-Ill.), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.)
The full text of the letter is available HERE and follows:
October 7, 2026
Honorable Frank Bisignano 
Chief Executive Officer
U.S. Internal Revenue Service
1111 Constitution Avenue NW
Washington, DC 20224
Honorable Scott Bessent
Secretary
U.S. Department of the Treasury 
1500 Pennsylvania Ave, NW 
Washington, DC 20220
Dear Secretary Bessent and CEO Bisignano,
We write to express our strong opposition to the proposed rule on the Application of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) to the Refunded Portion of Certain Federal Refundable Tax Credits. The rules regarding the eligibility criteria for refundable tax credits are clearly defined by Congress in the Internal Revenue Code, and PRWORA was clearly never intended to separately address them. Yet, this proposed regulation would strip hundreds of thousands of people of their deserved tax refunds by redefining refundable tax credits as “Federal public benefits” under PRWORA, harming our constituents, their families, and our communities.
Congress has modified these credits since PRWORA was enacted (most recently in Public Law 119-21 (2025)) but never made the changes Treasury proposes in this rule. Therefore, Congress clearly did not intend to import PRWORA’s limits on eligibility for federal public benefits into these refundable tax credits. In fact, Congress’s decision in P.L. 119-21 to limit the American Opportunity Tax Credit to people with a valid Social Security number would be nonsensical under Treasury’s reading of the statute, because those without one would have already been excluded. The Congressional Budget Office would not have estimated this provision to reduce the deficit by $247 million had the assertions in this proposed rule been accurate. Similarly, Congress’s decision in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2018) to limit Child Tax Credit eligibility to people with a valid Social Security number would not have made sense if PRWORA already imposed a much stricter interpretation.
The administration’s apparent desire to change the law to attack immigrant communities does not change Congress’s intent when it passed PRWORA, nor does it change the law. As the notice of rulemaking states, “Section 401(c)(1)(B) of PRWORA (8 U.S.C. 1611(c)(1)(B)) defines the term “Federal public benefit,” in relevant part, as “any retirement, welfare, health, disability, public or assisted housing, postsecondary education, food assistance, unemployment benefit, or any other similar benefit for which payments or assistance are provided to an individual, household, or family eligibility unit by an agency of the United States or by appropriated funds of the United States. ” Tax credits are absent from that list, which clearly consists of direct assistance programs delivered through federally funded programs. Congress would have explicitly specified tax credits if it had intended their inclusion. Wholly adopting a novel and unsupported interpretation of PRWORA to fit President Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda goes directly against the law as written and congressional intent.
In fact, PRWORA separately addressed the issue of immigrants qualifying for refundable credits when it originally passed in 1996. Section 451 of PRWORA restricted the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) by barring those without a Social Security Number from the tax credit. The remaining eligible population is a much broader group than those deemed “qualified” immigrants under that law. If Congress intended to restrict refundable tax credits to only “qualified” immigrants, it would have not included this separate section in a distinct section of that law.
The proposed regulation relies on the 2020 Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel opinion stating that any payment to a taxpayer may be classified as a benefit under PRWORA regardless of congressional intent and history. The proposal fails to justify why this new interpretation, upending 30 years of precedent, is valid given Congress’s past decisions to make very clear which immigrants were or were not eligible for refundable tax credits. Had Congress intended to bar immigrants from taking advantage of refundable tax credits, it would have clarified the statute in any of the numerous changes made to PRWORA or refundable tax credits in the years since 1996.
We urge you to withdraw this proposed regulation, which has no basis in the law, upends decades of precedent and runs counter to congressional intent.
Sincerely,
###
title: Sánchez, House Democratic colleagues oppose rule denying legal immigrants tax credits

HOUSTON – A federal grand jury has indicted six alleged YNS gang members and affiliates, while 10 other face charges in federal criminal complaints.

A total of 16 alleged gang members and affiliates face charges of conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute cocaine, attempted possession with intent to distribute cocaine, conspiracy to interfere with commerce by robbery, and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime.

Jocquez Frye, 18; Darrell Sampson, 18; Jacob Barrett, 18; Kristian Winters, 18; Jaquan McClendon, 19; Triwayne Davison, 20; Donfarius Holmes, 24; Haven Duncan, 29; Jason Pittman, 34; Ledanyan Bennett, 19; Alex Davison, 32; Monterio Whitfield, 30; William Nolan-Waddell, 34; Javonte Hoyle, 28; Will Clark, 28; and Xzaveon Francis, 28, all of Houston, have made their initial appearances in federal court.

Frye, Sampson, Barrett, Winters, McClendon, and Triwayne Davison appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Dena Palermo Sept. 28. The court ordered them to remain in custody pending further criminal proceedings.

During the detention hearing, the court heard that YNS is a violent gang operating in Houston’s Greenspoint area and allegedly involved in homicides, assaults, home invasions, vehicle burglaries, and drug and firearms trafficking. The court also heard that authorities linked Frye to the Jan. 4 armed carjacking of a former Houston Texans player at his home.

The court reviewed social media posts and videos depicting alleged YNS members displaying firearms equipped with machinegun conversion devices, assaulting a rival gang member, and intimidating rivals outside their residences. The court also heard that the weapons posed a danger to innocent bystanders and that the alleged activities could provoke retaliatory violence in the Greenspoint area.

Social media posts and messages introduced into evidence allegedly showed members discussing past and planned violent crimes, firearms trafficking, and threats against rival gangs and groups.

The court also heard that YNS members allegedly planned to rob what they believed was a drug stash house containing 42 kilograms of cocaine. On July 23, several members met with a confidential informant before traveling to the location carrying firearms and wearing black clothing, masks, and gloves, according to the allegations.

Sampson, Barrett, and Winters allegedly planned a separate armed robbery at the time of their Sept. 23 arrests. The three allegedly intended to rob an individual at gunpoint following what they believed would be a large-scale cocaine transaction.

Holmes, Duncan, Pittman, Bennett, Alex Davison, Whitfield, Nolan-Waddell, Hoyle, Clark and Francis appeared before Judge Palermo for detention hearings Sept. 29-30.

During those hearings, the court heard that the defendants allegedly conspired to transport what they believed was 50 kilograms of cocaine to a buyer before robbing the individual following the delivery. At the time of their arrests, authorities discovered firearms, zip ties, and gloves in their possession.

If convicted, all 16 YNS members face up to life in prison and a possible $250,000 maximum fine.

FBI Houston and the Houston Police Department conducted the investigation with the assistance of the Texas Department of Public Safety, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, and U.S. Marshals Service.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sebastian Edwards and Samuel Blackington are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law.
title: 16 alleged YNS gang members and affiliates face federal drug trafficking, robbery, and firearms charges

Construction Business Owner Charged with Employment Tax Scheme and Failing to File Returns
A federal grand jury in Greenbelt, Maryland returned an indictment today charging a Maryland man with failing to account for and pay over employment taxes withheld from the wages of his company’s employees and failing to file tax returns.
According to the indictment, Martin Herrera Navarrete, of Glenn Dale, was the sole owner and sole corporate officer of Navarrete Brothers Construction, Inc., a commercial construction company. Navarrete was allegedly responsible for withholding Social Security, Medicare, and income taxes from his employees’ wages and paying those withholdings over to the IRS. From the first quarter of 2008 through the last quarter of 2025, Navarrete allegedly failed to pay any of the withheld taxes to the IRS. In total, the indictment alleges that Navarrete failed to pay more than $3 million in taxes owed to the IRS during this period. Additionally, from 2020 through 2024, Navarrete allegedly failed to file his own personal tax returns and corporate tax returns.
Navarrete is charged with failing to pay over and account for employment taxes, failing to file corporate tax returns, and failing to file personal tax returns. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison for each count of failing to account for and pay over employment taxes and a maximum penalty of one year in prison for each count of failing to file tax returns. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes of the District of Maryland made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case.
Trial Attorney Catriona Coppler of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Rosenthal of the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Barrigada Man Sentenced to 120 months in Federal Prison for Trafficking Methamphetamine
Hagåtña, Guam – SHAWN N. ANDERSON, United States Attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, announced that defendant Michael Joseph Salas, age 42, from Barrigada, Guam was sentenced in the U.S. District Court of Guam to 120 months imprisonment for Distribution of 50 or More Grams of Methamphetamine Hydrochloride, in violation of 21 U.S.C. § 841(a)(1). The Court also ordered five years of supervised release and a mandatory $100 special assessment fee. In addition, defendants convicted of a federal drug offense may no longer qualify for certain federal benefits.
On February 11, 2025, Salas agreed to sell three ounces of methamphetamine to a confidential informant. Salas had the informant drive him to a location to meet up with his source of supply. After receiving $3,300 from the informant, Salas met with his source and returned with a bag of methamphetamine. Upon returning to his residence, Salas packaged three ounces of the drug for the informant and kept an unknown quantity for himself. Salas previously sold one ounce of methamphetamine to the informant for $1,200. Federal agents executed a search warrant at the residence in March 2025. It resulted in the seizure of 34.22 additional grams of methamphetamine.
Salas has criminal convictions for possession of an unregistered firearm, second degree and third degree theft by receiving stolen property, and second degree promotion of major prison contraband.
“Repeat offenders who traffic drugs are prime targets for federal law enforcement,” stated United States Attorney Anderson. “They will face mandatory minimum sentences in federal court. Those sentences will be served at a Bureau of Prisons facility on the mainland, far from Guam. We will continue to aggressively prosecute those associated with this illicit activity.”
“Methamphetamine continues to ravage communities across the United States, extending beyond the mainland to Hawaii and territories such as Guam. Its trail of devastation leaves no corner untouched. Today’s sentencing proves to drug traffickers that they are not beyond the reach of the law," said David S. Olesky, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration Los Angeles Field Division, which covers Guam. "We will track them down and bring them to justice. DEA stands united with our federal partners to safeguard American lives.”
This investigation was conducted by the Drug Enforcement Administration. Assistant United States Attorney Devarup Rastogi prosecuted this case in the District of Guam.
title: Barrigada Man Sentenced to 120 months in Federal Prison for Trafficking Methamphetamine

Fort Myers, Florida –Desmond Belmer (25, Fort Myers) has been sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Sheri Polster Chappell to three years and five months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, for possessing a firearm as a previously convicted felon. Belmer previously pleaded guilty on June 25, 2026. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court records and documents, on June 17, 2025, Belmer—a previously convicted felon—unlawfully possessed a loaded Glock firearm. Then, on December 11, 2025, when law enforcement officers executed a search warrant at Belmer’s residence, they located and seized a loaded AR-style pistol and assorted ammunition and firearms-related accessories belonging to Belmer.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Fort Myers Police Department. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Simon Eth.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods. PSN is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

DALLAS — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould and FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock today announced today that federal agents have disrupted a major illicit laptop‑hosting network that enabled Democratic People's Republic of Korea IT workers to unlawfully access U.S. corporate systems using stolen or falsified American identities.

As part of Operation Lonestar Roundup, the FBI executed searches of over 40 residences in the State of Texas seizing 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices, all of which had operated as laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. In North Texas, agents seized approximately 100 devices that the DPRK workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used carry out the fraudulent scheme to obtain remote employment and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs.

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. “Operation Lonestar Roundup was aimed at disrupting malicious cyber activity perpetrated by the North Korean government with the purpose of supporting its WMD and ballistic missile programs, intelligence program, and nuclear program. Each laptop seized potentially represents one company that has hired a DPRK IT worker,” said FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock. “The FBI will continue to work with our law enforcement and private sector partners to combat this threat. We encourage any company, or individual, who has information on this scheme to come forward and file a report at ic3.gov.”

Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI
An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.
“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”
“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”
“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”
According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.
Recording Device 1
Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.
According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.
The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:
Image of Alfozan
Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.
The FBI is investigating the case.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker for the Northern District of California is prosecuting the case with valuable assistance from Trial Attorney Kate Tagert of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.
This prosecution is in support of National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) designed to support American superiority in super intelligence technology.
title: Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI

USDA Announces $86.6 Million Investment into the U.S. Specialty Crop Industry
(Washington, D.C., October 13, 2026) – The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) today announced it is awarding $86.6 million in grant funding to support the specialty crop industry through the Specialty Crop Block Grant Program (SCBGP). The program funds innovative projects designed to enhance the competitiveness of specialty crops.
“Today I am proud to announce USDA will be investing more than $86 million across 56 states and territories through the Specialty Crop Block Grant Program. These 609 state projects represent the Trump Administration’s commitment to innovation, marketing, and research—ensuring specialty crop businesses are at the forefront of markets all around the world,” said Secretary Brooke L. Rollins. “Putting farmers first will continue to drive economic growth and strengthen the fabric of rural communities across America.”
States and territories are providing subawards to projects that address the needs of U.S. producers of fruits, vegetables, tree nuts, dried fruits, horticulture, and nursery crops. The funded projects help businesses throughout the specialty crops distribution chain by enhancing food safety, supporting research, developing new and improved seed varieties and specialty crops, fighting pests and diseases, educating communities about healthy eating, and making it easier and more affordable to get specialty crops to market.
USDA’s Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) is investing $86.6 million in approximately 609 state projects across 56 states and territories.
Projects include:
- Michigan will use over $2.64 million through subawards to enhance the competitiveness of specialty crops including apples, asparagus, beans, blueberries, Christmas trees, herbs, mushroom, and grapes throughout the state.
- Georgia will use over $1.7 million across 2 research projects, 9 education and outreach projects, and 2 marketing projects in support of the state's pecan, blueberry, pepper, strawberry, peach, apple, Vidalia onion, and citrus growers.
- Ohio will use over $800,000 for projects to enhance competitiveness of apples, leafy greens, brassicas, herbs, maple syrup, honey, and nuts throughout the state.
- Pennsylvania will use over $1.1 million on research, education and outreach, and marketing of mushrooms, potatoes and apples.
- Texas will use over $2 million for projects to enhance competitiveness of grapes, watermelons, pecans, onions, and spinach.
- Florida will use over $4.3 million on research, education and outreach, and marketing of mangoes, blueberries, sweet corn, and muscadine grapes.
- North Carolina will use over $1.5 million to enhance competitiveness of sweet potatoes, fir trees, tomatoes, blueberries, apples, canary melons, and centipede grass seed.
For more information and to view a complete list of funded projects, visit the AMS SCBGP webpage.
AMS supports U.S. food and agricultural product market opportunities, while increasing consumer access to fresh, healthy foods through applied research, technical services, and congressionally funded grants.
To learn more about AMS’s investments in enhancing and strengthening agricultural systems, visit www.ams.usda.gov/grants.
