WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Carolina Performance Fabrics, S.A. de C.V. (Carolina), located in the state of Guanajuato, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Carolina facility, which manufactures specialized, high-performance textiles for the automotive industry.
Background
The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 10, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from a Mexican union affiliated with the Confederación Central Nacional (COCENA). The petition alleges that Carolina has violated workers’ rights by interfering in union activity and retaliating against workers because of their attempts to organize for COCENA, including through harassment, threats, and unlawful dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.
After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Carolina are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Carolina.
Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.
A copy of the request for review can be found here.
A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.
Information about previous requests can be found here.
###
title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Carolina Performance Fabrics

Connecticut Congressional Delegation Announces $75.3 Million in LIHEAP Funding to Connecticut
Hartford, CT — Today, Reps. John B. Larson (CT-01), Joe Courtney (CT-02), Rosa DeLauro (CT-03), Jim Himes (CT-04), and Jahana Hayes (CT-05), and Senators Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy announced over $75.3 million in Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) funding to Connecticut for FY27 allocated through the Continuing Resolution. This funding comes after the Trump Administration’s proposed FY27 budget included the elimination of the LIHEAP program and as Connecticut families are dealing with skyrocketing costs to heat their homes due to the war in Iran.
“LIHEAP is a lifeline to nearly 100,000 Connecticut families, including children and seniors, helping them to heat their homes. As this war of choice in Iran causes oil costs to soar, more and more families will struggle to afford their utility bills. As a delegation, we have fought to protect and strengthen LIHEAP, especially under threats of elimination by President Trump. We are proud to have secured $75.3 million for Connecticut’s first round of funding from LIHEAP – one of the earliest releases of funding in years. We will continue to deliver the resources Connecticut families depend on and defend this funding from this administration’s attacks so no one has to choose between heating their home and buying groceries,” said the delegation.
Connecticut residents can apply for energy assistance through the Connecticut Department of Social Services, available here.
title: Connecticut Congressional Delegation Announces $75.3 Million in LIHEAP Funding to Connecticut

Congressman Gonzalez Secures Nearly $1 Million in Federal Funds for City of Raymondville
Contact: Alexis Torres
Raymondville, Texas—Today, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), joined by the City of Raymondville and Mayor Gilbert Gonzales, delivered $965,467 in Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) Community Project Funding to renovate and improve safety at multiple parks as part of the city-wide park improvement plan. This investment will support improvements at Pool Park, Pocket Park and Smiley Face Park, including new restrooms, exercise stations, nature trails, and additional parking.
“Over the past year, I worked with local partners across our district to pass into law funding for 15 community projects that improve the lives of South Texas families,” said Congressman Vicente Gonzalez. “With this nearly $1 million investment into Raymondville, we are creating opportunities to promote a healthier future while advancing economic and community development tied to the City’s parks and recreation system. Thank you to all our city leaders for their outstanding leadership. I remain committed to ensuring federal resources make their way to our smaller communities just as much as in big cities.”
“The Mayor, along with the Raymondville Board of Commissioners, and the City of Raymondville, would like to take this opportunity to thank Congressman Gonzalez and his staff in working hard in obtaining funding for our community. This investment which consists of park improvements throughout the City and will assist us in enhancing the quality of life for our community, promote health well-being, and help in the fight against diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. These improvements consist of walking trails, inclusive playground equipment, lighting, parking, and ADA restrooms. Once again, our greatest gratitude and appreciation to Congressman Gonzalez and his staff for always supporting our local community,” said Raymondville Mayor Gilbert Gonzales.
As a Member of the U.S. House of Representatives, Congressman Gonzalez successfully secured $12.6 million in federal funds for 15 community projects this past year, including Raymondville’s city-wide park improvement plan.
title: Congressman Gonzalez Secures Nearly $1 Million in Federal Funds for City of Raymondville

KANSAS CITY, KANSAS – Systemair MFG, Inc., a Florida Corporation with its principal place of business in Lenexa, Kansas, has agreed to pay $2,357,709.00 to resolve allegations that it submitted a false claim to obtain a Paycheck Protection Program loan.

The Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act established the PPP to provide forgivable loans to eligible small businesses affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. The U.S. Small Business Administration administered the loan program.

To qualify for a First Draw PPP loan, businesses were generally required to meet size limits, including having fewer than 500 employees of affiliated entities. When applying for PPP loans, borrowers were required to certify that they were eligible for the requested loans and that the information they provided was true and accurate.

The settlement resolves allegations that Systemair MFG exceeded the size limits when it obtained a First Draw PPP loan in June 2020 and later sought loan forgiveness. At the time, Systemair MFG was a wholly owned subsidiary of Systemair AB, a company based in Sweden that owns other businesses throughout the world. According to the allegations, Systemair MFG, with these affiliated companies exceeded the program size limits, making the company ineligible for the loan.

“The Paycheck Protection Program was designed to grant relief to small businesses. The Department of Justice and our agency partners continue to review these loans for fraud and those who took advantage of these programs,” said United States Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “Make no mistake, those who use the compassion of the American taxpayer to unjustly enrich themselves will be held to account.”

The settlement stems from a qui tam or whistleblower complaint filed under the False Claims Act which permits a private party to file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The case is United States ex rel . Verity Investigations, LLC v. Systemair MFG. Inc., Case No. 2:25-cv-02244.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office conducted the investigation in coordination with the Small Business Administration. The investigation was led by Assistant United States Attorney Jon Fleenor.

Individuals with information about allegations of fraud involving COVID-19 are encouraged to report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form

The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.
title: Florida company agrees to pay over $2.3 Million to resolve false claims act allegations involving improper Paycheck Protection Program

Kaptur, Latta Introduce Bipartisan Legislation Honoring Fremont’s Rutherford B. Hayes Library and Museums
Fremont, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09) and Congressman Bob Latta (OH-05) introduced a bipartisan resolution in recognition of the United States’ first Presidential library, the Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library and Museums. This year marks the 110th Anniversary of the Library and Museums and the 150th Anniversary of Rutherford B. Hayes’ Presidential campaign.
“The Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library and Museums have left an indelible mark on our region throughout its 110 years, and I am honored to celebrate an institution that serves as a model for preserving and celebrating Ohio and American history,” said Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09). “In creating the first Presidential Library, Hayes’ descendants showed the nation how to commemorate history in a manner that honors the sacrifices of those that came before and that seeks to teach future generations of the responsibility of citizenship.”
“I’m proud to co-lead this resolution to honor and celebrate the 110th anniversary of the Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library & Museums in Fremont, Ohio and the 150th anniversary of his Presidential campaign,” said Congressman Bob Latta (OH-05). "The Hayes Library was our nation’s first Presidential Library, and beginning in the 120th Congress, this historic place will call Ohio’s Fifth Congressional District home. President Hayes was a devoted public servant who dedicated his career to Ohio and our nation. It’s important that we preserve significant elements of American history, such as the Hayes Library, to ensure future generations can learn about the lives of figures who have had a positive impact on our country."
Born in Delaware, Ohio in 1822, Hayes served as a Governor of Ohio and as the 19th President of the United States. After his death, Hayes’ children cemented their father’s legacy by creating the Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library and Museums at the Hayes’ residence at Spiegel Grove in Fremont, Ohio. The library and museums were the first of their kind, and they preserve the former President’s personal library, his military service records, and materials and artifacts from his Presidency. The museums also takes careful effort to preserve and collect materials that showcase life along Lake Erie’s south shoreline, along with artifacts from Ohio’s history and other former presidents. It was used as a model for constructing the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum in New York, the first official Federal Presidential library. Following the path of the Hayes and Roosevelt institutions, 16 Federal Presidential libraries exist today.
A full copy of the resolution can be found by clicking here. More information on the Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library and Museums can be found by clicking here.
# # #
title: Kaptur, Latta Introduce Bipartisan Legislation Honoring Fremont’s Rutherford B. Hayes Library and Museums

text:
Since the early 2000s, Tehran's construction of gas centrifuge uranium enrichment facilities has generated widespread concern in Congress that Tehran is pursuing nuclear weapons. According to past U.S. intelligence assessments, Tehran had the capacity to produce nuclear weapons at some point but had halted its nuclear weapons program and had not mastered all of the necessary technologies for building such weapons.
The status of Iran's nuclear program is unclear. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) withdrew inspectors from Iran after June 2025 U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. The extent to which these attacks, as well as U.S.-Israeli airstrikes that began in February 2026, affected Iran's ability to produce nuclear weapons is unclear. Prior to the 2026 airstrikes, Iran "was intending to try to recover from the devastation of its nuclear infrastructure," the 2026 Annual Threat Assessment (ATA) of the U.S. Intelligence Community states. A June 2026 memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the United States and Iran states that "Iran reaffirms that it shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons." Iranian government statements since February 2026 indicate that the government has no intention of developing nuclear weapons.
Gas centrifuges enrich uranium by spinning uranium hexafluoride (UF6) gas at high speeds to increase the concentration of the uranium-235 (u-235) isotope. Such centrifuges can produce both low-enriched uranium (LEU), which can be used in nuclear power reactors, and highly enriched uranium (HEU), which is one of the two types of fissile material used in nuclear weapons. Tehran has asserted that its enrichment program is only meant to produce fuel for peaceful nuclear reactors.
The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which effectively is no longer in force, has required Iran to implement various physical restrictions on its nuclear program, as well as to accept specific monitoring and reporting requirements. During the first Trump Administration, the President announced in May 2018 that the United States was ending U.S. participation in the JCPOA. Over time, Iran stopped implementing many of its JCPOA obligations and scaled back JCPOA-required IAEA monitoring. Beginning in July 2019, the IAEA verified that some of Iran's nuclear activities were exceeding JCPOA limits. In February 2021, Iran stopped allowing the agency to implement JCPOA-mandated verification and monitoring activities, according to a June 4, 2026, report from IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi. Since 2021, the IAEA has implemented inspections and monitoring in Iran pursuant to Tehran's comprehensive safeguards agreement only.
Tehran's expansion of an enrichment program beginning in 2019 has decreased the time needed to produce enough weapons-grade HEU for a nuclear weapon—an action frequently termed "breakout." According to U.S. assessments, Iran halted its nuclear weapons program in late 2003. This program's goal, according to U.S. officials and the IAEA, was to develop an implosion-style nuclear weapon for Iran's Shahab-3 ballistic missile. A 2025 public U.S. intelligence assessment stated that "Iran is not building a nuclear weapon" and that the then supreme leader had "not reauthorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003." Grossi stated on March 4, 2026, that the IAEA in June 2025 had no "information indicating that there was a structured systematic [Iranian] program to build or to construct a nuclear weapon."
The U.S. government assessed prior to the JCPOA that Iran had not mastered all the necessary technologies for building a nuclear weapon. Tehran may have resumed conducting work on such technologies. The 2024 ATA observed that "Iran is not currently undertaking the key nuclear weapons-development activities necessary to produce a testable nuclear device." This phrase is absent from 2024 and 2025 Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) assessments of Tehran's nuclear program. The 2026 ATA states that the United States is "monitoring Iranian WMD-related capabilities and actions following" the 2026 attacks; the ATA does not address Iran's nuclear weapons activities.
The JCPOA-mandated restrictions on Iran's nuclear program, as well as the agreement's Iran-specific monitoring and reporting requirements, supplemented Tehran's obligations pursuant to the government's comprehensive IAEA safeguards agreement. Such agreements empower the agency to detect the diversion of nuclear material from peaceful purposes and to detect undeclared nuclear activities and material. These agreements require governments to declare their entire inventory of certain nuclear materials and related facilities. Safeguards include agency inspections and monitoring of declared nuclear facilities.
Prior to and after the JCPOA's January 2016 implementation, IAEA and U.S. officials expressed confidence in the ability of both the IAEA and the U.S. intelligence community to detect an Iranian breakout attempt using either Tehran's IAEA-monitored facilities or clandestine facilities. An ODNI spokesperson stated that the U.S. intelligence community was capable of detecting Iranian efforts to build a nuclear weapon, according to an August 9, 2024, press report.
U.S. estimates concerning Iranian nuclear weapon development account for the time necessary to produce a sufficient amount of weapons-grade HEU and complete the remaining steps necessary for an implosion-style nuclear device suitable for explosive testing. Such a device, according to the Office of Technology Assessment, uses "a shell of chemical high-explosive surrounding the nuclear material ... to rapidly and uniformly compress the nuclear material to form a supercritical mass" necessary for a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
The time needed to produce enough weapons-grade HEU for a nuclear weapon is a function of a nuclear program's enrichment capacity, as well as the mass and u-235 content of the UF6 stockpile fed into the enrichment process. LEU used in nuclear power reactors typically contains less than 5% u-235; research reactor fuel can be made using enriched uranium containing 20% u-235; HEU used in nuclear weapons typically contains about 90% u-235.
The JCPOA has mandated restrictions on Iran's declared enrichment capacity and requires that Iran's enriched uranium stockpile must not exceed 300 kilograms (kg) of UF6 containing 3.67% u-235 "or the equivalent in other chemical forms." These restrictions constrained Iran's nuclear program so that Tehran, using its declared enrichment facilities, would, for at least 10 years, have needed a minimum of 1 year to produce enough weapons-grade HEU for 1 nuclear weapon. This timeline would have begun to decrease after JCPOA restrictions on Iran's enrichment capacity, as well as the mass and u-235 content of the UF6 stockpile, began to expire. The agreement scheduled these expirations to begin in January 2026.
Before the June 2025 strikes on Iran, Tehran's number of installed centrifuges, the mass and u-235 concentration of Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile, and number of enrichment locations exceeded JCPOA-mandated limits. Iran was also conducting JCPOA-prohibited enrichment research and development, as well as centrifuge manufacturing and installation.
A November 2024 ODNI report explained that Iran's fissile material stockpile would, if further enriched, have been sufficient for "more than a dozen nuclear weapons." The U.S. government estimated that Iran would have needed as little as one week to produce enough weapons-grade HEU for one nuclear weapon, according to a State Department (DOS) official in March 2022. The Defense Intelligence Agency assessed in May 2025 that Iran would have needed "probably less than one week" to produce this amount of HEU.
Had resumed implementing its JCPOA obligations, this fissile material production timeline would have increased but would have been less than one year, according to DOS officials. This estimate reflected Iran's accumulation of knowledge gained by operating more sophisticated centrifuges. Former National Intelligence Council official Eric Brewer noted in an October 2021 publication that, absent this experience, Iran probably would have used less efficient centrifuges for a breakout attempt.
The IAEA, according to Grossi, assesses that Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile remains in the country. The IAEA estimates that this stockpile includes 184.1 kg of UF6 containing up to 20% u-235 and 440.9 kg of UF6 containing up to 60% u-235. The latter two categories of UF6 are of particular concern because relatively little additional effort would be necessary to produce weapons-grade HEU using UF6 containing these amounts of u-235. Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi stated on March 15, 2026, that the country's enriched uranium is "under the rubble" created by the June 2025 attacks on Iran's enrichment facilities. Iran has "no plan" to recover this material, he added. In 2026, U.S. and Iranian officials have said that Iran has not resumed enriching uranium.
When JCPOA negotiations concluded, the U.S. intelligence community assessed that Iran would have needed one year to complete the necessary steps, excluding fissile material production, for producing a nuclear weapon. This estimate assumed Iran could complete fissile material production and weaponization in parallel. Iran, therefore, would have needed about one year to produce a nuclear weapon.
A DOS official told CRS in an April 2022 email that Iran would have needed approximately one year to complete the necessary weaponization steps. This timeline took "into consideration assessed knowledge gaps" and reflected the intelligence community's "view of Iran's fastest reasonable path to overcome them," the official added. The then Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Army General Mark Milley testified in March 2023 that Iran would need "several months to produce an actual nuclear weapon." He did not explain the assumptions underlying this estimate. The current assessed timeline is unclear.
IAEA reports have indicated that Iran does not yet have a viable nuclear weapon design or a suitable explosive detonation system. Tehran may also lack sufficient experience in producing uranium metal; weapons-grade HEU metal for use in a nuclear weapon is first "cast and machined into suitable components for a nuclear core."
The one-year fissile-material breakout estimate assumed that Iran would use its declared nuclear facilities to produce fissile material for a weapon. Because the estimate did not account for a potential covert nuclear program, it did not completely measure Tehran's potential to produce nuclear weapons. The U.S. government has assessed that Iran was more likely to use covert, rather than declared, facilities to produce the requisite fissile material; whether this is still the U.S. assessment is unclear. Neither the U.S. government nor the IAEA have publicly described evidence that Iran is conducting covert fissile material production nuclear activities.
In JCPOA negotiations, the breakout timeline was an unclassified proxy measure of Iranian nuclear weapons capabilities. A DOS official described the breakout "concept" in a September 2021 email to CRS as "a useful metric to help quantify" U.S. negotiating goals and as "a useful analytic framework to structure the negotiation of technical measures related to enrichment."
In considering potential congressional action concerning Iran, Congress may request or require intelligence community briefings on the status of Tehran's nuclear program, including Iranian plans, if any, to develop a nuclear weapon.
title: Iran and Nuclear Weapons Production

Coast Guard searching for missing kayaker near San Diego
U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Public Affairs: (206) 815-6689
SAN DIEGO —The Coast Guard is searching for a missing kayaker, 27-year-old Samantha Youngs, who was reported missing near Torrey Pines Gliderport in La Jolla, California, Tuesday morning. 
Anyone who may have information regarding Youngs’ location is asked to call the Joint Harbor Operations Center at 619-278-7057. 
At 6:00 a.m., watchstanders at Coast Guard Sector San Diego received notification that Youngs’ family reported her missing, along with her kayak. Her car was found at the Torrey Pines Gliderport cliffside parking lot. 
Coast Guard vessels and aircraft are actively searching waterside in the vicinity of Torrey Pines Natural reserve and La Jolla shores, along with partner agencies, San Diego Lifeguard Service and the San Diego Police Department. 
—USCG—
title: Coast Guard searching for missing kayaker near San Diego

BOSTON – A Dominican national unlawfully residing in Worcester, Mass. has been charged by a federal grand jury with healthcare benefit fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Santo Escolastico Cuello, 56, was indicted on three counts of making false statements relating to health care matters and one count of aggravated identity theft. Cuello will be arraigned at a later date. In June 2026, Cuello was charged by criminal complaint.

According to court filings, Cuello used the stolen identity of a U.S. citizen, including the citizen’s social security number, to obtain government benefits. Specifically, it is alleged that Cuello represented that he was a U.S. citizen when applying for healthcare benefits in Massachusetts and submitted a sworn affidavit falsely alleging the same. According to the criminal complaint, Cuello allegedly obtained approximately $162,180 in MassHealth benefits using the stolen identity. Cuello is alleged to have identified himself to law enforcement as the individual whose identity he had stolen during prior arrests.

The charge of making false statements relating to a health care program provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a mandatory two-year sentence to run consecutively to any other sentence imposed, one year of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting, Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; and Roberto Coviello, Special Agent in Charge of the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Colin T. Missett of the Health Care Fraud Unit is prosecuting the case.

On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621).

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law
title: Illegal Alien Charged with Healthcare Benefit Fraud and Aggravated Identity Theft

Austin Couple Indicted for Running Fake ID Websites
An Austin couple were charged today with running websites that purported to sell fake identification documents and evading the payment of their federal income taxes.
According to court documents and statements made in court, Jerrod Lochmiller and Christina Linden allegedly owned and operated several websites that purported to sell fraudulent identification documents (“Fake IDs”), including driver’s licenses and identification cards. They also allegedly owned and operated websites that purported to provide Search Engine Optimization (SEO) services. Lochmiller and Linden operated their websites in the names of aliases and nominees. In order to obtain clients, Linden and Lochmiller hired SEO services to improve the Fake ID websites’ visibility in search engine results and created websites that reviewed and recommended their Fake ID websites. To conceal the source of their income, Linden and Lochmiller allegedly primarily received payment from customers via cryptocurrency and then transferred the cryptocurrency through multiple addresses before ultimately moving the cryptocurrency to exchange accounts in their names. Lochmiller and Linden then allegedly converted the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars, and deposited the money into their bank accounts. Clients who purchased the Fake IDs allegedly did not receive the Fake IDs.
Between 2017 and 2024, Lochmiller and Linden allegedly received over $6 million in mostly cryptocurrency income from their Fake ID and SEO websites. During that same time period, Lochmiller and Linden allegedly did not file any federal income tax returns and allegedly failed to report their income to the IRS.
Linden and Lochmiller face a maximum penalty of twenty years for the conspiracy to commit wire fraud and the wire fraud charges, five years in prison for conspiracy to defraud the IRS, six years in prison for tax evasion, and one year in prison for willfully failing to file a tax return.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division made the announcement.
IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case.
Senior Litigation Counsel Michael C. Boteler and Trial Attorney Michael Jones of the National Fraud Enforcement Division prosecuted the case with assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Alan Buie of the Western District of Texas.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

INDIANAPOLIS- Andrew Scott Whitaker, Jr., 30, of Indianapolis, has been sentenced to 19.5 years in federal prison, followed by 15 years of supervised release, after pleading guilty to distribution and possession of child sexual abuse material. Whitaker was also ordered to pay restitution to each of 15 identified victims, totaling $47,500.

According to court documents, on December 27, 2024, Whitaker sent multiple images and videos containing child sexual abuse material to several individuals using the social media messaging application Kik. On March 27, 2025, law enforcement officers executed a search warrant at Whitaker’s residence and recovered a cellphone containing approximately 2,279 images and 1,109 video files of child sexual abuse material. Investigators also discovered a second Kik account Whitaker used to facilitate the same criminal conduct.

At the time of his 2024 arrest, Whitaker was on federal supervised release stemming from a 2021 conviction in the Southern District of Indiana for possession of and access with intent to view child sexual abuse material.

“This dangerous offender exploited a social media platform to circulate the horrific abuse of the most vulnerable among us, all while already on federal supervised release for the same reprehensible conduct,” said Tom Wheeler, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana. “Those who gather online to revel in the exploitation of children should know that we will identify you, we will find you, and we will hold you accountable.”

“Distribution and possession of child sexual abuse material is a serious crime that causes significant pain and trauma to victims, families and the community, and it carries significant penalties, as this case demonstrates,” said Special Agent in Charge Ike Barnes, of the U.S. Secret Service’s Indianapolis Field Office. “The U.S. Secret Service is committed to using its resources to pursue those who choose to engage in such nefarious online behavior. Thank you to the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department, the Indiana Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force and the U.S. Attorney’s Office of the Southern District of Indiana for their work in helping to bring this repeat offender to justice.

The United States Secret Service and Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department investigated this case. The sentence was imposed by Chief U.S. District Judge James R. Sweeney, II.

U.S. Attorney Wheeler thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys MaryAnn Mindrum, who prosecuted this case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood , a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims.

If you are a victim of child sexual exploitation, please contact your local police department. Resources for victims of child exploitation can be found on our website at https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdin/project-safe-childhood

This investigation was conducted by the Indiana Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, a multiagency task force led by the Indiana State Police that investigates and prosecutes persons who use the internet to sexually exploit or entice children. Each year, Indiana ICAC investigators evaluate thousands of tips, investigate hundreds of cases, and rescue dozens of children from ongoing sexual abuse. Visit https://www. internetcrimesagainstkids.com to learn more about their efforts.

On July 20, 2015, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2231 (2015) to implement the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) and other provisions concerning Iran's nuclear program, Tehran's development of missiles, and arms transfers to and from Iran. In August 2020, the United States invoked the resolution's "snapback" mechanism, which required the Security Council to reimpose UN sanctions lifted pursuant to Resolution 2231 and the JCPOA. (CRS Report R40094, Iran's Nuclear Program: Tehran's Compliance with International Obligations.) Although that effort failed, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom (UK), collectively known as the "E3," invoked the snapback mechanism on August 28, 2025, resulting in the sanctions' reimposition on September 27, 2025.
Resolution 2231 stipulated that the council, "seized of the Iranian nuclear issue" since 2006, was to end consideration of the matter on October 18, 2025. The resolution's snapback mechanism then would have ceased to operate. The JCPOA effectively is no longer in force; snapback reimposed previously terminated UN sanctions and indefinitely extended both the sanctions and Iran's nuclear program as a subject of Security Council consideration.
Prior to June 2025 U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, including those associated with Tehran's enrichment program, Tehran's expansion of that program had decreased the amount of time necessary for Iran to produce enough fissile material for use in a nuclear weapon. (CRS In Focus IF12106, Iran and Nuclear Weapons Production.) The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) withdrew inspectors from Iran after the strikes. The extent to which either the 2025 strikes or subsequent 2026 U.S.-Israeli strikes have impacted Iran's enrichment program is unclear.
The JCPOA, finalized in July 2015 by Iran and China, France, Russia, the UK, the United States, and Germany (collectively known as the "P5+1"), required Iran to implement constraints on its uranium enrichment and heavy water nuclear reactor programs, as well as allow the IAEA to monitor Tehran's compliance with the agreement. These programs have caused international concern because they could produce fissile material for use in nuclear weapons.
Prior to the JCPOA, Iran was improving its ability to produce such fissile material, despite what U.S. officials characterized as UN and other sanctions' apparent success in slowing Tehran's nuclear program. At the time, IAEA and U.S. officials observed that IAEA safeguards on Iran's declared nuclear facilities likely would have detected an Iranian attempt to use them for producing nuclear weapons. (CRS Report R43333, Iran Nuclear Agreement and U.S. Exit.)
Pursuant to the JCPOA, Tehran received relief from sanctions imposed by the European Union, United Nations, and United States. On January 16, 2016, the agreement's Implementation Day, the Security Council terminated the provisions of seven resolutions: 1696 (2006), 1737 (2006), 1747 (2007), 1803 (2008), 1835 (2008), 1929 (2010), and 2224 (2015). The first six of these resolutions required Iran to take several steps, such as cooperating fully with an IAEA investigation of Tehran's nuclear activities as well as suspending sensitive nuclear activities. These resolutions also imposed sanctions on Iran. In May 2018, President Donald Trump issued a memorandum stating that the United States would no longer participate in the JCPOA and would reimpose sanctions that had been suspended pursuant to the agreement. Arguing that subsequent efforts by the remaining JCPOA participants, known as the "P4+1," were inadequate to sustain the agreement's benefits for Iran, Tehran undertook nuclear activities that exceeded JCPOA-mandated limits.
Beginning in July 2019, the IAEA verified that some of Iran's nuclear activities were exceeding JCPOA-mandated limits; according to agency reports, Iran's government subsequently increased the number of such activities. In February 2021, Iran stopped allowing the IAEA "to conduct verification and monitoring activities in relation to the JCPOA," according to a February 27, 2026, report from IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi. Iran's JCPOA commitments supplement Tehran's obligations pursuant to its IAEA comprehensive safeguards agreement and the nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT). (CRS Report R40094, Iran's Nuclear Program: Tehran's Compliance with International Obligations.)
The NPT, which Iran ratified in 1970, prohibits Iran from obtaining or producing nuclear weapons. The treaty also requires countries such as Iran to conclude a comprehensive IAEA safeguards agreement. Such agreements empower the agency to detect the diversion of nuclear material from declared nuclear facilities and to detect undeclared nuclear activities and material.
In February 2021, Iran ceased implementing the Additional Protocol to its comprehensive safeguards agreement. Such protocols provide the IAEA with additional authority to inspect certain nuclear-related facilities and demand information from member states. Iran had been implementing provisionally its additional protocol pursuant to the JCPOA, which also required Tehran to seek the Iranian parliament's ratification of the protocol no later than October 2023. Iran had signed such an additional protocol in late 2003 but stopped implementing it in early 2006.
On September 1, 2026, Grossi reported on the IAEA's JCPOA-mandated monitoring of Iranian compliance with agreement-specific restrictions. The agency currently monitors Iranian compliance with the Security Council resolutions adopted between 2006 and 2010, as well as a September 9, 2026, IAEA Board of Governors resolution.
In addition to the JCPOA-related provisions, Resolution 2231 (2015) imposes other requirements on Iran, some of which have expired. For example, the resolution restricted exports of missile-rated items to Iran until October 2023; other restrictions concerning Iranian imports and exports of conventional weapons expired in October 2020. Despite lacking a direct connection to the country's nuclear program, previous arms restrictions, the first of which were imposed by Security Council Resolution 1747 (2007), were part of a broad U.S.-led approach of pressuring Iran to comply with relevant council resolutions.
According to Resolution 2231, a JCPOA participant could, after notifying the Security Council of an issue that the government "believes constitutes significant non- performance of [JCPOA] commitments," trigger an automatic draft resolution to keep sanctions relief in effect. The United States in August 2020 initiated the snapback process, but the P4+1 governments and the Security Council president argued that the United States lacked the right to proceed with snapback because Washington had ceased participating in the JCPOA.
Despite a September 19, 2020, U.S. contention that snapback had reinstated previously terminated sanctions, UN Secretary General António Guterres wrote that the uncertainty about U.S. snapback initiation required the Secretary General to refrain from proceeding on the matter. In February 2021, the Biden Administration reversed the U.S. position on snapback. President Trump's February 4, 2025, National Security Presidential Memorandum/NSPM-2 directed the U.S. Permanent Representative to the UN to "work with key allies to complete the snapback of international sanctions and restrictions on Iran."
The E3 invoked the snapback mechanism in an August 28, 2025, letter. The Security Council president introduced a draft resolution on September 19, 2025, that would have maintained sanctions relief. The council did not adopt the resolution. China and Russia introduced a resolution on September 26, 2025, that would have effectively extended the end of Security Council consideration of the "Iranian nuclear issue" until April 18, 2026, with "a possibility for a further extension." The council did not adopt the resolution. The conclusion of the snapback process resulted in the sanctions' reimposition on September 27, 2025. The same day, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the E3 action as "an act of decisive global leadership."
In an October 18, 2025, letter to the Security Council, China, Iran, and Russia argued that the E3 lacks standing to invoke the snapback mechanism because the three governments had "ceased to perform" their JCPOA and Resolution 2231 commitments. The E3 failed to "exhaust the procedures" of a dispute resolution mechanism contained in the JCPOA, according to the letter, which stipulates that both Resolution 2231's provisions and the council's "consideration of the Iranian nuclear issue" have ended. The dispute concerning the resolution's status has continued in council meetings, most recently on September 10.
In addition to reimposing sanctions and other Security Council resolutions' requirements, snapback has ended the process by which the council was to have ceased in 2025 its consideration of the Iranian nuclear issue. The Security Council had adopted Resolution 2231, as well as all the resolutions that had imposed sanctions on Iran, under Chapter VII, Article 41, of the UN Charter. This provision enables the Security Council to adopt "measures not involving the use of armed force," including sanctions, "to give effect to its decisions" concerning "threats to the peace, breaches of the peace, and acts of aggression." Since adopting Resolution 1737 (2006), the council has been considering the Iranian nuclear issue pursuant to Article 41.
The September 2026 IAEA board resolution reports Iran's noncompliance to the Security Council and requests the IAEA Director General to report on the implementation of Iran's IAEA safeguards agreement, as well as "the verification activities as required by the relevant" IAEA and Security Council resolutions.
Reacting to the invocation of snapback, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated on September 30, 2025, that "Iran's Supreme National Security Council will assess the situation and ultimately adopt 'the right and well-calculated decisions' in line with national interests." Iran is bound by its NPT obligations, but not by the JCPOA transparency measures governing, or physical constraints on, the government's enrichment program.
Iran has cited JCPOA Paragraph 36 as grounds for Tehran's decision to end all JCPOA-mandated transparency measures that supplement the government's IAEA safeguards agreement. The agency currently implements inspections and monitoring in Iran pursuant to Tehran's comprehensive safeguards agreement only, which is of indefinite duration; as noted, Tehran has ceased implementing the Additional Protocol to that safeguards agreement.

Office of the Spokesman

October 13, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Samarkand, Uzbekistan; Mumbai, India; and Jamnagar, India from October 17-22.

In Uzbekistan, Secretary Rubio will participate in the C5+1 Ministerial to highlight how strategic cooperation through this diplomatic platform promotes a more peaceful and prosperous future for the United States and the countries of Central Asia. The Secretary will also participate in bilateral engagements with senior officials from all C5 countries – Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Kyrgyz Republic. On this historic visit, Secretary Rubio will lead a U.S. commercial delegation comprised of over 200 business leaders, ushering in a new era of strengthened commercial cooperation for the United States and Central Asia.

The Secretary will then travel to India for his second official visit this year. He will meet with senior government officials to strengthen the U.S.-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation. Secretary Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation.

Crow Presses Pentagon Over Civilian Casualties during Trump’s Iran War
AURORA — Congressman Jason Crow (D-CO), a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who serves on the House Armed Services Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, is demanding answers on a strike that resulted in civilian casualties at a wedding in Iran, reported to have been carried out by the U.S. military during Trump’s war of choice.
According to The New York Times, at least five people were killed, including two children, and nearly 70 more were injured while attending a wedding due to a military strike in the town of Kuhestak, Iran. Additional reporting indicates a high likelihood that the bomb used was launched by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran.
Joining Crow in his letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are Congresswomen Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) and Sara Jacobs (D-CA). The group previously led their Democratic colleagues pressing the Administration for answers on a U.S. strike on an Iranian girls’ elementary school where at least 175 civilians, many of them children, were killed. The Pentagon has yet to provide a sufficient update on the incident.
“We demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran,” Crow and his colleagues wrote. “The consequences of this American strike have been devastating: 5 civilians were killed as a result of the strike in Kuhestak, including a 4-year-old boy and a 16-year-old boy, and dozens of civilians were injured.”
They continued, “We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department. Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.”
Crow, Co-Chair of the Protection of Civilians in Conflict Caucus, has demanded answers on Secretary Hegseth’s attempts to dismantle civilian protections at the Pentagon.
Crow’s service as a combat veteran in Iraq and Afghanistan informs much of his work in Congress aimed at increasing civilian protection in combat. He helped pass legislation codifying the creation of the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, and has passed major portions of his Protection of Civilians in Military Operations Act and Department of Defense Civilian Harm Transparency Act.
A PDF of the letter can be found here, with full text appearing below:
Dear Secretary Hegseth,
We are once again writing with grave concern regarding the conduct of the administration’s war in Iran. Specifically, there are devastating reports of civilian casualties at a wedding in the town of Kuhestak, Iran, on September 1, 2026. This is the latest in an alarming pattern of civilian casualty incidents in strikes carried out by the United States in Iran since the war began on February 28, 2026. While the Department has not publicly acknowledged responsibility for this incident, the Washington Post recently reported that there is a “high likelihood” that the U.S. was responsible for the incident, citing an official familiar with the operations. Furthermore, analysis from U.S. weapons experts has suggested that the explosion was caused by a U.S. glide bomb.
The Post reported that six U.S. Navy aircraft-launched weapons targeted a communications complex near the home where the wedding was taking place and that one weapon missed its intended target. Accordingly, we demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the Department is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran. The consequences of this American strike have been devastating: 5 civilians were killed as a result of the strike in Kuhestak, including a 4-year-old boy and a 16-year-old boy, and dozens of civilians were injured.
This incident is regrettably among the latest in a string of civilian casualty incidents arising from the U.S.-led war in Iran. This includes a strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war that killed a reported 175 civilians, including 120 children. While it has been reported that a preliminary investigation by the Department found that the U.S. military was responsible for the strike, over six months later the Department has still not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike nor released the findings of its investigation. Similarly, reporting and independent analysis indicate that U.S. forces were responsible for a strike at a youth sports hall in Lamerd, Iran, that killed 21 civilians, including 7 children, on February 28. While the Department has denied responsibility, analysis by weapons experts found that the damage pattern is consistent with that of an American Precision Strike Missile (PrSM).
We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department. Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.
This is why it is all the more alarming that amid these devastating incidents, the Department has also severely degraded the civilian harm mitigation and response (CHMR) programs and personnel designed to prevent, respond to, and learn from civilian harm. Understanding the civilian environment – including the location of civilian objects and critical infrastructure such as schools and gymnasiums, and patterns of life including large gatherings such as weddings – was intended to be a key aspect of this program. Yet CHMR staff at CENTCOM have reportedly dwindled from over 10 to just one full-time staff. The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, which was mandated by Congress and designed to support combatant commands in this life saving work, has been cut from over thirty down to just seven.
On March 12, 2026, 121 Members of the U.S. House of Representatives wrote to you demanding answers regarding civilian casualties caused by Operation Epic Fury and the Department's civilian protection efforts. The Department refused to provide any answers, simply stating “The United States Central Command (USCENTCOM) has initiated an investigation of this incident and appointed an investigating officer from outside the USCENTCOM chain of command. USCENTCOM will share the results of this investigation with Congress once it is completed.” Nearly seven months into the war, Congress and the American public still lack basic information about the findings of that investigation and the measures the Department has taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring again.
The strike in Kuhestak makes that failure all the more troubling. In response to the reports regarding U.S. responsibility for the strike in Kuhestak, a spokesperson for the U.S. Central Command stated “The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.” Similarly, Vice President Vance said at a press briefing recently that he was “skeptical” of reports that the U.S. was responsible for the bombing, while acknowledging that the incident was under investigation.We are concerned this lack of transparency from this Administration is becoming a pattern, given the Department also initially denied responsibility for the Minab strike and has yet to release the investigation related to that incident.
The American people deserve answers on not just this strike, but the Department’s pattern of civilian harm resulting from U.S. military operations in Iran. To that end, we insist on answers to the following questions no later than October 26, 2026.
- Did U.S. forces carry out the September 1, 2026 strike in Kuhestak, Iran, that killed 5 civilians and injured dozens? If so, what was the target and why was the decision taken to execute the strikes? What was the assessed civilian harm risk of the strikes, and what steps were considered or taken to prevent civilian harm?
- Has the Department formally initiated an investigation into the September 1 strike in Kuhestak? If so, please provide the date on which the investigation began, the office responsible for conducting it, whether the investigating officer is independent of the operational chain of command, and the expected timeline for completion.
- What is the status of the USCENTCOM investigation into the February 28 strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab? On what date will the Department provide Congress with the full findings of that investigation, including its conclusions regarding U.S. responsibility and the circumstances that led to the reported civilian casualties? On what date will the unclassified version of these findings be made available to the public?
- Did the Department conduct an initial review of whether it is possible the U.S. was involved in the Lamerd strike on February 28, 2026? What were the results of that initial review? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all?
  - Did the Department conduct a civilian harm assessment of whether it is more likely than not that civilian harm occurred as a result of this strike? What were the results of this assessment? Was additional information provided after the fact, and did this alter the initial review results at all?
  - Has the Department conducted an administrative investigation, such as an AR 15-6, into the strike? If so, when was the investigation initiated, when are the findings due to the commander, and when will its findings be provided to Congress and released publicly?
- What steps, if any, has the Department taken to prevent civilian harm in targeting practices since the apparent U.S strikes in Minab on February 28, 2026? Please detail any specific policies that have been implemented.
- How many U.S. investigations, initial reviews, and civilian harm assessments into civilian casualties arising from operations in Iran have been initiated since February 28, 2026 and how many have been completed? Please provide details of all ongoing and completed investigations.

HAMMOND – Courteau D. Givens, 38 years old, of Merrillville, Indiana, was sentenced by United States District Court Judge Philip P. Simon after pleading guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, announced United States Attorney Adam L. Mildred.

Givens was sentenced to 70 months in prison followed by 2 years of supervised release.

“Courteau Givens has a lengthy history of being unable or unwilling to comply with the law.

During a disturbance on February 5, 2023, Courteau Givens armed himself with a firearm and threatened a person. When police arrived, they discovered the gun and retrieved it. Being a convicted felon, Givens could not legally possess a firearm. His aggressive behavior towards others shows a willingness to use guns and violence as tools to get what he wants, making him a danger to the community. Enforcing this law is paramount to ensuring that our neighborhoods remain safe and our homes remain sanctuaries. By strictly prosecuting felon-in-possession cases, law enforcement and prosecutors remove illegally held weapons from our streets before they can be used to commit further violent acts. This prosecution is a direct result of the Project Safe Neighborhoods initiative, a collaborative strategy involving federal, state, and local law enforcement to target the most violent offenders and reduce gun crime. Prosecuting these cases is one of our most effective tools for preventing gun violence before it strikes. We remain fully committed to working alongside our law enforcement partners to hold illegal gun possessors accountable, take firearms out of the wrong hands, and secure the peace and safety that every resident deserves,” said United States Attorney Adam L. Mildred.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, with assistance from the Merrillville Police Department. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Caitlin M. Padula.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season to make landfall in the conterminous United States. It made landfall in the Florida Panhandle as a Category 2 hurricane the night of Friday, October 9, 2026, and brought high wind, significant rainfall, flooding, and power outages to many areas across the Southeast.
On October 9, President Trump issued several emergency declarations for certain counties in Florida, Alabama, and Georgia. These emergency declarations authorized federal assistance to save lives, protect property, and other measures that may prevent the incident from becoming a major disaster. Such measures include evacuations, emergency food and shelter, and the pre-positioning of rescue equipment. The situation remains dynamic; additional declaration requests or amendments to existing requests (i.e., addition of counties) may be forthcoming as states such as Florida are still assessing hurricane-related damage.
Presidential declarations of emergency or major disaster made pursuant to the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (the Stafford Act, P.L. 93-288, as amended; 42 U.S.C. §§5121 et seq.) may authorize FEMA to provide assistance through a suite of disaster programs:
Emergency declarations may authorize more limited forms of assistance than major disaster declarations.
The authorized forms of assistance may vary by designated area, per the declaration (subject to amendment). The President can also amend emergency and major disaster declarations to reduce the affected state's cost-share requirements for PA.
Information about state and county disaster assistance authorizations is published in FEMA's declaration database. Additional releases may be posted to FEMA Blog.
Hurricane damage can be caused by wind, water, or both, but these hazards are insured separately. A Stafford Act declaration is not required for policyholders to make insurance claims.
Wind is generally included as a covered peril in standard homeowners insurance policies. Homeowners insurance policies are sold by private insurance companies, which are regulated at the state level. Because hurricanes can cause significant damage, many states require a separate deductible for hurricane damage. To some degree, depending on the state, insurance companies determine the level of this hurricane deductible and when it should apply; however, the Florida hurricane deductible is set by statute and all insurance companies in Florida are generally required to offer hurricane deductible options.
Homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; homeowners must purchase separate coverage for flood losses. The NFIP is the primary source of flood insurance coverage for residential properties. The NFIP is operated by FEMA and is currently authorized until December 11, 2026. Homeowners and tenants with NFIP flood insurance can make flood damage claims using the normal NFIP claims process. FEMA may institute a claims process specific to Hurricane Isaias at a later date.
FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) is the primary funding source for federal government response and recovery activities. As a result, its level of unobligated funds is often used as a proxy for the overall federal resources available for response and recovery.
As of the end of FY2026, roughly $8.3 billion was available in the DRF to pay the costs associated with major disaster declarations. Under the terms of the continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103, Division A) providing interim funding for federal government operations during the first months of FY2027, an additional $26.4 billion is also available until the continuing resolution expires or is replaced by an enacted annual appropriations measure covering FEMA.
The United States takes a "bottom-up" approach to emergency management, and when a state's capacity to manage incident response has been exceeded, it may request assistance from the federal government. Some Members of Congress may be concerned about both state and federal capacity for emergency management.
Regarding federal capacity, congressional concerns may center on whether FEMA is sufficiently staffed, as the Government Accountability Office recently identified staffing gaps within FEMA's disaster workforce. Additional concerns may relate to whether the current Administration is approving declarations in line with historic trends, and whether FEMA's disaster and mitigation programs are operating as they have historically (e.g., no new funding has been approved or obligated for any HMA programs since March 2025).
Regarding state capacity, the Trump Administration has suggested states should take on additional responsibilities related to disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. Further, the FEMA Review Council provided recommendations to this effect, including recommending changes to FEMA's criteria for evaluating whether the President should declare a major disaster authorizing PA and IA (e.g., increasing the PA per capita indicator to account for historic inflation). While implementation would require changes to FEMA's regulations, in the interim, the FEMA Review Council's final report states, "the President could direct through executive action that generally only requests above higher thresholds may be considered." The Administration has also been unusually late to issue notices of funding opportunities and has changed certain policies, including related to the Emergency Management Performance Grant program, which can fund emergency management staff, resulting in some states experiencing uncertainty about funding availability. (FEMA was later directed to amend certain award terms and conditions and disperse allowable costs.)
Regarding insurance, Congress may take interest in the solvency, reform, and reauthorization of the NFIP as well as the state of insurance markets, which have seen insurers raising premiums or withdrawing from certain markets due to elevated risks.
For more information, see CRS Report R46408, Hurricane Events: CRS Experts, and CRS Report WMR10001, CRS Guide to Federal Emergency Management.
title: Hurricane Isaias: Brief Overview of FEMA Programs, Resources, and Selected Issues

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressmen Rob Menendez (NJ-08) and Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08) sent a letter to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. calling on HHS to update federal research and guidance on high-caffeine energy drinks and conduct a comprehensive assessment of their consumption and health effects among school-aged children.
“Kids are consuming more caffeine than ever, and Sarah Katz’s tragic death exposed how dangerous poor labeling and hidden caffeine levels can be,” said Congressman Menendez. “We are calling on HHS to update federal caffeine guidelines, protect our children, and ensure parents and teachers have the information they need to keep children safe.”
“Energy drink use among kids is at record levels, while caffeine-related emergency room visits among middle and high school students have roughly doubled,” said Congressman Krishnamoorthi. “These products can pose serious health risks to children, yet the federal government is still relying on outdated research and guidance. Our government needs to catch up and give parents, schools, and health care providers the information they need to keep kids safe.”
In 2022, 21-year-old Jersey City native Sarah Katz died after drinking an energy drink that was improperly labeled. Congressman Menendez reintroduced the bipartisan Sarah Katz Caffeine Safety Act last year to increase transparency of caffeine in food and beverages. The bill would also require the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) to conduct a safety review for caffeine and support a study to examine how caffeine impacts vulnerable populations, including children.
Today, nearly one in four high school seniors consume energy drinks daily, up from one in six in 2022. From 2017 to 2023, caffeine-related emergency department visits among middle and high school students roughly doubled. Despite this uptick, official CDC guidance still relies in part on a 2013 SAMHSA report using emergency department visit data from 2007 to 2011. 
The lawmakers also raised concerns about a lack of federal oversight and caffeine labeling requirements for energy drinks. FDA guidance is over ten years old, nonbinding, and provides no recommended caffeine limit for children or adolescents.
Menendez and Krishnamoorthi requested that HHS conduct a comprehensive assessment of energy drink consumption and its health effects among school-aged children and provide answers to the following questions:
The lawmakers called on HHS to make the assessment publicly available so parents, schools, and healthcare providers can understand the risks these products pose and the steps being taken to address them.
To read the full letter, please click here.
Congressman Menendez currently serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Subcommittees on Energy, the Environment, and Communications and Technology. Since coming to Congress, he has advocated for transparency in caffeine labeling and reintroduced the Sarah Katz Caffeine Safety Act during the 119th Congress.
title: Menendez and Krishnamoorthi Push for Stronger Energy Drink Safety Rules to Protect Kids

Representative April McClain Delaney Joined 99 Democratic Lawmakers in Slamming Department of Education for Failure to Enforce Title IX and Protect Student Survivors
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Democratic Women’s Caucus (DWC) member Maxine Dexter (OR-03), DWC member Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), DWC Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03) and Rep. Mark Takano (CA-41) led a letter to the Office of the Inspector General at the Department of Education. The letter urges the Acting Inspector General to open an investigation into the Department’s gutting of the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and Title IX rollbacks and its impact on the Department’s ability to enforce Title IX protections for student survivors of sexual assault and harassment. 99 House Democrats joined the effort.
The call for the investigation comes after Jane Doe’s story from Cornell University and Kendall Francis’ story from Louisiana State University (LSU) sparked a national outcry about the high rate of sexual violence on college campuses. Additionally the survivors’ stories have renewed scrutiny of how colleges and universities respond, and how the Department of Education enforces Title IX protections for survivors.
One in four undergraduate women experience sexual assault or rape while in college. Sexual violence against women on college campuses is a public health crisis, yet significant barriers remain that block accountability and protections for students. Changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities under the Trump administration have only made that worse and have undermined the Department’s ability to properly investigate complaints and enforce Title IX protections.
As of January 2025, OCR reportedly faced a backlog of nearly 12,000 civil rights cases, while the administration reduced OCR’s workforce by nearly half. The Department has closed zero college sexual harassment or sexual violence cases. The Department also formalized weaker protections and processes for student survivors: narrowing the definition of sexual harassment, reducing school liability, and implementing intimidating investigative and hearing procedures that are retraumatizing to survivors.
Without proper federal enforcement and institutional accountability, Title IX protections become just words on a page. The Department of Education is failing student survivors. Protections for survivors are not partisan and should always be a priority, however the Department’s rollback of vital protections creates additional barriers for survivors and is leaving them to fend for themselves in their most vulnerable moments.
In their letter, the members explained how the Department’s changes will leave student survivors vulnerable and why an investigation is necessary:
“We urge the Office of Inspector General to immediately open an investigation into the Department’s failure to adequately enforce Title IX protections for survivors of sexual harassment and assault, including whether changes in staffing, resources, case-processing, and enforcement priorities have undermined the Department’s ability to protect students, investigate complaints in a timely manner, and hold institutions accountable.”
The members outlined the Department’s policies that have weakened protections for student survivors:
“At the same time that OCR’s staff and regional capacity were substantially reduced, the Department announced and pursued Title IX enforcement priorities concerning transgender students’ participation in athletics and access to sex-separated facilities, and also dismantling Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) programs. These reprioritizations do nothing to address the backlog of sexual violence cases.”
The letter also explains how reprioritizations and restructuring by the Department have decreased OCR’s capacity to investigate cases of sexual violence on campus:
“This restructuring threatens to further delay investigations, erode OCR’s institutional expertise, and create additional barriers for survivors seeking accountability. These reprioritizations, staff reductions, and the interagency agreement raise significant questions about whether OCR has sufficient capacity to investigate Title IX complaints, communicate with complainants, and fulfill its civil rights enforcement responsibilities in a timely and effective manner.”
The members also outlined what they are urging the Inspector General to investigate:
- Examining whether the Department has fulfilled its legal and administrative responsibilities to investigate and resolve Title IX complaints in a timely and effective manner.
- The causes and consequences of the absence of resolution agreements involving college sexual harassment and assault complaints since January 2025.
- Whether reductions in OCR staffing, the closure of regional offices, or changes in enforcement priorities have contributed to delays, backlogs, or failures to resolve these complaints.
- Examining whether OCR has sufficient staffing, resources, policies, and procedures to effectively enforce Title IX and protect students from sex discrimination, including sexual harassment and violence.
- Identifying how survivors have been harmed by these changes.
Lastly, the members asked the Inspector General to answer the following questions:
- How many Title IX sexual harassment and sexual violence complaints are currently pending before OCR, and how long have they been pending?
- How have processing times, case closures, investigations, and resolution agreements changed since January 2025?
- Have staffing reductions or office closures affected OCR’s ability to investigate complaints or communicate with survivors?
- Have Department officials directed, formally or informally, OCR personnel to deprioritize certain categories of Title IX complaints?
- What safeguards are currently in place to ensure Title IX complaints involving sexual violence receive timely and appropriate review?
- What corrective actions are necessary to ensure the Department is meeting its obligations to protect students under Title IX?
Read the full letter here.
The letter was signed by: Amo, Gabe; Ansari, Yassamin; Balint, Becca; Barragán, Nanette; Beatty, Joyce; Beyer, Donald; Bonamici, Suzanne; Brownley, Julia; Brown, Shontel; Bynum, Janelle; Carter, Troy; Castor, Kathy; Chu, Judy; Clarke, Yvette; Craig, Angie; Crockett, Jasmine; Davids, Sharice; Dean, Madeleine; DeGette, Diana; DeSaulnier, Mark; Dexter, Maxine; Dingell, Debbie; Elfreth, Sarah; Escobar, Veronica; Espaillat, Adriano; Evans, Dwight; Fletcher, Lizzie; Foster, Bill; Foushee, Valerie; Frankel, Lois; Frost, Maxwell; Garamendi, John; Garcia, Sylvia; Goldman, Daniel; Goodlander, Maggie; Grijalva, Adelita; Houlahan, Chrissy; Hoyle, Val; Ivey, Glenn; Jackson, Jonathan; Jayapal, Pramila; Johnson, Julie; Kamlager-Dove, Sydney; Kelly, Robin; Kennedy, Timothy; Khanna, Ro; Landsman, Greg; Latimer, George; Lee, Summer; Leger Fernandez, Teresa; Lynch, Stephen; Magaziner, Seth; Matsui, Doris; McBride, Sarah; McClain Delaney, April; McClellan, Jennifer; McIver, LaMonica; Mejia, Analilia; Menefee, Christian; Meng, Grace; Mfume, Kweisi; Morelle, Joseph; Mullin, Kevin; Nadler, Jerrold; Norton, Eleanor; Omar, Ilhan; Pelosi, Nancy; Pettersen, Brittany; Pingree, Chellie; Quigley, Mike; Ramirez, Delia; Randall, Emily; Raskin, Jamie; Ross, Deborah; Salinas, Andrea; Scanlon, Mary Gay; Schakowsky, Janice; Scholten, Hillary; Sewell, Terri; Simon, Lateefah; Stansbury, Melanie; Stanton, Greg; Stevens, Haley; Strickland, Marilyn; Subramanyam, Suhas; Sykes, Emilia; Takano, Mark; Thompson, Bennie; Thompson, Mike; Titus, Dina; Tlaib, Rashida; Tokuda, Jill; Tonko, Paul; Trahan, Lori; Velázquez, Nydia; Walkinshaw, James; Watson Coleman, Bonnie; Williams, Nikema; Wilson, Frederica.
