Many of today's federal lands are located on the ancestral homelands of federally recognized Tribes ("Tribes"). Many Tribes maintain ongoing physical, cultural, spiritual, and economic relationships with their ancestral homelands. Tribes may seek access to federal lands or input into federal land management decisions because of the large amount of land currently owned by the federal government that once was tribal land. In addition, Tribes with lands close to federal lands also may seek to influence federal land management. These tribal interests may complement, or they may conflict with the preferences of other stakeholders' preferences for land management.
Tribes have historically had the opportunity to provide input on federal land management decisions through a variety of mechanisms. Historically, Congress ratified treaties in which Tribes reserved rights to access resources on their ceded lands (which are now federal lands), forming the basis for partnerships. In certain instances, Congress has required federal-tribal consultation. Congress also has passed site-specific laws encouraging cooperation or co-management on particular federal lands, such as national monuments. More broadly, Congress has authorized federal land management agencies to partner with nonfederal entities including Tribes using various legal instruments and has provided tribal-specific authorities such as Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act contracts or compacts.
In recent decades, many Tribes have advocated for a more robust, long-term, and formal role in managing federal lands to which they have a connection. This type of tribal involvement in federal land management is referred to as federal-tribal co-management. Although there is no statutory definition, generally, co-management refers to the sharing of management power and responsibility between the federal government and nonfederal entities, typically through a formal agreement. In general, tribal co-management involves varying degrees of tribal influence in federal decisionmaking, as shown below:
The U.S. Departments of the Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, and Defense are among the federal executive agencies that have implemented tribal co-management of natural, historical, and cultural resources on federal lands. This co-management has ranged from upholding tribal treaty fishing rights in the Pacific Northwest to managing subsistence wildlife in Alaska to restoring watersheds within national forests. These departments and Tribes have also co-managed historic and cultural resources on national monuments.
Congress may continue to consider the suitability and effectiveness of federal-tribal co-management of federal lands. Federal-tribal co-management on federal lands may help federal agencies achieve congressional priorities. It can provide an opportunity to integrate unique Indigenous knowledge with contemporary resource management policies to meet mutual objectives. At the same time, Congress and agencies may also find it challenging to weigh various tribal interests, such as protecting tribal sacred sites, with other statutory mandates and interests. Congress also may consider the scope of activities allowed under co-management agreements on federal lands, including whether agencies may delegate certain activities to Tribes. Finally, Congress may consider the administrative and financial benefits and challenges facing agencies and Tribes in implementing these agreements.
Many of today's federal lands are located on the ancestral homelands of federally recognized Tribes ("Tribes").1 Many Tribes maintain ongoing physical, cultural, spiritual, and economic relationships with their ancestral homelands. Tribes may seek access to federal lands or input into federal land management decisions because of the large amount of land currently owned by the federal government that once was tribal land.2 In addition, Tribes with tribal lands close to federal lands also may seek to influence federal land management.3
Tribes have historically had the opportunity to provide input on federal land management decisions through a variety of mechanisms. Historically, Congress ratified treaties in which Tribes reserved rights to access resources on ceded lands (which are now federal lands), forming the basis for partnerships. In certain instances, Congress has required federal-tribal consultation. Congress also has passed site-specific laws encouraging cooperation or co-management on particular federal lands, such as national monuments. More broadly, Congress has authorized federal land management agencies to partner with nonfederal entities including Tribes using various legal instruments, such as cooperative agreements, memoranda of agreement and understanding, or other arrangements. Whereas some laws provide broad authority to agencies to partner with nonfederal entities on a range of management areas, others provide for partnering with entities or Tribes to perform particular activities.
In recent decades, many Tribes have advocated for a more robust, long-term, and formal role in managing federal lands to which they have a connection.4 This type of tribal involvement in federal land management is referred to as federal-tribal co-management, though different entities use the term to refer to different types of involvement. Tribal co-management of federal lands differs from federal partnerships with other entities, in part due to Tribes' unique, government-to-government relationship with the federal government. The federal government may have certain responsibilities with respect to Tribes that affect co-management, such as the federal trust responsibility, consultation, and certain tribal treaty hunting, fishing, and gathering rights.
Federal-tribal co-management on federal lands may help federal land management agencies achieve federal priorities.5 It can provide an opportunity to integrate Indigenous knowledge into contemporary resource management policies to address issues and meet mutual objectives. At the same time, Congress and agencies may find it challenging to weigh various tribal interests, such as protecting tribal sacred sites, with other statutory mandates and interests. For example, some Tribes may want to co-manage a federal land area to limit development or limit access to non-tribal members, whereas other stakeholders, such as those interested in resource, mineral, and recreational development, may want to access and/or develop the area.6
This report provides an overview of federal-tribal co-management by explaining the historical underpinnings of tribal interest in, and potential rights to, co-managing federal lands; the spectrum of co-management types and their underlying authorities; and examples of how co-management has been used with respect to certain natural and cultural resources.7 The report concludes with an overview of issues and options for Congress regarding the suitability and effectiveness of federal-tribal co-management of federal lands.
Tribes have inhabited North America for millennia, developing deep cultural, spiritual, and subsistence ties to the landscape, which many Tribes have attempted to maintain.8 Tribal support for increased co-management of federal land generally stems from this history of tribal connection to lands now owned by the federal government and Tribes' unique relationship to the federal government. These historical foundations inform how Tribes may claim access to, or inform the management of, resources on federal lands in a co-management arrangement.
The federal government removed many Tribes from their ancestral homelands in the 18th and 19th centuries through treaties and other means. From 1774 to about 1871, the United States negotiated 375 tribal treaties.9 In some of these treaties, Tribes ceded lands but reserved their rights to hunt, fish, trap, and gather on those lands.10 In addition, Tribes may retain rights, including rights of access, on ceded lands even if they are not currently located near their ceded lands.11 Whether or the degree to which a specific treaty provides a basis for co-management is a matter of legal interpretation for federal agencies and courts. The federal government no longer enters into treaties with Tribes, so any co-management authority derived from treaty rights would be based on existing treaties.
In addition to treaty rights influencing co-management of federal lands, some Tribes assert that federal land management agencies should obtain tribal consent, or at least consult, on federal actions due to the federal trust responsibility.12 The federal trust responsibility is a legal obligation under which the United States, through treaties, acts of Congress, and court decisions, "has charged itself with moral obligations of the highest responsibility and trust" toward Tribes.13 It can include obligations to protect tribal treaty rights, lands, assets, and resources on behalf of Tribes and tribal members. Regardless of treaty or trust obligations, many Tribes maintain ongoing physical, cultural, spiritual, and economic relationships with their ancestral homelands now under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Tribes may seek access to federal lands or input into federal land management decisions to continue using the lands for historic cultural, religious, or subsistence purposes.
Federal land management agencies can collaborate with Tribes in different ways. As a result, the concept of co-management has been used to refer to a wide variety of federal-tribal collaborations on federal lands. Although there is no statutory definition, generally, co-management refers to the sharing of management power and responsibility between the federal government and nonfederal entities, typically through a formal agreement.14 This section presents a framework or spectrum for understanding the various types of arrangements and agreements categorized as co-management, as illustrated in Figure 1.
Historically, federal agencies generally had discretion regarding how much to involve Tribes in federal decisionmaking. Many Tribes assert that, in practice, there was generally little to no tribal influence in many federal land management decisions.15 Others assert that several laws adequately provide for "careful consideration" of tribal values in federal land management.16 For the purpose of this framework, the absence of tribal influence in federal land management is the baseline against which other types of co-management arrangements are compared.
One way Congress and agencies have provided for tribal input in agency decisionmaking is through federal-tribal consultation requirements for federal land management decisions. In certain instances, Congress has required federal-tribal consultation. For example, the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA, 54 U.S.C. §§300101 et seq.) requires federal agencies to take into account the effects of projects they carry out, license, or financially assist (collectively referred to as undertakings) on historic properties.18 As part of that consideration, federal agencies must consult with any Tribe that "attaches religious and cultural significance" to historic properties that may be affected by the undertaking.19
Some federal land management agencies, such as the Department of the Interior (DOI) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), have entered into formal agreements with Tribes to endeavor that agency decisionmaking complies with the NHPA. Consultation-related agreements have the potential to both support statutory compliance and increase collaboration between Tribes and federal land management agencies in decisionmaking. For example, the Forest Service's (FS's) Ozark-St. Francis National Forests and Ouachita National Forest have entered into a series of NHPA Programmatic Agreements with nonfederal entities (including Tribes) that provide a framework for managing cultural resources, including a process for addressing the discovery of human remains and any associated funerary objects.20
In other instances, the executive branch has directed agencies—through executive orders, regulations, agency guidance, and other administrative actions—to consult with Tribes in the development of federal policies with tribal implications.21 This has included requiring some federal agencies responsible for administering federal lands and waters to establish consultation procedures with Tribes. For example, both USDA and DOI have tribal consultation policies that direct their agencies to provide Tribes the opportunity for consultation and coordination in policy development and program activities that have tribal implications.22 However, each agency has different consultation policies and processes, which can result in inconsistent levels and types of tribal consultation in federal decisionmaking on federal lands.23
CRS searched the United States Government Publishing Office's Compilation of Presidential Documents website and found no evidence that the Trump Administration has rescinded any presidential directives related to tribal consultation as of October 5, 2026.24 Therefore, it appears that the presidential directives related to tribal consultation from prior Administrations remain in effect. However, offices within the Executive Office of the President, such as the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), have directed federal agencies to limit tribal consultation in certain contexts. For example, OMB Memorandum M-25-36, "Streamlining the Review of Deregulatory Actions," states that federal agencies should consider deregulatory actions as "presumptively not triggering" consultation requirements. Furthermore, it states that "[i]f there exists a particular reason for specific government-to-government consultations," agencies should presume that these consultations "should take place as part of the normal opportunity for stakeholder participation."25
A co-management approach with more direct tribal involvement in the decisionmaking process entails agencies entering into agreements with Tribes to enable Tribes to conduct specific activities on federal lands. Congress has both mandated this type of co-management and provided agencies with discretion to engage in this type of co-management on federal lands. For example, when Congress established the Grand Portage National Monument in 1958, it provided a specific preference for employing tribal members in construction, maintenance, visitor services, "or any other service within the monument for which they are qualified."26 Congress has also allowed DOI and FS to contract or compact with Tribes to manage certain federal programs under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, as outlined in the textbox below.
Another type of co-management is long-term partnerships between federal agencies and Tribes, which enable more tribal influence. In certain instances, federal agencies have entered into agreements to facilitate consistent coordination and cooperative management with Tribes based on tribal treaties and Tribes' historical ties to agency lands. On a regional scale, DOI, the Department of Commerce (DOC), and the Department of Defense (DOD) have worked with Tribes to give effect to tribal treaty fishing rights in the Pacific Northwest, and DOI has worked with Alaska Natives to manage subsistence wildlife on federal lands in Alaska (for more on these examples, see "Co-Managing Natural Resources").27 At a local level, the FS and the Tribes that are members of the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission used a memorandum of understanding to establish standards by which the parties would "act consistently across national forest lands within areas ceded in the treaties of 1836, 1837, and 1842."28 In particular, the parties sought to ensure "the meaningful exercise" of tribal treaty rights, facilitate "consistent and timely communication," and foster effective tribal participation in relevant forest plans.29
Federal agencies have used the terms "co-management" and "co-stewardship" to refer to long-term partnerships, although each term has been defined slightly differently.30 In a 2016 secretarial order, DOI defined co-management as "a situation where there is a specific legal basis that requires the delegation of some aspect of Federal decision-making" but did not define delegation in that context.31 In addition to co-management, during the Biden Administration, USDA and DOI encouraged co-stewardship, which focused on proactively identifying and entering into agreements with Tribes. For example, in November 2021, USDA and DOI issued Secretarial Order (SO) 3403, which directed agencies to collaborate with Tribes based on the treaty, religious, subsistence, and cultural interests of Tribes in the co-stewardship of federal lands and waters.32 In 2022, DOI included this direction in departmental guidance, and NPS, BLM, and FWS released a series of follow-up policy memoranda encouraging co-stewardship.33 In December 2024, DOI reported that more than 400 co-stewardship agreements had been signed.34 In addition, FS's 2023 Tribal Action Plan entitled "Strengthening Tribal Consultations and Nation-to-Nation Relationships" committed to a co-stewardship strategy.35 This strategy included "expanding scope and scale of Tribal involvement in agency work, planning, and decision making, as well as Tribal self-determination."36 The USDA, DOC, and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) have not publicly defined the term co-management.
Federal land management agencies have entered into co-management arrangements for a variety of different resources. The type of co-management and the relevant authorization often depend on the type of resource being managed. This section provides selected examples of DOI, USDA, DOC, and DOD co-management with Tribes of natural, cultural, and historic resources on federal lands. The examples below are categorized based on the primary activity, although many co-management agreements include a range of activities.
Many Tribes maintain Indigenous knowledge ("IK") about their ancestral lands and associated plants, fish, and wildlife, having relied on harvesting these resources for thousands of years.37 Some communities are more reliant on certain resources due to their geographic location, seasonality, and cultural traditions. Co-management of federal lands can provide Tribes with the opportunities to provide input on federal decisions affecting these natural resources and to advocate for access to them. In addition, through co-management, policymakers can potentially learn about this knowledge, including tribal values, culture, and ways of life, which could improve land management outcomes.38 At the same time, some Indigenous peoples may want to control or limit information sharing for various reasons.39
Due to their historical connection to salmon and other native fish, some of the Tribes in the Pacific Northwest reserved rights to continue hunting, fishing, or gathering on lands they ceded to the federal government by treaty. Many Tribes retain treaty-reserved rights to hunt or fish in "usual and accustomed" places.40 Courts have affirmed these rights even when the usual and accustomed places are not located within the boundaries of a reservation.41 Courts also have held that the right to fish by extension includes a right to protect the habitat on which the fish rely.42
Congress has acknowledged or protected regional tribal fishing rights, such as by ensuring a tribal role in managing fish in federal waters. The Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, as amended, specifies certain Tribes as members on the Pacific Fishery Management Council.43 The act specifies that the Secretary of Commerce (or designee) shall appoint at least one Pacific Fishery Management Council member "from an Indian Tribe with Federally recognized fishing rights from California, Oregon, Washington, or Idaho."44 This tribal representation rotates among Tribes in the area, taking into account "the various rights of the Indian Tribes involved and judicial cases that set forth how those rights are to be exercised."45 Due to this tribal representation, the Pacific Fishery Management Council has described the Tribes as co-managers of the fisheries overseen by the council, alongside the states and federal government.46
As another example, in 1985 Congress provided for the implementation of the Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and Canada through the Pacific Salmon Treaty Act of 1985.47 The treaty governs the overall harvest and allocation of salmon stocks in the region, and the statute established the Pacific Salmon Commission to implement the treaty.48 The act mandated that regional "treaty Indian tribes" have representatives on the commission.49 The act defined a treaty Indian tribe as "any of the federally recognized Indian tribes of the Columbia River basin, Washington coast or Puget Sound areas having reserved fishing rights to salmon stocks subject to the Treaty under treaties with the United States Government."50 Each year, commission representatives from the Canadian and U.S. governments, U.S. states, First Nations (i.e., Canadian Indigenous peoples), and treaty Indian tribes meet to discuss and review management of commercial, sport, and subsistence fisheries relative to the Pacific Salmon Treaty requirements.51
Many Pacific Northwest Tribes have sought to maintain fisheries by working with federal agencies. Tribes and others have argued that effective conservation of salmon, in particular, requires federal-tribal co-management, drawing on both IK and Western science.52 DOI and other federal agencies have often collaborated with Tribes to ensure compliance with tribal treaty rights and other laws providing for tribal management of fisheries and access to fish harvests. For example, throughout the 20th century, the Nez Perce Tribe (NPT), the United States, the State of Idaho, and local communities and water users in Idaho worked to resolve the Tribe's water rights claims in the Snake River Basin (NPT claimed water rights for instream flows to protect the Tribe's treaty-reserved fisheries).53 In 2004, Congress passed a law to implement a tribal water rights settlement and authorize tribal co-management of federal fisheries in the Pacific Northwest.54 That law specifically provided for tribal co-management of the Dworshak National Fish Hatchery, which was built by the USACE and operated by FWS on the NPT Reservation.55 In 2022, FWS transferred its fishery management responsibilities to the NPT. USACE continues to own the facility, and the FWS committed to continuing to provide administrative support.56 Tribal members are allowed to harvest salmon and steelhead trout in tribal fishing grounds adjacent to the hatchery.57
Alaska Natives have been treated distinctly from other Tribes because Congress has recognized that Alaska and its inhabitants are distinct from the rest of the country—for example, due to Alaska's late joinder to the union, size, distinct geography, and separation from the contiguous United States. One example of this distinct treatment is that, rather than treaties and reservations, Congress resolved Alaska Native land claims via a settlement mechanism: the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971 settled outstanding Alaska Native lands claims by providing Alaska Natives with 45 million acres and a monetary payment.58 ANCSA divided the majority of that land among more than 200 village corporations and 12 regional corporations (Alaska Native Corporations).59
Through various laws, Congress has directed federal agencies to ensure Alaska Native access to fish and wildlife on federal lands. For example, the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) of 1980 aimed to provide access to fish and wildlife on federal lands for rural subsistence needs, including for Alaska Natives.60 Generally, a subsistence use is when rural Alaskan residents use fish and wildlife resources for traditional purposes such as consumption, shelter, transportation, or some commerce.61 The act acknowledged Alaska Native subsistence use in particular as "essential to Native physical, economic, traditional, and cultural existence."62
ANILCA also established multiple federally protected areas in Alaska, including the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge.63 The proximity of the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge to certain Alaska Native communities has enabled co-management through ISDEAA agreements. Under ISDEAA, the FWS may enter annual or multiyear funding agreements for Tribes to assume certain FWS duties on units of the National Wildlife Refuge System or the National Fish Hatchery System. Several Alaska Native villages lying within or adjacent to the refuge maintain long-standing hunting and fishing (subsistence) uses.64 In 1998, a regional consortium of Alaska Natives known as the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments requested an expanded role in management of the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge through an ISDEAA agreement.65 In 2004, FWS entered into an ISDEAA agreement with the council to conduct refuge activities, including subsistence-related activities.66 In FY2019, the parties agreed to collaborate on Yukon Flats moose management, among other activities.67
Through the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 (MMPA), Congress provided Alaska Natives with an exemption allowing for the subsistence use of marine mammals.68 The MMPA also allows the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior to enter into cooperative agreements with Alaska Native organizations "to conserve marine mammals and provide co-management of subsistence use by Alaska Natives."69 These agreements can include grants to collect and analyze data on marine mammal populations for subsistence uses, and to develop "marine mammal co-management structures" with federal and state agencies.70
The MMPA does not define co-management, but the agencies and Alaska Natives have delineated the term through implementation. For example, the Marine Mammal Commission (comprising representatives of FWS, NOAA Fisheries, and Alaska Natives) characterized its work implementing the MMPA as an example of co-management: "two or more entities, each having legally established management responsibility, working together to actively protect, conserve, enhance, or restore fish and wildlife resources."71 In the 2006 memorandum of agreement on negotiating individual co-management cooperative agreements, NOAA Fisheries, FWS, and the Indigenous Peoples Council for Marine Mammals included a goal of "shared decision-making" for agreements that would be reached "through consensus, based on mutual respect."72 In addition, the parties agreed to use the best available scientific information and traditional and contemporary Alaska Native knowledge and wisdom for all decisions regarding Alaska marine mammal co-management.
Congress also provided some Alaska Natives with an exemption allowing for the subsistence use of migratory birds in the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA).73 The MBTA implements four bilateral treaties governing migratory birds. Although the law generally prohibits the taking of migratory birds, the MBTA authorizes FWS to issue regulations as needed to ensure Alaska Natives may take migratory birds and collect their eggs for their own nutritional and other essential needs during seasons established by FWS.74
In 1997, the Senate ratified a protocol amending the MBTA treaty with Canada to provide for co-management of migratory birds by Alaska Natives, the State of Alaska, and the federal government.75 The protocol stated that Alaskan Indigenous inhabitants "shall be afforded an effective and meaningful role in the conservation of migratory birds" through participating in "management bodies."76 This protocol led to the creation of the Alaska Migratory Bird Co-Management Council, which comprises representatives from the federal government, the State of Alaska, and Alaska Natives, "as equals," from 12 regional management areas.77 This council develops recommendations identifying certain subsistence harvest areas, which the FWS considers in developing its regulations on spring and summer subsistence harvesting of migratory birds and their eggs in Alaska.78 In line with the protocol's acknowledgement that IK should be considered in managing migratory birds, the council also is authorized to develop recommendations for the research and use of that knowledge related to the subsistence harvest of migratory birds.79
For decades, Tribes have coordinated with FS to manage forests and associated watersheds. For example, FS has collaborated with the Tulalip Tribes for many years to manage the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, which FS has recognized as the Tribes' ancestral homeland. FS has noted that its goal is to "create and maintain meaningful relationships between the Forest Service and local Indigenous communities."80 The agency has worked with the Tribes on wildlife reintroduction, huckleberry enhancement, and watershed enhancement. In 2007, the agency signed a memorandum of agreement with the Tulalip Tribes which laid out the parties' intent to "identify opportunities for collaboration between the Parties; so as to further the protection and conservation of natural, cultural, and archaeological resources for future generations."81
In 2020, the parties entered into a new kind of agreement. Under the Tribal Forest Protection Act (TFPA), which was first authorized in 2004, a Tribe may propose a project on FS or BLM lands that border, or are adjacent to, forested tribal trust or restricted fee lands to protect the tribal land from threats such as fire, insects, and disease.82 The Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 farm bill) authorized FS and BLM to enter into self-determination contracts under ISDEAA to perform "administrative, management, and other functions" of TFPA projects.83 The act stated that these would be "demonstration projects" but did not define that term or the scope of these projects.
In 2020, the Tulalip Tribes became the first Tribe to use this expanded TFPA authority to enter into a self-determination contract with FS. Under the contract, the Tulalip Tribes agreed to annually reintroduce beavers into salmon habitat to help with watershed restoration. FS explained that beaver dams can help maintain healthy habitat and water quality.84 Furthermore, improving instream and riparian landscapes could help support endangered salmon, which the Tribe claims is a treaty resource.85 As of November 2023, a total of 22 TFPA self-determination contracts totaling $41.7 million had been executed nationwide.86
Many Tribes maintain ongoing cultural and spiritual relationships with their ancestral homelands. Tribes may seek access to federal lands to continue practicing traditional ceremonies, and they may argue against certain activities on federal lands that may impede their ability to continue those practices or may affect lands they hold sacred.87 In contrast to co-management of natural resources, which generally focuses on the use and development of natural resources, co-management of federal lands for historical and cultural purposes would provide Tribes with the opportunity to weigh in on federal decisions to advocate for protection of federal areas and the Tribes' continued access.88
The federal government and the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa have collaborated for almost a century to preserve the unique heritage around Grand Portage, MN. In addition to being tribal traditional homelands, Grand Portage is a historical fur trading area.89 The Band advocated for the creation of the Grand Portage National Monument, and the Band donated about half of the land that became the monument.90 In the enabling legislation for the monument, Congress acknowledged that the area contained "unique historical values," and provided a specific preference for tribal employment in construction, maintenance activities, and "any other service within the monument for which they are qualified."91
After the monument's establishment in 1958, NPS collaborated with the Band through various agreements. In 1999, the Band and NPS reached an initial ISDEAA agreement for the Tribe to conduct maintenance on the monument.92 Between 1985 and 2016, NPS and the Band had completed more than 200 projects together.93 The Band's construction program has helped build park housing, a maintenance facility, a heritage center, and park administration offices. In 2022, DOI testified that a tribal youth organization called the "Grand Portage Conservation Crew" had engaged in "co-management practices and projects," including preserving historic structures, archaeological and wildlife surveys, plant restoration, and timber stand improvement.94
The Bears Ears National Monument in southern Utah is an example of the consultative and co-management role of multiple Tribes with cultural and historical ties to the area. Due in part to the significance of the area to many Tribes, President Obama issued a proclamation to reserve approximately 1.35 million acres as a national monument in December 2016.95 The proclamation established a Bears Ears Commission with members from several Tribes "to provide guidance and recommendations on the development and implementation of management plans and on management of the monument."96
Presidential proclamations in 2017 and 2021 modified the national monument to reduce or expand its size. In 2017, President Trump issued a proclamation reducing the Bears Ears National Monument by 1.15 million acres to ensure it was the "smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects of historic or scientific interest to be protected."97 In 2021, President Biden issued a proclamation that generally reestablished the terms and boundaries of the 2016 President Obama proclamation, also highlighting the spiritual, cultural, prehistoric, and historic legacy of the area.98
In addition, President Biden directed the federal agencies to issue a new management plan and reestablished the commission to ensure that "management decisions affecting the monument reflect expertise and traditional and historical knowledge" of Tribes.99 In June 2022, BLM and FS signed an intergovernmental cooperative agreement with the Bears Ears Commission.100 The agreement provides the Tribe with a co-management role, ensuring management decisions for the monument "reflect the expertise and traditional and historical knowledge of interested Tribal Nations and people."101 The agreement created a framework for communication that includes regular meetings and a timeline for tribal input in the monument planning process. BLM and FS worked with the Bears Ears Commission to develop a monument management plan, which was issued in January 2025.102 Among other things, the plan states that "the agencies' co-stewardship relationship with the [Commission] facilitates, enhances, and supplements coordination and cooperative management of the federal lands within [the Monument]; however, the agencies retain decision-making authority."103
In 2026, President Trump issued a proclamation that modified the monument in several ways. It reduced the monument by more than 1.2 million acres to approximately 121,096 acres comprising two units: the Shash Jáa Unit and the Indian Creek Unit. It also directed BLM and FS to develop new management plans, and that they "shall provide for public involvement in the development of any management plan, including consultation with federally recognized Tribes and State and local governments." The proclamation also disbanded and terminated the commission.104 On September 2, 2026, several Tribes and environmental groups sued the Administration to overturn this action.105
Congress may continue to consider the suitability and effectiveness of federal-tribal co-management of federal lands. For example, Congress may continue to consider whether certain federal lands may be managed or protected through co-management agreements, or whether certain lands would not be available for co-management. Congress also may consider the scope of activities governed by co-management agreements on federal lands, including whether there are certain activities that agencies may not delegate to Tribes. Additionally, Congress may consider the administrative and financial benefits and challenges facing agencies and Tribes in these agreements.
Due to their historical connections, many Tribes maintain IK about their ancestral landscapes. Although there is no single definition, one scholar defined IK as "a cumulative body of knowledge, practice, and belief ... handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of living beings (including humans) with one another and with their environment."106 Some tribal groups have asked Congress to direct federal agencies to include Tribes (and their IK) in land management decisions to bring together "the expertise of diverse perspectives to build a collective and participatory framework that can benefit everyone."107
For the past several decades, some scientists working on natural resources and land management topics and some federal agencies have been collecting and using IK to varying degrees.108 Appreciation for using IK began to change in the 1980s, potentially due to increasingly visible Indigenous political movements and an increased scientific recognition of IK.109 For example, federal land managers can potentially learn from IK, including tribal values, culture, and ways of life, which could improve land management outcomes.110 Starting in the 1980s, some federal agencies began to consider and incorporate IK into their decisions and activities. More recently, the Biden Administration issued government-wide guidance on IK and specifically encouraged the incorporation of IK in federal land management.111 For example, Executive Order 14072 established a policy to support IK and cultural and subsistence practices in national forests; the Trump Administration revoked this executive order in 2025.112
Congress has several options regarding the federal use of IK in federal land management planning. Congress could maintain the status quo, which would allow most federal agencies to continue to consider IK on an ad hoc basis. Alternatively, Congress could consider directing federal agencies to consider IK in specific contexts. Some Members of Congress have introduced legislation that would have required federal land management agencies to consult with Tribes in developing management plans on federal lands.113 Several bills specifically referenced the integration of IK into these management plans.114 For example, H.R. 3444 from the 119th Congress would provide a new authority for the Secretary of Agriculture to enter into agreements with Tribes to conduct certain activities on FS lands. When considering whether to enter into such an agreement, the Secretary of Agriculture was directed to "give special consideration" to the IK and skills of the Tribe. In the 119th Congress, at least two bills also include provisions requiring DOI and/or USDA to protect IK, for example from disclosure.115
Many Tribes continue to seek access to federal lands to practice traditional ceremonies in culturally important areas.116 A basic legal framework exists at the federal level to protect tribal religious, historic, and cultural sites and objects.117 For example, under the NHPA, federal agencies must consult with any Tribe that "attaches religious and cultural significance" to historic properties that may be affected by agency projects.118 However, absent specific legislative language, the protection of sacred sites on federal lands is largely up to agency discretion.

Stanton, Ansari, Grijalva Press GardaWorld Over Unanswered Questions After Company Secures New $1.2 Billion ICE Contract
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Greg Stanton (AZ-04) led Representatives Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03) and Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07) in demanding answers from GardaWorld Federal Services (GWFS) following its latest $1.2 billion contract to expand immigration detention facilities in Florence, Arizona. The lawmakers also pressed the company to answer questions it failed to address in a previous inquiry related to the Surprise warehouse facility.
The new contract, awarded September 21, raises fresh concerns about transparency and coordination with local governments. According to reporting, the Town of Florence was not notified of the planned expansion and had no additional information about the contract.
"It is deeply concerning that, despite the significant scale of these projects and their potential impact on surrounding communities, local governments continue to learn about them only after contracts have been awarded," the lawmakers wrote.
The letter also presses GWFS on questions left unanswered from the lawmakers’ March 2026 inquiry into its contract with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to convert a warehouse in Surprise into an immigration detention facility. In its April response, GWFS deferred many questions to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and failed to address basic questions about its own detention experience, staffing, facility assessments, and subcontracting plans. The lawmakers are demanding full answers.
The lawmakers also raised concerns about GWFS' previously undisclosed role in the environmental review of the Surprise warehouse. The City of Surprise revealed that a company representative had requested information for the assessment, despite neither GWFS nor federal agencies publicly disclosing its involvement.
The lawmakers are requesting written responses within 15 business days of receipt of the letter, including answers about:
- Experience and staffing: GWFS' qualifications to manage both projects, personnel overseeing operations, and plans to subcontract construction, medical care, staffing, or facility management.
- Facility safety: Structural and code-compliance assessments of the Surprise warehouse, including plans for ventilation, extreme heat mitigation, fire safety, and medical care.
- Environmental review: GWFS' role in the Surprise environmental assessment and its experience conducting comparable federal reviews.
- Florence expansion: Specific projects, facilities, and task orders planned under the $1.2 billion contract, including their scope and cost.
- Local coordination: Consultations with Surprise, Florence, Maricopa and Pinal counties, school districts, and public safety agencies.
- Taxpayer costs: Whether GWFS or DHS will cover increased demands for emergency medical services, fire protection, and law enforcement rather than shifting those costs to local taxpayers.
"The communities surrounding the Surprise and Florence facilities deserve transparency," the lawmakers concluded.
Read the full letter HERE.
title: Stanton, Ansari, Grijalva Press GardaWorld Over Unanswered Questions After Company Secures New $1.2 Billion ICE Contract

One Year After Trump Promised Full Reversal of Funding Cuts, First Responders Statewide are Still Without Millions in Federal Investments 
BUFFALO, N.Y. – Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26), Ranking Member of the House Homeland Security Committee’s Subcommittee on Emergency Management and Technology, led members of the New York Congressional Delegation in urging the Department of Homeland Security to immediately release $87 million in FY2025 Homeland Security Grant Program (HSGP) funding that is still owed to New York. Their letter, sent to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton, highlights the danger of withholding this funding from one the largest states in the nation and a top target for international and domestic terrorism.
“One year ago, President Trump promised to restore New York counterterrorism funding in full after slashing the state’s allocation by nearly 90 percent. Yet today, DHS refuses to release $87 million that is still missing,” said Congressman Kennedy. “As Ranking Member of the Emergency Management and Technology Subcommittee, I know how critical these preparedness investments are. They help law enforcement and first responders across New York, from Buffalo to Manhattan, plan for emergencies, train for real world terrorism threats, and get the equipment they need to keep our communities safe. These preparedness grants were born out of the aftermath of the deadliest terror attack in American history, a tragedy that changed New York State forever. DHS’s refusal to restore $87 million for the state is not just reckless – it poses a direct threat to public safety.”
In September 2025, DHS issued HSGP award notifications that cut New York’s allocation by 86 percent, or $187 million, leaving the state with just $30 million compared to roughly $220 million in FY24. In October 2025, following bipartisan advocacy, President Trump committed to restoring full funding at approximately $220 million. After a court order in Noem v. Illinois that found Trump unlawfully cut emergency grant funding, the administration released $100 million, but $87 million is still owed to New York.
The missing funds affect every county in the state, including Erie and Niagara, and represent $11 million in losses for New York City. The letter warns that without full restoration, DHS is severely limiting local law enforcement’s ability to plan, train tactical teams, procure equipment, and conduct operations. Created in the wake of the September 11th attacks, HSGP has protected New York State for decades. The delegation underscored that the funds are due 25 years after 9/11 and one year after the President’s promise.
The full text of the letter can be found here. 
 
###
title: Kennedy, New York Delegation Demand DHS Release $87 Million in Counterterrorism Funding Still Owed to New York

Trump Administration Announces More Than $177 Million to Recruit Rural Healthcare Workers, Expand Mobile Care, and Modernize Services Across Nebraska
This federal investment will bring new providers to rural communities, deploy remote-monitoring technology at dozens of healthcare facilities, and create hundreds of community health positions across Nebraska
Today, the Trump Administration announced more than $177 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to strengthen rural healthcare delivery across Nebraska. This investment will expand access to care, support healthcare workforce development, modernize rural healthcare technology, and bring services closer to home for rural and frontier communities.
This transformational funding is supporting rural communities across Nebraska. Recruitment and retention awards have already resulted in signed contracts with providers across 51 counties, helping build and sustain a healthcare workforce that serves the needs of rural communities. Forty-five healthcare facilities have gained access to remote-monitoring technology, with 68 devices deployed so far, and more than 200 community health worker and supervisor positions have been created to help residents navigate care, manage chronic disease, and connect with local providers. During Nebraska’s 2026 wildfires, 19 crisis debriefing sessions provided community mental health support, and rural law enforcement and first responders are also being equipped with app-based telehealth tools that provide direct access to trained mental health professionals during a crisis.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is expanding access to quality healthcare, regardless of a patient’s zip code, and equipping first responders with the lifesaving resources they need when every second counts. This funding will make critical investments to strengthen rural healthcare, expand access to lifesaving services, and bring modern technology to communities across Nebraska.
“President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”
“President Trump made a historic commitment to rural America, and these investments are turning that commitment into better care for patients in communities across Nebraska,” said Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “This is what rural health transformation should look like: federal investment that is putting patients first, driving lasting improvements and expanding healthcare for the hardworking Americans who call these communities home.”
Today’s investment was made possible through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act — passed by Republicans in Congress and unanimously opposed by Democrats — delivering a historic $50 billion investment to help states transform the way healthcare is delivered in America.
“Nebraska’s successful first year of the Rural Health Transformation Program reflects the strength of our federal state partnership. This funding is already expanding access to care, addressing critical workforce needs, and supporting prevention focused, technology enabled solutions in our rural communities,” said Gov. Jim Pillen. “It is laying the foundation for a more sustainable health care system. A system that supports healthier families, stronger local economies, and thriving rural communities for generations to come.”
“The Rural Health Transformation Fund was created by Republicans to support rural communities across the country. I was proud to vote to create this program, and I welcome this much-needed funding coming home to Nebraska to expand access to quality health care,” said Sen. Deb Fischer.
“Nebraskans deserve access to quality care regardless of their zip code. Thank you to CMS for this further investment in our state to help strengthen rural healthcare in our communities. I look forward to continuing our work together to deliver on Nebraskans’ priorities and support the Good Life,” said Sen. Pete Ricketts.
“Growing rural Nebraska means protecting quality healthcare close to home. I voted to create the Rural Health Transformation Program to strengthen the hospitals and clinics our small towns depend on. This investment will help Nebraska healthcare facilities grow their workforce, expand mobile and behavioral health services, and keep vital care within reach for rural communities,” said Rep. Mike Flood.
“Rural Nebraskans deserve quality health care close to home, and this $177 million investment will help make that possible,” said Rep. Don Bacon. “This funding will strengthen our rural health workforce, expand technology and mobile health services, and put a greater emphasis on prevention so Nebraska families can get the care they need. I thank the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for this important investment in the health and future of rural Nebraska.”
“I was proud to support the Working Families Tax Cuts, which created the Rural Health Transformation Program, and am pleased to see this vital program continue to invest in rural communities across Nebraska. Moving forward, I will continue to work to ensure that every Nebraskan has access to quality care close to home, regardless of their ZIP code,” said Rep. Adrian Smith.
Today’s announcement is one part of the larger overall funding amount awarded to Nebraska for fiscal year 2026.
Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:
- Building the rural healthcare workforce: Supporting recruitment, training, and retention strategies to strengthen the pipeline of healthcare professionals serving rural communities.
- Strengthening rural facilities and access: Supporting partnerships, operational improvements, and care-delivery changes that help rural providers maintain essential services and improve access.
- Advancing innovative care and payment models: Supporting new approaches to delivery and financing designed to improve quality, strengthen primary care, and support sustainable rural healthcare.
- Expanding community-based and preventive care: Investing in school-based care, mobile services, and other community strategies that improve prevention, address chronic disease, and expand access to care.
- Modernizing rural healthcare technology: Expanding remote care and data-driven tools to improve coordination and extend healthcare services to rural communities.
The Trump Administration is delivering on its commitment to strengthen rural America by investing in solutions that modernize technology to promote health and well-being for rural communities. Led by CMS, the RHTP is moving beyond the failed one-size-fits-all approach and giving rural communities the tools to build stronger, more innovative, and more sustainable health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes for the Americans they serve.
For more information about the RHTP, visit: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health.

CLEVELAND – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio has announced the unsealing of a 58-page indictment charging U.S. citizens and Chinese nationals for their roles in an IT worker conspiracy affecting more than 70 U.S. companies. These charges are the result of a year-long investigation.

A federal grand jury returned an indictment Oct. 1, 2026, charging the following defendants with Wire Fraud Conspiracy, Money Laundering Conspiracy, Conspiracy to Commit Identity Theft, and Aggravated Identity Theft:

Sun Sheng Ming, 37, Dandong City, China

Pei Li Guang, age unknown, Liaoning, China

Weng Shou Cheng, age unknown, Liaoning, China

Han Guo Bin, age unknown, Dandong City, China

Wang Jian Jun, 34, Dandong City, China

Sheng Zhang Kun, age unknown, Shenzhen, China

Zhang Wei Ping, age unknown, Dandong City, China

Zhang Li Ping, age unknown, unknown location

Yu Yang, 40, age unknown, Dandong City, China

Jin Long, 35, unknown location

Michael James Bostelle, 31, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, 37, San Juan, Texas

Carrillo and Bostelle were recently arrested and are expected to make their initial appearances in court in the Northern District of Ohio in the near future. All other defendants in this case remain at large. Two defendants remain under seal.

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“Today’s indictment underscores the pervasive danger targeting America’s businesses and the lengths at which threat actors and criminal networks will engage to undermine U.S. companies and augment nation-state interests,” said FBI Cleveland Special Agent in Charge Joshua DelManzo. “The FBI remains unyielding in its mission to defend not only Ohio businesses and companies across the country, but also to defend the United States against criminal and national security threats and will continue to investigate threats wherever they originate and ensure those responsible are held accountable.”

According to the allegations in the indictment, the defendants conspired to participate in a multi-year fraudulent scheme to obtain remote IT work to generate revenue for the government of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), which is more commonly referred to as North Korea.

The scheme was allegedly carried out by facilitators in the United States who assisted others working on behalf of the DPRK to be hired as remote IT workers with U.S. companies. Among the ways used to carry out the scheme, U.S. facilitators received and hosted multiple laptop computers—issued by victim U.S. companies—at their residences in the U.S., referred to as “laptop farms.”

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK.

Victim entities included companies serving a broad array of industries and services including health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing companies. Victim businesses were located not only in Ohio, but also across much of the U.S. including in Massachusetts, California, New York, New Jersey, Florida, Georgia, Minnesota, Maryland, North Carolina, Illinois, Virginia, Michigan, Texas, Arkansas, Pennsylvania, Washington, and the District of Columbia.

In addition to the unsealing of the indictment, the FBI has issued an alert for the business community regarding the hiring of remote IT workers. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter and adapt to improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. For more information about the FBI’s alert to U.S. businesses, visit https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA261013 .

The FBI is actively investigating remote IT worker fraud schemes throughout the country, including FBI’s Cleveland Division in the Northern District of Ohio.

Assistant United States Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the Criminal Division’s National Security Section are leading the prosecution.

An indictment is only a charge and is not evidence of guilt. Defendants are entitled to a fair trial in which it will be the government’s burden to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
title: 14 Indicted in North Korean Remote IT Worker Conspiracy Affecting More than 70 U.S. Companies

MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that Marquise Javon Walker, 30, of Lakeville, Minnesota, was sentenced to 60 months in prison for conspiracy to distribute fentanyl.

Walker was sentenced before U.S. District Judge John R. Tunheim on October 13, 2026. He is one of three defendants in a drug trafficking conspiracy, and he previously pleaded guilty on April 3, 2026. Walker’s co-defendants, La’Veal O. Allen, 40, of Minneapolis, and Michaela K. McKinney , 38, of New Hope, Minnesota, are currently awaiting sentencing.

According to court documents, starting no later than March 31, 2024, and continuing through at least September 10, 2024, Walker entered into an agreement or understanding with others to distribute fentanyl and other controlled substances. On March 31, 2024, the defendant drove from the Twin Cities metro area to Bemidji, Minnesota, to assist a co-conspirator’s drug distribution activities.

On April 13, 2024, the defendant’s co-conspirator sold approximately 48 grams of fentanyl to a buyer. Following the sale, law enforcement stopped the defendant while he was driving in his vehicle with his co-conspirator in the passenger seat. Officers searched the vehicle and found inside the passenger-side glove compartment the defendant’s Glock .45 caliber handgun.

In the following months, law enforcement seized an additional approximately 267 grams of fentanyl as well as 29.5 grams of methamphetamine from the defendant’s co-conspirator through a series of controlled purchases.

“For years, this defendant took advantage of addiction to make money. My office is committed to disrupting the flow of drugs into northern Minnesota and the Red Lake Indian Reservation,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen.

“For too long, individuals from outside northern Minnesota have exploited our communities, taking advantage of addiction, economic hardship, and the increased profitability of distributing narcotics in rural areas. Those times are gone. If you bring fentanyl into our region to distribute and profit from the suffering of others, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, gather evidence against you, and hold you accountable. This conviction is a direct result of that commitment and the hard work, dedication, and professionalism of our agents and the local, state, tribal, and federal partners involved in this investigation,” said Paul Bunyan Drug Task Force Commander and Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office Sergeant David Hart.

This case was the result of an investigation by the Paul Bunyan Drug Task Force, FBI Headwaters Task Force, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office, Bemidji Police Department, Hubbard County Sheriff’s Office, Morrison County Sheriff’s Office, Morrison County Attorney’s Office, Lakes Area Drug Investigative Division, and the Minnesota State Patrol.

Assistant United States Attorney Garrett S. Fields prosecuted the case.

Note: Previous press release on the indictment here .
title: First Defendant in Conspiracy Sentenced to Five Years’ Imprisonment for Trafficking Fentanyl to Bemidji

FBI Sacramento Reports Regional Results from Operation Summer Heat 2.0
The FBI Sacramento Field Office and its local, state, and federal law enforcement partners arrested 123 individuals for violent crimes between June 1 and September 30, 2026, as part of Operation Summer Heat 2.0, the FBI’s nationwide effort to reduce violent crime.
“This second year of Operation Summer Heat clearly demonstrates the FBI’s focus on crushing violent crime and the whole-of-government approach necessary to ensure safer communities,” said FBI Sacramento Special Agent in Charge Brian Tosh. “We are surging resources and working shoulder-to-shoulder with our law enforcement partners at all levels to remove violent crime and dangerous drugs from the communities we serve.”
Operation Summer Heat 2.0 was a collaborative, four-month nationwide effort focused on apprehending violent criminals and fugitives, dismantling violent gangs, identifying and rescuing child victims, and resolving violent crime cases in Indian Country.
Nationally, the operation led to 8,927 arrests, the recovery of 5,013 illegal weapons, the seizure of 687 kilograms of deadly fentanyl and 27,512 kilograms of cocaine. Additionally, agents, task force officers, and intelligence analysts investigating violent crimes against children identified or located 1,410 child victims.
Within the 34-county region served by the FBI Sacramento Field Office, these efforts resulted in 123 arrests, the recovery of 30 illegal weapons and the location or identification of 15 children. Additionally, 69 drug seizures resulted in the removal of illegal drugs from communities, including 7.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 562.03 kilograms of methamphetamine, 56.63 kilograms of cocaine and nearly one kilogram of MDMA.
Operation Summer Heat 2.0 follows historic drops in crime across the United States, according to the FBI’s 2025 UCR Summary of Reported Crimes in the Nation.
title: FBI Sacramento Reports Regional Results from Operation Summer Heat 2.0

Today, Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary. The briefing, which generated wall-to-wall coverage, served as a strong introduction to her tenure and highlighted the Trump Administration’s record of delivering historic successes for the American people.

We love new media, and we want to be able to embrace it.” (Watch)

text:
The Department of Justice Announces Results of Law Enforcement and Private Industry Joint Disruption Week Targeting Online Scam Accounts and Transnational Criminal Networks Operating in West Africa
Note: B-roll and photos related to the enforcement actions can be obtained at: https://spaces.hightail.com/space/UACsRDqzHp
Transnational criminal scam networks operating from West Africa suffered major disruptions last week during a coordinated international “Joint Disruption Week,” an effort that produced arrests, seizures, and the largest-ever takedown of fraudulent social media accounts linked to scam centers in the region, announced the Department of Justice.
“Criminals beware: Law enforcement from around the world are working together, and with private industry, to find you, stop your schemes, and bring you to justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI) was built for this brand of collaboration. The millions of bogus social media accounts taken down and dozens of arrests that took place as part of Joint Disruption Week are just the beginning. I want to thank the United Kingdom (UK)’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and its Director General, Graeme Biggar, for hosting this effort, as well as everyone who participated. I am especially grateful to the courageous law enforcement officers in Ghana and Nigeria who put themselves in harm’s way to seize evidence and arrest the criminals who prey on innocent people.”
“Transnational fraud demands a transnational response,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia, founder of the Scam Center Strike Force. “I have partnered with the NCA and the Crown Prosecutor for England and Wales to push forward cases on both sides of the Atlantic; criminals are not hindered by borders and neither are we. We will deploy our team wherever in the world transnational criminals target innocent victims.”
The “Joint Disruption Week” events mark the first coordinated effort focused specifically on West Africa, underscoring the growing global commitment to dismantling increasingly sophisticated transnational scam networks.
The operation included members of the U.S. Department of Justice, the Scam Center Strike Force under the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, FBI, U.S. Secret Service, U.S. Department of the Treasury, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), the UK’s NCA, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force - National Cybercrime Center, Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority, and private sector partners.
Additional participants included law enforcement agencies from Australia, Canada, Ghana, India, New Zealand, Nigeria, along with INTERPOL and additional cybercrime units. Several tech giants also played a key role. The large-scale effort was hosted by the UK NCA in London.
“Thanks to brilliant partnership with the Department of Justice and the private sector, across multiple African countries, we arrested dozens of criminal actors, seized hundreds of devices, identified at least $11 million in potentially freezable funds, and truly saved lives,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This is what happens when law enforcement executes with precision across the interagency. We are demolishing Scam Centers across the globe and crushing a criminal industry preying on American citizens.”
“Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it,” said Nick Sharp, Deputy Director of Fraud at the NCA. “Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilize the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud. Fraudsters can operate from anywhere and will target victims both domestically and globally. The NCA will continue to work with international and private sector partners to tackle fraudsters working upstream, overseas and online. Collaborating in this way sends a clear signal to criminals that the combined capabilities of law enforcement and industry means that we will relentlessly pursue them and the infrastructure they rely on no matter where they operate.”
During the week beginning Oct. 6, investigators and industry partners exchanged real-time intelligence across jurisdictions, enabling rapid identification and disruption of scam centers in Nigeria, Ghana, and other African countries. Many of the targeted operations were tied to schemes victimizing individuals in the United States, UK, and other countries around the world.
Several private industry partners, including Meta, Adobe, Binance, Coinbase, Cyjax, Elliptic, Chainalysis, Flashpoint, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Silent Push, Starlink and TRM Labs collaborated with international law enforcement in the event, and voluntarily took action on their own networks to disrupt scammers using their platforms to perpetrate fraud. These companies reported to the Department that they “removed more than 3.7 million accounts, Pages and Groups targeting people in the U.S., UK and beyond, and shared leads on over 30 suspected scam centers with law enforcement, resulting in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and cryptocurrency seizures. In total over $11 million dollars in potential freezable funds were identified by the private sector partners. Meta played a key role in coordinating the event and encouraging broad private sector participation to maximize scam compound disruption.
Among the key accomplishments:
A consortium of international law enforcement agencies made 28 arrests of individuals tied to the criminal scam operations, including:
- In Ghana, in the Accra suburb of Sasaabi, authorities arrested 19 individuals and seized 303 electronic devices. In addition, authorities identified 117 victims of human trafficking that are now pending repatriation to Nigeria. An additional 89 victims of the scam were identified with an approximate loss of $8.3 million. During the last week of September alone, authorities made scores of arrests at six locations, identified 34 trafficking victims, and seized 129 electronic devices. The Ghana operation was led by the Ghana Cyber Security Authority, Ghana Police Service Criminal Investigation Department, National Security Service, with support from the NCA, FBI, and Nigeria’s Economic and Financial Crimes Commission.
- In Nigeria, authorities arrested nine individuals during the enforcement period, and 53 electronic devices.
- The disrupted schemes included law enforcement impersonation scams, digital “arrest” extortion schemes, cryptocurrency investment fraud (also known as “pig butchering”), and a variety of other online fraud operations targeting global victims.
According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), investment scams were reported 72,984 times in 2025, with cryptocurrency investment fraud comprising 72 percent of that category. Reported losses from these scams rose from $3.96 billion in 2023 to $5.8 billion in 2024. Reported losses for investment scams with a cryptocurrency nexus rose 24 percent in 2025 to over $7.2 billion, according to IC3’s released 2025 annual report. Those figures, based largely on victim reports, are believed to significantly underrepresent actual losses, as many victims do not report to law enforcement. According to one government report, a conservative estimate of the annual value of funds stolen by scam syndicates worldwide approached $64 billion as of the end of 2023.
Strengthening Accountability for Transnational Scam Operations
Criminal scam centers operating in West Africa mirror those uncovered in Southeast Asia — highly organized enterprises that recruit workers, train them in social engineering, and deploy multi‑platform fraud campaigns targeting global victims. While technology companies can significantly disrupt online infrastructure used to perpetuate these schemes, true accountability requires sustained law enforcement action against the individuals and organizations behind them.
The FBI, The Scam Center Strike Force, and its international partners remain committed to advancing this model of public‑private collaboration and expanding global efforts to dismantle criminal networks responsible for online fraud.
On March 6, 2026, President Trump signed an Executive Order directing the Administration to prioritize cybercrime, fraud, and predatory schemes draining American families of their life savings. Through the Executive Order, President Trump is unleashing every available tool to stop foreign-backed criminal networks that exploit vulnerable Americans through cyber-enabled fraud. The Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative, Scam Center Strike Force under U.S. Attorney Pirro, and the Homeland Security Task Force National Coordination Center (NCC) are critical in executing the mission outlined in the President’s Order.
The Department of Justice’s Criminal Division, through its Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI), works to disrupt and stop cyber-enabled criminal networks that prey on Americans. CSI brings together expert prosecutors from across the Division to accelerate the prosecution of cyber-enabled financial crimes, including investment and crypto scams, government imposter schemes, romance and inheritance scams, financially motivated sextortion, lottery and sweepstakes scams, and other predatory schemes. With nationwide jurisdiction and global reach, CSI leverages every available tool to dismantle criminal operations, pursue bad actors, recover criminal proceeds, and obtain justice for victims. The Criminal Division partners with U.S. Attorney’s Offices across the country.
The Scam Center Strike Force was officially launched by U.S. Attorney Pirro in November 2025 to address the growing threat posed by Chinese organized crime syndicates operating scam centers, primarily in Southeast Asia. The Strike Force targets cryptocurrency investment fraud, cyber-enabled fraud, human trafficking, and money laundering operations that have cost American victims billions of dollars. The Scam Center Strike Force has been joined in its work by the FBI, the U.S. Secret Service, Justice Department’s Criminal Division, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, IRS Criminal Investigation, and HSI, as well as the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Districts of Alaska, Hawaii, Eastern North Carolina, Rhode Island, and Western Washington. The Strike Force works in collaboration with other federal agencies, including the Treasury and State Departments. The Strike Force works in strategic partnership with private industry and calls on all U.S. businesses to take more proactive steps to protect users from scam operations.
The Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF)’s NCC, established by Executive Order, is responsible for coordinating Federal efforts to detect, disrupt, dismantle, and deter — including by involving the private sector as appropriate — cyber-enabled criminal activity conducted by foreign Transnational Criminal Organizations and associated networks that target U.S. persons, businesses, critical infrastructure, or public services.
title: The Department of Justice Announces Results of Law Enforcement and Private Industry Joint Disruption Week Targeting Online Scam Accounts and Transnational Criminal Networks Operating in West Africa

ROANOKE, Va. – First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci today announced the release of the first Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) Annual Report highlighting the district’s ongoing efforts to reduce violent crime by enhancing law enforcement partnerships across federal, state, and local agencies, including Virginia sheriff’s offices, police departments, and Commonwealth’s Attorney’s.

This year’s report underscores the significant impact of three major PSN operations conducted in Danville, Roanoke, and Lynchburg. Each of these initiatives focused on identifying and prioritizing drivers of violent crime and removing them from the community, as well as seizing illegal firearms and narcotics from our streets.

The report reflects the Department of Justice’s renewed emphasis on deepening collaboration with law enforcement at every level. By unifying resources, intelligence, and investigative capabilities, PSN aims to enhance the effectiveness of crime reduction strategies to promote community safety and the role of law.

“The extraordinary success of combined law enforcement operations in Danville, Roanoke, and Lynchburg over the last year is a direct result of the cooperation, dedication and professionalism of our local, state, and federal partners. This office will seek maximum accountability against those who violate federal law in the Western District of Virginia and further enhance partnerships to ensure that every citizen of this district can live with safety and dignity in their communities,” First Assistant United States Attorney Tracci said today.

The PSN initiative remains the Department of Justice’s flagship program for reducing violent crime, built on the principles of evidence-based strategies, targeted enforcement, and rapid response to violent crime.

The full Project Safe Neighborhoods Report for the Western District of Virginia is now available to the public and can be found here .
