U.S. Marshals Massachusetts Fugitive Task Force Arrests Fugitive Wanted for Trafficking Children
For immediate release
Dennis Matulewicz, Acting U.S. Marshal
Boston, MA – The U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) District of Massachusetts (DMA) announced today a multi-agency coordinated arrest in Nantucket, Massachusetts, of a fugitive wanted for trafficking children.
Rigoberto Chavez-Regaldo, 40, was arrested in the morning hours of October 8, 2026, in connection with alleged criminal activity that occurred in Brockton and elsewhere in Eastern Massachusetts involving the trafficking of minors. Chavez was charged in Plymouth County with Sexual Conduct for a Fee (two counts), Aggravated Rape - Serious Bodily Injury, Aggravated Statutory Rape of a Child, Rape of a Child with Force, Trafficking Person for Sexual Servitude (two counts), Indecent Assault and Battery on person over 14, Sell/Deliver Liquor to person under 21, and Enticing a Child under 16.
Chavez was arraigned on the charges in Brockton District Court late that day. The Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office moved for a dangerousness hearing to be held. Chavez is being held without bail pending the outcome of a dangerousness hearing on Tuesday, October 13, 2026.
Investigators worked diligently across Eastern Massachusetts to apprehend Chavez, and he was arrested without incident in Nantucket, Massachusetts. The arrest was the result of a coordinated effort by members of the USMS DMA Fugitive Task Force, Brockton Police, Massachusetts State Police (MSP) Violent Fugitive Apprehension Section (VFAS), MSP Air Wing, and the Nantucket Police. This arrest would not have been possible without the assistance of the MSP Air Wing, and the rapid response by the MSP Air Wing was critical to the safe and successful apprehension.
“Allegations concerning the sexual exploitation and trafficking of children are arguably the most disturbing we encounter. Protecting young people from predators is our highest obligation as a society, and the USMS and our law enforcement partners will use every resource at our disposal to pursue anyone who preys on them,” said Dennis Matulewicz, head of the USMS for the District of Massachusetts. “Our Fugitive Task Force represents the very best of collaborative law enforcement. Today's arrest reflects the strength of those partnerships and our shared commitment to our communities and public safety. Our thoughts and prayers are with the children affected by these alleged crimes as they heal and move forward.”
In order to protect the privacy of the minor victims involved, additional details will not be released.
USMS DMA Fugitive Task Force participants include the USMS DMA, Massachusetts State Police, Boston Police, Brockton Police, Cambridge Police, Chicopee Police, Hampden County Sheriff’s Department, Haverhill Police, Lowell Police, Middlesex Sheriff’s Department, New Bedford Police, Plymouth County Sheriff's Department, Quincy Police, Randolph Police, Rochester Police, Springfield Police, Suffolk County Sheriff’s Department, West Springfield Police, Worcester Police, Massachusetts National Guard Counter Drug Program, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, and the Drug Enforcement Administration.
The USMS and its law enforcement partners remain committed to identifying, locating, and apprehending violent fugitives, developing actionable intelligence, and working collaboratively to enhance public safety throughout Massachusetts and across the nation.
The USMS reminds the public that criminal charges and allegations are accusations, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.
If you have any information regarding the whereabouts of any state or federal fugitive, please contact the USMS at 1-877-WANTED2 or submit a tip by emailing usmstips@usdoj.gov

Ohio Today
This summer, 14 students participated in a unique local internship experience. Since 2026 marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, the Central Region Humanities Center (CRHC) recruited Ohio University students to create exhibits that connect this national event with Southeast Ohio history and stories.
The CRHC supports university research and experiential learning in the humanities, connecting that to Southeast Ohio and the surrounding regional communities. Mariana Dantas, associate professor and director of the CRHC, was thrilled to involve students in this milestone event.
“The biennial conference was a great opportunity to develop a stronger relationship between the CRHC, our students, and the amazing local public humanities organizations in our city and county,” Dantas said. “When students have the chance to take their skills and knowledge into the community to promote the work they do and help them tell their stories, they get a taste of the wonderful things they can accomplish with their education.”
The student experiences were funded by a grant of almost $200,000 from the National Endowment for the Humanities, allowing the CRHC to fund research and opportunities for their interns surrounding the 250th anniversary.
Read more at Ohio Today.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives Lou Correa (CA-46) and Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) today reintroduced a resolution remembering and honoring the life and legacy of Alex Odeh. The resolution acknowledges Alex's impact on his community and the country, and reaffirms the importance of pursuing justice against those responsible for his death.
“Alex Odeh was a teacher, a poet, and a man of peace, and he was murdered in our community simply for speaking up for civil and human rights,” said Correa. “He was a voice for peace and dignity in Orange County. Remembering him is the least we can do, and pursuing justice for his family is our obligation.”
Rep. Correa represents the district where Alex and his family lived and where the attack took place.
“Alex Odeh dedicated his life to achieving true equality and equity for all. For daring to push for a better tomorrow, Alex was assassinated by members of the Jewish Defense League, and his killers have yet to be brought to justice,” said Tlaib. "This horrific act of anti-Arab and anti-Palestinian violence was, and is not, new. But this violence will never silence us. Those who continue to fear-monger and incite hate against us will not win. Arab and Palestinian Americans are still here, loud and proud, carrying on Alex’s legacy.”
Read the bill text here.
About Alex Odeh
Alex was born in Jifna, Palestine, and lived in Orange County, California, for most of his adult life, including Santa Ana. He was a peace activist who worked to promote civil liberties for Arab-Americans in the United States. Alex Odeh was the Southern California Regional Director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC).
On October 11, 1985, Alex was killed when a pipe bomb exploded as he entered the ADC regional office in Santa Ana, California. Although the primary suspects have long been known, no one has been brought to justice. The investigation remains open.
title: CORREA, TLAIB REINTRODUCE RESOLUTION HONORING ALEX ODEH

SANTA ANA – A previously removed illegal alien was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison for possessing with intent to distribute methamphetamine, unlawfully possessing ammunition as a felon, and illegally reentering the United States after prior deportations.

The case was investigated as part of Operation Guardian Angel, an initiative targeting violent offenders, narcotics trafficking, and previously removed criminal aliens operating in local communities.

Juan Jose Guerra‑Renteria, 46, a Mexican national who had been deported in 2006 and again in 2020, was sentenced on October 8, 2026, for possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, being a felon in possession of ammunition, and illegal reentry.

United States District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani sentenced him to 120 months’ imprisonment on the drug trafficking and firearms counts and 29 months on the illegal reentry count, to be served concurrently.

“Thanks to Operation Guardian Angel, criminal illegal aliens like Guerra‑Renteria are being identified and removed from our communities,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “This sentence reflects the seriousness of defendant’s conduct and his repeated disregard for federal law. My office will continue to work with our law enforcement partners to safeguard our communities and ensure that dangerous criminal illegal aliens are held accountable with federal prison time.”

According to the plea agreement, on October 14, 2025, law enforcement conducted a traffic stop on Guerra‑Renteria in Orange County, during which officers located over 211.9 grams of methamphetamine and 56 rounds of .45‑caliber ammunition.

At the time he possessed the ammunition, Guerra‑Renteria had multiple prior felony convictions, making it illegal for him to possess ammunition under federal law. Following his 2020 removal, he knowingly and voluntarily reentered the United States without authorization from the Attorney General or the Department of Homeland Security.

This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Orange Police Department.

Assistant United States Attorney Kevin Y. Fu of the Orange County Office prosecuted the case.

USPS responds to Delaware delegation on future of Ocean View Post Office
USPS confirms search for potential new location as delegation continues push for permanent solution, greater transparency
OCEAN VIEW, Del. — U.S. Representative Sarah McBride and U.S. Senators Chris Coons and Lisa Blunt Rochester (all D-Del.) today announced that they have received a formal response from the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) regarding the continued closure and future of the Ocean View Post Office.
The response follows a letter from the delegation to Postmaster General David Steiner demanding greater transparency, a clear timeline, improved interim services, and a permanent solution for Ocean View residents who have been without a fully functioning local Post Office for more than a year.
The Ocean View Post Office closed for emergency repairs in October 2025 after problems with the facility were identified. USPS initially announced plans to repair the building, then announced in June that further evaluations had determined a full rebuild was necessary, with construction expected to begin in spring 2027 and conclude that fall.
In its latest response to the delegation, however, USPS said additional engineering concerns prompted officials to further evaluate their plans. USPS is now conducting a search for existing properties in the Ocean View community to determine whether leasing a new location would be preferable to constructing a new facility on the existing property.
“For more than a year, the people of Ocean View have dealt with changing plans and far too much uncertainty about the future of their Post Office,” said Congresswoman McBride and Senators Coons and Blunt Rochester. “We appreciate that USPS is seriously analyzing every option to restore full postal service to Ocean View, however that looks. But residents still deserve what we asked for in our letter: a permanent solution, a clear timeline, and regular, transparent communication about how USPS intends to get there. We will continue pressing USPS until Ocean View has the reliable, fully functioning Post Office this community deserves.”
USPS also addressed concerns raised by the delegation regarding interim postal services. The agency said it is preparing to replace the existing collection box at 220 Atlantic Avenue with a larger collection box, though the 11 a.m. pickup time will remain unchanged. USPS had previously announced in April that the larger box would be installed by May 30. The agency acknowledged the delay and said it expects the new box to be installed soon.
While the Ocean View facility remains closed, retail and Post Office Box services continue to operate through the Bethany Beach Post Office, just over two-and-a-half miles away, while carrier delivery continues through the Sussex County Carrier Annex in Frankford.
The delegation had also requested an in-person meeting with Postmaster General Steiner. USPS indicated that it is willing to meet with the delegation and committed to contacting congressional staff when it has a substantive update regarding the facility search. The delegation will continue working with USPS, state and local officials, and Ocean View residents to press for a timely permanent solution and ensure the community is kept informed as the process moves forward.
###
title: USPS responds to Delaware delegation on future of Ocean View Post Office

BURLINGTON – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Vermont stated that on October 6, 2026, Paul Conneh, 39, of Moncton, New Brunswick, Canada, was sentenced by United States District Judge William K. Sessions III to serve a 33-month term of imprisonment for his three weeks of participation in the “grandparent scam.” Judge Sessions also ordered him to pay $256,000 in restitution to the victims of the offense. Previously, on May 28, 2026, Conneh pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit wire fraud and conspiring to launder monetary instruments in connection with the grandparent scam.

According to court records, Conneh participated in the grandparent scam by recruiting “bail bondsmen” to travel to the United States, laundering the money they took from elderly Americans, and distributing the money to co-conspirators. Conneh participated in the grandparent scam for three weeks during July and August 2023, victimizing approximately 20 elderly Americans. Conneh was arrested in Costa Rica on January 23, 2025 at the request of the United States, and was extradited to the United States.

First Assistant United States Attorney Jonathan A. Ophardt commended the investigative work of Vermont-based agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), United States Customs and Border Protection, and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, and recognized the assistance provided by HSI in Panama, Interpol, the United States Department of Justice’s Office of International Affairs, the United States Embassy in Costa Rica, and Costa Rica’s Judicial Investigation Department (Organismo de Investigación Judicia) in efforts to secure the arrest and December 2025 extradition.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Nate Burris and Michelle Arra. Conneh was represented by Chandler Matson, Esq.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Vermont is comprised of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the Diplomatic Security Service, the Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation, and state and local partner agencies, with prosecutions being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Vermont.

If you or someone you know has been a victim of elder fraud, help is standing by at the National Elder Fraud Hotline (833-FRAUD-11). This hotline is a free resource created by the U.S. Department of Justice, Office for Victims of Crime for people to report fraud against anyone age 60 or older.
title: Canadian Man Sentenced to Prison for Participation in “Grandparent Scam”

text:
Seattle – A 54-year-old former attorney was sentenced yesterday in U.S. District Court in Seattle to two years in prison for wire fraud for his theft of more than $1.5 million from an estate he was hired to probate, announced Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd. Duncan Connelly voluntarily surrendered his law license as part of his plea agreement on March 5, 2026. At the sentencing hearing U.S. District Judge Jamal N. Whitehead said, “We talk about these financial crimes as if they’re just money,.. but as one of the victim’s wrote, ‘this was the money of someone I loved’… (The victims) had trust in you…. What we’re really talking about is theft. And then you covered it up.”

“Mr. Connelly not only stole from his victims, he lied to them about his embezzlement for nearly two years,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd. “His crime was predatory, prolonged, and planned. The victims will likely not be made whole and will have to live the final years of their lives without the financial security that was rightfully theirs.”

According to records filed in the case, in July 2020 Connelly was hired by the executor of the estate of a Port Townsend, Washington, woman who left some $3.7 million to six nieces and nephews, with nine specific gifts to various entities. The executor was one of the relatives - all of whom lived overseas - and all were unfamiliar with all of the legal steps necessary to distribute the funds and close the estate. The executor hired Connelly, who then worked at a large prestigious law firm, because of rankings on the firm’s website.

Initially, Connelly handled the affairs of the estate appropriately while billing significant legal fees. However, in 2021, Connelly was fired from his large prestigious law firm and went out on his own as a solo practitioner.

Connelly began delaying payments and failing to respond to inquiries from the heirs. In February 2023 he began stealing money from the estate. He wrote himself checks from the estate and tried to make it look as if it was a specific bequest. He would deposit the money in his firm account and then transfer it to his personal account to pay his personal expenses. The first check was for $10,000 but the next one in May was for $50,000. Again, he used amounts that made it appear he was paying a specific bequest. All the while he continued to bill fees – some $6,000 for his “work” on the case.

Finally in August 2023 Connelly stole $1.5 million from the estate account which he labeled “transfer for investment” to make it look legitimate. But the investment was in risky online day trading and Connelly lost the money. He made some additional partial payments to some of the victims but by July 2024 there was just a little over $500 left in the estate, despite owing the beneficiaries well over $1 million. At this point Connelly stopped responding to the beneficiaries.

Connelly ultimately reported his theft to the FBI and federal prosecutors and agreed to give up his law license as part of his guilty plea.

In asking for a 30-month sentence prosecutors wrote to the court, “Connelly used his unique position of being the estate’s attorney to commit his crime, knowing his clients had no knowledge of the legal system or estate procedures of this country. Instead of helping the client he was actively billing and ethically required to help, he exploited their inexperience. Connelly had other clients, other opportunities to embezzle client funds, but he chose these victims because they had a large estate and they were uniquely unprepared to challenge Connelly’s lies or detect his fraud from afar.”

Judge Whitehead ordered three years of supervised release to follow prison and $1,369,462 in restitution, which accounts for some of the money Connelly paid back after the theft.

The case was investigated by the FBI and was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Grace Zoller.
title: Former attorney sentenced to two years in prison for stealing from estate he was to probate

WASHINGTON — Prasan Nepal, 21, also known by the online moniker “Trippy,” of High Point, North Carolina, pleaded guilty yesterday to conspiracy to commit sexual exploitation of a child.

“This is the latest victory in the FBI’s work with partners to dismantle the violent 764 network,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Prasan Nepal, a leader of 764, pleaded guilty for his role in exploiting juveniles - not only breaking the law himself but recruiting others to participate in the heinous conduct targeting kids online through sexual assault, pornography, animal crushing, and more. Dismantling 764 and their online network has been a top priority for this FBI, with a nearly 500% increase in 764 related arrests last year with our state and local partners. We are finding these criminal actors all over the country no matter where they operate. Let there be no doubt that the FBI and our partners will use all our resources to protect children and bring to justice those who commit acts of terrible abuse.”

“Nepal used his leadership role within 764 to orchestrate the systematic exploitation, torture, and psychological destruction of children for the twisted satisfaction of an online network built on cruelty and chaos,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He directed unspeakable crimes and then treated the suffering of the group’s victims as currency to be traded among his co-conspirators. We will not rest until every member of this network, and others like it, are held accountable.”

“This case exposes a world where cruelty is currency, violence is entertainment, and children are treated as targets in a game of domination and control,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “What Nepal and his co‑conspirators built was not just a criminal operation, it was a deliberate campaign to corrupt the vulnerable and dismantle the guardrails of civilized society. Yesterday’s plea is a victory for every child they sought to harm, and a warning to anyone who believes they can hide behind an encrypted screen: we will find you, and we will stop you.”

Nepal operated as a senior leader within “764,” a nihilistic violent extremist network that, according to court documents, engaged in a wide range of criminal conduct across the United States and abroad — including coordinated efforts to exploit minors, extort vulnerable victims, and inflict psychological harm as part of an organized ideology promoting chaos and societal destabilization.

According to court documents, Nepal and co‑defendant Leonidas Varagiannis, known as “War,” served as core leaders of 764 and its inner subgroup, 764 Inferno.

From approximately 2021 through 2025, Nepal and others used encrypted platforms to coordinate the exploitation of minors worldwide. They directed members, enforced “rules,” managed recruitment, and oversaw the production and circulation of materials used to manipulate and coerce victims.

Membership in 764 required prospective recruits to produce “content” that furthered the group’s extremist and abusive aims. Individuals who complied gained status; those who did not were excluded. Nepal and Varagiannis maintained strict control over membership, monitored activity, and issued instructions designed to expand the network’s reach and increase the volume of exploitative material.

Court documents detail the involvement of co‑conspirators operating inside the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area. One D.C.-based individual allegedly stored network material on digital devices within the District and participated in conduct aimed at coercing minor victims. Other U.S.-based co‑conspirators engaged in coordinated online extortion schemes that targeted minors in multiple states and foreign jurisdictions.

The stored content included images of the words “764 Kills” written in red on a wall and a video of 15-year-old minor victim standing topless with her breasts exposed, talking to someone on a live chat while she poured bleach on her arm and set her arm on fire.

Federal investigators have identified more than a dozen active co‑conspirators associated with Nepal and Varagiannis, many of whom operated under aliases and interacted regularly in encrypted group channels. Their activities reflected an organized, hierarchical structure designed to recruit vulnerable victims, generate exploitative material, and cultivate notoriety within the network.

764 and 764 Inferno were built on a shared extremist ideology that embraced social collapse and celebrated violence. Members used encrypted applications to:

Identify vulnerable minors online,

Manipulate victims into compliance,

Coerce individuals using threats and intimidation,

Distribute extremist and exploitative content, and

Promote members based on the severity of material they helped generate.

The defendants and their co-conspirators around the world used the Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) and other gore and violent material to create digital “Lorebooks,” which were used as digital currency within the 764 network, traded, archived in encrypted “vaults,” and used as a means to recruit new members or maintain status within the network.

The defendants instructed other members in grooming tactics and set content production expectations for new recruits. In multiple instances, defendants threatened and caused their victims to engage in self-mutilation, online and in-person sexual acts, harm to animals, sexual exploitation of siblings and others, acts of violence, threats of violence, suicide, and murder.

According to court documents, the defendants exploited at least eight minor victims across multiple jurisdictions, with some content traced back to children as young as 13-years old. The network’s activities spanned from late 2020 through early 2025.

Nepal joined 764 in or around early 2021, and worked with others known and unknown, including Individual 1, to establish the group. After Individual 1’s arrest on or about Aug. 25, 2021, Nepal emerged as a leader of 764 and remained in that position through April 2025.

In his capacity as a member and leader of 764, Nepal used several online monikers, including, “Leather Jacket,” “Rebirth,” “Indras Jester,” and “KingKrampus,” but he was most widely known in 764 Inferno as “Trippy.”

Nepal was arrested in 2025 and charged alongside Varagiannis as part of a sweeping international investigation involving the District of Columbia, federal field offices across the United States, and law enforcement authorities abroad. Yesterday’s plea represents one of the most significant developments yet in dismantling 764’s leadership structure.

Variagiannis is currently being held at Grevena Prison in northern Greece and is expected to have a trial in the next six months on charges related to child pornography and participation in a criminal organization.

Nepal faces a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison and a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison. Sentencing is set for March 5, 2027.

This case is being investigated by the FBI Washington Field Office with significant assistance from the FBI New York Field Office, FBI Charlotte Field Office, and international partners. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of North Carolina also provided invaluable assistance.

The case is being prosecuted by Trial Attorneys Justin Sher and James Donnelly of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Karen Shinskie and Janani Iyengar for the District of Columbia.

The Justice Department remains vigilant against the threat of NVE networks like 764 that operate within the United States and around the globe. NVEs often target vulnerable individuals, including minors, using social media platforms to share CSAM and gore material, and groom victims toward committing acts of violence. Victims are often extorted, coerced, compelled, and blackmailed into complying with NVE demands, including self-mutilation, online and in-person sexual acts, harm to animals, sexual exploitation of siblings and others, acts of violence, threats of violence, suicide, and murder. For more information on how to protect children and others, read about the online risks here: https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/parents-and-caregivers-protecting-your-kids and the FBI’s March 2025 public service announcement.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

Illinois Woman Sentenced to 31 Months in Prison for Distributing and Conspiring to Create and Distribute Sexual Torture and Mutilation Videos of Baby Monkeys
Amanda Leigh Fourez, of Catlin, Illinois, was sentenced yesterday to 31 months in prison and three years of supervised release in connection with her involvement with online groups dedicated to creating and distributing videos depicting acts of extreme violence and sexual abuse against monkeys in violation of the federal Animal Crushing statute.
Fourez pleaded guilty in April to distributing animal crush videos and conspiring with others to create and distribute the videos.
According to court documents and statements made during the sentencing hearing, Fourez paid thousands of dollars to commission bespoke sexual torture videos of monkeys, and later she distributed the obscene crush videos online. She was a member of several chat groups and private payment groups dedicated to the creation, distribution, and discussion of sexual and violent videos depicting monkeys being tortured, including baby and adult monkeys being burned and their genitals mutilated.
During the sentencing hearing, the court denied Fourez’s motion for a downward variance. The court observed that the videos that Fourez created and distributed were “shocking and violent” and documented “agonizing torture” of animals. The court further noted that the sentence should deter others from this serious conduct.
Another member of these groups, Joseph Garrett Buckland, of Mount Pleasant, Pennsylvania, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to create and distribute animal crush videos in April and is set to be sentenced on Jan. 13, 2027 for his role in the conspiracy ring.
“We stand ready to prosecute this depraved conduct,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of the Justice Department’s Energy and Natural Resources Division (ENRD). “We appreciate the collaboration of HSI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office in rooting out this conspiracy and prosecuting the case.”
“Amanda Fourez commissioned mutilation of helpless animals on video, and then disseminated those gruesome videos to an online community of people who were seeking content that portrayed the infliction of severe pain and suffering,” said U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti for the Western District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentencing demonstrates the ongoing commitment of the Department of Justice and our law enforcement partners to investigating and prosecuting these serious federal crimes involving cruelty to animals.”
“The conduct in this case was unimaginably cruel and highlights the depraved nature of the online networks HSI is committed to dismantling,” said Special Agent in Charge Matt Wright of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New Orleans. “HSI will continue to utilize advanced investigative techniques and vital law enforcement partnerships to track those who facilitate these heinous crimes across international borders.”
HSI New Orleans’ Cyber and Human Exploitation Investigations investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Emily R. Stone of ENRD’s Environmental Crimes Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alyssa Angotti and Kelly M. Locher for the Western District of Pennsylvania are prosecuting the case.
title: Illinois Woman Sentenced to 31 Months in Prison for Distributing and Conspiring to Create and Distribute Sexual Torture and Mutilation Videos of Baby Monkeys

Frankfort, Ky. – A Shelbyville man, Natividad Aguilera Garcia, 40, pleaded guilty on Friday, October 9, 2026, before Chief U.S. District Judge David L. Bunning to receipt of child sexual abuse material, inducing illegal immigration, making false statements to the United States, and presenting false documentation to the United States.

According to his plea agreement, Garcia, a Honduran citizen and legal permanent resident of the United States, met a minor while visiting family in Honduras. The minor reported that, while in Honduras, Garcia courted her. Upon his return to the United States, Garcia received sexually explicit images of the minor. The minor reported, and electronic evidence shows, that Garcia persuaded the minor to illegally enter the United States. Once in the United States, the minor went to a shelter for unaccompanied alien children, overseen by the Office of Refugee Resettlement (“ORR”), a sub-agency of Health and Human Services. Thereafter, Garcia falsely represented to ORR that he was the minor’s uncle, also presenting a false Honduran birth certificate to establish the familial relationship. ORR relied on these falsehoods and decided to place the minor in Garcia’s care. Garcia picked the minor up from the Louisville airport. Days after picking up the minor, Garcia’s ex-wife reported Garcia’s conduct to the shelter, prompting law enforcement’s investigation. Garcia’s plea agreement does not contain admissions regarding his conduct with the minor after he picked her up from the airport. However, soon after law enforcement contacted Garcia about the minor’s whereabouts, Garcia searched the internet for information about how long after intercourse sexual contact can be detected.

Garcia was indicted in March 2024. The court docket indicated several delays associated with Garcia obtaining new counsel.

“This prosecution demonstrates federal law enforcement’s commitment to protecting children outside of our borders from conduct that originates within our borders; ensuring the integrity of our borders; and deterring those who would lie to the United States government to gain custody of an alien child for nefarious purposes,” said Jason Parman, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Kentucky.

“HSI is committed to protecting vulnerable individuals - including unaccompanied alien children - and holding accountable those who use deception, fraud, and exploitation to victimize others,” said HSI Nashville acting Deputy Special Agent in Charge Michael Perez. “Working alongside our federal, state, and local partners, we will continue to investigate these complex cases, support victims, and pursue those who violate the law.”

“Today’s guilty plea underscores the critical importance of protecting vulnerable children from those who seek to exploit them,” said Jason E. Meadows, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships with Homeland Security Investigations, the Kentucky State Police, and the Shelbyville Police Department. Together, we remain steadfast in our commitment to pursuing those who prey upon minors, holding those who commit such crimes accountable, and safeguarding the integrity of federal programs designed to protect children.”

Jason Parman, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Kentucky; Dennis M. Fetting, Special Agent in Charge, Homeland Security Investigations-Nashville; Jason E. Meadows, Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Inspector General; Phillip J. Burnett, Jr., Commissioner of the Kentucky State Police; and Bruce W. Gentry, Shelbyville Police Department; jointly announced the guilty plea.

The investigation was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General, Shelbyville Police Department, and Kentucky State Police. The U.S. Attorney’s Office was represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mary Melton and Aubrey Girouard.

Garcia is scheduled to be sentenced on February 10, 2027. He faces a minimum of five years and a maximum of twenty years in prison, in addition to a $250,000 fine (if applicable). However, any sentence will be imposed by the Court, after its consideration of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and the federal sentencing statutes.

This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov .

— END —

D.C. Safe Task Force Continues the Crime Fight
For immediate release
Office of Public Affairs
Usms.mediadesk@usdoj.gov
Washington, DC – The D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force made over 200 arrests this week since Sunday. This unprecedented level of sustained zero-tolerance collaboration against crime will continue. This weekend is no exception, as task force members will be out in full force seeking out and arresting those looking to harm residents and visitors of our Nation’s capital.
On Sunday, Task Force Officers arrested Kenneth Brock-Smith for Homicide following a reported stabbing. The victim was transported to Med Star hospital where he succumbed to his injuries. A knife was recovered at the scene.
A Sunday traffic stop for a violation of tinted windows led to the arrest of David Thompson for Possession with Intent to Distribute while Armed, Felon in Possession, Carrying Pistol without a License, Possession of Unregistered Firearm/Ammunition Large Capacity Feeding Device and Contempt of Court.
Mouhamed Lam was arrested on Tuesday for Carrying a Pistol without a License, Possession of an Unregistered Firearm/Ammunition, Possession with Intent to Distribute Controlled Substances, Felon in Possession, and an outstanding warrant following a traffic stop for parking in a no parking zone.
Tim McCrae was arrested on a warrant for 1st degree murder on Wednesday. The charge was related to a homicide which happened on August 4, 2026. Task Force Officers located McCrae at a residence and knocked on the door for him to exit. McCrae eventually came to the door and was arrested.
Also arrested for 1st degree murder related to the same incident on August 4, 2026, was Henry Buchanan. Task Force Officers located Buchanan at his jobsite and he was arrested without incident.
Also on Wednesday, Task Force Officers observed a Nissan driving recklessly at a high rate of speed in reverse. Officers attempted a traffic stop, but the driver, Deshawn Grant, did not comply. He drove into oncoming traffic, colliding with 2 police vehicles and a guardrail. After the traffic stop, it was discovered Grant had two active warrants. The Nissan was found to have been stolen. Grant was charged with Assault and Battery on a Police Officer and the two arrest warrants.
Donnel Craig was charged with Armed Car Jacking. Craig was arrested by D.C. Safe Task Force Officers after a search for a vehicle that was reported stolen. Craig was suspected of the violent armed carjacking that left the victim brutally beaten. Officers located the vehicle occupied by Craig who was then arrested and charged for his involvement in the carjacking.
Darrel Dark was arrested following the execution of a Search Warrant for Unlawful Possession of an Unregistered Firearm and Ammunition, and Possession of Controlled Substances. During the search, Officers recovered 3 Firearms, Crack Cocaine, Marijuana, PCP, and THC Resin.
The D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force has made 18,344 arrests since August 2025, seizing 2157 firearms in the process.
"Crime in D.C. will end! These arrests show why we must enforce all laws in our nation’s capital! D.C. Safe Task Force will be in full force this weekend aggressively enforcing all laws and making D.C. safe for everyone!" said United States Marshals Service Director Gadyaces S. Serralta.
The D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force will continue the mission of to make the Nation’s Capital the safest and most beautiful city in the nation.

EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi Wraps Two-Day Swing in Virginia, Joins Representative Kiggans to Announce Over $90 Million for Chesapeake Bay Program
WASHINGTON — Last week, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi was joined by U.S. Representative Jen Kiggans (R-VA-02) to announce more than $90 million in funding for 83 projects in Smithfield, Va. The funding coming from Small Watershed Implementation and Innovative Nutrient and Sediment Reduction grants and matching funds, will help to improve water quality and reduce nutrient and sediment pollution throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed. The pair got to see firsthand the impact the funding can have during a tour of the living shoreline at Windsor Castle Park, a key project providing a tangible example of how federal investments support practical, on-the-ground restoration and coastal resilience.
“My visit to Virginia was yet another example of why it’s so important to meet with state and local leaders and speak directly to them about how EPA can best support their communities,” said EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi. “Our announcement on Friday to provide tens of millions of dollars in additional funding to the Chesapeake Bay program proves how the Trump Administration is investing in improving water quality, reducing nutrients and sediment entering the watershed, and keeping our ecosystems healthy for generations to come.”
The announcement was part of a two-day swing in Virginia where he met with state and local leaders to discuss how the Trump EPA can continue advancing cooperative federalism with the state to protect human health and the environment. On Thursday, Deputy Administrator Fotouhi met with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Norfolk District following the completion of the Norfolk Harbor and Thimble Shoal Channel deepening project. Port-related activity like this supports more than 570,000 jobs and approximately $63 billion in Virginia gross state product annually. As the port continues to expand its infrastructure, Deputy Administrator Fotouhi and USACE focused on how efficient permitting and coordination among federal agencies can help ensure these projects continue.
Next, Deputy Administrator Fotouhi traveled to Virginia Beach to meet with Mayor Bobby Dyer and City Manager Patrick Duhaney. Mayor Dyer is a newly appointed member of EPA’s Local Government Advisory Committee (LGAC), an advisory group comprised of state and local officials who help advance the agency's core mission while Powering the Great American Comeback. Their discussion focused on local infrastructure priorities and the federal-local partnership.
Deputy Administrator Fotouhi ended his trip with a visit at the Atlantic Wood Industries Superfund Site. This site is a 50-acre industrial waterfront property along the Southern Branch of the Elizabeth River, where EPA has led a multi-phase cleanup addressing contaminated soil, groundwater and more than 30 acres of river sediment, including the dredging of approximately 360,000 cubic yards of contaminated sediment. The visit highlighted progress of the cleanup and ongoing efforts to measure its impact on the health of the Elizabeth River ecosystem, including through tissue sampling of oysters and other aquatic species. The Trump EPA’s Superfund Solutions initiative aims to expedite cleanups at sites across the country so that they can return to productive reuse in their communities.
title: EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi Wraps Two-Day Swing in Virginia, Joins Representative Kiggans to Announce Over $90 Million for Chesapeake Bay Program

RELEASE: Gottheimer Urges FDA to Establish Clear Standards for Rare Disease Status
Protect Patients with Sarcoidosis and Other Serious Illnesses Bipartisan Letter Warns That Unclear Standards Could Strip Rare Disease Status From Conditions Like Sarcoidosis
WASHINGTON, DC — U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), Founder and Co-Chair of the Congressional Sarcoidosis Caucus, and thirty-eight of his colleagues sent a bipartisan letter to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and U.S. Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Marty Makary urging the agencies to establish clear, consistent standards for defining rare disease patient populations.
“When 95 percent of rare diseases do not have cures, we cannot risk discouraging innovation in areas where scientific progress is rapidly outpacing regulatory adaptation,” the letter reads. “These challenges are not merely technical — they have real implications for patients… This means if the FDA considers prevalence rate with the higher estimate as the prevailing rate, diseases like Sarcoidosis are no longer capable of receiving crucial rare disease funding to find cures even though the patient population that needs treatment is well below the current FDA standard for rare.”
The letter raises concerns about the lack of clear, consistent FDA standards on how patient populations should be defined, how prevalence should be measured, and what evidentiary standards sponsors must meet. Advances in genomics and precision medicine are enabling researchers to identify increasingly specific disease subtypes, but the FDA has no clear roadmap for how to characterize those populations in regulatory submissions. The letter warns that this uncertainty can lead to unpredictable regulatory outcomes and discourage investment in therapies for small or complex patient populations.
This lack of clarity is already causing harm. Diseases like sarcoidosis, multiple myeloma, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and pulmonary hypertension — serious, often life-altering conditions — risk losing rare disease status depending on how patient populations are counted. For example, while some estimates place sarcoidosis prevalence just above 200,000, only about 60,000 patients actually require treatment. If the FDA relies on the higher estimate, diseases like sarcoidosis could lose access to rare disease-specific research funding and incentives, even though the population that needs treatments is well below the 200,000-person threshold.
The lawmakers urge HHS and the FDA to:
- Establish standardized definitions for how patient populations are delineated, including the role of genetic, biomarker, and clinical criteria.
- Issue clear guidance on acceptable methodologies for calculating and submitting prevalence data, including preferred data sources, timeframes, and analytic approaches.
- Outline how real-world data and registry-based studies should be incorporated into regulatory submissions.
- Provide greater transparency into how population definitions and prevalence estimates are evaluated during review.
- Clarify the role of treatment-eligible patient populations in determining rare disease status.
- Engage patient groups, researchers, and industry to develop consensus-driven best practices for population identification and data submission.
The letter is co-signed by Reps. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA), Don Bacon (R-NE), Nanette Díaz Barragán (D-CA), Wesley Bell (D-MO), André Carson (D-IN), Yvette Clarke (D-NY), Steve Cohen (D-TN), Jim Costa (D-CA), Danny Davis (D-IL), Don Davis (D-NC), Madeleine Dean (D-PA), Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), Lois Frankel (D-FL), Maggie Goodlander (D-NH), Adam Gray (D-CA), Adelita Grijalva (D-AZ), French Hill (R-AR), Jim Himes (D-CT), Jonathan Jackson (D-IL), Hank Johnson (D-GA), Ro Khanna (D-CA), Darin LaHood (R-IL), Mike Lawler (R-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Sarah McBride (D-DE), Max Miller (R-OH), Kelly Morrison (D-MN), Seth Moulton (D-MA), Jimmy Panetta (D-CA), Mark Pocan (D-WI), Linda Sánchez (D-CA), Eric Sorensen (D-IL), Darren Soto (D-FL), Tom Suozzi (D-NY), Shri Thanedar (D-MI), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL).
The letter builds on Gottheimer’s longstanding work on sarcoidosis and rare diseases. He has led an annual bipartisan appropriations letter urging research funding for sarcoidosis through the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), founded the Bipartisan Congressional Sarcoidosis Caucus, and has met with patients, advocates, and leading medical professionals from across New Jersey to discuss the disease. Importantly, Gottheimer secured language in the Fiscal Year 2027 Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education appropriations bill that passed out of committee this year. The language encourages the NHLBI to advance research into sarcoidosis — the first-ever mention of the disease in this appropriations bill.
Gottheimer, a Rare Disease Caucus member, is also leading Gwenn’s Law, which would increase the number of women in NIH clinical research trials to help drive treatments and cures for rare diseases, and Cameron’s Law, which would restore the Orphan Drug Tax Credit to support rare disease drug development.

USDA Encourages Producers and Residents to Prepare for Hurricane Isaias
(Washington, D.C., October 9, 2026) – The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) reminds communities, farmers and ranchers, families and small businesses in the path of Hurricane Isaias that USDA has programs that provide assistance in the wake of disasters. USDA staff in regional, state, and county offices stand ready to assist as conditions develop and to support recovery.
USDA’s Disaster Resource Center and Disaster Assistance Discovery Tool offer easy access to information on programs that support recovery from natural disasters. USDA also encourages residents and producers to contact their local USDA Service Center to determine which programs may meet their needs.
Food safety guidance:
Heavy winds, flooding, and power outages can jeopardize stored food. USDA recommends the following steps to keep food safe:
- A refrigerator will keep food below 40°F for up to 4 hours during an outage. A full freezer stays cold for about 48 hours (24 hours if half full). Keep doors closed as much as possible.
- Keep an appliance thermometer in both the refrigerator and freezer to check temperatures if power is lost.
- Freeze containers of water ahead of the storm or make ice in containers to help keep food cold in the refrigerator and freezer.
- Freeze refrigerated items you may not need immediately—such as leftovers, milk, and fresh meat or poultry—to extend their safe storage time.
- Consider purchasing 50 pounds of dry or block ice if a long outage is expected; this can keep an 18-cubic-foot freezer cold for two days.
- Group foods together in the freezer to help them stay cold longer.
- Keep several days’ worth of ready-to-eat foods that do not require cooking or cooling.
For food safety questions, call the Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-674-6854 (Monday–Friday, 10 a.m.–6 p.m. ET), or email MPHotline@usda.gov. Meat and poultry businesses may contact the FSIS Small Plant Help Desk online 24/7, call 1-877-FSIS-HELP (1-877-374-7435) or email InfoSource@usda.gov.
Protecting pets and livestock:
The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) urges everyone in the potential path of the hurricane to prepare now:
- Plan for evacuation—know how you will evacuate and where you will go. If it is not feasible to evacuate livestock, provide strong shelter and adequate food and water.
- If moving livestock across state lines, contact the receiving state’s State Veterinarian’s Office. APHIS Veterinary Services state offices can also assist.
- Follow instructions from emergency officials and evacuate if asked to do so.
Risk management and disaster assistance for agricultural operations:
USDA offers several programs to help producers recover from hurricane impacts. Producers with Federal Crop Insurance or Noninsured Crop Disaster Assistance Program (NAP) coverage should report losses to their crop insurance agent or local Farm Service Agency (FSA) office within 72 hours of discovering damage and follow up in writing within 15 days.
Other key programs from USDA include:
- Livestock Indemnity Program and Emergency Assistance for Livestock, Honeybees, and Farm-raised Fish.
- Tree Assistance Program for damaged orchards and vineyards.
- Emergency Conservation Program and Emergency Forest Restoration Program for land and forest recovery.
- Producers should document all losses and contact their local USDA Service Center as soon as possible.
The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) also provides financial and technical assistance through the Environmental Quality Incentives Program and can support local governments through the Emergency Watershed Protection Program.
FSA also offers financial support to farmers and ranchers impacted by natural disasters, including:
- Direct and guaranteed farm loans, including operating and emergency farm loans, to producers unable to secure commercial financing.
- Low interest emergency loans for producers in designated disaster areas to help recover from production and physical losses.
- Loan servicing options for borrowers unable to make scheduled payments due to circumstances beyond their control.
Loans help producers replace property, livestock, equipment, feed and seed, cover living expenses, refinance farm-related debts and more.
Producers can also use tools on farmers.gov, including the Disaster Assistance Discovery Tool and Disaster Assistance-at-a-Glance fact sheet, to identify applicable recovery programs. For crop insurance claims, contact your insurance agent. For FSA or NRCS programs, reach out to your local USDA Service Center.
USDA’s Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) also works closely with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and stands by to support requests from state and local authorities for emergency nutrition assistance. In disaster situations, FNA helps communities meet immediate nutrition needs when it matters the most.
###
title: USDA Encourages Producers and Residents to Prepare for Hurricane Isaias

SAN DIEGO – Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of California filed 99 border-related cases this week, including charges of bringing in aliens for financial gain, reentering the U.S. after deportation, and importation of controlled substances.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California is the fourth-busiest federal district, largely due to a high volume of border-related crimes. This district, encompassing San Diego and Imperial counties, shares a 140-mile border with Mexico. It includes the San Ysidro Port of Entry, the world’s busiest land border crossing, connecting San Diego (America’s eighth largest city) and Tijuana (Mexico’s second largest city).

In addition to reactive border-related crimes, the Southern District of California also prosecutes a significant number of proactive cases related to terrorism, organized crime, drugs, white-collar fraud, violent crime, cybercrime, human trafficking and national security. Recent developments in those and other significant areas of prosecution can be found here .

A sample of border-related arrests this week:

On October 3, 2026, Efrain Antonio Avalos, a United States citizen, was arrested and charged with Transportation of Illegal Aliens. According to a complaint, Border Patrol Agents attempted to conduct a vehicle stop on a Hyundai suspected of transporting illegal aliens. Defendant failed to yield and instead sped up to about 105 miles per hour. Border Patrol Agents deployed a vehicle immobilization device and the vehicle’s left tires made positive contact with the device. Defendant continued to flee at a high rate of speed, failed to stop at a stop sign and collided into an oncoming vehicle. The Defendant exited the vehicle after the collision Border Patrol Agents observed the material witness crawling away from the Hyundai with carpet coverings on his feet and his head covered in blood. The Hyundai then caught on fire.

On October 5, 2026, Victor Hugo Gutierrez De La Torre, a Mexican citizen, was arrested and charged with Importation of Controlled Substance. According to a complaint, Customs and Border Protection officers discovered 1,038 pounds of methamphetamine concealed in the fuel tank of the 2020 Volvo VNL 760 tractor the defendant was driving as he applied for entry to the U.S. at the Otay Mesa Port of Entry.

September 6, 2026, Justin Jimenez, a United States citizen, was arrested and charged with Importation of Controlled Substance. According to a complaint, Customs and Border Protection officers discovered 91 pounds of Xanax concealed in the floorboards of his Volkswagen Jetta GLI the defendant was driving as he applied for entry to the U.S. at the San Ysidro Port of Entry.

The immigration cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE ERO), Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), with the support and assistance of state and local law enforcement partners.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: U.S. Attorney’s Office Filed 99 Border-Related Cases This Week

text:
Greenbelt , Maryland – A federal grand jury indicted a Maryland man, today, in connection with a COVID-19 healthcare fraud scam.

Marc Aaron Potash, 57, of Rockville, is charged with conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud and seven counts of healthcare fraud. The charges stem from Potash submitting false and fraudulent claims to Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP), and other insurers for at-home, self-administered COVID-19 tests. Potash is also charged with five counts of conducting transactions in criminally derived proceeds. This prosecution is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the indictment with Special Agent in Charge Darren B. Cox, FBI Washington Field Office; Inspector General T. March Bell, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG); and Michael R. Esser, Deputy Inspector General Performing the Duties of the Inspector General, Office of Personnel Management, Office of the Inspector General (OPM-OIG).

According to the indictment, between January 2022 and May 2026, Potash allegedly conspired with others to personally enrich himself and maximize the financial success of Tiero, LLC, a company located in Gaithersburg, Maryland. Through the conspiracy, Potash, Tiero’s founder and chief executive officer, and his co-conspirators schemed to obtain money through false and fraudulent representations to insurers.

The indictment further alleges that as part of the healthcare fraud scheme, Potash and his co-conspirators sent false emails, letters, and paperwork to the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) to obtain a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) certification for Tiero. As part of the conspiracy, Potash and his co-conspirators submitted documents that falsely portrayed Tiero’s medical providers performing on-site COVID-19 testing at the company’s purported lab. The co-conspirators then used Tiero’s CLIA license to submit fraudulent claims to insurers that listed false dates of service, a fake place of service, and a phony rendering provider for COVID-19 tests that would have been administered or analyzed by a provider at Tiero.

However, in reality, Potash and his co-conspirators merely shipped over-the-counter, self-administered COVID-19 tests to insured individuals across the country. In total, Potash and his co-conspirators caused the submission of more than $100 million in false and fraudulent healthcare claims, resulting in more than $50 million in insurance payments to Tiero.

The indictment also alleges that Potash engaged in multiple monetary transactions in criminally derived property. This included Potash purchasing a Range Rover, Mercedes-Benz, and $4 million real property in Beallsville, Maryland, along with two security transfers totaling more than $4 million and $8 million, respectively.

An indictment is not a finding of guilt. Individuals charged by indictment are presumed innocent until proven guilty at a later criminal proceeding.

If convicted, Potash faces a maximum of 10 years in federal prison for conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud, each count of healthcare fraud, and each count of conducting transactions in criminally derived proceeds.

Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes commended the FBI, HHS-OIG, and OPM-OIG for their work in the investigation. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys Megan S. McKoy and Joshua Rosenthal, who are prosecuting this federal case.

For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to report fraud, please visit justice.gov/usao-md and justice.gov/usao-md/report-fraud .

title: Maryland Man Facing Federal Indictment for Role in COVID-19 Healthcare Fraud Scheme Totaling More Than $100M

Schakowsky, Trahan, Kean Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Protect FTC Whistleblowers as The Social Reckoning Hits Theaters
WASHINGTON– As The Social Reckoning, a new film about Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, hits theaters nationwide, Congresswoman Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03), and Congressman Tom Kean, Jr. (NJ-07) today introduced bipartisan legislation to protect whistleblowers who disclose wrongdoing at their current or former workplaces that fall under the jurisdiction of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).
The FTC Whistleblower Act of 2026 would protect current and former employees from retaliation when they disclose violations of consumer protection and antitrust laws to the FTC. The legislation would also establish incentives for whistleblowers to come forward with information about unlawful conduct.
“Frances Haugen took an enormous risk when she came forward with information about what was happening inside Facebook,” said Congresswoman Jan Schakowsky. “Her courage helped expose serious concerns about the impact of social media on our children and families. But no worker should have to choose between doing the right thing and losing their livelihood. Our bipartisan bill makes sure whistleblowers who expose wrongdoing to the FTC have the protections they deserve.”
“When something goes wrong inside a company, the workers there are often the first to know. Today, if they bring that information to the FTC, they take the risk alone,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan. “The FTC Whistleblower Act gives them real protections and a real reason to come forward. That’s good for workers, good for families, and good for the companies doing things the right way. Frances Haugen showed what one person can do. Nobody should have to be that brave just to tell the truth.”
“The FTC Whistleblower Act would empower workers to safely report corporate misconduct without fear of retaliation. By protecting whistleblowers who report misconduct, the bill will allow the FTC to uncover violations and build strong enforcement cases,” said Congressman Tom Kean, Jr. “With increased transparency into harmful practices, the bill ensures companies can’t operate in the shadows and protects workers from retaliation.”
The FTC is the federal agency responsible for enforcing a broad range of consumer protection and antitrust laws. Unlike some other federal agencies, the FTC does not have a comprehensive whistleblower protection and award program for employees who report violations within its jurisdiction.
“This legislation is an excellent opportunity for Congress to apply cohesive rights across federal agencies, including the FTC, in accordance with their sustained leadership on whistleblower protections. The FTC’s ability to protect consumers and keep big businesses in check goes hand in hand with whistleblowers keeping Americans safe. Providing protections and best practice incentives for whistleblowers coming forward with original information to the Commission is a nonpartisan issue and essential to good governance,” said Maya Efrati, Director of Legislation & Congressional Affairs at Government Accountability Project.
“Whistleblowers are our most effective safeguard against corporate fraud and corruption. This bill strengthens essential protections and incentives so that insiders can more safely expose wrongdoing that harms American families and consumers. POGO appreciates Congresswoman Schakowsky’s leadership on this crucial bill that will enhance regulatory oversight, hold powerful corporations more accountable, and protect the public’s trust," said Joe Spielberger, Senior Policy Counsel, Project On Government Oversight.
The need for stronger protections was highlighted by Haugen’s 2021 disclosures of internal Facebook documents, which became known as the “Facebook Files.” Haugen later testified before Congress about the company’s practices and their potential impact on young people.
###
title: Schakowsky, Trahan, Kean Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Protect FTC Whistleblowers as The Social Reckoning Hits Theaters

text:
Forging a Frontline Ally: Royal Australian Navy Maintainers Learn U.S. Submarine Sustainment to Bolster Pacific Readiness
Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii - In the summer of 2025, in a corner of a machine shop at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PHNSY & IMF), Able Seaman Colby Morley disassembled a pressure valve for testing. It’s the kind of hands-on job he’d rarely get to do back home as an avionics technician with the Royal Australian Navy.
As part of a first-of-its-kind training rotation, Morley was one of 20 Royal Australian Navy Fleet Support Unit (FSU) sailors who trained in Hawaii to learn how to maintain U.S. nuclear-powered attack submarines. The cross-functional team was stationed in Pearl Harbor from June through October of last year and completed an intensive U.S.-led training rotation before returning home to support USS Vermont’s (SSN 792) submarine maintenance period at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia in November 2025.
“The team is a small but very important cog in the wheel for AUKUS. Our main goal is making sure Australia is self-reliable when it comes to the maintenance of these newer assets,” said Royal Australian Navy Chief Petty Officer Steven Sheakey, the deployed maintenance team’s senior technical officer. “The fleet support units are going to play an important role in delivering maintenance to the U.S. assets that are going to be rotating through HMAS Stirling. So, the knowledge, experiences and cohesive relationships we’ve got with U.S. personnel—both civilian and in uniform—are going to play a vital role moving forward to ensure we’re interoperable in the future.”
In the U.S., the FSU team’s mission was to gain maintenance experience on U.S. platforms, build technical interoperability and prepare to sustain U.S. and U.K. nuclear-powered submarines. Under the AUKUS agreement, the U.S. and U.K. are supporting Australia’s efforts to acquire, maintain and sustain its own sovereign fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines—a departure from Australia’s current fleet of diesel-electric submarines.
Submarine Rotational Force-West, or SRF-West, is one of the AUKUS partnership’s key outcomes. The initiative will see U.S. Virginia-class and U.K. Astute-class submarines rotate out of the Royal Australian Navy’s submarine base in the Indian Ocean, HMAS Stirling, for an extended period, starting in 2027.
Strategic Sustainment Starts with People
The team sent to Hawaii was drawn from across the Royal Australian Navy’s five FSUs and selected through a competitive, skills-based screening process. The sailors’ specialties range from electronics to propulsion to weapons, reflecting the future workforce Australia will need to support Australian-flagged nuclear-powered submarines.
“We needed a team that could embed anywhere, adapt quickly and represent the full scope of Navy engineering,” said Royal Australian Navy Lt. Zachery Telfser, officer in charge of the deployed maintenance team. “This isn’t just submarine work—it’s about building a broad, interoperable sustainment workforce that can flex with future mission demands.”
Some sailors, like Morely, are outside the traditional submarine pipeline. But as Australia expands its readiness to support nuclear propulsion, the Royal Australian Navy is pulling from across its engineering enterprise to identify who can contribute to the overall mission.
“We’re stress-testing the system,” Sheakey said. “In Australia, we multi-train our sailors so they can wear more than one hat. That kind of flexibility is essential to building interoperable teams who can deliver complex submarine maintenance packages at SRF-West.”
Fleet Support Unit-West sailors will serve as SRF-West's primary uniformed maintenance workforce. More than 200 personnel from the Australian Submarine Agency’s civilian sustainment partner, ASC Pty. Ltd., are also training in Hawaii to lead intermediate- and depot-level maintenance work on Australia’s future fleet of fast-attack submarines. Both the Fleet Support Unit and ASC teams put their newfound skills to the test during the November 2025 submarine maintenance period at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia.
“This joint workforce approach combining the U.S. Navy, Royal Australian Navy and Australian civilians is central to how SRF-West will operate,” said Elizabeth Tolin, the deputy division head for SRF-West at the U.S. Navy’s AUKUS Integration and Acquisition program office. “Our work with Australia is enabling us to build a cohesive, interoperable sustainment enterprise.”
These joint efforts align directly with the Department of War’s May 2026 announcement formally establishing Naval Support Activity Stirling and reestablishing Submarine Squadron 3. PHNSY &IMF, which was previously named the lead maintenance activity for SRF-West, is actively preparing to deploy its maintenance detachment to Western Australia where American personnel will continue working alongside their FSU and ASC maintenance counterparts.
Learning to Work Together, Technically and Culturally
For Royal Australian Navy Leading Seaman Jayden Webb, an electronics technician, the rotation was his second stint working with the U.S. Navy, and another opportunity to refine shared maintenance insights.
“We’re doing more than just fixing systems,” he said in an interview alongside Morely last August. “We’re learning how the U.S. Navy thinks about readiness, risk and reporting. That’s what it’ll take to maintain and sustain these platforms safely and confidently back in Australia.”
Webb embedded with the U.S. Navy’s Performance Monitoring Team, which performs rigorous testing and diagnostics aboard submarines. Others, like Morely, worked in the shipyard’s machine shop, rebuilding and testing valves under the mentorship of experienced U.S. tradesmen.
“At home, we’re used to getting a tech order that tells us what’s wrong,” Morely said. “At Pearl, we’re learning how to troubleshoot from scratch. It’s taught me to be more comfortable with uncertainty and more deliberate about communication.”
From Pearl Harbor to Perth
In October 2025, the team returned to Western Australia to complete their mission by performing maintenance aboard USS Vermont during its planned submarine maintenance period.
The submarine maintenance period, which lasted through November, marked a historic milestone underscoring the momentum of AUKUS and its vision for enhanced deterrence and industrial resilience in the Indo-Pacific. For Australia, it’s also an opportunity to evaluate its long-term investment in submarine sustainment and sovereign capability.
“The submarine maintenance period was a big step forward from when we had a U.S. submarine tender, USS Emory S. Land (AS 39) across the pier from USS Hawaii (SSN 776) in August 2024 to oversee and execute the submarine tendered maintenance period,” said Rear Adm. Doug Adams, director, AUKUS, International & Systems. “For Vermont, we had a larger work package, a truly blended maintenance workforce led by Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Activity, and when that boat left to operate in the Indo-Pacific region, it was ready for any tasking.”
As Australia continues to build capacity to own, operate and maintain nuclear-powered submarines, sailors from the FSU will continue to support U.S. submarine maintenance periods, including the next one scheduled to occur in Western Australia by the end of 2026.
“We’ve still got a lot of work ahead,” said Sheakey. “Australia’s got to grow its infrastructure, procedures and people. But, we’re proving we’re up to the task, and that we’re a capable, committed partner.”
For sailors like Morely and Webb, the experience has also reshaped how they think about their roles in a trilateral security framework.
“To me, AUKUS is about bringing our forces together, not just in strategy, but in day-to-day operations,” said Webb. “It’s exciting to be part of something this big.”
“This was my first time outside Australia,” Morely added. “To be in Hawaii, working with the U.S. Navy on something that’s going to have such a big impact back home—that means a lot.”
-30-
title: Forging a Frontline Ally: Royal Australian Navy Maintainers Learn U.S. Submarine Sustainment to Bolster Pacific Readiness
