MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that yesterday a federal jury found Alejandro Rojas Garcia, 65, a Mexican national in the United States illegally, guilty of attempted production of child pornography.

The guilty verdict was returned after a four-day trial starting on October 5, 2026, before U.S. District Judge John R. Tunheim. Sentencing will be set at a later date and Garcia faces a mandatory minimum of 180 months in prison. The defendant is also facing state criminal charges for related conduct.¹

Photo of Alejandro Rojas Garcia

“Garcia is a predator. A verdict cannot undo the evil he brought on two innocent girls, but it is justice,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen.

According to federal court documents, evidence presented during trial, and as alleged in public state court documents, in early April 2024, law enforcement began an investigation into Garcia after receiving information that he had sexually assaulted two sisters, including Minor Victim 1 and Minor Victim 2, both of whom were then under the age of 13.

Garcia was a longtime family friend of the victims’ family, and the family trusted Garcia to care for the children a few days of the week. When Garcia provided childcare for the minor victims, they spent time at Garcia’s apartment. Minor Victim 1 stated that in the spring of 2024, Garcia sexually assaulted her and was violent.

Minor Victim 2 stated that, on multiple instances, Garcia would sexually assault her and that he caused her pain.

On April 5, 2024, Garcia was arrested. Officers conducted a search of Garcia’s apartment pursuant to a search warrant. The officers seized multiple cellphones, cameras, laptop computers, flash drives, other data storage devices, and a massage gun. Garcia had several hidden cameras placed throughout his apartment, including five cameras hidden in the bathroom. Cameras were aimed at the genital area of a person sitting on the toilet and towards the shower and bath area.

Electronic Storage Devices Found in Garcia’s Apartment

Officers searched the various storage devices Garcia had stashed in his apartment and found numerous child sexual abuse material, including that of Minor Victim 1 and of other unknown child victims. While searching Garcia’s apartment, an electronic storage detection dog indicated the presence of evidence in a wooden crucifix hanging on a wall in Garcia’s bedroom. Inside the crucifix, behind a bottle of holy water, was a micro-SD card which contained child sexual abuse material involving Minor Victim 1.

Front of Crucifix

Inside Crucifix Depicting Holy Water and Micro-SD Card

At trial, Garcia testified. Under oath, he claimed that he was unaware of the child sexual abuse material on the various devices in his apartment. Regarding the child sexual abuse material involving Minor Victim 1 found on the micro-SD card inside the crucifix, Garcia acknowledged that he put the material on the micro-SD card but denied producing the material with the intent of gratifying his sexual desire.

This case was the result of an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations and the Stillwater Police Department, with assistance from Washington County Child Protective Services.

Assistant United States Attorneys Dana M. Joseph, Echo D. Fatsis, and William C. Mattessich are prosecuting the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

¹ Garcia has been charged by complaint in Washington County District Court File No. 82-CR-24-1329 on two counts of Criminal Sexual Conduct in the 1st Degree.

ICYMI in HousingWire | HUD Action Ensures FHA Loans are for Americans Only
Following HUD Action, Homeownership Loans for Illegals and Non-Residents Drop
October 9, 2026
WASHINGTON - New data reveals Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans for non-permanent residents and illegals fell from 6% to nearly zero after the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development revoked their eligibility in May 2025.
“President Trump promised to put Americans first, and HUD delivered,” said Secretary Turner. “We are preventing illegals and non-residents from accessing taxpayer-backed programs at the expense of American homebuyers. Today, that share is zero. Make no mistake — exploit our citizens, and HUD will act.”
Watch Secretary Turner break down what this means for Americans:
Learn more from HousingWire:
Changes to residency requirements for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans have sharply reduced the share of FHA purchase mortgages made to non-permanent residents, according to origination data from Intercontinental Exchange (ICE).
In March 2025, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued Mortgagee Letter 2025-09 and Title I Letter 490, removing the “non-permanent resident” category from FHA’s Single Family Title I and Title II programs, effective May 25, 2025.
Before the policy changes took effect, non-permanent residents accounted for about 5.8% of FHA purchase originations and 5.6% of purchase mortgages across the broader market, according to ICE data shared with HousingWire. After the changes, their share of FHA purchase loans fell to about 0.1%, while their share of purchase mortgages across all loan types declined by 2.2 percentage points to 3.4%, the data shows.
“President Trump promised to put Americans first, and HUD delivered,” Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. “We are preventing illegals and non-residents from accessing taxpayer-backed programs at the expense of American homebuyers. Today, that share is zero. Make no mistake — exploit our citizens, and HUD will act.”
Market-specific impacts
The changes have had a larger impact in some markets where non-permanent residents had previously represented a relatively significant share of FHA purchase activity.
ICE evaluated markets with the highest non-permanent resident alien share of purchase originations prior to the FHA policy change (measured from second-quarter 2024 through first-quarter 2025) and filtered to the 100 largest U.S. markets and 33 markets along the U.S. borders with Mexico and Canada.
Utah markets recorded some of the largest declines. In Salt Lake City, non-permanent residents accounted for 26% of FHA purchase originations before the changes, compared with 0.15% afterward (Q4 2025 to the present). In Provo, the share fell from 20% to less than 0.5%.
Florida markets also saw declines. In Orlando, the pre-policy share went from 16.1% to a post-policy share of 0.2%. Lakeland went from 13.6% to 0.16%, and both Cape Coral and Miami went from 10% to less than 1%.
Other markets also recorded significant declines. Raleigh‘s share fell from 11.1% to 0.8%, while San Jose’s fell from about 10% to 0%.
The data suggests that conventional lending has not fully offset the decline in FHA lending to non-permanent residents. ICE data shows that non-permanent resident volume across conventional prime conforming loans remained relatively stable rather than increasing by a comparable amount.
“This new policy has definitely had an impact on families that would have qualified before May 2025,” said Michael Brown, a Tennessee-based home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage. “Many of these borrowers are doing conventional loans now because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac permit lawful non-permanent residents to obtain financing.”
Brown said that non-QM loans are another option for non-permanent residents, but that the new policy limits affordable financing options. “Some of these non-permanent residents will end up having to put more money down, work on improving their credit scores to qualify, or simply will need to wait until they obtain permanent-resident status,” he said.
Isaac Schultz, a Michigan-based home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, echoed that the only options for non-permanent residents are conventional financing or “some flavor of non-qualified mortgage financing.”
“I am currently working on a loan in one such scenario, and it does make it far more difficult for the borrower to qualify. For better or for worse, that was the main desired result of the policy change,” Schultz said.
Home price declines
It is unclear whether the declines have affected affordability, but most markets in the ICE dataset recorded lower prices after the policy changes took effect, according to HousingWire Data.
In Salt Lake City, the median list price for a single-family home ranged from $619,900 to $795,000 from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025. From Q4 2025 to the present, prices ranged from $620,000 to $742,450.
In Provo, the median list price ranged from $630,000 to $877,400 from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025, compared with $589,900 to $699,950 from Q4 2025 to the present.
Prices also shifted in Florida markets. In Orlando, the median list price ranged from $490,000 to $544,950 before the policy change, then dropped to a range of $489,000 to $525,000 afterward.
The change appeared to have no impact on prices in Lakeland, where they ranged from $350,000 to $374,999 before the change, and from $357,000 to $375,000 afterward. In Cape Coral, however, prices ranged from $475,000 to $510,000 before the policy changes, compared with $420,000 to $467,450 afterward.
In Raleigh, the median list price for a single-family home ranged from $579,900 to $699,000 before the change, but later dropped to $522,000 to $624,900.
San Jose, one of the nation’s most expensive markets, saw a smaller shift. The median list price for a single-family home there ranged from $1.56 million to $1.70 million from Q2 2024 through Q1 2025. From Q4 2025 to the present, prices ranged from $1.498 million to $1.70 million.

Hoyer Statement on Trump Administration Decision to Lift Sanctions on Russian Diesel
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement after President Donald Trump announced a 180-day suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel and indicated that the U.S. may purchase large quantities of the fuel:
"It is outrageous for the President of the United States to purchase tons of diesel from Russia in direct contravention of legislation he signed three weeks ago imposing the toughest sanctions on Russia’s oil and gas. Doing so would fuel the very war of aggression in Ukraine that our sanctions are meant to stop. It is a sudden and mendacious shift in policy from the pressure of our sanctions to actively aiding and abetting the war effort of Russia against Ukraine - and an infusion of economic assistance to Russia. Both of these are the exact opposite of Congress’s intent and the President’s statement in enacting and signing the Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act three weeks ago. This action bails out both Putin and Trump - for Putin, his faltering war effort and economy; for Trump, the consequences of a war of choice in Iran: exorbitant fuel costs for Americans.
"President Trump’s action of helping Russia while at the same time asking our allies to shoulder more of the burden of support for Ukraine is clearly duplicitous.
“Congress must take action, drawing on the strong bipartisan support behind the sanctions law, to prevent a penny of American funds from being used to purchase Russian petroleum products, on which Putin relies to fund his war.”

SAN DIEGO – Isaac Jimenez, a U.S. citizen residing in Tijuana, was sentenced in federal court today to 12 years in prison for his role in a human smuggling conspiracy whose members kidnapped migrants and extorted their families for ransom.

Two victims in unrelated kidnappings—a father of four U.S. citizen children and a 21-year-old woman from Tijuana—were never heard from again. The woman was found dead in Tijuana; the man is believed to have been killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

Jimenez crossing the border to pick up ransom money from victim's wife

U.S. District Judge Janis L. Sammartino also ordered Jimenez to pay $24,500 in restitution to family members of the victims for funeral and related expenses and for a portion of the ransom payments made during the conspiracy.

Judge Sammartino imposed the sentence after the government detailed Jimenez’s extensive history of alien smuggling and his knowing participation in the Tijuana-based organization that used kidnapping, threats and violence against migrants who had paid to be smuggled into the United States.

“There’s a fantasy of human smugglers as being on the side of the vulnerable. Then there’s the truth: They are liars, blackmailers and killers. You want proof, keep reading,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon.

“Today’s sentencing holds the defendant accountable for knowingly supporting a human smuggling organization that exploited vulnerable people through kidnapping, extortion, threats, and violence,” said Kevin Murphy, Special Agent in Charge of HSI San Diego. “Human smuggling networks profit from human suffering and show a callous disregard for the lives they endanger. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement partners on both sides of the border to identify, investigate, and dismantle those responsible for these crimes.”

At today’s hearing, Judge Sammartino described the case events as “the most deliberate and unnecessary loss of life I’ve seen in a very long time.” Addressing Mr. Jimenez, she said, “You preyed upon the most vulnerable people.”

Jimenez, who previously lived in Escondido before moving to Tijuana, had been involved in alien smuggling for years before joining the organization in 2024. He was convicted of alien-smuggling offenses in 2015 and 2017 and was arrested again in 2022 in connection with another smuggling investigation. In early 2024, after being released from custody in Mexico, Jimenez began working for members of a Tijuana-based organization, transporting migrants from the border area to locations in the United States for payment.

As Jimenez became more involved, he learned that the organization was holding migrants against their will and demanding additional payments from them and their families as a condition of their release. He also received photographs and videos depicting kidnappings and murders involving members of the organization. Despite this knowledge, Jimenez continued to participate in the conspiracy.

In September 2024, the organization agreed to smuggle C.G.C., a father of four U.S. citizen children who had previously resided in Southern California, into the United States from Mexico. Instead of being smuggled into the United States, C.G.C. was held captive in Mexico while his kidnappers demanded $30,000 from his family and threatened to kill him.

At the direction of his coconspirators, Jimenez collected $15,000 in ransom payments from C.G.C.’s wife, transported the money to Tijuana and delivered it to the kidnappers. Additional ransom demands followed, including demands for money and vehicles. When the family could no longer pay, the kidnappers threatened to provide the location of C.G.C.’s body. Communications eventually ceased. C.G.C. remains missing and, according to court documents, is presumed to have been killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

Three months later, Jimenez agreed to coordinate the smuggling of V.A.E., a 21-year-old Mexican woman, for $7,000. Jimenez was to earn a $1,000 commission. Instead, his coconspirators took V.A.E. to a safe house and held her captive, demanding $30,000 from her family for her release. The kidnappers sent videos showing V.A.E. being threatened with firearms and beaten; they threatened to kill her if the ransom was not paid.

V.A.E.’s family eventually paid approximately $10,000, but she was never released. Her skeletal remains were discovered in the Tijuana area in November 2025 and were identified through DNA testing. According to court documents, V.A.E. was likely killed in Mexico by Jimenez’s coconspirators.

At today’s hearing, Judge Sammartino described the case events as “the most deliberate and unnecessary loss of life I’ve seen in a very long time.” Addressing Mr. Jimenez, she said, “You preyed upon the most vulnerable people.”

Even after the two victims disappeared, Jimenez continued working with the organization and coordinating smuggling operations. Investigators recovered messages from his phone reflecting his continued involvement and awareness of the organization’s use of threats and violence. In one exchange, Jimenez discussed an unidentified woman who was not cooperating and suggested taking her to an office. Other communications among members of the organization referred to making people disappear and torture. Investigators also recovered a video showing a man with his wrists bound as though he had been detained or kidnapped.

As part of his guilty plea, Jimenez admitted coordinating alien-smuggling events and collecting ransom payments from family members of migrants who were instead held captive by his coconspirators.

The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Escondido Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert J. Miller and former Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alex Biggs and Samson Schatz prosecuted the case.

DEFENDANT Case Number 25cr2648-JLS

Isaac Jimenez Age: 30 San Diego, CA

SUMMARY OF CHARGES

Conspiracy to Bring in Certain Aliens – Title 18, U.S.C., Section 371, and Title 8, U.S.C., Section 1324(a)(2)(B)(ii)

Maximum penalty: Five years in prison and $250,000 fine

Bringing in Aliens for Financial Gain – Title 8, U.S.C., Section 1324(a)(2)(B)(ii)

Maximum penalty: Ten years in prison (and a mandatory minimum three years) and $250,000 fine

INVESTIGATING AGENCY

Homeland Security Investigations

This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF San Diego comprises agents and officers from FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, DEA, ATF, U.S. Marshals, Department of Defense, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Naval Criminal Investigative Service, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Interpol, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California.

Scott, DeSaulnier Demand Answers from Trump Administration on Ability to Protect 155 Million Workers’ Benefits
WASHINGTON – House Committee on Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10) demanded the Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) Assistant Secretary Daniel Aronowitz share a detailed accounting of the agency’s staffing, the damage done by the Trump-Musk federal workforce cuts, and its actions to effectively enforce the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA).
ERISA governs 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 retirement plans, and 521,000 other employee benefit plans that cumulatively cover 155 million Americans. However, under the Trump Administration, EBSA has experienced chronic underfunding, reduced staff, and weakened enforcement capacity, allowing bad actors to evade accountability for harming workers’ hard-earned benefits.
“The chaotic nature of the Trump Administration’s campaign to slash the federal workforce has also obscured the exact scope and severity of the damage imposed on the Agency’s workforce. Over the last 20 months, we have had to rely on media reports and top-line figures in annual budget requests to ascertain EBSA’s capacity, which are often vague or outdated. Moreover, your responses to the Committee’s questions for the record after your appearance failed to provide any substantive information on staffing. In order for the Committee to evaluate EBSA’s ability to effectively carry out its mission, as well as to advocate for more resources, it is imperative we have a robust and up-to-date picture of the Agency’s workforce changes and composition,” wrote Ranking Members Scott and DeSaulnier.
The Ranking Members requested the agency turn over documents and information related to this request no later than October 22, 2026.
Background:
On November 18, 2025, the Ranking Members urged the Trump Administration to adequately staff EBSA to ensure it can fulfill its enormous mission and called on Secretary Aronowitz to tackle wrongful claim denials by group health plans and insurance companies and secure coverage for working people under ERISA.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – Dominican authorities extradited Patricia Joanna Almonte-Frías and her partner Rineldys Feliciano Díaz-Cuevas to the United States to face cyberstalking and sextortion conspiracy charges filed in the District of Puerto Rico, announced Héctor Ramírez-Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico. The defendants were arrested in the Dominican Republic on August 19, 2026, at the request of the United States, and extradited to Puerto Rico on September 30, 2026.

According to court documents, Patricia Joanna Almonte-Frías and Rineldys Feliciano Díaz-Cuevas operated an international, financially motivated “sextortion” scheme that conspired to engage in, and did engage in, cyberstalking and intestate threats.

The defendants, operating from the Dominican Republic, identified and sextorted victims using Facebook, WhatsApp, and other social media platforms. Almonte-Frías used her image to encourage victims in Puerto Rico to share online sexually explicit photos and videos (which were secretly recorded). Subsequently, defendant Díaz-Cuevas and other co-conspirators then extorted victims to send money under threat of exposing the compromising images to the victims’ family and friends. In some instances, the defendants created photo collages by combining the victim’s sexually explicit images with images of minors, thereby giving the false impression that victims were involved in sexual relationships with minors.

On multiple occasions, the victims paid the demanded amounts, emptied their accounts, and the defendants still carried out the threats and distributed the victims’ sexual images to the victims’ online network of friends and family members.

“These defendants ran a calculated scheme that preyed on trust, fear, and vulnerability, leaving lasting harm in its wake,” said Héctor Ramírez‑Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico. “Sextortion is a ruthless crime, and today’s prosecution makes clear that those who exploit victims—no matter where they hide—will be identified, pursued, and held to account.”

“In today’s ever-changing digital environment, criminals will develop creative ways to target victims and exploit them. Extortion is a serious crime that can cause lasting financial and psychological harm to its victims,” said Carlos R. Goris, Special Agent in Charge of FBI San Juan. “The FBI encourages all citizens to remain vigilant online and report to the authorities if you suspect you have been a victim of extortion. Your report will help law enforcement disrupt these networks and prevent others from becoming victims. The FBI demonstrates once again that no matter where you are, we will find you and bring you to justice.”

Almonte-Frías and Díaz-Cuevas are charged with conspiracy to cyberstalk and send interstate threats in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 371. The defendants made their initial court appearances on October 1, 2026 before U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcos E. López of the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of five years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The FBI in San Juan, Puerto Rico investigated the case.

The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, FBI Legal Attaché in Santo Domingo, the U.S. Marshals Service, and law enforcement partners in the Dominican Republic provided substantial assistance in securing the arrest and extradition to the United States of Almonte-Frías and Díaz-Cuevas.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Julián Radzinschi, of the Financial Fraud and Public Corruption Division, is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

WASHINGTON – Darae Vaughn, 31, of the District of Columbia, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 96 months in federal prison in connection with his role in a narcotics trafficking conspiracy that distributed fentanyl and crack cocaine in Northeast D.C., announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“Darae Vaughn trafficked fentanyl and crack cocaine while armed, putting lives at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Now he’s going to prison for eight years. If you push deadly drugs into our community while armed, you will be held accountable. You will go to prison.”

“Darae Vaughn trafficked fentanyl and crack cocaine while armed, putting lives at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Now he’s going to prison for eight years. If you push deadly drugs into our community while armed, you will be held accountable. You will go to prison.”

Vaughn, aka “Rae,” pleaded guilty June 30, 2026, before Judge Trevor N. McFadden to conspiracy to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl, to possession with intent to distribute 28 grams or more of cocaine base, and to distribution and possession of 10 grams or more of fentanyl. In addition to the 96-month prison term, Judge McFadden ordered Vaughn to serve five years of supervised release.

According to court documents, in March 2025 the FBI Safe Streets Task Force began an investigation into reports of narcotics trafficking on the 2000 block of 19th Place SE, particularly counterfeit M30 fentanyl pills.

The investigation revealed that from at least April 2025 through September 2025, during nine recorded transactions, Vaughn sold hundreds of fentanyl pills, and quantities of crack cocaine, carfentanyl, and methamphetamine while he was armed with a Glock 43x pistol.

In January 2025, codefendant Charles Dixon and Vaughn exchanged text messages discussing pills that Vaughn had supplied to Dixon. Dixon argued with Vaughn about how many pills Vaughn owed him. On April 8, 2025, Dixon participated in the sale of 96 fentanyl pills. On July 3, 2025, Dixon was involved in the sale of 163 fentanyl pills.

Dixon was sentenced on October 6 to 33 months in prison for his role in the conspiracy.

This investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Iris McCranie and Kate Naseef.

This case is part of the Department of Justice’s broader efforts to combat fentanyl trafficking and drug related violence in the District of Columbia. Fentanyl remains one of the deadliest substances circulating in the illegal drug supply, and counterfeit pills containing fentanyl pose extreme risks to unwitting users and the community at large.

NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit. On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations.
“In alignment with the President’s National Space Policy, NASA is committed to maintaining a sustained American presence in low Earth orbit long after the International Space Station retires,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
Building on the agency’s Ignition event earlier this year, NASA regularly has engaged with private industry to shape the agency’s future direction in low Earth orbit. This included publishing two Requests for Information in March to gather industry’s perspective on low Earth orbit destinations and transportation. The agency also published a draft Request for Proposals in July, followed by an industry day and one-on-one meetings that allowed interested companies to review and comment on the planned acquisition approach.
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” said Isaacman. “Since Ignition, we have spent a lot of time listening to industry and working through what it will take to make this transition successful. The opportunity is significant, but the economics ultimately have to work. We want to see credible plans, strong technical execution, and companies prepared to invest in destinations that can serve NASA while developing additional customers and markets of their own.”
Proposals are due Tuesday, Dec. 8, with contract awards expected in spring 2027.
Under the solicitation, NASA outlines requirements for companies interested in designing, building, testing, certifying, and operating commercial low Earth orbit destinations capable of providing end-to-end destination and transportation services for human spaceflight use.
NASA intends to award firm-fixed-price, multi-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts supporting development, certification, and services for continued low Earth orbit research and exploration. This will allow NASA to select two or more contractors through early development, followed by a competitive task order for final design, test, and evaluation, as well as certification and services from one or more contractors.
Learn more about NASA’s missions on the agency’s website:

DAVENPORT, Iowa – Rock Island men were sentenced to federal prison for conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, distribution of a controlled substance, possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, and felon in possession of a firearm.

According to public court documents and evidence presented at sentencing, on June 12, 2025, all three men drove together to sell marijuana to a confidential source.

Daquez Deasante Howard, 22, remained in the car and possessed money from the drug sale, a loaded, Taurus pistol with an extended magazine, and 20.83 grams of marijuana on his seat. On July 8, 2026, Howard was sentenced to a 68-month prison term, followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Darryl Lee Smith, Jr., 23, was apprehended by police after he ran from the car and possessed a loaded revolver with the hammer cocked back. On May 13, 2026, Smith was sentenced to a 57-month prison term, followed by a three-year term of supervised release

Darryl Benard Shears, III,24, ran on foot, escaping the police. Inside the car, police found a loaded pistol, 35.10 grams of cocaine, 14.31grams of crack cocaine, and two functioning scales where Shears had been seated in the car before and after the drug deal. On June 29, 2025, Shears was arrested. Shears again attempted to flee from police on the Arsenal Bridge, crashing into multiple police cars, and jumping into the Mississippi river. Shears also possessed a loaded pistol with a round in the chamber. On October 8, 2026, Shears was sentenced to a 204-month prison term, followed by a six-year term of supervised release.

There is no parole in the federal system.

United States Attorney David C. Waterman of the Southern District of Iowa made the announcement. The Davenport Police Department investigated the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. For more information about Project Safe Neighborhoods, please visit Justice.gov/PSN.

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Darrell Dee Faver, Jr., age 41, of McAlester, Oklahoma, entered a guilty plea to an Information of two counts of Abusive Sexual Contact in Indian Country, punishable by a term of imprisonment up to life on each count.

The Information alleged that beginning in or about September 2017, and continuing until in or about October 2019, Faver knowingly engaged in and caused sexual contact with two victims who had not attained the age of 12 years, with an intent to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade, and gratify the sexual desire of any person.

The charges arose from an investigation by the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

Fact Sheet

Office of the Spokesman

October 9, 2026

Political reconciliation talks between the interim Venezuelan government and 2015 National Assembly representatives are producing tangible reforms in civil liberties and political rights, laying the groundwork for credible elections and a democratic transition. Two rounds of talks have already taken place, producing significant results: a wholesale reform and reconstruction of an independent Venezuelan Supreme Court, the restoration of access to more than 70 previously blocked internet domains, and the reform of a key repressive law. The interim government has also released more than 1,000 political prisoners and announced the release of nearly 200 more.

The talks bring together representatives of Venezuela’s 2015 National Assembly, led by its President Dinorah Figuera, and representatives of the interim government, led by current National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez. The 2015 National Assembly was Venezuela’s last democratically elected legislative body recognized by all Venezuelan political parties and by the international community.

The delegations held two rounds of talks in Caracas in August and September, with another round scheduled to begin October 14. The parties have decided to remain in session to maintain the momentum they have achieved.

The United States supports this Venezuelan-led process to create the conditions for a peaceful democratic transition, which is only possible because of President Trump’s bold leadership. Early accomplishments include the following:

Rebuilding an Independent Supreme Court:

Following the talks, the 2026 National Assembly published a law reforming the Supreme Court selection process, with 32 new judges to be selected by December. The Supreme Court will adjudicate any challenges to Venezuela’s future election results, underscoring the importance of a credible selection process.

The talks led to the creation of a seven-member Credentials Council, an unprecedented all-judge body that will screen candidates and send only qualified jurists to the Judicial Nominations Committee. Importantly, the 2015 National Assembly chose a majority of the Council.

The Judicial Nominations Committee, made up of 11 current National Assembly members and 12 civil society members, will choose the 32 nominees from the Credentials Council’s approved list.

This selection process increases transparency and enshrines protections to ensure the new judges will be qualified and not tied to the Maduro regime.

Expanding Freedom of Expression:

The interim government has restored or partially restored access to more than 70 previously blocked internet domains, including El Tiempo , EFE , Revista Semana , El Pitazo , Efecto Cucuyo , among others.

Reforming Repressive Laws:

The National Assembly established a commission to reform and decriminalize penalties contained in the repressive 2017 Law Against Hatred, which was notorious for its use by the Maduro regime to jail opposition leaders and those who spoke out against the regime.

The law established penalties of up to 20 years in prison for the “promotion or incitement of hatred, discrimination, or violence,” although in practice it was used to punish criticism of the regime.

Releasing Political Prisoners:

The interim government has released over 1,000 political prisoners since Operation Absolute Resolve. Since the political reconciliation talks began in August, the interim government has announced the release of an additional 177 political prisoners, an important step toward restoring fundamental political freedoms.

Prominent political prisoners released since January 3 include Juan Pablo Guanipa, advisor to Maria Corina Machado and former First Vice President of the National Assembly; Freddy Superlano, ex-gubernatorial candidate and former National Assembly member; and Enrique Márquez, ex-presidential candidate and former Vice President of the National Electoral Council.

Exiled opposition figures Claudia Macero and Omar González Moreno, who fled the threat of detention due to political motivated charges, have also returned to Venezuela.

What Comes Next

The third round of reconciliation talks is scheduled to begin October 14. The delegations will focus on finalizing the Supreme Court selection process and providing individuals and political parties participation guarantees necessary for credible elections.

Future rounds of dialogue will address reform of the National Electoral Council, repealing remaining repressive laws, and opening political space so all political parties and leaders can return and participate in political life.

We welcome the joint efforts with Venezuela’s interim government to recover the gold in the United Kingdom.

The Trump Administration will continue to support this Venezuelan-led process as it moves from dialogue to durable democratic institutions.

For media inquiries, please contact the Office of the Spokesman.

LOS ANGELES – A Santa Clarita man was charged today in a federal criminal complaint alleging he intentionally set a wildfire in the Angeles National Forest that burned more than 1,000 acres of federally owned land, the Justice Department announced.

Rodney Ameile Saba, 70, of Santa Clarita, was charged with arson involving federal property. He is expected to make his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in downtown Los Angeles.

According to the complaint, on October 3, 2026, at approximately 2:13 p.m., Saba allegedly ignited what became known as the “Bouquet Fire” behind his residence on Bouquet Canyon Road. Moments before the fire started, Saba allegedly warned a neighbor to expect a loud sound like a shotgun blast. Witnesses then heard a powerful explosion followed by Saba yelling for help and a fire rapidly spreading up the hillside.

The complaint alleges that Saba admitted to law enforcement that he threw a cigarette from his porch onto fireworks, causing them to explode and start the fire. Investigators later recovered a lighter, cigarettes, shotgun ammunition, and an aerial mortar firework from Saba’s cabin.

Fire investigators with the U.S. Forest Service determined that the Bouquet Fire, which ultimately burned approximately 1,048 acres of federal land, was “probably caused by fireworks” after excluding lightning, campfires, debris burning, and other potential causes.

The complaint further alleges that Saba has multiple prior felony convictions, including mayhem, vandalism, possession of a controlled substance, criminal threats, manufacture or possession of a dangerous weapon, and possession of a stolen vehicle.

Saba was arrested on October 3, 2026, by local law enforcement on related state charges. Today’s federal complaint formally charges him in federal court.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

If convicted, Saba would face a statutory maximum sentence of up to 20 years in federal prison.

The United States Forest Service is investigating this matter, with assistance from Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department – Arson Explosives Detail.

Assistant United States Attorneys Alexandra Sloan Kelly of the Environmental Crimes and Consumer Protection Section and Brenda N. Galván of the Transnational Organized Crime Section are prosecuting the case.
title: Santa Clarita Man Charged with Federal Arson Offense Alleging He Set Wildfire that Burned Over 1,000 Acres of National Forest Land

Neal Slams Trump’s Latest Fed Stunt
SPRINGFIELD, MA— Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal (D-MA) released the following statement after President Trump announced he’d create a committee to search for pretext to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook:
“The Trump Administration should be focused on bringing diesel back from record highs, lowering prices at the pump and grocery store, and ending their failed war with Iran. Instead, the president’s attention is consumed by a grudge he can’t let go of. Despite being told no by the Supreme Court and his handpicked Fed Chair, Trump’s commitment to bend monetary policy to his will and put Americans’ financial stability at more risk is relentless.
“Fed independence isn’t up for debate, no matter how many tricks Donald Trump tries in an effort to put his thumb on the scale. By creating this so-called committee, he is wasting resources and time on a debunked fishing expedition that should instead be spent making your life easier. The Fed works for the American people, and we will keep fighting the president’s desperate claw for power.”
###

CHICAGO — A man has been indicted in federal court for allegedly aiming a laser pointer at a Chicago Police Department helicopter.

IGNACIN RAMOS, 36, of Chicago, knowingly aimed the beam of a laser pointer at the CPD helicopter on Aug. 11, 2026, according to an indictment returned Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Chicago. The indictment charges Ramos with one count of aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft in the special aircraft jurisdiction of the United States.

Ramos pleaded not guilty during his arraignment on Thursday in federal court in Chicago. A status hearing was scheduled for Dec. 3, 2026, at 9:30 a.m., before U.S. District Judge Mary M. Rowland.

The indictment was announced by Andrew S. Boutros, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, and Ryan Whalen, Special Agent-in-Charge of the Chicago Field Office of the FBI. Valuable assistance was provided by the Chicago Police Department and the Cook County Sheriff’s Office. The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Davis Price Shugrue.

The public is reminded that an indictment is not evidence of guilt. The defendant is presumed innocent and entitled to a fair trial at which the government has the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The charge in the indictment is punishable by up to five years in federal prison. If convicted, the Court must impose a reasonable sentence under federal statutes and the advisory U.S. Sentencing Guidelines.
title: Man Indicted in Federal Court for Allegedly Aiming Laser Pointer at Chicago Police Helicopter

A North Hollywood man was sentenced today to 70 months in federal prison for his role in a series of fraud schemes that caused nearly $5 million in losses to federal COVID 19 relief and small business lending programs.
Sarkis Sarkisyan, a.k.a. “Samuel Shaw,” 38, of North Hollywood, was sentenced by United States District Judge Cynthia Valenzuela.
Sarkisyan pleaded guilty on April 29 to two counts of wire fraud and one count of transactional money laundering arising from his fraudulent application for a $786,457 Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan and a subsequent $25,000 laundering transaction. In addition, the government’s investigation revealed that he also orchestrated additional fraud involving Small Business Administration (SBA) Preferred Lender Program loans totaling more than $4 million, as well as attempted to obtain two Economic Injury Disaster Loans of $500,000 each.
According to court records, Sarkisyan fabricated businesses, payrolls, IRS tax forms, and financial records to obtain federally backed loans intended to support legitimate small businesses during the COVID 19 pandemic. He and his co schemers then transferred the proceeds through shell companies and associates to conceal the origin of the illicit funds.
In total, Sarkisyan and his co-schemers received $4,866,457 in fraudulently obtained loan proceeds, most of which ultimately benefited him personally.
Sarkisyan “participated in a massive scheme to defraud multiple banks and, ultimately, taxpayers, out of almost $5 million in funds from lending programs designed to benefit small businesses and those in need during the COVID-19 pandemic,” prosecutors argued in their sentencing memorandum. His scheme “involved fabricating out of whole cloth businesses to make them appear legitimate entities whose funds taxpayers would expect to be an engine for the greater economy or in need of dire assistance during the pandemic,” and by doing so, defendant “exploited the goodwill of lenders and taxpayers.”
A deferred restitution hearing is set for December 4.
SBA-OIG, IRS Criminal Investigation, and HSI are investigating this matter.
Assistant United States Attorneys Andrew M. Roach and David C. Lachman of the Major Frauds Section are prosecuting this case.
title: North Hollywood Man Sentenced to Over 5 Years in Federal Prison for COVID-19 Fraud

Coast Guard medevacs cargo ship crew member offshore Hawaii
Coast Guard Oceania District External Affairs - (808) 271-6543
HONOLULU — The Coast Guard medevaced an ailing cargo ship crew member 86 miles offshore Hawaii Wednesday.
An MH-65 Dolphin helicopter crew from Coast Guard Air Station Barbers Point hoisted a 55-year-old man at 8:35 a.m. and safely transferred him to higher medical care at Hilo International Airport.
Joint Rescue Coordination Center Honolulu watchstanders received a notification at 7:50 a.m. Tuesday from a crew member of the Ocean Gladiator, a 545-foot U.S.-flagged cargo ship, requesting a medevac for a crew member who had been experiencing a medical condition aboard the vessel which was 540 miles southeast Big Island, Hawaii.
After conferring with the duty flight surgeon, who recommended a medevac, watchstanders established regular communications with the vessel’s crew to monitor the patient's status and planned a medevac when the vessel was 86 miles offshore Big Island.
For more information follow us on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
-USCG-

Department of Justice Announces Updates to Emergency Scheduling Actions for 7-OH and Related Opioid Substances
The Department of Justice today announced updated emergency scheduling actions targeting 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and three potent opioid substances related to 7-OH: mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), MGM-15, and MGM-16.
“Dangerous and addictive opioids do not belong behind convenience store counters,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Our nation’s children and communities deserve protection from harmful substances like 7-OH and other powerful synthetic drugs. The actions taken by the Department of Justice today reflect our commitment to keeping Americans safe and holding drug traffickers accountable.”
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is issuing two new Notices of Intent based on new scientific information and recommendations provided by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The updated HHS analysis supports a revised threshold approach for 7-OH and MGPI designed to distinguish products containing trace amounts of these substances from formulations that have been intentionally enhanced or concentrated.
The two Notices of Intent address:
- MGM-15 and MGM-16: DEA will reissue the Notice of Intent without changing the current scheduling approach for these substances.
- 7-OH and MGPI: DEA will issue a new Notice of Intent incorporating HHS' updated scientific recommendation for concentration and ratio thresholds applicable to both substances.
HHS recommended that 7-OH and MGPI be subject to Schedule I control when either substance alone, or their combined amount when both are present, exceeds 1 milligram per gram in solid products or 1 milligram per milliliter in liquid products, or when the ratio of mitragynine to 7-OH, MGPI, or their combined amount is less than 100 to 1. HHS recommended this approach to better distinguish products intentionally enhanced or concentrated in these opioid substances from products whose alkaloid composition is more consistent with botanical kratom.
The updated HHS analysis confirms that 7-OH occurs naturally in botanical kratom at relatively low levels and identifies additional scientific information suggesting MGPI may also occur at trace levels in some botanical or kratom-derived products. HHS noted that the science concerning the presence of MGPI continues to develop but recommended applying a threshold approach to both 7-OH and MGPI.
DEA temporarily placed MGPI, MGM-15, and MGM-16 into Schedule I on August 26, 2026. Those controls will remain in effect during the new 30-day Notice of Intent period and until DEA issues a new temporary scheduling order.
For 7-OH, DEA had not yet issued a temporary scheduling order. DEA will reissue a new Notice of Intent reflecting HHS’ updated scientific recommendation.
Press Release Number: 26-1165
title: Department of Justice Announces Updates to Emergency Scheduling Actions for 7-OH and Related Opioid Substances

Rep. Subramanyam Issues Statement on Livestream Execution of Fort Hood Shooter Nidal Hasan
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Representative Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), Ranking Member of the Military and Foreign Affairs Oversight Subcommittee, issued the following statement on the Pentagon’s announcement that they would be livestreaming the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan. Nidal Hisan killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009.
“Regimes in Iran, North Korea, and ISIS carry out public executions, not America. Nidal Malik Hisan should face consequences, but livestreaming his execution is blatantly un-American and against what our country stands for. When we do this, we lose our moral standing on the global stage and set a horrible precedent. The Administration must stop this, and Secretary Hegseth needs to be removed. History will not judge this action kindly,” said Ranking Member Suhas Subramanyam.
###

Medical Supply Company Owner Sentenced to 14 Years in Prison for $30M Medicare, TRICARE, and CHAMPVA Fraud
An Oklahoma business owner and chiropractor was sentenced yesterday to 14 years in prison for his role in a years-long scheme that attempted to bilk Medicare, TRICARE, and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) out of over $30 million for orthotics braces, continuous glucose monitors, and other durable medical equipment (DME) that beneficiaries did not want or need.
“Yesterday's 14-year sentence shows that health care fraud does not pay,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Department of Justice's National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The Department is committed to bringing to justice those who corrupt our health care system by paying illegal kickbacks, submitting false claims, deceiving programs that serve our seniors, service members, and veterans, and treating sensitive patient information like a commodity to be bought and sold.”
“Fraud against federal health care programs is a direct attack on the public’s trust and on the vulnerable individuals these programs are meant to protect, and the jury’s verdict and sentencing of Mark Loftis demonstrate that schemes of this kind will be met with decisive action and significant consequences,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General. “HHS-OIG will not hesitate to investigate and dismantle criminal conduct wherever it threatens the integrity of federal programs, and this case reflects the unwavering commitment of our agency and our law-enforcement partners to safeguard taxpayer dollars and ensure that those who defraud the government are held fully accountable.”
“Healthcare fraud drains millions of dollars from federally funded programs, and we all pay the price,” said Special Agent in Charge Rodney Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office. “Today’s sentence underscores the FBI’s steadfast commitment to aggressively pursuing those who engage in kickback schemes and other fraudulent practices.”
“As the law enforcement arm of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS) is committed to safeguarding the integrity of the TRICARE program,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Nakia M. Alexander of the DCIS Southeast Field Office. “This investigation is an example of a healthcare fraud scheme that directly affected American service members and their families. I applaud the collaborative work of the investigative agencies and the Department of Justice that led to today’s sentencing.”
“Fraud schemes targeting VA programs and services compromise their integrity and divert funds from veterans who rely on these benefits,” said Inspector General Cheryl L. Mason, Department of Veterans Affairs. “The VA OIG works every day with our law enforcement partners to identify fraudsters and hold them accountable.”
According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Dr. Mark Loftis, 39, of Cushing, Oklahoma, and his co-conspirators did not disclose to Medicare the ownership and management of the DME company Back Pain Home Supplies LLC dba EZ Medical Supply. Loftis and his co-conspirators hid from Medicare that unenrolled entities were billing claims through the DME company. Lofits paid over a million dollars in illegal kickbacks, including through a shell marketing company, to marketers, purported telemedicine companies, and a call center that persuaded elderly and disabled Americans to disclose their personal information and receive DME they did not need. Loftis and his co-conspirators also purchased sham doctors’ orders for orthotic braces, continuous glucose monitors, and DME that were generated by telemedicine doctors and nurse practitioners who never examined, and often never spoke to, the beneficiaries. Loftis and his co-conspirators submitted over $30 million in false and fraudulent claims and were paid over $8 million. Loftis and his co-conspirators frequently billed for multiple orthotic braces at a time, including in one example eight braces for a single beneficiary.
After a 12-day jury trial ending in July 2026, Loftis was convicted of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud. In addition to the prison sentence, Loftis was ordered to pay over $8 million in restitution and to forfeit over $560,000.
HHS-OIG, FBI, DCIS, and VA-OIG investigated the case.
Assistant Deputy Chief Catherine Wagner and Trial Attorney Raymond Beckering III of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Health Care Fraud Section prosecuted the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
title: Medical Supply Company Owner Sentenced to 14 Years in Prison for $30M Medicare, TRICARE, and CHAMPVA Fraud

Op-Ed: Health care premiums continue to rise. Congress can lower them
By Rep. Joe Courtney (Published in the Day, October 9th, 2026)
Last month, Connecticut’s state insurance department officially approved an 11.3% average rate increase in 2027 for state-regulated, individual and small business health care coverage plans.
This double-digit increase, far above an already high general inflation rate, has justifiably been met with deep frustration from both individual patients and health care plan administrators, with small businesses in particular feeling the squeeze.
It is clear from the persistent high trajectory of the state insurance department rate increases that the mounting cost of health care is creating a burden that will not be sustainable over the long term. It is time for policy makers to stop this trend by digging deeper into these decisions to identify which health services are spiking in cost.
The 2026 rate decision could not be clearer. A leading driver of this year’s health care premium increase is prescription drug cost increases. According to the Connecticut Department of Insurance, 30% of a Connecticut health care premium dollar is consumed by prescription drug costs. This amount has doubled since 2010.
That trend screams out for action, not just in Hartford, but also in Washington, where over the last four years, real reductions in drug costs have been achieved because of Medicare price negotiations.
Along those lines, I am a co-sponsor of the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act (H.R. 6166), which would empower the Medicare program to negotiate with pharmaceutical companies for lower prescription drug costs, not just for Americans 65 and older, but for all Americans on employer-based plans and individual ACA marketplace plans (Access Health CT here in Connecticut).
This bill builds on the price negotiation success of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which by law has saved both patients and Medicare billions. As a result of price negotiations, the diabetes drug Januvia saw its price lowered from $527 to $113, blood thinners Eliquis and Xarelto went from $521 to $231 and $517 to $197, respectively, and the Asthma and COPD drug Trelegy went from $654 to $175, to name just a few.
Expanding drug price regulation has strong public support. At least two-thirds of U.S. adults across all parties, including 68% of Republicans, say that there is not enough government regulation when it comes to the price of prescription drugs, according to 2026 polling by KFF.
Even President Trump and Congressional Republicans clearly recognize the success and popularity of drug price negotiation.
In 2025, when they cut nearly $1 trillion from the Medicaid program in their so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” (H.R. 1) and allowed Affordable Care Act marketplace (Access Health CT) premiums to skyrocket for middle-class Americans, Trump and the GOP very carefully left the Biden-era Medicare drug price negotiation in intact.
What about Trump Rx, the three-year deal with big pharma, you might ask? A close look at the Trump Rx portal that claims to provide lower drug prices in most cases recycles drug coupons for discounted prices that already exist.
In addition, Americans are only able to use Trump Rx to purchase drugs outside of their commercial health plans, meaning it does nothing to lower Connecticut premium rates. After three years, the Trump Rx deal expires, unlike the statutory permanence of the 2022 law that will expand the list of drugs subject to price reduction.
It is very clear, to lower Connecticut health care premiums, Congress should pass the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act into law and create cost-saving parity for working age Americans on par with Medicare. It’s simple and it will work.
title: Op-Ed: Health care premiums continue to rise. Congress can lower them

On Sept. 10th, the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base flightline welcomed a tailwheel turboprop aircraft with a wingspan broader than that of an A-10 Thunderbolt II and equipped with twice as many radios as an F-15E Strike Eagle. Air Force Special Operations Command’s newest combat platform, the OA-1K Skyraider II, touched down for an exclusive "Pet-the-Aircraft" event, bringing the acquisition community face-to-face with the aircrew and the combat capability they have worked for years to build.
The aircraft was flown directly from Will Rogers Air National Guard Base, Oklahoma, where operators have been refining the platform’s specialized capabilities. It was commanded and piloted by an Air Force captain and supported by the weapons systems officer, another Air Force captain. For the remainder of the afternoon, the aircraft served as a centerpiece for multidisciplinary technical evaluation, workforce recognition, and family appreciation.
For the engineers, program managers, logisticians, financial managers, and contracting officers of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center's Attack Systems Division, operating under the Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance and Special Operations Forces (ISR & SOF) Directorate, the visit transformed engineering diagrams, contract lines, and technical data packages into operational reality.
The Genesis of Armed Overwatch: Meeting the Call of the Warfighter
The OA-1K's arrival at Wright-Patterson AFB marks the culmination of a deliberate, rapid acquisition journey initiated in 2020 by USSOCOM.
To execute special operations missions in alignment with the National Defense Strategy, USSOCOM recognized an urgent operational deficit: the need for a sustainable, cost-effective aircraft, designed to be adaptable across mission requirements, whether it be close air support, precision strike, or armed intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Historically, high-end fighters and strike platforms carried immense operating costs and heavy logistical tails that strained resources during long-loiter counter-violent extremist operations. USSOCOM required a rugged, crewed system that could operate from austere, unimproved dirt strips with minimal maintenance that could adapt to mission requirements.
To meet this requirement without decades of costly developmental cycles, USSOCOM deployed an aggressive, three-phased acquisition framework:
Phase 1: Market Research and Industry Screening: In early 2020, USSOCOM assessed over 50 initial industry white papers and conducted extensive contractor facility assessments, alongside independent RAND Corporation studies, to down-select the field to five viable flying prototypes.
Phase 2: Prototype Flight Demonstrations: In early 2021, leveraging Title 10 U.S.C. § 4022 Middle Tier of Acquisition (MTA) Rapid Prototyping authority to conduct flight trials across five competitive aircraft at Eglin AFB, Florida, narrowing the selection to three finalists.
Phase 3: Production Solicitation and Contract Award: From summer 2021 to summer 2022, the process transitioned from MTA to Major Capability Acquisition Milestone C. A competitive production solicitation was issued, culminating in a best-value contract award to L3Harris for the AT-802U integrated weapon system.
In late 2022, the aircraft earned its official military type designation, OA-1K, and in February 2025, AFSOC formally christened it the "Skyraider II," a historic homage to the famed Douglas A-1 Skyraider that protected downed airmen and supported troops in contact during the Korean and Vietnam wars.
Bridging the Gap: PMO Technical Q&A with the Aircrew
A highlight of the event was an interactive, open-forum Q&A session between the Wright-Patterson Program Management Office team and the visiting pilot and WSO. This session provided an invaluable feedback loop, allowing program managers, engineers, contracting specialists, financial managers, and logisticians to hear directly from the aviators flying the aircraft daily.
This direct technical exchange gave the PMO real-world user feedback to refine future system reviews, tackle engineering bottlenecks, and streamline the upcoming transition of the fleet from Block-1 to the combat-ready Block-2 standard.
Built for the Austere Edge: Crop Duster to Combat Workhorse
The OA-1K Skyraider II represents a masterclass in militarizing proven commercial utility designs.
Manufactured initially by Air Tractor in Olney, Texas, as the AT-802 utility airframe, the platform is modified into a combat-ready weapon system.
- Powerplant and Performance: Pratt and Whitney PT6A Turboprop – delivers high-torque performance, high loiter persistence, and low operating costs per flying hour.
- Runway Independence: Ruggedized tailwheel fixed landing gear and Short Takeoff and Landing capability – takes off and lands on austere dirt, gravel, or grass airstrips.
- Combat Payload: Missionized equipment across external hardpoints – standard loadouts feature pods for air-launched rockets, air-to-ground missiles, and precision-guide munitions.
- Mission Architecture: The pilot and WSO stations have independent, full control of flight systems, sensors, and munitions.
- Expeditionary Mobility: Rapid breakdown and reassembly design – can be disassembled in hours by a small crew, loaded into a single cargo aircraft, and rapidly reassembled in theater.
With the aircraft returning to its training lines in Oklahoma, the Wright-Patterson AFB acquisition team turns its focus back to contract milestones, technical reviews, and sustainment packages that will ensure the OA-1K Skyraider II stands ready when the call comes downrange.
OA-1K Skyraider II Fast Facts: 
- Primary Mission: Close Air Support, Armed ISR, and Precision Strike
- Lead Commands: Air Force Special Operations Command and U.S. Special Operations Command
- Program Management: AFLCMC/WID Attack Systems Division supporting USSOCOM PEO Fixed Wing
- Crew: 2 (Pilot in front seat, Weapon Systems Officer in rear seat)
title: OA-1K Skyraider II lands at Wright-Patterson AFB for hands-on acquisition review

Minnesota Woman Convicted in $3.6M Scheme to Defraud Medicaid Housing Services Program
A federal jury in St. Paul convicted a Minnesota woman yesterday for executing a scheme to steal $3.6 million from the now-defunct Minnesota Medicaid Housing Stabilization Services (HSS) Program.
“The Fraud Division has arrived in Minnesota — and we are here to stay,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The jury’s guilty verdict in this case sends a clear message that those who steal from programs meant to help our most vulnerable will be held accountable. As proven at trial, Meadows falsified records to enrich herself while preventing critical services from reaching those in need. Her fraud scheme — and others like it — forced Minnesota’s Housing Stabilization Services Program to shut down entirely after costs of the program outran estimates by four thousand percent. I commend the dedicated prosecutors, agents, and support staff who worked tirelessly to deliver justice in this case.”
“The defendant chose to defraud millions from a program meant to help vulnerable Minnesotans,” said U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota. “My office is committed to prosecuting those who steal from the American taxpayer.”
According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Sharmaine Meadows, 45, of Lake Elmo, Minnesota, orchestrated a scheme to bill the HSS Program for housing services that were meant to transition the unhoused and assist them in sustaining that housing. Instead, these services were not actually provided. The HSS Program permitted providers to bill up to 150 hours for transitional services and 150 hours for sustaining services per eligible Medicaid beneficiary. Meadows routinely emphasized to her employees that they were required to maximize the billings to that 150-hour cap, even if the hours of services were never provided.
Agenda from Meadows’ company staff meeting in July 2022 at which “Maximizing of Hours” was discussed
The evidence presented at trial also proved that Meadows and her company billed the HSS Program for in-person hours supposedly provided by employees who were in other states, like Illinois, and in other countries, like the Philippines, where the defendant paid only $6.00 per hour and explicitly offered no benefits.
Employment Offer Letter from Meadows’ Company to Individual in the Philippines
She also submitted claims for services that could not have been provided because beneficiaries were in the hospital. And through data analysis, evidence showed that Meadows billed as if her employees were working more than 20 hours per day, every day, for weeks.
Summary of billing for “Impossible Days” by Meadows’ company Summaries of billing for “Impossible Days” by Meadows’ company
At the same time, Medicaid beneficiaries testified that they received little to no services from Meadows’ company. These beneficiaries testified that they were routinely told by Meadows’ employees that despite having received no assistance, they had run out of available hours in the HSS Program.
As a result of the fraud scheme, the HSS Program paid Meadows’ company over $3.6 million between 2020 and 2025 into accounts that Meadows exclusively controlled.
The jury convicted Meadows of three counts of health care fraud. She is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date and faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on each count. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s Fraud Division; U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota; Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson of the FBI Minneapolis Field Office; Special Agent in Charge Thomas Ethridge of the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG); and Special Agent in Charge Adam Jobes of the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Chicago Field Office, made the announcement
FBI, HHS-OIG, and IRS-CI investigated the case.
Trial Attorneys Brant Cook and Emily Reeder-Ricchetti of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section, with the assistance of Health Care Fraud Section Trial Attorney Jody King and Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Murphy for the District of Minnesota, are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

Fort Myers, Florida – A federal jury has found Jesus Pujol Hernandez (Naples, 42), Miguel Marquez Romero (Naples, 30), and Paulo Sabon Montero (Naples, 55) guilty of conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and use of interstate facilities for murder-for-hire. Each faces up to 20 years in federal prison. The sentencing hearings will be held on January 27, 2027. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court records, testimony, and evidence presented at trial, in April 2025, the FBI was investigating Marquez in an unrelated investigation in the Southern District of Florida. On April 16, 2025, agents learned that Marquez had advised Sabon that he had a “sweet play” which involved a millionaire in Marco Island who wanted to kill their brother for $30,000. Marquez made plans to introduce Sabon to Hernandez—the person who put him onto the murder-for-hire—the following day. Sabon agreed and requested they receive payment upfront. As part of the investigation, FBI Miami coordinated with FBI Fort Myers and the Collier County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO) to monitor Marquez’s apartment in Naples. Marquez, Hernandez, Sabon, and another individual were later detained.

Upon arrest, the FBI searched Hernandez’s pockets and located a large printed out photograph of the intended victim. The FBI also located latex gloves, a mask, a bandana, and more than $2,300 in Marquez’s vehicle. Subsequent investigation also revealed that Hernandez was on the phone with the intended victim’s brother when the group had met up in a grocery store parking lot earlier.

This case was investigated by the FBI (Miami Field Office) and FBI (Fort Myers Resident Agency), with assistance from the Collier County Sheriff’s Office. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Matt Redavid, Jesus M. Casas, and Patrick Darcey.
title: Jury Convicts Trio for Conspiracy to Commit Murder-for-Hire

The Federal Trade Commission today announced Greenway Auto Group has agreed that its price advertisements will prominently include the actual price a consumer must pay for a vehicle, excluding only charges the government requires consumers to pay, to settle the Commission’s lawsuit alleging the company advertised prices that were thousands of dollars below what it actually charged.
In addition to requiring price transparency and prohibiting deceptive prize mailers, the proposed order prohibits specific misrepresentations, including whether charges, fees, taxes, products or services are optional or required and whether any type of or source for financing is required.
“Truthful advertising in the auto industry is vital because purchasing a car is one of the most significant financial decisions consumers make,” said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Consumers can’t make informed choices when the actual price is hidden. Price transparency is critical to a properly functioning market and is a top priority for the Trump FTC.”
According to the complaint, Greenway inflated the amount it charged the overwhelming majority of consumers by tacking on to the advertised price mandatory fees, packages and penalties that cost consumers thousands.
The complaint alleges Greenway charged consumers more than $3,350, on average, over the advertised price in over 92% of transactions. The fees Greenway allegedly imposed on top of the advertised price included so-called administrative fees, dealer fees, delivery fees and processing fees. Greenway’s advertised prices at times also allegedly reflected conditional rebates and discounts available only to a subset of consumers.
In addition, the FTC alleges Greenway lured consumers into dealerships with scam mailers representing that recipients had won thousands of dollars in cash prizes that could be collected at a Greenway dealership, but the prizes were not real.
In a March 2026 letter, the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection warned Greenway about its misleading advertising practices, advising the company to ensure that the “price consumers see in advertising is the actual price they will pay.” According to the complaint, however, Greenway responded by adding false assurances of price transparency to their websites while continuing to advertise vehicles for thousands less than their actual prices.
The Commission continues to promote price transparency across several markets, including grocery delivery, rental housing, sports and concert ticketing as well as auto sales and leasing.
The Commission vote authorizing the staff to file the complaint and stipulated final order was 2-0. The FTC filed the complaint and stipulated final order in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, Orlando Division.
NOTE: Stipulated orders have the force of law when approved and signed by the District Court judge.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: FTC Secures Settlement with Auto Dealership Group in Price Transparency Win for Consumers
