- $1 billion in estimated eligible FEMA Public Assistance funding.
- $744 million available through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program.
- $3.1 billion approved in U.S. Small Business Administration low-interest disaster loans.
- $2.4 billion provided to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for debris removal.
  - More than 2.7 million tons of debris removed.

FEMA remains committed to helping affected communities recover efficiently and responsibly while reducing the impacts and costs of future disasters.

Shelton Lapointe, age 36, from Sioux City, Iowa, was sentenced on October 6, 2026, to 360 months’ imprisonment. Lapointe was convicted by a jury on April 29, 2026, on one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and aiding and abetting another to do so. Lapointe had prior convictions in Woodbury County District Court for possession with intent to deliver methamphetamine, in 2018 and again in 2022, serving time in state prison after each conviction.

The evidence at trial showed that on July 17, 2024, law enforcement agents were conducting surveillance at WinnaVegas Casino. They saw a car traveling away from the casino while driving over the speed limit. The agents attempted to stop the car. The car then took off at speeds ranging from 100 to 140 mph. During the flight, two packages of methamphetamine and one of marijuana were thrown out of the car. Law enforcement officers found and seized approximately ½ pound of methamphetamine and several ounces of marijuana in the packages. Lapointe, who was driving the car, handed his co-conspirator the drugs and instructed him to throw it out the window in an attempt to avoid getting caught with the drugs in their possession. Lapointe conspired with at least five other people to traffic methamphetamine from about 2022 through July 2024.

United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand sentenced Lapointe to 360 months’ imprisonment to be followed by 10 years of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Lapointe remains in custody of the U.S. Marshals until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Shawn S. Wehde and was investigated by the DEA Tri-State Drug Task Force based in Sioux City, Iowa, that consists of law enforcement personnel from the Drug Enforcement Administration; Sioux City Police Department; Homeland Security Investigations; Woodbury County Sheriff’s Office; South Sioux City Police Department; Nebraska State Patrol; Iowa National Guard; Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement; United States Marshals Service; South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation; and Woodbury County Attorney’s Office.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 24-4078.

Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.
title: Sioux City Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for 30 Years for Meth Convictions

text:
Two Fugitives Arrested in the Brutal Stabbing of NYPD Detective
For immediate release
Tracy Amaladas, Supervisory Deputy U.S. Marshal
New York, NY — The U.S. Marshals Service for the Southern District of New York and the District of Massachusetts announced the arrest of two fugitives wanted for the stabbing of a New York City Police Department (NYPD) detective this past Friday. The fugitives were taken into custody in Massachusetts following an intensive, non-stop multi-jurisdictional manhunt.
Dangelo Caraballo and Sneider Mejia were positively identified as the suspects wanted in this vicious stabbing. The case was turned over to the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) NY/NJ Regional Fugitive Task Force (NY/NJ RFTF) to locate and apprehend the fugitives. The moment the case was received, task force investigators worked tirelessly and developed intelligence indicating that the fugitives had fled the New York area together. USMS task force members tracked the pair to Massachusetts, where a targeted operation was conducted with the assistance of the U.S Marshals Service in the District of Massachusetts, the Massachusetts State Police, and the Lynn Police Department. Late Tuesday night, both individuals were taken into custody without further incident or injuries.
“When individuals commit violent, unprovoked acts against members of law enforcement, there is nowhere they can hide. From the second this case was assigned, the USMS in the Southern District of New York and the NY/NJ Regional Fugitive Task Force worked around the clock, tracking these suspects across state lines to ensure they were apprehended without further violence. We will always stand shoulder-to-shoulder with our police officers to hold violent offenders fully accountable,” said U.S. Marshal Ricky J. Patel.
“The attempted murder of an off-duty NYPD detective is an attack on every member of law-enforcement, and these two fugitives will now face justice,” said Dennis Matulewicz, head of the U.S. Marshals Service for the District of Massachusetts. “These arrests are the result of the exceptional teamwork between the U.S. Marshals Service Fugitive Task Forces and our outstanding state and local partners who worked tirelessly on this investigation.
The U.S. Marshals Service will always relentlessly pursue those who commit acts of violence, and our prayers are with the NYPD detective for a fast and full recovery.”
The fugitives are currently in custody of the Massachusetts State Police awaiting extradition to New York.
The NY/NJ RFTF began operations in April 2002 and was the first regional fugitive task force to become fully operational following the Presidential Threat Protection Act of 2000. The NY/NJ RFTF was the flagship that has allowed seven other regional fugitive task forces to be created across the country. With partnership agreements with over 90 federal, state, or local agencies and 13 fully operational offices, the NY/NJ RFTF has successfully apprehended over 95,000 fugitives since inception.
title: Two Fugitives Arrested in the Brutal Stabbing of NYPD Detective | U.S. Marshals Service

PORTLAND, Ore.—United States Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced the continued work of the District of Oregon’s Government Fraud Task Force, bringing together federal law enforcement agencies and inspectors general to strengthen efforts to identify, investigate, and prosecute fraud against government programs and American taxpayers.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office hosted the task force’s most recent meeting on Monday, October 5, attended by federal prosecutors and representatives from participating agencies. The meeting focused on expanding intelligence and data sharing, developing new methods for identifying fraud, prioritizing investigative leads, and ensuring law enforcement resources are directed toward significant fraud schemes.

“Fraud against government programs is theft from the American taxpayer, and we are committed to using every tool available to identify and prosecute those who exploit these programs for personal gain,” said U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford. “By bringing our federal, state, and local partners together to share intelligence, prioritize the strongest cases, and strategically deploy investigative resources, we will more effectively detect fraud, hold offenders accountable, and protect taxpayer dollars.”

The agencies joining the Government Fraud Task Force at the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Oregon include:

Federal Bureau of Investigation

IRS Criminal Investigation

U.S. Department of Agriculture

U.S. Department of Education

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs

U.S. Office of Inspector General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Units

U.S. Small Business Administration

U.S. Social Security Administration

Key priorities of the Government Fraud Task Force include:

Expanding information and data sharing among participating agencies to identify potential fraud schemes;

Cross-referencing government databases and benefit records to identify suspicious activity and potentially ineligible or fraudulent recipients;

Prioritizing and ranking fraud leads and referrals so investigative resources can be directed toward the strongest and most significant cases;

Deploying investigative resources strategically to address fraud leads in areas where agencies may lack sufficient personnel;

Using data analytics and financial investigative tools to identify unusual billing, benefit, grant, and contracting activity; and

Conducting annual reviews to evaluate the task force’s impact and identify opportunities to strengthen fraud enforcement.

The Government Fraud Task Force focuses on fraud affecting federal programs and taxpayer dollars, including health care fraud, government benefits fraud, Small Business Administration loan fraud, Social Security fraud, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program fraud, trade fraud, and student aid fraud.

Participating agencies are also working together to investigate suspicious financial activity, False Claims Act referrals, and government claims data; and identifying connections between government beneficiaries and other law enforcement and government records.

These efforts support the U.S. Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative, and creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”), to enhance coordination among federal agencies and strengthen the government’s ability to detect and prosecute fraud.

Federal prosecutors and representatives of federal law enforcement agencies in the Government Fraud Task Force attended the October 5, 2026, meeting at the Mark O. Hatfield U.S. Courthouse in Portland.
title: U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Oregon Announces Continued Work of the Government Fraud Task Force

U.S. Marshals Capture 14-year Iowa Fugitive Using Alias
For immediate release
Wade Jackson, Deputy U.S. Marshal
Davenport, IA – The U.S. Marshals (USMS) arrested a man wanted on several outstanding warrants from the Southern District of Iowa in the Mission Beach area of San Diego, California, October 6.
In 2013, Brian Anthony Williams, 50, was charged in the Southern District of Iowa for unlawful flight to avoid prosecution related to a 2012 Davenport Iowa Kidnapping case.
Williams was charged in Scott County October 26, 2012, for first-degree kidnapping, assault willful injury causing serious injury, conspiracy to commit a felony and first-degree arson for his alleged role in the October 8, 2012, assault where Williams and other coconspirators are alleged to have kidnapped, assaulted and shot a woman before leaving her in a northwest Davenport, Iowa, field.
The Davenport Police Department requested assistance from the USMS Southern Iowa Fugitive Task Force (SIFTF) in locating and arresting Williams.
Williams has remained a fugitive for nearly 14 years, appearing on local new stations in the Quad Cities as a most wanted fugitive as well as being posted on the United States Marshals Service Southern District of Iowa’s webpage.
In September 2026, the U.S. Marshals Service developed information indicating Williams was living in San Diego under the assumed identity of “Troy Williams” and working as a chef. Additional investigation showed that the individual believed to be Williams had appeared in local publications and television news reports under that assumed identity.
On October 6, U.S. Marshals from San Diego went to the 3700 block of Mission Boulevard in Mission Beach California where they located Williams inside the business and took him into custody without incident. Williams will remain in USMS custody pending his extradition to Iowa.
“This arrest is a perfect example of those who think they have bested law enforcement and evaded arrest,” said U.S. Marshal Ted Kamatchus, U.S. Marshal for the Southern District of Iowa. “Deputy U.S. Marshals remain resolute in their relentless pursuit of the most dangerous offenders in our society.”
U.S. Marshals Service task forces combine the efforts of federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies to locate and arrest our nation’s most dangerous fugitives. These task forces are dedicated to reducing violent crime by locating and apprehending wanted criminals. They also serve as the central point for agencies to share information on fugitive matters. In 2025, the U.S. Marshals arrested 73,323 fugitives, cleared 87,984 warrants, which averaged out to around 293 fugitives arrested per day in 2025 alone.

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, announced the conviction by jury of JONATHAN SPALLETTA, a/k/a “Cthulhon,” a/k/a “Jspalletta,” for computer fraud and money laundering in connection with his hacks of the decentralized cryptocurrency exchange Uranium Finance (“Uranium”). SPALLETTA was convicted on all counts of the Indictment following a six day jury trial before U.S. District Judge Jed S. Rakoff.

“As a unanimous Manhattan jury has found, Jonathan Spalletta repeatedly exploited vulnerabilities in the code of a decentralized cryptocurrency platform to steal tens of millions of dollars,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Spalletta’s own words are indicative of his dangerously misguided indifference for his victims and the hardships he caused, saying: ‘Crypto is just fake internet money anyway.’ As Spalletta’s many victims know, those words could not be further from the truth. Spalletta’s crimes cost real people to lose real money—over $50 million dollars—and caused an entire crypto platform to collapse. Our prosecutors of the Office and our agency partners have done outstanding work to ensure Spaletta’s virtual world criminal conduct ended in his real-world criminal conviction.”

“As a unanimous Manhattan jury has found, Jonathan Spalletta repeatedly exploited vulnerabilities in the code of a decentralized cryptocurrency platform to steal tens of millions of dollars,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Spalletta’s own words are indicative of his dangerously misguided indifference for his victims and the hardships he caused, saying: ‘Crypto is just fake internet money anyway.’ As Spalletta’s many victims know, those words could not be further from the truth. Spalletta’s crimes cost real people to lose real money—over $50 million dollars—and caused an entire crypto platform to collapse. Our prosecutors of the Office and our agency partners have done outstanding work to ensure Spaletta’s virtual world criminal conduct ended in his real-world criminal conviction.”

According to the Indictment, public filings, and evidence presented at trial:

Uranium was a decentralized cryptocurrency exchange that allowed users to deposit and exchange different kinds of cryptocurrencies via liquidity pools. In April 2021, SPALLETTA committed two separate hacks of Uranium.

In the first hack, on April 8, 2021, SPALLETTA engaged in a deceptive series of transactions with Uranium’s smart contract that SPALLETTA used to withdraw far more “rewards” in cryptocurrency than he was authorized to receive. He repeated those transactions over and over until he had drained the liquidity pool of nearly all its rewards tokens. In total, SPALLETTA successfully extracted cryptocurrency worth approximately $1.4 million in the first hack. Approximately two weeks after he fraudulently obtained the funds, SPALLETTA told another individual in writing, “I did a crypto heist of $1.5MM a couple of weeks ago . . . There was a bug in a smart contract, and I exploited it . . . Crypto is all fake internet money anyway.” SPALLETTA subsequently extorted Uranium into agreeing to allow him to keep approximately $386,000 of the money he stole as a sham “bug bounty” to help him evade prosecution in exchange for return of the remainder of the stolen money to Uranium.

In the second hack, on April 28, 2021, SPALLETTA exploited an error in the Uranium smart contract that governed how much cryptocurrency he could withdraw in a liquidity pool on Uranium. SPALLETTA exploited that issue across multiple separate Uranium liquidity pools, fraudulently obtaining approximately $53.3 million in cryptocurrency and causing Uranium to shut down due to lack of funds.

SPALLETTA then laundered the funds he had fraudulently obtained from Uranium through a complex series of cryptocurrency transactions, including by using the cryptocurrency mixer Tornado Cash.

After laundering the funds, SPALLETTA used the money he had fraudulently obtained to purchase personal collectable items, including but not limited to (i) rare cards for the trading card game Magic: The Gathering (“Magic Cards”); (ii) rare cards for the trading card game Pokémon (the “Pokémon Cards”); and (iii) antique Roman coins (the “Antique Coins”), among other items. In particular, SPALLETTA used the fraudulently obtained funds to purchase: (i) a “Black Lotus” Magic Card for approximately $500,000; (ii) 18 packs of sealed “Alpha Booster” Magic Cards for approximately $1,512,500; (iii) one sealed box of first edition “Booster” Pokémon Cards for approximately $257,500; (iv) one first edition complete base set of Pokémon Cards for approximately $750,000; (v) a piece of fabric from the original Wright brothers’ airplane that was subsequently transported to the surface of the moon by astronaut Neil Armstrong on the first moon landing, for approximately $137,500; (vi) one “Eid Mar Denarius,” an Antique Coin commemorating the assassination of Julius Caesar, for approximately $601,545.

Photographs of the Black Lotus Magic Card, the piece of fabric from the original Wright brothers’ airplane that was subsequently transported to the surface of the moon by astronaut Neil Armstrong, and certain of the Antique Coins, all of which were seized from the residence of SPALLETTA pursuant to a judicially-authorized search warrant, are below.

In addition, on February 24, 2025, law enforcement seized pursuant to a judicially-authorized seizure warrant cryptocurrency worth approximately $31 million at the time of seizure that SPALLETTA had fraudulently obtained from Uranium.

If you believe you have been a victim of the Uranium hack, please contact UraniumVictims@hsi.dhs.gov.

* * *

SPALLETTA, 36, of Rockville, Maryland, was convicted of one count of computer fraud, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison; and one count of money laundering, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

The maximum potential sentences in this case are prescribed by Congress and provided here for informational purposes only, as any sentencing of the defendant will be determined by a judge.

Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding work of HSI.

The case is being prosecuted by the Office’s Complex Frauds and Cybercrime Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kevin Mead, William C. Kinder, and Shaun Werbelow are in charge of the prosecution.
title: Jonathan Spalletta Convicted For Defrauding Crypto Exchange Of Over $50 Million In Hacks

The Federal Task Force to Combat Antisemitism Announces First Stop on The American Tour Against Hate
Today, the Department of Justice Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism announced the first stop of the American Tour Against Hate will be in Southfield, Michigan on Wednesday, October 14. The Task Force’s national campaign reflects the Trump Administration’s steadfast commitment to eradicating antisemitism across the country. “President Trump has made clear that this Administration will not tolerate antisemitism, and the Department of Justice is committed to implementing that directive,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “This national tour is an important step in ensuring communities across the country know the federal government stands ready to work with them to confront antisemitic threats, protect public safety, and uphold civil rights.”
"No American should live in fear of unjust discrimination or violence,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. “The Department of Justice is working tirelessly to protect and defend all Americans’ right to freedom of speech and free exercise of religion. Reps. Davids (D), Crane (R) Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Improve Housing Access for Tribal Veterans
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Yesterday, Representative Sharice Davids (D-KS-03) and Eli Crane (R-AZ-02) introduced bipartisan legislation to improve how unused housing vouchers are managed and distributed. The legislation would allow Tribes to voluntarily give back vouchers they do not plan to use, so the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) can redirect assistance to Tribal communities facing a shortage.
"Native veterans hold a special place in my heart,” said Davids, a member of the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin. “My mom and grandfather both served in the Army, and as a Native person, I know how much our communities value the veterans who have served our country. Tribal Nations know best what their communities and veterans need, and respecting Tribal sovereignty means giving them the flexibility and resources to meet those needs. I'm grateful to work with Rep. Crane on this bipartisan effort to ensure more Native veterans get the housing they need after returning home.”
"The Tribal HUD-VASH program helps house Tribal veterans in need, but the current system is not as efficient as it should be,” said Representative Eli Crane (R-AZ-02). “Some Tribes have leftover vouchers they cannot use while others lack the resources to take care of our veterans. Our legislation aims to resolve this longstanding issue by getting unused vouchers into the hands of Tribes that can put them to use. This is a sensible approach that makes better use of existing support without expanding the size and scope of the federal government. As the representative for more than half of the Tribes in Arizona, I'm honored to advocate for these heroes by reforming and modernizing this process. I appreciate Rep. Davids' willingness to work across the aisle. We've made real progress together before, and I look forward to building on that success with this bill.”
Native American veterans experience some of the highest rates of homelessness in the United States. To address this, Congress created the Tribal HUD-Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing (Tribal HUD-VASH) demonstration program, which provides rental assistance and supportive services to Native veterans who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
Although the program has helped many veterans secure stable housing, it lacks a clear process for Tribes to return vouchers they cannot use or to request additional ones. As a result, valuable housing support sits idle while veterans in other Tribal communities wait for help.
The new Tribal Veterans Voucher Flexibility Act directs HUD to establish a voluntary program for reallocating unused Tribal HUD-VASH vouchers to Native veterans who need them most. Under the bill, Tribes and Tribally Designated Housing Entities (TDHEs) can notify HUD via digital, phone, or mail correspondence if they have surplus vouchers or request additional assistance for their communities without impacting their future allocations.
Required to launch within 180 days of enactment, the program creates a streamlined process to strengthen Tribal HUD-VASH and expand Native veterans' access to earned housing assistance. Within that same timeframe, HUD must submit a congressional report detailing voucher usage and shortfall metrics, distribution recommendations, and an assessment of whether to increase overall program funding.
This is not the first time Davids and Crane have partnered on legislation to assist Tribal communities. Davids previously introduced the Native American Entrepreneurial Opportunity Act, which would bolster U.S. Small Business Administration outreach to Tribal entrepreneurs navigating the unique complexities of running a business on a reservation. Crane co-led the measure, and it has twice passed the House with strong bipartisan support.
title: Reps. Davids (D), Crane (R) Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Improve Housing Access for Tribal Veterans

BLM Targets Invasive Weeds to Reduce Wildfire Risk in Southwestern Idaho
Organization:
Media Contact:
BOISE, Idaho—In a proactive step to reduce wildfire risk and invest in healthy, resilient public lands, the Bureau of Land Management Boise District in southwestern Idaho, partnering with the U.S. Wildland Fire Service, will conduct the following aerial herbicide treatments:
- Approximately 9,800 acres of lands managed by the BLM Bruneau Field Office within Owyhee County.
- Approximately 6,000 acres of lands managed by the BLM Owyhee and Four Rivers Field Offices within Ada and Owyhee Counties.
Treatments are scheduled to begin the second week of October 2026, depending on weather, wildfire activity and other operational conditions. They are intended to reduce invasive annual grasses and hazardous fine fuels, maintain strategic fuel breaks, support vegetation recovery following wildfire, and improve the establishment and long-term success of desirable perennial vegetation. By strengthening landscapes before wildfire strikes, the work helps reduce wildfire risk and the potential costs of large, damaging fires while protecting wildlife habitat, rangelands, watersheds and other public resources.
Treatments will use the BLM-approved herbicide imazapic. Application rates will vary by project area based on vegetation and management objectives.
The public may see low-flying aircraft over designated treatment areas and should avoid those areas while applications are underway. USWFS employees will be present in project areas before and during application. Federal officials appreciate the public’s cooperation as these treatments invest in the long-term health and resilience of public lands and reduce wildfire risk.
Rangelands in Idaho and across the West have been heavily impacted by destructive wildfires, exacerbated by drought, insects, and disease, leaving millions of acres vulnerable to future wildfires. Since 2000, wildfires have burned an average of 7.3 million acres annually, with BLM lands seeing an average of 236,530 acres affected each year. This year alone, wildfires have devastated over 3.3 million acres of BLM-managed lands, and 9 million acres of all jurisdictions nationwide.
The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.
title: BLM Targets Invasive Weeds to Reduce Wildfire Risk in Southwestern Idaho

WASHINGTON -- FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance is available to the territory of Guam to supplement recovery efforts in the areas affected by Super Typhoon Bavi from July 4-12, 2026.
The President's action makes federal funding available to affected individuals in Guam. Assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help individuals and business owners recover from the effects of the disaster.
Individuals and families who sustained losses in the designated areas should first file claims with their insurance providers and then apply for assistance online at www.DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling the local, toll-free line 671-735-1050, calling the FEMA Helpline 1-800-621-3362 or by using the FEMA App. If you use a relay service, such as video relay service (VRS), captioned telephone service or others, provide FEMA the number for that service.
Federal funding is also available to territorial and eligible local governments and certain private nonprofit organizations on a cost-sharing basis for emergency work and the repair or replacement of facilities damaged by Super Typhoon Bavi.
Teresa Y. Serata has been named the Federal Coordinating Officer for federal recovery operations in the affected areas. Additional designations may be made at a later date if warranted by the results of damage assessments.

DETROIT – Brian Mitchell was sentenced today to 33 months in federal prison after having pleaded guilty to executing a multi-million-dollar commodities trading fraud scheme, United States Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon, Jr. announced.

Gorgon was joined in the announcement by Special Agent in Charge Jennifer Runyan, Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Mitchell, 44, of Ann Arbor, previously pleaded guilty to wire fraud and admitted that he defrauded multiple third-party investors, causing a loss of over $2.7 million.

“This defendant caused regular folks to lose millions of dollars. That was not enough for him, so he targeted a church to cover his scheme. He is shameless,” stated U.S. Attorney Gorgon.

“This defendant built a multi-million-dollar fraud scheme on lies, false promises, and the hard-earned money of people who trusted him. Those who make a business out of stealing from investors should expect the FBI to make a case out of them,” said Jennifer Runyan, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Detroit Field Office. “Our FBI Ann Arbor Resident Agency conducted a meticulous investigation that helped expose this scheme and bring justice for the victims.

According to court records, Mitchell acknowledged that he caused false representations to be made regarding the security, profitability, and use of investor funds. Mitchell used various entities to solicit investor money, including “Young Pros Investment Group” (“YPIG”) and “My Nest Egg.” As part of his scheme, Mitchell made—and caused—repeated misrepresentations that investor principal was protected against loss and was “guaranteed.” Mitchell also made, and caused, misrepresentations regarding future earnings. After suffering significant trading losses, Mitchell lied to investors about why their investment principal was no longer guaranteed, as he had previously claimed. Mitchell falsely told investors that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) had seized assets that he described as “back-up money.”

While executing his fraud scheme, Mitchell entered into a settlement with the CFTC relating to earlier violations of the Commodity Exchange Act that occurred between January 2018 and January 2019. Under that settlement, Mitchell was barred for three years from engaging in commodity futures trading activity and from soliciting, receiving, and accepting funds for such activity. Despite that ban, Mitchell continued to solicit, accept, and trade third-party investment funds in commodity futures and failed to disclose his trading bar to investors.

Mitchell solicited and obtained a $150,000 investment from a local church while he was suspended from trading activity. Mitchell falsely promised that church a 72% annual rate of return, which he claimed would result in investment earnings of $4,798,153 over five years.

Mitchell admitted that his conduct violated his prior settlement agreement with the CFTC and the regulatory requirements of the Commodity Exchange Act.

According to court records, Mitchell’s scheme victimized at least 128 individuals and organizations.

Mitchell was ordered to pay restitution of $2,749,210.60 and serve 2 years on supervised release following the completion of his custodial sentence.

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Andrew J. Yahkind.
title: Suspended Ann Arbor Commodities Trader Sentenced To 33 Months in Federal Prison After Defrauding Local Church and Over 100 Other Victims in Multi-Million-Dollar Fraud Scheme

RALEIGH, N.C. - A federal judge sentenced Kenneth Omar Roger Chung, also known as “Skully”, 53, of Raleigh, NC, to 27 years in federal prison for distributing fentanyl that led to the overdose death of a 26-year-old Raleigh man. In addition, he was also sentenced for conspiracy to possess with intent to sell fentanyl, meth, and cocaine. Chung pleaded guilty to the charges on May 20, 2026.

“When you sell drugs, you know people can die. This isn’t just everyday dealing. He chose profit over human life. Chung kept pushing poison even after he knew someone had died, just went right back out looking for his next customer. This 27-year federal sentence protects the people of the Eastern District of North Carolina for decades and delivers the serious punishment his actions deserved and demanded. The message is simple: Drugs kill. Prison follows. Do the right thing,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle.

“When you sell drugs, you know people can die. This isn’t just everyday dealing. He chose profit over human life. Chung kept pushing poison even after he knew someone had died, just went right back out looking for his next customer. This 27-year federal sentence protects the people of the Eastern District of North Carolina for decades and delivers the serious punishment his actions deserved and demanded. The message is simple: Drugs kill. Prison follows. Do the right thing,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle.

On March 28, 2023, the Raleigh Police Department responded to a 911 call and found a 26-year-old man dead from a drug overdose. Officers seized heroin, purple fentanyl powder, and 11 Xanax pills from his backpack. An autopsy confirmed he died from a fentanyl overdose. Evidence on his cell phone showed Chung had delivered the drugs the night before. Soon afterward, law enforcement conducted several controlled drug buys, including purple fentanyl, directly from Chung and his co-defendant, Jermaine Robinson.

On October 7, 2023, Chung delivered crack cocaine to a man in Cary, who later died from an overdose.

On October 23, 2023, Raleigh Police Department officers responded to another 911 call at Chung’s apartment. Officers found his roommate unresponsive, and the roommate later died from an overdose.

Following these incidents, investigators intensified their efforts to determine the extent of Chung’s drug dealing activity. On October 25, 2023, Raleigh Police officers executed a search warrant at his apartment and seized 57 grams of marijuana, 29.06 grams of fentanyl, 5.09 grams of cocaine, 9.96 grams of heroin, 23.75 grams of meth, and four guns. Officers then arrested Chung, seizing additional drugs and $5,541 during the arrest.

“The dangers of illegal narcotics are absolutely real and often fatal,” said ATF Special Agent in Charge Alicia Jones. “Illegal possession of firearms adds to that danger and the threats against our community. ATF and our law enforcement partners are committed to identifying those that endanger our safety and shutting down their lawless operations.”

“The Raleigh Police Department extends its sincere gratitude to our exceptional public safety partners whose dedication and teamwork were instrumental throughout this investigation. Together, we worked to disrupt the illegal drug trade, remove dangerous drugs from our community, and protect the people we serve,” said Raleigh Police Chief Rico Boyce. “We are especially grateful for our strong partnership with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina. This collaboration reflects our shared commitment to holding those responsible accountable, keeping dangerous drugs off our streets, and making our community safer.”

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

W. Ellis Boyle, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina, made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III. The ATF, the Raleigh Police Department, and the Cary Police Department investigated the case.

A copy of this press release is located on our website . Related court documents and information can be found on the website of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina or on PACER by searching for case number 5:25-CR-00124-D.
title: Raleigh Dealer Receives 27-Year Federal Prison Sentence for Fatal Fentanyl Overdose

JOHNSTOWN, Pa. – A resident of Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Pittsburgh on a charge of theft of government property, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.

The one-count Indictment named George Grist, 65, as the sole defendant.

According to the Indictment, from on or about April 30, 2021, to July 16, 2025, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, Grist did embezzle, steal, purloin and knowingly convert to his own use property of the Social Security Administration to which Grist was not entitled. The Indictment alleges that Grist stole a total of approximately $68,048.71 in the form of more than 50 separate benefit payments made to another person.

The law provides for a maximum total sentence of up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed would be based upon the seriousness of the offense and the prior criminal history, if any, of the defendant.

Assistant United States Attorney Arnold P. Bernard Jr. is prosecuting this case on behalf of the government.

The Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General conducted the investigation leading to the Indictment.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

An indictment is an accusation. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.
title: Punxsutawney Man Indicted for Social Security Fraud

Rep. Sykes Announces $33,000 for Canal Fulton-Lawrence Township Fire Department
CANAL FULTON, OH — Today, U.S. Representative Emilia Sykes (OH-13) announced that the Canal Fulton – Lawrence Township Fire Department is receiving two Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) grant awards that will fund new firefighting equipment and a community fire safety training tool. Congresswoman Sykes supported both grant applications with letters of support.
The City of Canal Fulton received the following awards:
- $17,055.55 in federal funding for a regional fire hose replacement, with a local share of $852.78, for a total project investment of $17,908.33. The project will replace attack and supply hose within the departments' shared response system.
- $16,737.14 in federal funding for a fire extinguisher training system, with a local share of $836.86, for a total project investment of $17,574.00. The project will provide an augmented-reality training system that allows hands-on public education without live fire, smoke, chemical discharge, or cleanup.
Together, the awards provide $33,792.69 in federal funding toward a total investment of $35,482.33 in public safety projects.
“Our firefighters and EMS crews show up to keep our neighbors safe every day, and they must have the tools to do their jobs safely. I am proud to have supported Canal Fulton's grant applications, and I congratulate Chief Yerian and the entire department on these well-earned awards,”said Congresswoman Sykes.
“Receiving these FEMA awards is tremendous news for the Canal Fulton community and our regional fire service,” said Shawn Yerian, Fire Chief of the Canal Fulton – Lawrence Township Fire Department. “The funding will allow us to replace outdated fire hose that our firefighters rely on every day, while also providing a new fire extinguisher training system that addresses one of the most frequent safety-training requests we receive from local businesses.
“These are important investments in both firefighter safety and community education, and they are projects we would not have been able to move forward with at this time without federal assistance. We are extremely grateful for Congresswoman Sykes' support of our applications and her continued support of local fire and EMS services. Her assistance helped make it possible for us to bring these resources back to the community we serve.”
Congresswoman Sykes congratulates Chief Yerian and the entire Canal Fulton - Lawrence Township Fire Department on these awards and thanks them for their service to the community.
title: Rep. Sykes Announces $33,000 for Canal Fulton-Lawrence Township Fire Department

BENTON, Ill. – A district court judge sentenced an Olney man to 40 years in federal prison after he admitted to producing child pornography.

George T. Grove, 49, pleaded guilty to two counts of production of child pornography for creating child sexual abuse material of a 13-year-old victim.

“Sex crimes are vile offenses. There is no amount of prison time sufficient for those who violate children,” said U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft.

“Sex crimes are vile offenses. There is no amount of prison time sufficient for those who violate children,” said U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft.

According to court documents and information discussed at hearings, Grove admitted to creating two videos of child sexual abuse material with a cell phone of a 13-year-old victim in July 2024. During the investigation, officers discovered the defendant was exchanging alcohol, money and drugs with minors for nude photos and sex.

The Richland County Sheriff’s Office, the Olney Police Department and Homeland Security Investigations contributed to the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney David Sanders prosecuted the case.

text:
Speech

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

The Pnyx

Athens, Greece

October 7, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO: There are great ruins all across the world. In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.

But the Acropolis is different.

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world. Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it – they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget. But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory. They call us back to them, again and again.

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch. Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island. But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home. So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days. They were eventually overwhelmed. The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow. And the progeny of the men who built it – the sons of Athens and Rome – have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish.

The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity. Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city. The city where our Constitution was born – Philadelphia – is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours. They were exceptionally well-read in history – they were vividly aware of their unique place in it – but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity. Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist. No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders – and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them. Most of us are familiar with the basic history. Athens gave us democracy. Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy. Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states. Even much of our political vocabulary – words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself – found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true. But the things we owe to this place – as Americans, and as Westerners – are actually far far deeper. These institutions and ideas – these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks – qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory. An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos. An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.

These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy. They were the characteristic of a people – expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man. The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself. Much about – much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new. It was this trait – it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown canbe known. The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood – and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology – of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology – a common view of man and his place in the universe. Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.

For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence. They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft. The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle – to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel. The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat. Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best. We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things. The ancient Greek city-states were filled. They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict. But from that constant struggle for distinction – from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos , as the ancient Greeks called it – the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride – is the heart of great civilization. And without it? Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.

Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality. Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional. We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt. We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness.

The word “nationalism” became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history. And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit. In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness. And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.

Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility. To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive. They understood that nations have interests. They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail. They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.

We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague.

Greece has been at the center of this shift. The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.

And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example.

Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them. Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can. Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum. Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts. It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland – an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO. All three partners in that deal emerged victorious. All of Europe – and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together. We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people. And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else.

They believed – fiercely – in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds. But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself. The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life. We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans – surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia – who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty. And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life – but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These – these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination. From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country. Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes – our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death. It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles. Now, we take the West’s conception of these things – heroism, honor, duty – we take these things for granted. We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places. They are not. They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it. A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence. The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo. The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.

And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew. An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition. The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit. The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world.

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit. We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization.

The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions. War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace. Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again. There is new competition between great powers again. There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again.

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them. And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece. In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.

Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation. When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle. Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them. This is what he said in his speech; he said: “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them. And all of us – not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West – must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece – the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse – it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms. The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud – that we should be intensely proud – of where we come from. We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside. The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West. From them – from them – we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.

Thank you.

(Applause.)

NEWARK, N.J. – A Hudson County woman, who is a naturalized citizen who immigrated to the United States from the Dominican Republic, was charged with illegally voting in a federal election and unlawfully procuring citizenship, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced today.

Lizabeth Almonte Rosa, 24, of West New York, New Jersey was charged by criminal complaint with voting by an alien in a federal election and unlawfully procuring citizenship. Almonte Rosa had her initial appearance on October 7, 2026, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Stacey D. Adams in federal court in Newark.

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court:

Almonte Rosa was a non-citizen when she was registered to vote. The answers provided in her voter registration form falsely certified and attested that she was a United States citizen. In order to register, and to vote in federal elections, a person must be a United States citizen.

Almonte Rosa voted in-person in the primary election held in June 2022 and the general election held in November 2022. At the time she cast her ballots, Almonte Rosa, who entered the United States from the Dominican Republic on an IR2 visa, was not a United States citizen and was therefore not authorized to vote in federal elections.

After illegally voting in federal elections, Almonte Rosa applied to become a United States citizen by submitting an application for naturalization (an N-400). An N-400 requires the applicant to swear under penalty of perjury that the information provided in the application is complete, true, and correct. In her N-400 application, Almonte Rosa falsely claimed that she had never registered to vote or voted in any federal elections.

The count of voting by an alien carries a maximum sentence of 1 year’s imprisonment, and a fine of up to $100,000. The count of unlawfully procuring citizenship carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $250,000.

U.S. Attorney Frazer credited special agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy; Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Michael McCarthy; and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, with the investigation.

The case was brought under the United States Attorney’s Office’s Election Integrity Task Force, a coalition of federal law enforcement partners focused on preserving and protecting the integrity of elections conducted in the District of New Jersey.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin D. Bleiberg of the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s Criminal Division.

The charges and allegations contained in the complaint are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

title: Hudson County Woman Charged with Illegally Voting in Federal Election and Unlawful Procurement of U.S. Citizenship

Gainesville, Florida – Stephen Lamar Jones, 43, of Gainesville, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, heroin, and cocaine. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “I applaud the excellent investigative work by the DEA and the Alachua County Sheriff’s Office that supported this successful prosecution by my office. This repeat offender sought to profit from the devastation caused by meth and other drugs, but now he’ll remain locked away in federal prison where he belongs.”

Court records indicate that the defendant was found in possession of 284 grams of methamphetamine. The defendant also had heroin and cocaine in his possession. The defendant has a prior conviction for Trafficking in Amphetamines.

Jones faces a minimum mandatory sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment, and up to life imprisonment.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Alachua County Sheriff’s Office. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Christie Utt and Tyler Fleming.

Sentencing is scheduled for December 8, 2026, at the United States Courthouse in Gainesville before Chief United States District Judge Allen C. Winsor.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime, human and drug trafficking.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

ST. LOUIS – A convicted felon on Wednesday admitted possessing about 25 kilograms of meth and robbing two St. Louis County banks.

Otis Frazier, 37, pleaded guilty in two separate cases: to one count of bank robbery in one case and in the other to one count of possession with the intent to distribute methamphetamine and one count of possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime.

On Feb. 6, 2025, a St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department Anti-Crime Task Force detective targeting stolen vehicles spotted a white Genesis GV70 that appeared to have been stolen. The detective followed the Genesis, but stopped when the driver began to drive erratically. The next day, the detective located the vehicle again and confirmed the license plate was a stolen dealer plate. When Frazier parked at a store on Jennings Station Road, officers detained him after a brief struggle and found two handguns, about 4.7 kilograms of methamphetamine and about 14.31 grams of fentanyl in the vehicle.

In an interview with Drug Enforcement Administration agents the next day, Frazier said he was a large-scale drug distributor and had more meth and two guns at a friend’s house. There the DEA found the guns and a little over 20 kilograms of meth.

Frazier was indicted in U.S. District Court in St. Louis on March 12 and a warrant for his arrest was issued.

On July 31, 2025, Frazier robbed a bank on North Highway 67 in St. Louis County. Frazier said something along the lines of, “It’s happening,” while gripping the butt of what appeared to be a handgun in his pocket. He forced two employees into the back of the bank and demanded entry to the vault. Frazier threatened employees, telling them if the police arrived, everyone would die, his plea says. After stealing cash, Frazier fled on a bicycle, discarding the clothing he was wearing in a nearby dumpster.

On Sept. 24, 2025, Frazier entered a bank on Dunn Road in St. Louis County and said, “You know what this is, right,” while keeping his hand in his pocket. When bank employees told Frazier the vault was locked, a frustrated Frazier made threats before accepting cash from a teller’s cash drawer. He fled the scene on a motorized scooter. Frazier was arrested and a court-approved search of Frazier’s girlfriend’s home found a 9mm pistol gun with his DNA on it.

Frazier is scheduled to be sentenced on the bank robbery charge on January 7. Bank robbery is punishable by up to 20 years in prison. He will also be ordered to repay the money. Both the U.S. Attorney’s office and Frazier’s lawyer have agreed to recommend a sentence of 15 years for the drug case, which is set to be sentenced on January 13.

The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the FBI, and the St. Louis County Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Nichole Frankenberg and Dane Rennier are prosecuting the case.
title: Man Admits Dealing Meth and Robbing Two St. Louis County Banks

text:
Top Air Force and Space Force leaders, joined by their spouses, offered observations during a panel at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference into the lives of military families and how that dynamic contributes to readiness and defense of the nation.
The discussion included Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach and his wife, Cindy; Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess and his wife, Debbie; Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe and his wife, Dr. Doniel Wolfe; and Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John Bentivegna and his wife, Cathy. Retired U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Burt Field, president and CEO of the Air and Space Forces Association, moderated the panel at the association’s conference on Sept. 16.
The panelists underscored a central theme: “Readiness begins at home.” They agreed that strong families build strong units and a stronger national defense.
Evolving Perspectives on Leadership
Wilsbach explained how his view of leadership has changed over his 41-year career and 26 moves with his spouse. “When you start out earlier in your career, you’re very focused on the mission,” he said. “As I’ve gained rank and responsibility the people piece really expands.”
Mrs. Wilsbach shared a memorable example from their time at Kadena Air Base in 2009. While meeting with deployed spouses, she noticed one woman who answered she was “fine” when asked by her husband but clearly was not.
“After watching the interaction, I knew she wasn’t fine, so I stepped back and said, ‘Is everything okay?’, and it wasn’t okay. She had a child with a health problem and was far away from family,” she recounted. “That shows me the value of what I bring to this table. I sometimes see things, and I’m told things that he’s not.”
“All our family members are part of a team. When John gets deployed, that's his away game and he's busy taking care of his away-game family,” Mrs. Bentivegna said. “But the other teammates are still at home with roles to play. We still have our own goals, and in order to keep a successful team, we have to have good communication. We have to understand the mission, what's going on, and keep everyone, especially our kids, involved to feel part of the team."
Dr. Wolfe highlighted the power of simple kindness, quoting a lesson she learned: “If you treat everybody you meet as if they are going through some big trouble in their life, more than half the time you’ll be right.” She encouraged everyone to make saying “hello” a regular practice.
Family Stability Equals Warfighter Readiness
The panelists stressed that families directly impact the ability of Airmen and Guardians to focus on the mission. Gen. Schiess noted the unique challenges for a large portion of Space Force personnel who are employed in place.
"I learned early on that if I understand 'the why,' then I can invest more and I can support better as a spouse,” Mrs. Schiess said. “And so, taking the time to fill me in, even if he can't give me the details, to say, 'there's something big going on at work and stress levels are high.' Those kind of pieces of information help me to better support him, and I encourage other military members to do the same."
The spouses and their counterparts in the other services are members of the Military Spouse Commission, which President Donald Trump established to advise and assist the president on policies that affect military spouses and families.
Panelists discussed multiple programs aimed at supporting military families, notably the Global Military Spouse Connection, STARBASE, and the AFPASS Card Initiative.
Global Military Spouse Connection
The Global Military Spouse Connection is a pilot initiative designed to strengthen connections between qualified Department of the Air Force spouses and federal employment opportunities. It is being tested at the following installations across the world:
- Luke Air Force Base, Glendale, Arizona
- Goodfellow AFB, San Angelo, Texas
- Laughlin AFB, Del Rio, Texas
- Mountain Home AFB. Mountain Home, Idaho
- Travis AFB, Fairfield, California
- Patrick Space Force Base, Satellite Beach, Florida
- Ramstein AB, Ramstein-Miesenbach
- RAF Croughton, United Kingdom
- RAF Mildenhall, U.K.
- RAF Lakenheath, U.K.
- RAF Feltwell, U.K.
- Kadena AB, Okinawa, Japan
The program is designed to target military spouse unemployment, which currently has rates around 20%, largely due to frequent permanent change of station moves. GMSC aims to improve career continuity by connecting qualified spouses with DAF civilian employment opportunities before they arrive at their new duty station.
“It is a good start,” said CMSAF Wolfe. “With the four spouses here being involved in the [Presidential] Military Spouse Commission, we have an opportunity to make some real change to laws that currently prevent us from hiring people fast enough and putting people in positions and jobs.”
STARBASE and STEM Support for Military Children
Another family-oriented program mentioned during the panel was STARBASE, a Department of War STEM education program that delivers hands-on, immersive experiences primarily to fifth grade students from military-connected, at-risk and underserved communities. The program seeks to spark interest and inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers and future defense professionals.
“Our kids have to live with the decisions of their parents, and I think we owe them the best we possibly can provide,” said CMSAF Wolfe. He stressed the importance of the Air Force investing in educational opportunities for military children, using Starbase as a positive example. The program exposes military youth to the technological environments and positive civilian and military roles found on active, Guard, and Reserve military bases and installations.
AFPAAS Card for Spouse Roster
Each spouse discussed the challenge in spouse outreach, especially during times when connecting with family is most essential such as deployments and crises.
One solution mentioned was an Air Force Personnel Accountability and Assessment System Card, which provides unit leaders with instructional pocket cards and guidance for accessing current personnel and family contact information through the AFPAAS, maintaining accurate recall rosters and securely sharing appropriate roster data with key support liaisons.
Improving access to timely contact information, the initiative supports faster outreach to newly arriving spouses and families of deployed Airmen and Guardians, strengthens assistance during permanent change of station moves, deployments, exercises and emergencies and closes gaps in family-support communication. Participation respects privacy, as spouses may opt out of routine contact, while enabling stronger grassroots support networks and unit resilience.
Advice to the Next Generation
Panelists were asked what advice they would give to young Airmen, Guardians, and their spouses who are just beginning their military journey:
- Take every opportunity to grow professionally and personally
- Build and nurture strong relationships
- Recognize that military service is a family service to the nation
- Prioritize physical fitness, financial responsibility and emotional resilience
- Understand the “why” behind the mission to support one another more effectively
- Never underestimate the power of simple human connection
"You have to really embrace the preciousness of time because you can't get it back,” said CMSSF Bentivegna. “We're always focusing on that next assignment, next rotation, or the next deployment. You think, 'I've got plenty of time to focus on my finances, education, family, relationships … but you can't get that time back. Make the most of it."
title: DAF leaders, their spouses highlight families’ role in mission success
