For the first time, the Air Force Office of Special Investigations has certified a cadre of special agents to both operate and instruct others on the Skydio X10D as part of a broader effort to expand small unmanned aircraft system operations across the agency.
Last month, six personnel completed a weeklong course at AFOSI headquarters in Quantico, Virginia, creating the first group of instructors positioned to bring the capability back to technical operations units in the field.
“We not only learned how to operate the drones, but also how to properly instruct other individuals on how to fly successfully to meet mission needs,” said Special Agent Logan Trigg, assigned to the 2nd Field Investigations Squadron Technical Operations Program.
That instructor qualification is what gives the course its broader impact. Rather than returning to their units as individual operators, the six graduates can now begin building additional capacity across AFOSI.
“My plan is to train the entire 2 FIS Technical Operations flight on drone operations because it enables every member to carry out the mission regardless of where or when the capability is needed,” Trigg said. “Having everyone certified creates the ability to attack the mission effectively.”
That train-the-trainer model is central to how AFOSI intends to grow the program. The capability could support surveillance, outdoor crime scenes, protective-service support and other missions requiring what Trigg called an “an eye in the sky.”
The work to build AFOSI’s agency-level capability has been an ongoing effort since early 2024, with Detachment 111 at Edwards Air Force Base, California, serving as a working pilot program well before the five X10Ds will be used by Technical Operations agents in January 2027.
Creating multipliers
The course was structured around more than basic flight instruction. Agents first completed roughly 16 hours of classroom work covering airspace, Federal Aviation Administration requirements, mission planning and the administrative requirements behind government sUAS operations.
“After the classroom portion, we transitioned to the field for hands-on flight operations,” said Special Agent Scott Zawacki, AFOSI Technical Operations program manager. “We focused on the fundamentals of takeoff and landing, then progressed to the system’s autonomous capabilities and how those features can be applied to meet operational requirements.”
Once students were comfortable with the aircraft, the training shifted to approximately 16 hours of flight scenarios built around AFOSI missions.
In one exercise, students lifted to roughly 400 feet, identified a vehicle’s license plate and tracked the vehicle for roughly a mile. In another, they used the aircraft’s thermal camera at night to locate a person concealed in a wooded area.
“The real advantage is our ability to design highly specialized training scenarios that directly support AFOSI’s unique mission requirements,” Zawacki said.
By the end of the week, all six had qualified as both operators and instructors. The course was the latest step in an effort that began years earlier at Edwards AFB.
Building the program
At Edwards AFB, Anthony Zutten, AFOSI Det. 111 criminal indexing and investigations specialist, in coordination with Zawacki, developed a sUAS capability before AFOSI moved to establish a broader program in 2024.
To do this, Zutten worked through the approvals, funding and training requirements needed to stand up the local effort, which soon moved beyond demonstration flights.
Prior to the latest training, agents at Edwards AFB used drones to support reconnaissance related to illegal marijuana growing operations near the installation, map the site of a recent B-52 crash for the 412th Test Wing and assist with search-and-rescue efforts across the installation’s expansive operating area.
In one case, Zutten said a drone helped narrow the search area for a 12-year-old believed to be in danger before the child was eventually located. Those missions gave AFOSI early proof of concept for how sUAS could support investigations and other operational needs.
Meanwhile, at AFOSI headquarters, Zawacki examined the same capability from an agency-wide perspective. The two efforts eventually converged.
“Det. 111 helped establish the proof of concept for a broader expansion,” Zawacki said.
As AFOSI’s new MAJCOM sUAS program manager, Zawacki, in collaboration with Zutten, brought the Edwards AFB effort under the developing AFOSI structure, building on roughly two years of policy work, testing, coordination and funding efforts to establish a broader command capability. Zutten’s experience also made him a natural choice to lead AFOSI’s first broader operator-instructor course.
“He did a lot of the legwork in finding the policy, finding the people to talk to, coordinating everything and helping get this off the ground,” Zawacki said.
Drone technology also shows potential for detailed crime-scene documentation, he said. In one demonstration, operators captured 126 images that were stitched together to develop two- and three-dimensional crime-scene models.
“When reviewing crime-scene map captures, the detail is so clear you can zoom in and see each individual bullet casing, easily identify placards and see exactly where key evidence rests in relation to the scene,” Zutten said.
With compatible software, agents can also mark evidence and measure distances using spatial data captured through the drone’s imagery, incorporate telemetry data and upload the information directly into AFOSI’s case management system.
“By utilizing sUAS to assist with crime scenes, we can effectively cut tens of hours of work from our field agents by digitizing everything on scene in real time,” Zutten said.
AFOSI has not yet used that capability in an actual case. For now, demonstrations are helping officials determine where the technology can best support field operations.
“Our job is to give agents the capabilities they need to accomplish the mission,” Zutten said. “If this technology can help us collect detailed information faster, reduce risk to our people and better support a case or operation, then that’s where its value shines.”
title: AFOSI certifies first drone operator-instructor cadre ahead of X10D fielding

Baltimore, Maryland – A Baltimore County softball coach pled guilty in federal court, today, to charges connected to sexually abusing a former player who was a minor at the time.

Michael Joseph Pusateri, 59, of Nottingham, pled guilty to coercion and enticement of a minor. Pusateri also recently pled guilty to sexual child abuse against the same victim in Baltimore County Circuit Court, resulting in a 10-year sentence.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul, FBI Baltimore Field Office; Baltimore County State’s Attorney Scott Shellenberger; and Chief Robert McCullough, Baltimore County Police Department (BCPD).

According to the guilty plea, from at least March 2025, through July 2025, Pusateri coerced and enticed a minor victim, who was 16 and 17 years old at the time of the abuse. Pusateri groomed the minor victim through text messages and coerced and enticed the child into sending him sexual images. He then saved the messages and CSAM on his cellphone. Additionally, Pusateri sent the minor victim several pictures of his genitals.

After law enforcement seized his cellphone, BCPD uncovered over 400 phone calls between Pusateri and the minor victim from March 21, through July 25. The minor victim met the Baltimore County softball coach when she was approximately 8 years old. The victim joined Pusateri’s club softball team, when she was 11 or 12 years old, where he coached her through the time of the abuse.

This case is part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit justice.gov/psc . For more information about Internet safety education, please visit justice.gov/psc and click on the “Resources” tab on the left of the page.

Pusateri faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years, with a maximum of life in federal prison, for coercion and enticement. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. Sentencing is set for Tuesday, Feb. 9, 2027, at 2:30 p.m.

A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

U.S. Attorney Hayes commended the FBI, the Baltimore County State’s Attorney’s Office, and BCPD for their work in the investigation. Ms. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Colleen Elizabeth McGuinn who is prosecuting the federal case.

For more information on the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to help the community, please visit justice.gov/usao-md .

The German American story began on October 6, 1683, when 13 families from Krefeld, after braving the Atlantic in search of opportunity, landed on our shores and soon founded Germantown, Pennsylvania—the first permanent German settlement in America.
In the centuries since, German Americans have farmed the fields of our heartland and powered the industries that turned our young country into the mightiest economic powerhouse in the world. Their sons and daughters have defended American freedom in every era, serving valiantly in both World Wars and standing watch through the long struggle against communism during the Cold War. In our own time, their descendants continue to serve in our Armed Forces, work the factories and family farms that sustain our Nation, and lead the businesses and communities that keep the American Dream alive for all of our citizens.
This spirit endures in the long-standing relationship between the United States and Germany—a relationship sustained by our mutual respect, and a shared desire for peace and prosperity. As President, I have led a historic renewal of the NATO alliance, securing a historic commitment from our NATO allies to increase their investment in our common defense. Since that historic summit in The Hague last year, Germany has taken bold steps toward the realization of a stronger, more balanced NATO. The impact of this commitment will be felt beyond Europe, as billions of dollars in new investments strengthen the transatlantic defense industrial base and create thousands of high-paying jobs for American workers.
Today, we give thanks for the generations of German Americans whose labor and love of liberty helped make the United States the greatest Nation on Earth. Their story is woven into the fabric of America, and together, we commit ourselves to building on this legacy to create an even brighter, more prosperous future for all Americans.
title: Presidential Message on German American Day

RICHMOND, Va. – A Petersburg man was sentenced today to five years and 11 months in prison for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

According to court documents, on Oct. 4, 2025, Richmond Police Officers responded to a report of random gunfire in the area of Gilpin Court. When officers arrived, they observed Tynell Jones, 34, discharge a firearm three times. Jones was immediately detained. The firearm had a round in the chamber and was equipped with a 30-round magazine with 10 rounds remaining.

Jones was previously convicted of, among other crimes, assault, assault and battery, and possession of controlled substances. As a convicted felon, Jones cannot legally possess firearms or ammunition. Jones was convicted in 2018 in the Eastern District of Virginia for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Anthony A. Spotswood, Special Agent in Charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Washington Field Division, made the announcement after sentencing by Senior U.S. District Judge John A. Gibney Jr.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Eric Gilliland and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Jeremiah Johansen prosecuted the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

text:
Elected leaders who hailed the reopening of the state’s second freestanding birth center earlier this year may have celebrated prematurely.
The Cambridge Health Alliance Birth Center, which closed in March 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, was scheduled to reopen on July 6 with the aim of welcoming 100 babies in the first year. CHA said the center would serve all patients but have a “special focus on vulnerable and underserved populations who will benefit most from midwifery care and a birth center experience.”
But no deliveries happened this summer, even as supporters of the 2024 maternal health law tried to create new urgency around bolstering access to care and removing healthcare disparities for people of color.
“The Birth Center has been open for prenatal and outpatient visits,” CHA spokesperson David Cecere told the News Service Thursday. “We are anticipating our first delivery this week — they had been on hold as we worked through a leadership transition.”
Cecere said that “unexpected turnover” prompted the center to “hold deliveries until we established a plan to ensure high quality care and an exceptional patient experience.”
A spokesperson for the Department of Public Health, asked whether it was aware of any paused operations or staffing issues, said DPH had called the birth center and was told it was “taking clients.”
CHA has said the reopening would not have been possible without $1 million in state funding, which Cambridge Rep. Marjorie Decker helped secure in the fiscal 2024 budget. The center also received a grant from Beth Israel Lahey Health to help cover training, equipment, and community education and outreach.
The birth center, situated in a Victorian home with three renovated birthing rooms, held an open house on June 17 with more than 200 attendees, according to CHA. Speakers included Decker, U.S. Rep. Katherine Clark, Sen. Sal DiDomenico, Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui and Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein.
“Too often we are talking about the closure of maternity services, but today we get to celebrate a spectacular rebirth – and one that I hope will be followed by many more,” Goldstein said in a statement at the time. “Expanding access to community-based, relationship-centered care is key in advancing health equity. The reopening of the CHA Birth Center supports families who deserve more options for culturally responsive maternity care.”
Clark said the reopening was a “signal to women everywhere that we can and will keep making progress on maternal health.”
“We’re going to keep fighting for a healthcare system worthy of every mother in this community and a future worthy of the children who will begin their lives at CHA,” she said.
Michele Helgeson, a member of the Community Coalition for the Cambridge Birth Center, said everything had seemed “very positive” and “very, very upbeat” surrounding the open house. The coalition has met with CHA leaders to advocate for community interests and promote a midwifery model of care.
“There was no indication that there was any reason to stop or pause at that point,” said Helgeson, who added she wants to see CHA conduct community outreach and assure patients about available services at the birth center.
Birth centers are seen as alternatives to hospital deliveries, particularly in low-risk pregnancies. The facilities offer a home-like environment and are staffed by midwives who can provide more personalized care.
The 2024 law removed regulatory barriers to opening freestanding birth centers and created a pathway for certified professional midwives to become licensed. The state started accepting applications for temporary CPM licensure last month, as DPH expects to issue regulations for “standard” licensure in early 2027.
Until the CHA Birth Center returned to the maternal health landscape, Massachusetts was home to only one such freestanding facility in Northampton. But Seven Sisters Midwifery and Community Birth Center faces intense financial pressure due to low reimbursement rates compared to services provided in hospitals, according to owner and clinical director Ginny Miller.
Legislation (S 784) to ensure that certified nurse midwives, certified professional midwives and licensed freestanding birth centers are not paid less than physicians and hospitals delivering the same services has been lodged in the Senate Ways and Means Committee since April.
Kimberly Amsley-Camp was the CHA’s director of midwifery from August 2025 through September 2026, and she managed a staff of 20 certified nurse midwives and nurse practitioners, according to her LinkedIn profile. Working with a “multi-disciplinary” team, Amsley-Camp wrote she “planned and developed reopening of a hospital owned freestanding birth center.”
Amsley-Camp did not respond to a News Service request for comment.
Cecere said consultant and certified nurse midwife Erin Stein is now overseeing “daily operations” of the CHA Birth Center. She’s working alongside Dr. Tara Singh, chief of obstetrics and gynecology, and Allisyn Brady, senior director of OB/GYN.
Helgeson said the coalition wants to meet with CHA leaders and get an update on birth center operations, though she expects that won’t happen until November due to scheduling logistics.
“There is definitely support for the sustainability of the birth center, and that’s really what we’re hoping to achieve in the long run,” Helgeson said. “The opening is important, but we really want it to succeed in the long-term as well.”

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. – A Springfield, Mo., man was sentenced today for the crimes of mail fraud, aggravated identity theft, and money laundering in federal court for his role in a scheme that involved submitting false documents to the Missouri Department of Revenue in an effort to obtain mechanics liens and titles for vehicles that had previously been stolen.

Dennis Arthur Cleveland, 76, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Stephen R. Bough on one count of mail fraud, one count of aggravated identity theft, and one count of money laundering. Cleveland received a sentence of 120 months for the mail fraud and money laundering counts that will run concurrently, an additional 24 months for aggravated identity theft that will run consecutively to the other counts, and an additional nine months’ incarceration for his violations of his post release supervision from a prior conviction for Clean Air Act offenses in 2023. Overall, Cleveland was sentenced to a total of 153 months incarceration, to be followed by three years of post-release supervision, payment of a $300 special assessment, payment of a restitution in the amount of $37,049 to the victims, a full order of forfeiture in the amount of $37,049, and the payment of $400,000 in fines assessed by the court against the defendant.

“Government records and title systems exist to establish legitimate ownership, not to provide an easy way for criminals to turn stolen vehicles into profit,” said R. Matthew Price, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Missouri. “The defendant didn’t simply commit a harmless paperwork offense; he manipulated records for personal greed. Today’s sentence makes it clear that those who try to defraud government processes at any level in the Western District of Missouri, will be held accountable and aggressively prosecuted.”

Cleveland, as the owner of Affordable Towing, directed his employees, who he knew were submitting fraudulent documents, to send those documents to the Missouri Department of Revenue. The purpose of the documents was to obtain substitute or replacement mechanics liens and vehicle titles that would allow Cleveland to sell the vehicles. In each instance, the documents submitted by Cleveland and his employees claimed to have received permission from the vehicle’s owner. Upon reviewing the documents, it was discovered that none of the listed vehicle owners gave Cleveland or Affordable Towing permission to seize or sell their vehicle. Further, in all these documents, a signature in the name of the vehicle’s owner was provided and was confirmed to be a forgery. In those instances that Cleveland obtained a replacement lien or title, he would sell the vehicle at a used car dealership. In those instances that Cleveland failed to receive a replacement title or mechanics lien, he would send the vehicle to a local scrapyard. Under either circumstance, Cleveland took all the proceeds from sale or scrapping of a vehicle for himself, totaling several million dollars. Each of the vehicles involved in this scheme were confirmed to have been reported stolen and neither Cleveland nor Affordable Towing had permission to possess, sell, or scrap any of these vehicles.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Patrick Carney. It was investigated by the Missouri Department of Revenue, Compliance and Investigation Bureau, the Environmental Protection Agency-Criminal Investigation Division, the Missouri Department of Natural Resources, the United States Post Inspection Service, and the Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation.
title: Springfield Man Sentenced to 153 Months in Federal Prison for Submitting False Documents to the Missouri Department of Revenue

WASHINGTON -- FEMA announced today that federal disaster assistance is available to the state of Florida to supplement state, tribal and local response efforts due to the emergency conditions resulting from Hurricane Isaias on beginning Oct. 6, 2026, and continuing.
The President’s action authorizes FEMA to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts to alleviate the hardship and suffering caused by the emergency on the local population, and to provide appropriate assistance to save lives, to protect property, public health and safety and to lessen or avert the threat of a catastrophe.
The assistance is for Baker, Bay, Calhoun, Citrus, Columbia, Dixie, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gilchrist, Gulf, Hamilton, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Leon, Levy, Liberty, Madison, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Wakulla and Washington counties.
Specifically, FEMA is authorized to identify, mobilize, and provide at its discretion, equipment and resources necessary to alleviate the impacts of the emergency. Emergency protective measures, limited to direct federal assistance, will be provided at 75% federal funding.
Brett H. Howard has been named the Federal Coordinating Officer for federal response operations in the affected area. Designations may be made later if requested by the state and warranted by the results of further damage assessments.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández visitó Vimenti, en el Residencial Ernesto Ramos Antonini en San Juan, donde presentó $1,031,000 en fondos federales que aseguró para desarrollar el Next Generation STEM Learning Lab Accelerator. La iniciativa ampliará las oportunidades de educación STEM para estudiantes de Vimenti School y otras tres escuelas del programa de Escuelas Comunitarias de Servicio Completo.

El Comisionado Residente aseguró los fondos mediante una solicitud de Financiamiento para Proyectos Comunitarios (Community Project Funding) presentada ante el Comité de Asignaciones de la Cámara de Representantes. Los recursos serán canalizados a través de la Oficina de STEM Engagement de la NASA.

“Llevo semanas diciendo que tenemos que priorizar lo básico, y la educación es básica. Nuestros niños fracasan en las materias básicas de español, inglés, ciencias y matemáticas. Este tipo de asignación ayuda a resolver ese problema.”, dijo el Comisionado Residente.

“Agradecemos al comisionado residente, Pablo José Hernández Rivera, y a su equipo, por la confianza depositada en este proyecto. Este logro reafirma nuestro compromiso de seguir identificando y allegando recursos que permitan que más escuelas públicas de Puerto Rico cuenten con espacios, herramientas y oportunidades educativas de excelencia para sus estudiantes, maestros y familias”, expresó Bárbara Rivera Batista, directora ejecutiva de Vimenti.

“Esta subvención confirma lo que puede lograr el modelo de Escuela Comunitaria de Servicio Completo cuando se le brinda el respaldo necesario. Nuestro compromiso es que estos recursos y espacios STEM se queden en cada escuela, sostenidos por sus propios equipos, mucho después de que termine el financiamiento”, indicó Lola Yglesias Quiñones, directora de Expansión de Vimenti.

A través del proyecto, las escuelas podrán desarrollar nuevos espacios educativos con herramientas de robótica y programación, astronomía y ciencias espaciales, ciencias de la Tierra, análisis de datos e inteligencia artificial. La iniciativa también contempla capacitación y acompañamiento para maestros, con el objetivo de fortalecer la capacidad de las escuelas para mantener y ampliar estos programas a largo plazo.

Durante su visita, el Comisionado Residente también sostuvo un conversatorio con estudiantes, familias y maestros sobre el modelo de Vimenti, los resultados que ha alcanzado la organización y la importancia de ampliar el acceso a oportunidades educativas en áreas STEM.

Según datos provistos por Vimenti, durante el año escolar 2023-2024 sus estudiantes alcanzaron un 54% de dominio en matemáticas, frente a un 11% a nivel de Puerto Rico. Entre los estudiantes con discapacidades, el dominio en matemáticas alcanzó un 63%, comparado con tasas de entre 10% y 18% a nivel estatal.

Vimenti atiende a estudiantes y familias mediante un modelo de dos generaciones que integra educación, salud y bienestar, desarrollo laboral, capacidad financiera, emprendimiento y mentoría. De acuerdo con su estudio de impacto de siete años, la organización ha generado cerca de $59 millones en impacto económico mediante sus operaciones y proyecta otros $97 millones asociados a iniciativas futuras.

PITTSBURGH, Pa. - A resident of Valencia, in Butler County, Pennsylvania, has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Pittsburgh on a charge of receiving a firearm and ammunition, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the firearm and ammunition would be used to commit a felony or a Federal crime of terrorism, including providing, attempting to provide, and conspiring to provide material support or resources to a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO), United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced today.

The one-count Indictment named Jonathan Hunter Kramer, 21, as the sole defendant. Kramer previously was charged with that crime by federal criminal complaint (read the complaint news release here ) and remains detained pending trial.

According to the Indictment, on or about September 12, 2026, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, Kramer knowingly received a semiautomatic rifle, .223 caliber ammunition, and 5.56 caliber ammunition, knowing and having reasonable cause to believe that the firearm and ammunition would be used to commit a felony or a Federal crime of terrorism, including providing, attempting to provide and conspiring to provide material support and resources to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated FTO. As alleged in the affidavit filed in support of the complaint, Kramer had been using the online persona of “Hamza Al Rashid” who claimed affiliation with ISIS, offered to share explosive manuals with others, and, just a few days prior to September 12, expressed his intent to prepare for his “mission” and that he was only missing a “weapon.”

The affidavit further details that, on September 12, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) observed Kramer quickly depart his residence while carrying a bag. Thereafter, he acquired a long black bag from the trunk of another individual’s vehicle in the parking lot of a retail store, booked a hotel room, and visited the gun counter at a sporting goods store. FBI agents interdicted Kramer as he returned to the hotel in possession of three 30-round capacity rifle magazines and five boxes of rifle ammunition. Subsequently, the FBI executed federal search warrants upon Kramer’s person, hotel room, and residence, which resulted in the seizure of a semiautomatic rifle, five rifle magazines (two loaded and the other three each offering a 30-round capacity), a rifle bipod and scope, a total of 190 rounds of rifle ammunition, and other items, along with a handwritten note stating “DoNt look For me[.] IDK what I did buT I cant live In constant Fear[.]”

The law provides for a maximum total sentence of up to 15 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both. Under the federal Sentencing Guidelines, the actual sentence imposed would be based upon the seriousness of the offense and the prior criminal history of the defendant.

Assistant United States Attorneys Brendan J. McKenna and Alyssa R. Angotti of the Western District of Pennsylvania and Trial Attorneys Andrew Briggs and Matthew Hracho of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division are prosecuting this case on behalf of the United States.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, with assistance from numerous state and local counterparts, conducted the investigation leading to the Indictment.

An indictment is an accusation. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

BANGOR, Maine: A Mexican man pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Bangor to illegally reentering the country after a prior removal.

According to court records, on September 10, 2026, a U.S. Border Patrol agent was traveling in Franklin County when he observed a cargo van operating with temporary license plates. The agent followed the van to a fast-food restaurant in Farmington and spoke with the occupants. Ramon Delgado-Guerrero , 29, was a passenger in the vehicle. Delgado-Guerrero is a citizen of Mexico and had previously been removed from the United States on two separate occasions in 2017.

Delgado-Guerrero faces up to two years in prison and a $250,000 fine. He will be sentenced after the completion of a presentence investigation report by the U.S. Probation Office. A federal district judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case.

U.S. Marshals: 2 Federal Escapees Captured in Mexico and Returned to the United States
For immediate release
Josh Warvel, Deputy U.S. Marshal
Corpus Christi, TX – The U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) Gulf Coast Violent Offenders Fugitive Task Force – Corpus Christi Division announces the apprehension of two federal escapees in Mexico following separate fugitive investigations and coordination with U.S. and Mexican law enforcement partners.
Daniel Pena escaped from the satellite camp adjacent to the Federal Correctional Institution Three Rivers in Live Oak County on March 10 while serving a 70-month federal sentence for possession with intent to distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. Deputy U.S. Marshals determined Pena had fled to Matamoros, Tamaulipas, Mexico, where he was living and working as a mechanic. Through coordination with the USMS Office of International Operations – Mexico Foreign Field Office and Mexican authorities, Pena was apprehended in Matamoros on Sept. 23, ending his more than six months as a federal fugitive.
Hugo Gilberto Aguilar remained a fugitive for more than three years after escaping federal custody in Three Rivers while serving a sentence of more than 120 months for possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance. The investigation spanned the United States, Colombia, and Mexico, where investigators determined Aguilar had used an assumed identity and fraudulent Mexican government identification to evade capture.
Aguilar was initially detained at Monterrey International Airport but was later erroneously released from Mexican federal immigration. U.S. Marshals continued the investigation and, through coordination with Mexican law enforcement, located Aguilar in Nayarit, Mexico, where local authorities apprehended him on Sept. 28, ending his more than three years as a fugitive.
Both fugitives are expected to face further judicial proceedings related to their outstanding federal warrants and escapes.
The U.S. Marshals Service remains committed to pursuing fugitives wherever they flee and working with domestic and international law enforcement partners to bring them to justice.
The U.S. Marshals led Gulf Coast Violent Offenders Fugitive Task Force in Corpus Christi, Texas, is integrated by remarkable investigators from the Texas Department of Public Safety, Texas Department of Criminal Justice, Corpus Christi Police Department, Aransas County Sheriff’s Office, Jim Wells County Sheriff’s Office, Nueces County Sheriff’s Office, Kleberg County Attorney’s Office, and other partner federal agencies that work together for the protection of our communities.

EXIM Announces $547 Million Loan Guarantee to Support Tele-Fonika Cable Americas Proposed Manufacturing Facility in Texas
WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) announced a $547 million loan guarantee to support Tele-Fonika Cable Americas’ (TFCA) growing manufacturing investment in the United States. Santander and Erste Bank Polska acted as sole arrangers for this financing. EXIM’s loan guarantee will support TFCA’s inaugural production of rubber-insulated cables in the United States. The cables, which will be made in Waller, Texas, are the arteries of modern infrastructure, carry power through the data centers, mines, and industrial facilities on which the American economy runs. TFCA’s cables will be manufactured by American workers for customers in the United States and around the world. The loan guarantee will be provided under the Bank’s Make More in America Initiative, which extends EXIM financing to export-oriented domestic manufacturing projects, especially in sectors critical to national security, to compete on a global scale.
“EXIM’s innovative tools like Make More in America help U.S. workers win around the globe and at home. Winning means building, and President Trump is delivering at unprecedented speed and scale. This financing will help Tele-Fonika Cable Americas reshore U.S. jobs and put Americans to work building the industries of the future,” said EXIM Chairman Jovanovic.
“EXIM’s approval of the $547 million loan guarantee is a key step for Tele-Fonika Kable Group’s investment in Waller, Texas,” said Bartłomiej Zgryzek, CFO of Tele-Fonika Kable Group. “This investment is a clear result of the Make More in America Initiative. Building a manufacturing facility in the United States from the ground up is a significant operational challenge, and we are taking it on. We expect continued growth in the U.S. market, particularly in data centers, mining and industrial infrastructure, and we intend to serve that demand with cables made in Texas.”
Tele-Fonika Cable Group is the third-largest electrical cable manufacturer in Europe and one of the largest in the world, employing more than 2,500 people and selling its products in more than 80 countries. The proposed Waller, Texas facility would be the company's first manufacturing operation in North America and reflects confidence in American workers and the U.S. industrial base. The facility is expected to boost employment in Texas, employing up to 500 people and several hundred construction workers.
EXIM’s first loan guarantee under the Make More in America Initiative is an important milestone in supporting export-oriented domestic manufacturing and strengthening the U.S. industrial base. The investment remains subject to all required regulatory approvals and permits, the securing of financing, compliance with all applicable conditions.
ABOUT EXIM:
As the United States government’s official export credit agency, the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) supports American jobs by facilitating U.S. exports. As an independent agency, EXIM plays a critical role in supporting economic growth, securing critical supply chains, and ensuring American businesses are given a fighting chance. To achieve this mission, EXIM offers financing including export credit insurance, working capital guarantees, loan guarantees, and direct loans. Learn more at www.exim.gov.

text:
Reps. Castro, Cisneros Honor Hispanic and Latino Storytellers
WASHINGTON D.C. — Reps. Joaquin Castro (TX-20) and Gil Cisneros (CA-31) introduced a resolution to honor and celebrate the cultural impacts of Hispanics and Latinos in film, television, and streaming.
Hispanics and Latinos represent 21% of the total population of the United States but Hispanics and Latinos in film, television, and streaming account for less than 7% of on-screen roles and less than 5% of off-screen roles. However, television series and films featuring Hispanic and Latino talent consistently rank among the most watched and financially successful productions.
El Cine, the Hispanic Heritage Foundation, the Latino Film Institute, the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), the National Association of Latino Independent Producers (NALIP), the National Hispanic Foundation for the Arts (NHFA), and the National Hispanic Media Coalition (NHMC) signed on as supporting organizations.
“Latino artists have helped shape American film and television for generations, and Latinos are one of the largest and fastest-growing audiences in this country," said Congressman Castro. "Yet we are still underrepresented on screen and in the writing rooms and leadership roles where decisions are made. Latino film festivals across the country are doing important work to support Latino storytellers, and the industry should invest in that talent. I'm proud to join Congressman Cisneros in recognizing these contributions and calling for more Latino representation on and behind the big screen.”
“Latinos and Hispanics represent some of the biggest stars and the most important stories of the century. The time when actors like Rita Hayworth, Anthony Quinn or Martin Sheen had to change their names has given way to mainstream stars like Selma Hayek, Eva Longoria, Diego Luna, and Selena Gomez,” said Congressman Cisneros. “Hispanic and Latino storytellers have enriched our media with diverse stories, artistic excellence, and economic growth and they deserve recognition for their talent. I’m proud to introduce this resolution to celebrate and honor the success of Hispanics and Latinos in film, television, and streaming and recognize their past, present, and future contributions to the United States.”
“One of the biggest dangers our culture faces is erasure,” said Mariana Da Silva, Founder of El Cine. “We are taught to hide parts of ourselves, our language, our histories, and the stories that make us who we are. At El Cine, we create space for those stories to be seen, heard, and passed on. Latin culture is American culture. We’re proud to support this resolution because recognizing our contributions also means making room for the next generation to tell their stories without having to hide who they are.”
“Fifty-nine percent of Latino adults went to a movie theater last year, more than any other group,” said Juan Proaño, Chief Executive Officer of LULAC. “Latinos are the profit margin of this industry. Yet we hold just 5 percent of the roles on screen, 2.8 percent of the lead roles, and one half of one percent of the writing credits, and 44 percent of top films have no Latino speaking character at all. LULAC is proud to support Congressman Cisneros's resolution, which honors the artists who opened doors and calls on the industry to reflect the audiences who sustain it. When we tell our own stories, the whole country sees itself more clearly.”
“Thirty years ago, Jimmy Smits, Sonia Braga, Esai Morales, Merel Julia and I founded the National Hispanic Foundation for the Arts (NHFA), when Latinos were one in ten Americans and almost nowhere on screen," said Felix R. Sánchez, Chair and Co-founder of NHFA. "Today we are one in five, and we hold fewer than three of every hundred lead roles in Hollywood's top films. The country changed, the screen has not.”
“Latino Americans are intertwined in the fabric of the United States – including in film, television, and streaming,” said Brenda Victoria Castillo, President and CEO of National Hispanic Media Coalition (NHMC). “With the highest per capita consumption in entertainment, representing 24% of film ticket sales, 29% of daily mobile television viewers, and 24% of streaming subscribers, it's no wonder that our stories resonate, inspire, and are central to modern American culture. NHMC thanks Congressmen Cisneros and Castro for recognizing our community and continuing to be allies to increase Latino representation in media.”
“From a fifth grader's first film to a fellow's first credit to a festival premiere, Latino Film Institute is building the workforce of American film, television, and streaming,” said Axel Caballero, Chief Executive Officer of the Latino Film Institute. “And we are preparing it for what comes next: new kinds of stories, told on platforms that are still taking shape. Through YCP, our fellowships, and LALIFF, that talent is being readied and celebrated. We thank Congressman Cisneros, Congressman Castro, and all the cosponsors, and LFI is proud to support this resolution.”
Read the full text of the resolution here.

WILMINGTON, Del. – On October 1, 2026, a federal judge convicted Deborah Evans Mott, 71, of Ormond Beach, Florida, of making false statements under penalty of perjury in a bankruptcy proceeding, announced U.S. Attorney Benjamin L. Wallace.

U.S. District Judge Maryellen Noreika returned the verdict following a four-day bench trial held June 22 through June 25, 2026, after Mott waived her right to a jury trial.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Mott was the controlling and majority member of Team Systems International, LLC (“TSI”). In January 2022, after a federal jury in Florida returned a judgment of more than $6 million against the company, TSI filed a voluntary petition for relief under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware (No. 22-10066-CTG). Mott knew about, and intentionally failed to disclose, several closed TSI bank accounts and more than $3 million in transfers to herself and other company insiders, including Mott’s family members. She then gave TSI’s bankruptcy lawyers financial information for TSI’s Statement of Financial Affairs that omitted those accounts and transfers, reviewed the paperwork TSI’s lawyers prepared that omitted that information, and signed the paperwork for TSI under penalty of perjury.

The court found Mott guilty on one count of making false statements under penalty of perjury in a bankruptcy proceeding and acquitted her on a second count of making false statements under oath during a deposition in the bankruptcy. Mott faces a maximum prison term of five years and a maximum fine of $250,000. Sentencing is scheduled for February 4, 2027. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after taking into account the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

“Deborah Mott decided to pay herself and her favored circle rather than her company’s creditors. She then tried to cover her tracks by lying to TSI’s lawyers, TSI’s creditors, the Chapter 7 Trustee, and the Bankruptcy Court. That abuse of our judicial system has now earned Mott a federal felony conviction. We thank the District Court for the care and thought it exhibited in serving as the trier of fact in this bench trial, and we look forward to advocating for a just sentence for Mott in the coming months.”

“Honesty is not optional in the federal bankruptcy system,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Providing false information under penalty of perjury undermines the integrity of the process. This conviction demonstrates the FBI’s commitment to holding accountable those who abuse the bankruptcy system for personal gain.”

The investigation was conducted by the FBI’s Wilmington Resident Agency. Assistant U.S. Attorney Claudia L. Pare and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Hannah J. McCollum prosecuted the case.

A copy of this press release is located on the website of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Delaware. Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the District of Delaware or on PACER by searching for Case No. 1:24-cr-00077-MN.

SAN JOSE – Dr. Raghava Reddy Ghosala pleaded guilty in federal court yesterday to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States.

Ghosala, 65, of North Wales, Pennsylvania, was charged by information on May 5, 2026. Under the plea agreement, Ghosala pleaded guilty to all counts. In pleading guilty, Ghosala admitted he was the President of the non-profit organization North American Telugu Association, Inc. (also known as NATA) from 2019 through 2022. During this period, and under Ghosala’s leadership, NATA defrauded multiple employers’ corporate matching programs by causing employees to request and secure millions of dollars’ worth of corporate matching payments for purported charitable contributions which did not qualify for matching payments, usually because the contributions were refunded to the employees by NATA, often via cash or payments to intermediaries (rather than to employees directly). Ghosala also admitted he worked with others to falsify NATA’s tax returns for 2019 through 2021 by fraudulently reclassifying expenditures which were actually used to reimburse donors as legitimate expenses. Ghosala then authorized the filing of those tax returns despite the fact that he knew they were false.

Another defendant, Venkateswara Kalluri, was charged in connection with this scheme in case No. 5:25-cr-00066-EJD. Kalluri pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States on June 23, 2025.

United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian, IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) San Francisco Field Office Acting Special Agent in Charge David Lowe, and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Special Agent in Charge Scott Schelbe made the announcement.

Ghosala’s sentencing hearing is scheduled for February 22, 2027, at 1:30 PM before U.S. District Judge Edward J. Davila. Ghosala faces a maximum statutory penalty of 20 years in prison as to the wire fraud conspiracy count, and 5 years in prison as to the conspiracy to defraud the United States count. Any sentence will be imposed by the court after consideration of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and the federal statute governing the imposition of a sentence, 18 U.S.C. § 3553.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael G. Pitman is prosecuting the case with the assistance of Sahib Kaur. The prosecution is the result of an investigation by IRS-CI, and the FBI.

LEXINGTON, Ky. – Two Richmond, Ky., residents, Destiny Burns, 24, and Aaron Whittamore, 33, were sentenced to 11 years and 12 years in prison, respectively, on Monday, October 5, 2026, by U.S. District Judge Chad Meredith for conspiracy to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine.

Beginning in June 2025, law enforcement used a confidential informant to conduct a series of controlled purchases of methamphetamine from Burns. The investigation culminated in a traffic stop of Burns and Whittamore on August 22, 2025, after law enforcement observed Whittamore entering Burns’s vehicle carrying multiple bags. During the traffic stop, officers located multiple gallon- sized Ziplock bags containing a total of approximately 2,035 grams of methamphetamine, along with $1,109 in U.S. currency. As part of their individual plea agreements, Burns and Whittamore each admitted to engaging in a conspiracy to and possessing with the intent to distribute methamphetamine.

MIAMI – U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida received the League of Prosecutors’ President’s Award at the organization’s 2026 Justice Award Dinner in Miami.

The President’s Award recognizes distinguished contributions to the justice system, public service, and the community. The League honored Reding Quiñones for a career of service spanning more than two decades in the military, on the bench, in national security, and as a federal prosecutor, as well as for his continued commitment to the work ahead as U.S. Attorney.

“I am deeply grateful to the League of Prosecutors for this honor,” said U.S. Attorney Reding Quiñones. “Ideas do not prevail simply because they are right. They endure because people are willing to stand up for them and fight for them. Every day, prosecutors are in the trenches fighting for the idea and the principle of justice, and I am proud to be in that fight with them. I have had the privilege of serving our country in uniform, serving our community from the bench, and serving alongside extraordinary prosecutors and law enforcement officers throughout my career. This award is not a finish line. It is a reminder of the responsibility we carry and the work still ahead.”

Founded in 2002, the League of Prosecutors brings together current and former prosecutors and members of the broader justice community. For more than two decades, the organization has supported and mentored generations of prosecutors, educated the public about issues affecting the justice system, and recognized judges, prosecutors, law enforcement officers, and other public servants for their contributions to the community and the administration of justice.

Reding Quiñones was sworn in as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida on Aug. 13, 2025. An Air Force Colonel with more than 23 years of military service, he previously served as a Florida trial judge, as a national security official in the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, and as a federal prosecutor in both the Eastern District of Virginia and the Southern District of Florida.

As U.S. Attorney, Reding Quiñones serves as the chief federal law enforcement officer for the Southern District of Florida. He oversees the prosecution of federal crimes and the representation of the United States in civil matters throughout the district.

BANGOR, Maine: A Tremont man pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Bangor to failing to report a motor vehicle accident, failing to maintain control of a motor vehicle, and carrying or storing an open container of alcohol inside a vehicle.

According to court records, in August 2025, Gregory Harper , 42, crashed his pickup truck into a tree on the Seal Cove Road in Acadia National Park and fled the scene. A witness called 911 and reported the accident. Harper was not present when National Park Service rangers arrived, but he turned himself in two days later. During a search of his truck, rangers located open alcohol cans. When interviewed, Harper said he swerved to avoid a deer.

Harper faces up to six months in prison, a maximum fine of $5,000, and up to five years of probation on each count. He will be sentenced after the completion of a presentence investigative report by the U.S. Probation Office. A U.S. Magistrate Judge will determine any sentence after considering statutory sentencing factors.

The National Park Service investigated the case with assistance from the Southwest Harbor Police Department.

After delivering more than 11,000 pounds of supplies, science experiments, and other cargo to the International Space Station for NASA, Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL spacecraft is scheduled to depart Friday, Oct. 9, as part of the company’s Commercial Resupply Services-24 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-24.

Watch NASA’s live coverage of departure beginning at 12:30 p.m. EDT through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:

https://www.nasa.gov/live

Flight controllers on the ground will send commands for the space station’s Canadarm2 robotic arm to detach the Cygnus XL spacecraft from the Unity module’s Earth-facing port and maneuver it into position for release at 12:45 p.m. NASA astronaut Luke Delaney will monitor the operation from aboard the orbital complex.

Loaded with thousands of pounds of disposal items and other unneeded cargo, Cygnus XL will deorbit Monday, Oct. 12, for a destructive re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere, where it will safely burn up. NASA will not provide coverage of the spacecraft’s deorbit.

The resupply spacecraft launched on April 11 on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Oct. 6, 2026
BETHESDA, MD — Today the U.S. Postal Service issued a semipostal stamp, Know the Facts About Fentanyl, at a ceremony held at the National Institutes of Health.
The stamp will raise funds to advance research and raise awareness to combat this ongoing epidemic while providing a message encouraging hope, healing and recovery.
The stamp was dedicated by Peter Pastre, USPS government relations and public policy vice president.
“Fentanyl contributes to some 80,000 overdose deaths each year, with devasting impacts to families and communities across the nation,” he said. “This semipostal stamp is priced higher than the standard 1-ounce letter rate to help raise money for causes in the national interest. The net proceeds from this stamp will be distributed to the National Institute on Drug Abuse —the world’s largest provider of research into substance abuse, addiction treatment, and recovery support.”
Pastre was joined by Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health.
“Fentanyl represents one of the most urgent public health challenges of our time, and confronting it requires the full weight of scientific inquiry, innovation and national resolve,” he said. “At NIH, we are committed to funding the rigorous research needed to understand addiction, develop new treatments and save lives. This stamp is a uniquely meaningful way to remind every American that this fight belongs to all of us, and that science offers real hope for the future.”
Dr. Nora D. Volkow, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, also spoke at the dedication.
“Addiction research has shown that recovery is sustained through meaningful interpersonal connections — the support of families, friends and peers in recovery. It is fitting to convey that message through a postage stamp, because stamps travel and connect one person to another. This stamp will travel through homes, workplaces and communities across the country, carrying a reminder that community matters, treatment works, recovery is possible, and nobody has to confront addiction by themselves,” she said.
Most of the approximately 80,000 annual overdose deaths in the United States involve fentanyl and other extremely potent synthetic opioids. In 2023, the U.S. saw a reduction in drug overdose deaths for the first time in years. Data released in 2024 showed deaths involving fentanyl declined at a historic rate, down more than 30 percent over the previous year. Sustained research to prevent and treat addiction, deploy overdose interventions, and sustain recovery is critical to build on current progress.
When working on the stamp design, Antonio Alcalá, an art director for USPS, said he wanted to convey the idea of supporting people while avoiding imagery of pills, which could be triggering to those recovering from misuse.
He reached out to illustrator Whitney Sherman, who created the art for the wildly successful Breast Cancer Research Semipostal.
The art focuses on a person in the center of the stamp surrounded by a diverse group of supporters. This emphasizes how fentanyl can affect one person yet also has an impact on the community. The group shows care and comfort to the central figure, reflecting their love and support. The central figure accepts their support without shame or embarrassment.
“The word ‘hope’ was dominant in my mind as it presents possibilities and positive outcomes,” Sherman said. “If you look at each person, they have an intention. They come from various places in the figure’s life. They are expressing care with their eyes and hand gestures. Some are looking at us, suggesting an invitation to also be caring, some are showing their commitment to the central figure that a family member or close friend may give, others offer a sympathetic glance.”
While Alcalá said working on any stamp is meaningful, this one is a little more special.
Know the Facts About Fentanyl is a semipostal stamp. The price of a semipostal stamp pays for the First-Class single-piece postage rate in effect at the time of purchase plus an amount to fund causes that have been determined to be in the national public interest. By law, revenue from sales (minus postage and the reasonable reimbursement of costs to the Postal Service) is to be transferred to a selected executive agency or agencies. Net proceeds from this stamp will be distributed to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
News of the Know the Facts About Fentanyl semipostal stamp is being shared with the hashtag #FentanylSemipostalStamp.
Postal Products
Customers may purchase stamps and other philatelic products through The Postal Store at usps.com/shopstamps, by calling  844-737-7826, by mail through USA Philatelic, or at Post Office  locations nationwide. For officially licensed stamp products, shop the USPS  Officially Licensed Collection on Amazon. Additional information on stamps, first-day-of-issue ceremonies and stamp-inspired products can be found at stampsforever.com.

Congresswoman Scholten Introduces COIN Act to Help Small Businesses Evaluate Uses of Digital Assets
WASHINGTON, DC – This week, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03), member of the House Small Business Committee, introduced the Currency Options, Information, and Navigation (COIN) Act. This legislation would direct the Small Business Administration (SBA) to create learning modules to help small businesses learn how to evaluate the use of digital assets, such as cryptocurrency, for their operations. According to PayPal, 39 percent of American merchants currently accept cryptocurrency at checkout, and 84 percent believe payments using cryptocurrency will become common within the next five years.
“Small businesses keep our state and country running, but too many owners are being asked to navigate rapidly changing technology without clear, reliable guidance or learning opportunities,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “Digital assets like cryptocurrency are becoming more and more common at checkout counters, which is why I’m proud to introduce the COIN Act to make sure Main Street businesses have what they need to adapt and succeed.”
The bill requires these learning modules to be made with detailed information on the benefits and drawbacks of digital assets, and would provide entrepreneurs information on the logistics involving this technology, including tax implications and security risks if they choose to adopt any kind of digital asset. Additionally, this bill directs the SBA Administrator to work with relevant agencies to achieve accuracy in the information provided, with the goal of creating a comprehensive resource for small businesses. Finally, the bill establishes an Advisory Working Group made up of members from academia, industry, and financial consumer advocates to inform the creation of these learning modules.
This bill reflects the Congresswoman’s ongoing efforts to support small business owners in Michigan and across the country. Earlier this year, Congresswoman Scholten’s bipartisan Investing in All of America Act was signed into law, and her Main Street Competes Act, AI WISE Act, and AI for Main Street Actall passed the House.

LOS ANGELES – A ranking member of a San Fernando Valley-based wing of the transnational criminal organization Mara Salvatrucha 13 (MS-13) was sentenced today to life in federal prison for participating in two murders of MS-13 associates who violated gang rules and were taken to remote areas of Los Angeles County, where they were killed.

Walter Chavez Larin, 27, a.k.a. “Delito,” of Panorama City, was sentenced by United States District Judge Stanley Blumenfeld, Jr. to life in prison.

At the conclusion of a nine-week trial, a jury in November 2025 found Chavez guilty of one count of racketeering conspiracy and two counts of violent crimes in aid of racketeering (VICAR) murder. Four other defendants were convicted during this trial.

According to evidence presented at trial, Chavez and his co-defendants murdered their victims who had violated MS-13 rules. The trial centered on MS-13 Los Angeles cliques that implemented gang rules that required its members to use murder to rise within its ranks.

In June 2017, a victim – identified in court documents as “E.H.” – who allegedly overstated his position in the gang. The victim was confronted by Chavez and other MS-13 gang members at an abandoned property, known as a “destroyer,” disarmed of his machete, and assaulted the victim. The victim was taken to Angeles National Forest, where he was stabbed and hacked to death. Several MS-13 members tried decapitating him but found it too difficult. They doused the body with rubbing alcohol under the belief it destroyed forensic evidence. After murdering E.H., they eventually threw the victim’s body over a ridge.

In January 2019, another victim – identified in court documents as “O.F” – who was a teenager targeted by MS-13. Chavez put a “green light” on this victim, meaning the victim should be killed on sight for disobeying gang rules.

The victim was taken from a North Hollywood park to Santa Clarita where he was executed by MS-13 members, including Edwin Martinez and Carlos Daniel Orellana, under the direction of Chavez.

Martinez, who was convicted at trial with Chavez of one count of racketeering conspiracy and three counts of VICAR murder, was sentenced to life in federal prison.

Orellana pleaded guilty in August 2025 to one count of racketeering conspiracy and is serving a federal prison sentence of 33 years and nine months.

Federal prosecutors have secured 34 convictions in this case.

The FBI, the Los Angeles Police Department, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office investigated this matter.

Assistant United States Attorneys William M. Larsen and Suria M. Bahadue of the Criminal Appeals Section, Jason C. Pang of the Transnational Organized Crime Section, Sara Vargas of the General Crimes Section, and Special Assistant United States Attorney Eric W. Siddall of the Major Crimes Section prosecuted this case.

text:
Fast Facts
Quantum computers have the potential to solve problems much faster than standard computers. But they could also break cryptography—the mathematical processes that can “lock,” “unlock,” or authenticate information—on federal systems. This could put sensitive data at risk.
Experts believe a quantum computer capable of breaking such cryptography could be developed as soon as the 2030s. To protect their data, federal agencies need to transition their systems to more secure cryptography. But they haven't gotten ready to do this, by, for example, fully identifying vulnerable systems or testing quantum-resistant algorithms.
A person holding a small electronic device with the words "Quantum computing" on it with several computer icons overlayed on the image.
Reissued with Revisions Oct 14, 2026
Errata statement - Revised on October 14, 2026 to clarify the summary on the highlights page as well as pages 5 and 43 of our coordination with executive branch agencies to obtain agreement that sensitive information was appropriately removed.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Quantum computers leverage qubits (the quantum equivalent of classical computer bits) to solve specific problems significantly faster than classical computers. However, the emergence of quantum computers could undermine the cryptography (e.g., encryption) that federal agencies use to secure their systems. Today’s quantum computers cannot yet break this cryptography. But a future quantum computer of sufficient size and sophistication—referred to as a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC)—could potentially do so for certain cryptography.
Most industry experts believe that a CRQC will be developed, possibly as soon as the 2030s. However, development estimates vary widely due to several factors, such as uncertainty in the rate of growth for qubits and how many qubits will be needed. Once a CRQC is developed, its use could have devastating impacts to federal systems reliant on vulnerable cryptography. For example, a malicious actor could use a CRQC tocompromise systems that ensure the authenticity of system users—thus allowing the actor to
- gain access to sensitive information; and
- decrypt (or unlock and view) data that the actor acquires and stores prior to the development of such a computer.
To address the threat posed by a CRQC, it is important that agencies transition existing systems to more secure cryptography (referred to as post-quantum cryptography). Using Office of Management and Budget guidance, GAO created an evaluation framework of three practices that agencies should address to prepare for this transition. However, none of the 24 selected agencies fully addressed these practices (see figure).
Extent to Which the 24 Chief Financial Officer Act Agencies Addressed Preparatory Practices for Migrating to Quantum Computing
The incomplete implementation of these practices is due in part to a lack of (1) cryptography expertise, (2) processes for developing cryptography inventories and identifying funding needed to transition to post-quantum cryptography, and (3) plans to guide post-quantum cryptography testing. Until the selected agencies address these weaknesses, they will not be well-positioned to address the threat of CRQCs to cryptography that agencies rely on to protect sensitive information.
Why GAO Did This Study
Federal agencies rely on cryptography to protect sensitive data and systems. However, some experts predict that a quantum computer capable of breaking certain cryptography may be developed within the next 10 to 20 years.
GAO was asked to review the threat of quantum computing to federal agency cryptography. This report describes (1) the threats quantum computers pose to cryptography on federal agencies’ information systems and (2) the extent to which federal agencies have begun preparing for this threat consistent with federal guidance.
GAO also evaluated cryptography inventories, funding assessments, and other planning documentation at each of the 24 Chief Financial Officer Act agencies to determine the extent to which they had addressed transition preparatory practices consistent with federal guidance.
This is a public version of a sensitive report that GAO issued in September 2025. GAO coordinated with the executive branch agencies included in this review from September 2025 through September 2026 to obtain concurrence that sensitive information was appropriately removed.
Reissued with revisions on Oct. 14, 2026
Errata statement - Revised on October 14, 2026 to clarify the summary on the highlights page as well as pages 5 and 43 of our coordination with executive branch agencies to obtain agreement that sensitive information was appropriately removed.
Recommendations
In the sensitive report, GAO made 89 recommendations to 23 agencies to, among other things, establish and implement processes to develop inventories of vulnerable cryptography and identify funding for post-quantum cryptography.
Twelve agencies agreed with GAO’s recommendations, two partially agreed, seven neither agreed nor disagreed, and one disagreed with three of its four recommendations. GAO maintains that all recommendations are warranted.
GAO is not making any additional recommendations in this public version.
title: Quantum Computing: Federal Actions Needed to Prepare for Emerging Cyber Threat [Reissued with revisions on Oct. 14, 2026]

text:
Moore, Bonamici, Frost, Grijalva, and Pocan Blast Regulations Paving the Way for National Voucher Scheme
The Treasury Department recently released regulations on their national voucher scheme, which was established through the Republicans’ Big Ugly Bil (HR 1). That law allowed Americans to receive a tax credit, up to $1,700, for donations to eligible scholarship-granting organizations, including religious schools. These regulations will double the credit amount for married couples. Representatives Gwen Moore (WI-04), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), and Mark Pocan (WI-02) have introduced HR 9289, the Keep Public Funds in Public Schools Act, which would repeal the H.R .1 voucher scheme.
In states across the country, taxpayer supported voucher programs operate with little oversight and fund private schools who lack civil rights and other protections for students. In Wisconsin, the current voucher program at the state level will cost state taxpayers more than $700 million this year alone. Nearly all the students receiving a voucher in Wisconsin attend private, religious schools. 
Republicans are working to enact and expand this flawed system at the national level. So far, six states have resisted, including Wisconsin. 
“Despite what Republicans claim, these regulations make it clear this voucher scheme is designed to prop up private schools– at the expense of our public schools. Public schools serve every student who walks through its doors. Our tax dollars should not be funneled to schools that can discriminate against students who try to enroll. That is why I am proud to spearhead legislation to reverse this voucher scheme,” said Representative Gwen Moore (WI-04).
"The Treasury Department's school voucher regulations clearly demonstrate that the Trump administration has no interest in supporting public schools or the students they serve," said Representative Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01). "Diverting public resources into private schools - including religious schools -  that can pick and choose which students they enroll is unjust and irresponsible. Alarmingly, the regulations actually prohibit states from implementing additional oversight, reporting, accountability, or civil rights protections. The vast majority of students in this country attend public schools. We should be strengthening public education, not destroying it."
“This voucher scheme sends public money to private schools with less accountability for how that money is spent," said Representative Maxwell Frost (FL-10)."We’ve already seen the consequences in Florida, where the state struggled to track hundreds of millions of dollars in voucher funds and cases of fraud surfaced. Now the Treasury Department and Trump administration want to take that same model nationwide. We shouldn’t be making it easier to lose track of taxpayer dollars; we should be making sure every dollar is accountable to the public.” 
“Arizona’s fraud-ridden school voucher program should serve as a warning to the rest of the country. Instead, the Trump Administration is moving full steam ahead with a national voucher scheme while failing to include even basic safeguards to prevent taxpayer dollars from being wasted or abused. Arizona has already seen where this road leads. That’s why Congress must act to ensure federal taxpayer dollars strengthen the public schools that serve the overwhelming majority of America’s children, not subsidize privatization schemes rife with fraud,” said Representative Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07).
“As a proud public school graduate, I know firsthand the value and importance of our public education system,” said Representative Mark Pocan (WI-02). “Fixing this blatant abuse of the tax system will help kids across the country, not just those whose parents are members of Mar-a-Lago. I applaud my friend, Rep. Moore, for spearheading this legislation, and I’m glad to be part of this effort to keep public funds in public schools.”
title: Moore, Bonamici, Frost, Grijalva, and Pocan Blast Regulations Paving the Way for National Voucher Scheme

text:
Do Not Pay Reaches 99% of Federal Programs and New Safeguards Verify Over $3.7 Trillion in Payments
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Bureau of the Fiscal Service announced significant Fiscal Year 2026 results from Treasury’s efforts to prevent fraud and improper payments to better protect taxpayer dollars, fulfilling key requirements of Executive Order 14249, Protecting America's Bank Account Against Fraud, Waste, and Abuse, issued by President Trump on March 25, 2025.
“Treasury continues to transform how the federal government protects taxpayer dollars by using better data, stronger controls, and advanced technology to stop fraud and improper payments before money goes out the door,” said Secretary Scott Bessent. “In the past year alone, Treasury built and deployed new safeguards that verified more than $3.7 trillion in federal payments and increased Do Not Pay access from 4 percent of programs to 99 percent, ensuring agencies have access to the data they need. We are moving beyond ‘pay and chase’ and making prevention the federal government’s first line of defense.”
Over the past year, Treasury streamlined access to Do Not Pay’s fraud prevention tools, added nine new data sources to the Do Not Pay program, and deployed a new government-wide payment verification process.
MORE THAN TWENTYFOLD INCREASE IN DO NOT PAY REACH
Treasury significantly expanded the reach and capabilities of the Do Not Pay program, which provides federal agencies and federally funded state-administered programs with data and tools to help verify identity and eligibility for the purpose of preventing fraud and improper payments.
During FY2026, Treasury:
- Expanded Federal Programs’ Access to Do Not Pay Data by More Than Twentyfold. Approximately 99 percent of federal programs can now access all Do Not Pay data sources for which they are legally authorized, compared with approximately 4 percent at the end of FY2025. Most remaining programs are on track to complete onboarding in early FY2027. Treasury achieved this progress by streamlining the Do Not Pay onboarding process and partnering with federal agencies to accelerate the data-sharing and privacy compliance work necessary to expand access. All access to and use of Do Not Pay data is governed by strict privacy, security, and user access controls.
- Screened Over 2.3 Billion Records Against Do Not Pay Data Sources, a nearly four-fold increase from the 641 million records screened in FY2025. The increase reflects expanded use of Do Not Pay across the federal government, the implementation of payment verification, and additional screenings conducted for states through the Public Assistance Reporting Information System (PARIS).
- Added Nine New Datasets, expanding the breadth and depth of information available to agencies for payment, identity, and eligibility screening. New sources include company registration information through OpenCorporates, select verification against the Social Security’s Numident data, and grantee audit findings from the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, among others.
MOVING FROM “PAY AND CHASE” TO PREVENTION AND VERIFICATION
Treasury also implemented a new payment verification process during FY2026, establishing additional safeguards to verify critical payment information before federal payments are disbursed. During the fiscal year, Treasury screened more than 1.1 billion federal payments totaling approximately $3.7 trillion. Through these screenings, Treasury identified and returned approximately 13,500 payments totaling $175 million that would have gone to deceased individuals.
Treasury developed and implemented these safeguards in close collaboration with federal agencies, with controls designed to protect legitimate payments while ensuring payment data is used responsibly and securely.
Treasury piloted additional verification capabilities during FY2026 to validate bank account ownership and the presence and format of Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TINs) associated with federal payments. These capabilities became fully operational on September 30, 2026, enabling Treasury to identify and return payments that fail established verification requirements before funds are disbursed.
Together, these improvements provide agencies with earlier access to authoritative and high-value data, strengthening their ability to identify potential fraud and improper payments before awards are made and payments are issued. Treasury will continue working with federal agencies to expand the data available through Do Not Pay, strengthen payment verification capabilities, and further embed fraud prevention into government-wide payment and program integrity controls.
###
title: Treasury Reports Major Progress in Preventing Fraud and Improper Payments
