Release Number 9307-26
CFTC Seeks Public Comment on Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Relating to Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets
October 05, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today published an Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to provide notice of, and seek public comment regarding, its intent to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework comprised of fit-for-purpose rules concerning section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act and retail commodity transactions described thereunder involving crypto assets (such transactions, “CTXs”).
“Today’s action is a critical step in the CFTC’s ongoing efforts to ensure America remains the crypto capital of the world,” Chairman Michael S. Selig said. “The American people deserve clarity, certainty, and consumer protections in the crypto asset markets and the agency is committed to delivering this by incorporating crypto asset transactions into its uniform national market regulatory framework. The Commission’s announcement begins our process of new rulemakings grounded in the CEA’s purpose and President Trump’s directive to propose a federal crypto asset regulatory market structure using the CFTC’s existing statutory authorities. Under my leadership, the Commission will take every necessary step to establish regulations that are designed to prevent, rather than only prosecute after the fact, fraudulent schemes such as FTX.”
Among other topics, the ANPRM solicits comment on the manners in which the Commission can: (i) prevent abusive practices in crypto asset markets and CTXs under a uniform national regime; (ii) provide market participants with crypto asset-specific contextual information concerning certain requirements and practices that are commonly accepted in the industry and have been found, based on the Commission’s experience in overseeing aspects of crypto asset markets since 2014, to represent industry best practices for compliance with the regulatory requirements that attach to CTXs; and (iii) codify through rulemaking a subcategory of designated contract market registration, known as a crypto asset market, that is purpose-built specifically for CTXs.
The Commission intends to use the information and comments received to inform potential future agency action, such as a rulemaking, with respect to section 2(c)(2)(D) and CTXs.
Comments must be in writing and received within 60 days of the ANPRM’s publication in the Federal Register. Comments received will be posted on Regulations.gov.
-CFTC-
title: CFTC Seeks Public Comment on Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Relating to Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets

Today, Congresswoman Maxine Waters (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, along with Representatives Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA) and Sam Liccardo (D-CA), sent a letter to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chairman Paul S. Atkins strongly opposing the Commission’s proposal to eliminate the March 2024 climate-related disclosure rules.
In the letter, the lawmakers warn that eliminating the rules would deprive investors of critical information about the financial risks companies face from climate change at a time when climate-related events are becoming increasingly more common and disruptive to businesses and the broader economy. They argue that the SEC has a responsibility to ensure investors have consistent, standardized information necessary to evaluate these risks and make informed decisions with their money.
“Stripping away these rules denies investors the information they need to accurately assess a company’s long-term value and to make sound, well-informed decisions with their hard-earned money,” the lawmakers wrote.
The lawmakers also dispute the Commission’s argument that the SEC exceeded its statutory authority in adopting the rules. They point to the SEC’s longstanding authority under federal securities laws to determine what information public companies must disclose to investors, as well as the Commission’s decades-long history of requiring disclosures in response to evolving market risks and economic conditions. The letter notes that the SEC has required various forms of environmental disclosure dating back to the 1970s and argues that climate-related disclosures fall within the Commission’s traditional role of ensuring investors have relevant information when making investment decisions.
The lawmakers added, “…nothing in the governing statutes, case law, or legislative history has changed since March 2024, and Congress has amended neither the Securities Act nor the Exchange Act. The only thing that has changed is the composition of the Commission.”
The letter also pushes back on arguments that climate disclosures are unnecessary or immaterial to investors. The lawmakers point to data showing that companies actively managing climate risks can realize significant financial benefits, while 80 percent of investors want the opportunity to invest in companies that consider environmental sustainability. Investors and financial institutions representing hundreds of trillions of dollars in assets have also sought climate-related information from companies to inform their investment and financing decisions.
The lawmakers conclude by urging the Commission to maintain the existing disclosure framework and withdraw its proposal to rescind the rules.
Full list of signers includes: Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA), Sam Liccardo (D-CA).
Read the full letter HERE.
Background:
    - June 16, 2021 — Passed climate-risk disclosure legislation through the House. Then Chairwoman Waters led House passage of a broader ESG disclosure package, which would require public companies to disclose financial and business risks associated with climate change. Read Waters' floor statement on passage of the legislation. 
- March 21, 2022 — Applauded the SEC's proposed climate-disclosure rule after years of Committee action. Then-Chairwoman Waters joined committee Dems in a letter to commending the SEC's proposed rule requiring climate-related disclosures by public companies. Waters highlighted that, under her leadership, the Committee had already held four hearings on the issue and advanced legislation from Committee Democrats over the previous two Congresses. Read Waters and Committee Dems statement on the proposed SEC rule. 
- October 6, 2023 — Pressed SEC Chair Gary Gensler to quickly finalize the rule. Waters urged Gensler to finish the long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule, warning that climate change and transition risks threatened Americans' investments, retirement savings, businesses and broader financial stability. She argued that investors needed consistent and comparable information to understand those risks. Read Waters' letter urging Gensler to finalize the climate-risk disclosure rule. 
- March 7, 2024 — Supported the SEC's final climate-disclosure rule while pushing for stronger protections. After the SEC finalized the rule, Waters welcomed the creation of standardized climate-risk disclosures but criticized the Commission for significantly weakening its original proposal. She specifically raised concerns about the treatment of Scope 1 and 2 emissions and the elimination of Scope 3 requirements, while emphasizing the real financial consequences of climate change for investors, homeowners and renters. Read Waters' statement on the final SEC climate-disclosure rule.
- April 10, 2024 — Defended the climate rule against Republican attacks in a full Committee hearing. At a Republican-led hearing titled “Beyond Scope: How the SEC's Climate Rule Threatens American Markets,” Waters defended the rule as a commonsense investor protection, arguing that climate change affects companies' financial health and investors have a right to understand how the companies they own are responding to those risks. Read Waters' opening statement defending the SEC climate rule. 
- June 5, 2024 — Led 36 lawmakers with Senator Elizabeth Warren in pressing the SEC to defend and enforce the rule. Waters and Warren led 36 lawmakers urging the SEC to remain focused on climate risk despite litigation challenging the rule. They called on the Commission to enforce its existing climate-risk guidance while the rule was stayed, use every available resource to defend the rule in court and robustly implement it once the stay was lifted. Read the Waters-Warren letter and Committee release. 
- September 17–19, 2024 — Fought Republican legislation restricting the SEC's disclosure authority. Waters opposed H.R. 4790, warning that it would restrict the SEC's authority to determine what information public companies must disclose, including environmental and climate-related information, and undermine investors' access to information about the companies they own. She testified against the legislation before the Rules Committee on September 17 and opposed it again on the House floor on September 19. Read Waters' September 17 testimony against H.R. 4790. Read Waters' September 19 floor statement. 
- December 29, 2025 — Demanded SEC oversight after Chairman Paul Atkins abandoned the climate-rule defense. Waters called for a long-overdue oversight hearing with Atkins amid sweeping changes at the SEC, including the Commission's retreat from climate-risk disclosure. The request put the Administration's reversal of climate-related investor protections squarely within the Committee Democrats' broader oversight of Atkins' leadership. Read Waters' request for an SEC oversight hearing. 
- February 11, 2026 — Confronted Atkins directly over halting the SEC's defense of the climate rule. When Atkins finally appeared before the Committee, Waters criticized his SEC for having “halted the SEC's defense of the climate disclosure rule” even as the California wildfires demonstrated the material financial risks associated with climate change. She placed the decision within a broader critique that Atkins' SEC was prioritizing Wall Street and billionaires over investors. Read Waters' February 2026 opening statement confronting Atkins.

Congressman Don Davis Introduces Bill to Ban Federal Candidates from Betting on Their Own Elections
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman Don Davis (NC-01) introduced the No Betting on Your Own Race Act, which would ban federal candidates seeking elected office from trades tied to their own races.
The No Betting on Your Own Race Act would prohibit federal candidates, their spouses or dependent children, and authorized campaign committees from buying, selling, acquiring, disposing of, or holding contracts tied to the candidate’s election.
"We don't want our athletes to bet on their games. A candidate running for federal elected office should be treated exactly the same and should not be allowed to trade on their own election," said Congressman Don Davis. "The No Betting on Your Own Race Act aims to prevent market interference, insider trading, as well as candidates and their family members from cashing in. To establish consistency and ensure all federal candidate campaign committees understand this, Congress must pass this common-sense legislation."
Violators will incur a $10,000 civil penalty for each violation. If there is a net financial gain, the penalty will be three times the gain, or $10,000, whichever is greater. The new law also provides that a candidate who is running for office at the federal level must be notified during the filing period.
The legislative text can be found HERE.
title: Congressman Don Davis Introduces Bill to Ban Federal Candidates from Betting on Their Own Elections

Washington, D.C.— Today, U.S. Reps. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25), Scott Franklin (FL-18), Darren Soto (FL-09) and Kat Cammack (FL-03) introduced the Restore Agricultural Investment, Stability and Expansion (RAISE) Act of 2026, to provide the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) with the standing authority to help American farmers and growers recover after natural disasters by issuing block grants.
“Congress needs to have the back of America’s farmers, and I’m proud to work across the aisle to make sure the crops and agricultural resources that fuel American families are protected from increasingly extreme weather threats, something our own citrus industry faces in Florida,” said Wasserman Schultz. “From timber to food on our tabletops, we need every tool at hand to help farmers recover from natural disasters.”
“The devastating freeze Florida farmers faced this past February was another reminder of how quickly a natural disaster can threaten years of hard work,” said Franklin. “Our growers face hurricanes, freezes, droughts, floods and other disasters, and they need a reliable way to recover when disaster strikes. This bill gives USDA permanent authority to provide flexible block grants for high-value and specialty crop losses so assistance can reach producers faster. I’m pleased we secured this provision in the House-passed Farm Bill and will continue working with Congresswoman Wasserman Schultz to get it across the finish line.”
“Glad to join Reps. Franklin, Wasserman Schultz, and Soto on this effort to support our Florida producers,” said Cammack. “When extreme weather threatens our crops, as is often the case in the Sunshine State, we must be prepared to help our farmers recover and continue the important work of feeding our nation.” 
“In Central Florida, our farmers, ranchers, and growers have struggled after devastating hurricanes,” said Soto. “As these natural disasters get stronger, we must work to ensure that they have the resources to recover, maintain their livelihoods, and keep feeding America.”
“Florida's citrus industry knows firsthand the devastating impacts of freezes, hurricanes and other disasters on crops. In times of disaster, America's growers and farmers need timely support to recover and replant,” said Matt Joyner, EVP and CEO of Florida Citrus Mutual. “Florida's citrus growers are grateful to our state’s Congressional members, including Debbie Wasserman Schultz, Kat Cammack, Darren Soto and Scott Franklin, for their leadership and commitment to advancing the RAISE Act. The legislation seeks to give the United States Department of Agriculture tools to quickly deliver block grant assistance in the wake of disasters, helping Florida citrus and the greater agriculture industry recover and continue producing for America's families.”
More than 90 percent of all Florida citrus production was impacted by hurricanes in 2022, totaling 375,302 acres. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services expects these devastating losses to cost the industry as much as $675 million. Florida citrus generates $6.8 billion in annual revenue and supports 33,000 jobs.
Click here for the full text of the legislation.

California Woman Arrested on Charges Alleging She Acted as Agent of China and Spied on Relatives of U.S. Based High-Ranking Taiwanese Government Official
Wanying Zhang, 34, also known as Heather Zhang, of Irvine, California, was arrested Sunday on a one count complaint charging her with acting in the United States as an unregistered agent of the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), including by conducting surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official.
“The central allegation here — that Zhang, at the behest of the People’s Republic of China, covertly surveilled relatives of a high-ranking foreign government official in the United States — is deeply troubling,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division and U.S. Attorney’s Offices, along with the FBI and other law enforcement partners, will remain vigilant against threats like this on our soil.”
“Protecting our national security means confronting foreign governments that engage in covert operations in our nation,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Ms. Zhang is charged with acting at the direction of Chinese government officials to spy on the family of a senior Taiwanese official here in the United States. She violated our laws and will be held accountable in our courts. We will aggressively investigate and prosecute illegal foreign operations on American soil.”
“The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Wanying Zhang’s arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China’s authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI’s unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government — and any foreign adversary — to conduct transnational repression within our borders.”
Zhang was arrested prior to her planned departure from Los Angeles International Airport, where she planned to board a flight to China. She is expected to make her initial appearance and be arraigned this afternoon in U.S. District Court in downtown Los Angeles.
According to the complaint, from June 2025 to September 2025, Zhang acted as an agent of the PRC without prior notification to the Attorney General of the United States, as required by federal law.
At the direction and control of PRC officials, Zhang coordinated with other individuals to promote the interests of China by, among other things, conducting surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official at their residence in the United States.
In June 2025, Zhang traveled from Southern California to China, where she met with PRC officials and was tasked with conducting surveillance in the United States.
On Aug. 29, 2025, Zhang and another individual flew from John Wayne Airport in Orange County to Las Vegas. On Sept. 1, 2025, they flew from Las Vegas to the Pacific Northwest, where the victims reside. On that date, Zhang messaged a PRC official that she was “Boarding now” and sent a photograph of her boarding pass.
Upon their arrival, Zhang and the other individual traveled to the victims’ residence and conducted surveillance. Zhang sent the same PRC official the following message: “Saw him, young male, it’s the young one.” When this official asked her to join an audio call, she replied, “I am videorecording.”
Zhang also sent the same official the license plate numbers for the two vehicles parked in front of the victims’ home.
If convicted, Zhang would face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
The FBI Los Angeles Field Office is investigating the case.
Senior Counsel Scott M. Lara of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda B. Elbogen and Colin S. Scott for the Central District of California are prosecuting the case.
A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
Justice Department Announces Actions Advancing Two Challenges to State and Local Natural Gas Bans in Colorado and Illinois
The Justice Department’s Energy and Natural Resources Division (ENRD) last week received a favorable decision regarding its statement of interest filing in a Colorado case. ENRD also filed an amicus brief opposing a natural gas ban by a Chicago-area municipality.
At issue in both cases is the ability of American families and businesses to continue relying on federally regulated gas stoves, furnaces, water heaters, dryers, and other appliances. In recent years, a growing patchwork of state and local regulations concerning the energy use and efficiency of appliances threatens to undermine those national standards.
“These efforts to support consumer choice and cut energy costs deliver on the President’s commitment to unleash American energy and protect consumer choice,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of ENRD. “The Department of Justice will continue prioritizing the fight against radical state and local overreach.”
Colorado Statement of Interest
The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado last week allowed to advance a challenge to certain Colorado and Denver regulations, holding as plausible that the measures are preempted by the federal Energy Policy and Conservation Act (EPCA). Earlier last month, ENRD filed a statement of interest in the case which expressed support for the challenge against the Colorado and Denver provisions. The court agreed with ENRD’s argument that if municipalities try to set building-wide energy use targets — which are largely a result of how much energy appliances in the building use — such efforts have an “impermissible connection with” the energy use and efficiency of appliances that federal standards already regulate.
Seventh Circuit Amicus Brief
ENRD filed an amicus brief last week in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit advancing arguments against a natural gas ban by the Village of Oak Park, Illinois. Plaintiffs challenged Oak Park’s “Climate Ready Oak Park” as being preempted by the EPCA. The brief by ENRD argues that “EPCA’s broad preemption provision bars local measures, like Oak Park’s, that prohibit products subject to a federal energy conservation standard from using a type of energy or that impose specific requirements concerning appliances’ energy use or efficiency.”
These developments reflect the latest action from ENRD and the Justice Department fighting back against state and local gas bans. Earlier this year, the department sued a New Jersey Township and successfully sued two California cities, for similar natural gas bans.
Deputy Assistant Attorney General Charles Roberts of ENRD handled both filings.
title: Justice Department Announces Actions Advancing Two Challenges to State and Local Natural Gas Bans in Colorado and Illinois

Davids Fights Washington Healthcare Cuts with Plan to Lower Costs, Protect Kansas Hospitals
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Representative Sharice Davids (KS-03) introduced a comprehensive package of healthcare legislation that directly counters Washington’s recent healthcare rollbacks, which are increasing monthly costs and closing rural hospitals. Davids’ efforts would protect Kansas families from rising medical costs, block new federal red tape, and keep local hospitals and health clinics open.
“At a time when families are stretching every dollar to cover groceries, energy, and housing, Washington shouldn't be making healthcare more expensive just to give billionaires a tax break,” said Davids. “I’m fighting back because hard-working Kansans deserve practical solutions, not higher medical bills and shuttered clinic doors. My healthcare package focuses on what actually matters to our neighbors: bringing down out-of-pocket costs, cutting through bureaucratic red tape, and making sure our local hospitals and birthing centers stay open.”
Last year, Davids voted against the extreme, partisan budget law, which included the largest cuts to Medicaid in American history. The law strips health coverage from 92,937 Kansans, puts six rural hospitals at risk of closure, restricts reproductive healthcare, and increases ACA premiums by an average of $708 per year for families in Kansas’ Third District.
Medicaid is a lifeline for Kansas hospitals, especially in rural communities, and the cuts could take more than $78 million a year from hospitals, increasing uncompensated care costs and potentially forcing Kansans to travel farther for emergency or specialized care. Higher ACA premiums could also push healthier people out of the insurance market, driving costs even higher for those who remain.
While party leaders in D.C. continue pushing partisan legislation that raises costs on working families, Davids’ package is focused on common-sense, bipartisan solutions that deliver tangible savings and protect access to care across Kansas.
- Restoring eliminated tax credits: The Healthy Communities Act would permanently restore enhanced ACA tax credits, saving Kansas families an average of $700 a year on premiums. It would also eliminate new Medicaid paperwork requirements, increase incentives for states like Kansas to expand coverage to working adults, and close Kansas’ Medicaid coverage gap, giving thousands of low-income Kansans access to ACA tax credits.
- Keeping rural operating rooms open: The Rural Surgery Sustainability Act would raise the federal reimbursement cap for surgical procedures at critical access hospitals, helping hospitals afford the nurse anesthetists needed to keep surgical services running.
  - “Access to local surgical procedures and maternity care is essential for rural Kansas communities, and maintaining a reliable anesthesia care team is critical to providing those services. However, the current Medicare reimbursement threshold has not been updated in more than two decades despite significant increases in the cost of recruiting and retaining these professionals. Updating this outdated policy would give rural hospitals greater flexibility to sustain these essential services and better meet the needs of their communities,” said Chad Austin, President and CEO, Kansas Hospital Association.
- Protecting seniors from insurance discrimination: The Guaranteeing Access to Supplemental Plans Act would give seniors an annual opportunity to switch Medicare Supplement plans without being denied coverage or charged more because of a pre-existing condition.
  - “My husband and I have been experiencing Medigap premium increases that are quite high considering how frequent they are. We are penalized for having a couple of minor “pre-existing” conditions, one of which requires no treatment. We are held hostage by our insurance providers because we cannot change companies without underwriting, resulting in even higher rates or refusal of coverage. Who at 65 or older does not have some form of a pre-existing condition? I appreciate Rep. Davids’ efforts to address this problem and work toward a solution that gives seniors more options and protects us from being trapped by our insurance providers,” said Shelly Toft, Lenexa resident.
- Protecting rural hospitals from sudden funding cuts: The Long-Term Rural Health Investment Act would phase in reimbursement changes and prevent abrupt federal payment limits from putting rural emergency care at risk.
- Keeping local clinics open when hospitals close: The Access to Community Care Act would prioritize federal grants for safety-net clinics that take on patients displaced by nearby healthcare facility closures, helping families maintain access to local primary care.
- Keeping maternity care close to home: The Maternity Care for Rural Communities Act would protect labor and delivery services at rural and Tribal hospitals from federal funding cuts, helping prevent new maternity care deserts.
- Making healthcare available to people with early-onset Alzheimer’s: The Early-Onset Alzheimer’s Coverage Act would allow adults diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s who do not qualify for Social Security Disability to buy into Medicare and access treatment, prescriptions, and specialized care.
  - “When my husband was diagnosed with younger-onset Alzheimer’s, our world turned upside down — and finding out he didn't qualify for Medicare because they spent years raising our children at home felt like a punch in the gut. Stay-at-home parents sacrifice so much for their families, and they shouldn't be cut off from life-saving healthcare when tragedy strikes. This bill is a true lifeline. I am so grateful to Representative Davids for standing up for families like mine, listening to our pain, and taking real action to fix this broken system,” said Nina Westvold, Overland Park resident.
"Healthcare costs are putting an enormous strain on Kansas families,” said April Holman, Executive Director, Alliance for a Healthy Kansas. “We hear from Kansans who are putting off needed care, rationing medication, or going without necessities to afford basic medical care. As premiums and deductibles continue to rise, so do medical debt. We need comprehensive solutions to lower costs, protect access to care in rural communities, and ensure every Kansan has access to affordable, quality healthcare in every stage of life."
“The high cost of living is crippling Kansas families, and the soaring costs of health care are a top concern," said David Jordan, President and CEO of the United Methodist Health Ministry Fund. "Unfortunately, health care costs will only go up for Kansans due to HR 1 and the failure of Congress to extend enhanced premium tax credits. Representative Sharice Davids’ (KS-03) comprehensive health care package will help reverse harmful cuts and help make care more affordable. The package will also help protect vulnerable rural Kansas hospitals and help keep maternity care close to home. This package is win for Kansas families, Kansas hospitals and providers, and Kansas communities.”
Throughout her time in Congress, Davids has championed policies to make healthcare more affordable and accessible. She voted to cap insulin costs at $35 per month for Medicare recipients, extend tax credits that help families afford insurance through the Affordable Care Act, and cap annual out-of-pocket drug costs for seniors. She also supported giving Medicare the power to negotiate drug prices — saving 74,000 Kansans up to 79 percent — and led efforts to ban surprise medical billing and increase transparency from insurers to help patients avoid costly out-of-network care.
title: Davids Fights Washington Healthcare Cuts with Plan to Lower Costs, Protect Kansas Hospitals

Reps. Houlahan, Smith Lead Members of Congress Demanding Answers on End to Tenured Appointments at Military Service Academies
  
  
    
      Washington,
      October 5, 2026
    
    
    
    
  
  
  
  
  
  
    
      
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Representatives Chrissy Houlahan (PA-06) and Adam Smith (WA-09) demanded answers on the Department of Defense’s decision to end appointments to tenured positions at military service academies. Specifically, the lawmakers questioned Secretary Pete Hegseth about the Department’s legal authority for this action, its intended application, and effects on existing faculty.  
“Congress has long recognized that the service academies have a dual mission: preparing cadets and midshipmen for military service while providing a rigorous academic education,” wrote the lawmakers. “Civilian faculty play an important role in making that possible.” 
The lawmakers continued, “Given this statutory and institutional history, we are concerned about the legal basis for the Department’s new policy and whether the directive is intended to prohibit future grants of tenure or to alter the status and employment protections of faculty who are currently tenured.” 
Rep. Houlahan is Ranking Member of the House Military Personnel Subcommittee and Rep. Smith is Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee. The Members were joined by Representatives Bobby Scott (VA-03), Ranking Member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, Pat Ryan (NY-18), representing the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, Sarah Elfreth (MD-03), representing the U.S. Naval Academy, Joe Courtney (CT-02), representing the U.S. Coast Guard Academy, and Chris Deluzio (PA-17).   
Secretary Hegseth is asked to provide a response by October 16, 2026. The full letter can be found here.

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the New York Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (“HSI”), Pete Gizas, Director of the New York Field Office of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”), Francis J. Russo, and Commissioner of the New York City Police Department (“NYPD”), Jessica S. Tisch, announced today that MIGUEL FRANCISCO MORA NUNEZ and CHRISTHIAN AYBAR-BERROA were sentenced to 180 months and 151 months in prison, respectively, for possession of ammunition as illegal aliens in connection with the shooting of an off-duty U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) Officer in Manhattan last summer. MORA NUNEZ and AYBAR-BERROA previously pled guilty before U.S. District Judge Loretta A. Preska, who imposed today’s sentences.

“Today’s sentences reflect our Office’s commitment to removing violent criminals from our streets,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Last summer, Mora Nunez and Aybar-Berroa, who were illegally in the United States, attempted to murder a member of the law enforcement community. Their actions shocked our city and caused devastating, lasting harm to the victims of their indiscriminate violence.”

“Today’s sentences reflect our Office’s commitment to removing violent criminals from our streets,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Last summer, Mora Nunez and Aybar-Berroa, who were illegally in the United States, attempted to murder a member of the law enforcement community. Their actions shocked our city and caused devastating, lasting harm to the victims of their indiscriminate violence.”

“This cold-blooded act of violence nearly cost a heroic officer his life simply because of the defendants’ indiscriminate targeting of innocent citizens,” said HSI New York Acting Special Agent in Charge Pete Gizas. “The defendants’ actions were an affront to every New Yorker who deserves to feel safe, and these sentences serve as a direct message that those who bring this level of danger to our streets will be held fully accountable. Working in lockstep with our law enforcement partners, HSI New York will never back down from investigating and pursuing those whose violence compromises the wellbeing and security of our citizens.”

“Today’s sentencing brings us another step closer to full justice for our officer and our entire community,” said CBP Director of Field Operations Francis J. Russo. “While our brave officer continues his courageous recovery, this resolution sends an unmistakable message that violence against law enforcement will be met with the full weight of the law. We are deeply grateful to the Southern District of New York, Homeland Security Investigations, and the New York City Police Department for their unwavering partnership throughout this process, ensuring that those responsible are held fully accountable for their heinous actions.”

According to the charging instruments and statements made in public filings and public court proceedings:

On July 19, 2025, at approximately 11:50 p.m., MORA NUNEZ shot an off-duty CBP Officer in Fort Washington Park in Manhattan. A bullet MORA NUNEZ fired struck the CBP Officer in the face and right arm. The CBP Officer returned fire, hitting MORA NUNEZ twice, before MORA NUNEZ fled on a motorbike driven by AYBAR-BERROA. AYBAR-BERROA later tried to get rid of the clothing he was wearing during the shooting because it was bloody and discussed with a relative of MORA NUNEZ that they needed to get rid of AYBAR-BERROA’s bloody clothes.

Both MORA NUNEZ and AYBAR-BERROA entered the United States illegally, are in the United States unlawfully, and are subject to orders of removal from the United States.

* * *

In addition to their prison terms, MORA NUNEZ, 22, and AYBAR-BERROA, 23, each of the Dominican Republic, were both sentenced to three years of supervised release.

Mr. McDonald thanked HSI, CBP, and the NYPD for their assistance in this case.

This case is being handled by the Office’s General Crimes Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mostafa Khairy, Samantha Fry, Meredith Foster, and Christy Slavik are in charge of the prosecution.
title: Two Dominican Republic Nationals Sentenced To 180 Months And 151 Months In Prison For Possession Of Ammunition By An Illegal Alien In Connection With The Shooting Of An Off-Duty CBP Officer

Today, Representatives Suzan DelBene (WA-01), Emily Randall (WA-06), Rick Larsen (WA-02), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Kim Schrier, M.D. (WA-08), Adam Smith (WA-09), Marilyn Strickland (WA-10), Jared Huffman (CA-02), Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), and Andrea Salinas (OR-06) sent a letter to U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz demanding answers and transparency regarding recent immigration enforcement activities on U.S. Forest Service (USFS) lands. 
This letter comes after a shocking incident over Labor Day weekend where U.S. Forest Service Law Enforcement Officers (LEO) may have coordinated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to arrest five men who were camping with their families in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. 
As of October 1, 2026, four of the five men arrested remain in detention at the Tacoma NW ICE Detention Center.   
“As Members of Congress representing the Pacific Northwest and Democratic leadership of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, the House Natural Resources Committee, and the House Agriculture Committee, we are concerned that the U.S. Forest Service is misusing taxpayer dollars by neglecting their mission and directing career staff to prioritize immigration enforcement on federal public lands. Particularly during a difficult wildfire season, we want to express our gratitude to the Forest Service for fighting wildfires in the Pacific Northwest and across the country,” the lawmakers wrote.  
The U.S. Forest Service has undergone significant funding cuts and reorganization efforts since the start of Trump’s second term. Since 2025, the USFS has lost nearly 6,000 workers through DOGE cuts and other factors, raising concerns about wildfire preparedness, forest health research, and public land management. Earlier this year, USFS announced consolidation efforts to shutter research and development facilities nationwide. USFS backtracked on its original proposal to close 57 out of 77 research labs after public outcry. In September 2026, USFS announced it would still close 23 labs.   
The 2026 wildfire season is still underway, and Washington state has recorded one of its worst wildfire seasons to date, with almost 900,000 acres being burned as of early September.  
The lawmakers concluded the letter by demanding answers to the following questions by October 15, 2026:
Questions for the U.S. Forest Service:  
    - Which agency first identified those arrested as targets for investigation, when were they identified, and what information about the targets was used to justify the raid? 
- Can you confirm that the law enforcement officers that first approached the families were employees of the USFS?  
- To what extent did USFS participate in the raid, and under what authority? Please provide any agreement or memorandum that governs cooperation between the U.S. Forest Service and DHS. 
- Please provide any agreement or memorandum between the U.S. Forest Service and DHS that governs the collection and sharing of visitors' identification and reservation data with DHS or ICE. 
- What other immigration raids has the U.S. Forest Service participated in since January 21, 2025? 
- What appropriations account(s) has the USFS used to fund its participation in immigration enforcement operations since January 21, 2025, and how much funding has been obligated or expended for this purpose? 
- Has any USFS law enforcement personnel time, budget, or resources been reallocated from other law enforcement priorities (e.g., resource protection, search and rescue, wildfire-adjacent enforcement) to support immigration enforcement operations? If so, how much of this reallocation has been disclosed to Congress since these funds were appropriated for land management and resource protection purposes rather than immigration enforcement? 
- Given limited agency resources, why is it a priority of the USFS to use employees in the targeting of families on public land? 
The full letter can be found 
here
.

LOS ANGELES – A Koreatown man pleaded guilty today to assaulting security officers assisting federal law enforcement by throwing two Molotov cocktails inside a federal building in downtown Los Angeles, and to possessing additional unregistered destructive devices.

José Francisco Jovel, 54, pleaded guilty to one count of assault on a person assisting federal officers and employees and one count of possession of unregistered or unlawfully manufactured destructive devices.

Jovel has been in federal custody since December 2025.

According to his plea agreement, on the morning of December 1, 2025, Jovel approached a federal building located in the Civic Center of downtown Los Angeles, carrying multiple bags containing a flame torch, two airsoft guns, five knives, pepper spray, and seven additional Molotov cocktails he had constructed. Each device was made using a glass Nescafe jar, ignitable liquid, and a fabric wick.

While standing outside the employee entrance, Jovel yelled at federal officers and security guards assisting them, stating that if children were not present, he would “kill them.” After waiting for an employee to exit the doorway, Jovel reached into a bag and threw a Molotov cocktail at one of the security guards. The device shattered, spreading glass and ignitable liquid toward law enforcement officers and members of the public.

Jovel then threw a second Molotov cocktail through the public entrance of the building, where individuals were waiting to go through security. That device rolled across the floor inside the building.

Jovel admitted that he intentionally threw the devices at federal officers and those assisting them, intending and attempting to inflict injury, and that his actions caused reasonable apprehension of immediate bodily harm. He also admitted that the Molotov cocktails were destructive devices that were not registered with the National Firearm Registration and Transfer Record.

United States District Judge Otis D. Wright II scheduled a sentencing hearing for January 28, 2027 at 8:00 a.m. at which time, Jovel will face a statutory maximum sentence of 30 years in federal prison.

The FBI is investigating this matter with assistance from the Federal Protective Service, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Homeland Security Investigations, the Los Angeles Police Department, and the Los Angeles Fire Department.

Assistant United States Attorney Lana Morton Owens and Jenna W. Long of the National Security Division are prosecuting this case.
title: Koreatown Man Pleads Guilty to Throwing Molotov Cocktails at Security Guards Inside Federal Building in Downtown L.A.

United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods announced that Joshua Hollum, 47, of Yankton, South Dakota, was sentenced on September 24, 2026, in federal court in Lincoln, Nebraska, for one count of possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine actual and one count of possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. United States District Judge Susan M. Bazis sentenced Hollum to a total of 180 months’ imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system. After Hollum’s release from prison, he will begin a 5-year term of supervised release.

On February 4, 2025, Nebraska State Troopers responded to reports of a hit and run on Interstate-80 in Buffalo County. They found a silver vehicle with heavy front-end damage and smoke coming out of its engine. Hollum was identified as the driver and sole occupant of the vehicle. When directed to exit the vehicle, he had a loaded syringe sticking out of the breast pocket on his t-shirt. The syringe was seized and the liquid inside tested positive for methamphetamine.

Troopers arrested Hollum and his vehicle was searched. Troopers found a backpack on the passenger seat, which contained methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, fentanyl, 9 clonazepam pills, 8 buprenorphine pills, marijuana, a loaded Sig Sauer P320 handgun with an extended magazine containing 17 9mm rounds, an additional extended magazine containing 30 9mm rounds, unused plastic bags, and a digital scale with drug residue on it.

The controlled substances were sent to the State Patrol Crime Laboratory. The lab confirmed at least 400 grams of methamphetamine actual, 0.9 grams of cocaine, 1.2 grams of heroin, and 4 grams of fentanyl.

This case was investigated by the TRIDENT and CODE Task Forces which is made up of law enforcement agencies throughout a 22-county area in west-central/southwest Nebraska and includes the North Platte Police Department, Lexington Police Department, Dawson County Sheriff’s Office, Ogallala Police Department, Nebraska State Patrol, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).

text:
MATSUI, DUCKWORTH, SCHUMER LEAD BIPARTISAN CALL REQUIRING FAA TO GUARANTEE EVERY EMERGENCY MEDICAL KIT ABOARD FLIGHTS INCLUDE LIFE-SAVING EPINEPHRINE
WASHINGTON D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Doris Matsui (D-CA-07), Co-Chair of the Congressional Food Allergy Research Caucus, U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL),Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation, and U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) led a group of 20 bipartisan, bicameral lawmakers in calling on the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to guarantee that emergency medical kits (EMK) on every commercial aircraft include epinephrine, a life-saving medication to treat passengers who go into anaphylactic shock. Today is the final day for the American people to submit public comments on the FAA’s dangerous new proposed rule that would result in medications being less consistent and dependable for passengers experiencing health emergencies on commercial flights—a severely misguided proposal that prioritizes flexibility for air carriers over the safety of the flying public.
“Without proper medications that can easily be administered on board, medical emergencies happening while 35,000 feet in the air could turn deadly,” wrote the lawmakers in their official public comment to the FAA’s proposed rule. “The provisions outlined in the FAA’s proposed rule threaten the safety of airline passengers traveling with allergies and reverse previous FAA action to ensure the safety of all passengers.”
In the landmark 2024 FAA Reauthorization Law that Congresswoman Matsui supported, the FAA requires commercial airlines to have adequate emergency medical kits on board to treat conditions like anaphylaxis. And yet, the FAA’s proposed rule would not require them to carry epinephrine—the only medication that reliably treats this medical emergency—in delivery methods that can be easily self-administered by individuals without medical training.
The lawmakers continued, “If a passenger is experiencing anaphylaxis, they could have mere seconds until they are unable to breathe. Without FDA-approved epinephrine delivery methods designed to be easily self-administered, passengers rely on the chance that there will be a good Samaritan on the flight who is a trained medical professional, or a flight attendant, in consultation with a medical professional on the ground, to quickly measure an appropriate dose of epinephrine using a vial and syringe. This is both risky and unnecessary; it is why the FAA’s working group recommended ‘pre-measured auto-delivery device’ be on the EMK contents list.”
In their letter, the lawmakers hammered the FAA’s proposed rule for ignoring expert recommendations, creating an even greater lack of transparency and consistency in EMKs for the flying public—who rely on EMKs during a medical emergency—and for needlessly putting the lives of commercial airline passengers at greater risk.
“To ensure the safety of all airline passengers, we must guarantee that U.S.-based airlines include FDA-approved epinephrine delivery methods designed for self-administration on every flight,” the lawmakers concluded.
In light of the FAA’s misguided and dangerous proposed rule change, Matsui, Duckworth, and Schumer are calling on the FAA to heed their concerns—as well as the more than 1,500 public comments that have been submitted to express deep concern over this would-be policy failure that would place cost cutting and convenience for air carriers over the safety of the flying public.
In addition to Matsui, the letter is co-signed in the House by U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA-01), Maxwell Frost (D-FL-10), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX-29), Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ-05), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-08), LaMonica McIver (D-NJ-10), Kelly Morrison (D-MN-03) and Mike Quigley (D-IL-05). In addition to Duckworth and Schumer, the letter is co-signed in the Senate by U.S. Senators Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Jack Reed (D-RI) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI).
Full text of the letter can be found below and HERE.
Dear Administrator Bedford:
We write to provide our comments on the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published on August 5, 2026, which would make drastic changes to how the FAA determines the composition of the emergency medical kit (EMK) carried aboard aircraft. The proposed rule is opaque and dangerous, and it threatens to undermine previous work the FAA has done to ensure the safety of the traveling public.
EMKs are supposed to enable initial treatment of a passenger experiencing moderate to severe injuries or illnesses until the aircraft can land and the passenger can be transferred to emergency medical personnel. Without proper medications that can easily be administered on board, medical emergencies happening while 35,000 feet in the air could turn deadly.
The proposed rule would make harmful steps to reverse work done at the agency to direct operators to include epinephrine in aircraft EMKs. Having multiple doses of epinephrine on every aircraft, in delivery methods that can be easily self-administered by individuals without medical training, is more urgent than ever. This is due to the on-flight presence of food items containing unlabeled allergens, a steady increase in the number of children with food allergies, the increased prevalence of a tick-borne illness that could create life-threatening allergies and the very real possibility that more than one passenger may require epinephrine during a single flight.
The provisions outlined in the FAA’s proposed rule threaten the safety of airline passengers traveling with allergies and reverse previous FAA action to ensure the safety of all passengers.
Our concerns about the proposed rule are outlined below:
Lack of Alignment with Previous Recommendations
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 directed the FAA to assemble a panel of experts to make recommendations on EMKs and issue a proposed rule. The FAA Onboard Medical Kits Working Group included aerospace medicine experts and physicians, physiologists, psychologists, human factors specialists, cabin safety professionals and researchers. This working group submitted its report, dated May 1, 2025, to the FAA. The report stated:
“The items proposed … are intended to provide initial stabilizing Basic Life Support (BLS) care for immediately life-threatening conditions such as cardiac arrest, airway emergencies, major hemorrhage, andanaphylaxis (emphasis added), as well as to facilitate provision of limited basic first-aid interventions for minor injuries and illnesses that are known to occur in-flight.”
Importantly, the proposed EMK content list in the report includes both “pre-measured auto-delivery device” or “vial-drawn kit.” Yet, just one year later, the FAA publicly defied the recommendations in this report developed by the expert working group the FAA itself commissioned.
No Clear Requirement for Epinephrine
Through rulemaking, the Trump administration is seeking to downgrade the EMK content list, from a binding requirement to mere optional guidance. The proposed rule would allow operators to determine what components should be included in EMKs, so long as the EMK is “practical and sufficient” to address nine conditions, including anaphylaxis:
“…FAA recommends sufficient resources for anaphylaxis (sudden/acute severe allergic reaction), which may include the following signs and symptoms: hives; swelling of the mouth, throat, or tongue; difficulty breathing, rapid or weak pulse, dizziness; stomach pain; nausea or vomiting; or loss of consciousness. Treatment options could (emphasis added) include medication such as epinephrine.”
Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. The final rule must contain a clear directive that EMKs shall include epinephrine.
No Requirement for Epinephrine in Easily Self-Administered Forms
If a passenger is experiencing anaphylaxis, they could have mere seconds until they are unable to breathe. Without Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved epinephrine delivery methods designed to be easily self-administered, passengers rely on the chance that there will be a good Samaritan on the flight who is a trained medical professional, or a flight attendant, in consultation with a medical professional on the ground, to quickly measure an appropriate dose of epinephrine using a vial and syringe. This is both risky and unnecessary; it is why the FAA’s working group recommended “pre-measured auto-delivery device” be on the EMK contents list.
Currently, JetBlue, Southwest, Breeze and Frontier stock their EMKs with epinephrine auto-injectors, and American Airlines’ EMKs include both adult- and pediatric-dose epinephrine auto-injectors. Delta is in the process of transitioning its fleet to include auto-injectors in their EMKs by September 2027, and, this year, United Airlines and Allegiant Airlines will begin the work to include auto-injectors in EMKs. Even with tight profit margins, including epinephrine in delivery methods that can be easily self-administered, is possible. Through the rulemaking process, the FAA must direct airlines to include epinephrine in delivery methods that can be easily administered and not reverse course from its previous recommendations by abandoning the requirement to include epinephrine in EMKs in entirety.
Lack of Transparency on Compliance
The proposed rule would eliminate the exemption process, which was created to account for challenges in stocking EMKs due to drug shortages and allow airlines to substitute drugs, “without requesting an FAA exemption.” Airlines are not required to publicly or centrally report the real-time inventory and exact contents of their EMKs and have continued to operate under exemptions granted by the FAA for years. EMK suppliers and airlines can track when an EMK is opened and needs restocking, but only in instances where the kit was used. There is no means of systematically tracking incidents of allergic reactions or anaphylaxis, especially when passengers use their own epinephrine. For medical conditions that can be treated by multiple, accessible options, eliminating the need for the exemption process may make sense. However, epinephrine is the only first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. The public also deserves to know when certain items are not included in a flight’s EMK, and a rationale for the exclusion.
Conclusion
The proposed rule will reduce public safety and trust when flying by increasing ambiguity, subjectivity and opacity of EMK components. The proposed rule argues that increased flexibility is needed to keep up with advances in medicine but, without appropriate reporting and tracking, the Trump administration is significantly increasing the risk of major inconsistencies in EMKs from flight to flight. Predictability, consistency and transparency are all necessary to ensure passengers’ safety, particularly in cases of anaphylaxis, when minutes, or even seconds, matter.
To ensure the safety of all airline passengers,we must guarantee that U.S.-based airlines include FDA-approved epinephrine delivery methods designed for self-administration on every flight.
We call on the FAA to address the concerns outlined in this letter.
title: MATSUI, DUCKWORTH, SCHUMER LEAD BIPARTISAN CALL REQUIRING FAA TO GUARANTEE EVERY EMERGENCY MEDICAL KIT ABOARD FLIGHTS INCLUDE LIFE-SAVING EPINEPHRINE

text:
Pou Demands Answers After 5,500-Gallon Data Center Diesel Spill
Record-setting leak fouled creek connected to Hackensack River
PATERSON, NJ – Congresswoman Nellie Pou (D-NJ-09) is seeking answers from the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) following a massive diesel fuel spill at an Equinix data center in Secaucus that contaminated local waterways in her district.
Pou called for a full accounting of the roughly 5,500-gallon spill, its environmental impact, and the safeguards being put in place to prevent another data center disaster.
“This spill in the Ninth District was the largest data center fuel spill on record in our state. The scale of this disaster demands a full accounting. We need to understand how it happened, ensure the cleanup is complete, and put protections in place to prevent another one happening again. Our residents deserve clear answers now,” Congresswoman Pou writes to New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection Commissioner Ed Potosnak.
Secaucus and surrounding communities have lived with pollution for decades. Contamination from industrial sites and landfill runoff led the Environmental Protection Agency to designate the Lower Hackensack River a Superfund site in 2022. Now as a major cleanup is underway, the September 11 Equinix spill has dumped another 5,500 gallons of diesel into the local environment.
The Secaucus spill comes amid growing national concern over the environmental impact and public costs of rapidly expanding data centers. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and can require significant water for cooling. Also, as seen in Secaucus, they can often store large quantities of diesel to power backup generators.
Data center electricity demand is rising rapidly, raising questions about energy costs and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve these facilities. The Secaucus spill highlights what can happen when the systems designed to keep these massive facilities running fail.
Pou concludes, “NJDEP has a vital role in protecting New Jersey’s environment and holding data centers and their owners accountable when safeguards fail. The scale of this disaster demands a full accounting. . . . Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
A copy of Congresswoman Pou’s letter is below.
Dear Commissioner Potosnak:
I write to express my concern about the recent fuel spill at the Equinix data center in Secaucus that contaminated nearby waterways. Over the last decade, several data centers have experienced large-scale fuel spills, including several in New Jersey. In 2017, roughly 600 gallons of fuel spilled into Clifton’s storm drains from the Digital Realty EWR21 Data Center. Then, in 2022, more than 1800 gallons leaked from an Equinix-owned data center in North Bergen. Now, just weeks ago, Secaucus has experienced the largest data center diesel spill on record in our state. Residents and local officials deserve to know how this happened, what damage it caused, and what safeguards will keep this from happening again.
Secaucus and the surrounding communities have a long history of dealing with pollution. Decades of contamination from manufacturing plants and landfill runoff into the Hackensack River prompted the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to designate the Lower Hackensack River as a Superfund site in 2022. The river is already undergoing a major cleanup after those years of contamination.
Against that backdrop, the September 11 spill is especially alarming. According to public reports, roughly 5,500 gallons of diesel fuel escaped the Equinix data center into a creek and tributary connected to the Hackensack River.5 The spill reportedly occurred during an automated fuel-recycling process and has been attributed to a “computer glitch.”
Three weeks later, the public still lacks a full accounting of the spill’s impact on local waterways and wildlife. The incident also raises broader questions about the environmental risks posed by data centers, including the storage and handling of large quantities of backup fuel. Those questions are particularly urgent here given the major federal cleanup underway on the Hackensack River.
I appreciate that NJDEP is working to investigate and address the spill. But NJDEP must provide a clear account of exactly what happened and what is being done to prevent another spill to ensure transparency and accountability. To that end, please provide answers to the following questions no later than October 9, 2026.
1) Please identify the best available timeline for when each of the following events occurred on September 11, 2026 and any days thereafter:
a) Equinix began its fuel recycling process.
b) The system failed, and fuel began spilling.
c) Equinix first identified the spill.
d) The flow of fuel was stopped.
e) Equinix first contacted emergency responders.
f) Equinix first notified NJDEP.
g) The emergency response team arrived on site.
h) Crews began containment efforts to prevent the diesel from spreading.
i) NJDEP first notified Secaucus officials about the spill and the response.
j) Any barges or other cleanup equipment that were removed from the site, and the basis for determining they were no longer needed.
2) Has NJDEP continued to brief Secaucus on the containment and cleanup? If so, please provide the dates of those communications. If not, please explain why.
3) Following the spill, has NJDEP required Equinix or other data centers to adopt human, on-site monitoring and other safeguards for automated fuel systems or other risks to the community? If so, please describe those requirements. If not, please explain why.
4) Has NJDEP determined whether diesel from the spill reached the Hackensack River? If so, please provide its findings and any information on remediation and cleanup.
5) When does NJDEP expect to complete its investigation and issue a final public report on the spill?
NJDEP has a vital role in protecting New Jersey’s environment and holding data centers and their owners accountable when safeguards fail. This spill in the Ninth District was the largest data center fuel spill on record in our state. The scale of this disaster demands a full accounting. We need to understand how it happened, ensure the cleanup is complete, and put protections in place to prevent another one happening again. Our residents deserve clear answers now.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your prompt response.
Sincerely,
Nellie Pou
Member of Congress
###
title: Pou Demands Answers After 5,500-Gallon Data Center Diesel Spill

An investigation conducted by ICE Homeland Security Investigations Dallas, police departments in Arlington and Forney, as well as sheriff’s offices in Green and Hays Counties, discovered Sahi was producing and was in possession of child sexual abuse material.
Sahi pleaded guilty to the charges on April 1 and has been sentenced to 35 years in federal prison.
President Trump has made it a top priority to make our nation secure and our communities safer. By restoring law and order and locking up the worst of the worst, ICE HSI is delivering on the President’s promise to the American people. There is no room for child predators and those who commit such heinous crimes will be found and prosecuted.

“This lengthy sentence sends a resounding message: Child predators will find no safe harbor in the Northern District of Texas,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “We will find them and ensure they face the full weight of federal prosecution. Our commitment to protecting children is absolute, and we hope this outcome serves as a clear deterrent to anyone contemplating similar crimes.”
According to court documents, authorities arrested Sahi for sexual assault of a child on Feb. 28, 2025. Law enforcement believed Sahi was communicating with a 14-year-old girl from his residence in Arlington. Sahi would pick up the girl outside her home in Forney and transport her to various locations to sexually assault her.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Eugene Vindman (D-Va.-07) joined Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.-10) and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) in a letter warning the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) about the potential consequences of the proposed merger between NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) and Dominion Energy (“Dominion”), and urged the regulator to closely examine the deal and block it if it would increase consumers’ energy costs or otherwise fail to meet public interest requirements.
On May 18, 2026, NextEra announced a $66.8 billion deal to merge with Dominion. The proposed deal would eliminate a competitor in the energy generation market and create the largest regulated electric utility in the world. It would be the fourth largest merger of all time and would create a company worth $420 billion.
A NextEra-Dominion entity would serve about 10 million homes and businesses across Virginia, Florida, North Carolina, and South Carolina, but the effects of the merger — including higher electricity rates — could extend even further. Residential electricity prices have risen 15 percent since January 2025, and families are projected to spend an average of $110 more on electricity bills in 2026 than they did last year.
The full text of the letter can be found here.
“The merger would give the combined company control over approximately a quarter of the electricity in the New England region, leading to considerable negotiating leverage over states and the ability to demand abusive terms at the expense of households,” wrote the lawmakers. “This megamerger may consolidate competitive power markets and raise electricity rates even more for American families.”
Under the Federal Power Act, FERC shall approve a merger of public utilities only if the applicants demonstrate that the merger is in the public interest and does not pose a risk of harmful cross-subsidization, and may block a merger that is not “consistent with the public interest.”
“Our fundamental concern is that this new entity will be both a gigantic power generator and a gigantic power-providing utility,” wrote the lawmakers. “We urge you to closely scrutinize this merger and block it if the Commission determines it would increase market concentration or have an adverse effect on costs for consumers—or if the acquisition is otherwise not in the public interest.”
The lawmakers are concerned that a NextEra-Dominion merger would create an even larger vertically integrated electricity utility and electricity generator that will squash competition and raise prices. Previous utility mergers have coincided with increases in household electricity costs. Additionally, a merger increasing the market share of already vertically integrated utility companies could make it even easier for the combined entity to engage in improper “cross-subsidization,” a practice by which corporations unfairly shift onto consumers the cost of transactions between utility companies and affiliate companies, which researchers say forces households to pay higher electricity rates.
“The consequences of failing to address utility merger harms, including by imposing insufficient mitigation measures, are not theoretical: when FERC allows utility companies to gain enough power to stamp out competition in an entire region, higher prices have followed,” wrote the lawmakers.
The lawmakers also warned that large utility companies that are intertwined with generating entities have strong incentives to oppose building transmission connections to bring in cheaper power from other regions, a problem that could get worse with the creation of a giant like NextEra-Dominion. New England states have accused NextEra of using its existing power to obstruct new transmission infrastructure projects.
“We therefore urge FERC to closely examine whether this deal may decrease competition or cause electricity rates for households to climb even higher; to remain skeptical of mitigation conditions that have historically failed to blunt the negative impacts of large utility merges; and to deny the application unless the applicants demonstrate that the transaction will have no adverse effect, now or in the future, on competition, rates, or regulation and will not result in impermissible cross-subsidization or the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets,” concluded the lawmakers. “If the present record is insufficient to make those findings, the Commission should deny the application.”
Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Representatives Chris Deluzio (Pa.-17), Maggie Goodlander (N.H.-2), Raja Krishnamoorthi (Ill.-08), and Seth Magaziner (R.I.-02) also signed the letter.
BACKGROUND
In August, Congressman Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) was the first member of the Virginia delegation to speak out against the proposed merger. He sent a letter to members of the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) urging them to reject the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra energy. In the letter, Vindman warned that the deal would put Wall Street profits ahead of Virginia families, weaken local accountability, and increase costs for consumers. You can read his letter here.
Later that month, Vindman launched a district-wide survey asking for constituents’ thoughts on the proposed merger. The results were clear: of 950 respondents, the overwhelmingly majority opposed the merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy, underscoring widespread concerns about the deal’s potential impact on Virginia ratepayers.

BOSTON – A West Bridgewater man was sentenced today in federal court in Boston for drug conspiracy and firearm charges, following a series of arrests targeting gangs in the Brockton and Randolph areas.

Lue Andrade, a/k/a “Poncho,” 31, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Brian E. Murphy to 80 months in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release. In July 2026 , Andrade pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances and four counts of being a felon in possession of a firearm. In February 2026 , federal complaints were unsealed against seven defendants charged with drug and firearm crimes.

Andrade was arrested on Dec. 17, 2025, following searches at numerous residences and stash houses associated with the Brockton-based Harvard Street Gang and their Randolph-based affiliates including Andrade’s residence in West Bridgewater and his stash house in Brockton. In his residence, two handguns, ammunition, multiple pounds of marijuana and packaging materials were seized. The stash location was a second-floor apartment that was set up as drug repackaging workshop. The apartment contained dozens of pounds of marijuana, some of which was discovered in hidden compartments within the walls. In the basement, two rifles, a pistol, an extended magazine and various ammunition were also seized. Andrade was prohibited from possessing firearms due to a prior state conviction for drug dealing from 2016.

The drug conspiracy to which Andrade pleaded guilty went back to March 2023, when authorities executed search warrants at Andrade’s then-residence in Bridgewater and a different stash apartment in Brockton. In that stash location, a backpack containing hundreds of grams of fentanyl and cocaine were recovered.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; and Colonel Geoffrey D. Noble, Superintendent of the Massachusetts State Police made the announcement. Valuable assistance was provided by Homeland Security Investigations, Boston Division; the Abington, Acushnet, Ashland, Boston, Braintree, Bridgewater, Brockton, Chelsea, East Bridgewater, Medford, Quincy, Randolph, Raynham, Stoughton, Taunton and West Bridgewater Police Departments; Plymouth and Suffolk County Sheriff’s Departments; Massachusetts Department of Correction; and the Plymouth, Norfolk and Suffolk County District Attorney’s Offices. Assistant U.S. Attorneys David Cutshall and Philip A. Mallard of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit prosecuted the case.

California Woman Arrested on Charges Alleging She Acted as Agent of China and Spied on Relatives of U.S. Based High-Ranking Taiwanese Government Official
Wanying Zhang, 34, also known as Heather Zhang, of Irvine, California, was arrested Sunday on a one count complaint charging her with acting in the United States as an unregistered agent of the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), including by conducting surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official.
“The central allegation here — that Zhang, at the behest of the People’s Republic of China, covertly surveilled relatives of a high-ranking foreign government official in the United States — is deeply troubling,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division and U.S. Attorney’s Offices, along with the FBI and other law enforcement partners, will remain vigilant against threats like this on our soil.”
“Protecting our national security means confronting foreign governments that engage in covert operations in our nation,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Ms. Zhang is charged with acting at the direction of Chinese government officials to spy on the family of a senior Taiwanese official here in the United States. She violated our laws and will be held accountable in our courts. We will aggressively investigate and prosecute illegal foreign operations on American soil.”
“The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Wanying Zhang’s arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China’s authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI’s unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government — and any foreign adversary — to conduct transnational repression within our borders.”
Zhang was arrested prior to her planned departure from Los Angeles International Airport, where she planned to board a flight to China. She is expected to make her initial appearance and be arraigned this afternoon in U.S. District Court in downtown Los Angeles.
According to the complaint, from June 2025 to September 2025, Zhang acted as an agent of the PRC without prior notification to the Attorney General of the United States, as required by federal law.
At the direction and control of PRC officials, Zhang coordinated with other individuals to promote the interests of China by, among other things, conducting surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official at their residence in the United States.
In June 2025, Zhang traveled from Southern California to China, where she met with PRC officials and was tasked with conducting surveillance in the United States.
On Aug. 29, 2025, Zhang and another individual flew from John Wayne Airport in Orange County to Las Vegas. On Sept. 1, 2025, they flew from Las Vegas to the Pacific Northwest, where the victims reside. On that date, Zhang messaged a PRC official that she was “Boarding now” and sent a photograph of her boarding pass.
Upon their arrival, Zhang and the other individual traveled to the victims’ residence and conducted surveillance. Zhang sent the same PRC official the following message: “Saw him, young male, it’s the young one.” When this official asked her to join an audio call, she replied, “I am videorecording.”
Zhang also sent the same official the license plate numbers for the two vehicles parked in front of the victims’ home.
If convicted, Zhang would face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
The FBI Los Angeles Field Office is investigating the case.
Senior Counsel Scott M. Lara of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda B. Elbogen and Colin S. Scott for the Central District of California are prosecuting the case.
A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
