SEC’s Division of Examinations Announces New Exam Handbook
Washington D.C., Oct. 1, 2026 —
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Examinations today published its new handbook, “The SEC Exam Handbook: A Practical Guide on Process and Engagement,” which replaces and expands upon the previous examination brochure by providing registrants with more insight and detail about what to expect during an examination.
The new handbook provides a clear roadmap of the process used by division examiners across the country to help ensure consistency and is designed to emphasize the Commission’s commitment to approach each examination with an accessible and collaborative mindset. In addition to supporting the SEC’s mission, division examinations are designed to improve industry practices and compliance, monitor risk, and prevent fraud.
“The Division of Examinations is a crucial part of how the SEC provides market oversight and protects investors. The Division’s new handbook clarifies the examination process, offering regulated entities greater insight into what to expect during an exam and establishing clear expectations,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “The transparency this handbook provides will make examinations more effective and further help the SEC fulfill its mission of protecting investors, facilitating capital formation, and maintaining fair, orderly, and efficient markets.”
“The division’s goal to be more accessible provides registrants and the Commission with a more efficient and effective examination program,” said Keith Cassidy, Director of the SEC’s Division of Examinations. “By answering the call from registrants to provide more clarity to the exam process, we aim to make the process more consistent and predictable for everyone involved.”
The Examination Process Handbook covers each stage of an exam, from the risk assessment process through to the disposition letter, along with several avenues to provide feedback or ask questions. The handbook also provides registrants with practical tips and helpful resources to prepare for an exam and stay current on compliance obligations.
###

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Tyler Daugherty, age 32, of York County, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on September 29, 2026, to 78 months’ imprisonment by United States District Judge Jennifer P. Wilson for receiving child pornography. The court also ordered Daugherty to serve a five-year term of supervised release following his release from prison and required him to pay victims $9,000 in restitution.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, Daugherty obtained child pornography by using the “Tor” browser to access the “dark” web and was discovered to be in possession of hundreds of images and videos of child pornography when the FBI searched his Mount Wolf home in 2025.

When imposing the 78-month sentence, Judge Wilson highlighted that Daugherty had acquired child pornography over more than six years and that some of the images he possessed depicted the sexual abuse of toddlers. Judge Wilson also referred to victim impact statements that had been submitted prior to sentencing, which she noted attested to the lasting harms caused by those who possess and view child pornography.

The FBI Philadelphia’s Capital Area Resident Agency investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Christian T. Haugsby prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC.

San Diego, CA – Last week, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) hosted a virtual training event with Rep. Juan Vargas (CA-52) and representatives from Kids Belong in Classrooms and Immigrant Defenders Law Center. The webinar helped ensure community members understand how to safely interact with federal law enforcement officers, what to do if they or their loved ones are detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and what resources are available to San Diego’s immigrant community.

During the week of September 7th, San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) and San Diego City College both informed the Congressman's office of ICE arrest activity outside their schools. These are in addition to a dramatic increase in ICE activity across San Diego County, especially around sensitive locations like schools, childcare facilities, hospitals, courthouses, and places of worship.

“Regardless of your immigration status, you have certain rights in this country,” said Rep. Peters. “These resources are more important than ever as community members continue to navigate frightening and lawless interactions with federal law enforcement officers under the Trump Administration. Until ICE operations change to responsibly target dangerous criminals instead of hardworking families, I will continue to push for real reforms and hold the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accountable for the fear it has inflicted on my constituents and communities across the country.”

“Everyone has constitutional rights when interacting with ICE or law enforcement – regardless of immigration status. As ICE continues to target our communities, it’s more important than ever that people know their rights and understand how to exercise them,” said Rep. Juan Vargas. “Thank you to my colleague, Rep. Scott Peters, for holding this important Know Your Rights training to help us look out for one another.”

Watch and share a recording of the training here. Additional resources from Kids Belong in Classrooms and Immigrant Defenders Law Center can be accessed below:

Toolkit for Organizing in Your School Community

Spanish Kids Belong in Classrooms Toolkit

How to Talk to Your Kids About ICE Enforcement

How to Make a Family Preparedness Plan

San Diego Immigration Hotline: (858) 751-7553. The Hotline is monitored Monday-Friday from 9am-6pm

Further Background:

Rep. Peters joined his California colleagues to call on DHS to end ICE enforcement activity around schools and educational institutions in San Diego County.

Rep. Peters is an original cosponsor of the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would bar immigration enforcement within 1,000 feet of schools, hospitals, and churches except in true emergencies. He also introduced the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, a bill to make our communities safer by establishing a stronger standard for Federal immigration agents' use of force. Rep. Peters has pushed Congress to pass these commonsense reforms, but they have been blocked by the Republican majority.

U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Phone: 206-815-6689
LOS ANGELES — The Coast Guard, L.A. County Fire Department and L.A. County Sheriff’s Department are responding to a helicopter crash offshore Pebbly Beach, Santa Catalina Island, Wednesday night.
Coast Guard Sector Los Angeles-Long Beach command center watchstanders received a notification from Baywatch Avalon personnel at approximately 7:50 p.m. that an Airbus H-135 medical helicopter with five people aboard crashed offshore Pebbly Beach.
Watchstanders diverted a Coast Guard Air Station Ventura MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew and coordinated the launch of a Coast Guard Station Los Angeles-Long Beach 45-foot Response Boat-Medium crew.
L.A. County Fire Department personnel coordinated the launch of crews from Baywatch Avalon, Baywatch Cabrillo, Baywatch Isthmus and multiple air assets.
Four individuals were recovered from the water. Two of the individuals were transferred to a hospital on the mainland and two were pronounced deceased.
One individual is still unaccounted for and the search remains ongoing.

Bill Text (PDF)

BOSTON, MA – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) and Congressman Eugene Vindman (VA-07) introduced the Wigs for Warriors Act, legislation that would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss.

“When individuals in our military families experience severe hair loss, they should be met with the support and care they need to feel like their authentic selves,” said Rep. Pressley. “Through my own experience with alopecia areata, I understand the psychological, social, and economic impact that comes with navigating severe hair loss—and I know that we can do something to lighten the load. For some, accessing medical-grade wigs can make all the difference. That’s why I’m proud to lead the Wigs for Warriors Act alongside Rep. Vindman and bring much-deserved relief and support to TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata and other hair loss conditions.”

“I heard directly from a constituent, a 16-year-old from Prince William County and daughter of a U.S. Marine, who lost all of her hair to alopecia areata by the end of second grade. She told my team how a medical-grade wig could have helped her navigate the emotional and social challenges of losing her hair, but that these wigs can be incredibly expensive,” said Vindman. “This bill, which I am proud to lead alongside Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, will help ensure TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata, like my constituent, have access to the care and support they need to feel comfortable and confident.”

TRICARE, the insurance for servicemembers and military families, has extremely limited coverage for individuals experiencing severe hair loss. Currently, patients with alopecia areata receive no coverage for a cranial prosthesis — a medical-grade, custom-fitted wig designed to address medically related hair loss.

The bill would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss, as certified by a physician. Coverage would also extend to hair loss resulting from chemotherapy, regardless of the underlying condition being treated.

The legislation would also eliminate TRICARE’s current lifetime limit of one prosthesis per patient, allowing cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy to receive coverage for multiple wigs as medically necessary.

The Wigs for Warriors Act is supported by the National Alopecia Areata Foundation (NAAF).

“The National Alopecia Areata Foundation applauds the introduction of the Wigs for Warriors Act of 2026 and thanks Representative Vindman for his efforts to improve the lives of members of the military and their families living with the autoimmune disease alopecia areata,” said Ryan Reczek, President & CEO of the National Alopecia Areata Foundation. “This legislation is critical to ensure that medically necessary cranial prostheses, also known as medical wigs, that are used to restore well-being and support mental health, are affordable and accessible under TRICARE.”

“This act is life changing for both the military and medical hair loss communities, allowing for better mental health of our service members and their families,” said a 16-year-old resident of Prince William County with alopecia areata. “Representative Vindman and his team not only took the time to listen to my story but have moved forward to resolving the issue. I am forever grateful.”

Text of the bill can be accessed here.

BACKGROUND

Alopecia areata is a common autoimmune disease that causes the immune system to attack a person’s hair follicles, resulting in patchy or complete hair loss across the scalp and body. Nearly 6.7 million people in the United States are directly affected by alopecia areata, with about 700,000 currently living with active disease. The remaining millions have had the disease or will likely develop it at some point.

Alopecia areata carries a substantial mental health burden and wigs are a documented, effective way to manage it. The psychological impact of alopecia areata can be profound, with elevated rates of anxiety and depression, increased time off work, and impaired quality of life, stemming largely from the fact that hair plays a crucial role in shaping an individual’s identity, self-esteem, and social interactions. This burden is especially acute for young people who develop the condition.

Congresswoman Pressley has been steadfast in her advocacy for women’s health, ending race-based hair discrimination, and introducing policies that affirm the right of women to show up in the world as their full, authentic selves.

On March 18, 2026, Congresswoman Pressley, alongside Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) and Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04) reintroduced the Recognition of Traction Alopecia in Service Women Act, legislation that would support and expand medical coverage of traction alopecia in the military.

Rep. Pressley is a lead co-sponsor of the Creating a Respectful and Open World for Natural Hair (CROWN) Act, legislation with Reps. Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Barbara Lee (CA-13) and Ilhan Omar (MN-05) that would ban discrimination based on hair textures and hairstyles that are commonly associated with a particular race or national origin.

Congresswoman Pressley, alongside Congresswomen Brown and Velázquez, have led congressional efforts to ban formaldehyde in hair products. In March 2026, Rep. Pressley, alongside Congresswoman Shontel Brown (OH-11) and Congresswoman Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), introduced the Health Hair Act, legislation to effectively ban formaldehyde from hair products. Last year, they sent a letter to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requesting an update on delays in implementation of a rule to ban formaldehyde and other formaldehyde-releasing chemicals in hair products. In October 2023, the FDA proposed the ban of formaldehyde in hair products following a letter led by Reps. Pressley and Brown, which called on the agency to investigate the health risks associated with the chemical. However, the implementation of the ban has continuously been delayed.

In February 2026, Rep. Pressley, alongside Rep. Jim McGovern (MA-02) and Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), led their colleagues in re-introducing the Wigs as Durable Medical Equipment Act, legislation to help individuals affected by Alopecia Areata and patients with cancer who are undergoing chemotherapy by allowing medical wigs and other head coverings to be covered under the Medicare program.

Rep. Pressley leads the Anti-Racism in Public Health Act, a bicameral bill to declare structural racism a public health crisis and confront its public health impacts through two bold new programs within the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Rep. Pressley originally introduced the bill in September 2020.

In 2020, the House passed an amendment introduced by Congresswoman Pressley to provide $5 million dollars for the National Institutes of Health’s National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases to fund research on the causes, impacts, and possible treatments of Alopecia areata.

In December 2019, Rep. Pressley and her colleagues sent a letter to Johnson & Johnson Chairman and CEO Alex Gorsky seeking information on the targeted marketing and sale of the company’s talc-based baby powder and its potential to cause harm, particularly to women, teenage girls, and people of color, due to asbestos contamination.

###
title: Pressley, Vindman Introduce Legislation to Expand Alopecia Support for Military Families

U.S. Marshals in Wyoming Close Out ‘Operation Spring Cleaning’ with Arrest of Longstanding Fugitive
For immediate release
Michael J. Thomas, Ph.D., Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal
Cheyenne, WY — The U.S. Marshals Service District of Wyoming, in coordination with state and local law enforcement partners, apprehended Adrian Cunningham today, bringing a fugitive investigation spanning more than five years to a close and marking the conclusion of Operation Spring Cleaning.
Cunningham was wanted on a felony warrant for probation violation stemming from a burglary case. The warrant was issued in January 2021. His criminal history includes offenses involving firearms, narcotics, domestic assault, burglary, and probation violations.
Earlier this year, the District of Wyoming launched Operation Spring Cleaning, a multiagency initiative focused on locating individuals wanted on violent and other high-priority warrants while assisting Laramie County authorities in resolving longstanding fugitive cases. The operation resulted in multiple apprehensions in Wyoming and across the country.
Cunningham remained the final outstanding target of the operation.
Through continued investigative efforts, the task force developed information indicating Cunningham was in the Cheyenne area and may have been in possession of firearms, including a rifle. Investigators also learned that several children, including an infant, were present at the residence where Cunningham had been staying.
Investigators subsequently located Cunningham away from the residence and attempted to take him into custody. Cunningham fled in a U-Haul truck, resulting in a vehicle pursuit. Personnel from the Cheyenne Police Department, Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, and Wyoming Highway Patrol coordinated the response and deployed tire-deflation devices. The pursuit concluded on the east side of Cheyenne, where Cunningham was taken into custody without further incident.
“Today’s apprehension reflects the persistence of our investigators and the strength of our law enforcement partnerships,” said Michael Thomas, Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal for the District of Wyoming. “For more than five years, Cunningham remained wanted, but the passage of time did not diminish our commitment to this case. Operation Spring Cleaning demonstrates what can be accomplished when federal, state, county, and local agencies work together with a shared commitment to public safety and accountability.”
Cunningham’s apprehension officially concludes Operation Spring Cleaning and represents the culmination of months of coordinated investigative and enforcement efforts resulting in multiple arrest and violent crime reduction throughout the nation and the great state of Wyoming.
The U.S. Marshals Service District of Wyoming recognizes the Cheyenne Police Department, Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, Wyoming Highway Patrol, and all participating law enforcement personnel for their professionalism, coordination, and commitment to public safety.
All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.
title: U.S. Marshals in Wyoming Close Out ‘Operation Spring Cleaning’ with Arrest of Longstanding Fugitive | U.S. Marshals Service

BOSTON – A Queens, N.Y., man has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston for allegedly travelling across state lines to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a 13-year-old minor in Massachusetts.

Andre Jamal Bennett, 33, was indicted on one count of sexual exploitation of children and one count of interstate travel to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor. Bennett was arrested and charged by criminal complaint with one count of interstate travel to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor in August 2026 . He remains in federal custody.

According to the charging documents, Bennett was employed by Delta Air Lines as a ground controller at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York. In September 2025, Bennett allegedly created multiple social media accounts – including two Instagram accounts and a Snapchat account – using the fictitious name “Chris.” Using the accounts, Bennett allegedly falsely presented himself to be a 16-year-old boy in order to contact the minor victim.

In November 2025, Bennett allegedly took a flight from New York City to Boston. Upon landing in Boston, Bennett who had allegedly previously contacted the minor victim, informed her that he was in the area and coerced her into meeting him in person, sending her an Uber to her house. It is alleged that Bennett, still purporting to be a 16-year-old male boy, met the minor victim wearing a hooded sweatshirt concealing his face.

It is further alleged that Bennett brought the minor victim to a hotel and raped her. Bennett also allegedly recorded the sexual assault on his phone. Following the encounter, Bennett allegedly continued to contact the minor victim through social media over the course of several months and sought to entice her to meet with him again, including by offering to pay her. The minor victim refused.

The charge of sexual exploitation of children provides for a sentence of at least 15 years and up to 30 years in prison, at least five years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct provides for a sentence of up to 30 years in prison, at least five years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; and Michael Cox, Commissioner of the Boston Police Department made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the FBI’s New York Field Office and United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York. Assistant U.S. Attorney Luke A. Goldworm, of the Major Crimes Unit and Project Safe Childhood Coordinator Unit is prosecuting the case.

The case is brought as part of Project Safe Childhood. In 2006, the Department of Justice created Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative designed to protect children from exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov .

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: New York Man Indicted for Child Exploitation

BOSTON – As part of the United States Attorney’s ongoing enforcement priority to investigate and prosecute benefit fraud involving federal and state assistance programs, a Worcester, Mass. man has been indicted by a federal grand jury for using the identity of a deceased U.S. citizen to obtain Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, MassHealth benefits and a Massachusetts identification card.

“John Doe,” whose true identity is unknown at this time, is charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits, false representation of a Social Security number, false statements relating to health care matters and aggravated identity theft. The defendant was previously arrested in April 2026 after being charged by criminal complaint. He remains detained in federal custody.

According to the charging documents, since at least 2001, John Doe has been living in Massachusetts under the identity of a U.S. citizen from Puerto Rico who died in 2006. It is alleged that under the deceased citizen’s identity, the defendant fraudulently obtained a Massachusetts identification card, as well as MassHealth benefits.

According to court documents John Doe has criminal convictions in Massachusetts under the deceased citizen’s identity, including assault and drug convictions. Specifically, in September 2012, John Doe was convicted in Worcester Superior Court of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon (gun) as well as trafficking cocaine, for which he was sentenced to state prison for 8-10 years and 11-15 years in state prison, respectively.

Upon his release from prison in January 2022, the defendant allegedly used the stolen identity to apply for SNAP benefits. It is alleged that, in connection with his SNAP application, John Doe spoke with an employee of the Massachusetts Department of Transitional Assistance (DTA) in April 2022, claiming that he was the individual listed on the application, that he was a U.S. citizen and verified his purported Social Security number. According to the charging documents, the DTA employee noted in the file: “Death match ??? – reviewing with supervisor [sic]” – apparently indicating that the Social Security number that John Doe allegedly provided corresponded to a deceased person. However, the application was ultimately approved by Massachusetts DTA, and John Doe allegedly proceeded to collect SNAP benefits.

In total, from April 2022 through February 2026, John Doe allegedly applied for and obtained approximately $12,623 in SNAP benefits under the stolen deceased citizen’s identity.

The charge of unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of misrepresenting a Social Security number provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of false statements relating to health care matters provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, up to three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a sentence of at least two years in prison, up to one year of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; Amy Connelly, Special Agent in Charge of the Social Security Administration, Office of Inspector General, Office of Investigations, Boston Field Division; Charmeka Parker, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Agriculture - Office of Inspector General, Northeast Region; and Roberto Coviello, Special Agent in Charge of the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan O’Shea of the Worcester Branch Office is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.

text:
ST. LOUIS – Three men who were involved in a conspiracy to steal checks from the mail and deposit them into fraudulently-opened bank accounts were sentenced to prison Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Joshua M. Divine sentenced Isaiah W. Douglas, 25, of Champaign, Ill. to 39 months in prison, Luis A. Franco-Gonzalez, 26, of Rantoul, Ill., to 34 months in prison and Isaiah B. Handford, 28, to 33 months.

Douglas and others stole checks, or caused them to be stolen, from U.S. Postal Service collection boxes in and around St. Louis. Handford and Franco-Gonzalez then posed as representatives of the victim businesses and opened or tried to open bank accounts with fraudulent documents supplied by Douglas.

On June 12, 2023, Handford entered a St. Louis bank and applied to open a business account by falsely claiming that he was an owner and registered agent of one of the victim businesses. Suspicious bank officials refused to open the account. That same day, Franco-Gonzalez was successful in opening an account at a different bank in Chesterfield and depositing a $312,677 check.

The following day, Franco-Gonzalez unsuccessfully tried to open an account at a bank in Creve Coeur before fleeing the bank on foot. Police arrested Handford in a getaway car close to the bank and then found and arrested Franco-Gonzalez in a Ford Explorer in the parking lot of a nearby hotel. The Explorer contained a handgun and fraudulent paperwork in the name of one of the victims. Officers found Douglas at the hotel, carrying a backpack and a duffel bag that contained more fraudulent paperwork, a handgun and 53 loose checks, money orders, and envelopes that had been stolen from collection boxes. In hotel rooms used by the conspirators, police found more stolen mail and an additional stolen check.

Douglas and his co-defendants admitted that they intended to cause a loss of at least $581,123, based on the value of stolen checks deposited into unauthorized business accounts and the stolen checks recovered by police. They ultimately failed to make any money from the scheme, however.

The case is the latest prosecution of those responsible for mail theft and whose conduct takes advantage of the public's reliance on a vital government service, Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Clow wrote in sentencing memo.

“The sentencing in this case illustrates that individuals who engage in mail theft will be held accountable for their actions,” stated Inspector in Charge, Nicholas Bucciarelli, who leads the Chicago Division, which includes the St. Louis Domicile Office. “The Postal Inspection Service is proud to work with our local, state, and federal partners to bring mail theft perpetrators to justice and prevent financial crimes targeting local citizens, postal customers, and financial institutions.”

Douglas pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud and one count of possession of stolen mail matter. Franco-Gonzalez and Handford pleaded guilty to one count of making a false statement to a financial institution.

The Creve Coeur Police Department and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Clow prosecuted the case.
title: Three Sentenced for Bank Fraud Conspiracy Involving Checks Stolen from the Mail

WASHINGTON – Yesterday, the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche held a press conference to announce federal charges against ten aliens for unlawful voting and registration offenses in Minnesota.
Following an investigation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) St. Paul, a federal grand jury returned ten indictments against ten foreign nationals, including NINE counts of illegal voting by an alien and NINE counts of making a false claim of citizenship in order to vote. The defendants are accused of voting in recent elections such as the 2022 and 2024 elections, and even as recently as the primary election in August 2026. Nine of the defendants were arrested in Minnesota while the tenth was arrested in Massachusetts.
Secretary Mullin and Attorney General Blanche were joined at the press conference by Daniel N. Rosen, U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota.
“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” said Secretary Mullin. “Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration will never allow the votes of American citizens to be cancelled out by non-citizens illegally voting in our elections. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.”
“Today's charges allege that ten foreign nationals committed voter fraud in Minnesota, one voting illegally as recently as this August's primary,” said Attorney General Blanche. “The law is clear, only American citizens may vote in American elections, and enforcing this law is fundamental to our democracy. That should not be a partisan concept.”
“Voting in American elections is a privilege of American citizenship,” said Attorney Rosen. “Stealing that privilege is a crime. When, in order to obtain a ballot, a non-citizen swears he or she is a citizen, we will prosecute.”
The ten suspects are:
Bhator Konah Bryant, a Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR), from Liberia
Edvile Vaidoto Edmunds, LPR, from Lithuania
Joshua Edzie, LPR, from Ghana
Alan Barbu Kargbo, LPR, from Liberia
Fadil Rasim Rasim Ozegovic, LPR, from Bosnia and Herzegovina
Aparecido Donizetti Padovan, LPR, from Brazil
- Paul Kras, LPR, from Germany
- Chris Adam Pettiquoui, LPR, from Liberia
- Christian Liam Schenk, LPR, from Canada
- Hester Sophia Weihmann, LPR, from South Africa
First Assistant United States Attorney Joseph S. Teirab is prosecuting these cases.
This is part of the Trump Administration’s broader focus on stopping non-citizens from voting in American elections. Recent examples include:
- In September, HSI and the FBI arrested Sanata Coulibaly, an alien from Senegal, who admitted to voting in 2020 and 2024 in New Jersey.
- In September, an HSI investigation lead to the conviction of Evelyn Novelles Miller, an alien from the Philippines, who illegally voted in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania.
- In September, HSI arrested Ludwig Uriel Espejo-Carrillo, an alien from Mexico, and charged him with unlawful voting and false claim to U.S. citizenship after illegally voting in American elections in 2015.
- In September, ICE arrested Anthony Tyrone Higgs, an alien from the Bahamas who had illegally voted in the 2020 election, and whose criminal history includes convictions for TWO counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime, TWO counts of grand larceny, armed robbery with a deadly weapon, criminal domestic violence, assault on a police officer, and resisting arrest.
- In September, ICE arrested Mariana Alexandra Dewey, an alien from Peru, for illegally misrepresenting herself as a U.S. citizen to vote in the 2024 election in Kansas.
- In August, Carlos Felipe Jaramillo-Grajales, a criminal illegal alien from Colombia, was sentenced to three years in prison after an ICE investigation led to him pleading guilty to committing identity theft to illegally vote in elections for more than 20 years.
- In July, HSI arrested Marian Charitun, an alien from Slovakia who had illegally voted in the 2022 election in New Jersey.
- In July, an HSI investigation led to the arrest of Denise Nataly Migliore, an alien from Australia who illegally voted in the 2022 and 2024 elections in Louisiana.
- In May, DHS and the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced charges against four non-citizens in New Jersey who illegally voted in federal elections and made false statements while applying for U.S. citizenship.
- In April, Jose Ceballos, an alien from Mexico, pleaded guilty to THREE counts of disorderly election conduct after illegally voting multiple times and falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen in Kansas.
- In March, ICE arrested Mahady Sacko, a criminal illegal alien from Mauritania who had been illegally voting in the United States since 2008.
In recent months, DHS has taken additional steps to safeguard the integrity and security of American elections. These measures include:
- In September, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan: Securing the Next 250.
- In July, Secretary Mullin sent letters to secretaries of state in several states across the country warning that tens of thousands of non-citizens are registered to vote.
- In July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) announced that grant recipients will be required to take several key actions on election integrity.
- In June, DHS directed ICE to enforce stricter penalties for non-citizens who illegally vote in American elections, including deportation.

text:
The US Supreme Court handed Donald Trump a significant victory on Tuesday by letting his administration immediately resume rapid deportations of migrants to third countries, triggering outrage from critics who branded the emergency order 'evil' and the policy 'reckless cruelty'.
A federal court had blocked those removals unless migrants had a chance to challenge them, including over fears of persecution or torture. The unsigned Supreme Court order lets the administration resume the policy ahead of arguments scheduled for December.
Supreme Court Grants Relief
Third-country deportations send immigrants to nations other than their own. Critics warn that people could be forced into dangerous destinations, including countries accused of human rights abuses. The government sought emergency permission to restart those rapid removals while the legal dispute continues.
The three liberal justices said they would have denied the administration's request. The order allows the government to proceed while the court prepares to hear arguments on the policy.
The Trump administration has sent more than 25,000 people to third countries, including Liberia, Equatorial Guinea and the Central African Republic, the New York Times reported.
The earlier federal court restriction concerned migrants' opportunity to object before being removed. It required that they be able to raise fears of persecution or torture in the country to which they would be sent.
Criticism of Supreme Court Order
Those reactions appeared on X and Bluesky, with critics challenging both the administration's choice of destinations and the court's decision to let removals restart.
Colorado Democratic representative Brittany Pettersen focused on the risks of sending people somewhere they had never lived, without family connections or assurances about their safety. 'Deporting someone to a country they've never set foot in, with no family, no ties, and no guarantee of safety, is reckless cruelty,' Pettersen wrote on X.
'The Supreme Court's decision to allow this is deeply heartbreaking & dangerous. We cannot treat human lives like this. I will never stop fighting for basic due process, oversight, and an immigration system that actually respects and honors the rights of EVERY person.'
Her statement called for due process and oversight, linking her criticism of the court's decision to the protections available to people facing removal. Podcaster and rural healthcare advocate Michelle Rathman condemned the decision on Bluesky, using the word 'evil' and warning that deportees could face fatal consequences.
'The horror of this I really don't know if there are words to describe how evil this is,' Rathman wrote. 'Without any due process, thousands of people will be sent to die. SCOTUS [is] rubber stamping death sentences.' Those comments predicted deaths rather than identifying deaths resulting from Tuesday's emergency order.
Political scientist Norm Ornstein directed his response at the court's conservative majority, calling the justices 'six monstrous partisan hacks'.
Supreme Court Arguments in December
The reactions ranged from Pettersen's demands for safeguards to direct criticism of the justices. The liberal members' opposition, meanwhile, concerned whether to grant the government's emergency request.
The order addresses the government's request to restart removals, allowing the administration to proceed while the policy itself remains in dispute. The permission granted on Tuesday applies to rapid deportations to countries other than the immigrants' own. The court is preparing to hear arguments on the policy in December.
title: Supreme Court Hands Trump a Major Win With 'Evil' Emergency Order Described as 'Reckless Cruelty'

SCRANTON - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Reinaldo Gonzalez, Jr., age 32, of Wayne County, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on September 30, 2026, to 51 months’ imprisonment by United States District Judge Joseph F. Saporito, Jr. for accessing with intent to view child pornography. The court also ordered Gonzalez to serve a seven-year term of supervised release following his release from prison.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, in July 2022, Gonzalez utilized a Snapchat account to upload and view child pornography. Gonzalez’s actions generated a CyberTip which was sent from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) to the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s Office for further investigation. During an interview with federal law enforcement officers, Gonzalez acknowledged having a sexual attraction to children and admitted to trading child pornography with others on various internet-based platforms, including Snapchat, Kik, and Facebook.

Homeland Security Investigations and the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s Office investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Tatum R. Wilson prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

DENTON, Texas – This week, FEMA awarded nearly $65 million in grant funding to fire departments and first responder organizations in Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas. These awards will enable agencies to get the equipment, staff and support they need to carry out their critical, life-saving missions. This week’s fire grant funding brings the total amount awarded to Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas this year to more than $84 million. “Firefighters and other first responders are everyday heroes, helping their neighbors and communities when they need it most,” said FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton. “Through this grant funding, FEMA is building the capability of these local organizations to respond to disasters and emergencies. By empowering fire departments to get the staff, training and equipment they need, FEMA is strengthening the resilience of American communities nationwide.”
FEMA is administering these funds through its Assistance to Firefighters Grants and its Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response grant program. Examples of awards issued this week include:
- Nearly $10 million to the Houston Fire Department in Houston, Texas to hire more firefighters.
- More than $2.6 million to the City of Shreveport Fire Department in Shreveport, Louisiana to hire more firefighters.
- More than $1.7 million to the Oklahoma State Firefighters Association for national, state, local or federal recruitment and retention.

Justice Department Files Complaint Against the State of Maryland, Prince George’s County, MD and Montgomery County, MD Challenging Mask Ban and Identification Requirements for Federal Officers
Today, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the State of Maryland, Maryland Attorney General Anthony G. Brown, the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission, Prince George’s County, and Montgomery County, challenging their unconstitutional attempt to regulate federal law enforcement officers by prohibiting federal officers from wearing masks and requiring they provide identification in the manner prescribed by Md. Code Ann., Pub. Safety §§ 3-207, 3-535, 3-536, Prince George’s Co., Md Code § 18-124, and Montgomery Co., Md. Code § 35-13E.
Not only are these laws illegal attempts to regulate the federal government, but, as alleged in the complaint, the laws threaten the safety of federal officers who have faced an unprecedent wave of harassment, doxing, and even violence. Threatening officers with prosecution for simply protecting their identities and their families also chills the enforcement of federal law and compromises sensitive law enforcement operations.
“Under the U.S. Constitution, the Supremacy Clause provides that states and localities do not have the authority to regulate the Federal Government,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. “And they certainly cannot enact laws that place the safety of federal law enforcement at risk and undermine federal operations. We will never tolerate the doxxing or harassment of federal officers, or any law like those in Maryland that enables violent behavior against federal law enforcement officers and their families.”
“These Maryland state and local laws are a direct regulation of federal law enforcement operations and threaten severe consequences for officers and public safety alike,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “The Federal Government, not state and local governments, gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties.”
Attorney General Blanche has instructed the Department’s Civil Division to identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal laws or impede lawful federal operations. Today’s lawsuit is the latest in a series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division targeting illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country, including in New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, California, Philadelphia, and Milwaukee. The United States has secured preliminary relief from each court to have ruled on mask ban / ID requirements so far.
Note: The complaint can be viewed here.
Press Release Number: 26-1124

BILLINGS – A Billings man who was part of a large-scale drug ring operating out of Mexico that trafficked significant amounts of methamphetamine into Montana was sentenced today to 14 years and two months in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced.

Joshua Jacob Best, 41, pleaded guilty in May 2026 to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine.

U.S. District Judge Susan P. Watters presided.

The government alleged in court documents that a drug smuggling ring run out of Mexico and operating in Wyoming, South Dakota, California, and Montana, had operators in Billings. Billings police learned through an informant in June 2023 that Raymond Best (Joshua Best’s brother) was bringing “pounds of meth” and other drugs into Billings.

Over the course of the next several months, investigators learned Joshua Best was helping move cash and drugs between Mexico and Billings. During a DEA undercover operation in October 2023, Joshua Best arranged to deliver $67,000 to a co-conspirator (actually an undercover agent) in the Walmart parking lot, on the premise he would then transport the money to their supplier in the Los Angeles area. Best showed up and made the drop in a black Chevy Camaro.

In January 2024, DEA learned that Joshua Best had rented a car and arranged for a courier to drive it from Des Moines, Iowa, to Billings. DEA tipped off law enforcement, who pulled the car over after it had left Des Moines. They discovered 57 pounds of methamphetamine, approximately 1 kilogram of cocaine, and approximately 2 pounds of marijuana. Joshua Best was the contact to pick up the drugs once they reached Billings.

Joshua Best crashed a black Chevy Camaro on Monad Road in March 2024. He ran from the scene, dropping two heat-sealed bags as he fled. With a warrant, officers searched the Camaro and found a vacuum sealed bag containing roughly a pound of methamphetamine on the driver’s side floor. Also in the car were numerous documents belonging to Joshua Best even though he was not the car’s registered owner.

Best was eventually apprehended in Mexico after fleeing the country. Working closely with Mexican authorities, the DEA and U.S. Marshals Service captured Best and brought him back to the U.S. to face prosecution.

“DEA and its partners worked relentlessly to ensure our region now has one less drug trafficker putting poison into our communities,” said Mark Putnam, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Rocky Mountain Field Division Special Agent in Charge. “We appreciate the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Montana, for prosecuting this case.”

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Montana comprises agents and officers from a number of federal agencies as well as drug task forces throughout the state, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Montana.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case. The Billings Police Department, DEA, and Eastern Montana High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area Task Force conducted the investigation as part of the HSTF.
title: Billings man sentenced to more than 14 years in prison for trafficking meth as part of drug ring

CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas – A 45-year-old Hutchinson, Kansas, resident will serve federal prison time for his role in an alien smuggling conspiracy.

Jesse Antonio Villa pleaded guilty Aug. 20, 2025.

U.S. District Judge Nelva Gonzales Ramos ordered Villa to serve 65 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by three years of supervised release. At the hearing, the court heard additional testimony that Villa recruited at least 10 drivers from Hutchinson and supplied drivers who helped transport more than 100 illegal aliens. Villa sent the drivers to Houston, where Edgar Ruiz-Briones helped coordinate alien smuggling trips from the Rio Grande Valley through checkpoints into Houston.

Between May 2023 and November 2024, Villa recruited drivers in Kansas to support an alien smuggling organization led by Ruiz-Briones. Villa sent the drivers to the Rio Grande Valley, where Ruiz-Briones coordinated transportation for illegal aliens crossing the southern border.

The drivers communicated with both men to set up trips, report progress, and coordinate Houston drop-offs following successful smuggling operations. They picked up illegal aliens from various stash houses and transported them to Houston, where they met with Ruiz-Briones before the aliens were moved farther into the United States.

Ruiz-Briones was previously sentenced to 120 months for his role in the conspiracy.

Villa has been and will remain in custody pending transfer to a Federal Bureau of Prisons facility to be determined in the near future.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation with the assistance of Border Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney Joseph Griffith prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigrants, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.
title: Kansas man heads to prison for role in human smuggling organization involving transportation of over 100 illegal aliens

text:
MIAMI – A federal jury in Miami found a Margate man guilty of participating in a murder-for-hire scheme that culminated in the November 2023 death of Suren Seetal.

According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Avin Seetaram, also known as “Smalls,” 27, of Margate, conspired with Somjeet Christopher Singh, also known as “Lil Chris,” 32, of Coral Springs, to have Seetal killed over business dealings. The conspirators first targeted Seetal in July 2023. After tracking his whereabouts through an electronic device placed in the vehicle he was using, they sent a gunman and driver to kill him. The gunman opened fire on Seetal, who returned fire. No one was struck, and the gunman and the driver fled.

After that attempt failed, Seetaram and Singh arranged a second plot. On Nov. 2, 2023, they lured Seetal to a business location, where a newly hired gunman was waiting. The gunman ambushed Seetal and shot him to death. Seetaram and Singh then paid the gunman as promised and coordinated efforts to conceal the crime, including transporting and disposing of Seetal’s body in the Everglades.

“This was not a spontaneous act of violence. It was a deliberate, persistent, and cold-blooded murder-for-hire scheme,” said U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida. “The defendants tracked Suren Seetal, sent armed men to kill him, tried again after the first attempt failed, and ultimately had him ambushed and murdered. They then paid the gunman and helped dispose of Seetal’s body in the Everglades. One conspirator is already serving life in federal prison, and a jury has now convicted Seetaram for his role in this brutal crime.”

The jury convicted Seetaram of murder-for-hire conspiracy, murder for hire, stalking resulting in death, discharging a firearm in furtherance of a crime of violence, conspiracy to use and carry a firearm during a crime of violence, and causing the death of a person through the use of a firearm during a crime of violence. He faces up 20 years in federal prison on the conspiracy to use and carry a firearm during a crime of violence count and up to life in prison on the remaining counts. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Singh previously pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire conspiracy, murder for hire, kidnapping conspiracy, kidnapping, stalking resulting in death, conspiracy to use and carry a firearm during a crime of violence, causing the death of a person through the use of a firearm during a crime of violence, and obstruction of justice. U.S. District Judge Roy K. Altman sentenced Singh to concurrent terms of life in federal prison on six counts, 140 months on the firearm conspiracy count, and 120 months on the obstruction of justice count.

U.S. Attorney Reding Quiñones and Special Agent in Charge Brett D. Skiles of the FBI Miami Field Office made the announcement.

FBI Miami is investigating the case, with assistance from the Fort Lauderdale Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Abbie D. Waxman and Michael Gilfarb are prosecuting the case.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Southern District of Florida at www.flsd.uscourts.gov or at http://pacer.flsd.uscourts.gov , under case number 23-cr-20483.

text:
Fast Facts
In 2020, the Food and Drug Administration began regulating millions of e-cigarettes and other tobacco products already on the market. In response, FDA received a surge of applications seeking authorization to remain on the market. This led to a backlog of over 25 million applications that were awaiting review.
FDA has made progress reducing this backlog. However, it didn't meet its goals for timely reviews, or collect the data necessary to monitor these goals.
We recommended that FDA collect this data. More timely reviews will help clarify which products are legally marketed and allow FDA to take action against unauthorized products.
A person using an e-cigarette.
Highlights
What GAO Found
In 2016, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its authority to oversee all tobacco products, including millions of e-cigarettes that were already on the market. In response, it received a surge of applications from manufacturers in 2020 for products seeking authorization to remain on the market legally. Specifically, it received over 25 million applications in 2020 and 2021, compared to just over 1 thousand applications in 2018 and 2019. This led to a backlog of applications. While FDA has since reviewed most of the applications submitted during this period, almost 132 thousand remained without a completed review as of December 31, 2025. (See figure.)
Figure: FDA Tobacco Product Application Reviews, Calendar Year (CY) 2018-2025
From CY2018 to CY2025, FDA took an average of 507 days to complete its review of tobacco product applications. FDA has goals for each phase of the review process, ranging from 7 to 180 days. For the screening phase, FDA did not meet its goals, although it has made progress toward them. FDA also has goals for the last phase of review, when it must review an application’s scientific information. However, FDA’s data system was not designed to track steps in this part of the review process. Thus, it does not collect the data necessary to monitor whether it is meeting these goals. According to practices identified in prior GAO work, collecting performance information and using it to monitor performance are needed to assess if programs and activities are achieving intended goals. Meeting these goals will help FDA ensure a more predictably timed application process, and more completed reviews will help clarify which products are legally marketed, thus allowing FDA to take action against unauthorized products.
FDA has taken steps to improve review timeliness. For example, since the surge of applications, it issued multiple guidance documents for manufacturers to improve application quality, as it found that poor quality applications slowed the review process. In September 2025, the agency also created a pilot program aimed at streamlining the review process for nicotine pouches and plans to apply lessons learned from that pilot to other product types. However, the changes are too recent to know whether they will increase the timeliness of reviews.
Why GAO Did This Study
FDA has regulated certain tobacco products, such as cigarettes, since 2009. A surge of new product applications soon after led to an application backlog and significant delays, as GAO reported in 2013. FDA took steps to address these challenges and implemented performance measures for review timeliness. However, the 2016 expansion of FDA’s authority to oversee all tobacco products once again raised questions about timeliness.
GAO was asked to provide an update on FDA’s efforts to review applications and provide timely responses. This report examines (1) the status of FDA’s reviews of tobacco product applications submitted 2018 through 2025, (2) the extent to which it met its timeliness goals for reviewing these applications, and (3) the steps FDA took to improve the timeliness of these reviews, among other topics.
GAO analyzed FDA tobacco product application data for submissions FDA received in 2018 through 2025, reviewed agency documents, and interviewed FDA officials and tobacco representatives.
Recommendations
GAO recommends FDA collect the data necessary to monitor whether it is meeting its timeliness goals for reviewing scientific information in all tobacco product applications. HHS agreed with the recommendation.
title: Tobacco Products: FDA Should Monitor Timeliness of Application Reviews

The Federal Reserve Taps GSA to Lead HQ Renovations as Chairman Warsh Moves to Rein in Costs
Chairman Warsh Partners with GSA Following Explosive OIG Report Finding Federal Reserve Renovation Costs Rose from $1.3B to $2.4B Under Previous Chairman Powell’s Leadership
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Yesterday, Federal Reserve Board (the Fed) Chairman Kevin Warsh announced that the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) will serve as Project Executive for the central bank’s renovation of their headquarters located in the Eccles and East Buildings. In a letter to Inspector General Horowitz [PDF - 798 KB], Warsh stated he was enlisting GSA to work with the Fed “in the task of finally bringing the renovations to a speedy and successful completion.”
“GSA fully supports Chairman Kevin Warsh’s efforts to bring greater accountability, cost discipline, and effective project management to major renovation work across Federal Reserve facilities,” said GSA Administrator Edward C. Forst. “As the federal government’s primary real estate and building management agency, GSA will work closely with the Chairman and bring its expertise in construction, project management, and federal real estate to get these projects back on track. Together, we will focus on delivering better value for taxpayers and ensuring the Federal Reserve’s facilities are positioned to better serve the American people.”
The move follows a highly critical report by the Office of Inspector General (OIG), which found serious mismanagement of the Federal Reserve’s renovation of the Eccles and East Buildings under former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. According to the OIG, project costs ballooned from an initial estimate of $1.3 billion in 2020 to $2.4 billion by December 2024 during Chairman Powell’s tenure, with uncertainty remaining over how much further costs have climbed since. The report also found that the Federal Reserve failed to establish a guaranteed maximum price for the project.
Exclusive Coverage by Fox News here.

About GSA: GSA provides centralized procurement and shared services for the federal government, managing approximately 360 million rentable square feet, overseeing over $126 billion in products and services via federal contracts, and delivering technology services to millions of people across dozens of federal agencies. GSA’s mission is to deliver exceptional customer experience and value in real estate, acquisition, and technology. To address nearly $50 billion in delinquent maintenance, GSA is leading a coalition of every cabinet agency and many federal leaders urgently advocating for full Federal Buildings Fund access and raising the prospectus threshold from $3.96 million to $75 million. For more information, visit GSA.gov and follow @USGSA.

BOLTON, MS — Today, Congressman Bennie G. Thompson (MS-02) announced that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has awarded $486,000 to Midtown Partners, Inc. in Jackson, Mississippi.

NORFOLK, Va. – A Chesapeake man was sentenced yesterday to 10 years and one month in prison for possession of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

According to court documents, on July 6, 2012, William Oyster, 50, was convicted in the Eastern District of Virginia of receipt of CSAM. Oyster was released from prison in November 2020 and began a term of supervised release that included provisions making his home and electronic devices subject to search at any time and prohibiting him from using or accessing online devices without prior approval of a probation officer.

On Nov. 12, 2025, a probation officer conducted a routine search of Oyster’s residence and observed an unapproved smartphone in plain view. Within the residence, Oyster also possessed another smartphone, an external hard drive, and two thumb drives. A review of the devices revealed that Oyster possessed CSAM.

When the U.S. Marshals Service arrested Oyster on Jan. 6, 2026, he was in possession of a loaded handgun. As a previously convicted felon, Oyster cannot legally possess firearms or ammunition.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Kai Wah Chan, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Washington, D.C., made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge Mark S. Davis. HSI and the U.S. Marshals Service investigated this case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Anthony C. Mozzi prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

For more information about HSI’s efforts to protect children from sexual predators, visit Know2Protect.gov.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:26-cr-33.
title: Previously convicted offender returning to prison for possession child sexual abuse material

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Amara Dukuly, 44, of Woodlyn, Pennsylvania, a former immigration officer employed by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”), was sentenced today to 12 months and one day in prison, three years of supervised release, a $6,000 fine, and $6,000 in restitution by United States District Judge John Milton Younge for accepting a $6,000 bribe.

The defendant was arrested on a criminal complaint and warrant in June of last year, indicted that July, and pleaded guilty in March to aiding and abetting the bribery of a public official in exchange for an official act.

As detailed in court filings and statements, from approximately 2015 to 2025, Dukuly used his status as a USCIS employee to solicit bribes from individuals in exchange for promises to help them obtain assistance with their immigration status.

On April 4, 2025, Dukuly received a $6,000 bribe from an individual to help him with the removal of “terrorist” references from the individual's immigration file. Dukuly promised the individual that after the “terrorist” references were removed, his file would be “clean.”

This case was investigated by the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General, Homeland Security Investigations, and the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Robert J. Livermore.
title: Former Immigration Officer Sentenced to a Year and a Day in Prison for Accepting $6,000 Bribe

Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Bennie G. Thompson (MS-02) issued the following statement following notification from the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) that Jackson Area Federal Credit Union (JAFCU) has been liquidated and that Five Star Credit Union has assumed its member share accounts:

“Jackson Area Federal Credit Union has served thousands of families, public employees, and members of the Jackson and Hinds County communities for decades. The liquidation of this longstanding institution is a serious development, and my primary concern remains protecting the members who entrusted their hard-earned money to this credit union.

“NCUA has assured my office that members transferring to Five Star Credit Union will experience no interruption in service and that federally insured accounts remain protected through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. Members deserve a transition that is orderly, transparent, and protects their access to their money.

“While protecting members must come first, the liquidation of Jackson Area Federal Credit Union also raises serious questions about the circumstances that brought the institution to this point. My office will continue engaging with NCUA to ensure there is full transparency and accountability regarding what occurred, how members were affected, and what steps are being taken to protect them moving forward.”

On September 30, NCUA facilitated a partial purchase and assumption agreement under which Five Star Credit Union purchased certain JAFCU assets and assumed its member share accounts. NCUA subsequently liquidated JAFCU.
title: Congressman Thompson Responds to Liquidation of Jackson Area Federal Credit Union

Pensacola, Florida – Tyronzia Roquza Levine, 45, of Pensacola, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and cocaine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “I applaud the excellent investigative work by the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office, with support from our federal law enforcement partners, which stopped this armed drug trafficker before he could continue peddling deadly drugs on our streets. My office is committed to aggressively prosecuting these cases to deliver the safe, drug-free streets that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that on September 19, 2025, deputies with the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office observed the defendant asleep in the driver’s seat of a parked vehicle. Deputies could plainly see a large amount of U.S. currency along with multiple bags in the cup holder, one of which contained a crystal-like substance. During the search of the vehicle, the deputies seized methamphetamine, cocaine, and a .22-caliber revolver.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, and the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant United States Attorneys Jessica Etherton and Jeffrey Tharp are prosecuting the case.

Sentencing is scheduled for November 23, 2026, at 1:00 p.m. at the United States Courthouse in Pensacola before United States District Judge M. Casey Rodgers.

Commander, Navy Installations Command Celebrates 23 Years as Foundation of Navy Readiness 01 October 2026 WASHINGTON, D.C. (Oct. 1, 2026) – U.S. Navy operations begin long before a ship gets underway, an aircraft launches, or a special operator deploys. These operations begin on the waterfront, airfield, training range, barracks, child development center, and installations where Sailors live, work, and train for every mission. Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC) today celebrates its 23rd anniversary, recognizing more than two decades of providing the shore infrastructure, installation services, and quality of service programs that enable the Navy’s global mission. Since its establishment on Oct. 1, 2003, CNIC has served as the Navy’s single shore installation management command, supporting 10 regions and 71 installations around the world. “For 23 years, our Sailors, civilians and partners have built an enterprise that quietly powers every Navy mission,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, commander of Navy Installations Command. “Whether supporting a carrier strike group, maintaining critical infrastructure or caring for Navy families, readiness begins with the strength of our installations.” This milestone comes as the Navy advances Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle’s Foundry, Fleet, Fight vision which is an effort to generate combat power by strengthening the industrial base, modernizing infrastructure, and accelerating readiness across the force. As the Navy’s Shore Type Command (TYCOM), CNIC provides the resilient foundation that allows operational forces to train, deploy, and sustain missions worldwide. Over the past year, CNIC has launched and expanded initiatives that strengthen both warfighting readiness and the daily lives of Sailors and their families, including: Accelerating the No Sailor Lives Ashore initiative by expanding barracks modernization and increasing quality housing opportunities for unaccompanied Sailors. Implementing Human Performance Optimization and enhanced shore food service pilots to improve nutrition, resilience, and operational performance. Realigning installation maintenance and public works under installation commanding officers to speed repairs and improve support across the Shore Enterprise. Expanding virtual counseling and family support services to provide greater access to behavioral health and quality of life resources regardless of duty station.
As CNIC enters its 24th year, the command is focused on building a more resilient, modern, and agile Shore Enterprise capable of supporting distributed maritime operations and the Navy’s future force. Priorities include modernizing aging waterfront infrastructure, strengthening energy resilience, improving installation security, accelerating barracks investments, and delivering smarter, data-informed services to Sailors and their families. “The Foundry, Fleet, Fight vision reminds us that combat power is built long before the first ship leaves the pier,” Collins said. “Our responsibility is to create the environments where people, platforms, and missions are ready to perform at their very best. That is the enduring value of the Shore Enterprise.” Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC) is responsible for worldwide U.S. Navy Shore installation management, designing and developing integrated solutions for sustainment and development of Navy shore infrastructure as well as quality of life programs. CNIC oversees 10 Navy regions, 71 installations, and approximately 63,000 employees who are focused on warfighting and manning, training, and equipping the Shore to fight and win. Navy installations are warfighting platforms essential to every fleet operation. Learn more: http://www.cnic.navy.mil.
title: Commander, Navy Installations Command Celebrates 23 Years as Foundation of Navy Readiness

CFTC Staff Extends Brexit-Related No-Action Positions
October 01, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Market Participants Division and Division of Market Oversight announced today they are extending temporary no-action positions in connection with the withdrawal of the United Kingdom from the European Union, known as Brexit. [See CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-28]
On February 25, 2019, the CFTC issued a statement in conjunction with the Bank of England, including the Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Financial Conduct Authority to provide regulatory certainty on the continuity of derivatives trading and clearing activities between the UK and the United States. [See CFTC Press Release No. 7876-19]
The letter announced today extends positions previously announced in CFTC Staff Letter No. 24-11, as amended by CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-10. It seeks to maintain the regulatory certainty established when the CFTC originally acted to issue EU comparability determinations and exemptive orders for certain EU entities. MPD and DMO continue to believe maintaining these no action positions is proper while the CFTC works with the relevant UK authorities to analyze relevant UK law and, where appropriate, issue UK comparability determinations and exemptive orders for certain UK entities.
-CFTC-

U.S. Congressman Everton Blair Introduces Legislation to Bring Deported U.S. Army Veteran Godfrey Oliver Wade Home
Media Contact:
Allison Phipps, Allison.Phipps@mail.house.gov ; Amya Enlow, Amya.Enlow@mail.house.gov
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Congressman Everton Blair (GA-13), introduced a bill for the relief of Godfrey Oliver Wade, a Jamaican-born U.S. Army veteran and Covington, Georgia resident who was deported in February 2026 after living in the United States for more than 50 years. The legislation seeks to grant Mr. Wade lawful status, allowing him to return home to his children, grandchildren and the nation he has served with distinction.
Mr. Wade entered the United States lawfully in 1975 as a teenager and has called the nation home ever since. He went on to enlist in the U.S. Army, serving four years on active duty, including three years overseas supporting vital operations during the final years of the Cold War, before receiving an honorable discharge.
Despite his decorated military service and deep ties to the community, Mr. Wade was held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody for nearly five months. He was deported earlier this year after an emergency stay of removal was denied, even while an appeal in his case remained pending.
"Godfrey Wade answered the call of service, enlisting in the U.S. Army, leaving behind a legacy of honorably protecting our nation," said Congressman Blair. "For over half a century, he built his life here as a lawful permanent resident, a father, and a grandfather. To deport an honorably discharged veteran while his legal appeals were still pending is a profound injustice. He fought for our country, so now it is time for us to fight for him and bring him home."
The relief bill would pave the way for Mr. Wade's immediate return to the United States and restore his status as a permanent resident.
###
title: U.S. Congressman Everton Blair Introduces Legislation to Bring Deported U.S. Army Veteran Godfrey Oliver Wade Home
