US Department of Labor awards $10.2 million to 67 organizations to promote workplace safety and health training
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration today announced the award approximately $10.2 million in grant funds to 67 organizations across the nation to support education and training focused on worker safety to help employees and employers recognize serious workplace hazards and employ safety and health programs.
Funded through the Susan Harwood Training Grant Program, the grants aim to advance worker safety and health by providing instructor-led training opportunities for workers and employers in small businesses with an emphasis on industries with high injury, illness, and fatality rates.
The grants will fund training and education on hazard awareness, prevention, and controls to protect workers from on-the-job hazards through the development of quality classroom-ready training and educational materials that identify and prevent workplace hazards.
The grants honor the legacy and work of Dr. Susan Harwood who, during her 17 years with OSHA, developed workplace safety guidelines for benzene, formaldehyde, bloodborne pathogens and lead in the construction industry. Harwood was also primary author of OSHA’s cotton dust standard which virtually eliminated byssinosis – a lung disease that causes asthma-like symptoms – among textile workers.

text:
Congressman Cohen Reintroduces the Police Training and Independent Review Act
Bill makes police more effective and accountable
WASHINGTON – Congressman Steve Cohen (TN-9), a senior member of the Judiciary Committee, today reintroduced the Police Training and Independent Review Act, legislation that would help restore trust between law enforcement officials and the communities they serve by helping prevent police-involved deaths and encouraging independent, impartial investigations into law enforcement officials’ use of deadly force.
Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois introduced a companion measure in the Senate last week.
Congressman Cohen made the following statement:
“Too many police encounters on our streets turn deadly. In my community, the death of Tyre Nichols at the hands of the Memphis police prompted protests and prosecutions. The names of Sonya Massey and Tyre Nichols have been added to the list of victims Philando Castille, Eric Garner, Michael Brown, Sandra Bland, Tamir Rice and Alton Sterling: all individuals who were killed during interactions with law enforcement. And those are just the cases that made national news. Further, we know a disproportionate number of those killed are African Americans. To regain the trust of the people, we must ensure that our law enforcement officers have the proper training and the justice system treats all fairly and equally.”
The Police Training and Independent Review Act would create financial incentives for states to require training for law enforcement officials on fair and impartial policing and best practices for working with members of the community who are disabled and have mental illnesses. Additionally, it would encourage communities to use independent prosecutors to investigate law enforcement officials’ use of deadly force. When implemented, the legislation would authorize the U.S. Attorney General to award grants to states that require an independent investigation and, if warranted, prosecution in cases where one or more of the alleged offenses result in death or serious bodily harm.
Senator Duckworth released the following statement:
“From Chicago to Louisville or anywhere in America, we cannot allow ourselves to accept that Black teenagers, men and women are still being unjustly executed at the hands of law enforcement without judge or jury. Laquan McDonald’s death was preventable, and Congress still has yet to do enough to ensure tragedies like his never happen again. In honor of Laquan's 29th heavenly birthday, I’m proud to lead Senate Democrats in reintroducing this overdue legislation that would help save lives and restore trust between law enforcement and local communities by increasing resources for training to help prevent such incidents, while promoting objective and independent investigations of police-involved uses of deadly force. Families like Laquan McDonald’s that have experienced heartbreak are no less deserving of justice than any other family. It’s time our country acts to ensure accountability within our law enforcement agencies and provide justice to those who have lost loved ones.”
Police in the United States kill more than 1,000 people each year, yet fewer than 3 percent of those killings result in an officer being charged with a crime. In much of the country, the officer's own department investigates a police killing while a local prosecutor—who works alongside that department every day—decides whether to bring charges, an inherent conflict of interest this legislation is designed to eliminate.
The types of independent investigation and prosecution of law enforcement that would be eligible for financial incentives under the Police Training and Independent Review Act include:
- The use of an independent agency, civilian review board or outside law enforcement department, such as the State Police, responsible for independently investigating and prosecuting all officer use of force allegations.
- The appointment of the State Attorney General, or a special prosecutor overseen by the State Attorney General, responsible for conducting the criminal investigation and prosecution.
- The use of an independent prosecutor, who does not reside or work in the same county as the county where the officer’s use of force was committed.
# # #
title: Congressman Cohen Reintroduces the Police Training and Independent Review Act

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Heather Lynn Harjo, age 40, formerly of Ada, Oklahoma, was sentenced to thirty-seven months in prison for one count of Involuntary Manslaughter in Indian Country.

The charge arose from an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Ada Police Department, the Chickasaw Lighthorse Police Department, the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation, and the U.S. Marshals Service.

On October 17, 2026, Harjo pleaded guilty to the charge. According to investigators, on April 28, 2025, while visiting an Ada residence, Harjo became involved in an altercation and—unreasonably believing herself to be in danger of imminent death or serious bodily injury—pulled a 9mm pistol and fired a single shot, striking and killing the victim. Harjo fled and was captured eight weeks later on a fugitive arrest warrant in Dallas, Texas.

The crime occurred in Pontotoc County, within the boundaries of the Chickasaw Nation Reservation, in the Eastern District of Oklahoma.

The Honorable John A. Woodcock, Jr., Senior Judge in the United States District Court for the District of Maine, sitting by designation, presided over the hearing in Muskogee, Oklahoma. Harjo will remain in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending transportation to a designated United States Bureau of Prisons facility to serve a non-paroleable sentence of incarceration.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Lewis M. Reagan represented the United States.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) and Ayanna Pressley (Mass.-07) today introduced the Wigs for Warriors Act, legislation that would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss.

“I heard directly from a constituent, a 16-year-old from Prince William County and daughter of a U.S. Marine, who lost all of her hair to alopecia areata by the end of second grade. She told my team how a medical-grade wig could have helped her navigate the emotional and social challenges of losing her hair, but that these wigs can be incredibly expensive,” said Vindman. “This bill, which I am proud to lead alongside Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, will help ensure TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata, like my constituent, have access to the care and support they need to feel comfortable and confident.”

“When individuals in our military families experience severe hair loss, they should be met with the support and care they need to feel like their authentic selves,” said Pressley. “Through my own experience with alopecia areata, I understand the psychological, social, and economic impact that comes with navigating severe hair loss—and I know that we can do something to lighten the load. For some, accessing medical-grade wigs can make all the difference. That’s why I’m proud to lead the Wigs for Warriors Act alongside Rep. Vindman and bring much-deserved relief and support to TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata and other hair loss conditions.”

TRICARE, the insurance for servicemembers and military families, has extremely limited coverage for individuals experiencing severe hair loss. Currently, patients with alopecia areata receive no coverage for a cranial prosthesis — a medical-grade, custom-fitted wig designed to address medically related hair loss.

The bill would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss, as certified by a physician. Coverage would also extend to hair loss resulting from chemotherapy, regardless of the underlying condition being treated.

The legislation would also eliminate TRICARE’s current lifetime limit of one prosthesis per patient, allowing cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy to receive coverage for multiple wigs as medically necessary.

“This act is life changing for both the military and medical hair loss communities, allowing for better mental health of our service members and their families,” said a 16-year-old resident of Prince William County with alopecia areata. “Representative Vindman and his team not only took the time to listen to my story but have moved forward to resolving the issue. I am forever grateful.”

The Wigs for Warriors Act is supported by the National Alopecia Areata Foundation (NAAF).

“The National Alopecia Areata Foundation applauds the introduction of the Wigs for Warriors Act of 2026 and thanks Representative Vindman for his efforts to improve the lives of members of the military and their families living with the autoimmune disease alopecia areata,” said Ryan Reczek, President & CEO of the National Alopecia Areata Foundation. “This legislation is critical to ensure that medically necessary cranial prostheses, also known as medical wigs, that are used to restore well-being and support mental health, are affordable and accessible under TRICARE.”

BACKGROUND

Alopecia areata is a common autoimmune disease that causes the immune system to attack a person’s hair follicles, resulting in patchy or complete hair loss across the scalp and body. Nearly 6.7 million people in the United States are directly affected by alopecia areata, with about 700,000 currently living with active disease. The remaining millions have had the disease or will likely develop it at some point.

Alopecia areata carries a substantial mental health burden and wigs are a documented, effective way to manage it. The psychological impact of alopecia areata can be profound, with elevated rates of anxiety and depression, increased time off work, and impaired quality of life, stemming largely from the fact that hair plays a crucial role in shaping an individual’s identity, self-esteem, and social interactions. This burden is especially acute for young people who develop the condition.

###
title: Vindman, Pressley Introduce Legislation to Expand Alopecia Support for Military Families

Justice Department Finds UCLA Law School Discriminates Based on Race in Admissions
The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division announced today investigative findings that the University of California-Los Angeles School of Law (UCLA Law) discriminated against white and Asian students in granting admission to its 2023, 2024, and 2025 incoming classes. UCLA Law’s discriminatory conduct violates Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race or color, and the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (SFFA), which banned race discrimination in admissions.
“Like many of its peer institutions, UCLA Law School runs a two-tiered admissions system whose academic bar for acceptance shifts up or down depending on the color of your skin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “The use of race as a thumb on the scale that helps or disadvantages any student is illegal. The Department will continue to enforce equal treatment under the law everywhere — including in our nation’s law schools.”
The Department’s investigation found that post-SFFA, UCLA Law’s application includes personal statements and essay prompts, which are designed to elicit information about race. And UCLA Law’s admissions staff instructed prospective applicants how to reveal their race in these sections of the application—during race-based recruitment efforts, such as its annual “Diversity Admissions Open House”.
The Department’s analysis revealed that UCLA Law rejected white and Asian applicants who had the same LSAT scores as admitted black and Hispanic applicants. Plainly, lower-scoring white and Asian applicants would have been admitted by UCLA Law if they were black or Hispanic. Further, in 2024 and 2025 (combined), half of the admitted black applicants had LSAT scores that were at or below 90% of the admitted white applicants.
As recipients of federal financial assistance, law schools are subject to federal non-discrimination laws. The Department will continue to investigate their compliance with Title VI, as interpreted by SFFA’s prohibition on race-conscious admissions. Where a violation has been found, the Department will engage in settlement negotiations to ensure the school’s admissions practices are brought into compliance. If those efforts fail, the Department will file suit.
Members of the public may report possible civil rights violations at www.civilrights.justice.gov/.
NOTE: Read the Department’s Findings Letter here.
title: Justice Department Finds UCLA Law School Discriminates Based on Race in Admissions

From frequent moves and deployments to balancing education and family responsibilities, military life can create unique childcare challenges for Airmen, Guardians and their families.
The Air and Space Forces Aid Society, the services’ official relief organization, offers several programs to help families with childcare costs during different stages of military life.
“Childcare can quickly become an added source of stress for military families, particularly during a move, deployment or other major transition,” said retired Command Chief Master Sgt. Kris Spencer, AFAS chief operating officer, who oversees the organization’s programs and support services. “Our goal is to provide practical support that gives families greater flexibility and helps relieve some of that burden.”
Childcare assistance available through AFAS includes:
Giving Parents a Break
Provides families up to $120 per dependent child over a three-month period to give parents an opportunity to take a much-needed break during periods of stress. To qualify, families must be referred by a unit commander, first sergeant, medical provider, chaplain or Military and Family Readiness Center personnel.
Childcare for PCS
Provides $200 per dependent child up to age 12, with a maximum of $1,000 per family, to help cover childcare during a permanent change of station. Assistance is also available for retirement, palace chase, and separation moves. All Air Force and Space Force families qualify regardless of rank or finances.
Education Childcare Grant
Provides up to $750 in childcare assistance for eligible military spouses approved for the AFAS Bee Arnold Spouse Tuition Program, helping offset childcare costs while they pursue education or career goals.
For these programs, approved funds are sent directly to families through Zelle or ACH, providing the flexibility to choose the childcare option that best meets their needs.
“We want Airmen, Guardians, and their families to know these resources are available and easy to access,” Spencer said. “When childcare is a challenge, AFAS is here to help.”
To learn more or to apply, visit afas.org.
title: AFAS offers childcare assistance to Air Force, Space Force families

MOBILE, AL – Tyler Matthew McIlwain, age 31, was sentenced to life in prison after entering guilty pleas to Sexual Exploitation of a Minor and Attempted Enticement of a Minor on March 25, 2026.

According to court documents, in October 2024 the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force received a tip that McIlwain was in possession of child pornography. During the investigation, MCSO obtained McIlwain’s social media accounts and his cell phone which contained numerous incidents of McIlwain distributing child pornography, including graphic images of the abuse of infants. McIlwain also communicated with other pedophiles about their shared desire to sexually abuse children and infants. On his cell phone, investigators discovered a video of McIlwain sexually abusing a minor. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) later identified the minor in the video.

At sentencing, United States District Judge Moorer imposed a life sentence and a 15-year term of supervised release in the unlikely event that McIlwain is ever released from prison. During his term of imprisonment, McIlwain will be subject to sex offender treatment and mental health treatment. McIlwain will be required to register as a sex offender and is to have no contact with minors. McIlwain was ordered to pay $15,000 in restitution and $200 in special assessments.

“Protecting children from predators like this defendant is one of the highest priorities of the Department of Justice,” said Sean P. Costello, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Alabama. “Today’s sentence ensures this criminal will never be free to exploit children in South Alabama or anywhere else. Working with our law enforcement partners and courageous victims, we will continue to relentlessly investigate and prosecute those who prey on children for their own sick ends. I am especially grateful for the excellent work done in this case by the FBI and the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office. The are steadfast partners in our commitment to doing justice on behalf of the victims.”

“Child exploitation inflicts lasting harm, and today’s sentencing underscores the FBI’s determination to protect victims and pursue those who commit these crimes,” said Christopher R. Flowers, Special Agent in Charge, FBI Mobile Division. “Quick action and a thorough investigation by Mobile Sheriff’s Investigators led to a request for FBI assistance. Strong partnerships like this are vital to bringing offenders to justice. The FBI remains committed to rebuilding public trust, and we urge the public to report suspected child exploitation at tips.fbi.gov.”

“Our ICAC investigators did outstanding work on this case from the very beginning,” stated Mobile County Sherrif Paul Burch. “Their investigation uncovered deeply disturbing criminal activity involving the exploitation of children and ultimately led to federal charges and a guilty plea. Cases like this demonstrate the critical importance of our Internet Crimes Against Children Unit. We will continue working with our federal partners to identify those who prey on children and hold offenders accountable.”

The Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kacey Chappelear prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.usdoj.gov/psc. For more information about Internet safety education, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc/publications-resources.

EPA and Partners Highlight Progress on Brownfields Cleanup of Infamous Illegal Dumping Site in Camden, NJ
$2.5 million EPA Brownfields grant will support cleanup of former S. Yaffa & Sons facility
NEW YORK — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and its local and state partners today joined forces to highlight a huge leap forward for the Brownfields cleanup and redevelopment efforts at the former S. Yaffa & Sons facility in Camden. The City of Camden is slated to receive a $2.5 million EPA Brownfields grant to drive final cleanup activities at the property, which has been the infamous site of illegal dumping. With these funds, EPA is delivering on the Trump Administration’s commitment to provide clean air, land, and water for Americans while providing economic growth and opportunity for communities.
During the event, EPA Regional Administrator Michael Martucci, Rep. Donald Norcross, Mayor of Camden Victor G. Carstarphen, Camden County Board of Commissioners Director Jeff Nash, and other officials celebrated progress and laid out planned cleanup activities and opportunities for continued community involvement. The work will advance Camden redevelopment efforts, support healthier neighborhoods, and create opportunities for economic growth.
“This site was for decades a terrible eyesore and posed a serious health hazard for nearby residents. Thanks to the collaboration of all levels of government, today this site is ready for the final phase of cleanup needed to return it to the community as a site that can be used productively and to the community’s advantage,” said EPA Regional Administrator Michael Martucci. “EPA has long been a partner in this endeavor and others across Camden and our Brownfields program is now set to provide the funding needed for this final phase that we celebrate today,”
“Leaving things in a better place than how you found them is a good rule to live by. Camden has benefitted greatly during my lifetime by leaders following that principle, and the team effort to earn this substantial funding for environmental cleanup is just the latest example,” Congressman Donald Norcross (NJ-01) said. “I’m proud to have advocated for this project since day one, and I’m even prouder to be part of the group of people making such a big difference for Camden.”
“We are delighted to announce the $2.5 million U.S. Environmental Protection Agency grant award which will aid in the cleanup of underground contamination and advance the ongoing redevelopment at the S. Yaffa & Sons/Weyhill site,” said Camden Mayor Victor G. Carstarphen. “In just five years, this location has been transformed from a nuisance property to an opportunity for community growth. The cleanup of the site has already spurred in new public-private investments throughout this area. We are grateful to Congressman Donald Norcross and EPA for this critical funding to improve the quality of life in Camden.”
The $2.5 million EPA Brownfields grant will fund cleanup activities, such as cleanup of the Former S. Yaffa & Sons facility, which has a history of automotive repair and illegal dumping. The grant will also support community engagement.
EPA’s Brownfields Program began in 1995 and, once these grants are awarded, will have provided over $3 billion in grant funding to assess and clean up contaminated properties and return blighted properties to productive reuse. To date, brownfields investments leveraged more than $45 billion in cleanup and redevelopment. Over the years, the relatively small investment of federal funding was able to leverage, from both public and private sources, more than 228,900 jobs. Through fiscal year 2025, on average, $19.47 was leveraged for each EPA Brownfields Grant dollar awarded through multipurpose, assessment, revolving loan fund and cleanup cooperative agreements.
To learn more, visit EPA Brownfields.

Rep. Lee, UNLV Announce New Program to Make Higher Education More Affordable, Lee’s Bipartisan Legislation to Expand Program Nationwide
LAS VEGAS, NV – Today, Congresswoman Susie Lee (NV-03) hosted a roundtable at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) with Earn to Learn and UNLV students and administrators to announce UNLV’s new Earn to Learn program that will make higher education more affordable for current and returning students, and to discuss Lee’s bipartisan Earn to Learn Act, which would expand implementation of this program nationwide.
“As a lifelong education advocate, I know that education is the key to opportunity. Unfortunately, the cost of higher education has skyrocketed, leaving many graduating with crippling student debt,” said Congresswoman Susie Lee. “I’m glad my commonsense bill will help Nevadans achieve the education and training they need without taking on crippling debt, and I look forward to continue working with UNLV to help higher education more attainable for students here in Nevada.”
In response to rising higher education costs nationwide, the Earn to Learn Act is common-sense legislation that would establish a matched-savings program to help low-income students, including adult learners, pay for tuition, books, fees, and other education-related expenses.
This bipartisan bill is a much-needed step to addressing the student loans crisis in the United States. Nearly 368,000 Nevadans together owe approximately $13.2 billion in student loan debt. Additionally, 93,000 Nevadans, or 25% of Nevadans with student loans, are in default—and Nevada borrowers in default owe more than $2 billion.
“Higher education creates a pathway to personal and career success, but affordability is a real concern for many attending or considering a return to college,” said Chris Heavey, UNLV interim president. “That’s why we’re proud to partner with Earn to Learn through our Destination Degree initiative to remove barriers to access and make the road to a UNLV degree more attainable. And we’re grateful to Congresswoman Lee for her continuing efforts to advance the Earn to Learn Act, which would reduce reliance on student loans, improve financial literacy, and make higher education possible for students in Nevada and nationwide.”
Modeled off the successful Earn to Learn program, the Earn to Learn Act helps Nevadans achieve the education and training they need without taking on crippling debt. Students who qualify save $500 of their own money toward their education. Their investment is then matched 8:1 through a combination of public and private support. The combination of the student’s savings and the match creates up to $4,500 in flexible scholarship support that can address unmet need and remove financial barriers to postsecondary completion.
“For more than a decade, Earn to Learn has seen the power of combining matched savings, financial education, and student support to help students invest in their own futures, complete their education, and build greater financial stability,” said Kate Hoffman, founder and chief executive officer of Earn to Learn. “The Earn to Learn Act creates an opportunity to bring this proven model to students across the country, while our partnership with UNLV demonstrates what is possible when higher education, government, philanthropy, and the private sector come together to invest in students. We are incredibly grateful to Congresswoman Lee for her leadership and to UNLV for helping bring this innovative approach to Nevada and expand pathways to education and economic opportunity.”
As seen during the program’s operations at the state level, Earn to Learn scholars have a first-year retention rate nearing 90%, and the majority of them graduate with little or no student loan debt. In fact, the majority of Earn to Learn students graduate with less than $10,000 in student loan debt. The demonstration program created by the bill would enable an estimated 250,000 scholarships over the course of five years.
Before coming to Congress, Lee spent two decades leading education non-profits – reducing dropout rates and making sure Nevada kids had the wrap-around services they needed to thrive.

IMAGERY AVAILABLE: Coast Guard, Air National Guard conduct long-range medevac 58 miles south of Adak, Alaska
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Coast Guard and the Alaska Air National Guard conducted a complex, long-range medevac of a 58-year-old man from a container ship approximately 58 miles south of Adak, Wednesday.
Coast Guard Arctic District watchstanders received a medevac request at approximately 6 a.m. Tuesday from the crew of the 991-foot Japanese-flagged container ship One Majesty. The vessel’s master was reportedly experiencing severe abdominal pain indicating a medical emergency.
Watchstanders directed the launch of a Coast Guard Air Station Kodiak MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter aircrew to medevac the man.
Due to the extreme travel distance of over 1,000 miles, about the same distance from Tampa Bay, Florida, to New York City, the transit required refueling stops in Dutch Harbor and Adak along the way.
To mitigate crew fatigue and ensure flight safety over the long transit, the mission also required a helicopter crew swap prior to the rescue. The Coast Guard requested the assistance of an AKANG HC-130J Combat King II aircrew with the 211th Rescue Squadron based out of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (JBER), who transported the following personnel to meet the helicopter crew in Adak:
- A relief Coast Guard helicopter crew from Air Station Kodiak.
- Two pararescuemen from the Alaska Air National Guard’s 212th Rescue Squadron, also based out of JBER.
For additional safety, a second Coast Guard MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew launched from Air Station Kodiak and staged in Cold Bay to provide cover in the event the primary helicopter crew required emergency assistance.
Once in Adak, the Coast Guard helicopter relief crew, carrying the two National Guard pararescuemen, launched from Adak alongside the HC-130J aircraft, which provided overhead flight cover.
The two aircrews then flew approximately 58 miles south from Adak to the One Majesty. The Coast Guard aircrew hoisted the patient and returned to Adak, transferring him to the care of the AKANG HC-130 aircrew. The AKANG aircrew then transported him to Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport where he was transferred to EMS personnel.
"I am incredibly proud of the resilience displayed by everyone involved in this long and complex rescue effort," said Jennifer Whitcomb, search and rescue mission coordinator at Coast Guard Arctic District. "The determination and collaborative efforts of the Coast Guard, Alaska Air National Guard and One Majesty crew were the vital keys to the success of this life-saving mission."
For media inquiries, please contact the Arctic District Public Affairs Office at uscgalaska@uscg.mil.
-USCG-

WASHINGTON – Three members of the Unknown Vice Lords (UVL), a violent street gang in Memphis, Tennessee, were sentenced to a total of over 42 years in prison for conspiring and attempting to commit a gang-related murder and firearms violations.

“These individuals showed a blatant disregard for public safety by engaging in a gang shooting in the middle of a residential neighborhood,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Gang violence terrorizes our communities, fosters fear, destabilizes neighborhoods, and endangers the lives of law-abiding residents. The Criminal Division is standing up for the rule of law. We will continue to dismantle these criminal organizations to zealously protect the safety and security of American citizens.”

“The days of criminal gangs controlling the streets of Memphis are over.” said U.S. Attorney D. Michael Dunavant for the Western District of Tennessee. “Gang culture, rivalries, and beefs beget more senseless gang violence that endangers innocent citizens. If you are a member of a criminal gang committed to a lifestyle of lawlessness, no matter your rank, role, or nickname - your days are numbered - there will be a reckoning.”

“ATF’s primary mission is to ensure public safety by combating violent crime,” said Special Agent in Charge James VanVliet of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Nashville Field Division. “Individuals who deliberately engage in violent activities such as retaliatory gang shootings render our communities vulnerable to great harm, instill fear, and ultimately diminish the quality of life for all citizens. The ATF will continue to work with our local, state, and federal law enforcement partners to aggressively investigate offenders who render our communities unsafe.”

The following individuals were sentenced:

Antwon Brown, also known as Yayo, 33, of Memphis, was sentenced to 300 months in prison for attempting to commit murder and discharging a firearm into an occupied residence.

Cordera Douglas, also known as Chuckie Dee, 37, of Memphis, was sentenced to 87 months in prison for conspiring to commit murder.

Willie Merriweather, also known as Willie, 42, of Antioch, Tennessee, was sentenced to 120 months in prison for conspiring to commit murder.

According to court documents, Brown, Douglas, and Merriweather were all ranked members of UVL, also known as The Ghost Mob, which is a criminal enterprise that controlled territory throughout Memphis, Arkansas, and Mississippi. Members of UVL committed murders, assaults, and drug trafficking on behalf of the enterprise.

Court documents allege that on Sept. 6, 2020, rival gang members opened fire on UVL members and their families, injuring four people. Merriweather, who was a high-ranking UVL leader, ordered a retaliatory attack. Douglas participated in a gang meeting planning retaliation. Shortly after midnight on Sept. 7, 2020, Brown traveled to the residence of the rival gang members armed with assault style rifles and wearing masks and gloves. Brown intentionally shot approximately 40-50 bullets into the residence with the rival gang members inside. Neighborhood security cameras captured the shooting. In the video, Brown is using, carrying, and firing multiple firearms into the residence.

Antwon Brown pictured on left

Co-defendant Ricky Rogers, Jr., also known as Double R, RR, 32, of Memphis, is set to be sentenced on Nov. 5.

Co-defendant Tevin Richardson, also known as Santana, 34, of Memphis, is set for trial on April 4, 2027.

The ATF and Memphis Police Department investigated the case.

Trial Attorneys Lisa M. Thelwell and Dennis Robinson of the Criminal Division’s Violent Crime and Racketeering Section are prosecuting the case, with substantial assistance from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Tennessee.

This case is part of the Criminal Division’s Violent Crime Initiative to prosecute violent crimes in Memphis, Tennessee, and surrounding areas. The Criminal Division and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Tennessee have partnered, along with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies, to confront violent crimes committed by gang members and associates through the enforcement of federal laws and use of federal resources to prosecute the violent offenders and prevent further violence.

ATF marks 10-year anniversary of Crime Gun Intelligence Governance Board
National leaders gather in Jacksonville to advance strategic integration of firearms technology, forensics, and violent crime reduction efforts
WASHINGTON - The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives concluded the semi-annual meeting of the National Crime Gun Intelligence Governance Board last week in Jacksonville, Florida, marking a decade of leading the nation’s crime gun intelligence strategy.
Held Sept. 21–22, the two-day meeting convened federal, state, local, and county law enforcement executives, prosecutors, and forensic experts to discuss future enhancements to crime gun intelligence operations nationwide, which capitalize on the 10 years of progress that the board has set into motion.
Crime Gun Intelligence Centers are interagency collaborations between ATF, local police departments, crime laboratories, and federal and state prosecutors. CGICs leverage technology, intelligence, and forensic analysis to investigate gun crime, identify armed violent offenders, and dismantle illicit firearms supply chains.
The Crime Gun Intelligence Governance Board provides strategic direction, policy oversight, and best practices for the operation and expansion of Crime Gun Intelligence Centers and the use of Crime Gun Intelligence across the country. CGICs combine automated ballistic identification technology, such as the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network, with trace data, forensic analysis, and intelligence mapping to rapidly identify serial shooters, disrupt illegal firearms trafficking networks, and apprehend violent offenders.
“Crime gun intelligence works, and the proof is in the numbers,” said ATF Director Rob Cekada. “As law enforcement increased NIBIN ballistics processing by over 13 percent last year, firearm-related crime dropped by 12 percent. The Governance Board has turned fired cartridge casings into actionable leads, empowering local, state, county and federal partners to stop retaliatory violence before it starts and keep our communities safe.”
Today, 25 ATF Crime Gun Intelligence Centers operate nationwide, serving key metropolitan areas including Philadelphia, St. Louis, Louisville, Boston, Nashville, and Denver. These centers function as regional hubs for multi-agency collaboration, connecting local police departments, federal prosecutors, and crime laboratories to ensure evidence collected from crime scenes is analyzed rapidly to prevent retaliatory violence.
The Governance Board has led to advancements in forensic capabilities, including automated firearms tracing, streamlining evidence processing workflows, and establishing priority metrics to expand CGIC support to rural and mid-sized law enforcement partners. During the Jacksonville meeting, board members: evaluated crime gun intelligence resources available to law enforcement partners looking to develop or improve upon the use of CGI in their violent crime reduction strategy; discussed outreach to expand NIBIN in areas that did not have adequate coverage; and the employment of technological advancements to enhance efficiencies in the acquisition and correlation of ballistic evidence.
The Board meets twice annually to address emerging trends impacting national crime gun intelligence strategy. In-person meetings are hosted at the Board’s dedicated facility on the Wichita State University campus, as well as in host cities nationwide like Jacksonville to support regional law enforcement collaboration.
For more information on ATF’s Crime Gun Intelligence initiative and NIBIN technology, visit www.atf.gov.
###
ATF protects American communities from violent crime driven by the illegal use of firearms, explosives, and acts of arson. Through crime gun intelligence, forensic analysis, and relentless investigation, we identify and arrest violent offenders and gang members, dismantle trafficking networks, and sever the supply chains arming cartels, prohibited persons, and terrorist organizations. We defend the rights of law-abiding citizens by safeguarding lawful commerce and upholding the Constitution of the United States. Learn more about what ATF is doing to reduce violent crime in your community by following us on X @ATFHQ, Instagram @ATFHQ, LinkedIn @ATF, and Facebook @HQATF, or on the web at www.atf.gov.
title: ATF marks 10-year anniversary of Crime Gun Intelligence Governance Board

text:
WASHINGTON—Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury took unprecedented action against the A7 Network, a shadow banking network with ties to Russia used by the Iranian regime to evade sanctions.
- Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed a rule that would prohibit transmittals of funds regarding transactions involving the A7 Network’s Sub-Agents.
- Additionally, FinCEN issued an Alert to help financial institutions detect and report suspicious activity related to the A7 Network.
- Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned the A7 Network as a significant transnational criminal organization.
“Treasury is dismantling the financial infrastructure that allows Iran and other adversaries to evade sanctions, move illicit funds, and undermine the integrity of the global financial system,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Today’s action targeting A7 continues Treasury’s unprecedented efforts to isolate Iran and its financial enablers and sends a clear message that if you facilitate illicit finance for America’s adversaries, you will lose access to the U.S. financial system.”
The A7 Network was created and backed by U.S.-sanctioned persons in order to evade sanctions. It has developed a global web of Sub-Agents, companies that are purpose-built to disguise payments linked to sanctioned sectors and persons as ordinary commercial activity. The A7 Network has been leveraged by Iran, including Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Today’s actions build on the August 14, 2025 designation of several A7 Network entities, such as A7 LLC and Old Vector LLC, by exposing the broader network itself to U.S. sanctions.
THE A7 NETWORK’S FACILITATION OF RUSSIAN ILLICIT FINANCE: CREATING A PARALLEL FINANCIAL SYSTEM
As set out in the notice of proposed rulemaking, the A7 Network’s Sub-Agents are a constellation of companies based in third-country jurisdictions designed to receive and remit payments to facilitate transactions for the A7 Network. These Sub-Agents form a core layer of the A7 Network’s operational architecture as a purpose-built sanctions evasion and money laundering mechanism connected to Russian illicit finance and exploited by other illicit finance threat actors, including Iran. The public comment period will close 30 days after the NPRM is published in the Federal Register.
The A7 Network exploits the international financial system by leveraging Sub-Agents, falsified trade documents, falsified import-export records, and misleading goods descriptions to make sanctioned or illicit payments appear to be ordinary commercial activity. By its own account, as of January 2026, the A7 Network claimed to process more than 2,000 transactions a day with a total transaction volume of more than 7.5 trillion rubles, the U.S. dollar equivalent of $91.5 billion or approximately 13 percent of the Russian Federation’s 2025 foreign trade transactions.
Today’s notice of proposed rulemaking, issued pursuant to section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act, is not limited to Russian sanctions evasion. The same A7 Network Sub-Agents that enable Russian illicit finance created pathways for other actors, including the Central Bank of Iran, the IRGC, and Iran-backed terrorist organizations, to move funds through the international financial system. Beyond state actors, A7 Network Sub-Agents also catered to cybercriminals, including ransomware and procurement actors seeking to obtain restricted goods, to move funds through the international financial system. FinCEN’s investigation identified that the A7 Network’s Sub-Agents processed more than $17 billion between January 2025 and June 2026, aggregated globally.
In addition, A7 Network Sub-Agents have been used to facilitate Iranian oil sales and weapons procurement efforts. For example, one A7 Network Sub-Agent directly transacted with entities involved in Iran’s “shadow fleet”—the network of tankers, shipping companies, and front companies used to transport and sell Iranian oil in contravention of U.S. and international sanctions; that same A7 Network Sub-Agent and its sister company received nearly $140 million from entities involved in Iranian sanctions evasion. A separate A7 Network Sub-Agent transferred approximately $1.6 million to a company linked to Iranian sanctions evasion and weapons procurement efforts.
FINCEN ISSUING KEY INDICATORS OF A7 NETWORK ACTIVITY
FinCEN’s Alert will assist financial institutions to be vigilant in detecting, identifying, and reporting suspicious activity and specifies a list of red flags to assist in identifying activity involving the A7 Network. The Alert describes the A7 Network’s use of foreign companies to facilitate its access to international payment systems.
FinCEN’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking can be found here.
FinCEN’s Alert can be found here.
Today’s action follows the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency’s August 31, 2026 Alert on A7 which describes the use of the A7 Network to facilitate sanctions evasion and illicit financial activity involving Russia and Iran.
For questions on FinCEN’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking or Alert, please contact FinCEN at http://www.fincen.gov/contact.
A7 DESIGNATED AS TRANSNATIONAL CRIMINAL ORGANIZATION
Today, OFAC is complementing FinCEN’s action against the A7 Network by sanctioning it as a significant transnational criminal organization. As described above, the A7 Network is a shadow banking network with ties to Russia that utilizes money laundering methodologies to fraudulently move vast sums of money in violation of sanctions and other laws in the jurisdictions in which it operates. The A7 Network is led by Ilan Mironovich Shor, a sanctioned and convicted criminal fraudster, and includes a constellation of companies known as Sub-Agents that it uses to disguise illicit transactions as legitimate trade. Today’s action in furtherance of Operation Economic Outcast underscores the A7 Network’s financial support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as well as Iranian proxies, such as Hamas. Furthermore, the A7 Network has been linked to Nobitex, Iran’s largest digital asset exchange, which OFAC designated on June 2, 2026, and has also facilitated transactions related to North Korean hacks of cryptocurrency exchanges and other illicit actors.
The A7 Network’s Sub-Agents are wholly controlled by A7 Network individuals. A7 Network Sub-Agents’ websites and bank accounts are controlled by A7 Network staff, who access Sub-Agent financial accounts using custom-built Virtual Private Networks that mask their true location and permit the rapid execution of payments.
The A7A5 token is a blocked, ruble-backed token issued by Old Vector LLC, which OFAC designated on August 14, 2025 and is part of the A7 Network. The A7 Network created the token for its members to evade sanctions and transact internationally while generating revenue for sanctioned infrastructure providers that profit from the token’s circulation.
SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS OF TODAY’S OFAC ACTION AGAINST THE A7 NETWORK
As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the A7 Network, including transactions involving Sub-Agents acting for or on behalf of the A7 Network, that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC. In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. Unless authorized by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons.
Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons. OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions. In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons. The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing or conspiring to cause U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades U.S. sanctions.
Individuals located in the United States or abroad who provide information to about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. As highlighted in FinCEN’s recent Bulletin, this includes information about violations of the Bank Secrecy Act or OFAC-administered sanctions programs that may involve the use of Iranian proxies and facilitators operating outside of Iran.

The Department of Justice Files Complaint Against the University of Delaware Challenging Policies that Provide In-State Tuition to Illegal Aliens
Today, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the University of Delaware for violating federal law by prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands. The Department is challenging the University of Delaware’s policy which grants in-state tuition for illegal aliens while denying reduced tuition to U.S. citizens. This policy unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate, which is in direct conflict with federal law.
“This Department of Justice’s efforts will not cease until we have challenged every state law or university policy that gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. “Congress long ago made clear that states cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans. When a state Attorney General allows her own state to violate federal law, this department must step in to enforce it.”
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”
In the complaint, the United States seeks to enjoin the University of Delaware from enforcing its policy that provides aliens who reside in Delaware with in-state tuition rates, regardless of whether those aliens are lawfully present in the United States. Additionally, the complaint seeks to enjoin the University of Delaware from enacting any new tuition policies that favor illegal aliens over U.S. citizens.
Today’s lawsuit brings the Department’s total to 26 lawsuits challenging in-state tuition for illegal aliens. Under the leadership of Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department’s efforts have delivered numerous wins for the American people, as six lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois, and Kansas have resulted in favorable orders permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional similar laws which gave reduced tuition to illegal aliens including an order from the Fifth Circuit.
Lawsuits against other states that are also violating federal law by putting illegal aliens ahead of U.S. citizens are pending across the country including Minnesota, Virginia, California, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland, Colorado, New York, Connecticut, Vermont, Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, Washington, Hawaii, the District of Columbia, Arkansas, and Utah.
For more information about the Enforcement & Affirmative Litigation Branch and its affirmative litigation efforts visit www.justice.gov/civil/enforcement-affirmative-litigation-branch.

WASHINGTON — Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, a resident of Richland, Washington, was arrested this morning and charged with attempting to provide material support or resources to the Houthis, a designated foreign terrorist organization. Ellaboudy is scheduled to make an initial appearance before a federal magistrate judge on Oct. 2 at 11:00 a.m. in Richland, Washington.

“As alleged, a U.S. government employee traveled overseas and used his specialized expertise in an attempt to aid the Houthis, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization backed by Iran,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Additionally, Ellaboudy acquired materials for the construction of explosive material and drones capable of delivering these explosives. These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination.”

“Protecting the American people is the FBI’s mission and the cornerstone of everything we do,” said W. Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Seattle field office. “We deeply value the partnership of the Department of Energy and the law enforcement agencies working with us on Joint Terrorism Task Forces throughout Washington, as well as the tireless efforts of our investigators to develop this case. Their work is a remarkable example of our shared commitment to protecting the state of Washington as well as the constant vigilance required to keep our state and nation safe.”

“The Hanford Field Office appreciates the leadership and diligence of the investigation conducted by the FBI. This matter did not involve an attempt to harm the Hanford Site or its workforce, and at no time was there a threat to the safety or security of the site,” said Office Manager Ray Geimer of the Department of Energy Hanford Field Office. “We remain committed to providing a safe and secure workplace as we move the Hanford mission forward.”

According to court records, Ellaboudy, who was a Department of Energy employee, came to the attention of the FBI after they received information that he had purchased precursor chemicals, components, and other materials commonly used in the construction of homemade explosive devices. In addition to the precursor chemicals, the investigation revealed Ellaboudy had also purchased parts used for the construction of drones and remotely operated aerial systems.

The complaint alleges that in December 2024, the FBI learned that Ellaboudy took sick leave from his employment, claiming that it was due to having been exposed to highly concentrated nitric acid, a common chemical used in the construction of explosive materials. In September 2025, Ellaboudy, using an official passport previously issued to him when employed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, traveled from Richland, Washington to Oman. Upon arriving in Oman, Ellaboudy used this same passport to cross the border into Yemen with the intent on traveling to Sanaa, Yemen, the country’s capital, which is under the control of the Houthis. Upon returning to the United States, Ellaboudy stated to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officers that he had travelled overseas on official government business. Subsequent information from Ellaboudy’s DOE supervisor revealed he did not have any authorized official government travel to that region.

During the investigation, Ellaboudy began communicating with an FBI confidential human source (CHS) who purported to be working for a Houthi “Colonel” to acquire communications equipment that would be sent to Yemen for use in a mobile communications center. Ellaboudy provided expert advice and assistance, based upon his background in electrical engineering, by helping the CHS test and modify solar power generators and communication equipment. Additionally, Ellaboudy provided guidance on how the power systems and communication system integrated, provided schematics and diagrams for the proper setup of the systems, and conducted research and provided guidance on other equipment that could be acquired to enhance the communications equipment of the Houthis.

If convicted, Ellaboudy faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

The FBI’s Inland Northwest Joint Terrorism Task Force investigated the case.

This matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lisa Cartier-Giroux for the Eastern District of Washington and Trial Attorneys Patrick Cashman and Ryan White of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

The charges contained in the complaint are only allegations. A person is presumed innocent unless and until he or she is proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Department of Energy Employee Arrested in Washington State on Charges of Attempted Material Support to Houthis

DETROIT - Two Detroit-area residents were indicted for their roles in a scheme to embezzle money from incapacitated persons, announced United States Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr.

Joining in the announcement was Special Agent in Charge Jennifer Runyan, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Detroit Field Division.

Kijuana Evans, 54, of Clinton Township and Lonnie Griffin, 57, of Harper Woods, were charged in an indictment with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering.

According to the indictment, probate courts regularly appoint guardians and conservators to manage the personal and financial affairs of adults, known as wards, who have been found by the court to lack the capacity to do so themselves. Guardians and conservators are fiduciaries who are obligated to act in the best interests of their wards. The indictment alleges that Kijuana Evans owned TriState Guardian Services, an agency that was appointed as a fiduciary by the Oakland County Probate Court for incapacitated wards. Lonnie Griffin operated Key to Life, a non-emergency transportation service, and was employed as a manager of TriState.

The indictment alleges that the defendants conspired to systematically embezzle funds from wards, and to obtain and retain money for themselves that rightly belonged to the wards and the wards’ estates. The indictment sets forth examples of the co-conspirators working together to misappropriate money belonging to wards. In one instance, Evans is alleged to have used $87,000 in a ward’s funds to purchase a transit van used by Griffin’s transportation company. In another, Evans and Griffin are alleged to have taken for themselves $180,000 in funds from the sale of a ward’s home. In yet another case, Evans and Griffin are alleged to have taken the proceeds of a ward’s lawsuit settlement and deposited it into their bank account.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Robert Moran. The investigation is being conducted by the FBI.

An indictment is only a charge and is not evidence of guilt. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. It is the government’s burden to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Washington, DC — Today, Congressmen Lou Correa (D-CA) and Jack Bergman (R-MI) reintroduced the VA Medicinal Cannabis Research Act. The bipartisan legislation directs the Department of Veterans Affairs to conduct clinical research on the safety and efficacy of medical cannabis in treating veterans’ post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic pain.

"With the opioid crisis raging across America, it is imperative to the health and safety of our veterans that we find alternative treatments for chronic pain and service-related injuries," said Correa. "Throughout my district, I consistently meet veterans who depend on cannabis to manage their pain. Numerous veterans attest to the treatment benefits of medical cannabis. It's time the VA did a formal study and began recognizing that cannabis can play a safe role in our veterans' healthcare."

The bill would:

Authorize VA to implement a comprehensive research plan, including clinical trials assessing the effectiveness of medicinal cannabis in treating chronic pain and PTSD.

Expand research into related factors in veterans' health, including improvements to mood and social functioning, impacts on other substance use, and overall quality of life.

Require clinical trials to examine different forms, potencies, and methods of cannabis administration, with veterans' health and safety prioritized throughout.

“Veterans struggling with PTSD and chronic pain deserve access to treatments backed by sound science and rigorous research. The VA Medicinal Cannabis Research Act will help us better understand whether medicinal cannabis can provide safe and effective relief while ensuring Veterans’ health and safety remain the top priority. We owe it to our Veterans to explore every responsible avenue that could improve their quality of life,” said Bergman.

Chronic pain affects one in five Americans and impacts veterans at a higher rate than the general population. Twenty-three percent of veterans receiving VA care have experienced PTSD at some point in their lives, and the two conditions are often linked — veterans with chronic pain have elevated rates of PTSD. This bill would mandate research that could lead to safer, more effective treatment options for veterans managing these conditions.

"Since 2017, IAVA has made empowering veterans who are calling for the medicinal use of cannabis one of our top priorities. Our members have said consistently and passionately that cannabis offers real help with the most pressing injuries we face when we come home, from chronic pain to PTSD to traumatic brain injury. Our national policies are lagging, research is lacking, and the stigma persists. The VA Medicinal Cannabis Research Act is how we start to change that. Every solution begins with research, and veterans have waited long enough for it," said Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA).

“The VFW supports the VA Medicinal Cannabis Research Act of 2023,” said Pat Murray, Director, National Legislative Service, Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW). “VFW members tell us that medicinal cannabis has helped them cope with chronic pain and other service-connected health conditions. They cannot receive these services at VA because of VA’s bureaucratic hurdles. VA uses evidence-based clinical guidelines to manage other pharmacological treatments of post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic pain, and substance use disorder because medical trials have found them effective. VA must expand research on the efficacy of non-traditional medical therapies, such as medicinal cannabis and other holistic approaches.”

View the bill text HERE.

text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández, responsabilizó hoy al Gobierno por el aumento en la factura de luz que entra en vigor hoy. Una familia que consume 800 kilovatios-hora al mes pagará unos $42 más. El Comisionado Residente presentó cuatro alternativas para aliviar a las familias a corto plazo.

"Hoy las familias puertorriqueñas empiezan a pagar 18% más por la luz, y no es por mala suerte. Es el resultado de una reconstrucción lenta, de plantas averiadas y de un sistema que depende de una sola empresa para recibir el gas. La gente no puede seguir pagando los errores de otros", expresó el Comisionado Residente.

Nueve años después del huracán María, el 75% de los $14,300 millones en fondos federales obligados para la red eléctrica sigue sin desembolsarse, según la Oficina de Rendición de Cuentas del Gobierno federal (GAO). Mientras tanto, las plantas averiadas obligan a quemar diésel, un combustible mucho más caro.

"El Gobierno negoció con New Fortress un contrato de gas que la propia Junta de Supervisión Fiscal criticó por falta de competencia. Hoy esa empresa controla el única terminal por donde entra el gas a San Juan. Desde el 16 de septiembre las unidades 5 y 6 de la Central San Juan no reciben gas y estamos quemando diésel, que es cuatro veces más caro. El Negociado de Energía ya dejó fuera de la factura, por ahora, unos $75 millones vinculados a alegados incumplimientos de New Fortress, e investiga $19 millones en gas que Genera, su subsidiaria, habría pedido de más. El conflicto en el Medio Oriente ha empeorado los precios, pero no lo explica todo: el propio Negociado señaló plantas fuera de servicio y fallas en la entrega de gas", añadió el Comisionado Residente.

El Comisionado Residente propuso cuatro medidas inmediatas:

Que New Fortress responda por sus alegados incumplimientos. El Negociado de Energía dejó fuera de la factura, por ahora, unos $75 millones vinculados a los alegados incumplimientos de New Fortress. Esos costos no deben pasar nunca a la factura del pueblo.

Que el Gobierno asegure la entrada del gas y tenga un plan B. La demanda que presentó el Gobierno contra New Fortress es un paso, pero no basta. Hay que resolver ya la entrada del gas a San Juan y tener otro suplidor con contrato firmado por si New Fortress vuelve a fallar. Cada día que se quema diésel se paga en la factura de enero. El gobierno debe garantizar el suministro de gas finalizando su contrato de respaldo y comenzando a utilizar a los otros proveedores de GNL en la isla.

Que ADSEF aclare cuántos fondos federales de LIHEAP tiene disponibles. Este programa federal ayuda a pagar la luz a participantes de TANF y a otras familias de bajos ingresos que cualifiquen. ADSEF debe informar cuánto dinero tiene y cuándo abre las ayudas, ahora que más familias las necesitan.

Que el Gobierno identifique recursos para un alivio temporero. Si se encontraron $554 millones para el cheque de alivio contributivo, debe poder identificar recursos para aliviar la factura de luz mientras dure esta crisis, junto con incentivos para que las familias ahorren energía. Otras posibles medidas incluyen la reducción de la crudita y el trabajo a distancia. No obstante, urge que los alivios mantengan el presupuesto balanceado y que cada pérdida sea subsanada mediante recortes en otras áreas del presupuesto.

"Desde el Congreso he exigido que los fondos federales para la red se usen ya: he llevado el reclamo al Departamento de Energía federal con apoyo de republicanos y demócratas, y a Vivienda federal. También seguiré defendiendo en el Congreso los fondos de LIHEAP. Mi agenda es priorizar lo básico, y no hay nada más básico que prender la luz sin tener que escoger entre pagarla y comer", concluyó el Comisionado Residente.

title: Comisionado Residente responsabiliza al Gobierno por el alza en la luz y presenta alternativas
