Fast Facts
More than a million veterans have limited or uncertain access to food. Eligible veterans can get Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to help, but they're less likely to participate than non-veterans. Federal, state, and relevant organizations' officials told us that veterans may have misconceptions about SNAP.
This Q&A reviews SNAP's veteran outreach. While the Department of Agriculture has taken steps to make veterans more aware of SNAP, it could do more. For example, it doesn't have veteran-friendly outreach materials with up-to-date information.
We recommended addressing this and more to help veterans access benefits.
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and EBT Food Stamp Benefits sign
Highlights
What GAO Found
According to a 2023 RAND report, an average of 1.4 million veterans faced food insecurity each year from 2015 to 2020, meaning their households did not have enough food for an active and healthy life. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) provides benefits to low-income households to buy food. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) administers SNAP in partnership with states. The share of veterans receiving benefits varies by state, according to GAO’s analysis of Census Bureau data.
Estimated Percentage of Veterans Who Lived in Households Receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Benefits by State in 2024
States have the option to conduct outreach to increase awareness of SNAP and may target outreach to certain groups, such as veterans. States must have a USDA-approved outreach plan to receive partial federal reimbursement for their outreach expenses. Most states with outreach plans in fiscal year 2026 (39 of 47) identified veterans as a target group.
However, stakeholders GAO interviewed reported that veterans' misconceptions about SNAP hinder outreach efforts. USDA has not developed outreach materials tailored to veterans in the past 5 years, despite recent program changes for veterans. Several stakeholders said that outreach materials, such as talking points dispelling myths about SNAP, would help them communicate more effectively with veterans. By developing and disseminating such materials, USDA could help ensure that trusted messengers, like veterans’ organizations, share accurate and up-to-date information on the program with food-insecure veterans.
The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and USDA established a memorandum of agreement (MOA) to address veteran food insecurity in September 2023. However, the agencies’ collaborative efforts have slowed since April 2025 following the loss of key staff at USDA, according to VA officials. Agency officials told GAO they consider the MOA to still be in place; however, the agencies have not reviewed the MOA as specified in the agreement, making the current status of the MOA unclear. By ensuring a formal mechanism is in place to guide their collaboration, VA and USDA can enhance their efforts to ensure low-income veterans and their families have access to the food they need through programs like SNAP.
Why GAO Did This Study
Research has shown that food-insecure veterans are less likely than their nonveteran peers to participate in SNAP.
GAO was asked to review states’ efforts to target SNAP outreach to veterans and work with veterans’ organizations to help connect veterans to the program. This report examines state and federal efforts to conduct SNAP outreach to veterans.
GAO reviewed relevant federal laws, regulations, and agency documentation. GAO also analyzed survey data on veteran households’ receipt of SNAP benefits and reviewed states’ most recent SNAP outreach plans and reports. In addition, GAO interviewed VA and USDA officials and representatives of 16 stakeholder organizations, including national organizations with expertise on food assistance or veterans issues, as well as state SNAP agencies, outreach partners, and VA medical centers from three states. GAO selected states that were actively conducting SNAP outreach to veterans and varied by geographic region and the share of veterans receiving SNAP benefits. GAO selected other stakeholder organizations for their national perspectives on veteran food security issues.
Recommendations
GAO is making four recommendations, including that USDA develops and disseminates additional SNAP outreach materials tailored to veterans and that VA and USDA ensure a formal mechanism is in place to collaborate on efforts to address veteran food insecurity. We provided a draft of this report to VA and USDA for review and comment. VA and USDA concurred with GAO’s recommendations.
title: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Federal Actions Needed to Help Veterans Access Benefits

Ranking Member Khanna Demands Answers from Bessent on Trump-Xi Summit and China’s Unfair Trade Practices
WASHINGTON – Today, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA), Ranking Member of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, sent a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demanding answers about the Trump Administration’s economic strategy toward the People’s Republic of China, arguing that President Trump’s recent summit with CCP leader Xi Jinping failed to produce meaningful progress on the structural economic challenges posed by Beijing’s unfair trading practices that have very real impacts on workers and American families.
In the letter, Khanna raised concerns that the summit resulted primarily in an extension of the existing trade truce rather than concrete commitments from Beijing to address industrial overcapacity, dumping, state subsidies, forced technology transfer, critical minerals, and other unfair economic practices.
“At a time when American families are struggling with high costs and American workers continue to lose good-paying jobs, the Administration cannot afford to substitute pageantry for a strategy that rebuilds American economic strength,” Khanna wrote.
Khanna pointed to continued U.S. dependence on critical minerals from the PRC, Beijing’s subsidization of automobile production, and the continued expansion of subsidized steel exports as examples of pressing challenges that the Trump Administration has failed to meaningfully address.
He also raised concerns about the Administration’s decision to extend the trade truce despite Beijing’s failure to fulfill prior trade commitments.
The letter asks Secretary Bessent to provide answers by October 29, 2026, including:
- What economic issues did President Trump raise with President Xi?
  - Please provide a detailed account of the discussion regarding industrial overcapacity, dumping, state subsidies, forced technology transfer, critical minerals, and other unfair economic practices.
- Why did the Administration not seek to make progress on more substantive commitments at the summit?
- Has this more cooperative orientation in the Administration’s approach to Beijing been formalized in any policy or strategy document?
- To what extent did the Administration seek input from stakeholders such as organized labor, Congress, industry, and civil society to inform the agenda for Xi’s visit?
- To what extent will public input be sought for further Board of Trade actions like the one announced on September 27, 2026?
“American workers need more than reassuring rhetoric and presidential pageantry,” Khanna concluded. “They need a government that recognizes the scale of China's industrial strategy and responds with a strategy of its own. The Administration should explain to Congress and the American people what that strategy is—and why President Trump did not use this summit to demand meaningful commitments from Xi Jinping on the economic threats we face today.”
Read the letter to Treasury Secretary Bessent HERE.

title: Ranking Member Khanna Demands Answers from Bessent on Trump-Xi Summit and China’s Unfair Trade Practices

Navy High-Speed Wi-Fi Reaches 90 Percent of Global Unaccompanied Housing
01 October 2026
The Navy’s initiative to provide free, high-speed Wi-Fi to all Navy-owned and -operated unaccompanied housing has reached 90 percent completion, with the service now available in 865 of 962 total buildings since launching the rollout in November 2025.
WASHINGTON D.C. (Oct. 1, 2026) — The Navy’s initiative to provide free, high-speed Wi-Fi to all Navy-owned and -operated unaccompanied housing has reached 90 percent completion, with the service now available in 865 of 962 total buildings since launching the rollout in November 2025.
The program, a partnership between Commander, Navy Installations Command and the Navy Exchange Service Command, continued its worldwide expansion with service going live across Navy bases throughout the continental United States, Europe, Asia, and the Pacific region.
Driven by a dedicated focus on improving the quality of service, well-being, and operational readiness of Sailors, this connectivity effort ensures warfighters remain connected to family, support networks, and educational resources while stationed abroad and in the homeland.
“Reliable connectivity is an important part of sustaining the force and ensuring Sailors have the support they need to remain ready and resilient,” said Adm. Scott Gray, Deputy Chief of Naval Operations for the Office of Navy Sustainment. “This milestone demonstrates the Navy’s continued investment in the infrastructure and services that enable our people to focus on the mission, wherever they serve.”
Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command, said the command will sustain the initiative’s momentum through completion and continue pursuing improvements across the Shore Enterprise.
“Across 71 installations, our responsibility is clear: deliver the safe, resilient, and reliable shore infrastructure and services Sailors need to succeed,” Collins said. “Completing this Wi-Fi initiative remains a priority, and we will build on this progress to raise the standard of service, strengthen quality of life, and ensure our shore enterprise keeps pace with the needs of a ready naval force.”
The remaining 10 percent of unaccompanied housing facilities located in isolated regions, such as Camp Lemonnier, Djibouti, and Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, are scheduled for completion in fiscal year 2027 due to necessary backbone and base infrastructure requirements.
The program continues to offer filtered free Wi-Fi as well as subsidized high-speed upgrades without long-term contracts or termination fees in full compliance with the Military Honor and Decency Act of 1996.
Program managers report that network operations continue to run smoothly, and Sailors experiencing connection issues are encouraged to contact the service provider help desk for immediate support.
Commander, Navy Installations Command is responsible for worldwide U.S. Navy Shore installation management, designing and developing integrated solutions for sustainment and development of Navy shore infrastructure as well as quality of life programs. CNIC oversees 10 Navy regions, 70 installations, and more than 63,000 employees who are focused on warfighting and manning, training and equipping the Shore to fight and win. Navy installations are warfighting platforms essential to every fleet operation.
title: Navy High-Speed Wi-Fi Reaches 90 Percent of Global Unaccompanied Housing

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that two foreign nationals unlawfully present in Oklahoma were sentenced on charges relating to a fraudulent payroll check scheme.

Bairon Nayn Cabrera-Martinez, 36, an illegal alien from Honduras unlawfully present in LeFlore County, Oklahoma, was sentenced to a term of 33 months in prison for one count of Conspiracy to Commit Bank Fraud, and 33 months in prison for one count of Unlawful Reentry of Removed Alien. The court set the terms to be served concurrently. On April 1, 2026, Cabrera-Martinez pleaded guilty to the charges in federal district court.

Carlos Eduardo Nuila-Ramos, 36, an illegal alien from El Salvador unlawfully present in LeFlore County, Oklahoma, was sentenced to 22 months in prison for one count of Conspiracy to Commit Bank Fraud and 22 months in prison for one count of Unlawful Reentry of Removed Alien. The court set the terms to be served concurrently. On May 20, 2026, Nuila-Ramos pleaded guilty to the charges in federal district court.

The court also ordered the defendants to pay restitution in the amount of $299,474.00.

On July 17, 2026, co-defendant Carlos Banegas-Contreras, 47, an illegal alien from Honduras, was sentenced to 27 months in prison for one count of Conspiracy to Commit Bank Fraud after entering a guilty plea to the charge on October 6, 2025.

The charges arose from an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, the United States Secret Service, the Indiana State Police, the Benton County, Indiana Sheriff’s Department, the Benton County, Indiana Prosecutor’s Office, the Poteau, Oklahoma Police Department, and the Houston, Texas Police Department.

According to investigators, in June of 2023, Cabrera-Martinez, Nuila-Ramos, Banegas-Contreras, and others conspired to use fake identification cards to cash 178 fraudulent paychecks totaling $299,474.00 at three check-cashing businesses and five branches of a local bank. The fraudulent paychecks were designed to look like they had been issued by a building materials supply company in the Eastern District of Oklahoma.

The Honorable John A. Woodcock, Jr., Senior Judge in the United States District Court for the District of Maine, sitting by designation, presided over the hearing in Muskogee, Oklahoma. The defendants will remain in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending transportation to a designated United States Bureau of Prisons facility to serve a non-paroleable sentence of incarceration.

Assistant U.S. Attorney T. Cameron McEwen represented the United States.

Representatives Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), and and Greg Casar (D-Texas), today sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Director David J. Venturella calling for answers and accountability following three Immigration and Customs Enforcement shootings in their congressional districts where agents failed to wear body cameras.

The full letter is available here.

The Members point to the shootings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas; Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine; and Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin, Texas. In the latest case, Garces Perez was shot in the back by an ICE agent in Austin on September 20. The agent had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it. A second agent was wearing a camera, but it did not capture the shooting.

The repeated failures come despite significant funding from Congress. Earlier this year, Congress appropriated $20 million specifically for procuring, deploying, and operating body-worn cameras for federal immigration enforcement officers.

That is on top of an unprecedented increase in funding for ICE. Congress provided ICE roughly $75 billion in supplemental funding in 2025, followed by another $38.5 billion in 2026 through the Secure America Act.

“Over and over again, we’ve seen DHS agents resort to deadly violence when conducting enforcement operations in our districts. And when we demand to see the body cam footage, they give us the same tired excuses. No more,” said Congresswoman Pingree. “The fact that DHS has failed to outfit its officers with body cameras—despite having hundreds of billions of dollars at its disposal and more than a year to procure and deploy this equipment—is totally unacceptable. There is simply no reason that a federal agency with more money than most countries’ entire GDPs is not held to the same standards as local law enforcement. We deserve the truth about why cameras weren’t deployed during these most recent shootings, including the one that took the life of my constituent, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Our demands are simple: Every immigration enforcement officer must have a working body camera, must be properly trained on how to use it, and be held accountable when that camera isn’t used.”

“ICE is not short on money. Congress has provided billions of dollars to this agency, and after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed in my district, we were told body cameras were coming. The money is there. The deadlines have passed. So why does this keep happening?” said Congresswoman Garcia. “This is completely unacceptable. When federal agents use deadly force, the public should not be left in the dark. There must be transparency, accountability, and answers for the families who are left behind. Lorenzo’s family deserves answers. They deserve justice. DHS and ICE need to explain why their body camera system keeps failing when it matters most.”

"Wilber Garces Perez was shot in the back in Austin by an ICE agent who wasn't wearing a body camera, weeks after DHS promised every officer in the field would have one," said Congressman Casar. "Secretary Mullin keeps making promises while his agents keep shooting people. Secretary Mullin must release every second of footage from that scene, so we can know the truth.”

The letter also points to commitments DHS made following the July 7 killing of Salgado Araujo in Houston. During a July 15 phone call with Congresswoman Garcia, Secretary Mullin said all federal immigration officers would have body-worn cameras within 45 to 60 days. That deadline passed in September.

Salgado Araujo, a Houston construction worker and father of three, was killed without available body camera footage capturing the shooting. Days later, ICE fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero. Agents involved in Guerrero’s shooting were also not wearing body cameras. Then, on September 20, Garces Perez was shot in Austin by an officer who had been issued a camera but was not wearing it.

Members are demanding DHS and ICE explain whether all federal immigration officers have been issued working body cameras and properly trained to use them. They also ask why the officer who shot Garces Perez was not wearing his issued camera, why the second officer’s camera failed to capture the shooting, whether other footage exists, and whether officers who fail to follow body camera rules will face disciplinary action.

The Members requested written answers from DHS and ICE by October 14, 2026.

###
title: Reps. Pingree, Garcia, Casar Call for Accountability After Three ICE Shootings and Body Camera Failures

Today, House Agriculture Committee Ranking Member Angie Craig (D-MN-02) released the following statement.
“Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran are increasing prices across the board. While congressional Republicans defend the president’s backward priorities and unpopular war, millions of Americans are struggling to afford groceries. Instead of making food affordable by restoring SNAP, banning AI-powered surveillance pricing or securing free school lunches for our kids, Republicans are doubling down,” said Ranking Member Craig.
“Starting today, states and counties will be responsible for an unfunded SNAP cost-shift, forced onto them by the so-called Big Beautiful Bill, which increased their share of administrative costs from 50 percent to 75 percent. The money Republicans took from administering SNAP did not go toward making SNAP more efficient or improving fraud mitigation efforts; it went toward tax breaks for billionaires and the corporations building data centers in our backyards. Since the Big Beautiful Bill went into effect, over 5 million Americans, including around 2 million children, have been kicked off food assistance. With today’s cost-shift to the states, the growing hunger and food affordability crisis in America will only get worse. Working people cannot afford Trump’s America,” Ranking Member Craig continued.
On April 24, 2025, House Agriculture Democrats were briefed by state and county administrators who warned that the looming SNAP cost-shift to the states could imperil food assistance access across the country and result in higher taxes and cuts to crucial state and local programs.
On June 24, 2025, 23 governors warned that continuing to implement the Big Beautiful Bill’s SNAP cuts would force states to withdraw from the program entirely. 
On January 21, 2026, House Agriculture Democrats hosted a public roundtable warning that this unfunded mandate would put a $65 billion hole in state budgets.
On January 22, 2026, House Agriculture Democrats introduced the Farm and Family Relief Act, which would address food affordability by restoring SNAP funding and ending the president’s tariffs, while also providing economic assistance to struggling family farmers.
title: Ranking Member Angie Craig: “Working people cannot afford Trump’s America”

WASHINGTON — Congressman Gil Cisneros (CA-31) and Puerto Rico Resident Commissioner Pablo José Hernández (D-PR) introduced the PROMISE for Small Businesses Act, legislation to enhance oversight of federal contracting and protect the commitments made to small businesses and their participation in subcontracting opportunities.

Currently, large companies and corporations that receive certain federal contracts are required to provide plans outlining how they will provide subcontracting opportunities to small businesses. This legislation directs the Small Business Administrator to conduct compliance reviews to ensure large contractors follow through on their promise to deliver opportunities to small businesses in their subcontracting plans.

“Small businesses are critical to our economy and they deserve a fair shot in the federal marketplace.” said Rep. Gil Cisneros. “I’m proud to join Rep. Pablo José Hernández to introduce the PROMISE for Small Businesses Act to make sure they are not being left out. If enacted, this legislation would strengthen oversight of federal contracts to help ensure that large prime contractors keep their promise to small businesses as outlined in subcontracting plans. It would direct reviews of subcontracting plans and require reporting to Congress on compliance, noncompliance trends, and any enforcement actions taken. We cannot allow our small businesses to be pushed out of federal contracting.”

“When companies receive federal contracts and commit to working with small businesses, we should make sure they follow through,” said Hernández. “These opportunities can help small businesses grow, create jobs, and build experience in the federal marketplace. Our bill strengthens accountability and helps ensure those opportunities reach them.”

Small businesses greatly benefit from competing in the federal marketplace, and this bill will ensure they’re able to continue to do so fairly.

The PROMISE for Small Businesses Act would require the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) to review at least 10 percent of contracts subject to these subcontracting plans at each federal agency every year to determine whether contractors are meeting their commitments.

The legislation would also require the SBA to report:

whether contractors complied with their small business subcontracting plans;

how many compliance reviews the agency conducted;

what compliance issues were identified; and

what additional actions or reviews the SBA took in response.

Full text of the bill can be found here.

Rep. Cisneros is a member of the House Committee on Small Business, the Ranking Member on the Subcommittee on Contracting and Infrastructure, and on the Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Regulations. He is a member of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and serves on its leadership team as the Freshman Representative.

###
title: Rep. Cisneros and Commissioner Hernández Introduce Bill to Strengthen Small Business Participation in Federal Contracts

BANGOR, Maine: An Oakland Gardens, New York, man was sentenced today in U.S. District Court in Bangor for cyberstalking.

U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann sentenced Dabin Jeon , 31, to 30 months in prison to be followed by three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay $40,181.72 in restitution to the victim. Jeon pleaded guilty on September 9, 2025.

According to court records, Jeon met the victim online in 2019 and the two began a relationship when they both lived in New York. At Jeon’s request, the victim began providing him with financial assistance until she moved back to Maine and told him she could no longer afford to give him money. In response, Jeon threatened to rape the victim’s mother, send explicit pictures he took of the victim to her employer, friends, and family, and harm her grandparents. Based on these threats, the victim continued sending money to Jeon. Jeon also demanded that the victim account for her whereabouts and gave her tasks to complete.

In December 2022, several of the victim’s friends and family received text messages containing clothed and unclothed pictures of her. The person sending the messages claimed to be the victim and offered approximately six other phone numbers with the opportunity to support her alleged OnlyFans account. Agents reviewed records provided by the service providers associated with the phone numbers and traced most of the numbers back to accounts opened by Jeon.

“Dabin Jeon was strategic in his cyber torment of his victim and her family. His targeted bullying was intended to inflict significant emotional harm and the fear of physical violence, and it did exactly that,” said Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Boston Division. “We commend this young woman’s courage in coming forward because Mr. Jeon’s behavior very well could have escalated. Sending threatening communications is a crime, which is why the FBI takes threats like these so seriously.”

“Online predators and stalkers believe their illegal and abusive behavior will be anonymized through the internet,” said U.S. Attorney Andrew Benson. “This federal prosecution and sentence demonstrate, however, that through the diligent work of the FBI and our other law enforcement partners, those who seek to injure, harass or intimidate others online will be held accountable for their actions and their victims will receive a measure of justice.”

The FBI investigated the case.

###
title: New York Man Sentenced for Cyberstalking

Tallahassee, Florida – David Christopher Jensen, 54, of Steinhatchee, Florida, has pleaded guilty in federal court to one count of possession with intent to distribute cocaine and marijuana and one count of possession of an unregistered firearm. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the plea.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Thanks to the excellent investigative work of the Taylor County Sheriff’s Office and ATF, this armed drug trafficker has been taken off our streets and the successful prosecution by my office will ensure he remains behind bars where he belongs.”

The investigation revealed that on September 25, 2025, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF), along with the Taylor County Sheriff’s Office, executed two federal search warrants on the defendant’s primary residence and his storage unit. During the execution of the search warrants, law enforcement seized cocaine and marijuana that was intended for distribution. Law enforcement also located several firearms, including a short-barreled rifle. During an interview with law enforcement, the defendant admitted ownership over the narcotics and firearms.

Jensen faces up to 20 years’ imprisonment for possession with intent to distribute cocaine and marijuana and up to 10 years’ imprisonment for possession of an unregistered firearm.

The case was jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and the Taylor County Sheriff’s Office. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Joseph A. Ravelo.

Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

The purpose of this funding is to support projects to improve the functioning of the criminal justice system, to prevent or combat juvenile delinquency, and to assist victims of crime.

Wellton Police Department awarded $324,000.

La Paz County Sheriff’s Department awarded $579,000.

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Miya Pack, 40, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was sentenced today to three years of probation and 75 hours of community service by United States District Judge Joshua D. Wolson for voting more than once in a federal election.

The defendant was charged with that offense by indictment in September 2025 and pleaded guilty this June, in connection with the 2024 presidential election.

As admitted by the defendant at her change of plea hearing, Pack was registered to vote in Bergen County, New Jersey, had been registered there since in or about 2004, and until October 2024 had no history of having voted in New Jersey. In 2016, Pack registered to vote in Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania.

On October 26, 2024, the defendant voted in person at an early voting location in Bergen County, New Jersey, casting a vote for the office of President of the United States of America.

On Election Day, November 5, 2024, Pack went to a polling place in Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania, and cast another ballot in the 2024 general election, including another vote for the office of President of the United States of America.

This case was investigated by the FBI, with assistance from the Office of the Superintendent of Elections for Bergen County, New Jersey, and the Office of Philadelphia City Commissioner Seth Bluestein, and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Nancy E. Potts.
title: Philadelphia Woman Sentenced for Election Fraud Offense

NEW ORLEANS — Julian Curo-Churata, a 47-year-old illegal alien from Peru, passed away in ICE custody Sept. 29, 2026, at Ochsner LSU Health Monroe Medical Center in Monroe, Louisiana. The preliminary cause of death is unknown. An autopsy will determine the official cause of death. On Sept. 28, Curo was found to be in medical distress. At approximately 8:14 p.m. CDT, facility staff transported Curo-Churata to Ochsner LSU Health Monroe Medical Center for advanced medical treatment. Despite life-saving efforts, an on-duty physician pronounced Curo deceased at 4:01 a.m. CDT.
His background includes convictions for driving with expired vehicle registration, and a separate court judgment against him in favor of the Comptroller of Maryland. Curo entered the United States at an unknown date and location without inspection. Enforcement and Removal Operations Baltimore arrested Curo during a targeted enforcement operation June 27, 2026, and served him with a Notice to Appear. ERO Baltimore transferred him to ERO New Orleans custody June 29, 2026, and detained him at Richwood Correctional Center. On Sept. 18, 2026, an immigration judge denied Curo’s applications for relief and voluntary departure. He reserved his right to appeal.
While in custody, Curo received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.
Consistent with ICE policy, ERO New Orleans notified the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility through the Joint Intake Center. ERO New Orleans also notified Curo-Churata’s spouse, his attorney, and the Consulate General of Peru.
ICE makes official notifications to Congress, non-governmental organization stakeholders and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.

Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility, access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care.

Davids, Alford Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Protect America’s Medical Supply Chains, Support Kansas City Innovation
Bill would help protect medicine, vaccine, and animal health science from foreign influence
Today, U.S. Representatives Sharice Davids (D-KS-03) and Mark Alford (R-MO-04) introduced the Critical Biomanufacturing Input Assessment Act. It’s a bipartisan bill that would help strengthen America’s biotechnology supply chains, support the growing medical industry in the Kansas City region, and address growing concerns about U.S. reliance on foreign suppliers — including China — for critical materials needed to produce medicines and other health products.
“Kansas City is creating the next generation of medicines, health products, and technologies that improve people’s lives — and we need to make sure American companies have the supplies they need to succeed,” said Davids. “This bipartisan bill will help us identify weaknesses in our supply chains, reduce our dependence on countries like China, strengthen American manufacturing, and create good-paying jobs while lowering healthcare costs. I appreciate Representative Alford’s partnership on this important, bipartisan effort.”
“As we work to bring more manufacturing back to American soil, we must ensure our biotechnology supply chains are secure, transparent and resilient,” said Congressman Mark Alford (R-MO-04). “This commonsense, bipartisan legislation will help identify vulnerabilities, reduce reliance on foreign adversaries like China, and protect the critical materials needed to produce lifesaving medicines and animal health products. I’m proud to partner with Representative Davids to strengthen innovation in the Kansas City region and safeguard our nation’s health and economic security.”
Many products that Americans rely on — including medicines, vaccines, and animal health products — are made using biotechnology. But many companies do not have a clear picture of where the materials and equipment they depend on come from. Some critical supplies are made overseas, including in China, creating potential risks for our economy and national security. This bill will help identify these vulnerabilities before a disruption occurs.
The Critical Biomanufacturing Input Assessment Act would require the Department of Commerce to regularly review America’s reliance on foreign sources for important biotechnology supplies and equipment.
The information collected through this review would help:
- Identify potential supply chain problems before they become emergencies;
- Help businesses make better decisions about where to source materials;
- Encourage more companies to manufacture critical supplies in the United States; and
- Strengthen America’s ability to compete in the global biotechnology industry.
The Kansas City region is one of the country’s fastest-growing biotechnology hubs. It is home to the KC BioHub, a partnership focused on making Kansas City a national leader in biotechnology research, innovation, and manufacturing. The region is also home to the Kansas City Animal Health Corridor, one of the largest concentrations of animal health companies in the world.
These companies and research institutions rely on specialized supplies and equipment to develop products that improve human and animal health. Making sure those supply chains are strong and reliable is critical to their continued success.
Davids has been a strong supporter of expanding Kansas City’s biotechnology industry. She helped champion the region’s application for the federal Regional Technology and Innovation Hub program and has worked with KC BioHub and other local partners to support investments in biotechnology, workforce development, and advanced manufacturing.
title: Davids, Alford Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Protect America’s Medical Supply Chains, Support Kansas City Innovation

KANSAS CITY, KAN. – A federal grand jury in Kansas City, Kansas, returned an indictment charging a Kansas woman for allegedly submitting fictitious information to the Small Business Administration (SBA) to receive pandemic-era financial assistance.

According to court documents, Christina Marie DeLeon, 42, of Wichita was indicted on two counts of wire fraud.

During the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic, the SBA provided emergency financial assistance for small businesses struggling to cover payroll and other business expenses through the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP). In the PPP loan applications, business owners were required to state their average monthly payroll expenses and number of employees.

DeLeon was the owner of a company called “Wicks Before Dicks”. In April 2020 and January 2022, DeLeon is accused of knowingly submitting false information about gross sales and the number of employees in order to receive PPP loans for $9,300 and $20,832, and then allegedly submitting false information again to receive loan forgiveness.

The Small Business Administration – Office of Inspector General (SBA-OIG) is investigating the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher Oakley is prosecuting the case.

OTHER INDICTMENTS

Victor Daniel Gomez-Hernandez, 51, an illegal alien from Mexico, was indicted on one count of unlawful reentry after deportation. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is investigating the case.

Jose Carlos Moreno-Aboytes, 29, an illegal alien from Mexico, was indicted on one count of reentry of a previously removed alien. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is investigating the case.

Jorge Paiva-Suarez, 33, an illegal alien from Venezuela, was indicted on one count of illegal alien in possession of a firearm. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is investigating the case.

Britney L. Smith-Stimach, 38, was indicted on count of felon in possession of a firearm. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) is investigating the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ###

WILLIAMSPORT- The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Ryan Edward Mills, age 54, of Northumberland County, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on September 29, 2026, to 121 months’ imprisonment by Chief United States District Judge Matthew W. Brann for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, Mills possessed firearms after having been convicted of multiple drug trafficking felonies. In January 2024, Mills was wanted for violating his terms of state parole and absconding. The United States Marshals Fugitive Task Force, with assistance from the Pennsylvania State Police and Milton Police Department, tracked down and arrested Mills. A subsequent search of his vehicle and residence revealed he possessed three firearms as a felon, specifically, a pistol, a 12-gauge shotgun, and an AR-style rifle.

When imposing the 121-month sentence, Chief Judge Brann noted Mills’s significant criminal history and his lack of respect for the law exhibited by his absconding from state parole.

The FBI Philadelphia’s Capital Area Resident Agency, Pennsylvania State Police, and Milton Police Department investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Kyle A. Moreno prosecuted the case.

text:
Crime Data Shows Progress; Partnership Remains Essential
This opinion piece by FBI New Haven Special Agent in Charge P.J. O’Brien was published by CT Insider on September 1, 2026.
The FBI’s latest Reported Crimes in the Nation Summary for 2025 shows significant decreases in both violent and property crimes across our country. Nationally, violent crime decreased by an estimated 9.3% from 2024 to 2025, including an 18.1% decrease in murder and nonnegligent manslaughter. These decreases represent the single largest yearto-year decreases in violent crime and murder since estimations began in 1936. Additional violent crime data shows an 18.5% decrease in robbery, a 7.6% decrease in rape, and a 7.2% decrease in aggravated assault were also estimated. The 2025 murder rate is tied with 1955 and 1956 for the lowest rate in recorded history. Property crimes followed a similar trend with an estimated 12.4% decrease. This includes a 22.7% decrease in motor vehicle theft, a decrease of 15.8% in burglary, and a 9.8% decrease in larceny. These numbers matter because they reflect the hard work being done by law enforcement at all levels; local, state, tribal, territorial, and federal, to keep those who we serve safe. Participating agencies, whose data contributes to the report, protect over 96% of the population. This report helps law enforcement identify trends, allocate resources, and better understand public safety challenges.
While most of the national estimates are positive, there continues to be a troubling trend regarding assaults on law enforcement officers. In 2025, 53 law enforcement officers were feloniously killed in the line of duty, with an additional 28 accidentally killed in the line of duty. During the same timeframe, over 90,000 assaults on law enforcement officers were reported; a ten-year high and an approximately 61% increase since 2016.
Here in Connecticut, already one of the safest states in the country, the violent crime and property crime trends are also highly encouraging. For 2025, the Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection (DESPP) reported a 7.4% decrease in violent crimes with only 70 murders state-wide; while DESPP does not calculate percent of change for values below 100, this would be about a 22% decrease from 2024 and a 49% decrease compared to 2023 data. Similarly, property crimes declined by 16.7%. These successes are a direct reflection of the hard work being done by the sworn law enforcement officers at all levels throughout the state; and the trend continues, as DESPP reported in the first quarter of 2026, violent crimes against declined nearly 15% when comparing the same period last year, with only 10 murders being reported.
A seminal aspect to addressing violent crimes is partnerships. The collaboration and cooperation among Connecticut law enforcement is second to none. The FBI New Haven Field OAice works every day with local, state, tribal and other federal partners across Connecticut combating violent crime as well as national security and cyber threats. The Task Force officers that work side by side with our Agents are critical to our success the task forces they support are a force multiplier that adds back to their communities. That cooperation is one of our greatest strengths. When working together we are greater than the sum of our parts. In a February press conference discussing Connecticut crime statistics, DESPP Commissioner Ronnell Higgins called for “more information sharing, more task forces, and more regional strategies instead of silos.” I could not agree more and look forward to the continued partnerships across the state.
Commissioner Higgins also emphasized the importance of getting crime data out more quickly so law enforcement can make better decisions and understand emerging trends. We agree. Accurate reporting and strong partnerships help us see the full picture. When communities report crime, when agencies share data, and when law enforcement work together, we are better positioned to protect the people we serve.
These national and local trends are important, but they do not mean the work is finished. Every crime has a victim, a family, and a community behind it. Even though many traditional crime categories have declined, Connecticut law enforcement continues to see serious threats from fraud, cyber-enables crime, hate crimes, crimes against children and other oAenses that harm Connecticut residents. Cybersecurity remains a persistent and growing public safety priority, aAecting individuals, businesses, schools, healthcare systems, and local governments across Connecticut and the nation. Like with violent crime, FBI New Haven stands ready to work with our partners to make meaningful impact against these threats as well.
The data shows tremendous progress. Our collective responsibility is to sustain and improve upon it.
title: Crime Data Shows Progress; Partnership Remains Essential

Two Minnesota Men Plead Guilty to Defrauding Medicaid Housing Services Program
Two Minnesota men pleaded guilty to defrauding Minnesota’s Housing Stabilization Services (HSS) program out of more than $500,000 by submitting fraudulent claims for services that were never provided. This case is part of the ongoing collaboration between the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota and the Health Care Fraud Strike Force to combat prolific fraud on government programs in Minnesota.
“This case is a stark reminder that fraud against public programs is not just a crime against government — it is a betrayal of the most vulnerable among us,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “By diverting resources meant for the elderly, mentally ill, and those suffering from substance abuse, the defendant undermined trust and jeopardized essential services. This guilty plea demonstrates our unwavering resolve to pursue justice, restore integrity, and ensure that taxpayer dollars are used to uplift — not exploit — our communities.”
“My office is committed to maintaining the integrity of public programs. The defendants’ guilty pleas bring us closer to obtaining accountability for the American taxpayer,” said U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota.
“These guilty pleas are the result of a continued, coordinated effort to stop the fraud plaguing our social services and healthcare benefits systems,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson of the FBI Minneapolis Field Office. “These programs are meant to provide critical services to those most in need, not to line the pockets of fraudsters. The FBI and our partners remain steadfastly committed to rooting out these frauds and defending the resources of the American taxpayer.”
“I want to emphasize that protecting programs designed to support vulnerable communities is a top priority for IRS Criminal Investigation,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Robert J. Kuszynski of IRS Criminal Investigation’s Chicago Field Office. “The deliberate submission of fraudulent claims undermines the trust placed in these vital services and diverts resources from those who truly need them. These guilty pleas demonstrate our unwavering resolve to pursue those who exploit public programs for personal gain. We will continue to work alongside our law enforcement partners to ensure accountability and safeguard taxpayer dollars.”
According to court documents, Hassan Ahmed Hussein, 29, and Ahmed Abdirashid Mohamed, 28, both of the Twin Cities area, enrolled Pristine Health LLC as a Medicaid provider, promising to help people with disabilities — including seniors and people suffering from mental illnesses and substance use disorders — find and maintain housing through the State’s now-defunct HSS program. Instead, Hussein and Mohamed submitted HSS claims to Medicaid for services that were never provided and significantly inflated the claims for higher reimbursement. Pristine Health enrolled approximately 90 Medicaid beneficiaries for HSS, including some who never agreed to receive the services. In total, Pristine Health billed Minnesota Medicaid more than $820,000.
Hussein entered a guilty plea on September 24, 2026, and Mohamed entered a guilty plea on October 1, 2026. Both pleaded to one count of wire fraud and face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Sentencing dates will be set by the Court at a later date.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s Fraud Division; U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota; Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson of the FBI Minneapolis Field Office; Special Agent in Charge Thomas Ethridge of the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG); and Special Agent in Charge Adam Jobes of the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Chicago Field Office, made the announcement
FBI, HHS-OIG, and IRS-CI investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Raymond E. Beckering III of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Murphy for the District of Minnesota are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
title: Two Minnesota Men Plead Guilty to Defrauding Medicaid Housing Services Program

I want to express my sincere gratitude to Congressman Mannion for securing this federal funding, which directly invests in the safety of every resident in Onondaga County and throughout Central New York. This Mobile Command Unit is not just a vehicle; it is a state-of-the-art operational backbone. WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congresswoman Madeleine Dean (PA-04) and Senator Brian Schatz (D-HI) reintroduced the Beyond the Box for Higher Education Act. The Beyond the Box Act would provide colleges and universities guidance on the removal of criminal and juvenile justice questions from their initial application for admissions.

Almost one out of three Americans have some kind of arrest or conviction record that would appear in a criminal background check. Individuals with criminal or juvenile justice involvement experience barriers to educational opportunities, decreased earnings, and increased poverty.

One significant barrier that these individuals face is that most colleges and universities ask criminal justice, juvenile justice, and/or school disciplinary questions in their admissions processes. People with felony convictions are forty percent less likely to complete college applications than people without, and the application rejection rates for individuals with felony convictions can be as high as 2.5 times the rate of those without.

“Every student deserves the chance to claim their education — and people who have made mistakes in the past and are looking for a fresh start are no exception,” Rep. Dean said. “As a former professor, I have seen firsthand how education can change lives, and we can ensure more Americans are afforded that chance. I am grateful for Senator Schatz’s continued partnership.”

The Beyond the Box for Higher Education Act directs the Department of Education to provide guidance on:

Whether criminal and juvenile justice questions are necessary in the initial application for admissions;

How to create a process to determine when criminal or juvenile justice information can be requested of students for non-admissions purposes; and

How colleges and universities that decide to keep criminal and juvenile justice questions can reduce their impact on the admissions process.

Congresswoman Dean and Senator Schatz previously introduced this bicameral legislation in 2021 and 2023.

Read the text of the bill here.

Rep. Madeleine Dean is a mother, grandmother, attorney, professor, former four-term member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, and U.S. Representative for the Fourth District of Pennsylvania.

Read the full letter HERE.

The Members point to the shootings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas; Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine; and Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin, Texas. In the latest case, Garces Perez was shot in the back by an ICE agent in Austin on September 20. The agent had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it. A second agent was wearing a camera, but it did not capture the shooting.

The repeated failures come despite significant funding from Congress. Earlier this year, Congress appropriated $20 million specifically for procuring, deploying, and operating body-worn cameras for federal immigration enforcement officers.

That is on top of an unprecedented increase in funding for ICE. Congress provided ICE roughly $75 billion in supplemental funding in 2025, followed by another $38.5 billion in 2026 through the Secure America Act.

“ICE is not short on money. Congress has provided billions of dollars to this agency, and after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed in my district, we were told body cameras were coming. The money is there. The deadlines have passed. So why does this keep happening?” said Congresswoman Garcia. “This is completely unacceptable. When federal agents use deadly force, the public should not be left in the dark. There must be transparency, accountability, and answers for the families who are left behind. Lorenzo’s family deserves answers. They deserve justice. DHS and ICE need to explain why their body camera system keeps failing when it matters most.”

“Over and over again, we’ve seen DHS agents resort to deadly violence when conducting enforcement operations in our districts. And when we demand to see the body cam footage, they give us the same tired excuses. No more,” said Congresswoman Pingree. “The fact that DHS has failed to outfit its officers with body cameras—despite having hundreds of billions of dollars at its disposal and more than a year to procure and deploy this equipment—is totally unacceptable. There is simply no reason that a federal agency with more money than most countries’ entire GDPs is not held to the same standards as local law enforcement. We deserve the truth about why cameras weren’t deployed during these most recent shootings, including the one that took the life of my constituent, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Our demands are simple: Every immigration enforcement officer must have a working body camera, must be properly trained on how to use it, and be held accountable when that camera isn’t used.”

"Wilber Garces Perez was shot in the back in Austin by an ICE agent who wasn't wearing a body camera, weeks after DHS promised every officer in the field would have one," said Congressman Casar. "Secretary Mullin keeps making promises while his agents keep shooting people. Secretary Mullin must release every second of footage from that scene, so we can know the truth.”

The letter also points to commitments DHS made following the July 7 killing of Salgado Araujo in Houston. During a July 15 phone call with Congresswoman Garcia, Secretary Mullin said all federal immigration officers would have body-worn cameras within 45 to 60 days. That deadline passed in September.

Salgado Araujo, a Houston construction worker and father of three, was killed without available body camera footage capturing the shooting. Days later, ICE fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero. Agents involved in Guerrero’s shooting were also not wearing body cameras. Then, on September 20, Garces Perez was shot in Austin by an officer who had been issued a camera but was not wearing it.

Members are demanding DHS and ICE explain whether all federal immigration officers have been issued working body cameras and properly trained to use them. They also ask why the officer who shot Garces Perez was not wearing his issued camera, why the second officer’s camera failed to capture the shooting, whether other footage exists, and whether officers who fail to follow body camera rules will face disciplinary action.

The Members requested written answers from DHS and ICE by October 14, 2026.
title: Reps. Garcia, Pingree, Casar Call for Accountability After Three ICE Shootings and Body Camera Failures

text:
The culprit was smuggling 11 illegal aliens into the country when he caused the fatal crash that killed a grandmother and her 7-year-old granddaughter
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after an investigation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) led to the sentencing of a smuggler to life in prison after he caused a fatal crash in Texas that killed four people while he was smuggling illegal aliens into the United States in 2023.
According to local reports, the fatal crash took place on March 13, 2023. The culprit, Rassian Nateray Comer, a United States citizen from Louisiana, was driving a vehicle with 11 illegal aliens from Mexico inside when a Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) trooper tried to pull him over. Comer fled, leading police on a chase that exceeded 100 miles per hour. Comer even streamed the chase on Facebook Live, showing the police cars in pursuit and showing off his speedometer reading 105.
Comer streamed the high-speed pursuit on Facebook Live
The chase ended in Ozona when Comer ran a red light and struck a pickup truck driven by Maria Tambunga, who had her 7-year-old granddaughter Emilia Brooke Tambunga with her. The crash killed both of them as well as two of the 11 illegal aliens in Comer’s vehicle, while the other nine illegal aliens suffered serious injuries. Comer was arrested at the scene, admitting that it was his fourth smuggling trip, and also admitting to possessing a stolen handgun that was found in his vehicle.
The vehicle that the victims, Maria Tambunga and her granddaughter Emilia Brooke Tambunga, were in during the crash
The vehicle that Comer was driving during the crash, which was smuggling 11 illegal aliens
On June 18, 2026, Comer pleaded guilty to one count ofconspiracy to transport illegal aliens resulting in death, 11 counts of transportation of an illegal alien resulting in death, and one count of possession of a stolen firearm. On September 25, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas announced that Comer was sentenced to life in prison.
“This horrific tragedy is almost beyond words,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “This monster was already trying to cause more chaos and destruction by smuggling illegal aliens into this country, then decided to lead police on a high-speed chase that claimed the lives of a grandmother and her granddaughter. Maria Tambunga and Emilia Brooke Tambunga should still be alive today, and they would be if it weren’t for this criminal who endangered so many lives just for profit. Thanks to our partners at the Department of Justice, this scumbag will spend the rest of his life behind bars, where he belongs. My thoughts and prayers are with the Tambunga family, who have suffered a loss that few of us can even imagine.”
“This case lays bare a heartbreaking human tragedy — a grandmother, a 7-year-old child and two Mexican nationals were all killed because of Mr. Comer’s criminal and depraved actions,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “These were innocent lives, stolen in an instant by an alien smuggler whose criminal actions showed complete disregard for everyone on the road. No sentence can restore what was lost, but it does send a clear message: when criminals gamble with human lives, we will respond with the full weight of the federal government to ensure victims receive justice.”
“Comer’s reckless actions turned a human-smuggling run into an unimaginable tragedy that took the lives of four people, including a grandmother and her young granddaughter,” said HSI Dallas Acting Deputy Special Agent in Charge Judy Pardo. “He showed a callous disregard for the lives of the people he transported, the law enforcement officers pursuing him, and the innocent family sharing the road that night. This sentence holds him accountable for that devastating choice. HSI will continue to work with our partners to pursue the smuggling networks that profit from human lives and leave tragedy in their wake.”
Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation with assistance from the Texas Department of Public Safety, the Crockett County Sheriff’s Office, the Texas Border Prosecution Unit, and the 112th Judicial District Attorney’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jeffrey R. Haag, West Texas Branch Chief, prosecuted the case.
# # #
title: HSI Investigation Leads to Life Sentence for Smuggler Who Killed Four in High-Speed Pursuit While Smuggling Illegal Aliens
